The Bodhisattva path involves practicing the paramitas (perfections) such as generosity, morality, patience, effort, concentration, and wisdom.
qs.kf:
☛ Who is the founder of Buddhism? → Gautama Buddha
☛ Which concept is emphasized in Mahayana Buddhism? → Bodhisattva
☛ What does Bodhisattva literally mean? → Enlightened being
☛ What are the Four Noble Truths in Buddhism? → Suffering, origin, cessation, path
☛ How many paramitas are there for a Bodhisattva? → 6 or 10 paramitas

q: Which of the following festivals marks the birth of Prince Siddhartha Gautama, who founded a religion?
qs.e: Buddha Purnima, also known as Vaishakh Purnima, is celebrated as the day of Gautam Buddha's birth, enlightenment (Nirvana), and death (Mahaparinirvana). It is the most sacred festival in Buddhism. Prince Siddhartha Gautama was born in Lumbini (present-day Nepal), attained enlightenment in Bodh Gaya, and passed away in Kushinagar. On Buddha Purnima, Buddhists engage in prayer, meditation, and charity. The festival promotes the values of non-violence, compassion, and peace.
qs.kf:
☛ Birthplace of Gautam Buddha → Lumbini (Nepal)
☛ Enlightenment site of Gautam Buddha → Bodh Gaya (Bihar)
☛ Mahaparinirvana site of Gautam Buddha → Kushinagar (Uttar Pradesh)
☛ Founder of Buddhism → Gautam Buddha
☛ Alternate name of Buddha Purnima → Vaishakh Purnima

q: A festival of the Jain community, Deo Deepawali, which is celebrated 10 days after Deepawali to mark the attainment of nirvana (death) by Mahavira, is mainly celebrated at _____ in Bihar.
qs.e: Deo Deepawali is an important festival of the Jain community, celebrated 10 days after Deepawali. It marks the attainment of nirvana (death) by Lord Mahavira, the 24th Tirthankara of Jainism. The festival is mainly celebrated at Pawapuri in Bihar. Pawapuri, also known as Apapapuri, meaning 'the sinless town', is a significant Jain pilgrimage site. It is believed that Lord Mahavira attained nirvana here, and his last rites were performed at this place. The town is famous for its Jal Mandir, a beautiful temple built in the middle of a lotus pond. During Deo Deepawali, thousands of devotees gather at Pawapuri to light lamps and offer prayers. The festival symbolizes the spiritual light and the victory of knowledge over ignorance.
qs.kf:
☛ Who is the 24th Tirthankara of Jainism? → Mahavira Swami
☛ In whose memory is Deo Deepawali celebrated? → Mahavira Swami
☛ What is another name for Pawapuri? → Apapapuri
☛ Which famous temple is located in Pawapuri? → Jal Mandir
☛ How many days after Deepawali is Deo Deepawali celebrated? → 10 days

q: Gautam Buddha taught in which common language of the ordinary people, so that everybody could understand his messages?
qs.e: Gautam Buddha used Prakrit language to deliver his teachings so that common people could easily understand his messages. Prakrit was the vernacular language of the masses at that time, unlike Sanskrit, which was confined to the elite and scholars. Buddha aimed to spread his message to all sections of society regardless of caste or class. The Buddhist scriptures, the Tipitaka, were also written in Pali, which is a derivative of Prakrit. The word 'Prakrit' means 'natural' or 'common', reflecting its simplicity and accessibility. By using Prakrit, Buddha ensured his teachings were not limited by language barriers and could reach a wider audience. He also adapted to regional dialects, but Prakrit remained the primary medium.
qs.kf:
☛ In which language did Buddha preach? → Prakrit
☛ The Buddhist Tipitaka is written in which language? → Pali
☛ What does Prakrit mean? → Natural or common
☛ Sanskrit was confined to which class? → Elite and scholars
☛ What was Buddha's objective? → Spread dharma to all sections

q: Which of these festivals is considered the most sacred Buddhist festival, commemorating the birth, enlightenment and Mahaparinirvana (passing away) of Buddha Shakyamuni?
qs.e: Saga Dawa is the most sacred festival in Buddhism, commemorating the birth, enlightenment, and Mahaparinirvana (passing away) of Buddha Shakyamuni. It is observed on the full moon day of the fourth month of the Tibetan Buddhist calendar (Saga Dawa). On this day, Buddhists engage in meditation, fasting, and acts of merit. Other options: Tamladu is a Bodo festival, Sangken is a Buddhist festival of the Thoing community (Arunachal), and Ojiyale is a Muslim festival. Saga Dawa holds supreme importance in Tibetan Buddhism.
qs.kf:
☛ Which festival is most sacred in Buddhism? → Saga Dawa
☛ Saga Dawa commemorates what events of Buddha Shakyamuni? → Birth, enlightenment, and Mahaparinirvana
☛ In which month is Saga Dawa celebrated? → Fourth month of Tibetan calendar
☛ What practices are prominent during Saga Dawa? → Meditation, fasting, and good deeds
☛ Where did Buddha Shakyamuni attain Mahaparinirvana? → Kushinagar

q: The 'Mahavamsa', a Buddhist literary work, was originally written in which of the following languages?
qs.e: The Mahavamsa is a major historical chronicle of Sri Lanka related to Buddhism. It was originally written in the Pali language. This text is believed to have been composed by the monk Mahanama in the 6th century CE. The Mahavamsa describes the history of Sri Lankan kings and the Buddhist sangha. The Pali language is the primary language of Theravada Buddhist scriptures. This work was composed after the Dipavamsa and later continued as the Culavamsa.
qs.kf:
☛ Who composed the Mahavamsa? → Monk Mahanama
☛ Which country's historical chronicle is the Mahavamsa? → Sri Lanka
☛ Which language is used in Dipavamsa and Mahavamsa? → Pali
☛ What is the later part of Mahavamsa called? → Culavamsa
☛ In which language are Theravada Buddhist scriptures written? → Pali

q: The book ‘Sutta Pitaka’ contains the words of which religious preacher?
qs.e: Sutta Pitaka is a major text of Buddhism and a part of the Tripitaka. It contains the discourses and teachings of Lord Buddha. This text primarily includes Buddha's sermons on ethics, philosophy, and the path to enlightenment. Written in Pali language, Sutta Pitaka is considered highly sacred by Buddhist followers. It comprises five collections known as Nikayas: Digha Nikaya, Majjhima Nikaya, Samyutta Nikaya, Anguttara Nikaya, and Khuddaka Nikaya. The Sutta Pitaka elaborates on Buddha's life and core principles such as the Middle Way, Four Noble Truths, and Eightfold Path.
qs.kf:
☛ What are the three parts of Tripitaka? → Vinaya Pitaka, Sutta Pitaka, Abhidhamma Pitaka
☛ In which language was Sutta Pitaka composed? → Pali language
☛ How many Nikayas are there in Sutta Pitaka? → Five Nikayas
☛ Who founded Buddhism? → Gautam Buddha
☛ Which text contains the teachings of Buddha? → Sutta Pitaka

q: Which of the following statements is/are correct in the context of the religious development during the Gupta Empire?
I. Nalanda University was founded by Kumargupta I of the Gupta dynasty in the 5th century CE.
II. Narasimhagupta Baladitya was influenced by Mahayana Buddhism.
qs.e: During the Gupta period, Nalanda University was founded in the 5th century by Kumargupta I. It became a major center of Buddhist learning. Kumargupta I laid the foundation of Nalanda Mahavihara, which later developed into a university. On the other hand, Narasimhagupta Baladitya (c. 473-476 CE) was a Gupta ruler who was greatly influenced by Mahayana Buddhism. He also contributed to the development of Nalanda University. Thus, both statements are correct, reflecting the influence of Buddhism and support for education during the Gupta era.
qs.kf:
☛ Founder of Nalanda University → Kumargupta I
☛ Buddhist sect associated with Narasimhagupta Baladitya → Mahayana Buddhism
☛ Another name of Kumargupta I → Mahendraditya
☛ Century of Nalanda University's establishment → 5th century CE
☛ Order of Narasimhagupta Baladitya in Gupta dynasty → Third ruler

q: Which of the following buildings/architecture was used primarily for residential purpose for Buddhist Priests?
qs.e: In Buddhism, viharas were primarily used as residential quarters for monks. These were rectangular or square buildings with a central courtyard surrounded by cells where monks lived, meditated, and studied. Chaityas were prayer halls, stupas were built over Buddha's relics, and stambhas were commemorative pillars or religious symbols. Thus, viharas were the key architectural structures serving the residential purpose for Buddhist priests.
qs.kf:
☛ Residential place for Buddhist monks → Vihara
☛ Prayer and assembly hall → Chaitya
☛ Monument containing Buddha's relics → Stupa
☛ Religious pillar or column → Stambha
☛ Famous vihara sites → Nalanda, Vikramashila

q: A single narrative detailing one of Buddha's former existences is known by which of the following names?
qs.e: The stories of Buddha's previous births are called Jataka tales. These tales describe the Buddha's past lives as humans, animals, or deities in his previous existences. Each Jataka tale teaches a moral lesson and illustrates the paramitas (perfections) such as compassion, generosity, renunciation, and virtue. The Jataka tales are an important part of Buddhist literature and are especially prevalent in the Theravada Buddhist tradition. These stories have been depicted in art and literature across India, Sri Lanka, and other Southeast Asian countries. The term 'Jataka' means 'birth' or 'related to birth'. Hence, a single narrative detailing one of Buddha's former existences is known as a Jataka tale.
qs.kf:
☛ Stories of Buddha's previous births are called → Jataka tales
☛ Which Buddhist tradition emphasizes Jataka tales → Theravada Buddhism
☛ Meaning of the term Jataka → Birth
☛ Main purpose of Jataka tales → Moral teaching and description of paramitas
☛ Jataka tales are part of which literature → Buddhist literature

q: What is a notable characteristic of the carvings found at the entrances of the Sanchi Stupa?
o: Mythical creatures like yakshas and kinnaras
qs.e: The carvings on the four gateways (toranas) of the Sanchi Stupa prominently feature Jataka stories, which depict events from the previous lives of Buddha. Located in Madhya Pradesh, the stupa was originally built during the Mauryan period under Emperor Ashoka, but the present carvings date to the Shunga and Satavahana periods. These carvings use symbolic representations (such as footprints, thrones) for Buddha rather than human form, as early Buddhist art avoided direct portrayal. The Jataka narratives convey moral teachings and compassion central to Buddhism.
qs.kf:
☛ In which state is Sanchi Stupa located? → Madhya Pradesh
☛ Who commissioned the construction of Sanchi Stupa? → Ashoka
☛ Sanchi Stupa is associated with which religion? → Buddhism
☛ How is Buddha represented in Sanchi carvings? → Symbolically
☛ What do Jataka stories describe? → Buddha's previous births

q: Which of the following is NOT a principle of Jainism?
o: The whole world, including stone and water, has life.
Rejection of the doctrine of Karma
Practice of non-injury to living beings
Monastic life is the only way to salvation.
qs.e: In Jainism, Karma is a fundamental principle. Jain philosophy considers Karma as subtle particles (pudgala) that attach to the soul and cause rebirth. Therefore, rejecting the doctrine of Karma cannot be a principle of Jainism. The other options align with Jainism: ahimsa (non-injury to living beings), syadvada (relative truth), and monastic life as the path to salvation. Jainism believes that every entity, including stone and water, possesses a soul (jiva).
qs.kf:
☛ Core principles of Jainism → Ahimsa, Satya, Asteya, Brahmacharya, Aparigraha
☛ Nature of Karma in Jainism → Pudgala particles attach to the soul
☛ Path to liberation in Jainism → Samyak Darshan, Samyak Jnana, Samyak Charitra
☛ Concept of Jiva in Jainism → All substances have a soul
☛ Key philosophical doctrine of Jainism → Syadvada (Anekantavada)

q: Which of the following is a Buddhist text containing stories related to the previous births of the Buddha?
qs.e: The Jatakas are a significant Buddhist text that contains stories about the previous births of the Buddha. These stories illustrate the paramitas (perfections) and moral principles of Buddhism. Written in Pali language, the Jatakas include around 550 tales where the Buddha appears as an animal, human, or deity, demonstrating virtues like generosity, compassion, truthfulness, and patience. The text is an important part of Buddhist literature, teaching ethical and philosophical concepts through simple narratives. The other options: Panchatantra is a Hindu collection of fables, Arthashastra is a political treatise by Kautilya, and Manusmriti is a Hindu legal code.
qs.kf:
☛ Buddhist text containing stories of Buddha's previous births → Jatakas
☛ Language of Jatakas → Pali
☛ Number of Jataka tales → Approximately 550
☛ Forms of Buddha in Jatakas → Animal, human, or deity
☛ Virtues highlighted in Jatakas → Generosity, compassion, truth, patience

q: In Jain religion, the Svetarnbara canon consists of how many of Agamas?
qs.e: In the Svetambara tradition of Jainism, the canonical literature consists of 45 Agamas. These Agamas are the scriptures containing the teachings of Mahavira and were compiled by the Ganadharas. The Svetambara canon includes 12 Angas, 12 Upangas, 10 Prakirnakas, 6 Chedasutras, 4 Mulasutras, and 1 Chulika. In contrast, the Digambara sect accepts only the 12 Angas as authoritative. The Svetambara Agamas cover ethics, philosophy, conduct, and karma theory, and are considered the most authentic source of Jain doctrine in the Svetambara tradition.
qs.kf:
☛ Total number in the Svetambara canon → 45
☛ Number of Agamas accepted by Digambaras → 12 (Angas)
☛ Main divisions of Svetambara Agamas → 12 Angas, 12 Upangas, 10 Prakirnakas, 6 Chedasutras, 4 Mulasutras, 1 Chulika
☛ Source of Jain Agamas → Teachings of Mahavira
☛ First Agama in Svetambara tradition → Acharanga Sutra

q: Which of the following Jain councils was held at Vallabhi (Gujarat) in 512 CE under the chairmanship of Devardhi Kshamasramana?
qs.e: The Second Jain Council was held in 512 CE at Vallabhi (Gujarat) under the chairmanship of Devardhi Kshamasramana. Its primary purpose was to compile and preserve the Jain scriptures, particularly the Agamas, in written form. The First Jain Council had been held earlier at Pataliputra around 300 BCE. After the Second Council, the Third Jain Council was also held at Vallabhi in the 5th century. The Second Council is crucial for the Shwetambara sect, as it systematically organized the 12 Angas and Upangas. Devardhi Kshamasramana was a prominent Acharya who contributed significantly to the preservation of Jain literature.
qs.kf:
☛ First Jain Council → Pataliputra, 300 BCE, Chairman: Sthulabhadra
☛ Second Jain Council → Vallabhi, 512 CE, Chairman: Devardhi Kshamasramana
☛ Third Jain Council → Vallabhi, 5th century
☛ Jain Agama texts → 12 Angas, 12 Upangas, 10 Prakirnakas, etc.
☛ Devardhi Kshamasramana → Shwetambara Acharya, compiler of Agamas

q: During the period of medieval Indian literature, which language began to decline as the dominant medium for Buddhist literary expression and scholarship?
qs.e: During the medieval period of Indian literature, Pali began to decline as the dominant medium for Buddhist literary expression and scholarship. Early Buddhist texts, such as the Tripitaka, were written in Pali, but medieval times saw a rise in the use of Sanskrit among Buddhist scholars. Universities like Nalanda and Vikramashila produced works in Sanskrit. Pali's usage became largely confined to the Theravada tradition. As a result, Pali's prominence diminished, and Sanskrit became the language of Buddhist philosophy and tantric literature.
qs.kf:
☛ Earliest language of Buddhist literature → Pali
☛ Language of Tripitaka → Pali
☛ Language of Hinayana Buddhism → Pali
☛ Language of Mahayana Buddhism → Sanskrit
☛ Chinese Buddhist pilgrim Faxian wrote in → Chinese

q: At what age did Gautama Buddha attain Enlightenment (Nirvana) at Bodh Gaya in Bihar?
qs.e: Gautama Buddha attained Enlightenment (Nirvana) at the age of 35 under a peepal tree at Bodh Gaya in Bihar. Before this, he had renounced his princely life at the age of 29 and practiced severe austerity for six years. After attaining Nirvana, he came to be known as the Buddha. He was born in 563 BCE in Lumbini, Nepal. The Mahabodhi Temple in Bodh Gaya is a major pilgrimage site for Buddhists and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
qs.kf:
☛ Birthplace of Gautama Buddha → Lumbini, Nepal
☛ Age of Renunciation → 29 years
☛ Place of Enlightenment → Bodh Gaya, Bihar
☛ Age of Enlightenment → 35 years
☛ Famous temple at Bodh Gaya → Mahabodhi Temple

q: The Visuddhimagga, a key Buddhist text, was written by which of the following scholars?
qs.e: The Visuddhimagga, meaning 'Path of Purification', is a key text in Theravada Buddhism. It was composed by the scholar Buddhaghosa in the 5th century CE. The text systematically summarizes the teachings of the Buddha and provides a detailed commentary on the Abhidhamma. Buddhaghosa is regarded as the greatest commentator of the Theravada tradition, and he also wrote commentaries on the Tripitaka. Nagarjuna and Aryadeva are associated with the Madhyamaka philosophy, while Vasubandhu is linked to the Yogacara school. Hence, the Visuddhimagga is correctly attributed to Buddhaghosa.
qs.kf:
☛ Author of Visuddhimagga → Buddhaghosa
☛ Buddhaghosa belongs to which tradition → Theravada
☛ Period of Buddhaghosa → 5th century CE
☛ Nagarjuna is associated with which philosophy → Madhyamaka
☛ Vasubandhu is associated with which school → Yogacara

q: During which period of Indian history were the stupas of Sanchi and Sarnath built, reflecting its architectural style?
qs.e: The stupas of Sanchi and Sarnath are outstanding examples of architecture from the Mauryan period. They were built by Emperor Ashoka (c. 268-232 BCE). Sanchi Stupa, located in Madhya Pradesh, is renowned for its large hemispherical dome and ornate gateways (toranas). Sarnath Stupa, in Uttar Pradesh, marks the site where Buddha delivered his first sermon. Mauryan stupa architecture reflects the influence of Buddhism, along with exquisite stone carving and grandeur. Ashoka's edicts are also a significant heritage from this period. The Mauryan rule was marked by centralized administration and patronage of art and religion.
qs.kf:
☛ Who built the Sanchi Stupa? → Emperor Ashoka
☛ What is Sarnath famous for? → Buddha's first sermon
☛ Major architectural style of Mauryan period? → Stupa construction
☛ In which script are Ashoka's edicts written? → Brahmi script
☛ Who was the last ruler of Mauryan dynasty? → Brihadratha

q: The artistic and architectural style evident in the Bagh Caves of Madhya Pradesh, India, is predominantly associated with which of the following faiths?
qs.e: The Bagh Caves, located on the banks of the Bagh River in Madhya Pradesh, are associated with Buddhism. These caves were constructed around the 5th-6th century AD and consist of viharas (monastic residences) and a chaitya (prayer hall). The wall paintings found in the caves depict Buddhist themes such as the Jataka tales and scenes from the life of Buddha. The artistic style is heavily influenced by the Ajanta style of painting. Thus, the artistic and architectural style of the Bagh Caves is predominantly associated with Buddhism.
qs.kf:
☛ Period of construction of Bagh Caves → 5th-6th century AD
☛ State where Bagh Caves are located → Madhya Pradesh
☛ Who resided in these caves → Buddhist monks
☛ Painting style influencing Bagh Caves → Ajanta style
☛ What stories are depicted in Bagh Caves → Buddhist Jataka tales

q: Name the Buddhist text that comprises rules for monks.
qs.e: In Buddhism, the Tripitaka is a collection of three major texts. The Vinaya Pitaka deals with the rules of discipline and conduct for monks and nuns. It contains detailed codes of conduct to be followed during spiritual practice. Among the other options, the Sutta Pitaka is a collection of the Buddha's discourses, while the Abhidhamma Pitaka is a philosophical and psychological text. The Tipitaka is the collective name for all three, not a single text. Hence, the Vinaya Pitaka comprises rules for monks.
qs.kf:
☛ How many rules are in the Vinaya Pitaka? → 227 rules (for a full monk)
☛ How many sections are in the Vinaya Pitaka? → Three: Suttavibhanga, Khandhaka, Parivara
☛ Who founded the Buddhist Sangha? → Gautama Buddha
☛ How many Nikayas are in the Sutta Pitaka? → Five Nikayas
☛ How many books are in the Abhidhamma Pitaka? → Seven books

q: In which state of India can we find the preserved Buddhist caves called 'Karla'?
qs.e: The Karla Caves are ancient Buddhist rock-cut caves located in the state of Maharashtra, India. Situated near Lonavala in the Pune district, these caves date back to the 2nd century BCE to the 5th century CE. The Karla Caves are renowned for their magnificent chaityagriha (prayer hall), which is one of the largest and best-preserved ancient cave temples in India. The cave complex features exquisite sculptures and inscriptions, reflecting both Hinayana and Mahayana traditions of Buddhism. The Karla Caves are a protected monument of national importance and attract numerous tourists and historians.
qs.kf:
☛ Which state are the Karla Caves located in? → Maharashtra
☛ When were the Karla Caves constructed? → 2nd century BCE to 5th century CE
☛ What is the main structure in Karla Caves? → Chaityagriha
☛ Which religion do the Karla Caves belong to? → Buddhism
☛ Which city is near the Karla Caves? → Lonavala

q: Which statement from the given options is NOT correct?
o: Buddhist scriptures werer written in Pali.
Charak was the personal physician of Gautam Buddha.
Upagupta influence Ashoka to embrace Buddhism.
The birth place of Gautam Buddha is in Nepal.
qs.e: Charak was not the personal physician of Gautam Buddha. Charak was an ancient Indian physician who authored the Charaka Samhita, a foundational text of Ayurveda, and lived around the 2nd century BCE. Buddha's personal physician was Jivaka, who also served as a physician to Lord Mahavira. The other statements are correct: Buddhist scriptures were written in Pali, Upagupta influenced Ashoka to embrace Buddhism, and Gautam Buddha was born in Lumbini (Nepal).
qs.kf:
☛ Language of Buddhist scriptures → Pali
☛ Personal physician of Gautam Buddha → Jivaka
☛ Author of Charaka Samhita → Charak
☛ Monk who influenced Ashoka to embrace Buddhism → Upagupta
☛ Birthplace of Gautam Buddha → Lumbini (Nepal)

q: Which of the following statements is true about the Sutta Pitaka?
o: It is Buddhist text that was written in Sri Lanka.
It deals with the conversation between the ruler of Magadha and the Buddha.
It is about the rules and regulations for those who joined the Buddhist monastic order.
It is the biography of the Buddha.
qs.e: The Sutta Pitaka is one of the three main texts of Buddhism, known as the Tipitaka. It contains the discourses of the Buddha and his disciples. Specifically, within the Sutta Pitaka, the Digha Nikaya includes suttas like the 'Samannaphala Sutta', which describes a conversation between the ruler of Magadha, Ajatashatru, and the Buddha. This text was originally written in the Pali language and is preserved in the Theravada tradition. Other options are incorrect: the first is false because it claims the text was written in Sri Lanka, whereas it was originally composed in India; the third option relates to the Vinaya Pitaka, which deals with monastic rules; the fourth is false because the biography of the Buddha is found in texts like the Buddhacharita, not the Sutta Pitaka.
qs.kf:
☛ What are the three divisions of the Tripitaka? → Vinaya Pitaka, Sutta Pitaka, Abhidhamma Pitaka
☛ In which language was the Sutta Pitaka written? → Pali language
☛ How many Nikayas are in the Sutta Pitaka? → Five Nikayas (Digha, Majjhima, Samyutta, Anguttara, Khuddaka)
☛ What does the Vinaya Pitaka deal with? → Rules and code of conduct for Buddhist monks
☛ What does the Abhidhamma Pitaka deal with? → Buddhist philosophy and psychology

q: At which of the following places did Gautam Buddha attain enlightenment?
qs.e: Gautam Buddha attained enlightenment under a peepal tree at Bodh Gaya, located in the state of Bihar. He lived approximately from 563 BCE to 483 BCE. After attaining enlightenment, he became known as the Buddha. Bodh Gaya is one of the four major pilgrimage sites of Buddhism. The Mahabodhi Temple here is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. At Sarnath, he delivered his first sermon; at Kushinagar, he attained Mahaparinirvana; and at Lumbini (Nepal), he was born.
qs.kf:
☛ Birthplace of Gautam Buddha → Lumbini (Nepal)
☛ Place of Enlightenment → Bodh Gaya (Bihar)
☛ Place of First Sermon → Sarnath (Uttar Pradesh)
☛ Place of Mahaparinirvana → Kushinagar (Uttar Pradesh)
☛ Famous temple at Bodh Gaya → Mahabodhi Temple

q: The worship of images of Buddha became an important tradition in:
qs.e: The worship of images of Buddha became an important tradition in Mahayana Buddhism. Mahayana, meaning 'Great Vehicle', is a major branch of Buddhism. In Mahayana, Buddha is revered as a divine being and emphasis is placed on the concept of bodhisattvas who work for the liberation of others. In contrast, Hinayana Buddhism places less emphasis on image worship and focuses more on individual salvation. Vajrayana is tantric Buddhism which evolved from Mahayana, and Nyingma is a sect of Tibetan Buddhism. Mahayana popularized image worship, making Buddhism accessible to the common people. This tradition included the creation of Buddha statues and stupas for veneration.
qs.kf:
☛ In which branch of Buddhism is image worship prominent? → Mahayana
☛ What does Mahayana mean? → Great Vehicle
☛ Which Buddhist branch emphasizes the concept of Bodhisattva? → Mahayana
☛ What does Hinayana mean? → Small Vehicle
☛ From which branch did Vajrayana evolve? → Mahayana

q: The concept of Bodhisattva is associated with:
qs.e: The concept of Bodhisattva is associated with Mahayana Buddhism. Mahayana, meaning 'Great Vehicle', is a major branch of Buddhism. A Bodhisattva is an enlightened being who postpones Nirvana to help all sentient beings achieve liberation, guided by compassion and bodhicitta. The Bodhisattva path emphasizes the practice of the paramitas (perfections: generosity, morality, patience, vigor, meditation, wisdom). In contrast, Hinayana (Theravada) focuses on becoming an Arhat, not a Bodhisattva. Jainism and Sikhism do not have the concept of Bodhisattva. Thus, the Bodhisattva ideal is central to Mahayana Buddhism, distinguishing it from other traditions. Competitive Exam Special One-liners: ☛ One who follows the Bodhisattva path → Bodhisattva ☛ Mahayana Buddhism is also called → Great Vehicle ☛ Qualities of a Bodhisattva → Paramitas ☛ Main ideal of a Bodhisattva → Compassion and bodhicitta ☛ Goal of Hinayana Buddhism → Becoming an Arhat

q: Vinaya and Sutta Pitaka are the compilations of whose teachings?
qs.e: The Vinaya Pitaka and Sutta Pitaka are two major parts of the Tripitaka, which is the compilation of the teachings of Gautam Buddha. The Tripitaka consists of three sections: the Vinaya Pitaka (rules for monastic discipline), the Sutta Pitaka (discourses of the Buddha), and the Abhidhamma Pitaka (philosophical analysis). These scriptures are written in the Pali language and are considered the foundational texts of Buddhism. The Vinaya Pitaka details the code of conduct for monks and nuns, while the Sutta Pitaka contains the sermons delivered by Buddha. These texts are highly revered in the Theravada Buddhist tradition.
qs.kf:
☛ In which language is the Tripitaka composed? → Pali
☛ Who founded Buddhism? → Gautam Buddha
☛ What does Abhidhamma Pitaka deal with? → Philosophical analysis
☛ What is described in the Vinaya Pitaka? → Rules for monastic discipline
☛ Whose teachings are compiled in the Sutta Pitaka? → Gautam Buddha

q: Which of the following universities is acclaimed as the 'Oxford of Mahayanism'?
qs.e: Nalanda University is acclaimed as the 'Oxford of Mahayanism'. It was a major Buddhist learning center in ancient India, flourishing from the 5th to 12th century. Nalanda became the epicenter for the study and propagation of Mahayana Buddhism, attracting scholars from across the world. Subjects taught included Mahayana philosophy, Buddhist scriptures, logic, and grammar. Its prestige and academic excellence earned it the title 'Oxford of Mahayanism'. Nalanda is also a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
qs.kf:
☛ Most famous ancient university of India → Nalanda
☛ Founder of Nalanda → Kumaragupta I (Gupta dynasty)
☛ Who destroyed Nalanda → Bakhtiyar Khilji (1193 CE)
☛ Founder of Vikramashila University → Dharmapala (Pala dynasty)
☛ Taxila known for → Medicine and Political Science

q: Jataka tales are related to _____
qs.e: Jataka tales are related to Buddhism. These stories describe the previous births of Gautama Buddha, where he is born as various beings and imparts moral lessons. Each Jataka tale depicts the actions and consequences of Buddha's past lives, helping to understand Buddhism's principles of karma and rebirth. Jataka tales are an important part of Buddhist literature and are used to explain the ethical and philosophical aspects of Buddhism in simple language.
qs.kf:
☛ Which religion are Jataka tales related to? → Buddhism
☛ What is the main subject of Jataka tales? → Previous births of Gautama Buddha
☛ What is the purpose of Jataka tales? → Moral and philosophical teaching
☛ Which tales explain karma and rebirth in Buddhism? → Jataka tales
☛ Jataka tales are part of which literature? → Buddhist literature

q: Lord Mahavira's original name is _________.
qs.e: Lord Mahavira was born in 540 BCE in Kundagrama near Vaishali to a Kshatriya family. His father was Siddhartha and mother Trishala. As a child, he was named Vardhamana, meaning 'one who grows'. He is the 24th and last Tirthankara of Jainism. At the age of 30, he renounced worldly life and after 12 years of severe penance attained Kevala Jnana (omniscience). He then became known as Mahavira (Great Hero). He preached in Prakrit language and advocated five principles: Ahimsa, Satya, Asteya, Brahmacharya, and Aparigraha. His teachings form the core of Jain philosophy. He attained Nirvana at Pavapuri in 468 BCE.
qs.kf:
☛ Father of Mahavira → Siddhartha
☛ Mother of Mahavira → Trishala
☛ Birthplace of Mahavira → Kundagrama (Vaishali)
☛ 24th Tirthankara of Jainism → Mahavira
☛ Place of Mahavira's Nirvana → Pavapuri

q: Which of the following is an ancient Buddhist text?
qs.e: ✅ Correct Answer: (D) Abhidharma kosha

q: Where was Gautama Buddha born?
qs.e: Gautama Buddha was born in 563 BCE in Lumbini (present-day Nepal). This site is located 27 km from Kapilavastu, the capital of the Shakya Republic. His mother, Queen Mahamaya, was traveling from Kapilavastu to her parental home in Devadaha when she stopped in the Sal grove of Lumbini and gave birth to him. Later, Emperor Ashoka visited Lumbini in 249 BCE and erected a pillar there, which serves as evidence of this event. The site is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
qs.kf:
☛ Birthplace of Gautama Buddha → Lumbini (Nepal)
☛ Name of Buddha's father → Shuddhodhana
☛ Name of Buddha's mother → Mahamaya
☛ Childhood name of Buddha → Siddhartha
☛ Ashoka pillar at Lumbini erected in → 249 BCE

q: The famous Buddhist structure, Dhamekh Stupa was originally constructed during ________ dynasty.
qs.e: The Dhamekh Stupa is a famous Buddhist structure located in Sarnath, Uttar Pradesh, India. It was originally constructed during the Mauryan dynasty by Emperor Ashoka. This stupa marks the spot where Gautama Buddha delivered his first sermon, known as the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta (Setting in Motion the Wheel of Dharma). The present structure saw several additions and renovations later during the Gupta period. The Dhamekh Stupa has a cylindrical shape and features intricate stone carvings and geometric patterns on its walls. It is one of the prominent Buddhist monuments at Sarnath and forms part of the Sarnath complex, which is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
qs.kf:
☛ Where is Dhamekh Stupa located? → Sarnath, Uttar Pradesh
☛ Who built the Dhamekh Stupa? → Mauryan Emperor Ashoka
☛ Where did Gautama Buddha deliver his first sermon? → Sarnath
☛ Which period is credited with the renovation of Dhamekh Stupa? → Gupta period
☛ Which is the largest stupa in Sarnath? → Dhamekh Stupa

q: In the context of Buddhist architecture, what is a ‘chaitya’?
o: A hall for prayer and assembly
qs.e: ✅ Correct Answer: (D) A hall for prayer and assembly

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (06/06/2025) Shift 3
q: The Abhidhamma Pitaka explores which of the following areas in depth?
o: Ethics, mental phenomena, and psychological insights
qs.e: The Abhidhamma Pitaka is the third part of the Buddhist Tripitaka, focusing on philosophical and psychological analysis. It deeply explores ethics, mental phenomena, and psychological insights. It includes a systematic examination of consciousness, mental factors, and the nature of reality. Other options like political history, folk tales, and animal stories are not subjects of the Abhidhamma. The Abhidhamma Pitaka provides the foundation for Buddhist philosophy and helps develop a deep understanding of the mind.
qs.kf:
☛ What are the three parts of the Tripitaka? → Vinaya Pitaka, Sutta Pitaka, Abhidhamma Pitaka
☛ What does the Abhidhamma Pitaka deal with? → Philosophy and psychology
☛ How many books are in the Abhidhamma Pitaka? → 7 books
☛ When was the Abhidhamma Pitaka compiled? → Third Buddhist Council (c. 250 BCE)
☛ In which language was the Abhidhamma Pitaka written? → Pali language

q: One of the best preserved Buddhist caves, Karla, is in which of the following states?
qs.e: Karla Caves are an ancient Buddhist cave complex located in the Pune district of Maharashtra state. They are renowned for their large chaitya griha (prayer hall) containing a stupa and intricate carvings. Dating back to the 1st century BCE, these caves belong to the Hinayana sect of Buddhism. Karla Caves are considered one of the best-preserved Buddhist cave complexes in India. Situated in the Sahyadri hills, they showcase the architectural skills of ancient India.
qs.kf:
☛ In which state are the Karla Caves located? → Maharashtra
☛ Karla Caves are associated with which religion? → Buddhism (Hinayana)
☛ Which structure is prominent in Karla Caves? → Chaitya griha and stupa
☛ To which century do the Karla Caves belong? → 1st century BCE
☛ Who built the Karla Caves? → Satavahana kings

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (19/06/2025) Shift 1
q: The relics of Buddha are found inside which of the following Buddhist architectures?
qs.e: In Buddhist architecture, Stupas are the structures that contain relics of Buddha. A stupa is a dome-shaped monument that preserves parts of Buddha's body or objects associated with him. It is considered a center of worship in Buddhism. The most famous stupa is the Sanchi Stupa in Madhya Pradesh, built by Emperor Ashoka. Stupas are surrounded by railings (vedika) and gateways (torana). Other options: Rock Edicts are related to royal decrees, Chaitya Halls are prayer halls, and Ashokan Pillars bear inscriptions, but none of them contain relics.
qs.kf:
☛ Relics of Buddha are found in? → Stupas
☛ Who built the Sanchi Stupa? → Ashoka
☛ What is the shape of a stupa? → Dome-shaped
☛ What surrounds a stupa? → Railing (vedika) and gateways (torana)
☛ Chaitya Halls are used for? → Prayer

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (24/06/2025) Shift 1
q: Which of the following stupas marks the spot where Buddha gave his first sermon?
qs.e: The Dhamek Stupa is located in Sarnath, Uttar Pradesh, India. It marks the spot where Lord Buddha delivered his first sermon, known as the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta (Turning of the Wheel of Dharma), to his first five disciples after attaining enlightenment. The stupa was originally built by Emperor Ashoka and later enlarged during the Gupta period. It is renowned for its massive structure and intricate stone carvings. Dhamek Stupa is one of the four major pilgrimage sites for Buddhists.
qs.kf:
☛ Where did Buddha give his first sermon? → Sarnath
☛ What does Dhammacakkappavattana mean? → Turning the Wheel of Dharma
☛ Who built the Dhamek Stupa? → Emperor Ashoka
☛ Who were the first listeners of Buddha's sermon? → Five disciples
☛ In which language did Buddha give his first sermon? → Pali

q: Which of the following kings convened the fourth Buddhist Council in Kashmir?
qs.e: Kanishka was the most famous ruler of the Kushana dynasty. During his reign, the Fourth Buddhist Council was convened at Kundalavana in Kashmir. The council was presided over by Vasumitra, with Ashvaghosha as vice president. This council formalized the split between Mahayana and Hinayana schools of Buddhism. The teachings of the Buddha were compiled, and commentaries on the Tripitaka were written. Kanishka patronized Buddhism and built a massive stupa at Peshawar.
qs.kf:
☛ First Buddhist Council → Rajgir (presided by Mahakashyapa)
☛ Second Buddhist Council → Vaishali (presided by Sabbakami)
☛ Third Buddhist Council → Pataliputra (presided by Moggaliputta Tissa)
☛ Fourth Buddhist Council → Kashmir (presided by Vasumitra)
☛ Kanishka's court poet → Ashvaghosha

q: Which of the following sermons of Gautama Buddha known as Fire Sermon?
qs.e: Gautama Buddha's Adittapariyaya Sutta is famously known as the 'Fire Sermon'. The Buddha delivered this sermon to five monks in Gaya, explaining that everything is burning - eyes, forms, consciousness, contact, and sensations - all are aflame with the fire of attachment, aversion, and ignorance. This sutta emphasizes the concept of anatta (non-self) and teaches detachment from all conditioned phenomena. It is one of the early sermons given after Buddha's enlightenment and is found in the Samyutta Nikaya of the Sutta Pitaka. The Fire Sermon uses the metaphor of fire to illustrate the unsatisfactoriness of clinging and the path to liberation.
qs.kf:
☛ Which sutta is known as the Fire Sermon? → Adittapariyaya Sutta
☛ Which was Buddha's first sermon? → Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta
☛ Which sutta focuses on anatta (non-self)? → Anatta-lakkhana Sutta
☛ Buddha's teachings are collected in which pitaka? → Sutta Pitaka of Tripitaka
☛ Adittapariyaya Sutta belongs to which nikaya? → Samyutta Nikaya

q: At which of the following places did Gautam Buddha attain enlightenment?
qs.e: Gautam Buddha attained enlightenment (Bodhi) under a Peepal tree at Bodh Gaya, located in the Gaya district of Bihar. After 49 days of intense meditation and ascetic practices, he achieved Nirvana at this site. It is one of the four major pilgrimage sites in Buddhism. The other three are: Lumbini (birth), Sarnath (first sermon), and Kushinagar (Mahaparinirvana). The Mahabodhi Temple at Bodh Gaya is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The sacred Bodhi tree, under which Buddha meditated, is still worshipped here. This place holds immense significance in Buddhist history and attracts pilgrims from around the world.
qs.kf:
☛ Where did Gautam Buddha attain enlightenment? → Bodh Gaya
☛ Which is the birthplace of Buddha? → Lumbini
☛ Where did Buddha give his first sermon? → Sarnath
☛ Where did Buddha attain Mahaparinirvana? → Kushinagar
☛ Which temple at Bodh Gaya is a UNESCO World Heritage Site? → Mahabodhi Temple

q: What was the real name of Buddha?
qs.e: Gautama Buddha was born in 563 BCE in Lumbini (Nepal). His real name was Siddhartha and he was a prince of the Shakya clan. His father's name was Shuddhodhana and mother's name was Maya Devi. At the age of 29, he left the palace in search of truth. After six years of severe penance, he attained enlightenment under a peepal tree at Bodh Gaya and became known as 'Buddha'. His first sermon was delivered at Sarnath, known as Dhammachakka Pavattana. Buddha preached the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path.
qs.kf:
☛ Real name of Gautama Buddha → Siddhartha
☛ Clan of Buddha → Shakya
☛ Mother of Buddha → Maya Devi
☛ Place of enlightenment → Bodh Gaya
☛ Place of first sermon → Sarnath

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (17/06/2025) Shift 3
q: The maximum number of Buddhist stupas had been built by which of the following rulers?
qs.e: Ashoka (268-232 BCE), the third emperor of the Maurya dynasty, embraced Buddhism after the Kalinga War. He commissioned the construction of a large number of Buddhist stupas and pillars across India and regions like Nepal, Sri Lanka, and Afghanistan. Texts like 'Divyavadana' and 'Ashokavadana' mention that Ashoka built 84,000 stupas. Famous stupas like Sanchi Stupa and Bharhut Stupa belong to his period. Pushyamitra Sunga was anti-Buddhist, Chandragupta Maurya was a Jain, and Bimbisara followed Buddhism but built fewer stupas than Ashoka. Thus, Ashoka built the maximum number of stupas.
qs.kf:
☛ Number of stupas built by Ashoka → 84,000
☛ Ashoka's Buddhist teacher → Upagupta
☛ Language of Ashoka's edicts → Prakrit
☛ Location of Sanchi Stupa → Madhya Pradesh
☛ Famous stupa built by Ashoka → Sanchi Stupa

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (24/06/2025) Shift 2
q: The Bagh caves, which contain Buddhist mural paintings, are located in which of the following states of India?
qs.e: The Bagh caves are located in the Dhar district of Madhya Pradesh. These caves are famous for their Buddhist mural paintings, which date back to the Gupta period (around 5th-7th century AD). There are a total of 9 caves, out of which only 5 contain preserved paintings. These paintings are similar to those in the Ajanta caves but on a smaller scale. The Bagh caves were built by Buddhist monks during the Gupta period. They are historically significant for their architecture and painting.
qs.kf:
☛ In which state are the Bagh caves located? → Madhya Pradesh
☛ Which religion is associated with the Bagh caves? → Buddhism
☛ During which period were the Bagh caves built? → Gupta period
☛ In which district are the Bagh caves located? → Dhar district
☛ How many caves are there in Bagh? → 9

q: The Jain monastic establishments are called as:
qs.e: In Jainism, monastic establishments are called 'Basadis' (or Basadi). This term is mainly used in South India for Jain monasteries and temples where Jain monks reside and perform religious rituals. 'Aparigraha' is a Jain principle emphasizing non-attachment to possessions. 'Svetambara' is a major sect of Jainism. 'Tirth' refers to a holy place in Jainism, especially associated with Tirthankaras. The word 'Basadi' is derived from Sanskrit 'Vasati', meaning a dwelling or residence. These establishments have been centers for the spread of Jain teachings and education. Basadis are distinct from other Jain structures and play a key role in the community's religious life.
qs.kf:
☛ Jain monastic establishments are called → Basadis
☛ What is Aparigraha? → Jain principle of non-attachment
☛ What is Svetambara? → A sect of Jainism
☛ Holy places in Jainism → Tirth
☛ Origin of word Basadi → Sanskrit 'Vasati'

q: What is the primary function of ‘viharas’ in Buddhist architecture?
o: To serve as residential places for Buddhist priests
qs.e: In Buddhist architecture, viharas primarily functioned as residential places for Buddhist monks. These were monasteries where monks lived, studied, and meditated. Viharas were often located near stupas and chaityas. Early viharas were made of wood, but later cave viharas (e.g., Ajanta and Ellora) became common. They typically included cells for monks, prayer halls, and courtyards. Serving as meditation halls was the primary function of chaityas, while stupas housed relics. Thus, the main purpose of viharas was to provide accommodation for the monastic community.
qs.kf:
☛ Primary function of vihara → Residence for Buddhist monks
☛ Primary function of chaitya → Meditation and prayer hall
☛ Primary function of stupa → Preservation of Buddhist relics
☛ Ajanta and Ellora caves → Excellent examples of viharas
☛ Three major forms of Buddhist architecture → Stupa, Chaitya, Vihara

q: Gautam Buddha is associated with which famous place of the following?
qs.e: Gautam Buddha was born in 563 BCE in Lumbini, which is located in present-day Nepal in the Rupandehi district. This site is one of the four major pilgrimage sites of Buddhism. Buddha was born as Prince Siddhartha in the Shakya clan. Lumbini has been declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Its main attractions are the Maya Devi Temple and the Ashoka Pillar. Bardoli, Srirangapatnam, and Pawapuri are other religious or historical sites but are not directly associated with Buddha.
qs.kf:
☛ Birthplace of Buddha → Lumbini
☛ Year of Buddha's birth → 563 BCE
☛ Clan of Buddha at birth → Shakya republic
☛ Country where Lumbini is located → Nepal
☛ Major pillar in Lumbini → Ashoka Pillar

q: Which Buddhist text, from the 1st century BCE, records the dialogues of the Buddha?
qs.e: The Sutta Pitaka, part of the Tipitaka, contains the discourses and dialogues of the Buddha. It was compiled around the 1st century BCE in Sri Lanka at the Alu-Vihara during the Fourth Buddhist Council. Written in Pali, it includes about 10,000 suttas. The Vinaya Pitaka contains monastic rules, the Abhidhamma Pitaka philosophical analysis, and Jataka Tales stories of the Buddha's previous lives. The Sutta Pitaka expounds core Buddhist doctrines like the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path.
qs.kf:
☛ Which part of Tipitaka deals with rules? → Vinaya Pitaka
☛ Where are the Buddha's life stories found? → Jataka Tales
☛ Which Pitaka contains philosophical analysis? → Abhidhamma Pitaka
☛ Where was the Fourth Buddhist Council held? → Sri Lanka (Alu-Vihara)
☛ In which language is the Sutta Pitaka written? → Pali

q: Which Buddhist text, compiled around the 1st century CE, narrates stories of the Buddha’s past lives?
qs.e: The Jataka Tales are Buddhist texts compiled around the 1st century CE. They narrate stories of the Buddha's previous births, where he appears in various forms and imparts moral teachings. There are 547 Jataka tales, highlighting the importance of ethics and compassion in Buddhism. Originally written in the Pali language, they were later translated into other languages. The Jataka Tales are a significant part of Buddhist literature, emphasizing virtues such as generosity, patience, and self-sacrifice. These stories not only entertain but also serve as moral lessons for followers of Buddhism.
qs.kf:
☛ In which language were the Jataka Tales written? → Pali
☛ How many Jataka tales are there? → 547
☛ When were the Jataka Tales compiled? → 1st century CE
☛ Which religion are the Jataka Tales associated with? → Buddhism
☛ Which text contains stories of Buddha's past lives? → Jataka Tales

q: The study of Inscriptions is called
qs.e: The study of inscriptions is called Epigraphy. It is a crucial historical source that provides information about ancient civilizations, kings, events, and social life. Epigraphy involves the study of inscriptions engraved on stones, copper plates, pillars, and other materials. In India, the Edicts of Ashoka are famous, offering important evidence about the Mauryan Empire. Other options: Ecology studies the environment, Hydrology studies water, and Sociology studies society.
qs.kf:
☛ Study of inscriptions is called → Epigraphy
☛ Language of Ashoka's edicts → Prakrit
☛ Specialist in epigraphy is called → Epigraphist
☛ Study of copper plate inscriptions → Under epigraphy
☛ Famous epigraphist of India → James Prinsep

q: The construction of the “Sanchi Stupa” was commissioned by which Mauryan Emperor?
qs.e: The Sanchi Stupa, located in Madhya Pradesh, is a prominent Buddhist monument. Its construction was commissioned by the Mauryan Emperor Ashoka (c. 268-232 BCE) in the 3rd century BCE. After embracing Buddhism following the Kalinga War, Ashoka built numerous stupas across India, with the Sanchi Stupa being one of the most important. The stupa originally housed relics of Lord Buddha. Later, during the Shunga period, it was expanded and the famous gateways (toranas) were added. Sanchi Stupa is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and an excellent example of Buddhist architecture.
qs.kf:
☛ Where is Sanchi Stupa located? → Madhya Pradesh
☛ After which war did Ashoka adopt Buddhism? → Kalinga War
☛ During which period were the toranas added to Sanchi Stupa? → Shunga period
☛ Who was Ashoka's spiritual teacher? → Upagupta
☛ In which architectural style was Sanchi Stupa built? → Buddhist stupa style

q: In whose court was Chanakya a minister?
qs.e: Chanakya, also known as Kautilya or Vishnugupta, was a great ancient Indian scholar, teacher, and politician. He guided Chandragupta Maurya in becoming a king and served as the prime minister in his court. Chanakya authored the famous text Arthashastra, which is an important source of politics, economics, and military strategy. His policies and wisdom played a crucial role in establishing the Mauryan Empire. Thus, Chanakya was a minister in the court of Chandragupta Maurya.
qs.kf:
☛ Real name of Chanakya → Vishnugupta
☛ Text authored by Chanakya → Arthashastra
☛ Birthplace of Chanakya → Taxila
☛ Educational institution of Chanakya → Taxila University
☛ Empire established by Chanakya → Mauryan Empire

q: Name the daughter of one of the most important rulers in early Indian history, Chandragupta II.
qs.e: Chandragupta II (Vikramaditya) was one of the most powerful rulers of the Gupta dynasty. His daughter Prabhavatigupta was married to the Vakataka king Rudrasena II. After Rudrasena's death, Prabhavatigupta ruled as regent on behalf of her sons, a period lasting about 20 years. During this time, she extended Gupta influence into the Deccan region. Thus, Prabhavatigupta was not only the daughter of Chandragupta II but also an influential queen in the Vakataka dynasty. Her rule symbolizes the political and cultural exchange between the Gupta and Vakataka empires.
qs.kf:
☛ Daughter of Chandragupta II → Prabhavatigupta
☛ Prabhavatigupta married to → Rudrasena II (Vakataka)
☛ Prabhavatigupta's reign → about 20 years as regent
☛ Golden age of Gupta dynasty → Chandragupta II (Vikramaditya)
☛ Vakataka dynasty → powerful in the Deccan region

q: What is meant by Epigraphy?
qs.e: Epigraphy is the study of ancient inscriptions and writings on durable materials like stone and metal. It is a crucial branch of archaeology and history that helps decode past civilizations. Inscriptions record royal edicts, religious texts, and social norms. Notable examples include Emperor Ashoka's edicts, the Hatigumpha inscription, and the Girnar inscription. Epigraphists require knowledge of scripts such as Brahmi and Kharosthi to read them. The field also aids in deciphering ancient scripts like the Indus Valley script. Epigraphy provides primary sources for reconstructing political, cultural, and economic histories.
qs.kf:
☛ In which language are Ashoka's edicts primarily written? → Prakrit
☛ Which is the most ancient script? → Brahmi
☛ To which king does the Hatigumpha inscription belong? → Kharavela
☛ Which ruler's inscription is the Girnar inscription? → Rudradaman
☛ What is the study of Epigraphy? → Inscriptions

q: Who was the teacher of Chandragupta Maurya?
qs.e: The teacher of Chandragupta Maurya was Vishnu Gupta, also known as Chanakya or Kautilya. Chanakya was a great scholar, economist, and politician who taught Chandragupta politics, warfare, and administration. He played a crucial role in ending the Nanda dynasty and establishing the Maurya Empire. Kalhan was a historian of Kashmir, Vishnu Sharma authored the Panchatantra, and Skandgupta was a ruler of the Gupta dynasty. Chanakya composed the Arthashastra, a key text on statecraft and economics. Thus, the teacher of Chandragupta Maurya was Vishnu Gupta (Chanakya).
qs.kf:
☛ What was the real name of Chanakya? → Vishnu Gupta
☛ By what other name is Chanakya known? → Kautilya
☛ Which famous book was written by Chanakya? → Arthashastra
☛ Which dynasty did Chandragupta Maurya establish? → Maurya dynasty
☛ Which ruler did Chanakya defeat to establish the Maurya Empire? → Dhanananda (Nanda dynasty)

q: Who among the following was the last Mauryan King?
qs.e: Brihadratha was the last Mauryan emperor, who ruled around 187-180 BCE. He was the ruler during the decline of the Mauryan Empire. Brihadratha was assassinated by his commander-in-chief Pushyamitra Shunga during a military parade, after which Pushyamitra established the Shunga dynasty. During Brihadratha's reign, the Mauryan Empire had already weakened and faced challenges to its authority. Brihadratha was a descendant of Chandragupta Maurya, the founder of the Mauryan dynasty. His death marked the end of the Mauryan Empire and the beginning of the Shunga rule in India.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the last Mauryan king? → Brihadratha
☛ Who killed Brihadratha? → Pushyamitra Shunga
☛ Who founded the Shunga dynasty? → Pushyamitra Shunga
☛ What was the reign period of Brihadratha? → Around 187-180 BCE
☛ Which dynasty came after the Mauryan Empire? → Shunga dynasty

q: Who was the successor of Chandragupta Maurya?
qs.e: After Chandragupta Maurya, his son Bindusara succeeded to the Mauryan throne. Bindusara reigned from approximately 297 BCE to 273 BCE. He was also known by the title 'Amitraghata' (slayer of enemies). Bindusara expanded the empire into the southern part of India, conquering most of the peninsula except for Kalinga. Chanakya continued to serve as his minister during his reign. Bindusara was a follower of Jainism and under his rule the Mauryan Empire reached its zenith. He was succeeded by his son Ashoka.
qs.kf:
☛ Successor of Chandragupta Maurya → Bindusara
☛ Title of Bindusara → Amitraghata
☛ Bindusara's reign → 297-273 BCE
☛ Religion of Bindusara → Jainism
☛ Bindusara's successor → Ashoka

q: The 'lion-colored pillar-head' in Sarnath was built by whom?
qs.e: The 'lion-colored pillar-head' at Sarnath was built by the Mauryan emperor Ashok. This pillar is one of several pillars erected by Ashok to propagate dharma. It is famously known as the 'Sarnath Lion Capital'. The most distinctive feature of this capital is the four lions standing back to back. This capital was adopted as the National Emblem of India. Ashok erected such pillars across his empire, inscribed with his edicts. The Sarnath pillar is made of sandstone and is renowned for its artistic excellence and historical significance. It currently resides in the Sarnath Museum near Varanasi.
qs.kf:
☛ Who built the Sarnath Lion Capital? → Ashok
☛ How many lions are on the Sarnath pillar? → Four
☛ From which pillar is India's National Emblem taken? → Sarnath Lion Capital
☛ What material are Ashokan pillars made of? → Sandstone
☛ Where is the Sarnath pillar now located? → Sarnath Museum, Varanasi

q: During whose reign Chinese traveler Fa-Hienya, who visited India?
qs.e: The Chinese Buddhist monk Fa-hien visited India during the reign of Chandragupta II (also known as Vikramaditya) of the Gupta Empire, between 399-414 CE. He came in search of Buddhist scriptures and traveled extensively across the Indian subcontinent, visiting places like Pataliputra, Kannauj, Mathura, and Takshashila. His travelogue, 'Fo-kuo-ki' (Account of Buddhist Kingdoms), provides valuable insights into the Gupta period's society, economy, religion, and administration. Fa-hien mentioned the coexistence of Hinduism and Buddhism, efficient governance, and social welfare activities. He also noted the absence of severe punishments and the prevalence of vegetarianism among the people. His account is a crucial primary source for understanding ancient Indian history.
qs.kf:
☛ During whose reign did Fa-hien visit India? → Chandragupta II
☛ What was the purpose of Fa-hien's visit to India? → To obtain Buddhist scriptures
☛ What is the name of Fa-hien's travelogue? → Fo-kuo-ki (Account of Buddhist Kingdoms)
☛ Which country did Fa-hien belong to? → China
☛ Which Gupta ruler was given the title 'Vikramaditya'? → Chandragupta II

q: Which of the following officers was known as Akaradhyaksha during the Mauryan period?
qs.e: In the Mauryan administration, Akaradhyaksha was the Superintendent of Mines, responsible for the production, tax collection, and management of mineral resources. Kautilya's Arthashastra mentions various officials such as Sitadhyaksha (in-charge of agriculture), Panyadhyaksha (Superintendent of Markets), and Lohadhyaksha (Superintendent of Iron). These positions highlight the efficient administrative system of the Mauryan Empire. The management of mines was crucial for state revenue and economic stability.
qs.kf:
☛ Sitadhyaksha → Officer in-charge of Agriculture
☛ Panyadhyaksha → Superintendent of Market
☛ Lohadhyaksha → Superintendent of Iron
☛ Akaradhyaksha → Superintendent of Mines
☛ Navadhyaksha → Head of the Navy Department

q: Who was responsible for District administration in the Maurya empire?
qs.e: In the Maurya Empire, the administrative system was highly organized under Emperor Chandragupta Maurya. According to Kautilya's Arthashastra, the empire was divided into provinces (managed by Kumaras or Aryaputras), which were further subdivided into districts called Aharas. Each district was administered by an officer known as Pradeshika. The Pradeshika was responsible for revenue collection, law and order, and judicial functions at the district level. The other options: Yukta was an officer for village administration, Purohit was the chief priest handling religious affairs, and Koshadhyaksha managed the royal treasury.
qs.kf:
☛ Head of district administration in Maurya empire → Pradeshika
☛ Revenue officer at village level → Yukta
☛ Head of religious affairs in Maurya period → Purohit
☛ Treasury manager → Koshadhyaksha
☛ Mauryan administrative treatise → Arthashastra

q: What was the capital of the Maurya Empire during the rule of Ashoka?
qs.e: During the reign of Ashoka, the capital of the Maurya Empire was Pataliputra (modern-day Patna). Situated on the banks of the Ganges river, it was the administrative and economic center of the empire. Ashoka ruled from Pataliputra and expanded the empire. The Greek ambassador Megasthenes described the grandeur of Pataliputra, which was protected by a wooden fort and moat. Ashoka issued his edicts promoting Buddhism from here. The Third Buddhist Council was also convened in Pataliputra under Ashoka's patronage.
qs.kf:
☛ What was the capital of the Maurya Empire? → Pataliputra
☛ Which dynasty did Ashoka belong to? → Maurya dynasty
☛ Which Greek ambassador wrote about Pataliputra? → Megasthenes
☛ What is the main source of Ashoka's reign? → Ashokan edicts
☛ Who founded the Maurya Empire? → Chandragupta Maurya

q: Who among the following was the son of Chandragupta Maurya?
qs.e: Chandragupta Maurya was the founder of the Maurya dynasty. His son Bindusara ascended the throne in 298 BCE. Bindusara was also known as 'Amitraghata' (destroyer of enemies). He expanded the empire with the help of Chanakya. During his reign, provinces like Taxila and Ujjain were administered by his sons Ashoka and Susima. Bindusara established diplomatic relations with the Greek ruler Antiochus I. He died in 273 BCE, after which a succession war led to Ashoka's coronation. Thus, Bindusara was the direct son and successor of Chandragupta Maurya.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the son of Chandragupta Maurya? → Bindusara
☛ By what name was Bindusara known? → Amitraghata
☛ With which Greek ruler did Bindusara establish ties? → Antiochus I
☛ Which province did Ashoka administer under Bindusara? → Ujjain
☛ When did Bindusara die? → 273 BCE

q: Who was the third ruler of the Maurya Empire?
qs.e: The Maurya Empire was founded by Chandragupta Maurya in 322 BCE. His son Bindusara became the second ruler, reigning from 298-272 BCE. The third ruler was Ashoka the Great, son of Bindusara, who ruled from 268-232 BCE. Ashoka was also known as Devanampriya and Priyadarshi. After the Kalinga War in 261 BCE, he embraced Buddhism and propagated the policy of non-violence.
qs.kf:
☛ Founder of Maurya Empire → Chandragupta Maurya
☛ Second Mauryan ruler → Bindusara
☛ Third Mauryan ruler → Ashoka
☛ Title of Ashoka → Devanampriya Priyadarshi
☛ Ashoka's famous war → Kalinga War (261 BCE)

q: Arrange the following Mauryan Emperors in chronological order.
I. Bindusara
II. Brihadratha
III. Samprati
IV. Ashoka
qs.e: The correct chronological order of Mauryan emperors is: Bindusara (298-272 BCE), Ashoka (268-232 BCE), Samprati (224-215 BCE), and Brihadratha (187-180 BCE). Bindusara was the son of Chandragupta Maurya. Ashoka was the son of Bindusara, known for embracing Buddhism after the Kalinga war. Samprati was the grandson of Ashoka and a patron of Jainism. Brihadratha was the last Mauryan ruler, assassinated by Pushyamitra Shunga. Thus, the correct sequence is Bindusara, Ashoka, Samprati, Brihadratha.
qs.kf:
☛ Who founded the Maurya dynasty? → Chandragupta Maurya
☛ In which script were Ashoka's edicts written? → Brahmi
☛ Which religion did Samprati patronize? → Jainism
☛ Who was the last Mauryan ruler? → Brihadratha
☛ What was Bindusara's nickname? → Amitraghata

q: Which of the following refers to tax paid only in cash during the Mauryan period?
qs.e: During the Mauryan period, various types of taxes were imposed. Hiranya was a tax that was paid only in cash (coins). In contrast, Bhaga was a tax paid in kind, as a share of the agricultural produce. Bali was a voluntary offering or gift to the king, not a regular tax. Kara was a general tax that could be collected in cash or kind. The Mauryan administration had a systematic revenue collection system, and Hiranya was specifically designated for cash payments. This tax was primarily levied on traders and the urban population.
qs.kf:
☛ Which tax was paid only in cash during Mauryan period? → Hiranya
☛ What was the basis of Bhaga tax? → Crop yield
☛ What type of contribution was Bali? → Voluntary offering
☛ What was the general term for tax in Mauryan administration? → 'Kara'
☛ Hiranya tax was mainly levied on which class? → Traders

q: Which of the following was the smallest administrative unit in the Mauryan Empire?
qs.e: In the Mauryan Empire, the administrative structure was hierarchical. The smallest unit was the village, headed by an official called gramika or gramani. Several villages formed a sangrahana, administered by a sangrahanadhyaksha. The next level was vithi, comprising multiple sangrahanas. The largest administrative unit was the province (called rajya or pradesh). This hierarchy ensured coordination between the central and local levels. Detailed information about this administrative system is found in Chanakya's Arthashastra.
qs.kf:
☛ Smallest administrative unit in Mauryan Empire? → Village
☛ Head of a village called? → Gramika or Gramani
☛ Group of villages called? → Sangrahana
☛ Head of a Sangrahana? → Sangrahanadhyaksha
☛ Main source describing Mauryan administration? → Arthashastra

q: Which of the following Gupta rulers defeated Shaka King Rudrasimha III and captured his kingdom?
qs.e: The Gupta ruler Chandragupta II (also known as Vikramaditya) defeated the Shaka Kshatrapas and established control over western India. He vanquished the Shaka king Rudrasimha III and annexed regions such as Gujarat, Kathiawar, and Malwa into the Gupta Empire. This victory was one of the most significant achievements of Chandragupta II's reign, greatly expanding the Gupta territory. After this conquest, he assumed titles like 'Vikramaditya' and 'Shakari' (destroyer of Shakas). Chandragupta II is regarded as the most powerful ruler of the Gupta dynasty, under whom the empire reached its zenith in both political power and cultural prosperity.
qs.kf:
☛ Title of Chandragupta II → Vikramaditya
☛ Capital of Shaka Kshatrapas → Ujjain
☛ Court poet of Chandragupta II → Kalidasa
☛ Founder of Gupta dynasty → Sri Gupta
☛ Goddess depicted on Chandragupta II's coins → Lakshmi

q: Who was an ambassador sent to the court of Chandragupta by the Greek ruler of West Asia?
qs.e: Megasthenes was a Greek ambassador sent by Seleucus Nicator, the Greek ruler of West Asia, to the court of Chandragupta Maurya. He visited India and wrote the book Indica, which provides valuable information about the Mauryan Empire, including its administration, society, and geography. Megasthenes described the city of Pataliputra (modern Patna) and its governance. His accounts are crucial historical sources for understanding the Mauryan period. Seleucus and Chandragupta had a treaty after the Seleucid-Mauryan war, which included a marriage alliance and exchange of gifts.
qs.kf:
☛ Who sent Megasthenes to India? → Seleucus Nicator
☛ What is the name of Megasthenes' book? → Indica
☛ In whose court was Megasthenes an ambassador? → Chandragupta Maurya
☛ What did Chandragupta give to Seleucus? → 500 elephants
☛ Which city did Megasthenes describe? → Pataliputra

q: Who founded the Gupta empire?
qs.e: The Gupta Empire was founded by Chandragupta I. He was the third ruler of the Gupta dynasty and started the Gupta era in 320 CE. He assumed the title 'Maharajadhiraja' and expanded his kingdom through marriage alliances. He married the Lichchhavi princess Kumaradevi to strengthen his position. The Gupta period is known as the Golden Age of India due to advancements in art, literature, and science. After Chandragupta I, Samudragupta and Chandragupta II further expanded the empire.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the founder of the Gupta dynasty? → Shri Gupta
☛ When did the Gupta era begin? → 320 CE
☛ What was the title of Chandragupta I? → Maharajadhiraja
☛ Name the wife of Chandragupta I? → Kumaradevi
☛ What is the Gupta period known as? → Golden Age

q: Which of the following Mauryan rulers is known for his support of Buddhism and spreading its teachings?
qs.e: The Mauryan emperor Ashoka (268-232 BCE) is renowned for his patronage and propagation of Buddhism. After the devastating Kalinga War (261 BCE), Ashoka embraced Buddhism and renounced violence. He promoted the principles of Dhamma and sent Buddhist missionaries across India and to regions like Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Nepal, and Afghanistan. His edicts inscribed on rocks and pillars spread Buddhist teachings. Ashoka built the Mahabodhi Temple in Bodh Gaya and the Lion Capital of Ashoka at Sarnath. He also convened the Third Buddhist Council at Pataliputra to purify the sangha. Ashoka's support made Buddhism a major world religion.
qs.kf:
☛ Mauryan emperor who adopted Buddhism after Kalinga War → Ashoka
☛ Script used in Ashokan edicts → Brahmi
☛ Famous Buddhist missionary sent by Ashoka → Mahendra (to Sri Lanka)
☛ Buddhist council held during Ashoka's reign → Third
☛ Ashoka's son who became a Buddhist monk → Mahendra

q: Who looked after markets and checked wrong practices in the Maurya empire?
qs.e: In the Mauryan empire, the economy was regulated by specific officials. The Samsthadhyaksha (Market Superintendent) was responsible for overseeing markets, checking weights and measures, ensuring the quality of goods, and preventing malpractices like adulteration and fraud. Detailed references to this role are found in Kautilya's Arthashastra. This officer also controlled pricing, collected sales taxes, and regulated profit margins for merchants. Other officials mentioned included the Annapala (food controller), Rajjukas (land surveyors and boundary setters), and Durgapala (fort guardian). The Samsthadhyaksha played a key role in maintaining fair trade and consumer protection in Mauryan markets.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the market superintendent in the Maurya Empire? → Samsthadhyaksha
☛ What was the main duty of Samsthadhyaksha? → Market supervision and checking malpractices
☛ Who managed food supplies in Mauryan administration? → Annapala
☛ What was the role of Rajjukas? → Land measurement and boundary setting
☛ In which text is Samsthadhyaksha mentioned? → Arthashastra

q: The Lion Capital located at Sarnath, which is adopted as the national emblem of the Republic of India, was erected by which of the following Mauryan kings?
qs.e: The Lion Capital at Sarnath was erected by the Mauryan emperor Ashoka around 250 BCE. It features four lions standing back to back on a pillar. The base has carvings of an elephant, horse, bull, and lion. On January 26, 1950, it was adopted as the National Emblem of India. The motto "Satyameva Jayate" below it is taken from the Mundaka Upanishad. The capital symbolizes the Dharmachakra Pravartana (the first sermon of Buddha). It is one of the finest examples of Mauryan art and architecture.
qs.kf:
☛ Who built the Sarnath pillar? → Ashoka
☛ Where was the National Emblem taken from? → Lion Capital at Sarnath
☛ When was the Ashoka pillar at Sarnath erected? → 250 BCE
☛ What is written on the National Emblem? → Satyameva Jayate
☛ Which Upanishad is Satyameva Jayate taken from? → Mundaka Upanishad

q: Which of the following officials toured Mauryan provinces every five years to inspect administration and submit reports on provincial governance?
qs.e: In the Mauryan administration, there were three categories of officials: Pradeshika, Rajuka, and Nagarika. The Pradeshika was a high-ranking officer who toured the provinces every five years to inspect the administration and submit reports on provincial governance. This tour was primarily meant for review and reporting. The Rajuka was responsible for judicial matters and land measurement. The Nagarika was in charge of city administration. Amatya were ministers or high-ranking officials. Thus, the task of provincial inspection was assigned to the Pradeshika.
qs.kf:
☛ Mauryan official for provincial inspection → Pradeshika
☛ Interval of Pradeshika's tour → Five years
☛ Main duty of Rajuka → Justice and land measurement
☛ Nagarika's jurisdiction → City administration
☛ Amatya's position → Minister or high official

q: Who was the founder of the Mauryan Empire and established a centralised administrative system?
qs.e: The Mauryan Empire was founded by Chandragupta Maurya around 322 BCE. With the help of Chanakya (Kautilya), he defeated the Nanda dynasty and established a centralized administrative system. This system is detailed in the Arthashastra. Chandragupta unified most of northern India and created a strong central government. His reign saw the expansion of the empire and the division of administration into various departments. Later, his son Bindusara succeeded him, and his grandson Ashoka took the empire to its zenith.
qs.kf:
☛ Founder of the Mauryan Empire → Chandragupta Maurya
☛ Guru and advisor of Chandragupta → Chanakya (Kautilya)
☛ Text describing centralized administration → Arthashastra
☛ Highest administrative body under Mauryas → Council of Ministers
☛ Successor of Chandragupta Maurya → Bindusara

q: Which of the following kings of Kalinga in the 2nd century B.C. professed Jainism in India?
qs.e: In the 2nd century B.C., the king of Kalinga, Kharavela, was a follower of Jainism. He is famous for the Hathigumpha inscription, which describes his military achievements and devotion to Jainism. Kharavela played a significant role in the promotion and protection of Jainism. Among other options, Ashoka adopted Buddhism, Samprati was a Jain but belonged to the Maurya dynasty and not Kalinga, and Bindusara was a follower of Ajivika. Thus, Kharavela is the correct answer.
qs.kf:
☛ Which king is associated with the Hathigumpha inscription? → Kharavela
☛ Which Kalinga king adopted Jainism? → Kharavela
☛ Kharavela belonged to which dynasty? → Mahameghavahana dynasty
☛ Which religion did Ashoka follow? → Buddhism
☛ Samprati belonged to which dynasty? → Maurya dynasty

q: Which of the following is/are an ancient set of inscriptions, promoting moral values and governance principles and is considered one of the earliest written records in Indian history?
qs.e: The Edicts of Ashoka are among the earliest written records in Indian history. They were commissioned by Emperor Ashoka (268–232 BCE), a ruler of the Mauryan dynasty. These inscriptions primarily promote moral values, the principles of Dhamma (righteousness), and governance ideals. They emphasize non-violence, truth, compassion, and social welfare. Found across India and beyond (e.g., Afghanistan), they are written in ancient scripts like Brahmi and Kharosthi. These edicts are crucial sources for understanding ancient Indian history, culture, and the spread of Buddhism. They reflect Ashoka's transformation from a conqueror to a benevolent ruler after the Kalinga war.
qs.kf:
☛ How many major rock edicts of Ashoka are there? → 14 major rock edicts
☛ What script is used in Ashokan edicts? → Brahmi and Kharosthi
☛ What religion did Ashoka follow? → Buddhism
☛ What is the main message of Ashoka's edicts? → Dhamma and non-violence
☛ Which ruler is mentioned in the edicts? → Emperor Ashoka

q: The Mauryan empire was founded by Chandragupta Maurya in which of the following years?
qs.e: Chandragupta Maurya founded the Mauryan Empire around 322 BCE after defeating the Nanda ruler Dhanananda and capturing Magadha. He was guided by his mentor Chanakya (Kautilya), who authored the famous treatise Arthashastra. The Mauryan Empire became the largest empire in Indian history, with its capital at Pataliputra (modern Patna). Chandragupta defeated Seleucus I Nicator and established matrimonial ties, extending the empire to the northwestern regions. Later, he embraced Jainism and performed sallekhana (fast unto death) at Shravanabelagola. The Mauryan administration was highly centralized and divided into provinces for efficient governance.
qs.kf:
☛ Who founded the Mauryan Empire? → Chandragupta Maurya
☛ Who was the mentor of Chandragupta Maurya? → Chanakya (Kautilya)
☛ Which famous text did Chanakya write? → Arthashastra
☛ What was the capital of the Mauryan Empire? → Pataliputra
☛ Which religion did Chandragupta Maurya adopt? → Jainism

q: Which Buddhist scripture explicitly states “All dhammas are without self,” affirming the doctrine of Anatta?
qs.e: The Dhammapada is a key Buddhist scripture belonging to the Theravada tradition. It contains the essence of the Buddha's teachings. In Chapter 6 (Yamaka Vagga), it explicitly states: "Sabbe dhamma anatta" meaning "All dhammas are without self". This affirms the core Buddhist doctrine of Anatta (no-self), which denies the existence of a permanent, independent self in any phenomenon. This principle fundamentally distinguishes Buddhism from Hindu philosophy. The other options—Kalpa Sutra, Bhagavati Sutra, and Uttaradhyayana—are Jain scriptures and are unrelated to Buddhist teachings.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Buddhist scripture states "All dhammas are without self"? → Dhammapada
☛ How many chapters are in the Dhammapada? → 26 chapters
☛ Who propounded the doctrine of Anatta? → Gautam Buddha
☛ In which language is the Dhammapada composed? → Pali language
☛ What is the primary scripture of Theravada Buddhism? → Tripitaka (which includes Dhammapada)

q: During the Mauryan period, the village headman in North India was known by ______.
qs.e: During the Mauryan period, the smallest unit of rural administration was the village, and its headman was called Gramika. The Gramika was responsible for village administration, tax collection, and maintaining law and order. He was appointed by the king and assisted by the village assembly. References to Gramika are found in Kautilya's Arthashastra. Among the other options, 'Gavunda' was the village headman in South India, 'Mununda' was associated with certain regions of North India, and 'Pattakila' was a military or defense-related position. Thus, in North India during the Mauryan period, the village headman was known as Gramika.
qs.kf:
☛ Title of village headman in Mauryan North India → Gramika
☛ Text that mentions Gramika → Arthashastra
☛ Smallest unit of rural administration in Mauryan period → Village
☛ Who appointed the Gramika → King
☛ Village headman in South India during Mauryan era → Gavunda

q: By what name was the administrative head of the Mauryan city administration, as described in the Arthashastra, addressed?
qs.e: The administrative head of the Mauryan city administration, as described in the Arthashastra by Kautilya, was called Nagarika. The Nagarika was responsible for the revenue, security, population control, and management of various departments of the city. He supervised officials in charge of wards and gates. Under the Nagarika, there were Gopas (village-level officers) and Sthanikas (regional officers). The position of Nagarika was the highest in city administration, and he reported directly to the king or the chief minister.
qs.kf:
☛ Head of Mauryan city administration → Nagarika
☛ Text mentioning Nagarika → Arthashastra
☛ Officers under Nagarika → Gop and Sthanika
☛ Gop was an officer of → Rural administration
☛ Mauryan city fort in-charge → Nagarika

q: Who among the following was the first ruler who inscribed his message on stone surfaces for his subjects and officials?
qs.e: The tradition of inscribing messages on stone surfaces in India was begun by Emperor Ashoka of the Maurya dynasty. He had Edicts of Ashoka carved on rocks and pillars across his empire, containing messages on governance, morality, and compassion. These inscriptions were written in Prakrit language using Brahmi script. Ashoka's edicts provide valuable insights into the extent and administration of the Mauryan empire. Chandragupta Maurya, Harshavardhan, and Chandragupta I did not use stone inscriptions for royal messages.
qs.kf:
☛ In which language are Ashoka's edicts? → Prakrit
☛ Which script was used in Ashoka's edicts? → Brahmi
☛ Which edict of Ashoka mentions the Kalinga War? → 13th Rock Edict
☛ What title is used for Ashoka in the edicts? → Devanampriya (Beloved of the Gods)
☛ On what materials are Ashoka's edicts inscribed? → Rock and pillar

q: Asoka, arguably the most famous ruler of early India, conquered Kalinga. He was the grandson of _____.
qs.e: Asoka was the third emperor of the Mauryan dynasty. He was the grandson of Chandragupta Maurya, who founded the Mauryan Empire. Asoka ruled approximately from 268 to 232 BCE. After the Kalinga War (c. 261 BCE), he renounced violence and embraced Buddhism. Asoka's edicts and pillars are important sources of his reign. Chandragupta Maurya, with the help of Chanakya, defeated the Nanda dynasty and laid the foundation of the Mauryan Empire. Asoka is known for spreading Dhamma (righteousness). He appointed Dhamma Mahamatras (officers). His son Mahendra and daughter Sanghamitra propagated Buddhism in Sri Lanka.
qs.kf:
☛ Who founded the Mauryan dynasty? → Chandragupta Maurya
☛ Who was the guru of Asoka? → Upagupta
☛ Which war did Asoka fight? → Kalinga War
☛ In which script are Asoka's edicts inscribed? → Brahmi
☛ Who was the last Mauryan ruler? → Brihadratha

q: Who mentioned Adhyakshas as the superintendents of different departments in the Mauryan administration?
qs.e: Kautilya, in his treatise Arthashastra, provided a detailed description of the superintendents (Adhyakshas) of various departments in the Mauryan administration. According to him, there were 18 types of superintendents appointed for different state functions, such as the treasurer, agriculture superintendent, commerce superintendent, etc. Megasthenes, in his book Indica, described the Mauryan administration but did not mention the Adhyakshas. Strabo and Pliny also wrote about India, but they did not provide a detailed account of administrative posts. Thus, the earliest and most detailed mention of departmental superintendents in the Mauryan administration is found in Kautilya's Arthashastra.
qs.kf:
☛ Author of Arthashastra → Kautilya (Chanakya)
☛ Number of Adhyakshas in Mauryan administration → 18
☛ Author of Indica during Mauryan period → Megasthenes
☛ Original name of Kautilya → Vishnugupta
☛ One of the departments described in Arthashastra → Sita (Agriculture department)
