q: Which Ashokan Rock Edict mentions of Ashoka's triumph in Kalinga?
qs.e: Among Ashoka's rock edicts, the Thirteenth Rock Edict (Rock Edict XIII) is the one that describes the Kalinga War. The devastating consequences of this war deeply affected Ashoka, leading him to abandon violence, embrace Buddhism, and propagate Dhamma. This edict is crucial for understanding the transformation in his rule and his policy of peace.
qs.kf:
☛ Rock Edict mentioning Kalinga War → Thirteenth
☛ Rock Edict introducing Ashoka's Dhamma policy → Second
☛ Total number of Major Rock Edicts → 14
☛ Smallest Rock Edict → First (Bhabru)
☛ Scripts used in Ashoka's edicts → Brahmi and Kharosthi

q: To which dynasty did Ashoka belong?
qs.e: Ashoka was the third emperor of the Maurya dynasty, who ruled from 268 to 232 BCE. He was the grandson of Chandragupta Maurya and son of Bindusara. The Maurya dynasty was founded by Chandragupta Maurya in 322 BCE and was the largest empire in ancient India. Ashoka is famous for his Dhamma policy and adopting Buddhism after the Kalinga War. He erected edicts and pillars throughout the Indian subcontinent. The Nanda, Gupta, and Kanva dynasties are distinct from the Maurya dynasty. The Nanda dynasty preceded the Mauryas, the Gupta dynasty emerged later, and the Kanva dynasty arose after the decline of the Mauryas.
qs.kf:
☛ Who founded the Maurya dynasty? → Chandragupta Maurya
☛ What was the name of Ashoka's father? → Bindusara
☛ After which event did Ashoka adopt Buddhism? → Kalinga War
☛ In which script were Ashoka's edicts inscribed? → Brahmi script
☛ What was the capital of the Maurya Empire? → Pataliputra

q: Bindusara ruled between which of the following periods?
qs.e: Bindusara was the second ruler of the Maurya dynasty, succeeding Chandragupta Maurya. His reign is generally considered to be from 297 B.C.E. to 273 B.C.E. This period was crucial for the expansion and consolidation of the Mauryan Empire. Bindusara was also known as Amitraghata (destroyer of enemies). He conquered parts of the Deccan, extending the empire southward. He was a follower of the Ajivika sect. During his reign, friendly relations were maintained with the Greek ruler Antiochus I. He had several sons, with Ashoka succeeding him as the most famous Mauryan emperor.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the founder of the Maurya dynasty? → Chandragupta Maurya
☛ What was the name of Bindusara's son? → Ashoka and Susima
☛ How did Bindusara die? → During Ashoka's coronation
☛ Who was the Greek ruler contemporary to Bindusara? → Antiochus I
☛ What was Bindusara's other name? → Amitraghata

q: Who among the following kings became the follower of the Jainism towards the later stages of his life?
qs.e: Chandragupta Maurya was the founder of the Maurya dynasty. In the later stages of his life, he embraced Jainism. He became a disciple of Bhadrabahu and went to Shravanabelagola in South India, where he performed Sallekhana (fast unto death). A famous statue of him exists there. Bindusara and Ashoka did not adopt Jainism; Ashoka patronized Buddhism. Kunal was Ashoka's son and had no direct connection with Jainism. Chandragupta Maurya's conversion is a significant event in Indian history.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the guru of Chandragupta Maurya? → Bhadrabahu
☛ Where did Chandragupta Maurya give up his body? → Shravanabelagola
☛ Which religion did Chandragupta Maurya adopt in his later life? → Jainism
☛ Who was the founder of the Maurya dynasty? → Chandragupta Maurya
☛ Who is the 24th Tirthankara of Jainism? → Mahavira Swami

q: Which of the following was NOT an artisan guild during the Mauryan period?
qs.e: During the Mauryan period, several artisan guilds (shrenis) existed, such as potters, carpenters, bankers and merchants. These guilds played a crucial role in economic and social life. Potters made earthenware, carpenters worked with wood, and bankers and merchants were involved in commerce and financial activities. Astrologer was not an artisan guild; it was a professional group related to astronomy and prediction. The Mauryan administration regulated these guilds, which helped organize production and trade. Guilds also acted as trade unions, ensuring quality control and settling disputes among members.
qs.kf:
☛ What were artisan guilds called in the Mauryan period? → Shreni
☛ Does Kautilya's Arthashastra mention artisan guilds? → Yes
☛ What was the head of a merchant guild called in Mauryan times? → Shreshthi
☛ Which guild was most powerful during the Mauryan period? → Bankers and Merchants
☛ What was the main function of guilds in the Mauryan period? → Regulation of trade and production

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (10/06/2025) Shift 2
q: Chandragupta Maurya is said to have converted to:
qs.e: Chandragupta Maurya is said to have converted to Jainism in the later part of his life. He became a disciple of the Jain monk Bhadrabahu and followed the practice of Santhara (fasting unto death) at Shravanabelagola (Karnataka). This event is recorded in Jain texts and some historical inscriptions. Though Buddhist texts suggest he leaned towards Buddhism, most evidence points to Jainism. Chandragupta renounced his throne and adopted the ascetic life of a Jain monk. This conversion highlights the influence of Jainism in ancient India.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the guru of Chandragupta Maurya? → Bhadrabahu
☛ Where did Chandragupta Maurya spend his last days? → Shravanabelagola
☛ Who is the founder of Jainism? → Mahavira (24th Tirthankara)
☛ Santhara is associated with which religion? → Jainism
☛ Who founded the Maurya Empire? → Chandragupta Maurya

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (10/06/2025) Shift 3
q: Who discovered the Maski Ashoka Inscription?
qs.e: The Maski Ashoka Inscription is located in the Raichur district of Karnataka. It was discovered in 1915 by C Beadon. This inscription is significant because it clearly mentions Ashoka's name as 'Devanampriya Ashoka', which confirmed the identity of Ashoka. The language of this inscription is Prakrit and the script is Brahmi. Before this discovery, James Prinsep was credited with deciphering Ashokan edicts, but the Maski inscription provided definitive proof of Ashoka's identity. Maski is one of the minor rock edicts of Ashoka and contains teachings about non-violence and Dhamma.
qs.kf:
☛ Discoverer of Maski inscription → C Beadon
☛ Language of Maski inscription → Prakrit
☛ Script of Maski inscription → Brahmi
☛ Name of Ashoka mentioned → 'Devanampriya Ashoka'
☛ State → Karnataka (Raichur district)

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (11/06/2025) Shift 1
q: Who succeeded Ashoka to the throne?
qs.e: After Emperor Ashoka's death in 232 BCE, the Mauryan throne was succeeded by his grandson Dasharatha Maurya. Dasharatha was the son of Kunala, who was Ashoka's son but was blind and thus could not ascend the throne. Dasharatha ruled from 232 BCE to 224 BCE. He was a follower of Buddhism and is known for constructing the Barabar Caves, which were dedicated to the Ajivika sect. His reign marked the beginning of the decline of the Mauryan Empire. After Dasharatha, his successor was Samprati, another grandson of Ashoka. Thus, the immediate successor of Ashoka was Dasharatha, not Chandragupta II or Bindusara.
qs.kf:
☛ Dasharatha Maurya's reign period → 232-224 BCE
☛ Dasharatha Maurya associated with which sect → Buddhism
☛ Who built the Barabar Caves → Dasharatha Maurya
☛ Why Kunala did not become king → He was blind
☛ Last ruler of Mauryan Empire → Brihadratha

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (11/06/2025) Shift 2
q: The Maski Ashoka Inscription is situated in which state of India?
qs.e: The Maski Ashoka Inscription is located in the Indian state of Karnataka. It is one of the 14 Major Rock Edicts of Emperor Ashoka and was discovered in 1915 by C. B. Lewis. The Maski inscription is significant because it mentions Ashoka by name as 'Devanampriya' and 'Ashoka', which helped confirm the identity of the emperor. The inscription is written in Brahmi script and the language is Prakrit. Maski is situated in the Raichur district of Karnataka.
qs.kf:
☛ In which state is the Maski Ashoka Inscription located? → Karnataka
☛ Who discovered the Maski inscription? → C. B. Lewis (1915)
☛ What name of Ashoka is mentioned in the Maski inscription? → Devanampriya and Ashoka
☛ In which script is the inscription written? → Brahmi script
☛ Maski is located in which district? → Raichur district

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (19/06/2025) Shift 3
q: Who were the 'Rajukas' during the Mauryan period?
qs.e: During the Mauryan period, Rajukas were provincial officials responsible for land measurement, boundary determination, and judicial functions. They are mentioned in Chanakya's Arthashastra. Rajukas were a key part of the regional administrative framework of the empire. Their duties included revenue collection, surveying agricultural land, and administering justice. The provinces in the Mauryan empire were called Janapadas, and Rajukas were the chief officials of these Janapadas. They were appointed by the central government.
qs.kf:
☛ Which period does Rajukas belong to? → Mauryan period
☛ Which text mentions Rajukas? → Arthashastra
☛ What was the main function of Rajukas? → Land measurement and judicial administration
☛ What was a province called during the Mauryan period? → Janapada
☛ Who appointed the Rajukas? → Central government

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (20/06/2025) Shift 1
q: Ashoka appointed special officers to spread Dhamma, known as:
qs.e: Emperor Ashoka appointed special officers to propagate Dhamma across his empire, known as Dhamma Mahamatras. These officers were responsible for spreading Ashoka's principles of moral governance and ensuring the welfare of the people. They also carried out missionary work in border regions and neighboring kingdoms. While Mahamatras were general administrative officials, Dhamma Mahamatras were specifically designated for religious and ethical matters. Rajukas were concerned with land and justice, while Purohits performed religious rites. Thus, the special officers appointed for spreading Dhamma were called 'Dhamma Mahamatras'.
qs.kf:
☛ Ashoka's special officers for Dhamma propagation → Dhamma Mahamatras
☛ Main source of Ashoka's Dhamma → His edicts (rock and pillar)
☛ Year of appointment of Dhamma Mahamatras → Around 250 BCE
☛ Major administrative officers in Ashoka's empire → Rajukas, Yuktas, Mahamatras
☛ Essence of Ashoka's Dhamma → Non-violence, truth, compassion, social harmony

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (21/06/2025) Shift 1
q: The Mauryan period saw the development of which script for inscriptions?
qs.e: The Mauryan period saw the development of the Brahmi script for inscriptions. This script was primarily used in Ashoka's edicts. Brahmi script later evolved into Devanagari and other Indian scripts. The Kharosthi script was used in the northwestern regions, while Grantha script belongs to a later period, and Pali is a language, not a script. Most of Ashoka's inscriptions are written in Brahmi. James Prinsep successfully deciphered the Brahmi script in 1837. Thus, during the Mauryan period, the development of Brahmi script for inscriptions was significant.
qs.kf:
☛ In which script are most of Ashoka's edicts inscribed? → Brahmi
☛ Which scripts evolved from Brahmi? → Devanagari and other Indian scripts
☛ Who first deciphered Brahmi script? → James Prinsep
☛ Which script was used in northwestern regions during Mauryan period? → Kharosthi
☛ What is Pali? → A language, not a script

q: Ashok Pillar of Delhi has baffled scientists as it weathers all vagaries of weather and yet does not rust or corrode. Which is it made of?
qs.e: The Ashok Pillar of Delhi is made of iron, which has baffled scientists because it has not rusted or corroded despite being exposed to the elements for about 1600 years. This pillar was built during the Gupta period (around 402 AD) and stands 7.21 meters tall, weighing approximately 6 tonnes. The secret of its preservation lies in its high phosphorus content and the formation of a thin protective layer of iron oxide that prevents further oxidation and moisture from reaching the metal. It is located in the Qutub Minar complex in Delhi.
qs.kf:
☛ Ashok Pillar (Delhi) material → Iron
☛ Age of the pillar → About 1600 years
☛ Reason for preservation → High phosphorus content and protective oxide layer
☛ Location → Qutub Minar complex, Delhi

q: The earliest deciphered epigraphy of Ashoka's inscription in India was written in which script?
qs.e: Ashoka's edicts were primarily written in the Brahmi script, which is one of the oldest scripts of India. Brahmi was first deciphered by James Prinsep in 1837. Most of Ashoka's inscriptions are in Brahmi, while some in the northwestern regions are in Kharoshthi. Brahmi is the ancestor of Devanagari and many other Indian scripts. The Harappan script remains undeciphered.

q: Which dynasty was overthrown by Chandragupta Maurya to establish the Mauryan Empire?
qs.e: Chandragupta Maurya overthrew the Nanda Dynasty by defeating its last ruler Dhanananda to establish the Mauryan Empire around 321 BCE. With the help of his mentor Chanakya (Kautilya), Chandragupta attacked Pataliputra and ended Nanda rule. The Nanda dynasty was founded by Mahapadma Nanda and was a powerful kingdom in Magadha. The Mauryan Empire became the first large empire in India, with its capital at Pataliputra.

q: Whom did Chandragupta II marry after defeating the Saka king?
qs.e: After defeating the Saka king Rudrasimha III, Chandragupta II ('Vikramaditya') married the Saka princess Kubernaga. This marriage was a political move to strengthen Gupta-Saka relations and consolidate control over western India. Kubernaga was the daughter of the Saka king, and this alliance helped bring stability to the Gupta Empire's western frontiers. Chandragupta II was one of the greatest rulers of the Gupta dynasty, known for his patronage of art, literature, and military conquests. His court housed the 'Navaratnas' (nine gems), including the renowned poet Kalidasa.

q: An internal trade route during the post-Mauryan empires, Uttarapatha, connected the:
o: western and southern parts of India
southern and eastern parts of India
northern and southern parts of India with the northwestern region
northern and eastern parts of India with the northwestern region
qs.e: During the post-Mauryan period, Uttarapatha was a major internal trade route. This route connected the northern and eastern parts of India (such as Pataliputra) with the northwestern region (such as Taxila). It ran parallel to the foothills of the Himalayas and facilitated trade, travel, and cultural exchange. Many towns and commercial centers were located along this route. In contrast, Dakshinapatha was a route associated with southern India. Thus, Uttarapatha specifically linked the north-east to the north-west.

q: Which Mauryan ruler sent Buddhist missionaries to foreign countries?
qs.e: Mauryan emperor Ashoka embraced Buddhism after the Kalinga War and sent Buddhist missionaries to foreign countries to spread the religion. He sent his son Mahendra and daughter Sanghamitra to Sri Lanka, where King Devanampiya Tissa adopted Buddhism. Missions were also sent to Egypt, Syria, Macedonia, and Thailand. Ashoka's edicts (Dharmalipis) mention these missions. Thus, Ashoka was the first ruler to make organized efforts for religious propagation.

q: What was Ashoka's relation to Bindusara?
qs.e: Ashoka was the son of Mauryan Emperor Bindusara. Bindusara was the son of Chandragupta Maurya, the founder of the Maurya dynasty. Ashoka succeeded Bindusara as the ruler of the Mauryan Empire in 268 BCE after his father's death. Bindusara sent Ashoka to suppress rebellions in Ujjain and Taxila, where he displayed administrative skill. Ashoka was one of Bindusara's sixteen sons. Under Bindusara's reign, the empire expanded, and Ashoka later took it to its zenith. Ashoka is famously known for adopting Buddhism after the Kalinga War.

q: Chandragupta was succeeded by which of the following rulers, who ruled between 297 and 273 BCE?
qs.e: After Chandragupta Maurya, his son Bindusara ruled from 297 to 273 BCE. Bindusara was also known as 'Amitraghata' (slayer of enemies). He expanded the Mauryan Empire into southern India, conquering 16 kingdoms. During his reign, a rebellion occurred in Taxila, which was suppressed by his son Ashoka. The Greek ambassador Deimachus visited his court. Bindusara was a follower of the Ajivika sect. His rule strengthened the empire and consolidated the administrative system laid by his father.

q: What was the name of Ramagupta's widow whom Chandragupta II marry after defeating the Saka king?
qs.e: Chandragupta II, also known as Vikramaditya, married Dhruvadevi, the widow of his brother Ramagupta, after defeating the Saka king Rudrasimha III. Ramagupta was a weak ruler who offered Dhruvadevi to the Saka king after being defeated, but Chandragupta II opposed this, killed the Saka king, and rescued Dhruvadevi. This event is recorded in the history of the Gupta Empire. Dhruvadevi became Chandragupta II's wife, and their son Kumaragupta I later succeeded the throne. This marriage is considered significant in Gupta politics. The drama 'Devichandraguptam' by Vishakhadatta also mentions this story.

q: ‘Pradeshtris’ word is used for which officers during the Mauryan Empire?

qs.e: During the Mauryan Empire, 'Pradeshtris' were officers responsible for the suppression of criminals and maintaining law and order. They were stationed in provinces and their main duties included investigating crimes and punishing offenders. They are mentioned in Kautilya's Arthashastra. Pradeshtris were also known as 'Pradestri' and performed both judicial and police functions. These officers were appointed by the king and had the authority to arrest, investigate, and punish criminals. The position of Pradeshtri was crucial in the Mauryan administration as they ensured peace and security in the empire.

q: After which battle did Ashoka embrace Buddhism?
qs.e: Emperor Ashoka embraced Buddhism after the Kalinga War (261 BCE). This was one of the bloodiest wars in history, with about 1.5 lakh killed and over 1.5 lakh wounded. Witnessing the carnage, Ashoka was filled with remorse and renounced violence. He was influenced by the Buddhist monk Upagupta and adopted the policy of Dhamma, based on non-violence, compassion, and morality. Ashoka gave royal patronage to Buddhism and sent missionaries across Asia to spread the religion. His edicts on pillars and rocks propagated moral principles.

qs.e: Chandragupta Maurya overthrew the Nanda dynasty with the assistance of Chanakya, also known as Kautilya or Vishnugupta. Chanakya was a renowned economist, political strategist, and author of the ancient Indian treatise 'Arthashastra', which covers statecraft, economic policy, and military strategy. He guided Chandragupta in building an army and formulating strategies to defeat the Nanda ruler Dhanananda around 322 BCE. Chanakya's mentorship and diplomatic acumen were instrumental in establishing the Maurya Empire, which became one of the largest empires in Indian history. The alliance between Chandragupta and Chanakya marked a turning point, leading to the downfall of the Nanda dynasty and the rise of the Mauryan rule.

q: Which metal was extensively used for coinage in the Mauryan Empire?
qs.e: In the Mauryan Empire, silver coins called 'pana' and 'karshapana' were extensively used. These silver coins were also known as 'rupya'. They played a crucial role in trade and tax collection. While copper coins were also in circulation, silver was the primary metal for coinage. Kautilya's Arthashastra provides detailed accounts of the weight and purity of silver coins. Gold coins were rare and mainly used for gifts or honors. Iron was not used for coinage in the Mauryan period.

q: Which of the following is true regarding the materials of construction used for Ashokan pillars?
o: They were largely made of stone.
They were largely made of wood.
They were largely made of concrete.
They were largely made of iron.
qs.e: Ashokan pillars were primarily made of a single block of sandstone. These pillars are exemplary of the exquisite craftsmanship of the Mauryan period. They were quarried from Chunar (Uttar Pradesh) and then transported to various locations for erection. Each pillar weighed around 50 tonnes, reflecting their grandeur. The inscriptions on the pillars are in Brahmi script and pertain to dharma and administration. Ashokan pillars are important sources of Indian history and art, showcasing the technological and cultural achievements of the Mauryan Empire.

q: Chandra Gupta Maurya was the founder of the Mauryan Dynasty. Which of the following statements regarding his rule in the History of India is INCORRECT?
o: Chandra Gupta Maurya is credited with the setting up of the first nearly pan-India Empire.
Bairam Khan was his best ally, mentor, and guide.
Archaeological evidence of the empire shows existence of a number of towns and cities, the most prominent being the capital city of Pataliputra.
He met Alexander and served in his army so as to learn the Macedonian way of warfare.
qs.e: Chandra Gupta Maurya founded the Mauryan Dynasty, establishing the first nearly pan-Indian empire. His chief mentor and guide was Chanakya (Kautilya), who helped him gain the throne and authored the Arthashastra. Bairam Khan was the regent of the Mughal emperor Akbar in the 16th century, not associated with Chandra Gupta Maurya. Hence, statement 2 is incorrect. Archaeological evidence of the Mauryan empire shows towns and cities, with the capital Pataliputra being most prominent. Chandra Gupta Maurya is said to have met Alexander and possibly served in his army, as per Greek sources. Thus, only option 2 is historically wrong.

q: The royal title used by Chandragupta I was:
qs.e: Chandragupta I was a ruler of the Gupta dynasty who reigned around 320 CE. He adopted the title 'Maharajadhiraja', meaning 'Great King of Kings', which signified supreme imperial authority. This title was used during the Gupta period to denote the highest sovereign power. Chandragupta I strengthened his position by marrying the Lichchhavi princess Kumaradevi. His coins also bear this title. Other options like 'Maharaj' and 'Samrat' were of lower status, while 'Chakravartin' was used later. Thus, the royal title of Chandragupta I was Maharajadhiraja.

q: What does 'Dhamma' primarily refer to in Ashoka’s inscriptions?
qs.e: In Ashoka's inscriptions, the term 'Dhamma' primarily refers to Moral law or a code of conduct. It focused on practical ethical principles for the common people, rather than the deeper philosophical aspects of Buddhism. Ashoka promoted 'Dhamma' through principles like non-violence, truth, compassion, and social harmony. He expected his subjects to respect parents, teachers, and elders, practice charity, and be kind to all living beings. The aim of 'Dhamma' was to establish unity and peace among different religions and communities. It was not a specific religious doctrine but a universal moral code that Ashoka considered essential for governance and social order. The 'Dhamma' was propagated through edicts inscribed on pillars and rocks, and special officers known as Dhamma Mahamatras were appointed to spread its message.

☛ Which of Ashoka's edicts clearly explains 'Dhamma'? → 13th Major Rock Edict
☛ How is Ashoka's 'Dhamma' different from Buddhism? → Emphasizes social ethics rather than spiritual liberation

Dasharatha Maurya preserved Buddhism during his reign and constructed the Nagarjuna caves. He described the city planning of Pataliputra (modern Patna) and the efficient Mauryan bureaucracy. According to him, Chandragupta was a capable ruler and the empire had a well-organized administrative system with seven categories of officials. Megasthenes' writings are a key source for understanding Mauryan India.

Brahmi was one of the major scripts of ancient India, used in Ashoka's edicts. Princep studied the Hathigumpha inscription of Kalinga and various coins to crack the script. q: Which of the following administrative features was a key characteristic of the Mauryan Empire under Chandragupta Maurya?
qs.e: Under Chandragupta Maurya, the defining administrative feature of the Mauryan Empire was a centralised bureaucracy guided by the Arthashastra (written by Kautilya). This system had the king as supreme, with provinces administered by governors who were not hereditary. The empire was divided into provinces, districts, and villages, with a detailed hierarchy of officials overseeing tax collection, law and order, irrigation, and trade. The Arthashastra provided the framework for administration, economy, and military strategy, ensuring efficient governance. Unlike feudal or religious systems, this state-controlled bureaucracy was highly structured and documented.

☛ Where was the Mauryan capital located? → Pataliputra

q: What was the name given to the special officials appointed by Ashoka to spread his policy of Dhamma?
qs.e: Emperor Ashoka appointed special officials known as Dhamma Mahamattas to spread his policy of Dhamma throughout his empire. These officers were responsible for propagating the principles of Dhamma, including non-violence, morality, and social welfare, among the people. They not only enforced the emperor's orders but also listened to the grievances of the people and provided solutions. The Dhamma Mahamattas were sent to various regions to promote religious tolerance, mutual respect, and charitable acts. This was a key aspect of Ashoka's administrative system, reflecting his commitment to ethical governance and the well-being of his subjects.
qs.kf:
☛ Officials appointed by Ashoka to spread Dhamma → Dhamma Mahamattas
☛ Ashoka's religion is known as → Dhamma
☛ Scripture of Ashokan edicts → Brahmi
☛ War after which Ashoka embraced Dhamma → Kalinga War
☛ Main principles of Ashoka's Dhamma → Non-violence and good conduct

q: Which of the following officials in the Mauryan administration was primarily responsible for supervising state agriculture and cultivation on crown lands?
qs.e: In the Mauryan administration, the Sitadhyaksha was primarily responsible for supervising state agriculture and cultivation on crown lands (Sita land). This official managed agricultural production, seed distribution, irrigation, and crop oversight, as detailed in the Arthashastra. The Panyadhyaksha was in charge of commerce and markets, the Samaharta handled revenue collection and accounts, and the Aksapataladhyaksha was the keeper of royal records. Thus, the Sitadhyaksha was the key authority for agricultural management.
qs.kf:
☛ Chief official for state agriculture in Mauryan period → Sitadhyaksha
☛ Land supervised by Sitadhyaksha → Sita land (crown land)
☛ Head of commerce and markets → Panyadhyaksha
☛ Duty of Samaharta → Revenue collection and accounts
☛ Role of Aksapataladhyaksha → Custodian of royal records

name: All Questions · Q1–27
sub: Ancient History - Post-Mauryan Dynasties (Shunga, Kushan, Satavahana)

q: Kanishka was the great king of which dynasty?
qs.e: Kanishka was the most powerful and renowned ruler of the Kushan dynasty in ancient India. He ascended the throne around 78 CE, and his reign is associated with the beginning of the Shaka era. Kanishka's empire extended from Central Asia to North India, with his capital at Purushapura (modern-day Peshawar). He was a patron of Buddhism and convened the Fourth Buddhist Council. Kanishka's coins feature various deities and his own image. The Kushan dynasty was founded by Kujula Kadphises and ruled until the Huna invasions.
qs.kf:
☛ What was the capital of Kanishka? → Purushapura (Peshawar)
☛ Which religion did Kanishka patronize? → Buddhism
☛ Which Buddhist council was convened by Kanishka? → Fourth Buddhist Council
☛ Who founded the Kushan dynasty? → Kujula Kadphises
☛ Which era is believed to have started with Kanishka's reign? → Shaka era

q: Which dynasty did Kanishka belong to?
qs.e: Kanishka was the most famous ruler of the Kushan dynasty in ancient India. The Kushan dynasty was founded by the Yuezhi tribe and ruled from around 30 CE to 375 CE. Kanishka's reign began around 78 CE, which marks the beginning of the Shaka era. He established his capital at Purushpura (modern Peshawar) and Mathura. Kanishka was a great patron of Buddhism and convened the Fourth Buddhist Council in Kundalvan, Kashmir. His empire included parts of North India, Central Asia, and Iran. Coins and inscriptions from his time reflect his military conquests and cultural contributions. The Kushan period was significant for trade along the Silk Route and artistic development, especially the Gandhara and Mathura schools of art.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the founder of the Kushan dynasty? → Kujula Kadphises (Kadphises I)
☛ What was the capital of Kanishka? → Purushpura (Peshawar)
☛ Which religion did Kanishka patronize? → Buddhism
☛ Who were the scholars in Kanishka’s court? → Ashvaghosha, Nagarjuna, Vasumitra
☛ Where was the Fourth Buddhist Council held? → Kundalvan, Kashmir

q: Which dynasty succeeded the Muaryas? A. Shunga B. Gupta
C. Sisunaga D. Chola
qs.e: After the decline of the Mauryan Empire, the Shunga dynasty rose to power in northern India. It was founded in 185 BCE by Pushyamitra Shunga, who was a Mauryan general. The Shunga dynasty ruled the Magadha region for about 112 years. The Gupta dynasty came much later, not immediately after the Mauryas. The Sisunaga dynasty preceded the Mauryas. The Chola dynasty was a contemporary or later southern power.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the founder of the Shunga dynasty? → Pushyamitra Shunga
☛ What was the capital of the Shunga dynasty? → Pataliputra
☛ Who was the last ruler of the Shunga dynasty? → Devabhuti
☛ What was the period of the Shunga dynasty? → 185 BCE to 73 BCE
☛ Which literary work mentions the Shungas? → Malavikagnimitra

q: The Hathigumpha inscription was engraved by whom?
qs.e: The Hathigumpha inscription was engraved by King Kharavela of Kalinga. This inscription is located in the Udayagiri hills near Bhubaneswar, Odisha. It is written in Prakrit language and uses Brahmi script. The inscription provides detailed information about Kharavela's life, military campaigns, and religious activities. It mentions Kharavela as the third ruler of the Kalinga dynasty. The Hathigumpha inscription dates back to the 1st century BCE and is a crucial source for understanding ancient Indian history, especially the history of Kalinga.
qs.kf:
☛ In which language is the Hathigumpha inscription written? → Prakrit
☛ Which script is used in the Hathigumpha inscription? → Brahmi
☛ Where is the Hathigumpha inscription located? → Udayagiri (Odisha)
☛ To which dynasty does the Hathigumpha inscription belong? → Kalinga dynasty
☛ What is the time period of the Hathigumpha inscription? → 1st century BCE

q: The last ruler of the Maurya Empire was killed by whom?
qs.e: The last ruler of the Maurya Empire was Brihadratha Maurya. He was killed by his commander-in-chief Pushyamitra Shunga in 185 BCE. Pushyamitra Shunga then established the Shunga dynasty. Brihadratha Maurya was the grandson of Ashoka. Pushyamitra Shunga assassinated Brihadratha during a military parade.
qs.kf:
☛ Who founded the Maurya dynasty? → Chandragupta Maurya
☛ Who was the most famous Mauryan ruler? → Ashoka
☛ Who founded the Shunga dynasty? → Pushyamitra Shunga
☛ Who was the last Mauryan ruler? → Brihadratha Maurya
☛ When was Brihadratha Maurya killed? → 185 BCE

q: The Shaka dynasty in India was founded by _____.
qs.e: The Shaka dynasty in India was founded by Maues (Moga) around 120 BCE. Maues was a prominent Shaka ruler who ruled over the Gandhara and Swat regions. The Shakas were originally nomadic tribes from Central Asia who invaded and settled in India. Maues' coins were widely circulated in the Gandhara region. The Shaka dynasty had a significant influence in northwestern India. Later, Rudradaman I became a powerful Shaka ruler. Nahapana was a ruler of the Western Kshatrapas. Menander I was an Indo-Greek ruler.
qs.kf:
☛ Who founded the Shaka dynasty? → Maues (Moga)
☛ Where did the Shakas come from? → Central Asia
☛ Who was a famous Shaka ruler? → Rudradaman I
☛ Who was an Indo-Greek ruler? → Menander I
☛ Who was the prominent ruler of the Western Kshatrapas? → Nahapana

q: The title Devaputra, used by the Kushana rulers, implies which of the following?
o: Divine origin or claim to divinity
qs.e: The title 'Devaputra', used by the Kushana rulers, literally means 'son of God'. This title was employed by Kushana kings to assert their divine origin and claim to divinity. It is believed to be influenced by the Chinese concept of 'Son of Heaven'. The founder of the Kushana empire, Kujula Kadphises, adopted this title. Prominent Kushana rulers like Kanishka also bore the title 'Devaputra'. Through this title, the Kushana rulers sought to legitimize their authority by giving it a religious and divine character, thereby enhancing their influence over the people. This reflects the synthesis of Central Asian and local traditions within the Kushana empire. The title signifies the ruler's claim to be a divine or semi-divine being, rather than a mere hereditary monarch or protector of dharma.
qs.kf:
☛ Meaning of 'Devaputra' title in Kushana period → Divine origin or claim to divinity
☛ First Kushana ruler to adopt 'Devaputra' title → Kujula Kadphises
☛ Which Kushana ruler used the title 'Devaputra'? → Kanishka
☛ Concept that influenced the Kushana title 'Devaputra' → Chinese 'Son of Heaven' concept
☛ Capital of Kushana empire → Purushapura (Peshawar)

q: After the fall of the Mauryan Empire, which dynasty was founded by Pushyamitra Shunga, the general who killed the last Mauryan ruler?
qs.e: After the fall of the Mauryan Empire, the last Mauryan ruler Brihadratha was killed by his general Pushyamitra Shunga in 185 BCE. Pushyamitra Shunga established the Shunga Dynasty, which lasted from 185 BCE to 73 BCE. The capital of this dynasty was Pataliputra. Pushyamitra Shunga performed the Ashwamedha Yajna and patronized Brahminical religion. During the Shunga period, art and culture flourished, exemplified by the stupas of Bharhut and Sanchi. The last ruler of this dynasty was Devabhuti, who was killed by his minister Vasudeva Kanva, leading to the establishment of the Kanva Dynasty.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the founder of the Shunga dynasty? → Pushyamitra Shunga
☛ What was the capital of the Shunga dynasty? → Pataliputra
☛ Who was the last ruler of the Shunga dynasty? → Devabhuti
☛ Which dynasty succeeded the Shunga dynasty? → Kanva dynasty
☛ Which yajna did Pushyamitra Shunga perform? → Ashwamedha Yajna

q: Which of the following dynasties initiated the practice of land grants to Brahmanas?
qs.e: The Satavahana dynasty initiated the practice of land grants to Brahmanas. This practice was first started in South India by the Satavahanas, as evidenced by the Nasik inscription. Satavahana rulers like Gautamiputra Satakarni and Vasishthiputra Pulamavi granted land to Brahmanas. These grants were called Agrahara, which provided tax-free land to Brahmanas. The purpose of this practice was to gain the support of Brahmanas and encourage their religious activities. Later, during the Gupta period, this practice became more widespread.
qs.kf:
☛ First dynasty to grant land to Brahmanas → Satavahanas
☛ Famous inscription of Satavahanas → Nasik inscription
☛ Satavahana ruler who granted land → Gautamiputra Satakarni
☛ Land grants were known as → Agrahara
☛ Capital of Satavahanas → Pratishthana (Paithan)

q: ‘Milind Panho’ is a post-Mauryan text which contains the conversations between the Indo-Greek ruler Menander and the scholar and Buddhist monk ___________.
qs.e: 'Milind Panho' is a significant post-Mauryan Buddhist text that contains dialogues between the Indo-Greek king Menander (Milind) and the Buddhist monk Nagasena. Written in Pali language, it discusses various aspects of Buddhist philosophy. Nagasena converted Menander to Buddhism. This text highlights the cultural and religious exchange between Indian and Greek traditions.
qs.kf:
☛ In which language is 'Milind Panho' written? → Pali
☛ Menander belonged to which dynasty? → Indo-Greek
☛ Nagasena was a monk of which religion? → Buddhism
☛ What is another name for 'Milind Panho'? → Milind's Questions
☛ How many questions are in this text? → 262

q: Which subject is dealt with in 'Sushruta Samhita'?
qs.e: The Sushruta Samhita is an ancient Indian text primarily dealing with medicine and surgery, especially surgery. It is one of the foundational texts of Ayurveda, authored by Sushruta, who is considered the father of surgery. The text contains 184 chapters, describing over 1120 diseases, 121 surgical instruments, and various surgical procedures. It emphasizes not only surgical techniques but also medical ethics and diagnosis. The Sushruta Samhita is often compared to the Charaka Samhita, which focuses on internal medicine.
qs.kf:
☛ Author of Sushruta Samhita → Sushruta
☛ Number of chapters in Sushruta Samhita → 184
☛ Sushruta is called the father of → Surgery
☛ Main surgical text of Ayurveda → Sushruta Samhita
☛ Charaka Samhita deals with → Internal medicine

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (09/06/2025) Shift 2
q: Which ruler of the Western Kshatrapas dynasty is primarily known for restoring the Sudarshana Lake in Kathiawar?
qs.e: Rudradaman I was a prominent ruler of the Western Kshatrapas dynasty, reigning in the mid-2nd century CE. He is primarily known for restoring the Sudarshana Lake in the Kathiawar region of Gujarat. The lake was originally built during the Maurya Empire under Chandragupta Maurya but later fell into disrepair. Rudradaman I undertook its renovation, as recorded in the Junagadh inscription. This inscription is written in Sanskrit and provides details of his reign, achievements, and administrative efficiency. Rudradaman not only repaired the lake but also improved irrigation facilities, boosting agriculture in the area. He was a skilled military leader and patron of arts. His rule is considered a golden period of the Western Kshatrapas.
qs.kf:
☛ Who built the Sudarshana lake originally? → Pushyagupta, a Vaishya, during Chandragupta Maurya's reign
☛ Who was the founder of the Western Kshatrapas dynasty? → Chashtana
☛ In which script is the Junagadh inscription written? → Brahmi script
☛ Who restored the Sudarshana lake? → Rudradaman I
☛ Who succeeded Rudradaman I? → Damajadaputra I

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (09/06/2025) Shift 3
q: The Scythians, or Shakas, originally came from _______.
qs.e: The Scythians, or Shakas, were originally nomadic tribes from Central Asia. They belonged to an Iranian-speaking group and migrated into India around the 2nd century BCE. The Shakas established several kingdoms in India, most notably the Western Satraps. They are known for their art, coinage, and cultural influence. The Shaka ruler Rudradaman is famous for the Junagadh inscription. Shaka culture had a deep impact on Indian art and architecture, contributing to the development of Gandhara art.
qs.kf:
☛ Where did the Shakas come from? → Central Asia
☛ Which language group did the Shakas belong to? → Iranian
☛ Who was a prominent Shaka ruler? → Rudradaman
☛ Art style associated with Shakas → Gandhara art
☛ Name of Shaka dynasty → Western Satraps

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (20/06/2025) Shift 1
q: Which of the following was the famous ruler of the Satavahana dynasty?
qs.e: Gautamiputra Satakarni was the most powerful and famous ruler of the Satavahana dynasty. He ruled approximately from 106 CE to 130 CE. He is also known as 'Hala'. He defeated the Shakas, Yavanas, and Pahlavas, expanding the Satavahana empire. His capital was Pratishthana (present-day Paithan, Maharashtra). He assumed the title 'Raja' and was honored with the title 'Trisamudra-toya-pita-vahana'. During his reign, the Satavahana empire spread widely across western and southern India. Gautamiputra Satakarni is considered the real founder of the Satavahana dynasty.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the founder of the Satavahana dynasty? → Simuka
☛ What was the capital of the Satavahana dynasty? → Pratishthana (Paithan)
☛ What was the name of Gautamiputra Satakarni's mother? → Gautami Balashri
☛ Which inscription is important from Gautamiputra Satakarni's reign? → Nasik inscription
☛ Who was the last ruler of the Satavahana dynasty? → Pulamavi IV

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (23/06/2025) Shift 1
q: Which dynasty replaced the Shungas in Magadha?
qs.e: After the Shunga dynasty, the Kanva dynasty ruled over Magadha. The last Shunga ruler Devabhuti was killed by his minister Vasudeva Kanva, who founded the Kanva dynasty. The Kanvas ruled from 72 BCE to 28 BCE for about 45 years. There were four Kanva rulers: Vasudeva, Bhumimitra, Narayana, and Susarman. The last ruler Susarman was defeated by the Satavahana ruler Simuka, after which the Satavahanas rose to power in Magadha. Thus, the Kanva dynasty was a short-lived ruling dynasty in Magadha with limited historical significance.
qs.kf:
☛ Who founded the Kanva dynasty? → Vasudeva Kanva
☛ What was the period of Kanva rule? → 72 BCE to 28 BCE
☛ Who was the last Kanva ruler? → Susarman
☛ Who ended the Kanva dynasty? → Satavahana ruler Simuka
☛ How many rulers did the Kanva dynasty have? → Four

q: Which native Indian dynasty issued their own coins with portraits of their rulers on them?
qs.e: The Satavahana Dynasty was a prominent native Indian dynasty that ruled the Deccan region. This dynasty is known for issuing coins with portraits of their rulers, which was a significant advancement in Indian coinage. The Satavahana coins were primarily made of lead, copper, and silver, and they featured portraits of kings along with symbols and inscriptions in Brahmi script. The Satavahana rulers patronized Buddhism and promoted trade. Their coins were widely circulated across the Indian subcontinent.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the founder of the Satavahana dynasty? → Simuka
☛ Who was the most famous ruler of the Satavahana dynasty? → Gautamiputra Satakarni
☛ Which metal were Satavahana coins made of? → Lead, copper, and silver
☛ What was the capital of the Satavahana dynasty? → Pratishthana (modern Paithan)
☛ Which region did the Satavahana dynasty rule? → Deccan region

q: What is a mixture of copper and silver used by Satvahanas ?
qs.e: The mixture of copper and silver used by the Satavahanas was called 'Putty'. This special alloy was used during the Satavahana period for making coins and ornaments. The use of this copper-silver mixture reflects the advanced metallurgical skills of the Satavahanas. The term 'Putty' is also found in ancient Indian texts. The Satavahana empire flourished in southern India from around 230 BCE to 220 CE. They issued coins made of lead, copper, and silver. This alloy was a distinctive feature of their coinage.
qs.kf:
☛ Satavahana copper-silver mixture → Putty
☛ Satavahana empire period → 230 BCE to 220 CE
☛ Capital of Satavahanas → Pratishthana (Paithan)
☛ Major Satavahana ruler → Gautamiputra Satakarni
☛ Metals used in Satavahana coins → Lead, Copper, Silver

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (05/06/2025) Shift 3
q: The Shakas were defeated by which tribal group before entering India?
qs.e: The Shakas (Scythians) migrated to India from Central Asia. Before entering India, they were defeated by the Yueh-chis (also known as the Kushans). This conflict occurred around the 2nd century BCE. The Yueh-chis drove the Shakas from their original territories, forcing them to move southward into India, where they later established kingdoms in the western regions. The Shakas ruled areas like Ujjain and Mathura. The Yueh-chis themselves later entered India and founded the Kushan Empire, which controlled a large part of the Indian subcontinent. Thus, the Yueh-chis' defeat of the Shakas paved the way for the latter's entry into India.
qs.kf:
☛ By what other name are the Yueh-chis known? → Kushans
☛ Which two major regions did the Shakas rule in India? → Ujjain and Mathura
☛ Which empire did the Yueh-chis establish in India? → Kushan Empire
☛ In which century did the Shakas enter India? → 1st century BCE
☛ What was the original homeland of the Yueh-chis and Shakas? → Central Asia

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (06/06/2025) Shift 1
q: Kanishka, the Kushana ruler, was a patron of which religion?
qs.e: The Kushana ruler Kanishka (c. 78-144 CE) was a great patron of Buddhism, specifically of the Mahayana school. Under his patronage, the Fourth Buddhist Council was held at Kundalavana in Kashmir, presided over by Vasumitra with Ashvaghosha as vice-president. This council resulted in the translation of Buddhist texts into the Tibetan language. Kanishka's reign saw the flourishing of Gandhara and Mathura schools of art. He also built a large stupa at Purushapura (modern Peshawar).
qs.kf:
☛ Capital of Kanishka → Purushapura (Peshawar)
☛ State religion of Kanishka → Buddhism
☛ Reign of Kanishka → 78 CE (start of Shaka era)
☛ Chairman of Fourth Buddhist Council → Vasumitra
☛ Court scholars of Kanishka → Ashvaghosha, Nagarjuna, Vasumitra

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (23/06/2025) Shift 3
q: Demetrius, a Bactrian-Greek ruler, came into conflict with ______.
qs.e: Demetrius was a Bactrian-Greek ruler who invaded India around 200 BCE. He came into conflict with Pushyamitra Shunga, the founder of the Shunga dynasty. Pushyamitra established his rule around 185 BCE after the decline of the Maurya Empire. Demetrius had occupied the Indus Valley and Punjab regions, leading to a direct confrontation between the two powers. This conflict is a significant chapter in Indo-Greek history. Pushyamitra Shunga was a follower of Vedic religion and resisted Greek invasions. The term Yavana was used in ancient India to refer to Greeks. Thus, the struggle between Demetrius and Pushyamitra Shunga holds historical importance.
qs.kf:
☛ Which dynasty did Demetrius belong to? → Bactrian-Greek
☛ Who founded the Shunga dynasty? → Pushyamitra
☛ After which empire's decline did Pushyamitra rise? → Maurya Empire
☛ With whom did Demetrius conflict in India? → Pushyamitra Shunga
☛ What were Greeks called in ancient India? → Yavana

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (05/06/2025) Shift 1
q: The Takht-i-Bahi inscription refers to which Parthian ruler?
qs.e: The Takht-i-Bahi inscription is found at an ancient Buddhist monastery site in the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province of Pakistan. This inscription is associated with the rule of the Parthian king Gondophernes. Gondophernes was a ruler of the Indo-Parthian kingdom in the 1st century CE. The inscription mentions the 26th year of Gondophernes' reign, making it one of the earliest dated inscriptions from the Indian subcontinent. The inscription is written in the Kharosthi script and provides historical evidence of the spread of Buddhism in the region.
qs.kf:
☛ Where is the Takht-i-Bahi site located? → Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan
☛ In which script is this inscription? → Kharosthi script
☛ To which dynasty did Gondophernes belong? → Indo-Parthian dynasty
☛ Which century did Gondophernes rule in? → 1st century CE
☛ Which year of Gondophernes' reign is mentioned in the Takht-i-Bahi inscription? → 26th year

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (13/06/2025) Shift 1
q: Rudradaman, who ruled in the middle of second century AD territories of Mathura and Gujarat belonged to which dynasty?
qs.e: Rudradaman, who ruled in the middle of the second century AD over Mathura and Gujarat, belonged to the Shaka dynasty, also known as the Western Kshatrapas. The Shakas were originally from Central Asia and established their rule in western parts of India. Rudradaman is renowned for his military campaigns and administrative skills. He recorded his achievements in the Junagadh rock inscription, an important source for the history of Shaka rulers. This inscription was written in Sanskrit, indicating the literary development of that period. Rudradaman is considered the most powerful Shaka ruler, having conquered several kingdoms and expanded his empire.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the most powerful Shaka ruler? → Rudradaman
☛ Which inscription mentions Rudradaman? → Junagadh rock inscription
☛ What is the other name for Shaka dynasty? → Western Kshatrapas
☛ In which language did Rudradaman write his inscription? → Sanskrit
☛ Where did the Shakas originally come from? → Central Asia

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (23/06/2025) Shift 2
q: The last ruler of the Shunga dynasty was:
qs.e: The last ruler of the Shunga dynasty was Devabhuti, who reigned from 83 BCE to 73 BCE. His reign marked the decline of the Shunga empire. He was assassinated by his minister Vasudeva Kanva, who later founded the Kanva dynasty. The Shunga dynasty was established by Pushyamitra Shunga in 185 BCE after the fall of the Mauryan empire. With the murder of Devabhuti, the Shunga dynasty ended, and a new dynasty began in Indian history.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the founder of the Shunga dynasty? → Pushyamitra Shunga
☛ Who founded the Kanva dynasty? → Vasudeva Kanva
☛ What was the capital of the Shunga dynasty? → Pataliputra
☛ Which is the famous Shunga monument? → Bharhut Stupa
☛ Who killed the last Shunga ruler? → Vasudeva Kanva

q: Amravati architecture was first protected by which rulers?
qs.e: The Satavahana Dynasty was the first to protect and patronize the Amravati architecture, particularly the famous Amravati Stupa located in Guntur district, Andhra Pradesh. The Satavahana rulers were great patrons of Buddhism and undertook the construction and expansion of the Amravati Stupa. The art of this period reflects Sangam period influences. The Amravati style of architecture developed during the Satavahana rule, which was later also patronized by the Ikshvaku and Vijayanagara rulers.
qs.kf:
☛ Where is Amravati Stupa located? → In Guntur district, Andhra Pradesh
☛ Which dynasty first patronized Amravati architecture? → Satavahana dynasty
☛ Who was the founder of the Satavahana dynasty? → Simuka
☛ What material is the Amravati Stupa made of? → Marble and limestone
☛ What was the capital of the Satavahana dynasty? → Pratishthana (modern Paithan, Maharashtra)

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (19/06/2025) Shift 2
q: The Indo-Greek king who issued coins with bilingual inscriptions was:
qs.e: Demetrius I was the Indo-Greek king who first issued bilingual coins (Greek and Kharosthi). He ruled around 200-180 BCE and is credited with initiating this practice in the Indian subcontinent. These coins featured his name and image in Greek script on one side and local language in Kharosthi script on the other, reflecting cultural fusion. Later rulers like Menander I also issued bilingual coins. Demetrius' coins are significant not only administratively but also as evidence of syncretism between Greek and Indian cultures. His kingdom covered parts of modern Afghanistan and Punjab.
qs.kf:
☛ First Indo-Greek king to issue bilingual coins? → Demetrius I
☛ Scripts used on Demetrius' coins? → Greek and Kharosthi
☛ Which Indo-Greek king issued the most coins? → Menander I
☛ Region ruled by Demetrius? → Afghanistan and Punjab
☛ Where was Kharosthi script prevalent? → Gandhara and Central Asia

q: Which Shaka ruler is credited with repairing the Sudarshana Lake without imposing any tax?
qs.e: The Shaka ruler Rudradaman (2nd century CE) is credited with repairing the Sudarshana Lake in Gujarat without imposing any tax. The lake, originally built during the Mauryan period, was damaged by floods. Rudradaman used his own treasury for the repairs, as recorded in the Junagadh inscription. This inscription is written in Sanskrit and is considered Rudradaman's most famous edict. He belonged to the Western Kshatrapa dynasty.
qs.kf:
☛ Who built the Sudarshana Lake? → Chandragupta Maurya
☛ In which script is the Junagadh inscription written? → Brahmi script
☛ To which dynasty did Rudradaman belong? → Western Kshatrapa
☛ Who repaired the Sudarshana Lake? → Rudradaman (without tax) and Skandagupta (with tax)
☛ What is Rudradaman's famous inscription? → Junagadh inscription

q: King Kharavela belonged to which of the following dynasties?
qs.e: King Kharavela was a powerful ruler of the Chedi dynasty who ruled over Kalinga (present-day Odisha) around the 1st century BCE or CE. His detailed account is found in the Hathigumpha inscription at Udayagiri, which describes his military campaigns, religious tolerance, and administrative achievements. The inscription mentions his father as Chetaraja (king of Chedi). The Chedi dynasty is also referenced in the Mahabharata. Kharavela is the most famous ruler of this dynasty. The Kanva dynasty ruled Magadha, the Satavahana dynasty ruled the Deccan, and the Shunga dynasty ruled central India, making them incorrect options.
qs.kf:
☛ Where is Kharavela's inscription located? → Hathigumpha (Udayagiri, Odisha)
☛ Which assembly did Kharavela address? → Nagar Sabha (city assembly)
☛ Which religion was patronized by Kharavela? → Jainism

q: Who is the author of the drama 'abhignanashakuntalam'?
qs.e: Abhignanashakuntalam is a famous Sanskrit drama written by the great poet Kalidas. The play is based on the love story of King Dushyanta and Shakuntala, the daughter of sage Vishwamitra and the celestial nymph Menaka. Kalidas is regarded as the greatest poet and dramatist in Sanskrit literature. His notable works include the dramas Malavikagnimitram, Vikramorvashiyam, and the epic poems Kumarasambhavam and Raghuvamsham. He is often referred to as the 'Shakespeare of India'. Though his exact period is uncertain, he is believed to have lived during the Gupta period. His mastery of language and vivid descriptions of nature and emotions make his works timeless.
qs.kf:
☛ Author of Abhignanashakuntalam → Kalidas
☛ Dramas written by Kalidas → Malavikagnimitram, Vikramorvashiyam
☛ Epic poems by Kalidas → Kumarasambhavam, Raghuvamsham
☛ Kalidas is known as → Shakespeare of India
☛ Characters of Abhignanashakuntalam → Dushyanta and Shakuntala

q: Who was the Chinese pilgrim who visited India during the Gupta period?
A. Hiuen Tsang
B. Fa Hien
C. I ching
D. Li Xiu
qs.e: Fa Hien was a Chinese Buddhist monk who visited India during the Gupta period (around 399-414 AD). He arrived during the reign of Chandragupta II (Vikramaditya) and traveled to places like Patna, Kapilavastu, Varanasi, and Pataliputra. He wrote an account of his travels in the book Fo-kwo-ki (Record of Buddhist Kingdoms), which is an important source of social, religious, and economic life during the Gupta era. Fa Hien carried copies of the Pali Tripitaka back to China and contributed to the spread of Buddhism. Hiuen Tsang came in the 7th century during Harshavardhana's reign, while I Ching came in the late 7th century. Li Xiu visited during the Tang dynasty.
qs.kf:
☛ Chinese pilgrim who visited India during Gupta period? → Fa Hien
☛ Name of Fa Hien's book? → Fo-kwo-ki
☛ Under which Gupta ruler did Fa Hien visit India? → Chandragupta II
☛ Chinese pilgrim who visited Harshavardhana's court? → Hiuen Tsang
☛ Century in which I Ching visited India? → Late 7th century

q: Who was the founder of the Gupta Empire?
A. Chandragupta II
B. Samudragupta
C. Sri Gupta
D. Ghatookacha
qs.e: The Gupta Empire was founded by Sri Gupta, who was the first ruler of the Gupta dynasty. He ruled around the late 3rd century CE, with his kingdom centered in the Magadha region. Sri Gupta adopted the title of 'Maharaja', indicating he was a minor chieftain. His successor was Ghatokacha, who expanded the territory. The actual establishment of the empire is attributed to Chandragupta I, the grandson of Sri Gupta, but the founder of the dynasty remains Sri Gupta. The Gupta period is often referred to as the 'Golden Age' of ancient India due to advancements in art, literature, and science.
qs.kf:
☛ Who founded the Gupta dynasty? → Sri Gupta
☛ Who was the first great ruler of the Gupta Empire? → Chandragupta I
☛ Who is considered the most famous Gupta ruler? → Samudragupta
☛ What is the Gupta period known as? → Golden Age of India
☛ What title did Sri Gupta assume? → Maharaja

q: Who is known as the 'Napoleon of India'?
qs.e: Samudragupta is known as the 'Napoleon of India'. He was one of the greatest rulers of the Gupta dynasty. His reign (c. 335-380 CE) is considered the golden age of the Gupta Empire. Samudragupta conducted many military campaigns and expanded his empire. Due to his military genius and conquests, historians compare him to Napoleon. He also performed the Ashvamedha sacrifice and held the title 'Kaviraj'. His policies strengthened the Gupta Empire. The Prayag Prashasti inscription describes his achievements.
qs.kf:
☛ Who is known as the Napoleon of India? → Samudragupta
☛ Samudragupta belonged to which dynasty? → Gupta dynasty
☛ What was the reign period of Samudragupta? → 335-380 CE
☛ What title did Samudragupta hold? → Kaviraj
☛ Who was the court poet of Samudragupta? → Harishena

q: Vikramaditya is another name of which famous Gupta ruler?
qs.e: Chandragupta II, also known as Vikramaditya, was a prominent ruler of the Gupta Empire. His reign (c. 375–415 CE) is considered the Golden Age of the Gupta Empire. He is renowned for his patronage of art, literature, and culture. His court was adorned by the Navaratnas (nine gems), including poet Kalidasa, physician Dhanvantari, and astronomer Varahamihira. Chandragupta II defeated the Western Kshatrapas and expanded his empire. The title Vikramaditya reflects his valor and wisdom.
qs.kf:
☛ What is the other name of Chandragupta II? → Vikramaditya
☛ Which Gupta ruler had Navaratnas in his court? → Chandragupta II
☛ Under whose reign did the Gupta Empire experience a Golden Age? → Chandragupta II
☛ Which kingdom did Chandragupta II defeat? → Western Kshatrapas
☛ Who bore the title Vikramaditya? → Chandragupta II

q: Bhukti, Bhoga, Visaya, Vithi and Mandal were:
o: great saints of the Mauryan period
administrative divisions in the Gupta period
qs.e: During the Gupta period, the administrative system was divided into several levels. The largest unit was Bhukti, governed by an Uparika. Bhukti was subdivided into Bhoga, headed by a Bhogapati. Bhoga was further divided into Visaya (district), headed by a Visayapati. Within Visaya, smaller units like Vithi and Mandal existed. Thus, these terms represent different administrative divisions of the Gupta empire.
qs.kf:
☛ Largest administrative unit in Gupta period → Bhukti
☛ Head of Bhukti → Uparika
☛ Head of Bhoga → Bhogapati
☛ District-level unit → Visaya
☛ Head of Visaya → Visayapati

q: Who ascended the Gupta throne after Chandragupta I?
qs.e: Chandragupta I (c. 319-335 CE) was the grandson of the Gupta dynasty founder Sri Gupta and son of Ghatotkacha. After his death, his son Samudragupta ascended the throne. Samudragupta is often called the 'Napoleon of India' for his military conquests. He assumed the title 'Kaviraj' (king of poets). During his reign, the Gupta Empire reached its zenith. The Prayag Prashasti (Allahabad Pillar Inscription) composed by Harisena details his achievements. He was a great warrior and patron of arts.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the founder of the Gupta dynasty? → Sri Gupta
☛ Which title was assumed by Samudragupta? → Kaviraj
☛ Who composed the Prayag Prashasti? → Harisena
☛ By what name is Samudragupta known in history? → Napoleon of India
☛ Which Lichchhavi princess did Chandragupta I marry? → Kumaradevi

q: Which period has been described as the Golden Age of Indian history?
qs.e: The Gupta period (approximately 320-550 CE) is known as the Golden Age of Indian history. This era witnessed unprecedented progress in art, literature, science, and culture. Rulers like Chandragupta Vikramaditya and Samudragupta expanded the empire. Luminaries such as Kalidasa and Aryabhata flourished during this period. The Nalanda University was also established in this age. Due to peace, prosperity, and cultural advancement, it is called the Golden Age.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the founder of the Gupta Empire? → Sri Gupta
☛ What was the official language of the Gupta period? → Sanskrit
☛ Who was the famous physician of the Gupta period? → Sushruta
☛ Who established Nalanda University during the Gupta period? → Kumaragupta I
☛ Who first called the Gupta period the Golden Age? → William Jones

q: Which of the following kings of the Gupta Empire was also a good Veena player?
qs.e: Samudragupta was a great ruler of the Gupta Empire, often called the 'Napoleon of India'. He was not only a skilled warrior but also a lover of arts and music. His coins depict him playing the veena, showcasing his musical talent. He held titles like 'Kaviraj' and 'Veenaavadan'. He expanded his empire by defeating many kings. The court poet Harishena wrote inscriptions praising him. Other Gupta rulers like Chandragupta Vikramaditya, Chandragupta I, and Kumaragupta I were not known for veena playing.
qs.kf:
☛ Gupta king playing veena → Samudragupta
☛ Samudragupta's nickname → Napoleon of India
☛ Samudragupta's coin with veena → Veenavadan mudra

☛ Founder of Gupta Empire → Sri Gupta

q: Who was the son of Shakuntala in Kalidasa's drama of Abhijnana Shakuntalam?
qs.e: In Kalidasa's Sanskrit play Abhijnana Shakuntalam, the son of Shakuntala is Bharata. The play is based on the love story of King Dushyanta and Shakuntala. After their marriage, Shakuntala receives a curse from sage Durvasa due to which Dushyanta forgets her. Shakuntala arrives at the royal court with her son Bharata, and after finding the ring of remembrance, Dushyanta recalls everything. The name Bharatavarsha (India) is believed to be derived from King Bharata. Thus, Shakuntala's son was Bharata.

☛ India is named after which king → Bharata

☛ Kalidasa is known as → Indian Shakespeare

q: Who among the following was called as the "Indian Napoleon"?
qs.e: Samudragupta (335-380 CE) was called the 'Indian Napoleon'. He was the greatest ruler of the Gupta dynasty, and his reign is considered the golden age of the Gupta Empire. He conducted extensive military campaigns, conquering most of the kingdoms in northern India, and also sent expeditions to southern India. His victories are described in the Prayag Prashasti (Allahabad pillar inscription), composed by his court poet Harishena. Samudragupta was also a patron of music and arts; his coins depict him playing the veena, which is evidence of his cultural interests.
qs.kf:
☛ Who is called the Indian Napoleon? → Samudragupta
☛ Who was the court poet of Samudragupta? → Harishena

☛ Samudragupta belonged to which dynasty? → Gupta dynasty

q: Which metal coins of the Gupta period were known as 'Rū paka'?
qs.e: During the Gupta period, silver coins were known as 'Rū paka'. The Gupta rulers issued coins in various metals: gold coins were called 'Dī nā ra', silver coins were called 'Rū paka', and copper coins were called 'Kā ṣika'. Rū paka coins were primarily made of silver and depicted the Gupta rulers and various deities. Silver coins played a significant role in the Gupta economy and were used in trade and commerce. The study of Gupta coins provides valuable insights into the culture, administration, and economic conditions of that era. The term 'Rū paka' later evolved into the modern word 'rupee', reflecting the historical continuity of Indian currency.
qs.kf:
☛ What were Gupta gold coins called? → Dī nā ra
☛ What were Gupta copper coins called? → Kā ṣika
☛ Which metal's coins were called 'Rū paka' in Gupta period? → Silver

☛ Whose images were mainly depicted on Gupta coins? → Rulers and deities

q: The Gupta Period saw the development of which important systems in Mathematics?
qs.e: The Gupta period (approximately 4th-6th century CE) is considered the Golden Age of Indian mathematics. During this time, the decimal notation system was developed, which included the use of zero as a placeholder. Mathematicians like Aryabhata and Brahmagupta advanced this system. Without decimal notation, modern mathematics would be unimaginable. It simplified arithmetic and algebra, revolutionizing trade and astronomy.
qs.kf:
☛ Which system of mathematics was developed during the Gupta period? → Decimal notation
☛ What was used as a placeholder in the decimal system? → Zero (0)

☛ Which fields were revolutionized by the decimal system? → Arithmetic, algebra, trade, and astronomy
☛ What is the Gupta period known as in mathematics? → Golden Age

q: Who among the following was the court poet of Samudragupta?
qs.e: The court poet of Samudragupta was Harishena. Harishena was a renowned poet, minister, and general. He composed the Prayag Prashasti (Allahabad Pillar Inscription), which describes the military campaigns and achievements of Samudragupta. This inscription is written in Sanskrit and is a crucial source of Gupta history. Harishena bestowed titles such as 'Kaviraj' and 'Lichchhavi Dauhitra' upon Samudragupta. The inscription details Samudragupta's conquests, cultural patronage, and administrative capabilities. Among the other options, Vatsyayana authored the Kamasutra, Bharavi wrote Kiratarjuniya, and Kalidasa was the court poet of Chandragupta II.
qs.kf:
☛ Who composed the Prayag Prashasti? → Harishena
☛ Which titles were given to Samudragupta? → Kaviraj and Lichchhavi Dauhitra
☛ Which is the most famous inscription of the Gupta period? → Prayag Prashasti (Allahabad Pillar)
☛ Kalidasa was the court poet of which Gupta ruler? → Chandragupta II
☛ Which epic was written by Bharavi? → Kiratarjuniya

q: Who was the first ruler of the Gupta dynasty to adopt the grand title of Maharajadhiraja?
qs.e: In the Gupta dynasty, Chandragupta I (319–335 CE) was the first ruler to adopt the grand title of Maharajadhiraja (King of Kings). Earlier rulers like Ghatotkacha and Sri Gupta used lesser titles such as Maharaja. Chandragupta I strengthened his position by marrying the Lichchhavi princess Kumaradevi, which gave the Gupta dynasty political prestige. He initiated the Gupta era, also known as the Chandragupta I era, during his reign. His coins bear the title Maharajadhiraja, reflecting his supremacy over other kings. Thus, Chandragupta I established the Gupta Empire as an imperial power.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the founder of the Gupta dynasty? → Sri Gupta
☛ Who was the first independent ruler of the Gupta dynasty? → Ghatotkacha
☛ With which dynasty did Chandragupta I establish a marital alliance? → Lichchhavi
☛ What title appears on Chandragupta I's coins? → Maharajadhiraja
☛ Who started the Gupta era? → Chandragupta I

q: The Iran stone inscription states that Samudragupta was chosen as king by his father because of his _____________.
qs.e: The Iran stone inscription (also known as the Allahabad pillar inscription) states that Samudragupta was chosen as king by his father Chandragupta I because of his devotion, pious conduct, and heroism. This inscription is a crucial source for Gupta history. Samudragupta is often called the 'Napoleon of India' for his military conquests. During his reign, the Gupta Empire expanded significantly. The inscription is written in Sanskrit and details his achievements and character. It highlights that his qualities were the reason for his selection over other sons.
qs.kf:
☛ What title is Samudragupta known by? → Napoleon of India
☛ In which language is the Iran stone inscription written? → Sanskrit
☛ Who founded the Gupta dynasty? → Srigupta
☛ Who was the father of Samudragupta? → Chandragupta I
☛ Which horse sacrifice did Samudragupta perform? → Ashvamedha yajna

q: Which Gupta emperor was known as the 'Napoleon of India' due to his military conquests and strategic warfare?
qs.e: Samudragupta is known as the 'Napoleon of India' due to his military conquests and strategic warfare. He was one of the greatest rulers of the Gupta dynasty, expanding his empire from North India to South India. His victories are described in the Prayag Prashasti (Allahabad Pillar Inscription), composed by his court poet Harishena. Samudragupta also performed the Ashvamedha Yajna. He was also proficient in playing the veena and composing poetry.
qs.kf:

☛ Who was the court poet of Samudragupta? → Harishena
☛ Who wrote the Prayag Prashasti? → Harishena
☛ Which musical instrument was Samudragupta proficient in? → Veena
☛ Who was the founder of the Gupta dynasty? → Sri Gupta

q: What was the other name of Chandragupta II, the renowned ruler of the Gupta dynasty?
qs.e: Chandragupta II, the renowned ruler of the Gupta dynasty, was also known as Vikramaditya. He reigned from 380 to 415 CE and brought the Gupta Empire to its zenith. Vikramaditya means 'valiant like the sun'. Chandragupta II conquered regions like Malwa, Gujarat, and Kathiawar. His court was adorned with Navaratnas (nine gems), including poet Kalidasa and astronomer Varahamihira. He defeated the Huns and strengthened the empire through matrimonial alliances. His rule is considered a golden age of art, literature, and culture.
qs.kf:
☛ Chandragupta II's epithet → Vikramaditya
☛ Chandragupta II's reign period → 380-415 CE
☛ Navaratnas in Chandragupta II's court → Kalidasa, Varahamihira, etc.
☛ Enemy defeated by Chandragupta II → Huns
☛ Regions conquered by Chandragupta II → Malwa, Gujarat, Kathiawar

q: Which military division had become rare in warfare during the Gupta period despite being part of the army in texts?
qs.e: During the Gupta period, the army consisted of four divisions: infantry, cavalry, elephants, and chariots. Although texts mention chariots as part of the army, their use in warfare had become rare. The main reasons were the slow speed of chariots, high maintenance costs, and changing warfare strategies. The Gupta period emphasized cavalry and elephants more. Chariots were used only for ceremonial or symbolic purposes. Thus, the chariot was the military division that, despite being part of the army in texts, became rare in actual combat.
qs.kf:
☛ What were the four divisions of the Gupta army? → Infantry, cavalry, elephants, and chariots
☛ Which military division became rare in warfare during the Gupta period? → Chariot
☛ Which divisions were most important in the Gupta army? → Cavalry and elephants
☛ Why did the use of chariots decline in the Gupta period? → Slow speed and high maintenance
☛ What was the main division of the Gupta army? → Infantry and cavalry

q: In the Gupta period, the term Udranga referred to ______.
qs.e: During the Gupta period, the term Udranga referred to a type of land tax. It was imposed on agricultural land and collected regularly from landowners. The Gupta rulers established a centralized administrative system where land tax served as the primary source of revenue. The rate of Udranga was fixed and typically constituted a portion of the agricultural produce. Other contemporary taxes included Karana (tax on trade), Haladhani (tax on plows), and Pindakara (tax on commodities). References to Udranga are found in Gupta inscriptions and literature, highlighting its importance in the revenue system.
qs.kf:
☛ Gupta period land tax → Udranga
☛ Gupta period trade tax → Karana
☛ Gupta period plow tax → Haladhani
☛ Gupta period commodity tax → Pindakara
☛ Main revenue source in Gupta period → land tax

q: The village headman during the Gupta period was commonly known as _____.
qs.e: During the Gupta period, the village headman was known as Gramadhyaksha. This position was the chief of village administration. Mahattara referred to village elders or prominent persons, while Uparika was a provincial governor. Amatyas were ministers or high officials. The Gramadhyaksha was responsible for revenue collection, law and order, and administrative duties in the village. In Gupta administration, the village was called grama and its head was termed Gramadhyaksha or Gramika.
qs.kf:
☛ What was the village headman called in the Gupta period? → Gramadhyaksha
☛ What was the provincial governor called in the Gupta period? → Uparika
☛ What were ministers called in the Gupta period? → Amatyas
☛ What was the main function of Gramadhyaksha? → Revenue collection and administration
☛ What was the village called in the Gupta period? → Grama

q: Which of the following officers managed stores and the supply of weapons like spears and swords during the Gupta period?
qs.e: During the Gupta period, the officer called Ranabhandagarika managed stores and the supply of weapons like spears and swords. This position was a key part of military administration. Sandhivigrahika was the minister for peace and war, Kumaramatya was a high administrative post often serving as guardian of princes, and Mahadandanayaka was the commander of the army or judicial officer. The term Ranabhandagarika is derived from 'rana' (war) and 'bhandara' (store), indicating management of war materials. The Gupta empire had a well-organized military system with distinct roles for various officers.
qs.kf:
☛ Officer for weapon supply in Gupta period → Ranabhandagarika
☛ Gupta minister for peace and war → Sandhivigrahika
☛ Guardian of princes in Gupta administration → Kumaramatya
☛ Army chief in Gupta period → Mahadandanayaka
☛ Meaning of 'rana' in Gupta context → war

q: Which of the following statements about succession in the Gupta dynasty is true?
o: Sons had to prove their eligibility before an assembly
The eldest son was always crowned Yuvraj at priority
Only the eldest son could become king
The ruler always declared himself divine to get the throne
qs.e: In the Gupta dynasty, succession was not based on primogeniture. After the king's death, sons had to prove their eligibility before an assembly of ministers, commanders, and high officials. The eldest son was not always crowned; merit was prioritized. Rulers like Chandragupta II and Kumaragupta exemplified this. While Gupta kings often declared themselves divine (e.g., as 'Paramabhagavata'), it was not a requirement for succession. The assembly played a crucial role in selecting the most capable heir, ensuring stability. This flexible system allowed capable rulers to ascend, contributing to the dynasty's golden age. Thus, the correct statement is that sons had to prove their eligibility before an assembly.
qs.kf:
☛ What was the basis of succession in the Gupta dynasty? → Merit, not seniority
☛ What was the assembly that decided succession in Gupta period called? → Council of ministers
☛ Which Gupta ruler ascended the throne on merit? → Chandragupta II
☛ What did Gupta rulers declare themselves as? → Divine or Paramabhagavata
☛ Who was the last major ruler of the Gupta dynasty? → Skandagupta

q: What is the height of the Allahabad pillar which bears inscriptions associated with Samudragupta?
qs.e: The Allahabad pillar, also known as the Prayag Prashasti, has a height of 35 feet. This pillar is famous for the inscription composed by Harishena, the court poet of Samudragupta. The inscription is in Sanskrit and describes the expansion of the Gupta Empire and Samudragupta's conquests. The pillar was originally erected by Ashoka, and later Samudragupta had his inscription engraved on it. This pillar is located in present-day Prayagraj (Allahabad). Its height of 35 feet makes it a significant epigraph of the Gupta period.
qs.kf:
☛ Height of Allahabad pillar → 35 feet
☛ Who inscribed on Allahabad pillar → Samudragupta
☛ Who composed the inscription → Harishena
☛ Who erected the pillar originally → Ashoka
☛ Where is Allahabad pillar located → Prayagraj (Allahabad)

q: Who among the following kings of the Gupta dynasty married the Lichchhavi princess (Kumari devi)?
qs.e: The founder of the Gupta dynasty was Srigupta, followed by his son Ghatotkacha, whose son Chandra Gupta I married the Lichchhavi princess Kumari Devi. This marriage enhanced the political and social prestige of the Gupta dynasty. The Lichchhavis were a respected Kshatriya clan that previously ruled in Vaishali. Chandra Gupta I initiated the Gupta Era in 320 CE, which is mentioned on coins as 'Chandragupta-Kumardevi'. He was the first Gupta ruler to assume the title Maharajadhiraja. His son Samudra Gupta further expanded the empire.

☛ First Gupta ruler to adopt the title Maharajadhiraja? → Chandra Gupta I
☛ Husband of Lichchhavi princess Kumari Devi? → Chandra Gupta I
☛ Father of Chandra Gupta I? → Ghatotkacha

q: Which official in the Gupta administration was responsible for peace and war matters?
qs.e: In the Gupta administration, the official responsible for peace and war matters was the Sandhi-Vigrahika. The literal meaning of this term is 'minister of peace and war'. This official was in charge of foreign policy, treaties, and war strategies. Other options: Vishayapati was the head of district administration, Mahapratihara was the palace guard or gatekeeper, and Mahadandanayaka was the chief judicial and military officer. The Sandhi-Vigrahika worked at the central level and played a crucial role in the Gupta bureaucratic system.

q: The 'Tirabhukti' mentioned in Gupta inscriptions corresponds to present-day ______.
qs.e: The term 'Tirabhukti' mentioned in Gupta inscriptions corresponds to the present-day region of Bihar. 'Tirabhukti' means 'the region on the bank' or 'riverine area'. It was a province of the Gupta Empire located in northern Bihar. It is mentioned in the Prayag Prashasti and other Gupta inscriptions. Tirabhukti included important areas like Vaishali, Mithila, and Tirhut. In the 3rd century, Samudragupta annexed this region into his empire. In modern times, it covers the northeastern part of Bihar state. Tirabhukti is also known as Tirhut. It was one of the administrative divisions of the Gupta period.

q: The Maitrakas of Valabhi were initially the:
qs.e: The Maitrakas of Valabhi were initially subordinates of the Gupta Empire. The Maitraka dynasty was founded by Bhatarka in the 5th century CE, who served as a provincial ruler under the Gupta emperors. They acknowledged Gupta suzerainty and used Gupta coinage. Later, as the Gupta Empire declined, the Maitrakas became independent. Their capital was Valabhi in the Saurashtra region of Gujarat. During Maitraka rule, Valabhi developed into an important center of learning and was known for its Buddhist university.
