q: The governor of a province (bhukti) in the Pala and Pratihara empire was called:
qs.e: In the administrative system of the Pala and Pratihara empires, a province was called a 'bhukti'. The governor appointed to administer this bhukti was known as 'Uparika'. The main duties of an Uparika included maintaining law and order, collecting taxes, and ensuring loyalty to the central authority. This position was appointed by the central power and oversaw several districts (vishayas), each administered by a Vishayapati. While Rashtrapati was a higher rank sometimes in charge of provinces in other empires, and Koshtapala was a treasurer, the Uparika specifically governed the bhukti. Thus, the term Uparika was used for the provincial governor in the Pala-Pratihara administration.
qs.kf:
☛ What was a province called in the Pala empire? → Bhukti
☛ Who was the governor of a bhukti? → Uparika
☛ Who administered a district in the Pratihara empire? → Vishayapati
☛ What was the role of Koshtapala in Pala administration? → Treasurer
☛ Which empire is associated with the term Rashtrapati? → Gupta empire

q: Which Rajput ruler founded the Gurjara-Pratihara dynasty in Malwa during the 8th century CE?
qs.e: The Gurjara-Pratihara dynasty was founded in the 8th century CE by Nagabhatta I in the Malwa region. This dynasty was one of the prominent Rajput dynasties of medieval India and successfully resisted Arab invasions. Nagabhatta I established the Gurjara-Pratihara empire with Ujjain and Kannauj as its capitals. Notable later rulers include Vatsaraja, Nagabhatta II, and Mihira Bhoja. Mihira Bhoja is considered the most powerful ruler of this dynasty. The Gurjara-Pratiharas played a significant role in northern India from the 8th to the 11th century CE.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the founder of the Gurjara-Pratihara dynasty? → Nagabhatta I
☛ What was the capital of the Gurjara-Pratihara dynasty? → Kannauj
☛ Which Gurjara-Pratihara ruler defeated the Arabs? → Nagabhatta I
☛ Who was the most famous ruler of the Gurjara-Pratihara dynasty? → Mihira Bhoja
☛ In which region did the Gurjara-Pratiharas rule? → North India (Malwa, Kannauj)

q: The Tripartite Struggle was a prolonged conflict among the Gurjara-Pratiharas, Palas, and which southern Indian dynasty?
qs.e: The Tripartite Struggle was a prolonged conflict among the Gurjara-Pratiharas, Palas, and Rashtrakutas for control over Kannauj, which was a strategic and cultural center in early medieval India. This struggle lasted from the 8th to the 10th century and significantly drained the resources of all three powers. The Rashtrakutas were a Deccan dynasty based at Manyakheta, while the Palas ruled Bengal (east) and the Gurjara-Pratiharas ruled Rajasthan-Gujarat (west). The conflict centered on Kannauj because of its prestige and location in the Gangetic plains. The continuous warfare led to the weakening of all three dynasties, paving the way for other powers like the Chandellas and Ghaznavids.
qs.kf:
☛ Who were the three parties in the Tripartite Struggle? → Gurjara-Pratiharas, Palas, and Rashtrakutas
☛ Which city was the center of the struggle? → Kannauj
☛ What was the capital of the Rashtrakutas? → Manyakheta
☛ Which Pala ruler expanded the empire? → Dharmapala
☛ Who was a famous Gurjara-Pratihara ruler? → Mihira Bhoja

q: When was the Gurjara Pratihara dynasty founded by Nagabhatta I in the region of Malwa?
qs.e: The Gurjara Pratihara dynasty was founded by Nagabhatta I around 730 CE in the Malwa region, which falls in the 8th century. This dynasty emerged as a major power in North India and played a crucial role in halting Arab invasions. Nagabhatta I laid the foundation of the Gurjara Pratihara empire, which later made Kannauj its capital. The most famous ruler of this dynasty was Mihira Bhoja. The Pratiharas ruled for about three centuries.
qs.kf:
☛ Founder of Gurjara Pratihara dynasty → Nagabhatta I
☛ Period of Gurjara Pratihara foundation → 8th century (c. 730 CE)
☛ Capital of Gurjara Pratiharas → Kannauj
☛ Famous ruler of Gurjara Pratihara dynasty → Mihira Bhoja
☛ Contribution of Gurjara Pratiharas → Stopping Arab invasions

q: Among which of the following powers did the ‘Tripartite Struggle’ take place during the 8 th and 9th centuries?
qs.e: The Tripartite Struggle during the 8th and 9th centuries in India was fought among three major dynasties: the Palas (Bengal), the Pratiharas (northwestern India), and the Rashtrakutas (Deccan). The main objective of this conflict was to gain control over Kannauj, a strategically important and prosperous region in the Gangetic plains. Pala ruler Dharmapala initially captured Kannauj by defeating Pratihara Vatsaraja and Rashtrakuta Dhruva, but later Pratihara Nagabhata II and Rashtrakuta Govinda III recaptured it. The struggle lasted for over a century, with the Pratiharas eventually emerging as the dominant power. This event is also known as the Kannauj Tripartite Struggle.
qs.kf:
☛ Who were involved in the Tripartite Struggle? → Palas, Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas
☛ What was the cause of the struggle? → Control over Kannauj
☛ Pala ruler who conquered Kannauj? → Dharmapala
☛ Pratihara ruler who regained Kannauj? → Nagabhata II
☛ Rashtrakuta ruler who defeated Dharmapala? → Dhruva

q: Which of the following dynasties was NOT involved in the struggle for the control of the prosperous city of Kannauj in northern India?
qs.e: The struggle for control of the prosperous city of Kannauj in northern India involved the tripartite struggle among the Pratihara, Pala, and Rashtrakuta dynasties. This conflict lasted from the 8th to the 10th century. The Pallava dynasty was based in southern India with its capital at Kanchipuram and was not part of the Kannauj struggle. The Pratiharas were from western India, Palas from eastern India, and Rashtrakutas from the Deccan. All three fought for dominance over Kannauj.
qs.kf:
☛ Dynasties involved in tripartite struggle → Pratihara, Pala, Rashtrakuta
☛ Period of struggle for Kannauj → 8th-10th century
☛ Capital of Pallava dynasty → Kanchipuram
☛ Region of Pratihara dynasty → Western India
☛ Region of Rashtrakuta dynasty → Deccan

q: During the expansion of the Gurjara-Pratihara dynasty, which of the following cities became the capital of Vatsaraja?
qs.e: During the Gurjara-Pratihara dynasty, Vatsaraja (c. 780-800 CE) expanded the kingdom. He made Ujjain his capital, an important city in the Malwa region. Vatsaraja fought against the Pala king Dharmapala and the Rashtrakuta king Dhruva. Although later rulers shifted the capital to Kannauj, during Vatsaraja's reign Ujjain was the main center. Ujjain is an ancient city and part of Malwa region, but Malwa is a region, not a city. Mathura and Kannauj were also in Pratihara territory, but Vatsaraja's capital was Ujjain.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the founder of the Gurjara-Pratihara dynasty? → Nagabhata I
☛ Who made Kannauj the capital of the Pratihara dynasty? → Nagabhata II
☛ Which Pala ruler did Vatsaraja defeat? → Dharmapala
☛ Which Rashtrakuta ruler defeated Vatsaraja? → Dhruva
☛ Which river is Ujjain located on? → Shipra

q: Between the ninth and eleventh centuries, the_________ style was used for the sculptures in Bengal (including Bangladesh) and Bihar.
qs.e: Between the ninth and eleventh centuries, the Pala style was used for sculptures in Bengal (including Bangladesh) and Bihar. This style developed during the rule of the Pala dynasty (c. 750-1161 CE), known for patronizing Buddhism. Pala style sculptures mainly depict Buddhist deities like Buddha, Tara, and Avalokiteshvara. These sculptures exhibit simplicity, balance, and grace. The Pala style also flourished at Buddhist universities like Nalanda and Vikramashila. This style later influenced Tibet and Southeast Asia.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the founder of the Pala dynasty? → Gopala
☛ What was the capital of the Pala dynasty? → Munger (Mudgagiri)
☛ Which religion was associated with the Pala style? → Buddhism
☛ Which site is famous for Pala style sculptures? → Nalanda
☛ Where did the Pala style influence? → Tibet and Southeast Asia

q: Second Battle of Panipat took place in the year-
qs.e: The Second Battle of Panipat was fought on November 5, 1556, between Akbar (Mughal Empire) and Hemus (a Hindu king). Hemu had captured Delhi and assumed the title 'Vikramaditya'. The Mughal army was led by Bairam Khan. Hemu was hit by an arrow and fell unconscious, later being captured. Akbar's victory re-established the Mughal Empire in North India. The three Battles of Panipat (1526, 1556, 1761) are significant in Indian history.
qs.kf:
☛ First Battle of Panipat → 1526 (Babur vs Ibrahim Lodi)
☛ Third Battle of Panipat → 1761 (Ahmad Shah Abdali vs Marathas)
☛ Hemu's real name → Hemchandra Vikramaditya
☛ Akbar's age during Second Panipat → 14 years
☛ Bairam Khan's title → Khan-e-Khana

q: Who among the following founded Gurjara-Pratihara dynasty after winning Kannauj in the tripartite struggle?
qs.e: The Gurjara-Pratihara dynasty was founded by Nagabhata I after winning Kannauj in the tripartite struggle. This struggle took place between the Pala, Pratihara, and Rashtrakuta dynasties. Nagabhata I successfully repelled Arab invasions and expanded his kingdom. His successor was Vatsaraja, while Mihira Bhoja was the most famous ruler of the Pratihara dynasty. Rampal was the last ruler of the Pala dynasty.
qs.kf:
☛ Founder of Gurjara-Pratihara dynasty → Nagabhata I
☛ Dynasties involved in tripartite struggle → Pala, Pratihara, Rashtrakuta
☛ Most famous Pratihara ruler → Mihira Bhoja
☛ Invaders repelled by Nagabhata I → Arabs
☛ Capital of Pratiharas → Kannauj (Uttar Pradesh)

q: Which of the following Gurjara-Parthihara kings was highly praised by the Arabian scholar Sulaiman for keeping his empire safe from robbers?
qs.e: The Gurjara-Pratihara king Mihira Bhoja (r. 836-885 CE) was highly praised by the Arab scholar Sulaiman in his book 'Silsilat-ut-Tawarikh'. Sulaiman noted that during Bhoja's reign, there were no thieves and the empire was completely safe from robbers. He considered the Pratihara kingdom as one of the most powerful states in India. Mihira Bhoja made Kannauj (Kanyakubja) his capital and assumed the title 'Adivaraha'. His empire extended from Multan in the west to Bengal in the east. He was a devout follower of Vishnu.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the founder of the Gurjara-Pratihara dynasty? → Nagabhata I
☛ What was the title of Mihira Bhoja? → Adivaraha
☛ Which Pratihara king was praised by Arab scholar Sulaiman? → Mihira Bhoja
☛ What was the capital of Mihira Bhoja? → Kannauj
☛ Who was the greatest ruler of the Pratihara empire? → Mihira Bhoja

q: Who among the following had one of their capitals at Benaras?
qs.e: The Gahadavala dynasty emerged in the 11th century in Kannauj and had its capital at Varanasi (Benaras) among other places. Prominent rulers of this dynasty include Chandradeva, Govindachandra, and Jayachandra. Chandradeva founded the Gahadavala dynasty in 1089 CE and made Varanasi his capital. Varanasi is referred to as 'Kashi' or 'Varanasi' in Gahadavala inscriptions. The Gahadavala rulers were patrons of art and literature. They primarily ruled the Gangetic plains.
qs.kf:
☛ Who founded the Gahadavala dynasty? → Chandradeva
☛ What were the capitals of the Gahadavala dynasty? → Kannauj and Varanasi
☛ In which battle was Gahadavala king Jayachandra killed? → Battle of Chandawar (1194 CE)
☛ Who ended the Gahadavala dynasty? → Muhammad Ghori
☛ Which religion were the Gahadavala rulers patrons of? → Hinduism (especially Shaivism and Vaishnavism)

q: Arrange the following rulers of the Pala dynasty in the chronological order
qs.e: The Pala dynasty was founded by Gopala. After him, Dharamapala (770-810 CE) ruled and expanded the empire in Bengal. Then Devapala (810-850 CE) succeeded, considered the most powerful Pala ruler. After a period of weak rulers, Mahipala I (988-1038 CE) revived the Pala dynasty. Finally, Nayapala (1038-1055 CE) ruled. Thus, the correct chronological order is Dharamapala, Devapala, Mahipala, Nayapala.
qs.kf:
☛ Founder of Pala dynasty → Gopala
☛ Famous university established by Dharamapala → Vikramshila
☛ Court poet of Devapala → Vajradatta
☛ Mahipala I is known as → Second founder of Pala dynasty
☛ Which invader attacked Bengal during Nayapala's reign → Kalachuri ruler Karna

q: Which of the following battles was fought in the year 1191 AD?
qs.e: The First Battle of Tarain was fought in 1191 AD between Prithviraj Chauhan and Muhammad Ghori. In this battle, Prithviraj Chauhan defeated Muhammad Ghori. This battle took place at a place called Tarain. The Battle of Chandawar was fought in 1194 AD, the Battle of Kasahrada in 1178 AD, and the First Battle of Panipat in 1526 AD. Thus, the battle fought in 1191 AD is the First Battle of Tarain.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Second Battle of Tarain fought? → 1192 AD
☛ Who won the First Battle of Tarain? → Prithviraj Chauhan
☛ Who won the Second Battle of Tarain? → Muhammad Ghori
☛ Between whom was the Battle of Chandawar fought? → Jayachandra and Muhammad Ghori
☛ Between whom was the First Battle of Panipat fought? → Babur and Ibrahim Lodi

q: The mother of Jahangir was a Kachhwaha princess, a daughter of Rajput ruler of ___________.
qs.e: The mother of Jahangir was Mariam-uz-Zamani, who was the daughter of Raja Bharmal (Bhagwandas), the Rajput ruler of Amber (present-day Jaipur). Raja Bharmal belonged to the Kachhwaha dynasty. Akbar sought an alliance with the Rajputs through matrimony, resulting in the marriage of his son Salim (later Jahangir) to the Kachhwaha princess. This marriage strengthened Mughal-Rajput relations and brought stability to the empire. Mariam-uz-Zamani was given high status in the Mughal court and influenced Jahangir's character with Hindu traditions. Thus, this relationship is a key example of Mughal-Rajput cooperation.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was Mariam-uz-Zamani's father? → Raja Bharmal of Amber
☛ Which Rajput dynasty did Jahangir's mother belong to? → Kachhwaha dynasty
☛ What strategy did Akbar use to build relations with Rajputs? → Matrimonial alliances
☛ Who was the contemporary ruler of Amber allied with Akbar? → Raja Bharmal
☛ What was the original name of Mariam-uz-Zamani? → Harkha Bai

q: The Pala King of Bengal, Dharamapala was defeated by which of the following Rashtrakuta kings?
qs.e: The Pala king Dharamapala (770-810 CE) established a strong empire in Bengal. He was involved in the Tripartite Struggle for Kannauj. The Rashtrakuta king Dhruva Dharavarsha (780-793 CE) defeated Dharamapala during his northern campaign around 790 CE. Dhruva also defeated the Gurjara-Pratihara king Vatsaraja. He was the son of Dantidurga, the founder of the Rashtrakuta dynasty. Dhruva expanded the Rashtrakuta empire to northern India.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the founder of the Pala dynasty? → Gopala
☛ Which university was founded by Dharamapala? → Vikramashila
☛ Who founded the Rashtrakuta dynasty? → Dantidurga
☛ Which dynasties were involved in the Tripartite Struggle for Kannauj? → Palas, Pratiharas, and Rashtrakutas
☛ What was the reign period of Dhruva Dharavarsha? → 780–793 CE

q: Which of the following dynasties did NOT participate in tripartite struggle over Kannauj?
qs.e: The tripartite struggle over Kannauj took place between the 8th and 10th centuries among the Palas, Gurjara-Pratiharas, and Rashtrakutas. These three powers fought for control over Kannauj, which was a strategic and commercial center in northern India. The Palas ruled eastern India (Bihar, Bengal), the Gurjara-Pratiharas dominated western and central India, while the Rashtrakutas were based in the Deccan. The Chola dynasty, although a major power in southern India, did not participate in this struggle. The Cholas were primarily engaged in conflicts with the Pandyas and Chalukyas in the south and remained largely uninvolved in the politics of northern India. Therefore, the Chola dynasty was not a participant in the tripartite struggle over Kannauj.
qs.kf:
☛ Dynasties involved in Kannauj tripartite struggle → Palas, Gurjara-Pratiharas, Rashtrakutas
☛ Cause of tripartite struggle → Political and economic control over Kannauj
☛ Founder of Pala dynasty → Gopala
☛ Greatest ruler of Gurjara-Pratihara dynasty → Mihir Bhoja
☛ Prominent Rashtrakuta rulers → Dantidurga, Govinda III, Amoghavarsha

q: The tripartite struggle for Kannauj was among the:
qs.e: The tripartite struggle for Kannauj took place between the Palas, Gurjara-Pratiharas, and Rashtrakutas from the 8th to the 10th century. This struggle was for control over Kannauj, which was a symbol of imperial power in North India. The Palas ruled in eastern India, the Gurjara-Pratiharas in western and central India, and the Rashtrakutas in the Deccan. The Pratiharas emerged as the most successful, retaining Kannauj for the longest period. This conflict significantly influenced the political balance in early medieval India.
qs.kf:

q: Who was the founder of the Gurjara - Pratihara dynasty?
qs.e: The Gurjara-Pratihara dynasty was founded by Nagabhata I around 730 CE. This dynasty flourished in northwestern India with its capital at Kannauj. Nagabhata I successfully repelled Arab invasions and expanded his kingdom. His successors included Vatsaraja, Nagabhata II, and Bhoja I, who were prominent rulers. The dynasty remained powerful from the 8th to the 11th century and played a key role in the Tripartite Struggle. Although Bhoja I is considered the greatest ruler, Nagabhata I was the founder of the dynasty.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the first ruler of the Gurjara-Pratihara dynasty? → Nagabhata I
☛ Which invasion did Nagabhata I face? → Arab invasion
☛ What was the capital of the Gurjara-Pratihara dynasty? → Kannauj
☛ Who was the most powerful ruler of the Gurjara-Pratihara dynasty? → Bhoja I
☛ Which dynasties were involved in the Tripartite Struggle? → Gurjara-Pratihara, Rashtrakuta, and Pala

q: Which of the following is the correct chronology of these rulers?
A. Timur
B. Mahmud of Ghazni
C. Genghis Khan
D. Muhammad Ghori
qs.e: The correct chronology of these rulers is based on their reign periods. Mahmud of Ghazni (998-1030 CE) was the ruler of the Ghaznavid Empire who conducted 17 raids into India. Muhammad Ghori (1173-1206 CE) laid the foundation of Muslim rule in India, defeating Prithviraj Chauhan in the Second Battle of Tarain (1192). Genghis Khan (1206-1227 CE) founded the Mongol Empire. Timur (1370-1405 CE) was the ruler of the Timurid Empire who invaded India in 1398. Thus the order is: Mahmud of Ghazni (11th century), Muhammad Ghori (12th century), Genghis Khan (13th century), Timur (14th century).
qs.kf:
☛ How many invasions did Mahmud of Ghazni make on India? → 17
☛ When was the First Battle of Tarain fought? → 1191
☛ What was the real name of Genghis Khan? → Temujin
☛ In which year did Timur invade India? → 1398
☛ Which dynasty was founded by Muhammad Ghori? → Slave Dynasty

q: Manyakheta was the capital of which of following dynasties during the eighth century AD?
qs.e: During the 8th century AD, Manyakheta (present-day Malkhed, Karnataka) was the capital of the Rashtrakuta dynasty. The Rashtrakutas initially had their capitals at Halihippi and Nasirabad, but later shifted to Manyakheta. Dantidurga (735-756 AD) founded the Rashtrakuta dynasty. The most famous ruler, Amoghavarsha I (814-878 AD), patronized Kannada literature and authored the 'Kavirajamarga'. The Rashtrakutas of Manyakheta participated in the tripartite struggle for Kannauj against the Palas and Pratiharas. Their reign saw architectural marvels like the Kailash Temple at Ellora, built during Krishna I's rule. The dynasty declined after the death of Krishna III in 973 AD, succeeded by the Western Chalukyas.
qs.kf:
☛ Which dynasty had Manyakheta as its capital? → Rashtrakuta
☛ Who founded the Rashtrakuta dynasty? → Dantidurga
☛ Which Rashtrakuta ruler wrote 'Kavirajamarga'? → Amoghavarsha I
☛ Under whose rule was the Kailash Temple built? → Krishna I
☛ Which region did the Rashtrakutas rule? → Southern India

q: Pala Rulers were primarily great patrons of which religion/sect?
qs.e: The Pala dynasty (8th-12th century) was a significant kingdom in the Bengal region. The Pala rulers were great patrons of Buddhism. The founder of the dynasty, Gopala, adopted Buddhism, and his successors, especially Dharmapala and Devapala, contributed significantly to the construction of Buddhist monasteries and universities. They established the Vikramashila University, which became a major center of Buddhist learning. The Palas also patronized the Nalanda University. They followed Mahayana Buddhism and also encouraged Tantric Buddhism (Vajrayana). Thus, Buddhism was the primary religion patronized by the Pala rulers, while other religions like Vaishnavism, Shaivism, and Jainism were tolerated but not given as much patronage.
qs.kf:
☛ Founder of Pala dynasty → Gopala
☛ Most famous Pala rulers → Dharmapala and Devapala
☛ Famous Buddhist university established by Palas → Vikramashila
☛ Ancient university patronized by Palas → Nalanda
☛ Buddhist sect followed by Pala rulers → Mahayana and Vajrayana

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (06/06/2025) Shift 3
q: Mihira Bhoja, a famous ruler of the Pratiharas, adopted which title?
qs.e: The famous Pratihara ruler Mihira Bhoja (c. 836-885 AD) adopted the title Adivaraha. He was one of the most powerful rulers of the Pratihara dynasty and expanded his empire significantly. 'Adivaraha' means 'first boar' or 'boar incarnation', associated with the incarnation of Lord Vishnu. Mihira Bhoja was a devotee of Vishnu. He also inscribed the title 'Adivaraha' on his coins. Other titles like Vikramaditya, Parmeshwara, and Adityavardhana were used by different rulers. Under Mihira Bhoja, the Pratihara empire reached its zenith.
qs.kf:
☛ Title of Mihira Bhoja → Adivaraha
☛ Founder of Pratihara dynasty → Harishchandra
☛ Capital of Pratiharas → Kannauj
☛ Pratihara ruler who stopped Arabs → Nagabhata I
☛ Title on Mihira Bhoja's coins → Adivaraha

q: Which term is used to describe the conflict between the Gurjara-Pratiharas, Palas, and Rashtrakutas over the control of northern India?
qs.e: The prolonged struggle among the Gurjara-Pratihara, Pala, and Rashtrakuta dynasties for control of northern India is known as the Tripartite struggle. This conflict lasted from the 8th to the 10th century and was primarily over the possession of Kannauj, which was a symbol of imperial power. The Gurjara-Pratiharas ruled western India, the Palas ruled eastern India, and the Rashtrakutas ruled the Deccan. The constant warfare exhausted these kingdoms, weakening northern India and paving the way for invasions by Mahmud of Ghazni. The term "tripartite" refers to the three parties involved in this conflict.
qs.kf:
☛ Which dynasties were involved in the Tripartite struggle? → Gurjara-Pratihara, Pala, and Rashtrakuta
☛ Which city was the center of the Tripartite struggle? → Kannauj
☛ During which centuries did the Tripartite struggle occur? → 8th to 10th century
☛ Who founded the Gurjara-Pratihara dynasty? → Nagabhata I
☛ Who founded the Pala dynasty? → Gopala

q: Which dynasty ruled over Kannauj during the Tripartite Struggle?
qs.e: The Tripartite Struggle (8th-10th century) involved the Palas, Rashtrakutas, and Gurjara-Pratiharas fighting for control of Kannauj. Kannauj was a strategic trade center in the Ganga-Yamuna doab, often called the 'City of Three Seas.' The Gurjara-Pratihara dynasty ruled Kannauj for a long period. Key rulers like Nagabhata I and Bhoja Pratihara played crucial roles. The Pratiharas also halted Arab invasions in western India. Their capital was initially Ujjain, later moved to Kannauj. This struggle highlighted the political importance of Kannauj in medieval India.
qs.kf:
☛ Which three dynasties were involved in the Tripartite Struggle? → Palas, Rashtrakutas, Gurjara-Pratiharas
☛ Which dynasty made Kannauj its capital? → Gurjara-Pratiharas
☛ Who was a famous Pratihara ruler? → Bhoja Pratihara
☛ What was the main cause of the Tripartite Struggle? → Control of Kannauj
☛ Which invasion did the Gurjara-Pratiharas stop? → Arab invasions

q: Which of the following rulers of the Gurjara-Pratihara dynasty is credited with resisting Arab invasions effectively?
qs.e: Nagabhata I (c. 730-760 CE) of the Gurjara-Pratihara dynasty is credited with effectively resisting Arab invasions. He defeated the Arabs, who were advancing from Sindh, in the Malwa region. This victory protected northern India from Arab expansion. Nagabhata I laid the foundation of the Pratihara empire, which was later strengthened by rulers like Mihira Bhoja. This successful resistance against the Arabs is considered a pivotal event in Indian history.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the founder of the Gurjara-Pratihara dynasty? → Nagabhata I
☛ Which Arab commander did Nagabhata I defeat? → Junayd
☛ Who was the most famous ruler of the Pratihara dynasty? → Mihira Bhoja
☛ What was the capital of Mihira Bhoja? → Kannauj
☛ Who protected northern India from Arab invasions? → Nagabhata I

q: Vikramshila University located in the Bhagalpur district of Bihar was founded by which of the following rulers?
qs.e: Vikramshila University was founded by Dharampala, a ruler of the Pala dynasty, in the 8th century (c. 783-820 CE). It is located on the banks of the Ganga River in Bhagalpur district, Bihar. It was a major Buddhist learning center in ancient India, specializing in Tantric Buddhism. The renowned scholar Atisha Dipankara studied here. The university had 108 temples and 6 hostels. It was destroyed by Bakhtiyar Khilji in 1203 CE. The founder of the Pala dynasty was Gopala, while Devapala and Mahipala were later rulers.
qs.kf:
☛ Founder of Vikramshila University → Dharampala
☛ Founder of Pala dynasty → Gopala
☛ Vikramshila is located in → Bhagalpur district, Bihar
☛ Vikramshila was destroyed by → Bakhtiyar Khilji (1203 CE)
☛ Scholar associated with Vikramshila → Atisha Dipankara

q: Mahmud Begada was a famous sultan of which Sultanate?
qs.e: Mahmud Begada was the famous sultan of the Gujarat Sultanate. His real name was Sultan Mahmud Shah I and he belonged to the Muzaffarid dynasty of the Gujarat Sultanate. He ruled from 1458 to 1511 CE. The title 'Begada' was given to him because he captured two major forts. He conquered the forts of Champaner and Junagadh. Mahmud Begada shifted his capital from Ahmedabad to Muhammadabad (present-day Champaner). He was a skilled military commander and administrator. During his reign, the Gujarat Sultanate reached its peak of power. He also fought against the Portuguese. His reign marked significant expansion and consolidation of the sultanate.
qs.kf:
☛ Who founded the Gujarat Sultanate? → Zafar Khan (Muzaffar Shah I)
☛ Which city did Mahmud Begada make his capital? → Muhammadabad (Champaner)
☛ Which European power attacked Gujarat Sultanate during Mahmud Begada's reign? → Portuguese
☛ When did the Mughals annex Gujarat Sultanate? → 1573 CE (by Akbar)
☛ Which two forts did Mahmud Begada capture? → Champaner and Junagadh

q: Who among the following introduced the practice of branding of horses?
qs.e: Allauddin Khilji (1296-1316) introduced the practice of branding horses. This was part of his administrative and military reforms. The purpose of this practice was to identify royal horses and prevent fraud in the army. A special mark was branded on each horse's body, indicating its ownership and quality. This maintained discipline in the army and ensured availability of horses during wars. This reform was a significant aspect of Allauddin's efficient administrative policies.
qs.kf:
☛ Delhi Sultanate ruler who introduced branding of horses → Allauddin Khilji
☛ Reign of Allauddin Khilji → 1296-1316 CE
☛ Allauddin's administrative reforms included → market control, land revenue reforms
☛ Another practice introduced by Allauddin → paying soldiers in cash
☛ Purpose of branding horses → identification and quality control of horses

q: The Bahamani state was the most powerful under whose rule?
qs.e: The Bahamani state was most powerful under the rule of Mahmoud Gavan, a prime minister (Vazir) who effectively controlled the administration. From 1466 to 1481, he implemented administrative reforms, strengthened the military, and expanded the kingdom's territory. He conquered important regions like Goa and Bidar. Under his leadership, the Bahamani Sultanate reached its peak in military power and economic prosperity. He led successful campaigns against the Vijayanagara Empire and neighboring states. Although not a sultan, his policies made the Bahamani state a dominant force in the Deccan. After his execution, the kingdom weakened and eventually fragmented. His period is considered the golden era of the Bahamani Sultanate.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the most powerful ruler of the Bahamani state? → Mahmoud Gavan (Vazir)
☛ Under which sultan did Mahmoud Gavan serve? → Muhammad Shah III
☛ What administrative reform did Mahmoud Gavan introduce? → Reorganization of provinces
☛ What was the capital of the Bahamani state under Mahmoud Gavan? → Bidar
☛ Who ordered the execution of Mahmoud Gavan? → The Sultan

q: In which of the following year did Aamir Taimur invade Delhi?
qs.e: Amir Taimur invaded Delhi in 1398 AD. Taimur was a Central Asian conqueror who founded the Timurid Empire. He defeated Nasir-ud-din Mahmud Shah, the ruler of the Delhi Sultanate. Taimur's invasion was devastating for Delhi, resulting in massive plunder and massacre. He looted vast amounts of wealth and resources from Delhi, exposing the weakness of the Delhi Sultanate. After the invasion, Taimur did not establish his rule in India but returned to Samarkand. Taimur's invasion laid the foundation for the decline of the Delhi Sultanate.
qs.kf:
☛ When did Taimur invade Delhi? → 1398 AD
☛ Which empire was Taimur associated with? → Timurid Empire
☛ By which title is Taimur known? → Timur the Lame
☛ How long was Taimur's India campaign? → About 6 months
☛ Who was the Sultan of Delhi during Taimur's invasion? → Nasir-ud-din Mahmud Shah

q: Who among the following was a famous slave of Allauddin Khilji?
qs.e: Malik Kafoor was a famous slave of Allauddin Khilji who later became his chief general. He is regarded as the prominent commander of the Khilji dynasty. Malik Kafoor led successful campaigns in South India, conquering kingdoms like Devagiri, Warangal, and Madura. Between 1308 and 1311 AD, he commanded Allauddin's southern expeditions. He was also known as 'Hazar Dinari' because he was bought for a thousand dinars. After Allauddin's death, he briefly seized power but was soon killed.
qs.kf:
☛ Slave of Allauddin Khilji → Malik Kafoor
☛ Nickname of Malik Kafoor → Hazar Dinari
☛ Leader of South India campaigns → Malik Kafoor (1308-1311 AD)
☛ Sultan after Allauddin → Malik Kafoor (short reign)
☛ Amir Khusro → Patron Allauddin Khilji, not a slave

q: Which of these famous cities was formed by Firoz Shah Tughlaq?
qs.e: Firoz Shah Tughlaq (1351-1388 AD) founded the city of Hisar in 1354 AD. This city is located in the state of Haryana. Firoz Shah Tughlaq undertook several construction projects during his reign, including canals, forts, mosques, and cities. The original name of Hisar was 'Hisar-e-Firoza', meaning 'the fort of Firoz'. The city also has a famous fort built by Firoz Shah. The purpose of establishing Hisar was to protect the northwestern frontier and promote trade. Firoz Shah Tughlaq is also known for building irrigation canals and public buildings.
qs.kf:
☛ Who founded Hisar city? → Firoz Shah Tughlaq
☛ What was the ancient name of Hisar? → Hisar-e-Firoza
☛ In which state is Hisar located? → Haryana
☛ What was the reign period of Firoz Shah Tughlaq? → 1351-1388 AD
☛ Which dynasty did Firoz Shah Tughlaq belong to? → Tughlaq dynasty

q: Who did Iltutmish chose to declare as his successor?
qs.e: Iltutmish chose his daughter Razia Sultana as his successor. She became the first and only female ruler of the Delhi Sultanate. Iltutmish found his sons incompetent and selected Razia, who was skilled in administration and military affairs. Razia ruled from 1236 to 1240. During her reign, she broke gender norms by holding court in male attire. However, opposition from nobles and Turkish chiefs led to her death in battle. This event was a turning point in the history of the Delhi Sultanate.
qs.kf:
☛ First female ruler of Delhi Sultanate → Razia Sultana
☛ Successor of Iltutmish → Razia
☛ Razia's reign period → 1236-1240 CE
☛ How did Razia die → Killed in battle
☛ Dynasty of Iltutmish → Slave Dynasty

q: Which of the following Sultans of Delhi is known for its market control policy?
qs.e: Allauddin Khilji (1296-1316) was the Sultan of Delhi known for his economic reforms and market control policy. He implemented a strict administrative system to control prices of essential commodities like food grains, cloth, horses, and other goods. He appointed officials such as 'Diwan-i-Riyasat' and 'Shahna-i-Mandi' to monitor the markets. Allauddin imposed severe punishments for black marketing and hoarding to enforce price controls. His policy aimed to maintain a large army at low salaries and defend against Mongol invasions. Under this policy, all traders had to register, and prices were fixed by the government. This system is considered one of the earliest examples of state-controlled markets in medieval India.
qs.kf:
☛ What was the purpose of Allauddin Khilji's market control policy? → To maintain a large army at low cost and defend against Mongols
☛ Which department did Allauddin establish for price control? → Diwan-i-Riyasat
☛ What was the market inspector called? → Shahna-i-Mandi
☛ Which commodities did Allauddin control prices of? → Food grains, cloth, horses, weapons
☛ What was the reign period of Allauddin Khilji? → 1296-1316 CE

q: Under whose rule was the Charminar monument built in Hyderabad?
qs.e: The Charminar is a historic monument in Hyderabad, built by Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah in 1591. He was the fifth ruler of the Qutb Shahi dynasty. The monument was constructed to mark the end of a plague and the founding of the city. Charminar features four grand minarets and is an excellent example of Indo-Islamic architecture. The Mecca Masjid is located nearby. Today, Charminar is a symbol of Hyderabad and a major tourist attraction.
qs.kf:
☛ Who built the Charminar? → Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah
☛ In which year was the Charminar built? → 1591
☛ Which architectural style does Charminar represent? → Indo-Islamic
☛ On which river is Charminar located? → Musi River
☛ Who was the last ruler of the Qutb Shahi dynasty? → Abdullah Qutb Shah

q: Who among the following did NOT belong to the Slave Dynasty?
qs.e: The Slave Dynasty (1206-1290 AD) was founded by Qutbuddin Aibak. Prominent rulers of this dynasty include Iltutmish, Balban, and Kaiquabad. Hammir was a ruler of the Yadava dynasty of Devagiri, who lived during the time of Alauddin Khilji. He belongs to the Khilji dynasty period, not the Slave Dynasty. Hence, Hammir did not belong to the Slave Dynasty.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the founder of the Slave Dynasty? → Qutbuddin Aibak
☛ Who was the last ruler of the Slave Dynasty? → Muizuddin Kaiquabad
☛ What was the full name of Balban? → Ghiyasuddin Balban
☛ Which coinage system did Iltutmish introduce? → Tanka (silver) and Jital (copper)
☛ Which dynasty did Hammir belong to? → Yadava dynasty

q: Who was the only female ruler of Delhi Sultanate?
A. Chand Bibi
B. Noor Jahan
C. Razia Sultan
D. Mumtaz Mahal
qs.e: The only female ruler of the Delhi Sultanate was Razia Sultan, who reigned from 1236 to 1240 CE. She belonged to the Mamluk Dynasty (Slave Dynasty) and was the daughter of Iltutmish. Recognizing the incompetence of his sons, Iltutmish appointed Razia as his successor. Razia Sultan abandoned the purdah system and personally led the army. She was known for her justice, foresight, and administrative skills. During her reign, she faced rebellions from nobles and Turkish chiefs. Eventually, she was killed in a rebellion by the governor of Bhatinda.
qs.kf:
☛ To which dynasty did Razia Sultan belong? → Mamluk Dynasty (Slave Dynasty)
☛ Who was Razia Sultan's father? → Iltutmish
☛ What was the reign period of Razia Sultan? → 1236-1240 CE
☛ Where did Razia Sultan die? → Bhatinda
☛ Who was the first and last female ruler of Delhi Sultanate? → Razia Sultan

q: Where did Muhammad Bin Tughlaq shift his capital to from Delhi?
A. Daulatabad
B. Aurangabad
C. Allahabad
D. Shaharanpur
qs.e: Muhammad bin Tughlaq (1325-1351) shifted his capital from Delhi to Daulatabad (Maharashtra) in 1327, then known as Devagiri. His aim was better control over the entire Indian subcontinent and to suppress revolts in the south. He ordered the entire population of Delhi to march to Daulatabad on foot, causing many deaths. This decision failed due to lack of water and other issues in Daulatabad. Later, he had to shift the capital back to Delhi. This event is considered one of his ill-conceived policies. Daulatabad was originally founded by Ramdevar Yadav and later renamed by Muhammad bin Tughlaq.
qs.kf:
☛ Muhammad bin Tughlaq's capital shift → Daulatabad
☛ Reign of Muhammad bin Tughlaq → 1325-1351
☛ Ancient name of Daulatabad → Devagiri
☛ Daulatabad is in which state → Maharashtra
☛ Token currency introduced by Muhammad bin Tughlaq → Copper coins

q: Mecca Masjid, Hyderabad was completed by:
A. Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah
B. Jahangir
C. Qutb Shahi
D. Aurangzeb
qs.e: Mecca Masjid in Hyderabad was started by Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah in 1617 but was completed under the reign of Aurangzeb in 1694. It is one of the largest mosques in India and is located near the Charminar in Hyderabad. The mosque gets its name because bricks used for its construction were made from soil brought from Mecca.
qs.kf:
☛ Who started the construction of Mecca Masjid? → Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah
☛ Where is Mecca Masjid located? → Hyderabad, India
☛ When was Mecca Masjid construction started? → 1617
☛ When was Mecca Masjid completed? → 1694
☛ What is special about bricks used in Mecca Masjid? → Made from soil brought from Mecca

q: Construction of the Qutub Minar, the world’s tallest brick minaret commenced in 1193, under the orders of ______ the founder of the Delhi Sultanate.
A. Firoz Shah Tughlaq.
B. Qutub-ud-din Aibak.
C. Iltutmish.
D. Quli Qutub Shah.
qs.e: The construction of the Qutub Minar, the world's tallest brick minaret, began in 1193 under the orders of Qutub-ud-din Aibak, the founder of the Delhi Sultanate. The minaret stands at a height of about 73 meters. Its design was inspired by the Minaret of Jam in Afghanistan. Aibak only built the first storey, and later Iltutmish added three more storeys. In 1368, Firoz Shah Tughlaq repaired the minaret and added a dome and fifth storey. The Qutub Minar is located in Delhi and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
qs.kf:
☛ Who founded the Delhi Sultanate? → Qutub-ud-din Aibak (Slave Dynasty)
☛ What is the height of Qutub Minar? → 73 meters
☛ Who completed the construction of Qutub Minar? → Iltutmish
☛ Who added the fifth storey to Qutub Minar? → Firoz Shah Tughlaq
☛ Where is Qutub Minar located? → Delhi

q: Who among the following ended the Kakatiya dynasty rule?
qs.e: The Kakatiya dynasty ruled in southern India from the 12th to the 14th century with its capital at Warangal. The last ruler was Prataparudra II. The Delhi Sultanate under Alauddin Khilji attacked Kakatiya territories in 1303 and 1310. Later, Muhammad bin Tughlaq launched a decisive invasion in 1323 AD, which ended the Kakatiya dynasty. Thus, the Delhi Sultanate was responsible for ending Kakatiya rule.
qs.kf:
☛ Capital of Kakatiya dynasty → Warangal
☛ Last ruler of Kakatiya dynasty → Prataparudra II
☛ Delhi Sultan who ended Kakatiya dynasty → Muhammad bin Tughlaq (1323 AD)
☛ Founder of Kakatiya dynasty → Prola Raja (father of Ganapati Deva) around 1083 AD
☛ Major ruler of Kakatiya dynasty → Ganapati Deva (1199-1262 AD)

q: Which ruler wanted to build the Alai Minar near the Qutub Minar, but could not complete it?
qs.e: Ala-ud-Din Khilji planned to build a minar twice the height of the Qutub Minar, known as the Alai Minar. It is located to the north of the Qutub Minar. However, after his death, the construction remained incomplete. The Alai Minar stands at a height of about 24.5 meters, far less than the intended height. It is made of red sandstone and is an important example of the architecture of the Delhi Sultanate. Ala-ud-Din Khilji belonged to the Khilji dynasty and is known for his empire expansion and administrative reforms.
qs.kf:
☛ Who started the construction of Alai Minar? → Ala-ud-Din Khilji
☛ Where is the Alai Minar located? → Near Qutub Minar, Delhi
☛ What material is the Alai Minar made of? → Red sandstone
☛ Which dynasty did Ala-ud-Din Khilji belong to? → Khilji dynasty
☛ What is the height of Alai Minar? → About 24.5 meters

q: Who established Sera-i-Adl, an exclusive market in Delhi for manufactured and exported goods to be sold at prices fixed by administration?
qs.e: Alauddin Khalji established Sera-i-Adl, an exclusive market in Delhi for manufactured and exported goods to be sold at prices fixed by the administration. During his reign (1296-1316 CE), Alauddin implemented a price control system regulating the prices of grain, cloth, and other commodities. Sera-i-Adl was part of this policy, where merchants sold goods at predetermined rates. The market aimed to regulate trade and ensure consumers got goods at fair prices. Other options like Muhammad bin Tughlaq, Shershah Suri, and Qutbuddin Mubarak Shah did not establish such a market system.
qs.kf:
☛ Who introduced price control in the Delhi Sultanate? → Alauddin Khalji
☛ Who established Sera-i-Adl? → Alauddin Khalji
☛ What was Alauddin Khalji's market control department called? → Diwan-i-Riyasat
☛ What was the reign period of Alauddin Khalji? → 1296-1316 CE
☛ Under which system did Alauddin fix prices? → Price control system

q: During which period did the Sultanate ruler, Ghiyas-ud-din Balban, take over and rule the throne of Delhi?
qs.e: Ghiyas-ud-din Balban was a powerful ruler of the Delhi Sultanate. Originally a slave purchased by Iltutmish, Balban ascended the throne of Delhi in 1266 AD and ruled until 1287 AD. He is known for eliminating the influence of the 'Chalisa' group, implementing irrigation projects, and the policy of 'Bando-basti'. He also repelled Mongol invasions and strengthened the borders of the Sultanate. Balban adopted the title of 'Zill-e-Ilahi' (Shadow of God). During his reign, the central administration was strengthened, and royal dignity was emphasized. He is also famous for his strict justice under the policy of 'blood and iron'. Balban's rule marked the consolidation of the Delhi Sultanate after the initial slave dynasty rulers.
qs.kf:
☛ What title did Balban adopt? → Zill-e-Ilahi (Shadow of God)
☛ What was Balban's original name? → Baha-ud-din
☛ Which group did Balban eliminate? → Chalisa (Group of forty nobles)
☛ What policy did Balban follow? → Policy of Bando-basti (settlement)
☛ Who was the chief poet in Balban's court? → Amir Khusrau

q: Ibn Battuta, a famous Moroccan traveller visited India during the time of:
qs.e: The famous Moroccan traveler Ibn Battuta visited India in the 14th century. He documented his travels in the book 'Rihla'. He arrived in Delhi during the reign of Muhammad bin Tughlaq and was appointed as a Qazi (judge). The Tughlaq dynasty was part of the Delhi Sultanate. Ibn Battuta provided detailed accounts of India's social, cultural, and administrative life. He also traveled to China and recorded his journeys.
qs.kf:
☛ Book by Ibn Battuta → Rihla
☛ Ibn Battuta visited India under → Muhammad bin Tughlaq
☛ Ibn Battuta's country of origin → Morocco
☛ Last dynasty of Delhi Sultanate → Lodi dynasty
☛ Establishment of Delhi Sultanate → 1206 AD (Qutb-ud-din Aibak)

q: Who founded the Bahmani kingdom?
qs.e: The Bahmani kingdom was founded by Alauddin Bahman Shah, also known as Hasan Gangu, in 1347 AD. He was a rebel chief under the Delhi Sultanate ruler Muhammad bin Tughlaq. After a rebellion in the Deccan, he declared an independent state. The capital of the Bahmani kingdom was Gulbarga (Ahsanabad). This kingdom lasted for about 200 years and later split into five states. Alauddin Bahman Shah implemented administrative reforms and promoted cultural development.
qs.kf:
☛ Who founded the Bahmani kingdom? → Alauddin Bahman Shah (Hasan Gangu)
☛ What was the capital of the Bahmani kingdom? → Gulbarga (Ahsanabad)
☛ Who was the last ruler of the Bahmani kingdom? → Kalimullah Shah
☛ When was the Bahmani kingdom established? → 1347 AD
☛ What was Hasan Gangu's full name? → Alauddin Bahman Shah

q: Who completed the construction of the Qutub Minar?
qs.e: The construction of Qutub Minar was started by Qutub-ud-Din Aibak and completed by Iltutmish. Later, Firoz Shah Tuglak carried out repairs and rebuilt the top stories in 1368 AD. The height of the minar is 72.5 meters and it is located in the Mehrauli area of Delhi. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Firoz Shah Tuglak constructed the fourth and fifth storeys.
qs.kf:
☛ What is the height of Qutub Minar? → 72.5 meters
☛ Who started the construction of Qutub Minar? → Qutub-ud-Din Aibak
☛ Who completed the construction of Qutub Minar? → Iltutmish
☛ Who rebuilt the top stories of Qutub Minar? → Firoz Shah Tuglak
☛ Where is Qutub Minar located? → Mehrauli, Delhi

q: Who among the following built the "Adhai din ka Jhopara" at Ajmer?
qs.e: Adhai Din Ka Jhopara is a historic mosque located in Ajmer, Rajasthan. It was built by Qutubuddin Aibak in 1199 AD. The mosque was constructed using the remains of Sanskrit and Jain temples, which were demolished and their materials reused. Its most notable feature is the grand arch and intricate carvings. The name 'Adhai Din Ka Jhopara' originates from the legend that it was built in just two and a half days. It is one of the oldest mosques in India and exemplifies the architecture of the Delhi Sultanate period. Qutubuddin Aibak was the first ruler of the Delhi Sultanate and also initiated the construction of the Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque and the Qutub Minar.
qs.kf:
☛ Who built Adhai Din Ka Jhopara? → Qutubuddin Aibak
☛ Where is Adhai Din Ka Jhopara located? → Ajmer
☛ Qutubuddin Aibak belonged to which dynasty? → Slave Dynasty
☛ Who was the first ruler of Delhi Sultanate? → Qutubuddin Aibak
☛ Which other mosque was built by Qutubuddin Aibak? → Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque

q: Amir Khusrau was born at ________ in Uttar Pradesh.:
qs.e: Amir Khusrau was born in Patiyali, a town in the Etah district of Uttar Pradesh, in 1253 AD. He was a renowned Sufi poet, musician, and scholar associated with the courts of several Delhi Sultanate rulers. He is considered the father of Hindavi literature and made significant contributions to Persian poetry. In music, he is credited with developing the khayal and tarana styles. He was a disciple of the famous Sufi saint Hazrat Nizamuddin Auliya. His major works include 'Tughlaqnama', 'Khazainul Futuh', and 'Kiranus Sadain'.
qs.kf:
☛ By which title was Amir Khusrau honoured? → Tuti-e-Hind
☛ Which musical instrument did Amir Khusrau invent? → Sitar
☛ Which Sufi saint was the teacher of Amir Khusrau? → Hazrat Nizamuddin Auliya
☛ Which is the famous book of Amir Khusrau? → Kiranus Sadain
☛ Which musical styles did Amir Khusrau develop? → Khayal and Tarana

q: Who built the famous city of Jaapnah?
qs.e: The famous city of Jaapnah was built by Muhammad bin Tughluq. He was a prominent Sultan of the Delhi Sultanate who ruled from 1325 to 1351. He attempted to shift his capital from Delhi to Daulatabad. Jaapnah was a walled city located near Delhi. Its purpose was to create a secure and well-organized administrative center. This city served as an important hub during his reign.
qs.kf:
☛ Who built the city of Jaapnah? → Muhammad bin Tughluq
☛ When was Jaapnah city constructed? → 14th century
☛ To which city did Muhammad bin Tughluq shift his capital? → Daulatabad
☛ What was the main purpose of Jaapnah city? → Administrative center
☛ What was the reign period of Muhammad bin Tughluq? → 1325-1351

q: Which of the following popular Sultan of Delhi built the Alai Darwaza?
qs.e: The Alai Darwaza was built by Allauddin Khilji in 1311 AD as the southern gateway of the Quwwat-ul-Islam Mosque in the Qutub Minar complex, Delhi. It is a masterpiece of Indo-Islamic architecture, constructed using red sandstone and featuring a magnificent dome. Allauddin Khilji, a powerful ruler of the Khilji dynasty, commissioned this structure to enhance the mosque's grandeur. The Alai Darwaza is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The other options—Firozshah Tughlaq, Muhammad bin Tughluq, and Balban—were not responsible for its construction; thus, Allauddin Khilji remains the correct answer.
qs.kf:
☛ Builder of Alai Darwaza → Allauddin Khilji
☛ Construction year → 1311 AD
☛ Location → Qutub Minar complex, Delhi
☛ Material used → Red sandstone
☛ Architectural style → Indo-Islamic

q: Which of the following dynasties was the last to rule the Delhi Sultanate of India?
qs.e: The last dynasty to rule the Delhi Sultanate was the Lodi dynasty. It was founded by Bahlul Lodi in 1451 CE. The last ruler of this dynasty was Ibrahim Lodi, who was defeated by Babur in the First Battle of Panipat in 1526 CE. This battle marked the end of the Delhi Sultanate and the beginning of the Mughal Empire. Other dynasties such as the Khilji dynasty (1290-1320), Tughlaq dynasty (1320-1414), and Sayyid dynasty (1414-1451) ruled earlier. Thus, the Lodi dynasty was the fifth and final dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate.
qs.kf:
☛ Founder of Lodi dynasty → Bahlul Lodi
☛ Last ruler of Delhi Sultanate → Ibrahim Lodi
☛ First Battle of Panipat → 1526 CE, Babur vs Ibrahim Lodi
☛ First dynasty of Delhi Sultanate → Slave dynasty
☛ Total dynasties of Delhi Sultanate → 5 (Slave, Khilji, Tughlaq, Sayyid, Lodi)

q: Who became the emperor of Delhi in 1414 AD?
qs.e: In 1414 AD, Khizr Khan became the emperor of Delhi. He was the founder of the Sayyid dynasty, which took power after the decline of the Tughlaq dynasty. Khizr Khan was appointed as the governor of Delhi by Timur and ruled from 1414 to 1421 AD. He did not claim the title of Sultan but styled himself as a representative of Timur's descendants. His reign marked the beginning of the Sayyid dynasty, though his empire was limited and he faced several rebellions. He was succeeded by his son Mubarak Shah after his death.
qs.kf:
☛ Who founded the Sayyid dynasty? → Khizr Khan
☛ Who appointed Khizr Khan as governor of Delhi? → Timur
☛ How long did Khizr Khan rule? → 1414 to 1421 AD
☛ Which dynasty of Delhi Sultanate lasted the shortest period? → Sayyid dynasty
☛ Who was the last ruler of the Tughlaq dynasty? → Nasir-ud-din Mahmud

q: Who was the last ruler of the Sayyid dynasty?
qs.e: The Sayyid dynasty was the fourth dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate, ruling from 1414 to 1451 CE. The founder was Khizr Khan, a former governor of Timur. He was succeeded by Mubarak Shah and then Muhammad Shah. The last ruler was Alauddin Alam Shah (1445-1451 CE), during whose reign the power of the Sayyid dynasty declined. He was an incompetent and weak ruler, which led to Bahlol Lodi capturing Delhi in 1451 CE and establishing the Lodi dynasty. Alauddin Alam Shah abdicated without a fight and retired to Badaun. Thus ended the Sayyid dynasty.
qs.kf:
☛ Founder of Sayyid dynasty → Khizr Khan
☛ Last ruler of Sayyid dynasty → Alauddin Alam Shah
☛ Period of Sayyid dynasty → 1414-1451 CE
☛ Who ended the Sayyid dynasty → Bahlol Lodi
☛ Where was Alauddin Alam Shah exiled → Badaun

q: Who was the ruler of Delhi when Babur invaded?
qs.e: Babur invaded India in 1526 AD. At that time, the ruler of Delhi was Ibrahim Lodi, the last Sultan of the Lodi dynasty. The First Battle of Panipat was fought between Babur and Ibrahim Lodi on April 21, 1526, in which Ibrahim Lodi was defeated and killed. Babur used the Tughluma war tactic in this battle. Ibrahim Lodi was unpopular due to his harsh rule and poor treatment of nobles, which led to officials like Daulat Khan Lodi inviting Babur to invade. This battle marked the beginning of the Mughal Empire in India.
qs.kf:
☛ When did the First Battle of Panipat take place? → 1526 AD
☛ Ibrahim Lodi belonged to which dynasty? → Lodi dynasty
☛ Which war tactic did Babur use? → Tughluma
☛ Who founded the Lodi dynasty? → Bahlol Lodi
☛ Which empire did Babur establish in India? → Mughal Empire

q: According to Ibn Battuta, a Moroccan traveller to India during the Delhi Sultanate, the method of postal system in which the royal horses were used to transfer packages, is called:
qs.e: According to Ibn Battuta's travelogue 'Rihla', the postal system of the Delhi Sultanate was called 'Uluq'. It primarily used royal horses for transferring packages and messages. Relay stations were established at regular intervals (a few miles apart) where fresh horses were kept ready, enabling rapid communication. Foot runners were also employed alongside. This system ensured swift delivery of official correspondence and parcels, playing a vital role in maintaining administrative control over the vast empire. It was an efficient network that connected the sultanate's key regions, facilitating quick decision-making and surveillance.
qs.kf:
☛ Name of the postal system in Delhi Sultanate → Uluq
☛ Main mode of transport in Uluq → Royal horses
☛ Ibn Battuta's travelogue → Rihla
☛ Primary purpose of Uluq → Quick message and parcel delivery
☛ Location of relay stations in Uluq → Every few miles

q: Which of the following was a military division during the reign of Alauddin Khalji?
qs.e: Alauddin Khalji introduced military reforms and established Diwan-e-Arz as the military department during his reign. This department was responsible for recruitment, salary, and discipline of the army. It also introduced the branding of horses to prevent corruption. Other options: Diwan-e-Insha (correspondence), Diwan-e-Wizarat (finance), and Diwan-e-Risalat (religious affairs) were non-military departments.
qs.kf:
☛ Military department under Alauddin Khalji → Diwan-e-Arz
☛ Finance department under Alauddin Khalji → Diwan-e-Wizarat
☛ Founder of Khalji dynasty → Jalaluddin Khalji
☛ Purpose of horse branding under Alauddin Khalji → Prevent corruption
☛ Function of Diwan-e-Arz → Army management

q: Which department of the Delhi Sultanate was responsible for military organisation and administration of the empire’s army?
qs.e: In the Delhi Sultanate, the Diwan-i-Arz was the military department responsible for the organisation, recruitment, salary, and administration of the army. Its head was called Ariz-i-Mumalik. The Sultanate had seven main departments: Diwan-i-Wizarat (revenue), Diwan-i-Insha (correspondence), Diwan-i-Risalat (religious affairs), Diwan-i-Qaza (justice), Diwan-i-Arz (army), Diwan-i-Bandagan (slaves), and Diwan-i-Khairat (charity). This department became more active during the reigns of Alauddin Khalji and Muhammad bin Tughlaq.
qs.kf:
☛ Head of Diwan-i-Arz → Ariz-i-Mumalik
☛ Function of Diwan-i-Insha → Royal correspondence
☛ Function of Diwan-i-Risalat → Religious affairs
☛ Function of Diwan-i-Qaza → Justice administration
☛ Function of Diwan-i-Wizarat → Revenue management

q: Which department, headed by Dabir-i-Khas, handled royal correspondence and official communication during the Delhi Sultanate?
qs.e: During the Delhi Sultanate, the Diwan-i-Insha department handled royal correspondence and official communication. The head of this department was called Dabir-i-Khas, who was responsible for drafting state letters, treaties, and royal orders. This department played a crucial role in administrative communication and record-keeping. The Dabir-i-Khas held a highly trusted position close to the Sultan. Other options include Diwan-i-Riyasat (revenue department), Diwan-i-Arz (military department), and Barid-i-Mumalik (intelligence department).
qs.kf:
☛ Department of royal correspondence → Diwan-i-Insha
☛ Head of Diwan-i-Insha → Dabir-i-Khas
☛ Military department → Diwan-i-Arz
☛ Intelligence department → Barid-i-Mumalik
☛ Revenue department → Diwan-i-Riyasat

q: Market control under Alauddin Khilji aimed mainly to ________.
o: check price inflation for army provisions
qs.e: Alauddin Khilji (1296-1316 AD) implemented a market control system to maintain his large army and extensive conquests. The primary objective was to stabilize prices of essential commodities, especially food grains, so that soldiers could afford basic goods despite low salaries. This helped check inflation and allowed the administration to control military expenditure. Alauddin divided Delhi's markets into four categories and appointed officers to fix prices. Prices of grains, cloth, horses, weapons, etc., were regulated. The system was enforced through strict punishments, with dishonest traders facing severe penalties. This market control was crucial for sustaining his military campaigns and maintaining political stability.
qs.kf:
☛ When did Alauddin Khilji start market control? → Around 1296 AD
☛ Who was the chief officer for price regulation? → Shahna-i-Mandi
☛ Which commodity's price was most strictly controlled? → Food grains
☛ How many main markets were there in Delhi under Alauddin? → Four
☛ What was the main aim of market control? → Ensure cheap goods for the army

q: Which Delhi Sultan captured Bukka and Harihara after the fall of the Kakatiya Kingdom?
qs.e: After the fall of the Kakatiya Kingdom, Bukka and Harihara were captured by Muhammad bin Tughlaq. These two brothers served under the Kakatiya ruler and later founded the Vijayanagara Empire. Muhammad bin Tughlaq was a powerful Sultan of the Delhi Sultanate, who ruled from 1325 to 1351. He pursued an expansionist policy in South India and annexed Kakatiya territories. Bukka and Harihara were taken captive and forced to convert to Islam, but they later escaped and succeeded in establishing the Vijayanagara Empire. This event is significant in Indian history as it laid the foundation for a major Hindu empire in the South.
qs.kf:
☛ Who were the founders of the Vijayanagara Empire? → Harihara and Bukka
☛ What was the reign period of Muhammad bin Tughlaq? → 1325-1351 CE
☛ What was the capital of the Kakatiya Kingdom? → Warangal
☛ Who captured Bukka and Harihara? → Muhammad bin Tughlaq
☛ When was the Vijayanagara Empire founded? → 1336 CE

q: Who among the following Delhi sultans accidentally died during a game of polo in the year 1210?
qs.e: The founder of the Delhi Sultanate, Qutbuddin Aibak (1206–1210), died in 1210 in Lahore after falling from his horse while playing polo (chowgan). He was the first ruler of the Slave Dynasty and originally a slave of Muhammad Ghori. He constructed the Quwwat-ul-Islam Mosque in Delhi and the Adhai Din Ka Jhonpra in Ajmer. He was also known as Lakhbaksh (giver of lakhs). After his death, his son Aram Shah briefly succeeded him but was soon deposed by Iltutmish.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Delhi sultan died while playing polo? → Qutbuddin Aibak
☛ To which dynasty did Qutbuddin Aibak belong? → Slave Dynasty
☛ What was the title of Qutbuddin Aibak? → Lakhbaksh
☛ Which mosque was built by Qutbuddin Aibak? → Quwwat-ul-Islam Mosque
☛ Where did Qutbuddin Aibak die? → Lahore

q: Alauddin Khilji introduced the Dagh and Huliyah systems to control the army. What was Huliyah associated with?
qs.e: Alauddin Khilji (r. 1296–1316 AD) introduced the Dagh and Huliyah systems to strengthen the army and prevent corruption. The Dagh system involved branding horses to ensure their identity during battle. The Huliyah system recorded the physical description of each soldier (e.g., height, complexion, marks) to prevent the enlistment of fake or mercenary soldiers. This system helped maintain the quality and discipline of the army. Alauddin also replaced land grants with cash payments directly from the treasury to ensure loyalty and reduce corruption. The Dagh and Huliyah systems were pioneering reforms in medieval Indian military administration.
qs.kf:
☛ What was the Dagh system associated with? → Horse branding
☛ What was recorded under the Huliyah system? → Soldier's physical description
☛ How were soldiers paid during Alauddin Khilji's reign? → In cash
☛ Who was the market control officer under Alauddin Khilji? → Diwan-i-Riyasat
☛ How did Alauddin assess land revenue? → Based on actual produce

q: Who headed the Diwan-i-Arz and was responsible for managing soldiers, branding horses, and administering war provisions?
qs.e: In the administrative system of the Delhi Sultanate, the head of the Diwan-i-Arz was called Ariz-i-Mumalik. This department was responsible for military affairs, including recruitment, salary, and discipline of soldiers. The Diwan-i-Arz also managed the branding of horses (dagh) and the muster roll (talika) of soldiers. During wars, it handled weapons, logistics, and food supply. The Ariz-i-Mumalik was accountable directly to the Sultan and played a crucial role in maintaining the army's strength. This position was highly prestigious in the Sultanate period.
qs.kf:
☛ Head of Diwan-i-Wazarat → Wazir
☛ Head of Diwan-i-Risalat → Dabir-i-Khas
☛ Head of Diwan-i-Insha → Dabir-i-Mumalik
☛ Head of Diwan-i-Qaza → Qazi-ul-Quzat
☛ Head of Diwan-i-Istifa → Mustaufi-i-Mumalik

q: Who among the following Delhi Sultans controlled the prices of food; horses, ponies, cattle and slaves; cloth and fruit; and articles for domestic consumption and personal use?
qs.e: Alauddin Khalji (r. 1296-1316 CE) implemented a rigorous price control system in his empire. He fixed the prices of food, horses, ponies, cattle, slaves, cloth, fruit, and articles for domestic consumption. This policy aimed to provide cheap supplies to his army and curb inflation. To monitor prices, he appointed officials like Diwan-i-Riyasat (market department) and Shahna-i-Mandi (market superintendent). He also registered merchants and imposed strict penalties for violations. This was a unique experiment in price regulation during the Delhi Sultanate.
qs.kf:
☛ Department related to Alauddin Khalji's market control → Diwan-i-Riyasat
☛ When was Alauddin Khalji's coronation? → 1296 CE
☛ Which tax did Alauddin abolish? → Zakat
☛ Main objective of Alauddin's price control policy → To ensure army supplies
☛ Which famous gate was built by Alauddin Khalji? → Alai Darwaza

q: Which king of Bengal was defeated by Bakhtiyar Khilji in the 13th century?
A. Mahipal
B. Lakshmanasen
C. Shashank
D. Grihavarman
qs.e: Bakhtiyar Khilji was a Turkish general who invaded Bengal in the early 13th century. In 1204 AD, he defeated Lakshmanasen, the last ruler of the Sena dynasty, and established Turkish rule in Bengal. This event marked the beginning of Muslim rule in Bengal. The Sena dynasty was a Hindu dynasty that ruled Bengal and Bihar.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was defeated by Bakhtiyar Khilji? → Lakshmanasen
☛ Lakshmanasen belonged to which dynasty? → Sena dynasty
☛ Which river was crossed by Bakhtiyar Khilji to attack Nalanda? → Ganges (Actually, Nalanda's destruction occurred around 1197-1200 AD)
☛ What was the original name of Bakhtiyar Khilji? → Muhammad Bakhtiyar Khilji
☛ After Bakhtiyar Khilji, which dynasty ruled Bengal? → Khilji dynasty (part of Delhi Sultanate)

q: Which emperor shifted his capital from Delhi to Daulatabad?
qs.e: Muhammad Bin Tughlaq (1325-1351) shifted his capital from Delhi to Daulatabad (Devagiri). The main reasons were to better control the Deccan region and to protect the capital from Mongol invasions. He ordered the entire population of Delhi to move to Daulatabad, causing immense suffering and loss of life. The plan failed, and he later had to move the capital back to Delhi. This decision is considered one of his most controversial policies.
qs.kf:
☛ Who shifted the capital from Delhi to Daulatabad? → Muhammad Bin Tughlaq
☛ What was the ancient name of Daulatabad? → Devagiri
☛ Under which plan did Muhammad Bin Tughlaq shift the capital? → Daulatabad Scheme
☛ What was the reign period of Muhammad Bin Tughlaq? → 1325-1351 CE
☛ Who founded the Tughlaq dynasty? → Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq

q: Haidar Ali was the ruler of:
qs.e: Haidar Ali was the ruler of Mysore. He ascended the throne of Mysore in 1761 and built a powerful army. With the help of the French, he modernized his army and fought several wars against the British. Under his rule, Mysore emerged as a major power in South India. After Haidar Ali, his son Tipu Sultan became the ruler of Mysore, known as the 'Tiger of Mysore'. Both Haidar Ali and Tipu Sultan fiercely resisted British expansion in India.
qs.kf:
☛ Which kingdom did Haidar Ali rule? → Mysore
☛ Who was Haidar Ali's successor? → Tipu Sultan
☛ Which European power assisted Haidar Ali? → French
☛ What is Tipu Sultan popularly known as? → Tiger of Mysore
☛ When did Haidar Ali ascend the throne? → 1761

q: Who died while playing chaugan?
qs.e: Qutubuddin Aibak was the first ruler of the Delhi Sultanate, reigning from 1206 to 1210. Originally a slave, he became a general under Muhammad Ghori. Aibak died in 1210 after falling from a horse while playing Chaugan (polo). Chaugan is an ancient horseback sport popular in Central Asia. Aibak is known for constructing the Quwwat-ul-Islam Mosque in Delhi and the Adhai Din Ka Jhonpra in Ajmer. His tomb is located in Lahore. He was also called 'Lakh Baksh' (giver of lakhs) due to his generosity. His sudden death led to a succession crisis in the Delhi Sultanate.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the first ruler of the Delhi Sultanate? → Qutubuddin Aibak
☛ Where is the tomb of Qutubuddin Aibak located? → Lahore
☛ Qutubuddin Aibak was known by which title? → Lakh Baksh
☛ What is the ancient name of the game Polo? → Chaugan
☛ Who built the Quwwat-ul-Islam Mosque? → Qutubuddin Aibak

q: In the fourteenth century India who used token currency of cheap metals in place of regular currencies of gold and silver?
qs.e: In the fourteenth century, Muhammad Bin Tughlaq introduced token currency made of cheap metals like copper and brass to replace gold and silver coins. This decision was taken due to economic crisis, but the experiment failed because the government could not ensure the real value of token currencies. People devalued these coins and started forging them. This failure caused huge losses to the treasury, and ultimately the token currency had to be withdrawn. Muhammad Bin Tughlaq was an educated and visionary ruler, but some of his policies, such as tax increase in the Doab region and transfer of capital, were also controversial.
qs.kf:
☛ Who introduced token currency? → Muhammad Bin Tughlaq
☛ Which metals were used in token currency? → Copper and brass
☛ What was the result of token currency? → Economic failure and loss
☛ What was Muhammad Bin Tughlaq's original name? → Jauna Khan
☛ In which region did Muhammad Bin Tughlaq increase taxes? → Doab

q: The Iqta system was introduced by _____ in Delhi sultanate in institutional form.
qs.e: The Iqta system was institutionalized in the Delhi Sultanate by Iltutmish. It was a land revenue system where military officers and officials were assigned land (iqta) in lieu of salary. The holders, called iqtadars or muqtis, collected taxes and remitted the surplus to the central treasury after meeting their expenses. Iltutmish formalized this system to strengthen administration and ensure regular revenue. Later, Balban and Alauddin Khalji introduced reforms. The iqta system became the backbone of the Sultanate's economy and governance, helping maintain a large army without heavy cash expenditure.
qs.kf:
☛ Who institutionalized the Iqta system? → Iltutmish
☛ What were Iqta holders called? → Iqtadars or Muqtis
☛ Which rulers reformed the Iqta system? → Balban and Alauddin Khalji
☛ Which sultan first introduced Iqta informally? → Qutb-ud-din Aibak
☛ What was the main purpose of the Iqta system? → Paying soldiers through land revenue

q: Ibn-Battuta was born in _________.
qs.e: Ibn-Battuta was a famous Muslim traveler and geographer, born in 1304 AD in Tangier, Morocco. He is best known for his travelogue 'Rihla', which describes his journeys across Africa, Asia, and Europe. He visited India during the reign of Muhammad bin Tughlaq and served as a judge in the Delhi Sultanate. Ibn-Battuta is considered one of the greatest travelers of the 14th century.
qs.kf:
☛ Birthplace of Ibn-Battuta → Morocco
☛ Famous book by Ibn-Battuta → Rihla
☛ Which Indian ruler did he serve under? → Muhammad bin Tughlaq
☛ Birth year of Ibn-Battuta → 1304 AD
☛ Profession of Ibn-Battuta → Traveler and geographer

q: During Delhi Sultanate period who brought capital back from Lahore to Delhi?
qs.e: During the early Delhi Sultanate period, Qutbuddin Aibak had shifted the capital to Lahore. Later, Iltutmish (r. 1211–1236 AD) brought the capital back to Delhi. Iltutmish is regarded as the real founder of the Delhi Sultanate. He moved the capital to Delhi to avoid Mongol invasions and to centralize the empire. Iltutmish formed the Chalisa (Turkan-e-Chihalgani), a military group, and introduced coins like Tanka (silver) and Jital (copper). He was the third Mamluk ruler, and his reign is known for expansion and consolidation of the Sultanate.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the first ruler of Delhi Sultanate? → Qutbuddin Aibak
☛ Which currency was introduced by Iltutmish? → Tanka (silver) and Jital (copper)
☛ Who formed the Chalisa group? → Iltutmish
☛ Who shifted the capital of Delhi Sultanate from Lahore to Delhi? → Iltutmish
☛ Where is the tomb of Iltutmish located? → Delhi

q: In which of the following years was the battle of Bannihatti fought?
qs.e: The Battle of Bannihatti was fought in 1565 CE. It is considered part of the Battle of Talikota, also known as the Battle of Rakshasi-Tangadi. This war was fought between the Vijayanagara Empire and the Deccan Sultanates. The Vijayanagara Empire suffered a decisive defeat in this battle, which became a major factor in the decline of the empire. The Battle of Bannihatti was fought in present-day Karnataka. It was the result of a joint campaign by the Deccan Sultanates against the Vijayanagara Empire.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Battle of Bannihatti fought? → 1565
☛ Between whom was the Battle of Bannihatti fought? → Vijayanagara Empire and Deccan Sultanates
☛ What is the other name of this battle? → Battle of Talikota or Battle of Rakshasi-Tangadi
☛ Who was the last ruler of Vijayanagara Empire? → Sadashiva Raya
☛ Which sultanate led the Talikota war? → Ahmadnagar Sultanate

q: Delhi Sultanate signifies the rule over India with capital as Delhi, of which community?
qs.e: The Delhi Sultanate (1206-1526) was established by rulers of Turkish origin. It was founded by Qutb-ud-din Aibak, a Turkish slave. The sultanate included the Slave, Khilji, Tughlaq, Sayyid, and Lodi dynasties, most of whom had Turkish or Turko-Afghan roots. These rulers came from Central Asia and are known for spreading Islam and introducing administrative systems. The Delhi Sultanate brought Turkish culture, architecture, and military techniques to India.
qs.kf:
☛ Founder of Delhi Sultanate → Qutb-ud-din Aibak (Turkish)
☛ Last dynasty of Delhi Sultanate → Lodi dynasty (Turko-Afghan)
☛ Capital of Delhi Sultanate → Delhi (initially Lahore also)
☛ Period of Delhi Sultanate → 1206 to 1526 CE
☛ Main religion brought by Turkish rulers → Islam

q: Which of the following Sultans of Delhi adopted the policy of Blood and Iron?
qs.e: The policy of 'Blood and Iron' was adopted by Ghiyasuddin Balban during the Delhi Sultanate. He was a stern ruler who emphasized the use of force to secure the empire's frontiers and suppress rebellions. Balban followed this policy to counter Mongol invasions and maintain law and order in the kingdom. His reign lasted from 1266 to 1287 CE, and he was a slave of Iltutmish. Balban introduced practices such as 'Sijda' and 'Pabos' to enhance the dignity of the king. He strengthened the royal army and built forts near Delhi. Thus, Balban's policy protected the Delhi Sultanate from internal and external threats.
qs.kf:
☛ Which ruler of the Delhi Sultanate is known for the 'Blood and Iron' policy? → Ghiyasuddin Balban
☛ What practices did Balban introduce to enhance royal dignity? → Sijda and Pabos
☛ What was the reign period of Ghiyasuddin Balban? → 1266-1287 CE
☛ Balban was the slave of which Sultan? → Iltutmish
☛ To counter which invasion did Balban adopt the 'Blood and Iron' policy? → Mongol invasions

q: The first Turkish ruler who introduced pure Arabic coins in India was ________________.
qs.e: Iltutmish, the third ruler of the Delhi Sultanate, was the first Turkish ruler to introduce pure Arabic coins in India. He issued the silver tanka and the copper jital. The tanka weighed 175 grains and remained in use until the Mughal period. Before him, Qutubuddin Aibak had founded the Sultanate but did not reform the coinage. Iltutmish also claimed to be the representative of the Caliph and inscribed Arabic legends on his coins. This monetary reform strengthened trade and administration.
qs.kf:
☛ Which coins did Iltutmish introduce? → Silver tanka and copper jital
☛ What was the weight of the tanka? → 175 grains
☛ Who was the first ruler of the Delhi Sultanate? → Qutubuddin Aibak
☛ Iltutmish belonged to which dynasty? → Slave dynasty
☛ From which Caliph did Iltutmish seek recognition? → Caliph of Baghdad

q: Who among the following established the Khalji dynasty?
qs.e: The Khalji dynasty was founded by Jalaluddin Khalji in 1290 AD. He was the first Khalji ruler of the Delhi Sultanate. He seized power by defeating Shamsuddin Kayumars, the last ruler of the Slave dynasty. Jalaluddin was known for his liberal policies and religious tolerance. During his reign, he faced Mongol invasions. Later, his nephew and son-in-law Alauddin Khalji assassinated him and took over the throne. The Khalji dynasty ruled from 1290 to 1320 AD and played a crucial role in expanding the Delhi Sultanate.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the founder of the Khalji dynasty? → Jalaluddin Khalji
☛ Which dynasty did Jalaluddin Khalji overthrow? → Slave dynasty
☛ When did Alauddin Khalji assassinate Jalaluddin? → 1296 AD
☛ Who was the last ruler of the Khalji dynasty? → Mubarak Shah Khalji
☛ What was the period of the Khalji dynasty in Delhi Sultanate? → 1290-1320 AD

q: Bhanudeva II, the ruler of Jajnagar in Orissa helped Rai Rudra Dev of Warangal in his battle against ____________, the Sultan of Delhi.
qs.e: Bhanudeva II was the ruler of Jajnagar in Orissa (Eastern Ganga dynasty). He helped Rai Rudra Dev (Prataparudra II), the Kakatiya ruler of Warangal, in his battle against Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq, the Sultan of Delhi. Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq (1320-1325 AD) was the founder of the Tughlaq dynasty and pursued an expansionist policy in South India. In 1323 AD, he invaded Warangal, leading Rai Rudra Dev to seek military aid from Bhanudeva II. This event highlights the conflict between the Delhi Sultanate and southern kingdoms. Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq conquered Warangal, ending the Kakatiya dynasty.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the founder of the Tughlaq dynasty? → Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq
☛ What was the reign period of Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq? → 1320-1325 AD
☛ Which Kakatiya ruler was defeated by Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq? → Prataparudra II (Rai Rudra Dev)
☛ What was the capital of the Eastern Ganga dynasty? → Jajnagar (Orissa)
☛ How did Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq die? → Collapse of a pavilion built by his son Muhammad bin Tughlaq

q: Qutb ud-Din Aibak was fond of which of the following outdoor sports?
qs.e: Qutb ud-Din Aibak was the first ruler of the Delhi Sultanate and the founder of the Slave Dynasty. He was also known as 'Lakh Baksh' for his generosity. Aibak was especially fond of the outdoor sport of Polo (also called Chaugan). Polo is an equestrian sport where players on horseback strike a ball with long-handled mallets. This sport originated in Central Asia and was popular among Turkic rulers. Aibak was seriously injured when he fell from his horse while playing polo, and later died from his injuries. Thus, polo was his favorite outdoor sport, which also led to his death.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the first ruler of the Delhi Sultanate? → Qutb ud-Din Aibak
☛ Who founded the Slave Dynasty? → Qutb ud-Din Aibak
☛ What was Qutb ud-Din Aibak's nickname? → Lakh Baksh
☛ What is another name for Polo? → Chaugan
☛ How did Qutb ud-Din Aibak die? → Fell from horse while playing polo

q: In 1309, who invaded the Kakatiya kingdom?
qs.e: In 1309, Malik Kafur, the general of Sultan Alauddin Khalji of the Delhi Sultanate, invaded the Kakatiya kingdom in southern India. This campaign was part of Alauddin's southern conquests. Malik Kafur defeated the Kakatiya king Prataparudra II and forced him to accept the suzerainty of the Delhi Sultanate. The invasion caused heavy losses to the Kakatiyas, who had to surrender their treasure and elephants to Alauddin. This event marked the beginning of the decline of the Kakatiya empire, which was later completely annexed by Muhammad bin Tughlaq in 1323.
qs.kf:
☛ What was the capital of the Kakatiya kingdom? → Warangal
☛ Which Sultan did Kakatiya king Prataparudra II pay tribute to? → Alauddin Khalji
☛ In which year did Malik Kafur invade Devagiri? → 1307
☛ What was Malik Kafur's nickname? → Hazar Dinari
☛ Who was the founder of the Kakatiya dynasty? → Beta Raja I

q: Who was considered as the viceroy of Muhammad Ghori and overall commander of the army in India?
qs.e: After his conquests in India, Muhammad Ghori appointed Qutbuddin Aibak as his viceroy and overall commander of the army in India. Aibak was a capable military leader who laid the foundation of Ghori's Indian empire. After Ghori's death, Aibak founded the Slave Dynasty and became the first Sultan of Delhi. His original name was Qutbuddin, and he was originally a slave purchased and trained by Ghori. He started the construction of the Qutub Minar in Mehrauli. Aibak ruled from 1206 to 1210.
qs.kf:
☛ First ruler of Delhi Sultanate → Qutbuddin Aibak
☛ Who started the construction of Qutub Minar → Qutbuddin Aibak
☛ Founder of the Slave Dynasty → Qutbuddin Aibak
☛ Viceroy of Muhammad Ghori → Qutbuddin Aibak
☛ Death of Qutbuddin Aibak → 1210 AD while playing polo

q: Who among the following was the successor of Sultan Iltutmish in Delhi Sultanate?
qs.e: Sultan Iltutmish (r. 1211-1236 CE) of the Delhi Sultanate appointed his daughter Raziya as his successor during his lifetime, preferring her over his sons due to her competence. After Iltutmish's death in 1236 CE, Raziya ascended the throne and became the first and only female ruler of the Delhi Sultanate, ruling until 1240 CE. The other options are incorrect: Alauddin Khilji was a ruler of the Khilji dynasty (late 13th century), Feroz Tughlaq belonged to the Tughlaq dynasty (14th century), and Alptekin was a Ghaznavid general. Thus, Raziya is the correct successor.
qs.kf:
☛ Daughter of Iltutmish → Raziya
☛ First female ruler of Delhi Sultanate → Raziya
☛ Reign of Raziya → 1236-1240 CE
☛ When did Iltutmish appoint Raziya as successor? → Around 1231 CE
☛ Who defeated Raziya? → Bahram Shah
