This post was equivalent to the finance minister and its duties included revenue collection, expenditure control, and implementing financial policies. Akbar reformed the revenue system under the Dahsala system, which involved land survey and tax assessment based on crops. The notable officer who held this position was Todar Mal, who played a key role in revenue reforms. Among other options, Vakil was the prime minister, Subadar was the provincial governor, and Mir Bakhshi headed the military department. Hence, Diwan-i-Kul was the correct authority for financial oversight.
qs.kf:
☛ Which post was the central finance minister? → Diwan-i-Kul
☛ Who was associated with revenue reforms? → Todar Mal
☛ Who introduced the Dahsala system? → Akbar
☛ What was the role of Subadar? → Provincial administration
☛ Which department did Mir Bakhshi head? → Military

q: Who among the following officials was responsible for maintaining law and order in a village during Sher Shah’s administration?
qs.e: In Sher Shah Suri's administration, the official responsible for maintaining law and order at the village level was the Muqaddam. The Muqaddam was the village headman who handled revenue collection, security, and dispute resolution. Among the other options, Qazi was a judicial officer, Shiqqdar was a district administrator, and Fotedar was a treasurer. Sher Shah introduced efficient administrative reforms including land revenue system, postal system, and road construction. The Muqaddam played a crucial role in rural administration and was empowered to maintain peace and order in the village.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the village headman? → Muqaddam
☛ Who was the revenue officer? → Fotedar
☛ Who was the district administrator? → Shiqqdar
☛ Who was the judicial officer? → Qazi
☛ Which famous road was built by Sher Shah? → Grand Trunk Road

q: Sher Shah divided his empire into shiqqs, equivalent to which administrative division under the Mughals?
qs.e: Sher Shah Suri divided his empire into administrative units called shiqqs. This division was equivalent to the Sarkar under the Mughals. Sher Shah's administrative system served as a model for the Mughals. He divided his empire into subas (provinces), which were further divided into shiqqs, and then into parganas. The Mughal emperor Akbar adopted this system, dividing subas into sarkars and then into parganas. Thus, Sher Shah's shiqq corresponded to the Mughal sarkar.
qs.kf:
☛ Sher Shah's shiqq was equivalent to which Mughal unit? → Sarkar
☛ What were the administrative units under Sher Shah? → Suba, Shiqq, Pargana
☛ What was the head of a Mughal sarkar called? → Faujdar
☛ Sher Shah's silver coin was called? → Rupaya
☛ Which animal did Sher Shah use for his postal system? → Horse

q: When were Bahadur Shah Zafar and his wife Begum Zinat Mahal sent to prison in Rangoon?
qs.e: After the failure of the 1857 revolt, the last Mughal emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar was captured by the British. He was tried for sedition and convicted. As punishment, the emperor and his wife Begum Zinat Mahal were exiled to Rangoon (modern-day Yangon, Myanmar) in October 1858. This exile was intended to prevent them from leading any further rebellion. Bahadur Shah Zafar died in Rangoon in 1862, marking the end of the Mughal Empire. Begum Zinat Mahal also lived there until her death. This event is a significant turning point in Indian history.
qs.kf:
☛ When was Bahadur Shah Zafar exiled? → October 1858
☛ Where was Bahadur Shah Zafar exiled? → Rangoon
☛ When did Bahadur Shah Zafar die? → 1862
☛ Bahadur Shah Zafar was the last Mughal emperor. → True
☛ Bahadur Shah Zafar was charged with? → Sedition

q: During Shahjahan’s rule, how many mansabdars out of 8000 were higher ranking mansabdars who received 61.5% of the total estimated revenue of the empire as salaries for themselves and their troopers?
qs.e: Under the Mughal Mansabdari system, officers were classified based on their rank (zat) and number of soldiers (sawar). During Shahjahan's rule (1628-1658), there were a total of 8000 mansabdars, out of which only 445 were higher ranking mansabdars (i.e., zat 500 and above). These 445 mansabdars received 61.5% of the total estimated revenue of the empire as salaries for themselves and their troopers. This figure highlights the unequal distribution of income in the Mughal administration, where the bulk of the revenue went to top officials. The remaining 7555 lower ranking mansabdars received only 38.5% of the revenue.
qs.kf:
☛ What were zat and sawar in the Mughal Mansabdari system? → Zat indicated rank and sawar indicated number of soldiers
☛ How many total mansabdars were there during Shahjahan's reign? → 8000
☛ How many higher ranking mansabdars were there? → 445
☛ What percentage of revenue did higher ranking mansabdars receive? → 61.5%
☛ Which system caused unequal distribution of revenue in the Mughal period? → Mansabdari system

q: Abu’l Fazl was the court historian of which of the following rulers?
qs.e: Abu'l Fazl was the court historian of the Mughal emperor Akbar. He was one of the Navaratnas (nine gems) of Akbar's court. He authored the famous work Akbarnama, which is a detailed history of Akbar's reign. The third volume of this work is Ain-i-Akbari, which provides administrative, cultural, and social information. Abu'l Fazl was also considered a close advisor of Akbar. Later, he was assassinated on the orders of Salim (Jahangir).
qs.kf:
☛ Which text was written by Abu'l Fazl? → Akbarnama
☛ What is the third volume of Akbarnama called? → Ain-i-Akbari
☛ Which Mughal emperor included Abu'l Fazl among his Navaratnas? → Akbar
☛ Who ordered the assassination of Abu'l Fazl? → Jahangir (Salim)
☛ Which is the main source for Akbar's reign? → Akbarnama

q: Babur, the first Mughal ruler, was related to two of the medieval world's greatest conquerors. If he was related to the Mongol conqueror Genghis Khan on his maternal side, to whom was he related on his paternal side?
qs.e: Babur was the founder of the Mughal dynasty. On his maternal side, his mother Qutlugh Nigar Khanum was the daughter of Yunus Khan, a Mongol ruler descended from Genghis Khan, making Babur a descendant of Genghis Khan. On his paternal side, Babur was related to Timur (Timur Lang), as his father Umar Sheikh Mirza was a great-grandson of Timur. Timur was a Turco-Mongol conqueror who founded the Timurid Empire in 1370 CE. Babur established the Mughal Empire in India after defeating Ibrahim Lodi in the First Battle of Panipat in 1526 CE. Thus, Babur was a descendant of two of the greatest medieval conquerors: Genghis Khan and Timur, giving him a strong lineage and legacy.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the founder of the Mughal Empire? → Babur
☛ To whom was Babur related on his maternal side? → Genghis Khan
☛ To whom was Babur related on his paternal side? → Timur
☛ When was the Timurid Empire founded? → 1370 CE
☛ When was the First Battle of Panipat fought? → 1526 CE

q: Which foreign ruler invaded India in 1739, leading to the massacre of Delhi and further weakening the Mughal Empire?
qs.e: Nadir Shah was the ruler of Persia (Iran) who invaded India in 1739. He defeated the Mughal emperor Muhammad Shah at the Battle of Karnal and entered Delhi. After a rebellion in Delhi, Nadir Shah ordered a brutal massacre that killed about 30,000 people. He looted the Peacock Throne and the Kohinoor diamond and took them to Persia. This invasion severely weakened the Mughal Empire, paving the way for further foreign invasions and the eventual decline of Mughal rule in India.
qs.kf:
☛ Persian ruler who invaded India in 1739 → Nadir Shah
☛ Mughal emperor during Nadir Shah's invasion → Muhammad Shah
☛ Famous diamond taken from India by Nadir Shah → Kohinoor
☛ Battle where Nadir Shah defeated the Mughals → Battle of Karnal
☛ Famous throne looted by Nadir Shah from Delhi → Peacock Throne

q: The Buland Darwaza at Fatehpur Sikri was erected by Akbar to celebrate his conquest of ______.
qs.e: The Buland Darwaza is a massive gateway located in Fatehpur Sikri, built by the Mughal emperor Akbar in 1601 AD to commemorate his victory over Gujarat. It is the highest gateway in the world with a height of 54 meters. The structure is made of red sandstone and includes white marble inlays. A Persian inscription on the door quotes a saying of Jesus. The Buland Darwaza is an outstanding example of Mughal architecture and has been declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
qs.kf:
☛ Who built the Buland Darwaza? → Akbar
☛ Where is Buland Darwaza located? → Fatehpur Sikri
☛ Buland Darwaza was built to commemorate which victory? → Gujarat victory
☛ What is the height of Buland Darwaza? → 54 meters
☛ Buland Darwaza is made of which stone? → Red sandstone

q: Who founded the city of Agra?
qs.e: The city of Agra was founded by Sikander Lodhi in 1504 AD. He was the second ruler of the Lodhi dynasty. Sikander Lodhi made Agra his capital and developed it as an important administrative and cultural center. After the First Battle of Panipat (1526), Mughal emperor Babur captured Agra. Later, Mughal emperor Akbar built the Agra Fort (Red Fort) here. Sikander Lodhi also conquered the Bihar region. He died in Agra in 1517 AD.
qs.kf:
☛ Who founded Agra? → Sikander Lodhi (1504 AD)
☛ Who founded the Lodhi dynasty? → Bahlol Lodhi
☛ When was the First Battle of Panipat fought? → 1526 AD
☛ Who built the Agra Fort? → Akbar
☛ Where did Sikander Lodhi die? → Agra

q: Who was the last Mughal emperor of India?
qs.e: The last Mughal emperor of India was Bahadur Shah II (1837-1857). He was the 20th and final ruler of the Mughal dynasty. After the Indian Rebellion of 1857, the British deposed him and exiled him to Rangoon (now Yangon, Myanmar), where he died in 1862. During his reign, the Mughal Empire had become nominal, with real power held by the British East India Company. Bahadur Shah II was also a poet and a Sufi saint, writing poetry in Urdu and Persian. His defeat marked the formal end of the Mughal Empire, leading to the direct rule of the British Crown in India.
qs.kf:
☛ Last Mughal Emperor → Bahadur Shah II
☛ Exile Location → Rangoon (Myanmar)
☛ Reign Period → 1837-1857
☛ Father → Akbar Shah II
☛ Death → 1862, Rangoon

q: In which year was the East India Company granted 'Diwani rights' (right to collect revenues and decide civil cases of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa) by Mughals?
qs.e: In 1765, the Mughal emperor Shah Alam II granted the East India Company the Diwani of Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa. This right allowed the Company to collect revenues and adjudicate civil cases. The grant formalized under the Treaty of Allahabad, negotiated by Robert Clive. This event marked a turning point, giving the Company a stable revenue base and political dominance in India. The Diwani rights effectively made the Company the de facto ruler of these provinces.
qs.kf:
☛ Mughal emperor who granted Diwani → Shah Alam II
☛ Governor at the time of Treaty of Allahabad → Robert Clive
☛ Regions covered under Diwani rights → Bengal, Bihar, Orissa
☛ Meaning of Diwani → Revenue collection and civil justice
☛ Year of Diwani grant → 1765

q: Who took away the Peacock Throne from India?
qs.e: India's famous Peacock Throne was built by Mughal emperor Shah Jahan. It was taken away by Nadir Shah, the ruler of Persia (Iran), when he invaded India in 1739 CE. Nadir Shah defeated Mughal emperor Muhammad Shah Rangeela in the Battle of Karnal and captured Delhi. He took the Peacock Throne, the Kohinoor diamond, and other treasures to Persia. The throne was known for two peacocks with a large diamond between them. No original version of the Peacock Throne exists today. Nadir Shah was assassinated by his own soldiers in 1747 CE. After his death, the Peacock Throne disappeared.
qs.kf:
☛ Who built the Peacock Throne in India? → Shah Jahan
☛ Battle of Karnal was fought between whom? → Nadir Shah and Muhammad Shah Rangeela
☛ When did Nadir Shah invade India? → 1739 CE
☛ What is the world's largest cut diamond? → Kohinoor
☛ Nadir Shah was the ruler of which country? → Iran (Persia)

q: The historical Grand Trunk road was developed by many rulers. What was it called during the reign of the Mauryas?
qs.e: The historical Grand Trunk Road was called Uttarpath during the Mauryan period. This road was a major trade and military route in ancient India, connecting the eastern and western parts. The Mauryan rulers Chandragupta Maurya and Ashoka developed and maintained this route. 'Uttarpath' means northern path. Later, Sher Shah Suri renamed it 'Badshahi Sadak', and the British called it Grand Trunk Road. 'Rajpath' and 'Poorvipath' are names of other ancient routes. During the Mauryan era, this route ran from Pataliputra to Taxila.
qs.kf:
☛ What was the Grand Trunk Road called during the Mauryan period? → Uttarpath
☛ Which ruler reconstructed the Grand Trunk Road? → Sher Shah Suri
☛ What was the road built by Sher Shah Suri called? → Badshahi Sadak
☛ What is the approximate length of the Grand Trunk Road? → 2400 km
☛ Which countries does the Grand Trunk Road pass through? → India, Pakistan, Bangladesh

q: Takht-e-Akbari, Platform on which Akbar was crowned as emperor lies in State of ________
qs.e: Takht-e-Akbari is the platform where Akbar was crowned as emperor in 1556 at the young age of 13. This historical site is located in Punjab state, specifically in Gurdaspur district at a place called Kalanur. Akbar ascended the throne of Delhi after the death of his father Humayun, but his coronation took place in Kalanur because the Mughal Empire was in crisis at that time and he was in the Punjab region. His regent Bairam Khan proclaimed Akbar as emperor on this occasion. This site holds great significance in Mughal history as it marks the beginning of Akbar's reign, who later became one of the greatest rulers of India.
qs.kf:
☛ Where was Akbar crowned? → Kalanur, Punjab
☛ What was Akbar's age at coronation? → 13 years
☛ Who was Akbar's regent? → Bairam Khan
☛ When did Akbar's reign begin? → 1556 CE
☛ In which state is Takht-e-Akbari located? → Punjab

q: The Battle of Chausa between Humayun and Sher Shah Suri was fought in the year:
qs.e: The Battle of Chausa between Humayun and Sher Shah Suri was fought in 1539 CE. This battle took place at Chausa in Bihar, on the banks of the Ganges river. In this battle, Sher Shah Suri decisively defeated Humayun, forcing him to jump into the Ganges to save his life. According to a story, a boatman saved him, and Humayun granted him a promise in return. This battle strengthened Sher Shah Suri's power and weakened the Mughal Empire. Later, in 1540, Sher Shah Suri again defeated Humayun at the Battle of Kannauj. The Battle of Chausa is a significant event in Indian history.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Battle of Chausa fought? → 1539
☛ Who defeated Humayun at Chausa? → Sher Shah Suri
☛ Where was the Battle of Chausa fought? → On the banks of Ganges in Bihar
☛ When was the Battle of Kannauj fought? → 1540
☛ Who were the famous painters in Humayun's court? → Mir Sayyid Ali and Abdus Samad

q: The battle of Haldighati was fought in:
qs.e: The Battle of Haldighati was fought on 18 June 1576. It was fought between Maharana Pratap and the Mughal army of Emperor Akbar. The Mughal forces were led by Man Singh. This battle is historically significant as it symbolizes the struggle between Rajput pride and Mughal expansionism. Although the Mughals claimed victory, Maharana Pratap escaped and continued guerrilla warfare. Haldighati is located in the Rajsamand district of Rajasthan.
qs.kf:
☛ Date of Battle of Haldighati → 18 June 1576
☛ Mughal commander in the battle → Man Singh
☛ Location of Haldighati → Rajsamand, Rajasthan
☛ Name of Maharana Pratap's horse → Chetak
☛ Famous elephant used in the battle → Elephant of Madari Miyan

q: Tulughama is a:
o: water conservation method used by Akbar
punishment given to criminals by Jahangir
qs.e: Tulughama was a famous military strategy used by Babur during his battles in India. It was a type of enclosure formation where the army was protected by forming a circular structure using horses and bullock carts. The purpose was to defend the soldiers from enemy arrows and attacks. Babur successfully employed this strategy in the First Battle of Panipat (1526) against Ibrahim Lodi. This strategy was based on Central Asian warfare and involved effective use of artillery. Tulughama reflects Babur's military expertise and strategic acumen.
qs.kf:
☛ In which battle was Tulughama used? → First Battle of Panipat
☛ From where did Babur learn Tulughama? → Central Asia
☛ What is the meaning of Tulughama? → Enclosure or circular defense formation
☛ Who was Babur's opponent in the First Battle of Panipat? → Ibrahim Lodi
☛ Which new weapon did Babur use in Tulughama? → Artillery

q: Who among the following was one of the finest calligraphers at Akbar's court, who was honoured with the title 'Zarrin Qalam' (golden pen)?
qs.e: Muhammad Husayn was one of the finest calligraphers at Akbar's court, honored with the title 'Zarrin Qalam' (golden pen). He was a master of the Nastaliq script, a prominent style of Persian calligraphy. During Akbar's reign, art and culture flourished, and calligraphy received special patronage. Husayn worked on several important manuscripts, including the 'Razmnama' (the Persian translation of the Mahabharata). His work is noted for its beauty and precision. Abul Fazal was a historian, while Daswant and Basawan were painters.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was called 'Zarrin Qalam' in Akbar's court? → Muhammad Husayn
☛ Which calligraphic style was Muhammad Husayn expert in? → Nastaliq
☛ On which famous manuscript did Muhammad Husayn work at Akbar's court? → Razmnama
☛ Who were the leading painters in Akbar's court? → Daswant and Basawan
☛ Who was the chief historian at Akbar's court? → Abul Fazal

q: What is the real name of Babur?
qs.e: Babur's real name was Zahir-ud-din Muhammad. He was the founder of the Mughal Empire in India and defeated Ibrahim Lodi in the First Battle of Panipat in 1526. Born in 1483 in Fergana (present-day Uzbekistan), he was a descendant of Timur and Genghis Khan. He wrote his autobiography Baburnama in Turkish. Babur was a skilled military leader and poet. He died in 1530 in Agra.
qs.kf:
☛ Original name of Babur → Zahir-ud-din Muhammad
☛ Founder of Mughal Empire → Babur
☛ Autobiography written by Babur → Baburnama
☛ First Battle of Panipat → 1526, Babur vs Ibrahim Lodi
☛ Babur's death → 1530 CE in Agra

q: In 1717, which Mughal emperor issued an inspection to the East India Company?
qs.e: In 1717, Mughal emperor Farrukhshiyar issued a famous firman to the East India Company. Under this decree, the company was granted trade concessions and inspection rights in Bengal, Hyderabad, and Gujarat. Additionally, the company was allowed to inspect goods at Masulipatnam, Kasimbazar, Patna, and other places. Farrukhshiyar ruled as Mughal emperor from 1713 to 1719, and during his reign, the decline of the Mughal Empire began. This firman was a major political and economic success for the East India Company, paving the way for the expansion of British power in India.
qs.kf:
☛ Reign of Farrukhshiyar → 1713 to 1719
☛ Emperor who issued the 1717 firman → Farrukhshiyar
☛ When did the East India Company get inspection rights → 1717
☛ Successor of Farrukhshiyar → Muhammad Shah
☛ Dynasty of Farrukhshiyar → Timurid dynasty

q: Which ruler has created Taj Mahal?
qs.e: The Taj Mahal was built by Mughal Emperor Shah Jahan in memory of his wife Mumtaz Mahal. This monument is located in Agra, Uttar Pradesh, and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Its construction started in 1632 and was completed in 1653. The chief architect was Ustad Ahmad Lahauri. The Taj Mahal is made of white marble and is considered a masterpiece of Mughal architecture.
qs.kf:
☛ Where is the Taj Mahal located? → Agra, Uttar Pradesh
☛ In which year was the Taj Mahal completed? → 1653
☛ Who was the chief architect of the Taj Mahal? → Ustad Ahmad Lahauri
☛ In which year was the Taj Mahal declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site? → 1983
☛ For whom did Shah Jahan build the Taj Mahal? → Mumtaz Mahal

q: Babur assumed the title of Ghazi after the success of-
qs.e: After defeating the Rajput confederation led by Rana Sanga at the Battle of Khanwa in 1527, Babur assumed the title of 'Ghazi'. This title, meaning a warrior fighting for Islam, was used by Babur to legitimize his campaigns against the Hindu rulers and to boost the morale of his troops. The Battle of Khanwa was crucial as it consolidated Babur's power in North India after his initial victory at Panipat. By calling himself a Ghazi, Babur aimed to present his conquest as a holy war, thus gaining support from his followers. This title also helped him in distinguishing his rule from previous Turkic and Afghan rulers.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Battle of Khanwa fought? → 1527
☛ Who led the Rajputs against Babur at Khanwa? → Rana Sanga
☛ After which battle did Babur assume the title Ghazi? → Battle of Khanwa
☛ What is another name for the Battle of Khanwa? → Battle of Bayana
☛ How many major battles did Babur fight in India? → Four (Panipat, Khanwa, Chanderi, Ghaghra)

q: Which Mughal emperor was also known as Salim?
qs.e: The Mughal emperor Jahangir was born in 1569 and was named Salim. He was the son of Akbar. Salim ascended the throne in 1605 and took the title Jahangir (Conqueror of the World). His reign lasted from 1605 to 1627. He was a patron of arts and Mughal painting flourished during his time. His wife Nur Jahan had a strong influence on state affairs.
qs.kf:
☛ Birth name of Jahangir → Salim
☛ Father of Jahangir → Akbar
☛ Wife of Jahangir → Nur Jahan
☛ Reign of Jahangir → 1605-1627
☛ Meaning of Jahangir's title → Conqueror of the World

q: Who among the following Mughal Prince allied with Malik Ambar and revolted against his father?
qs.e: Mughal Prince Shah Jahan revolted against his father Jahangir in 1623 AD. In this revolt, he allied with Malik Ambar, the powerful commander of the Deccan. Malik Ambar was the vizier of the Nizam Shahi Sultanate of Ahmednagar and was famous for his military prowess and guerrilla warfare tactics. Shah Jahan aimed to dethrone his father, but the rebellion failed, and he had to seek forgiveness. Later, after Jahangir's death in 1627, Shah Jahan became the Mughal emperor.
qs.kf:
☛ Which sultanate was Malik Ambar the vizier of? → Nizam Shahi Sultanate (Ahmednagar)
☛ When did Shah Jahan revolt? → 1623 AD
☛ Who was Shah Jahan's father? → Jahangir
☛ What warfare technique was Malik Ambar known for? → Guerrilla warfare
☛ When did Shah Jahan become Mughal emperor? → 1627 AD

q: Which of the following was the original name of Sher Shah Suri, the founder of Suri dynasty?
qs.e: Sher Shah Suri, who founded the Suri dynasty in 1540 AD, was originally named Farid Khan. He was an Afghan ruler who defeated the Mughal emperor Humayun and captured Delhi. Sher Shah implemented significant administrative and revenue reforms, such as introducing the rupee (silver coin) and building roads, most notably the Grand Trunk Road. He used jarib for land measurement and strengthened the agricultural system. His governance model was later adopted by Akbar.
qs.kf:
☛ Founder of Suri dynasty → Sher Shah Suri
☛ Original name of Sher Shah → Farid Khan
☛ Title of Sher Shah → Sher Khan (later Sher Shah)
☛ Coin introduced by Sher Shah → Rupee
☛ Road built by Sher Shah → Grand Trunk Road (GT Road)

q: Who among the following was appointed as the Governor of Chitor after Akbar invaded it in 1567?
qs.e: In 1567, Mughal Emperor Akbar attacked Chittor, the capital of Mewar ruled by Rana Udai Singh II. After a long siege and capture of the fort, Akbar appointed Asaf Khan as the Governor of Chittor. Asaf Khan was a relative of Bairam Khan and a prominent noble in Akbar's administration. The Mughal army was led by Akbar himself, while the defense of Chittor was bravely led by Jaimal Rathore and Patta Sisodia. The capture of Chittor strengthened Mughal control over Rajputana.
qs.kf:
☛ Year of Akbar's invasion of Chittor → 1567
☛ Ruler of Mewar during the attack → Rana Udai Singh II
☛ Rajput commanders who defended Chittor → Jaimal Rathore and Patta Sisodia
☛ First Mughal Governor of Chittor → Asaf Khan
☛ Title assumed by Akbar after Chittor victory → Ghazi

q: Under the reign of which of the following Mughal Emperors did Bahadur Shah attack Chittor?
qs.e: Bahadur Shah (Sultan of Gujarat) attacked Chittor in 1535 during the reign of the Mughal Emperor Humayun. Humayun (1530-1540 and 1555-1556) was the second ruler of the Mughal Empire. At that time, Chittor was under the rule of Rana Sangram Singh (Rana Sanga), who sought help against Bahadur Shah's invasion. Although Humayun did not directly attack Chittor, the invasion occurred during his reign. Later, Humayun defeated Bahadur Shah and annexed Gujarat. This event is part of the Mughal-Rajput conflicts. Thus, the correct answer is Humayun because Bahadur Shah's attack on Chittor took place while Humayun was the Mughal emperor.
qs.kf:
☛ When did Bahadur Shah attack Chittor? → 1535 CE
☛ What was Humayun's reign period? → 1530-1540 and 1555-1556
☛ Which kingdom did Bahadur Shah rule? → Gujarat
☛ Who was the ruler of Chittor? → Rana Sangram Singh (Rana Sanga)
☛ Which Mughal emperor was Humayun? → Second

q: In the 15th century, Babur made the game ______ popular in India.
A. Golf
B. Polo
C. Kabaddi
D. Karate
qs.e: Babur, the founder of the Mughal Empire, popularized the game of Polo in India during the 15th century. Polo is an equestrian sport where players use long-handled mallets to hit a ball into the opponent's goal. Babur was very fond of Polo and introduced it to the Mughal court. The game originated in Central Asia and spread to the Indian subcontinent under his rule. Golf, Kabaddi, and Karate have no connection with Babur.
qs.kf:
☛ What was the ancient name of Polo? → Chaugan
☛ What is the name of Babur's autobiography? → Baburnama
☛ When was the Mughal Empire established in India? → 1526 (First Battle of Panipat)
☛ Which game is called the King of Sports? → Polo
☛ In which battle did Babur defeat Ibrahim Lodi? → First Battle of Panipat

q: Which of the following is not a historical monument in Fatehpur Sikri?
A. Buland Darwaza
B. Ibadat Khana
C. Gol Gumbaj
D. Panch Mahal
qs.e: Gol Gumbaj is not a historical monument in Fatehpur Sikri; it is located in Bijapur (Karnataka) and is the mausoleum of Muhammad Adil Shah. Fatehpur Sikri houses Buland Darwaza, Ibadat Khana, and Panch Mahal. Buland Darwaza is a victory gate, Ibadat Khana was a hall for religious discussions, and Panch Mahal is a five-story palace. Thus, Gol Gumbaj is the correct answer.
qs.kf:
☛ Who founded Fatehpur Sikri? → Akbar
☛ Why was Buland Darwaza built? → To commemorate the victory over Gujarat (1573)
☛ What is the architectural style of Panch Mahal? → Mixed Hindu-Islamic
☛ Where is Gol Gumbaj located? → Bijapur, Karnataka
☛ What type of dome does Gol Gumbaj have? → Second largest in the world

q: Which Mughal emperor's original name was Zahir-ud-Din Muhammad?
qs.e: The founder of the Mughal Empire, Babur, was originally named Zahir-ud-Din Muhammad. He was born in 1483 in the Fergana Valley and was a descendant of Timur and Genghis Khan. Babur established the Mughal Empire in India after defeating Ibrahim Lodi at the First Battle of Panipat in 1526. He wrote his autobiography, the Baburnama, in the Turkish language, which was later translated into Persian. His reign lasted from 1526 to 1530, and he died in Agra.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the founder of the Mughal dynasty? → Babur
☛ What was Babur's original name? → Zahir-ud-Din Muhammad
☛ Which dynasty did Babur belong to? → Timurid and Mongol
☛ When was the First Battle of Panipat fought? → 1526
☛ In which language was the Baburnama written? → Turkish

q: In which year was the Second battle of Panipat fought between Akbar and Hemu?
qs.e: The Second Battle of Panipat was fought on 5 November 1556 between Akbar and Hemu. Hemu, also known as Hemchandra Vikramaditya, had captured Delhi and Agra. Akbar's army was led by Bairam Khan. During the battle, Hemu was wounded, captured, and later executed. This victory strengthened Akbar's Mughal Empire and ended Hemu's rule. The battle was a turning point in Mughal history, consolidating Akbar's authority in North India.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Second Battle of Panipat fought? → 1556
☛ Between whom was the Second Battle of Panipat fought? → Akbar and Hemu
☛ What was Hemu's full name? → Hemchandra Vikramaditya
☛ Who led Akbar's army in the Second Battle of Panipat? → Bairam Khan
☛ What was the result of the Second Battle of Panipat? → Akbar's victory and Hemu's death

q: Which of the following monuments is NOT located in Delhi?
qs.e: Buland Darwaza is not located in Delhi; it is situated in Fatehpur Sikri (Uttar Pradesh). It was built by Mughal Emperor Akbar in 1601 AD to commemorate his victory over Gujarat. It is the tallest gateway in the world (54 meters). The other monuments are located in Delhi: Humayun's Tomb (early example of Mughal architecture), India Gate (memorial for World War I soldiers), and Alai Darwaza (located in the Qutub Minar complex, built by Alauddin Khalji).
qs.kf:
☛ Where is Buland Darwaza located? → Fatehpur Sikri, Uttar Pradesh
☛ Who built Buland Darwaza? → Akbar
☛ Who built Humayun's Tomb? → Haji Begum (Akbar's wife)
☛ Who designed India Gate? → Edwin Lutyens
☛ Alai Darwaza is built in which style? → Indo-Islamic style

q: Humayun-Nama was written by _____
qs.e: The Humayun-Nama is a historical work that describes the life of Humayun, the second Mughal emperor. It was written by Gulbadan Begum, the daughter of Babur and sister of Humayun. The book is written in Persian and provides a first-hand account of events during Humayun's reign. Gulbadan Begum was a learned woman who composed this text at the request of Akbar, Humayun's son. The Humayun-Nama is a key source for understanding Mughal history.
qs.kf:
☛ Who wrote the Humayun-Nama? → Gulbadan Begum
☛ Whose daughter was Gulbadan Begum? → Babur
☛ In which language was the Humayun-Nama written? → Persian
☛ Whose life is described in the Humayun-Nama? → Humayun
☛ Gulbadan Begum was related to which rulers? → Babur and Humayun

q: Who was the revenue minister of Emperor Akbar?
qs.e: During Emperor Akbar's reign, Raja Todar Mal served as the Revenue Minister. He was one of the Navaratnas (nine gems) of Akbar's court. Todar Mal reformed the revenue system based on land surveys. His famous system, the Dahsala System (or Todar Mal Bandobast), fixed revenue according to crop yield and prices. This system was implemented across the Mughal Empire and later adopted by the British administration. Todar Mal appointed officers like Kanungo (revenue record keeper) and Patwari (village accountant) to ensure proper collection. His reforms strengthened the economic foundation of the Mughal Empire.
qs.kf:
☛ Base of Mughal revenue system → Dahsala System (Todar Mal Bandobast)
☛ Department of Akbar's Navaratna Raja Todar Mal → Revenue Minister
☛ Types of land under Dahsala System → Polaj, Parati, Banjar, Chachar
☛ Birthplace of Raja Todar Mal → Lahore, Punjab
☛ Famous Hindu noble in Akbar's court → Raja Todar Mal

q: In which city is the tomb of Emperor Akbar situated?
qs.e: The tomb of Emperor Akbar is located in Agra, Uttar Pradesh, at a place called Sikandra, a suburb of Agra. Akbar himself started the construction of this tomb during his lifetime, and it was completed by his son Jahangir between 1605 and 1613. The tomb is an excellent example of Mughal architecture, using red sandstone and marble. It is surrounded by a vast garden laid out in the Charbagh style. The tomb is included in the tentative list of UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
qs.kf:
☛ Where is Akbar's tomb located? → Agra (Sikandra)
☛ Who completed the construction of Akbar's tomb? → Jahangir
☛ Which stones are used in Akbar's tomb? → Red sandstone and marble
☛ What is the garden style of Akbar's tomb? → Charbagh
☛ Akbar's tomb is an example of which architecture? → Mughal architecture

q: In which year "Ibadat - Khana (House of Worship) was erected by Akbar?
qs.e: Akbar built the Ibadat Khana (House of Worship) in 1575 at Fatehpur Sikri. It was a place for religious discussions where scholars from different faiths were invited to debate. Akbar was known for his religious tolerance and he invited representatives from Hinduism, Islam, Christianity, Jainism, Zoroastrianism and other religions. The discussions held here influenced Akbar's religious views and later led to the idea of Din-i-Ilahi, a syncretic religion. The Ibadat Khana is an important symbol of religious dialogue and tolerance during the Mughal period.
qs.kf:
☛ Builder of Ibadat Khana → Akbar
☛ Year of construction → 1575
☛ Location → Fatehpur Sikri
☛ Purpose → Religious discussions
☛ Outcome → Idea of Din-i-Ilahi

q: Who was the next successor of the Mughal Empire after Aurangzeb?
qs.e: After Aurangzeb's death in 1707, the next ruler of the Mughal Empire was Bahadur Shah I. His real name was Shah Alam and he was the son of Aurangzeb. He ascended the throne after defeating his brothers in the war of succession. Bahadur Shah I's reign lasted from 1707 to 1712 and is considered a symbol of the decline of the Mughal Empire. During his rule, there were conflicts with the Sikh leader Guru Gobind Singh and wars with the Rajputs. Bahadur Shah I was a liberal and tolerant ruler who maintained good relations with Hindus.
qs.kf:
☛ Who became the Mughal ruler after Aurangzeb? → Bahadur Shah I
☛ What was the real name of Bahadur Shah I? → Shah Alam
☛ What was the reign period of Bahadur Shah I? → 1707-1712
☛ When did Bahadur Shah I die? → 1712
☛ Who was the father of Bahadur Shah I? → Aurangzeb

q: What was the battle of Kannauj fought between?
qs.e: The Battle of Kannauj was fought in 1540 AD between Mughal Emperor Humayun and Sher Shah Suri. It was fought near Bilgram and is also known as the Battle of Bilgram. In this battle, Sher Shah Suri decisively defeated Humayun, forcing him to flee India and take refuge in Iran. This victory led to the establishment of the Suri Dynasty and Sher Shah's rule over North India. The battle marked a major setback for the Mughals, though Humayun later reclaimed his throne in 1555.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Battle of Kannauj fought? → 1540 AD
☛ What is the other name for the Battle of Kannauj? → Battle of Bilgram
☛ Who won the Battle of Kannauj? → Sher Shah Suri
☛ Which dynasty was established by Sher Shah Suri? → Suri Dynasty
☛ Where did Humayun flee after the Battle of Kannauj? → Iran

q: Who was the ruler that Babur defeated in the First Battle of Panipat?
qs.e: The First Battle of Panipat was fought on 21 April 1526 between Babur and Ibrahim Lodi. This battle marked the foundation of the Mughal Empire in India. Babur used artillery and advanced tactics to defeat Ibrahim Lodi's large army. Ibrahim Lodi was killed in the battle, and Babur captured Delhi and Agra, establishing the Mughal dynasty. This battle is notable for Babur's effective use of gunpowder weapons.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the First Battle of Panipat fought? → 1526
☛ Who fought the First Battle of Panipat? → Babur vs Ibrahim Lodi
☛ Who died in the First Battle of Panipat? → Ibrahim Lodi
☛ Which dynasty was founded after the First Battle of Panipat? → Mughal Empire
☛ What new technology did Babur use at Panipat? → Artillery

q: The Grand Trunk Road in Medieval India was built by whom?
qs.e: The Grand Trunk Road (Sadak-e-Azam) is one of the most important roads of medieval India. It was built by Sher Shah Suri between approximately 1540-1545 CE. The road stretched from Bengal (Chittagong) to Punjab (Sohawa). Sher Shah constructed it for trade and administrative convenience. Later, the British expanded it. For the convenience of travelers, the road had sarais (inns), wells, and trees. This road still connects India, Pakistan, and Afghanistan. Sher Shah is known for road construction and administrative reforms. He also introduced the postal system.
qs.kf:
☛ Old name of Grand Trunk Road → Sadak-e-Azam
☛ When was Grand Trunk Road built → 1540-1545 CE
☛ Extent of Grand Trunk Road → Chittagong to Sohawa (Punjab)
☛ Sher Shah's reign → 1540-1545 CE
☛ Another system started by Sher Shah → Postal system

q: Which Mughal ruler started Din - i - Elahi ?
qs.e: Din-i-Ilahi was a religious movement started by Mughal emperor Akbar in 1582 AD. Its aim was to create a syncretic religion incorporating elements from Islam, Hinduism, Christianity, Zoroastrianism, Jainism, and others. Akbar named it 'Tawhid-i-Ilahi' or 'Din-i-Ilahi'. It was not a mass religion; only select courtiers and followers could join. Akbar built the 'Ibadat Khana' at Fatehpur Sikri for religious discussions. Din-i-Ilahi did not survive after Akbar's death.
qs.kf:
☛ Who founded Din-i-Ilahi? → Akbar
☛ When was Din-i-Ilahi established? → 1582 AD
☛ Which building was built by Akbar for religious discussions? → Ibadat Khana
☛ What is the other name of Din-i-Ilahi? → Tawhid-i-Ilahi
☛ Which religion's element was NOT included in Din-i-Ilahi? → Buddhism

q: What does the word 'factory' mean in medieval India?
qs.e: In medieval India, the word 'factory' referred to an imperial workshop, also known as 'karkhana'. These state-run workshops were prominent during the Mughal period, producing a variety of goods such as weapons, textiles, jewelry, and carpets. Managed by the state, they were centers of economic activity. European traders also used the term 'factory' for their trading posts in India. In the Mughal Empire, karkhanas were the main source of production, employing skilled artisans. These workshops supplied items for the royal treasury and also facilitated trade. The term 'factory' thus denoted a place where goods were manufactured under imperial patronage.
qs.kf:
☛ What were imperial workshops called in the Mughal period? → Karkhana
☛ Which Mughal emperor organized the karkhanas? → Akbar
☛ What were European trading centers in India called? → Factory
☛ What was mainly produced in Mughal karkhanas? → Weapons, textiles, jewelry
☛ From which language is the word 'factory' derived? → Latin

q: Who is the founder of the Mughal Empire?
qs.e: The Mughal Empire was founded by Babur in 1526 after defeating Ibrahim Lodi at the First Battle of Panipat. Babur was a descendant of Timur and Genghis Khan. He ruled until 1530. His son Humayun succeeded him. The Mughal Empire is a significant period in Indian history and contributed greatly to architecture, art, and culture.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the founder of the Mughal Empire? → Babur
☛ In which year did the First Battle of Panipat take place? → 1526
☛ Name of Babur's father? → Umar Sheikh Mirza
☛ Name of Babur's autobiography? → Baburnama
☛ Which dynasty did Babur belong to? → Timurid

q: Around which year did the construction of Taj Mahal Complex begin
qs.e: The Taj Mahal was built by Mughal Emperor Shah Jahan in memory of his wife Mumtaz Mahal. Construction began in 1632 AD and was completed in 1653 AD, taking about 22 years. The chief architect was Ustad Ahmad Lahauri. The Taj Mahal is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and is considered one of the Seven Wonders of the World.
qs.kf:
☛ Who built the Taj Mahal? → Shah Jahan
☛ Who was the chief architect of Taj Mahal? → Ustad Ahmad Lahauri
☛ On which river is the Taj Mahal located? → Yamuna River
☛ In which year did Taj Mahal become a UNESCO World Heritage Site? → 1983
☛ In which city is the Taj Mahal located? → Agra

q: When was Akbar became the emperor?
qs.e: Akbar was born in 1542 AD. He became the emperor in 1556 AD at the age of just 13. This event occurred immediately after the death of his father Humayun. Akbar was crowned under the guardianship of Bairam Khan. This was a crucial turning point in the history of the Mughal Empire. After his accession in 1556 AD, he fought the Second Battle of Panipat (1556 AD) against Hemu and defeated him. Akbar ruled for nearly 50 years and expanded his empire significantly.
qs.kf:
☛ When was Akbar born? → 1542 AD
☛ When did Akbar ascend the throne? → 1556 AD
☛ Who was Akbar's regent? → Bairam Khan
☛ When did Akbar fight the Second Battle of Panipat? → 1556 AD
☛ Against whom did Akbar fight the Second Battle of Panipat? → Hemu

q: Arrange the following historical events in their chronological order.
A. Nadir Shah invades Indian and attacks Delhi.
B. The Diwani of Bengal is transferred to the East India Company.
C. Humayun regains lost territories.
D. Ahmad Shah Abdali defeats the Marathas in the third battle of Panipat.
qs.e: The correct chronological order is: Humayun regained lost territories from the Sur Empire in 1555 (C). Then Nadir Shah invaded India and attacked Delhi in 1739 (A). Thereafter, Ahmad Shah Abdali defeated the Marathas in the Third Battle of Panipat in 1761 (D). Finally, the Diwani of Bengal was transferred to the East India Company in 1765 (B). This sequence reflects the decline of the Mughal Empire and the rise of British rule in India.
qs.kf:
☛ Humayun's restoration → occurred in 1555 CE.
☛ Nadir Shah's invasion → attacked Delhi in 1739 CE.
☛ Third Battle of Panipat → fought in 1761 CE.
☛ Diwani of Bengal → granted to British in 1765 CE.
☛ Maratha defeat at Panipat III → by Ahmad Shah Abdali.

q: In which year was the battle of Haldighati fought?
qs.e: The Battle of Haldighati was fought on 18 June 1576 AD. It was fought between Maharana Pratap and the army of Mughal Emperor Akbar. The Mughal army was led by Man Singh. The battle took place at the Haldighati pass near Gogunda in Rajasthan. The Mughals won the battle, but Maharana Pratap escaped and later continued guerrilla warfare. This battle symbolizes the conflict between Rajput valor and Mughal expansionism.
qs.kf:
☛ Date of Haldighati battle → 18 June 1576 AD
☛ Mughal commander → Man Singh
☛ Maharana Pratap's horse name → Chetak
☛ Haldighati located in → Rajasthan (near Gogunda)
☛ Battle result → Mughal victory

q: Tomb of Sher Shah Suri is situated in ________.
qs.e: The tomb of Sher Shah Suri is located in Sasaram, Bihar. It was built in memory of Sher Shah Suri, the founder of the Sur Empire. The construction was completed in 1545 AD. The tomb is situated in the middle of an artificial lake, making it unique. It is an excellent example of Indo-Islamic architecture. Sher Shah Suri also constructed the Grand Trunk Road. The height of the tomb is about 122 feet.
qs.kf:
☛ Tomb of Sher Shah Suri → Sasaram (Bihar)
☛ Reign of Sher Shah Suri → 1540–1545 AD
☛ Road constructed by Sher Shah Suri → Grand Trunk Road
☛ Currency introduced by Sher Shah Suri → Rupee
☛ Real name of Sher Shah Suri → Farid Khan

q: What was Akbar's idea of Sulh-i-kul?
qs.e: Akbar's idea of Sulh-i-kul is based on 'Universal peace'. It means 'peace with all' or 'absolute peace'. By adopting this principle, Akbar promoted religious tolerance and treated people of all religions equally. He invited scholars from all religions to the Ibadat Khana for discussions and later founded Din-i-Ilahi. The goal of Sulh-i-kul was to maintain communal harmony in the empire. It was the cornerstone of Akbar's religious policy.
qs.kf:
☛ What is the meaning of Sulh-i-kul? → Peace with all
☛ Which religious principle did Akbar adopt? → Sulh-i-kul
☛ Venue for religious discussions in Akbar's court? → Ibadat Khana
☛ Religion founded by Akbar? → Din-i-Ilahi
☛ Reign of Akbar? → 1556-1605

q: Which of the following was NOT built by Shah Jahan?
qs.e: Buland Darwaza, located in Fatehpur Sikri, was built by the Mughal emperor Akbar in 1601 AD to commemorate his victory over Gujarat. It was not constructed by Shah Jahan. Shah Jahan built the Red Fort in Delhi between 1638-1648 AD, the Jama Masjid in Delhi in 1656 AD, and the Shalimar Gardens in Kashmir in 1619 AD (though some sources link it to Akbar or Jahangir, major expansion occurred under Shah Jahan). Buland Darwaza is the highest gateway in the world, with a height of 54 meters. Hence, the correct answer is Buland Darwaza as it was not built by Shah Jahan.
qs.kf:
☛ Who built Buland Darwaza? → Akbar
☛ Where is Buland Darwaza located? → Fatehpur Sikri
☛ Buland Darwaza commemorates which victory? → Gujarat victory
☛ What is the height of Buland Darwaza? → 54 meters
☛ Who built Red Fort and Jama Masjid? → Shah Jahan

q: Who among the following was the ruler of Gujarat when Humayun attacked the kingdom in 1532?
qs.e: In 1532, when Mughal emperor Humayun attacked Gujarat, the ruler of Gujarat was Bahadur Shah. He was a powerful sultan of the Gujarat Sultanate who reigned from 1526 to 1537. Humayun launched this campaign to annex Malwa and Gujarat into the Mughal Empire. Bahadur Shah resisted the Mughal advance and maintained his independence for a period. However, in 1535, Humayun again invaded and captured Mandu and Champaner. Bahadur Shah sought an alliance with the Portuguese to counter the Mughal threat. He was eventually killed in a conflict with the Portuguese in 1537.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the last ruler of Gujarat Sultanate? → Muzaffar Shah III
☛ When did Humayun conquer Gujarat? → 1535 AD
☛ Who founded the Gujarat Sultanate? → Zafar Khan Muzaffar (1407 AD)
☛ How did Bahadur Shah die? → In a conflict with the Portuguese in 1537 AD
☛ With whom did Bahadur Shah ally against the Mughals? → The Portuguese

q: _____was Bairam Khan's son, who became an important person in Akbar's court.
qs.e: Abdul Rahim Khan-i-Khanan was the son of Bairam Khan, Akbar's guardian and commander. He was one of the Navratnas in Akbar's court and a renowned poet and writer. He composed in Hindavi and Persian, and his Rahim's couplets are famous. He was also a skilled general who led Akbar's armies in many battles. His tomb is located in Delhi.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was Bairam Khan the guardian of? → Akbar
☛ Who was the father of Abdul Rahim Khan-i-Khanan? → Bairam Khan
☛ How many Navratnas were in Akbar's court? → 9
☛ What is the language of Rahim's couplets? → Hindavi (Brajbhasha)
☛ Where is Abdul Rahim Khan-i-Khanan's tomb? → Delhi

q: In which of the following cities is the Tomb of Sheikh Salim Chisti located?
qs.e: The Tomb of Sheikh Salim Chisti is located in Fatehpur Sikri, Uttar Pradesh. It was built by Mughal Emperor Akbar in 1571. Sheikh Salim Chisti was a famous Sufi saint who predicted the birth of Akbar's son Jahangir. The tomb is made of white marble and is situated in the courtyard of the Jama Masjid. It was later reconstructed in marble by Jahangir.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Mughal emperor was contemporary of Sheikh Salim Chisti? → Akbar
☛ Who founded Fatehpur Sikri? → Akbar
☛ What material is the Tomb of Sheikh Salim Chisti made of? → White marble
☛ In which state is Fatehpur Sikri located? → Uttar Pradesh
☛ To which Sufi order did Sheikh Salim Chisti belong? → Chishti

q: The famous Jama Masjid was built by which ruler?
qs.e: The famous Jama Masjid in Delhi is one of the largest mosques in India. It was built by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan between 1650 and 1656. The mosque was inaugurated in 1656. It is constructed using red sandstone and marble. The mosque has three large gates, four minarets, and two minars. The main prayer hall has 11 arches. It is a prime example of Mughal architecture.
qs.kf:
☛ Who built Jama Masjid? → Shah Jahan
☛ Where is Jama Masjid located? → Delhi
☛ When was Jama Masjid built? → 1656
☛ Construction material of Jama Masjid? → Red sandstone and marble
☛ Famous monument adjacent to Jama Masjid? → Red Fort

q: The famous composition 'Totinama' was created during the reign of _____________.
qs.e: 'Totinama' (or 'Tuti-nama') is a Persian illustrated manuscript containing 52 miniature paintings. It was created during the reign of the Mughal emperor Akbar. The book is a Persian translation of the Sanskrit text 'Shuka-Saptati' (Seventy Tales of the Parrot), originally written by Ziyauddin Nakhshabi. Akbar's reign was a golden age for Persian literature and miniature painting. The Mughal atelier, under the supervision of masters like Mir Sayyid Ali and Abdus Samad, produced this exquisite work. The 'Totinama' reflects the early Mughal painting style, blending Persian and Indian elements. Akbar established a royal library (Kitabkhana) where many important texts were translated and illustrated, and 'Totinama' is one of the most notable surviving examples from this period.
qs.kf:
☛ During whose reign was 'Totinama' created? → Akbar
☛ In which language was 'Totinama' written? → Persian
☛ What is the original Sanskrit source of 'Totinama'? → Shuka-Saptati
☛ Who wrote 'Shuka-Saptati'? → Ziyauddin Nakhshabi
☛ Who supervised the illustration of 'Totinama' in Akbar's court? → Mir Sayyid Ali and Abdus Samad

q: At which of the following places is the tomb of Sher Shah located?
qs.e: The tomb of Sher Shah Suri is located at Sasaram in Bihar. It was built in 1545 AD. The tomb is situated in the middle of an artificial lake and is considered an excellent example of Indo-Islamic architecture. It was designed by the architect Mir Muhammad Aliwal. The tomb is made of red sandstone and its height is about 101 feet. Sher Shah Suri founded the Suri Empire and ruled Delhi from 1540 to 1545.
qs.kf:

☛ Which empire did Sher Shah Suri establish? → Suri Empire
☛ Who built Sher Shah's tomb? → Mir Muhammad Aliwal
☛ What was Sher Shah Suri's reign period? → 1540-1545 AD
☛ What architectural style is mixed in Sher Shah's tomb? → Indo-Islamic

q: The Mughal empire was founded by -
qs.e: The Mughal Empire was founded by Babur in 1526 after defeating Ibrahim Lodi in the First Battle of Panipat. Babur was a descendant of Timur and Genghis Khan. He established the Mughal dynasty in India, which ruled for nearly 300 years. Babur ruled until his death in 1530. He was succeeded by Humayun, but Babur is regarded as the founder of the empire.

☛ Babur's father → Umar Sheikh Mirza

q: The famous Asphan Jahi dynasty is related to which regional empire?
qs.e: The Asfhan Jahi dynasty ruled the princely state of Hyderabad, founded in 1724 by Mir Qamar-ud-din Khan Siddiqi (Nizam-ul-Mulk). After the decline of the Mughal Empire, this dynasty established independent rule in the Deccan region. The Nizams ruled until Hyderabad's merger with the Indian Union in 1948. The title "Asfhan Jah" was conferred upon Nizam Ali Khan by Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II. The dynasty is known for its significant contributions to Hyderabad's culture and architecture, including iconic structures like the Charminar and Golconda Fort. The Nizams were among the wealthiest rulers in Indian history.
qs.kf:

q: Mahmud Gawan was granted the title of Chief of the Merchants or Malik-ut-Tujjar by __________.
qs.e: Mahmud Gawan was a prominent minister and general of the Bahmani Sultanate. He was granted the title of 'Malik-ut-Tujjar' (Chief of the Merchants) by Humayun Shah, the Bahmani sultan who ruled from 1458 to 1461 AD. Mahmud Gawan played a key role in expanding the empire and reorganizing the army. He led campaigns against the Vijayanagara Empire. After Humayun Shah's death, his son Nizam Shah and later Muhammad Shah became sultans. Mahmud Gawan was later executed during the reign of Muhammad Shah. The title reflects his administrative skills and contributions to trade. This fact is important for understanding the administrative structure of the Bahmani Sultanate.
qs.kf:
☛ Who founded the Bahmani Sultanate? → Alauddin Bahman Shah
☛ Which sultan was Mahmud Gawan a minister of? → Humayun Shah

☛ What was the reign of Humayun Shah? → 1458-1461 AD
☛ Who executed Mahmud Gawan? → Muhammad Shah

q: Which ruler regained his lost kingdom by 1555 after defeating Sher Shah Suri's successors, thereby marking the end of the Second Afghan Empire?
qs.e: Humayun was the second Mughal emperor who lost his throne to Sher Shah Suri in 1540 and spent 15 years in exile. During his exile, he sought refuge in Persia under Safavid ruler Shah Tahmasp I and rebuilt his army. In 1555, Humayun defeated Sher Shah Suri's successors at the Battle of Sirhind, reasserting Mughal control over Delhi and Agra. This victory marked the end of the Second Afghan Empire (Suri dynasty) and restored the Mughal Empire. Humayun's regained rule lasted only a year as he died in 1556, but his successful campaign laid the foundation for his son Akbar to expand and consolidate the empire. Humayun's return is a key event in Mughal history, showcasing resilience and strategic alliances.
qs.kf:
☛ When did Sher Shah Suri defeat Humayun and capture Delhi? → 1540
☛ Where did Humayun take refuge during exile? → Persia (Safavid Empire)
☛ In which battle did Humayun defeat Sher Shah’s successors? → Battle of Sirhind (1555)
☛ Who founded the Second Afghan Empire? → Sher Shah Suri
☛ When did Humayun die? → 1556

q: Which of the following materials has been mainly used for building the Jahangiri Mahal in Agra Fort?
qs.e: The Jahangiri Mahal, located inside the Agra Fort on the banks of the Yamuna River, was built primarily for Emperor Jahangir. The main construction material used is red sandstone, which gives the palace its distinctive reddish hue. This material was chosen for its durability and aesthetic appeal. The Jahangiri Mahal is a fine example of Mughal architecture, blending Hindu and Islamic styles. Although later, Shah Jahan used white marble for his palaces, the Jahangiri Mahal remains predominantly built of red sandstone, visible in its walls, pillars, and ceilings. The palace is part of the Agra Fort, a UNESCO World Heritage site.
qs.kf:
☛ Where is Jahangiri Mahal located? → Inside Agra Fort
☛ Who built Jahangiri Mahal? → Emperor Akbar

☛ Which material did Shah Jahan use for his palaces later? → White marble

q: In which of the following buildings/towns constructed by the Mughals is Salim Chishti's tomb situated?
qs.e: Salim Chishti's tomb is located in Fatehpur Sikri. This tomb was built by Mughal Emperor Akbar. Salim Chishti was a Sufi saint whose blessings Akbar sought for the birth of his son Salim (Jahangir). The tomb was constructed between 1580-1581 CE and is made of white marble. It is situated in the courtyard of the Jama Masjid and is renowned for its intricate lattice work.

☛ Where is Salim Chishti's tomb located? → Fatehpur Sikri
☛ Who built the tomb? → Akbar
☛ Construction period → 1580-1581 CE
☛ Material used → Marble
☛ In which mosque's courtyard is it? → Jama Masjid

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (24/06/2025) Shift 1
q: ’Top-khanah’ was the general name given to the military/artillery branch of which of the following?
qs.e: In the Mughal Empire, the military administration was divided into several branches. The artillery branch was commonly known as 'Top-khanah'. It was a vital part of the Mughal army, responsible for the production, maintenance, and use of cannons in warfare. Mughal emperors, especially Akbar, Jahangir, and Shah Jahan, emphasized the development of artillery. The term 'Top-khanah' is derived from Persian, meaning 'house of cannons' or 'artillery department'. The other options—Vijayanagara Empire, Ghurid Dynasty, and Delhi Sultanate—did not use the term 'Top-khanah' for their artillery branch.
qs.kf:
☛ Head of Mughal artillery → Mir-Atish
☛ Akbar's artillery workshop → Fatehpur Sikri
☛ Supreme commander of Mughal army → Sipahsalar
☛ Major cannon used in Mughal period → Zabbura
☛ Mughal military department head → Bakhshi

q: Which of the following statements about Aurangzeb is INCORRECT?
o: Aurangzeb's death led to the collapse of the Mughal empire in the mid-18th century.
He was the second son of Shah Jahan and Mumtaz Mahal.
He was also known as Alamgir.

In his struggle for power, Aurangzeb decisively defeated his brother \(% MathType!MTEF!2!1!+- % feaahqart1ev3aaatCvAUfeBSjuyZL2yd9gzLbvyNv2CaerbuLwBLn % hiov2DGi1BTfMBaeXatLxBI9gBaerbd9wDYLwzYbItLDharqqtubsr % 4rNCHbGeaGqiVu0Je9sqqrpepC0xbbL8F4rqqrFfpeea0xe9Lq-Jc9 % vqaqpepm0xbba9pwe9Q8fs0-yqaqpepae9pg0FirpepeKkFr0xfr-x % fr-xb9adbaqaaeGaciGaaiaabeqaamaabaabaaGcbaGaamiramaana % aabaGaamyyaaaacaWGYbWaa0aaaeaacaWGHbaaaaaa!39A1! D\overline a r\overline a \) in a battle and confined his father in his own palace at Agra.
qs.e: Aurangzeb was the third son of Shah Jahan and Mumtaz Mahal, not the second. His elder brothers were Dara Shikoh and Shah Shuja, and his younger brother was Murad Baksh. The correct statements include that Aurangzeb's death led to the decline of the Mughal empire in the mid-18th century, he was also known as Alamgir, and he defeated Dara Shikoh in battle and confined his father. Dara Shikoh was defeated at the Battle of Samugarh (1658).
qs.kf:
☛ Which son of Shah Jahan was Aurangzeb? → Third son
☛ What was Aurangzeb's title? → Alamgir
☛ In which battle was Dara Shikoh defeated? → Battle of Samugarh (1658)
☛ Where did Aurangzeb imprison his father? → Agra Fort
☛ When did the Mughal empire begin to decline? → Mid-18th century

q: Identify the option that arranges the chronology of Mughal emperors in the correct order.
qs.e: The correct chronological order of major Mughal emperors is Akbar (1556-1605), Jahangir (1605-1627), Shah Jahan (1628-1658), and Aurangzeb (1658-1707). Akbar strengthened the empire and promoted religious tolerance. Jahangir patronized arts and culture. Shah Jahan's reign saw the construction of the Taj Mahal and other architectural marvels. Aurangzeb expanded the empire but faced rebellions due to his policies. This sequence is crucial for competitive exams.
qs.kf:
☛ Reign of Akbar → 1556-1605 CE
☛ Reign of Jahangir → 1605-1627 CE
☛ Reign of Shah Jahan → 1628-1658 CE
☛ Reign of Aurangzeb → 1658-1707 CE
☛ Founder of Mughal dynasty → Babur (1526-1530)

q: Who wrote 'Ain-i-Akbari'? It is a 16th-century detailed document recording the administration of the Mughal Empire under Emperor Akbar.
qs.e: ‘Ain-i-Akbari’ is a detailed administrative document written by Abul Fazl, the court historian of Mughal Emperor Akbar. It is the third volume of the Akbarnama, and it records the administration, revenue system, military, judiciary, and social structure of Akbar's reign. It also includes information about Akbar's Navratnas, religious policies, and various provinces. Written in Persian, this 16th-century work is a primary source for understanding the Mughal Empire under Akbar.
qs.kf:
☛ Who wrote the Akbarnama? → Abul Fazl
☛ Which volume of Akbarnama is Ain-i-Akbari? → Third volume
☛ In which language was Ain-i-Akbari written? → Persian
☛ Who was the chief historian of Akbar’s court? → Abul Fazl
☛ Which work details Mughal administration under Akbar? → Ain-i-Akbari

q: From which Asian country did Ahmad Shah Abdali come to India?
qs.e: Ahmad Shah Abdali, also known as Ahmad Shah Durrani, was the ruler of Afghanistan. He founded the Durrani Empire and launched several invasions into India during the 18th century. The most notable of these was the Third Battle of Panipat (1761), where he defeated the Maratha Empire. Abdali hailed from the Kandahar region of Afghanistan and expanded his power into India following the decline of the Mughal Empire. He is regarded as a symbol of Afghan nationalism and his invasions significantly impacted the political landscape of the Indian subcontinent.
qs.kf:
☛ Birthplace of Ahmad Shah Abdali → Multan (now in Pakistan)
☛ Capital of Durrani Empire → Kandahar
☛ Third Battle of Panipat → 1761 between Abdali and Marathas
☛ Main rival of Abdali → Maratha Empire
☛ Successor of Abdali → Timur Shah Durrani

q: Which 16th-century CE heritage site near Agra was commissioned by Emperor Akbar as a planned capital city?
qs.e: Fatehpur Sikri is a 16th-century heritage site located in the Agra district of Uttar Pradesh. It was commissioned by Emperor Akbar in 1571 CE as the capital of the Mughal Empire. The city is built primarily from red sandstone and includes structures like Buland Darwaza, Jama Masjid, Panch Mahal, and Diwan-i-Khas. Akbar established the Ibadat Khana (House of Worship) here for religious discussions. Due to water scarcity, the capital was moved to Lahore in 1585 CE. It was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1986. Fatehpur Sikri stands as a fine example of Mughal architecture.
qs.kf:
☛ Who founded Fatehpur Sikri? → Emperor Akbar
☛ In which year was Fatehpur Sikri founded? → 1571 CE
☛ When was Fatehpur Sikri declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site? → 1986
☛ Which famous gate is located in Fatehpur Sikri? → Buland Darwaza
☛ To where did Akbar shift the capital from Fatehpur Sikri? → Lahore

q: In the Chola empire, the tax-free lands donated to Brahmins where they settled were known as ___________.
qs.e: In the Chola empire, the tax-free lands donated to Brahmins for their settlement were known as Agraharam. These were villages or plots of land where Brahmins resided and were exempted from taxes. This practice was a significant form of religious endowment, providing social and economic support to the Brahmin community. The Chola rulers actively promoted the development of Agraharams, which helped in fostering education and culture. The other options: Mahasabha was the village assembly, Garbhagriha is the inner sanctum of a temple, and Valanadu was an administrative division.
qs.kf:
☛ Village assembly in Chola administration → Mahasabha
☛ Holies part of a temple → Garbhagriha
☛ Administrative division in Chola empire → Valanadu
☛ Tax-free lands donated to Brahmins → Agraharam
☛ Greatest Chola ruler → Rajaraja I

q: Which 17th-century CE monument in Agra, built by Shah Jahan, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site?
qs.e: The Taj Mahal is a 17th-century monument located in Agra, built by Mughal emperor Shah Jahan in memory of his wife Mumtaz Mahal. Construction began in 1632 CE and was completed in 1653 CE. It is made of white marble and showcases a blend of Persian, Islamic, and Indian architectural styles. The Taj Mahal was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1983. It is considered a symbol of love and is one of the Seven Wonders of the World. Situated on the banks of the Yamuna River, it attracts millions of tourists annually.
qs.kf:
☛ On which river is the Taj Mahal located? → Yamuna River
☛ Who was the architect of the Taj Mahal? → Ustad Ahmad Lahauri
☛ What is the Taj Mahal made of? → White marble
☛ When was the Taj Mahal declared a UNESCO site? → 1983
☛ Which architectural style does the Taj Mahal represent? → Mughal architecture

q: Which Mughal court historian authored the Akbarnā ma, the official chronicle of Emperor Akbar’s reign?
qs.e: Abul Fazl was the court historian and chief advisor of the Mughal Emperor Akbar. He authored the Akbarnā ma, a three-volume official chronicle of Akbar's reign. The third volume is the Ain-i-Akbari, detailing the empire's administration, culture, and resources. Born in 1551 CE, Abul Fazl was one of Akbar's Navratnas (nine gems). Written in Persian, the Akbarnā ma is a key source for understanding Akbar's policies and ideas, completed in 1602 CE. Abul Fazl played a crucial role in shaping Akbar's religious and administrative reforms.
qs.kf:
☛ Who wrote the Akbarnā ma? → Abul Fazl
☛ Which text is part of the Akbarnā ma? → Ain-i-Akbari
☛ Under which emperor did Abul Fazl serve? → Akbar
☛ In which language was the Akbarnā ma written? → Persian
☛ When was Abul Fazl born? → 1551 CE

q: Which of the following ministers was the Commander of the entire military under the king during the Mughal rule?
qs.e: In the Mughal Empire, Mir Bakshi was a key minister who served as the Commander of the entire military under the king. This position was established by Akbar during his administrative reforms. Mir Bakshi was responsible for recruitment, salary, and discipline of the army, and he reported directly to the emperor. Other options: Mir Saman (in charge of royal construction and supplies), Diwan-i-Insha (in charge of royal correspondence), and Sadr-us-Sudur (in charge of religious affairs and endowments). The Mir Bakshi's role was crucial both during war and peace, and it symbolized central control over Mughal military power. This minister also oversaw the mansabdari system and ensured loyalty of the nobles through jagir assignments.
qs.kf:
☛ What was the role of Wazir in Mughal administration? → Prime Minister and Finance Minister
☛ What was the main function of Sadr-us-Sudur? → Religious affairs and grants
☛ Which department did Diwan-i-Insha head? → Royal correspondence and records
☛ Which officers were under Mir Bakshi in the Mughal army? → Faujdars and Qiladars
☛ For what was Mir Saman responsible? → Royal factories and supplies

q: In the Mansabdari system introduced by Akbar, the term Mansab refers to which of the following?
o: Rank or position of an official
qs.e: In the Mansabdari system introduced by Akbar in the 1570s, the term 'Mansab' refers to the rank or position of an official. It was a numerical system that determined the official's military responsibility and salary. Each Mansabdar was assigned a Zat (personal rank) and a Sawar (number of horsemen). This system formed the backbone of Mughal administration.
qs.kf:
☛ Who introduced the Mansabdari system? → Akbar
☛ What does Mansab mean? → Rank or position
☛ What are Zat and Sawar related to? → Mansabdari system
☛ When was the Mansabdari system implemented? → 1570s
☛ How were Mansabdars paid? → Cash or Jagir

q: Which of the following did Emperor Akbar NOT construct?
qs.e: Emperor Akbar did not construct the Jama Masjid of Delhi; it was built by Shah Jahan in 1656 AD. This mosque is the largest in Delhi. Akbar is known for constructing Agra Fort (1565-73), Buland Darwaza (at Fatehpur Sikri commemorating the victory of Gujarat, 1601), and Fatehpur Sikri (1571). Akbar reigned from 1556 to 1605 AD and was the third Mughal emperor. Buland Darwaza is a symbol of grandeur, and Agra Fort is a UNESCO World Heritage site.
qs.kf:
☛ Who built Jama Masjid of Delhi? → Shah Jahan
☛ Who built Buland Darwaza? → Akbar
☛ Who built Agra Fort? → Akbar
☛ Who founded Fatehpur Sikri? → Akbar
☛ What was Akbar's reign period? → 1556-1605 AD

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (05/06/2025) Shift 2
q: Which ruler, upon his death in 1530, left behind a newly established empire that stretched across northern India—from the Indus River in the west to Bihar in the east, and from the Himalayas in the north to Gwalior in the south?
qs.e: Babur (1526-1530) founded the Mughal Empire after defeating Ibrahim Lodi at the First Battle of Panipat in 1526. Upon his death in 1530, he left an empire extending from the Indus River in the west to Bihar in the east, and from the Himalayas in the north to Gwalior in the south. Babur was a descendant of Timur and Genghis Khan. He wrote his autobiography, the Baburnama, in Chagatai Turkic. His army effectively used guns and cannons. Alauddin Khalji (1296-1316) belonged to the Khalji dynasty, Aurangzeb (1658-1707) was a later Mughal ruler, and Qutb ud-Din Aibak (1206-1210) founded the Slave Dynasty.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the founder of the Mughal Empire? → Babur
☛ When and where did Babur die? → 1530, Agra
☛ What is the name of Babur's autobiography? → Baburnama
☛ Whom did Babur defeat in the First Battle of Panipat (1526)? → Ibrahim Lodi
☛ To which dynasty did Babur belong? → Timurid dynasty

name: All Questions · Q1–23
sub: Medieval History - Vijayanagara, Bahmani & Regional Kingdoms

q: Which famous empire was established by Harihar and Bukka?
qs.e: Harihar and Bukka, the founders of the Sangama dynasty, established the Vijayanagara Empire in 1336 CE. Located on the banks of the Tungabhadra River in South India, this empire lasted for about 300 years. Harihar I served as the first ruler. The empire is renowned for its patronage of Hinduism and development of South Indian culture. It successfully resisted the Deccan Sultanates and made significant contributions to art, architecture, and literature. The empire's capital was also named Vijayanagara (modern-day Hampi), which is a UNESCO World Heritage site.
qs.kf:
☛ Who founded the Vijayanagara Empire? → Harihar and Bukka
☛ What was the capital of the Vijayanagara Empire? → Vijayanagara (Hampi)
☛ Which dynasty did Harihar I belong to? → Sangama dynasty
☛ Which river is associated with Vijayanagara? → Tungabhadra
☛ Who was the last ruler of the Vijayanagara Empire? → Ramaraya

q: Which of the following famous rulers is related to the Tuluva dynasty?
qs.e: The Tuluva dynasty was one of the four major dynasties of the Vijayanagara Empire. This dynasty was founded by Tuluva Narasa Nayaka. Krishna Dev Rai was the most famous ruler of this dynasty, reigning from 1509 to 1529. His reign is considered the golden age of the Vijayanagara Empire. He was a great patron of art, literature, and architecture. His court had eight famous poets known as Ashtadiggajas. Tenali Raman was a renowned poet and court jester, not a ruler. Dev Rai I belonged to the Sangama dynasty, and Bukka Rai was also one of the founders of the Sangama dynasty.
qs.kf:
☛ What were the four dynasties of Vijayanagara Empire? → Sangama, Saluva, Tuluva, Aravidu
☛ Who founded the Tuluva dynasty? → Tuluva Narasa Nayaka
☛ Which dynasty did Krishna Dev Rai belong to? → Tuluva dynasty
☛ What is Krishna Dev Rai's reign called? → Golden age of Vijayanagara Empire
☛ What were the eight poets in Krishna Dev Rai's court called? → Ashtadiggajas

q: Golconda Fort was built during ______.
A. Vijayanagara Empire
B. Qutb Shahi dynasty
C. Satavahana dynasty
D. Hoysala Dynasty
qs.e: Golconda Fort is located near Hyderabad in the Indian state of Telangana. It was built during the rule of the Qutb Shahi dynasty in the 16th century. Initially a mud fort, it was later strengthened with stone. The fort is famous for its acoustics, circular layout, and beauty. The famous Kohinoor diamond was found here. The fort contains several palaces, mosques, and gardens.
qs.kf:
☛ Which dynasty built Golconda Fort? → Qutb Shahi dynasty
☛ Where is Golconda Fort located? → Telangana (near Hyderabad)
☛ What is a special feature of Golconda Fort? → Acoustic design
☛ Which diamond was found at Golconda Fort? → Kohinoor diamond
☛ Golconda Fort was initially built with? → Mud and stone

q: The Charminar of Hyderabad was built by:
qs.e: The Charminar of Hyderabad was built by Muhammad Quli Qutab Shah in 1591 AD. It is a symbol of the Qutb Shahi dynasty and is located in the heart of the city. The structure was built to mark the end of a plague epidemic and the founding of the new capital, Hyderabad. It is a mosque with four minarets, 45 prayer spaces, and a bustling market. Charminar is an excellent example of Indo-Islamic architecture.
qs.kf:
☛ Who built the Charminar? → Muhammad Quli Qutab Shah
☛ Where is Charminar located? → Hyderabad, Telangana
☛ When was Charminar built? → 1591 AD
☛ What was the capital of Qutb Shahi dynasty? → Golconda (later Hyderabad)
☛ How many minarets does Charminar have? → Four

q: _______ is the city of Karnataka in India that stands as a reminder of glory of the Vijayanagar empire.
qs.e: Hampi is a historic city in Karnataka, once the capital of the Vijayanagar Empire that flourished in South India from the 14th to the 17th century. It boasts magnificent structures like the Virupaksha Temple and Vittala Temple, showcasing the empire's wealth and artistic excellence. Hampi is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and lies on the banks of the Tungabhadra River. Pattadakal is known for Chalukya architecture, Gokak for its waterfall, and Basavakalyan was a Chalukya capital. Thus, Hampi is the correct answer as the iconic reminder of the Vijayanagar glory.
qs.kf:
☛ What was the capital of Vijayanagar Empire? → Hampi
☛ Which river flows near Hampi? → Tungabhadra
☛ In which state is Hampi located? → Karnataka
☛ Who founded the Vijayanagar Empire? → Harihara and Bukka
☛ Hampi is a UNESCO World Heritage Site since which year? → 1986

q: The famous Gol Gumbaz is located in:
qs.e: The famous Gol Gumbaz is located in Bijapur (Vijayapura) in the state of Karnataka, India. It is the mausoleum of Mohammed Adil Shah, built in 1656 AD. The dome of Gol Gumbaz is one of the largest in the world, with a diameter of 44 meters. A unique feature is the suspended echo inside the dome, where a sound made in one corner can be heard clearly 37 meters away. This architectural marvel is a prime example of the Adil Shahi dynasty's building style and represents the Deccan architecture tradition.
qs.kf:
☛ Who built Gol Gumbaz? → Mohammed Adil Shah
☛ What is the diameter of Gol Gumbaz dome? → 44 meters
☛ Gol Gumbaz is an example of which architectural style? → Deccan architecture
☛ Whose tomb is inside Gol Gumbaz? → Mohammed Adil Shah
☛ When was Gol Gumbaz added to UNESCO tentative list? → 2014

q: Who was the ruler of the Vijayanagara dynasty who ruled in the 16th century?
qs.e: Krishnadeva Raya was the most famous ruler of the Vijayanagara Empire, reigning in the 16th century (1509-1529 CE). He belonged to the Tuluva dynasty and his reign is considered the golden age of the empire. He promoted art, literature, and architecture. His court was adorned by eight scholars known as Ashtadiggajas, including Tenali Ramakrishna. He defeated the Sultan of Bijapur and expanded the empire. Other options: Pulakeshin II (Chalukya dynasty, 7th century), Raja Raja Chola (Chola dynasty, 11th century), Adi Shankara (philosopher).
qs.kf:
☛ Most powerful ruler of Vijayanagara → Krishnadeva Raya
☛ Dynasty of Krishnadeva Raya → Tuluva dynasty
☛ Reign period of Krishnadeva Raya → 1509-1529 CE
☛ Eight scholars in Krishnadeva Raya's court → Ashtadiggajas
☛ Founder of Vijayanagara Empire → Harihara and Bukka

q: The Vijayanagara empire was founded in the:
qs.e: The Vijayanagara Empire was founded in 1336 CE by Harihara I and Bukka I of the Sangama dynasty. It was a major empire in South India that lasted until about 1646 CE. Its capital was Vijayanagara (present-day Hampi, Karnataka). The empire rose after the decline of the Hoysala Empire and preserved Hindu culture in South India. The Vijayanagara Empire was ruled by four major dynasties: Sangama, Saluva, Tuluva, and Aravidu.
qs.kf:
☛ Who founded the Vijayanagara Empire? → Harihara and Bukka
☛ What was the capital of the Vijayanagara Empire? → Vijayanagara (Hampi)
☛ Who was the most famous ruler of Vijayanagara? → Krishnadevaraya
☛ On which river was Vijayanagara located? → Tungabhadra
☛ Which was the last dynasty of Vijayanagara? → Aravidu dynasty

q: Kulottunga I was a king of which of the following dynasties?
qs.e: Kulottunga I was a prominent king of the Chola dynasty, who ruled from 1070 CE to 1122 CE. He was the son of Rajendra Chola II and successfully conquered Sri Lanka, Kalinga, and the Kakatiya regions. He established diplomatic relations with Chinese rulers and promoted trade. His reign is considered the golden age of the Chola empire, marked by advancements in art, literature, and architecture. He renovated the Chidambaram Temple and strengthened the irrigation system in the Kaveri delta.
qs.kf:
☛ With which country did Kulottunga I establish diplomatic relations? → China
☛ What was the reign period of Kulottunga I? → 1070 CE to 1122 CE
☛ Who was the father of Kulottunga I? → Rajendra Chola II
☛ Which temple did Kulottunga I renovate? → Chidambaram Temple
☛ Which regions were conquered during Kulottunga I's reign? → Sri Lanka, Kalinga, and Kakatiya

q: Which of the following kings of the Vijayanagara Empire assumed the title of Yavanarajya Sthapanacharya?
qs.e: The greatest king of the Vijayanagara Empire, Krishnadevaraya, assumed the title 'Yavanarajya Sthapanacharya' as part of his foreign policy to control the Portuguese. The title means 'Establishment-maker of the Yavana (foreign) kingdom'. It symbolized his military and political power. He made a treaty with the Portuguese, gaining benefits while keeping their influence in check. This title is considered one of the significant achievements of his reign. The Vijayanagara Empire was located on the banks of the Tungabhadra River, and Krishnadevaraya extended special patronage to Telugu literature.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the guru of Krishnadevaraya? → Tatacharya
☛ Who is called Andhra Bhoja? → Krishnadevaraya
☛ What was the capital of Vijayanagara? → Hampi
☛ Name of Krishnadevaraya's queen? → Chinnadevi
☛ Telugu work composed by Krishnadevaraya? → Amuktamalyada

q: What was the role of Nayakas under the Amara-Nayaka system of Vijayanagar administration?
qs.e: The Amara-Nayaka system of the Vijayanagar Empire was a military-feudal system. Under this system, Nayakas were granted land (amara) in exchange for providing military service to the king. Their primary role was as an Army Commander, meaning they led troops during wars. They also collected revenue from their territories, but that was a secondary function. Their duties did not include being the Head of Spies or Village Head. This system was crucial for maintaining the empire's military strength. It later contributed to the decline of the Vijayanagar Empire as Nayakas became increasingly independent. The system was particularly strengthened under the rule of Krishnadevaraya.
qs.kf:
☛ What was the main purpose of the Amara-Nayaka system in Vijayanagar? → Military security
☛ What was the land grant given to Nayakas called? → Amara
☛ Which Vijayanagar ruler strengthened the Amara-Nayaka system? → Krishnadevaraya
☛ What was the primary duty of a Nayaka? → To lead the army
☛ The Amara-Nayaka system was a __________ system. → Military-feudal

q: Arrange the following rulers of the Sharqi dynasty in the chronological order.
o: Hussain Shah < Ibrahim Shah < Mubarak Shah < Mahmud Shah
Mahmud Shah < Hussain Shah < Mubarak Shah < Ibrahim Shah
Hussain Shah < Mubarak Shah < Ibrahim Shah < Mahmud Shah
Mubarak Shah < Ibrahim Shah < Mahmud Shah < Hussain Shah
qs.e: The Sharqi dynasty was founded by Malik Sarwar in 1394 AD, who assumed the title of Khwaja-i-Jahan. The correct chronological order of its major rulers is: Mubarak Shah (1399-1401) ruled first, followed by Ibrahim Shah (1401-1440), who had a long reign and promoted the Sharqi style of architecture. After him, Mahmud Shah (1440-1457) ascended the throne, and the last ruler was Hussain Shah (1457-1479), under whom the sultanate expanded and later ended after defeat by Bahlol Lodi.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the founder of the Sharqi dynasty? → Malik Sarwar (Khwaja-i-Jahan)
☛ What was the capital of the Sharqi dynasty? → Jaunpur
☛ Under which ruler did the Sharqi empire expand? → Hussain Shah
☛ Who ended the Sharqi dynasty? → Bahlol Lodi (1479 AD)
☛ Which art did Ibrahim Shah promote? → Architecture (Sharqi style)

q: Zain - ul - Abidin was known for his tolerant thoughts. What was the sultan of which empire?
qs.e: Zain-ul-Abidin was the Sultan of the Kashmir empire. He ruled from 1420 to 1470 CE. He is also known as 'Bud Shah' (Great King). He was renowned for his religious tolerance and liberal policies. He treated Hindus and Muslims equally and allowed the construction of many temples. He implemented administrative reforms, promoted agriculture, and patronized literature. He was a scholar himself and knew Persian, Sanskrit, and Kashmiri languages. He commissioned the translation of 'Rajatarangini' into Persian. His tolerant attitude strengthened communal harmony in Kashmir.
qs.kf:
☛ Reign of Zain-ul-Abidin → 1420-1470 CE
☛ Title of Zain-ul-Abidin → Bud Shah
☛ Work translated by Zain-ul-Abidin → Rajatarangini (into Persian)
☛ Reason for Zain-ul-Abidin's fame → Religious tolerance
☛ Languages known to Zain-ul-Abidin → Persian, Sanskrit, Kashmiri

q: Who was the founder of the Vijayanagar empire?
o: Achyuya Ram Rai and Krishna Dev Rai
qs.e: The Vijayanagar Empire was founded in 1336 AD by two brothers, Harihar and Bukka. They belonged to the Sangama dynasty and were initially feudatories of the Kakatiya kingdom. With the guidance of sage Vidyaranya (Madhavacharya), they established a powerful empire in South India. The capital was Vijayanagar (present-day Hampi, Karnataka).
