sub: Medieval History - Medieval Art, Architecture & Literature

q: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched (important foreign travellers to the ruler's reign or dynasty when the travellers visited India)?
qs.e: John Jurdan (also known as John of Montecorvino) visited India in the 14th century during the reign of Muhammad bin Tughlaq of the Delhi Sultanate, not Shah Jahan. Marco Polo visited the Pandya Kingdom in the 13th century. Abdur Razzak, a Persian ambassador, came in 1443-44 during the rule of Devaraya II of the Vijayanagara Empire. Ralph Fitch, an English merchant, travelled to India between 1584-1591 during the reign of Akbar. Therefore, the pair John Jurdan - Shah Jahan is incorrectly matched.
qs.kf:
☛ During whose reign did John Jurdan visit India? → Muhammad bin Tughlaq
☛ Marco Polo visited which kingdom in India? → Pandya Kingdom
☛ Abdur Razzak visited which ruler's court? → Devaraya II
☛ Ralph Fitch visited India during which Mughal ruler's reign? → Akbar
☛ Who was the first English traveller to India? → Ralph Fitch

q: Rudreswara Temple or Veyisthambala Gudi (thousands pillars temple) was built by Rudra Deva. Which dynasty does Rudra Deva belong to?
qs.e: The Rudreswara Temple, also known as Veyisthambala Gudi (temple of a thousand pillars), was built by Rudra Deva (Rudradeva). He belonged to the Kakatiya dynasty. This temple is located in Hanamkonda, Telangana. The Kakatiya dynasty ruled parts of South India from the 12th to the 14th centuries. Rudra Deva (1158–1195) was a prominent ruler of this dynasty. He promoted temple architecture. The temple is renowned for its intricate carvings and pillars. The capital of the Kakatiya dynasty was Warangal.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the founder of the Kakatiya dynasty? → Prolaraja I
☛ Who was the last ruler of the Kakatiya dynasty? → Prataparudra II
☛ Who built the Warangal Fort? → Kakatiya rulers
☛ Where is the Rudreswara Temple located? → Hanamkonda, Telangana
☛ What was the emblem of the Kakatiya dynasty? → Nandi (bull)

q: Pulakeshin II was the most illustrious ruler of which dynasty?
qs.e: Pulakeshin II was the most illustrious ruler of the Badami Chalukya dynasty. He reigned from 610 to 642 CE. He was the son of Kirtivarman I. Pulakeshin II defeated Harshavardhana on the banks of the Narmada River. His court poet was Ravikirti, who composed the Aihole inscription, which details Pulakeshin's achievements. He fought against the Pallava king Narasimhavarman I, and eventually the Pallavas captured Vatapi (Badami). The Chalukya dynasty ruled over parts of southern India from the 6th to the 8th century.
qs.kf:
☛ Court poet of Pulakeshin II → Ravikirti
☛ Language of Aihole inscription → Sanskrit and script Kannada
☛ Pulakeshin II defeated → Harshavardhana
☛ Capital of Chalukya dynasty → Badami (Vatapi)
☛ Founder of Chalukya dynasty → Jayasimha

q: Which of the following Nawabs of Awadh built the Bara Imambara in Lucknow?
qs.e: The Bara Imambara, also known as the Asafi Imambara, is a historical building in Lucknow, India. It was built by Nawab Asaf-ud-Daula of Awadh in 1784. It is one of the largest unsupported structures in India. Nawab Asaf-ud-Daula commissioned it as a famine relief project to provide employment to the people during a severe famine. It is said that about 20,000 workers worked during the day and demolished the structure at night so that more people could get employment. The building has three gateways, a large hall, and a labyrinth of passages known as the Bhool Bhulaiya.
qs.kf:
☛ Who built Bara Imambara? → Asaf-ud-Daula
☛ Where is Bara Imambara located? → Lucknow
☛ When was Bara Imambara built? → 1784
☛ What is the other name of Bara Imambara? → Asafi Imambara
☛ What is the architectural style of Bara Imambara? → Mughal architecture

q: The rulers Pulakeshin I and Pulakeshin II were related to which of the following dynasties?
qs.e: Pulakeshin I and Pulakeshin II were prominent rulers of the Chalukya dynasty, which ruled large parts of South India from the 6th to 12th centuries. Pulakeshin I founded the Badami Chalukya kingdom in 543 AD. Pulakeshin II is considered the most powerful king of this dynasty; he defeated the northern emperor Harshavardhana on the banks of the Narmada River. The Chalukya dynasty is renowned for its architecture, including the temples at Badami, Aihole, and Pattadakal.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the founder of the Chalukya dynasty? → Pulakeshin I
☛ Which emperor did Pulakeshin II defeat? → Harshavardhana
☛ What was the capital of the Chalukya kings? → Badami (Vatapi)
☛ In which region did the Chalukya dynasty rule? → South India
☛ Which are the major architectural sites of the Chalukya period? → Aihole, Badami, Pattadakal

q: The famous traveler Nicolo Conti was from which country?
qs.e: Nicolo Conti was a famous Italian traveler and merchant who journeyed to India and Southeast Asia in the 15th century. He spent about 25 years traveling across various parts of Asia and recorded his experiences. His travel accounts were later documented by order of Pope Eugene IV. Conti's writings provide detailed descriptions of the Vijayanagara Empire, the Malabar Coast, and Sumatra. He was a native of Venice, which was a major trading hub at the time. His travels significantly contributed to European knowledge of Asia during the Renaissance period.
qs.kf:
☛ Main region of Nicolo Conti's travels → India and Southeast Asia
☛ Who ordered the recording of Nicolo Conti's travels → Pope Eugene IV
☛ Which empire did Nicolo Conti describe → Vijayanagara Empire
☛ Which city was Nicolo Conti from → Venice
☛ Which century did Nicolo Conti travel → 15th century

q: Quwwat-al-islam mosque is nearest to which of the following historical monuments?
qs.e: The Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque is located in the Mehrauli area of Delhi and is part of the Qutub Minar complex. Its construction was started by Qutb-ud-din Aibak in 1192 AD. The mosque is adjacent to the Qutub Minar, a 72.5-meter tall minaret. Humayun's Tomb is in Nizamuddin, Tughlakabad Fort is in South Delhi, and Jama Masjid is in Old Delhi. The Qutub Minar is a UNESCO World Heritage site, and the mosque is within the same complex, making it the nearest monument.
qs.kf:
☛ Height of Qutub Minar → 72.5 meters
☛ Builder of Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque → Qutb-ud-din Aibak
☛ Who completed Qutub Minar → Iltutmish
☛ UNESCO World Heritage declared → 1993
☛ Qutub Minar complex located → Mehrauli, Delhi

q: Who among the following was the last Pallava ruler?
qs.e: The last Pallava ruler was Aparajitavarman, who ruled from 880 to 897 CE. The Pallava dynasty was a major power in South India from the 3rd to the 9th century, with its capital at Kanchipuram. During Aparajitavarman's reign, the Pallava empire ended when the Chola king Aditya I defeated him. The Pallavas are renowned for their contributions to art and architecture, especially rock-cut temples and rathas (chariot temples). They also patronized Sanskrit and Tamil literature.
qs.kf:
☛ Last Pallava ruler → Aparajitavarman
☛ Pallava capital → Kanchipuram
☛ Chola king who defeated Pallavas → Aditya I
☛ Major art form of Pallava period → Rathas and cave temples
☛ Famous Pallava king → Narasimhavarman I (Mamalla)

q: Match the following Rulers with their titles correctly. Set – I Set - II a. Tarikh-i-Sindh 1. Nizamuddin Bakshi b. Tarikh-i-Kashmir
2. Arif kandhari c. Tabaqat-i-Akbari 3. Mirza Massom d. Tarikh-i-Akbari 4. Mirza Haider
qs.e: Tarikh-i-Sindh (a) is authored by Mirza Massom (3), dealing with the history of Sindh. Tarikh-i-Kashmir (b) is authored by Mirza Haider (4), covering the history of Kashmir. Tabaqat-i-Akbari (c) is written by Nizamuddin Bakshi (1), a detailed history of Akbar's reign. Tarikh-i-Akbari (d) is authored by Arif Kandhari (2), also about Akbar's period. These are important Mughal historical texts, and correct matching of authors is crucial for understanding sources of Mughal history.
qs.kf:
☛ Who wrote Tarikh-i-Sindh? → Mirza Massom
☛ Who wrote Tarikh-i-Kashmir? → Mirza Haider
☛ Who wrote Tabaqat-i-Akbari? → Nizamuddin Bakshi
☛ Who wrote Tarikh-i-Akbari? → Arif Kandhari
☛ Which region does Tarikh-i-Sindh pertain to? → Sindh

q: Angkor Vat temple, which is dedicated to the god Vishnu, was built in the 12th century by __________, the king of Kambuja (Cambodia).
qs.e: Angkor Wat temple, located in the Angkor region of Cambodia, is a massive Hindu temple dedicated to Lord Vishnu. It was built in the early 12th century by King Suryavarman II of the Khmer Empire. The construction took about 30 years and is a masterpiece of Khmer architecture. The walls are adorned with carvings depicting scenes from the Ramayana and the Mahabharata. Although originally a Hindu temple, it was later converted into a Buddhist temple. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and is also depicted on the national flag of Cambodia.
qs.kf:
☛ Builder of Angkor Wat → Suryavarman II
☛ Dedicated deity of Angkor Wat → Vishnu
☛ Location of Angkor Wat → Cambodia
☛ Religion of Angkor Wat (originally) → Hindu
☛ Century of Angkor Wat → 12th century

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (09/06/2025) Shift 2
q: The Chalukyas of Badami were founded by:
qs.e: The Chalukya dynasty of Badami was founded by Pulakesin I in the 6th century CE. He established Vatapi (modern Badami) as their capital and laid the foundation of the Chalukya empire. Pulakesin I performed the Ashvamedha sacrifice and assumed the title 'Maharajadhiraja'. His son Kirttivarman I succeeded him and expanded the kingdom. The most famous ruler of this dynasty was Pulakesin II, who defeated Harsha on the banks of the Narmada River. The Chalukyas were pioneers in art and architecture, as seen in the cave temples of Badami. The dynasty ruled for over two centuries and left a lasting impact on South Indian history.
qs.kf:
☛ Who founded the Badami Chalukya dynasty? → Pulakesin I
☛ What was the capital of the Badami Chalukyas? → Vatapi (Badami)
☛ Which Chalukya king defeated Harsha? → Pulakesin II
☛ Which sacrifice did Pulakesin I perform? → Ashvamedha
☛ Where are the Chalukya cave temples located? → Badami

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (10/06/2025) Shift 1
q: The Takht-i-Bahi inscription is associated with which region?
qs.e: The Takht-i-Bahi inscription is associated with the Gandhara region (present-day Khyber Pakhtunkhwa in Pakistan). This inscription dates back to the reign of the Kushan king Kanishka and records the construction of a monastery. It is an important source for understanding the Gandhara civilization and the spread of Buddhism. Takht-i-Bahi is an ancient Buddhist monastic complex and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
qs.kf:
☛ Takht-i-Bahi is related to which religion? → Buddhism
☛ Takht-i-Bahi inscription is associated with which king? → Kanishka
☛ What is the modern name of Gandhara region? → Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan
☛ Kushan king Kanishka belonged to which dynasty? → Kushan dynasty
☛ Which is the most famous inscription of Kanishka? → Takht-i-Bahi inscription

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (10/06/2025) Shift 2
q: Which of the following architectures has been built in the 'Charbagh' style?
qs.e: Charbagh style is a distinct Mughal architectural style where a garden is divided into four parts separated by pathways or water channels. This style was derived from Persian architecture. The Taj Mahal, built by Shah Jahan between 1632-1653 AD, is an excellent example of this style. The main tomb is not at the center but at the northern end near the Yamuna River, yet the garden is divided into four parts. The Gumbaj of Bijapur represents Deccan architecture, while the Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque and Qutub Minar reflect the architecture of the Delhi Sultanate period.
qs.kf:
☛ Who introduced the Charbagh style in India? → Babur
☛ What does Charbagh mean? → A garden with four parts
☛ Who built the Taj Mahal? → Shah Jahan
☛ Where is the tomb located in a Charbagh? → Center or edge
☛ From where did the Charbagh style originate? → Persia

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (23/06/2025) Shift 1
q: The famous building 'Qutub Minar' has been built under which style of architecture?
qs.e: Qutub Minar is the tallest minaret in India, started by Qutb-ud-din Aibak in 1193 and completed by Iltutmish. It is an excellent example of the Mamulek (Slave Dynasty) style of architecture. This style uses red sandstone and marble, featuring Islamic calligraphy and Quranic verses. The balconies are adorned with muqarnas (honeycomb vaulting), a hallmark of this style. The Mamulek style laid the foundation of Turkish architecture in India, which later evolved into the Mughal style. The structure is also a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1993.
qs.kf:
☛ Height of Qutub Minar → 72.5 meters
☛ Builders → Qutb-ud-din Aibak and Iltutmish
☛ Material → Red sandstone and marble
☛ Style → Mamulek (Slave Dynasty)
☛ UNESCO World Heritage → Inscribed in 1993

q: From the given options, which dynasty developed shipping ventures in Southeast Asia?
qs.e: The Chola Dynasty (c. 300 BCE – 1279 CE) developed shipping ventures in Southeast Asia. The Cholas built a powerful navy and conducted trade expeditions. King Raja Raja Chola I and his son Rajendra Chola I invaded the Srivijaya Empire (present-day Indonesia). The Cholas established trade relations with the Malay Peninsula, Sumatra, and Java. Their fleet was active in the Bay of Bengal and the South China Sea. The Chola navy is considered one of the most powerful navies of its time.
qs.kf:
☛ Famous ruler of Chola dynasty → Raja Raja Chola and Rajendra Chola
☛ Capital of Cholas → Thanjavur
☛ Famous temple built by Cholas → Brihadeeswarar Temple
☛ Which country did Cholas invade? → Srivijaya (Indonesia)
☛ Main area of Chola navy → Southeast Asia

q: Which of the following traveller came in the court of Krishna Dev Rai?
qs.e: Domingo Paes was a Portuguese traveller who visited the court of Krishna Dev Rai, the ruler of the Vijayanagara Empire, in 1520 CE. His detailed account provides valuable insights into the empire's prosperity, administration, and military strength. He praised the grandeur of the city of Hampi and the generosity of the king. Paes' writings are considered a crucial source for the history of the Vijayanagara Empire. Among the other options, Nicolò de Conti visited Vijayanagara in the 15th century, before Krishna Dev Rai's reign. William Hawkins came to the Mughal court in the 17th century, and Abdur Razzaq visited Vijayanagara during the Sangama dynasty in the 15th century.
qs.kf:
☛ Portuguese traveller to Vijayanagara → Domingo Paes
☛ Traveller in Krishna Dev Rai's court → Domingo Paes
☛ Year of Domingo Paes' visit → 1520 CE
☛ City described by Domingo Paes → Hampi
☛ Abdur Razzaq came from → Persia (Timurid Empire)

q: The famous Uttarmaram inscription is related to which dynasty?
qs.e: The famous Uttarmaram inscription is associated with the Chola dynasty of South India. This inscription dates back to the reign of the Chola emperor Rajaraja I (985-1014 CE), who built the Brihadeeswarar Temple in Thanjavur and was a great administrator. The Uttarmaram inscription provides detailed information about the administrative, revenue, and social aspects of the Chola empire. It was discovered in the Pudukkottai district of Tamil Nadu and records land grants, tax collection, and temple management. The Chola dynasty is renowned for its efficient administration, magnificent temple architecture, and contributions to literature.
qs.kf:
☛ The Uttarmaram inscription belongs to which dynasty? → Chola
☛ Under which Chola ruler was the Uttarmaram inscription issued? → Rajaraja I
☛ Where was the Uttarmaram inscription found? → Pudukkottai (Tamil Nadu)
☛ What was the capital of the Chola dynasty? → Thanjavur
☛ Who built the Brihadeeswarar Temple? → Rajaraja I

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (13/06/2025) Shift 2
q: The Rashtrakutas dominated which part of India after the Guptas?
qs.e: After the decline of the Gupta Empire, the Rashtrakutas dominated the Deccan region (south-central India) from around 753 CE to 982 CE. Their capital was Manyakheta (modern-day Karnataka). The Rashtrakuta empire extended from the Narmada River in the north to the Kaveri River in the south. They succeeded the Chalukyas and at their peak controlled parts of western Deccan, Maharashtra, Karnataka, and Madhya Pradesh. Dantidurga was the founder of the Rashtrakuta dynasty, while Amoghavarsha I and Krishna III were notable rulers. The Rashtrakutas patronized art, literature, and architecture, including the construction of the Kailasanatha Temple at Ellora.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the founder of the Rashtrakuta dynasty? → Dantidurga
☛ What was the capital of the Rashtrakutas? → Manyakheta
☛ Which famous temple was built by the Rashtrakutas? → Kailasanatha Temple at Ellora
☛ Which dynasty ended the Rashtrakuta rule? → Chalukyas
☛ Who was the most famous Rashtrakuta ruler? → Amoghavarsha I

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (21/06/2025) Shift 2
q: The Badami caves in Karnataka have been built by which of the following rulers?
qs.e: The Badami caves are located in Bagalkot district of Karnataka. They were built by the Chalukya dynasty, especially during the reign of Pulakeshin I and his successors. These caves are associated with Hinduism, Jainism, and Buddhism and are famous for their architecture. Badami was the capital of the Chalukyas. The Chalukya dynasty ruled from around the 6th to 8th centuries.
qs.kf:
☛ Badami cave builder dynasty → Chalukyas
☛ Badami was the capital of which dynasty? → Chalukyas
☛ Which king defeated Harshavardhana? → Pulakeshin II
☛ Examples of Chalukya architecture → Badami caves, Virupaksha temple
☛ Number of Badami caves → Four

q: Kanchi was the capital of _________.
qs.e: The city of Kanchi was one of the major historical sites in South India. It served as the capital of the Pallava dynasty. The Pallavas ruled parts of South India from approximately the 6th to 9th centuries. Their capital was located at Kanchi (present-day Kanchipuram). The Pallavas were patrons of art and architecture, exemplified by the Ratha temples at Mahabalipuram and the Kailashnath Temple. Although later the Cholas took over Kanchi, it was originally the capital of the Pallavas. The Chalukyas had their capital at Badami, and the Rashtrakutas at Manyakheta. Thus, Kanchi is famously known as the capital of the Pallavas.
qs.kf:
☛ Capital of the Pallava dynasty → Kanchipuram
☛ Capital of the Chola dynasty → Thanjavur
☛ Capital of the Chalukya dynasty → Badami
☛ Capital of the Rashtrakuta dynasty → Manyakheta
☛ Famous Pallava architectural site → Mahabalipuram

q: By which of the following dynasties was the Brihadeswara temple built?
qs.e: The Brihadeeswarar Temple, also known as Rajarajeswaram Temple, is located in Thanjavur, Tamil Nadu. It was built by the Chola dynasty ruler Raja Raja Chola I between 1003 and 1010 AD. The temple is dedicated to Lord Shiva and is famous for its massive vimana (tower), which rises to a height of 66 meters. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and an outstanding example of Chola architecture. The temple walls feature inscriptions and sculptures from the Chola period.
qs.kf:
☛ Who built the Brihadeeswarar Temple? → Raja Raja Chola I
☛ Which god is the Brihadeeswarar Temple dedicated to? → Shiva
☛ Where is the Brihadeeswarar Temple located? → Thanjavur, Tamil Nadu
☛ When was the Brihadeeswarar Temple built? → 1003-1010 AD
☛ Who was the founder of the Chola dynasty? → Vijayalaya

q: Which of the following monuments was built by Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah is said to be built to commemorate the eradication of plague?
qs.e: The Charminar was built in 1591 AD by Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah. It is located in Hyderabad, Telangana. It is said to have been constructed to commemorate the end of a plague epidemic in the city. This four-towered structure is an excellent example of Indo-Islamic architecture. Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah was the fifth ruler of the Qutb Shahi dynasty and shifted his capital from Golconda to Hyderabad. The Charminar has four minarets, each 56 meters tall, and is built using granite and lime mortar.
qs.kf:
☛ Builder of Charminar → Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah
☛ Year of construction of Charminar → 1591 AD
☛ Location of Charminar → Hyderabad, Telangana
☛ Reason for building Charminar → Commemoration of plague eradication
☛ Number of minarets in Charminar → Four

q: Who is considered the greatest of the early Chola kings?
qs.e: Among the early Chola kings, Karikala is considered the greatest. He flourished around the first century CE. Karikala undertook large-scale flood control and irrigation projects along the banks of the Kaveri River. He defeated the Kalabhras and expanded the Chola kingdom. His capital was Uraiyur. Karikala also invaded Sri Lanka and brought 12,000 captives to use them in building a dam across the Kaveri delta. During his reign, the Chola empire became economically and militarily strong. He is glorified in Sangam literature, especially in the poems Pattinappalai and Porunaraatruppadai.
qs.kf:
☛ Greatest early Chola king → Karikala
☛ Karikala's capital → Uraiyur
☛ Karikala's period → 1st century CE
☛ Dam built by Karikala → on Kaveri River
☛ Karikala's achievement → Defeated Kalabhras

q: Who built the Lingaraj Temple?
o: Rulers of the Rajput Chandela Dynasty
qs.e: The Lingaraj Temple is a famous Hindu temple located in Bhubaneswar, Odisha, dedicated to Lord Shiva. It was built in the 11th century by King Yayati Keshari of the Somavamshi dynasty. The temple is an excellent example of Kalinga architecture. Its main sanctum is 55 meters high. It is considered the 'Kashi of North India' and one of the 'Saptarudra' temples. Later, King Anantavarman Chodaganga Deva renovated the temple, but the original construction was done by Yayati Keshari.
qs.kf:
☛ Where is Lingaraj Temple located? → Bhubaneswar, Odisha
☛ Which deity is it dedicated to? → Lord Shiva
☛ What is its architectural style? → Kalinga architecture
☛ How high is its main sanctum? → 55 meters
☛ Who renovated it later? → King Anantavarman Chodaganga Deva

q: 'Amir-al-Khayl' is an Arabic title that is usually translated 'Commander of the Faithful' or 'Leader of the Faithful'. Who among the following was given this designation?
qs.e: Amir-al-Khayl means 'Commander of the Faithful'. This title was given to Jamal-ud-Din Yaqut, an Abyssinian slave who served under the Delhi Sultanate ruler Razia Sultana. He was appointed as the chief of the cavalry. This appointment caused discontent among the Turkish nobles, who resented a non-Turkish slave holding such a high position. This dissatisfaction led to a rebellion against Razia Sultana, ultimately resulting in her death. Yaqut was bestowed this title during Razia Sultana's reign (1236-1240 AD).
qs.kf:
☛ Who was Razia Sultana's father? → Iltutmish
☛ Where was Razia Sultana killed? → Kaithal, Haryana
☛ Who did Razia Sultana marry? → Malik Ikhtiar-ud-din Altunia
☛ Who was the first female ruler of Delhi? → Razia Sultana
☛ What was Jamal-ud-Din Yaqut's ethnicity? → Abyssinian (Habshi)

q: Who established the Rashtrakuta dynasty?
qs.e: The Rashtrakuta dynasty was founded by Dantidurga in the 8th century. He was a feudatory of the Badami Chalukyas and established his capital at Manyakheta (modern Malkhed) around 752 CE. The Rashtrakutas created a powerful empire in southern India that lasted for about 200 years. Dantidurga's successor, Krishna I, expanded the empire. The Rashtrakuta period saw flourishing art, literature, and architecture, including the construction of the Kailasa temple at Ellora by Krishna I. Other options: Pulakeshin was from the Chalukya dynasty, Rajaraja Chola from the Chola dynasty, and Agniputra is associated with Rajput clans.
qs.kf:
☛ Founder of the Rashtrakuta dynasty → Dantidurga
☛ Capital of the Rashtrakutas → Manyakheta (Malkhed)
☛ Kailasa temple at Ellora built by → Krishna I
☛ Famous Rashtrakuta rulers → Amoghavarsha I, Indra III
☛ Decline of the Rashtrakutas → Overthrown by the Chalukyas in the 10th century

q: Which of the following cities was the capital of Chalukya?
qs.e: The capital of the Chalukya dynasty (6th-8th century) was Badami (also known as Vatapi), located in present-day Karnataka. The dynasty was founded by Pulakeshin I in 540 CE, who made Badami the capital. The Chalukyas ruled over the Deccan region and are known for their cave temples at Badami. Tanjore was the capital of the Cholas, Kanchipuram of the Pallavas, and Madurai of the Pandyas.
qs.kf:
☛ Where was the capital of the Chalukya dynasty? → Badami
☛ What is the ancient name of Badami? → Vatapi
☛ Who founded the Chalukya dynasty? → Pulakeshin I
☛ What are the Badami cave temples famous for? → Architecture
☛ In which region was the Chalukya empire located? → Deccan

q: Quwwat-al-islam mosque is located in which of the following cities?
qs.e: Quwwat-ul-Islam Mosque is one of the oldest existing mosques in India, located in the Mehrauli area of Delhi. Its construction was started in 1193 AD by Qutb-ud-din Aibak. The mosque is part of the Qutb Complex, which also includes the Qutb Minar. The name 'Quwwat-ul-Islam' means 'Might of Islam'. The mosque was built using materials from 27 demolished Hindu and Jain temples. Later, Alauddin Khalji and Iltutmish expanded it. It is a significant example of the architectural style of the Delhi Sultanate period.
qs.kf:
☛ Who built the Qutb Minar? → Qutb-ud-din Aibak (started) and Iltutmish (completed)
☛ Which period does the Iron Pillar in Qutb Complex belong to? → Gupta period (Chandragupta II)
☛ Which mosque was expanded by Alauddin Khalji? → Quwwat-ul-Islam Mosque
☛ Which was the first mosque of Delhi Sultanate? → Quwwat-ul-Islam Mosque
☛ Where is Quwwat-ul-Islam Mosque located? → Mehrauli, Delhi

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (17/06/2025) Shift 3
q: Which of the following architectures was built by Aurangzeb?
qs.e: Bibi-ka-Maqbara was built by Aurangzeb in memory of his wife Dilras Banu Begum. Located in Aurangabad, it was constructed between 1651 and 1661. It is often called the "Mini Taj Mahal" because it was designed on the lines of the Taj Mahal. Other options: Qutub Minar was started by Qutub-ud-din Aibak, Taj Mahal was built by Shah Jahan, and Humayun's tomb was built by Haji Begum (Humayun's wife).
qs.kf:
☛ Where is Bibi-ka-Maqbara located? → Aurangabad
☛ In whose memory was Bibi-ka-Maqbara built? → Dilras Banu Begum
☛ Which Mughal emperor built Bibi-ka-Maqbara? → Aurangzeb
☛ Which famous tomb inspired the design of Bibi-ka-Maqbara? → Taj Mahal
☛ What is the nickname of Bibi-ka-Maqbara? → Mini Taj Mahal

q: King Simhavishnu belonged to the ______ dynasty.
qs.e: King Simhavishnu was a prominent ruler of the Pallava dynasty. He is considered the founder of the Pallava empire in the late 6th century. Simhavishnu revived Pallava power and made Kanchipuram his capital. He defeated the Kalabhras and expanded the Pallava kingdom. During his reign, Pallava architecture flourished, and he was the father of Mahendravarman I. The Pallava dynasty holds a significant place in South Indian history.
qs.kf:
☛ Capital of Pallava dynasty → Kanchipuram
☛ Last ruler of Pallava dynasty → Aparajitavarman
☛ Major rivals of Pallavas → Chalukyas
☛ Author of Mattavilasa Prahasana (Pallava period) → Mahendravarman I
☛ Famous temple of Pallava style → Kailasanathar Temple (Kanchipuram)

q: The magnificent temple of Khajuraho was built by ________ rulers.
qs.e: The Khajuraho temples were built by the Chandel rulers. These temples are located in the Chhatarpur district of Madhya Pradesh and are renowned for their Nagara-style architecture and erotic sculptures. The Chandellas constructed these temples between the 9th and 12th centuries AD. The Khajuraho group of temples is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Originally, there were about 85 temples, of which only 22 remain today. The Kandariya Mahadeva Temple is the largest and most magnificent temple in the complex. The Chandel dynasty was ended by Qutb-ud-din Aibak of the Delhi Sultanate.
qs.kf:
☛ What style are the Khajuraho temples built in? → Nagara style
☛ Which is the largest temple in Khajuraho? → Kandariya Mahadeva Temple
☛ What was the capital of the Chandel dynasty? → Khajuraho and Mahoba
☛ Who was the last ruler of the Chandel dynasty? → Kirtivarman
☛ When was Khajuraho declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site? → 1986

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (19/06/2025) Shift 1
q: Which powerful ruler of the Pallavas constructed the Shore Temple at Mahabalipuram?
qs.e: The Shore Temple at Mahabalipuram was built by the powerful Pallava ruler Narasimhavarman II (also known as Rajasimha) in the 8th century. This temple is a rock-cut structure dedicated to Lord Shiva. Narasimhavarman II is known for his patronage of art and architecture; he also built the Kailasanathar Temple at Kanchipuram. The Shore Temple is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site group of monuments at Mahabalipuram. It is renowned for its intricate carvings and picturesque location on the shores of the Bay of Bengal.
qs.kf:
☛ Who built the Shore Temple at Mahabalipuram? → Narasimhavarman II (Rajasimha)
☛ Who was the last powerful ruler of the Pallava dynasty? → Narasimhavarman II
☛ Who built the Kailasanathar Temple at Kanchipuram? → Narasimhavarman II
☛ What was the capital of the Pallava dynasty? → Kanchipuram
☛ Which god is the Shore Temple at Mahabalipuram dedicated to? → Shiva

q: Which of the following is NOT an important monument inside the Daulatabad Fort Maharashtra, India?
qs.e: Daulatabad Fort is a historic fort located in Aurangabad district of Maharashtra, India. Inside the fort, there are several important monuments including Jami Masjid, Bharatmata Mandir, and Chand Minar. Jami Masjid is an ancient mosque, while Chand Minar is a tall minaret that enhances the fort's beauty. Bharatmata Mandir is also situated within the fort premises. However, Sikandra Fort is not located inside Daulatabad Fort; it is a separate fort situated in Agra. Therefore, Sikandra Fort is NOT an important monument inside Daulatabad Fort.
qs.kf:
☛ Daulatabad Fort is located in which state? → Maharashtra
☛ Main minaret inside Daulatabad Fort? → Chand Minar
☛ Mosque inside Daulatabad Fort? → Jami Masjid
☛ Where is Sikandra Fort located? → Agra
☛ Old name of Daulatabad Fort? → Devagiri

q: Select the INCORRECT combination of the books and their respective authors.
qs.e: The author of Tughlaq Nama is Amir Khusro, not Abul Fazal. Abul Fazal is the author of Akbarnama and Ain-i-Akbari. Prithviraj Raso was composed by Chand Bardai, a court poet of Prithviraj Chauhan. Gita Govinda is a famous Sanskrit poetic work by Jayadeva Goswami, centered on the love of Radha and Krishna. Baburnama is the autobiography of Babur, written by himself in Turkish and later translated into Persian. Thus, only the combination of Tughlaq Nama is incorrect.
qs.kf:
☛ Author of Prithviraj Raso → Chand Bardai
☛ Author of Akbarnama → Abul Fazal
☛ Author of Gita Govinda → Jayadeva Goswami
☛ Author of Baburnama → Babur
☛ Author of Tughlaq Nama → Amir Khusro

q: After visiting India and learning about Indian culture, Al-Biruni wrote which book?
qs.e: Al-Biruni (973-1048 AD) was a great Persian scholar, mathematician, and historian. He accompanied Mahmud of Ghazni to India and stayed here for about 13 years. He deeply studied Indian culture, religion, philosophy, science, and society. As a result of this study, he wrote the famous book 'Kitab-Ul-Hind' (or 'Tarikh-Ul-Hind') in Arabic. This book presents a detailed account of India's social, religious, and scientific life. In this text, Al-Biruni shed light on Indian philosophy, astronomy, mathematics, medicine, and customs. This book is considered an important source for understanding medieval Indian history and culture.
qs.kf:
☛ Full name of Al-Biruni → Abu Rayhan Muhammad ibn Ahmad al-Biruni
☛ During whose reign did Al-Biruni visit India → Mahmud of Ghazni
☛ Language of Kitab-Ul-Hind → Arabic
☛ Other name of Kitab-Ul-Hind → Tarikh-Ul-Hind
☛ Apart from India, Al-Biruni wrote on which subjects → Mathematics, Astronomy, Geography

q: What was a major administrative feature in the military governance system of early South Indian kingdoms, such as the Chalukyas and Rashtrakutas?
o: Feudatory chiefs were assigned military and administrative duties
Temple authorities directly recruited soldiers for village defence
District leaders were rotated annually by royal decree
Military governance was entirely centralised under the royal council
qs.e: A major administrative feature in the military governance system of early South Indian kingdoms like the Chalukyas and Rashtrakutas was the assignment of military and administrative duties to feudatory chiefs. These chiefs, known as 'Mandaleshwar' or 'Rashtrapati', were responsible for tax collection, justice, local peace, and overseeing military campaigns in their territories. They provided military support to the king in exchange for land grants and political autonomy. This system facilitated the expansion of the empire by incorporating local chiefs into governance, leading to decentralization of administration. It was a kind of feudal structure that strengthened the central military rule. Other options, such as recruitment by temple authorities or annual rotation of district leaders, were not key features of these kingdoms. Military governance was not entirely centralized under the royal council; instead, it was decentralized through feudatory chiefs.
qs.kf:
☛ What were the feudatory chiefs called in Chalukya administration? → Mandaleshwar or Rashtrapati
☛ What was the land grant system in the Rashtrakuta empire called? → Shasana or Agrahara
☛ What was the capital of the Chalukyas? → Vatapi (Badami)
☛ Which famous temple was built by the Rashtrakutas? → Kailasa temple (Ellora)
☛ What was a characteristic of South Indian feudalism? → Decentralization of military and administrative duties

q: Which Chalukya ruler defeated Harshavardhana on the banks of the Narmada?
qs.e: The most powerful ruler of the Chalukya dynasty, Pulakesin II, defeated Harshavardhana on the banks of the Narmada River around 618-619 CE. This battle took place between the Chalukyas of Vatapi (modern Badami, Karnataka) and Harshavardhana of Kannauj. Pulakesin II expanded the Chalukya empire in southern India and made his capital Vatapi a powerful center. His victories are described in the Aihole inscription (634 CE) by Ravikirti. Preventing Harshavardhana from crossing the Narmada was a testament to Pulakesin II's military superiority. After this battle, Pulakesin II assumed titles like Parameshwara and Dakshinapateshwara. He is considered the greatest ruler of the Chalukya dynasty.
qs.kf:
☛ Founder of the Chalukya dynasty → Jayasimha
☛ Court poet of Pulakesin II → Ravikirti
☛ Language and script of Aihole inscription → Sanskrit and Kannada
☛ Capital of Harshavardhana → Kannauj
☛ Capital of the Chalukyas → Vatapi

q: The Rashtrakutas were primarily known for which architectural marvel?
qs.e: The Rashtrakuta ruler Krishna I (756-773 CE) built the Kailasa Temple at Ellora, Maharashtra. This temple is a monolithic structure carved out of a single rock and is considered a masterpiece of Indian architecture. The temple is 84 feet high and 154 feet long, aligned north-south, and built in the rathakara style. It took about 8,000 laborers 18 years to complete. The Ellora caves are a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The Rashtrakutas also patronized Buddhist, Jain, and Hindu faiths. The Kailasa Temple is dedicated to Lord Shiva and is known for its intricate sculptures and massive size.
qs.kf:
☛ Who built the Kailasa Temple? → Rashtrakuta king Krishna I
☛ How many caves are there at Ellora? → 34 caves
☛ What is the height of Kailasa Temple? → 84 feet
☛ Who founded the Rashtrakuta dynasty? → Dantidurga
☛ What is the architectural style of Kailasa Temple? → Rathakara style

q: Which 13th-century 1193 CE monument was built by Qutb-ud-din Aibak?
qs.e: The construction of Qutub Minar was started by Qutb-ud-din Aibak in 1193 CE. Located in Delhi, this historic minaret is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The height of Qutub Minar is approximately 73 meters with 379 steps. It is built of red sandstone and marble, adorned with intricate carvings and inscriptions in Arabic and Nagari scripts. Qutb-ud-din Aibak established the Delhi Sultanate and was the first ruler of the Slave Dynasty. Qutub Minar was not built by Mughals but during the Sultanate period.
qs.kf:
☛ Who started the construction of Qutub Minar? → Qutb-ud-din Aibak
☛ What is the height of Qutub Minar? → Approximately 73 meters
☛ How many steps are in Qutub Minar? → 379
☛ What material is Qutub Minar made of? → Red sandstone and marble
☛ Which dynasty is Qutb-ud-din Aibak associated with? → Slave Dynasty

q: The Chalukya Utsava was revived in December 2025 in which of the following historic regions?
qs.e: In December 2025, the Chalukya Utsava was revived on a large scale in Badami, Karnataka. This festival showcases the cultural and historical heritage of the Chalukya dynasty. Badami, formerly known as Vatapi, served as the capital of the Chalukyas. The Badami Cave Temples and other structures here are prime examples of Chalukya architecture. The festival included dance, music, and cultural programs aimed at preserving the art and culture of this ancient dynasty. The event was also intended to boost tourism in the region.
qs.kf:
☛ Capital of Chalukya dynasty → Badami
☛ Ancient name of Badami → Vatapi
☛ Language of Chalukya dynasty → Kannada
☛ Badami Cave Temples belong to which dynasty → Chalukya
☛ Month of Chalukya Utsava revival → December

q: Which language was predominantly used by Amir Khusrau in his literary compositions during the Delhi Sultanate period?
qs.e: Amir Khusrau (1253-1325 CE) was a great poet, musician, and scholar of the Delhi Sultanate period. He is known for composing in both Hindavi (early Hindi-Urdu) and Persian, but his major literary works are predominantly in Persian, which was the court and literary language of that time. Khusrau authored famous works like 'Tughlaq Nama', 'Khazain ul-Futuh', and 'Afzal ul-Fawaid', all in Persian. He also contributed to music, inventing the khyal and tarana styles. While he wrote some poetry in Hindavi, his most significant and celebrated compositions are in Persian.
qs.kf:
☛ Birth year of Amir Khusrau → 1253 CE
☛ Name of Amir Khusrau's spiritual guide → Nizamuddin Auliya
☛ Major Persian work by Amir Khusrau → Tughlaq Nama
☛ Royal patron of Amir Khusrau → Sultan Alauddin Khalji
☛ Title given to Amir Khusrau → Tuti-e-Hind (Parrot of India)

q: The Pallava dynasty had its capital at which of the following places?
qs.e: The Pallava dynasty was a prominent South Indian dynasty that ruled from approximately 275 CE to 897 CE. Their capital was Kanchipuram (in present-day Tamil Nadu), also known as 'Kanchi'. This city was a center of learning, art, and religion. The Pallava rulers built many temples here, including the Kailasanathar Temple and Vaikuntha Perumal Temple. They promoted Dravidian architecture and their inscriptions are found in Sanskrit and Tamil languages. Other options: Vatapi and Badami were capitals of the Chalukya dynasty, while Madurai was the capital of the Pandya dynasty.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the founder of the Pallava dynasty? → Simhavishnu
☛ Who was the greatest Pallava ruler? → Narasimhavarman I
☛ What script did the Pallavas use? → Grantha script
☛ Which famous Sanskrit play was written during the Pallava period? → Mattavilasa Prahasana
☛ Who was the last Pallava ruler? → Aparajita Varman

q: Vijayalaya, the founder of the Chola dynasty, was the first feudal -
qs.e: The founder of the Chola dynasty, Vijayalaya, was initially a feudatory of the Pallavas. He ruled under the Pallava supremacy during the mid-9th century and later captured Thanjavur and established the Chola kingdom. Vijayalaya built the Nishumbhasudini temple at Thanjavur. The Chola dynasty went on to rule over much of South India for about four centuries, known for their administrative efficiency, literature, and temple architecture. The Pallavas had a major influence on early Chola art and culture. The Chola Empire reached its zenith under kings like Rajaraja I and Rajendra I.
qs.kf:
☛ Who founded the Chola dynasty? → Vijayalaya
☛ Vijayalaya was a feudatory of which dynasty? → Pallavas
☛ What was the capital of the Cholas? → Thanjavur
☛ Which temple did Vijayalaya build? → Nishumbhasudini temple
☛ What time period did the Cholas rule? → 9th to 13th century

q: Where did Rani Lakshmi Bai die fighting the British?
A. Varanasi
B. Gwalior
C. Morar
D. Jhansi
qs.e: Rani Lakshmi Bai was born in 1828 in Varanasi. She played a pivotal role in the 1857 Rebellion. After defending Jhansi, she moved to Kalpi and then to Gwalior. On 17 June 1858, she died fighting the British at Kotah-ki-Sarai or Kundhdan field in Gwalior. Varanasi is her birthplace, Jhansi her kingdom, Kalpi is where she met Tatya Tope, while Morar is a place in Gwalior where the army revolted. Her martyrdom took place in Gwalior.
qs.kf:
☛ Rani Lakshmi Bai's birthplace → Varanasi
☛ Place of her death → Gwalior
☛ Date of her death → 17 June 1858
☛ Name of her husband → Raja Gangadhar Rao
☛ Her adopted son → Damodar Rao

q: The Battle of Gulnabad was led by Mahmud Hotaki and fought in the year _____.
qs.e: The Battle of Gulnabad was fought in the year 1722. It was led by Mahmud Hotaki. This battle took place between the Safavid dynasty of Iran and the Afghan Hotaki dynasty. Mahmud Hotaki defeated the Safavid ruler Shah Husain in this war, gaining control over Iran and capturing Isfahan. After this victory, Mahmud Hotaki declared himself the Shah of Iran. This battle is an important event in Afghan history, as it established the power of the Hotaki dynasty.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Battle of Gulnabad fought? → 1722
☛ Who led the Battle of Gulnabad? → Mahmud Hotaki
☛ Between which groups was the Battle of Gulnabad fought? → Safavid dynasty and Hotaki dynasty
☛ Whom did Mahmud Hotaki defeat? → Shah Husain
☛ After the victory at Gulnabad, what did Mahmud Hotaki do? → Declared himself Shah of Iran

q: In Indian history, who was called "Badshah Khan"?
qs.e: Khan Abdul Gaffar Khan was known as 'Badshah Khan' or 'Frontier Gandhi'. He was a freedom fighter and Pashtun leader who led a non-violent movement. He founded the Khudai Khidmatgar (Red Shirt movement), which was associated with the Indian National Congress. Inspired by Mahatma Gandhi, he spread the message of non-violence and unity. He opposed the partition of India and raised his voice regarding Jammu and Kashmir. He was awarded the Bharat Ratna in 1987.
qs.kf:
☛ What was the nickname of Khan Abdul Gaffar Khan? → Frontier Gandhi
☛ Who started the Khudai Khidmatgar movement? → Khan Abdul Gaffar Khan
☛ Which national award did Khan Abdul Gaffar Khan receive? → Bharat Ratna (1987)
☛ When did Badshah Khan die? → 20 January 1988
☛ Which region is associated with Badshah Khan? → Present-day Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (Pakistan)

q: Who built the celestial observatory in Jantar Mantar in Delhi?
qs.e: The Jantar Mantar in Delhi is an astronomical observatory built by Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II in 1724 AD. He was a Kachwaha Rajput ruler of Amber (Jaipur). Jai Singh II constructed five observatories across India: Delhi, Jaipur, Ujjain, Mathura, and Varanasi. The Delhi observatory houses various instruments to measure celestial positions, such as the Samrat Yantra and Jai Prakash Yantra. It represents a significant post-Mughal scientific structure.
qs.kf:
☛ Who built the Jantar Mantar in Delhi? → Jai Singh II
☛ How many observatories did Jai Singh II build? → Five
☛ When was Delhi Jantar Mantar built? → 1724 AD
☛ Jai Singh II was the ruler of which state? → Amber (Jaipur)
☛ What is the purpose of Jantar Mantar? → Astronomical observation and calculation

q: Which of the following was the capital of Satavahana Dynasty?
qs.e: The Satavahana dynasty (230 BCE – 220 CE) was a prominent ancient Indian dynasty ruling the Deccan region. Its capital was Pratishthana, now known as Paithan, located on the banks of the Godavari River in Aurangabad district, Maharashtra. The Satavahanas rose to power after the decline of the Mauryan Empire and ruled for about 450 years. They were patrons of Buddhism and promoted the Prakrit language. During their rule, important art centers like Amaravati and Nagarjunakonda flourished. Other options: Taxila (capital of Gandhara), Pataliputra (Mauryan capital), Ujjain (important in Gupta period).
qs.kf:
☛ Capital of Satavahana Dynasty → Paithan (Pratishthana)
☛ Patronage of Satavahanas → Buddhism and Prakrit language
☛ Most famous Satavahana ruler → Gautamiputra Satakarni
☛ Stupa built during Satavahana period → Amaravati Stupa
☛ Last Satavahana ruler → Yajna Sri Satakarni

q: Who was the commander-in-chief of Nana Saheb?
qs.e: Nana Saheb was a prominent leader of the 1857 Revolt. His commander-in-chief was Tatya Tope, a skilled warrior and strategist. Tatya Tope fought several important battles against the British during the revolt, including the Battle of Kanpur and the Battle of Gwalior. He was adept at guerrilla warfare and continued to challenge the British for a long time. Eventually, he was captured and executed. Tatya Tope's real name was Ramchandra Pandurang Tope.
qs.kf:
☛ Commander-in-chief of Nana Saheb in 1857 Revolt → Tatya Tope
☛ Birthplace of Tatya Tope → Yola, Pune
☛ Place of execution of Tatya Tope → Shivpuri
☛ Original name of Tatya Tope → Ramchandra Pandurang Tope
☛ Adept in guerrilla warfare → Tatya Tope

q: Who among the following propagated the motto 'Back to the Vedas'?
qs.e: Swami Dayanand Saraswati propagated the motto 'Back to the Vedas'. He founded the Arya Samaj and considered the Vedas as infallible truth. He opposed idol worship, caste system, and child marriage. His famous book is 'Satyarth Prakash'. Through this slogan, he emphasized returning to Vedic culture and pure Hinduism.
qs.kf:
☛ Who founded the Arya Samaj? → Swami Dayanand Saraswati
☛ Who wrote 'Satyarth Prakash'? → Swami Dayanand Saraswati
☛ What was Dayanand's main message? → Back to the Vedas
☛ Which social evils did Dayanand oppose? → Idol worship and caste system
☛ In which state was Dayanand born? → Gujarat

q: In the Pallava administration, which was the smallest administrative unit directly managed by local self-governing assemblies?
qs.e: In the Pallava administration, Ur was the smallest administrative unit directly managed by local self-governing assemblies. It referred to a village or a small settlement. The Pallava system comprised three main territorial divisions: Kottam (district), Nadu (administrative subdivision), and Ur (village). The state was divided into several Kottams for administrative convenience, which were further subdivided into Nadus. The Ur assemblies oversaw local matters such as land management, tax collection, and judicial functions. These autonomous assemblies enabled local control over resources and dispute resolution. Thus, the Ur system ensured effective governance at the grassroots level.
qs.kf:
☛ What was the largest administrative unit under the Pallavas? → Kottam
☛ What was the local assembly in Pallava villages called? → Ur Sabha
☛ What area was managed by the Ur assembly? → A village
☛ What did 'Nadu' mean in Pallava administration? → Administrative subdivision
☛ What modern division corresponds to a Kottam? → District

q: During the Satavahana Empire, the terms 'Ahara' or 'Rashtra' referred to
qs.e: ✅ Correct Answer: (D) District

q: Which of the following administrative features was common to both Pallava and Pandya kingdoms?
o: Division of the kingdom into Mandalams and Nadus
Village assemblies were called Sabha and Ur
qs.e: A common administrative feature of both the Pallava and Pandya kingdoms was that village assemblies were known as Sabha and Ur. In the Pallava kingdom, villages were organized into administrative units, and village assemblies played a key role in local governance. Similarly, in the Pandya kingdom, the same system existed where village assemblies were called Sabha and Ur. The other options are incorrect: rule by elected monarchs was not practiced in either kingdom; the division into Mandalams and Nadus was a characteristic of the Chola dynasty; abolition of land revenue taxes did not occur in these kingdoms. Thus, the correct answer pertains to the nomenclature of village assemblies.
qs.kf:
☛ Capital of Pallava dynasty → Kanchipuram
☛ Capital of Pandya dynasty → Madurai
☛ Famous Pallava ruler → Mahendravarman I
☛ Famous Pandya ruler → Nedunjeliyan
☛ Famous site of Pallava art → Mamallapuram

q: The Battle of Plassey 1757 was fought between the British forces led by Robert Clive and the Nawab of Bengal _____.
qs.e: The Battle of Plassey was fought on 23 June 1757 between the British East India Company and the Nawab of Bengal Siraj-ud-Daula. Led by Robert Clive, the British won with the help of traitors like Mir Jafar. This battle laid the foundation of British rule in India. Siraj-ud-Daula was the grandson of Alivardi Khan and ascended the throne in 1756. He ordered the British not to fortify their positions, which led to conflict. Despite having a larger army, the Nawab was defeated due to betrayal. After the battle, Mir Jafar was made the Nawab of Bengal.
qs.kf:
☛ Date of Battle of Plassey → 23 June 1757
☛ Cause of war → Siraj-ud-Daula's capture of Calcutta (1756)
☛ British commander → Robert Clive
☛ Traitor → Mir Jafar
☛ Outcome → Beginning of British rule in India

q: In Brahmadeya villages under the Pallavas, which caste predominantly managed the local Sabha assemblies?
qs.e: In the Pallava period, Brahmadeya villages were those donated to Brahmanas. The management of the local Sabha assembly in these villages was predominantly carried out by the Brahmana caste. Brahmadeya was a form of land grant where the king tax-free land to Brahmanas, for religious and social reasons. The Sabha was a local self-governing body that oversaw village administration, tax collection, and judicial matters. Brahmanas held a prominent role due to their education and training in religious affairs. This system was a key part of rural administration under the Pallava empire.
qs.kf:
☛ What is Brahmadeya? → Land donated to Brahmanas
☛ Where did the local Sabha exist in Pallava period? → In Brahmadeya villages
☛ Which caste managed the Sabha? → Brahmanas
☛ What was the capital of the Pallavas? → Kanchipuram
☛ Which religion did Pallava kings mainly follow? → Mainly Shaivism

q: Which Indo-Greek ruler's envoy Heliodorus installed a pillar in Vidisha and was a devotee of Lord Krishna?
qs.e: Heliodorus, the envoy of the Indo-Greek ruler Antialkidas, installed a pillar in Vidisha (ancient Bhelsa) in Madhya Pradesh. This pillar is known as the Garuda Pillar and bears an inscription in Brahmi script, where Heliodorus describes himself as a Bhagavata (devotee of Lord Vishnu/Krishna). This shows the influence of Indian religions in the courts of Greek rulers. Antialkidas ruled around 115-95 BCE and was the ruler of the western part of the Indo-Greek kingdom. The pillar is also called the Besnagar Pillar. It is a significant archaeological evidence of cultural exchange between India and the Hellenistic world.
qs.kf:
☛ Where is the Heliodorus pillar located? → Vidisha (Madhya Pradesh)
☛ Who was Heliodorus a devotee of? → Lord Vishnu/Krishna (Bhagavata)
☛ In which script is the Heliodorus pillar inscribed? → Brahmi script
☛ Who installed the Garuda pillar? → Heliodorus
☛ Which dynasty did Antialkidas belong to? → Indo-Greek dynasty

q: What was the main source of revenue for the Pallava empire, used for maintaining their army and administrative expenses?
qs.e: In the Pallava empire, the main source of revenue was the land tax, known as 'kara' or 'bhaga'. It was a fixed share of the agricultural produce. This tax funded the army and administrative expenses. The Pallava rulers developed a system of land surveys and records. Agriculture was the primary economic activity, and most of the population were farmers. Besides land tax, other taxes like irrigation tax and craft tax existed, but land tax was the principal source.
qs.kf:
☛ What was the main revenue source of the Pallavas? → Land tax
☛ What was the land tax called in Pallava period? → Kara or Bhaga
☛ What type of tax system did the Pallavas adopt? → Land revenue system
☛ What was the base of the Pallava economy? → Agriculture
☛ Which tax did Pallava rulers survey? → Land tax

q: The five village committees (variyams) such as neernilai variyam and needhi variyam were a unique administrative feature of which of the following dynasties?
qs.e: The Pandya dynasty was one of the ancient Tamil dynasties of South India, with its capital at Madurai. Their administrative system featured five village committees (variyams) at the village level, including Neernilai Variyam (water management) and Needhi Variyam (finance). These committees were responsible for efficient local governance. The Pandyas emphasized local self-government, and these variyams were formed through an electoral process with fixed tenures. This system of village committees was a unique feature of the Pandya administration. Other dynasties like the Guptas, Satavahanas, and Mauryas did not have such well-organized village committees. The variyams managed various aspects of village life and contributed to effective decentralization.
qs.kf:
☛ What was the capital of the Pandya dynasty? → Madurai
☛ What was Neernilai Variyam related to? → Water management
☛ What was the function of Needhi Variyam? → Finance management
☛ How were village committees formed under the Pandyas? → Through elections
☛ What was a unique feature of Pandya administration? → Five village committees (variyams)

q: Which of the following was NOT a kingdom based on the modern-day Tamil Nadu?
qs.e: The Rashtrakuta dynasty was centered in modern-day Karnataka, not Tamil Nadu. The Chola, Chera, and Pandya were three ancient Tamil dynasties that ruled over the Tamil Nadu region. The Chola kingdom was based in the Kaveri Delta, the Chera kingdom in Kerala and western Tamil Nadu, and the Pandya kingdom in southern Tamil Nadu with its capital at Madurai. The Rashtrakutas ruled the Deccan plateau from the 8th to the 10th century, with their capital at Manyakheta (modern Karnataka). Thus, the Rashtrakutas were not a kingdom based in Tamil Nadu.
qs.kf:
☛ Capital of Chola Empire → Thanjavur
☛ Capital of Pandya Empire → Madurai
☛ Capital of Chera Empire → Vanji (Kerala)
☛ Capital of Rashtrakuta Empire → Manyakheta (Karnataka)
☛ Founder of Rashtrakuta dynasty → Dantidurga

q: Rajendra Chola I is known for his naval expeditions on the revived Sri Vijaya empire of:
qs.e: Rajendra Chola I (reigned 1014-1044 CE) was one of the greatest rulers of the Chola dynasty. He built a powerful navy and conducted naval expeditions in Southeast Asia. His most famous campaign was against the Sri Vijaya empire, which was centered on the island of Sumatra in present-day Indonesia. The Sri Vijaya empire was a major maritime trading power. Rajendra Chola attacked and defeated the ports of Sri Vijaya, extending Chola influence into Southeast Asia. This campaign is mentioned in the Thanjavur inscription.
qs.kf:
☛ Reign of Rajendra Chola I → 1014-1044 CE
☛ Where is Sri Vijaya empire located today? → Indonesia (Sumatra)
☛ Chola king who attacked Sri Vijaya → Rajendra Chola I
☛ Against which empire did Rajendra Chola's naval expedition take place? → Sri Vijaya empire
☛ Capital of Chola empire → Thanjavur

q: On which of the following states of India did Siraj-ud-Daula, Mir Jafar and Mir Qasim rule in the 18th century?
qs.e: In the 18th century, the three prominent Nawabs of Bengal were Siraj-ud-Daula (1756–1757), Mir Jafar (1757–1760), and Mir Qasim (1760– 1763). Siraj-ud-Daula was the last independent Nawab of Bengal. He lost his throne after his defeat in the Battle of Plassey in 1757 against Robert Clive. Mir Jafar was installed as the Nawab by the East India Company, but later replaced by Mir Qasim. Mir Qasim faced defeat in the Battle of Buxar in 1764. All three rulers governed the Bengal region, which included present-day West Bengal, Bangladesh, and parts of Bihar.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Battle of Plassey fought? → 1757
☛ Who installed Mir Jafar as Nawab? → Robert Clive
☛ Who was defeated in the Battle of Buxar? → Mir Qasim
☛ Who was the last independent Nawab of Bengal in the 18th century? → Siraj-ud-Daula
☛ Which region did Mir Jafar rule? → Bengal

q: Who was the last ruler of the Chola dynasty?
qs.e: The last ruler of the Chola dynasty was Rajendra Chola III (1246–1279 CE). During his reign, the Chola empire began to decline. He was not as powerful as his predecessors, and the empire gradually shrank. Eventually, the Pandyas defeated the Cholas and captured their territories. After Rajendra Chola III, the Chola dynasty came to an end. The Chola dynasty was founded by Vijayalaya Chola in the 9th century, and its greatest rulers were Rajaraja Chola I and Rajendra Chola I.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the founder of the Chola dynasty? → Vijayalaya Chola
☛ Who was the greatest Chola ruler? → Rajaraja Chola I
☛ What caused the decline of the Chola empire? → Invasions by Pandyas and Hoysalas
☛ What was the capital of the Chola dynasty? → Thanjavur
☛ Which city was founded by Rajendra Chola I? → Gangaikonda Cholapuram

q: Who fought the Battle of Plassey against the East India Company?
qs.e: The Battle of Plassey was fought on 23 June 1757 between the Nawab of Bengal Siraj-ud-Daula and the British East India Company. The conflict arose mainly due to the Nawab's succession dispute and the Company's growing influence. The Company's forces were led by Robert Clive. The Nawab's commander Mir Jafar betrayed him by ordering the army to retreat, giving the British an easy victory. The British suffered only 23 casualties, while the Nawab's forces faced heavy losses. This victory laid the foundation of British rule in India and enabled the Company to intervene in Bengal's politics.
qs.kf:
☛ Date of Battle of Plassey → 23 June 1757
☛ British commander in the battle → Robert Clive
☛ Traitor commander of the Nawab → Mir Jafar
☛ Main cause of the battle → Succession dispute and trade rights
☛ New Nawab of Bengal after Plassey → Mir Jafar

q: Which of the following places was made the capital of the Rashtrakutas by Dantidurga?
qs.e: The founder of the Rashtrakuta dynasty, Dantidurga, made Manyakheta (present-day Malkhed in Karnataka) his capital. After defeating the Chalukyas in the 8th century, Dantidurga established the Rashtrakuta empire and declared Manyakheta as its capital. This city later flourished under rulers like Amoghavarsha I and became a major political and cultural center in the Deccan region. Manyakheta remained the capital for most of the Rashtrakuta rule, from which they controlled large parts of southern and central India.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the founder of the Rashtrakuta dynasty? → Dantidurga
☛ What was the capital of the Rashtrakutas? → Manyakheta (Malkhed)
☛ Which dynasty did Dantidurga defeat to establish his empire? → Chalukyas
☛ Who was a famous Rashtrakuta ruler? → Amoghavarsha I
☛ With which region are the Rashtrakutas associated? → Deccan

q: Which of the following was NOT a part of Shailendra Empire, founded in the South East Asia, in the 8th Century CE?
qs.e: The Shailendra Empire was a prominent maritime empire in Southeast Asia from the 8th to 9th century CE, controlling key trade routes. It was primarily centered on the islands of Java and Sumatra, where it built magnificent Buddhist monuments like Borobudur. The Shailendra rulers also exerted influence over the Malay Peninsula and parts of Champa. However, Sri Lanka was never part of this empire; it was under the Anuradhapura Kingdom and was a separate political entity, though there were trade and cultural exchanges between the two regions.
qs.kf:
☛ Where was the Shailendra Empire centered? → Java and Sumatra
☛ Famous Buddhist stupa built by Shailendra kings? → Borobudur
☛ Which religion did the Shailendra dynasty patronize? → Buddhism (Mahayana)
☛ Century of Shailendra Empire's establishment? → 8th Century CE
☛ Regions under Shailendra rule? → Java, Sumatra, Malay Peninsula, Champa

q: The kings of which among the following dynasties defeated the kings of Malaya, Java and Sumatra?
qs.e: The rulers of the Chola dynasty defeated the kings of Malaya, Java and Sumatra. The Chola Empire expanded its influence to Southeast Asia through its powerful navy. The most famous Chola emperor, Rajendra Chola I, in the 11th century, invaded and defeated the Srivijaya Empire, which controlled Malaya, Java and Sumatra. This expedition is known as the Kedah expedition. The Chola navy was one of the strongest in the region, dominating the Bay of Bengal and establishing Chola supremacy in Southeast Asia. The Pandya, Rashtrakuta and Chera dynasties did not possess such naval power or reach.
qs.kf:
☛ What is the name of Rajendra Chola's Southeast Asian campaign? → Kedah expedition
☛ What was the capital of the Chola dynasty? → Thanjavur
☛ Who was the greatest Chola emperor? → Raja Raja Chola I
☛ Which empire did the Cholas defeat in Southeast Asia? → Srivijaya Empire
☛ Who founded the Chola dynasty? → Vijayalaya Chola

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (10/06/2025) Shift 3
q: Who was the head of the Kayastha community?
qs.e: In ancient India, the head of the Kayastha community was called Prathamakayastha. This position was the chief of administrative and accounting functions. The term is found in inscriptions of the Gupta period. Under Prathamakayastha, other Kayasthas worked. Uparika was a provincial governor, Pustapala was the keeper of records, and Prathamakulika was not the head of a community. Thus, the head of the Kayastha community was known as Prathamakayastha.
qs.kf:
☛ What was the head of the Kayastha community called? → Prathamakayastha
☛ What did Prathamakulika refer to? → Head of clans
☛ In which period was the post of Uparika prevalent? → Gupta period
☛ What was the function of Pustapala? → To protect records and documents
☛ In which text is the term Kayastha mentioned? → Brihaspati Smriti

q: Which of the following empires had their own ancient harbor in Korki?
qs.e: The ancient harbor of Korki (Korkai) belonged to the Pandya Empire. Located on the coast of Tamil Nadu, Korkai was famous for pearl fishing and trade with the Roman Empire. It also served as an early capital of the Pandyas. Ancient Tamil literature mentions Korkai as a significant port. Other empires like Pallava, Chola, and Chera had their own harbors such as Kaveripattinam (Chola), Muziris (Chera), and Mamallapuram (Pallava), but Korkai is specifically associated with the Pandya dynasty.
qs.kf:
☛ Which empire had the ancient harbor of Korkai? → Pandya
☛ What was the capital of the Pandya empire? → Madurai (later), Korkai (early)
☛ Which Tamil ports were famous for Roman trade? → Korkai, Muziris, Arikamedu
☛ Pandya's famous port → Korkai
☛ Korkai is located at the mouth of which river? → Thamirabarani

q: The founder of the Chola empire, Vijayalaya, was the feudatory of which of the following South Indian powers?
qs.e: The founder of the Chola empire, Vijayalaya, was originally a feudatory of the Pallava rulers. In the mid-9th century, he captured Thanjavur and laid the foundation of the Chola empire. The Pallava dynasty was a major South Indian power that ruled from the 3rd to the 9th century. Vijayalaya served as a vassal under the Pallava king Nandivarman III. Gradually gaining strength, he conquered the region north of the Kaveri River and established the Chola empire. This event marks the rise of the medieval Chola dynasty in Indian history.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the founder of the Chola empire? → Vijayalaya
☛ Vijayalaya was a feudatory of which dynasty? → Pallavas
☛ Who was the last great Pallava king? → Nandivarman III
☛ Which city became the capital of the Cholas? → Thanjavur
☛ Under whom did the medieval Chola empire reach its zenith? → Rajaraja I

q: Which of the following was the correct ascending order of administration units of the Rashtrakuta dynasty?
qs.e: The ascending order of administrative units under the Rashtrakuta dynasty was Bhukti, Vishaya, and Rashtra. The smallest unit was Bhukti, equivalent to a district. Above it was Vishaya, a group of several Bhuktis. The largest unit was Rashtra, functioning as a province. Thus, the correct ascending order is Bhukti < Vishaya < Rashtra. The Rashtrakuta empire flourished in South and Central India from the 6th to the 10th century, with its capital at Manyakheta (modern Malkhed). The king was supreme, aided by a council of ministers.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the founder of the Rashtrakuta dynasty? → Dantidurga
☛ What was the capital of the Rashtrakutas? → Manyakheta
☛ Which Rashtrakuta ruler built the Kailash Temple at Ellora? → Krishna I
☛ Which language was patronized by the Rashtrakutas? → Kannada
☛ What was the smallest administrative unit in the Rashtrakuta period? → Bhukti

name: Set 1 · Q1–41
