q: The final war of Wandivash was fought between whom?
qs.e: The Battle of Wandivash was fought in 1760 between the English and the French in India. It was the final and decisive battle of the Carnatic Wars. In this battle, the English forces led by Sir Eyre Coote defeated the French forces under Comte de Lally. This victory permanently weakened the French power in India and strengthened British dominance. Wandivash (or Vandavasi) is located in present-day Tamil Nadu's Tiruvannamalai district. After this battle, the French were confined to only small territories in India.
qs.kf:
☛ When did the Battle of Wandivash take place? → 1760
☛ Who was the English commander? → Sir Eyre Coote
☛ Who was the French commander? → Comte de Lally
☛ Which war was it a part of? → The Third Carnatic War
☛ Which Nawab of Carnatic supported the English? → Muhammad Ali Wallajah

q: Which of the following started the Goa Carnival in India?
qs.e: The Goa Carnival was started by the Portuguese in the 18th century. It is an annual festival celebrated before Lent, the Christian fasting period. Goa was under Portuguese rule for about 500 years, and Portuguese influence is evident in its culture, cuisine, and festivals. The carnival features colorful parades, music, dance, and traditional costumes. It is based on the Portuguese tradition called 'Entrudo'. The festival symbolizes Goa's rich cultural heritage and attracts tourists from all over the world.
qs.kf:
☛ Who started the Goa Carnival? → Portuguese
☛ On which tradition is Goa Carnival based? → Entrudo
☛ Before which period is Goa Carnival celebrated? → Lent
☛ How long did Portuguese rule in Goa? → About 500 years
☛ What does Goa Carnival include? → Colorful parades, music, dance, and traditional costumes

q: Where was the ﬁrst session of the Indian National Congress?
qs.e: The first session of the Indian National Congress was held from 28 to 31 December 1885 at Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College in Bombay (now Mumbai). The session was presided over by Womesh Chandra Bonnerjee. A total of 72 delegates attended the session. The INC was founded by Allan Octavian Hume, a retired British civil servant. Initially, its aim was to seek reforms from the British government, not to attain independence. Subsequent sessions were held in Kolkata, Madras, Allahabad, etc.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the first session of INC held? → 1885
☛ Who was the president of the first session? → Womesh Chandra Bonnerjee
☛ Who founded the INC? → A.O. Hume
☛ How many delegates attended the first session? → 72
☛ Where is Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College located? → Bombay

q: Where was the ﬁrst session of the Indian National Congress?
qs.e: The first session of the Indian National Congress (INC) was held on December 28, 1885 at Bombay (now Mumbai) in the Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College. The session was presided over by Womesh Chandra Bonnerjee and was attended by 72 delegates. The INC was founded by A.O. Hume, a retired British civil servant, with the aim of creating a platform for educated Indians to exchange views and cooperate with the British government. The first session primarily discussed political rights, administrative reforms, and Indian participation in civil services. This session is considered the foundation of the Indian national movement.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the first president of INC? → Womesh Chandra Bonnerjee
☛ When was INC founded? → 1885
☛ Who founded INC? → A.O. Hume
☛ How many delegates attended the first session? → 72
☛ Where was the first INC session held? → Bombay

q: The inspiration of Liberty, Equality and Fraternity was derived from ________
qs.e: The ideals of Liberty, Equality and Fraternity were derived from the French Revolution (1789). This slogan became the cornerstone of the revolution and later inspired many constitutions worldwide. The Preamble of the Indian Constitution also enshrines these values. The French Revolution abolished monarchy and established a republic, emphasizing fundamental rights. This ideology influenced Dr. B.R. Ambedkar and other framers of the Indian Constitution.
qs.kf:
☛ What was the main slogan of the French Revolution? → Liberty, Equality, Fraternity
☛ Which words are used in the Preamble of Indian Constitution? → Liberty, Equality, Fraternity
☛ When did the French Revolution occur? → 1789 AD
☛ Who was the President of the Indian Constituent Assembly? → Dr. Rajendra Prasad
☛ From which country was the term 'Fraternity' taken in the Preamble? → France

q: Match the following monuments/places with their exact location. Monuments Place P) Golconda Fort a. Hyderabad Q) Buland Darwaza b. Fatehpur Sikri R) Humayun's Tomb c. New Delhi S) Rani ki Vav d. Patan
A. P-a, Q-b, R-c, S-d B. P-a, Q-c, R-b, S-d C. P-d, Q-b, R-c, S-a D P-d, Q-c, R-b, S-a
qs.e: Golconda Fort is located in Hyderabad, Telangana. Buland Darwaza is located in Fatehpur Sikri, Uttar Pradesh, built by Mughal emperor Akbar to commemorate his victory over Gujarat. Humayun's Tomb is located in New Delhi, built by his widow Haji Begum, and is the first garden tomb in Mughal architecture. Rani ki Vav is located in Patan, Gujarat, built by Queen Udayamati of the Solanki dynasty in the 11th century. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
qs.kf:
☛ Where is Golconda Fort located? → Hyderabad
☛ Where is Buland Darwaza located? → Fatehpur Sikri
☛ Where is Humayun's Tomb located? → New Delhi
☛ Where is Rani ki Vav located? → Patan
☛ Which monument is a UNESCO World Heritage Site? → Rani ki Vav

q: Who among the following is known as the Father of Civil Services in India?
A. Lord Cornwallis
B. Warren Hastings
C. Lord Wellesley
D. Lord William Bentinck
qs.e: Lord Cornwallis is known as the Father of Civil Services in India. He served as Governor-General of India from 1786 to 1793 and implemented several reforms to strengthen the administration. He prohibited civil servants from engaging in trade and private gain, laying the foundation for a professional and impartial bureaucracy. He also emphasized merit and hierarchy in appointments in coordination with the Court of Directors. During his tenure, the Permanent Settlement of Bengal was introduced. Thus, he is recognized as the founder of the Indian civil services.
qs.kf:
☛ Who is the Father of Indian Civil Services? → Lord Cornwallis
☛ What did Lord Cornwallis prohibit civil servants from? → Trade and private profit
☛ Under whose tenure was the Permanent Settlement introduced? → Lord Cornwallis
☛ What was Lord Cornwallis's tenure as Governor-General? → 1786-1793
☛ Who laid the foundation of modern bureaucracy in India? → Lord Cornwallis

q: Which of the following incidents took place after the victory of the British in the Battle of Plassey, in 1757?
o: No new buildings and institutions were developed.
Trade of the British East India Company expanded.
The port cities of Madras, Calcutta and Bombay were destroyed.
People stayed away from the colonial cities of Madras, Calcutta and Bombay.
qs.e: The victory of the British in the Battle of Plassey (1757) established their control over Bengal. Following this, the East India Company greatly expanded its commercial activities. They developed port cities like Calcutta, Madras, and Bombay, constructing new buildings, institutions, and trade centers. People were attracted to these colonial cities. Hence, option 2 is correct.
qs.kf:
☛ When did the Battle of Plassey take place? → 1757
☛ Who fought the Battle of Plassey? → Siraj-ud-Daulah and the British
☛ Who led the British in the Battle of Plassey? → Robert Clive
☛ What was the result of the Battle of Plassey? → British control over Bengal
☛ Which company's trade expanded after the Battle of Plassey? → British East India Company

q: Siraj ud-Daulah, the Nawab of Bengal, was defeated in the battle of Plassey in the year:
qs.e: The Battle of Plassey was fought on 23 June 1757 between the Nawab of Bengal, Siraj ud-Daulah, and the British East India Company. The battle was won largely due to the betrayal of the Nawab's commander Mir Jafar. This victory laid the foundation of British rule in India.
qs.kf:
☛ Date of Battle of Plassey → 23 June 1757
☛ Siraj ud-Daulah's commander → Mir Jafar
☛ British commander → Robert Clive
☛ Result of Plassey → British control over Bengal
☛ Successor of Siraj ud-Daulah → Mir Jafar (puppet Nawab)

q: The Subsidiary Alliance was a non-intervention policy devised by _______ in 1798.
qs.e: The Subsidiary Alliance system was devised by Lord Wellesley in 1798. It was a non-intervention policy that placed Indian states under British protection. Under this system, the Indian ruler had to disband his own army and accept British troops for his state's protection. The state had to pay for the maintenance of the British troops or cede territory. Lord Wellesley (1798-1805) was the Governor-General of British India and through this policy he expanded British influence across India. Several states such as Hyderabad, Awadh, Tanjore, etc. came under British control through this alliance. This policy helped the British to establish indirect control over Indian states without direct annexation.
qs.kf:
☛ Who introduced the Subsidiary Alliance? → Lord Wellesley
☛ When was Subsidiary Alliance introduced? → 1798
☛ Which was the first Indian state to accept the Subsidiary Alliance? → Hyderabad
☛ What did the state need to provide under the Subsidiary Alliance? → Subsidy or territory
☛ What British policy was promoted by the Subsidiary Alliance? → Expansionist policy

q: In 1798, who became the Governor General and built a massive palace, Government House, for himself in Calcutta?
qs.e: Lord Wellesley became the Governor-General of India in 1798. He built a massive palace, Government House, in Calcutta (now Kolkata). This building was designed as a symbol of British power. Wellesley is famous for his 'Subsidiary Alliance' policy, under which many Indian states came under British control. During his tenure (1798-1805), British expansion occurred in Mysore, Maratha, and Awadh. Government House is now known as Raj Bhavan.
qs.kf:
☛ Who built Government House in Calcutta? → Lord Wellesley
☛ Subsidiary Alliance system is associated with? → Lord Wellesley
☛ What was Lord Wellesley's tenure? → 1798-1805
☛ Who constructed Raj Bhavan, Kolkata? → Wellesley
☛ In which war did Wellesley defeat Tipu Sultan? → Fourth Anglo-Mysore War (1799)

q: In which year did King George-III establish the Supreme Court in Madras?
qs.e: King George III established the Supreme Court in Madras in 1800. This was part of the judicial system in India during the British East India Company rule. The Madras Supreme Court was the third such court established in the Presidency towns, after Calcutta (1774) and Bombay (1823). It consisted of a Chief Justice and three puisne judges. The court followed English legal procedures and had jurisdiction mainly over Madras city and its surrounding areas. Its establishment aimed to provide better legal remedies and control over the local population under British administration.
qs.kf:
☛ Year of establishment of Madras Supreme Court → 1800
☛ Year of establishment of Calcutta Supreme Court → 1774
☛ Year of establishment of Bombay Supreme Court → 1823
☛ First Supreme Court in India → Calcutta (1774)
☛ First Chief Justice of Madras Supreme Court → Sir Thomas Strange

q: In which year did the East India Company acquire 'Diwani' rights over Bengal and Bihar?
qs.e: The East India Company acquired the Diwani rights over Bengal, Bihar, and Odisha in 1765 from the Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II. This right was obtained after the Battle of Buxar (1764), where the combined forces of Mir Qasim, Shuja-ud-Daulah, and Shah Alam II were defeated. Diwani meant the right to collect revenue. With this, the Company became the de facto ruler of Bengal. This event is considered the foundation of British rule in India. The rights were granted under the Treaty of Allahabad in 1765, giving the Company control over Bengal's revenues.
qs.kf:
☛ When did the Battle of Buxar take place? → 1764
☛ Under which treaty were Diwani rights granted? → Treaty of Allahabad (1765)
☛ Which Mughal emperor granted Diwani? → Shah Alam II
☛ Who was the last independent Nawab of Bengal? → Siraj-ud-Daulah
☛ When did the Battle of Plassey take place? → 1757

q: The song of lament 'the life has gone out of the body' is associated with Nawab ________ of the State of Awadh.
qs.e: This song of lament is associated with the last Nawab of Awadh, Wajid Ali Shah, and his exile. When the British annexed Awadh in 1856, they deposed Wajid Ali Shah and exiled him to Kolkata. His supporters composed this sorrowful song describing the downfall of Awadh. The line 'the life has gone out of the body' metaphorically represents the death of the kingdom. Wajid Ali Shah was a patron of arts, especially Thumri music and Kathak dance.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the last Nawab of Awadh? → Wajid Ali Shah
☛ When did the British annex Awadh? → 1856
☛ Where was Wajid Ali Shah exiled? → Kolkata
☛ Which dance form was patronized by Wajid Ali Shah? → Kathak
☛ Which music style was patronized by Wajid Ali Shah? → Thumri

q: The 'Third Mysore War' was fought between the years:
qs.e: The Third Mysore War (1790-92) was fought between the British East India Company and Tipu Sultan, the ruler of the Mysore Kingdom. The Company was aided by the Maratha Empire and the Nizam of Hyderabad. The main cause of the war was Tipu's expansionist policies and his conflict with the British. The war ended with the Treaty of Seringapatam in 1792, under which Tipu had to cede half of his territory. The territories were divided among the British, Marathas, and the Nizam. This war significantly weakened Tipu's power and increased British influence in South India.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Third Mysore War fought? → 1790-92
☛ Who fought the Third Mysore War? → British East India Company and Tipu Sultan
☛ When was the Treaty of Seringapatam signed? → 1792
☛ Which Mysore War led to Tipu Sultan's defeat? → Third Mysore War
☛ Who were the allies of the British in the Third Mysore War? → Marathas and Nizam

q: In the Battle of Plassey, who led the troops of the British East India Company?
qs.e: The Battle of Plassey was fought on 23 June 1757 between the Nawab of Bengal Siruj-ud-Daulah and the British East India Company. The Company's forces were led by Robert Clive, while the Nawab's army was commanded by Mir Jafar, who was already part of a conspiracy. The Company won the battle, and Mir Jafar was installed as the Nawab of Bengal. This victory laid the foundation of British rule in India.
qs.kf:
☛ Year of Battle of Plassey → 1757
☛ Guardian of Nawab Siraj-ud-Daulah → Alivardi Khan
☛ Company's commander → Robert Clive
☛ Conspirator commander → Mir Jafar
☛ Result of the battle → British victory

q: Which battle laid the foundation of British colonialism in India?
qs.e: The Battle of Plassey was fought on 23 June 1757 between the British East India Company led by Robert Clive and the Nawab of Bengal, Siraj-ud-Daulah. Clive secured victory through conspiracy with Mir Jafar and other traitors. This win granted the Company political dominance in Bengal and extensive trade privileges. The battle is widely regarded as the foundation of British colonial rule in India, as it allowed the Company to gradually expand control over the entire subcontinent.
qs.kf:
☛ Date of Battle of Plassey? → 23 June 1757
☛ Nawab of Bengal at Plassey? → Siraj-ud-Daulah
☛ British commander at Plassey? → Robert Clive
☛ Who became Nawab after Plassey? → Mir Jafar
☛ Significance of Plassey? → Laid foundation of British rule in India

q: During the Quit India Movement, Aruna Asaf Ali hoisted the National Congress Flag in:
qs.e: During the Quit India Movement (1942), Aruna Asaf Ali hoisted the National Congress Flag at Gowalia Tank Maidan in Bombay (now Mumbai) on 9 August 1942. This event is known as the hoisting of the 'flag of independence'. She was a prominent leader of the Indian freedom struggle and led the movement while underground. She was honored with titles like 'Nightingale of India' and 'Grand Old Lady'. Later, she became the first woman Mayor of Delhi.
qs.kf:
☛ Where did Aruna Asaf Ali hoist the flag? → Gowalia Tank Maidan, Bombay
☛ When did the Quit India Movement start? → 8 August 1942, Mumbai
☛ What title was given to Aruna Asaf Ali? → Bharat Kokila (Nightingale of India)
☛ Of which city did Aruna Asaf Ali become the first woman Mayor? → Delhi
☛ Who passed the Quit India resolution? → Indian National Congress

q: When was Goa captured by the Portuguese?
qs.e: The Portuguese captured Goa in 1510 AD under the command of Afonso de Albuquerque. At that time, Goa was under the rule of the Bijapur Sultanate. Albuquerque made Goa the capital of Portuguese India, and it remained a Portuguese colony until 1961. The capture of Goa was a significant milestone in the expansion of the Portuguese Empire, giving them a strong foothold on the western coast of India and control over the spice trade.
qs.kf:
☛ Portuguese capture of Goa → 1510 AD
☛ Portuguese commander → Afonso de Albuquerque
☛ Ruler before capture → Bijapur Sultanate
☛ Liberation of Goa from Portuguese → 1961 AD

q: When did the British army under Eyre Coote defeat Haider Ali at Porto Novo and save Madras?
qs.e: The British army under Sir Eyre Coote defeated Haider Ali at the Battle of Porto Novo (present-day Parangipettai, Tamil Nadu) on 1 July 1781. This battle was part of the Second Anglo-Mysore War (1780-1784). Haider Ali had launched an attack on Madras, but Eyre Coote's decisive victory saved the city and strengthened British dominance in South India. Eyre Coote was a skilled commander known for his tactics in the Carnatic region. After this defeat, Haider Ali's power declined, and he died in 1782, succeeded by his son Tipu Sultan. The battle marked a turning point in the war, preventing Mysore from capturing Madras.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Battle of Porto Novo fought? → 1 July 1781
☛ Who led the British army at Porto Novo against Haider Ali? → Sir Eyre Coote

☛ When did Haider Ali die? → 1782
☛ Which British company did Eyre Coote serve? → British East India Company

q: In which of the following places did the English open their 'factory' in 1611 on east coast of India?
qs.e: In 1611, the English (East India Company) established their first 'factory' on the east coast of India at Masulipatnam (in present-day Andhra Pradesh). This factory was primarily used for trade in textiles and spices. Later, in 1639, the English built Fort St. George in Madras (Chennai). Tuticorin and Yanam were under Dutch and French influence, respectively. The Masulipatnam factory served as a crucial base for English commercial expansion in eastern India.
qs.kf:
☛ First English factory on east coast of India → Masulipatnam (1611)
☛ Fort St. George in Madras established → 1639
☛ Masulipatnam is located in which state → Andhra Pradesh

☛ Yanam was under control of → French

q: Who was the Nawab of Bengal during the Battle of Plassey?
qs.e: The Battle of Plassey was fought in 1757 between the British East India Company and the Nawab of Bengal, Siraj ud-Daulah. This battle marked the beginning of British political control in India. Siraj ud-Daulah ascended the throne in 1756 after his grandfather Alivardi Khan. The main reasons for conflict were the Company's misuse of trade privileges and the fortification of Fort William. During the battle, Mir Jafar, the commander of Siraj's army, betrayed him by siding with the Company. After his defeat, Siraj ud-Daulah was captured and executed, and Mir Jafar was installed as the new Nawab. The Battle of Plassey is a key example of political treachery and the expansion of colonialism in Indian history.
qs.kf:
☛ Year of Battle of Plassey → 1757
☛ Who became Nawab after Siraj ud-Daulah's death? → Mir Jafar
☛ Cause of Battle of Plassey → Dispute over trade privileges
☛ Successor of Alivardi Khan → Siraj ud-Daulah
☛ Leader of Company forces at Plassey → Robert Clive

q: In which city of India did the East India Company set up their first trading center?
qs.e: The East India Company established its first trading center in India at Surat. In 1612, the company obtained permission from Mughal Emperor Jahangir and set up a factory in Surat. Surat was a major port and commercial hub at that time, dealing in spices, textiles, and other goods. This establishment is considered the beginning of British colonial presence in India. Later, the company set up centers in other places like Mumbai, Kolkata, and Madras.
qs.kf:

☛ Mughal emperor who allowed factory at Surat → Jahangir
☛ First Governor of East India Company → Thomas Smythe
☛ First English factory in India → Surat
☛ River on which Surat is located → Tapi River

q: In which year was the British East India Company formed?
qs.e: The British East India Company was founded on 31 December 1600 under a charter granted by Queen Elizabeth I of England. Its full name was the Governor and Company of Merchants of London Trading into the East Indies. The company received a monopoly on trade with India. It was a joint-stock company primarily aimed at trading spices, silk, and other goods. Over time, it became a political power in India, eventually leading to the establishment of British Raj.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the British East India Company founded? → 1600
☛ Who granted the charter? → Elizabeth I
☛ Full name of the company? → Governor and Company of Merchants of London Trading into the East Indies

☛ First factory in India? → Surat (1613)

q: The second Anglo-Mysore war ended under which agreement?
qs.e: The Second Anglo-Mysore War (1780-1784) was fought between the British East India Company and the Kingdom of Mysore under Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan. The war ended in 1784 with the Mangalore Accord, which was signed by the British and Tipu Sultan. This treaty ensured the mutual restoration of territories captured by both sides. It was a significant event in Indian history as it brought temporary peace. However, it did not end Mysore's challenge to British dominance in South India.

☛ Cis-Sutlej region referred to → South of Sutlej

q: In 1759, Ahmed Shah Abdali returned to India to seek revenge from ____________.
qs.e: In 1759, Ahmed Shah Abdali invaded India to seek revenge from the Marathas before the Third Battle of Panipat (1761). The Marathas had interfered in the Punjab region under Abdali's control and removed his governor. Abdali aimed to weaken Maratha power and maintain his dominance. This battle proved decisive for the Maratha Empire, after which Abdali left India.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Third Battle of Panipat fought? → 1761
☛ Which dynasty did Ahmed Shah Abdali belong to? → Durrani Empire
☛ Who founded the Maratha Empire? → Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj
☛ In which battle were the Marathas defeated by Ahmed Shah Abdali? → Third Battle of Panipat
☛ Between whom was the Third Battle of Panipat fought? → Marathas and Ahmed Shah Abdali

q: Who abolished the practice of Sati in India?
qs.e: The practice of Sati was abolished in India by Lord William Bentinck in 1829. Sati involved the immolation of a widow on her husband's funeral pyre. Bentinck declared the practice illegal and punishable as a crime. Social reformer Raja Ram Mohan Roy campaigned against this practice. Due to Bentinck's efforts, this cruel practice was ended. Bentinck served as Governor-General of India from 1828 to 1835.
qs.kf:
☛ When was Sati abolished? → 1829
☛ Who opposed Sati? → Raja Ram Mohan Roy
☛ Lord William Bentinck's tenure → 1828-1835
☛ When was the Child Marriage Restraint Act passed? → 1929
☛ Who enacted the Widow Remarriage Act? → Lord Dalhousie

q: Who among the following Governor Generals is associated with Subsidiary Alliance System?
qs.e: Lord Wellesley (1798-1805) introduced the Subsidiary Alliance System in India. Under this system, Indian states had to maintain British troops and pay for their maintenance. In return, the British government took responsibility for their external defense, but the states lost their internal autonomy and came under British control. The first alliance was signed with the Nizam of Hyderabad in 1798, followed by states like Mysore, Tanjore, Awadh, and the Maratha Empire. Lord Dalhousie is associated with the Doctrine of Lapse, Lord Cornwallis with the Cornwallis Code, and Lord Mayo with financial decentralization.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Governor General introduced the Subsidiary Alliance System? → Lord Wellesley
☛ Which state signed the first Subsidiary Alliance? → Hyderabad (1798)
☛ Which major states accepted the Subsidiary Alliance? → Hyderabad, Mysore, Tanjore, Awadh, Maratha
☛ Which Governor General is associated with the Doctrine of Lapse? → Lord Dalhousie
☛ What is Lord Cornwallis famous for? → Cornwallis Code and Permanent Settlement

q: What was the major impact of British policies on Indian handicrafts?
o: Decline due to competition with British goods
qs.e: The major impact of British policies on Indian handicrafts was their decline. The British turned India into a source of raw materials and a market for British goods. Policies under Lord Wellesley and other Governor-Generals made raw materials expensive for Indian artisans while cheap machine-made British imports flooded the market. Events like the Bengal Famine of 1770 and the trade monopoly of the East India Company further weakened handicrafts. As a result, famous craft centers like Dhaka, Murshidabad, and Varanasi saw their handloom and other artisanal industries destroyed.
qs.kf:
☛ Lord Wellesley → Second Anglo-Maratha War
☛ Bengal Famine of 1770 → Killed about 10 million people
☛ Dhaka Muslin → Industry destroyed by British policies
☛ Trade Monopoly → Policy of British East India Company

q: In 1917, which Irish woman along with Annie Besant and Sarojini Naidu founded the Women's Indian Association (WIA) in Adyar, Madras, to bring awareness among women?
qs.e: Margaret Cousins, an Irish woman, along with Annie Besant and Sarojini Naidu, founded the Women's Indian Association (WIA) in Adyar, Madras in 1917. The aim was to bring political and social awareness among women. It marked a significant beginning of the women's movement in India. Margaret Cousins also actively fought for women's suffrage and was a founding member of the All India Women's Conference. WIA worked in the areas of education, health, and political rights for women.
qs.kf:
☛ When was Women's Indian Association (WIA) founded? → 1917
☛ Where was WIA founded? → Madras (Adyar)
☛ Who were the founders of WIA? → Margaret Cousins, Annie Besant, and Sarojini Naidu
☛ Which country did Margaret Cousins belong to? → Ireland
☛ Which movement did Margaret Cousins notably contribute to? → Women's suffrage movement

q: Which British officer fought in the famous Battle of Chinhat?
qs.e: The Battle of Chinhat was fought on 30 June, 1857 near Lucknow during the Indian Rebellion of 1857. The British forces were led by Henry Lawrence, who was the Resident of Lucknow and Chief Commissioner. He was a British military officer and administrator who played a crucial role in the defense of Lucknow during the rebellion. The British suffered a heavy defeat in this battle, and Lawrence was wounded, dying a few days later. This event was a significant part of the rebellion's early phase.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Battle of Chinhat fought? → 30 June 1857
☛ Which rebellion was it a part of? → Indian Rebellion of 1857
☛ What was Henry Lawrence's position? → Resident of Lucknow
☛ What was the outcome of the battle? → British defeat
☛ When did Henry Lawrence die? → 4 July 1857

q: Which of the following territories was annexed by the British Governor General Lord Dalhousie before the 1857 revolt that fueled the First War of Independence?
qs.e: Lord Dalhousie annexed Awadh in 1856 under the pretext of 'misgovernment', though it was not under the 'Doctrine of Lapse'. The Nawab of Awadh, Wajid Ali Shah, was deposed and exiled. This annexation deeply angered the local nobility, landlords, and soldiers. A large number of soldiers in the Bengal Army were from Awadh, and the annexation directly fueled the 1857 revolt. Dalhousie also annexed other states like Punjab, Assam, and Gwalior during his tenure, but Awadh's annexation was the most significant in causing the rebellion. The annexation of Awadh is considered a major immediate cause of the First War of Independence, as it united various sections of Indian society against British rule.
qs.kf:
☛ Which states were annexed under Dalhousie's Doctrine of Lapse? → Satara, Jhansi, Sambalpur, Baghat, Nagpur
☛ When was Awadh annexed? → February 7, 1856
☛ Who was the last Nawab of Awadh? → Wajid Ali Shah
☛ What excuse did Dalhousie use for annexing Awadh? → Misgovernment
☛ From which region did the maximum number of soldiers in the 1857 revolt come? → Awadh

q: Where was the Battle of Chinhat in 1857 fought?
qs.e: The Battle of Chinhat was fought near Lucknow on 30 June 1857 during the Indian Rebellion of 1857. The battle took place between the British forces led by Sir Henry Lawrence and the rebellious Indian soldiers. The British suffered a decisive defeat, with Lawrence being mortally wounded. This defeat forced the British to retreat to the Residency in Lucknow, where they were besieged. The battle strengthened the rebellion in the Awadh region and became a major event in the history of the revolt. The site of Chinhat is strategically located near Lucknow, and the battle demonstrated the strength of the Indian resistance against British rule.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Battle of Chinhat fought? → 30 June 1857
☛ Who led the British forces at Chinhat? → Sir Henry Lawrence
☛ Which revolt was the Battle of Chinhat a part of? → Indian Rebellion of 1857
☛ Who won the Battle of Chinhat? → The rebel Indian soldiers
☛ Where did the British take shelter after Chinhat? → Lucknow Residency

q: In addition to Awadh, which of the following were the other territories annexed by the British under various pretexts?
qs.e: The British used the 'Doctrine of Lapse' to expand their empire in India. Under this policy, if a princely state's ruler had no son, the state would be annexed by the British Empire. Lord Dalhousie implemented this doctrine most vigorously. Jhansi and Satara were prominent territories annexed by the British under this policy. Jhansi was annexed in 1853, and Satara in 1848. Awadh was annexed in 1856 under the pretext of 'misgovernment'. Assam and Nagaland were annexed through other processes. Mysore and Hyderabad came under British control through the subsidiary alliance system.
qs.kf:
☛ Who implemented the Doctrine of Lapse? → Lord Dalhousie
☛ When was Jhansi annexed by the British? → 1853
☛ When was Satara annexed by the British? → 1848
☛ Under what pretext was Awadh annexed? → Misgovernment (1856)
☛ Under which treaty did Mysore come under British control? → Subsidiary Alliance

q: Who among the following British officers introduced the policy of Subsidiary Alliance, one of the reason of 1857 revolt?
qs.e: The policy of Subsidiary Alliance was introduced by Lord Wellesley (1798-1805). Under this policy, Indian states were required to maintain British troops and bear their expenses, leading to loss of independence. They lost control over foreign relations and accepted British supremacy. This policy brought many states under British control, causing discontent among local rulers. Economic exploitation and cultural interference further fueled public anger, contributing to the 1857 Revolt.
qs.kf:
☛ First state to accept Subsidiary Alliance → Hyderabad
☛ First state to reject Subsidiary Alliance → Mysore
☛ Lord Wellesley's tenure → 1798-1805
☛ Immediate cause of 1857 Revolt → Greased cartridges
☛ Start of the revolt → 10 May 1857, Meerut

q: Womesh Chandra Bonnerjee represented Calcutta University in the Bengal Legislative Council during _________.
qs.e: Womesh Chandra Bonnerjee was the first president of the Indian National Congress. He was a lawyer at the Calcutta High Court and represented Calcutta University in the Bengal Legislative Council. He served as the university's representative in the council during the period 1894-1895. He was also a fellow of Calcutta University. Bonnerjee played a key role in Indian politics and was instrumental in the formation of the Congress. He advocated for constitutional agitation against British rule.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the first president of the Indian National Congress? → Womesh Chandra Bonnerjee
☛ Which university did Womesh Chandra Bonnerjee represent in the Bengal Legislative Council? → Calcutta University
☛ At which High Court did Womesh Chandra Bonnerjee practice as a lawyer? → Calcutta High Court
☛ Where was the first session of the Indian National Congress held? → Bombay
☛ When was Womesh Chandra Bonnerjee born? → 1844

q: The Nizam of Hyderabad accepted British subsidiary alliance under ________________.
qs.e: Lord Wellesley (1798-1805) introduced the Subsidiary Alliance system in India. Under this, the Nizam of Hyderabad accepted the treaty in 1798. The Nizam had to disband his own army and maintain a British army, for whose expenses he had to cede territories. This alliance brought Hyderabad under British control. Lord Wellesley used this policy to subordinate many Indian princely states.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the founder of Subsidiary Alliance? → Lord Wellesley
☛ When did Hyderabad accept Subsidiary Alliance? → 1798
☛ Which was the first state to accept Subsidiary Alliance? → Hyderabad
☛ What was Lord Wellesley's tenure? → 1798-1805
☛ What was the condition of Subsidiary Alliance? → State to maintain British army and pay expenses

q: In which of the following Indian cities was the Prarthana Samaj, which believed in the spiritual equality of all castes, founded in the 19th century?
qs.e: The Prarthana Samaj was founded in Bombay (now Mumbai) in 1867. It was established by Atmaram Pandurang and later led by Keshab Chandra Sen. The society believed in the spiritual equality of all castes and emphasized the removal of caste discrimination. It supported social reforms such as widow remarriage, prevention of child marriage, and women's education. The Prarthana Samaj was inspired by the Brahmo Samaj but was more active in western India. It played a key role in the social reform movement of 19th-century India.
qs.kf:
☛ Founder of Prarthana Samaj → Atmaram Pandurang
☛ Year of establishment → 1867
☛ Place of establishment → Bombay
☛ Main objective → Spiritual equality and abolition of caste discrimination
☛ Key social reform → Widow remarriage and women's education

q: The Dutch East India Company established its first factory in India in _________.
qs.e: The Dutch East India Company (VOC) established its first factory in India at Petapuli in present-day Andhra Pradesh in 1606. The Dutch primarily traded in spices, pepper, and textiles. Later, they established factories at Surat (1616), Nagapattinam (1658), and Cochin (1663). Their main rival in India were the Portuguese. The Dutch influence declined in the 18th century due to Anglo-Dutch rivalry.
qs.kf:
☛ First factory of Dutch East India Company in India → Petapuli (1606)
☛ Second factory established by Dutch in India → Surat (1616)
☛ Major Dutch port in India → Nagapattinam
☛ Full name of Dutch Company → Vereenigde Oost-Indische Compagnie (VOC)
☛ Last Dutch fort in India → Sadras

q: Joseph Francois Dupleix was the governor who led the forces of which of the following European powers?
qs.e: Joseph Francois Dupleix was the governor of the French East India Company and led the French forces in India. He is known for his efforts to expand French influence in India, particularly during the Carnatic Wars (1746-1763). Dupleix formed alliances with local rulers and used military strategy to challenge British dominance. Despite his initial successes, the British ultimately prevailed and established control over India.
qs.kf:
☛ Dupleix was the governor of which European power? → French
☛ Who was the French governor in India? → Joseph Francois Dupleix
☛ Between whom were the Carnatic Wars fought? → British and French
☛ What was Dupleix's main objective? → Expand French influence in India
☛ With which wars is Dupleix associated? → Carnatic Wars

q: Which of the following European powers was the first to arrive in India by sea route?
qs.e: The Portuguese explorer Vasco da Gama was the first European to reach India by sea in 1498. He sailed around the Cape of Good Hope and landed at Calicut (Kerala). Before this, European trade was primarily overland. The Portuguese later established Goa as their main settlement in India. The Dutch, English, and French arrived in India after the Portuguese.
qs.kf:
☛ First European to reach India by sea → Vasco da Gama (Portuguese)
☛ Place where Vasco da Gama landed in India → Calicut (Kerala)
☛ First Portuguese settlement in India → Goa
☛ Second European power to arrive in India → Dutch
☛ Year of discovery of sea route to India → 1498

q: In which of the following years was Indian Universities Act enacted to impose stiff control over Indian Universities?
qs.e: The Indian Universities Act was enacted in 1904 during the tenure of Lord Curzon. The main objective of this Act was to impose strict government control over Indian universities. It brought changes in the governance structure of universities, reduced the number of fellows, and increased government intervention. This Act was introduced to strengthen British government interference in the field of education. Earlier, in 1857, the universities of Calcutta, Madras, and Bombay were established. The 1904 Act brought universities under greater bureaucratic control.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Indian Universities Act enacted? → 1904
☛ Under whose tenure was this Act passed? → Lord Curzon
☛ What was the main objective of the Act? → To increase government control over universities
☛ Which universities were established in 1857? → Calcutta, Madras, Bombay
☛ What did the 1904 Act reduce? → The number of fellows

q: In which of the following years was the first British East India Company founded in India?
qs.e: The British East India Company was founded on December 31, 1600, during the reign of Queen Elizabeth I of England. It was granted the name 'Governor and Company of Merchants of London Trading into the East Indies'. The company received a monopoly on trade with India, valid for 15 years. Sir James Lancaster was its first governor. The primary objective of the company was to trade in spices, silk, cotton cloth, and other goods. Later, this company became the foundation of the British Empire in India.
qs.kf:
☛ British East India Company founded → 1600
☛ Ruler → Queen Elizabeth I
☛ First Governor → Sir James Lancaster
☛ Initial monopoly period → 15 years
☛ Main trade items → Spices, silk, cotton cloth

q: Dating back to 1639-1640 CE, which construction, located in Chennai, India, is historically known as the primary English defense post?
qs.e: Fort St. George was built during 1639-1640 CE by the British East India Company. It is located in Chennai (formerly Madras) and is historically recognized as the first English defense post in India. The construction of this fort laid the foundation for the city of Madras and it became the early administrative center of British India. Sadras Dutch Fort was built by the Dutch, while Fort St. David is located in Cuddalore and Gingee Fort is associated with Maratha rulers. Hence, Fort St. George is the correct answer.
qs.kf:
☛ When was Fort St. George built? → 1639-1640 CE
☛ Where is Fort St. George located? → Chennai (Madras)
☛ Which company built Fort St. George? → British East India Company
☛ Which is the first English fort in India? → Fort St. George
☛ What is the significance of Fort St. George? → Early administrative center of British India

q: Who was the first Portuguese explorer to reach India in 1498, arriving at Calicut on the Malabar Coast?
qs.e: Vasco da Gama was a Portuguese explorer who reached India in 1498 by sea route, arriving at Calicut (now Kozhikode) on the Malabar Coast. His voyage established the first direct sea route from Europe to Asia, giving Portugal control over the spice trade. This event marked a turning point in world history, as it initiated the era of European colonialism in India. Da Gama's expedition was sponsored by King Manuel I of Portugal. He later returned to India as viceroy in 1524. Calicut was a major trading port for spices like pepper and cardamom, which were highly valued in Europe.
qs.kf:
☛ First Portuguese explorer to reach India by sea → Vasco da Gama (1498)
☛ Landing place of Vasco da Gama in India → Calicut (Kerala)
☛ Purpose of Vasco da Gama's voyage to India → Spice trade
☛ Portuguese governor who strengthened Portuguese power in India → Albuquerque
☛ Arab navigator who helped Vasco da Gama return to Portugal → Ibn Majid

q: Which of the following statements regarding the Ryotwari settlement is correct? 1.It was developed by Thomas Munro. 2. The settlement was made directly with the cultivators, not zamindars. 3.It was tested on a small scale in the annexed territories of Tipu. 4. Finding it successful, it was then applied in the Ganga plains. Select the correct combination:
qs.e: The Ryotwari settlement was developed by Thomas Munro, where revenue was collected directly from the cultivators, bypassing zamindars. It was first tested on a small scale in the territories annexed from Tipu Sultan. However, this system was confined to southern India and was not applied in the Ganga plains, where the Permanent Settlement and Mahalwari system were implemented. Thus, statement 4 is incorrect.
qs.kf:
☛ Who developed the Ryotwari system? → Thomas Munro
☛ From whom was revenue collected in Ryotwari? → Directly from cultivators
☛ Where was Ryotwari first tested? → Tipu's territories
☛ Where was Ryotwari not applied? → Ganga plains
☛ Which settlements were applied in Ganga plains? → Permanent and Mahalwari

q: Pondicherry was captured by the Dutch in 1693 but was returned to the French company by the Treaty of Ryswick in _______.
qs.e: Pondicherry was captured by the Dutch in 1693, which was a major blow to the French East India Company. However, under the Treaty of Ryswick signed in 1697, the Dutch returned Pondicherry to the French company. This treaty was concluded to end the Nine Years' War (1688– 1697), which involved several European powers including France and England. According to the Treaty of Ryswick, most territories conquered during the war were restored to their original owners. Thus, Pondicherry was handed back to the French in 1699. The French East India Company later made Pondicherry its main center in India.
qs.kf:
☛ In which year was the Treaty of Ryswick signed? → 1697
☛ What was the duration of the Nine Years' War? → 1688-1697
☛ In which year did the Dutch capture Pondicherry? → 1693
☛ What was the main center of the French East India Company? → Pondicherry
☛ Which treaty ended the Nine Years' War? → Treaty of Ryswick

q: What was the capital of Awadh when it was established in 1722?
qs.e: Awadh was established in 1722 by Saadat Khan (Burhan-ul-Mulk), who became the first Nawab of Awadh after the decline of the Mughal Empire. He made Faizabad his capital, which was about 130 km east of Lucknow. Later, in 1775, Shuja-ud-Daula shifted the capital to Lucknow. Awadh was a prosperous region that became an important independent state as the Mughal Empire weakened. The history of Awadh includes many significant events, including its eventual annexation by the British in 1856. Faizabad was situated on the banks of the Yamuna River and served as a major trading center during that period. The city remained the capital for about 53 years before being replaced by Lucknow.
qs.kf:
☛ Who founded Awadh in 1722? → Saadat Khan (Burhan-ul-Mulk)
☛ Where was the capital of Awadh shifted in 1775? → Lucknow
☛ What was the initial capital of Awadh? → Faizabad
☛ When did the British annex Awadh? → 1856
☛ Who was the last Nawab of Awadh? → Wajid Ali Shah

q: In which of the following years did Vasco da Gama land in Calicut on the Malabar Coast for the second time?
qs.e: Vasco da Gama first landed in Calicut on the Malabar Coast in 1498. He returned for the second time in 1502 with a large fleet and clashed with the ruler of Calicut. Vasco da Gama discovered the sea route to India, which transformed trade between Europe and Asia. As a Portuguese navigator, he was the first European to reach India by sea. His voyages played a crucial role in the expansion of the Portuguese Empire.
qs.kf:
☛ When did Vasco da Gama first come to India? → 1498
☛ When did Vasco da Gama come to India for the second time? → 1502
☛ When did Vasco da Gama come to India for the third time? → 1524 (as Governor)
☛ Vasco da Gama was a sailor of which country? → Portugal
☛ Where did Vasco da Gama first set foot in India? → Calicut, Malabar Coast

name: Set 3 · Q83–123
sub: Modern History - Advent of Europeans & Expansion of British Rule

q: In which of the following cities was the Paramhansa Mandali founded to work for the abolition of caste?
qs.e: The Paramhansa Mandali was founded in 1849 in Bombay (now Mumbai). Its aim was the abolition of caste system and social reform. The founder was Dadoba Pandurang. The organization emphasized monotheism and equality of all humans. Members had to follow rules like feeding Brahmins and dining with untouchables. The Mandali worked secretly and promoted women's education and widow remarriage. It later merged with the Prarthana Samaj.
qs.kf:
☛ Who founded the Paramhansa Mandali? → Dadoba Pandurang
☛ When was the Paramhansa Mandali founded? → 1849
☛ What was the main objective of Paramhansa Mandali? → Abolition of caste system
☛ In which city was Paramhansa Mandali founded? → Bombay
☛ Which society did Paramhansa Mandali merge into? → Prarthana Samaj

q: Who introduced the Permanent Settlement in British India?
qs.e: The Permanent Settlement, also known as the Zamindari System, was introduced in British India by Lord Cornwallis in 1793. Under this system, zamindars were recognized as landowners and were required to pay a fixed revenue to the British. The main objectives were to ensure a stable revenue and encourage agricultural improvement. Lord Cornwallis also implemented judicial reforms and laid the foundation of the civil service. The Permanent Settlement was initially implemented in Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa. This system ultimately led to the exploitation of peasants and the decline of agriculture.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Permanent Settlement introduced? → 1793
☛ What was the fixed revenue share under the Permanent Settlement? → 10/11 of the produce
☛ In which province was the Permanent Settlement not implemented? → Madras
☛ What was the major drawback of the Permanent Settlement? → Exploitation of peasants
☛ What was the principle behind the Permanent Settlement? → Private ownership of land

q: Who was the first Portuguese governor in India, sent in 1505 to establish naval supremacy?
qs.e: De Almeida was the first Portuguese governor in India, sent in 1505 to establish Portuguese naval supremacy in the Indian Ocean. He built several forts along the western coast of India and controlled trade routes. In 1509, he defeated a combined fleet of Egypt and Gujarat at the Battle of Diu, which ensured Portuguese dominance at sea. After him, Albuquerque took over as governor in 1509. De Almeida's tenure is considered crucial for laying the foundation of the Portuguese Empire in India. His focus on naval power and strategic fortifications helped Portugal control key maritime trade routes for decades.
qs.kf:
☛ First Portuguese governor in India → De Almeida (1505)
☛ Second Portuguese governor in India → Albuquerque (1509)
☛ Famous battle of De Almeida → Battle of Diu (1509)
☛ Main objective of Portuguese naval supremacy → Control of Indian Ocean trade
☛ Start of Portuguese rule in India → Arrival of De Almeida in 1505

q: Who piloted Vasco da Gama’s ship to Calicut during his first successful voyage to India in 1498?
qs.e: Vasco da Gama undertook his first successful voyage to India in 1498. His pilot was a Gujarati Muslim navigator named Abdul Majid, who was familiar with the trade routes of the Indian Ocean. Abdul Majid guided Vasco da Gama's ship from the eastern coast of Africa to Calicut (present-day Kozhikode). This journey was crucial in establishing a sea route between Portugal and India, marking the beginning of European colonialism in Asia. Abdul Majid's navigational expertise ensured the success of this historic voyage.
qs.kf:
☛ Birth of Vasco da Gama → 1460, Sines, Portugal
☛ Arrival in India → 20 May 1498, Calicut
☛ Ruler of Calicut → Zamorin
☛ Death of Vasco da Gama → 1524, Cochin
☛ Purpose of voyage → To find a sea route for spice trade

q: Where was the first British presidency established in India?
qs.e: The first British presidency in India was established at Surat in 1612, when the East India Company obtained trading privileges from Mughal Emperor Jahangir. Subsequently, presidencies were set up in Mumbai (1687) and Kolkata (1690). The Surat presidency laid the foundation for British colonization and remained the center of British activities until 1636. Goa was under Portuguese control, not British.

☛ When did the Surat presidency end? → 1687 (shifted to Mumbai)

☛ Who established the Mumbai Presidency? → East India Company, 1687
☛ Who was the administrative head of British presidencies? → Governor

q: When was the French East India Company set up?
qs.e: The French East India Company (Compagnie des Indes Orientales) was established in 1664 during the reign of King Louis XIV of France, under the patronage of his minister Jean-Baptiste Colbert. Its purpose was to trade with India and East Asia and to establish French colonies. The company set up its first factory in Surat in India and later made Pondicherry (in 1673) its main headquarters. The arrival of the French East India Company led to rivalry with the British, eventually resulting in the Carnatic Wars. The company was dissolved in 1769, but it laid the foundation for French influence in India, especially in the southern regions.

☛ Which became the main French settlement in India? → Pondicherry

q: Who discovered the sea route to India?
qs.e: Vasco da Gama, a Portuguese explorer, discovered the sea route to India in 1498 by sailing around the Cape of Good Hope in Africa. He landed at Calicut (present-day Kozhikode, Kerala), establishing a direct maritime trade route between Europe and India. This discovery gave Portugal a monopoly over the spice trade and marked the beginning of European colonialism in India.

q: Subsidiary Alliance, through which the British were responsible for protecting their Indian allies from external and internal threats to their power, was devised by:
qs.e: The Subsidiary Alliance system was devised by Lord Wellesley (Governor-General from 1798 to 1805). Under this system, Indian states had to disband their own armies and pay for British military protection. In return, the British pledged to protect them from external and internal threats. This effectively ended the sovereignty of Indian states and brought them under British control. The first subsidiary alliance was signed with the Nizam of Hyderabad in 1798. Later, states like Mysore, Tanjore, and Awadh also accepted this alliance. Lord Wellesley used this policy to expand British influence in India without direct war.
qs.kf:
☛ Who is called the father of Subsidiary Alliance? → Lord Wellesley
☛ Which state signed the first Subsidiary Alliance? → Hyderabad (1798)
☛ What were Indian states prohibited from under Subsidiary Alliance? → Maintaining their own army
☛ Who called Subsidiary Alliance a 'trap of slavery'? → Ranjit Singh (Punjab rejected it)
☛ Which Nawab was deposed by Lord Wellesley? → Nawab of Awadh (for non-payment of military expenses)

q: In which year did the British achieve political power in India?
qs.e: The British achieved political power in India in 1757 after the Battle of Plassey. In this battle, the East India Company, led by Robert Clive, defeated the Nawab of Bengal, Siraj-ud-Daulah. This victory granted the Company political control over Bengal, laying the foundation of British rule in India. The year 1657 saw no significant event; the 1857 revolt was against British rule; and India gained independence in 1947. Hence, 1757 is the correct answer.
qs.kf:
☛ Battle of Plassey → 1757
☛ Leader of British East India Company → Robert Clive
☛ Nawab of Bengal → Siraj-ud-Daulah
☛ Outcome of Plassey → Start of British political power
☛ Foundation of British rule in India → 1757

q: Quit India movement was launched at the ______ session of the All India Congress Committee.
qs.e: The Quit India Movement was launched on 8 August 1942 under the leadership of Mahatma Gandhi. This historic decision was taken at the Bombay session of the All India Congress Committee. In this session, Gandhi gave the call of 'Do or Die' and urged a mass movement against British rule. The movement garnered widespread public support across the country and marked a crucial turning point in the Indian freedom struggle. Although Congress leaders were arrested immediately, the people continued the movement. Thus, the Bombay session remains a significant event in India's struggle for independence.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Quit India Resolution passed? → 8 August 1942
☛ Who gave the slogan of this movement? → Mahatma Gandhi
☛ Which movement is associated with 'Do or Die'? → Quit India Movement
☛ Who was the President of the AICC Bombay session? → Abul Kalam Azad
☛ Who was the Viceroy of India during Quit India Movement? → Lord Linlithgow

q: Henry Lawrence is associated with the battle of:
qs.e: Henry Lawrence was a British commander at Lucknow during the Indian Rebellion of 1857. He is associated with the Battle of Chinhat (30 June 1857), fought near Lucknow. In this battle, the British forces suffered a severe defeat at the hands of Indian rebels. Lawrence later led the defense of the Residency in Lucknow and was mortally wounded on 4 July 1857. The Battle of Plassey (1757) is associated with Robert Clive, Haldighati (1576) with Maharana Pratap, and Chausa (1539) with Sher Shah Suri.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Battle of Chinhat fought? → 30 June 1857
☛ When did Henry Lawrence die? → 4 July 1857
☛ Where was Henry Lawrence commander? → Lucknow
☛ Which rebellion was the Battle of Chinhat part of? → Indian Rebellion of 1857
☛ What was Henry Lawrence's full name? → Sir Henry Montgomery Lawrence

q: Who defected against Siraj-ud-Daulah in the battle of Plassey?
qs.e: The Battle of Plassey was fought on 23 June 1757 between the Nawab of Bengal Siraj-ud-Daulah and the British East India Company. In this battle, Mir Jafar, who was the commander of Siraj-ud-Daulah's army, defected and sided with the British. He made a secret pact with the Company, which led to the British victory. This battle is considered the foundation of British rule in India. Mir Jafar was later made the Nawab of Bengal. Among other options, Murshid Quli Khan was the first Nawab of Bengal, Alivardi Khan was Siraj's grandfather, and Mir Qasim became Nawab later.
qs.kf:
☛ Year of Battle of Plassey → 1757
☛ British leader in the battle → Robert Clive
☛ Cause of the battle → Denial of trade privileges to British
☛ Traitor commander → Mir Jafar
☛ Result → Foundation of British Empire in India

q: Who introduced the policy of Paramountcy?
qs.e: The policy of Paramountcy was introduced by Lord Hastings (Governor-General from 1813 to 1823). Under this policy, the British East India Company claimed supreme authority over Indian princely states, asserting its right to intervene in their internal affairs. Hastings used this policy to wage wars against Nepal (1814-16), the Marathas (1817-18), and the Pindaris. Later, Lord Dalhousie implemented the Doctrine of Lapse, which was an extension of Paramountcy. This policy effectively established British dominance over the entire Indian subcontinent.
qs.kf:
☛ Father of Paramountcy policy → Lord Hastings
☛ Lord Hastings' tenure → 1813-1823
☛ Who introduced Doctrine of Lapse → Lord Dalhousie
☛ Nepal War (1814-16) took place under whom → Lord Hastings
☛ Who suppressed the Pindaris → Lord Hastings

q: The Chauri-Chaura incident during Non Cooperation Movement occurred in which district of Uttar Pradesh?
qs.e: The Chauri-Chaura incident occurred on February 4, 1922, in the Goarkhpur district of Uttar Pradesh at a place called Chauri-Chaura. This event took place during the Non Cooperation Movement, when protesters set fire to a police station, killing 22 policemen. As a result, Mahatma Gandhi called off the Non Cooperation Movement on February 12, 1922, citing the violation of the principle of non-violence. This incident had a profound impact on the strategy of non-violent resistance in the Indian independence movement.
qs.kf:
☛ Date of Chauri-Chaura incident → February 4, 1922
☛ District of Chauri-Chaura → Gorakhpur, Uttar Pradesh
☛ Number of policemen killed → 22
☛ Leader who called off the movement → Mahatma Gandhi
☛ Date of suspension of movement → February 12, 1922

q: Name the Dutch who helped Raja Ram Mohan Roy in the promotion of modern education in India?
qs.e: David Hare was a Dutch-born educationist who worked with Raja Ram Mohan Roy to promote modern education in India. He arrived in Calcutta in 1800 and played a significant role in spreading Western education. Together with Raja Ram Mohan Roy, he helped establish the Hindu College (later renamed Presidency College) in 1817. This college was the first institution of Western education in India. David Hare worked in the field of education until his death in 1853. He also contributed to the establishment of the Calcutta School Book Society and the School Society. His efforts were instrumental in introducing secular and scientific education in India.
qs.kf:
☛ David Hare belonged to which country? → Netherlands (Dutch)
☛ Which college did David Hare help establish? → Hindu College, Kolkata
☛ When was Hindu College founded? → 1817
☛ With which society was David Hare associated? → Calcutta School Book Society
☛ Who collaborated with Raja Ram Mohan Roy in education? → David Hare

q: The first textile mill in India was established at Fort Gloster near in 1818.
qs.e: The first textile mill in India was established in 1818 at Fort Gloster, located near Calcutta (now Kolkata). The mill was set up by British traders and was known as the 'Bengal Mill'. However, it was not commercially successful and eventually closed down. The first successful textile mill was established later in 1854 in Bombay (now Mumbai), named the 'Bombay Spinning and Weaving Mill'. Both Calcutta and Bombay played crucial roles in the development of the Indian textile industry. The establishment of the first mill marked the beginning of modern industrialisation in India.
qs.kf:
☛ Where was India's first cotton textile mill established? → Fort Gloster near Calcutta
☛ When and where was the first successful textile mill established? → 1854 in Bombay
☛ What was the name of the first textile mill? → Bengal Mill
☛ In which state is Fort Gloster located? → West Bengal
☛ Which state has the largest textile industry in India? → Tamil Nadu

q: Vasco da Gama of ______ had discovered a new sea route from India to Europe.
qs.e: Vasco da Gama was a Portuguese explorer who discovered the sea route from Europe to India in 1498. He sailed under the patronage of King Manuel I of Portugal, rounding the Cape of Good Hope and reaching Calicut in Kerala. This discovery established a direct maritime link between Europe and India, giving Portugal a monopoly over the spice trade. Vasco da Gama's voyage is considered a landmark in the history of geography and global trade, paving the way for European colonization and trade expansion in Asia.
qs.kf:
☛ Which country did Vasco da Gama belong to? → Portugal
☛ When did Vasco da Gama reach India? → 1498
☛ Which Indian port did Vasco da Gama first land at? → Calicut (Kerala)
☛ Who was the King of Portugal who sent Vasco da Gama to India? → Manuel I
☛ What trade route did Vasco da Gama open? → Sea route from Europe to India

q: Which of the following was related to the first Anglo-Maratha war?
qs.e: The First Anglo-Maratha War (1775-1782) was fought between the British East India Company and the Maratha Empire. This war ended with the Treaty of Salbai (1782), signed between Warren Hastings and Nana Fadnavis. Under this treaty, both parties restored each other's territories and established peace for 20 years. The Treaty of Madras (1769) is related to the First Anglo-Mysore War, the Treaty of Paris (1763) to the Seven Years' War, and the Treaty of Mangalore (1784) to the Second Anglo-Mysore War.
qs.kf:
☛ Treaty ending First Anglo-Maratha War → Treaty of Salbai (1782)
☛ Treaty of Second Anglo-Maratha War → Treaty of Bassein (1802)
☛ Result of Third Anglo-Maratha War → Abolition of Peshwa office
☛ Governor-General at Treaty of Salbai → Warren Hastings
☛ Maratha representative at Treaty of Salbai → Nana Fadnavis

q: In which year did King George V and Queen Mary of Britain visit India, and the announcement regarding the transfer of India's capital from Calcutta (Kolkata) to Delhi take place?
qs.e: King George V and Queen Mary visited India in January 1911. On 12 December 1911, during the Delhi Durbar, the King announced the transfer of India's capital from Calcutta to Delhi. This decision was made to bring the colonial administration closer to the geographical center of British India. Delhi also held historical and symbolic significance. King George V was the only British monarch to visit India during the colonial period. The actual shift of the capital began in 1912, but the announcement was made in 1911.
qs.kf:
☛ Delhi Durbar announcement date → 12 December 1911
☛ Year of capital transfer announcement → 1911
☛ Inauguration of New Delhi → 13 February 1931
☛ Reason for shift from Calcutta to Delhi → Administrative convenience and central location
☛ Monarch who made the announcement → King George V

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (09/06/2025) Shift 3
q: VO Chidambaram Pillai was actively involved in the revolutionary movement in which of the following areas?
qs.e: V.O. Chidambaram Pillai (1872-1936) was a prominent Indian freedom fighter and revolutionary who was primarily active in the Madras Presidency (present-day Tamil Nadu). He was a member of the Indian National Congress and later became involved in revolutionary activities. Pillai led the Swadeshi movement and established an Indian shipping company in Tuticorin, which challenged the British monopoly. He was arrested on charges of sedition against the British Empire and sentenced to life imprisonment. His contributions were significant in the revolutionary movement, particularly in South India.
qs.kf:
☛ V.O. Chidambaram Pillai → Revolutionary from Madras Presidency
☛ Swadeshi Shipping Company → Established in Tuticorin
☛ British monopoly → Challenged by Indian shipping
☛ Sedition charges → Led to life imprisonment
☛ Revolutionary movement → Active in South India

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (10/06/2025) Shift 2
q: Which of the following companies built Fort St George in Chennai in the 1640s and later established the Madras Presidency in 1684?
qs.e: The construction of Fort St George in Chennai began in 1644 by the British East India Company. It was their first major fortification in India and later became the headquarters of the Madras Presidency. In 1684, the company formally established the Madras Presidency, which became a key center of British influence on the Coromandel Coast. The fort protected trading activities and strengthened the company's role in regional politics. Other companies like the Portuguese or French were active in other parts of India, but the Chennai fort was built exclusively by the British East India Company.
qs.kf:
☛ Who built Fort St George? → British East India Company
☛ Where is Fort St George located? → Chennai, Tamil Nadu
☛ When was the Madras Presidency established? → 1684
☛ Which was the first Indian fort of the British East India Company? → Fort St George
☛ What was the capital of Madras Presidency? → Fort St George

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (11/06/2025) Shift 1
q: Which of the following companies assisted the Raja of Cochin in expelling the Portuguese from his kingdom in 1663?
qs.e: In 1663, the Raja of Cochin expelled the Portuguese from his kingdom with the help of the Dutch East India Company. The Dutch East India Company (VOC) was a major European power in India during the 17th century. They allied with local rulers to seize control of coastal regions from Portuguese colonists. Cochin was an important port city, and the Dutch helped eliminate Portuguese influence there. After this victory, the Dutch became the dominant European power in Cochin until 1795, when they were defeated by the British. Other companies like the French, British, and Spanish East India Companies were not involved in this specific event.
qs.kf:
☛ European power that expelled Portuguese from Cochin → Dutch East India Company
☛ Headquarters of Dutch East India Company in India → Surat
☛ First European power to defeat Portuguese in India → Dutch
☛ Year of Battle of Cochin → 1663
☛ Establishment of Dutch East India Company → 1602

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (19/06/2025) Shift 3
q: Under whose administration was the practice of Sati officially abolished in British India?
qs.e: The practice of Sati, where a widow was immolated on her husband's funeral pyre, was a cruel social custom. It was officially abolished during the tenure of Lord William Bentinck as Governor-General of India (1828-1835). He passed the Bengal Sati Regulation (Regulation XVII) on December 4, 1829, banning the practice. This reform was supported by social reformers like Raja Ram Mohan Roy and Christian missionaries. Bentinck's move marked a significant step in social reform in India, protecting women's rights and ending a brutal tradition.
qs.kf:
☛ When was Sati officially abolished? → 1829
☛ Who was the Governor-General during the abolition of Sati? → Lord William Bentinck
☛ Which regulation banned Sati? → Bengal Sati Regulation (Regulation XVII)
☛ Who was the prominent reformer supporting the abolition? → Raja Ram Mohan Roy
☛ What was Lord William Bentinck's tenure as Governor-General? → 1828-1835

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (20/06/2025) Shift 2
q: Which of the following was formed in 1600 through a charter that granted it the exclusive privilege of trading with the area east of the Cape of Good Hope for 15 years?
qs.e: On December 31, 1600, the English East India Company was granted a royal charter by Queen Elizabeth I, giving it the exclusive privilege of trading with the regions east of the Cape of Good Hope for 15 years. This marked the beginning of English involvement in India, leading eventually to colonial rule until 1858. The other options—Austrian, Danish, and Spanish East India companies—were formed later and did not receive such a charter in 1600.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the East India Company chartered? → 31 December 1600
☛ Who granted the charter? → Queen Elizabeth I
☛ Which region was covered by the exclusive privilege? → East of Cape of Good Hope
☛ What was the duration of the privilege? → 15 years
☛ When did the Company's rule in India end? → 1858

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (21/06/2025) Shift 1
q: Which Princely State was ruled personally by the Nizam and had the 'Sarf khas' estate?
qs.e: The princely state of Hyderabad was under the personal rule of the Nizam. 'Sarf khas' referred to the private estate of the Nizam, separate from the state treasury. The Nizam was the title of the ruler of Hyderabad, one of the wealthiest rulers in India. Hyderabad remained a princely state until its annexation into India in 1948.

☛ When was Hyderabad annexed to India? → 1948
☛ Who founded the Hyderabad state? → Asaf Jah I

q: Even before East India Company consolidated power, India was exporting fine textiles made of:
qs.e: Before the East India Company consolidated power, India was exporting fine textiles made of cotton and silk. Indian cotton textiles like muslin, calico, and chintz were renowned worldwide. Similarly, Bengal silk was in high demand. These textiles were handcrafted and woven by skilled artisans. Nylon is a synthetic fiber developed much later, making that option incorrect. India's textile industry was advanced since ancient times, and these exports were a major source of economic prosperity.
qs.kf:

☛ Famous silk from Bengal → Bengali silk
☛ Indian textiles popular in Europe → Calico and chintz
☛ Major textile export centers in India → Gujarat, Bengal, and South India
☛ Reason for demand of Indian textiles → High quality and craftsmanship

q: Who was known as the father of civil services in British India?
qs.e: Charles Cornwallis is known as the father of civil services in British India. After becoming Governor-General in 1786, he implemented administrative reforms. He prohibited private trade, reducing corruption, and provided high salaries to civil servants. He introduced the position of District Collector and created separate departments. His reforms professionalised the civil services in India.
qs.kf:
☛ Who is called the father of civil services in India? → Charles Cornwallis
☛ Cornwallis banned civil servants from what? → Private trade
☛ Which post was created by Cornwallis? → District Collector
☛ In which year did Cornwallis become Governor-General? → 1786
☛ What did Cornwallis do to reduce corruption in civil services? → Provided high salaries

q: In which year was Battle of Plassey fought?
qs.e: The Battle of Plassey was fought on 23 June 1757. This battle took place between the British East India Company and the Nawab of Bengal, Siraj-ud-Daulah. The Company forces were led by Robert Clive. The British bribed the Nawab's commander Mir Jafar, who betrayed the Nawab. After the battle, Mir Jafar was made the Nawab of Bengal. This battle laid the foundation of British rule in India.
qs.kf:
☛ Between whom was the Battle of Plassey fought? → British and Nawab of Bengal Siraj-ud-Daulah
☛ Who commanded the British in the Battle of Plassey? → Robert Clive
☛ Who betrayed in the Battle of Plassey? → Mir Jafar
☛ What was the immediate cause of the Battle of Plassey? → Attack on Fort William and the Black Hole incident
☛ Who became Nawab after the Battle of Plassey? → Mir Jafar

q: In which area did the Wadiyar dynasty emerge?
qs.e: The Wadiyar dynasty emerged in the region of Mysore (present-day Karnataka). It was founded in 1399 CE by Yaduraya, who initially established the capital at Hebbar village. In the 16th century, Chamaraja Wadiyar III shifted the capital to Mysore city. The dynasty ruled the princely state of Mysore from 1799 to 1950. The Wadiyars were known for patronizing art, culture, and education. Mysore was merged into the Indian Union in 1950. The Wadiyars belonged to the Kshatriya caste.
qs.kf:
☛ Who founded the Wadiyar dynasty? → Yaduraya (1399 CE)
☛ What was the first capital of Mysore? → Hebbar village
☛ Which Wadiyar ruler shifted the capital to Mysore? → Chamaraja Wadiyar III
☛ When was Mysore merged into India? → 1950
☛ What caste did the Wadiyars belong to? → Kshatriya

q: Who implemented the double rule policy in Bengal?
qs.e: The Dual Government system in Bengal was implemented by Robert Clive in 1765 after the Treaty of Allahabad. Under this system, the East India Company obtained the Diwani rights (revenue collection), while the Nizamat (administration and justice) remained with the Nawab. This arrangement allowed the company to secure revenue without administrative responsibility, leading to chaos and misrule in Bengal. The system was abolished by Warren Hastings in 1772.
qs.kf:
☛ Father of Dual Government in Bengal → Robert Clive
☛ Year of implementation of Dual Government → 1765
☛ What the Company got under Dual Government → Diwani rights (revenue)
☛ Who abolished Dual Government → Warren Hastings (1772)
☛ Last Nawab of Bengal under Dual Government → Najm-ud-Daula

q: In 1765, which state was conferred on British by British?
qs.e: In 1765, the Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II granted the Diwani (revenue rights) of Bengal, Bihar and Odisha to the British East India Company through the Treaty of Allahabad (1765). This treaty was signed between Robert Clive and Shah Alam II. Under this, the Company was allowed to collect revenue from these regions, while administrative authority remained with the Nawab of Bengal. This marked a crucial step in the establishment of British rule in India. Later, in 1772, Warren Hastings took over both the Diwani and Nizamat (administrative) functions, effectively bringing the region under British control.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Treaty of Allahabad signed? → 1765
☛ Who received the Diwani rights? → British East India Company
☛ Which region retained Nizamat rights? → Nawab of Bengal
☛ Who signed the treaty on behalf of the British? → Robert Clive
☛ Who was the last independent Nawab of Bengal? → Siraj-ud-Daulah

q: When did Vasco De Gama come to India?
qs.e: Vasco da Gama, a Portuguese explorer, became the first European to reach India by sea when he arrived in Calicut (present-day Kozhikode) in 1498. His primary goal was to establish a direct trade route for spices. He traveled via the Cape of Good Hope in Africa, a significant maritime route to the East. This expedition laid the foundation for trade relations between Europe and India. Vasco da Gama's arrival marked the beginning of European colonialism in India. His journey is considered a remarkable achievement in world history.
qs.kf:
☛ When did Vasco da Gama reach India? → 1498
☛ Which country did Vasco da Gama belong to? → Portugal
☛ At which port did Vasco da Gama land? → Calicut, Kerala
☛ What was Vasco da Gama's main objective? → Spice trade
☛ Who was the first European to reach India by sea? → Vasco da Gama

q: After which of the following wars did the British company rule formally begin in India?
qs.e: The Battle of Plassey was fought in 1757 between the British East India Company led by Robert Clive and the Nawab of Bengal, Siraj-ud-Daulah. After this victory, the Company established its influence in Bengal. However, the formal beginning of British rule is considered after the Battle of Buxar in 1764, where the Company gained the Diwani rights of Bengal, Bihar, and Odisha. Plassey laid the foundation for British expansion, while Buxar provided administrative control. Thus, the battle after which British company rule formally began in India is the Battle of Plassey, as it marked the start of political dominance.
qs.kf:
☛ Year of Battle of Plassey → 1757
☛ Year of Battle of Buxar → 1764
☛ British commander at Plassey → Robert Clive
☛ British commander at Buxar → Hector Munro
☛ Year of Diwani Rights → 1765

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (12/06/2025) Shift 3
q: Which of the following companies founded in 1602 is also known as the 'Verenigde Oostindische Compagnie (VOC)'?
qs.e: The Verenigde Oostindische Compagnie (VOC) is also known as the Dutch East India Company. Founded in 1602 in the Netherlands, it is considered the first multinational corporation in the world. It played a major role in establishing the Dutch trading empire in Asia, particularly in the spice trade. VOC was also the first company to issue stocks on a public stock exchange. It was involved in colonial activities in India, Indonesia, Sri Lanka, and other Asian regions. The company was dissolved in 1799 after financial decline.
qs.kf:
☛ Full name of VOC → Verenigde Oostindische Compagnie
☛ Year of establishment → 1602
☛ Headquarters → Amsterdam
☛ First public company → VOC

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (17/06/2025) Shift 2
q: Which Princely State had a representative assembly from as early as 1881?
qs.e: The princely state of Mysore had a representative assembly as early as 1881, known as the 'Mysore Representative Assembly'. It was the first legislature established in any princely state of India. It was founded in 1881 during the reign of Maharaja Chamaraja Wodeyar X. The assembly was an advisory body with limited powers, consisting of elected and nominated members. This assembly laid the foundation for the later Mysore Legislative Assembly. Other princely states like Hyderabad, Patiala, and Gwalior established their representative assemblies later.

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (13/06/2025) Shift 2
q: During the colonial period, India's industrial development was the result of British policies. Which of the following options best describes the nature of industrial development in India at the eve of independence?
o: Balanced regional distribution of heavy industries
Strong domestic capital goods industry in all provinces
Widespread industrial growth across rural and urban areas
Limited industrial activity, mainly concentrated in a few cities like Calcutta and Bombay
qs.e: During the colonial period, British policies were designed to keep India as a supplier of raw materials and a market for finished goods. This resulted in a limited and unbalanced industrial development. Heavy industries were discouraged, and only light industries like textiles were allowed to grow. These industries were concentrated in port cities such as Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras, which were convenient for export and import. Rural areas saw almost no industrial growth. By the time of independence, India had a very narrow industrial base, with most activity limited to a few urban centers. This pattern of limited, concentrated industrialization is best described by Option 4.
qs.kf:

q: The Nizam of Hyderabad tried to project his rule as:
qs.e: The Nizam of Hyderabad tried to project his rule as a Muslim sovereignty in Deccan. After the decline of the Mughal Empire, the Nizam emerged as an independent ruler and liked to be called the "true emperor of Deccan". He promoted Islamic traditions and Persian culture, linking his rule with Muslim identity. Although Hyderabad was a British protectorate, the Nizam maintained autonomy in internal affairs and emphasized his sovereignty. As a Muslim ruler in a Hindu-majority region, he presented an image of Muslim sovereignty. His state had its own currency, army, and postal system, reinforcing this projection.

q: In which year did the English East India Company pass a new law that required every new person who took up employment in the Company’s army to serve overseas if required?
qs.e: In 1856, the English East India Company passed a new law requiring every new recruit in the Company's army to serve overseas if needed. This law was highly objectionable to Indian soldiers because crossing the sea was considered a religious and social taboo at that time. The law increased discontent among the sepoys and became one of the causes of the 1857 rebellion. The Company implemented this law to enhance military efficiency, but it eroded the trust of Indian soldiers. The law was introduced under the governance of Lord Canning.

q: Which power suffered a decisive defeat in the Malabar region during the Battle of Colachel in 1741?
qs.e: The Battle of Colachel in 1741 was fought between the Kingdom of Travancore and the Dutch East India Company. King Marthanda Varma of Travancore decisively defeated the Dutch forces, ending Dutch colonialism in Kerala. This battle marked the first major military victory of an Indian state over a European power. The Dutch commander, Eustachius De Lannoy, was captured and later served as a general in the Travancore army. The victory established Travancore as a powerful kingdom and effectively ended Dutch influence in the Malabar region.
