qs.e: The 'Doctrine of Lapse', implemented during Lord Dalhousie's tenure (1848-1856), allowed the British to annex any princely state whose ruler died without a natural male heir. This policy denied the traditional right of adopted sons to inherit the throne. Major states like Satara (1848), Nagpur (1854), Jhansi (1854), and Awadh (1856) were annexed under this policy. It caused widespread discontent among Indian rulers, becoming a key factor in the 1857 Rebellion. The doctrine was seen as a direct violation of Indian customs and a tool for British expansionism.
qs.kf:
☛ Who introduced the Doctrine of Lapse? → Lord Dalhousie
☛ First state annexed under this doctrine? → Satara (1848)
☛ Meaning of this policy? → Annexation of states without natural heirs
☛ When was Jhansi annexed? → 1854
☛ Under what pretext was Awadh annexed? → Alleged misgovernment

q: Who among the following was the leader of the 1857 Revolt from Kullu?
qs.e: Raja Pratap Singh was the ruler of the Kullu princely state who led the 1857 Revolt against the British. He was the last ruler of Kullu and led an armed rebellion against British rule. During the Revolt of 1857, discontent spread in the Kullu region as well, and Raja Pratap Singh took the lead. Under his leadership, soldiers from Kullu fought against the British. However, the revolt was suppressed and Raja Pratap Singh was captured. He was sentenced to death by the British on charges of treason. Raja Pratap Singh's contribution is considered significant in the history of Kullu.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the leader of the 1857 Revolt from Kullu? → Raja Pratap Singh
☛ Which princely state did Raja Pratap Singh rule? → Kullu
☛ What was the contribution of Kullu in the 1857 Revolt? → Revolt led by Raja Pratap Singh
☛ What punishment was given to Raja Pratap Singh? → Death sentence
☛ When did the 1857 Revolt take place in Kullu? → 1857

q: Who led the rebellions of 1857 at Allahabad?
qs.e: During the Rebellion of 1857, the leadership in Allahabad was taken by Maulvi Liyakat Ali. He raised the banner of revolt against the British and captured Allahabad. However, the British later recaptured Allahabad. Maulvi Liyakat Ali was a prominent rebel leader who also played a significant role in the Awadh region. He is counted among the important leaders of the 1857 struggle. Kunwar Singh led the rebellion in Bihar, Khan Bahadur Khan in Bareilly, and Lakshmi Bai and Tantia Tope in Jhansi and Gwalior.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the leader of 1857 revolt in Awadh? → Begum Hazrat Mahal
☛ Who led the 1857 revolt in Bareilly? → Khan Bahadur Khan
☛ Who led the 1857 revolt in Bihar? → Kunwar Singh
☛ Who led the 1857 revolt in Jhansi? → Rani Lakshmi Bai
☛ What was the immediate cause of the 1857 revolt? → Greased cartridges

q: Mirza Wajid Ali Shah was the king of which of the following regions during the Indian Rebellion of 1857?
qs.e: During the Indian Rebellion of 1857, Mirza Wajid Ali Shah was the king of Awadh. Awadh was annexed by the British in 1856 under Lord Dalhousie's 'Doctrine of Lapse', and Wajid Ali Shah was exiled to Calcutta. His deposition and the annexation of Awadh sparked widespread resentment among Indian rulers and soldiers, contributing significantly to the outbreak of the 1857 rebellion. Wajid Ali Shah was a patron of arts and music; he developed the dance form 'Parikhana'. His son Birjis Qadr led the rebellion in Awadh after his father's exile, making Awadh a major center of the uprising, particularly under the leadership of Begum Hazrat Mahal.
qs.kf:
☛ When was Awadh annexed under the Doctrine of Lapse? → 1856
☛ Where was Wajid Ali Shah exiled? → Calcutta
☛ Who led the revolt in Awadh during 1857? → Birjis Qadr and Begum Hazrat Mahal
☛ Which dance form did Wajid Ali Shah develop? → Parikhana
☛ Who propounded the Doctrine of Lapse? → Lord Dalhousie

q: Where did the sepoys go after their mutiny in Meerut?
qs.e: The revolt of 1857 began in the Meerut cantonment on 10 May 1857. The sepoys revolted against the use of greased cartridges by the British. After the mutiny, the sepoys marched overnight from Meerut to Delhi. They reached Delhi on 11 May 1857 and went to the Red Fort to meet the Mughal emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar. They proclaimed him as the Emperor of India and asked him to lead the revolt. Thus, Delhi became the epicenter of the revolt. While uprisings also occurred in Lucknow, Bareilly, and Kanpur, the Meerut sepoys directly proceeded to Delhi.
qs.kf:
☛ What was the immediate cause of the 1857 revolt? → Use of greased cartridges
☛ What is the date of the Meerut revolt? → 10 May 1857
☛ Who led the revolt in Delhi? → Bahadur Shah Zafar
☛ Which city was made the capital of the revolt in 1857? → Delhi
☛ How many days did the Meerut sepoys take to reach Delhi? → One night (11 May 1857)

q: Which of the following languages was/were used in proclamations calling people to join the 1857 Revolt?
qs.e: During the 1857 Revolt, proclamations were issued to rally people in different regions. These proclamations used Hindi, Urdu and Persian languages. Persian was the court language of the Mughals, while Hindi and Urdu were widely spoken by the masses. Leaders like Bahadur Shah Zafar issued appeals in these languages to mobilize diverse groups. English and Sanskrit were not used because English was not understood by the rebels and Sanskrit was not a common language at that time.
qs.kf:
☛ Which languages were used in 1857 proclamations? → Hindi, Urdu and Persian
☛ Which was the court language during 1857? → Persian
☛ Bahadur Shah Zafar issued appeals in which languages? → Urdu and Persian
☛ Pamphlets were distributed in which languages during 1857? → Hindi and Urdu
☛ Were English and Sanskrit used? → No

q: General Service Enlistment Act was passed in which of the following years?
qs.e: The General Service Enlistment Act was passed in 1856 AD. This act forced Indian soldiers to serve overseas if needed, which was against their religious beliefs as crossing the sea was considered a threat to their caste and religion. It was passed during the tenure of Lord Canning, the Governor-General of India. The Act was one of the major causes of the Indian Rebellion of 1857. Indian soldiers had never been required to serve abroad before, and this act created widespread resentment among them, as it interfered with their traditional practices and led to a feeling of betrayal. The Act, combined with other grievances like the Enfield rifle cartridge issue, sparked the rebellion.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the General Service Enlistment Act passed? → 1856 AD
☛ Under which Governor-General was this Act passed? → Lord Canning
☛ What was the main provision of this Act? → Indian soldiers were required to serve overseas
☛ Which rebellion did this Act help trigger? → The 1857 Rebellion
☛ What did Indian soldiers fear? → Loss of caste and religion due to sea voyage

q: Which of the following was the most significant development after the revolt of 1857?
o: Indian people formed associations, societies, and organisations which led to the formation of Indian National Congress.
Indian people dropped the idea of liberating themselves.
Indian people formed close relationship with the British empire.
Indians started reorganising themselves for another armed revolt.
qs.e: After the failure of the 1857 revolt, Indians realized that armed struggle against the British was not feasible. This led to the rise of a new political consciousness, where educated Indians began to voice their demands through constitutional and peaceful means. Consequently, in 1885, the Indian National Congress was formed, which became a major platform for the Indian freedom movement. The other options are incorrect because Indians did not abandon the idea of liberation, nor did they form close ties with the British empire; instead, they reorganised politically. The formation of the Congress was a significant development that channeled nationalist sentiments into organised political action.
qs.kf:
☛ What was the change in Indian politics after the 1857 revolt? → Start of constitutional movements
☛ When was the Indian National Congress founded? → 1885
☛ Who was the first president of the Indian National Congress? → Womesh Chunder Bonnerjee
☛ What was the immediate cause of the 1857 revolt? → Greased cartridge issue
☛ What was the nature of the 1857 revolt? → A military revolt that turned into a popular uprising

q: Who was the chief commissioner of Awadh in 1857?
qs.e: At the time of the 1857 revolt, the Chief Commissioner of Awadh was Sir Henry Lawrence. He assumed the position after the annexation of Awadh in 1856 and commanded the British forces in Lucknow. During the revolt, he was besieged in the Lucknow Residency and was mortally wounded by a shell fragment on 4 July 1857. After his death, Major General Sir James Outram took over command. Sir Henry Lawrence is remembered for his military and administrative acumen, and his role in shaping British policy in Oudh.
qs.kf:
☛ When was Awadh annexed? → 1856
☛ Who led the British during the siege of Lucknow? → Sir Henry Lawrence
☛ When did Sir Henry Lawrence die? → 4 July 1857
☛ Who was the last Nawab of Awadh? → Wajid Ali Shah
☛ Who was the Governor General during the 1857 revolt? → Lord Canning

q: Who fought in the famous Battle of Chinhat with the Britishers during the Revolt of 1857?
qs.e: The Battle of Chinhat was fought on 12 July 1857 near Lucknow during the Revolt of 1857. In this battle, Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah led the rebel forces against the British and defeated them. He was a prominent rebel leader from Faizabad, who fought against the British contingent commanded by Henry Lawrence. With the support of the Nawab of Nawabganj, Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah inflicted a heavy defeat on the British, forcing them to retreat. He continued to be a major threat to the British in the Awadh region until he was captured and executed on 5 June 1858.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Battle of Chinhat fought? → 12 July 1857
☛ Which British officer was involved in the Battle of Chinhat? → Henry Lawrence
☛ With which district is Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah associated? → Faizabad
☛ What was the outcome of the Battle of Chinhat? → Rebel victory
☛ When did Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah die? → 5 June 1858

q: Which of the following places did Kunwar Amar Singh of Arrah make his battlefield in the revolt of 1857?
qs.e: Kunwar Amar Singh was a zamindar of Arrah (Shahabad) in Bihar. During the Revolt of 1857, he fought against the British. After the suppression of the revolt, he moved to the Azamgarh and Ghazipur regions, where he continued guerrilla warfare. These areas were in the eastern part of the United Provinces (present-day Uttar Pradesh). He defeated the British army several times there. His army included many local peasants and soldiers. Later, in 1859, he fled to Nepal. His contribution is considered significant in the Indian freedom struggle.
qs.kf:
☛ Where was Kunwar Amar Singh a zamindar? → Arrah (Shahabad), Bihar
☛ What type of warfare did Amar Singh use in the 1857 revolt? → Guerrilla warfare
☛ In which province were Azamgarh and Ghazipur located? → United Provinces (Uttar Pradesh)
☛ Where did Amar Singh finally flee? → Nepal
☛ What does the name Kunwar Amar Singh mean? → Warrior prince

q: Which commander in chief of British army captured Lucknow during the revolt of 1857?
qs.e: Sir Colin Campbell was the Commander-in-Chief of the British Army during the Revolt of 1857. He captured Lucknow in November 1857, defeating the rebel forces loyal to the Nawab. His campaign restored British control in the region. After the revolt, he became the Governor-General of India. Campbell's strategic acumen played a key role in suppressing the uprising in Oudh.
qs.kf:
☛ Who captured Lucknow in 1857? → Sir Colin Campbell
☛ What was Campbell's position in India? → Commander-in-Chief
☛ When did the Revolt of 1857 start? → 10 May 1857
☛ Who was the Nawab of Lucknow? → Wajid Ali Shah
☛ What did Campbell become later? → Governor-General of India

q: The British adopted which of the following policies with respect to landlords and zamindars after the Revolt of 1857?
o: The policy of confiscation of property
Policies that protected their rights and provided security over their lands
qs.e: After the Revolt of 1857, the British completely changed their administrative policy in India. They realized that zamindars and landlords had supported the revolt, but to ensure stability, they needed to win them over. Therefore, they adopted policies that protected the rights of zamindars and provided security over their lands. The aim was to create a loyal class that would support British rule. Under this policy, zamindars were given legal rights over their lands and were involved in local administration. This strengthened the zamindar class, increased pressure on peasants, and ensured the zamindars remained loyal to the British Crown. The policy was a strategic shift from earlier punitive measures to a more collaborative approach.
qs.kf:
☛ Main objective of British policy after 1857 → To make local ruling class their supporters
☛ Result of protecting zamindars' rights → Increased exploitation of peasants
☛ Indian Permanent Settlement Act of 1861 → Secured zamindars' rights in Bengal
☛ Benefit of British policy → Zamindars became pillars of British rule
☛ Long-term impact of this policy → Increased inequality in land ownership

q: When was Awadh brought under the control of the Britishers after the uprising of the First War of Independence?
qs.e: After the 1857 uprising, Awadh was brought under direct British control in 1858. During the rebellion, Awadh was a major center of resistance led by figures like Nana Saheb, Tatya Tope, and Begum Hazrat Mahal. After the failure of the uprising, Awadh was annexed into the British Raj and made a province. This step was part of the British policy to consolidate power and annex Indian states. In 1858, the Government of India Act was also passed, transferring the governance of India from the East India Company to the British Crown.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Act was passed in 1858? → Government of India Act 1858
☛ Who annexed Awadh? → Lord Dalhousie
☛ Who led Awadh in the 1857 revolt? → Begum Hazrat Mahal
☛ Who was the last Nawab of Awadh? → Wajid Ali Shah
☛ What did the Government of India Act 1858 abolish? → Rule of East India Company

q: Who led the revolt of 1857 in the city of Farrukhabad?
qs.e: The revolt of 1857 in the city of Farrukhabad was led by Tafazzul Hussain Khan, who was the Nawab of Farrukhabad. He played a key role in organizing the rebellion against the British East India Company. Under his leadership, the rebels in Farrukhabad actively fought against British forces, making the region an important center of the uprising. However, the British eventually suppressed the revolt, and Tafazzul Hussain Khan was captured. His leadership and courage made him a prominent figure in the First War of Indian Independence. The revolt in Farrukhabad was part of the larger 1857 uprising, which saw participation from various leaders across India, such as Nana Saheb in Kanpur, Begum Hazrat Mahal in Lucknow, and Rani Lakshmibai in Jhansi.
qs.kf:
☛ Who led the 1857 revolt in Farrukhabad? → Tafazzul Hussain Khan
☛ Tafazzul Hussain Khan was the Nawab of which state? → Farrukhabad
☛ Who led the 1857 revolt in Kanpur? → Nana Saheb
☛ Who led the 1857 revolt in Lucknow? → Begum Hazrat Mahal
☛ Who was the Rani of Jhansi in 1857? → Lakshmibai

q: Which of the following was/were the consequences of the Revolt of 1857?
I. Reorganisation of the army
II. Agrarian reforms
III. Free trade policy
IV. The Arms Act was passed
qs.e: After the Revolt of 1857, the British government reorganised the army, increasing the number of European soldiers and excluding Indians from key positions. Additionally, the Arms Act of 1878 was passed, which restricted Indians from keeping weapons. Agrarian reforms and free trade policy were not direct consequences of the revolt. Although some agrarian reforms were introduced later, free trade policy had already been in place since the Charter Act of 1813. Hence, only I and IV are correct.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Act after 1857 restricted Indians from keeping arms? → Arms Act (1878)
☛ What was the change in the army after 1857? → Increase in European soldiers and removal of Indians from artillery
☛ What policy did the British adopt after 1857? → Divide and Rule
☛ What was the immediate cause of the Revolt of 1857? → Use of greased cartridges
☛ Who called the Revolt of 1857 a 'Sepoy Mutiny'? → British historians

q: Who led the rebellions from Dhule district, Maharashtra in 1857?
qs.e: During the 1857 rebellion, Khaza Singh led the uprising from Dhule district in Maharashtra. He was a local zamindar who raised the banner of revolt against the British. Under his leadership, rebels in the Dhule region posed a strong challenge to the British forces. Rani Laxmi Bai led from Jhansi, Tatya Tope from Central India, and Khan Bahadur from Rohilkhand. Khaza Singh's contribution is significant among the tribal and peasant rebellions in Maharashtra.
qs.kf:
☛ Who led the 1857 rebellion from Dhule? → Khaza Singh
☛ Dhule district is in which state? → Maharashtra
☛ Who was Khaza Singh? → Local zamindar
☛ Where did Rani Laxmi Bai lead the 1857 revolt? → Jhansi
☛ Which region was Tatya Tope associated with? → Central India

q: Who among the following was the leader of the Revolt of 1857 from Mathura?
qs.e: During the Revolt of 1857, Devi Singh led the uprising from Mathura. He was a landlord (zamindar) of Mathura and played a key role in mobilizing the revolt in the region. Devi Singh organized rebels and fought against the British forces. His rebellion was eventually crushed, and he was executed by the British. Maulvi Liyakat Ali led the revolt in Allahabad, Raja Pratap Singh was associated with Mainpuri, and Firoz Shah was linked to Delhi.
qs.kf:
☛ Leader of Revolt of 1857 from Mathura → Devi Singh
☛ Maulvi Liyakat Ali's area → Allahabad
☛ Raja Pratap Singh's location → Mainpuri
☛ Firoz Shah's association → Delhi
☛ Devi Singh's background → Zamindar

q: Which of the following was NOT a reason for the unrest among Indian soldiers for the British before 1857?
o: The annexation of Indian territories by the British
qs.e: Before 1857, the unrest among Indian soldiers was primarily due to the British annexation of Indian territories (like Dalhousie's 'Doctrine of Lapse'), disregard for Indian customs (such as forbidding soldiers to cross the sea), and poor pay with bad conditions. However, support for the Mughal emperor was not a reason for the unrest; instead, Bahadur Shah Zafar was made a symbolic leader during the revolt. The soldiers revolted to protect their religious and social rights, not due to loyalty to the Mughal emperor.
qs.kf:
☛ Immediate cause of the 1857 Revolt → Use of greased cartridges
☛ Who implemented the Doctrine of Lapse → Lord Dalhousie
☛ Center of the 1857 revolt against the British → Meerut
☛ Governor General of India during the 1857 Revolt → Lord Canning
☛ Role of Bahadur Shah Zafar → Symbolic leader

q: Who is credited with starting the rumour about cartridges coated with cow and pig fat, which resulted in the outbreak of the First War of Independence in India in 1857?
o: A low-caste khalasi working in Dum Dum
qs.e: The rumour that the new Enfield rifle cartridges were greased with cow and pig fat was started by a low-caste khalasi (labourer) working at the Dum Dum arsenal. This rumour deeply offended both Hindu and Muslim sepoys, as cows were sacred to Hindus and pigs were considered unclean by Muslims. The khalasi reportedly shared this information with a Brahmin sepoy, who then spread it further. British officials attempted to quash the rumour by investigating, but by then it had already caused widespread anger. This incident is considered the immediate spark of the 1857 rebellion. Thus, a low-caste khalasi from Dum Dum is credited with originating the rumour.
qs.kf:
☛ Who started the grease cartridge rumour in 1857? → A low-caste khalasi in Dum Dum
☛ Which rifle used these greased cartridges? → Enfield rifle
☛ Immediate cause of the 1857 revolt → Greased cartridge controversy
☛ Dum Dum is located in → West Bengal (near Kolkata)
☛ Where did Mangal Pandey revolt? → Barrackpore

q: On which day was Delhi declared captured by the British during the suppression of the Revolt of 1857?
qs.e: During the Revolt of 1857, Delhi was recaptured by the British on 21 September 1857. The British forces, led by General Wilson, breached the city through the Kashmir Gate and other entry points. Before this, the rebels had taken control of Delhi and declared Bahadur Shah Zafar as their nominal leader. The fall of Delhi was a major setback for the revolt, as it was the center of Mughal authority. After the capture, Bahadur Shah Zafar was arrested and exiled, and the British government took direct control of Delhi. This event marked a turning point in the suppression of the revolt.
qs.kf:
☛ Date of British capture of Delhi in 1857 → 21 September 1857
☛ British commander during the capture of Delhi → General Wilson
☛ Where was Bahadur Shah Zafar exiled after the capture → Rangoon (Yangon)
☛ Who was declared the leader of the 1857 revolt in Delhi → Bahadur Shah Zafar
☛ Who was the British Commander-in-Chief during the capture of Delhi → Colin Campbell

q: Who mobilised the headmen and cultivators of chaurasee des, moving at night from village to village, urging people to rebel against the British during the Revolt of 1857?
qs.e: During the Revolt of 1857, Shah Mal mobilised the headmen and cultivators of Chaurasee Des (a region in present-day Bijnor district, Uttar Pradesh). He moved at night from village to village, urging people to rebel against the British. Shah Mal was a local leader who opposed the injustices and tax policies of the British Raj. He united the peasants and led them in rebellion against the British forces. His revolt was primarily concentrated in the districts of Bijnor, Moradabad, and Saharanpur. Shah Mal is remembered as a prominent peasant leader of the 1857 uprising.
qs.kf:
☛ Which region was associated with Shah Mal? → Bijnor, Uttar Pradesh
☛ In which year did Shah Mal lead the revolt? → 1857
☛ Where is Chaurasee Des located? → Bijnor district
☛ Who mobilised peasants in the 1857 revolt? → Shah Mal
☛ Against whom did Shah Mal rebel? → The British

q: When did the sepoys in the cantonment of Meerut break out in mutiny?
qs.e: The sepoy mutiny in the cantonment of Meerut broke out on 10 May 1857. This event marked the beginning of the Indian Rebellion of 1857. The immediate cause was the introduction of greased cartridges allegedly made with cow and pig fat, which offended both Hindu and Muslim sepoys. The Meerut sepoys rebelled, marched to Delhi, and proclaimed Bahadur Shah Zafar as their leader. This incident sparked the rebellion across large parts of North India.
qs.kf:
☛ When did the Revolt of 1857 start? → 10 May 1857
☛ What was the immediate cause of the Meerut mutiny? → Greased cartridges
☛ Who was proclaimed leader by the rebels in Delhi? → Bahadur Shah Zafar
☛ Which animal fats were allegedly used in the cartridges? → Cow and pig fat
☛ Where did the Meerut sepoys go after the mutiny? → Delhi

q: The Revolt of 1857 ended with the British victory in:
qs.e: The Revolt of 1857, also known as India's First War of Independence, ended with a British victory in 1858. The revolt began in May 1857 at Meerut and spread across northern India. The British East India Company suppressed the uprising through intense military action by 1858. Following the revolt, the Government of India Act 1858 was passed, which abolished the Company's rule and transferred the administration of India directly to the British Crown. Key leaders of the revolt included Bahadur Shah Zafar, Rani Lakshmibai, and Nana Sahib. The event marked a turning point in Indian history, leading to the establishment of the British Raj.
qs.kf:
☛ Official end year of 1857 Revolt → 1858
☛ Act that brought India under British Crown → Government of India Act 1858
☛ Place of origin of 1857 Revolt → Meerut
☛ Last Mughal emperor involved in the revolt → Bahadur Shah Zafar
☛ Region associated with Rani Lakshmibai → Jhansi

q: Which of the following is NOT the social cause of the Revolt of 1857?
qs.e: Social causes of the Revolt of 1857 included British policies that interfered with religious and social customs. Forced conversions, activities of Christian missionaries, and religious interference (e.g., abolition of Sati, Widow Remarriage Act) created widespread discontent. These were all social causes. In contrast, the decline of traditional industries was an economic cause resulting from British industrial policies destroying Indian handicrafts and textiles. Hence, it does not belong to social causes.
qs.kf:
☛ Immediate cause of Revolt of 1857 → Use of greased cartridges
☛ Political cause of the revolt → Doctrine of Lapse and policy of annexation
☛ Economic cause of the revolt → Decline of traditional industries and heavy taxation
☛ Military cause of the revolt → Discrimination against Indian soldiers
☛ Religious cause of the revolt → Missionary activities and social reform laws

q: Who was the Governor-General of India during the First War of Independence of 1857?
qs.e: During the First War of Independence of 1857, the Governor-General of India was Lord Canning (Charles Canning). He served from 1856 to 1862. After the revolt, the Government of India Act 1858 was passed, transferring the administration of India from the East India Company to the British Crown. Lord Canning also became the first Viceroy of India. During the revolt, he adopted a policy of suppression and later implemented a policy of clemency.
qs.kf:
☛ British Prime Minister during 1857 revolt → Lord Palmerston
☛ Mughal Emperor during 1857 revolt → Bahadur Shah Zafar
☛ After the revolt, India's administration transferred to? → British Crown
☛ When was the Government of India Act passed? → 1858
☛ Lord Canning's tenure → 1856-1862

q: Which of the following was the primary form of resistance used by the rebels during the Revolt of 1857?
qs.e: The Revolt of 1857 was primarily an armed revolt where rebels took up arms against British rule. They attacked military cantonments, forts, and administrative centers. Leaders like Mangal Pandey, Rani Lakshmibai, Bahadur Shah Zafar, and Nana Saheb organized both soldiers and civilians. British policies such as Lord Dalhousie's Doctrine of Lapse and social reforms fueled discontent, leading to a widespread uprising. The rebels lacked a unified political agenda but shared a common enemy, resorting to armed struggle. Other options like political negotiations or non-violent protest were not the primary mode of resistance. The revolt spread across northern and central India, causing significant casualties and resistance for months.
qs.kf:
☛ What was the immediate cause of the 1857 Revolt? → Use of greased cartridges
☛ Who led the revolt in Delhi? → Bahadur Shah Zafar
☛ Who implemented the Doctrine of Lapse? → Lord Dalhousie
☛ Who led the revolt in Kanpur? → Nana Saheb
☛ Which queen led the revolt in Jhansi? → Rani Lakshmibai

q: Which of the following events shook the foundation of British rule in India and led to the end of the East India Company's rule?
qs.e: The 1857 Revolt was the most significant event that shook the foundation of British rule in India and led to the end of the East India Company's rule. Also known as the 'Sepoy Mutiny' or the 'First War of Indian Independence', this uprising forced the British Crown to take direct control of India through the Government of India Act 1858. The immediate cause of the revolt was the introduction of the Enfield rifle cartridges greased with animal fat, which offended both Hindu and Muslim sepoys. The revolt began in Meerut on May 10, 1857, and quickly spread to many parts of North and Central India. Although it failed due to lack of unity and better British military strength, it ended the Company's rule and led to the beginning of the British Raj.
qs.kf:
☛ Official cause of the revolt → Greased cartridges of Enfield rifle requiring to be bitten
☛ Start of the revolt → May 10, 1857, at Meerut
☛ Key leaders → Bahadur Shah Zafar (Delhi), Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi, Tantia Tope
☛ Result of the revolt → End of East India Company rule, India under British Crown
☛ Main reason for failure → Lack of unity among Indian leaders and superior British military power

q: Which of the following was the immediate cause of the Revolt of 1857?
qs.e: The immediate cause of the Revolt of 1857 was the introduction of the Enfield Rifle. The cartridges had to be bitten open before use, and a rumor spread that they were greased with pig and cow fat, offending both Hindu and Muslim soldiers. On 29 March 1857, Mangal Pandey revolted at Barrackpore over this issue. The rebellion soon spread across northern India. Other options like Doctrine of Lapse or spreading Western civilization were deeper causes, but the immediate spark was the Enfield rifle.
qs.kf:
☛ Immediate cause of Revolt of 1857 → Greased cartridges of Enfield Rifle
☛ Mangal Pandey revolted on → 29 March 1857 at Barrackpore
☛ Cartridges greased with fat of which animals → Cow and Pig
☛ British name for Revolt of 1857 → Sepoy Mutiny
☛ Revolt of 1857 began from → Meerut Cantonment, 10 May 1857

name: Set 3 · Q91–135
sub: Modern History - Revolt of 1857 & Early Uprisings

q: Who was the king of Jagdishpur during the Revolt of 1857?
qs.e: During the Revolt of 1857, the king of Jagdishpur was Kunwar Singh. He was the ruler of Arrah district in Bihar and led the rebellion against the British at the age of 80. He belonged to the Ujjaini Rajput clan. Kunwar Singh defeated British forces multiple times, notably in the battle of Arrah. He was mortally wounded and died on 23 April 1858. He is regarded as a great hero of the Indian freedom struggle.
qs.kf:
☛ Kunwar Singh's birth place → Jagdishpur village in Bhojpur district, Bihar
☛ Kunwar Singh belonged to which clan → Ujjaini Rajput
☛ Kunwar Singh died on → 23 April 1858
☛ Kunwar Singh's age during the revolt → 80 years
☛ Kunwar Singh was associated with which region → Bihar, Arrah (Jagdishpur)

q: To which of the following countries did Nana Saheb flee after being defeated in the Revolt of 1857?
qs.e: After the failure of the Revolt of 1857, Nana Saheb (also known as Dhondu Pant) fled to Nepal to escape the British. He was the adopted son of the exiled Peshwa Baji Rao II and a key leader of the rebellion in Kanpur. The British announced a reward for his capture, but he was never caught. The then ruler of Nepal, Jung Bahadur Rana, granted him asylum, though later under British pressure he had to leave Nepal. Nana Saheb's final days remain mysterious; some sources claim he died in Nepal, while others believe he escaped. This event is a significant part of the early phase of India's struggle for independence.
qs.kf:
☛ Original name of Nana Saheb → Dhondu Pant
☛ Nana Saheb was the adopted son of → Peshwa Baji Rao II
☛ Where did Nana Saheb lead the Revolt of 1857 → Kanpur
☛ Nepali ruler who gave asylum to Nana Saheb → Jung Bahadur Rana
☛ Escape route of Nana Saheb → Kanpur to Nepal

q: The British response after the Indian Rebellion of 1857 was to:
o: all the princely states were annexed under British rule
provide economic aid to Indian farmers
community, caste, tribal and provincial loyalties were promoted in the army
qs.e: After the rebellion of 1857, the British government restructured the Indian army. They adopted the policy of divide and rule by promoting community, caste, tribal and provincial loyalties. During recruitment, emphasis was placed on caste and regional identity so that Indian soldiers would not remain loyal to each other and any potential revolt could be suppressed. This policy deepened divisions in Indian society and ensured British control over the army.
qs.kf:
☛ What policy did the British adopt after the 1857 rebellion? → Divide and rule
☛ What was the main objective of restructuring the Indian army? → Eliminate the possibility of revolt
☛ Which act transferred the administration of India to the British Crown? → Government of India Act 1858
☛ Which communities were preferred in the army after 1857? → Jats, Gujars, Khatris and Punjabi Muslims
☛ Who was the last Governor-General of India after 1857? → Lord Canning

q: Who among the following was one of the personalities related to Meerut during the 1857 Revolt?
qs.e: During the 1857 Revolt, Kadam Singh was a prominent personality associated with Meerut. He was one of the leaders of the rebellion in Meerut and its surrounding areas. Kunwar Singh was associated with Arrah (Bihar), Nana Saheb with Kanpur, and Man Singh with Delhi. Kadam Singh played a key role in the uprising against the British and led the rebels in Meerut.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the leader of Meerut in the 1857 Revolt? → Kadam Singh
☛ Which place was Kunwar Singh associated with? → Arrah (Bihar)
☛ Which place was Nana Saheb associated with? → Kanpur
☛ Which place was Man Singh associated with? → Delhi
☛ Which revolt was Kadam Singh associated with? → 1857 Revolt

q: The Revolt of 1857 symbolically ended with the fall of which major city?
qs.e: The Revolt of 1857, also known as India's First War of Independence, symbolically ended with the fall of Delhi. Delhi was the political and military center of the revolt, where Bahadur Shah Zafar was proclaimed as the leader of the rebels. The British recaptured Delhi on 21 September 1857, after which Bahadur Shah Zafar was arrested. This event marked the symbolic end of the revolt, although fighting continued in other regions. The fall of Delhi was a major success for the British as it broke the morale of the rebels and signaled the return of Company rule. It also led to the abolition of the Mughal dynasty and the eventual transfer of power from the East India Company to the British Crown through the Government of India Act 1858.
qs.kf:
☛ Center of the 1857 Revolt → Delhi
☛ Symbolic end of the Revolt → Fall of Delhi (September 1857)
☛ Leader of the Revolt in Delhi → Bahadur Shah Zafar
☛ British commander who recaptured Delhi → John Nicholson
☛ End of Company rule and beginning of British Raj → Government of India Act 1858

q: Who among the following was the British resistance at Gwalior during the Revolt of 1857?
qs.e: During the Revolt of 1857, the British resistance at Gwalior was led by Hugh Rose. He was a prominent British army officer who played a crucial role in the Gwalior campaign. In 1858, Hugh Rose confronted the combined forces of Rani Lakshmibai and Tatya Tope to re-establish British control over Gwalior. On 17 June 1858, he defeated the rebels at the Battle of Kotah-ki-Serai, where Rani Lakshmibai was martyred. Later, Hugh Rose also subdued Tatya Tope and consolidated British rule in Gwalior. Henry Lawrence was active in Lucknow, John Nicholson in Delhi, and William Taylor in other parts of Central India.
qs.kf:
☛ Who led the rebels in Gwalior during the Revolt of 1857? → Tatya Tope and Rani Lakshmibai
☛ What was Hugh Rose's main contribution in the Revolt of 1857? → Recapturing Gwalior
☛ When did the Battle of Kotah-ki-Serai take place? → 17 June 1858
☛ Where did Rani Lakshmibai die? → Near Kotah-ki-Serai, Gwalior
☛ Who became the ruler of Gwalior after the Revolt of 1857? → Scindia (under British suzerainty)

q: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? Place Leader of 1857 Revolt
I. Lucknow - Begum Hazrat Mahal
II. Jhansi Rani - Lakshmi Bai
III. Gwalior - Tatya Tope
IV. Allahabad - Kunwar Singh
qs.e: In the 1857 revolt, the leader of Allahabad was Liaqat Ali, not Kunwar Singh. Kunwar Singh was the leader of Arrah (Bihar region). Begum Hazrat Mahal was associated with Lucknow, Rani Lakshmi Bai with Jhansi, and Tatya Tope with Gwalior. These three pairs are correctly matched. Thus, only the fourth pair (Allahabad - Kunwar Singh) is incorrect. Kunwar Singh was a zamindar who led the revolt at Arrah against the British forces.
qs.kf:
☛ Leader of Lucknow → Begum Hazrat Mahal
☛ Rani of Jhansi → Lakshmi Bai
☛ Leader of Gwalior → Tatya Tope
☛ Leader of Bihar (Arrah) → Kunwar Singh
☛ Leader of Allahabad → Liaqat Ali

q: Which of the following statements is/are correct in the context of the causes of failure of the 1857 Revolt?
I. No active support of Princely states.
II. Lack of effective leadership of rebels.
qs.e: The main causes of the failure of the 1857 Revolt include the lack of active support from princely states and the absence of effective leadership among the rebels. Most major princely states, such as Gwalior, Patiala, and Hyderabad, supported the British, depriving the revolt of a wide base. Furthermore, the revolt lacked a unified command; Bahadur Shah Zafar was a nominal leader, and there was poor coordination among key figures like Nana Saheb, Rani Lakshmibai, and Tantia Tope. The rebels had no clear political goal or centralized leadership. Hence both statements are correct.
qs.kf:
☛ What was the immediate cause of the 1857 Revolt? → Use of greased cartridges
☛ Where did the revolt begin? → Meerut (10 May 1857)
☛ Who was the last Mughal emperor during the revolt? → Bahadur Shah Zafar
☛ Which princely states supported the British? → Gwalior, Patiala, Hyderabad
☛ What was the main center of the revolt? → Delhi

q: Who among the following was the British resistance at Lucknow during the Revolt of 1857?
qs.e: During the Revolt of 1857, the British resistance at Lucknow was led by Henry Lawrence. He was the British Resident of Awadh and organized the defense of the Residency, protecting British soldiers and civilians. He was fatally wounded by a shell fragment on 2 July 1857 and died on 4 July. His brother, Sir Henry Montgomery Lawrence, was also a prominent British officer in India. Among the other options, William Taylor was active in Bengal, Colonel Oncell is not associated with this event, and John Nicholson played a key role in the siege of Delhi.
qs.kf:
☛ Who led British resistance at Lucknow? → Henry Lawrence
☛ When did Henry Lawrence die? → 4 July 1857
☛ What was Henry Lawrence's position? → British Resident of Awadh
☛ Who led the rebellion in Lucknow? → Begum Hazrat Mahal
☛ John Nicholson is famous for? → Siege of Delhi

q: Which of the following was NOT one of the reasons for the failure of the First War of Independence?
o: Lack of unity among the rebels
Limited geographical spread of the rebellion
qs.e: The failure of the First War of Independence (1857) was due to several factors, including lack of unity among rebels, superior British military technology, and limited geographical spread. The rebellion was mostly confined to North India and did not involve the entire country. The British had modern weapons, better organization, and effective communication. The rebels lacked a common national objective and were divided by regional and local interests. However, strong support from foreign powers was not a reason for failure; in fact, the rebels received no substantial foreign assistance. Thus, this option was NOT a cause of failure.
qs.kf:
☛ What was the immediate cause of the 1857 revolt? → Greased cartridges
☛ Who was the symbolic leader of the 1857 revolt? → Bahadur Shah Zafar
☛ Who called the 1857 revolt a 'National Revolt'? → VD Savarkar
☛ What was the major outcome of the 1857 revolt? → Direct British Crown rule in India
☛ Who was the Governor-General during the 1857 revolt? → Lord Canning

q: Which of the following movements is also known as the 'Ulgulan' or the 'Great Tumult' movement?
qs.e: Ulgulan or 'Great Tumult' is the Munda uprising led by Birsa Munda from 1899 to 1900 against British rule and the zamindari system. Birsa Munda aimed to protect the land and rights of the Munda tribe. The rebels preached the 'Birsaite' religion and fought guerrilla warfare against the British. Eventually, Birsa Munda was captured and died in jail. This movement is a significant example of tribal contribution to the Indian freedom struggle.
qs.kf:
☛ Who led the Ulgulan movement? → Birsa Munda
☛ When did the Ulgulan movement occur? → 1899-1900
☛ Which tribe is associated with Ulgulan? → Munda
☛ What religion did Birsa Munda propagate? → Birsaite
☛ What does Ulgulan mean? → Great Tumult

q: The ‘Kundara Proclamation’ which openly called for taking up arms against the British, is associated with which of the following freedom fighters?
qs.e: The Kundara Proclamation was issued by Velu Thampi in 1809. Velu Thampi was the Diwan of Travancore and strongly opposed the growing influence of the British East India Company. At Kundara, he convened a public meeting and called upon the people to take up arms against the British. This proclamation is considered one of the earliest calls for armed rebellion in Indian history. Velu Thampi led a revolt against British authorities but eventually committed suicide to avoid capture. The proclamation remains a significant symbol of early resistance against colonial rule in India.
qs.kf:
☛ Who issued the Kundara Proclamation? → Velu Thampi
☛ Velu Thampi was the Diwan of which state? → Travancore
☛ In which year was the Kundara Proclamation issued? → 1809
☛ How did Velu Thampi die? → Suicide
☛ Travancore is now part of which Indian state? → Kerala

q: Which 18th-century revolt was led by Raja Chait Singh against British interference in the Benares region in 1781?
qs.e: In 1781, Raja Chait Singh led the Benares Revolt against British interference in the Benares region. The revolt was sparked by excessive taxation and political meddling by the British East India Company. Chait Singh, the ruler of Benares, was threatened with deposition by Governor-General Warren Hastings. This led to an armed uprising, which was brutally suppressed by the Company. Chait Singh was forced to flee, and Benares came under direct British control. The revolt is a significant example of local resistance against British expansion in India.
qs.kf:
☛ Who led the Benares Revolt? → Raja Chait Singh
☛ When did the Benares Revolt take place? → 1781
☛ Who was the Governor-General during the Benares Revolt? → Warren Hastings
☛ What was the main cause of the Benares Revolt? → British interference and tax policies
☛ What was the outcome of the Benares Revolt? → British control over Benares was established

q: The association of Devi Chaudhurani and Bhawani Pathak with the Fakir-Sanyasi rebellion in India indicates which of the following?
o: These rebellions were purely religious in nature.
There was participation of all religions and genders in this rebellion.
In Bengal, only tribal groups led such resistance.
The movement was dominated by the upper caste elite.
qs.e: The Fakir-Sanyasi rebellion (1760-1800) was a peasant uprising in Bengal against the British, involving Hindu sannyasis and Muslim fakirs fighting together. The presence of female leaders like Devi Chaudhurani and Bhawani Pathak indicates the inclusive nature of this revolt. It was not purely religious but had economic causes like heavy taxation and exploitation. The rebellion saw participation from different castes, religions, and genders, all affected by British policies. Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay's novels 'Anandamath' and 'Devi Chaudhurani' popularized this movement.
qs.kf:
☛ What was the period of Fakir-Sanyasi rebellion? → 1760-1800
☛ What was the main cause of this rebellion? → British economic exploitation and tax policy
☛ Which novels popularized this rebellion? → 'Anandamath' and 'Devi Chaudhurani'
☛ Who was Devi Chaudhurani? → A female leader involved in the rebellion
☛ Who was Bhawani Pathak? → A female leader of the Fakir-Sanyasi rebellion

q: What negative consequences did the Revolt of 1857 create in Indian society?
o: Mistrust developed between the Hindu and Muslim communities.
There was a decline in Indian handicrafts.
The tribal and peasant movements were weakened.
There was a decline in Indian language and culture.
qs.e: After the 1857 Revolt, the British adopted the policy of Divide and Rule. They blamed the Muslim community as the main instigator of the revolt, breaking the Hindu-Muslim unity. Under this policy, Muslims were suppressed and Hindus were given preference in jobs and opportunities, leading to mistrust between the two communities. This mistrust deepened the division in Indian society and later gave rise to communalism. It was a major success for the British as it weakened Indian unity and nationalism.
qs.kf:
☛ What policy did the British adopt after the 1857 Revolt? → Divide and Rule
☛ Which community was blamed for the 1857 Revolt? → Muslim community
☛ What was the main objective of the Divide and Rule policy? → To break Hindu-Muslim unity
☛ Which community was given preference in jobs after 1857? → Hindu community
☛ Which unity weakened in Indian society after the 1857 Revolt? → Hindu-Muslim unity

q: The Devi Movement took place in which of the following regions of India?
qs.e: The Devi Movement took place in the South Gujarat region of India. It was a socio-religious movement launched by the tribal community in 1922-23. The movement was led by Motilal Tejawat. Its objective was to keep tribals away from alcohol and superstition. The movement also supported Gandhian ideology. The Devi Movement is also known as the Bhagat Movement.
qs.kf:
☛ Who started the Devi Movement? → Motilal Tejawat
☛ Which community was associated with the Devi Movement? → Tribal
☛ Region of the Devi Movement? → South Gujarat
☛ Other name of the Devi Movement? → Bhagat Movement
☛ Main objective of the Devi Movement? → Oppose alcohol and superstition

q: Which of these was NOT a cause of popular resentment against British rule before 1857?
qs.e: Before the 1857 revolt, major causes of popular resentment against British rule included high taxes, low wages, and racial discrimination. Heavy taxes imposed by the British economically ruined peasants and zamindars. Indian soldiers received low wages and faced racial discrimination, being denied higher positions. In contrast, religious tolerance was not a cause of resentment; in fact, British policies that hurt religious sentiments, such as the use of greased cartridges, caused anger. However, religious tolerance itself was a positive aspect that did not generate resentment. Therefore, this option is inconsistent with the causes of popular anger before 1857.
qs.kf:
☛ What was the immediate cause of the 1857 revolt? → Use of greased cartridges
☛ What was the Permanent Settlement of Bengal related to? → Exploitation of peasants through high taxes
☛ Under which policy did Indian soldiers face low wages? → Discriminatory pay policy in the British army
☛ What was an example of racial discrimination? → Denying higher posts to Indians
☛ What type of resentment existed against British rule before 1857? → Economic, social, and political

q: The Wahabi Movement was started by Syed Ahmad, of _____.
qs.e: The Wahabi Movement was founded by Syed Ahmad, who was born in Rae Bareli district of Uttar Pradesh. This movement emerged in the 19th century, inspired by Islamic reforms and anti-British sentiment. Syed Ahmad propagated the Wahabi ideology in India, which was influenced by Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab of Saudi Arabia. The movement aimed to purify Islam and oppose British rule. Syed Ahmad called for jihad against the Sikh Empire and was martyred in the Battle of Balakot in 1831. The Wahabi Movement later inspired several uprisings against the British.
qs.kf:
☛ Founder of Wahabi Movement → Syed Ahmad of Rae Bareli
☛ Influenced by → Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab
☛ Main objectives → Islamic reform and anti-British stance
☛ Place of death → Battle of Balakot (1831)
☛ Region of movement → Primarily North India

q: Which of the following is NOT a major cause of the people’s revolts before 1857?
o: Exploitation of rural society by corrupt officers.
qs.e: Major causes of the people's revolts before 1857 included socio-economic discontent arising from colonial policies. Exploitation of rural society by corrupt officers, destruction of indigenous industries, and colonial land revenue settlements (e.g., Permanent Settlement, Ryotwari) led to heavy taxation and land alienation for peasants and artisans. While conversion programs were part of missionary activities and became a spark for the 1857 revolt, it was not a major cause in earlier revolts (e.g., Santhal, Chuar, Polygar) which were primarily against economic and administrative oppression rather than religious issues. These uprisings were rooted in grievances over revenue, land rights, and social exploitation.
qs.kf:
☛ First major tribal revolt before 1857 → Santhal rebellion (1855-56)
☛ Main cause of 'Indigo revolt' in Bengal → Oppression of peasants for indigo cultivation
☛ Region of Chuar rebellion → Jungle Mahal area of West Bengal
☛ Under whose rule did the Polygar revolts occur → East India Company rule
☛ Which pre-1857 revolt saw significant role of a 'religious guru' → Wahabi movement in Faizabad

q: What was the name of the legend who spearheaded the Munda Rebellion?
qs.e: Birsa Munda was a legendary tribal leader who spearheaded the Munda Rebellion in 1899-1900 against British rule and the oppressive landlords. He started the 'Ulgulan' (Great Rebellion) to fight for the rights of the Munda community, demanding reduction in land revenue and ownership over forests. The British government placed a bounty of 500 rupees on his head. He died mysteriously in Ranchi Jail on June 9, 1900. Birsa Munda is remembered as a significant symbol of India's freedom struggle.
qs.kf:
☛ Who led the Munda Rebellion? → Birsa Munda
☛ When did the Munda Rebellion take place? → 1899-1900
☛ Where was Birsa Munda born? → Ulihatu, Jharkhand
☛ Which rebellion is called 'Ulgulan'? → Munda Rebellion
☛ Where did Birsa Munda die? → Ranchi Jail

q: Who among the following was declared the leader of the rebellion by the rebels against British tyranny during the First War of Independence of 1857?
qs.e: During the First War of Independence in 1857, the rebels declared the Mughal Emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar as their leader. After capturing Delhi, they recognized him as the Emperor and issued decrees in his name. Bahadur Shah Zafar was the last emperor of the Mughal dynasty. He led the rebellion, but the British army recaptured Delhi. He was arrested and exiled to Rangoon (Yangon), where he died in 1862. His leadership gave the rebellion a national character.
qs.kf:
☛ 1857 First War of Independence → Also known as the Sepoy Mutiny
☛ Bahadur Shah Zafar's exile → Rangoon (present-day Yangon, Myanmar)
☛ Start of 1857 rebellion → Meerut
☛ Sepoy Mutiny → Another name for 1857 Revolt
☛ Bahadur Shah Zafar → Last emperor of the Mughal dynasty

q: Which of the following freedom fighters led the Rampa Rebellion of 1922 against forest laws?
qs.e: The Rampa Rebellion (1922-24) took place in the forest regions of Andhra Pradesh and was led by Alluri Sitarama Raju. The rebellion was against the British forest laws that prohibited tribals from collecting forest produce and practicing shifting cultivation. Alluri Sitarama Raju used guerrilla warfare and mobilized the tribal communities. He was popularly known as 'Manyam Veerudu' (Hero of the Jungle). He was captured and executed in 1924. Other options: Ashfaqullah Khan was associated with the Kakori Conspiracy, Jatindra Nath Das with hunger strikes, and Surya Sen with the Chittagong Armoury Raid.
qs.kf:
☛ Who led the Rampa Rebellion? → Alluri Sitarama Raju
☛ When did the Rampa Rebellion start? → 1922
☛ Against what was the Rampa Rebellion fought? → Forest laws
☛ What was Alluri Sitarama Raju known as? → Manyam Veerudu
☛ When was Alluri Sitarama Raju executed? → 1924

q: Who led the Tamar tribal revolts against the British in India?
qs.e: The Tamar tribal revolt (1830-1831) was led by Bhola Nath Sahay against the British. This uprising occurred in the Tamar region of the Bengal Presidency due to oppressive British policies, including high taxes and forest laws that threatened the livelihoods of the tribal communities. Bhola Nath Sahay, a local zamindar, organized the tribals and led the revolt. The British brutally suppressed the rebellion, capturing and executing Bhola Nath Sahay by hanging. The Tamar revolt is a significant chapter in the history of tribal resistance against British colonial rule in India, highlighting the early struggles for rights and autonomy.
qs.kf:
☛ Leader of Tamar revolt → Bhola Nath Sahay
☛ Year of Tamar revolt → 1830-1831
☛ Region of Tamar revolt → Bengal Presidency (now Jharkhand)
☛ Death of Bhola Nath Sahay → Hanging
☛ Cause of revolt → High taxes and forest laws

q: Which of the following rebellions was led by traditional land soldiers (foot soldiers) in Odisha?
qs.e: The Paika rebellion was a significant uprising in Odisha led by traditional land soldiers (foot soldiers) known as Paikas. These soldiers served under the Gajapati kings of Odisha. The rebellion occurred in 1817 against the British East India Company. It was led by Bakshi Jagabandhu Bidyadhar. The main causes were excessive taxation, land revenue policies, and the erosion of Paikas' privileges. Though the rebellion was suppressed, it is considered an early precursor to the 1857 War of Independence.
qs.kf:
☛ Who led the Paika rebellion? → Bakshi Jagabandhu Bidyadhar
☛ When did the Paika rebellion occur? → 1817
☛ Who were the Paikas? → Land soldiers of the Gajapati kings of Odisha
☛ Against whom was the Paika rebellion? → British East India Company
☛ What is the significance of the Paika rebellion? → Early precursor to the 1857 rebellion

q: Which of the following was a tribal rebellion led by Birsa, a leader from Ranchi, that began as a religious movement and later turned into a fight against colonial land settlement, moneylenders and forest contractors?
qs.e: This rebellion was led by Birsa Munda from 1899-1900 in the Ranchi region of present-day Jharkhand. Birsa started a religious movement called Birsait or Birsa Panth, which later turned into a fight against colonial land settlement, moneylenders, and forest contractors. The Munda tribe was exploited by the British and local landlords, leading to this uprising. Birsa Munda used guerrilla warfare tactics and was eventually captured by the British in 1900. He died in jail. This rebellion is significant in India's freedom struggle as a tribal resistance against colonial oppression.
qs.kf:
☛ When was Birsa Munda born? → 1875
☛ When did Birsa Munda die? → 1900
☛ Which tribal community did Birsa Munda belong to? → Munda
☛ Which region was affected by the Munda uprising? → Ranchi (Jharkhand)
☛ What was the name of Birsa Munda's religious movement? → Birsait

q: The brothers Sidhu and Kanhu were the leaders of which of the following tribal uprisings?
qs.e: The brothers Sidhu and Kanhu were the leaders of the Santhal Rebellion (1855-56). This uprising took place in the Santhal Pargana region of Jharkhand. The Santhal tribals revolted against the oppressive land revenue policies of the British, the usury of moneylenders, and the tyranny of zamindars. Sidhu and Kanhu united the Santhals and fought against the British. Although the rebellion was eventually crushed by the British army, it played a significant role in India's freedom struggle.
qs.kf:
☛ Leader of Santhal Rebellion → Sidhu and Kanhu
☛ Year of Rebellion → 1855-56
☛ Region → Santhal Pargana (Jharkhand)
☛ Cause → Land revenue policy and usury
☛ Outcome → Suppressed by British

q: The Santhal Revolt of 1855-56 was against which groups along with the British officials?
qs.e: The Santhal Revolt of 1855-56 was primarily against British officials, zamindars (landlords), and moneylenders. The Santhal tribe rose in rebellion against the British land revenue policies and the exploitation by zamindars and moneylenders. The revolt was led by Sidhu and Kanhu Murmu. The main cause was the Mahalwari system imposed by the British, which strengthened zamindars and moneylenders. The Santhals revolted in the Damin-i-Koh region, which was allocated to them. The British army brutally suppressed the revolt, but it inspired future peasant movements.
qs.kf:
☛ Who led the Santhal Revolt? → Sidhu and Kanhu Murmu
☛ In which region did the Santhal Revolt occur? → Damin-i-Koh (Sahibganj and Bhagalpur)
☛ Who were the opponents of the Santhal Revolt? → British, zamindars, moneylenders
☛ What was the main cause of the Santhal Revolt? → Land revenue policy and exploitation
☛ Which state is the main habitat of Santhal tribe? → Jharkhand, West Bengal, Odisha

q: After a hundred years of conquest and administration, the English East India Company faced a massive uprising that took place in _________.
qs.e: After a hundred years of conquest and administration, the English East India Company faced a massive uprising in 1857, known as the Revolt of 1857 or the First War of Indian Independence. The revolt began on 10 May 1857 at Meerut and rapidly spread across large parts of northern India. Key leaders included Mangal Pandey, Rani Lakshmibai, Bahadur Shah Zafar, and Nana Saheb. The immediate cause was the use of greased cartridges which offended religious sentiments. Although the revolt failed, it led to the end of Company rule and the beginning of direct British Crown rule in India in 1858.
qs.kf:
☛ Where did the Revolt of 1857 begin? → Meerut
☛ When did the Revolt of 1857 begin? → 10 May 1857
☛ What was the immediate cause of the Revolt of 1857? → Greased cartridges
☛ Which Mughal emperor was made the leader of the 1857 revolt? → Bahadur Shah Zafar
☛ When did the Company rule end after the 1857 revolt? → 1858

q: Pick the INCORRECT statement regarding the life of Birsa Munda.
o: He urged people to destroy the Europeans.
He advised his people to bring back the Golden Age of Mundas.
Birsa was born in the forests of Madhya Pradesh.
He had joined the local missionary school.
qs.e: Birsa Munda was born on 15 November 1875 in Ulihatu village, Ranchi district, Jharkhand (then part of Bengal Presidency). He belonged to the Munda tribe and led a rebellion against the British and missionaries. He urged people to destroy the Europeans and bring back the Golden Age of Mundas. He also joined the local missionary school. Therefore, the statement about his birth in the forests of Madhya Pradesh is incorrect.
qs.kf:
☛ Birsa Munda's birth place → Ulihatu, Ranchi, Jharkhand
☛ Objective of Birsa Munda's movement → Restoration of Munda rule and opposition to British
☛ Rebellion associated with Birsa Munda → Ulgulan rebellion (1899-1900)
☛ Birsa Munda's death → 9 June 1900, Ranchi jail
☛ Cause of Birsa Munda's death → Cholera

q: Who among the following sent a telegram on 6 August 1857 stating, 'Our men are cowed by the numbers opposed to them and the endless fighting. Every village is held against us, the zamindars have risen to oppose us'?
qs.e: Lieutenant Colonel Tytler sent this telegram from Delhi on 6 August 1857 during the Revolt of 1857, highlighting the difficulties faced by the British forces. The message indicates that the British were facing opposition from every village and the zamindars. Tytler was a British army officer in Delhi at the time and sent this telegram to Viceroy Lord Canning. In the telegram, he stated that his men were intimidated by the large numbers of rebels and the continuous fighting. This event is important for understanding the situation of the British administration during the Revolt of 1857. Tytler's message reflects the widespread impact of the revolt.
qs.kf:
☛ Who sent the telegram on 6 August 1857? → Lieutenant Colonel Tytler
☛ From where was the telegram sent? → Delhi
☛ To whom was the telegram sent? → Viceroy Lord Canning
☛ What did the telegram state? → Villages and zamindars were against the British
☛ Which revolt is this related to? → Revolt of 1857

q: During the Revolt of 1857, Rani Laxmibai led the rebellion from:
qs.e: During the Revolt of 1857, Rani Laxmibai led the rebellion from Jhansi. She was the queen of Jhansi and fought against the British policy of annexation. The rebellion in Jhansi started in June 1857, and she led her army against the British forces. She employed guerilla warfare tactics and ultimately died fighting near Gwalior in 1858. Rani Laxmibai is considered one of the leading figures of the Indian independence movement, known for her bravery and leadership.
qs.kf:
☛ Birthplace of Rani Laxmibai → Varanasi
☛ Original name of Rani Laxmibai → Manikarnika
☛ Rani Laxmibai married to → Raja Gangadhar Rao
☛ British officer in Jhansi during 1857 → Hugh Rose
☛ Place of death of Rani Laxmibai → Kotah-ki-Sarai near Gwalior

q: Which of the following was NOT a consequence of the Revolt of 1857?
o: Policies that favoured zamindars and landlords were struck down.
Lands and properties of Muslims were confiscated en masse.
The strength of Indian soldiers in the army was reduced.
The Governor-General of India was given the title 'Viceroy'.
qs.e: After the Revolt of 1857, the British government strengthened policies that favoured zamindars and landlords, rather than striking them down. Lord Canning abolished the 'Doctrine of Lapse' and assured zamindars of their rights to gain their support. The other options were actual consequences: Muslim lands and properties were confiscated, the number of Indian soldiers in the army was reduced, and the Governor-General was given the title 'Viceroy'. Hence, striking down pro-zamindar policies was not a consequence of the revolt.
qs.kf:
☛ Which doctrine was abolished after the Revolt of 1857? → Doctrine of Lapse
☛ Who was the first Viceroy of India? → Lord Canning
☛ What was the ratio of British to Indian soldiers maintained after 1857? → 1:2
☛ Which act transferred control of India from the Company to the Crown? → Government of India Act 1858
☛ How were Muslims treated after the 1857 revolt? → They faced repression and confiscation of property

q: Which of the following was the biggest armed resistance to colonialism in the 19th century in India?
qs.e: The biggest armed resistance to colonialism in 19th-century India was the Sepoy Mutiny (1857), also known as the First War of Indian Independence. It began on May 10, 1857 at Meerut and rapidly spread across northern India. Major causes included the controversy over greased cartridges, Lord Dalhousie's Doctrine of Lapse, and British administrative oppression. Leaders like Bahadur Shah Zafar, Rani Lakshmibai, and Tatya Tope led the revolt. Although ultimately unsuccessful, it laid the foundation for Indian nationalism. Other options: First Anglo-Maratha War (1775-82) and Battle of Buxar (1764) belong to the 18th century, while Quit India Movement (1942) is from the 20th century.
qs.kf:
☛ Immediate cause of 1857 Revolt → Use of greased cartridges
☛ Place of origin of the revolt → Meerut
☛ Major centers of revolt → Jhansi, Kanpur, Lucknow, Delhi
☛ Queen who led the revolt → Lakshmibai
☛ British Governor General during 1857 → Lord Canning

q: What was the ultimate promise made by Bhagirath Majhi to the Santhals if they followed his teachings?
o: Access to modern education and jobs
qs.e: Bhagirath Majhi was a leader of the Santhal Rebellion (1855-56). He rallied the Santhals against British oppression. His ultimate promise was that if they followed his teachings, they would regain their lost lands and receive divine protection. This promise was rooted in religious and cultural beliefs, assuring the Santhals that God would protect them and return their land. The rebellion was a major tribal uprising before the 1857 War of Independence.
qs.kf:
☛ Who led the Santhal Rebellion? → Sidhu and Kanhu Murmu
☛ When did the Santhal Rebellion occur? → 1855-56
☛ Which rebellion is Bhagirath Majhi associated with? → Santhal Rebellion
☛ What was the main cause of the Santhal Rebellion? → Land revenue and zamindari oppression
☛ Where is the Santhal region located? → Parts of Jharkhand and Bengal

q: Which tribal revolt in 1831-32 was led by Buddho Bhagat and targeted exploitative landlords and British officials?
qs.e: The Kol Revolt of 1831-32 was led by Buddho Bhagat against exploitative landlords and British officials. The Kol tribe, primarily from the Chotanagpur region of present-day Jharkhand, rose in rebellion due to oppressive British policies, including heavy taxation and the Permanent Settlement system that transferred land rights to non-tribal landlords. The revolt was marked by attacks on moneylenders, zamindars, and British officials. The British eventually suppressed the revolt with military force, but it remains a significant example of tribal resistance against colonial rule.
qs.kf:
☛ Who led the Kol Revolt → Buddho Bhagat
☛ When did the Kol Revolt occur → 1831-32
☛ What was the target of the Kol Revolt → Exploitative landlords and British officials
☛ Which region is associated with the Kol tribe → Jharkhand
☛ In which year was the Kol Revolt suppressed → 1832

q: The Kherwar movement was led by which charismatic leader?
qs.e: The Kherwar movement (1870s) was led by Bhagirath Manjhi. This movement took place in the Santhal Pargana region of Jharkhand against the oppression of the British and zamindars. Bhagirath Manjhi united the Kherwar tribe and demanded tax relief, land rights, and self-governance. The movement was based on peaceful civil disobedience. Although the movement did not succeed, it laid the foundation for later tribal struggles. Other options: Birsa Munda (Ulgulan), Sidhu Murmu (Santhal rebellion), and Tilka Manjhi (freedom fighter) are associated with different movements.
qs.kf:
☛ Leader of Kherwar movement? → Bhagirath Manjhi
☛ Region of Kherwar movement? → Santhal Pargana, Jharkhand
☛ Objective of the movement? → Tax relief, land rights
☛ Method of movement? → Peaceful civil disobedience
☛ Kherwar is a tribe? → Yes, Kherwar tribe

q: During the 1857 Revolt, Indian sepoys declared which of the following as their symbolic leader?
qs.e: During the 1857 Revolt, Indian sepoys declared the Mughal emperor Bahadur Shah II as their symbolic leader. He was in Delhi, and the rebels recognized him as the emperor. Although Bahadur Shah II had no real power, his name was used to legitimize the revolt. After the revolt was suppressed, he was exiled to Rangoon. Other options like Tantia Tope, Rani Lakshmibai, and Nana Saheb were important leaders but were not declared as symbolic leaders.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the symbolic leader of the 1857 Revolt? → Bahadur Shah II
☛ Where was Bahadur Shah II exiled? → Rangoon
☛ Where did Nana Saheb lead the 1857 Revolt? → Kanpur
☛ Where did Rani Lakshmibai lead the revolt? → Jhansi
☛ Who was Tantia Tope associated with? → Nana Saheb

q: Which tribal leader led the Munda Ulgulan (rebellion) in the 1890s?
qs.e: Birsa Munda led the Munda Ulgulan (rebellion) in 1899-1900 against British rule and the exploitation by zamindars. The revolt aimed at establishing Munda Raj and opposing land taxes, forced labor, and forest laws. Birsa Munda mobilized the tribal community and is revered as a deity by them. He was captured and died in jail in 1900.
qs.kf:
☛ Who led the Munda Ulgulan? → Birsa Munda
☛ Birthplace of Birsa Munda? → Ulihatu, Jharkhand
☛ When did Birsa Munda die? → 1900 (in jail)
☛ Year of Munda Ulgulan? → 1899-1900
☛ Which movement is Birsa Munda associated with? → Tribal revolt

q: Which of the following is not a reform suggested by Birsa Munda to the Munda tribal community during the Munda rebellion?
o: Not believing in magic and witchcraft
qs.e: Birsa Munda suggested several reforms to the Munda tribal community, which included quitting drinking alcohol, cultivating their land, and not believing in magic and witchcraft. He urged the tribals to stop living in the past and instead focus on present reforms and struggle. 'Stop living in the past' was not one of his suggested reforms. Birsa Munda led the Munda rebellion from 1899 to 1900 against British rule and oppressive landlords. He called for 'Ulgulan' (the great revolution) and encouraged social and religious reforms among the tribal community.
qs.kf:
☛ Birsa Munda's movement known as → Ulgulan (the great revolution)
☛ Year of Munda rebellion → 1899-1900
☛ Against whom did Birsa Munda rebel → British rule and landlords
☛ Birsa Munda's birthplace → Ulihatu, Jharkhand
☛ Which community did Birsa Munda organize → Munda tribal community

q: Which policy was adopted by the British in the post-1857 revolt in India due to distrust of Hindu-Muslim unity?
qs.e: After the 1857 revolt, the British felt threatened by the growing unity between Hindus and Muslims. To break this unity, they adopted the policy of Divide and Rule. This policy aimed to create communal divisions by promoting separate electorates, religious representation, and communal organizations. The British encouraged differences between the two communities to weaken the national movement. Doctrine of Lapse and Subsidiary Alliance were policies before 1857. Forward Policy related to frontier expansion. Hence, Option 4 is correct. The policy was systematically implemented through laws, educational institutions, and political concessions.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Divide and Rule policy adopted? → After the 1857 revolt
☛ What was the objective of this policy? → To break Hindu-Muslim unity
☛ Which act was passed under this policy? → Indian Councils Act 1909 (Minto-Morley Reforms)
☛ Who is credited with implementing Divide and Rule in India? → Lord Minto
☛ What was the impact of this policy on Indian independence? → Led to Partition in 1947

q: The Sannyasi-Fakir Rebellion commenced in the second half of which of the following centuries?
qs.e: The Sannyasi-Fakir Rebellion was a peasant and religious revolt against the British in India, mainly spread in the Bengal and Bihar regions. This rebellion started in the second half of the 18th century, especially between 1763 and 1800. Its main causes were the oppressive policies of the East India Company, increased land revenue, and restrictions on religious freedom. The Sannyasis (Hindu ascetics) and Fakirs (Muslim saints) jointly fought guerrilla warfare against the British. Prominent leaders included Bhavani Pathak, Devi Chowdhurani, Musa Shah, and Majnu Shah. This revolt became a symbol of popular awakening against British rule.
qs.kf:
☛ In which century did the Sannyasi-Fakir Rebellion begin? → 18th
☛ What was the main cause of this revolt? → Oppressive policies of East India Company
☛ Who were the prominent leaders? → Bhavani Pathak and Devi Chowdhurani
☛ Which regions were affected by this rebellion? → Bengal and Bihar
☛ Around which year did the rebellion start? → 1763

q: The Moplah Rebellion took place between the years:
qs.e: The Moplah Rebellion took place between 1921 and 1922 in the Malabar region of Kerala. It was a peasant uprising against British colonial rule and Hindu landlords, led by the Moplahs (Muslims of Kerala). The immediate trigger was the Khilafat movement, but the main causes were related to tenant rights and heavy land revenue. Thousands were killed in the rebellion, and the British Army brutally suppressed it. This event is a significant chapter in India's freedom struggle.
qs.kf:
☛ Where did the Moplah Rebellion occur? → Malabar region, Kerala
☛ Who were the Moplahs? → Muslims of Kerala
☛ What was the immediate cause of the Moplah Rebellion? → The Khilafat movement
☛ Who were the leaders of the Moplah Rebellion? → Ali Musliyar and Variamkunnath Kunhammed Haji
☛ The Moplah Rebellion was related to? → Peasant tenant rights and land revenue

q: Who was responsible for introducing Enfield rifles that used the greased cartridges which became the immediate reason of 1857 revolt?
qs.e: The immediate cause of the 1857 revolt was the use of greased cartridges in the Enfield rifles. The decision to introduce these rifles into the Indian army was taken during the tenure of Governor-General Lord Henry Hardinge (1844-1848). Although the rifles were actually distributed during the time of Lord Canning, the order for their import and training was given by Hardinge. The rumor that the greased cartridges contained cow and pig fat hurt the religious sentiments of Hindu and Muslim soldiers, sparking the rebellion. Among the other options, Captain Hearsey and Francis Grant were not directly associated with the introduction of these rifles.
qs.kf:
☛ Who introduced greased cartridges? → Lord Henry Hardinge
☛ What was the immediate cause of 1857 revolt? → Use of greased cartridges in Enfield rifles
☛ When were Enfield rifles introduced? → 1856 (under Lord Canning)
☛ Which fats were used in greased cartridges? → Cow and pig fat
☛ When did the revolt start at Meerut? → 10 May 1857

q: Which Indian sepoy in the British army played a key part in events immediately preceding the outbreak of the Indian rebellion of 1857?
qs.e: Mangal Pandey was a sepoy in the 34th Bengal Native Infantry regiment. On 29 March 1857 at Barrackpore, he refused to use the new Enfield rifle cartridges, rumored to be greased with cow and pig fat. He attacked his British officers and sparked the rebellion. This incident ignited widespread discontent across northern India, soon escalating into the great rebellion of 1857. Mangal Pandey was hanged on 8 April 1857. He is regarded as one of the first martyrs in India's freedom struggle.
qs.kf:
☛ Who started the 1857 rebellion? → Mangal Pandey
☛ Which regiment was Mangal Pandey in? → 34th Bengal Native Infantry
☛ When was Mangal Pandey hanged? → 8 April 1857
☛ What animal fats were used in the Enfield rifle cartridges? → Cow and pig
☛ Where did Mangal Pandey's revolt occur? → Barrackpore

q: Which of the following chronological order of events of the freedom struggle is correct?
o: Non cooperative movement – Sepoy mutiny – Champaran movement – Partition of Bengal
Sepoy mutiny - Partition of Bengal - Champaran movement - Non cooperative movement
Non cooperative movement - Champaran movement - Partition of Bengal - Sepoy mutiny
Non cooperative movement - Champaran movement - Sepoy mutiny - Partition of Bengal
qs.e: The Sepoy Mutiny (1857) was the first major revolt against British rule. This was followed by the Partition of Bengal in 1905 by Lord Curzon, which led to the Swadeshi movement. The Champaran movement (1917) was Mahatma Gandhi's first successful satyagraha against the exploitation of indigo farmers. The Non-Cooperation Movement (1920-22) was a mass movement launched by Gandhi urging non-cooperation with the British. This is the correct chronological order.
qs.kf:
☛ Sepoy Mutiny → 1857
☛ Partition of Bengal → 1905
☛ Champaran movement → 1917
☛ Non-Cooperation movement → 1920
☛ Gandhi's first satyagraha → Champaran, 1917
