☛ Who founded INC? → A.O. Hume

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (16/06/2025) Shift 3
q: What was the main issue debated during the 1905 Banaras Session of the INC, right after the announcement of Bengal’s partition?
o: Formation of All India Muslim League
Immediate resignation of British administrators in Bengal
qs.e: At the 1905 Banaras Session of the Indian National Congress, immediately after the announcement of Bengal's partition, the main issue debated was the use of Swadeshi and Boycott. Chaired by Dadabhai Naoroji, this session saw strong advocacy from the Garam Dal leaders for the boycott of British goods and promotion of indigenous products. The demand for Swaraj was raised later at the 1906 Calcutta Session. The All India Muslim League was formed in 1906. Thus, the core issue in 1905 was the use of Swadeshi and Boycott as a protest against the partition.
qs.kf:
☛ When was Bengal Partition announced? → 1905
☛ Who presided over the 1905 Banaras Session? → Dadabhai Naoroji
☛ What was the slogan of Swadeshi Movement? → Swadeshi, Boycott, National Education
☛ Who was the Viceroy during Bengal Partition? → Lord Curzon
☛ When was All India Muslim League founded? → 1906

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (21/06/2025) Shift 3
q: Which moderate leader, often referred to as the 'Grand Old Man of India,' became the first Indian elected to the British House of Commons and helped shape the early nationalist movement?
qs.e: Dadabhai Naoroji is known as the 'Grand Old Man of India'. He became the first Indian to be elected to the British House of Commons in 1892 from Finsbury Central. As a moderate leader, he played a crucial role in the early years of the Indian National Congress and served as its president three times. His famous 'Drain of Wealth' theory exposed the economic exploitation of India under British rule. He advocated for Swaraj and helped shape the early nationalist movement. He also wrote the influential book 'Poverty and Un-British Rule in India'.
qs.kf:
☛ Who propounded the 'Drain of Wealth' theory? → Dadabhai Naoroji
☛ How many times was Dadabhai Naoroji president of INC? → 3 times (1886, 1893, 1906)
☛ Which famous book did Dadabhai Naoroji write? → Poverty and Un-British Rule in India
☛ Who is called the 'Grand Old Man of India'? → Dadabhai Naoroji
☛ Who was the first Indian elected to the British House of Commons? → Dadabhai Naoroji

q: Which session of the congress gave a call to the attainment of 'Swaraj'?
qs.e: The 1906 Calcutta session of the Indian National Congress, presided over by Dadabhai Naoroji, gave the first call for the attainment of 'Swaraj' (self-rule). In his presidential address, Naoroji declared that India needed self-government. This session marked a significant shift in the Congress from moderate to militant nationalism. It was a turning point in the Indian freedom movement. Following this, the Congress split at the 1907 Surat session. The demand for Swaraj became a central theme in the struggle for independence. Dadabhai Naoroji, known as the Grand Old Man of India, played a key role in articulating the political aspirations of Indians.
qs.kf:
☛ Who first raised the demand for Swaraj in Congress? → Dadabhai Naoroji at the 1906 Calcutta session
☛ Who was the president of the 1906 Congress session? → Dadabhai Naoroji
☛ In which session did the Congress split? → 1907 Surat session
☛ What is Dadabhai Naoroji known as? → Grand Old Man of India
☛ What does Swaraj mean? → Self-rule or right to self-determination

q: The first national flag of India is said to have hoisted at _______ in 1906.
qs.e: The first national flag of India was hoisted on 7 August 1906 at Parsi Bagan Chowk (now Baratiya Bhavan Square) in Kolkata. The flag had three colors: green, yellow, and red, with eight lotus flowers, a crescent moon, and a sun. It was also known as the Bharat Swabhiman Flag. The flag was unfurled by Shachindra Prasad Bose and Sukhalal Yadav. This event took place during the Swadeshi movement, symbolizing the boycott of British goods. Later, in 1917, Madam Bhikaji Rustom Cama unfurled another version of the Indian flag.
qs.kf:
☛ Where was India's first national flag hoisted? → Kolkata
☛ When was the first flag hoisted? → 7 August 1906
☛ What were the flag's colors? → Green, yellow, red
☛ What symbols were on the flag? → Eight lotuses, crescent, sun
☛ Who hoisted the first flag? → Shachindra Prasad Bose and Sukhalal Yadav

q: Who among the following was the first Indian member of The British Parliament?
qs.e: Dadabhai Naoroji was a prominent Indian politician, economist, and social reformer. He was elected to the British Parliament in 1892, becoming the first Indian member of the British House of Commons. He represented the Finsbury Central constituency as a member of the Liberal Party. During his parliamentary tenure, he criticized British policies towards India and advocated for Indian interests. He is known for his 'Drain of Wealth' theory, which highlighted the economic exploitation of India under British rule. He also served thrice as the President of the Indian National Congress. His book 'Poverty and Un-British Rule in India' remains a significant critique of colonial economics.
qs.kf:
☛ Dadabhai Naoroji → First Indian member of the British Parliament (1892)
☛ Dadabhai Naoroji → Propounded the 'Drain of Wealth' theory
☛ Dadabhai Naoroji's book → 'Poverty and Un-British Rule in India'
☛ Dadabhai Naoroji → Three times President of Indian National Congress
☛ Dadabhai Naoroji's constituency → Finsbury Central, London

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (05/06/2025) Shift 3
q: Which of the following statements is/are correct regarding the Indian National Congress (INC)? a) The INC was founded in 1885 by Allan Octavian Hume. b) The first session of the INC was held in Pune under the presidency of WC Bonnerjee.
qs.e: The Indian National Congress (INC) was founded in 1885 by Allan Octavian Hume. The first session of the INC was held in Bombay (now Mumbai) at the Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College, not in Pune. The session was presided over by W.C. Bonnerjee. Thus, statement a is correct, while statement b is incorrect because the venue was Bombay, not Pune.
qs.kf:
☛ When was INC founded? → 1885
☛ Who founded INC? → Allan Octavian Hume
☛ Where was the first INC session held? → Bombay (Mumbai)
☛ Who was the first President of INC? → W.C. Bonnerjee
☛ How many delegates attended the first session? → 72

q: Who was chosen as the first president of the Indian National Congress (INC) during its first session?
qs.e: The Indian National Congress (INC) was founded in 1885. Its first session was held from 28 to 31 December 1885 at the Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College in Bombay (now Mumbai). In this session, Womesh Chandra Bonnerjee was chosen as the first president. He was a prominent barrister and politician. The session was attended by 72 delegates. The INC became a major platform for the Indian independence movement. Surendranath Banerjee became Congress president in 1895, Bipin Chandra Pal was a leader of the Garam Dal, and Pherozeshah Mehta also became president later.
qs.kf:
☛ Where was the first session of INC held? → Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College, Bombay
☛ When was INC founded? → 1885
☛ Who founded INC? → A. O. Hume
☛ How many delegates attended the first session? → 72
☛ What was Womesh Chandra Bonnerjee's profession? → Barrister

q: In which year was Bal Gangadhar Tilak arrested by the British authorities for writing a seditious article in the newspaper ‘Kesari’?
qs.e: Bal Gangadhar Tilak, a prominent Indian freedom fighter, was arrested by the British authorities in 1908 for writing seditious articles in his Marathi newspaper Kesari. In June 1908, he published an article praising Khudiram Bose and Prafulla Chaki, who had attempted to assassinate a British magistrate. The British government charged him with sedition and he was tried. In July 1908, he was sentenced to six years of imprisonment and was sent to Mandalay Prison in Burma. This event greatly enhanced Tilak's popularity and strengthened the Indian independence movement.
qs.kf:
☛ Name of Bal Gangadhar Tilak's newspaper → Kesari (Marathi) and Maratha (English)
☛ Sentence given to Tilak → Six years imprisonment
☛ Prison where Tilak was kept → Mandalay Jail, Burma
☛ Charge against Tilak → Sedition
☛ Famous slogan of Tilak → Swaraj is my birthright

q: Who was popularly known as the ‘Lion of Punjab’ during the Extremist phase?
qs.e: Lala Lajpat Rai was popularly known as the 'Lion of Punjab'. He was a prominent leader of the Extremist phase of the Indian freedom struggle. He was part of the Lal-Bal-Pal trio along with Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Bipin Chandra Pal. He was associated with Arya Samaj and raised the slogan of Swaraj. In 1928, during the Simon Commission protest, he was severely injured in a lathi charge and later died. He played a key role in the establishment of Dayanand Anglo-Vedic (DAV) College.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was known as 'Lion of Punjab'? → Lala Lajpat Rai
☛ Who was 'Pal' in Lal-Bal-Pal? → Bipin Chandra Pal
☛ Who died due to lathi charge during Simon Commission protest? → Lala Lajpat Rai
☛ Which organization was Lala Lajpat Rai associated with? → Arya Samaj
☛ Who is associated with the establishment of DAV College? → Lala Lajpat Rai

q: Which of the following institutions was set up during the Swadeshi movement?
qs.e: During the Swadeshi movement (1905-1908), several institutions were established to promote patriotism and national education. Bengal National College was founded in 1906 in Calcutta, with Aurobindo Ghosh as its first principal. Its aim was to provide national education as an alternative to the British education system. Other options: Bethune School (1849, women's education), Banaras Hindu University (1916), and Shantiniketan (1901, by Rabindranath Tagore) were established before or after the Swadeshi movement. Hence, Bengal National College is the institution set up during the Swadeshi movement.
qs.kf:
☛ First principal of Bengal National College → Aurobindo Ghosh
☛ Year of Swadeshi movement → 1905-1908
☛ Institution associated with national education movement → Bengal National College
☛ Year of establishment of Bethune School → 1849
☛ Founder of Banaras Hindu University → Pandit Madan Mohan Malaviya

q: At which session of the Indian National Congress did the party formally split into the Moderates and the Extremists?
qs.e: The Indian National Congress session at Surat in 1907 witnessed the formal split of the party into the Moderates and the Extremists. The Moderates were led by Gopal Krishna Gokhale, while the Extremists were led by Bal Gangadhar Tilak. The main reasons for the split were differences over the approach to national education, the Swadeshi movement, and the proposal by Tilak for the party presidency. This split marked a significant turning point in the history of the Congress, leading to separate strategies by both factions. The session is historically important as it divided the national movement into two distinct ideological streams.
qs.kf:
☛ 1907 Surat session → Congress split
☛ Moderate leader → Gopal Krishna Gokhale
☛ Extremist leader → Bal Gangadhar Tilak
☛ Reason for split → ideological differences
☛ Tilak's proposal → for party presidency

q: Which among the following slogans was popularised by Bal Gangadhar Tilak?
o: Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it
Give me blood and I will give you freedom
Freedom is our goal and we shall achieve it
Liberty is our dream and we must attain it
qs.e: Bal Gangadhar Tilak popularised the slogan 'Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it'. This slogan became a rallying cry in the Indian freedom struggle. Tilak was a staunch nationalist and a strong advocate of Swaraj (self-rule). He inspired Indians to demand self-governance as their birthright. Through his writings in 'Kesari' and public speeches, he spread this message widely. Tilak was a leader of the extremist faction in the Indian National Congress. His slogan ignited the spirit of patriotism among millions. The concept of Swaraj was central to his political philosophy. Tilak believed that Indians had an inherent right to rule themselves and must fight to achieve it.
qs.kf:
☛ Famous slogan of Bal Gangadhar Tilak → Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it
☛ Tilak belonged to which ideological group → Extremist / Garam Dal
☛ Newspapers founded by Tilak → Kesari (Marathi) and Mahratta (English)
☛ Birthplace of Bal Gangadhar Tilak → Ratnagiri, Maharashtra
☛ Movement during which Tilak was arrested → Swadeshi Movement (earlier) / Quit India Movement (later)

q: Which leader famously declared 'Swaraj is my birth right and I shall have it' during the Extremist Phase of the Indian National Movement?
qs.e: The famous slogan 'Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it' was declared by Bal Gangadhar Tilak in 1916. Tilak was a prominent leader of the Extremist (Garamb) faction of the Indian National Movement. He asserted that Swaraj was the birthright of every Indian, thereby igniting national consciousness and the demand for self-rule. Tilak popularized the concept of Swaraj among the masses and made it the central goal of India's freedom struggle. This slogan inspired widespread opposition to British rule. He also established the Home Rule League in 1916 to further the demand for self-government. Tilak used public festivals like Ganesh Utsav and Shivaji Utsav to mobilize people and spread nationalist ideas.
qs.kf:
☛ What was Bal Gangadhar Tilak's title? → Lokmanya
☛ Which newspapers did Tilak start? → Kesari (Marathi) and Maratha (English)
☛ Which jail was Tilak sent to? → Mandalay Jail (Burma)
☛ Which book of Tilak supports Swaraj? → Geeta Rahasya
☛ Who were the 'Lal-Bal-Pal' trio? → Lala Lajpat Rai, Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal

q: Which of the following principle was most emphasized by Bal Gangadhar Tilak during the Extremist Phase?
o: Swaraj as the birthright of every Indian
Complete armed revolution against the British
qs.e: During the Extremist Phase (1905-1908), Bal Gangadhar Tilak emphasized that Swaraj (self-rule) was the birthright of every Indian. He popularized the slogan, 'Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it.' Tilak viewed Swaraj not just as political independence but as a symbol of self-reliance and national pride. He mobilized mass support through the Home Rule League (1916) and used traditional festivals like Ganesh Chaturthi to spread nationalist ideas. Unlike moderates, he rejected reliance on British benevolence and advocated for direct action and resistance. However, he did not support complete armed revolution but favored constitutional agitation and mass movements. His emphasis on Swaraj as a birthright became the core ideology of the Indian freedom struggle.
qs.kf:
☛ Tilak's famous slogan → Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it
☛ Home Rule League founded in → 1916
☛ Extremist trio → Lal-Bal-Pal
☛ Festivals popularized by Tilak → Ganesh Utsav and Shivaji Utsav
☛ Newspapers published by Tilak → Kesari (Marathi) and The Mahratta (English)

q: Which form of nationalist protest emerged in response to the Partition of Bengal in 1905 that integrated economic, social, and political action?
o: Pursuing constitutional agitation within legislative councils
Submitting petitions to the British Parliament for reversal
Boycotting British goods and promoting indigenous industries
Organising armed resistance against colonial authorities
qs.e: In response to the Partition of Bengal in 1905, the Swadeshi and Boycott Movement emerged, integrating economic, social, and political action. It called for boycotting British goods and promoting indigenous industries. Starting in Bengal, it spread across India, strengthening national consciousness and emphasizing economic self-reliance. Leaders like Bal Gangadhar Tilak and later Mahatma Gandhi supported it. This movement laid the groundwork for future mass movements like the Non-Cooperation Movement.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Partition of Bengal? → 1905
☛ Who was the Viceroy during the partition? → Lord Curzon
☛ What was the key slogan of the Swadeshi movement? → Vande Mataram
☛ When was the partition of Bengal annulled? → 1911
☛ Who was a prominent leader of the Swadeshi movement? → Bal Gangadhar Tilak

q: Which demand advanced by the Moderate leadership of the Indian National Congress (1885–1905) most clearly reflected their objective of expanding Indian involvement within colonial decision-making structures?
o: Expansion of legislative councils for Indian representation
Immediate transfer of political authority to Indian hands
Preferential allocation of bureaucratic appointments to Indians
qs.e: The Moderate leadership (1885-1905) primarily aimed to increase Indian participation within colonial decision-making structures. Their most prominent demand was the expansion of legislative councils and the introduction of elected Indian members. This was partially achieved through the Indian Councils Act of 1892, which allowed indirect elections. The Moderates sought proportional representation to ensure Indian voices influenced law-making. While demands like tax reduction and job preferences were important, the demand for council expansion most clearly reflected their objective of expanding Indian involvement in governance.
qs.kf:
☛ What was the major constitutional reform demanded by Moderates? → Indian Councils Act 1892
☛ What did the Indian Councils Act 1892 provide? → Indirect elections to legislative councils
☛ What was the main political objective of Moderates? → Indian participation in colonial administration
☛ What is the time period of Moderate phase? → 1885-1905
☛ Who were the prominent Moderate leaders? → Dadabhai Naoroji, Gopal Krishna Gokhale

q: Which of the following statements is INCORRECT with respect to Indian socio-political movements and their leaders?
o: The Home Rule League was founded by Aurobindo Ghosh.
The Poona Sarvajanik Sabha was associated with Mahadev Govind Ranade.
The Self-Respect Movement was launched by E. V. Ramasamy.
The Abhinav Bharat Society was founded by Vinayak Damodar Savarkar.
qs.e: The Home Rule League was not founded by Aurobindo Ghosh but by Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Annie Besant in 1916. Tilak established his league in April 1916 in Maharashtra, while Besant formed hers in September 1916 covering the rest of India. The Poona Sarvajanik Sabha was founded in 1870 and was associated with Mahadev Govind Ranade. The Self-Respect Movement was launched in 1925 by E. V. Ramasamy (Periyar) in Tamil Nadu, focusing on anti-caste and social equality. The Abhinav Bharat Society was founded in 1904 by Vinayak Damodar Savarkar and his brother, as a revolutionary organization.
qs.kf:
☛ Who were the founders of the Home Rule League? → Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Annie Besant
☛ When was the Poona Sarvajanik Sabha established? → 1870
☛ Who launched the Self-Respect Movement? → E. V. Ramasamy (Periyar)
☛ Who founded the Abhinav Bharat Society? → Vinayak Damodar Savarkar
☛ What was the objective of the Home Rule League? → To attain self-government for India

q: Who among the following leaders founded the Indian National Association in 1876?
o: Surendranath Banerjee and Ananda Mohan Bose
Dadabhai Naoroji and Gopal Krishna Gokhale
Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Bipin Chandra Pal
qs.e: The Indian National Association was founded in 1876 by Surendranath Banerjee and Ananda Mohan Bose in Kolkata. It was a significant political organization that advocated for Indian rights through constitutional means. The association played a key role in the early nationalist movement and paved the way for the formation of the Indian National Congress. Surendranath Banerjee was known as the 'Father of Indian Nationalism', while Ananda Mohan Bose contributed to education and politics. The association aimed to unite Indians and promote national consciousness against British rule.
qs.kf:
☛ Who founded the Indian National Association in 1876? → Surendranath Banerjee and Ananda Mohan Bose
☛ Where was the Indian National Association established? → Kolkata
☛ Which organization preceded the Indian National Congress? → Indian National Association
☛ Which body supported the Indian National Association? → British Indian Association
☛ What is Surendranath Banerjee known as? → Father of Indian Nationalism

q: Which of the following statements is INCORRECT in the context of the Indian National Congress (INC)?
o: Womesh Chandra Bonnerjee was the first Hindu President of the INC
Badruddin Tyabji was the first Jainist President of the INC
George Yule was the first non-Indian President of the INC
Dadabhai Naoroji was the first Parsi President of the INC
qs.e: This statement is incorrect because Badruddin Tyabji belonged to the Muslim community, not Jainist. He was the first Muslim President of the INC, presiding over the 1887 Madras session. Womesh Chandra Bonnerjee was the first President of the INC and was Hindu. George Yule, a British businessman, became the first non-Indian President (1888). Dadabhai Naoroji was the first Parsi President (1886 and 1893). The INC was founded in 1885, and its early presidents represented diverse communities.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the first President of INC? → Womesh Chandra Bonnerjee
☛ First Muslim President of INC? → Badruddin Tyabji (1887)
☛ First non-Indian President of INC? → George Yule (1888)
☛ First Parsi President of INC? → Dadabhai Naoroji (1886)
☛ First woman President of INC? → Annie Besant (1917)

q: Which of the following statements is INCORRECT regarding the Atmiya Sabha?
o: The Atmiya Sabha was established in 1824
The Atmiya Sabha laid the foundation for the Brahmo Samaj
The Atmiya Sabha was established at Calcutta
The Atmiya Sabha was founded by Raja Ram Mohan Roy
qs.e: The Atmiya Sabha was founded by Raja Ram Mohan Roy in 1815, not 1824, at Calcutta. It was a philosophical discussion group that later laid the foundation for the Brahmo Samaj (established in 1828). Its aim was to promote social reform, monotheism, and Vedic principles. Therefore, the statement mentioning 1824 is incorrect.
qs.kf:
☛ Founder of Atmiya Sabha → Raja Ram Mohan Roy
☛ Year of establishment of Atmiya Sabha → 1815
☛ Place of establishment of Atmiya Sabha → Calcutta
☛ Successor of Atmiya Sabha → Brahmo Samaj (1828)
☛ Objective of Atmiya Sabha → Monotheism and social reform

q: Which of the following methods was characteristically adopted by the Moderates during the early phase of the Indian national movement?
o: Boycott of foreign goods and institutions
qs.e: During the early phase of the Indian national movement (1885-1905), the Moderates characteristically adopted the method of constitutional reforms. They remained loyal to the British Crown and sought changes through petitions, prayers, and delegations. Their approach was to educate public opinion and present demands before the British government. Leaders like Dadabhai Naoroji, Ferozeshah Mehta, and Gopal Krishna Gokhale advocated for reforms in Indian Councils Acts, civil services, and economic policies. They aimed for gradual self-government within the British Empire. The Moderates were criticized by later extremists for their soft approach, but they laid the groundwork for political awakening. The Swadeshi and Boycott movements were later adopted by the Extremists after 1905.
qs.kf:
☛ Key Moderate leader → Dadabhai Naoroji
☛ Main method of Moderates → Petition and prayer
☛ Goal of Moderates → Gradual constitutional reforms
☛ Limitation of Moderates → Not lack of patriotism, but strategy
☛ Boycott movement started by → Extremists in 1905

q: Which of the following pairs of leaders were closely associated with the signing of the Lucknow Pact of 1916?
o: Lala Lajpat Rai and Bipin Chandra Pal
Gopal Krishna Gokhale and Annie Besant
Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Muhammad Ali Jinnah
qs.e: The Lucknow Pact of 1916 was a historic agreement between the Indian National Congress and the Muslim League. The pact was signed under the leadership of Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Muhammad Ali Jinnah. Tilak had successfully reunited the moderate and extremist factions of the Congress, while Jinnah was a prominent leader of the Muslim League. Under the pact, the Muslim League supported the Congress's demand for self-government, and the Congress accepted separate electorates for Muslims. This agreement fostered Hindu-Muslim unity in the Indian national movement.
qs.kf:
☛ Chief architects of the Lucknow Pact → Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Muhammad Ali Jinnah
☛ Year of the pact → 1916
☛ Venue of the pact → Lucknow
☛ Congress President at that time → Ambika Charan Mazumdar
☛ Muslim League President at that time → Muhammad Ali Jinnah

q: Which Indian nationalist leader emerged as a prominent figure of the extremist phase of the freedom movement, emphasizing direct action and mass mobilisation?
qs.e: In the extremist phase of the Indian freedom movement, Bal Gangadhar Tilak emerged as a prominent leader who emphasized direct action and mass mobilization. He popularized the slogan "Swaraj is my birthright" and used public festivals like Ganesh Utsav and Shivaji Utsav to unite people. Tilak was the editor of newspapers 'Kesari' and 'Maratha'. In 1908, he was sentenced to six years in Mandalay jail for sedition. He represented the radical faction within the Indian National Congress, contrasting with the moderates like Gokhale.
qs.kf:
☛ Which party was Bal Gangadhar Tilak associated with? → Indian National Congress (Garam Dal)
☛ Which newspapers did Tilak found? → Kesari (Marathi) and Maratha (English)
☛ What was Tilak's famous slogan? → Swaraj is my birthright
☛ Which event led to the split in Congress in 1907? → Surat session (Moderate-Extremist split)
☛ In which jail was Tilak imprisoned? → Mandalay Jail (Burma)

q: Which of the following best explains the Indian National Congress’s stance on communal politics during the Moderate phase?
o: Accepted political demands based on religious identities
Maintained a secular approach in its programmes and demands
Aligned itself with leaders of specific religious communities
Limited organisational participation to a single religious group
qs.e: During the Moderate phase (1885-1905), the Indian National Congress adopted a secular stance and did not support demands based on religious identities. Leaders like Dadabhai Naoroji, Firozeshah Mehta, and Gopal Krishna Gokhale believed in uniting people of all religions. They focused on issues such as administrative reforms, economic exploitation, and civil rights, rather than communal matters. The Congress promoted Hindu-Muslim unity and opposed communal representation. Thus, the Congress maintained a secular approach in its programmes and demands during the Moderate phase, seeking equal rights for all religious communities.
qs.kf:
☛ Time period of Moderate phase → 1885-1905
☛ Moderate leaders → Dadabhai Naoroji, Gopal Krishna Gokhale, Firozeshah Mehta
☛ Key demand of Moderates → Administrative reforms and opposition to economic exploitation
☛ Meaning of secularism → State neutrality in religious matters
☛ Congress stance on communalism → Opposition to politics based on religious identity

q: Who gave the slogan "Jai Jawan Jai Kisan"?
qs.e: This slogan was given by Lal Bahadur Shastri during the 1965 India-Pakistan war. It aimed to boost the morale of both soldiers (jawans) and farmers (kisans), as the country faced war and food shortage simultaneously. The slogan became a symbol of national unity and patriotism. Shastri ji highlighted the importance of both the army and agriculture through this slogan. He was the second Prime Minister of India, serving from 1964 to 1966.
qs.kf:
☛ Who gave the slogan 'Jai Jawan Jai Kisan'? → Lal Bahadur Shastri
☛ During which war was this slogan given? → 1965 India-Pakistan war
☛ What was Lal Bahadur Shastri's tenure? → 1964-1966
☛ Which number Prime Minister was Shastri ji? → Second
☛ What was the purpose of this slogan? → To boost morale of soldiers and farmers

q: When was 'Dandi March' organized?
qs.e: The Dandi March, also known as the Salt Satyagraha, began on 12 March 1930 and ended on 6 April 1930. It was led by Mahatma Gandhi as a nonviolent protest against the British salt monopoly. Gandhi, along with 78 followers, marched from Sabarmati Ashram in Ahmedabad to the coastal village of Dandi, covering a distance of 240 miles (390 km). Upon reaching Dandi, Gandhi violated the salt law by making salt from seawater. This movement sparked the Civil Disobedience Movement across India and became a pivotal event in the Indian independence struggle.
qs.kf:
☛ Who led the Dandi March? → Mahatma Gandhi
☛ In which year did the Dandi March start? → 1930
☛ Against which law was the Dandi March? → Salt Law
☛ What was the distance of the Dandi March? → 240 miles (390 km)
☛ What is the alternative name for Dandi March? → Salt Satyagraha

q: By what name was the Bhoodan-Gramadan movement started by Vinoba Bhave?
qs.e: Vinoba Bhave started the Bhoodan-Gramadan movement under the name Bloodless Revolution. This movement began in 1951 in the Telangana region of Andhra Pradesh. Its aim was to obtain land from landowners without any violence and donate it to the landless. Vinoba Bhave was a follower of Mahatma Gandhi and followed Gandhian principles for social reform through non-violent means. In the Bhoodan movement, land was taken as donation from landowners, while in Gramdan, entire villages were donated. This movement was an important part of land reforms in India.
qs.kf:
☛ Who started the Bhoodan movement? → Vinoba Bhave
☛ In which year did the Bhoodan movement start? → 1951
☛ What title was given to Vinoba Bhave? → Acharya
☛ In which state did the Bhoodan movement start? → Andhra Pradesh (Telangana)
☛ Who was Vinoba Bhave a disciple of? → Mahatma Gandhi

q: When was the Lahore session held?
qs.e: The Lahore session was the historic convention of the Indian National Congress held in December 1929 in Lahore, presided over by Jawaharlal Nehru. At this session, the Congress passed the Purna Swaraj (complete independence) resolution and decided to celebrate 26 January 1930 as the first Independence Day. This session marked a turning point in India's freedom struggle, paving the way for the Civil Disobedience Movement against British rule.
qs.kf:
☛ Who presided over the Lahore session? → Jawaharlal Nehru

q: When was the Third Round Table Conference held?
qs.e: The Third Round Table Conference was held in London from 17 November 1932 to 24 December 1932. It was convened to discuss constitutional reforms for India. The Indian National Congress did not participate as its leaders were in prison. The conference was chaired by British Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald. Its outcome was the Communal Award, which provided separate electorates for minorities.

q: Who held the chairmanship of the interim cabinet built in 1946?
qs.e: In 1946, the British government decided to form an interim government in India. The chairmanship of this interim cabinet was held by Pt Jawaharlal Nehru. This government was formed on 2 September 1946 and functioned until 15 August 1947. Nehru was appointed as the Vice President of the Viceroy's Executive Council, which was equivalent to the Prime Minister. The cabinet included Vallabhbhai Patel as Home Minister, Dr. Rajendra Prasad as Food and Agriculture Minister, and C. Rajagopalachari as Education Minister. This government was formed after the elections to the Constituent Assembly and served as a temporary administration until India's independence. Thus, the chairman of the interim cabinet was Pt Jawaharlal Nehru.
qs.kf:

☛ Who was the Home Minister in the interim cabinet? → Vallabhbhai Patel

☛ When did the interim government end? → 15 August 1947

q: Who was the founder of the newspaper 'Indian Opinion'?
qs.e: The newspaper 'Indian Opinion' was founded by Mahatma Gandhi in 1903 in South Africa. Its purpose was to raise issues concerning the Indian community in South Africa and spread the idea of non-violent resistance. Through this journal, Gandhi promoted the principles of Satyagraha and non-cooperation. 'Indian Opinion' was initially published weekly in Gujarati, Hindi, Tamil, and English. It served as a crucial medium for Gandhi, later influencing the Indian independence movement. Gandhi remained its editor until 1914, and under his leadership, the paper became the voice of the Indian struggle in South Africa.
qs.kf:

☛ Where was Indian Opinion published? → South Africa

q: In which of the following cities did the Jallianwala Bagh massacre take place?
qs.e: The Jallianwala Bagh massacre took place in the city of Amritsar on 13 April 1919. It was a protest against the Rowlatt Act. British officer General Dyer ordered his troops to fire on unarmed civilians. Hundreds of people were killed in the incident. This event accelerated the Indian independence movement. Rabindranath Tagore returned his knighthood in protest. Udham Singh later assassinated General Dyer as revenge.

q: With which of the following movements is the slogan "Do or Die" associated?
qs.e: The slogan "Do or Die" was given by Mahatma Gandhi during the Quit India Movement in 1942. This movement was a major civil disobedience campaign against British rule during World War II. Gandhi ji proclaimed the slogan on August 8, 1942, at Gowalia Tank Maidan in Mumbai, inspiring the nation to fight for freedom. The British arrested Congress leaders, but the masses continued the movement without leadership. It is considered the most powerful movement in India's freedom struggle. The Quit India Movement laid the foundation for India's independence in 1947.

q: Who was the first person to observe 'Individual Satyagraha'?
qs.e: The Individual Satyagraha was launched by Mahatma Gandhi in 1940. Its purpose was to demonstrate that the Indian people could offer non-violent resistance against British rule. In this movement, satyagraha was to be observed individually, not collectively. Vinoba Bhave was chosen as the first satyagrahi of this movement. He started his satyagraha on 17 October 1940. Gandhi himself did not observe satyagraha; rather, he led the movement. Vinoba Bhave was a follower of Gandhi and is known for the Bhoodan Movement.

☛ Conclusion of Individual Satyagraha → 1941

q: Who among the following was popularly known as the ‘Frontier Gandhi?'
qs.e: Abdul Ghaffar Khan, popularly known as the 'Frontier Gandhi', was a prominent Indian independence activist and Pashtun leader. He led a non-violent movement and founded the Khudai Khidmatgar (Red Shirts) movement. He was a follower of Mahatma Gandhi and was active in the freedom struggle in the North-West Frontier Province (now Khyber Pakhtunkhwa). His dedication to non-violence and similarity to Gandhi earned him this title.

q: Mahatma Gandhi organized 'Dandi March' in 1930 against the-
qs.e: Mahatma Gandhi organized the Dandi March in 1930 to protest against the salt tax imposed by the British government. The march began on March 12, 1930 from Sabarmati Ashram and reached Dandi (Gujarat) on April 6, 1930. Gandhi broke the law by making salt on the seashore, marking the start of the Civil Disobedience Movement. Around 78 followers accompanied him, and the march lasted 24 days. Gandhi called the salt tax unjust and oppressive to the poor. This movement was a turning point in India's freedom struggle.

q: Which political leader was popularly known as 'Chacha?'
qs.e: Jawaharlal Nehru was popularly known as 'Chacha' due to his immense love and affection for children. He was the first Prime Minister of India and a close associate of Mahatma Gandhi. His fondness for children was such that his birthday, 14 November, is celebrated as Children's Day across India. He was a prominent freedom fighter and a leader of the Indian National Congress. Nehru played a key role in shaping India's policies, including the Five-Year Plans and the Non-Aligned Movement. He served as Prime Minister from 1947 until his death in 1964.

A. C. Rajagopalachari
B. Motilal Nehru
C. Lala Lajpat Rai
D. Mahatma Gandhi
qs.e: The Swaraj Party was founded in 1923 by Motilal Nehru and Chittaranjan Das after the withdrawal of the Non-Cooperation Movement. It aimed to enter legislative councils and oppose the British government from within. C. Rajagopalachari was a prominent member but not a founder. Lala Lajpat Rai and Mahatma Gandhi were not directly associated with its formation. The party performed well in the 1923 elections and remained active until 1926. The Swaraj Party represented a shift in Congress strategy, combining constitutional participation with nationalist demands.

q: In order to avenge whom, Bhagat Singh and his associates killed the British officer John Saunders?
A. Death of Ramprasad Bismil
B. Villagers' death in Chauri Chaura incident
C. Death of Lala Lajpat Rai
D. Massacre at Jallianwala Bagh
qs.e: Bhagat Singh and his associates killed the British officer John Saunders to avenge the death of Lala Lajpat Rai. Lala Lajpat Rai was subjected to a severe lathi charge during a protest against the Simon Commission, which led to his critical injuries and subsequent death on 17 November 1928. This incident is part of the 'Simon Go Back' movement. Bhagat Singh, along with Sukhdev and Rajguru, planned the assassination of John Saunders, which occurred on 17 December 1928 in Lahore. This event is famously known as the Lahore Conspiracy.

q: Who among the following was one of the founders of the Swaraj Party?
A. Motilal Nehru
B. Lala Lajpat Rai
C. Subhas Chandra Bose
D. Dadabhai Naoroji
qs.e: The Swaraj Party was founded on 1 January 1923. Its founders were Motilal Nehru and Chittaranjan Das. It emerged as a faction within the Indian National Congress, advocating a policy of non-cooperation with the British government by entering the legislative councils and obstructing the government from within. The party aimed to change the earlier policy of boycotting legislatures and instead enter them to disrupt the government. The Swaraj Party achieved success in the 1923 elections, becoming the largest party in the Central Legislative Assembly. Motilal Nehru later served as the President of the Indian National Congress.

q: The Gandhi-Irwin pact was signed in the year
qs.e: The Gandhi-Irwin Pact was signed on 5 March 1931 between Mahatma Gandhi and the Viceroy of India, Lord Irwin. It marked a crucial turning point in the Indian independence movement. Under the pact, the Congress agreed to suspend the Civil Disobedience Movement, and all political prisoners were released. Additionally, the ban on salt making was lifted, and Congress was allowed to participate in the Second Round Table Conference. However, the pact did not include the demand for complete independence (Purna Swaraj), which later led to dissent.

☛ What was a major limitation of the pact? → Did not mention complete independence

q: Which movement was called off following the violence at 'Chauri Chaura' incident?
A. Khilafat Movement
B. Quit India Movement
C. Non co-operation Movement
D. Home Rule Movement
qs.e: In 1922, at Chauri Chaura (Gorakhpur, Uttar Pradesh), protesters set fire to a police station, killing 22 policemen. Disturbed by this violence, Mahatma Gandhi called off the Non-co-operation Movement on 12 February 1922, as it violated the principle of non-violent Satyagraha. This movement had started in 1920, aiming at peaceful resistance against British rule. The Chauri Chaura incident challenged the ethos of non-violence, prompting Gandhi to halt the movement. Later, leaders like Chittaranjan Das and Motilal Nehru criticized this decision, leading to the formation of the Swaraj Party.

q: The salt satyagraha is notable for at least three reasons. Which of the following is not one of them?
o: the young population in India began to attend schools
It bought Mahatma Gandhi to the world's attention.
nationalist movement in which a large number of women participated.
The British had to realize that their monarchy would not last forever.
qs.e: The Salt Satyagraha of 1930, led by Mahatma Gandhi, was a major civil disobedience movement against the British salt tax. It is notable for three key reasons: first, it brought Mahatma Gandhi and India's freedom struggle to the world's attention; second, it was a nationalist movement in which a large number of women participated; third, it made the British realize that their rule would not last forever. The option about the young population attending schools is unrelated to the Salt Satyagraha, as it pertains to educational expansion rather than the political protest against the salt tax.

q: Which of the following was stated in the 'Gandhi-Irwin Pact' signed in March 1931?
o: All Indians would get good education.
The manufacture of salt along the coast would be stopped.
The Civil Disobedience Movement would be called off.
qs.e: The Gandhi-Irwin Pact was signed on March 5, 1931, between Mahatma Gandhi and Viceroy Lord Irwin. Under this pact, the Congress agreed to call off the Civil Disobedience Movement and participate in the Second Round Table Conference. The government promised to release political prisoners, relax the salt laws, and withdraw all ordinances. However, the pact was not fully satisfactory, and later the Congress continued its demand for complete independence. This pact showed that the British government was compelled to acknowledge the pressure of the Indian national movement. It was a significant step in the Indian freedom struggle as it marked a temporary truce between the British and the Congress.

q: Which of the following was a result of the Non-Cooperation and Khilafat movements?
o: Students went to schools and colleges run by the government.
The working class went on strike in many towns and cities.
Peasants carried loads for colonial officers.
qs.e: During the Non-Cooperation and Khilafat movements (1920-22), the working class participated in large-scale strikes, especially in cities like Bombay, Madras, and Calcutta. These movements were led by Mahatma Gandhi, who advocated non-violent non-cooperation. Workers showed their support through strikes and boycotts of British goods. In contrast, lawyers boycotted courts, students did not attend government-run institutions, and peasants refused to work for colonial officials. Thus, the working class strike was a significant result of these movements.

qs.e: The First Round Table Conference began on 12 November 1930 and concluded on 19 January 1931 in London. Its purpose was to discuss constitutional reforms for India. The Indian National Congress boycotted the conference as its leaders were in prison. British Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald chaired the conference. Participants included the Muslim League, Hindu Mahasabha, and representatives of princely states. The conference failed to reach a consensus on communal representation.

q: Who among the following made the remark "South Africa was the making of the Mahatma"?
qs.e: Chandran Devanesan wrote the book 'The Making of the Mahatma', which extensively describes the life and struggles of Mahatma Gandhi in South Africa. In this book, he remarked that South Africa was the making of the Mahatma, meaning that Gandhi's experiences in South Africa shaped him into a great leader and social reformer. Gandhi went to South Africa in 1893 and there he laid the foundation of Satyagraha and non-violent resistance against racial discrimination and injustice. His experiences in South Africa deeply influenced his political and social ideas, which later guided India's freedom struggle. The book highlights how Gandhi's early activism in South Africa was crucial in developing his philosophy of non-violence and civil disobedience.

q: Under whose presidency did the Indian National Congress declare Poorna Swaraj as its ultimate goal on December 19, 1929, at Lahore?
qs.e: On December 19, 1929, the Indian National Congress held its annual session at Lahore under the presidency of Jawaharlal Nehru. In this historic session, the Congress passed the Poorna Swaraj resolution, declaring complete independence as its ultimate goal, thus abandoning the demand for Dominion Status. Consequently, 26 January 1930 was celebrated as the first Independence Day. Nehru was elected president due to his progressive and youthful vision, which aligned with the growing demand for full independence. This resolution marked a major turning point in India's freedom struggle, shifting the focus from constitutional reforms to complete self-rule.

q: In which of the following cities is the famous Jallianwala Bagh located?
qs.e: Jallianwala Bagh, infamous for the 1919 massacre, is located in the city of Amritsar, Punjab. Earlier, in 1928, the Congress had demanded Dominion Status through the Nehru Report. However, in 1929, the resolution for complete independence was passed. q: In which year was Delhi officially announced as the Capital of British India by then Emperor George V?
qs.e: In 1911, during the Delhi Durbar, Emperor George V announced the transfer of the capital from Calcutta to Delhi. The announcement was made on 12 December 1911. Key reasons included: Delhi's central geographical location, appeasing opposition to the Partition of Bengal, and choosing the former Mughal capital as a symbol of British rule. The foundation stone of the new capital 'New Delhi' was laid in 1912, and it was inaugurated in 1931. This decision elevated Delhi's political significance and it remained the capital of British India until India's independence.

qs.e: After returning from South Africa in 1915, Mahatma Gandhi made his first major public appearance in India at the opening ceremony of Banaras Hindu University (BHU) in February 1916. q: Name the major revolt inspired by Mahatma Gandhi against the forced cultivation of indigo.
qs.e: The Champaran Satyagraha (1917) was Mahatma Gandhi's first successful satyagraha in India. In Bihar's Champaran district, British landlords forced peasants to cultivate indigo. The peasants received meager payment for indigo and were deeply in debt. Rajkumar Shukla informed Gandhi about this injustice. Gandhi protested peacefully, demanded a government inquiry, and eventually forced the end of forced indigo cultivation. This satyagraha became a model for civil disobedience and non-violence.

q: Name the leader whose opposition led to the disappearance of all hopes of compromise between the Congress and the Muslim League in 1928.
qs.e: In 1928, efforts for a compromise between the Congress and the Muslim League over the Nehru Report were thwarted primarily due to the opposition of M. R. Jayakar. Jayakar was an Indian politician and a prominent lawyer in Bombay who represented the Hindu Mahasabha. He strongly opposed any agreement with the Muslim League, especially on issues of communal representation and reservations. The Nehru Report had rejected separate electorates for minorities in provinces, which Jayakar objected to. His stance effectively ended hopes of a united front between the two major political parties before the Round Table Conferences. This failure deepened communal divisions and set the stage for future conflicts.

☛ Why did the Muslim League reject the Nehru Report? → Demand for separate electorates was not met
☛ When did Jinnah present his Fourteen Points? → 1929
☛ When was the Gandhi-Irwin Pact signed? → 1931

q: Which newspaper did Mahatma Gandhi start in South Africa?
qs.e: Mahatma Gandhi started the newspaper Indian Opinion in South Africa in 1903. It was published in Gujarati, Hindi, Tamil, and English to reach the diverse Indian community. The newspaper aimed to highlight the issues faced by Indians in South Africa and promote unity among them. Gandhi used Indian Opinion as a tool to spread the principles of Satyagraha and non-violence. It played a crucial role in mobilizing the Indian diaspora and was published until 1914. Other options include 'Indian Sociologist' started by Shyamji Krishnavarma, 'Common Weal' by Annie Besant, and 'National Herald' by Jawaharlal Nehru, which have no direct connection to Gandhi's South African movement.
qs.kf:
☛ Newspaper started by Gandhi in South Africa in 1903 → Indian Opinion
☛ Languages of Indian Opinion → Gujarati, Hindi, Tamil, English
☛ Purpose of Indian Opinion → To protect Indian rights in South Africa
☛ Newspaper that spread Gandhi's ideas → Indian Opinion
☛ Founder of Indian Sociologist → Shyamji Krishnavarma

q: Which one of the following is NOT associated with the Indian Freedom Struggle?
qs.e: The New Deal was a series of economic policies implemented by U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt in 1933 to combat the Great Depression. It has no connection to the Indian Freedom Struggle. In contrast, the Wavell Plan (1945), Cripps Mission (1942), and Simon Commission (1928) were all proposals or commissions introduced by the British government to address constitutional reforms or deal with the independence movement in India. Hence, these three options are associated with the Indian Freedom Struggle.
qs.kf:
☛ Not associated with Indian Freedom Struggle → New Deal
☛ Who proposed the Wavell Plan? → Lord Wavell
☛ What was the purpose of Cripps Mission? → To secure Indian cooperation in WWII
☛ When was Simon Commission established? → 1928
☛ New Deal was the policy of which country? → United States of America

q: Who along with Motilal Nehru formed the Swaraj Party within the Congress to argue for a return to council politics?
qs.e: CR Das along with Motilal Nehru formed the Swaraj Party in 1923 within the Indian National Congress. The party aimed to argue for a return to council politics by entering the legislative councils to oppose British policies from within. The Swaraj Party was formed after Mahatma Gandhi called off the Non-Cooperation Movement. Das and Nehru believed that the government could be challenged more effectively inside the councils. This marked an ideological split within the Congress, with one faction favoring council entry. The Swaraj Party later achieved success in the Central Legislative Assembly elections.
qs.kf:
☛ Who founded the Swaraj Party? → CR Das and Motilal Nehru
☛ When was the Swaraj Party founded? → 1923
☛ What was the main objective of the Swaraj Party? → To enter legislative councils and oppose the government
☛ After which movement was the Swaraj Party formed? → After the withdrawal of the Non-Cooperation Movement
☛ Who was the leader of the Swaraj Party? → CR Das as President and Motilal Nehru as Secretary

q: At which university did Mahatma Gandhi make his first public appearance in 1916 after returning from South Africa to India?
qs.e: Mahatma Gandhi returned to India from South Africa in 1915. In 1916, he made his first public appearance at the inauguration ceremony of Banaras Hindu University (BHU). The speech was delivered on February 6, 1916, where Gandhi spoke on nationalism, education, and self-rule. BHU was founded by Madan Mohan Malaviya in 1916. This speech is famously known as the 'Banaras Hindu University Speech'.
qs.kf:
☛ Who founded BHU? → Madan Mohan Malaviya
☛ When was BHU established? → 1916
☛ Where did Gandhi give his first public speech in India after returning? → Banaras Hindu University
☛ Which movement did Gandhi start after returning from South Africa? → Champaran Satyagraha (1917)
☛ Who was Gandhi's political mentor? → Gopal Krishna Gokhale

q: Who among the following has initially drafted the 'Quit India' resolution of the Indian National congress in 1942?
qs.e: The 'Quit India' resolution of the Indian National Congress in 1942 was initially drafted by Mahatma Gandhi. It was passed on August 8, 1942, during the All India Congress Committee session in Bombay. Gandhi gave the slogan 'Do or Die' and demanded an immediate end to British rule. The movement led to widespread protests and strikes across India. The British government responded by arresting Gandhi and other leaders. This movement marked a crucial turning point in India's struggle for independence.
qs.kf:
☛ Who drafted the Quit India resolution? → Mahatma Gandhi
☛ When was the Quit India resolution passed? → August 8, 1942
☛ What was the slogan of Quit India movement? → Do or Die
☛ Where was the Quit India resolution passed? → Bombay
☛ Who was the Viceroy during Quit India movement? → Lord Linlithgow

q: Which great freedom fighter was known as Deshbandhu?
qs.e: Chittaranjan Das, popularly known as Deshbandhu (Friend of the Nation), was a prominent Indian freedom fighter, politician, and lawyer. He was a key leader of the Swaraj movement in Bengal and played a crucial role in founding the Swaraj Party. Das also served as President of the Indian National Congress and actively participated in the Non- Cooperation Movement. He was renowned for his oratory skills and nationalist ideals. He also worked to promote education and social reforms in Bengal.
qs.kf:
☛ Who is known as Deshbandhu? → Chittaranjan Das
☛ Which party was associated with Chittaranjan Das? → Swaraj Party
☛ Which movement did Chittaranjan Das participate in? → Non-Cooperation Movement
☛ Which province was Chittaranjan Das from? → Bengal
☛ What is the birth year of Chittaranjan Das? → 1870

q: Clement Attlee who later became Prime Minister of Britain came to India as a member of ________.
qs.e: Clement Attlee, who later became Prime Minister of Britain, visited India in 1928 as a member of the Simon Commission. The Simon Commission was formed in 1927 to review constitutional reforms in India. It was chaired by Sir John Simon. Since it had no Indian members, it was widely opposed by Indians. During the protest, Lala Lajpat Rai succumbed to injuries from a lathi charge. Attlee later served as Prime Minister of Britain from 1945 to 1951 and was instrumental in passing the Indian Independence Act 1947.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the chairman of Simon Commission? → Sir John Simon
☛ When did the Simon Commission visit India? → 1928
☛ What was the slogan against Simon Commission? → Simon Go Back
☛ During which protest did Lala Lajpat Rai die? → Simon Commission protest
☛ Under which British Prime Minister was the Indian Independence Act 1947 passed? → Clement Attlee

q: Lala Lajpat Rai died protesting which British government decision?
qs.e: Lala Lajpat Rai died protesting the Simon Commission. On 30 October 1928, he led a demonstration in Lahore against the Commission, which had no Indian members and was seen as an insult. During the protest, Police Superintendent James Scott ordered a lathi charge, and Lajpat Rai was severely injured. He succumbed to his injuries on 17 November 1928. His death led to the revenge killing of Scott by Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev, and Rajguru. The Simon Commission, appointed in 1927 and arriving in 1928, was boycotted across India with the slogan 'Simon Go Back'. Lajpat Rai's sacrifice became a turning point in India's freedom struggle.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Simon Commission appointed? → 1927
☛ Who was the chairman of Simon Commission? → Sir John Simon
☛ When did Lala Lajpat Rai die? → 17 November 1928
☛ Who ordered the lathi charge? → James Scott
☛ What was the slogan against Simon Commission? → 'Simon Go Back'

q: In the year 1937, the Congress session was held for the first time in a village at:
qs.e: In 1937, the Indian National Congress held its session for the first time in a village, at Faizpur in Maharashtra's Jalgaon district. The session was presided over by Jawaharlal Nehru. It was historic because it was the first rural venue, reflecting the Congress's effort to connect with the peasantry. The session focused on issues of farmers and laborers, emphasizing agrarian reform. Faizpur played a key role in linking the Congress with the masses and strengthening the national movement. The venue choice was deliberate to symbolize the party's commitment to rural India.
qs.kf:
☛ 1937 Congress session venue? → Faizpur village (Maharashtra)
☛ President of that session? → Jawaharlal Nehru
☛ Issues highlighted at Faizpur? → Farmers and laborers
☛ Why was Faizpur historic? → First session in a village
☛ Faizpur is in which state? → Maharashtra

q: How many Indian members were there in the Simon Commission?
qs.e: The Simon Commission was a seven-member British commission sent to India in 1928 to evaluate constitutional reforms. It had no Indian members, leading to widespread protests and the slogan 'Simon Go Back'. The absence of Indians made it known as the 'White Commission'. Lord Birkenhead had challenged Indians' ability to draft a constitution, prompting Indian leaders to create the Nehru Report. The commission was chaired by Sir John Simon. Its recommendations formed the basis of the Government of India Act 1935. The all-white composition reflected British reluctance to include Indian representatives in decision-making, sparking demands for self-rule and influencing the Indian independence movement.
qs.kf:
☛ What was the Simon Commission also known as? → White Commission
☛ Who chaired the Simon Commission? → Sir John Simon
☛ What slogan was raised against the Simon Commission? → Simon Go Back
☛ Which report was prepared after the Simon Commission? → Nehru Report (1928)
☛ When did the Simon Commission arrive in India? → 1928

q: The person who was instrumental in bringing Mahatma Gandhi to Champaran in 1917 was:
qs.e: In 1917, it was Raj Kumar Shukla, a peasant from Champaran, who was instrumental in bringing Mahatma Gandhi to Champaran. He met Gandhi at a conference in Lucknow and persuaded him to visit Champaran to address the exploitation of farmers under the indigo plantation system. This marked Gandhi's first successful Satyagraha in India, leading to the abolition of the oppressive system. The Champaran Satyagraha established Gandhi as a prominent leader in India's freedom struggle and laid the foundation for his future movements like non-cooperation and civil disobedience.
qs.kf:
☛ When did the Champaran Satyagraha take place? → 1917
☛ What was the main cause of Champaran Satyagraha? → Exploitation in indigo cultivation
☛ Who invited Gandhi to Champaran? → Raj Kumar Shukla
☛ Which committee was formed after Champaran Satyagraha? → Brampton Committee
☛ What is Champaran Satyagraha considered as? → Gandhi's first Satyagraha in India

q: The Khilafat Movement originated in ________.
qs.e: The Khilafat Movement (1919-1924) was a political campaign launched by Indian Muslims to protect the position of the Caliph of Turkey after Turkey's defeat in World War I. The Allied powers planned harsh terms on Turkey, weakening the Caliph's authority. Indian Muslims saw this as an injustice to their religious leader. The movement was led by the Ali brothers, Maulana Muhammad Ali and Maulana Shaukat Ali. Later, Mahatma Gandhi linked it with the Non-Cooperation Movement, making it a major national struggle. The movement ended in 1924 when Turkey abolished the Caliphate.
qs.kf:
☛ What was the main aim of the Khilafat Movement? → To protect the Caliph of Turkey
☛ Who were the leaders of the Khilafat Movement? → Maulana Muhammad Ali and Shaukat Ali
☛ In which year did the Khilafat Movement start? → 1919
☛ Which movement was the Khilafat Movement linked with? → Non-Cooperation Movement (1920)
☛ When did the Khilafat Movement end? → 1924 (Turkey abolished the Caliphate)

q: The Salt march was launched by Mahatma Gandhi in the year:
qs.e: Mahatma Gandhi launched the Salt March on March 12, 1930 from Sabarmati Ashram. It was a major movement against the British salt tax. After a 24-day journey, Gandhi broke the law by making salt at Dandi on April 6, 1930. This movement gave a new direction to the Indian freedom struggle and created mass awareness across the country. The Salt March is also known as the Dandi March. It was part of the Civil Disobedience Movement, which challenged the British rule.
qs.kf:
☛ Date of start of Salt March → March 12, 1930
☛ Date when Gandhi made salt at Dandi → April 6, 1930
☛ Other name of Salt March → Dandi March
☛ Which movement it was part of → Civil Disobedience Movement
☛ Main objective of Salt March → Opposing British salt tax

q: Where was the All India Khilafat conference held in 1919?
qs.e: The All India Khilafat Conference was held in Delhi in 1919. This conference was a crucial part of the Khilafat Movement, which aimed to protect the status of the Turkish Caliph after World War I. The conference was presided over by Maulana Abul Kalam Azad. Mahatma Gandhi also participated and proposed the Non-Cooperation Movement. The Khilafat Conference strengthened Hindu-Muslim unity and accelerated India's freedom struggle. The Delhi conference laid the foundation for a united struggle against the British government.
qs.kf:
☛ Objective of Khilafat Movement → Protect the status of the Turkish Caliph
☛ Chairman of 1919 Khilafat Conference → Maulana Abul Kalam Azad
☛ Who proposed Non-Cooperation in the conference → Mahatma Gandhi
☛ Period of Khilafat Movement → 1919 to 1924
☛ Formation of Khilafat Committee → 1919 in Bombay

name: Set 2 · Q50–98
sub: Modern History - Gandhian Era (Non-Cooperation to Quit India)

q: Which of the following 'ashrams' was NOT established by Mahatma Gandhi?
qs.e: Paunar Ashram was established by Vinoba Bhave, not by Mahatma Gandhi. Gandhi established Tolstoy Farm in South Africa (1910), Sabarmati Ashram in India (1917), and Sevagram Ashram (1936). Sabarmati Ashram is located on the banks of Sabarmati River in Ahmedabad, from where Gandhi started the famous Salt Satyagraha in 1930. Sevagram Ashram is in Wardha. Paunar Ashram, in Maharashtra, was the center of Vinoba Bhave's Bhoodan Movement.
qs.kf:
☛ In which year was Sabarmati Ashram established? → 1917
☛ In which country is Tolstoy Farm located? → South Africa
☛ In which state is Sevagram Ashram located? → Maharashtra
☛ Who founded Paunar Ashram? → Vinoba Bhave
☛ From which ashram did Gandhi start the Salt Satyagraha? → Sabarmati Ashram

q: Karachi session of Indian National Congress was held in 1931. It was presided over by:
qs.e: The 46th annual session of the Indian National Congress was held in Karachi from March 26 to 28, 1931. It was presided over by Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel. This session took place after the Gandhi-Irwin Pact, which led to the suspension of the Civil Disobedience Movement. During this session, resolutions on Fundamental Rights and National Economic Policy were passed, which later formed the basis of the Indian Constitution. Jawaharlal Nehru and Mahatma Gandhi also participated, but the presidency was held by Sardar Patel. This session was a significant milestone in the Indian freedom struggle.
qs.kf:
☛ Who presided over the 1931 Karachi session of INC? → Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel
☛ When was the Gandhi-Irwin Pact signed? → 5 March 1931
☛ What resolution was adopted at the Karachi session? → Fundamental Rights and Economic Policy
☛ Which Civil Disobedience Movement ended in 1931? → Second Civil Disobedience Movement
☛ Where was the 46th INC session held? → Karachi

q: Which of the following movements began with the Dandi March?
qs.e: The Dandi March began on March 12, 1930 under the leadership of Mahatma Gandhi, marking the start of the Civil Disobedience Movement. The march lasted 24 days from Sabarmati Ashram to Dandi, where Gandhi broke the salt law. The movement aimed to protest the British salt tax and other unjust laws. Gandhi chose this march as a symbolic and nonviolent protest against British rule. Millions of Indians participated, putting pressure on the British. The Champaran Movement occurred in 1917, Non Co-operation Movement from 1920-22, and Quit India Movement in 1942.
qs.kf:
☛ When did the Dandi March start? → March 12, 1930
☛ Where did the Dandi March start from? → Sabarmati Ashram
☛ Who led the Dandi March? → Mahatma Gandhi
☛ How many days did the Dandi March last? → 24 days
☛ Where did the salt law breaking occur? → Dandi

q: Who observed the Pratyaksh Karyawahi Diwas (Direct Action Day) on 16 August 1946?
qs.e: The Direct Action Day (Pratyaksh Karyawahi Diwas) was observed on 16 August 1946 by the Muslim League. Its purpose was to strengthen the demand for a separate Pakistan. This day was initiated under the leadership of Muhammad Ali Jinnah, the president of the Muslim League. The campaign resulted in the Calcutta riots, in which thousands of people were killed. This event was one of the key incidents that led to the partition of India.
qs.kf:
☛ When was Direct Action Day observed? → 16 August 1946
☛ Who observed Direct Action Day? → Muslim League
☛ Under whose leadership was Direct Action Day started? → Muhammad Ali Jinnah
☛ Which riots resulted from Direct Action Day? → Calcutta riots
☛ What was the purpose of Direct Action Day? → To strengthen the demand for a separate Pakistan

q: Mahatma Gandhi came to Champaran in:
qs.e: Mahatma Gandhi came to Champaran in 1917. The Champaran Satyagraha was Gandhi's first successful Satyagraha in India. It was organized in the Champaran district of Bihar against the exploitation of indigo farmers. The farmers were forced by British landlords to grow indigo, which caused them heavy financial losses. Gandhi visited Champaran at the request of Rajkumar Shukla and studied the farmers' condition. As a result, the government was compelled to amend laws in favor of the farmers. The Champaran Satyagraha laid the foundation of Gandhi's leadership in the Indian freedom struggle. This event established Satyagraha as a powerful political weapon.
qs.kf:
☛ Champaran Satyagraha was related to which crop? → Indigo
☛ Who invited Gandhi to Champaran? → Rajkumar Shukla
☛ In which year did Champaran Satyagraha occur? → 1917
☛ Champaran is currently in which state? → Bihar
☛ Which was Gandhi's first Satyagraha in India? → Champaran Satyagraha

q: In which year did Mahatma Gandhi organise a satyagraha to support the peasants of the Kheda district?
qs.e: Mahatma Gandhi organized the Kheda Satyagraha in 1918 to support the peasants of Kheda district who were facing crop failure but were denied remission of land revenue. Under Gandhi's leadership, the peasants refused to pay the revenue, and Vallabhbhai Patel actively assisted him. This was one of Gandhi's first major successful satyagrahas in India, leading to a temporary suspension of revenue collection for the affected farmers. The movement strengthened the foundation for the later Non-Cooperation Movement and highlighted the power of nonviolent resistance.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the leader of Kheda Satyagraha? → Mahatma Gandhi
☛ Who assisted Gandhi in Kheda Satyagraha? → Vallabhbhai Patel
☛ Which crop crisis triggered the Kheda Satyagraha? → Crop failure
☛ In which year did the Kheda Satyagraha occur? → 1918
☛ What was the main issue of Kheda Satyagraha? → Land revenue remission

q: Which Indian Nationalist leader spearheaded the peasants' agitation known as the Bardoli Satyagraha?
qs.e: Bardoli Satyagraha (1928) was a peasants' movement led by Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel. It was against the increased land revenue in Bardoli taluka of Bombay Presidency. Patel organized the farmers to refuse tax payment, forcing the government to negotiate. This success earned Patel the title 'Sardar'.
qs.kf:
☛ Who led the Bardoli Satyagraha? → Vallabhbhai Patel
☛ When did Bardoli Satyagraha occur? → 1928
☛ What was the cause of Bardoli Satyagraha? → Increase in land revenue
☛ From which movement did Vallabhbhai Patel get the title 'Sardar'? → Bardoli Satyagraha
☛ In which state did Bardoli Satyagraha take place? → Gujarat

q: In which year did Indian National Congress observe 26 January as Independence Day for the first time?
qs.e: The Indian National Congress first observed 26 January as Independence Day in 1930. This decision was taken at the Lahore Session of Congress in December 1929, presided over by Jawaharlal Nehru. The session declared Purna Swaraj (complete independence) as the goal and decided to celebrate 26 January 1930 as the first Independence Day. On this day, the tricolor was hoisted across the country and a pledge for independence was taken. Later, after independence in 1947, the Constitution of India came into effect on 26 January 1950, which is now celebrated as Republic Day.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the president of the Lahore Session (1929)? → Jawaharlal Nehru
☛ When was Purna Swaraj declared? → 1929 at Lahore Session
☛ When was 26 January first observed as Independence Day? → 1930
☛ When did the Constitution of India come into effect? → 26 January 1950
☛ Who moved the Purna Swaraj resolution? → Jawaharlal Nehru

q: In which year did Gandhiji begin a defiant march to the sea to protest against the British monopoly on salt?
qs.e: Gandhiji began the famous Dandi March from Sabarmati Ashram to Dandi on 12 March 1930. This march was part of the Salt Satyagraha, a nonviolent protest against the British salt monopoly. Gandhiji walked for 24 days with 78 followers and reached Dandi on 6 April 1930, where he broke the law by picking up salt from the seashore. The march sparked the Civil Disobedience Movement across India and drew global attention to the Indian freedom struggle. It was a pivotal event in India's fight for independence.
qs.kf:
☛ When did the Dandi March start? → 12 March 1930
☛ What was the main aim of the Dandi March? → To protest against the British monopoly on salt
☛ How many followers accompanied Gandhiji? → 78
☛ How many days did the Dandi March last? → 24 days
☛ Which movement did the Dandi March initiate? → Civil Disobedience Movement

q: The Jallianwala Bagh massacre took place on _______.
qs.e: The Jallianwala Bagh massacre took place on 13 April 1919 in Amritsar, Punjab. On this day, a peaceful gathering was held to celebrate the festival of Baisakhi. British army commander General Dyer ordered his troops to fire on unarmed civilians without any warning. The firing lasted for about 10 minutes, resulting in thousands of deaths. This incident intensified the Indian independence movement. Rabindranath Tagore returned his knighthood in protest of the massacre. The massacre was a direct consequence of the repressive Rowlatt Act.
qs.kf:
☛ When did the Jallianwala Bagh massacre occur? → 13 April 1919
☛ Who ordered the firing at Jallianwala Bagh? → General Dyer
☛ Who returned his knighthood in protest? → Rabindranath Tagore
☛ In which city did this event take place? → Amritsar, Punjab
☛ Which British act led to this massacre? → Rowlatt Act

q: The Poona Pact was signed between:
o: M K Gandhi and M A Jinnah
M K Gandhi and B R Ambedkar
M K Gandhi and S C Bose
M K Gandhi and Lord Irwin
qs.e: The Poona Pact was signed on 24 September 1932 between Mahatma Gandhi and Dr. B. R. Ambedkar. It came after Gandhi's fast unto death against the Communal Award, which proposed separate electorates for depressed classes (Dalits). Gandhi believed this would divide the nation. The pact replaced separate electorates with reserved seats for Dalits in provincial legislatures. It also enhanced the number of seats for them. This agreement was crucial in the Indian freedom movement as it preserved national unity while addressing Dalit political representation.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Poona Pact signed? → 24 September 1932
☛ Which award did the Poona Pact oppose? → Communal Award
☛ What did the Poona Pact grant to Dalits? → Reserved seats (not separate electorates)
☛ Where did Gandhi fast before the Poona Pact? → Yerwada Jail (Pune)
☛ What issue did the Poona Pact resolve? → Political representation of depressed classes

q: What is correct about the Khilafat Movement in India?
o: It was a movement in demand of Pakistan
It was a movement in support of the Turkish Sultan
It was a movement against the massacre of Jallianwala Bagh
It was a movement to restore the Mughal Royal family in India
qs.e: The Khilafat Movement (1919-1924) was launched by Indian Muslims to support the Turkish Sultan (Caliph), who was threatened with abolition by Britain and its allies after World War I. The movement was led by leaders like Shaukat Ali, Muhammad Ali, and Maulana Azad. Mahatma Gandhi linked it with the Non-Cooperation Movement to strengthen Hindu-Muslim unity. The movement ended in 1924 when Mustafa Kemal Pasha abolished the caliphate in Turkey. This movement was not about demanding Pakistan, protesting the Jallianwala Bagh massacre, or restoring the Mughal dynasty.
qs.kf:
☛ What was the main objective of the Khilafat Movement? → To protect the Turkish Caliph
☛ Who were the main leaders of the Khilafat Movement? → Shaukat Ali and Muhammad Ali
☛ Which movement did Gandhi link with the Khilafat Movement? → Non-Cooperation Movement
☛ When did the Khilafat Movement end? → 1924
☛ Who abolished the caliphate in Turkey? → Mustafa Kemal Pasha

q: Rabindranath Tagore gave up his knighthood because of the:
qs.e: Rabindranath Tagore relinquished his knighthood in 1919 to protest the Jallianwala Bagh massacre. On April 13, 1919, British troops under General Dyer fired on unarmed Indians, killing hundreds. Tagore condemned the act as unjust and inhuman, returning the title conferred by the British government. This was a significant symbolic protest of the time. Tagore was a great poet, writer, and is known as Gurudev. He won the Nobel Prize for Literature in 1913. This incident further strengthened the Indian independence movement.
qs.kf:
☛ When did the Jallianwala Bagh massacre occur? → 13 April 1919
☛ Who ordered the firing at Jallianwala Bagh? → General Dyer
☛ When did Tagore renounce his knighthood? → 1919
☛ In which year did Tagore win the Nobel Prize? → 1913
☛ Which national anthem was composed by Tagore? → Jana Gana Mana

q: Who had called for Direct Action Day?
qs.e: Direct Action Day was called by Muhammad Ali Jinnah on 16 August 1946. The Muslim League observed it as a day of strike and protest to demand the creation of a separate Muslim state of Pakistan. Jinnah aimed to pressure the British and the Indian National Congress into accepting the partition of India. The day turned violent, especially in Calcutta (Kolkata), leading to widespread riots and thousands of deaths. This event accelerated the process of India's partition and the eventual creation of Pakistan in 1947.
qs.kf:
☛ When was Direct Action Day observed? → 16 August 1946
☛ Who called for Direct Action Day? → Muhammad Ali Jinnah
☛ Which city witnessed the worst violence on Direct Action Day? → Calcutta (Kolkata)
☛ What was the main purpose of Direct Action Day? → Support for the demand of Pakistan
☛ Which plan was announced after Direct Action Day? → 3 June Plan (Partition Plan)

q: When was the Poona Pact signed?
qs.e: The Poona Pact was signed on 24 September 1932. It was an agreement between Mahatma Gandhi and Dr. B. R. Ambedkar that ended the demand for separate electorates for the depressed classes and instead provided for reserved seats. This pact was made during Gandhi's fast in Yerwada Central Jail. The Poona Pact granted reserved seats for the depressed classes in provincial legislatures but rejected communal separate electorates. It marked a significant turning point in the Indian independence movement. The British government accepted this agreement as an amendment to the Communal Award.
qs.kf:
☛ Year of Poona Pact signing → 1932
☛ Signatories of Poona Pact → Mahatma Gandhi and Dr. B. R. Ambedkar
☛ Poona Pact related to → Reservation for depressed classes
☛ Place of Poona Pact → Yerwada Central Jail, Poona
☛ Outcome of Poona Pact → End of separate electorates and provision for reserved seats

q: The Quit India movement started in:
qs.e: The Quit India Movement was launched on August 8, 1942, at Bombay (now Mumbai). Mahatma Gandhi gave the call of 'Do or Die' at Gowalia Tank Maidan, initiating the mass civil disobedience movement. The British immediately arrested Gandhi and other Congress leaders. This movement, during World War II, was the largest mass uprising demanding the British to leave India. It spread across the country and played a crucial role in the final phase of India's independence struggle.
qs.kf:
☛ Date of Quit India Movement → August 8, 1942
☛ Slogan → Do or Die
☛ Venue → Gowalia Tank Maidan, Bombay
☛ Initiator → Mahatma Gandhi
☛ Key leaders → Jawaharlal Nehru, Sardar Patel, Abdul Ghaffar Khan

q: Which Prime Minister sent the Cripps Mission to India in 1942?
qs.e: In 1942, British Prime Minister Winston Churchill sent the Cripps Mission to India. The mission was led by Sir Stafford Cripps. Its purpose was to secure Indian cooperation during World War II. The mission proposed granting India Dominion status after the war, but it failed because the Congress and the Muslim League could not agree. Churchill was opposed to Indian independence.
qs.kf:
☛ When did the Cripps Mission come? → 1942
☛ Who led the Cripps Mission? → Sir Stafford Cripps
☛ What was the objective of the Cripps Mission? → To secure Indian cooperation in the war
☛ Who rejected the Cripps Mission proposal? → Congress and Muslim League
☛ Which movement followed the failure of the Cripps Mission? → Quit India Movement

q: The Quit India Movement started in the year:
qs.e: The Quit India Movement started on 8 August 1942 under the leadership of Mahatma Gandhi. It is also known as the 'August Revolution'. Gandhi gave the call of 'Do or Die' at Gowalia Tank Maidan in Mumbai. The main objective was to end British rule immediately. Leaders like Aruna Asaf Ali, Jayaprakash Narayan, and Liaquat Ali Khan participated. The British arrested Gandhi and many Congress leaders. The movement lasted until 1945 and paved the way for India's independence.
qs.kf:
☛ When did the Quit India Movement start? → 8 August 1942
☛ Who gave the slogan 'Do or Die'? → Mahatma Gandhi
☛ Which woman leader participated in the Quit India Movement? → Aruna Asaf Ali

q: When did the All-India Khilafat Committee pass a resolution declaring that no Muslim should serve in the British-Indian army?
qs.e: The All-India Khilafat Committee passed a resolution in July 1921 declaring that no Muslim should serve in the British-Indian army. This decision was taken during the Khilafat Movement, which was launched in protest against the dismemberment of the Ottoman Empire and the abolition of the Caliphate after World War I. The movement was led by leaders like Muhammad Ali Jinnah, Shaukat Ali, and Maulana Azad. It was part of the Non-Cooperation Movement supported by Mahatma Gandhi. The resolution aimed to pressure the British government to secure the position of the Turkish Caliph and respect the religious sentiments of Muslims.

q: Who was known as the ‘Iron Man of India'?
qs.e: Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel was known as the 'Iron Man of India'. He was the first Deputy Prime Minister and Home Minister of India. He played a crucial role in the integration of India by merging 562 princely states into the Indian Union. He was born on 31 October 1875 in Nadiad, Gujarat. Along with being an active participant in the freedom struggle, he was an able administrator. His firmness and iron will earned him the title 'Iron Man'. He is also remembered for his efforts in nation-building and unity.

q: What was the main reason for calling off the Non-Cooperation Movement by Gandhiji in 1922?

A police station at Chauri Chaura in Uttar Pradesh was set on fire by a mob
The movement was completed by achieving the target
qs.e: Gandhiji called off the Non-Cooperation Movement in February 1922 primarily due to the Chauri Chaura incident in Uttar Pradesh's Gorakhpur district. On 4 February 1922, a mob of protesters set fire to a police station, killing 22 policemen. Gandhiji viewed this as a violation of the principle of non-violence and withdrew the movement. He insisted on complete adherence to ahimsa (non-violence). This event highlighted the importance of civil disobedience in India's freedom struggle.

In Amritsar, a meeting was organized at Jallianwala Bagh to protest the Rowlatt Act. General Dyer ordered the troops to open fire on the unarmed crowd, killing hundreds.
