q: With which of the following organisations were Ram Prasad Bismil, Chandrashekhar Azad and Bhagat Singh associated?
qs.e: Ram Prasad Bismil, Chandrashekhar Azad, and Bhagat Singh were associated with the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (HSRA). HSRA was founded in 1928 at Firoz Shah Kotla Maidan in Delhi. Its aim was to achieve complete independence from British rule in India. This organization was known for its revolutionary activities. Chandrashekhar Azad was its prominent leader. As members of HSRA, Bhagat Singh participated in events like the Kakori Conspiracy and the Assembly Bomb Incident. Ram Prasad Bismil was a key revolutionary involved in the Kakori Conspiracy. HSRA also worked for social and political equality.
qs.kf:
☛ Full form of HSRA → Hindustan Socialist Republican Association
☛ Year of establishment of HSRA → 1928
☛ Key leader of HSRA → Chandrashekhar Azad
☛ Organization associated with Kakori Conspiracy → HSRA
☛ Name associated with Assembly Bomb Incident → Bhagat Singh and Batukeshwar Dutt

q: Which revolutionary organisation was founded by Barindra Kumar Ghosh in Bengal?
qs.e: The revolutionary organisation Anushilan Samiti was founded in Bengal in 1902 by Barindra Kumar Ghosh and his brother Aurobindo Ghosh. Its aim was armed struggle against British rule. The Samiti provided physical and political training to youths. It later strengthened under Sri Aurobindo's guidance. In 1908, the Alipore Bomb Case led to Barindra's arrest and the Samiti was banned. Other options: Brati Samiti (linked to Bal Gangadhar Tilak), Swadesh Bandhab Samiti (by Ashwini Kumar Datta), and Sadhana Samaj (by Sri Aurobindo) are incorrect.
qs.kf:
☛ Founder of Anushilan Samiti → Barindra Kumar Ghosh
☛ Major case linked to Anushilan Samiti → Alipore Bomb Case (1908)
☛ Barindra Kumar Ghosh's brother → Aurobindo Ghosh
☛ Year of founding → 1902
☛ Ban on Anushilan Samiti → 1908

q: Which of the following was NOT a part of the revolutionary movement for Indian Independence?
qs.e: The Indian independence movement included several revolutionary organizations. Anushilan Samiti (1902) was founded by Pramathanath Mitra in Kolkata and was a center of revolutionary activities. Jugantar (1906) was a revolutionary group that emerged from Anushilan Samiti and used bombs and violence. Abhinav Bharat (1904) was founded by Veer Savarkar and his brother Ganesh Savarkar in Maharashtra. Young Party was not a revolutionary organization; it was a political party formed in 1919 by C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru, which was moderate and did not follow revolutionary methods. Thus, Young Party was not part of the revolutionary movement.
qs.kf:
☛ Founder of Anushilan Samiti → Pramathanath Mitra
☛ Jugantar's association → Revolutionary violence
☛ Founder of Abhinav Bharat → Veer Savarkar
☛ Leaders of Young Party → C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru
☛ Ideology of Young Party → Moderate

q: Which freedom fighter shot General Michael O'Dwyer?
qs.e: Udham Singh shot General Michael O'Dwyer in London on 13 April 1940, avenging the Jallianwala Bagh massacre of 1919, which occurred under O'Dwyer's authority. Hundreds of unarmed Indians were killed in that massacre. Udham Singh waited 21 years to take revenge. After the assassination, he was arrested and hanged on 31 July 1940. He was a prominent Indian freedom fighter and revolutionary.
qs.kf:
☛ Date of Jallianwala Bagh massacre → 13 April 1919
☛ Date of General O'Dwyer's assassination → 13 April 1940
☛ Date of Udham Singh's execution → 31 July 1940
☛ Udham Singh's birthplace → Sunam, Punjab
☛ Real name of Udham Singh → Sher Singh

q: Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (HSRA) was founded in 1928 in which of the following cities?
qs.e: The Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (HSRA) was founded in 1928 in Delhi during a secret meeting at Firoz Shah Kotla Ground. It was formed as a reorganisation of the earlier Hindustan Republican Association (HRA). Prominent members included Bhagat Singh, Chandrashekhar Azad, and Sukhdev. The HSRA aimed to achieve complete independence from British rule through a socialist ideology. The organisation is known for events like the Lahore Conspiracy Case and the Central Assembly Bombing Case in Delhi. Delhi was chosen as the founding location because it was a politically active area and provided cover from government surveillance.
qs.kf:
☛ What was the full name of HSRA? → Hindustan Socialist Republican Association
☛ What is the founding year of HSRA? → 1928
☛ Who were the key founding members of HSRA? → Bhagat Singh, Chandrashekhar Azad, Sukhdev
☛ The HSRA was a reorganisation of which earlier organisation? → Hindustan Republican Association (HRA)
☛ What was the main objective of HSRA? → Complete independence based on socialist principles

q: Who was the founder of the Forward Bloc party?
qs.e: The Forward Bloc party was founded on 3 May 1939 by Subhas Chandra Bose. It emerged as a left-wing faction within the Indian National Congress after Bose was forced to resign from the Congress presidency. Disagreeing with the Congress policies, he formed the All India Forward Bloc with the aim of uniting the struggle for complete independence against British rule. The party promoted socialist ideology and actively participated in anti-British activities during World War II. Later, Bose led the Azad Hind Fauj (Indian National Army), which played a significant role in India's freedom movement. The Forward Bloc sought to achieve a socialist state through a revolutionary approach, distinct from the non-violent methods of Mahatma Gandhi.
qs.kf:
☛ Date of formation of Forward Bloc → 3 May 1939
☛ Main objective of Forward Bloc → Complete independence and socialism
☛ Other organization founded by Subhas Chandra Bose → Azad Hind Fauj
☛ Slogan of Subhas Chandra Bose → 'Give me blood, and I will give you freedom'
☛ Reason for leaving Indian National Congress → Disagreement with Gandhian policies

q: Who among the following freedom fighters founded the 'Naujawan Bharat Sabha'?
qs.e: The Naujawan Bharat Sabha was founded in 1926 by Bhagat Singh and his comrades. The aim of this organization was to arouse youth against British rule and spread socialist ideology. Bhagat Singh established it in Lahore, and it was a precursor to the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (HSRA). Through this forum, he promoted revolutionary activities and mobilized young people for the freedom struggle.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Naujawan Bharat Sabha established? → 1926
☛ Who founded the Naujawan Bharat Sabha? → Bhagat Singh
☛ In which city did Bhagat Singh found the Naujawan Bharat Sabha? → Lahore
☛ What was the objective of the Naujawan Bharat Sabha? → To awaken youth against British rule
☛ Which revolutionary organization was Bhagat Singh a member of? → HSRA

q: The Abhinav Bharat Mandir (Young India Society) was founded by _____________ and his brother, as a secret organisation during the Indian War of Independence.
qs.e: The Abhinav Bharat Mandir (Young India Society) was founded by Vinayak Damodar Savarkar and his brother Ganesh Damodar Savarkar in 1904. It was a secret revolutionary organization aimed at freeing India from British rule. Through this organization, Savarkar inspired youth for revolution and promoted the ideology of Hindutva. He was a powerful orator, writer, and freedom fighter. He wrote the book 'The Indian War of Independence, 1857', where he described the 1857 uprising as India's first war of independence.
qs.kf:
☛ Who founded Abhinav Bharat Mandir? → Vinayak Damodar Savarkar and his brother Ganesh Savarkar
☛ Which movement was Savarkar associated with? → Revolutionary movement
☛ Which famous book did Savarkar write? → 'The Indian War of Independence, 1857'
☛ What was Savarkar's ideology? → Hindutva
☛ What punishment was given to Savarkar? → 50 years of imprisonment (Kala Pani)

q: Who among the following national leaders founded the Forward Block in the year 1939?
qs.e: Subhash Chandra Bose founded the Forward Bloc in 1939. This party was formed by left-wing members of the Indian National Congress. Bose had previously served as Congress president but left due to differences with Mahatma Gandhi. The Forward Bloc aimed to intensify the demand for complete independence and adopt socialist policies. It was active in anti-British activities during World War II. Bose later formed the Azad Hind Fauj to fight for India's freedom.
qs.kf:
☛ Who founded the Forward Bloc? → Subhash Chandra Bose
☛ When was the Forward Bloc established? → 1939
☛ What ideology did the Forward Bloc follow? → Left-wing / Socialist
☛ Which party did Subhash Chandra Bose form? → Forward Bloc
☛ What was the main aim of the Forward Bloc? → Complete independence and socialism

q: The first nationalistic revolutionary movement in British India emerged from _____.
qs.e: The first nationalistic revolutionary movement in British India emerged from Bengal. The partition of Bengal in 1905 intensified nationalist sentiments, leading to the Swadeshi movement and the rise of revolutionary activities in Bengal. Organizations like Anushilan Samiti (1902) and Jugantar laid the foundation for armed rebellion. Revolutionaries like Khudiram Bose and Prafulla Chaki hailed from this region. The Alipore Bomb Case of 1908 brought the revolutionary movement to national attention. Thus, Bengal became the birthplace of the first nationalistic revolutionary movement.
qs.kf:
☛ Date of Partition of Bengal → 1905
☛ Founder of Anushilan Samiti → Satyendranath Bose
☛ Accused in Alipore Bomb Case → Aurobindo Ghosh
☛ Formation of Jugantar Party → 1906
☛ Slogan of Swadeshi Movement → Vande Mataram

q: Subhash Chandra Bose was re-elected as the President of INC at the Tripuri Session in 1939 by defeating Gandhiji's candidate:
qs.e: The Tripuri Session of the Indian National Congress in 1939 was a landmark event. Subhash Chandra Bose defeated Pattabhi Sitaramayya, who was Gandhi's candidate, to be re-elected as President. This election highlighted the growing ideological differences within the Congress. Despite his popularity, Bose's differences with Gandhi led to his resignation and Rajendra Prasad was appointed as the new President. The Tripuri Session marked a turning point in the Indian freedom struggle, revealing the diverse political ideologies within the Congress.
qs.kf:
☛ Year of Tripuri Session → 1939
☛ Gandhi's candidate → Pattabhi Sitaramayya
☛ President after Bose's resignation → Rajendra Prasad
☛ Party formed by Bose → Forward Bloc
☛ Start of World War II → 1939

q: When was the Hindustan Republican Association formed?
qs.e: The Hindustan Republican Association (HRA) was founded in the year 1924. It was formed by revolutionaries who believed in armed struggle against British rule in India. Key founders included Ram Prasad Bismil, Ashfaqulla Khan, and Sachindra Nath Sanyal. The main objective of HRA was to attain complete independence for India. It carried out the Kakori Conspiracy in 1925, which posed a major challenge to the British government. Later, in 1928, the organization was renamed the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (HSRA).
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Hindustan Republican Association formed? → 1924
☛ Who were the founders of HRA? → Ram Prasad Bismil, Ashfaqulla Khan, Sachindra Nath Sanyal
☛ Which major event is associated with HRA? → Kakori Conspiracy (1925)
☛ What was HRA later renamed as? → Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (HSRA)
☛ When was HSRA formed? → 1928

q: Who was one of the co-founder of Ghadar Party?
qs.e: The Ghadar Party was founded in 1913 by Indian expatriates in the United States. One of its co-founders was Har Dayal, a revolutionary and intellectual. The party's main objective was to overthrow British rule through armed revolution. Har Dayal also published the 'Ghadar' newspaper, which played a crucial role in the Indian freedom struggle. During World War I, the party planned an uprising known as the 'Ghadar Conspiracy'.

☛ Main place of Ghadar Conspiracy → Planned uprising in Punjab

q: What was the name of the political party formed by Subhash Chandra Bose after he left Congress party?
qs.e: After resigning from the Indian National Congress in 1939, Subhash Chandra Bose founded the All India Forward Bloc (AIFB). This left-wing political party aimed to counter the conservative policies of the Congress leadership. Bose emphasized radical opposition to British rule and socialist principles. The Forward Bloc played an active role in anti-British activities during World War II and later became a significant part of the Indian freedom movement. The party advocated complete independence and was instrumental in mobilizing youth for the struggle.

q: Prafulla Chaki and Khudiram Bose are known for their attempt to assassinate which British official?
qs.e: Prafulla Chaki and Khudiram Bose were revolutionaries in the Indian independence movement. In 1908, they attempted to assassinate Douglas Kingsford, the British magistrate of Muzaffarpur. Kingsford was known for his harsh actions against anti-partition activists. However, the bomb was mistakenly thrown at a carriage carrying two European women instead of Kingsford, killing them. Khudiram Bose was arrested and hanged, while Prafulla Chaki committed suicide to avoid capture. This incident intensified revolutionary activities against British rule in Bengal. The Muzaffarpur conspiracy highlighted the growing discontent and radicalism among the youth.
qs.kf:

☛ When was Khudiram Bose hanged? → 11 August 1908
☛ How old was Khudiram Bose at the time of his execution? → 18 years
☛ Where did Prafulla Chaki commit suicide? → Mokama Railway Station (Bihar)
☛ What was Kingsford's official position? → Magistrate of Muzaffarpur

q: What was the name of the headquarters of the Ghadar Party?
qs.e: The Ghadar Party was founded in 1913 in San Francisco, USA. Its headquarters was called Yugantar Ashram. This ashram served as a hub for Indian immigrants and revolutionaries, where the newspaper Ghadar was published. The party aimed to overthrow British rule in India through armed revolution. Key leaders included Lala Hardayal, Sohan Singh Bhakna, and Kartar Singh Sarabha. The movement inspired many Indians abroad to join the freedom struggle.
qs.kf:

q: Why was the Ghadar Party’s revolutionary attempt during World War I largely unsuccessful?
o: Lack of support from international allies
Strong opposition from the Indian National Congress
Interception by British intelligence and internal betrayal
qs.e: The Ghadar Party's revolutionary attempt during World War I was largely unsuccessful because the Indian public was apathetic towards armed revolution. The Ghadar Party had organized overseas Indians, especially in the United States and Canada, to launch a revolt against British rule. However, when the revolutionaries returned to India under the Ghadar Conspiracy of 1915, they did not receive the expected support from the masses. Most Indians remained loyal to the British and cooperated with the war effort. Additionally, revolutionary activities were mostly confined to Bengal, and other regions lacked political awareness. This public apathy prevented the party from staging a large-scale uprising, while the British government carried out severe repression. Thus, public indifference was the primary reason for its failure.
qs.kf:
☛ When and where was the Ghadar Party founded? → In 1913 in the United States
☛ Who was the founder of the Ghadar Party? → Lala Hardayal
☛ What was the main objective of the Ghadar Party? → To end British rule in India through armed revolution
☛ Who were the key leaders of the Ghadar Conspiracy? → Rash Behari Bose and Sachindra Nath Sanyal
☛ What was the main newspaper of the Ghadar Party? → Ghadar (published in Urdu and Punjabi)

q: Which of the following leaders of the Indian National Movement was NOT associated with the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (HSRA)?
qs.e: The Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (HSRA) was a revolutionary organization founded in 1928 at Feroz Shah Kotla ground, Delhi. Its prominent members included Chandrasekhar Azad, Bhagat Singh, Batukeshwar Dutt, Rajguru, and Sukhdev. The organization aimed to achieve independence through revolution and armed struggle. Mahatma Gandhi was a proponent of non-violence and satyagraha, and he had no association with revolutionary activities. The HSRA revolutionaries were involved in events like the Lahore Conspiracy Case and the Kakori Incident. Gandhi's philosophy was fundamentally different from the revolutionary ideology of the HSRA.
qs.kf:
☛ What was the main objective of HSRA? → To establish a socialist republic in India
☛ When was HSRA founded? → 1928
☛ In which case was Bhagat Singh hanged? → Lahore Conspiracy Case
☛ Where did Chandrasekhar Azad die? → Alfred Park, Allahabad
☛ Which event was Batukeshwar Dutt involved in? → Central Assembly Bombing Case

q: Who among the following was NOT sentenced to death in the Kakori Conspiracy Case (1925)?
qs.e: In the Kakori Conspiracy Case (1925), four revolutionaries were sentenced to death: Ashfaqulla Khan, Rajendra Lahiri, Roshan Singh, and Ram Prasad Bismil. Sachindra Nath Bakshi was sentenced to life imprisonment (Kala Pani), not death. The incident occurred on August 9, 1925, at Kakori railway station, where members of the Hindustan Republican Association (HRA) looted a government treasury. Bismil, Lahiri, Khan, and Singh were hanged in December 1927. Bakshi later became involved in politics and remained a freedom fighter.
qs.kf:
☛ Date of Kakori Conspiracy → August 9, 1925
☛ Organization name → Hindustan Republican Association (HRA)
☛ Use of looted money → To buy weapons
☛ Four hanged → Bismil, Lahiri, Khan, Roshan Singh
☛ One given life imprisonment → Sachindra Nath Bakshi

q: Which of the following statements is INCORRECT about the newspaper “The Hitavada”?
o: It was established at Nagpur in 1911
It was an English daily newspaper
It was the mouthpiece of the Ghadar movement
It was founded by Gopal Krishna Gokhale
qs.e: The Hitavada was founded in 1911 at Nagpur by Gopal Krishna Gokhale. It was an English daily newspaper and a significant voice in the Indian national movement. The mouthpiece of the Ghadar movement was the newspaper Ghadar, published in Urdu and Punjabi, started in 1913. Thus, the third statement is incorrect.

☛ Year of establishment of The Hitavada? → 1911
☛ Place of publication of The Hitavada? → Nagpur
☛ Mouthpiece of Ghadar movement? → Ghadar newspaper
☛ Year of start of Ghadar movement? → 1913

q: Which of the following samitis was founded by Ashwini Kumar Dutt in Barisal?
qs.e: Ashwini Kumar Dutt was a prominent Bengali revolutionary and nationalist leader. In 1905, he founded the Swadesh Bandhab Samiti in Barisal (now in Bangladesh) to oppose the partition of Bengal. The samiti aimed to promote the Swadeshi movement, boycott foreign goods, and spread national awakening. Dutt focused on education, self-employment, and rural development. He was a popular leader and was known as the 'Lion of Barisal'. The Anushilan Samiti was founded by Pramathanath Mitra in Kolkata, while the Jugantar Samiti was formed by Barindra Ghosh and other revolutionaries. The 'Bharat Mata Samiti' is not associated with Ashwini Kumar Dutt.
qs.kf:
☛ Who founded the Swadesh Bandhab Samiti? → Ashwini Kumar Dutt
☛ Where was the Swadesh Bandhab Samiti founded? → Barisal
☛ Who founded the Anushilan Samiti? → Pramathanath Mitra
☛ Who founded the Jugantar Samiti? → Barindra Ghosh
☛ By what name is Ashwini Kumar Dutt known? → Lion of Barisal

q: Who was the ﬁrst British Governor General of India in 1833?
qs.e: Lord William Bentinck (1828-1835) was the first British Governor General of India, as the Charter Act of 1833 elevated the Governor General of Bengal to Governor General of India. Previously, the Governor General had authority only over the Bengal Presidency. Lord Bentinck is known for abolishing the practice of Sati (1829), suppressing thuggee, and promoting English education. He was a reformist Governor General. Other options: Lord Dalhousie (1848-1856), Lord Wellesley (1798-1805), Lord Warren Hastings (1773-1785) are incorrect.
qs.kf:
☛ Who became the first Governor General of India under the Charter Act of 1833? → Lord William Bentinck
☛ When did Lord William Bentinck abolish Sati? → 1829
☛ What was Lord William Bentinck's tenure? → 1828-1835
☛ Who was the last Governor General of India? → Lord Canning
☛ Who was the first Governor General of Bengal? → Lord Warren Hastings

q: Who is known as the father of the Panchayat constituency?
qs.e: Lord Minto is known as the father of the Panchayat constituency in India. Under the Indian Councils Act of 1909, also known as the Minto-Morley Reforms, Lord Minto introduced separate electorates for Muslims, which laid the foundation for communal representation. He also formalized the electoral constituencies at the village level, paving the way for Panchayati Raj institutions. The concept of a panchayat constituency ensured local governance representation, which later evolved into the modern Panchayati Raj system. Lord Minto served as the Viceroy of India from 1905 to 1910, and his reforms significantly impacted India's political structure by recognizing the need for community-based electoral representation.
qs.kf:
☛ Who is the father of Panchayat constituency? → Lord Minto
☛ What is the Indian Councils Act of 1909 commonly known as? → Minto-Morley Reforms
☛ Who demanded separate electorates? → Muslim League
☛ When was Panchayati Raj introduced in India? → 1992 (73rd Amendment)
☛ What was Lord Minto's tenure as Viceroy? → 1905-1910

q: "Portfolio System" implemented by whom?
qs.e: The Portfolio System was implemented by Lord Canning in 1858. This system was introduced during British rule in India, where each member of the Governor-General's council was assigned a specific department, such as revenue, army, or law. The aim was to increase administrative efficiency and accountability. Lord Canning served as the first Viceroy of India from 1858 to 1862, and he initiated several administrative reforms after the Revolt of 1857. The Portfolio System was later formalized under the Indian Councils Act of 1861. This system marked a shift towards a more organized and departmentalized governance structure in British India.
qs.kf:
☛ Government of India Act 1858 → Ended the East India Company's rule and transferred power to the British Crown.
☛ Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms → Introduced in 1919, establishing dyarchy in provinces.
☛ Indian Councils Act 1861 → Gave legal recognition to the Portfolio System.
☛ Lord Canning's tenure → 1858–1862, served as Viceroy after the 1857 revolt.
☛ First three Viceroys → Lord Canning, Lord Elgin, Lord Lawrence.

q: Belur Math is located at:
A. West Bengal
B. Maharashtra
C. Uttar Pradesh
D. Tamil Nadu
qs.e: Belur Math is located on the banks of the Hooghly River in the Howrah district of West Bengal. It was established in 1897 by Swami Vivekananda. It is the headquarters of the Ramakrishna Mission, which propagates the teachings of Ramakrishna Paramahamsa. Belur Math is known for its unique architecture, blending elements from Hindu, Muslim, Christian, and other religions. It attracts devotees and tourists from all over the world.

☛ Who founded Belur Math? → Swami Vivekananda
☛ Belur Math is the headquarters of which organization? → Ramakrishna Mission
☛ On which river is Belur Math situated? → Hooghly
☛ When was Ramakrishna Mission founded? → 1897

q: Who described the kingdom of Awadh as 'a cherry that will drop into our mouth one day'?
qs.e: Governor-General Lord Dalhousie (1848-1856) annexed several princely states under the Doctrine of Lapse. He described the kingdom of Awadh as "a cherry that will drop into our mouth one day", implying its annexation was inevitable soon. In 1856, Awadh was annexed on the grounds of misgovernance. This statement reflects Dalhousie's expansionist policy and his desire to bring fertile Awadh under British control, which later became a major cause of the 1857 Revolt.

q: Who was the First Governor General of free India?
qs.e: The first Governor General of independent India was Lord Mountbatten. He assumed this position on August 15, 1947, when India gained independence. He served as Governor General from 1947 to 1948. He was succeeded by C. Rajagopalachari, who became the last Governor General of India. The position of Governor General was abolished when India became a Republic on January 26, 1950. Lord Mountbatten also served as the last Viceroy of British India. He played a key role during the partition of India.

☛ First Governor General of free India → Lord Mountbatten

q: Who became the last governor-general and first viceroy of India during the rule of the British crown?
qs.e: After the Revolt of 1857, the rule of the East India Company was abolished, and India came directly under the British Crown. Lord Canning was the Governor-General at that time and became the last Governor-General of India. Under the Government of India Act 1858, the post of Governor-General was replaced by Viceroy, and Lord Canning was appointed as the first Viceroy of India. Thus, he held both positions. This change marked a significant shift in Indian administration, ending Company rule and beginning direct rule by the British Crown.

☛ Who was the first Viceroy of India? → Lord Canning

☛ What was Lord Canning's tenure? → 1856 to 1862

q: Who became the first Viceroy of India?
qs.e: The first Viceroy of India was Lord Canning, who served from 1858 to 1862. After the Revolt of 1857, the British government transferred the administration of India from the East India Company directly to the Crown through the Government of India Act 1858. Lord Canning was initially appointed as Governor-General but became the first Viceroy in 1858. The title Viceroy represented the British monarch in India. During his tenure, he focused on reconstruction and reconciliation after the revolt. The Indian Councils Act 1861 was passed during his time, which allowed the inclusion of Indians in the Viceroy's executive council for the first time.

☛ What was Lord Canning's tenure as Viceroy? → 1858-1862

q: In which year were the powers of the East India Company passed to the British crown by the British Parliament?
qs.e: The Government of India Act 1858 was passed by the British Parliament in 1858 to end the rule of the East India Company in India. This act transferred all powers and property of the Company to the British Crown, making India a direct colony of the British Empire. It abolished the Board of Control and the Court of Directors and created the post of Secretary of State for India. The first Secretary of State was Lord Stanley. This act was introduced after the Revolt of 1857, which exposed the failures of Company rule.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Government of India Act passed? → 1858

☛ Who was the first Secretary of State for India? → Lord Stanley

☛ Which act abolished the Board of Control? → Government of India Act 1858

q: Name the Viceroy of India who was associated with the controversial Ilbert Bill during the Indian freedom struggle.
qs.e: Lord Ripon (1880-1884) was the Viceroy of India associated with the controversial Ilbert Bill (1883). The bill aimed to give Indian judges the jurisdiction to try European offenders, leading to widespread opposition from the British community in India. Lord Ripon, known as a liberal viceroy, also promoted local self-government (1882) and introduced Factory Act (1881) to improve labor conditions. The Ilbert Bill controversy highlighted racial tensions between Indians and the British. Lord Ripon's tenure is remembered for his progressive reforms and his support for Indian representation.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Viceroy was associated with the Ilbert Bill? → Lord Ripon
☛ What was Lord Ripon's tenure? → 1880-1884
☛ Who introduced local self-government in India? → Lord Ripon (1882)
☛ When was the first Factory Act passed in India? → 1881, under Lord Ripon
☛ In which year was the Ilbert Bill introduced? → 1883

q: Who founded the Visva Bharati which later became a Central University?
qs.e: Visva Bharati was founded in 1921 by Rabindranath Tagore in Santiniketan, West Bengal. Tagore aimed at integrating Indian and Western cultures. In 1951, it was granted the status of a 'Central University' and renamed 'Visva Bharati University'. Tagore received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1913. The university is one of the premier educational institutions in India.

q: Name the Governor-General under whom a new policy of ‘paramountcy’ was initiated.
qs.e: Lord Hasting (1813-1823) initiated the policy of 'paramountcy', under which the British East India Company established its supremacy over Indian princely states. This policy allowed the Company to interfere in the internal affairs of the states. Lord Hasting achieved victory in the Maratha Wars (1817-1818) and ended the Peshwa rule. He also forced the Rajputana states to accept British suzerainty. Lord Dalhousie introduced the 'Doctrine of Lapse', Lord Wellesley started the 'Subsidiary Alliance' system, and Lord Cornwallis implemented the 'Permanent Settlement'.

q: Who among the following passed the widow remarriage Act in India?
qs.e: The Widow Remarriage Act, 1856 was passed during the tenure of Lord Canning. This act legalized remarriage of Hindu widows and was a major social reform. The act was largely driven by the efforts of Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar. Lord Canning served as Governor-General of India from 1856 to 1862. This legislation marked a significant step towards women's rights in India.

q: Who was the Viceroy of India when Indian National Congress was founded?
qs.e: The Indian National Congress (INC) was founded on 28 December 1885 in Bombay. At that time, Lord Dufferin (1884-1888) was the Viceroy of India. The INC was established by A.O. Hume, a retired British civil servant. The first session was held under the presidency of Womesh Chunder Bonnerjee. Lord Dufferin is known for annexing Burma after the Third Anglo-Burmese War (1885), which became part of the British Empire in 1886. Initially, Dufferin viewed the INC as a safe platform to voice public opinion to the government. However, when the Congress adopted a critical stance, he turned against it.

q: Who was the first Indian to join the Indian Civil Service?
qs.e: Satyendranath Tagore (1842-1923) was the first Indian to join the Indian Civil Service (ICS). He was the elder brother of Rabindranath Tagore. In 1863, he passed the ICS examination and was appointed as an officer in British India. He served in various provinces like Bombay, Bengal, and Assam. His selection was a historic achievement for Indians under British rule. He held positions such as judge, collector, and secretary. He contributed to social reforms, especially women's education. He died in 1923.

q: Who was the Viceroy of British India at the time India became independent in 1947?
qs.e: At the time of India's independence in 1947, the last Viceroy of British India was Lord Mountbatten. He was appointed in February 1947 and served until June 1948. Mountbatten played a crucial role in planning India's partition and independence. He announced the partition plan on June 3, 1947, known as the Mountbatten Plan, which led to the creation of two independent nations: India and Pakistan. After independence, Mountbatten became the first Governor-General of India, while Muhammad Ali Jinnah became the Governor-General of Pakistan. Mountbatten's tenure is historically significant in the context of Indian independence and partition.

q: In which year was the title 'Viceroy’ given to 'Governor-General’ of India?
qs.e: The title 'Viceroy' was given to the 'Governor-General' of India in 1858. This change occurred under the Government of India Act 1858, which ended the rule of the East India Company and established direct rule by the British Crown. After this Act, the Governor-General of India was also called the Viceroy, representing the British monarch. The first Viceroy was Lord Canning, who had been Governor-General since 1856 and became Viceroy in 1858. The title remained in use until 1947, when India gained independence.

q: Name the first Indian to join viceroy's executive council.
qs.e: Satyendra Prasanna Sinha was the first Indian to join the Viceroy's Executive Council in British India. He was appointed as the Law Member in 1909 by Lord Minto. He was a prominent lawyer, politician, and also served as the President of the Indian National Congress. Later, he became the first Indian Governor-General of India. His appointment marked a significant step in the inclusion of Indians in higher administrative positions.

q: Who was the successor to Lord Wavell as Viceroy of British India?
qs.e: Lord Wavell served as Viceroy of India from 1943 to 1947. He was succeeded by Lord Mountbatten in March 1947. Mountbatten was the last Viceroy and oversaw the partition and independence of India. Lord Irwin served from 1926-31, Lord Minto from 1905-10, and Lord Linlithgow from 1936-43. During Wavell's tenure, the Cabinet Mission arrived in 1946 and the Constituent Assembly was formed. Mountbatten presented the 3 June Plan, which led to the partition of India. He remained Viceroy until 15 August 1947 and then became the first Governor-General of independent India. Thus, Lord Mountbatten was the successor to Lord Wavell as Viceroy.

q: 'White Paper on Constitutional Reforms' was prepared by ____.
qs.e: The 'White Paper on Constitutional Reforms' was prepared by the Simon Commission in 1930. The Simon Commission, also known as the Indian Statutory Commission, came to India in 1928 to study constitutional reforms. It submitted its report in 1930, recommending provincial autonomy and the abolition of dyarchy. Based on this report, the Government of India Act 1935 was enacted.

q: Which governor general prepared "the principle of lapsed" (or grab policy) in British India?
qs.e: Lord Dalhousie (1848-1856) introduced the Doctrine of Lapse, a policy under which princely states without a natural heir were annexed to the British Empire. This policy became infamous as the 'grab policy'. Major states annexed included Satarra (1848), Sambalpur (1849), Udaipur (1852), Nagpur (1853), Jhansi (1854), and Awadh (1856). The Doctrine of Lapse was a key factor in fueling the Revolt of 1857. Dalhousie also initiated the introduction of railways, telegraph, and postal system in India.

q: Who was the Viceroy of India during the Jalianwala Bagh massacre in 1919?
qs.e: During the Jallianwala Bagh massacre in 1919, the Viceroy of India was Lord Chelmsford (Frederic Thesiger). The incident occurred on 13 April 1919 in Amritsar, Punjab, when Brigadier General Reginald Dyer ordered firing on unarmed Indian civilians, killing hundreds. Chelmsford supported Dyer's actions and had previously enforced the Rowlatt Act. This massacre intensified the Indian independence movement, leading Mahatma Gandhi to launch the Non-Cooperation Movement. Chelmsford served as Viceroy from 1916 to 1921.

q: In 1877, which Governor General hosted the court to accept Queen Victoria as Queen of India?
qs.e: In 1877, Viceroy Lord Lytton hosted the Delhi Durbar to proclaim Queen Victoria as the 'Empress of India' (Kaiser-i-Hind). The durbar was intended to assert British control over India after the end of the East India Company's rule. Lord Lytton's tenure (1876-1880) is known for its reactionary policies and the Second Anglo-Afghan War.

q: Who was the Viceroy of India during the Shimla Conference of 1945?
qs.e: The Shimla Conference of 1945 was convened by the Viceroy of India, Lord Wavell, to discuss constitutional reforms with Indian political leaders. The conference aimed to break the political deadlock between the Indian National Congress and the Muslim League. Key issues included the Muslim League's demand for Pakistan and the Congress's stance for a united India. Lord Wavell proposed the formation of an Executive Council, but the talks failed due to disagreements between Jinnah and Nehru. This conference was a significant event in India's freedom struggle, highlighting the deepening communal divide.

q: Who was the Viceroy of India when the Indian University Act of 1904 was passed?
qs.e: The Indian University Act of 1904 was passed during the viceroyalty of Lord Curzon. The act aimed to improve the standard of education in Indian universities and increase government control over them. Lord Curzon (1899-1905) implemented several educational reforms, with the University Act of 1904 being a significant one. This act brought changes in the functioning, curriculum, and administration of universities. Curzon's education policy sought to curb nationalist sentiments and strengthen British interests. The act reduced the autonomy of universities and centralized control.

q: When did the first train run in British India?
qs.e: The first train in India ran on 16 April 1853 between Bombay (now Mumbai) and Thane. It covered a distance of 34 kilometers and had 14 carriages carrying about 400 passengers. This railway line was inaugurated during the tenure of Governor General Lord Dalhousie, who is considered the father of Indian Railways. The train was pulled by three engines named Sahib, Sultan, and Sindh. This event marked the beginning of modern transportation in India.

q: In 1927, who was the President of the 'Indian Statutory Commission' appointed by the British Government?
qs.e: In 1927, the British Government appointed the Indian Statutory Commission, also known as the Simon Commission, to review constitutional reforms in India. The commission was headed by Sir John Simon, a British politician and lawyer. The commission consisted entirely of British members, which led to widespread protests and boycotts by all Indian political parties, including the Indian National Congress. The famous slogan 'Simon Go Back' was raised during these protests. The commission submitted its report in 1930, which later formed the basis for the Government of India Act 1935.

q: In which year, the Indian National Congress demanded a Constituent Assembly to create the Constitution of India?
qs.e: The Indian National Congress first demanded a Constituent Assembly to frame the Constitution of India in 1935. This demand was a direct opposition to the Government of India Act 1935, which the Congress rejected. The Congress believed that the constitution should be drafted by Indian representatives elected by the people, not by the British Parliament. Later, in 1946, the Constituent Assembly was formed under the Cabinet Mission Plan. The 1935 demand strengthened the Indian struggle for self-governance. It was Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru who first raised this demand.

q: Who told the 'Hindu Institution' to the Indian Constituent Assembly?
qs.e: The British politician who called the Indian Constituent Assembly a 'Hindu Institution' was Lord Viscount Simon. He was the chairman of the Simon Commission of 1928, which recommended constitutional reforms in India. While commenting on the structure and functioning of the Constituent Assembly, Simon remarked that it would be a 'Hindu institution', implying Hindu dominance. This remark was controversial as the Constituent Assembly included representatives from all religions and communities. The Simon Commission faced widespread opposition in India, and this comment further fueled criticism against Simon. The Constituent Assembly was formed in 1946 to draft India's constitution, and its composition was diverse, representing various interests.

He was the Governor-General at the time of the transfer and was appointed as Viceroy. During his tenure, the Indian army was reorganized and financial reforms were introduced. Lord Wellesley, Lord Cornwallis, and Lord Mayo were Governors-General, but not Viceroys.

q: Who is the father of communal election?
qs.e: Lord Minto is known as the father of communal election in India. In 1906, under the Indian Councils Act of 1909 (also known as Minto-Morley Reforms), Lord Minto introduced separate electorates for Muslims. This system sowed the seeds of communalism in Indian politics. Lord Minto was the Viceroy of India at that time, and Lord Morley was the Secretary of State for India. The separate electorate provision divided the society along religious lines, eventually contributing to the partition of India. Thus, Lord Minto is called the father of communal election.

q: Who first started the portfolio system in India?
qs.e: The portfolio system in India was first introduced by Lord Canning in 1859. Under this system, the functions of the government were divided into various departments (portfolios) such as Home, Finance, Military, Foreign Affairs, etc., and each department was assigned to a member of the Executive Council. This system was implemented after the Government of India Act 1858, when the British Crown assumed direct control over India. Lord Canning also served as the first Viceroy of India. The portfolio system made the administration more organized and efficient. Before this, all members of the Council were jointly responsible. This reform became a key feature of British Indian administration.

qs.e: The Samjhauti Riot Movement took place in 1927 in British India. This movement was in protest against the Simon Commission. At that time, the Viceroy of India was Lord Irwin. qs.e: The first Governor General of independent India was Lord Mountbatten. He served from 15 August 1947 to 21 June 1948. He was also the last Viceroy of India. q: Which of the following statements is/are correct in the context of the Government of India Act of 1858?

II. The power to control the Indian Territory was vested in the Queen.
qs.e: The Government of India Act of 1858, also known as the Act for the Good Government of India, ended the rule of the East India Company and transferred the control of Indian territories directly to the British Crown. The Act vested the power to control Indian territory in the Queen, who exercised it through the Secretary of State for India. Hence, both statements are correct. This Act was passed after the Revolt of 1857 and designated the Governor-General as the Viceroy of India.

q: Which of the following is NOT the provision of the Government of India Act, 1858?

However, making the Law Member a full member of the Executive Council was a provision of the Charter Act of 1853, not the 1858 Act. q: Which of the following Governor-Generals introduced the General Service Enlistment Act?
qs.e: The General Service Enlistment Act was introduced in 1856 during the tenure of Lord Canning as Governor-General of India. This act required Indian soldiers to serve outside the country if needed when enlisted in the British Army. Previously, sepoys only agreed to serve within India. q: In which year were the Indian Civil Service (ICS) and Indian Police (IP) replaced by the Indian Administrative Service (IAS) and Indian Police Service (IPS), later recognised as All-India Services?
qs.e: After India's independence in 1947, the Indian Civil Service (ICS) and Indian Police (IP) were replaced by the Indian Administrative Service (IAS) and Indian Police Service (IPS) respectively. These services are known as All-India Services, which serve both the central and state governments. The ICS was established in 1858 during British rule and was often called the 'steel frame'. Following independence, the IAS took its place. Similarly, the IP was converted into the IPS. The provision for All-India Services is under Article 312 of the Constitution. Currently, there are three All-India Services – IAS, IPS, and IFoS.
qs.kf:
☛ When was ICS established? → 1858
☛ Under which Article are All-India Services provided? → Article 312
☛ How many All-India Services exist today? → Three (IAS, IPS, IFoS)
☛ What was ICS known as? → Steel frame
☛ What does IFoS stand for? → Indian Forest Service

q: What was the effect of English education and western thought on Indian nationalism?
qs.e: English education and western thought significantly influenced Indian nationalism. It introduced Indians to modern political ideas such as democracy, liberty, and equality. Reformers like Raja Ram Mohan Roy and Swami Vivekananda used western education to voice against social evils. Organizations like the Indian National Congress were formed by English-educated Indians who led the national movement. Thus, western education ignited national awakening, rather than supporting casteism or encouraging partition.
qs.kf:
☛ Who introduced western education in India? → Lord William Bentinck (1835)
☛ Which act made English education official? → Macaulay's Minute (1835)
☛ What was the first Indian university? → Calcutta University (1857)
☛ When was the Indian National Congress founded? → 1885
☛ Which movement was strengthened by western education? → Swadeshi Movement (1905)

q: Who among the following passed an Act in 1898, making it an offence to provoke people against the British rulers?
qs.e: In 1898, the Viceroy of India Lord Curzon passed an Act that made it an offence to provoke people against the British rulers. This Act came as an amendment to the Indian Penal Code and Code of Criminal Procedure. Its main objective was to suppress anti-British activities and crush the nationalist movement. It is also known as the Sedition Act. Lord Curzon's tenure lasted from 1899 to 1905. During this time, he also carried out the controversial Partition of Bengal in 1905. This Act was used to suppress many nationalist leaders.
qs.kf:
☛ Who passed the Act of 1898? → Lord Curzon
☛ What did this Act criminalize? → Provoking people against British rulers
☛ What was Lord Curzon's tenure? → 1899-1905
☛ What other controversial act did Lord Curzon do? → Partition of Bengal (1905)
☛ What is this Act also known as? → Sedition Act

q: Which organisation was established in 1817 to promote Western education among Indians?
qs.e: In 1817, Hindoo College (later renamed Presidency College) was established in Calcutta to promote Western education among Indians. It was one of the first modern educational institutions in India, focusing on English language and Western sciences. The college played a crucial role in the intellectual awakening of Bengal, producing many reformers and freedom fighters. Raja Ram Mohan Roy and David Hare were instrumental in its foundation. Hindoo College laid the groundwork for the spread of Western thought in India.
qs.kf:
☛ When was Hindoo College established? → 1817
☛ Where was Hindoo College located? → Calcutta
☛ What is the later name of Hindoo College? → Presidency College
☛ What was the aim of Hindoo College? → To promote Western education
☛ Which reformer was associated with Hindoo College? → Raja Ram Mohan Roy

q: Which law allowed inter-caste and inter-religious marriages during the British period in India?
qs.e: The Act of 1872 (Act III of 1872) was the first law in British India to legalize inter-caste and inter-religious marriages. It introduced the concept of civil marriage, where no religious rites or caste customs were required. This law was intended for those who wanted to marry outside their caste or religion. Enacted by the British Parliament, it applied to all religions and castes. The Act marked a significant social reform and laid the groundwork for the later Special Marriage Act, 1954. It should not be confused with the Widow Remarriage Act (1856), which allowed widow remarriage, or the Sarda Act (1929), which banned child marriage.
qs.kf:
☛ What was the purpose of the Act of 1872? → To legalize inter-caste and inter-religious marriages
☛ What type of marriage did the Act of 1872 propose? → Civil marriage
☛ Who passed the Act of 1872? → British Parliament
☛ Which Act followed the Act of 1872? → Special Marriage Act, 1954
☛ Which Act legalized widow remarriage? → Widow Remarriage Act, 1856

q: The office of Governor-General was renamed after 1858 as ____.
qs.e: Under the Government of India Act 1858, the rule of the East India Company was abolished and the administration of India came directly under the British Crown. This act abolished the office of Governor-General and renamed it as Viceroy of India. The Viceroy was the representative of the British monarch and had extensive powers. The first Viceroy was Lord Canning, who held the office from 1858 to 1862. This change marked a major shift in British policy in India after the Revolt of 1857. The office of Viceroy continued until 1947 when India gained independence.
qs.kf:
☛ Name of the 1858 Act → Government of India Act 1858
☛ First Viceroy → Lord Canning
☛ Last Viceroy → Lord Mountbatten
☛ First Governor-General → Warren Hastings
☛ When did the office of Viceroy end → 1947

q: Who was the last Governor General of India?
A. Chakravarti Rajagopalachari
B. Warren Hastings
C. Louis Mountbatten
D. Edward Law
qs.e: The last Governor General of India was Chakravarti Rajagopalachari. He succeeded Lord Mountbatten in 1948 and served until 1950, when India became a republic and the office of Governor General was abolished. Rajagopalachari was a prominent freedom fighter, lawyer, and politician. He later served as India's Home Minister and Governor of West Bengal. He was also the first Indian to be awarded the Bharat Ratna. Thus, he holds the distinction of being the last Governor General of India.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the first Governor General of India? → Lord William Bentinck (in 1833)
☛ Who was the last Viceroy of India? → Lord Mountbatten (in 1947)
☛ Who was the first President of India? → Dr. Rajendra Prasad
☛ Who was the first recipient of Bharat Ratna? → Chakravarti Rajagopalachari (in 1954)
☛ Who was the last British Governor General of India? → Lord Mountbatten (1947-1948)

q: Jallianwala Bagh massacre took place during the term of Viceroy ___________.
qs.e: The Jallianwala Bagh massacre occurred on 13 April 1919 in Amritsar. It took place during the tenure of Lord Chelmsford as Viceroy of India (1916-1921). Lord Chelmsford had enforced the Rowlatt Act in 1919, against which people had gathered at Jallianwala Bagh. General Dyer ordered the troops to open fire on the unarmed crowd, resulting in hundreds of deaths. A Hunter Commission was appointed to inquire into the incident.
qs.kf:
☛ Date of Jallianwala Bagh massacre → 13 April 1919
☛ Officer who ordered firing → General Dyer
☛ Viceroy at that time → Lord Chelmsford
☛ When was Rowlatt Act passed? → 1919
☛ Name of the inquiry commission → Hunter Commission

q: Who said in the Constituent assembly debate on 27 August 1947, “I believe separate electorates will be suicidal to the minorities."
qs.e: On 27 August 1947, during the Constituent Assembly debate on minority rights, Govind Ballabh Pant stated, "I believe separate electorates will be suicidal to the minorities." He argued that separate electorates would isolate minorities from the mainstream and foster communalism. Pant advocated for integrated society with safeguards for minorities. This statement is a crucial part of the Constituent Assembly debates, reflecting India's commitment to secularism and inclusive democracy. His views shaped the decision to adopt joint electorates in the Indian Constitution, ensuring national unity over divisive politics.
qs.kf:
☛ Who opposed separate electorates? → Govind Ballabh Pant
☛ 27 August 1947 debate topic? → Minority rights
☛ Govind Ballabh Pant was first CM of Uttar Pradesh → 1950-54
☛ Member of Drafting Committee? → Govind Ballabh Pant
☛ Separate electorates ended after? → 1951 elections

q: Who among the following was NOT a member of Simon Commission?
qs.e: The Simon Commission (1927) was formed to review constitutional reforms in India. It was chaired by John Simon, and other members included Clement Attlee (later Prime Minister of Britain) and Harry Levy-Lawson. James A Scott was not a member of this commission; he was a British diplomat who served in various posts in India. As the commission had no Indian members, it faced widespread boycott in India.

q: Who was the first Governor General of Independent India?
qs.e: The first Governor General of Independent India was Lord Mountbatten. He served from 15 August 1947 to 21 June 1948. He was the Viceroy during the partition of India and later became the first Governor General of independent India. After him, C. Rajagopalachari became the last Governor General of India. Note that Warren Hastings was the first Governor General of Bengal (1773-1785), and Lord William Bentinck was the first Governor General of India (1833-1835). Lord Mountbatten played a crucial role in India's independence and partition.

☛ First Governor General of British India → Warren Hastings

☛ Lord Mountbatten's tenure → 15 Aug 1947 to 21 June 1948

q: Which kingdom was called "a cherry" by Governor General Lord Dalhousie?
qs.e: Lord Dalhousie called the Kingdom of Awadh 'a cherry' because it was a ripe and easily annexable territory for the British Empire. He annexed Awadh in 1856 under the pretext of misgovernance, using the doctrine of 'lapse' in a broader sense. Unlike other states, Awadh was not annexed through the Doctrine of Lapse but through direct annexation on grounds of internal mismanagement. The Nawab of Awadh, Wajid Ali Shah, was deposed and exiled to Calcutta. This annexation was a major event in British Indian history, contributing to the causes of the 1857 Revolt. Dalhousie's policy reflected British expansionism, prioritizing economic and strategic gains.
qs.kf:
☛ When was Awadh annexed? → 1856
☛ What was the reason for annexation of Awadh? → Alleged misgovernment
☛ Who was the Governor General during Awadh annexation? → Lord Dalhousie
☛ What did Dalhousie call Awadh? → A cherry (ripe fruit)
☛ Where was the Nawab of Awadh exiled? → Calcutta

q: Which of the following Viceroy of India did take initiative to create elected local government bodies?
qs.e: Lord Rippon (1880-1884) was the Viceroy of India who took the initiative to create elected local government bodies. In 1882, he passed a resolution recommending the inclusion of elected members in municipal and district boards. He is regarded as the father of local self-government in India. The resolution gave local bodies more powers and the right to levy taxes. Lord Rippon's step aimed to give Indians participation in administration and teach them responsibility. This reform laid the foundation for democratic institutions during British rule.
qs.kf:
☛ Who is known as the father of local self-government in India? → Lord Rippon
☛ When did Lord Rippon introduce elected members in local bodies? → 1882
☛ Which important resolution was passed during Lord Rippon's tenure? → Local Self-Government Resolution 1882
☛ Which Viceroy after Lord Rippon furthered local self-government? → Lord Dufferin
☛ For which administrative reform is Lord Rippon known? → Development of local self-government

qs.e: In 1915, a committee was appointed to examine the co-operative movement in India under the chairmanship of Sir Edward Maclagan. Based on its recommendations, the Indian Co-operative Societies Act was passed in 1919, providing a legal framework for registration and management of co-operatives. Sir Edward Maclagan was a British civil servant who later served as Governor of Punjab. His committee played a key role in strengthening the co-operative movement in India.

q: The Red Shirt Movement, also known as Khudai Khidmatgar, was led by which Indian freedom fighter in the North-West Frontier Province?
qs.e: Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan, also known as 'Frontier Gandhi' or 'Bacha Khan', led the Khudai Khidmatgar (Red Shirt) movement in the North-West Frontier Province (now Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan). q: When was the designation of the Governor General in India promoted as a Viceroy or Crown's representative?

The Act gave the Governor General the title of Viceroy, representing the British sovereign in India. The first Viceroy was Lord Canning, who had been Governor General since 1856 and became Viceroy in 1858. This Act was passed after the Revolt of 1857, which exposed the weaknesses of Company rule.

q: Who was the Governor General of India between 1848 and 1856?
qs.e: Lord Dalhousie served as Governor General of India from 1848 to 1856. He is famous for the 'Doctrine of Lapse', under which states like Satara, Jhansi, and Nagpur were annexed. He introduced modern infrastructure such as railways, telegraph, and postal system. During his tenure, the Second Anglo-Sikh War (1848-49) and the Second Burma War (1852) took place. He also passed the Widow Remarriage Act (1856). Other options: Lord William Bentinck (1828-35), Lord Minto (1807-13), and Lord Warren Hastings (1772-85) were not in office during this period.

☛ What was Lord Dalhousie's tenure? → 1848-1856

q: Who among the following viceroys announced the vague offer of 'Dominion Status' for India in 1929?
qs.e: Lord Irwin (1926-1931) issued a statement in October 1929 vaguely promising Dominion Status for India. This offer followed the failure of the Simon Commission (1928), which was boycotted by the Indian National Congress. Lord Irwin declared that the British government aimed to grant Dominion Status to India, but without any timeline or clarity. The Congress rejected this offer and demanded complete independence (Purna Swaraj). Lord Irwin's move is seen as a political gamble by the British government to pacify Indian leaders. Lord Cornwallis (1786-1793) introduced the Permanent Settlement, Lord Canning (1856-1862) implemented the Government of India Act 1858, and Lord Ripon (1880-1884) introduced local self-government reforms.
qs.kf:
☛ Who made the vague offer of Dominion Status? → Lord Irwin
☛ When did the Simon Commission visit India? → 1928
☛ What was Lord Irwin's tenure? → 1926-1931
☛ When was the vague Dominion Status offer made? → October 1929
☛ Who succeeded Lord Irwin as Viceroy? → Lord Willingdon

q: The Doctrine of Lapse was implemented by which Governor General ?
qs.e: The Doctrine of Lapse was implemented by Lord Dalhousie, who served as Governor General of India from 1848 to 1856. Under this policy, any princely state without a natural heir was annexed by the British East India Company. Dalhousie applied this doctrine to annex several states, including Satara (1848), Sambalpur (1849), Jhansi (1853), and Nagpur (1854). The policy caused widespread resentment among Indian rulers and is considered a major cause of the Revolt of 1857.
qs.kf:
☛ Who implemented the Doctrine of Lapse? → Lord Dalhousie
☛ When was Dalhousie Governor General? → 1848-1856
☛ First state annexed under Doctrine of Lapse? → Satara (1848)

☛ Which revolt was fueled by the Doctrine of Lapse? → Revolt of 1857

q: Which British Viceroy described the Congress as representing only a 'microscopic minority' of the Indian population, thereby dismissing its political relevance?
qs.e: Lord Dufferin (1884-1888) described the Indian National Congress as representing only a 'microscopic minority' of the Indian population, thereby dismissing its political relevance. This statement came shortly after the Congress's formation in 1885. Dufferin believed that the Congress represented only a small class of educated Indians, while the majority of Indians were rural and illiterate. He considered Congress's demands impractical and was not ready for democratic representation under British rule. This remark highlighted the early tension between the Congress and the British government. Significant events during Dufferin's tenure include the Third Anglo-Burmese War (1885) and the founding of the Indian National Congress (1885).

q: Who was the Viceroy when the Royal Commission on Civil Services was formed in 1912?
qs.e: In 1912, the British government formed a Royal Commission on the Indian Civil Services, known as the Islington Commission, to review recruitment, salaries, and service conditions. At that time, the Viceroy of India was Lord Hardinge (1910-1916). During his tenure, the Delhi Durbar of 1911 was held and the capital was shifted from Calcutta to Delhi. Lord Hardinge succeeded Lord Minto and was followed by Lord Chelmsford. The commission was chaired by Lord Islington.

q: The Cornwallis Code, introduced in 1793, is known for _______.
o: establishing uniform police and judiciary reforms
introducing English as the court language
qs.e: The Cornwallis Code, introduced in 1793 by Lord Cornwallis, brought uniformity to the police and judicial system in India. It appointed magistrates as police superintendents and clarified the hierarchy of courts. Civil and criminal justice were separated. The Sadar Diwani Adalat and Sadar Nizamat Adalat were made the apex courts. At the district level, criminal and civil courts were established. Kotwals and darogas were appointed to control the police. This code did not abolish the zamindari system; instead, it was implemented under the Permanent Settlement. It did not promote native Indians in the judiciary, nor did it introduce English as the court language.
qs.kf:
☛ What was the primary objective of the Cornwallis Code? → To bring uniformity in police and judiciary reforms
☛ The Sadar Diwani Adalat dealt with which type of cases? → Civil appeals
☛ The Sadar Nizamat Adalat dealt with which type of cases? → Criminal appeals
☛ Under which system did Cornwallis implement the zamindari system? → Permanent Settlement
☛ Who were the top police officers under the Cornwallis Code? → Magistrates

q: Who was the first Indian Governor General of Independent India?
qs.e: The first Indian Governor General of Independent India was C. Rajagopalachari, who assumed office on 21 June 1948. He was also the last Governor General of India, as India became a republic on 26 January 1950. Rajagopalachari was a freedom fighter, statesman, and writer. He also served as the Chief Minister of Madras Province. Before becoming Governor General, he was India's first Home Minister. He was awarded the Bharat Ratna in 1954. qs.e: India gained independence on 15 August 1947, but until then the country was led by British Governors General. After independence, Lord Mountbatten was appointed as the first Governor General of independent India from 15 August 1947 to 21 June 1948. His main task was to handle the partition and the transitional period after independence. Later, C. Rajagopalachari became the second and last Governor General on 21 June 1948. q: Consider the following statements.
1. Lord Mayo’s Resolution of 1870 on financial decentralization visualized the development of local self-government institutions.
2. Hobhouse was the Chairman of the Royal Commission on Decentralization.
3. Under the Government of India Act of 1919, local self-government became a reserved subject. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
qs.e: Lord Mayo's Resolution of 1870 on financial decentralization laid the foundation for the development of local self-government institutions in India. Hobhouse chaired the Royal Commission on Decentralization (1907), which recommended devolution of powers to provinces. Under the Government of India Act of 1919, local self-government was made a transferred subject, not a reserved subject. Reserved subjects (e.g., defence, foreign affairs) remained under the Governor-General's control. Thus, statements 1 and 2 are correct, while statement 3 is incorrect.
qs.kf:

☛ Who chaired the Royal Commission on Decentralization? → Hobhouse
☛ Under the 1919 Act, local self-government was which type of subject? → Transferred subject
☛ Reserved subjects under the 1919 Act were controlled by whom? → Governor-General
☛ Which resolution laid the foundation of local self-government in India? → Lord Mayo's Resolution of 1870
