q: Who was the leader of "Eka Movement" of Uttar Pradesh?
qs.e: The Eka Movement (1921-22) was a major peasant movement in the Awadh region of Uttar Pradesh. It was led by Madari Pasi, a lower-caste peasant leader. The main objective was to protest against high land revenue, forced labor (begar), and oppression by landlords. Peasants took an oath not to pay revenue, not to perform begar, and to disrespect zamindars. The movement also had support from some nationalist leaders like Baba Ramchandra. Under Madari Pasi's leadership, the movement remained non-violent yet effective. Later, government repression and arrests of leaders weakened the movement.
qs.kf:
☛ When did the Eka Movement occur? → 1921-22
☛ What was the main aim of the Eka Movement? → Struggle against high revenue and begar
☛ Which region is associated with the Eka Movement? → Awadh, Uttar Pradesh
☛ What is the meaning of 'Eka'? → Unity
☛ Which newspaper supported the Eka Movement? → Pratap

q: Where was Dadabhai Naoroji appointed as Professor of Mathematics and Physics?
A. Presidency College, Chennai
B. Presidency College, Kolkata
C. St. Xavier's College, Mumbai
D. Elphinstone College, Mumbai
qs.e: Dadabhai Naoroji was a prominent Indian intellectual, economist, and politician. He was a professor of Mathematics and Physics and was appointed as a professor at Elphinstone College, Mumbai in 1856. He was one of the first Indian professors at the University of Bombay. Naoroji later became the first Indian to be elected to the British Parliament and played a key role in the Indian nationalist movement. He is regarded as the father of economic nationalism and is known for his Drain Theory, which criticized the economic exploitation of India by the British.
qs.kf:
☛ Where was Dadabhai Naoroji appointed as Professor of Mathematics and Physics? → Elphinstone College, Mumbai
☛ What theory is Dadabhai Naoroji famous for? → Drain Theory
☛ From which constituency was Dadabhai Naoroji elected to the British Parliament? → Finsbury Central, London
☛ When was Dadabhai Naoroji born? → 1825
☛ Of which movement was Dadabhai Naoroji a founding member? → Indian National Congress

q: Which of the following banks was established in India at Calcutta under European Management (in 1770)?
qs.e: Bank of Hindustan was the first bank in India, established in 1770 in Calcutta (now Kolkata) under European management. It was founded by employees of the British East India Company. This bank ceased operations in 1832. Later, banks like Bank of Bengal (1809) and Bank of Bombay (1840) were established. Indus Bank of India and National Bank of India were founded later. Bank of India was established in 1906. Therefore, the bank established in 1770 in Calcutta is Bank of Hindustan.
qs.kf:
☛ Which was the first bank in India? → Bank of Hindustan (1770)
☛ Which is the oldest joint stock bank in India? → Bank of Bengal (1809)
☛ Where was Bank of Hindustan established? → Calcutta
☛ When did Bank of Hindustan close? → 1832
☛ Which was the first bank under European management in India? → Bank of Hindustan

q: Name the person who was appointed as the first Surveyor General of India in 1815.
qs.e: Colin Mackenzie was appointed as the first Surveyor General of India in 1815. He was a British army officer and orientalist who conducted extensive surveys and mapping of India. He documented numerous temples and monuments in South India and assembled the Mackenzie Collection, a significant archive of manuscripts. His work was foundational for the development of geographical knowledge in British India.
qs.kf:
☛ First Surveyor General of India → Colin Mackenzie (1815)
☛ Mackenzie Collection → Archive of Indian manuscripts and antiquities
☛ Establishment of Survey of India → 1767
☛ Great Trigonometrical Survey → William Lambton
☛ Modern mapping of India → Initiated by James Rennell

q: What among the following is the Primary purpose of The Chipko Andolan?
qs.e: The Chipko Andolan started in 1973 in the Chamoli district of Uttarakhand (then part of Uttar Pradesh). Its primary objective was to protect trees and forests from deforestation. Villagers, especially women, hugged trees to prevent them from being cut down, giving the movement its name 'Chipko' (to hug). The movement was led by activists like Sunderlal Bahuguna and Chandi Prasad Bhatt. It later became a global symbol for environmental conservation. Other options like conserving water, preventing global warming, or saving the Earth were not the primary aims but indirect benefits.
qs.kf:
☛ When did Chipko Andolan start? → 1973
☛ Who was the main leader of Chipko Andolan? → Sunderlal Bahuguna
☛ Where did Chipko Andolan take place? → Uttarakhand (Chamoli)
☛ What was the role of women in Chipko? → Hugging trees to protest
☛ What was the main aim of Chipko? → Forest conservation

q: Who coined the slogan “Jai Jawan Jai Kisan"?
qs.e: The slogan ‘Jai Jawan Jai Kisan’ was coined by India's second Prime Minister Lal Bahadur Shastri in 1965. He gave this slogan to boost the morale of soldiers and farmers during the India-Pakistan war. Shastri ji united the two key pillars of the nation – defence and agriculture – through this slogan. He was a freedom fighter and a symbol of simplicity. He was born on 2 October 1904 and died on 11 January 1966 in Tashkent after the Tashkent Agreement.
qs.kf:
☛ Who gave the slogan ‘Jai Jawan Jai Kisan’? → Lal Bahadur Shastri
☛ Which number Prime Minister of India was Lal Bahadur Shastri? → Second
☛ When was Lal Bahadur Shastri born? → 2 October 1904
☛ Where did Lal Bahadur Shastri die? → Tashkent
☛ Who was the Prime Minister of India during the 1965 India-Pak war? → Lal Bahadur Shastri

q: In which year was the Railway introduced by the British in India for passengers?
qs.e: The first passenger train in India ran between Mumbai and Thane on 16 April 1853. It was inaugurated during the tenure of Governor General Lord Dalhousie. The train covered a distance of 34 kilometers and was pulled by three engines named Sahib, Sindh, and Sultan. This marked the beginning of Indian Railways under British colonial rule, laying the foundation for modern transport in India. Over time, the network expanded to connect major cities and regions.
qs.kf:
☛ When did the first passenger train run in India? → 16 April 1853
☛ From which city did the first train start? → Mumbai
☛ What was the destination of the first train? → Thane
☛ Under which Governor General was the railway introduced? → Lord Dalhousie
☛ How many engines were used in the first train? → Three (Sahib, Sindh, Sultan)

q: Which structure was built as a war memorial to soldiers of the undivided Indian Army during the First World War?
o: Lahori Gate in the Red Fort
qs.e: India Gate is a war memorial located in Delhi, built to commemorate about 70,000 soldiers of the undivided Indian Army who died during the First World War (1914-1918). Designed by Edwin Lutyens, it was inaugurated in 1931. The memorial is made of red sandstone and stands 42 meters tall. After independence, the Amar Jawan Jyoti (Flame of the Immortal Soldier) was added beneath the arch.
qs.kf:
☛ Who designed India Gate? → Edwin Lutyens
☛ When was India Gate inaugurated? → 1931
☛ Which war is India Gate a memorial of? → World War I
☛ What flame is added at India Gate? → Amar Jawan Jyoti
☛ What material is India Gate made of? → Red sandstone

q: Which of the following methods did Holt Mackenzie develop for collecting revenue in India?
qs.e: Holt Mackenzie, a British official in India, developed the Mahalwari system for revenue collection. This system was implemented in the North-Western Provinces (modern-day Uttar Pradesh). In this system, the village or "mahal" (a group of one or more villages) was considered the revenue unit. The revenue was assessed based on the crop yield and quality of land, and it was periodically revised. The responsibility of revenue collection was given to zamindars or village heads. This system was introduced in 1822 and later revised in 1833. It was a middle path between the Permanent Settlement and the Ryotwari system.
qs.kf:
☛ Who is considered the father of the Mahalwari system? → Holt Mackenzie
☛ In which region was the Mahalwari system implemented? → North-Western Provinces
☛ What was the revenue unit in the Mahalwari system? → Mahal (village or group of villages)
☛ In which year was the Mahalwari system introduced? → 1822
☛ In which year was the Mahalwari system revised? → 1833

q: Which of the following is considered as the first Vernacular newspaper of India?
qs.e: India's first vernacular newspaper is considered to be Samachar Darpan. It was first published on 23 May 1818 from Kolkata. It was started by John Clark Marshman, a Baptist missionary. The newspaper was published in Bengali language. Madras Courier was the first English newspaper in India, while Bengal Gazette (Hickey's Gazette) was the first English newspaper in India. Samachar Darpan pioneered the use of local languages in Indian journalism.
qs.kf:
☛ India's first newspaper → Bengal Gazette (Hickey's Gazette) 1780
☛ India's first vernacular newspaper → Samachar Darpan 1818
☛ Publisher → John Clark Marshman
☛ Language → Bengali
☛ Place → Kolkata

q: Who was the founder of the News paper Bengal Gazette (1780 - India's first News paper?
qs.e: India's first newspaper, the Bengal Gazette (also known as Hicky's Bengal Gazette), was first published on January 29, 1780 in Kolkata. Its founder was James Augustus Hicky (J.K. Hicky), an Irish journalist. It was a weekly English-language paper that criticized officials of the British East India Company. As a result, the company tried to suppress it and eventually shut it down in 1782. Hicky was also imprisoned. This newspaper is considered the foundation of Indian journalism.
qs.kf:
☛ First newspaper of India → Bengal Gazette (1780)
☛ Founder of Bengal Gazette → J.K. Hicky
☛ Language of Bengal Gazette → English
☛ Place of publication of Bengal Gazette → Kolkata
☛ Type of Bengal Gazette → Weekly

q: In which Indian city was the first successful Cotton mill set up?
qs.e: India's first successful cotton mill was set up in Mumbai in 1854. It was named Bombay Spinning and Weaving Company. The mill was established by Cowasji Nanabhai Davar. This mill marked the beginning of the industrial revolution in India. The easy availability of cotton and port facilities in Mumbai contributed to its success. Later, Mumbai became the center of the textile industry.
qs.kf:
☛ First successful cotton mill established → 1854, Mumbai
☛ Name of the first successful cotton mill → Bombay Spinning and Weaving Company
☛ Founder → Cowasji Nanabhai Davar
☛ First jute mill in India established → 1855, Howrah (Bengal)
☛ First railway locomotive factory in India → Chittaranjan (1950)

q: Who was known as "Liberator of Indian Press"?
qs.e: Charles Metcalfe is known as the 'Liberator of the Indian Press'. In 1835, he passed the Press Ordinance which abolished censorship and licensing restrictions on the Indian press. Prior to this, the Adams Press Ordinance of 1823 had severely curtailed press freedom. Metcalfe's step gave new direction to Indian journalism and made him a symbol of liberal ideas. He served as Governor-General of India from 1835 to 1838.
qs.kf:
☛ Liberator of Indian Press → Charles Metcalfe
☛ Press Ordinance of 1835 → Passed by Charles Metcalfe
☛ Adams Press Ordinance → Enacted in 1823
☛ Governor-General who removed press censorship → Charles Metcalfe
☛ Charles Metcalfe's tenure → 1835-1838

q: The Journal started by William Jones is
qs.e: Sir William Jones was a renowned British scholar and orientalist. In 1784 CE, he founded the Asiatic Society in Kolkata. The society launched a journal called Asiatick Researches (Asiatic Research) as its official publication. This journal gained fame for publishing research on Asian history, culture, languages, and civilization. William Jones deeply studied ancient languages like Sanskrit and Persian and introduced Indian knowledge to the Western world. His contributions are considered the foundation of modern Indian historiography.
qs.kf:
☛ Which society did William Jones establish? → Asiatic Society
☛ When was the Asiatic Society founded? → 1784 CE
☛ Where is the Asiatic Society located? → Kolkata
☛ Which languages was William Jones expert in? → Sanskrit and Persian
☛ With which society is the Asiatic Research journal associated? → Asiatic Society

q: Who is the founder of the service committee?
qs.e: Hridaynath Kunjru was a renowned Indian social worker and educationist. He founded the Service Committee (Seva Samiti) in 1912, which is a non-governmental organization aimed at serving the underprivileged sections of society and providing assistance in education, health, and disaster relief. Kunjru studied at the University of Allahabad and later served as a member of the National Education Commission. He was awarded the Padma Vibhushan for his contributions to social work.
qs.kf:
☛ Founder of Service Committee → Hridaynath Kunjru
☛ Establishment year of Service Committee → 1912
☛ Award received by Hridaynath Kunjru → Padma Vibhushan
☛ Headquarters of Service Committee → Allahabad
☛ Objective of Service Committee → Social service and disaster relief

q: Which of the following statements best describes India’s foreign trade during the colonial period?
o: India’s trade was largely controlled by Britain, with limited trade with other nations like Sri Lanka, China and Iran.
India’s foreign trade greatly benefited the economy and eliminated shortages of essential goods.
India imported raw materials and exported finished goods.
India primarily traded with European nations other than Britain.
qs.e: During the colonial period, Britain had complete control over India's foreign trade. India exported raw materials like cotton, jute, tea, and indigo to Britain, while importing finished goods from Britain. This trade was structured to benefit British interests and harmed the Indian economy. Trade with other nations such as Sri Lanka, China, and Iran was limited and also under British control. India faced a trade deficit and shortages of essential goods. Thus, option 1 correctly describes British dominance and limited trade with other countries.
qs.kf:
☛ Control of colonial trade → by Britain
☛ Major exports of India → raw materials (cotton, jute, tea)
☛ Major imports of India → finished goods from Britain
☛ Impact on economy → harmed Indian economy
☛ Limited trade partners → Sri Lanka, China, Iran

q: What was the impact of the British land revenue system on Indian agriculture?
o: Reduced the burden of taxes on farmers
Created a class of landlords who exploited peasants
qs.e: The British land revenue system, such as the Permanent Settlement (1793) and the Ryotwari system, deeply impacted Indian agriculture negatively. It created a new class of zamindars or landlords who were only responsible for revenue collection. These zamindars extracted excessive rents from peasants, leading to widespread indebtedness. In the Permanent Settlement, the revenue was fixed, but zamindars were given extensive powers, enabling them to exploit peasants. In the Ryotwari system, the government collected taxes directly from the cultivator, but the burden was so high that peasants lived in poverty. This system hampered agricultural productivity and promoted commercialization of land, where cash crops replaced food crops. Consequently, peasants were exploited and agriculture remained underdeveloped.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Permanent Settlement introduced? → 1793
☛ Which areas were under the Ryotwari system? → Madras and Bombay
☛ What was the main objective of British land revenue system? → Revenue collection
☛ In which system did peasants pay tax directly to the government? → Ryotwari
☛ What was the impact of British policy on Indian agriculture? → Exploitation of peasants

q: The extremists believed that economic self-reliance was necessary to:
qs.e: The extremist leaders like Lala Lajpat Rai, Bal Gangadhar Tilak, and Bipin Chandra Pal believed that the main cause of India's economic misery was British exploitation. They considered economic self-reliance as an integral part of the Swadeshi Movement, which started in 1905 in protest against the Partition of Bengal. Their goal was to challenge British economic control by boycotting foreign goods and promoting indigenous industries. Thus, the aim of economic self-reliance was to fight British exploitation, not to increase taxes or boost exports. This was a key ideology of the extremist phase of the Indian national movement.
qs.kf:
☛ When did the Swadeshi Movement start? → 1905
☛ Who were the extremist leaders? → Lala Lajpat Rai, Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal
☛ When did the Partition of Bengal occur? → 1905
☛ What was the main objective of economic self-reliance? → Fight British exploitation
☛ What was the slogan of the extremists? → Swaraj

q: Which industry was the most prominent in India before the British rule, though it had significant regional variations?
qs.e: Before British rule, the cotton textile industry was the most prominent in India. Indian cotton fabrics, such as muslin and calico, were renowned worldwide. This industry flourished with regional variations —Bengal was famous for muslin, Gujarat for silk and cotton cloth, and South India for high-quality textiles under the Cholas. Merchants exported these fabrics to Persia, Europe, and Southeast Asia. Other industries like tea and coffee plantations, sugar mills, and mining existed in the pre-British era, but they were not as widespread or economically influential as cotton textiles. Before industrialization, textile manufacturing was the backbone of India's economy.
qs.kf:
☛ Major textile center of ancient India → Bengal
☛ Famous place for Indian muslin → Dhaka
☛ Major export hub for cotton textiles → Gujarat
☛ Chola period famous textiles → South Indian cotton
☛ Industry harmed by British policies → Cotton textiles

q: How did the drain of wealth theory, as proposed by Dadabhai Naoroji, explain India’s poverty under British rule?
o: Export of Indian resources and wealth to Britain without fair compensation
qs.e: Dadabhai Naoroji, through his 'Drain of Wealth' theory, explained that India's poverty under British rule was due to the continuous and unjust transfer of wealth from India to Britain. According to Naoroji, Britain exported Indian resources, raw materials, and goods without providing fair compensation, leading to the impoverishment of India. British policies deliberately deindustrialized India, turning it into a supplier of raw materials and a market for British manufactured goods. Naoroji detailed this theory in his book 'Poverty and Un-British Rule in India' (1901). The drain included salaries of British officials, home charges, and profits of British companies. This theory became the economic foundation of the Indian national movement.
qs.kf:
☛ Dadabhai Naoroji is known as the 'Grand Old Man of India' → He also served as President of the Indian National Congress.
☛ Naoroji's book 'Poverty and Un-British Rule in India' → Published in 1901.
☛ According to the Drain of Wealth theory → India's surplus was transferred to Britain.
☛ Naoroji called British rule 'un-British' → Because it was against Indian interests.
☛ This theory provided an economic argument for the Indian freedom struggle → It became a key foundation of the movement.

q: Under the British Colonial rule, what accounted for most of India’s exports by the 1850s?
o: Raw materials like raw cotton, opium and indigo
Processed goods like fine cotton and silk
qs.e: Under British colonial rule, by the 1850s, most of India's exports consisted of raw materials like raw cotton, opium, and indigo. Britain needed cheap raw materials for its Industrial Revolution. India's traditional handicraft and textile industries were deliberately destroyed, and India became a supplier of raw materials and a market for British manufactured goods. The export of raw cotton fed British textile mills, opium was smuggled into China to balance trade, and indigo was used as a dye. This policy led to a trade surplus for India but drained its wealth and stunted industrial growth.
qs.kf:
☛ Major exports of India by 1850s → Raw cotton, opium, indigo
☛ British colonial trade policy aim → India as source of raw materials and market for finished goods
☛ Opium export from India used for → Smuggling into China to finance British tea imports
☛ Indigo export importance → Dye for British textile industry
☛ Impact of raw material exports → Deindustrialization and economic exploitation of India

q: Which of the following statements accurately describes the land revenue systems implemented by the British in India and their impact on agriculture?
o: The Zamindari system, covering the majority of land, provided incentives for cultivators to invest in their farms.
The Zamindari system focused on high revenue collection by zamindars, leaving cultivators with little to reinvest in agriculture.
In the Mahalwari system, land was held by individual cultivators who had autonomy over their land management.
The Ryotwari and Mahalwari systems covered 4% and 38% of the land, respectively, and provided some development for improving land fertility.
qs.e: During British rule, three major land revenue systems were implemented: Zamindari (1793), Ryotwari (1820), and Mahalwari (1822). In the Zamindari system, zamindars were granted revenue collection rights, but they often extracted excessive taxes from peasants. This left cultivators with little surplus to reinvest in agriculture, leading to stagnation in productivity and high indebtedness. The Ryotwari system taxed individual cultivators directly, while Mahalwari made the village collectively responsible. Both systems introduced some improvements like irrigation, but the tax burden remained heavy. The Zamindari system, covering about 57% of British India, particularly discouraged investment as zamindars had no incentive to improve land they did not own, worsening rural poverty.
qs.kf:
☛ First permanent land revenue system in India → Permanent Settlement (1793)
☛ Role of zamindars → Revenue collectors, not landowners
☛ Regions under Ryotwari system → Madras, Bombay, Assam
☛ Revenue unit in Mahalwari system → Village (mahal)
☛ Worst impact of land revenue systems → Lack of agricultural capital and decline in output

q: Which of the following Governor Generals of British India introduced the Permanent Settlement of Land Revenue in 1793?
qs.e: The Permanent Settlement was introduced in 1793 by Lord Cornwallis. It was implemented in Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa. This system granted zamindars the right to collect land revenue. The revenue rate was fixed permanently, ensuring a regular income for the Company. Zamindars were recognized as landowners, while peasants became tenants. The policy aimed to promote agricultural development and improve revenue management, but it led to increased exploitation of peasants. Cornwallis is also considered the father of the civil service in India.
qs.kf:
☛ Another name for Permanent Settlement → Zamindari System
☛ When was Permanent Settlement introduced → 1793
☛ Where was Permanent Settlement implemented → Bengal, Bihar, Orissa
☛ Beneficiaries of Permanent Settlement → Zamindars
☛ Other reforms by Lord Cornwallis → Civil service, judicial reforms

q: Tilak believed that political rights could only be achieved through:
qs.e: Bal Gangadhar Tilak, popularly known as 'Lokmanya', was a prominent leader of the Indian freedom movement. He believed that political rights could only be achieved through courageous action and strong pressure against the British rule. Tilak advocated for aggressive nationalism and emphasized mass mobilization and resistance. He coined the famous slogan 'Swaraj is my birthright' and launched the Home Rule Movement in 1916. He opposed the policy of negotiation or compromise and considered direct action essential. Tilak was also a journalist and ran two newspapers, Kesari (Marathi) and Maratha (English), to spread nationalist ideas. His leadership greatly influenced the radical wing of the Indian National Congress.
qs.kf:
☛ What is Tilak popularly known as? → Lokmanya
☛ What was Tilak's famous slogan? → 'Swaraj is my birthright'
☛ Which movement was started by Tilak? → Home Rule Movement (1916)
☛ Which newspapers were run by Tilak? → Kesari (Marathi) and Maratha (English)
☛ What was Tilak's political philosophy based on? → Aggressive nationalism and direct action

q: What was the primary focus of the economic policies adopted by the colonial government in India?
o: Security and promotion of the economic interests of Britain
Estimating national and per capita income accurately
Development of agriculture and local industries
qs.e: The colonial economic policies were entirely focused on protecting and promoting Britain's economic interests. India was turned into a source of raw materials and a market for British manufactured goods. Import duties were kept zero or minimal for British goods, while heavy duties were imposed on Indian goods. Indian industries were deliberately destroyed. British companies were given control over land and resources. Wealth drain (Drain Theory) from India to Britain was a key feature. Agriculture was commercialized to supply British industries, not for Indian farmers' benefit.
qs.kf:
☛ Main objective of British economic policy → Protection of Britain's economic interests
☛ Proponent of Drain Theory → Dadabhai Naoroji
☛ Transfer of wealth from India to Britain is called → Economic drain
☛ India's trade surplus during British rule → Was sent to Britain
☛ Cause of decline of Indian industries → British industrial policy

q: Which of the following British officials found India as an uncivilised country and had to be civilised, following which the English Education Act of 1835 was introduced?
qs.e: Thomas Babington Macaulay sharply criticized Indian culture and civilization, calling India an 'uncivilised' country. His efforts led to the English Education Act of 1835, which established Western education in India. Macaulay's objective was to create 'a class who may be interpreters between us and the millions whom we govern—a class of persons Indian in blood and colour, but English in taste, in opinions, in morals, and in intellect.' The Act made English the medium of instruction and neglected oriental education. Macaulay's Minute (1835) laid the foundation of Indian education policy. This act was passed under Governor-General Lord William Bentinck and significantly shaped the British education system in India.
qs.kf:
☛ Who introduced the English Education Act of 1835? → Thomas Macaulay
☛ When were Macaulay's Minutes presented? → 1835
☛ What was Macaulay's view on India? → Considered India uncivilised and backward
☛ What was the main objective of the English Education Act? → To make English the medium of education
☛ Who were the pioneers of Western education in India? → Lord William Bentinck (Governor-General) and Thomas Macaulay

q: In which of the following regions did Rani Avantibai Lodhi of Ramgarh raise and lead an army of four thousand against the British, who had taken over the administration of her state?
qs.e: Rani Avantibai Lodhi was the queen of Ramgarh, located in the Mandla district of present-day Madhya Pradesh. During the 1857 rebellion, when the British took over the administration of her state, she raised an army of four thousand soldiers and led them against the British. She was a brave warrior who fiercely fought the British in the Mandla region. Eventually, when surrounded by British forces, she chose to commit suicide rather than surrender. This region is now part of Madhya Pradesh.
qs.kf:
☛ Rani Avantibai was the queen of which state? → Ramgarh (Madhya Pradesh)
☛ Which rebellion is Rani Avantibai associated with? → 1857 First War of Independence
☛ How many soldiers did Rani Avantibai raise? → 4000
☛ How did Rani Avantibai die? → Suicide (when surrounded by British)
☛ Ramgarh is located in which state? → Madhya Pradesh

q: The Faraizi Movement's no-tax campaign primarily targeted the ________.
qs.e: The Faraizi Movement's no-tax campaign primarily targeted indigo planters and zamindars. This movement was started by Haji Shariatullah in the first half of the 19th century in East Bengal. Its aim was to free peasants from oppression and unjust taxes imposed by indigo planters and zamindars. The movement also emphasized Islamic reform and gained widespread support in rural Bengal. Later, Dadu Mian (Shariatullah's son) took over the leadership and further strengthened it. The Faraizi Movement is considered an important peasant-reform movement in India's freedom struggle.
qs.kf:
☛ Founder of Faraizi Movement → Haji Shariatullah
☛ Main region of Faraizi Movement → East Bengal
☛ Main objective of Faraizi Movement → Islamic reform and anti-oppression
☛ Second leader of Faraizi Movement → Dadu Mian
☛ Meaning of Faraizi → One who follows the farz (compulsory duties) of Islam

q: The names of Dora Bisoi and Chakra Bisoi are associated with the uprising against political unrest, the unsuitability of British laws and regulations and the economic suffering of the Khonds in ______.
qs.e: Dora Bisoi and Chakra Bisoi were leaders of the Khond tribe who led an uprising in the Ghumusar region (present-day Odisha) against British rule. The revolt lasted from 1835 to 1856, primarily due to the unsuitability of British laws, political unrest, and the economic suffering of the Khonds. The Khonds were losing their agricultural land and forest resources, while the British administration ignored their traditions. This revolt holds an important place in the tribal resistance movements of Odisha.
qs.kf:
☛ Which uprising is associated with Dora Bisoi and Chakra Bisoi? → Ghumusar revolt (Odisha)
☛ Which is the main habitat of the Khond tribe? → Hilly regions of Odisha
☛ What was the time period of the Ghumusar revolt? → 1835-1856
☛ Who were the main leaders of the Khonds? → Dora Bisoi and Chakra Bisoi
☛ What was the cause of the Khond revolt? → Unsuitability of British laws and economic exploitation

q: The main objective of British economic policies in India was to:
qs.e: The main objective of British economic policies in India was to turn India into a source of raw materials and a market for finished goods for Britain. Under this policy, raw materials like cotton, indigo, and tea were exported from India at cheap prices, while finished textiles and industrial products from Britain were sold in India. This policy destroyed Indian industries, especially the handloom industry. British officials exploited India economically through land revenue systems and trade policies. This policy was contrary to Indian self-sufficiency and industrialisation. It ensured that India remained a supplier of raw materials and a consumer of British manufactured goods, thereby strengthening the British economy at the cost of India's economic development.
qs.kf:
☛ Main objective of British economic policy → Benefit British economy
☛ Major raw materials exported from India → Cotton, indigo, tea
☛ Indian industry most affected by British policies → Handloom industry
☛ Primary aim of British land revenue system → Revenue extraction and economic exploitation
☛ Impact of British trade policy → Decline of Indian industries and benefit to Britain

q: Which British policy promoted English education to create a loyal class serving British interests in India?
qs.e: The British government adopted the 'Education Policy' to promote English education in India, aiming to create a loyal and educated class that would assist in British administration. This policy was primarily based on Macaulay's Minute (1835), which prioritized Western education over traditional Indian learning. By providing education in English, the British planned to develop a 'middle class' loyal to British interests. This class was intended to strengthen British rule and spread British values in Indian society. Other options like 'Subsidiary Alliance' and 'Divide and Rule' were political policies, while 'Trade Policy' was related to economic objectives.
qs.kf:
☛ What was the main objective of Macaulay's Minute (1835)? → To promote English education and create a loyal class in India
☛ Which language was prioritized under British education policy? → English
☛ What type of class did the education policy aim to create? → Middle class
☛ What is 'Subsidiary Alliance' associated with? → Treaties with Indian princely states
☛ What was the purpose of 'Divide and Rule'? → To promote Hindu-Muslim division

q: What was the main motive of British colonial rule in India?
qs.e: The main motive of British colonial rule in India was economic exploitation. The British extracted raw materials from India and sold finished goods in Indian markets, destroying local industries. Through land revenue systems and heavy taxation, they impoverished farmers. India was turned into a market for British goods and a source of cheap raw materials. Social development, industrialisation, or welfare of farmers were never the real objectives.
qs.kf:
☛ Primary objective of British rule → Economic exploitation
☛ India's exports under British rule → Raw materials
☛ Imports into India → Finished goods
☛ Impact of land revenue system → Impoverishment of peasants
☛ Role of India in British empire → Market and source of raw materials

q: In the context of British plantations in India, what does the term ‘bigha’ refer to?
o: A unit of measurement of land
A plant that replaced indigo in Britain
An agreement made with the ryots
A revenue estate which has one or more villages
qs.e: In the context of British plantations in India, the term 'bigha' refers to a traditional unit of land measurement that varied across different regions of India. It was used during the Mughal and British periods for measuring agricultural land and determining revenue. The size of a bigha ranged from approximately 0.33 to 1 acre depending on the region. During British rule, it was used to measure land area for plantations such as indigo, tea, and coffee. This term does not refer to a plant, an agreement, or a revenue estate; it is strictly a unit of land measurement.
qs.kf:

☛ During the British period, what was the bigha used for? → Measuring land for plantations
☛ How many acres is one bigha approximately equal to? → 0.33 to 1 acre
☛ From which period has the term been in use? → Mughal period
☛ Is bigha an agreement or estate? → No, it is a land measurement unit

q: Who among the following strongly criticised British education for being too Western and disconnected from Indian realities?
qs.e: Rabindranath Tagore strongly criticised the British education system for being purely Western in its approach and disconnected from Indian realities, culture, and traditions. He believed that such education alienated students from their own roots and suppressed creativity and critical thinking. Tagore established an alternative education system at Shantiniketan, which emphasized nature, art, and Indian values. According to him, the purpose of education was not merely to secure jobs but to achieve holistic development of individuals. He opposed the compulsory use of English and the rote-learning method. His critique highlighted the need for an education system that respects local culture and fosters independent thought.
qs.kf:
☛ On what basis did Tagore criticise British education? → For being too Western and disconnected from Indian realities
☛ Which institution did Tagore establish for alternative education? → Shantiniketan
☛ What did Tagore’s education system focus on? → Nature, art, and Indian values
☛ What did Tagore consider the purpose of education? → Holistic development of individuals
☛ Which education method did Tagore oppose? → Rote-learning method

q: Who among the following Mughal rulers is considered to be the last powerful Mughal ruler?
qs.e: The last powerful Mughal ruler is considered to be Aurangzeb (reigned 1658–1707). He expanded the Mughal Empire to its greatest territorial extent, covering almost the entire Indian subcontinent. After his death, the empire declined rapidly due to weak successors and internal revolts. Aurangzeb abandoned the policy of religious tolerance and strictly enforced Islamic laws. He reimposed the jizya tax on non-Muslims and destroyed many Hindu temples, which led to widespread opposition from Marathas, Sikhs, and Rajputs. His prolonged wars in the Deccan drained the empire's resources. Hence, Aurangzeb is regarded as the last effective Mughal emperor.
qs.kf:
☛ Aurangzeb's reign period → 1658–1707
☛ Which tax did Aurangzeb reimpose? → Jizya tax
☛ Where did Aurangzeb die? → Ahmednagar
☛ Major Maratha leader who opposed Aurangzeb → Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj
☛ Aurangzeb's successor → Bahadur Shah I

q: Which system of land tenure prevalent before independence led to exploitation of farmers?
qs.e: The Zamindari system was introduced under the Permanent Settlement Act of 1793 during British rule. It granted ownership rights to zamindars, who collected excessive rent from peasants. This system was a major cause of farmer exploitation because zamindars had to pay a fixed revenue to the government, so they arbitrarily extracted high rents from cultivators. Peasants had no land rights and fell into debt due to high rents, interest, and famines. This system weakened the rural economy and increased social inequality. It was later abolished through land reforms in the 1950s.
qs.kf:
☛ Father of Zamindari system → Lord Cornwallis
☛ Ryotwari system implemented in → Bombay, Madras, Assam
☛ Father of Mahalwari system → Holt Mackenzie
☛ Abolition of Zamindari in India → Under land reforms in 1950s
☛ Cooperative farming is associated with → Five Year Plans

q: Land revenue systems under British rule varied regionally. Which land revenue system was primarily followed in Bombay and Madras Presidencies?
qs.e: Under British rule, land revenue systems varied regionally. The Bombay and Madras Presidencies primarily followed the Ryotwari system. In this system, the government directly collected revenue from the cultivator (ryot). The main proponent was Sir Thomas Munro, who introduced it in 1820. It involved a direct survey of land and issuing individual leases to each farmer. The revenue rate was based on soil fertility and crop type, and could be as high as 50%. This system was mainly applied in South and West India, while the Zamindari system prevailed in North India and the Mahalwari system in Punjab.
qs.kf:
☛ Who introduced the Ryotwari system? → Sir Thomas Munro
☛ In which Presidencies was Ryotwari implemented? → Bombay and Madras
☛ What was the maximum revenue rate in Ryotwari? → Up to 50%
☛ In which system did the government directly collect revenue from peasants? → Ryotwari
☛ Where was the Zamindari system mainly applied? → North India

q: Which Governor General of India Proposed the Vernacular press act in 1878?
qs.e: The Vernacular Press Act of 1878 was enacted during the tenure of Lord Lytton (1876-1880). This act aimed to control the Indian-language newspapers, especially those critical of the British government. It gave district magistrates the power to ban any vernacular newspaper. It was also known as the Gagging Act. The act was later repealed by Lord Ripon in 1882. Lord Lytton also organized the Delhi Durbar (1877) and introduced the Arms Act (1878).
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Vernacular Press Act passed? → 1878
☛ Who repealed it? → Lord Ripon (1882)
☛ What was Lord Lytton's tenure? → 1876-1880
☛ Who held the Delhi Durbar of 1877? → Lord Lytton
☛ Who introduced the Arms Act of 1878? → Lord Lytton

q: Bengal Gazette, the first major newspaper in India, started in the year ______.
qs.e: The Bengal Gazette, also known as Hickey's Bengal Gazette, was the first newspaper in India. It was founded by James Augustus Hickey and first published on 29 January 1780 from Kolkata. It was a weekly newspaper covering news about British rule and Indian affairs. However, due to criticism of the British administration, it was shut down in 1782. It remains a significant milestone in the history of Indian journalism.

☛ What type of newspaper was the Bengal Gazette? → Weekly

☛ Which was the first newspaper in India? → Bengal Gazette

q: Who shot dead Rand, the commissioner of Police, Poona due to failure to-check plagues towards the end of 19th century in India?
qs.e: In 1897, during a plague outbreak in Pune, the British government imposed harsh measures for plague control, including forcibly entering homes, burning belongings, and insulting women. This caused widespread public anger. Police Commissioner Rand became a symbol of these oppressive measures. The Chapekar brothers, especially Damodar Chapekar, assassinated Rand in protest against this tyranny. This event is considered the beginning of the extremist phase of the Indian independence movement. Damodar Chapekar was later executed by hanging.

q: The peasant struggle of the Warli tribe in the year 1945 occurred in which of the following states of India?
qs.e: The peasant struggle of the Warli tribe in 1945 took place in Thane district of Maharashtra. This movement was against the oppression of British rule and landlords. qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (10/06/2025) Shift 3
q: The British used education as a tool to ______.
qs.e: The British used education in India primarily as a tool to strengthen colonial rule. Their aim was to create a class of educated Indians proficient in English language and Western values, who would assist in administration and remain loyal to the British Crown. Through education, they sought to instill a sense of cultural superiority of the West, thereby ensuring the subjugation of Indian minds. Lord Macaulay's Minute on Education (1835) exemplified this policy, advocating the creation of a class who would be 'Indian in blood and colour, but English in taste, opinions, morals, and intellect'. The education system was designed not to reform Indian society or support empowerment, but to produce clerks and intermediaries who would serve the colonial administration efficiently and perpetuate British control.
qs.kf:
☛ Macaulay's Minute (1835) → Introduced English education officially
☛ Wood's Despatch (1854) → Laid foundation for education policy
☛ Permanent Settlement (Bengal) → Revenue system, not related to education
☛ Downward Filtration Theory → Education limited to upper classes
☛ Anglo-Indian Education System → Created administrative assistants through English medium

q: The 'Drain of Wealth' theory, which highlighted the economic exploitation of India under British rule, was prominently advocated by whom?
qs.e: Dadabhai Naoroji propounded the 'Drain of Wealth' theory in his book 'Poverty and Un-British Rule in India'. He argued that under British rule, India's wealth was continuously transferred to Britain, leading to India's impoverishment. This theory highlighted the economic exploitation through government expenses, trade policies, and investments. Naoroji was a prominent Indian nationalist, thrice president of the Indian National Congress (1886, 1893, 1906), and the first Indian to be elected to the British Parliament (1892, Liberal Party). His work provided an economic critique of colonialism and fueled the freedom movement. He is regarded as the father of Indian economic nationalism.
qs.kf:
☛ Propounder of Drain of Wealth Theory → Dadabhai Naoroji
☛ Major Book → Poverty and Un-British Rule in India
☛ Congress Presidency → Three times (1886, 1893, 1906)
☛ First Indian British MP → From Liberal Party (1892)
☛ Father of Indian Economic Nationalism → Dadabhai Naoroji

q: In which year was English education formally introduced in India by the British?
qs.e: English education was formally introduced in India by the British in 1835. This was based on Lord Macaulay's Minute presented in February 1835. Macaulay advocated for Western education to create a class of 'educated Indians' who would assist in British administration. The proposal was approved by Governor General Lord William Bentinck on March 7, 1835. This decision marked a revolutionary change in Indian education, making English the medium of instruction and sidelining traditional systems. The introduction of English education aimed at spreading Western knowledge and values, and it laid the foundation for modern education in India.

☛ Who approved English education in 1835? → Lord William Bentinck

☛ What was the medium of education before 1835? → Persian

q: British land revenue policies were deeply exploitative. Under which system were landlords required to pay a fixed revenue regardless of crop yield?
qs.e: The Zamindari system was introduced by Lord Cornwallis in 1793 in Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa. Under this system, zamindars were recognized as the owners of land and were required to pay a fixed revenue to the British regardless of crop yield. If a zamindar failed to pay the revenue by the due date, his land was auctioned. This system led to extensive exploitation of peasants. In contrast, the Ryotwari system collected revenue directly from cultivators, and the Mahalwari system from village communities. The Zamindari system harmed agricultural production and pushed peasants into poverty.
qs.kf:

☛ Year of introduction of Zamindari system → 1793
☛ Revenue rate in Zamindari system → 10/11th of total produce
☛ Provinces where Zamindari system was applied → Bengal, Bihar, Orissa, northern part of Madras
☛ Main drawback of Zamindari system → excessive exploitation of peasants

q: Prior to independence, the first Indian jute mill was set up in ________.
qs.e: The first jute mill in India was established in 1855 at Rishra in Bengal by George Auckland. It was known as the Bengal Jute Mill. Prior to independence, the jute industry was primarily concentrated in the Bengal province due to the abundant availability of raw jute and easy transportation via river routes. During British rule, jute export was a major trade. Later, many jute mills were set up around Kolkata. The industry was affected after the partition of India, as raw jute went to East Pakistan (now Bangladesh).

☛ Name of first Indian jute mill → Bengal Jute Mill

☛ Location of establishment → Rishra, Bengal
☛ Founder → George Auckland

q: When was the Indian Official Secrets Act passed which restricted the freedom of the press?
qs.e: The Indian Official Secrets Act was passed in 1904. This Act was enacted to restrict the freedom of the press by making it a punishable offense to publish government documents or information without authorization. It imposed strict penalties on anyone violating government confidentiality. The Act was part of British colonial rule aimed at suppressing the nationalist movement and critical press reporting. Under its provisions, any person obtaining or publishing government documents without authority faced imprisonment. The law continued even after independence and was later amended. The Act had a significant impact on the freedom of expression during the British era and remained a tool to control sensitive information.
qs.kf:

☛ Under which rule was it implemented? → British colonial rule

☛ Did it remain in force after independence? → Yes, with amendments

q: Which Bengali newspaper was founded and edited by Raja Rammohan Roy?
qs.e: Raja Rammohan Roy founded and edited the Bengali newspaper Sambad Kaumudi in 1821. It was a weekly publication that played a key role in advocating social reforms, especially the abolition of sati and support for widow remarriage. The newspaper criticized superstitions and social evils while promoting reason and rationalism. Rammohan Roy also founded the Brahmo Samaj and contributed to religious reform. q: The first English factory of Bengal was set up on the banks of the river _______ in 1651.
qs.e: The first English factory of Bengal was established on the banks of the Hugli river in 1651. This factory was set up by the East India Company and laid the foundation of English trade in Bengal. The company used this factory for trading cotton and silk textiles. Later, the company built Fort William (1696) and other forts, and developed the city of Calcutta. The Hugli river is a major distributary of the Ganga and flows through West Bengal.

q: The Poligars rebelled against the British in which Presidency, when the British tried to snatch away their military and land rights?
qs.e: The Poligars were feudal lords in the Madras Presidency, particularly in the southern districts of present-day Tamil Nadu. In the late 18th century, the British attempted to curtail their military power and land rights, leading to several rebellions, notably the Poligar War of 1799-1805. The British army under Colonel Agnew suppressed the uprising. Key leaders of the Poligars included Veerapandya Kattabomman and Puli Thevar. The rebellion took place in the Madras Presidency, not in any other British presidency like Bengal, Bombay, or Agra. The Poligars fiercely resisted British encroachment on their traditional rights and autonomy.

q: The Mahalwari system was prevalent in certain regions of northern and central India. From whom was the land revenue collected under the Mahalwari system?
qs.e: The Mahalwari system was proposed by Holt Mackenzie in 1822 and later implemented by William Bentinck. Under this system, the entire village or mahal was treated as a unit for revenue assessment. The village head or lambardar was responsible for collecting revenue from the villagers and depositing it with the British. This system was prevalent mainly in the North-Western Provinces, Punjab, and Central India. The revenue rate was based on soil fertility and produce, typically ranging from 50% to 75% of the total yield. Peasants did not own the land but only cultivated it, while the village head acted as an intermediary between the British and the cultivators.

q: What was the main focus of the Aligarh Movement?
qs.e: The Aligarh Movement was started by Sir Syed Ahmad Khan in the 19th century. Its main focus was to promote modern education among Indian Muslims so that they could progress under British rule. Sir Syed believed that the advancement of Muslims was possible only by adopting Western education. To achieve this, he established the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College in 1875 (later Aligarh Muslim University). The movement also promoted the Urdu language and advised Muslims to stay away from politics. It is known for bringing socio-educational awakening in the Muslim community.

☛ When was the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College founded? → 1875

☛ What was the main aim of the Aligarh Movement? → Modern education among Muslims

q: Whose famous quote is this? "If you cry because the sun has gone out of your life, your tears will prevent you from seeing the stars."
qs.e: This quote is by Rabindranath Tagore, a great Indian poet, writer, and philosopher. It is from his work 'Stray Birds'. Tagore expressed profound truths of life and human emotions in simple language. In this quote, he says that if you focus on loss, you will miss new possibilities. Tagore was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1913 for 'Gitanjali'. He also composed the Indian national anthem 'Jana Gana Mana'.

q: Who started the first newspaper in India?
qs.e: The first newspaper in India was the Bengal Gazette (also known as the Calcutta General Advertiser), started by James Augustus Hickey in 1780. It was a weekly English newspaper published during the British East India Company rule. Hickey printed it on his own press and it included trade news, general news, and advertisements. The newspaper criticized the colonial government, which led to its eventual closure and Hickey's imprisonment. The first Hindi newspaper in India was Udant Martand, started in 1826 by Jugal Kishore Shukla.

q: Wood's Dispatch was concerned with which of the following reforms?
qs.e: Wood's Dispatch was a historic document issued in 1854 during British rule, which was concerned with educational reforms in India. It is named after Sir Charles Wood, who was the President of the Board of Control at that time. This dispatch laid the foundation of the modern education system in India, emphasizing English medium education, establishment of universities, and teacher training. As a result, the universities of Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras were established in 1857. Wood's Dispatch aimed to propagate Western education and prepare Indians for administrative services. It is a significant milestone in the field of education, whereas railways, irrigation, and industry were not related to it.

q: Who among the following was instrumental in promoting English education in India?
qs.e: Thomas Babington Macaulay became the President of the Law Commission in India in 1834 and presented the 'Macaulay's Minute' in 1835, advocating for English as the medium of instruction in India. This Minute was accepted during the tenure of Governor-General Lord William Bentinck and led to the 1835 Education Resolution, which officially promoted English education. This policy significantly influenced the Indian education system.

q: India's trade structure under British colonial rule was molded to serve the economic interests of Britain. Which of the following best describes India's trade structure at the eve of Independence?
o: Export of capital, import of labour
Export of raw materials, import of manufactured goods
Export of industrial goods, import of food
Balanced two-way trade with Europe only
qs.e: Under British colonial rule, India's trade structure was shaped to serve Britain's economic interests. India primarily exported raw materials such as cotton, jute, tea, and indigo, while importing manufactured goods like textiles and machinery from Britain. This asymmetrical trade pattern hindered India's industrialization and allowed Britain to exploit India as a source of raw materials and a market for finished products. On the eve of Independence, this structure persisted, leading to a trade deficit and economic dependency. The colonial trade policy deindustrialized India and transformed it into an agrarian economy supplying raw materials to British industries.
qs.kf:

q: Which of the following, like the Chipko Movement, aims to protect forests in the Uttara Kannada district?
qs.e: Similar to the Chipko Movement, the Appiko Movement was a peaceful protest where villagers hugged trees to prevent them from being cut down. q: Who led the railway strike in 1974?
qs.e: The historic 1974 Indian railway strike was led by George Fernandes, a prominent socialist leader and head of the railway union. The strike was organized to demand better wages and working conditions for railway employees, and it involved approximately 1.7 million workers. It began on 8 May 1974 and lasted for 20 days, after which it was crushed by government repression. Fernandes was arrested on charges of sedition and later served as a Union Minister in the Indian government.

q: Who coined the slogan "Total Revolution"?
qs.e: Jayaprakash Narayan coined the slogan Total Revolution (Purna Kranti) during the 1975-77 Emergency period in India. This comprehensive movement sought fundamental changes in social, economic, and political spheres. Also known as Sampoorna Kranti, it aimed to unite the masses against corruption, unemployment, and inequality. The movement generated widespread opposition against the then-government and played a crucial role in the change of government at the center after the Emergency.

qs.e: Shaikh Moinuddin Chishti was one of the most prominent saints of the Chishti order. Born in 1141 CE in Sistan, Iran, he came to India and settled in Ajmer. q: According to Dadabhai Naoroji’s Drain of Wealth theory, what major economic issue needed to be addressed to end India’s exploitation under British rule?
o: Unequal economic exchange between India and Britain
Excessive land revenue imposed on peasants
qs.e: Dadabhai Naoroji's 'Drain of Wealth' theory highlighted that under British rule, India's wealth was continuously transferred to Britain. This unequal economic exchange occurred through the export of raw materials from India and import of finished goods from Britain. British policies destroyed Indian industries and turned India into a primarily agricultural economy. To end this exploitation, it was necessary to establish fair trade relations between India and Britain. Naoroji, referencing Thomas Mun's theory of balance of trade, argued that unequal exchange was the main cause of economic drain. Addressing this required promoting Indian industries and ensuring equitable economic interactions.
qs.kf:
☛ Propounder of Drain of Wealth Theory → Dadabhai Naoroji
☛ Main cause of drain → Unequal economic exchange between India and Britain
☛ Famous book by Naoroji → 'Poverty and Un-British Rule in India'
☛ Effect of drain → Continuous outflow of wealth from India
☛ Suggested solution → Fair trade and industrial development

q: Who jointly led the first ever no-tax campaign against the British Government in Bengal during the 1838-1848 Farazi Movement?
o: Titu Mir and Syed Ahmad Barelvi
qs.e: The Farazi Movement (1838-1848) was led by Shariatullah Khan, who organized peasants in Bengal against the oppressive taxes of the British government. His son Dadu Mian continued the movement and launched the first no-tax campaign, where peasants refused to pay land revenue. The movement spread across Faridpur, Bakarganj and Dhaka districts. The Farazi Movement combined Islamic reform with resistance against British exploitation. Shariatullah Khan interpreted the term Farazi as 'compliance with Islamic commandments' and presented the struggle against the British as a religious duty. Dadu Mian later led the movement with greater militancy.
qs.kf:
☛ Who founded the Farazi Movement? → Haji Shariatullah
☛ What does Farazi mean? → Compliance with Islamic commandments
☛ What was the real name of Dadu Mian? → Muhammad Mohsin
☛ Who led the no-tax campaign under Farazi Movement? → Shariatullah Khan and Dadu Mian
☛ Time period of Farazi Movement? → 1838-1848

q: Which freedom ﬁghter is popularly known as Lok Nayak?
qs.e: Jaiprakash Narayan is popularly known as Lok Nayak. He was a prominent freedom fighter and social reformer. He called for a Total Revolution and played a key role in opposing the Emergency in the 1970s. He was a follower of Gandhian ideology and fought for democratic values.
qs.kf:
☛ What title was awarded to Jaiprakash Narayan? → Lok Nayak
☛ Which movement was led by Jaiprakash Narayan? → Total Revolution
☛ Which ideology influenced Jaiprakash Narayan? → Gandhism
☛ When was Jaiprakash Narayan born? → 11 October 1902
☛ In which year was Jaiprakash Narayan awarded Bharat Ratna? → 1999 (posthumously)

q: Who among the following performed Manipuri dance in Santiniketan and brought back his fame?
qs.e: Rabindranath Tagore performed Manipuri dance in Santiniketan and revived this art form. He was the famous Bengali poet, philosopher, and artist who gave global recognition to Indian culture. Visva-Bharati University, established by Tagore in Santiniketan, promoted Manipuri dance as a major art form. Tagore preserved the classical and spiritual essence of Manipuri dance while presenting it on modern stage. This dance style is characterized by graceful hand gestures and rhythmic movements. Tagore's efforts brought national and international fame to Manipuri dance, which is one of the eight classical dances of India, known for its lyrical and devotional themes.
qs.kf:
☛ Who performed Manipuri dance in Santiniketan? → Rabindranath Tagore
☛ Who founded Visva-Bharati University? → Rabindranath Tagore
☛ Who wrote India's national anthem? → Rabindranath Tagore
☛ Who won the Nobel Prize for Literature for Gitanjali? → Rabindranath Tagore
☛ What is the characteristic of Manipuri dance? → Hand gestures and rhythmic movements

q: When was the Planning Commission set up?
qs.e: The Planning Commission was established on 15 March 1950. It was set up to create and implement Five-Year Plans for the country's economic development. Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru was its first chairman. The Planning Commission played a crucial role in guiding India's economic growth and launched the first Five-Year Plan in 1951. In 2014, Prime Minister Narendra Modi dissolved the Planning Commission and replaced it with the NITI Aayog (National Institution for Transforming India), which was officially formed in 2015.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Planning Commission established? → 1950
☛ Who was the first chairman of the Planning Commission? → Jawaharlal Nehru
☛ When was the first Five-Year Plan launched? → 1951
☛ Which body replaced the Planning Commission? → NITI Aayog
☛ When was NITI Aayog formed? → 2015

q: Concept of Chipko movement originally came from ________?
A. Rajasthan
B. Assam
C. Arunachal Pradesh
D. Mizoram
qs.e: The concept of the Chipko movement originally came from Rajasthan's Bishnoi community, where in 1730 AD, under the leadership of Amrita Devi Bishnoi, 363 people sacrificed their lives to protect trees. This historic event laid the foundation for environmental conservation. Later in 1973, the Chipko movement started in Uttarakhand's Chamoli district when villagers hugged trees to prevent felling, led by Gaura Devi and Chandi Prasad Bhatt. This movement became a symbol of forest conservation and was later expanded by environmentalists like Sunderlal Bahuguna.
qs.kf:
☛ Year of Chipko movement start → 1973
☛ Location of Chipko movement → Uttarakhand (Chamoli)
☛ Location of 1730 Bishnoi sacrifice → Rajasthan (Khejarli)
☛ Key female leader of Chipko movement → Gaura Devi
☛ Male leaders associated with Chipko movement → Chandi Prasad Bhatt and Sunderlal Bahuguna

q: Who developed the rock garden of Chandigarh?
A. Tara Chand
B. Nek Chand
C. Himanshu Parikh
D. Kamal Sagar
qs.e: The Rock Garden of Chandigarh is a famous garden developed by Nek Chand Saini. Located in Sector-1 of the city, this garden is known for its unique artwork made from waste materials, broken objects, and stones. It is an excellent example of recycling and creativity, spread over approximately 40 acres. The garden features man-made waterfalls, sculptures, and natural beauty. Nek Chand was honored with the Padmashri award for this contribution.
qs.kf:
☛ Founder of Rock Garden → Nek Chand Saini
☛ Location of Rock Garden → Sector-1, Chandigarh
☛ Specialty of Rock Garden → Built from waste and stones
☛ Award received by Nek Chand → Padmashri
☛ Area of Rock Garden → Approximately 40 acres

q: Who was the first recipient of the Bharat Ratna award and the founder of Swatantra Party (1959)?
qs.e: C Rajagopalachari was the first recipient of the Bharat Ratna award in 1954. He was also the last Governor-General of India. In 1959, he founded the Swatantra Party, a liberal political party that advocated for free-market policies and limited government intervention. Rajagopalachari was a prominent freedom fighter, statesman, and close associate of Mahatma Gandhi. He served as the Chief Minister of Madras State (now Tamil Nadu). His contributions to the nation were recognized with the highest civilian award. The Swatantra Party played a significant role in Indian politics during the 1960s and 1970s, opposing the socialist policies of the Congress party.
qs.kf:
☛ First recipient of Bharat Ratna → C Rajagopalachari (1954)
☛ Founder of Swatantra Party → C Rajagopalachari (1959)
☛ Last Governor-General of India → C Rajagopalachari
☛ First Chief Minister of Tamil Nadu → C Rajagopalachari (1952-54)
☛ Year of Bharat Ratna institution → 1954

q: The Gateway of India was built in the traditional ________ style to welcome King George V and Queen Mary to India in 1911.
qs.e: The Gateway of India is a historic monument located in Mumbai, built to commemorate the visit of King George V and Queen Mary to India in 1911. Its design was created by the architect George Wittet, and the construction was completed in 1924. The monument was built in the Indo-Saracenic style, which blends Hindu, Mughal, and Islamic architectural elements. This style is characterized by domes, arches, and intricately carved columns. The Gateway of India stands on the waterfront and served as a ceremonial entrance to India during British rule. It remains a major tourist attraction in Mumbai today.
qs.kf:
☛ Architect of Gateway of India → George Wittet
☛ Completion year of Gateway of India → 1924
☛ Location of Gateway of India → Mumbai
☛ Elements mixed in Indo-Saracenic style → Hindu, Mughal, Islamic
☛ Purpose of Gateway of India → Welcome King George V and Queen Mary

q: When was the Atomic Energy Commission set up to supervise atomic energy activities in India?
qs.e: The Atomic Energy Commission was set up in August 1948 to supervise atomic energy activities in India. It was established under the leadership of then Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru, and Dr. Homi Jehangir Bhabha was appointed as its first chairman. The main objective of the Commission was to promote the peaceful uses of atomic energy and develop nuclear research in the country. Subsequently, the Department of Atomic Energy was formed in 1954. The Atomic Energy Commission is responsible for policy formulation and monitoring of India's nuclear program.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Atomic Energy Commission established? → August 1948
☛ Who was the first chairman? → Dr. Homi Jehangir Bhabha
☛ Who was the Prime Minister at that time? → Jawaharlal Nehru
☛ When was the Department of Atomic Energy formed? → 1954
☛ What is the main objective? → Peaceful use of atomic energy

q: Which of the following monument is built with some influence of Gujarati style to welcome King George V and Queen Mary to India?
qs.e: The Gateway of India is a famous monument located in Mumbai, built in 1911 to welcome King George V and Queen Mary to India. Its design was prepared by architect George Wittet and clearly shows influence of Gujarati style. The monument is made of basalt stone and stands 26 meters high. Construction was completed in 1924. The Gateway of India is also a significant symbol of India's independence movement, as the last British troops left India through this route in 1947.

q: When did Sir William Jones found Asiatic Society?
qs.e: Sir William Jones, a renowned British philologist and jurist, founded the Asiatic Society on January 15, 1784 in Calcutta. The society aimed to study Asian culture, history, and languages. It later became known as the Asiatic Society of Bengal. Jones played a key role in translating ancient Indian texts and introducing Sanskrit to the Western world. He proposed that Sanskrit, Greek, and Latin shared a common origin, laying the foundation for the Indo-European language family theory. The establishment of the Asiatic Society marked the beginning of systematic Oriental studies in India.
qs.kf:
☛ Founder of Asiatic Society → Sir William Jones
☛ Year of establishment → 1784
☛ Place of establishment → Calcutta
☛ Key language studied by Jones → Sanskrit
☛ Language family proposed → Indo-European

q: A large marble building in Kolkata, built by the British whose design echoes the Taj Mahal is _______.
qs.e: The Victoria Memorial is a large marble building in Kolkata, built by the British between 1906 and 1921. Its design echoes the Taj Mahal, with white marble and a grand dome. It was built in memory of Queen Victoria, who died in 1901. The architect was William Emerson, and it houses a museum with artifacts and paintings from British India. The Victoria Memorial is one of Kolkata's top tourist attractions, surrounded by beautiful gardens. Writers Building is a government office, St. Paul's Cathedral is a church, and Fort William is a military fort, making them incorrect choices.
qs.kf:

☛ When was Victoria Memorial built? → 1906-1921

☛ Which building inspired the design of Victoria Memorial? → Taj Mahal

q: The Mysuru Palace in Karnataka was an official residence of which of the following dynasties?
qs.e: The Mysuru Palace in Karnataka was the official residence of the Wadiyar dynasty. The Wadiyars ruled the Kingdom of Mysore from 1399 to 1947. The palace, completed in 1912, is a prime example of the Indo-Saracenic style. The Wadiyar rulers were patrons of art, music, and culture. Today, the palace is a major tourist attraction and is especially illuminated during the Dasara festival. Notable Wadiyar rulers include those contemporary to Tipu Sultan and the modern-era Maharaja Jayachamaraja Wadiyar.

q: Kailash Satyarthi was the founder of:
qs.e: Kailash Satyarthi is a renowned Indian child rights activist who founded Bachpan Bachao Andolan (BBA) in 1980. This organization's primary goal is to combat child labor, child trafficking, and child exploitation. It is India's largest grassroots movement for child protection. Kailash Satyarthi was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2014 for his work against child labor. Stree Bachao Andolan, Beti Padhao Andolan, and Sabko Padhao Andolan are other social movements, but Kailash Satyarthi is associated with Bachpan Bachao Andolan.

☛ Year of establishment of Bachpan Bachao Andolan → 1980
☛ Kailash Satyarthi awarded Nobel Peace Prize → 2014

q: Asiatic Society of Bengal was established in the year:
qs.e: The Asiatic Society of Bengal was founded on 15 January 1784 by Sir William Jones in Kolkata. It is one of the oldest research institutions in India, aimed at studying Asian history, culture, language, and science. The society played a key role in archaeological surveys and translation of ancient texts. In 1816, its name was changed to Asiatic Society. Currently, it operates under the patronage of the Government of India and its headquarters is in Kolkata.

q: Which of the following nations was the part of 'Axis Powers' in World War II?
qs.e: During World War II (1939-1945), the three main Axis Powers were Germany, Italy, and Japan. These countries were united under the Tripartite Pact signed in 1940. Germany was led by Adolf Hitler and initiated the war by invading Poland in 1939. In contrast, the USA, Britain, and Russia (Soviet Union) were part of the Allied Powers, which fought against the Axis. Therefore, among the given options, only Germany was an Axis power.

q: Who founded the Asiatic Society of Bengal in 1784?
qs.e: The Asiatic Society of Bengal was founded by Sir William Jones on 15 January 1784 in Calcutta. He was a British judge and Orientalist scholar. The Society's main objective was to study Asian culture, language, and history. Sir William Jones deeply studied Sanskrit and introduced Indian philosophy to the Western world. q: Who was the founder of the Ahmadiya movement?
qs.e: The founder of the Ahmadiya movement was Mirza Ghulam Ahmed (1835-1908). He founded the movement in 1889 at Qadian, a town in Punjab. Mirza Ghulam Ahmed claimed to be the Messiah and a Mujaddid (reformer). His aim was to reform and revive Islam. He opposed the concept of Jihad and emphasized peaceful propagation. The Ahmadiya movement promoted education and modernity. It has two main branches: the Qadiani group and the Lahori group.

☛ When was Mirza Ghulam Ahmed born? → 1835

q: Magna Carta is the charter of rights issued by _____
qs.e: Magna Carta was issued in 1215 by King John of England. It is a historic charter that limited the powers of the king and granted certain rights to the people. Magna Carta is considered a foundation of modern democracy and the rule of law. It was signed at Runnymede. Key provisions include the right to a fair trial, protection from arbitrary taxation, and the freedom of the Church. This document influenced the constitutional development of England and inspired later documents such as the United States Constitution. Magna Carta introduced the idea that everyone, including the king, is subject to the law, which remains a pivotal concept in legal systems today.

☛ Where was Magna Carta signed? → Runnymede
☛ What was the main purpose of Magna Carta? → To limit the king's powers

☛ In which language was Magna Carta written? → Latin

q: Who founded the 'Asiatic Society of Bengal'?
qs.e: The Asiatic Society of Bengal was founded in 1784 by Sir William Jones. It was the first academic institution established in India, aimed at the study of Asian culture, history, and languages. William Jones was a British judge and orientalist. He deeply studied Sanskrit and demonstrated that Sanskrit, Greek, and Latin shared a common root, which gave strength to the concept of the Indo-European language family. q: Hockey was introduced in India by _______.
qs.e: Hockey was introduced in India by the British people. The British army brought the sport to India in the 19th century. The first hockey club was established in Kolkata in 1885. India's golden era in hockey lasted from 1928 to 1956, winning six consecutive Olympic gold medals. The Indian hockey team has won a total of 8 Olympic gold medals, the highest by any country. Major Dhyan Chand is known as the Wizard of Hockey for his extraordinary skills.

☛ Where was the first hockey club in India established? → Kolkata
☛ When did India win its first Olympic hockey gold? → 1928
☛ Who is known as the Wizard of Hockey? → Major Dhyan Chand

☛ When was India's last Olympic hockey gold? → 1980

q: Which of the following lyrics was written by Mohammad Iqbal?
qs.e: Mohammad Iqbal, also known as Allama Iqbal, was a renowned philosopher, poet, and politician. He wrote the poem 'Tarā nah-e-Hindī ' in 1904, whose opening line is 'Saare Jahan Se Achha Hindustan Hamara'. This song became a prominent patriotic song during India's freedom movement. 'Vande Mataram' was written by Bankim Chandra Chatterjee, 'Amar Sonar Bangla' by Rabindranath Tagore, and 'Jana Gana Mana' also composed by Tagore.

q: Ranjit Singh was the ruler of which province?
qs.e: Maharaja Ranjit Singh (1780-1839) was a renowned ruler of Punjab, who reigned from 1799 to 1839. He is also known as the 'Lion of Punjab'. He established a strong Sikh Empire in Punjab, which extended from the Sutlej River to Kashmir. Ranjit Singh played a key role in modernizing his army and improving administration. He also gilded the Golden Temple in Amritsar. After his death, the Sikh Empire weakened and was eventually annexed by the British.

q: Which of the following is the production of port wine?
qs.e: Port wine is a fortified wine produced in the Douro Valley region of Portugal. Its name comes from the city of Porto, the second largest city in Portugal, from where it is exported. The production method involves adding grape brandy to the grape must during fermentation, which stops fermentation and preserves the natural sweetness of the wine. Port wine is made from red and white grapes, but mostly red Port is well-known.

☛ What type of wine is port wine? → Fortified wine
☛ After which city is port wine named? → Porto
☛ What is added to stop fermentation in port wine? → Grape brandy
☛ Which valley region is known for port wine production? → Douro Valley

q: In 1971-72, which country adopted the song 'Amar Sonar Bangla' as its national anthem?
qs.e: In 1971-72, Bangladesh adopted the song 'Amar Sonar Bangla', written by Rabindranath Tagore, as its national anthem. This song was originally composed in 1905 to protest the partition of Bengal. After Bangladesh gained independence, it was officially adopted as the national anthem. The melody and lyrics reflect the culture and history of Bangladesh. Tagore also wrote India's national anthem 'Jana Gana Mana'.

☛ Composer → Rabindranath Tagore
☛ Year of adoption → 1971-72

☛ Tagore's title → Gurudev

q: Who is known to make an image of Mother India during the freedom struggle?
qs.e: Abanindranath Tagore created the iconic image of 'Bharat Mata' around 1905. This painting depicts Mother India as a saffron-clad ascetic holding a book, sheaves of rice, a mala, and a white cloth in her four hands. The image became a symbol of nationalist sentiment and inspired the freedom struggle. Abanindranath Tagore was the founder of the Bengal School of Art, which revived Indian artistic traditions. His art rejected Western naturalism in favor of indigenous styles. The 'Bharat Mata' painting evoked patriotism and unity among Indians. It remains a powerful representation of Indian nationalism.

☛ Founder of Bengal School of Art → Abanindranath Tagore
☛ Objects in Mother India's hands in the painting → Book, rice, mala, white cloth
☛ Rise of nationalist painting in India → With Bengal School
☛ Abanindranath Tagore's famous paintings → 'Bharat Mata' and 'Death of Shah Jahan'

q: Where did Vasco-D-Gamma land in India first?
qs.e: Vasco-da-Gama landed at Calicut (present-day Kozhikode, Kerala) on the western coast of India on 20 May 1498. At that time, Calicut was ruled by the Zamorin king. He was not the first European to arrive in India, but the first to reach India via the sea route from Portugal. This voyage opened the Europe-India maritime trade route and laid the foundation for Portuguese colonialism. Calicut was a major spice trade center, exporting pepper, cinnamon and other spices.
qs.kf:

☛ Where is Vasco-da-Gama buried in India? → Cochin (later moved to Lisbon)

q: Which of the following is known as World Kavi?
qs.e: Rabindranath Tagore is known as World Kavi due to his immense literary and poetic genius. He was a towering figure in Indian literature, awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1913 for his collection of poems 'Gitanjali'. His poetry encompasses spirituality, love for nature, and profound humanism. Tagore seamlessly blended Indian cultural traditions with Western thought, earning global recognition. He composed the national anthems of two nations: India's 'Jana Gana Mana' and Bangladesh's 'Amar Shonar Bangla'. He is also respectfully called 'Gurudev'. Tagore's contributions span literature, music, and art, making him a universal poet whose works continue to inspire generations worldwide.

☛ For which work did Tagore win the Nobel Prize? → Gitanjali
