☛ What is the other name of Rabindranath Tagore? → Gurudev
☛ Where was Rabindranath Tagore born? → Kolkata

q: Which of the following scientists is known as the Father of the Green Revolution in India?
qs.e: The Father of the Green Revolution in India is MS Swaminathan. In the 1960s, he developed high-yielding varieties of wheat and rice, which made India self-sufficient in food grains. His work led to a tremendous increase in production and saved the country from famine. Swaminathan is known as an agricultural scientist and played a crucial role in shaping agricultural policies. CV Raman is a Nobel laureate in physics, Vikram Sarabhai is the father of the Indian space program, and Homi Bhabha is the father of the nuclear energy program.
qs.kf:
☛ Who is the father of the Green Revolution in India? → MS Swaminathan
☛ When did the Green Revolution start? → In the 1960s
☛ Which crops were the focus of the Green Revolution? → Wheat and rice
☛ Which awards did MS Swaminathan receive? → Padma Shri, Padma Bhushan, Padma Vibhushan
☛ What was the main objective of the Green Revolution? → Increase food production and achieve self-sufficiency

q: What was the condition of India's industrial sector in 1947?
o: Underdeveloped and focused on traditional industries
qs.e: At the time of independence in 1947, India's industrial sector was underdeveloped and primarily focused on traditional industries like textiles, sugar, and cement. During British rule, India was used as a supplier of raw materials, which hindered the growth of heavy industries. The production of capital goods was negligible, and there was a severe lack of technological advancement. The textile industry dominated industrial output, while engineering and chemical industries were underdeveloped. After independence, the government adopted a mixed economy through the Industrial Policy of 1948 and emphasized the development of heavy industries.
qs.kf:
☛ What was the main characteristic of India's industrial sector in 1947? → Underdeveloped and focused on traditional industries
☛ How was India used during British rule in terms of industry? → As a supplier of raw materials
☛ Which industry was the largest at the time of independence? → Textile industry
☛ What type of economy did the Industrial Policy of 1948 adopt? → Mixed economy
☛ When was emphasis given to the development of heavy industries in India? → After independence

q: Which industry was most developed in India before Independence?
qs.e: Before independence, the textile industry was the most developed in India. India's cotton and silk textile industry was world-renowned. During the Mughal and British periods, Indian textiles had a global demand. However, after the Industrial Revolution, Britain adopted policies to suppress the Indian textile industry, yet it remained dominant. The jute industry was also significant, but the textile industry contributed the most to the economy.

☛ Reason for decline of textile industry → Import of British machine-made textiles

q: Who among the following became the first person to hoist the Indian flag on foreign soil during the International Socialist Conference in Stuttgart, Germany, in 1907?
qs.e: During the International Socialist Conference held in Stuttgart, Germany in 1907, Madam Bhikaiji Cama became the first person to hoist the Indian flag on foreign soil. The flag she unfurled had three stripes of green, yellow, and red, with the words 'Vande Mataram' inscribed on it. This flag later became a significant milestone in the evolution of the Indian national flag. Madam Cama was a prominent revolutionary in the Indian independence movement and played a key role in raising awareness about India's freedom struggle abroad. Her act of hoisting the flag symbolized the spirit of Indian nationalism on an international platform.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the first woman to hoist the Indian flag on foreign soil? → Madam Bhikaiji Cama
☛ Where did Madam Bhikaiji Cama hoist the Indian flag? → Stuttgart, Germany

☛ What was inscribed on Madam Cama's flag? → Vande Mataram
☛ Which movement was Madam Bhikaiji Cama associated with? → Indian Independence Movement

q: What was the time period of the Sayyid dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate?
qs.e: The Sayyid dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate was founded by Khizr Khan in 1414 CE after the decline of the Tughlaq dynasty. The last ruler of this dynasty was Alam Shah, who ruled until 1451 CE, after which the Lodhi dynasty came to power. The Sayyids predominantly ruled over Delhi and its surrounding regions. During this period, the sultanate's military strength weakened, and regional kingdoms gained influence. The Sayyid dynasty ruled for a total of 37 years.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the founder of the Sayyid dynasty? → Khizr Khan
☛ Who was the last ruler of the Sayyid dynasty? → Alam Shah
☛ How many years did the Sayyid dynasty rule? → 37 years
☛ Which dynasty succeeded the Sayyid dynasty? → Lodhi dynasty
☛ What was the time period of the Sayyid dynasty? → 1414–1451

q: The Faraizi Movement, led by Haji Shariatullah, focused on religious purification and resisting the British in which region?
qs.e: The Faraizi Movement was led by Haji Shariatullah in the 19th century. It was active in the Bengal region of India. The movement focused on religious purification in Islam and resistance against British rule. Haji Shariatullah urged Muslims to follow the true principles of Islam and oppose British colonial policies. The term 'Faraizi' means 'obligatory duties', emphasizing the fundamental practices of Islam. Later, the movement was led by his son Dadu Mian.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the leader of the Faraizi Movement? → Haji Shariatullah
☛ In which region did the Faraizi Movement take place? → Bengal
☛ What was the main objective of the Faraizi Movement? → Islamic purification and opposition to the British
☛ What was the name of Haji Shariatullah's son? → Dadu Mian
☛ What does 'Faraizi' mean? → Obligatory duties

q: Which of the following countries does NOT share a land border with India?
qs.e: India shares its land borders with Afghanistan in the northwest, China, Nepal, Bhutan in the north, and Bangladesh and Myanmar in the east. Thailand does not share a land border with India; it is located in Southeast Asia, bordering Myanmar, Laos, Cambodia, and Malaysia. India and Thailand only have a maritime border in the Andaman Sea. Thus, Thailand is not connected by land to India.
qs.kf:
☛ Total land border length of India → 15,106.7 km
☛ Country with longest land border with India → Bangladesh
☛ Country with shortest land border with India → Afghanistan
☛ Number of neighboring countries (land border) of India → 7
☛ Maritime border between India and Thailand → Andaman Sea

q: Pazhassi Raja was a freedom fighter from the modern _________ state.
qs.e: Pazhassi Raja, also known as Kerala Simham (Lion of Kerala), was a freedom fighter who led a revolt against the British East India Company in the late 18th century. He belonged to the modern state of Kerala, specifically the Kottayam region. He opposed the Company's tax collection and expansionist policies, and waged a guerrilla war from 1797 to 1805. He ultimately committed suicide in 1805 to avoid capture. He is considered an important figure in India's early freedom struggle.
qs.kf:
☛ Pazhassi Raja's title → Kerala Simham
☛ Pazhassi Raja is associated with which state → Kerala
☛ Pazhassi Raja fought against → British East India Company
☛ Pazhassi Raja's death year → 1805
☛ Warfare style used by Pazhassi Raja → Guerrilla warfare

q: The Tri-Color which was hoisted in Stuttgart by Madam Cama was smuggled into British India by:
qs.e: Madam Bhikaji Cama hoisted the first Indian tricolor at the International Socialist Conference in Stuttgart, Germany in 1907. This flag was smuggled into British India by Indulal Yagnik, a prominent freedom fighter and socialist leader. He safely brought the flag to India, where it later became a symbol of revolutionary activities. The flag had green, yellow, and red stripes with 'Vande Mataram' inscribed in the center.
qs.kf:
☛ Where was Madam Cama born? → Mumbai
☛ Date of hoisting the flag in Stuttgart? → 21 August 1907
☛ What was the design of the flag? → Green, yellow, red stripes with 'Vande Mataram'
☛ Indulal Yagnik was associated with which movements? → Indian freedom movement and socialist movement
☛ What was Bhikaji Cama's original name? → Bhikaji Rustom Cama

q: Which great personality of the world was also known as 'Fuehrer'?
qs.e: Adolf Hitler (1889-1945) was the dictator of Germany and leader of the Nazi Party, known as 'Führer', a German word meaning 'leader' or 'guide'. He ruled Germany from 1934 to 1945 and was responsible for World War II and the Holocaust. The title 'Führer' signified his absolute dictatorial power. Other options: Vladimir Lenin (Russian revolutionary), Joseph Stalin (Soviet dictator) and Napoleon Bonaparte (French emperor) were not called 'Führer'.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was called Führer? → Adolf Hitler
☛ Hitler's full name → Adolf Hitler
☛ Hitler's birth → 20 April 1889, Austria
☛ Hitler's title → Führer (leader)
☛ Hitler's death → 30 April 1945, suicide

q: On 25 April 1945, _____ governments met in San Francisco for a conference and started drafting the UN Charter.
qs.e: On 25 April 1945, 50 governments met in San Francisco for a conference and started drafting the United Nations Charter. This conference was held to maintain international peace and security after World War II. The Charter was signed on 26 June 1945 and came into force on 24 October 1945. The United Nations has six principal organs: the General Assembly, Security Council, Economic and Social Council, Secretariat, International Court of Justice, and Trusteeship Council. The headquarters of the United Nations is located in New York, USA.
qs.kf:
☛ Date of signing of UN Charter → 26 June 1945
☛ Date of entry into force of UN Charter → 24 October 1945
☛ Permanent members of UN Security Council → USA, UK, France, Russia, China
☛ Headquarters of United Nations → New York, USA
☛ Current number of UN member states → 193

q: Who laid down the foundation stone of Delhi during Delhi Darbar 1911?
qs.e: During the Delhi Darbar of 1911, the British Emperor George V laid the foundation stone of Delhi. The darbar was held on December 12, 1911, where it was announced that the capital of India would be transferred from Kolkata to Delhi. George V and his wife Queen Mary visited India for this occasion. The foundation stone ceremony took place in the Kingsway (now Rajpath) area of Delhi. Later, the design of New Delhi was prepared by architect Sir Edwin Lutyens. This event is significant in Indian history as it marked the beginning of the construction of New Delhi.
qs.kf:
☛ When was Delhi proclaimed as the capital of India? → 1911
☛ Who designed the layout of New Delhi? → Edwin Lutyens
☛ Which British emperor participated in the 1911 Delhi Darbar? → George V
☛ Where was the Delhi Darbar held? → Delhi
☛ Which was the capital of India before the shift to Delhi? → Kolkata

q: Whose reign saw the largest extension of Delhi Sultanate?
qs.e: The largest territorial expansion of the Delhi Sultanate occurred during the reign of Muhammad bin Tughluq (1325-1351 AD). His empire extended from Kashmir in the north to Madurai in the south, and from Bengal in the east to Sindh in the west. He shifted the capital from Delhi to Daulatabad (Devagiri) to better control the Deccan. Although his conquests made the sultanate the largest ever, his administrative experiments like the token currency and increased taxation in the Doab failed. The empire covered approximately 1.2 million sq km. Alauddin Khilji and Balban also expanded the sultanate, but the maximum extent was under Muhammad bin Tughluq.
qs.kf:
☛ What was the capital of Muhammad bin Tughluq? → Daulatabad
☛ Which dynasty did Muhammad bin Tughluq belong to? → Tughluq dynasty
☛ What was the reign period of Muhammad bin Tughluq? → 1325-1351 AD
☛ Under whom was the Delhi Sultanate the largest? → Muhammad bin Tughluq
☛ What is the ancient name of Daulatabad? → Devagiri

q: Which of the following options gives the correct chronological history of India? P - Gupta Kingdom Q - Mauryan Empire R - Mughals S - Delhi Sultanate
qs.e: The correct chronological order of Indian history is the Mauryan Empire, Gupta Kingdom, Delhi Sultanate, and Mughal Empire. The Mauryan Empire (321-185 BCE) was founded by Chandragupta Maurya. It was followed by the Gupta Empire (320-550 CE), founded by Chandragupta I, known as the Golden Age of India. The Delhi Sultanate (1206-1526 CE) included the Slave, Khilji, Tughlaq, Sayyid, and Lodi dynasties. Finally, the Mughal Empire (1526-1857 CE) was established by Babur.
qs.kf:
☛ Who founded the Mauryan Empire? → Chandragupta Maurya
☛ Which Gupta ruler is associated with the Golden Age? → Chandragupta II
☛ Who founded the Delhi Sultanate? → Qutb-ud-din Aibak
☛ When was the First Battle of Panipat fought? → 1526 CE
☛ Who was the last Mughal emperor? → Bahadur Shah Zafar

q: Who wrote the lyrics of the song 'Sare Jahan Se Achcha'?
qs.e: The lyrics of the song 'Sare Jahan Se Achcha' were written by the renowned poet and philosopher Mohammed Iqbal. This patriotic song was composed in 1904 and later published in his book 'Bang-e-Dara'. It symbolizes the diversity and unity of India and was written to instill a sense of patriotism among Indians during his time. The song is still sung on national occasions like Independence Day and Republic Day. Mohammed Iqbal is also known as 'Shair-e-Mashriq' (Poet of the East).
qs.kf:
☛ Who wrote 'Sare Jahan Se Achcha'? → Mohammed Iqbal
☛ When was it written? → 1904
☛ What is Iqbal's famous work? → Bang-e-Dara
☛ What is Iqbal's nickname? → Shair-e-Mashriq
☛ What does the song represent? → Patriotism and national unity

q: Who led India's first expedition to the Antarctic in 1982?
qs.e: India's first Antarctic expedition was launched in 1982 under the leadership of Dr. Syed Zahoor Qasim (Dr. SZ Qasim), a renowned marine biologist and polar explorer. This expedition laid the foundation for India's presence in Antarctica, leading to the establishment of the first Indian research station, Dakshin Gangotri, in 1983. Dr. Qasim also played a key role in setting up the National Centre for Antarctic and Ocean Research (NCAOR). The expedition marked India's entry into polar research and highlighted the country's commitment to scientific exploration in extreme environments.
qs.kf:
☛ When did India's first Antarctic expedition start? → 1982
☛ What is the name of India's first Antarctic station? → Dakshin Gangotri (1983)
☛ Dr. SZ Qasim was famous in which field? → Marine biologist
☛ What is India's second Antarctic station? → Maitri (1989)
☛ What is India's third Antarctic station? → Bharati (2012)

q: What is the importance of 22 July 1947?
o: Leaders' discussion for selection of national anthem
qs.e: The importance of 22 July 1947 is that on this day, the Constituent Assembly of India adopted the present National Flag. The flag is a tricolor with saffron, white, and green horizontal stripes, and the Ashoka Chakra in the center. It symbolizes freedom and unity. The national song 'Vande Mataram' was adopted on 24 January 1950. The national anthem 'Jana Gana Mana' was also adopted by the Constituent Assembly on 24 January 1950. Thus, 22 July 1947 is historically significant specifically for the adoption of the national flag.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the National Flag adopted? → 22 July 1947
☛ Who designed the National Flag? → Pingali Venkayya
☛ When was the National Anthem adopted? → 24 January 1950
☛ When was the National Song adopted? → 24 January 1950
☛ How many spokes does the Ashoka Chakra have? → 24 spokes

q: In which year Sir William Jones founded "Asiatic Society of Bengal"?
qs.e: Sir William Jones founded the Asiatic Society of Bengal on 15 January 1784 in Kolkata. It was the first scientific and cultural institution in India, aimed at studying Asian history, languages, literature, and culture. Sir William Jones was a British judge and orientalist who studied Sanskrit and proposed the theory of the Indo-European language family. The society played a key role in Indian archaeology and history. Later it was renamed Asiatic Society.
qs.kf:
☛ Year of founding of Asiatic Society of Bengal → 1784
☛ Founder of Asiatic Society → Sir William Jones
☛ First Indian president → Raja Radhakanta Deb
☛ Current name → Asiatic Society (Kolkata)
☛ Sir William Jones' contribution → Indo-European language family theory

q: Who wrote the famous song 'Sare Jahan Se Accha' in Urdu?
qs.e: The famous Urdu song 'Sare Jahan Se Accha' was written by Muhammad Iqbal. He wrote this song in 1904, and it is also known as 'Tarana-e-Hindi'. Muhammad Iqbal was a renowned philosopher, poet, and politician. In this song, he expressed the unity in diversity and patriotic spirit of India. It is still sung on Independence Day and Republic Day. Muhammad Iqbal is also known as 'Shayar-e-Mashriq' (Poet of the East).
qs.kf:
☛ Writer of 'Sare Jahan Se Accha' → Muhammad Iqbal
☛ Year of writing this song → 1904
☛ Muhammad Iqbal is also known as → Shayar-e-Mashriq
☛ Alternative name of 'Sare Jahan Se Accha' → Tarana-e-Hindi
☛ Iqbal was a famous poet in which languages → Urdu and Persian

q: When were privy purses officially abolished in India?
qs.e: Privy purses in India were officially abolished in 1971 through the 26th Constitutional Amendment, which came into effect on 28 December 1971. The privy purse was an annual payment made to former rulers of princely states in exchange for their agreement to merge their territories with the Indian Union. The Indira Gandhi government first attempted to abolish them in 1969, but the Supreme Court struck down the order. Subsequently, the Parliament passed the 26th Amendment in 1971, which removed the constitutional recognition of princely privileges and privy purses. The move was aimed at promoting social and economic equality and abolishing feudal privileges. The amendment also deleted Articles 291 and 362 from the Constitution, which had provided for the privy purse.
qs.kf:
☛ Amendment that abolished privy purses → 26th Amendment, 1971
☛ Prime Minister at that time → Indira Gandhi
☛ Objective → Social and economic equality
☛ Privy purse was for → Former rulers of princely states
☛ Why 1969 attempt failed → Struck down by the Supreme Court

q: Which Indian freedom fighter was one of the first to openly support Marxist and communist ideologies, and played a pioneering role in the labour movement and the formation of the Communist Party of India?
qs.e: M N Roy (Manabendra Nath Roy) was an Indian freedom fighter who was among the first to openly support Marxist and communist ideologies. He played a pioneering role in the labour movement and was a founder of the Communist Party of India. He organized Indian revolutionaries abroad and also founded the Communist Party in Mexico. He later moved towards Radical Humanism. His contribution remains significant in the history of the Indian communist movement. Despite ideological shifts, his early role in bringing communist thought to India was foundational. His efforts in uniting workers and peasants under a socialist framework were crucial for the growth of leftist politics in India.
qs.kf:
☛ Full name of M N Roy → Manabendra Nath Roy
☛ Ideology supported by him → Marxism and Communism
☛ Party founded by him → Communist Party of India
☛ Later philosophy adopted → Radical Humanism
☛ National labour organization associated → All India Trade Union Congress (AITUC)

q: What role did the Indian People’s Theatre Association (IPTA) play during the British rule?
qs.e: The Indian People's Theatre Association (IPTA) was founded in 1942. Its primary role was to express dissent against British rule through various art forms like drama, music, and dance. IPTA aimed to raise political awareness among the masses and critique British policies. It was influenced by Marxist ideology and included prominent artists like Balraj Sahni and K.A. Abbas. The association used cultural performances to mobilize support for the Indian freedom struggle, making art a medium for political expression and social change. IPTA played a crucial role in connecting the cultural movement with the nationalist movement, fostering a sense of unity and resistance against colonial oppression.
qs.kf:
☛ When was IPTA founded? → 1942
☛ What was the main objective of IPTA? → To raise awareness against British rule
☛ Who were prominent artists associated with IPTA? → Balraj Sahni, K.A. Abbas
☛ Which ideology influenced IPTA? → Marxism
☛ How did IPTA use art? → As a medium for political expression

q: What was the term for Anglo-Indian bureaucrats in the princely states?
qs.e: The term 'Non-Mulkis' was used for Anglo-Indian bureaucrats in princely states, who came from British India and were not local residents. The term 'Mulkis' referred to local residents. This distinction was particularly important in the princely state of Hyderabad, where Non-Mulkis were appointed to higher positions and received higher salaries and privileges. This system was part of the British policy of divide and rule. 'Jagirdars' and 'Zamindars' are land-related titles, while 'Mulkis' are local officials. Non-Mulkis often had better access to British authorities and played a key role in administration.
qs.kf:
☛ Meaning of Non-Mulkis → Anglo-Indian or outsider bureaucrats
☛ Meaning of Mulkis → Local bureaucrats
☛ Princely state where this distinction was prominent → Hyderabad
☛ Aim of Non-Mulki policy → Strengthen British control
☛ Benefits given to Non-Mulkis → Higher salary and privileges

q: Which of the following popular tourist destinations of India were built in 1911 to commemorate the visit of King George V and Queen Mary?
qs.e: The Gateway of India is a famous historical monument located in Mumbai. It was built in 1911 to commemorate the visit of King George V and Queen Mary to India. The foundation stone was laid on March 31, 1911. The design was prepared by architect George Wittet and the monument was completed in 1924. It is built in the Indo-Saracenic style, blending Hindu and Muslim architectural elements. The monument stands on the waterfront of the Arabian Sea in the Apollo Bunder area of Mumbai.
qs.kf:
☛ Where is Gateway of India located? → Mumbai, Maharashtra
☛ When was Gateway of India completed? → 1924
☛ Who was the architect of Gateway of India? → George Wittet
☛ In which style is Gateway of India built? → Indo-Saracenic style
☛ Why was Gateway of India built? → To commemorate the visit of King George V and Queen Mary

q: The first Indian flag to be hoisted on foreign soil was unfurled in _______ by Bhikaji Cama in 1907.
qs.e: In 1907, Bhikaji Cama unfurled the first Indian flag on foreign soil at the International Socialist Conference in Stuttgart, Germany. The flag was a symbol of India's independence, featuring green, yellow, and red stripes with 'Vande Mataram' inscribed in the middle. This event is considered a significant milestone in the Indian independence movement. Bhikaji Cama was a prominent revolutionary who worked to raise awareness for India's freedom abroad.
qs.kf:
☛ Where was the first Indian flag hoisted on foreign soil by Bhikaji Cama? → Germany (Stuttgart)
☛ When was the first Indian flag hoisted? → 1907
☛ At which conference did Bhikaji Cama unfurl the flag? → International Socialist Conference
☛ What was inscribed on the flag? → Vande Mataram
☛ What were the colors of the flag? → Green, Yellow, Red

q: What was the chipko agitation against?
qs.e: The Chipko movement was an environmental movement that started in the 1970s in India against deforestation. It mainly took place in the villages of Uttarakhand (then part of Uttar Pradesh), where villagers hugged trees to prevent them from being cut. The movement was led by activists like Chandi Prasad Bhatt and Gaura Devi. Its main goal was to protect forests and the rights of local communities. The Chipko movement raised environmental awareness globally.
qs.kf:
☛ In which year did the Chipko movement start? → 1973
☛ What was the main slogan of the Chipko movement? → Save trees, save environment
☛ Who was the prominent female leader of the Chipko movement? → Gaura Devi
☛ Which state is associated with the Chipko movement? → Uttarakhand
☛ What does the word 'Chipko' mean? → To hug

q: In 1784 AD, along with the start of archaeological work in India by the Europeans, the Asiatic Society of Bengal was formed. Who was its founder?
qs.e: The Asiatic Society of Bengal (now Asiatic Society) was founded on 15 January 1784 by Sir William Jones, a British judge and Oriental scholar. Its aim was the study of Asian culture, history, and languages. William Jones deeply studied Sanskrit and proposed the Indo-European language family theory. The Society played a key role in the development of Indian epigraphy and numismatics. James Prinsep deciphered the Brahmi and Kharosthi scripts, Alexander Cunningham is known as the father of Indian archaeology, and George Turnour translated the Mahavamsa. Hence, the correct answer is William Jones.
qs.kf:
☛ Who founded the Asiatic Society of Bengal? → William Jones
☛ When was the Asiatic Society founded? → 1784 AD
☛ Who deciphered Brahmi and Kharosthi scripts? → James Prinsep
☛ Who is the father of Indian archaeology? → Alexander Cunningham
☛ Who translated the Mahavamsa? → George Turnour

q: Who is the author of 'The Great Indian Novel,' published in 2011?
qs.e: 'The Great Indian Novel' was written by Shashi Tharoor and published in 1989, not 2011. The novel is a satirical retelling of the Indian epic Mahabharata, intertwined with 20th-century Indian political history. Tharoor is a renowned author and politician, having served as Under-Secretary-General at the United Nations. Among the other options, Kiran Nagarkar wrote 'Cuckold', Vikram Seth wrote 'A Suitable Boy', and Arundhati Roy wrote 'The God of Small Things'. The question's year (2011) is incorrect; the book was published in 1989.
qs.kf:
☛ Shashi Tharoor's famous book → 'The Great Indian Novel'
☛ Epic it is based on → Mahabharata
☛ Tharoor's political role → Union Minister
☛ Tharoor's UN position → Under-Secretary-General
☛ Year of publication → 1989

q: How many languages have been listed in 8th schedule of Indian constitution?
qs.e: The 8th Schedule of the Indian Constitution lists 22 languages. These languages represent the official languages of India. Originally, the Constitution had only 14 languages, but their number was increased through amendments. The 21st Amendment (1967) added Sindhi. The 71st Amendment (1992) included Konkani, Manipuri, and Nepali. The 92nd Amendment (2003) added Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, and Santhali. These languages are recognized by the Official Language Commission and Sahitya Akademi. The languages in the 8th Schedule are not part of the basic structure of the Constitution but reflect the linguistic diversity of states.
qs.kf:
☛ How many languages are currently in the 8th Schedule? → 22
☛ By which amendment was Sindhi added? → 21st Amendment (1967)
☛ Konkani, Manipuri, and Nepali were added by which amendment? → 71st Amendment (1992)
☛ Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, and Santhali were added by which amendment? → 92nd Amendment (2003)
☛ How many languages were originally in the 8th Schedule? → 14

q: In which of the following schedules the allocation of seats to the states and union territories in the Rajya Sabha is mentioned?
qs.e: The Rajya Sabha is the upper house of the Indian Parliament, consisting of representatives from states and union territories. The allocation of seats to states and union territories in the Rajya Sabha is mentioned in the Fourth Schedule of the Indian Constitution. This schedule is related to Article 4(1) and Article 80(2). Seats are allocated to states based on their population, while union territories have specific provisions. The maximum strength of the Rajya Sabha is 250 members, of which 238 represent states and union territories, and 12 are nominated by the President. The Fourth Schedule is periodically amended to reflect changes in the composition of states and union territories.
qs.kf:
☛ Schedule related to Rajya Sabha seat allocation → Fourth Schedule
☛ Maximum members in Rajya Sabha → 250
☛ Nominated members in Rajya Sabha → 12
☛ Article related to Rajya Sabha → Article 80
☛ Fourth Schedule associated with → Articles 4(1) and 80(2)

q: Which schedule of constitution gives the list of states and union territories?
qs.e: The First Schedule of the Indian Constitution provides the list of states and union territories along with their territories. It is covered under Articles 1 and 4 of the Constitution. Originally, it contained 29 states and 7 union territories, but after several amendments, there are now 28 states and 8 union territories. The Tenth Schedule deals with anti-defection law, the Second Schedule specifies salaries and allowances of the President, Governors, Chief Justice, etc., and the Seventh Schedule contains the Union, State, and Concurrent lists. Thus, the First Schedule is the correct answer as it directly lists the states and union territories.
qs.kf:
☛ What is in the First Schedule? → List and territories of states and UTs
☛ Which articles relate to the First Schedule? → Articles 1 and 4
☛ Which schedule deals with anti-defection? → Tenth Schedule
☛ What does the Second Schedule contain? → Salaries of President, Governor, etc.
☛ What is in the Seventh Schedule? → Union, State, and Concurrent lists

q: The concept of social, economic and political justice has been taken from which revolution?
qs.e: The Preamble of the Indian Constitution mentions social, economic and political justice, which is largely inspired by the Russian Revolution (1917). The Russian Revolution highlighted the struggle against exploitation, inequality and injustice, leading to the spread of communist ideology. The framers of the Indian Constitution adopted these ideals and incorporated the three dimensions of justice into the Constitution. This concept focuses on empowering weaker sections of society and ensuring equality.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the leader of the Russian Revolution? → Vladimir Lenin
☛ In which year did the Russian Revolution occur? → 1917
☛ How many types of justice are mentioned in the Preamble of the Indian Constitution? → Three (social, economic, political)
☛ By which amendment was the word 'justice' added to the Preamble? → 42nd Amendment (1976)
☛ From which revolution are the three dimensions of justice in the Indian Constitution inspired? → Russian Revolution

q: The oath or administration of state ministers comes under which schedule of the Constitution?
qs.e: The Third Schedule of the Indian Constitution contains the forms of oaths or affirmations for various office holders, such as the President, Vice President, members of the Council of Ministers, State Ministers, judges, etc. The oath format for state ministers is also included in this schedule. According to Article 164, before entering office, a state minister takes an oath in the form prescribed in the Third Schedule. This oath is administered by the Governor of the state. Therefore, the oath-taking of state ministers comes under the Third Schedule.
qs.kf:
☛ Oath of President → Third Schedule
☛ Oath of Vice President → Third Schedule
☛ Oath of Prime Minister → Third Schedule
☛ Oath of State Ministers → Third Schedule
☛ Oath of Supreme Court judges → Third Schedule

q: When was the Constituent Assembly formed in India?
qs.e: The Constituent Assembly of India was formed on 9 December 1946 under the Cabinet Mission Plan (1946). Its permanent chairman was Dr. Rajendra Prasad, while Dr. B.R. Ambedkar served as the chairman of the Drafting Committee. The assembly adopted the Constitution on 26 November 1949 and it came into effect on 26 January 1950. The assembly originally had 389 members, which reduced to 299 after the Partition in 1947. Mahatma Gandhi was not a member of the Constituent Assembly. The assembly held 11 sessions in total.
qs.kf:
☛ Date of first meeting of Constituent Assembly → 9 December 1946
☛ Permanent Chairman of Constituent Assembly → Dr. Rajendra Prasad
☛ Chairman of Drafting Committee → Dr. B.R. Ambedkar
☛ Date of adoption of Constitution → 26 November 1949
☛ Date of enforcement of Constitution → 26 January 1950

q: Business, commerce and movement within India are described in which part of the Constitution?
qs.e: Part-XIII of the Indian Constitution deals with 'Trade, Commerce and Intercourse within the territory of India'. It comprises Articles 301 to 307. Article 301 declares that trade, commerce and intercourse throughout India shall be free. However, states have the power to impose reasonable restrictions in public interest. This part ensures the free flow of goods and services across the country, promoting economic unity and national integration. Its objective is to prevent barriers to inter-state trade and maintain a single economic market. Part-IV relates to Directive Principles, Part-XI to Centre-State relations, and Part-XIV to Services under the Union and States.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 301 → Guarantees freedom of trade, commerce and intercourse throughout India.
☛ Article 302 → Allows Parliament to impose restrictions on trade in public interest.
☛ Article 303 → Prohibits states from giving discriminatory taxes or preferences.
☛ Article 304 → Allows states to impose reasonable restrictions on trade in public interest.
☛ Article 307 → Empowers Parliament to appoint authority for carrying out purposes of Articles 301-306.

q: From which Constitution, the ideas of freedom, equality and brotherhood given in the preamble of our Constitution have been taken?
qs.e: The ideas of 'liberty, equality and fraternity' in the Preamble of the Indian Constitution have been taken from the French Constitution. These three principles are derived from the ideals of the French Revolution (1789), which inspired democratic values worldwide. The framers of the Indian Constitution adopted these principles to establish a just and egalitarian society. The term 'fraternity' was added to emphasize national unity and integrity. It is noteworthy that the Concurrent List was taken from Australia, Emergency provisions from the Weimar Constitution (Germany), and Fundamental Rights from the USA.
qs.kf:
☛ Which amendment added 'Socialist' to the Indian Preamble? → 42nd Amendment (1976)
☛ From which constitution is the word 'Secular' taken in the Preamble? → US Constitution
☛ How many ideals are mentioned in the Preamble of the Indian Constitution? → Four: Justice, Liberty, Equality, Fraternity
☛ What other major element is taken from the French Constitution? → Republican system
☛ What does 'Sovereign' in the Preamble signify? → India is independent in internal and external matters

q: What is the principle policy of the state taken from the Constitution?
qs.e: The Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) in the Indian Constitution are taken from the Irish Constitution. The Irish Constitution incorporated the concept of social justice and a welfare state, which was adopted by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar in the Indian Constitution. These principles guide the government in making policies, though they are not enforceable by courts. Part IV (Articles 36-51) of the Indian Constitution contains 15 DPSP, based on Gandhian, Socialist, and Liberal-Intellectual principles. Other elements borrowed from the Irish Constitution include the method of election of the President and the nomination system. The DPSP aim to establish social and economic democracy.
qs.kf:
☛ From which country's constitution is DPSP borrowed? → Ireland
☛ Which part of the Indian Constitution deals with DPSP? → Part IV (Articles 36-51)
☛ What is the nature of DPSP? → Non-justiciable
☛ What is the main objective of DPSP? → To establish a welfare state
☛ Under which article are DPSP defined? → Article 36

q: The Constitution of India describes India as a
qs.e: Article 1 of the Constitution of India describes India as a 'Union of States'. This provision indicates that India is an indestructible union and states have no right to secede. The term 'Quasi-Federation' is often used to describe India's federal structure, but it is not mentioned in the Constitution. Terms like 'Federation of Independent States' or 'Dominion of Free States' do not correctly represent India's constitutional position. India has a federal system with a strong central government, making it a union of states that are not sovereign entities.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 1 → Describes India as 'Union of States'.
☛ Indian Constitution → Adopted on 26 November 1949.
☛ India's federal structure → A federation with unitary bias.
☛ Quasi-Federal → Term used by K. C. Wheare for India.
☛ States in India → 28 states and 8 union territories.

q: The Federal Court of India was setup in the year________
qs.e: The Federal Court of India was established in 1937 under the provisions of the Government of India Act 1935, which laid the foundation for a federal structure in India. The court was located in Delhi and initially consisted of a Chief Justice and six other judges. Its primary functions were to adjudicate disputes between provinces and the central government and to hear constitutional matters. The Federal Court played a crucial role in the development of India's judicial system. On 26 January 1950, when the Constitution of India came into effect, the Federal Court was replaced by the Supreme Court of India.
qs.kf:
☛ Federal Court of India established → 1937
☛ Constitution under which Federal Court was set up → Government of India Act 1935
☛ Location of Federal Court → Delhi
☛ Number of judges initially → Chief Justice + 6 judges
☛ Replaced by Supreme Court on → 26 January 1950

q: What kind of fraternity has been ensured in the preamble of the Indian Constitution?
o: Integrity and integrity of the person's dignity and nation
qs.e: The Preamble of the Indian Constitution uses the term 'fraternity' to foster a sense of brotherhood among all citizens. This fraternity aims to ensure the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the nation. The Preamble declares India as a sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic republic, guaranteeing justice, liberty, equality, and fraternity to its citizens. Fraternity implies mutual brotherhood and unity, which strengthens individual dignity and national unity and integrity. This is also reflected in the Fundamental Duties of the Constitution. The Preamble is considered the soul of the Constitution and is a key to understanding its philosophy.
qs.kf:
☛ Objective of fraternity in Preamble → Dignity of individual and unity & integrity of nation
☛ Words in Preamble → Sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic, republic
☛ Preamble adopted on → 26 November 1949
☛ Fraternity mentioned → In the concluding part of Preamble
☛ Types of justice in Preamble → Social, economic, political

q: The ideals of Liberty, Equality and Fraternity enshrined in the Constitution of India are borrowed from the constitution of ______.
qs.e: The ideals of Liberty, Equality and Fraternity in the Indian Constitution are borrowed from the French Constitution. These principles emerged during the French Revolution (1789) and were later enshrined in France's constitution. India incorporated them into the Preamble of its Constitution. These three principles are part of the basic structure of the constitution and are protected by the judiciary. Other elements borrowed from France include the republican form of government and the ideals of the Preamble. From Japan, India took the concept of procedure established by law; from the United States, Fundamental Rights; and from the Soviet Union, the Directive Principles of State Policy.
qs.kf:
☛ From which constitution are Liberty, Equality and Fraternity borrowed? → France
☛ From which country are Fundamental Rights borrowed? → USA
☛ From which country are Directive Principles borrowed? → USSR
☛ From which country is Procedure Established by Law borrowed? → Japan
☛ Which part of the Indian Constitution is influenced by France? → Preamble ideals

q: Who was the chairman of the Constitution Drafting Committee?
qs.e: The Chairman of the Drafting Committee of the Indian Constitution was Dr. B. R. Ambedkar. He was elected to this post by the Constituent Assembly on 29 August 1947. The committee had seven members including Ambedkar as chairman, N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar, Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar, K. M. Munshi, Syed Mohammad Saadulla, B. L. Mitter, and D. P. Khaitan. Later, N. Madhava Rao replaced B. L. Mitter. The Constituent Assembly adopted the Constitution on 26 November 1949, and it came into effect on 26 January 1950. Ambedkar is widely regarded as the chief architect of the Indian Constitution.
qs.kf:
☛ Chairman of Drafting Committee → Dr. B. R. Ambedkar
☛ Total members in Drafting Committee → 7
☛ First meeting of Constituent Assembly → 9 December 1946
☛ Date of adoption of Constitution → 26 November 1949
☛ Date of enforcement of Constitution → 26 January 1950

q: The directive principles of state policy in Indian’s constitution are borrowed from the constitution of ____.
qs.e: The directive principles of state policy (DPSP) in the Indian Constitution are borrowed from the Constitution of Ireland. These principles guide the government in policy-making but are not judicially enforceable. DPSP aims to establish social and economic democracy. They are enshrined in Part IV (Articles 36-51) of the Indian Constitution. Inspired by Ireland, Dr. B.R. Ambedkar described them as the 'conscience of the Constitution'. The main objective of DPSP is to establish a welfare state. These principles help the government achieve goals like social justice, economic equality, and freedom from exploitation.
qs.kf:
☛ Source of DPSP → Ireland
☛ Part IV of Indian Constitution → Articles 36-51
☛ Nature of DPSP → Non-justiciable but guiding
☛ Main objective of DPSP → Welfare state
☛ Inspiration for DPSP → Constitution of Ireland

q: When did the Constituent Assembly of India meet for the first time?
qs.e: The first meeting of the Constituent Assembly of India was held on 9th December 1946 in New Delhi. It was chaired by Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha, the interim president of the assembly. Later, Dr. Rajendra Prasad was elected as the permanent president. The Constituent Assembly was formed under the Cabinet Mission Plan. It had a total of 389 members, of which 296 were elected from provincial assemblies and 93 represented princely states. The Muslim League boycotted the first meeting. The assembly adopted the Constitution on 26th November 1949 and it came into effect on 26th January 1950.
qs.kf:
☛ Interim President of Constituent Assembly → Sachchidananda Sinha
☛ Permanent President of Constituent Assembly → Rajendra Prasad
☛ Plan under which Constituent Assembly was formed → Cabinet Mission Plan
☛ Total members in Constituent Assembly → 389
☛ Date of adoption of Constitution → 26th November 1949

q: The idea of a Constituent Assembly was given by:
qs.e: The idea of a Constituent Assembly was first proposed by M.N Roy in 1934. He was a prominent Indian revolutionary, philosopher, and political activist. Later, in 1935, the Indian National Congress formally adopted this idea. The Constituent Assembly was formed in 1946 under the Cabinet Mission Plan. Dr. Rajendra Prasad served as its President, B.R. Ambedkar was the Chairman of the Drafting Committee, and Maulana Azad was a freedom fighter. M.N Roy was the first to demand a Constituent Assembly for India.
qs.kf:
☛ Who proposed the idea of Constituent Assembly? → M.N Roy
☛ Who was the President of Constituent Assembly? → Dr. Rajendra Prasad
☛ Who chaired the Drafting Committee? → B.R. Ambedkar
☛ When was Constituent Assembly formed? → 1946
☛ M.N Roy was associated with which movement? → Indian revolutionary movement

q: Indian Constitution was adopted by the constituent assembly on-
qs.e: The Indian Constitution was adopted by the Constituent Assembly on 26 November 1949. This day is celebrated as Constitution Day. The Constituent Assembly held its first meeting on 9 December 1946. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar was the chairman of the Drafting Committee. The Constitution came into effect on 26 January 1950, celebrated as Republic Day. On 26 November 1949, the Assembly adopted and signed the Constitution. The entire process took 2 years, 11 months, and 18 days.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the first meeting of the Constituent Assembly? → 9 December 1946
☛ Who was the President of the Constituent Assembly? → Dr. Rajendra Prasad
☛ Who was the Chairman of the Drafting Committee? → Dr. B.R. Ambedkar
☛ When did the Constitution come into force? → 26 January 1950
☛ How long did it take to draft the Constitution? → 2 years, 11 months, 18 days

q: The Constitution of India is republic, because it-
qs.e: India is called a republic because the head of the state (the President) is not a hereditary position but an elected one. A republic is defined by the absence of hereditary rule and the election of the head of state. Other options such as adult franchise, a bill of rights, or an elected parliament are features of democracy, not specifically of a republic. The Constitution of India came into effect on 26 January 1950, establishing India as a sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic republic. The President is elected by an electoral college, ensuring that the head of state is chosen by the people, not by birth.
qs.kf:
☛ Key feature of a republic → Head of state is not hereditary
☛ Election of President in India → Indirectly elected by an electoral college
☛ Indian Constitution enacted on → 26 January 1950
☛ Difference between democracy and republic → Democracy: rule by people; Republic: elected head of state
☛ Citizenship in India → Single citizenship is provided

q: Which of the following Indian Presidents served the longest in office?
qs.e: India's first President Dr. Rajendra Prasad served the longest in office. He was in office from 26 January 1950 to 13 May 1962, for nearly 12 years. He is the only President to serve two full terms, having been re-elected in 1957. Dr. Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan served from 1962 to 1967 (5 years). R. Venkatraman served from 1987 to 1992 (5 years). Dr. Shankar Dayal Sharma served from 1992 to 1997 (5 years). Thus, Dr. Rajendra Prasad's tenure is the longest.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the first President of India? → Dr. Rajendra Prasad
☛ Who served as President for the longest duration? → Dr. Rajendra Prasad (nearly 12 years)
☛ Who is the only President to complete two terms? → Dr. Rajendra Prasad
☛ What was Dr. Rajendra Prasad's tenure? → 1950-1962
☛ When did Dr. Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan serve as President? → 1962-1967

q: Who succeeded Rajendra Prasad as the President of India?
qs.e: Dr. Rajendra Prasad was the first President of India, serving two full terms from 1950 to 1962. He was succeeded by Dr. Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan, who was elected President in 1962. Radhakrishnan was a renowned philosopher and educationist, and also served as India's first Vice President. He held the office of President from 1962 to 1967. His birthday on 5th September is celebrated as Teacher's Day in India. V.V. Giri became President in 1969, Giani Zail Singh in 1982, and N. Sanjiva Reddy in 1977. Thus, the correct successor to Rajendra Prasad was Radhakrishnan.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the first President of India? → Rajendra Prasad
☛ Who was the first Vice President of India? → Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan
☛ When is Teacher's Day celebrated in India? → 5th September
☛ Who was the second President of India? → Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan
☛ How many terms did Rajendra Prasad serve? → Two

q: Who presided over the inaugural meeting of the Constituent Assembly of India?
qs.e: The first meeting of the Constituent Assembly of India was held on 9 December 1946. It was presided over by Sachchidananda Sinha, who was the oldest member at that time. Later, on 11 December 1946, Dr. Rajendra Prasad was elected as the permanent chairman. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar was the chairman of the Drafting Committee, while P. Upendra was another member. Thus, Sachchidananda Sinha presided over the inaugural meeting.
qs.kf:
☛ Date of first Constituent Assembly meeting → 9 December 1946
☛ Permanent chairman of Constituent Assembly → Dr. Rajendra Prasad
☛ Chairman of the Drafting Committee → Dr. B.R. Ambedkar
☛ Temporary chairman of Constituent Assembly → Sachchidananda Sinha
☛ Total meetings of Constituent Assembly → 166 days over 11 sessions

q: The Constitution of India came into force on ______?
qs.e: The Constitution of India was adopted on 26 November 1949 but came into force on 26 January 1950. This date was chosen to commemorate the declaration of Purna Swaraj (complete independence) made by the Indian National Congress in 1930. With its enforcement, India became a sovereign, democratic republic. This day is celebrated as Republic Day. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar played a key role in drafting the Constitution. The original Constitution had 395 articles and 8 schedules.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Indian Constitution adopted? → 26 November 1949
☛ When is Republic Day celebrated? → 26 January
☛ Who was the President of the Constituent Assembly? → Dr. Rajendra Prasad
☛ Who was the Chairman of the Drafting Committee? → Dr. B.R. Ambedkar
☛ What did India become when the Constitution came into force? → Sovereign Democratic Republic

q: Which country has the longest written constitution in the world?
qs.e: India has the longest written constitution in the world. It was adopted by the Constituent Assembly on 26 November 1949 and came into effect on 26 January 1950. Originally it had 395 articles, 8 schedules and 22 parts, now it has 448 articles, 12 schedules and 25 parts. The constitution draws inspiration from various constitutions of the world, so it is often called a 'bag of borrowings'. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar was the chairman of the Drafting Committee of the Constituent Assembly.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Indian constitution adopted? → 26 November 1949
☛ When did the Indian constitution come into force? → 26 January 1950
☛ Who was the chairman of the Drafting Committee? → Dr. B.R. Ambedkar
☛ How many articles are there currently in the Indian constitution? → 448
☛ What is the Indian constitution known as? → Bag of Borrowings

q: Who among the following was NOT the member of Draft Committee of the Indian Constitution?
qs.e: The Draft Committee of the Indian Constitution was formed on 29 August 1947 under the chairmanship of Dr. B. R. Ambedkar. Its members included Dr. K. M. Munshi, Mr. N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar, Syed Mohammad Saadullah, Mr. Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar, Mr. B. L. Mitter, and Mr. N. Madhav Rao (who replaced B. L. Mitter). A. V. Thakkar was not a member of the Draft Committee. He was a member of the Constituent Assembly and served on other committees such as the Advisory Committee and the Minorities Sub-Committee. Therefore, A. V. Thakkar was not a member of the Draft Committee.
qs.kf:

☛ How many members were in the Draft Committee initially? → 7 members
☛ Who replaced B. L. Mitter? → N. Madhav Rao
☛ Which committees was A. V. Thakkar a member of? → Advisory Committee and Minorities Sub-Committee
☛ When was the Draft Committee formed? → 29 August 1947

q: Who was the President of the Constituent Assembly of India after independence?
qs.e: The Constituent Assembly of India was formed in 1946, and its President was Dr. Rajendra Prasad. He was elected to this post on 11 December 1946. The Assembly adopted the Constitution on 26 November 1949, which came into effect on 26 January 1950. Dr. Rajendra Prasad later became the first President of India. The Assembly held a total of 11 sessions. Dr. B. R. Ambedkar was the Chairman of the Drafting Committee, not the President of the Assembly. C. Rajgopalachari was a freedom fighter and Acharya Narendra Dev was a socialist leader.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the temporary President of the Constituent Assembly? → Sachchidananda Sinha
☛ When was the first meeting of the Constituent Assembly? → 9 December 1946
☛ Who was the Chairman of the Drafting Committee? → Dr. B. R. Ambedkar
☛ Who was the first President of India? → Dr. Rajendra Prasad
☛ What was the total number of members in the Constituent Assembly? → 389

q: In 1930, who organised the Dalits into the Depressed Classes Association and demanded separate electorates for them?
qs.e: In 1930, Dr. B.R. Ambedkar organised the Depressed Classes (Dalits) into the Depressed Classes Association to work for their social and political upliftment. He demanded separate electorates for Dalits, arguing that they needed independent political representation due to caste-based discrimination. This demand was a major point of contention with Mahatma Gandhi, who opposed separate electorates fearing division of Hindu society. The issue was resolved in the Poona Pact (1932), where Ambedkar agreed to reserved seats instead of separate electorates. Ambedkar's efforts focused on ensuring Dalits had a voice in the political process and access to education and employment.
qs.kf:
☛ Who founded the Depressed Classes Association? → BR Ambedkar
☛ Who demanded separate electorates for Dalits in 1930? → BR Ambedkar
☛ When was the Poona Pact signed? → 1932
☛ What was the outcome of the Poona Pact? → Reserved seats for Dalits
☛ Why is BR Ambedkar considered the leader of Dalits? → For his fight for social justice

q: How many parts are there in the Constitution of India as of October 2020?
qs.e: As of October 2020, the Constitution of India has 25 parts. The number of parts has increased over time through amendments. The original Constitution had 22 parts. After the 73rd and 74th Amendments (1992), Part IX (Panchayats) and Part IXA (Municipalities) were added, making it 24 parts. Subsequently, the 100th Amendment (2015) added Part IVA (Fundamental Duties), raising the total to 25. Currently, the Constitution consists of 25 parts, 448 articles, and 12 schedules. It is important to note that Parts do not include the Preamble or the Schedules.
qs.kf:
☛ Number of parts in original Constitution → 22
☛ Part added by 73rd Amendment → Part IX (Panchayats)
☛ Part added by 74th Amendment → Part IXA (Municipalities)
☛ Part added by 100th Amendment → Part IVA (Fundamental Duties)
☛ Total articles in current Constitution → 448 (originally 395)

q: In the Unitary States, the _______ government performs all the governmental functions.
qs.e: A unitary state is a system of government where all powers are concentrated in the central government. In such states, the central government performs all governmental functions, and administrative units (like states or provinces) are subordinate to the center. Examples include the United Kingdom, France, Japan, and China. In contrast, federal states (like India and the USA) divide powers between the central and state governments.
qs.kf:
☛ Where does supreme power reside in a unitary state? → Central government
☛ Examples of unitary states? → UK, France, Japan, China
☛ What type of state is India? → Federal state
☛ Constitution in a unitary state? → Single constitution
☛ Citizenship in a unitary state? → Single citizenship

q: How many articles are there in the Constitution of India as of October 2020?
qs.e: The Constitution of India originally had 395 articles divided into 22 parts and 8 schedules. Over time, amendments have increased the number of articles. As of October 2020, the Constitution contains 448 articles, organized into 25 parts and 12 schedules. This increase is due to various amendment acts that added new articles and modified existing ones. Despite having 448 articles currently, the original 395-article structure still serves as the foundation.
qs.kf:
☛ Original number of articles in Indian Constitution → 395
☛ Total articles as of October 2020 → 448
☛ Total parts of the Constitution → 25
☛ Total schedules of the Constitution → 12
☛ Part added by the latest amendment → Part IXB (Cooperative Societies)

q: Who chaired the commission that drafted the Indian Penal code which was enacted in 1860?
qs.e: The Indian Penal Code (IPC) was enacted in 1860. It was drafted by the First Law Commission chaired by Lord Macaulay (Thomas Babington Macaulay). The commission was established in 1833, and the draft was completed in 1837. However, due to various reasons, its implementation was delayed until 1860. The IPC came into effect on 1 January 1862. It is the foundational criminal code of India, largely based on English law principles. Macaulay's draft was comprehensive and served as the basis for criminal law in several other British colonies as well.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the IPC enacted? → 1860
☛ When did the IPC come into effect? → 1 January 1862
☛ Which commission drafted the IPC? → First Law Commission
☛ Who was the chairman of the First Law Commission? → Lord Macaulay
☛ What was the Act number of IPC? → Act No. 45 of 1860

q: Which Schedule of the Indian Constitution makes provision for the division of powers between Union and the States?
qs.e: The Seventh Schedule of the Indian Constitution provides for the division of legislative powers between the Union and the States. It contains three lists: the Union List (subjects under the exclusive jurisdiction of the Centre), the State List (subjects under the exclusive jurisdiction of States), and the Concurrent List (subjects on which both can legislate). This division reflects the federal character of the Constitution and ensures a clear demarcation of authority between the two levels of government. The Union List has 100 subjects (now 97), the State List 61 (now 66), and the Concurrent List 52 subjects.
qs.kf:
☛ Which part of the Constitution deals with Union-State relations? → Part XI (Articles 245-263)
☛ Which Schedule of the Constitution deals with land reforms? → Ninth Schedule
☛ Which Schedule of the Constitution deals with languages? → Eighth Schedule
☛ Which Schedule of the Constitution deals with allocation of seats in the Rajya Sabha? → Fourth Schedule
☛ Which Schedule of the Constitution deals with oaths? → Third Schedule

q: In which year did the Constitution of India come into force?
qs.e: The Constitution of India was adopted by the Constituent Assembly on 26 November 1949, but it came into full effect on 26 January 1950. This day is celebrated as Republic Day. With the enforcement of the Constitution, India became a sovereign, democratic republic. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar was appointed as the chairman of the Drafting Committee. The making of the Constitution took 2 years, 11 months, and 18 days. It is the longest written constitution in the world.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Constitution adopted by the Constituent Assembly? → 26 November 1949
☛ When is Republic Day celebrated? → 26 January
☛ Who was the chairman of the Drafting Committee? → Dr. B.R. Ambedkar
☛ How long did it take to frame the Indian Constitution? → 2 years, 11 months, 18 days
☛ What did India become after adopting the Constitution? → Sovereign democratic republic

q: The Constitution of India provides for a ________ structure of governance in the form of Parliamentary Democracy both at the Centre and the State.
qs.e: The Constitution of India provides for a federal structure of governance, with a division of powers between the Centre and the States. It operates as a parliamentary democracy, where the executive is responsible to the legislature. Key federal features include single citizenship, a written constitution, and a supreme court. However, it also contains unitary elements like central dominance and an integrated judiciary, often making it described as quasi-federal. Nevertheless, the fundamental structure remains federal, ensuring governance at two levels.
qs.kf:
☛ What type of governance structure does the Indian Constitution provide? → Federal
☛ Which system is the Supreme Court of India a part of? → Integrated judiciary
☛ Where is the division of powers between Centre and States found? → Federal system
☛ What type of citizenship does India have? → Single citizenship
☛ How is India often described in terms of its federal structure? → Quasi-federal state

q: Which of the following provinces had maximum representation in the constituent assembly of India as on 31st December, 1947?
qs.e: As of 31st December, 1947, the United Provinces (now Uttar Pradesh) had the maximum representation in the Constituent Assembly of India. The Constituent Assembly was formed under the Cabinet Mission Plan of 1946, with seats allocated to provinces in proportion to their population. The United Provinces, being the most populous province at that time, was allotted 55 seats. Other provinces had fewer seats: Madras had 49, Bombay had 21, and West Bengal had 19. Thus, the United Provinces had the highest representation. The Assembly was chaired by Dr. Rajendra Prasad, and the Drafting Committee was led by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar.
qs.kf:
☛ What was the total number of seats in the Constituent Assembly in 1946? → 389 (296 provinces + 93 princely states)
☛ When was the first meeting of the Constituent Assembly? → 9 December, 1946
☛ Who was the interim president of the Constituent Assembly? → Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha
☛ Who became the permanent president of the Constituent Assembly? → Dr. Rajendra Prasad
☛ How many seats were allotted to United Provinces? → 55

q: What was the total time taken to draft the Constitution of India?
qs.e: The Constitution of India was finalized on 26 November 1949. Its drafting began on 9 December 1946, when the first meeting of the Constituent Assembly was held. In total, it took 2 years, 11 months and 18 days to draft the Constitution. During this period, the Constituent Assembly held 11 sessions. The President of the Constituent Assembly was Dr. Rajendra Prasad, while the Chairman of the Drafting Committee was Dr. B.R. Ambedkar. The Constitution came into effect on 26 January 1950, celebrated as Republic Day. The original Constitution had 395 articles and 8 schedules.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the first meeting of the Constituent Assembly held? → 9 December 1946
☛ When was the Constitution finally adopted? → 26 November 1949
☛ When did the Constitution come into effect? → 26 January 1950
☛ Who was the President of the Constituent Assembly? → Dr. Rajendra Prasad
☛ Who was the Chairman of the Drafting Committee? → Dr. B.R. Ambedkar

q: The reason for the Constitution of India to be republican is that it:
qs.e: The Constitution of India is republican because it provides for an elected Head of State (the President) who is not hereditary. A republic means the head of state is elected. In India, the President is indirectly elected, which reflects the republican character. Adult franchise and a bill of rights are democratic elements, not exclusively republican. Absence of hereditary elements is also a feature, but the key reason is the provision for an elected President. Hence, the correct answer is provides for an elected President. The option in the question mentions 'elected Parliament' which is incorrect; Parliament is the legislature, not the head of state. The republican nature is defined by the head of state being elected.
qs.kf:
☛ How is the President of India elected? → Indirectly by an electoral college
☛ What is the definition of a republic? → A state where the head of state is elected
☛ Where are hereditary elements absent in India? → In the office of the President
☛ Which Article provides for the President in the Indian Constitution? → Article 52
☛ Difference between democracy and republic? → Democracy is rule by the people; republic has an elected head of state

q: Who was appointed as the Constitutional Advisor (Legal Advisor) of the Constituent Assembly?
qs.e: B. N. Rau was appointed as the Constitutional Advisor (Legal Advisor) of the Constituent Assembly. He was a distinguished civil servant and jurist who played a crucial role in drafting the Indian Constitution. He provided legal advice to the Assembly and prepared various drafts. Later, he became a judge at the International Court of Justice in the United Nations. B. R. Ambedkar was the Chairman of the Drafting Committee, while S. N. Mukherjee and H. V. R. Iyengar were other office bearers.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the Constitutional Advisor of the Constituent Assembly? → B. N. Rau
☛ Who was the Chairman of the Drafting Committee? → B. R. Ambedkar
☛ Who was the temporary President of the Constituent Assembly? → Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha
☛ Who was the permanent President of the Constituent Assembly? → Dr. Rajendra Prasad
☛ When was the Constituent Assembly formed? → 1946

q: Who was the Chief Architect of the Constitution of India?
qs.e: The Chief Architect of the Constitution of India was Dr. B.R. Ambedkar. He served as the Chairman of the Drafting Committee of the Constituent Assembly and played a pivotal role in drafting the Indian Constitution. The Constituent Assembly was formed in 1946, and its first meeting was held on 9 December 1946. Dr. Ambedkar was appointed as the Chairman of the Drafting Committee on 29 August 1947. He presented the final draft of the Constitution to the Assembly on 4 November 1948. The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came into effect on 26 January 1950. Dr. Ambedkar is widely regarded as the Father or Chief Architect of the Indian Constitution for his immense contribution.

☛ Date of enforcement of Constitution → 26 January 1950

q: Who, in contempt of the 'Drafting Committee', addressed it with a new word 'Drifting Committee'?
qs.e: During the Indian Constituent Assembly debates, Naziruddin Ahmed criticized the Drafting Committee and referred to it as the 'Drifting Committee' to mock its slow progress and lack of clarity. He was a member of the Constituent Assembly and belonged to the Muslim League. The committee was chaired by Dr. B. R. Ambedkar. Ahmed actively participated in discussions and proposed several amendments to the Constitution. His remark is recorded in the official proceedings of the Assembly. This incident highlights the intense debates and diverse viewpoints during the framing of the Indian Constitution.

☛ Which party did Naziruddin Ahmed belong to? → Muslim League

q: Drafting committe was established in the ____ year to draft the constitution.
qs.e: The Drafting Committee for drafting the Indian Constitution was established on 29 August 1947. The committee was chaired by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar. It took 2 months and 15 days to prepare the draft. The draft was presented to the Constituent Assembly on 21 February 1948. The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came into effect on 26 January 1950.

q: What is the number of schedules in the Constitution of India?
qs.e: The Constitution of India originally had 8 schedules, but after amendments, the number increased to 12. Currently, there are 12 schedules in the Constitution. These schedules deal with various administrative and constitutional aspects, such as territories of states and union territories, allocation of seats in the Rajya Sabha, lists of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, languages, land reforms, and forms of oaths. The 12th Schedule was added by the 74th Amendment (1992), which relates to municipalities. The 11th Schedule was added by the 73rd Amendment (1992), which relates to Panchayati Raj. These schedules are an integral part of the Constitution.
qs.kf:
☛ Current number of schedules in the Constitution of India → 12
☛ 12th Schedule deals with → Municipalities
☛ 11th Schedule deals with → Panchayati Raj
☛ Number of schedules in the original Constitution → 8
☛ 9th Schedule deals with → Land reforms and laws

q: The constitution of India describes India as ___________.
qs.e: The Constitution of India, in its Article 1, describes India as a 'Union of States'. This phrase indicates that India is an indestructible entity and the states have no right to secede. The term 'Union' was deliberately chosen to emphasize the unitary character of the Indian polity, although the government is federal in structure. The Constituent Assembly avoided the term 'Federation' because India is a multi-ethnic and multi-linguistic nation, where the central government is given more powers. The Constitution of India describes the country as a 'Union of States', not as a 'federal state' or 'quasi-federal'.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Article of the Indian Constitution describes India as a 'Union of States'? → Article 1
☛ From which country's constitution is the term 'Union of States' borrowed? → Canada
☛ Why is India called a 'Union of States'? → Because states have no right to secede
☛ Which part of the Indian Constitution deals with the Union and its territories? → Part 1
☛ Which Article defines the names and territories of states? → Article 3

q: The structural part of the Constitution of India is taken from ________.
qs.e: The structural part of the Constitution of India is mainly taken from the Government of India Act, 1935. This Act provided the federal structure, powers of the Governor, organization of the judiciary, and the Public Service Commission. The Constituent Assembly adopted many provisions of the 1935 Act, such as the federal system, provincial autonomy, and judicial review. However, the Constitution also incorporated democratic principles and fundamental rights, which were different from the 1935 Act. This Act is a milestone in India's constitutional development and shaped the administrative framework of the Constitution.
qs.kf:
☛ Constitutional provision taken from Government of India Act, 1935 → Federal structure, powers of Governor
☛ Main objective of Government of India Act, 1935 → Establish federal government in India
☛ Source of India's Constitution → Government of India Act, 1935
☛ Main provision of Government of India Act, 1919 → Dyarchy (Dual government)
☛ Feature of Government of India Act, 1909 → Morley-Minto Reforms

q: Constitution of India ________.
qs.e: The Constitution of India is the longest written constitution in the world. It was adopted by the Constituent Assembly on 26 November 1949 and came into effect on 26 January 1950. The original constitution had 395 articles, 22 parts, and 8 schedules. After amendments, it now has over 470 articles, 25 parts, and 12 schedules. It is a written document, not unwritten or pictorial. The United Kingdom has an unwritten constitution, whereas India's constitution is detailed and written. It is based on a federal system and includes Fundamental Rights, Directive Principles of State Policy, and Fundamental Duties.
qs.kf:
☛ What is the size of the Indian Constitution? → World's longest written constitution
☛ When did the Indian Constitution come into effect? → 26 January 1950
☛ How many articles in the original constitution? → 395
☛ How many parts are there currently? → 25
☛ What type of constitution is India's? → Written, supreme, and longest

q: Who was the calligraphist of the Constitution of India?
qs.e: The calligraphist of the Indian Constitution was Prem Bihari Narayan Riyazada. He handwrote the original manuscript of the Constitution in both English and Hindi. The decoration and illustration of the Constitution were done by Nand Lal Bose. Riyazada was a renowned artist and calligrapher who gave a beautiful form to this historic document. The Constitution of India was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came into effect on 26 January 1950. It is the longest written constitution in the world, originally containing 395 articles and 8 schedules (currently over 470 articles and 12 schedules). The President of the Constituent Assembly was Dr. Rajendra Prasad, while the Chairman of the Drafting Committee was Dr. B.R. Ambedkar.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the calligraphist of the Indian Constitution? → Prem Bihari Narayan Riyazada
☛ Who decorated the Constitution? → Nand Lal Bose
☛ Who was the President of the Constituent Assembly? → Dr. Rajendra Prasad
☛ Who was the Chairman of the Drafting Committee? → Dr. B.R. Ambedkar
☛ When did the Constitution come into effect? → 26 January 1950

q: What is the schedule of Indian Constitution related to anti-defection law?
qs.e: The Tenth Schedule of the Indian Constitution contains the Anti-Defection Law. It was added by the 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act in 1985. This schedule lays down provisions for disqualification of members of Parliament and state legislatures on grounds of defection. The main objective is to maintain political stability and prevent defections in democracy. According to the Tenth Schedule, a member can be disqualified if they voluntarily give up membership of their political party or vote against the party whip. However, the decision on defection lies with the Speaker or Chairman, which is final.
qs.kf:
☛ Which schedule contains the Anti-Defection Law? → Tenth Schedule
☛ Which amendment added the Tenth Schedule? → 52nd Amendment
☛ Who decides on defection cases? → Speaker or Chairman
☛ In which year was the Anti-Defection Law enacted? → 1985
☛ Where are provisions for disqualification on defection? → Tenth Schedule of the Constitution

q: Indian type of socialism is-
qs.e: Indian socialism is based on Democratic Socialism, which adapts socialist principles within a democratic framework. It is enshrined in the Preamble of the Indian Constitution and implemented through Planning Commission and Five-Year Plans. The aim of Indian socialism is to achieve economic equality and social justice, while respecting private property and individual freedom. It differs from Marxist socialism as it emphasizes gradual reform rather than violent revolution. Indian democratic socialism is influenced by Gandhian and Nehruvian ideologies.
qs.kf:
☛ What type of socialism is adopted in the Indian Constitution? → Democratic Socialism
☛ What is the main objective of socialism in India? → Economic equality and social justice
☛ Through which mechanism was socialism implemented in India? → Planning Commission and Five-Year Plans
☛ Which ideologies influenced Indian socialism? → Gandhian and Nehruvian ideologies
☛ What is respected in Indian socialism? → Private property and individual freedom

q: The word 'fraternity' word in the Indian Constitution means-
qs.e: The word 'fraternity' in the Preamble of the Indian Constitution means 'the spirit of brotherhood'. It represents one of the core objectives of the Constitution, aiming to foster unity and integrity among all citizens. The concept was strongly advocated by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, who believed it was essential for social equality and justice. The Constituent Assembly was inspired by the French ideals of 'Liberty, Equality, Fraternity' while incorporating it. Fraternity goes beyond personal relationships and symbolizes national unity and inclusiveness. It binds all Indians together, transcending caste, religion, or region. This spirit is crucial for maintaining the democratic fabric of the nation and ensuring that all citizens feel a sense of belonging and mutual respect.
qs.kf:
☛ From which language is the word 'fraternity' derived? → French
☛ What is the objective of fraternity? → To establish brotherhood and unity among all citizens
☛ How many objectives are in the Preamble? → Four: Justice, Liberty, Equality, Fraternity
☛ Why did Dr. Ambedkar emphasize fraternity? → For social equality and national unity
☛ In which Article does 'fraternity' appear? → In the Preamble, not in any Article

q: New words of 'socialist, secular and integrity' have been added in the preamble of the Constitution _____________.
qs.e: The words 'socialist', 'secular' and 'integrity' were added to the Preamble of the Indian Constitution by the 42nd Constitution Amendment Act, 1976. This amendment was enacted during the Emergency period under the government of Prime Minister Indira Gandhi. It changed the description of India from 'sovereign democratic republic' to 'sovereign socialist secular democratic republic' and replaced 'unity of the Nation' with 'unity and integrity of the Nation'. The 42nd Amendment is the most comprehensive amendment to the Indian Constitution, containing 59 clauses, and is often referred to as the 'Mini-Constitution'. It also added the Fundamental Duties and strengthened the executive over the judiciary.
qs.kf:
☛ Which three words were added to the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment? → Socialist, Secular, Integrity
☛ In which year was the 42nd Amendment passed? → 1976
☛ Under whose prime ministership was the 42nd Amendment enacted? → Indira Gandhi
☛ By what name is the 42nd Amendment popularly known? → Mini-Constitution
☛ What was 'unity of the Nation' changed to in the Preamble? → Unity and integrity of the Nation

q: The characteristics of the "Fundamental Rights" are taken from _______.
qs.e: The characteristics of Fundamental Rights in the Indian Constitution are taken from the Constitution of the United States. The US Constitution includes the Bill of Rights, which guarantees freedoms such as speech, religion, and judicial review. India incorporated these rights in Part III of its Constitution. These rights are justiciable, meaning citizens can approach the Supreme Court or High Courts for enforcement. Other features borrowed from the US Constitution include judicial review, impeachment procedure, and presidential powers. Thus, the concept of Fundamental Rights in India is primarily inspired by the US Constitution.
qs.kf:
☛ Fundamental Rights borrowed from? → USA Constitution
☛ Judicial Review borrowed from? → USA Constitution
☛ Fundamental Rights in which Part of Indian Constitution? → Part III
☛ Which part of US Constitution deals with rights? → Bill of Rights
☛ Where can citizens go for violation of Fundamental Rights? → Supreme Court or High Court

q: Who is the chairman of the draft committee set up in 1947?
qs.e: In 1947, a Drafting Committee was set up to prepare the draft of the Indian Constitution. The chairman of this committee was Dr. B.R. Ambedkar. He is known as the chief architect of the Indian Constitution. The Drafting Committee had a total of seven members. Dr. Ambedkar presented the draft in the Constituent Assembly and led detailed discussions on every article. His tireless efforts ensured that the Constitution was completed on time. He headed one of the most important committees of the Constituent Assembly.
qs.kf:
☛ Who is the chief architect of the Indian Constitution? → Dr. B.R. Ambedkar
☛ Who was the chairman of the Drafting Committee? → Dr. B.R. Ambedkar
☛ How many members were there in the Drafting Committee? → 7
☛ Who was the temporary president of the Constituent Assembly? → Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha
☛ Who was the permanent president of the Constituent Assembly? → Dr. Rajendra Prasad

q: The word 'socialist' was added to the preamble of the Indian Constitution-
qs.e: The word 'socialist' was added to the Preamble of the Indian Constitution by the 42nd Amendment Act of 1976. This amendment was passed during the Emergency (1975-77) under the leadership of Prime Minister Indira Gandhi. Along with 'socialist', the words 'secular' and 'integrity' were also added to the Preamble through the same amendment. The addition of 'socialist' aimed to orient the state towards socialist principles, emphasizing economic equality and social justice. Before this, the Preamble described India only as a 'Sovereign Democratic Republic'. The 42nd Amendment is considered one of the most comprehensive amendments to the Indian Constitution.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the word 'secular' added to the Preamble? → In 1976 (by 42nd Amendment)
☛ Which year was the 42nd Constitutional Amendment passed? → 1976
☛ When was the word 'integrity' added to the Preamble? → In 1976
☛ What was the purpose of adding 'socialist' to the Preamble? → To orient the state towards socialist policies
☛ Which major amendment was enacted during Indira Gandhi's tenure? → The 42nd Amendment
