q: Nehru asserted that the Constituent Assembly derived its strength primarily from
o: the will of the Indian people
qs.e: Jawaharlal Nehru asserted that the strength of the Constituent Assembly came from the will of the Indian people, not from British laws or western revolutions. He emphasized that the Assembly drew its legitimacy from the support of the masses, reflecting the democratic spirit of India's freedom struggle. The Constituent Assembly was formed in 1946 under the Cabinet Mission Plan. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar served as the Chairman of the Drafting Committee. Nehru's statement highlights that the Constitution's authority is rooted in the sovereignty of the people. This idea resonated with the Objective Resolution, which later formed the basis of the Preamble to the Constitution.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the first meeting of the Constituent Assembly held? → 9 December 1946
☛ Who was the interim President of the Constituent Assembly? → Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha
☛ How many members were in the Constituent Assembly initially? → 389 (in 1946)
☛ When was the Indian Constitution adopted? → 26 November 1949
☛ In which speech did Nehru make this statement? → Objective Resolution

q: The concept of Directive Principles of the Indian constitution is borrowed from the Constitution of which country?
qs.e: The Directive Principles of State Policy enshrined in Part IV of the Indian Constitution are borrowed from the Constitution of Ireland. The Irish Constitution also contains similar directive principles that guide the state towards social and economic justice. The framers of the Indian Constitution included these principles to establish a welfare state. These principles are non-justiciable, meaning they cannot be enforced by any court, but they are considered fundamental in the governance of the country. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar described them as the 'conscience of the Constitution.'
qs.kf:
☛ Source of Directive Principles → Irish Constitution
☛ Which part of Indian Constitution contains Directive Principles → Part IV
☛ Which amendment strengthened Directive Principles → 42nd Amendment (1976)
☛ Articles covering Directive Principles → Articles 36 to 51
☛ Which country's constitution gave the concept of Concurrent List → Australia

q: Provision for the Administration of Scheduled Areas and Tribal Areas is mentioned under which of the following articles?
qs.e: Article 244 of the Indian Constitution deals with the administration of Scheduled Areas and Tribal Areas. It is divided into two parts: Part 244(1) provides for the administration of tribal areas in the states of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram, while 244(2) refers to the administration of scheduled tribal areas in the rest of India. This article is linked to the Fifth and Sixth Schedules. Article 242 was related to Jammu and Kashmir, Article 246 deals with legislative powers of Parliament and state legislatures, and Article 248 deals with residuary powers.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 244(1) → Administration of tribal areas in northeastern states
☛ Article 244(2) → Administration of scheduled tribal areas in rest of India
☛ Fifth Schedule → Administration of scheduled areas under Article 244(2)
☛ Sixth Schedule → Administration of tribal areas under Article 244(1)
☛ Amendment to Article 244 → 89th Amendment established National Commission for Scheduled Tribes

q: Which of the following words were added in the Preamble of the Indian Constitution by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act?
qs.e: The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act of 1976 added the words Socialist, Secular, and Integrity to the Preamble of the Indian Constitution. Originally, the Preamble described India as a Sovereign Democratic Republic. After the amendment, it became a Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic. The word Integrity was also added to the phrase "unity of the nation". This amendment was passed during the Emergency period under Prime Minister Indira Gandhi. It explicitly declared India as a Socialist and Secular state.
qs.kf:
☛ Words added by 42nd Amendment → Socialist, Secular, Integrity
☛ Year of 42nd Amendment → 1976
☛ Original words in Preamble → Sovereign, Democratic, Republic
☛ Prime Minister at the time → Indira Gandhi
☛ Period of 42nd Amendment → Emergency (1975-77)

q: The list of all official languages is given in which Schedule of the Indian Constitution?
qs.e: The Eighth Schedule of the Indian Constitution contains the list of 22 official languages. These languages are included under Article 344(1) and 351 of the Constitution. Initially, the Eighth Schedule had only 14 languages, which were gradually increased to 22 through amendments. The 21st Amendment (1967) added Sindhi language. The 71st Amendment (1992) added Konkani, Manipuri, and Nepali. The 92nd Amendment (2003) added Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, and Santhali. This schedule forms the basis for the formation of the Official Language Commission and language-related policies in India.
qs.kf:
☛ How many languages are in the Eighth Schedule? → 22 languages
☛ Which languages were added last to the Eighth Schedule? → Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, Santhali (in 2003)
☛ Which articles relate to the Eighth Schedule? → Article 344(1) and 351
☛ Which amendment added Sindhi to the Eighth Schedule? → 21st Amendment (1967)
☛ How many languages were originally in the Eighth Schedule? → 14 languages

q: Which of the following Acts provided for the establishment of a federal, provincial and joint public service commission, Reserve Bank of India and a federal court?
qs.e: The Government of India Act, 1935 provided for the establishment of a federal, provincial and joint public service commission, the Reserve Bank of India, and a Federal Court. This act was designed to introduce a federal structure in India, granting greater autonomy to provinces. It also ended the system of diarchy at the provincial level and introduced provincial autonomy. The Federal Court was established as the apex court, which later became the Supreme Court. The Reserve Bank of India was also created under this act in 1935. The act was a significant step towards the constitutional development of India, though it was never fully implemented due to political opposition.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Act established the Reserve Bank of India? → Government of India Act, 1935
☛ Which Act provided for a Federal Court? → Government of India Act, 1935
☛ Which system was ended by the Government of India Act, 1935? → Diarchy
☛ How many public service commissions were established under the Act of 1935? → Three (federal, provincial, joint)
☛ When was the Federal Court established? → 1937

q: The Preamble of the Indian Constitution was amended in 1976 to include which of the following words?
qs.e: The Preamble of the Indian Constitution was amended in 1976 by the 42nd Amendment to include the words 'Socialist', 'Secular', and 'Integrity'. Before the amendment, the Preamble described India as a 'Sovereign Democratic Republic'. After the amendment, it became a 'Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic'. Additionally, the phrase 'Unity of the Nation' was changed to 'Unity and Integrity of the Nation'. This amendment was passed during the Emergency under the government of Prime Minister Indira Gandhi. The word 'Socialist' emphasizes economic and social justice, while 'Secular' means the state maintains equal distance from all religions. These words reflect the fundamental character of the Indian state and its commitment to equality and justice. The 42nd Amendment is often called the 'Mini Constitution' due to the extensive changes it made.
qs.kf:
☛ Which amendment added 'Socialist' and 'Secular' to the Preamble? → 42nd Amendment, 1976
☛ Who was the Prime Minister during the 42nd Amendment? → Indira Gandhi
☛ Where was the word 'Integrity' added in the Preamble? → As 'Unity and Integrity of the Nation'
☛ Is the Preamble a part of the Constitution? → Yes, as per Kesavananda Bharati case
☛ What does 'Secular' mean in the Preamble? → Equal treatment of all religions by the state

q: Which of the following were done by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act?
o: Limiting the size of Council of Ministers.
Lowering the voting age from 21 to 18
Addition of word secular in the Preamble
qs.e: The 42nd Amendment (1976), known as the 'Mini-Constitution', added the words Socialist, Secular and Integrity to the Preamble. Limiting the size of the Council of Ministers was done by the 91st Amendment (2003). Lowering the voting age from 21 to 18 was done by the 61st Amendment (1988). The anti-defection law was introduced by the 52nd Amendment (1985). Therefore, only the addition of 'secular' in the Preamble is a work of the 42nd Amendment.
qs.kf:
☛ Words added to Preamble by 42nd Amendment → Socialist, Secular, Integrity
☛ Amendment limiting size of Council of Ministers → 91st Amendment (2003)
☛ Amendment lowering voting age to 18 → 61st Amendment (1988)
☛ Amendment related to anti-defection law → 52nd Amendment (1985)
☛ 42nd Amendment is also known as → Mini-Constitution

q: Which of the following Acts was based on the Mountbatten plan?
qs.e: The Mountbatten Plan was announced on 3 June 1947, proposing the partition of India and the creation of two independent dominions (India and Pakistan). To implement this plan, the Indian Independence Act, 1947 was enacted by the British Parliament in July 1947. This Act granted independence to India on 15 August 1947 and dissolved the British suzerainty. The Government of India Act, 1935 was an earlier legislation; the Simon Commission arrived in 1927-28; and the Composition of Constituent Assembly was related to the plan but is not an Act. Thus, the correct answer is the Indian Independence Act, 1947.
qs.kf:
☛ Date of announcement of Mountbatten Plan → 3 June 1947
☛ Who passed the Indian Independence Act, 1947 → British Parliament
☛ Section 8 of Indian Independence Act related to → Composition of Constituent Assembly
☛ Last Viceroy of India → Lord Mountbatten
☛ When did Indian Independence Act come into effect → 15 August 1947

q: The Constitution was drafted in 1947 by how many representatives of different castes, regions, religions, genders, etc.?
qs.e: The Indian Constitution was drafted in 1947 by the Constituent Assembly which had 299 members. It included representatives from different castes, regions, religions, genders and backgrounds. The Constituent Assembly was formed in 1946 under the Cabinet Mission Plan. Dr. B. R. Ambedkar was the chairman of the Drafting Committee. The Assembly adopted the Constitution on 26 November 1949 and it came into effect on 26 January 1950. Among the 299 members, 15 were women, including prominent figures like Sarojini Naidu and Vijayalakshmi Pandit.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the first meeting of the Constituent Assembly held? → 9 December 1946
☛ Who was the interim President of the Constituent Assembly? → Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha
☛ Who was the permanent President of the Constituent Assembly? → Dr. Rajendra Prasad
☛ Who was the Chairman of the Drafting Committee? → Dr. B. R. Ambedkar
☛ How many women members were in the Constituent Assembly? → 15

q: Who among the following played a pivotal role in drafting the Indian Constitution and is often referred to as the 'Father of the Indian Constitution'?
qs.e: The Indian Constitution was framed by the Constituent Assembly formed in 1946. Dr Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar was appointed as the Chairman of the Drafting Committee, which prepared the final draft of the Constitution. For his pivotal role, he is honored as the Father of the Indian Constitution or Modern Manu of India. Dr Ambedkar was an economist, jurist, and social reformer who worked for the upliftment of Dalits and backward classes. Besides the Constitution, he was also involved in the establishment of the Reserve Bank of India. He emphasized fundamental rights and justice in the Constitution.
qs.kf:
☛ Who is known as the Father of the Indian Constitution? → Dr BR Ambedkar
☛ Who was the Chairman of the Drafting Committee? → Dr BR Ambedkar
☛ When was the Constituent Assembly formed? → 1946
☛ When was Dr Ambedkar born? → 14 April 1891
☛ Which award was conferred posthumously on Dr Ambedkar? → Bharat Ratna (1990)

q: On which date did the Constituent Assembly give the third reading of the Constitution?
qs.e: The Indian Constitution was drafted by the Constituent Assembly. The Constituent Assembly gave the third reading of the Constitution on 26 November 1949 and finalized it. On this day, the Constitution was adopted. The third reading was the stage of final discussion and voting on the draft Constitution. Thereafter, the Constitution was enforced on 26 January 1950. The Constituent Assembly was established in 1946 and completed the Constitution in 2 years, 11 months, 18 days. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar was the Chairman of the Drafting Committee.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the first meeting of the Constituent Assembly? → 9 December 1946
☛ When was the Constitution adopted? → 26 November 1949
☛ When did the Constitution come into force? → 26 January 1950
☛ Who was the Chairman of the Drafting Committee? → Dr. B.R. Ambedkar
☛ Who was the permanent President of the Constituent Assembly? → Dr. Rajendra Prasad

q: As of 26 November 2024, how many constitutional amendments have been made to the Constitution of India since it was first enacted in 1950?
qs.e: The Constitution of India was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came into effect on 26 January 1950. As of 26 November 2024, a total of 106 constitutional amendments have been made. The latest amendment, the 106th, was passed in August 2023, which extended the reservation for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in the Lok Sabha and state legislative assemblies for another 10 years. These amendments have addressed various issues, including fundamental rights, federal structure, and reservations.
qs.kf:
☛ Total constitutional amendments in India so far? → 106
☛ What is the latest constitutional amendment? → 106th Amendment
☛ What does the 106th Amendment deal with? → Extension of SC/ST reservation
☛ When did the Constitution come into effect? → 26 January 1950
☛ When was the Constitution adopted? → 26 November 1949

q: The concept of Directive Principles in the Indian Constitution is borrowed from the Constitution of which country?
qs.e: The concept of Directive Principles (Part IV) in the Indian Constitution is borrowed from the Constitution of Ireland. These principles serve as guidelines for the state in policy-making but are not enforceable by any court. Their aim is to establish social and economic democracy. The Irish Constitution also contains similar directive principles, which were adopted by the framers of the Indian Constitution. This concept is based on the ideology of a welfare state, where the government is directed to formulate policies to improve the standard of living of citizens.
qs.kf:
☛ In which part of the Indian Constitution are the Directive Principles located? → Part IV
☛ From which country is the inspiration for the Directive Principles taken? → Ireland
☛ Are the Directive Principles enforceable in a court of law? → No
☛ What is the objective of the Directive Principles in the Indian Constitution? → To establish social and economic justice
☛ What is the main basis of the Directive Principles? → Welfare state

q: Who among the following was the President of the Constituent Assembly?
qs.e: Dr. Rajendra Prasad was the permanent President of the Constituent Assembly. He was elected to this position on 11 December 1946. The first meeting of the Constituent Assembly was held on 9 December 1946, with Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha as the temporary President. Dr. Rajendra Prasad presided over the adoption of the Constitution on 26 November 1949. He later became the first President of India. The Constituent Assembly held 11 sessions, and the task of constitution-making was completed in 2 years, 11 months, and 18 days.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the temporary President of the Constituent Assembly? → Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha
☛ When was the first meeting of the Constituent Assembly held? → 9 December 1946
☛ When was the Constitution adopted by the Constituent Assembly? → 26 November 1949
☛ To which post was Dr. Rajendra Prasad elected? → First President of India
☛ How long did the constitution-making take? → 2 years, 11 months, 18 days

q: According to Article 46, the State shall promote the educational and economic interests of:
o: weaker sections, particularly Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes
qs.e: Article 46 of the Indian Constitution is a Directive Principle of State Policy that directs the State to promote the educational and economic interests of weaker sections, especially Scheduled Castes (SCs) and Scheduled Tribes (STs). It also mandates the State to protect them from social injustice and exploitation. This provision is based on the principles of social justice and equality, reflected in the Preamble and Fundamental Rights. Article 46 is part of the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) in Part IV of the Constitution, which guides the government in policy-making. It was strongly advocated by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar to uplift marginalised communities.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 46 → Protection of educational and economic interests of weaker sections
☛ Scheduled Castes (SC) → Defined under Article 341
☛ Scheduled Tribes (ST) → Defined under Article 342
☛ Directive Principles of State Policy → Part IV, Articles 36-51
☛ Article 46 → Strongly supported by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar

q: In India’s parliamentary system of government, the Prime Minister is regarded as the:
qs.e: In India's parliamentary system, the President is the ceremonial head of state (De jure executive), while the Prime Minister is the de facto executive authority. The Prime Minister is the head of the Council of Ministers and exercises real executive powers. He is the head of the executive, not the judiciary. According to Articles 74 and 75 of the Constitution, the Prime Minister is appointed by the President and remains in office as long as he enjoys the confidence of the Lok Sabha. Thus, the Prime Minister is regarded as the de facto executive authority.
qs.kf:
☛ Which article of the Indian Constitution deals with the appointment of the Prime Minister? → Article 75
☛ In the parliamentary system, who holds the real executive power? → Prime Minister
☛ Who is the ceremonial head of state in India? → President
☛ To whom is the Prime Minister responsible? → Lok Sabha
☛ From which country did India adopt the parliamentary system? → Britain

q: Which body has the constitutional mandate to investigate all matters relating to the safeguards provided for Scheduled Castes under the Constitution?
qs.e: The National Commission for Scheduled Castes is a constitutional body established under Article 338 of the Indian Constitution. Its primary mandate is to investigate all matters relating to the safeguards provided for Scheduled Castes under the Constitution. The Commission monitors the implementation of these safeguards and submits annual reports to the President and Parliament. The President appoints the Chairperson and other members. Other options like the Election Commission deal with elections, the National Commission for Minorities deals with minorities, and the National Human Rights Commission deals with human rights, but only the National Commission for Scheduled Castes has the constitutional mandate under Article 338 to specifically investigate safeguards for Scheduled Castes.
qs.kf:
☛ Under which Article is the National Commission for Scheduled Castes established? → Article 338
☛ To whom does the Commission submit its report? → President and Parliament
☛ Who appoints the members of the Commission? → President
☛ What is the main function of the Commission? → To investigate safeguards for Scheduled Castes
☛ Article 338 deals with which body? → National Commission for Scheduled Castes

q: Provision for the Administration and Control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes is mentioned under which of the following schedules?
qs.e: The Fifth Schedule of the Indian Constitution provides for the administration and control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes. This schedule is divided into Part A and Part B. Part A contains general provisions relating to the administration of Scheduled Areas, while Part B details the powers of the Union and States in administering these areas. This schedule is primarily applied under Article 244(1) and ensures special administrative arrangements for the development and protection of the interests of tribal communities in these areas. The Sixth Schedule, on the other hand, deals with the administration of tribal areas in the northeastern states of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Article is associated with the Fifth Schedule? → Article 244(1)
☛ Which Schedule deals with Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes? → Fifth Schedule
☛ What is in Part A of the Fifth Schedule? → General provisions for administration of Scheduled Areas
☛ What is in Part B of the Fifth Schedule? → Powers of Union and States
☛ Which states are covered under the Sixth Schedule? → Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram

q: Which Schedule of the Indian Constitution contains the list of recognised languages in India?
qs.e: The Eighth Schedule of the Indian Constitution contains the list of recognised languages. Originally it had 14 languages, which have been increased to 22 languages through amendments. Sindhi was added by the 21st Amendment (1967), Konkani, Manipuri and Nepali by the 71st Amendment (1992), and Bodo, Dogri, Maithili and Santhali by the 92nd Amendment (2003). These languages are important for official language commissions, parliamentary committees and government use. They include Hindi, Bengali, Urdu, Tamil, Telugu, Marathi, Gujarati, Punjabi, Kashmiri, etc. The schedule also influences the language policies of the Union and states.
qs.kf:
☛ How many languages are in the Eighth Schedule? → 22
☛ Which amendment added Sindhi? → 21st Amendment, 1967
☛ Which amendment added Konkani, Manipuri and Nepali? → 71st Amendment, 1992
☛ Which amendment added Bodo, Dogri, Maithili and Santhali? → 92nd Amendment, 2003
☛ Which language in the Eighth Schedule is also a classical language? → Tamil

q: Which Schedule of the Constitution deals with the administration of Scheduled Areas and Tribes?
qs.e: The Fifth Schedule of the Indian Constitution deals with the administration of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes. It comes under Article 244(1) and contains special provisions for the declaration, administration, and welfare of Scheduled Areas and tribes. Under this schedule, the Governor has special powers to make regulations for the peace and good governance of these areas, ensuring the protection of tribal interests. In contrast, the Sixth Schedule applies to tribal areas in northeastern states like Assam, Meghalaya, Mizoram, and Tripura. The Eleventh Schedule deals with Panchayati Raj, and the Ninth Schedule covers land reforms and other laws. Thus, the Fifth Schedule is the correct answer.
qs.kf:
☛ Under which Article does the Fifth Schedule fall? → Article 244(1)
☛ The Sixth Schedule applies to which region? → Tribal areas of northeastern states
☛ Who has special powers over Scheduled Areas? → Governor
☛ The Eleventh Schedule is related to which system? → Panchayati Raj
☛ The Ninth Schedule deals with what? → Land reforms and other laws

q: Which British law was a major influence on the Indian Constitution’s institutional framework?
qs.e: The institutional framework of the Indian Constitution was heavily influenced by the Government of India Act, 1935. This Act provided key provisions like a federal structure, provincial autonomy, a bicameral legislature, and an independent judiciary. The Constitution borrowed several features from this Act, such as the powers of the Governor, the Council of Ministers, the Public Service Commission, and financial relations between the centre and provinces. It served as the foundational document for India's constitutional development and was the primary source for the framers of the Constitution.
qs.kf:
☛ Major source of Indian Constitution → Government of India Act, 1935
☛ Federal system model → Derived from this Act
☛ Provincial autonomy → Granted greater powers to provinces
☛ Independent judiciary → First ensured by this Act
☛ Public Service Commission → Made mandatory at union and state levels

q: What was the Supreme Court's decision regarding the Kamla Nehru Memorial Trust's land allotment in Uttar Pradesh?
o: Cancelled the land allotment due to lack of public benefit assessment
Directed the state to provide alternative land
Upheld the land allotment due to considerable public benefit assessment
qs.e: The Supreme Court cancelled the land allotment to the Kamla Nehru Memorial Trust in Uttar Pradesh on the ground that there was no proper assessment of public benefit before the allotment. The Court held that the allotment of government land to private entities must be transparent and accountable, with public interest as the priority. In this case, the allotment lacked an evaluation of public benefit, which violated constitutional provisions. This decision clarified that public interest is paramount in the allotment of government property, and any allotment without proper assessment is invalid.
qs.kf:
☛ Supreme Court decision → Land allotment cancelled
☛ Reason → Lack of public benefit assessment
☛ Case → Kamla Nehru Memorial Trust vs. UP Government
☛ Principle → Government property allotment must be transparent
☛ Impact → Public interest given priority

q: Under which of the following conditions is a Tribal Advisory Council (TAC) established in a State?
o: If the State has any forest area
If there is at least one Scheduled Tribe
qs.e: A Tribal Advisory Council (TAC) is established in a state when there is at least one Scheduled Tribe residing in that state. This provision is given in the Fifth Schedule under Article 244(1) of the Indian Constitution. The TAC is constituted by the Governor and consists of 20 members, out of which three-fourths are representatives of the Scheduled Tribes. Its main objective is to advise the Governor on the administration and welfare of tribal areas.
qs.kf:
☛ Who constitutes the TAC? → Governor
☛ Total number of members in TAC? → 20
☛ Proportion of ST representatives in TAC? → Three-fourths
☛ Main objective of TAC? → To advise on administration and welfare of tribal areas
☛ Under which Article is TAC formed? → Article 244(1)

q: Through which amendment were the words 'socialist' and 'secular' added to the Preamble?
qs.e: The words 'socialist' and 'secular' were added to the Preamble of the Indian Constitution through the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976. This amendment was enacted during the Indira Gandhi government and is often called the 'Mini-Constitution'. It added the words 'socialist', 'secular', and 'integrity' to the Preamble. Additionally, it introduced the Fundamental Duties (Article 51A) and made changes to the powers of the judiciary. The Preamble now declares India as a Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic Republic. The 42nd Amendment is considered one of the most significant amendments to the Constitution.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the 42nd Amendment enacted? → 1976
☛ Which three words were added to the Preamble? → Socialist, Secular, Integrity
☛ What is the 42nd Amendment called? → Mini-Constitution
☛ Which amendment added Fundamental Duties? → 42nd Amendment
☛ What does 'socialist' in the Preamble mean? → Social and economic justice

q: Which Act provided separate legislative subjects for the Centre and Provinces with three distinct lists?
qs.e: The Government of India Act 1935 divided legislative subjects between the Centre and Provinces through three distinct lists: Federal List, Provincial List, and Concurrent List. This act is notable for introducing provincial autonomy in India. It gave the Centre exclusive powers over the Federal List, provinces over the Provincial List, and both shared the Concurrent List. The Federal List included defense, foreign affairs, currency; the Provincial List included education, health, agriculture; and the Concurrent List included criminal procedure, labor welfare, etc. This act was a crucial step in India's constitutional development under British rule.
qs.kf:
☛ Government of India Act 1935 → Introduced provincial autonomy
☛ Federal List → Subjects for central government
☛ Provincial List → Subjects for provincial governments
☛ Concurrent List → Subjects for both centre and provinces
☛ Government of India Act 1935 → Provided basis for Indian Constitution

q: In which of the following years were the Montagu– Chelmsford Reforms introduced by the British Government in India to gradually establish self-governing institutions?
qs.e: The Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms were introduced by the British government in 1919. Based on the report of Edwin Montagu, Secretary of State for India, and Lord Chelmsford, the Viceroy, these reforms were enacted as the Government of India Act 1919. They introduced dyarchy (dual government) in provinces, dividing subjects into reserved and transferred categories. At the centre, a bicameral legislature was established, and women were given voting rights in some provinces. The reforms aimed at gradual self-government but were criticized by Indian nationalists for being insufficient. The Act was implemented in 1921 and remained in effect until replaced by the Government of India Act 1935.
qs.kf:
☛ What is the other name of Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms? → Government of India Act 1919
☛ In which Act was dyarchy introduced? → Government of India Act 1919
☛ When was the Montagu-Chelmsford Report published? → 1918
☛ What legislature did this Act create at the centre? → Bicameral legislature (two houses)
☛ When did the Government of India Act 1919 come into effect? → 1921

q: Under the Fifth Schedule, which primary authority is granted to the Governor of a State regarding Scheduled Areas?
o: Power to dissolve the State Legislative Assembly
Power to regulate land, forests and social customs in Scheduled Areas
Power to amend the Constitution regarding Schedule amendments
Authority to appoint Members of Parliament from Scheduled Areas
qs.e: The Fifth Schedule of the Indian Constitution deals with the administration of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes. Under this, the Governor is granted the primary authority to regulate land, forests, and social customs in Scheduled Areas. The Governor can direct that any law applicable to these areas shall not apply or shall apply with modifications. This power is intended to protect the interests of Scheduled Tribes. Additionally, the Governor must submit an annual report to the President on the administration of Scheduled Areas. Other options like dissolving the assembly or amending the Constitution are not within the Governor's scope under the Fifth Schedule.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Schedule deals with Scheduled Areas? → Fifth Schedule
☛ To whom does the Governor submit the report? → President
☛ Who can modify laws for Scheduled Areas? → Governor
☛ How many states currently have Fifth Schedule areas? → 10 states
☛ Which schedules deal with tribal welfare? → Fifth and Sixth Schedules

q: Which Article of the Constitution mandates the establishment of the National Commission for Scheduled Castes?
qs.e: Article 338 of the Indian Constitution mandates the establishment of the National Commission for Scheduled Castes. This commission oversees the rights and welfare of Scheduled Castes. It is appointed by the President and consists of a Chairperson, Vice-Chairperson, and three members. The objective of Article 338 is to ensure the social, educational, and economic development of Scheduled Castes. Article 338 also provides for a National Commission for Scheduled Tribes under Article 338A.
qs.kf:
☛ Under which Article is the National Commission for Scheduled Castes constituted? → Article 338
☛ How many members are in the National Commission for Scheduled Castes? → Three members
☛ Who appoints the Chairperson of the National Commission for Scheduled Castes? → The President
☛ Which Article deals with the National Commission for Scheduled Tribes? → Article 338A
☛ Article 340 is related to which commission? → Backward Classes Commission

q: Under Article 244(2) of the Constitution of India, the provisions of the Sixth Schedule apply to the administration of tribal areas in which of the following sets of States?
o: Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and Chhattisgarh
Nagaland, Manipur, Meghalaya and Arunachal Pradesh
Bihar, Odisha, West Bengal and Assam
qs.e: Under Article 244(2) of the Constitution of India, the provisions of the Sixth Schedule apply to the administration of tribal areas in the states of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram. These are northeastern states with a significant scheduled tribe population. The Sixth Schedule provides special provisions for the administration of tribal areas, including district councils and regional councils, to protect the rights of tribal communities over land, forests and resources. Currently, only these four states have notified tribal areas under the Sixth Schedule. Other options like Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan etc. are governed under the Fifth Schedule via Article 244(1).
qs.kf:
☛ Article 244(1) → Administration of scheduled areas and tribes under the Fifth Schedule
☛ Article 244(2) → Administration of tribal areas under the Sixth Schedule
☛ States where Sixth Schedule applies → Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram
☛ Purpose of Sixth Schedule → Self-governance and protection of land-forest rights in tribal areas
☛ District Council → Local body established in tribal areas under the Sixth Schedule

q: The Fifth Schedule of the Indian Constitution contains provisions for the administration and control of which of the following?
o: Union and State Lists of the Seventh Schedule
Disqualification of legislators on grounds of defection
qs.e: The Fifth Schedule of the Indian Constitution contains provisions for the administration and control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes. It falls under Article 244(1) and grants special powers to the Governor regarding the administration of these areas. The primary objective of the Fifth Schedule is to protect the interests of Scheduled Tribes and ensure their socio-economic development. It provides for the establishment of a Tribes Advisory Council. Note that the Sixth Schedule deals with tribal areas in the northeastern states.
qs.kf:
☛ Fifth Schedule → Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes
☛ Article 244(1) → Provision for Fifth Schedule
☛ Sixth Schedule → Tribal areas in Northeast
☛ Governor's power → Administration of Scheduled Areas
☛ Tribes Advisory Council → Formed under Fifth Schedule

q: When was the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act (RERA) enacted to regulate and promote the real estate sector, ensuring transparency and accountability in transactions and protecting the interests of homebuyers?
qs.e: The Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act (RERA) was enacted by the Indian Parliament in the year 2016 to regulate and promote the real estate sector, ensuring transparency, accountability, and protection of homebuyers' interests. It came into effect on 1 May 2017, with 59 out of 68 sections being enforced initially. The remaining sections were implemented later. Under RERA, each state is required to establish a Real Estate Regulatory Authority (RERA) to register projects, resolve disputes, and monitor compliance. The act imposes penalties on developers for project delays and non-compliance, thereby safeguarding buyers from unfair practices. RERA has significantly improved the trust and efficiency in the real estate market by mandating project registration, quarterly progress reports, and clear title deeds.
qs.kf:
☛ When was RERA Act passed? → 2016
☛ When did RERA come into effect? → 1 May 2017
☛ What is the full form of RERA? → Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act
☛ What is the main objective of RERA? → Ensure transparency and accountability
☛ Which authority is established under RERA? → Real Estate Regulatory Authority

q: Which of the following acts was aimed at establishing a federal polity in India?
qs.e: The Government of India Act, 1935 was aimed at establishing a federal polity in India. It ended dyarchy in provinces and introduced provincial autonomy, while proposing a federal structure at the centre. The act created three lists (federal, provincial, and concurrent). Although the federal part was never implemented, this act became the blueprint for the Indian Constitution. It also provided for a federation of British Indian provinces and princely states, though it was never fully realized.
qs.kf:
☛ Which act laid the foundation of federal polity in India? → Government of India Act, 1935
☛ Which act granted provincial autonomy? → Government of India Act, 1935
☛ How many lists were created under the Government of India Act, 1935? → Three (federal, provincial, concurrent)
☛ Which act proposed a federation of Indian states? → Government of India Act, 1935
☛ Until when was the federal part of the 1935 Act not implemented? → Until independence

q: The Rajya Sabha seat distribution among states is found in which Schedule of the Indian Constitution?
qs.e: The Fourth Schedule of the Indian Constitution deals with the allocation of seats in the Rajya Sabha to states and union territories. It is linked to Article 80, which defines the composition of the Rajya Sabha. The Rajya Sabha has a total of 245 members, of which 233 represent states and union territories, and 12 are nominated by the President. The number of seats allocated to each state is based on its population. The Fourth Schedule has been amended over time to reflect changes such as the formation of new states or population shifts. Understanding this schedule is crucial for grasping the federal structure of the Indian Parliament.
qs.kf:
☛ Which schedule allocates Rajya Sabha seats to states? → Fourth Schedule
☛ Fourth Schedule is related to which Article? → Article 80
☛ Total members in Rajya Sabha? → 245
☛ Number of nominated members in Rajya Sabha? → 12
☛ Number of elected representatives from states and UTs in Rajya Sabha? → 233

q: Which of the following states come under the Fifth Schedule of the Indian Constitution?
qs.e: The Fifth Schedule of the Indian Constitution deals with the administration and control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes. It applies to states with significant tribal populations. Currently, ten states fall under the Fifth Schedule: Andhra Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Gujarat, Jharkhand, Himachal Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Odisha, Rajasthan, and Telangana. Among these, Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh are included. States like Mizoram, Manipur, Nagaland, Meghalaya, Assam, and Tripura come under the Sixth Schedule, which provides separate provisions for tribal areas in the northeastern states. The Fifth Schedule ensures special safeguards for Scheduled Tribes through the establishment of Tribes Advisory Councils and the governor's role in regulating laws related to land and resources.
qs.kf:
☛ How many states are under the Fifth Schedule? → Ten
☛ Which Schedule applies to Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram? → Sixth Schedule
☛ What body is set up in Fifth Schedule states for tribal welfare? → Tribes Advisory Council
☛ What is the purpose of the Fifth Schedule? → Special provisions for welfare and protection of Scheduled Tribes
☛ Which amendment included Chhattisgarh in the Fifth Schedule? → State Reorganization Act of 2000

q: Which of the following is NOT a feature of India’s federal system, thereby reflecting its unitary character?
o: Single citizenship for the entire country
Requirement of some Constitutional Amendments to be ratified by States
An upper house of Parliament (Rajya Sabha) representing the states
Division of powers between the Centre and States
qs.e: India's federal system features division of powers between Centre and States, supremacy of the Constitution, independent judiciary, and a bicameral legislature (Rajya Sabha representing states). Some Constitutional amendments require ratification by states, strengthening the federal structure. Single citizenship is a unitary feature as it emphasizes national unity, with no separate state citizenship. Federations like the USA have dual citizenship, while India grants equal rights to all citizens under Articles 5-11. Thus, single citizenship does not reflect federalism but unitary character. The other options—amendment ratification, Rajya Sabha, and division of powers —are federal features.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Article deals with Single Citizenship in India? → Articles 5-11
☛ Which feature of federal system protects states' rights? → Independent judiciary and constitutional ratification
☛ How is Rajya Sabha constituted? → Not equal representation, but proportional to population
☛ Where is the division of powers between Centre and States given? → Articles 245-255 and Seventh Schedule
☛ Single citizenship reflects which character of India? → Unitary character

q: According to Article 335 of the Constitution of India, claims of SCs and STs shall be taken into consideration in matters of:
qs.e: Article 335 of the Constitution mandates that claims of SCs and STs shall be taken into consideration in matters of public employment, while maintaining administrative efficiency. This provision is crucial for ensuring social justice and forms the legal basis for reservation in government jobs. Read with Article 16(4), it upholds the principle of equality while addressing historical inequalities. The 77th Amendment (2000) clarified that promotions for SCs/STs are also covered under Article 335. It balances the right to equality under Article 16 with the need for social upliftment. This ensures that weaker sections get adequate representation in public services without compromising efficiency.
qs.kf:
☛ What is the main subject of Article 335? → Consideration of claims of SCs/STs in public employment
☛ Why does Article 335 mention 'administrative efficiency'? → To balance reservation with efficiency
☛ Which amendment included promotions under Article 335? → 77th Amendment (2000)
☛ Article 335 is related to which fundamental right? → Article 16 (Right to Equality)
☛ Does Article 335 provide absolute right to reservation? → No, it is subject to conditions

q: Which of the following is NOT a function under the Twelfth Schedule of the Constitution?
qs.e: The Twelfth Schedule was added by the 74th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992. It lists 18 functions of Municipalities. Urban planning, urban poverty alleviation, and public health are included in this schedule. Foreign trade promotion is a subject of the central government, falling under the Union List (List I), not the Twelfth Schedule. This function is handled by the Ministry of Commerce, not by municipal bodies. Hence, it is NOT a function under the Twelfth Schedule.
qs.kf:
☛ Which amendment is related to municipalities? → 74th Amendment
☛ How many functions are in the Twelfth Schedule? → 18
☛ Where is urban planning listed? → Twelfth Schedule
☛ Which list does foreign trade belong to? → Union List
☛ Is public health in the Twelfth Schedule? → Yes

q: The provisions for salaries and emoluments of constitutional authorities are mentioned in which Schedule?
qs.e: The Second Schedule of the Indian Constitution contains provisions for salaries, allowances, and emoluments of constitutional authorities such as the President, Vice-President, Governors, Speakers of Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha, judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts, and the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG). It also lays down rules regarding the deduction of salaries of the President and Governors during a financial emergency. This schedule ensures financial security and independence of these high offices.
qs.kf:
☛ Which schedule deals with the salary of the President? → Second Schedule
☛ Provisions for Governor's salary are in which schedule? → Second Schedule
☛ Salary of Supreme Court judges is mentioned in which schedule? → Second Schedule
☛ Where are the emoluments of the CAG provided? → Second Schedule
☛ Which schedule covers salaries of constitutional authorities? → Second Schedule

q: Which example best reflects the need for the Constitution in daily life?
o: Buying groceries from a local store
Class deciding rules for representation and resource sharing
qs.e: A constitution is a document that defines the structure of government, its powers, and the rights of citizens. In daily life, the need for a constitution arises when a group requires shared rules and a decision-making process. A class deciding rules for representation and resource sharing is a microcosm of constitutional principles in practice, such as justice, equality, and democratic participation. It demonstrates how a constitution ensures order and fairness in society. Other options, like celebrating festivals or buying groceries, are personal or cultural activities that do not require a constitutional framework. This example best reflects the core purpose of a constitution: establishing a framework for collective decision-making and resource distribution.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Indian Constitution adopted? → 26 November 1949
☛ Who was the President of the Constituent Assembly? → Dr. Rajendra Prasad
☛ Who was the Chairman of the Drafting Committee? → Dr. B.R. Ambedkar
☛ How many schedules are in the Indian Constitution? → 12 (originally 8)
☛ Which country has the oldest written constitution? → United States (1787)

q: Which schedule of the Citizenship Act, 1955, contains the qualifications for naturalisation?
qs.e: The Third Schedule of the Citizenship Act, 1955 contains the qualifications for naturalisation. Naturalisation is a process by which a foreign citizen can acquire Indian citizenship. The applicant must have resided in India for at least 12 years, including the last 12 months immediately preceding the application. Additionally, the applicant must not be in the service of any foreign government, must be of good character, and must take an oath to uphold the Constitution of India. The Third Schedule details all these conditions for naturalisation.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Citizenship Act, 1955 enacted? → 1955
☛ What is the minimum residence period for naturalisation? → 12 years
☛ How many modes of acquiring citizenship are there in India? → Five (birth, descent, registration, naturalisation, incorporation of territory)
☛ Which schedule contains conditions for registration of citizenship? → Second Schedule
☛ Which Article defines who is a citizen of India? → Article 5

q: Which Schedule of the Constitution deals with the administration of Scheduled Areas in states, other than the Northeast?
qs.e: The Fifth Schedule of the Indian Constitution deals with the administration of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes in states other than the northeastern states. It empowers the Governor to make regulations for the peace and good governance of these areas and mandates the formation of a Tribal Advisory Council. The President has the authority to declare or alter the boundaries of Scheduled Areas. The schedule aims to protect the interests of Scheduled Tribes and ensure their socio-economic development. In contrast, the Sixth Schedule governs the administration of tribal areas in the northeastern states of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram. The Fifth Schedule is crucial for the special administrative framework in mainland India.
qs.kf:
☛ Fifth Schedule → Administration of Scheduled Areas in states except Northeast
☛ Sixth Schedule → Administration of tribal areas in Northeastern states
☛ Authority to declare Scheduled Areas → President
☛ Tribal Advisory Council → Formed under Fifth Schedule
☛ Seventh Schedule → Subject list for Center-State relations

q: Which of the following Articles of the Constitution of India empowers the President to declare Scheduled Areas?
qs.e: Article 244 of the Indian Constitution empowers the President to declare Scheduled Areas. This article relates to the Fifth Schedule, which deals with the administration and welfare of Scheduled Tribes. Under Article 244(1), the President can declare any area in a state as a Scheduled Area. Article 244(2) relates to the Sixth Schedule, which provides for the administration of tribal areas in the northeastern states. Article 370 granted special status to Jammu and Kashmir, now abrogated. Article 338 deals with the National Commission for Scheduled Castes. Article 146 pertains to officers and servants of the Supreme Court.
qs.kf:
☛ Provision for declaring Scheduled Areas → Article 244(1)
☛ Schedule associated with Article 244 → Fifth Schedule
☛ Article related to the Sixth Schedule → Article 244(2)
☛ Article granting special status to J&K → Article 370
☛ Provision for National Commission for SCs → Article 338

q: Which of the following Schedules deals with the administration and control of Scheduled Areas and Tribes?
qs.e: The Fifth Schedule of the Indian Constitution deals with the administration and control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes. It comes under Article 244(1) and applies to Scheduled Areas in states like Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Odisha, Rajasthan, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, and Himachal Pradesh. In contrast, the Sixth Schedule provides for the administration of tribal areas in the northeastern states of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram. The Seventh Schedule defines the distribution of powers between the Union and States, while the Ninth Schedule deals with land reforms and legal validity of certain laws.
qs.kf:
☛ Fifth Schedule relates to → Administration of Scheduled Areas and Tribes.
☛ Number of states under Fifth Schedule → 10 (currently).
☛ Constitutional provision for Fifth Schedule → Article 244(1).
☛ National Commission for Scheduled Tribes → Formed under Article 338A.
☛ Governor's role under Fifth Schedule → Submit report on administration of Scheduled Areas.

q: The division of subjects between the Union and the States is laid out in which Schedule of the Constitution?
qs.e: The Seventh Schedule of the Indian Constitution divides legislative powers between the Union and the States. It contains three lists: the Union List (100 subjects of national importance, e.g., defense, foreign affairs), the State List (61 subjects of regional significance, e.g., police, agriculture), and the Concurrent List (52 subjects where both can legislate, e.g., education, forests). This division establishes a federal structure, ensuring a clear demarcation of powers. The Union List takes precedence in case of conflict with the State List, while the Concurrent List allows cooperative legislation. The Seventh Schedule is crucial for understanding India's federal system and the distribution of authority between the central and state governments.
qs.kf:
☛ Seventh Schedule → Divides subjects into Union, State, and Concurrent Lists
☛ Total subjects in Union List → 100 (originally 97, amended)
☛ Total subjects in State List → 61 (originally 66)
☛ Total subjects in Concurrent List → 52 (originally 47)
☛ Latest addition to Concurrent List → Goods and Services Tax (GST) via 101st Amendment (2016)

q: In which Schedule are the forms of oath and affirmation for various constitutional offices specified?
qs.e: The Third Schedule of the Indian Constitution specifies the forms of oath and affirmation for various constitutional offices, such as the President, Vice-President, Ministers, Judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts, and Election Commissioners, etc. This schedule ensures that individuals assuming office swear allegiance to the Constitution, serve the country, and perform their duties honestly. It contains a total of 12 oath formats, which vary according to the nature of each office. The purpose of the Third Schedule is to maintain accountability and ethical standards among constitutional functionaries.
qs.kf:
☛ Which office's oath is NOT included in the Third Schedule? → Prime Minister (PM takes the oath as a minister)
☛ How many oath formats are in the Third Schedule? → 12
☛ Under which article can the Third Schedule be amended? → Article 368
☛ Which schedule contains the oath of the President? → Third Schedule
☛ Which part of the Constitution relates to oaths and affirmations? → Third Schedule (not part of any specific part)

q: The __________ of the Indian Constitution protects laws from being challenged in courts under judicial review.
qs.e: The Ninth Schedule of the Indian Constitution provides protection to laws from being challenged in courts under judicial review. It was added by the First Amendment in 1951 to shield land reform laws from litigation. Under Article 31B, laws placed in this Schedule cannot be declared invalid even if they violate fundamental rights. However, in the landmark case of I.R. Coelho vs State of Tamil Nadu (2007), the Supreme Court ruled that laws in the Ninth Schedule are still subject to judicial review if they violate the basic structure of the Constitution. Initially containing 13 laws, the Ninth Schedule now includes over 284 laws, covering various socio-economic reforms. This Schedule acts as a protective umbrella but with limitations regarding constitutional basic structure.
qs.kf:
☛ Which amendment added the Ninth Schedule? → First Amendment, 1951
☛ Which Article is related to the Ninth Schedule? → Article 31B
☛ From which protection do Ninth Schedule laws benefit? → Judicial review
☛ Which case removed the absolute bar on judicial review of Ninth Schedule laws? → I.R. Coelho case, 2007
☛ How many laws are currently in the Ninth Schedule? → Over 284

q: Which of the following states does not follow the Sixth Schedule of the Constitution which deals with the administration and control of tribal areas? A. Assam B. Nagaland
C. Meghalaya D. Tripura
qs.e: The Sixth Schedule of the Indian Constitution provides for the administration of tribal areas in the states of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram. These states have Autonomous District Councils (ADCs) to manage tribal regions. Nagaland does not come under the Sixth Schedule. Instead, Nagaland has a special provision under Article 371A, which requires the state legislature's consent before certain central laws are applied in matters of religious or social practices, Naga customary law, and ownership of land and resources. Therefore, Nagaland does not follow the Sixth Schedule.
qs.kf:
☛ States under Sixth Schedule → Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram
☛ Special provision for Nagaland → Article 371A
☛ Sixth Schedule deals with → administration of tribal areas and Autonomous Councils
☛ Powers of Autonomous District Councils → land, forest, water, social customs
☛ State not following Sixth Schedule → Nagaland

q: Who gave the idea of a constituent assembly of India for the first time?
qs.e: The idea of a Constituent Assembly for India was first proposed by M.N. Roy in 1934. He was a prominent revolutionary and political philosopher. Later, in 1935, the Indian National Congress formally adopted this demand. C. Rajagopalachari further advanced the idea in 1938. Ultimately, the Constituent Assembly was formed under the Cabinet Mission Plan (1946). M.N. Roy was the founder of the Radical Democratic Party and a key figure in India's communist movement. His proposal laid the foundation for drafting India's democratic constitution.
qs.kf:
☛ Who first proposed the idea of Constituent Assembly? → M.N. Roy (1934)
☛ Which party formally demanded a Constituent Assembly in 1935? → Indian National Congress
☛ When was the Cabinet Mission Plan announced? → 1946
☛ Under which plan was the Constituent Assembly formed? → Cabinet Mission Plan
☛ Which party was founded by M.N. Roy? → Radical Democratic Party

q: On being criticized for borrowing features from other countries for the constitution, who said the following- “Nobody holds any patent rights in the fundamental ideas of a constitution.
qs.e: When the Constituent Assembly criticized the Indian Constitution for borrowing features from other countries, Dr. B.R. Ambedkar made this famous statement. He argued that constitutional ideas are not the property of any one individual or nation; they are universal and can be borrowed by any country. He emphasized that the Indian Constitution is original in its fundamental concepts and was crafted by drawing from the best constitutions of the world. This statement reflects Ambedkar's pragmatic approach and his commitment to making the constitution modern and effective.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the President of the Constituent Assembly? → Rajendra Prasad
☛ Who was the Chairman of the Drafting Committee? → Dr. B.R. Ambedkar
☛ Total members of the Constituent Assembly? → 389
☛ When was the Indian Constitution adopted? → 26 January 1950
☛ When was the first meeting of the Constituent Assembly? → 9 December 1946

q: Which schedule of the Indian Constitution contains the list of states and union territories and their territories?
qs.e: The First Schedule of the Indian Constitution contains the list of states and union territories along with their territories. It is divided into two parts: Part I lists the states and Part II lists the union territories. This schedule defines the territorial boundaries of each state and union territory and has been amended several times to accommodate the formation of new states or changes in boundaries. Other schedules serve different purposes: the Second Schedule deals with salaries of President, Governors, etc.; the Fifth Schedule pertains to the administration of scheduled areas and tribes; the Eighth Schedule lists official languages; and the Twelfth Schedule deals with municipalities. The First Schedule is fundamental to the federal structure of India.
qs.kf:
☛ Which schedule lists states and union territories? → First Schedule
☛ How many parts does the First Schedule have? → Two parts: Part I (States) and Part II (Union Territories)
☛ Which schedule deals with official languages? → Eighth Schedule
☛ Which schedule deals with scheduled areas? → Fifth Schedule
☛ Which schedule deals with salaries of President and Governors? → Second Schedule

q: The Constitution of India came into force in:
qs.e: The Constitution of India was adopted by the Constituent Assembly on 26 November 1949, but it came into force with full effect on 26 January 1950. This day is celebrated as Republic Day in India. With the enforcement of the Constitution, India became a sovereign, democratic republic. The Constitution replaced the Government of India Act 1935. The Constituent Assembly took 2 years, 11 months and 18 days to draft it. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar was the Chairman of the Drafting Committee.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Constitution of India adopted? → 26 November 1949
☛ When is Republic Day celebrated in India? → 26 January
☛ How long did it take to draft the Constitution? → 2 years, 11 months, 18 days
☛ Who was the Chairman of the Drafting Committee? → Dr. B.R. Ambedkar
☛ Which Act was replaced by the Constitution? → Government of India Act 1935

q: Who was elected as Vice-President of the Constituent assembly in year 1946?
qs.e: In 1946, HC Mookherjee was elected as the Vice-President of the Constituent Assembly. He was a prominent leader and educationist from Bengal. The President of the Constituent Assembly was Dr. Rajendra Prasad, who later became the first President of India. The Constituent Assembly was formed under the Mountbatten Plan and had 389 members. It adopted the Constitution of India on 26 November 1949.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the first President of the Constituent Assembly? → Dr. Rajendra Prasad
☛ Who was the Vice-President of the Constituent Assembly? → HC Mookherjee
☛ Who was the Chairman of the Drafting Committee? → Dr. B.R. Ambedkar
☛ Under which plan was the Constituent Assembly formed? → Mountbatten Plan
☛ How many members were there in the Constituent Assembly? → 389

q: Who was the first President of Constituent Assembly of independent India?
qs.e: The Constituent Assembly of India was formed in 1946. Its first meeting was held on 9 December 1946, in which Dr Sachchidananda Sinha was elected as the temporary chairman (pro tem speaker). However, on 11 December 1946, Dr Rajendra Prasad was elected as the permanent President of the Constituent Assembly. Hence, Dr Rajendra Prasad was the first President of the Constituent Assembly of independent India. He later became the first President of India. Dr B.R. Ambedkar was the Chairman of the Drafting Committee, while Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru played a key role in the Assembly.
qs.kf:
☛ Date of first meeting of Constituent Assembly → 9 December 1946
☛ Temporary Chairman of Constituent Assembly → Dr Sachchidananda Sinha
☛ First President of Constituent Assembly → Dr Rajendra Prasad
☛ Chairman of Drafting Committee → Dr B.R. Ambedkar
☛ First President of India → Dr Rajendra Prasad

q: An introductory statement in a constitution that states the reasons and guiding values of the constitution is called:
qs.e: The Preamble is an introductory statement in a constitution that outlines the reasons, purposes, and guiding values behind the constitution. It acts as a key to understanding the framers' intent and the fundamental principles of the nation. The Indian Constitution's Preamble begins with 'We, the people of India' and declares justice, liberty, equality, and fraternity as core values. It is often called the soul of the constitution. The Preamble was amended in 1976 by the 42nd Amendment, adding the words 'socialist, secular, and integrity'. It is an integral part of the constitution and aids in judicial interpretation. The Preamble reflects the philosophy and basic structure of the constitution.
qs.kf:
☛ What does the term 'Sovereign' in the Preamble mean? → India is independent in internal and external affairs.
☛ How many ideals are mentioned in the Preamble? → Four: Justice, Liberty, Equality, Fraternity.
☛ Which amendment amended the Preamble? → The 42nd Amendment (1976).
☛ From which constitution was the Preamble borrowed? → The US Constitution.
☛ Is the Preamble enforceable by courts? → Yes, the Supreme Court held it as part of the constitution and enforceable.

q: Which of the following is NOT a source of the Indian Constitution?
qs.e: The Indian Constitution has borrowed many features from various constitutions. The Constitution of Ireland inspired the Directive Principles of State Policy. The Constitution of France provided the ideals of Republic and Liberty, Equality, Fraternity. The U.S. Constitution contributed Fundamental Rights, Judicial Review, and the impeachment of the President. However, the Constitution of Denmark is not a source of the Indian Constitution. India also drew from Britain, Canada, Australia, the Soviet Union, and South Africa, but Denmark had no direct influence. Hence, the Constitution of Denmark is not a source.
qs.kf:
☛ From which constitution were emergency provisions taken? → Weimar Constitution of Germany
☛ Federal system and appointment of Governor are borrowed from which constitution? → Constitution of Canada
☛ Concept of Concurrent List is taken from which constitution? → Constitution of Australia
☛ Fundamental Duties are inspired by which constitution? → Constitution of Soviet Union (USSR)
☛ Written constitution in India is inspired by which country? → United States of America

q: Who among the following has served as the Prime Minister of India for the longest time?
qs.e: Jawaharlal Nehru is the longest-serving Prime Minister of India, holding office for 16 years and 286 days from 15 August 1947 to 27 May 1964. He was the first Prime Minister of independent India and played a pivotal role in shaping the nation's democratic institutions, industrial policy, and foreign relations. Nehru championed the policy of non-alignment and initiated the Five-Year Plans to boost economic growth. His leadership saw India's transition from colonial rule to a republic. He is often referred to as Pandit Nehru.
qs.kf:
☛ Longest serving PM of India → Jawaharlal Nehru (16 years 286 days)
☛ Longest continuous tenure as PM → Jawaharlal Nehru
☛ Second longest serving PM → Manmohan Singh (10 years 4 days)
☛ Shortest serving PM → Gulzari Lal Nanda (acting, 13 days)
☛ First PM of independent India → Jawaharlal Nehru

q: Which country's constitution has been considered by India for the 'Principles of Liberty, Equality & Fraternity'?
qs.e: The principles of 'Liberty, Equality, and Fraternity' enshrined in the Preamble of the Indian Constitution are inspired by the French Constitution. These ideals originated from the French Revolution (1789) with the motto 'Liberté, Égalité, Fraternité'. The Indian Constituent Assembly adopted these principles between 1947-49. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar emphasized their importance for Indian society in the Assembly. Apart from France, India borrowed the parliamentary system from Britain, Directive Principles of State Policy from Ireland, and the concurrent list from Australia. The Preamble of India declares India as a Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic Republic, ensuring liberty, equality, and fraternity for all citizens.
qs.kf:
☛ France's principle adopted by India → Liberty, Equality, Fraternity
☛ Year of French Revolution → 1789
☛ Number of ideals in Indian Preamble → Four (Justice, Liberty, Equality, Fraternity)
☛ Article for 'Equality' in Indian Constitution → Article 14
☛ Where is 'Fraternity' mentioned in Indian Constitution? → End of Preamble

q: The Constituent Assembly formed the Drafting Committee to prepare a Draft Constitution of India on:
qs.e: The Constituent Assembly formed the Drafting Committee to prepare a Draft Constitution of India on 29th August 1947. The committee was chaired by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar. The Drafting Committee submitted the draft Constitution to the Constituent Assembly on 21st February 1948. The Constituent Assembly adopted the Constitution on 26th November 1949, and it came into effect on 26th January 1950. Members of the Drafting Committee included Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar, N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar, K.M. Munshi, Syed Mohammad Saadulla, B.L. Mitter, D.P. Khaitan, and T.T. Krishnamachari.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the chairman of the Drafting Committee? → Dr. B.R. Ambedkar
☛ When was the Drafting Committee formed? → 29th August 1947
☛ When was the Constitution adopted by the Constituent Assembly? → 26th November 1949
☛ When did the Constitution of India come into effect? → 26th January 1950
☛ How many members were in the Drafting Committee? → 7 members

q: Under which Indian Act has the Central Bureau of Investigation been empowered to apprehend and prosecute wildlife offenders?
o: Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960
qs.e: The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) has been empowered to apprehend and prosecute wildlife offenders under Section 58 of the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972. This Act is a comprehensive legislation enacted to protect wildlife and their habitats in India. It prohibits hunting of endangered species, illegal trade, and collection of wildlife products. The Act contains six schedules that provide varying degrees of protection to different species. Under this Act, the CBI investigates interstate and international wildlife crimes, thereby strengthening wildlife conservation efforts. The Act also establishes mechanisms for declaring wildlife sanctuaries and national parks, and provides penalties for violations.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Wild Life (Protection) Act enacted? → 1972
☛ Which section of the Wildlife Act empowers CBI? → Section 58
☛ How many schedules are in the Wildlife Act? → Six
☛ What is the National Animal of India? → Tiger
☛ Who declares a National Park for wildlife conservation? → State Government

q: Which of the following schedules of the Constitution of India has to be amended for the formation of a new state?
qs.e: The First Schedule of the Constitution of India contains the names of the states and union territories along with their territorial extents. Whenever a new state is formed or the boundaries of an existing state are altered, this schedule must be amended. Such an amendment can be passed by the Parliament by a simple majority, but bills related to the reorganization of states can be introduced only with the prior recommendation of the President. Article 3 empowers Parliament to form new states and alter the areas, boundaries, or names of existing states. Without amending the First Schedule, no formation or boundary change of a state is constitutionally valid. The schedule is crucial for maintaining the official list of all territorial units of India.
qs.kf:
☛ Which schedule is amended for formation of a new state? → First Schedule
☛ Which schedule contains names and territories of states? → First Schedule
☛ Which article provides for formation of new states? → Article 3
☛ When can a bill for state reorganization be introduced? → On President's recommendation
☛ What majority is needed to amend the First Schedule? → Simple majority

q: Which among the following is INCORRECT in the context of Federalism?
o: There is no scope of dual citizenship in the case of federal countries.
To prevent the conflict between the centre and state, there is an independent judiciary to settle disputes.
Each government is autonomous in its own sphere.
Federalism is an institutional mechanism to accommodate two sets of polities-one at the regional level and other at the national level.
qs.e: This statement is incorrect because many federal countries allow dual citizenship. For instance, the United States, Canada, and Australia permit their citizens to hold dual citizenship. While India has single citizenship, it is not a mandatory feature of all federal systems. The core feature of federalism is the division of power between the centre and states, not the type of citizenship. Independent judiciary to resolve disputes between centre and states and the autonomy of each government in its own sphere are correct characteristics of federalism.
qs.kf:
☛ Which federal country allows dual citizenship? → United States
☛ What type of citizenship does India have? → Single citizenship
☛ In federalism, power is divided between whom? → Centre and states
☛ What is essential for settling federal disputes? → Independent judiciary
☛ In which sphere are governments autonomous in a federal system? → Their respective spheres

q: The provision of a quasi-federal form of government for India was adopted from:
qs.e: The provision of a quasi-federal form of government in the Indian Constitution was adopted from Canada. In this system, there is a federal structure with a strong central government, often described as 'quasi-federal' or 'center-oriented' federalism. Despite its federal framework, India vests more powers in the center, including a unified judiciary, a single constitution, and emergency provisions. Inspired by Canada's constitution, this system helps unite India's diversity. Among the other options, Ireland provided the Directive Principles of State Policy, Russia inspired Fundamental Duties, and Britain contributed the parliamentary system.
qs.kf:
☛ From which country was the quasi-federal system adopted? → Canada
☛ Other features taken from Canada? → Appointment of governors, advisory jurisdiction of Supreme Court
☛ What is Indian federalism called? → Cooperative federalism
☛ Feature taken from Ireland? → Directive Principles of State Policy
☛ Main feature taken from Britain? → Parliamentary system and law-making procedure

q: Which of the following states is NOT governed by 6th schedule of Indian Constitution?
qs.e: The Sixth Schedule of the Indian Constitution provides for the administration of tribal areas in four states: Assam, Meghalaya, Mizoram, and Tripura. It allows the formation of Autonomous District Councils with legislative powers over land, forests, water, and social customs. Arunachal Pradesh is not covered under the Sixth Schedule; its tribal areas are designated as Scheduled Tribal Areas with a different administrative framework. The Sixth Schedule ensures tribal autonomy in hilly and remote regions of the Northeast, distinct from the Fifth Schedule applicable in other states. Understanding this distinction is crucial for governance and constitutional provisions.
qs.kf:
☛ States under Sixth Schedule → Assam, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Tripura
☛ Main purpose of Sixth Schedule → Formation of Autonomous District Councils for tribal governance
☛ Status of Arunachal Pradesh → Scheduled Tribal Area (not under Fifth or Sixth Schedule)
☛ Seventh Schedule relates to → Distribution of powers between Union, State, and Concurrent lists
☛ Fifth Schedule covers states → Andhra Pradesh, Jharkhand, Gujarat, Rajasthan, Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Odisha, Telangana, Himachal Pradesh, Chhattisgarh

q: Who was the vice-chairman of the constituent assembly that wrote the Indian constitution?
qs.e: The Constituent Assembly of India was formed in 1946. Its permanent chairman was Dr. Rajendra Prasad, while the vice-chairman was H. C. Mookherjee. H. C. Mookherjee was a prominent educationist and politician who played a significant role in drafting the constitution. The Constituent Assembly had 389 members, of which 292 were from provinces, 93 from princely states, and 4 from special categories. The assembly adopted the constitution on 26 November 1949, and it came into effect on 26 January 1950.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the chairman of the Constituent Assembly? → Dr. Rajendra Prasad
☛ Who was the vice-chairman of the Constituent Assembly? → H. C. Mookherjee
☛ When was the Constituent Assembly formed? → 1946
☛ When did the constitution come into effect? → 26 January 1950
☛ Who was the chairman of the Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights? → Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel

q: The idea of Rule of Law in the Indian Constitution has been borrowed from which of the following constitutions?
qs.e: The idea of 'Rule of Law' in the Indian Constitution has been borrowed from the British Constitution. This principle was propounded by British jurist A.V. Dicey. According to Dicey, Rule of Law has three main aspects: supremacy of law, equality before the law, and predominance of individual rights. Article 14 of the Indian Constitution provides for equality before the law, which is a part of the Rule of Law. This principle ensures that no one is above the law and all citizens are treated equally. The concept of Rule of Law is fundamental to the democratic framework of India.
qs.kf:
☛ Who propounded the Rule of Law? → A.V. Dicey
☛ Which Article of the Indian Constitution provides equality before law? → Article 14
☛ Which feature is borrowed from the British Constitution? → Parliamentary government and Rule of Law
☛ How many aspects of Rule of Law did Dicey mention? → Three
☛ Other names for Rule of Law? → Government by law and supremacy of law

q: How many schedules are there in Wildlife Protection Act, 1972 of India?
qs.e: The Wildlife Protection Act, 1972 of India has a total of 6 schedules. This act was enacted for the protection of wild animals, birds, and plants. Schedule I and II provide the highest level of protection to endangered species. Schedule III and IV include species that are not as critically endangered. Schedule V lists vermin and animals that can be hunted. Schedule VI includes plant species that are prohibited from cultivation. The act also establishes penalties for wildlife crimes and supports the creation of national parks and sanctuaries. It is a comprehensive law aimed at conserving India's biodiversity and preventing poaching and illegal trade of wildlife.
qs.kf:
☛ When was Wildlife Protection Act enacted? → 1972
☛ What is in Schedule I? → Endangered species
☛ What is in Schedule V? → Vermin and harmful animals
☛ What is in Schedule VI? → Plant species
☛ What does this act prohibit? → Illegal hunting and trade of wildlife

q: In which of the following Articles of the Constitution of India is it written that 'India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States'?
qs.e: Article 1 of the Indian Constitution declares that 'India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States'. This article is part of Part I (The Union and its Territory). It establishes that India is a union of states, not a confederation, and its sovereignty is indivisible. Article 2 deals with the admission or establishment of new states, Article 3 deals with the formation of new states and alteration of areas, boundaries, or names of existing states, and Article 4 deals with laws made under Articles 2 and 3. Thus, the article that describes India as a Union of States is Article 1.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Article calls India a 'Union of States'? → Article 1
☛ What nature of India does Article 1 reflect? → Federal nature with unitary bias
☛ What does Article 2 deal with? → Admission or establishment of new states
☛ What does Article 3 deal with? → Reorganization or boundary changes of states
☛ What does Article 4 deal with? → Laws made under Articles 2 and 3

q: In relation to the provisions of the administration of Scheduled Tribes and tribal areas, which paragraph of the Indian Constitution has been given?
qs.e: Article 244 of the Indian Constitution provides provisions for the administration of Scheduled Tribes and tribal areas. It is associated with the Fifth and Sixth Schedules of the Constitution. The Fifth Schedule deals with the administration of scheduled areas and scheduled tribes in states other than Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram. The Sixth Schedule provides separate provisions for the administration of tribal areas in these four states. The objective of Article 244 is to ensure the socio-economic development of these regions and protect the interests of tribal communities. Other given articles: Article 243 relates to Panchayati Raj, Article 241 relates to High Courts, and Article 233 relates to judicial appointments.
qs.kf:
☛ What is Article 244 related to? → Administration of Scheduled Tribes and tribal areas
☛ Which states are not covered under the Fifth Schedule? → Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram
☛ Which states are covered under the Sixth Schedule? → Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram
☛ What is Article 243 related to? → Panchayati Raj institutions
☛ What is Article 241 related to? → Provisions for High Courts

q: The characteristics of India's "Rule of Law" (law governance) are taken from which of the following constitution?
qs.e: The concept of 'Rule of Law' in the Indian Constitution is borrowed from the British Constitution. This principle establishes that law is supreme and no one is above the law. In India, it was elaborated by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar in the Constituent Assembly. British jurist A.V. Dicey divided the Rule of Law into three principles: supremacy of law, equality before the law, and predominance of individual rights. Article 14 of the Indian Constitution provides for equality before the law, which is based on this concept. This feature makes India a democratic republic.
qs.kf:
☛ From which constitution is 'Rule of Law' borrowed? → British Constitution
☛ Who propounded this principle? → A.V. Dicey
☛ Which article of Indian Constitution provides equality before law? → Article 14
☛ Who elaborated it in the Constituent Assembly? → Dr. B.R. Ambedkar
☛ What are the three principles of Rule of Law? → Supremacy of law, equality, and individual rights

q: In 1938, under whose chair was the National Planning Committee established?
qs.e: In 1938, the Indian National Congress established the National Planning Committee to promote economic development. Its chairmanship was assigned to Jawaharlal Nehru, who later became the first Prime Minister of independent India. This committee laid the foundation for industrialization and economic planning in the country.
