☛ Election of Rajya Sabha members → Indirect (by state legislative assembly members)
☛ Anti-defection law → Tenth Schedule
☛ Administration of tribal areas → Sixth Schedule
☛ Official languages → Eighth Schedule

q: The provision of 'Single citizenship' for all in the Indian Constitution is adopted from the constitution of which of the following countries?
qs.e: The concept of single citizenship in the Indian Constitution is adopted from the British Constitution. It means that every person in India enjoys only one citizenship, that of the Union, promoting unity and integrity. Unlike the United States, which has a system of dual citizenship (federal and state), India follows the British model. The provisions related to citizenship are detailed in Part II (Articles 5 to 11) of the Indian Constitution. This adoption helped in preventing regionalism and fostering a sense of national identity. The British system also influenced India's parliamentary system and legislative process.
qs.kf:
☛ From which country is 'single citizenship' adopted in Indian Constitution? → Britain
☛ Which Articles deal with citizenship in Indian Constitution? → Articles 5 to 11
☛ Which country has dual citizenship system? → USA
☛ Which Article defines citizenship at the commencement of Constitution? → Article 5
☛ What is the advantage of single citizenship? → Maintains national unity and integrity

q: The Constitution of India provided for how many types of emergencies in Part XVIII, from Articles 352 to 360?
qs.e: Part XVIII (Articles 352 to 360) of the Indian Constitution provides for three types of emergencies: National Emergency (Article 352), Failure of Constitutional Machinery in States or President's Rule (Article 356), and Financial Emergency (Article 360). National Emergency is proclaimed on grounds of war, external aggression, or armed rebellion. President's Rule is imposed when a state's constitutional machinery fails. Financial Emergency is declared when India's financial stability or credit is threatened. During these emergencies, fundamental rights are affected. The President has the power to proclaim these emergencies, and they require parliamentary approval.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Article deals with National Emergency? → Article 352
☛ Which Article deals with President's Rule? → Article 356
☛ Which Article deals with Financial Emergency? → Article 360
☛ How many times has National Emergency been imposed in India? → Three times (1962, 1971, 1975)
☛ How many times has Financial Emergency been imposed? → Never

q: Which Article of the Constitution of India provides for the establishment of the National Commission for Scheduled Castes (NCSC) to safeguard the rights of the Scheduled Castes?
qs.e: Article 338 of the Indian Constitution provides for the establishment of the National Commission for Scheduled Castes (NCSC) to safeguard the rights of Scheduled Castes. The Commission consists of a Chairperson, Vice-Chairperson, and three other members appointed by the President. Its primary role is to monitor constitutional and legal safeguards, investigate complaints, and make recommendations to the government regarding the welfare of Scheduled Castes. Article 330 deals with reservation of seats for SCs/STs in the Lok Sabha, Article 350 with linguistic minorities, and Article 340 with the commission for backward classes. The NCSC was originally a single commission for both SCs and STs, but was later bifurcated by the 89th Amendment (2003) into separate commissions for SCs and STs.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Article establishes the NCSC? → Article 338
☛ How many members does NCSC have? → Chairperson, Vice-Chairperson, and 3 other members (total 5)
☛ Who appoints the NCSC Chairperson? → President
☛ What does Article 330 relate to? → Reservation of seats for SCs/STs in the Lok Sabha
☛ What does Article 340 relate to? → Commission to investigate the condition of backward classes

q: The Preamble primarily serves as which of the following?
qs.e: The Preamble to the Indian Constitution is a brief introductory statement that embodies the fundamental values and philosophy of the Constitution, such as justice, liberty, equality, and fraternity. It is not enforceable by law, meaning it cannot be directly taken to court if violated. However, it serves as a guiding principle for interpretation. The Supreme Court has used the Preamble in many landmark judgments to interpret ambiguous constitutional provisions and to understand the intent of the framers. For example, in the Berubari Union case (1960), the Court held that the Preamble is not a source of power but a key to understanding the Constitution. Thus, its primary function is to guide interpretation and not to act as an enforceable legal provision or a schedule.
qs.kf:
☛ Enforceability of Preamble → Not enforceable in a court of law
☛ Amendment of Preamble → Amended only once by the 42nd Amendment in 1976
☛ Source of Preamble → Inspired by the US Constitution
☛ Number of words in Preamble → Approximately 80 words
☛ Key elements of Preamble → Three elements: people, objectives, and authority

q: The Preamble declares India to be which of the following?
qs.e: The Preamble of the Indian Constitution declares India to be a Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic Republic. 'Sovereign' means India is independent in internal and external affairs. 'Socialist' was added by the 42nd Amendment in 1976, emphasizing economic and social justice. 'Secular' means the state does not officially recognize any religion. 'Democratic' denotes a government elected by the people. 'Republic' means the head of the state is elected. The Preamble serves as an introduction to the Constitution and is considered its soul. It outlines the core values and objectives of the Indian polity, including justice, liberty, equality, and fraternity.
qs.kf:
☛ Number of words in the Preamble? → 52
☛ Key words in the Preamble? → Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic, Republic
☛ Which amendment added Socialist and Secular? → 42nd Amendment, 1976
☛ Which country's constitution inspired the Preamble? → USA
☛ What is the Preamble considered as? → Soul of the Constitution

q: Providing free legal aid under Article 39A indirectly promotes which Preamble objective?
qs.e: Article 39A directs the State to provide free legal aid to ensure equal justice. This provision makes the judicial system accessible to economically weaker sections. The Preamble enshrines Justice as social, economic, and political. Free legal aid promotes social and economic justice, thereby indirectly serving the objective of Justice. Sovereignty, Republic, and Secularism are not directly related to this provision.
qs.kf:
☛ What does Article 39A deal with? → Equal justice and free legal aid
☛ How many types of justice are mentioned in the Preamble? → Social, economic, and political
☛ Free legal aid is a part of which fundamental right? → Article 21 (Right to Life)
☛ Which constitutional amendment added Article 39A? → 42nd Amendment 1976
☛ Where does the word Justice appear in the Preamble? → In the opening line

q: What does the term 'Sovereign' in the Indian Constitution's Preamble signify for India?
qs.e: The term 'Sovereign' in the Preamble of the Indian Constitution means that India is not subject to any external authority. It signifies that India has complete independence in its internal and external affairs. Sovereignty implies that India is free from the control of any foreign power or organization. This word highlights India's independence and right to self-determination. Other options like religious freedom, power to appoint the President, or non-alignment are not synonyms of sovereignty; they are separate concepts.
qs.kf:
☛ First word of the Indian Constitution's Preamble → We, the people of India
☛ Word that follows 'Sovereign' in the Preamble → Socialist
☛ In whom does India's sovereignty reside → The people
☛ Who proposed the Preamble of the Constitution → Jawaharlal Nehru
☛ How many key terms are in the Preamble → Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic, Republic

q: Under which article can the Parliament set a condition for employment within the state or union territory?
qs.e: Article 16 of the Indian Constitution provides for equality of opportunity in public employment. Under clause (5) of this article, the Parliament can set a condition of residence within a state or union territory for employment in that area. This allows Parliament to pass a law requiring persons to be residents of a particular area to be preferred for certain posts. Article 16 is part of the Fundamental Rights and prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, descent, place of birth or residence. Clause (5) specifically empowers Parliament to require residence within a state or union territory for employment.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 16(1) → Equality of opportunity in public employment
☛ Article 16(2) → No discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, etc.
☛ Article 16(3) → Parliament may prescribe residence condition (state/UT)
☛ Article 16(4) → Reservation for backward classes
☛ Article 16(5) → Exemption for religious institutions

q: Under which article can the Supreme Court issue a writ?
qs.e: Under Article 32 of the Indian Constitution, the Supreme Court has the power to issue writs for the enforcement of fundamental rights. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar called it the 'heart and soul of the Constitution'. The Supreme Court can issue five types of writs: habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari, and quo warranto. Article 226 empowers the High Courts to issue writs, while Article 131 deals with the original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court, and Article 143 provides for the President's power to consult the Supreme Court.
qs.kf:
☛ Under which article can the Supreme Court issue writs? → Article 32
☛ Under which article can High Courts issue writs? → Article 226
☛ What is Article 32 called? → Heart and soul of the Constitution
☛ How many writs can the Supreme Court issue? → Five
☛ What does Article 143 deal with? → President's consultation with Supreme Court

q: Military law is protected under which Article of the Indian Constitution?
qs.e: Article 34 of the Indian Constitution deals with military law. It empowers the Parliament to indemnify any person for actions taken during the imposition of martial law in any area. Martial law is an extraordinary situation where military administration replaces civilian administration. Under Article 34, the Parliament can validate actions taken during martial law by passing a law. This article is an exception to fundamental rights. It is important to note that Article 34 is read along with Article 33, which grants exemptions to the armed forces from fundamental rights. Article 34 ensures that those who act under martial law are protected from legal prosecution.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 33 → gives exemption from fundamental rights to armed forces
☛ Article 34 → provides protection for actions during martial law
☛ Martial law → imposition of military rule during emergencies
☛ Article 35 → power to make laws for implementing fundamental rights
☛ Article 36 → definition of State for Directive Principles

q: According to the Child Labour Prevention Act (Amendment) 2016, child labour is prohibited below the age of________years.
qs.e: According to the Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Amendment Act, 2016, child labour is prohibited for children below the age of 14 years. This amendment strictly bans employment of children in any occupation and also prohibits adolescents (14-18 years) from working in hazardous occupations. For the first time, the act introduced the category of 'adolescent' and allows them to work only in non-hazardous occupations. However, helping family businesses after school hours or during vacations is not considered an offense. The act aims to ensure that children get access to education and a healthy development. It also aligns with the Right to Education Act, making 14 years the key age for compulsory education.
qs.kf:
☛ Minimum age for child labour prohibition under 2016 Act → 14 years
☛ Age group defined as adolescent → 14 to 18 years
☛ Hazardous occupations banned for → persons below 18 years
☛ Exception for family business → allowed after school hours or vacations
☛ Main objective of the Act → Ensure education and development of children

q: Indian Constitution prohibits the employment of children under ___________ years of age
qs.e: Article 24 of the Indian Constitution prohibits the employment of children below 14 years of age in factories, mines, or other hazardous work. This is a fundamental right under the Constitution aimed at protecting children from exploitation. Additionally, the Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986 bans the employment of children under 14 in all occupations. However, recent amendments prohibit children under 18 from working in hazardous occupations. The constitutional provision set the age limit at 14 years, which forms the basis for child protection laws. This right ensures the safeguarding of children's health, education, and development.
qs.kf:
☛ Constitutional article prohibiting child labour → Article 24
☛ Minimum age for employment under Child Labour Act → 14 years
☛ Age limit for hazardous occupations → 18 years
☛ Right under which child labour prohibition falls → Fundamental Right
☛ Places where child labour is banned under Article 24 → Factories, mines, hazardous work

q: The right to adopt, practice and propagate a religion belongs to which article of Indian Constitution?
qs.e: Article 25 of the Indian Constitution guarantees the freedom of conscience and the right to profess, practice and propagate religion. This right is subject to public order, morality and health. Article 25 ensures that every person has the liberty to adopt any religion of their choice, follow its teachings and propagate it. It strengthens the principle of secularism. Article 26 provides freedom to manage religious affairs, while Article 29 protects the interests of minorities. Article 23 prohibits human trafficking and forced labor. Article 25 is a fundamental right under Part III of the Constitution.
qs.kf:
☛ Right to adopt, practice and propagate religion → Article 25
☛ Freedom to manage religious affairs → Article 26
☛ Protection of interests of minorities → Article 29
☛ Prohibition of human trafficking and forced labor → Article 23
☛ Article 25 is a fundamental right → Part III

q: Which of the following Articles deals with 'Prohibition of traffic in human beings and forced labour'?
qs.e: Article 23 of the Indian Constitution prohibits traffic in human beings and forced labour. It is a fundamental right under the Right against Exploitation. This article bans begar (forced labour without payment) and other similar forms of exploitation. Any violation of this provision is punishable by law. The only exception is compulsory service for public purposes imposed by the state, provided it does not discriminate on grounds of religion, race, caste, class or sex. Article 23 protects all persons, not just citizens, from human trafficking and bonded labour. In contrast, Article 27 deals with exemption from taxes for religious promotion, Article 29 protects the cultural and educational rights of minorities, and Article 30 gives minorities the right to establish educational institutions.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Article prohibits human trafficking? → Article 23
☛ What is the exception to forced labour? → Compulsory service for public purposes imposed by the state
☛ Article 23 is part of which Part of the Constitution? → Part III (Fundamental Rights)
☛ Article 23 is a right against what? → Exploitation
☛ Who is protected under Article 23? → All persons (not just citizens)

q: Which of the following Articles in the Constitution grants us the Right to Equality?
qs.e: The Right to Equality is enshrined in Articles 14 to 18 of the Indian Constitution. Article 14 guarantees equality before law and equal protection of laws. Article 15 prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth. Article 16 ensures equality of opportunity in public employment. Article 17 abolishes untouchability and makes it a punishable offense. Article 18 abolishes titles except military and academic distinctions. These are part of Fundamental Rights (Part III) and are justiciable, allowing citizens to directly approach the Supreme Court for enforcement. This right forms the bedrock of Indian democracy, ensuring justice and fairness for all citizens.
qs.kf:
☛ Which articles cover Right to Equality? → 14-18
☛ Article for equality before law? → 14
☛ Abolition of untouchability is in which article? → 17
☛ Equality of opportunity in public employment? → 16
☛ Article 18 deals with? → Abolition of titles

q: According to the Constitution of India, which one of the following is not a fundamental right?
A. Right to freedom
B. Right to live
C. Right to equality
D. Right to protect the country
qs.e: Part 3 (Articles 12-35) of the Indian Constitution enumerates the fundamental rights. These include right to equality (Articles 14-18), right to freedom (Articles 19-22), and right to life (Article 21). The right to protect the country is not a fundamental right; it is a fundamental duty under Article 51A. Fundamental duties were added by the 42nd Amendment in 1976. Therefore, among the options, only the right to freedom, equality, and life are fundamental rights, while the right to protect the country is a duty, not a right.
qs.kf:
☛ Which part contains Fundamental Rights? → Part 3 (Articles 12-35)
☛ Which part contains Fundamental Duties? → Part 4A (Article 51A)
☛ When was the 42nd Amendment enacted? → 1976
☛ Which article covers the Right to Life? → Article 21
☛ Which articles cover the Right to Equality? → Articles 14-18

q: In accordance with the Indian Constitution, Protection of Life and Personal Liberty is granted under which Article?
A. Article 20
B. Article 21
C. Article 22
D. Article 23
qs.e: Article 21 of the Indian Constitution provides protection of life and personal liberty. It states that no person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law. This fundamental right has been interpreted broadly by the Supreme Court to include the right to live with dignity, right to privacy, right to a pollution-free environment, and many other essential rights. It is different from Article 20 (protection from conviction for offences), Article 22 (protection from arrest), and Article 23 (prohibition of human trafficking). Article 21 is considered the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution and is the most fundamental of all fundamental rights.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 21A → Free and compulsory education for children aged 6-14
☛ Article 20 → Protection from conviction for offences
☛ Article 22 → Protection from arrest and detention
☛ Article 23 → Prohibition of human trafficking and child labour
☛ Article 21 → Right to life and personal liberty

q: Right To Information (RTI) Act came into effect in the year
qs.e: The Right to Information (RTI) Act came into effect in India on 15 June 2005. This Act empowers citizens to access information from public authorities. Under the RTI Act, any citizen can request information from a public authority, and the authority must respond within 30 days. The Act was enacted to promote transparency and accountability in governance. Its primary goal is to reduce corruption and strengthen democracy. The RTI Act is a landmark legislation that empowers ordinary citizens to hold the government accountable.
qs.kf:
☛ When did RTI Act come into effect? → 15 June 2005
☛ What does RTI stand for? → Right to Information
☛ In which year was RTI Act passed? → 2005
☛ What is the time limit for providing information under RTI? → 30 days
☛ What is the main objective of RTI Act? → Transparency and accountability

q: Under which Article of the Constitution, the Supreme Court of India may issue a writ for enforcement of Fundamental Rights?
qs.e: Article 32 of the Indian Constitution empowers the Supreme Court to issue writs for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar called it the soul of the Constitution. Under this article, any person can directly approach the Supreme Court for violation of their fundamental rights. The Supreme Court can issue five types of writs: Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, and Quo Warranto. Article 32 provides original jurisdiction to the Supreme Court for the protection of fundamental rights. It is a guaranteed right and cannot be suspended except during a national emergency under Article 359.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Article gives the right to move the Supreme Court for Fundamental Rights? → Article 32
☛ Who called Article 32 the 'soul of the Constitution'? → Dr. B.R. Ambedkar
☛ How many types of writs can the Supreme Court issue? → Five
☛ Which writ is related to release from illegal detention? → Habeas Corpus
☛ Article 32 is for enforcement of which rights? → Fundamental Rights

q: In the context of the Indian Constitution, which of the following is correctly matched?
o: Part III - Directive Principles of State Policy
qs.e: Part III of the Indian Constitution (Articles 12-35) deals with Fundamental Rights. These rights protect citizens from arbitrary state action and are enforceable by courts. Citizenship is covered in Part II (Articles 5-11), Directive Principles of State Policy in Part IV (Articles 36-51), and Fundamental Duties in Part IVA (Article 51A). Thus, only Fundamental Rights are correctly matched with Part III. These rights include equality, freedom, against exploitation, freedom of religion, cultural and educational rights, and constitutional remedies.
qs.kf:
☛ How many articles are in Part III? → 24 (Articles 12-35)
☛ From which constitution are Fundamental Rights inspired? → USA
☛ Which article deals with suspension of Fundamental Rights? → Article 359
☛ Which is the first Fundamental Right? → Right to Equality (Articles 14-18)
☛ Under which article is reservation for SC/ST provided? → Article 15(4)

q: From which Constitution has the Fundamental Rights in the Indian Constitution drawn?
qs.e: The Fundamental Rights in the Indian Constitution are drawn from the United States Constitution. These rights are justiciable, meaning citizens can approach courts if they are violated. The list of Fundamental Rights in India includes right to equality, freedom, against exploitation, freedom of religion, cultural and educational rights, and constitutional remedies. Inspired by the US Constitution, India made these rights fundamental and justiciable. However, the right to property was originally a fundamental right but was removed by the 44th Amendment (1978).
qs.kf:
☛ From where were Fundamental Rights borrowed? → United States
☛ How many Fundamental Rights are there in the Indian Constitution? → Six (originally seven, now six)
☛ Which right was removed as a Fundamental Right? → Right to Property (by 44th Amendment)
☛ Which Article provides constitutional remedies? → Article 32
☛ From which Constitution was the Preamble's idea borrowed? → US Constitution

q: Name the writ under which the court orders that the arrested person should be presented before it or can order to set free an arrested person if the manner or grounds of arrest are NOT lawful or satisfactory.
qs.e: Habeas Corpus is a crucial writ under which the court orders that an arrested person be brought before it. If the manner or grounds of arrest are found unlawful or unsatisfactory, the court can order the immediate release of the person. This writ protects personal liberty and is also known as the 'Great Writ'. It can be issued by the Supreme Court under Article 32 and by High Courts under Article 226 of the Indian Constitution. The literal meaning of Habeas Corpus is 'you shall have the body'. Its primary purpose is to prevent illegal detention and ensure that no person is deprived of liberty without legal authority. Other writs include Certiorari, Quo Warranto, and Mandamus.
qs.kf:
☛ Which right does Habeas Corpus protect? → Personal liberty
☛ Under which articles can this writ be issued? → Article 32 and 226
☛ Which courts can issue this writ? → Supreme Court and High Courts
☛ What is the literal meaning of Habeas Corpus? → 'You shall have the body'
☛ Which writ is also called the 'Great Writ'? → Habeas Corpus

q: Which amendment in the Constitution of India deals with the abolition of Right to Property as a fundamental right?
qs.e: The 44th Amendment to the Constitution of India, enacted in 1978, abolished the Right to Property as a fundamental right. It removed Article 19(1)(f) and Article 31 from the fundamental rights chapter. Instead, it added Article 300A, making the right to property a constitutional right but not a fundamental right. This amendment was passed by the Morarji Desai government to facilitate land reforms and reduce legal hurdles. The 44th Amendment also modified several other provisions, including the powers of the President and the emergency provisions.
qs.kf:
☛ Amendment that removed Right to Property as fundamental right → 44th Amendment (1978)
☛ Current status of Right to Property → Constitutional right under Article 300A
☛ Article removed by 44th Amendment → Article 19(1)(f) and Article 31
☛ Prime Minister at the time of 44th Amendment → Morarji Desai
☛ Amendment that curtailed fundamental rights → 44th Amendment

q: Which of the following fundamental rights is NOT guaranteed by the Constitution of India?
qs.e: The Constitution of India guarantees Right to equality (Articles 14-18), Right to freedom (Articles 19-22), and Right to freedom of religion (Articles 25-28) as fundamental rights. However, Right to profession is not a fundamental right; it falls under the Directive Principles of State Policy in Part IV of the Constitution. Article 19(1)(g) provides freedom of trade, business, industry and profession, which is a fundamental right, but it is not specifically titled 'Right to profession'. Therefore, among the given options, 'Right to profession' is not a fundamental right guaranteed by the Constitution.
qs.kf:
☛ Number of Fundamental Rights → Originally 7, now 6 (Right to property removed)
☛ Right to equality → Articles 14-18
☛ Right to freedom → Articles 19-22
☛ Right to freedom of religion → Articles 25-28
☛ Right to profession → Not a fundamental right, it is a directive principle

q: ________ of the Indian Constitution deals with the protection of interests of minorities.
qs.e: Article 29 of the Indian Constitution deals with the protection of interests of minorities. It falls under Fundamental Rights (Part III) and grants any citizen or group residing in India the right to conserve their language, script, or culture. Under this article, no citizen shall be denied admission into any educational institution maintained or aided by the State on grounds only of religion, race, caste, or language. This article protects the cultural and educational rights of minority communities. It ensures that minorities can preserve their distinct language and culture, thereby maintaining India's diversity. Article 29 is often read with Article 30, which gives minorities the right to establish and administer educational institutions. Together, they form the cornerstone of minority rights in India.
qs.kf:
☛ What does Article 29 deal with? → Protection of interests of minorities
☛ Article 29 is part of which Part? → Part III (Fundamental Rights)
☛ What does Article 29(1) provide? → Right of any citizen to conserve their language, script, or culture
☛ What does Article 29(2) say? → No discrimination in admission to state institutions on grounds of religion, race, etc.
☛ Difference between Article 29 and 30? → Article 29 protects cultural rights, Article 30 gives right to establish educational institutions

q: Which fundamental right is violated if a group of people are NOT given permission to open a Telugu-medium school in Kerala?
qs.e: The Indian Constitution provides Cultural and Educational Rights to minorities under Articles 29 and 30. Article 29(1) grants any section of citizens the right to conserve their language, script, or culture. Article 30(1) gives religious or linguistic minorities the right to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice. A Telugu-speaking group in Kerala wanting to open a Telugu-medium school falls under this right. Denying permission violates these rights. These rights are specifically designed to protect the language and culture of minorities. Right to Equality, Freedom of Religion, or Right to Freedom are not directly applicable here as the core issue is about educational and cultural preservation.
qs.kf:
☛ Which article deals with the right of minorities to establish educational institutions? → Article 30
☛ Cultural and Educational Rights are covered under which articles? → Articles 29-30
☛ Article 29(1) protects which aspects? → Language, script, and culture
☛ Article 30 applies to which groups? → Religious and linguistic minorities
☛ Telugu is primarily spoken in which states? → Andhra Pradesh and Telangana

q: The 'right to property' is a:
qs.e: The 'right to property' in the Indian Constitution was originally a fundamental right, but the 44th Amendment (1978) removed it from the list of fundamental rights and placed it under Article 300A, making it a legal right. Now, it is only a constitutional legal right, meaning no person can be deprived of their property except by authority of law. It is no longer enforceable through the Supreme Court directly under fundamental rights. This change was made to balance individual property rights with the state's power of eminent domain for public welfare. Thus, the right to property currently exists as a legal right.
qs.kf:
☛ What type of right is the right to property? → Legal right
☛ Article related to right to property → Article 300A
☛ Which amendment removed the right to property from fundamental rights? → 44th Amendment (1978)
☛ Right to property was influenced by which country's constitution? → Ireland
☛ Right to property now comes under which category? → Legal right

q: Under which articles of the Constitution of India is the Right to Equality mentioned?
qs.e: The Right to Equality under the Indian Constitution is enshrined in Articles 14 to 18 of Part III (Fundamental Rights). Article 14 guarantees equality before the law and equal protection of the laws. Article 15 prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth. Article 16 provides for equality of opportunity in public employment. Article 17 abolishes untouchability and forbids its practice in any form. Article 18 abolishes titles, except military and academic distinctions. These provisions ensure legal equality and promote social justice by removing discriminatory practices. They form the cornerstone of a just and equitable society, binding both the state and individuals.
qs.kf:
☛ Which articles cover Right to Equality? → 14-18
☛ Which article abolishes untouchability? → 17
☛ Which article provides equality of opportunity in employment? → 16
☛ Which article ensures equality before law? → 14
☛ Which article abolishes titles? → 18

q: Which articles of Indian Constitution ensures the abolition of titles?
qs.e: Article 18 is part of the Fundamental Rights in the Indian Constitution that ensures the abolition of titles. It prohibits the state from conferring any titles except military or academic distinctions. It also prevents Indian citizens from accepting titles from foreign states. This provision was created to promote social equality and eliminate discrimination. Article 17 abolishes untouchability, Article 23 prohibits human trafficking, and Article 25 guarantees freedom of conscience and religion.
qs.kf:
☛ Main purpose of Article 18 → Abolition of titles
☛ Provision under Article 17 → Abolition of untouchability
☛ Prohibition under Article 23 → Human trafficking and forced labor
☛ Article 25 relates to → Freedom of conscience and religion
☛ Article 22 deals with → Protection against arbitrary arrest

q: In which of the following Articles the concept of equality is enshrined?
qs.e: Article 14 of the Indian Constitution provides the right to equality. It states that the State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India. This article applies to all persons, both citizens and non-citizens. Article 14 establishes the general principle of equality, while Articles 15-18 deal with specific aspects like prohibition of discrimination on grounds of caste, sex, religion, etc. Article 14 includes two concepts: 'equality before the law' and 'equal protection of the laws.' The first means no one is above the law, and the second ensures that laws are applied equally. It is a fundamental pillar of the Fundamental Rights under Part III of the Constitution.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Article of the Indian Constitution provides equality before the law? → Article 14
☛ How many concepts are included in Article 14? → Two: equality before the law and equal protection of the laws
☛ Which foreign constitutions inspired Article 14? → British and Irish
☛ Is Article 14 limited only to citizens? → No, it applies to all persons
☛ Is reasonable classification allowed under Article 14? → Yes, if based on intelligible differentia

q: Article of the Indian Constitution related to the Comptroller and Auditor General of India is-
qs.e: The article related to the Comptroller and Auditor General of India (CAG) is Article 148. This article provides for the appointment, oath, and service conditions of the CAG. The CAG is appointed by the President of India and takes an oath before the President. The term of office of the CAG is 6 years or until the age of 65 years, whichever is earlier. Article 149 defines the duties and powers of the CAG. Article 150 deals with the form of accounts of the Union and the States. Article 151 relates to the submission of CAG's reports to the President. The CAG is considered an independent authority under the Indian Constitution.
qs.kf:
☛ Article related to CAG → Article 148
☛ Who appoints CAG → President
☛ Term of CAG → 6 years or 65 years
☛ Article for duties of CAG → Article 149
☛ Article for CAG's report → Article 151

q: Which of the following paragraphs of Indian Constitution have the right to freedom?
qs.e: The right to freedom in the Indian Constitution is enshrined in Articles 19 to 22. Article 19 provides six freedoms: speech and expression, assembly, associations, movement, residence, and profession. Article 20 provides protection in respect of conviction for offenses. Article 21 protects the right to life and personal liberty. Article 21A provides the right to education. Article 22 provides protection against arrest and detention in certain cases. Articles 14-18 deal with the right to equality, Articles 23-24 deal with the right against exploitation, and Articles 29-30 deal with cultural and educational rights.
qs.kf:
☛ Right to Freedom → Articles 19-22
☛ Right to Equality → Articles 14-18
☛ Right against Exploitation → Articles 23-24
☛ Cultural and Educational Rights → Articles 29-30
☛ Which right is in Article 21 → Right to life and personal liberty

q: Part III of the Indian Constitution is related to ___________.
qs.e: Part III of the Indian Constitution, comprising Articles 12 to 35, deals with Fundamental Rights. These rights are justiciable, meaning they can be enforced in a court of law. Fundamental Rights include the Right to Equality, Right to Freedom, Right against Exploitation, Right to Freedom of Religion, Cultural and Educational Rights, and Right to Constitutional Remedies. They protect citizens against arbitrary state actions. Fundamental Duties are covered in Part IV-A, Elections in Part XV, and Citizenship in Part II of the Constitution.
qs.kf:
☛ Which part of the Constitution deals with Fundamental Rights? → Part III
☛ How many Fundamental Rights are there? → 6 rights (originally 7)
☛ Which articles cover Fundamental Rights? → Articles 12-35
☛ Which article defines Fundamental Rights? → Article 12
☛ Are Fundamental Rights justiciable? → Yes

q: Which one is the article of the Indian Constitution related to the protection of minorities?
qs.e: Article 29 of the Indian Constitution protects the interests of minorities. It provides that any section of citizens residing in any part of India having a distinct language, script or culture shall have the right to conserve the same. It prohibits denial of admission into educational institutions on grounds of religion, race, caste or language. Article 29 is placed under Cultural and Educational Rights. It guarantees minorities the right to preserve their identity. Article 26 deals with religious affairs, Article 24 prohibits child labour, and Article 17 abolishes untouchability.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 29 → Protection of culture, language and script of minorities
☛ Article 30 → Right of minorities to establish educational institutions
☛ Article 26 → Right to manage religious affairs
☛ Article 25 → Freedom of conscience and religion
☛ Article 15 → Prohibition of discrimination on grounds of religion, caste etc.

q: The Abolition of Untouchability comes under which fundamental right of Indian constitution?
qs.e: The abolition of untouchability is enshrined in Article 17 of the Indian Constitution. This article falls under the Right to Equality (Articles 14-18). Untouchability is abolished, and its practice in any form is a legal offense. This provision was designed to ensure social equality and eliminate discrimination. Thus, the fundamental right it belongs to is the Right to Equality, not the Right against Exploitation, Right to Life, or Right to Freedom of Religion.
qs.kf:
☛ Which article abolishes untouchability? → Article 17
☛ Under which part does Article 17 come? → Part 3 (Fundamental Rights)
☛ Which articles cover Right to Equality? → Articles 14-18
☛ Which article is responsible for social equality? → Article 15 and 17
☛ What is the practice of untouchability in India? → A legal offense

q: Which of the following is related to the abolition of titles in the Indian Constitution?
qs.e: Article 18 of the Indian Constitution deals with the abolition of titles. It falls under the Fundamental Rights (Articles 12-35) and specifically under the Right to Equality (Articles 14-18). Article 18 prohibits the state from conferring any titles on citizens and also prohibits Indian citizens from accepting titles from foreign states. However, military and academic distinctions are exempted from this provision. This article ensures equality among citizens and abolishes feudal practices. Other options: Article 24 relates to prohibition of child labour, Article 51 pertains to promotion of international peace, and Article 21A deals with the right to education.
qs.kf:
☛ Article for abolition of titles → 18
☛ Article 18 comes under which Right → Right to Equality (Articles 14-18)
☛ Exception to Article 18 → Military and academic titles
☛ Article 24 deals with → Prohibition of child labour
☛ Article 21A → Right to education (6-14 years)

q: Which part of the Indian Constitution is mentioned as 'Magna Carta of India'?
qs.e: Part 3 (Articles 12-35) of the Indian Constitution deals with Fundamental Rights. It is called the Magna Carta of India because it guarantees six fundamental rights to citizens: Right to Equality, Right to Freedom, Right against Exploitation, Right to Freedom of Religion, Cultural and Educational Rights, and Right to Constitutional Remedies. The Magna Carta (1215) was a British charter that limited the king's powers and laid the foundation of individual liberty. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar called Fundamental Rights the heart of the Constitution. Article 32 empowers the Supreme Court to enforce these rights. Originally, there were seven fundamental rights, but the Right to Property (Article 31) was removed by the 44th Amendment, 1978.
qs.kf:
☛ Which part of the Indian Constitution is called the 'Magna Carta of India'? → Part 3
☛ Which articles cover Fundamental Rights? → Articles 12-35
☛ How many Fundamental Rights were originally in the Constitution? → 7 (now 6)
☛ Which article is called the 'heart and soul of the Constitution'? → Article 32
☛ Who is the protector of Fundamental Rights? → Supreme Court

q: "No person can be punished more than one for the same crime." What is this principle called?
qs.e: This principle states that no person can be punished more than once for the same crime. It is called the principle of Double Jeopardy. It is a fundamental right provided under Article 20(2) of the Indian Constitution. According to this, if a person has already been convicted or punished for an offence, they cannot be prosecuted again for the same offence. This principle protects an individual from arbitrary actions of the state and ensures fairness in the judicial process. In the United States Constitution, this principle is included in the Fifth Amendment. The doctrine of double jeopardy is also recognized in many legal systems around the world, ensuring that once a person is acquitted or convicted, they are not subjected to repeated trials for the same alleged act.
qs.kf:
☛ Under which Article of the Indian Constitution is Double Jeopardy mentioned? → Article 20(2)
☛ What is the meaning of Double Jeopardy? → Not being punished more than once for the same crime
☛ Which Fundamental Right includes this principle? → Article 20 (Protection against Conviction)
☛ In the US, which amendment contains Double Jeopardy? → Fifth Amendment
☛ Who is protected by Double Jeopardy? → Any person who has been previously convicted or acquitted

q: Which writ can be issued against both public and private individuals?
qs.e: Habeas corpus writ can be obtained by any person who has been illegally detained. This writ can be issued against both public and private individuals because its purpose is to protect the liberty of an individual from any unlawful detention. The writ is issued by a court to bring the detained person before the court to examine the legality of the detention. It is one of the fundamental rights and can be issued by the Supreme Court under Article 32 and by the High Courts under Article 226 of the Indian Constitution. Habeas corpus literally means 'to have the body' and serves as a powerful safeguard against arbitrary arrests.
qs.kf:
☛ Under which Article is Habeas Corpus described? → Article 32 (Supreme Court)
☛ Against whom can Habeas Corpus be issued? → Both public and private individuals
☛ What is the meaning of Habeas Corpus? → To have the body
☛ Which right does Habeas Corpus protect? → Right to personal liberty
☛ Who can issue Habeas Corpus writ? → Supreme Court and High Courts

q: When did the Right to Information Act (RTI) come into force?
qs.e: The Right to Information Act (RTI) is a landmark legislation in India that empowers citizens to access information from public authorities. It came into force on 12 October 2005, replacing the earlier Freedom of Information Act, 2002. The RTI Act promotes transparency and accountability in the functioning of government bodies. Under this act, any citizen can request information from a public authority, which must reply within 30 days. The act is a powerful tool against corruption and strengthens democracy. The RTI Act was passed by Parliament on 15 June 2005 and received presidential assent on 21 June 2005. It applies to all constitutional authorities, including the executive, legislature, and judiciary, except certain intelligence and security organizations.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the RTI Act passed by Parliament? → 15 June 2005
☛ When did the RTI Act come into force? → 12 October 2005
☛ What is the time limit to provide information under RTI? → 30 days
☛ What is the objective of RTI Act? → Promote transparency and accountability
☛ Which fundamental right is related to RTI? → Article 19(1)(a)

q: The state's definition is given in which article of Indian Constitution?
qs.e: Article 12 of the Indian Constitution provides the definition of the State. This is a crucial preliminary article that clarifies the meaning of the term 'State' in Part III (Fundamental Rights) of the Constitution. According to this definition, the State includes the Government and Parliament of India, the Governments and Legislatures of the States, as well as all local or other authorities within the territory of India or under the control of the Government of India. This definition ensures that fundamental rights are enforceable not only against the central and state governments but also against other public authorities.
qs.kf:
☛ Which article defines the State? → Article 12
☛ Article 12's definition of State falls under which part? → Part III (Fundamental Rights)
☛ What is included in the State under Article 12? → Government of India, Parliament, State Governments, Legislatures, local authorities
☛ Is the judiciary considered a State under Article 12? → Yes, in certain contexts (e.g., A.D.M. Jabalpur case)
☛ Which word is defined in Article 12? → 'State'

q: According to the legal order of the Indian Constitution, which of the following words is literally 'presenting body (person)'?
qs.e: Under Articles 32 and 226 of the Indian Constitution, five types of writs are issued. 'Habeas Corpus' is a Latin term meaning 'presenting body (person)'. This writ is issued to bring a person who has been illegally detained before the court and to examine the legality of their detention. It protects the personal liberty of citizens. Among other writs, Mandamus means 'we command', Quo-Warranto means 'by what authority', and Certiorari means 'to be informed'. Habeas Corpus is considered a bulwark of individual freedom against arbitrary state action.
qs.kf:
☛ Which writ protects personal liberty? → Habeas Corpus
☛ Which writ examines the authority of a person holding a public office? → Quo-Warranto
☛ Which writ is used to quash the order of a lower court? → Certiorari
☛ Which writ commands a public authority to perform its duty? → Mandamus
☛ Writ of Habeas Corpus is issued in case of? → Illegal detention

q: Which of the following article of Indian Constitution is related to the right to elementary education?
qs.e: Article 21A of the Indian Constitution is related to the right to elementary education. It was inserted by the 86th Amendment Act, 2002 and provides free and compulsory education to all children aged 6 to 14 years. It is considered a fundamental right to education. For its implementation, the Right to Education Act, 2009 (RTE Act) was enacted. Article 16 deals with equality of opportunity in public employment, Article 19 with freedom of speech and expression, and Article 24 with prohibition of child labour.
qs.kf:
☛ Fundamental right to education → Article 21A
☛ 86th Amendment year → 2002
☛ Age group for free and compulsory education → 6-14 years
☛ RTE Act year → 2009
☛ Title of Article 21A → Right to elementary education

q: Which of the following is the first written document related to the fundamental rights of citizens?
qs.e: The Magna Carta (1215) is considered the first written document related to the fundamental rights of citizens. It was an agreement signed between King John of England and rebellious barons. It limited the king's powers and granted certain legal rights, such as fair trial and protection from arbitrary imprisonment. Later, it inspired many constitutions, including the American Constitution and the Constitution of India. The Government of India Act 1935 and the American Constitution came later.
qs.kf:
☛ In which year was Magna Carta signed? → 1215
☛ In which country was Magna Carta signed? → England
☛ Which king signed Magna Carta? → King John
☛ What was the main purpose of Magna Carta? → To limit the king's powers
☛ Which right originated from Magna Carta? → Right to fair trial

q: Which of the following articles is related to the right to property?
qs.e: The right to property in the Indian Constitution was originally under Article 31, but was removed from fundamental rights by the 44th Amendment (1978). Currently, it is a constitutional right under Article 300A. It stipulates that no person shall be deprived of his property except by authority of law. Article 42 relates to just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief. Article 272 was repealed earlier. Article 214 deals with High Courts.
qs.kf:
☛ Which article deals with the right to property? → Article 300A
☛ What type of right is the right to property? → Constitutional right
☛ Which amendment removed the right to property from fundamental rights? → 44th Amendment (1978)
☛ Which article originally contained the right to property? → Article 31 (now repealed)
☛ Under Article 300A, what is the condition for deprivation of property? → Only by authority of law

q: Who is called 'Magna Carta of India'?
qs.e: Fundamental Rights (Articles 12-35) in the Indian Constitution are called the 'Magna Carta of India'. This name is given because these rights protect citizens from government tyranny, just as the Magna Carta of 1215 AD restricted the absolute power of the English king. Fundamental Rights are justiciable, meaning citizens can approach the High Court or Supreme Court if these rights are violated. These rights are divided into Right to Equality, Right to Freedom, Right against Exploitation, Right to Freedom of Religion, Cultural and Educational Rights, and Right to Constitutional Remedies. Article 32 is known as the 'heart and soul of the Constitution'. The Supreme Court has declared Fundamental Rights as part of the basic structure of the Constitution, and they cannot be amended to destroy their essence.
qs.kf:
☛ Magna Carta of India → Fundamental Rights
☛ Fundamental Rights are in which Articles → Articles 12-35
☛ Heart and Soul of Constitution → Article 32
☛ Magna Carta belongs to which country → England
☛ How many types of Fundamental Rights → 6

q: "If the court will find that a person has held a public position that he is not an officer, then he can officially stop him from holding office or office." In what legal order is this written?
qs.e: This question relates to the writ of Quo Warranto, which is issued by the High Court when a person holds a public office illegally. The court asks 'by what authority' the person occupies the office. If the person fails to prove their right, they are removed from the office. This writ ensures that no unqualified person holds a public position. Other options like 'Permission', 'Trademark Articles', and 'Prohibition' are different legal writs used for various purposes. Quo Warranto is a powerful tool to prevent usurpation of public office.
qs.kf:
☛ What does Quo Warranto mean? → It means 'by what authority' and is used to challenge illegal occupancy of a public office.
☛ Under which article is this writ issued? → Article 226 (High Court) and Article 32 (Supreme Court).
☛ What is the purpose of Quo Warranto? → To prevent an unqualified person from holding a public office.
☛ Against whom is this writ issued? → Only against claimants of public offices.
☛ What are the other writs? → Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, and Quo Warranto.

q: Which article of the Indian Constitution provides for the provision of the Independent Election Commission?
qs.e: Article 324 of the Indian Constitution provides for the establishment and powers of the Election Commission of India. This commission is responsible for the conduct, supervision, and control of elections in the country. Under Article 324, the Chief Election Commissioner and other commissioners are appointed by the President. The Election Commission is an independent constitutional body that manages elections to Parliament, state legislatures, the President, and the Vice President. Article 320 relates to the Union Public Service Commission, Article 330 provides for reservation of seats for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, and Article 314 protects the rights of officers of the Indian Administrative Service. Thus, the correct answer is Article 324.
qs.kf:
☛ Which article provides for the Election Commission of India? → Article 324
☛ Who appoints the Chief Election Commissioner? → The President
☛ Article 320 relates to which body? → Union Public Service Commission
☛ What does Article 330 provide? → Reservation of seats for SCs and STs
☛ Article 314 protects the rights of which officers? → Officers of the Indian Administrative Service

q: Under which fundamental right are the freedom of speech and expression?
qs.e: The Indian Constitution in Part III enumerates fundamental rights. Article 19(1)(a) guarantees freedom of speech and expression, which falls under the Right to freedom (Articles 19-22). This right allows citizens to express their thoughts freely, but reasonable restrictions can be imposed in the interest of state security, public order, decency, contempt of court, defamation, etc. It is a cornerstone of democracy.
qs.kf:
☛ Under which Article is freedom of speech? → Article 19(1)(a)
☛ How many Articles in Right to freedom? → 4 (19-22)
☛ Is this right absolute? → No, subject to reasonable restrictions
☛ Which fundamental right is most comprehensive? → Right to freedom
☛ What does freedom of expression include? → Oral, written, publication, broadcast

q: What is the right to equality in the fundamental rights?
o: All people are equal before the law
People in the same community are the same
qs.e: The Right to Equality is enshrined in Articles 14 to 18 of the Indian Constitution. Article 14 states that the State shall not deny to any person equality before the law and equal protection of the laws within the territory of India. This means that all citizens, irrespective of their gender, caste, religion, or social status, are equal in the eyes of the law. The right to equality is a fundamental right that prohibits discrimination and ensures that no person is granted special privileges. While other options like gender equality or social quality are related, the core principle is equality before the law for all individuals.
qs.kf:
☛ Which articles cover the Right to Equality? → Articles 14 to 18
☛ What does Article 14 provide? → Equality before law and equal protection
☛ Is Right to Equality applicable to foreigners? → Yes, Article 14 applies to all persons
☛ What is an exception to Right to Equality? → Special privileges for President, Governors, etc.
☛ Which article abolishes untouchability? → Article 17

q: ________ is given religious independence.
qs.e: Under Article 25 of the Indian Constitution, all citizens are granted the fundamental right to religious freedom. This right is not limited to minorities or the majority but gives every citizen the equal right to profess, practice, and propagate any religion. However, this right is subject to reasonable restrictions based on public order, morality, and health. This ensures the state remains secular and treats all religions equally. Thus, the Indian Constitution universally applies religious freedom to all citizens.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Article grants the right to religious freedom? → Article 25
☛ On what grounds can religious freedom be restricted? → Public order, morality, and health
☛ What type of state is India? → Secular state
☛ Who is entitled to religious freedom? → All citizens
☛ Do minorities have special religious rights? → Yes, they have the right to establish cultural and educational institutions

q: What is the minimum period for the arrested person to be presented by the police in front of the nearest judge?
qs.e: According to Article 22(2) of the Indian Constitution, any arrested person must be produced before the nearest magistrate within 24 hours of arrest. This provision is part of the Fundamental Rights and protects individual liberty. It does not apply to cases where a person is arrested as an enemy alien or under preventive detention laws. Additionally, Section 57 and 167 of the Criminal Procedure Code (CrPC) also prescribe the same time limit. If the police fail to produce the person within this period, the detention becomes illegal, and the arrested person has the right to file a habeas corpus petition. This right ensures that no person is held in custody without being brought before a judicial authority promptly.
qs.kf:
☛ Time limit to produce arrested person before magistrate → 24 hours
☛ Constitutional article providing this safeguard → Article 22(2)
☛ Under which rights is this provision? → Fundamental Rights (Article 22)
☛ Cases where this provision does not apply → Preventive detention and enemy alien
☛ CrPC sections with same time limit → Section 57 and 167

q: Except for the status as per the procedure established by law, no person will be deprived of life and personal liberty "This is an established law and in what article of the Constitution is cited?
qs.e: Article 21 of the Indian Constitution deals with the fundamental right to life and personal liberty. It states that no person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to the procedure established by law. This provision protects every citizen from arbitrary action, ensuring that any state action follows legal procedure. In the landmark case of Maneka Gandhi vs Union of India (1978), the Supreme Court interpreted Article 21 expansively, incorporating both procedural and substantive due process. It is considered the most important article of the Constitution and falls under Part III (Fundamental Rights). This article is distinct from Article 19 (freedom of speech) and Article 20 (protection in respect of conviction for offenses).
qs.kf:
☛ Which case expanded the scope of Article 21? → Maneka Gandhi vs Union of India (1978)
☛ Which right is NOT included in the right to life under Article 21? → Right to die (Gian Kaur vs Punjab, 1996)
☛ Article 21 falls under which part of the Constitution? → Fundamental Rights (Part III)
☛ What is the main purpose of Article 21? → Protection of life and personal liberty of citizens
☛ Article 21 is similar to which amendment of the US Constitution? → 14th Amendment (but only procedural due process)

q: If your fundamental rights have been tarnished by the state, then what is the basic right that citizens can appeal to the court against?
qs.e: Under Article 32 of the Indian Constitution, citizens have the right to approach the Supreme Court and High Court in case of violation of fundamental rights. This is known as the Right to Constitutional Remedies and is also called the right to writs. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar described Article 32 as the soul and heart of the Constitution. Five types of writs can be issued: Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari and Quo Warranto. This right is also available under Article 226 for High Courts.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 32 → Right to Constitutional Remedies
☛ Soul of the Constitution → Article 32
☛ Article for writs in High Court → Article 226
☛ Habeas Corpus writ → Freedom from illegal detention
☛ Mandamus writ → Order to public servant to perform duty

q: Under which article does the Right to Information get an explanation for the offense being arrested for the offense?
qs.e: Article 22 of the Indian Constitution provides protection to individuals in case of arrest. Under this, the arrested person has the right to be informed of the grounds of arrest and must be produced before the nearest magistrate within 24 hours. It also guarantees the right to consult and be defended by a lawyer. Article 22 ensures that no person can be arrested without being told the reason, and it is a fundamental right that safeguards against arbitrary arrest. This article applies to all persons except those under enemy action. Thus, the provision for obtaining an explanation when arrested for an offense under the Right to Information is contained in Article 22.
qs.kf:
☛ Which article provides the right to know the grounds of arrest? → Article 22
☛ Which article grants the right to consult a lawyer for an arrested person? → Article 22
☛ Which article mandates producing an arrested person before a magistrate within 24 hours? → Article 22
☛ Article 22 deals with protection against what? → Arrest and detention
☛ Does Article 22 apply to enemy aliens? → No

q: What paragraph can not be suspended at the time of the emergency?
qs.e: Article 20 (Protection in respect of conviction for offences) and Article 21 (Protection of life and personal liberty) of the Indian Constitution cannot be suspended even during a national emergency. Article 20 ensures that no person can be punished twice for the same offence or compelled to be a witness against themselves. Article 21 guarantees that no person shall be deprived of their life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law. These two articles are part of the Fundamental Rights and remain protected during an emergency. Under Article 359, the President can suspend the right to move any court for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights during an emergency, but Article 20 and 21 can never be suspended. The 44th Amendment Act of 1978 further strengthened this protection. Thus, the correct answer is Article 20 and Article 21.
qs.kf:
☛ Which articles cannot be suspended during emergency? → Article 20 and 21
☛ What does Article 20 protect? → Protection against double jeopardy and self-incrimination
☛ What is the essence of Article 21? → No deprivation of life or liberty except by procedure established by law
☛ What does Article 359 allow? → Suspension of enforcement of Fundamental Rights during emergency
☛ After which amendment are Articles 20 and 21 immune from suspension? → 44th Amendment Act, 1978

q: Which of the following rights is called the soul and heart of the Indian Constitution?
qs.e: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar called the Right to Constitutional Remedies (Article 32) the soul and heart of the Indian Constitution. This right empowers citizens to directly approach the Supreme Court or High Courts in case of violation of fundamental rights. Article 32 itself is a fundamental right, without which other fundamental rights become meaningless. Under this, writs like Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, and Quo Warranto are issued. Thus, it provides judicial protection and upholds the supremacy of the constitution.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 32 → Right to Constitutional Remedies
☛ Ambedkar on soul of Constitution → Article 32
☛ Types of writs → Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, Quo Warranto
☛ During emergency → Article 32 remains suspended
☛ High Court → Can issue writs under Article 226

q: What is the meaning of religious freedom?
o: Freedom of management of religious activities; Freedom to give religious instructions to some institutions
qs.e: Article 25 of the Indian Constitution guarantees religious freedom, including the freedom of conscience and the right to profess, practice, and propagate religion. Article 26 grants every religious denomination the right to manage its own affairs in matters of religion, establish institutions for religious and charitable purposes, and give religious instructions. These rights are subject to public order, morality, and health. The correct option combines these two freedoms: management of religious activities (from Article 26) and giving religious instructions to some institutions (related to Article 26 and 30).
qs.kf:
☛ Which articles cover religious freedom in India? → Articles 25-28
☛ What does Article 25 protect? → Freedom of conscience and the right to practice religion
☛ What does Article 26 include? → Right to manage religious affairs and establish institutions
☛ What does Article 28 prohibit? → Religious instruction in state-funded institutions
☛ Is religious freedom absolute in India? → No, it is subject to public order, morality, and health

q: If the court thinks that a particular officer is not following his legal duties, in this case, what is the writ issued by the court?
qs.e: When a public officer fails to perform his legal duty, the court issues Mandamus. It is a writ that commands the officer to fulfill his duty. The literal meaning of Mandamus is 'we command'. This writ is directed to a lower court, government official, or public body. Article 32 of the Indian Constitution empowers the Supreme Court, and Article 226 empowers the High Court to issue this writ. Mandamus is issued only when the duty is legal and the officer is failing to perform it. It cannot be issued against discretionary duties or private individuals.
qs.kf:
☛ Under which article is Mandamus issued? → Articles 32 and 226
☛ What is the literal meaning of Mandamus? → 'We command'
☛ Against whom is Mandamus issued? → Public officer or lower court
☛ When is Mandamus not issued? → When the duty is discretionary
☛ How many writs are there in India? → Five: Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, Quo Warranto

q: Under which article of the Constitution was the office of the Comptroller and Auditor General established?
qs.e: The office of the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) was established under Article 148 of the Indian Constitution. CAG is the supreme audit institution of India, responsible for auditing government accounts. Article 149 specifies the duties and powers of the CAG, while Article 150 deals with the form of accounts of the Union and States. According to Article 151, the CAG's reports are submitted to the President. The CAG is appointed by the President and holds office for a term of six years or until the age of 65, whichever is earlier.
qs.kf:
☛ Who appoints the CAG? → President
☛ What is the term of office of CAG? → 6 years or until 65 years of age
☛ Which article is related to CAG? → Article 148
☛ To whom does CAG submit its report? → President
☛ Which article describes the duties of CAG? → Article 149

q: By what kind of majority can fundamental rights be amended?
o: Special majority of parliament with consent of states
qs.e: Under Article 368 of the Indian Constitution, fundamental rights can be amended by a special majority of Parliament. A special majority means that at least half of the total members of the House are present and at least two-thirds of those present vote in favor. Additionally, the consent of states is not required for amending fundamental rights. This process is subject to the basic structure doctrine, as established in the Kesavananda Bharati case.
qs.kf:
☛ What majority is required for constitutional amendment? → Special majority
☛ How is special majority defined? → Half of total members present and two-thirds voting
☛ Is state consent needed for amending fundamental rights? → No
☛ Article 368 deals with? → Constitutional amendment
☛ Kesavananda Bharati case is related to which doctrine? → Basic structure doctrine

q: On the basis of equality, the ban on discrimination comes under the fundamental rights of the Indian Constitution?
qs.e: The Right to Equality is enshrined in Articles 14 to 18 of the Indian Constitution. Under this, Article 15 prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth. This fundamental right ensures equal treatment in public places, employment, and education. The Right to Equality embodies the principles of justice and fairness mentioned in the Preamble. It prevents the state from making any unreasonable discrimination against citizens. This right is a cornerstone of Indian democracy, promoting social harmony and equal opportunity for all.
qs.kf:
☛ How many articles are under Right to Equality? → 5 (Articles 14-18)
☛ Which article prohibits discrimination? → Article 15
☛ What does Article 14 provide? → Equality before law
☛ Article 16 relates to? → Equality of opportunity in public employment
☛ What does Article 17 abolish? → Untouchability

q: According to our Constitution, which of the following rights is NOT a fundamental right?
qs.e: Originally, the right to property (Article 31) was a fundamental right under the Indian Constitution. However, the 44th Amendment Act of 1978 removed it from the list of fundamental rights and made it a legal right. Currently, it is a constitutional right under Article 300A in Part XII of the Constitution. The other three rights—right to freedom of religion (Articles 25-28), right against exploitation (Articles 23-24), and right to equality (Articles 14-18)—remain fundamental rights in Part III. The Constitution now guarantees six fundamental rights: equality, freedom, against exploitation, freedom of religion, cultural and educational rights, and constitutional remedies.
qs.kf:
☛ Which amendment removed the right to property from fundamental rights? → 44th Amendment (1978)
☛ Under which article is the right to property now? → Article 300A
☛ Which part contains fundamental rights? → Part III
☛ How many fundamental rights exist currently? → Six
☛ Which articles cover the right against exploitation? → Articles 23 and 24

q: Which of the following is NOT a Fundamental Right?
qs.e: The Fundamental Rights in the Indian Constitution (Articles 12-35) include Right against exploitation (Articles 23-24), Right to constitutional remedies (Article 32), and Cultural and educational rights (Articles 29-30). The Right to property was originally a Fundamental Right under Article 31, but the 44th Constitutional Amendment (1978) removed it from the list of Fundamental Rights and made it a constitutional right under Article 300A. Therefore, the Right to property is not a Fundamental Right currently; it is a legal right. Other options are all Fundamental Rights.
qs.kf:
☛ When was Right to property removed from Fundamental Rights? → 1978 (44th Amendment)
☛ Under which Article is Right to property now? → Article 300A
☛ Under which Articles is Right against exploitation? → Articles 23 and 24
☛ Under which Article is Right to constitutional remedies? → Article 32
☛ How many Fundamental Rights are there in India? → 6 (Right to property is not a Fundamental Right)

q: Which Article of Indian Constitution prohibits the employment of children in factories?
qs.e: Article 24 of the Indian Constitution prohibits the employment of children below the age of 14 years in factories, mines, or other hazardous occupations. It is part of the Right against Exploitation under Articles 23 and 24. This provision ensures the protection of children from economic exploitation and safeguards their physical and mental development. Any violation of Article 24 can lead to legal action under relevant labor laws. The article aims to reduce child labor and promote education for children. It complements laws like the Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986, which further specifies hazardous occupations.
qs.kf:
☛ Article prohibiting child labour → Article 24
☛ Minimum age for employment in factories → 14 years
☛ Right against Exploitation includes → Articles 23 and 24
☛ Article 24 is part of which fundamental right → Right against Exploitation (Articles 23-24)
☛ Child Labour (Prohibition & Regulation) Act, 1986 → Applies to factories, mines, and hazardous occupations

q: What is written in Article 1 of the Indian Constitution?
o: India will be a federal republic
India i.e. Bharat will be a single state
India i.e. Bharat will be a union of states
India i.e. Bharat will be a federation of states
qs.e: Article 1 states that India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States. The term 'Union' was deliberately chosen over 'Federation' to emphasize the indestructible nature of the Indian Union. Unlike a federation, states have no right to secede. This article is part of Part I of the Constitution (Articles 1 to 4), which deals with the Union and its territory. It declares the official names of the country as India and Bharat. The provision ensures that the Union is indestructible and the states are created or abolished only by the Parliament. Article 1 lays the foundation for India's federal structure with a unitary bias.
qs.kf:
☛ What is the constitutional name of India? → India, that is Bharat
☛ Why is 'Union' used in Article 1? → To indicate the indestructibility of states
☛ Which part contains Articles 1 to 4? → Part I: The Union and its Territory
☛ Is India a federation? → No, it is a union of states
☛ What is the significance of Article 1? → It declares India as a Union of States

q: Which of the following Articles of the Constitution was amended to include the Right to Education as a Fundamental Right?
qs.e: The Right to Education was originally a Directive Principle under Article 45 in Part IV of the Constitution. The 86th Constitutional Amendment Act (2002) made it a Fundamental Right by inserting Article 21A after Article 21. Article 21A provides free and compulsory education to children aged 6-14 years. It is an extension of Article 21 (Right to Life). This right was enforced through the Right to Education Act, 2009. Hence, the correct answer is Article 21.
qs.kf:
☛ Article related to Right to Education → 21A
☛ Year of 86th Amendment → 2002
☛ Year RTE Act came into force → 2009
☛ Age group for free education → 6-14 years
☛ Article 21A inserted after which Article → Article 21

q: Fundamental Rights have been provided in the Constitution under which Part?
qs.e: The Fundamental Rights are enshrined in Part III (Articles 12 to 35) of the Indian Constitution. These rights protect citizens from arbitrary state action. Originally, there were seven fundamental rights, but the 44th Amendment removed the Right to Property (Article 31) from Part III and made it a legal right. Currently, there are six fundamental rights. These rights are justiciable, meaning citizens can directly approach the Supreme Court or High Courts in case of violation. Article 32 provides the constitutional remedy for enforcement of fundamental rights.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Part of the Constitution contains Fundamental Rights? → Part III
☛ Which Articles cover Fundamental Rights? → 12 to 35
☛ Which amendment removed the Right to Property from Fundamental Rights? → 44th Amendment
☛ Which Article provides judicial remedy for violation of Fundamental Rights? → Article 32
☛ How many Fundamental Rights are there currently? → Six

q: Which of the following Articles of the Indian Constitution guarantees 'Equality before the Law' and 'Equal protection of the law'?
qs.e: Article 14 of the Indian Constitution guarantees 'Equality before the Law' and 'Equal protection of the laws'. It prohibits the State from denying any person equality before the law or equal protection of the laws within the territory of India. This Article falls under Fundamental Rights and ensures equality for all citizens. It is also applicable to foreigners. Article 14 is the foundation of the Right to Equality and any discrimination made under it is considered unconstitutional. It is included in Part III of the Constitution.
qs.kf:
☛ Article guaranteeing equality before law → Article 14
☛ Article 14 comes under which rights → Fundamental Rights
☛ Article 14 applies to → Citizens and foreigners both
☛ Basis of Right to Equality → Article 14
☛ Article 14 is in which part → Part III

q: Which of the following freedoms is NOT part of the 'Right to Freedom' under Article 19?
qs.e: Article 19 grants six freedoms: speech and expression, peaceful assembly, forming associations or unions, free movement throughout India, residence and settlement in any part of the country, and practicing any profession, occupation, trade or business. Freedom of conscience falls under Right to Freedom of Religion in Article 25, not under Article 19. The other options (forming associations, assembling peacefully, and moving freely) are explicitly listed under Article 19. Hence, the correct answer is Freedom of conscience.
qs.kf:
☛ How many freedoms are granted under Article 19? → Six
☛ Which Article deals with freedom of speech? → Article 19(1)(a)
☛ Under which Article is freedom of conscience protected? → Article 25
☛ Which Article protects the right to assemble peacefully? → Article 19(1)(b)
☛ Which Article guarantees the right to move freely? → Article 19(1) (d)

q: Which of the following Articles of the Constitution of India says that all public places are open to all citizens?
qs.e: Article 15 of the Indian Constitution prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth. Its clause (2) specifically states that no citizen shall be denied access to shops, public restaurants, hotels, places of public entertainment, or the use of wells, tanks, bathing ghats, roads and places of public resort maintained by the state or dedicated to public use, solely on these grounds. This provision is part of the Right to Equality (Articles 14-18) and ensures equal access to public spaces for all citizens. Article 30 deals with minority educational institutions, Article 21 with right to life and personal liberty, and Article 16(2) with equality of opportunity in public employment.
qs.kf:
☛ Article guaranteeing equal access to public places → Article 15(2)
☛ Forbidden grounds under Article 15 → Religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth
☛ Public places covered under Article 15(2) → Shops, restaurants, hotels, entertainment venues, wells, tanks, roads
☛ Part containing Article 15 → Part III (Fundamental Rights)
☛ Articles related to Right to Equality → 14 to 18

q: Which fundamental right has provided Prevention against Arbitrary Arrest and Detention to Indian citizens?
qs.e: The protection against arbitrary arrest and detention is provided under Article 22 of the Indian Constitution. This article is a part of the Right to Freedom (Articles 19-22). Article 22 ensures that any person arrested must be informed of the grounds of arrest, allowed to consult and be defended by a lawyer, and produced before a magistrate within 24 hours. This right applies to both citizens and foreigners. However, enemy aliens and persons arrested under preventive detention laws are not entitled to this protection. The provision safeguards individual liberty against arbitrary state action. It also lays down safeguards for preventive detention laws through Articles 22(3) to 22(7).
qs.kf:
☛ Article 22 → Protection against arbitrary arrest and detention
☛ Rights of arrested person → Informed of grounds, consult lawyer, produced before magistrate within 24 hours
☛ Right to Freedom → Articles 19 to 22
☛ Exceptions → Enemy aliens and persons under preventive detention laws
☛ Preventive detention → Special provisions under Article 22 clauses 3-7

q: Which of the following is true regarding the writ jurisdiction under Articles 32 and 226 of the Indian Constitution?
o: The writ of Quo Warranto can only be issued by the President of India.
Only the Supreme Court has the authority to issue writs for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
Under Article 32, Parliament has the power to allow other courts to issue writs for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
High Courts can issue writs under Article 226 only for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
qs.e: Article 32 of the Indian Constitution empowers the Supreme Court to issue writs for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights. It also allows Parliament to authorise any other court to exercise the same power within its territorial jurisdiction. In contrast, Article 226 empowers High Courts to issue writs not only for Fundamental Rights but also for other legal rights. The writ of Quo Warranto is not issued by the President; it is a judicial remedy. The Supreme Court does not have exclusive authority to issue writs for Fundamental Rights; High Courts can also do so under Article 226. Thus, option 3 is correct.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Article deals with Supreme Court's writ jurisdiction? → Article 32
☛ Which Article deals with High Court's writ jurisdiction? → Article 226
☛ What writs can be issued under Article 32? → Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, Quo Warranto
