☛ Can Parliament empower other courts to issue writs under Article 32? → Yes, by law
☛ Under Article 226, writs can be issued for which rights? → Both Fundamental and other legal rights

q: The 86th Constitutional Amendment Act added the Right to Education in the Constitution, under which Article?
qs.e: The 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002 added the Right to Education as Article 21A in the Indian Constitution. This amendment inserted a new Article 21A after Article 21, providing free and compulsory education for children aged 6 to 14 years. It was made a Fundamental Right. Additionally, Article 45 (Directive Principle) was amended to emphasize early childhood care and education, and Article 51A(k) was added as a fundamental duty of parents to provide educational opportunities to their children. This amendment forms the constitutional basis for the National Education Policy 2020 and the RTE Act 2009.
qs.kf:
☛ 86th Constitutional Amendment → Passed in 2002
☛ Right to Education → Fundamental Right under Article 21A
☛ Age group → Children aged 6 to 14 years
☛ RTE Act → Enacted in 2009 to enforce the right
☛ Article 45 → Amended to focus on early childhood care and education

q: Which of the following Articles of the Indian Constitution explicitly prohibits the State from making any law that violates Fundamental Rights?
qs.e: Article 13 of the Indian Constitution explicitly prohibits the State from making any law that violates Fundamental Rights (Part III). It declares that any law made by the State that is inconsistent with Fundamental Rights shall be void. Additionally, pre-constitutional laws are also invalid to the extent they conflict with Fundamental Rights. This article ensures constitutional supremacy. Article 32 provides remedies for enforcement of Fundamental Rights, Article 30 grants minorities the right to establish educational institutions, and Article 42 directs the State to ensure just and humane working conditions.
qs.kf:
☛ Which article declares laws violating Fundamental Rights as void? → Article 13
☛ Article 32 deals with what? → Right to Constitutional Remedies
☛ Article 30 protects which group? → Minorities
☛ Article 42 is related to what? → Just and humane work conditions
☛ Which article prohibits the State from making laws that violate Fundamental Rights? → Article 13

q: Under which Article of the Constitution can the President of India direct that the provisions related to the Public Service Commissions be extended to any Union Territory?
qs.e: Article 321 of the Indian Constitution empowers the President to direct that the provisions relating to Public Service Commissions be extended to any Union Territory. This article allows the extension of provisions from Articles 315 to 320 to Union Territories. Article 315 deals with the establishment of Public Service Commissions for the Union and states, while Article 321 specifically authorizes the President to expand the powers and functions of these Commissions. Thus, the President can issue directions under Article 321 to apply Public Service Commission provisions to a Union Territory. Other options: Article 335 relates to reservations, Article 315 establishes commissions, and Article 323 governs the administration of Union Territories.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 321 → Empowers the President to extend Public Service Commission provisions to Union Territories.
☛ Article 315 → Deals with establishment of Public Service Commissions for Union and states.
☛ Article 335 → Concerns reservations for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in public services.
☛ Article 323 → Relates to administration and legislature of Union Territories.
☛ President's power → Under Article 321, to apply Public Service Commission provisions to Union Territories.

q: In which period did Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay write 'Vande Mataram' as a hymn to the motherland?
qs.e: Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay wrote 'Vande Mataram' in the 1870s, which later became part of his novel 'Anandamath' published in 1882. The hymn was composed as a praise to the motherland and became a prominent symbol of the Indian independence movement. Bankim Chandra was a leading figure of the Bengal Renaissance and a renowned writer and poet. 'Vande Mataram' was first sung at the 1896 Congress session and was later adopted as the National Song of India in 1937. The song depicts India as a goddess and is considered a symbol of patriotism.
qs.kf:
☛ Which novel contains Vande Mataram? → Anandamath
☛ When was Vande Mataram published? → 1882
☛ When was Vande Mataram adopted as National Song? → January 24, 1950
☛ How is India depicted in Vande Mataram? → As a mother goddess
☛ When was Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay born? → June 27, 1838

q: The Right to Privacy was declared a Fundamental Right under which of the following Articles?
qs.e: The Right to Privacy was declared a Fundamental Right under Article 21 of the Indian Constitution. This landmark decision was given by a 9-judge bench of the Supreme Court in the Puttaswamy v. Union of India case in 2017. Article 21 protects the right to life and personal liberty. The Court held that privacy is an independent fundamental right under Part III of the Constitution and is an intrinsic part of Article 21. This judgment overruled earlier decisions that had denied privacy the status of a fundamental right.
qs.kf:
☛ Which case declared Right to Privacy a fundamental right? → Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017)
☛ Under which Article is Right to Privacy protected? → Article 21
☛ What does Article 21 guarantee? → Right to life and personal liberty
☛ How many judges were in the Puttaswamy bench? → 9 judges
☛ Which part of the Constitution includes the Right to Privacy? → Part III (Fundamental Rights)

q: With respect to the Indian Constitution, the Fundamental Rights are:
o: written in the Schedules of the Constitution
not written in the Schedules nor outside the Schedules of the Constitution
qs.e: The Fundamental Rights in the Indian Constitution are explicitly mentioned in Part III (Articles 12-35). These rights guarantee citizens a just and free life. They include the Right to Equality (Articles 14-18), Right to Freedom (Articles 19-22), Right against Exploitation (Articles 23-24), Right to Freedom of Religion (Articles 25-28), Cultural and Educational Rights (Articles 29-30), and Right to Constitutional Remedies (Article 32). These rights are part of the main text of the Constitution, not the Schedules. Hence, option 2 is correct.
qs.kf:
☛ In which Part of the Constitution are Fundamental Rights present? → Part III
☛ Which Articles cover Right to Equality? → 14-18
☛ Which Article covers Right to Constitutional Remedies? → 32
☛ Where are Fundamental Rights described? → Main text of Constitution
☛ Which Articles cover Right to Freedom? → 19-22

q: Who among the following has the power to enforce the Fundamental Rights under Article 32?
qs.e: The power to enforce Fundamental Rights under Article 32 lies with the Supreme Court. This Article is considered the 'soul of the Constitution' as it provides citizens the right to directly approach the Supreme Court in case of violation of Fundamental Rights. The Supreme Court can issue writs like Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, and Quo Warranto for enforcement. Article 32 itself is a Fundamental Right and cannot be suspended except during a national emergency under Article 359.
qs.kf:
☛ Which court has the power under Article 32? → Supreme Court
☛ Who called Article 32 the 'soul of the Constitution'? → Dr. B.R. Ambedkar
☛ How many types of writs can be issued under Article 32? → 5
☛ Is Article 32 a Fundamental Right? → Yes
☛ When can Article 32 be suspended? → During national emergency

q: Protection of life and personal liberty is contained under which Article of the Indian Constitution?
qs.e: Article 21 of the Indian Constitution provides for the protection of life and personal liberty. It states that no person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law. This article is part of Part III (Fundamental Rights). The Supreme Court has given it a wide interpretation, including the right to privacy, right to live with dignity, and right to a clean environment under its ambit. Article 21 protects individuals against the state and cannot be suspended even during a national emergency except when public order is threatened. It is one of the most vital fundamental rights ensuring a life of dignity and freedom.
qs.kf:
☛ Protection of life and personal liberty is under which Article? → Article 21
☛ Right to privacy is interpreted under which Article? → Article 21
☛ Article 21 is part of which Part of the Constitution? → Part III (Fundamental Rights)
☛ Right to a clean environment falls under which Article? → Article 21
☛ Article 21A deals with? → Right to Education

q: Right to Education is contained in which of the following Articles of the Indian Constitution?
qs.e: Article 21 A of the Indian Constitution provides free and compulsory education to children aged 6 to 14 years. It was added by the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002. This article makes the Right to Education a Fundamental Right. Article 51 A lists the Fundamental Duties of citizens. Article 17 abolishes untouchability. Article 19 protects rights like freedom of speech. The Right to Education Act (2009) implements this article.
qs.kf:
☛ Which article contains Right to Education? → Article 21 A
☛ Which amendment added Article 21 A? → 86th Amendment
☛ When did RTE Act come into force? → 1 April 2010
☛ Which age group does Article 21 A cover? → 6-14 years
☛ What type of right is Right to Education? → Fundamental Right

q: The Right to Vote is:
o: neither a Fundamental Right nor a legal right
qs.e: The Right to Vote in India is a legal and constitutional right, not a Fundamental Right. It is derived from Article 326 of the Indian Constitution, which provides for adult suffrage in elections to the Lok Sabha and Legislative Assemblies. This right is exercised under the Representation of the People Act, 1951 and other electoral laws. While Fundamental Rights like freedom of speech (Article 19(1)(a)) are enforceable by courts, the right to vote is subject to statutory provisions. The Supreme Court has affirmed that voting rights are governed by constitutional provisions and laws made by Parliament. Therefore, it is a legal right, not a Fundamental Right or Duty.
qs.kf:
☛ What type of right is the Right to Vote? → Legal and constitutional
☛ Which Article of the Indian Constitution provides for adult suffrage? → Article 326
☛ Which Act governs elections in India? → Representation of the People Act, 1951
☛ Is the Right to Vote a Fundamental Right? → No, it is a legal right
☛ Under which Part of the Constitution does the Right to Vote fall? → Part XV

q: The rights mentioned in Part III of the Indian Constitution are termed as _____.
qs.e: Part III (Articles 12-35) of the Indian Constitution grants Fundamental Rights to citizens. These rights are justiciable, meaning one can approach the courts if they are violated. Fundamental Rights are divided into six categories: Right to Equality (Articles 14-18), Right to Freedom (19-22), Right against Exploitation (23-24), Right to Freedom of Religion (25-28), Cultural and Educational Rights (29-30), and Right to Constitutional Remedies (32). These rights protect democracy and individual liberty. During a National Emergency, all Fundamental Rights except Articles 20 and 21 can be suspended.
qs.kf:
☛ What is Part III called? → Fundamental Rights
☛ Which Article deals with Right to Constitutional Remedies? → Article 32
☛ Which Fundamental Rights are not suspended during Emergency? → Articles 20 and 21
☛ From which country are Fundamental Rights borrowed? → USA
☛ Which Articles contain Fundamental Rights? → 12 to 35

q: Which of the following fundamental rights is mentioned from Article 25 to Article 28 of the Indian Constitution?
qs.e: Articles 25 to 28 of the Indian Constitution enshrine the Right to Freedom of Religion. This right grants every person the freedom to profess, practice, and propagate any religion of their choice. Article 25 guarantees freedom of conscience and free profession, practice, and propagation of religion. Article 26 provides freedom to manage religious affairs. Article 27 prohibits imposition of taxes for promotion of any particular religion. Article 28 ensures freedom from attendance at religious instruction. This right is crucial for maintaining religious harmony and protecting individual faith.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 25 → Freedom of conscience and free profession, practice, and propagation of religion
☛ Article 26 → Freedom to manage religious affairs
☛ Article 27 → Prohibition of taxes for promotion of any religion
☛ Article 28 → Freedom from attendance at religious instruction
☛ Right to Freedom of Religion → Foundation of secularism

q: The National Green Tribunals has been established for the enforcement for environmental rights emanating from which Article of the Indian Constitution?
qs.e: The National Green Tribunal (NGT) was established under the National Green Tribunal Act, 2010. It is created for the enforcement of the right to a clean and healthy environment, which emanates from Article 21 (Right to Life) of the Indian Constitution. The Supreme Court has interpreted Article 21 broadly to include the right to environmental protection. NGT ensures speedy disposal of environmental disputes and hears cases related to pollution control. Its chairperson is Justice Prakash Shrivastava, and it has five regional benches.
qs.kf:
☛ Under which Act was NGT established? → National Green Tribunal Act, 2010
☛ Who is the chairperson of NGT? → Justice Prakash Shrivastava
☛ How many regional benches does NGT have? → Five
☛ From which Article does NGT enforce environmental rights? → Article 21
☛ Where is the headquarters of NGT? → New Delhi

q: Right to Education is given in _____ of the Indian Constitution.
qs.e: Article 21A of the Indian Constitution provides the right to free and compulsory education for children aged 6 to 14. It was added by the 86th Constitutional Amendment (2002) and came into effect in 2010. This right makes education a fundamental right, obligating the state to provide primary education. Under Article 21A, private schools must reserve 25% of seats for economically weaker sections. It is linked to Right to Equality (Article 14) and Right to Life (Article 21).
qs.kf:
☛ Right to Education Act → Passed in 2009
☛ RTE implemented from → 1 April 2010
☛ Article 21A added by which amendment → 86th Amendment
☛ Seat reservation for weaker sections in private schools → 25%
☛ Age group covered under RTE → 6-14 years

q: The Comptroller and Auditor General of India is mentioned in which Article of the Indian Constitution?
qs.e: The Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) of India is mentioned in Article 148 of the Indian Constitution. CAG is an independent constitutional authority that audits the accounts of the Government of India and state governments. Article 148 provides for the appointment, oath, and service conditions of the CAG. To ensure independence, the CAG is appointed by the President of India and can be removed only through a process similar to that of a Supreme Court judge. The CAG submits its reports to the President, who then places them before both houses of Parliament. This plays a crucial role in ensuring financial discipline and transparency.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Article mentions CAG? → Article 148
☛ Who appoints the CAG? → President
☛ How is CAG removed? → Like a Supreme Court judge
☛ To whom does CAG submit its report? → President
☛ What is the term of CAG? → 6 years or age of 65, whichever is earlier

q: In which of the following years was the Right to Information Act passed?
qs.e: The Right to Information Act (RTI Act) in India was passed by Parliament in the year 2005. This act provides citizens with access to government information and enhances transparency and accountability. The RTI Act came into effect on 12 October 2005. Under this law, any citizen can request information from a public authority. It is a crucial tool for anti-corruption measures.
qs.kf:
☛ Year of RTI Act passage? → 2005
☛ Date of RTI Act enforcement? → 12 October 2005
☛ Time limit for information under RTI? → 30 days
☛ Full name of RTI Act? → Right to Information Act, 2005
☛ Type of right under RTI? → Legal right, not fundamental right

q: Article 19 of the Indian Constitution guarantees six freedoms. Which of the following is NOT one of them?
o: Freedom to form associations or unions
Freedom to move freely throughout the territory of India
qs.e: Article 19 provides six freedoms: (1) speech and expression, (2) peaceful assembly without arms, (3) forming associations/unions, (4) moving freely throughout India, (5) residing anywhere, (6) practicing any profession or occupation. 'Freedom from arrest' is covered under Article 22, not Article 19. It is part of the right to personal liberty under Articles 21 and 22. The six freedoms under Article 19 can be reasonably restricted in the interest of sovereignty, security, public order, decency, etc.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 19(1)(a) → Freedom of speech and expression
☛ Article 19(1)(b) → Freedom to assemble peaceably
☛ Article 19(1)(c) → Freedom to form associations
☛ Article 19(1)(d) → Freedom to move freely throughout India
☛ Article 19(1)(g) → Freedom to practice any profession

q: What makes basic rules in the Constitution effective?
o: They are based on popular customs only.
qs.e: The key factor that makes basic rules in the Constitution effective is their legal enforceability. The Constitution is the supreme law of the land, and its provisions, such as fundamental rights, can be enforced through courts. Article 32 allows citizens to directly approach the Supreme Court for the enforcement of fundamental rights. This enforceability makes the Constitution a living document rather than a mere moral code. Violation of constitutional rules can lead to legal consequences through judicial review, which ensures compliance. Other options like being based on popular customs or being secret do not align with the nature of the Constitution, which is a binding legal framework. The effectiveness of constitutional rules lies in their ability to be legally challenged and upheld in courts, thereby maintaining the rule of law.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Article provides for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights? → Article 32
☛ Which part of the Indian Constitution deals with Fundamental Rights? → Part III
☛ Who has the power of Judicial Review? → High Courts and Supreme Court
☛ Which principle ensures the supremacy of the Constitution? → Constitutional Supremacy
☛ Which Article provides for the writ jurisdiction of the Supreme Court? → Article 32

q: The 25th Amendment curtailed the right to property by amending which Article of Indian Constitution?
qs.e: The 25th Amendment (1971) to the Indian Constitution dealt with the right to property. It amended Article 31, which originally provided protection for the right to property. The amendment allowed the state to acquire any property for public purpose, and the amount of compensation was to be determined by the Parliament, not the courts. This curtailed the right to property. Later, the 44th Amendment (1978) removed the right to property from the list of Fundamental Rights and made it a legal right under Article 300A.
qs.kf:
☛ In which year was the 25th Amendment passed? → 1971
☛ Under which Article is the right to property currently? → Article 300A
☛ Under which Prime Minister was the 25th Amendment enacted? → Indira Gandhi
☛ Which Amendment removed the right to property as a Fundamental Right? → 44th Amendment (1978)
☛ Who determined compensation under the 25th Amendment? → Parliament

q: Which of the following is the main objective of the Right to Information Act?
o: To ensure secrecy in public administration
To provide private data to media houses
To prevent public access to government records
qs.e: The main objective of the Right to Information Act (RTI), 2005 is to promote transparency and accountability in the functioning of public authorities. It empowers citizens to access information held by government bodies, enabling them to monitor government actions and curb corruption. The Act replaces secrecy with openness and strengthens the right to information under Article 19(1)(a) of the Indian Constitution. It ensures that citizens can demand information to hold the government accountable.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Right to Information Act enacted in India? → 2005
☛ To whom is an RTI application submitted? → Public Information Officer
☛ Which committee reviewed the RTI Act? → H.D. Shourie Committee
☛ Which fundamental right is RTI linked to? → Article 19(1)(a)
☛ Which government passed the RTI Act? → UPA government

q: Which Fundamental Right protects citizens from being forced into labour or human trafficking?
qs.e: Under Articles 23 and 24 of the Indian Constitution, the Right against Exploitation is provided as a Fundamental Right. This right protects citizens from forced labour, human trafficking, and child labour. Article 23 prohibits human trafficking and begar (forced labour), while Article 24 prohibits the employment of children below the age of 14 in hazardous industries. This right is available against both the state and private individuals. Among the given options, this right specifically offers protection against exploitation in the form of forced labour or human trafficking.
qs.kf:
☛ Article prohibiting human trafficking → 23
☛ Forced labour is also known as → Begar
☛ Article prohibiting child labour → 24
☛ Total articles under Right against Exploitation → Two (23 and 24)
☛ Major law against human trafficking in India → Inter-State Migrant Workers Act

q: Which article of the Indian Constitution relates RTI to the fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression?
qs.e: Article 19(1)(a) of the Indian Constitution guarantees the fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression to all citizens. The Right to Information (RTI) is an integral part of this freedom, as it enables citizens to access information held by public authorities, making their expression meaningful. The Supreme Court has recognized RTI as a facet of Article 19(1)(a). Article 15(1) prohibits discrimination, Article 21 deals with right to life and personal liberty, and Article 32 provides the right to constitutional remedies. The RTI Act, 2005, empowers citizens to request information from public bodies, promoting transparency and accountability in governance. This connection between RTI and freedom of speech is crucial for a vibrant democracy, as informed citizens can participate effectively and hold the government accountable.
qs.kf:
☛ Which article links RTI to freedom of speech? → Article 19(1)(a)
☛ When was the RTI Act enacted? → 2005
☛ Article 19(1)(a) deals with which right? → Freedom of speech and expression
☛ RTI is considered which type of right? → Fundamental right
☛ Which article provides constitutional remedies? → Article 32

q: Which of the following Articles of the Indian Constitution is commonly cited as forming the constitutional basis for Judicial Review?
qs.e: Judicial Review empowers the judiciary to invalidate laws that violate the Constitution. In the Indian Constitution, Article 13 is commonly cited as its constitutional basis. It states that any law made after the commencement of the Constitution that infringes upon Fundamental Rights shall be void. Although the term 'Judicial Review' is not explicitly mentioned, Article 13 grants courts the authority to examine the constitutionality of laws. This provision was inspired by the American Constitution and upholds the supremacy of the Constitution. It ensures that legislative and executive actions do not override fundamental rights.
qs.kf:
☛ Basis of Judicial Review → Article 13
☛ Laws void under Article 13 → Those violating Fundamental Rights
☛ Scope of 'law' under Article 13 → Ordinance, order, rule, regulation, by-law
☛ Exceptions to Article 13 → Constitutional amendments (post 1st Amendment Act, 1951)
☛ Core principle behind Judicial Review → Supremacy of Constitution

q: Which Article empowers the High Courts to issue writs for the enforcement of Legal and Fundamental Rights?
qs.e: Article 226 of the Indian Constitution empowers the High Courts to issue writs for the enforcement of both Fundamental Rights and Legal Rights. These writs include habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto, and certiorari. Unlike Article 32, which only allows the Supreme Court to enforce fundamental rights, Article 226 gives High Courts broader jurisdiction. High Courts can issue writs to any person or authority within their territorial jurisdiction. This provision is crucial for ensuring judicial review and protecting citizens' rights. Article 226 is a key tool for upholding the rule of law and providing quick legal remedies against administrative actions.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 226 → Empowers High Courts to issue writs for legal and fundamental rights
☛ Article 32 → Empowers Supreme Court to issue writs for fundamental rights only
☛ Five writs → Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Quo Warranto, Certiorari
☛ Article 226 jurisdiction → Limited to territorial jurisdiction of the High Court
☛ Article 136 → Grants Supreme Court power to grant special leave petition

q: Which of the following Fundamental Rights is guaranteed under Article 25 of the Indian Constitution?
o: Right to move the Supreme Court
qs.e: Article 25 of the Indian Constitution guarantees freedom of conscience and the right to profess, practice, and propagate religion freely, subject to public order, morality, health, and other fundamental rights. This right extends to all persons, both citizens and non-citizens. Articles 25 to 28 collectively cover the Right to Freedom of Religion. Under Article 25, Hindus include Sikhs, Jains, and Buddhists. The State has the power to regulate religious activities. This right protects religious conversion but does not allow forced conversions. The Supreme Court has upheld the right to wear religious attire as part of this freedom.
qs.kf:
☛ Which religions are included under Article 25? → Hindu, Sikh, Jain, Buddhist
☛ What does Article 26 provide? → Freedom to manage religious affairs
☛ Article 27 prohibits what? → Taxation for promotion of any religion
☛ Article 28 deals with? → Prohibition of religious instruction in educational institutions
☛ What restrictions apply to freedom of religion? → Public order, morality, health

q: Which of the following Fundamental Rights is guaranteed under Article 14 of the Indian Constitution?
o: Protection of life and personal liberty
qs.e: Article 14 of the Indian Constitution guarantees Equality before the law and Equal protection of the laws. This Fundamental Right prevents the State from treating any person unequally before the law. It is available to all persons, not just citizens. Article 14 forms the basis of the Right to Equality and is read along with Articles 15, 16, 17, and 18. However, this right is not absolute; the State can make reasonable classifications, such as in reservation policies. The other options: 'Right to freedom of religion' falls under Article 25, 'Prohibition of child labour' under Article 24, and 'Protection of life and personal liberty' under Article 21.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 14 → Equality before the law
☛ Article 21 → Protection of life and personal liberty
☛ Article 24 → Prohibition of child labour
☛ Article 25 → Right to freedom of religion
☛ Article 15 → Prohibition of discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex etc.

q: Which Fundamental Right guarantees Freedom of Speech, Assembly and Movement?
qs.e: Under Article 19 of the Indian Constitution, the Right to Freedom grants citizens six freedoms, including Freedom of Speech and Expression, Freedom to Assemble Peaceably, and Freedom of Movement. This right is part of Part III of the Constitution. Article 19(1)(a) deals with freedom of speech, 19(1)(b) with assembly, and 19(1)(d) with movement. This fundamental right ensures personal development and democratic participation. However, these freedoms are subject to reasonable restrictions. The Right to Equality (Articles 14-18) protects against discrimination. Cultural Rights protect minority interests. The Right to Constitutional Remedies (Article 32) is a means to enforce other rights.
qs.kf:
☛ Which article guarantees Freedom of Speech? → Article 19(1)(a)
☛ Which article guarantees Freedom of Assembly? → Article 19(1)(b)
☛ Which article guarantees Freedom of Movement? → Article 19(1) (d)
☛ Which articles impose restrictions on Right to Freedom? → Articles 19(2) to 19(6)
☛ Which article provides Right to Constitutional Remedies? → Article 32

q: Why does a diverse society need a constitution?
o: To provide basic rules for coordination and assurance
To allow rulers to dominate others
qs.e: A diverse society consists of people from various religions, languages, castes, and cultures. The constitution provides fundamental rules that establish coordination among these diverse groups and gives them assurance about their rights and security. It ensures that no group is oppressed by the majority. The constitution is the supreme law that limits the powers of the government and guarantees the fundamental rights of citizens. Thus, it serves as a means to maintain unity in diversity.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Indian Constitution adopted? → 26 November 1949
☛ Which part of the Constitution deals with Fundamental Rights? → Part III
☛ Which amendment added Fundamental Duties? → 42nd Amendment
☛ Which Article provides the Right to Equality? → Article 14
☛ What is the source of the Indian Constitution? → Constituent Assembly

q: Which of the following statements about the Right to Property in India is correct?
o: It is a fundamental right under Article 31 (now omitted)
It was completely abolished by the Forty-Second Amendment (1976).
It is a fundamental right under Article 32 of the Constitution.
It is no longer a fundamental right.
qs.e: The Right to Property was originally a fundamental right under Article 19(1)(f) and Article 31 of the Indian Constitution. The 44th Amendment (1978) removed it from the list of fundamental rights and made it a constitutional right under Article 300A. This amendment came into effect in 1979. The 42nd Amendment (1976) did not abolish the right to property; it only expanded the scope of Article 31C. Currently, no person can be deprived of property except by authority of law. It is no longer a fundamental right but a legal/constitutional right.
qs.kf:
☛ Which amendment removed the Right to Property from fundamental rights? → 44th Amendment (1978)
☛ Under which Article is the Right to Property now protected? → Article 300A
☛ When did the 44th Amendment come into effect? → 1979
☛ What type of right is the Right to Property now? → Constitutional right
☛ Which Articles originally contained the Right to Property? → Articles 19(1)(f) and 31

q: For the implementation of which of the following did the Central Government estimate a total requirement of ₹2.31 lakh crore over a five year period from 2010-11 to 2014-15?
qs.e: The Central Government estimated a total requirement of ₹2.31 lakh crore for the implementation of the Right to Education Act (RTE Act) from 2010-11 to 2014-15. The RTE Act provides free and compulsory education to children aged 6-14 years. It was passed in 2009 and came into effect on April 1, 2010. The Act mandates 25% reservation in private schools for economically weaker sections. The goal is to achieve universal elementary education in India.
qs.kf:
☛ When did the RTE Act come into force? → April 1, 2010
☛ Which age group does the RTE Act cover? → 6 to 14 years
☛ What is the percentage of reservation in private schools under RTE? → 25%
☛ Under which Article is the RTE Act implemented? → Article 21A
☛ What is the full name of the RTE Act? → Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009

q: The Right to Protection in respect of conviction for offences (including protection from double jeopardy and self-incrimination) is covered under:
qs.e: Article 20 of the Indian Constitution provides protection in respect of conviction for offences. It includes three key safeguards: protection against ex post facto laws, double jeopardy, and self-incrimination. Ex post facto law means no person can be convicted for an act that was not an offence at the time of commission. Double jeopardy means no person can be prosecuted or punished for the same offence more than once. Protection against self-incrimination means no accused can be compelled to be a witness against themselves. Article 20 applies to both citizens and foreigners. It ensures fundamental fairness in criminal proceedings and upholds the rule of law.
qs.kf:
☛ How many protections are provided under Article 20? → Three: ex post facto law, double jeopardy, and self-incrimination
☛ Article 20 applies to whom? → Both citizens and foreigners
☛ Article 20(1) deals with? → Ex post facto law
☛ Article 20(2) deals with? → Double jeopardy
☛ Article 20(3) deals with? → Self-incrimination

q: The Right to Constitutional Remedies, allowing individuals to move the Supreme Court directly for the enforcement of rights, is given under:
qs.e: Article 32 of the Constitution provides the Right to Constitutional Remedies. It allows individuals to directly approach the Supreme Court for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar called it the 'heart and soul of the Constitution'. Under this article, the Supreme Court can issue writs like Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, and Quo Warranto. Article 32 can be suspended when a National Emergency is in effect. It is a crucial mechanism to ensure that fundamental rights are not violated.
qs.kf:
☛ Which article provides Right to Constitutional Remedies? → Article 32
☛ Who called Article 32 the 'heart and soul of the Constitution'? → Dr. B.R. Ambedkar
☛ How many writs can be issued under Article 32? → 5 writs
☛ During which emergency can Article 32 be suspended? → National Emergency
☛ What type of right is Article 32? → Fundamental Right

q: Which of the following Articles deals with the Right against Exploitation?
qs.e: The Right against Exploitation in the Indian Constitution is enshrined in Articles 23 and 24. Article 23 prohibits human trafficking, forced labor, and beggary, while Article 24 prohibits the employment of children below the age of 14 in factories, mines, or hazardous industries. These fundamental rights protect citizens from all forms of exploitation, ensuring social justice and human dignity. They are part of Part III of the Constitution. The other options: Articles 31–32 (Right to Property and Constitutional Remedies), Articles 25–28 (Right to Freedom of Religion), and Articles 29–30 (Cultural and Educational Rights of Minorities) are incorrect. Thus, Articles 23–24 are the correct answer.
qs.kf:
☛ Articles dealing with Right against Exploitation → 23 and 24
☛ Article 23 prohibits → human trafficking and forced labor
☛ Age limit for child labor prohibition under Article 24 → below 14 years
☛ Hazardous industries mentioned in Article 24 → factories, mines, etc.
☛ Part of the Constitution where these rights are found → Part III (Fundamental Rights)

q: Which of the following is the primary objective of the Right to Information (RTI) Act, 2005?
o: To promote transparency and accountability in government functioning
To regulate foreign investment in India
To control corruption in the judiciary
To ensure reservations for backwards classes
qs.e: The Right to Information (RTI) Act, 2005 is a landmark legislation in India that empowers citizens to access information held by public authorities. Its primary objective is to promote transparency and accountability in government functioning, enabling citizens to scrutinize government actions and reduce corruption. The Act provides a legal framework for citizens to request information from public bodies, thereby strengthening democracy. It is not directly related to regulating foreign investment, controlling corruption in the judiciary, or ensuring reservations for backward classes. The focus is solely on enhancing openness and responsibility in governance.
qs.kf:
☛ RTI Act enacted on → 12 October 2005
☛ Time limit to provide information under RTI → 30 days
☛ Objective of RTI Act → Transparency and accountability
☛ First appellate authority under RTI → First Appellate Authority
☛ Right to Information is a constitutional right → Under Article 19(1)(a)

q: In the case of Vihaan Kumar vs. State of Haryana, what constitutional violation led the Supreme Court to declare the arrest illegal?
o: Violation of Article 21 (Right to Life and Personal Liberty)
Violation of Article 22(1) (Failure to inform grounds of arrest)
qs.e: In the case of Vihaan Kumar vs. State of Haryana, the Supreme Court declared the arrest illegal because the police failed to inform the arrested person of the grounds of arrest. Article 22(1) mandates that no person shall be detained in custody without being informed of the grounds of arrest. This is a fundamental right that ensures personal liberty. The court held that the police's failure to comply with this constitutional requirement rendered the arrest unconstitutional. The judgment emphasized that violation of Article 22(1) automatically makes the arrest invalid. This case reaffirms the importance of procedural safeguards in arrests under the Indian Constitution.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 22(1) → Right to be informed of grounds of arrest
☛ Article 22(2) → Right to be produced before a magistrate within 24 hours
☛ Vihaan Kumar case → Arrest declared illegal due to violation of Article 22(1)
☛ Article 21 → Right to life and personal liberty, but main violation here was Article 22(1)
☛ Failure to inform grounds → Constitutes infringement of constitutional right

q: Which article of the Indian constitution grants the right to equal opportunity in public employment ?
qs.e: Article 16 of the Indian Constitution guarantees the right to equal opportunity in public employment. It is a fundamental right under Part III and ensures equality of opportunity for all citizens in matters relating to employment or appointment to any office under the State. Article 16 prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, descent, place of birth, residence or any of them. Article 15 prohibits social discrimination, Article 14 ensures equality before law, and Article 13 deals with inconsistent laws. Article 16 specifically grants the right to equal opportunity in public employment, with provisions for reservation (Article 16(4)), residence-based conditions (Article 16(3)), and exceptions for certain posts (Article 16(5)).
qs.kf:
☛ Right to equal opportunity in public employment → Article 16
☛ Equal opportunity for Indian citizens in public employment → Under Article 16
☛ Reservation provision in Article 16 → Article 16(4)
☛ Residence condition in Article 16 → Article 16(3)
☛ Article 16 is part of → Part III (Fundamental Rights)

q: Which of the following Articles of Indian Constitution provides Right against Exploitation?
qs.e: The Right against Exploitation is enshrined in Articles 23 and 24 of the Indian Constitution. Article 23 prohibits trafficking in human beings, beggar (forced labor without payment), and child labor. It is a fundamental right. Article 19 provides the Right to Freedom, Article 21 the Right to Life, and Article 14 the Right to Equality. The Right against Exploitation protects vulnerable sections of society from various forms of exploitation.
qs.kf:
☛ Which articles cover the Right against Exploitation? → Articles 23 and 24
☛ What does Article 23 prohibit? → Human trafficking and forced labor
☛ Which article prohibits child labor? → Article 24
☛ Which article provides the Right to Equality? → Article 14
☛ Which article provides the Right to Life? → Article 21

q: How many fundamental rights were enshrined in the Constitution of India of 1950?
qs.e: When the Constitution of India came into effect in 1950, it originally enshrined seven fundamental rights under Articles 12 to 35. These included Right to Equality (Articles 14-18), Right to Freedom (Articles 19-22), Right against Exploitation (Articles 23-24), Right to Freedom of Religion (Articles 25-28), Cultural and Educational Rights (Articles 29-30), Right to Constitutional Remedies (Article 32), and Right to Property (Article 31). Later, the 44th Amendment Act of 1978 removed the Right to Property from the list of fundamental rights, making it a legal right under Article 300A. Hence, currently there are six fundamental rights.
qs.kf:
☛ Number of fundamental rights in the original constitution → Seven
☛ Amendment that removed Right to Property → 44th Amendment, 1978
☛ Current number of fundamental rights → Six
☛ Fundamental rights borrowed from which country → United States
☛ Right to Constitutional Remedies is in which Article → Article 32

q: Which of the following is NOT listed as a 'fundamental right' in the Indian Constitution?
qs.e: The list of Fundamental Rights in the Indian Constitution includes Right to Equality (Articles 14-18), Right to Freedom (Articles 19-22), and Cultural and Educational Rights (Articles 29-30). The 'Right to Speech' is not a separate Fundamental Right; it is part of the Right to Freedom under Article 19(1)(a). Article 19 guarantees six freedoms: speech and expression, assembly, association, movement, residence, and profession. Thus, the right to speech is a component, not an independent Fundamental Right.
qs.kf:
☛ Total Fundamental Rights originally → 7, now 6 (right to property removed)
☛ Right to Equality → Articles 14-18
☛ Right to Freedom → Articles 19-22
☛ Cultural and Educational Rights → Articles 29-30
☛ Right to Speech → Under Article 19(1)(a)

q: Which of the following British policies triggered people to assemble at Jallianwala Bagh, Amritsar?
qs.e: The Rowlatt Act was passed by the British government in 1919, allowing arrest and detention without trial. This act caused widespread anger among Indians as it was seen as a violation of civil liberties. To protest the Rowlatt Act, a peaceful assembly was organized on April 13, 1919, at Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar. The assembly was surrounded by British troops under the command of General Dyer, who ordered firing without warning, killing hundreds of unarmed people.
qs.kf:
☛ In which year was the Rowlatt Act passed? → 1919
☛ When did the Jallianwala Bagh massacre occur? → April 13, 1919
☛ Who ordered the firing at Jallianwala Bagh? → General Dyer
☛ In which city is Jallianwala Bagh located? → Amritsar, Punjab
☛ What did the Rowlatt Act violate? → Fundamental rights and civil liberties

q: Article 17 of the Indian Constitution enforces the :
o: joint sitting of both houses in certain cases
abolition of the practice of untouchability
qs.e: Article 17 of the Indian Constitution abolishes the practice of untouchability and forbids its practice in any form. It is a fundamental right that ensures social equality for all citizens. Any discrimination arising out of untouchability is constitutionally invalid. This article was enacted to eradicate caste-based discrimination prevalent in Indian society. Practicing untouchability is a legal offense, and the guilty can be punished. This right upholds individual dignity and freedom.
qs.kf:
☛ What does Article 17 deal with? → Abolition of untouchability
☛ What is forbidden under Article 17? → Practice of untouchability
☛ Under which fundamental right is untouchability abolition covered? → Right to Equality
☛ What happens on violation of Article 17? → Legal offense and punishment
☛ Which act was made against untouchability? → Untouchability Offences Act, 1955

q: Who among the following said, "The Rowlatt Act is a preventive murder"?
qs.e: Edwin Samuel Montagu, who served as the Secretary of State for India from 1917 to 1922, called the Rowlatt Act a 'preventive murder'. The Act, passed in 1919 by the British government, allowed political prisoners to be arrested and detained without trial. Montagu criticized its harshness. Mahatma Gandhi described it as 'satanic' and 'unjust'. The Act became a major issue in the Indian freedom movement and led to the Rowlatt Satyagraha.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Rowlatt Act passed? → 1919
☛ Who started the opposition to the Rowlatt Act? → Mahatma Gandhi
☛ Which committee gave the report for the Rowlatt Act? → Rowlatt Committee (headed by Sir Sydney Rowlatt)
☛ Who called the Rowlatt Act a 'preventive murder'? → Edwin Samuel Montagu
☛ When did the Rowlatt Satyagraha begin? → 6 April 1919

q: When the Right to Property was removed from our 'fundamental rights' and was made a 'legal right'?
qs.e: The Right to Property was originally a fundamental right under Article 31 in Part-III of the Indian Constitution. It was removed from fundamental rights and made a legal right under Article 300A by the 44th Constitutional Amendment in 1978. This amendment was passed during the tenure of Prime Minister Morarji Desai and came into effect in 1979. Now, no person can be deprived of their property except by authority of law, but it is no longer a fundamental right.
qs.kf:
☛ Under which Article was the Right to Property a fundamental right? → Article 31
☛ Which Amendment made Right to Property a legal right? → 44th Amendment (1978)
☛ Under which Article is the legal Right to Property now? → Article 300A
☛ Who was the Prime Minister during the 44th Amendment? → Morarji Desai
☛ Which Amendment restricted judicial review? → 42nd Amendment

q: Which article of the Constitution of India covers 'Right to Life'?
qs.e: Article 21 of the Indian Constitution is part of Part III (Fundamental Rights). It states that no person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to the procedure established by law. The Supreme Court has expansively interpreted 'Right to Life' to include the right to live with dignity, health, education, clean environment, and livelihood. Article 20 deals with protection against conviction for offences, Article 34 restricts rights during martial law, and Article 32 provides the right to constitutional remedies. Therefore, the Right to Life is enshrined in Article 21.
qs.kf:
☛ Which article deals with Right to Life and Personal Liberty? → Article 21
☛ What does 'Life' under Article 21 include? → Right to live with dignity, health, education, clean environment
☛ Fundamental Rights are covered in which part of the Constitution? → Part III (Articles 12-35)
☛ Article 32 deals with which right? → Right to Constitutional Remedies
☛ Can Article 21 be suspended? → Yes, during National Emergency (Article 359)

q: Which of the following articles of the Indian Constitution deals with the protection of the interests of minorities?
qs.e: Article 29 of the Indian Constitution deals with the protection of the interests of minorities. It is part of Part 3 (Fundamental Rights) under the heading 'Cultural and Educational Rights'. Article 29(1) states that any section of citizens residing in any part of India having a distinct language, script, or culture has the right to conserve the same. Article 29(2) provides that no citizen shall be denied admission into any educational institution maintained by the State or receiving aid out of State funds on grounds only of religion, race, caste, or language. This provision safeguards the cultural identity and educational opportunities of minority communities.
qs.kf:
☛ Which article protects the interests of minorities? → Article 29
☛ Article 29 is in which part of the Constitution? → Part 3 (Fundamental Rights)
☛ What does Article 30 deal with? → Right of minorities to establish educational institutions
☛ What does Article 29(1) protect? → Language, script, and culture
☛ On what grounds does Article 29(2) prohibit discrimination? → Religion, race, caste, or language

q: Which of the following is described as the soul of the Constitution of India?
qs.e: The soul of the Indian Constitution is the 'Fundamental Rights'. They are enshrined in Part III (Articles 12–35) of the Constitution. Fundamental Rights protect citizens from arbitrary state action and form the bedrock of democracy. Dr. B. R. Ambedkar called them the soul of the Constitution because they ensure individual liberty and equality. These rights are justiciable, meaning citizens can approach the Supreme Court if they are violated. Fundamental Rights include Right to Equality, Right to Freedom, Right against Exploitation, Right to Freedom of Religion, Cultural and Educational Rights, and Right to Constitutional Remedies. Article 32, which grants the right to move the Supreme Court, is itself a fundamental right and is described as the heart of the Constitution.
qs.kf:
☛ What is called the soul of the Constitution? → Fundamental Rights
☛ Fundamental Rights are in which part? → Part III
☛ Who is the guardian of Fundamental Rights? → Supreme Court
☛ Who called Fundamental Rights the soul of the Constitution? → Dr. B. R. Ambedkar
☛ Which Article deals with Constitutional Remedies? → Article 32

q: Which article of the Indian Constitution talks about 'right to life'?
qs.e: The right to life is enshrined in Article 21 of the Indian Constitution. It is a fundamental right under Part III and states that 'No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law.' It has been termed the 'heart of fundamental rights' by the Supreme Court. Through judicial interpretation, its scope has been expanded to include the right to live with dignity, right to a clean environment, right to privacy, and right to speedy trial. This article imposes a duty on the state to protect the life and liberty of citizens from arbitrary action. It is the most extensively interpreted article of the Constitution.
qs.kf:
☛ Article related to right to life → Article 21
☛ Article 21 is in which part? → Part 3 (Fundamental Rights)
☛ Which article is called the 'heart of fundamental rights'? → Article 21
☛ The word 'procedure' in Article 21 refers to → Procedure established by law
☛ Which right is NOT included under Article 21? → Right to property

q: The fundamental rights described in the Indian Constitution have been taken primarily from ______.
qs.e: The Fundamental Rights enshrined in the Indian Constitution are primarily borrowed from the American Constitution. These rights are justiciable and protect citizens from state oppression. Part III (Articles 12-35) of the Indian Constitution includes six fundamental rights: Right to Equality, Right to Freedom, Right against Exploitation, Right to Freedom of Religion, Cultural and Educational Rights, and Right to Constitutional Remedies. The American Bill of Rights (first 10 amendments) inspired these rights. However, unlike the US, Indian fundamental rights are not absolute; the state can impose reasonable restrictions. The Right to Constitutional Remedies (Article 32) is called the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar. This borrowing reflects India's adaptation of global democratic principles to its unique socio-political context.
qs.kf:
☛ Which part of the Indian Constitution deals with Fundamental Rights? → Part III (Articles 12-35)
☛ How many Fundamental Rights are there in the Indian Constitution? → Six (originally seven, but Right to Property was removed)
☛ Which Article provides the Right to Constitutional Remedies? → Article 32
☛ What is the main source of inspiration for the Indian Constitution? → Government of India Act 1935
☛ What is the Bill of Rights in the US Constitution? → First ten amendments guaranteeing fundamental rights

q: Which of the following Articles is for "Protection of interests of Minorities”?
qs.e: Article 29 of the Indian Constitution deals with the protection of interests of minorities. It provides that any section of citizens residing in India having a distinct language, script, or culture shall have the right to conserve the same. It also prohibits discrimination in admission to any educational institution maintained by the State or receiving aid from the State on grounds of religion, race, caste, or language. Article 30 gives minorities the right to establish and administer educational institutions. Article 27 prohibits levying taxes for promotion of any particular religion. Article 26 deals with freedom to manage religious affairs. Hence, Article 29 is directly related to protecting minority interests.
qs.kf:
☛ Protection of interests of minorities → Article 29
☛ Right of minorities to establish educational institutions → Article 30
☛ Prohibition of taxes for religious purposes → Article 27
☛ Freedom to manage religious affairs → Article 26
☛ Fundamental Rights in Constitution → Articles 12 to 35

q: Article 17 of Indian Constitution deals with -
qs.e: Article 17 of the Indian Constitution deals with the abolition of untouchability. It is a fundamental right that abolishes untouchability and forbids its practice in any form. Discrimination based on untouchability is considered a constitutional offense. This provision is crucial for ensuring social equality and human dignity. Under this article, the state can enact laws to punish any disability arising from untouchability. It provides protection to Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 14 → Equality before law
☛ Article 15 → Prohibition of discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth
☛ Article 16 → Equality of opportunity in matters of public employment
☛ Article 17 → Abolition of untouchability
☛ Article 18 → Abolition of titles

q: Which writ is issued against executive and inferior judicial bodies to perform their duties which they have failed to perform?
qs.e: Mandamus is a prerogative writ issued by a higher court to a public authority, inferior court, or government official to perform a duty that they have failed to perform. It is a command requiring the performance of a public duty that is mandatory in nature. This writ is issued under Article 32 and Article 226 of the Indian Constitution for the enforcement of fundamental rights. Mandamus cannot be issued against the President, Governor, or private individuals unless they are performing public duties.
qs.kf:
☛ Which article provides for Mandamus? → Article 32 and 226
☛ What is Mandamus also known as? → 'Writ of Command'
☛ Against whom can Mandamus not be issued? → President and Governor
☛ What is the purpose of Mandamus? → To compel performance of public duty
☛ What does 'Mandamus' mean? → 'We command'

q: Article 19(1)(a) of the Indian Constitution refers to _________.
qs.e: Article 19(1)(a) of the Indian Constitution grants citizens the freedom of speech and expression. It is a fundamental right under Part III and is considered the cornerstone of democracy. This right allows individuals to express their views through any medium—oral, written, print, or electronic. However, it is subject to reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2), which include security of the state, foreign relations, public order, decency, and morality. This right is available only to citizens, not to foreigners. The Supreme Court has termed it as the 'bulwark of the temple of liberty'. The right also includes the freedom of the press and the right to information.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Article deals with freedom of speech and expression? → Article 19(1)(a)
☛ Restrictions on Article 19(1)(a) are under which Article? → Article 19(2)
☛ Who is not entitled to freedom of speech? → Foreigners
☛ Part III of the Constitution deals with? → Fundamental Rights
☛ What did Supreme Court call freedom of speech? → Bulwark of the temple of liberty

q: Which of the following Articles of the Indian Constitution guarantees protection against arrest and detention in certain cases?
qs.e: Article 22 of the Indian Constitution guarantees protection against arrest and detention in certain cases. This fundamental right applies when a person is arrested or detained, except in cases of anti-state activities. Article 22 grants the arrested person the right to be informed of the grounds of arrest, consult a lawyer, and be produced before a magistrate within 24 hours. It also provides safeguards in cases of preventive detention, though such laws are subject to certain limitations. Article 21 deals with right to life and personal liberty, while Article 20 provides protection against conviction for offences. Article 23 prohibits trafficking in human beings and forced labor.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Article deals with right to be informed of grounds of arrest? ➔ Article 22
☛ Which Article provides safeguards against preventive detention? ➔ Article 22
☛ Which Article deals with right to life and personal liberty? ➔ Article 21
☛ Which Article provides protection against conviction for offences? ➔ Article 20
☛ Which Article prohibits trafficking and forced labor? ➔ Article 23

q: In which of the following Articles are there provisions related to establishment of the Election Commission?
qs.e: Article 324 of the Indian Constitution deals with the establishment and powers of the Election Commission. It provides that the superintendence, direction, and control of elections to Parliament, State Legislatures, and the offices of President and Vice-President shall be vested in the Election Commission. The Commission consists of the Chief Election Commissioner and other Election Commissioners appointed by the President. Article 330 relates to reservation of seats for Scheduled Castes and Tribes in the Lok Sabha. Article 343 deals with the official language (Hindi). Article 353 pertains to the effect of a Proclamation of Emergency.
qs.kf:
☛ Which article provides for the establishment of Election Commission? → Article 324
☛ Who appoints the members of the Election Commission? → President
☛ What is the tenure of the Chief Election Commissioner? → 6 years or age 65, whichever is earlier
☛ What does Article 330 deal with? → Reservation of seats for SC/ST in Lok Sabha
☛ What does Article 343 deal with? → Provisions related to official language Hindi

q: Which of the following Articles of the Indian Constitution provides for the Protection of ‘Life and Personal Liberty’?
qs.e: Article 21 of the Indian Constitution provides for the protection of 'Life and Personal Liberty'. It states that no person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law. This Article is part of Part III (Fundamental Rights). The Supreme Court has termed it the 'heart' of the Constitution and the 'soul' of fundamental rights. The right to life under this Article is not merely about survival but includes the right to live with dignity. In the landmark case of Maneka Gandhi vs Union of India (1978), the Supreme Court gave a broad interpretation to this Article, linking it with Articles 14 and 19. Article 22 deals with protection against arrest and detention, Article 25 guarantees the right to religious freedom, and Article 18 abolishes titles.
qs.kf:
☛ Article that provides right to life and personal liberty → Article 21
☛ Article that provides protection against arrest → Article 22
☛ Article that guarantees religious freedom → Article 25
☛ Article that abolishes titles → Article 18
☛ Where are Fundamental Rights mentioned → Part III, Articles 12-35

q: Which of the following statements regarding Fundamental Rights is/are NOT CORRECT?
1. Fundamental Rights are described in Articles 12 to 36 in Part-3 of the Constitution.
2. This part is called the Magna Carta of India.
3. Their objective is to create a government of law in the country and not of individuals.
4. These are not absolute; the state can impose reasonable restrictions on them.
qs.e: Statement 1 is incorrect because Fundamental Rights are described in Articles 12 to 35, not 36. Statement 2 is correct: Part-3 is called the Magna Carta of India. Statement 3 is correct: Fundamental Rights aim to establish a government of law, not of individuals. Statement 4 is correct: These rights are not absolute; the state can impose reasonable restrictions. Hence, only statement 1 is false.
qs.kf:
☛ Fundamental Rights are described in → Part-3, Articles 12-35
☛ Magna Carta of India → Part-3 (Fundamental Rights)
☛ Objective of Fundamental Rights → Establish rule of law
☛ Are Fundamental Rights absolute? → No, state can impose reasonable restrictions
☛ Article 36 → Part of Directive Principles, not Fundamental Rights

q: If the court finds that a person is holding office but not entitled to hold that office, it issues the writ of ______ and restricts that person from acting as an office holder.
qs.e: The writ of Quo-Warranto literally means "by what authority." It is issued to prevent a person from holding a public office to which they are not entitled. Under Articles 32 and 226 of the Indian Constitution, the Supreme Court and High Courts can issue this writ. Through this writ, the court asks the office holder to show by what authority they hold the office. If the person has no valid authority, the court can remove them from the office. This writ applies only to public offices and not to private ones. It ensures that no one usurps a public office without lawful authority.
qs.kf:
☛ Purpose of Quo-Warranto → To remove a person illegally holding a public office
☛ Articles related to Quo-Warranto → Articles 32 and 226
☛ Applicability of Quo-Warranto → Only to public offices
☛ Literal meaning of Quo-Warranto → "By what authority"
☛ Courts that issue this writ → Supreme Court and High Courts

q: The provision of ‘Prohibition of Employment of Children in Hazardous Jobs’ is reflected in which of the following Fundamental Rights of the Indian Constitution?
qs.e: The Indian Constitution provides the Right against Exploitation under Articles 23 and 24. Article 24 specifically prohibits the employment of children in hazardous jobs. This right protects human dignity and prevents the exploitation of vulnerable groups. According to Article 24, children below the age of 14 cannot be employed in factories, mines, or other hazardous work. This provision is a crucial safeguard against child labor and ensures the protection of children's well-being. The Right against Exploitation also includes Article 23, which prohibits human trafficking and forced labor. Together, these articles uphold the fundamental principle of justice and equality in society.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 23 → Prohibits human trafficking and forced labor
☛ Article 24 → Prohibits employment of children in hazardous jobs
☛ Minimum age for child employment → 14 years
☛ Articles covering Right against Exploitation → Articles 23 and 24
☛ Jobs prohibited under Article 24 → Factory, mine, and hazardous work

q: Which of the following Articles of the Indian Constitution states that no person who is arrested shall be detained in custody without being informed?
qs.e: Article 22 of the Indian Constitution provides protection against arrest and detention. It states that no person who is arrested shall be detained in custody without being informed of the grounds of arrest. Also, the arrested person must be produced before the nearest magistrate within 24 hours. This right does not apply to preventive detention cases. Article 20 deals with protection in respect of conviction for offences, Article 21 deals with right to life and personal liberty, and Article 19 deals with six fundamental rights including freedom of speech.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Article provides for production of arrested person before magistrate within 24 hours? → Article 22
☛ Which protection under Article 22 is not available in preventive detention? → Right to be informed of grounds of arrest
☛ Article 20 deals with? → Protection in respect of conviction for offences
☛ Under Article 21, a person can be deprived of life or personal liberty only by? → Procedure established by law
☛ How many freedoms are included in Article 19? → Six

q: According to which of the following Articles of the Indian Constitution, there shall be a Comptroller and Auditor-General of India who shall be appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal?
qs.e: Article 148 of the Indian Constitution provides for the office of the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India (CAG). According to this article, the CAG is appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal. The CAG is the head of the Indian Audit and Accounts Service and audits the accounts of the government. Article 149 deals with the duties and powers of the CAG. The term of office of the CAG is 6 years or until the age of 65, whichever is earlier. He can be removed only by impeachment. This office is crucial for financial accountability in India.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Article provides for the appointment of the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India? → Article 148
☛ Who appoints the CAG? → The President
☛ What is the term of office of the CAG? → 6 years or 65 years of age, whichever is earlier
☛ How can the CAG be removed? → By impeachment
☛ Which Article describes the duties and powers of the CAG? → Article 149

q: Which Article of the Indian Constitution provides that 'It shall be the duty of the Union and the State Public Service Commissions to conduct examinations for appointments to the services of the Union and the services of the State, respectively'?
qs.e: Article 320 of the Indian Constitution defines the duties of the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) and State Public Service Commissions (SPSCs). It states that it shall be the duty of these commissions to conduct examinations for appointments to the services of the Union and the State, respectively. Additionally, Article 320 provides for advising on recruitment processes, promotions, transfers, and disciplinary matters. This article is crucial for ensuring transparency and merit in public services. Article 319 deals with conditions of service of members, Article 318 with appointment and service conditions, and Article 322 with expenses of the commissions.
qs.kf:
☛ Under which Article is the Union Public Service Commission constituted? → Article 315
☛ Who appoints the members of UPSC? → President
☛ Who appoints the members of State Public Service Commission? → Governor
☛ What is the term of office for the Chairman and members of UPSC? → 6 years or age 65, whichever is earlier
☛ Which Articles ensure the independence of Union and State Public Service Commissions? → Article 322 and 323

q: Which of the following articles of the Indian Constitution facilitates people to move freely throughout the territory of India?
qs.e: Article 19(1)(d) of the Indian Constitution grants citizens the right to move freely throughout the territory of India. This fundamental right is one of the six freedoms under Article 19, subject to reasonable restrictions imposed by the state. Article 19(1)(a) deals with freedom of speech and expression, (b) with the right to assemble peacefully, and (c) with the right to form associations. Thus, the right to free movement is specifically protected under Article 19(1)(d).
qs.kf:
☛ Article 19(1)(a) → Freedom of speech and expression
☛ Article 19(1)(b) → Right to assemble peaceably
☛ Article 19(1)(c) → Right to form associations or co-operative societies
☛ Article 19(1)(d) → Right to move freely throughout the territory of India
☛ Article 19(1)(e) → Right to reside and settle in any part of India

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (09/06/2025) Shift 2
q: The Supreme Court described itself as the "sentinel on the qui vive" in relation to ____________.
qs.e: The Supreme Court described itself as the 'sentinel on the qui vive' in relation to the protection of Fundamental Rights. This phrase signifies the Court's role as a vigilant guard over the Fundamental Rights enshrined in Part III of the Constitution. The Supreme Court is the protector of Fundamental Rights and can declare any law or executive action unconstitutional if it violates these rights. This power is derived from Article 32, which itself is a Fundamental Right. The Court ensures that no law or government action infringes upon the basic rights of citizens.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Article gives the Supreme Court the power to protect Fundamental Rights? → Article 32
☛ In which Part of the Constitution are Fundamental Rights mentioned? → Part III
☛ Who described the Supreme Court as the 'sentinel on the qui vive'? → The Supreme Court itself
☛ What does 'qui vive' mean? → To be alert or vigilant
☛ Article 32 is also known as the? → Right to Constitutional Remedies

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (10/06/2025) Shift 1
q: Which of the following Articles of the Constitution of India prohibits human trafficking?
qs.e: Article 23 of the Indian Constitution prohibits human trafficking and beggar (forced labor). It is a fundamental right that protects citizens from exploitation. Article 23(2) allows the State to impose compulsory service for public purposes without discrimination. This article falls under the Right against Exploitation. Article 24 prohibits child labor. Article 19 provides freedom of speech, and Article 21 deals with the right to life. Human trafficking is a serious crime, and this article provides constitutional protection against it. The prohibition applies to all forms of trafficking, including trafficking in women and children for prostitution or forced labor.
qs.kf:
☛ Article prohibiting human trafficking → Article 23
☛ Article prohibiting forced labor (beggar) → Article 23
☛ Article prohibiting child labor → Article 24
☛ Articles under Right against Exploitation → Article 23 and 24
☛ Exception under Article 23(2) → State can impose compulsory service for public purposes

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (10/06/2025) Shift 2
q: Which of the following is a key reason for judicial review in India?
o: To allow the judiciary to make laws
To maintain federal balance between Centre and States
To ensure the supremacy of the Parliament
To protect the supremacy of the Constitution and fundamental rights
qs.e: The primary purpose of judicial review in India is to protect the supremacy of the Constitution and fundamental rights. This power is vested in the Supreme Court and High Courts. Through judicial review, the judiciary can examine any law or executive action for conformity with the Constitution and declare it void if found unconstitutional. This power is essential for safeguarding the fundamental rights guaranteed under Part III of the Indian Constitution. While maintaining federal balance is also a function of judicial review, the core reason is to uphold constitutional supremacy and protect fundamental rights. Thus, judicial review ensures that the Constitution remains supreme in the democratic framework.
qs.kf:
☛ From which country is the power of judicial review derived in India? → USA
☛ Who is considered the father of judicial review? → Marshall
☛ Under which articles does judicial review operate in India? → Articles 13 and 32
☛ Which amendment curtailed judicial review initially? → 42nd Amendment (originally)
☛ Is judicial review unlimited in India? → No, it is limited by the basic structure doctrine

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (10/06/2025) Shift 3
q: Which Article of the Constitution of India prohibits Indian citizens from accepting any title from a foreign state?
qs.e: Article 18 of the Indian Constitution deals with the abolition of titles. It prohibits the state from conferring any title (except military or academic distinctions) and forbids Indian citizens from accepting titles from foreign states. It also restricts persons holding offices of profit under the state from accepting foreign titles without presidential consent. This article is part of the Right to Equality (Articles 14-18), aimed at eliminating feudal distinctions and ensuring social equality. Article 18 does not apply to titles like Bharat Ratna or Padma awards, as they are considered decorations, not titles. The provision reflects India's commitment to equal citizenship and non-discrimination.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 17 → Abolition of untouchability
☛ Article 18(1) → Prohibition on conferring titles by the state
☛ Article 18(2) → Prohibition on Indian citizens accepting foreign titles
☛ Article 18(3) → Restriction on office holders accepting foreign titles without permission
☛ Article 18(4) → Prohibition on accepting gifts or titles from foreign states for persons under the state

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (12/06/2025) Shift 1
q: Which Article of the Constitution of India prohibits the State from discriminating against the use of wells, tanks and places of public entertainment?
qs.e: Article 15(2)(b) of the Indian Constitution specifically prohibits the State from discriminating against any citizen on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth in the use of wells, tanks, bathing ghats, roads and places of public entertainment. This fundamental right falls under the Right to Equality (Articles 14–18). Article 15 deals exclusively with prohibition of discrimination, while Article 17 abolishes untouchability, Article 18 abolishes titles, and Article 14 provides equality before law. Article 16 ensures equality of opportunity in public employment. Thus, the correct answer is Article 15, not 16, 17 or 18.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 15(1) → State shall not discriminate against any citizen on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth.
☛ Article 15(2)(b) → Prohibits discrimination in use of wells, tanks, bathing ghats, roads and public resorts.
☛ Article 15(3) → State can make special provisions for women and children.
☛ Article 15(4) → Special provisions for advancement of SCs, STs and backward classes.
☛ Article 15(5) → Reservation in educational institutions for SCs, STs and backwards classes.

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (12/06/2025) Shift 2
q: Which Article of the Constitution of India prevents any child below the age of 14 years from being employed in the factory, mine or hazardous occupation?
qs.e: Article 24 of the Indian Constitution prohibits the employment of children below the age of 14 years in factories, mines, or hazardous occupations. It is part of the Right against Exploitation under Fundamental Rights. Article 21 (Right to Life) and Article 23 (Prohibition of Human Trafficking and Forced Labor) deal with different subjects. Article 24 specifically aims to prevent child labor and is reinforced by the Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986. This provision protects the physical and mental development of children.
qs.kf:
☛ Prohibition of child employment → Article 24
☛ Right against Exploitation → Articles 23 and 24
☛ Article 23 prohibits → human trafficking and forced labor
☛ Article 21 deals with → right to life and personal liberty
☛ Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986 → implements Article 24

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (20/06/2025) Shift 2
q: Which of the following Articles of the Indian Constitution states about the establishment of Election Commission in India?
qs.e: Article 324 of the Indian Constitution provides for the establishment and powers of the Election Commission. It states that the superintendence, direction, and control of elections to the offices of President, Vice-President, Parliament, and State Legislatures shall be vested in the Election Commission. As per Article 324(2), the Commission consists of the Chief Election Commissioner and Election Commissioners appointed by the President. Article 326 deals with adult suffrage, Article 325 prohibits discrimination in electoral rolls on grounds of religion, race, etc., and Article 327 empowers the legislature to make laws relating to elections. The Election Commission is an independent and impartial constitutional body that conducts free and fair elections in the country.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Article establishes the Election Commission? → Article 324
☛ Which Article deals with adult suffrage? → Article 326
☛ Which Article prohibits discrimination in electoral rolls? → Article 325
☛ Which Article empowers legislature to make election laws? → Article 327
☛ Who appoints the Chief Election Commissioner? → President

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (20/06/2025) Shift 2
q: Which of the following statements about the Supreme Court's writ jurisdiction is correct?
o: It extends to both Fundamental Rights and other legal rights.
It is exclusive and cannot be exercised by the High Courts.
It can only be invoked for enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
It allows the Court to issue writs only against the Central Government.
qs.e: Under Article 32 of the Indian Constitution, the Supreme Court has the power to issue writs for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights. This right is itself a Fundamental Right and is called the heart and soul of the Constitution. The Supreme Court's writ jurisdiction is limited only to Fundamental Rights, whereas High Courts under Article 226 can issue writs for both Fundamental Rights and other legal rights. The Supreme Court can issue writs against both private individuals and the government. This jurisdiction is not exclusive because High Courts also have parallel power. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar called Article 32 the heart and soul of the Constitution. The five types of writs are Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, and Quo Warranto.
qs.kf:
☛ Under which Article does the Supreme Court have writ jurisdiction? → Article 32
☛ Under which Article do High Courts have writ jurisdiction? → Article 226
☛ How many types of writs can the Supreme Court issue? → 5 types (Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, Quo Warranto)
☛ Who called Article 32 the heart and soul of the Constitution? → Dr. B.R. Ambedkar
☛ Can the Supreme Court issue writs against private individuals? → Yes, for violation of Fundamental Rights

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (23/06/2025) Shift 1
q: Which Article of the Constitution of India provides a right to profess, practice and propagate religion?
qs.e: Article 25 of the Indian Constitution provides the right to profess, practice and propagate religion. It is a fundamental right under Part III and guarantees every person the freedom to adopt, practice and spread any religion of their choice. This right is subject to public order, morality and health. Additionally, the State is empowered to regulate any economic, financial or political activities associated with religious practices. Article 25 lays the foundation of secularism in India, ensuring equal freedom for all religions. It protects individual conscience and allows the propagation of religious beliefs, while also enabling the State to make laws for social welfare and reform, such as prohibiting practices like untouchability or temple entry restrictions.
qs.kf:
☛ Right to profess, practice and propagate religion → Article 25
☛ Right to manage religious affairs → Article 26
☛ Secularism is part of basic structure → Kesavananda Bharati case
☛ Article 25 subject to public order, morality and health → Proviso
☛ Freedom of religion is a fundamental right → Part III

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (23/06/2025) Shift 1
q: Which of the following Articles of the Indian Constitution states about the duty of Union Public Service Commission to present its report annually to the President of India?
qs.e: Article 323 of the Indian Constitution deals with the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC). It mandates the UPSC to present an annual report of its work to the President of India, who then places it before both Houses of Parliament. This ensures accountability and transparency of the commission.
