Note that Article 321 deals with additional functions of UPSC, Article 322 with salaries and allowances of members, and Article 324 with the Election Commission. Hence, the duty to submit an annual report is specifically under Article 323.
qs.kf:
☛ UPSC submits annual report to → President (Article 323)
☛ State PSC submits annual report to → Governor (Article 323)
☛ Additional functions of UPSC → Article 321
☛ Salaries of UPSC members → Article 322
☛ Election Commission of India → Article 324

q: Which of the following is NOT a fundamental right of an Indian Citizen?
qs.e: The Right to Property was originally a fundamental right under Article 31 of the Indian Constitution. However, the 44th Amendment Act, 1978, removed it from Part III (Fundamental Rights) and placed it under Article 300A as a constitutional right. The remaining options—Right to Equality (Articles 14-18), Right to Freedom of Religion (Articles 25-28), and Right against Exploitation (Articles 23-24)—are still fundamental rights under Part III of the Constitution. Thus, the Right to Property is not a fundamental right today.
qs.kf:
☛ Under which Article is the Right to Property currently protected? → Article 300A
☛ Which amendment removed the Right to Property from fundamental rights? → 44th Amendment (1978)
☛ How many fundamental rights are there in the Indian Constitution? → 6 (originally 7)
☛ What type of right is the Right to Property now? → Constitutional right
☛ Which Part of the Constitution contains Fundamental Rights? → Part III

q: As per the Constitution of India, every person who is arrested and detained in custody shall be produced before the nearest magistrate within a period of ______ hours of such arrest, excluding the time necessary for the journey from the place of arrest to the court of the magistrate.
qs.e: According to Article 22 of the Constitution of India, every person arrested and detained must be produced before the nearest magistrate within 24 hours of arrest, excluding the time required for the journey from the place of arrest to the court. This provision is a fundamental right designed to protect individuals from arbitrary detention and ensure judicial oversight. It prevents police from holding a person unlawfully and provides the accused with an opportunity for judicial review. This safeguard is crucial in a democratic society to prevent abuse of power and uphold the rule of law.
qs.kf:
☛ Time limit to produce arrested person before magistrate → 24 hours
☛ Article that provides this protection → Article 22
☛ Is travel time included in the 24 hours? → No
☛ Which part of Constitution contains this right? → Fundamental Rights
☛ Article 22 deals with → Protection against arrest and detention

q: What is a mandamus writ?
o: Calling for an end to hearings
Making a government body do its duty
qs.e: A mandamus writ is a type of writ that orders a public authority or lower court to perform its public duty. It is issued by High Courts under Article 226 and the Supreme Court under Article 32 of the Indian Constitution. This writ is only granted when no alternative remedy exists and the failure to perform duty violates fundamental rights. The purpose of mandamus is to ensure accountability in administrative actions. It cannot be issued against private individuals, only against public authorities.
qs.kf:
☛ Under which article does the Supreme Court issue mandamus? → Article 32
☛ What is the purpose of mandamus? → To make a public authority perform its duty
☛ Against whom cannot mandamus be issued? → Private individuals
☛ When is mandamus granted? → When no alternative remedy exists
☛ Which right does mandamus relate to? → Violation of fundamental rights

q: Article 15 of the Constitution refers to the prohibition of discrimination on the basis of __________ of any citizen.
qs.e: Article 15 of the Indian Constitution is a fundamental right that prohibits the state from discriminating against any citizen on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth. It is an extension of the right to equality (Article 14) and aims to ensure social justice. This article also prohibits discrimination in access to public places, shops, hotels, and entertainment venues. However, it allows the state to make special provisions for women, children, Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, and other backward classes. Article 15 is crucial for promoting equality and preventing discrimination based on personal characteristics. It reinforces the secular and inclusive nature of the Indian Constitution.
qs.kf:
☛ Main objective of Article 15? → Prohibition of discrimination
☛ Grounds of discrimination prohibited under Article 15? → Religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth
☛ Article 15 is related to which right? → Right to Equality
☛ Can the state make special provisions for women? → Yes, under Article 15(3)
☛ Which article extends Article 15 to employment? → Article 16

q: Which article is included under the 9th Schedule of Indian Constitution?
qs.e: The 9th Schedule of the Indian Constitution was added by the First Amendment (1951). It includes acts that are protected from judicial review on the ground of violation of Fundamental Rights. Originally, it contained land reform laws. Article 31-B is specifically associated with the 9th Schedule. It states that any act listed in the 9th Schedule cannot be challenged in any court for infringing Fundamental Rights. However, in the I.R. Coelho case, the Supreme Court ruled that laws in the 9th Schedule are subject to the basic structure doctrine and can be reviewed if they violate Fundamental Rights under the basic structure. Other options: Article 4 deals with reorganization of states, Article 243 with Panchayati Raj, and Article 102 with disqualification of MPs.
qs.kf:
☛ Which amendment added the 9th Schedule? → First Amendment, 1951
☛ What protection do laws in the 9th Schedule receive? → Protection from judicial review
☛ Which article added the 9th Schedule? → Article 31-B
☛ Which case held that 9th Schedule laws are subject to basic structure? → I.R. Coelho case
☛ What type of laws were initially included in the 9th Schedule? → Land reform laws

q: What is the right to life in the Indian constitution?
qs.e: The right to life under Article 21 of the Indian Constitution is a Fundamental Right. It protects individuals from arbitrary deprivation of life, ensures the right to live with dignity, and safeguards personal liberty. The Supreme Court has given it a broad interpretation, including aspects such as education, health, clean environment, and livelihood. This distinguishes it from Directive Principles of State Policy, which are non-justiciable. The right to life is interconnected with other fundamental rights like equality and freedom of speech. It is not absolute and can be restricted by lawful procedures. This right is essential for the protection of individual freedom and human dignity.
qs.kf:
☛ Under which Article is the Right to Life? → Article 21
☛ Which court gave a broad interpretation of Right to Life? → Supreme Court
☛ Is Right to Life a Directive Principle? → No, it is a Fundamental Right
☛ What does Right to Life include? → Dignity, health, education
☛ Is Right to Life absolute? → No, it can be restricted by legal procedure

q: What is the defense against the arbitrariness of arrest is called protection against personal freedom?
qs.e: Habeas corpus is a fundamental constitutional remedy that protects an individual from unlawful or arbitrary arrest. It is a writ issued by a court ordering the person who has been arrested to be produced before the court. Its purpose is to ensure that no one is detained without legal process. This right is a cornerstone of personal liberty and can be invoked under Articles 32 and 226 of the Indian Constitution. It is a powerful tool of judicial review that provides immediate relief against arbitrary detention and is considered the strongest safeguard against arbitrary state action.
qs.kf:
☛ Literal meaning of Habeas Corpus → 'You shall have the body'
☛ Under which articles is this writ available → Articles 32 and 226
☛ Which writ protects against illegal arrest → Habeas corpus
☛ Most powerful tool of judicial review → Habeas corpus
☛ Which country suspended Habeas Corpus → India (during 1975-1977 Emergency)

q: Free and compulsory education has been ensured for children of which age group in India?
qs.e: Under Article 21A of the Indian Constitution, free and compulsory education is ensured for children aged 6 to 14 years. This right was implemented through the Right to Education Act (RTE), 2009, which makes primary education a fundamental right. The Act mandates free education in government schools and reserves 25% seats in private schools for economically weaker sections. The age group of 6 to 14 years corresponds to elementary education (Class 1 to 8). The 86th Constitutional Amendment added Article 21A to the Constitution.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 21A → Right to education for 6-14 years
☛ RTE Act, 2009 → Free & compulsory education for 6-14 years
☛ 86th Amendment → Made education a fundamental right
☛ RTE reservation → 25% seats in private schools for EWS
☛ Elementary education → Class 1-8 (6-14 years)

q: How many types of writs are there?
qs.e: Under Article 32 of the Indian Constitution, the Supreme Court, and under Article 226, the High Courts, have the power to issue five types of writs for the enforcement of fundamental rights. These writs are: Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Quo Warranto, and Certiorari. Habeas Corpus means "to produce the body" and is used for protection against illegal detention. Mandamus orders a public authority to perform its duty. Prohibition is an order to a lower court to stop proceedings. Quo Warranto examines the legality of a claim to a public office. Certiorari transfers a case from a lower court to a higher court.
qs.kf:
☛ Habeas Corpus → For release from illegal detention
☛ Mandamus → For performance of public duty
☛ Prohibition → To stop lower court proceedings
☛ Quo Warranto → To check validity of claim to public office
☛ Certiorari → Transfer of case from lower to higher court

q: Under which article of the Constitution is self-elitism (superimposition against self) evidence prohibited?
qs.e: Article 20 of the Indian Constitution provides protection in respect of conviction for offences. It includes three key rights: (1) No person shall be convicted of any offence except for violation of a law in force at the time of the act (protection against ex-post-facto law); (2) No person shall be prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once (protection against double jeopardy); and (3) No person accused of any offence shall be compelled to be a witness against himself (protection against self-incrimination). This third provision prohibits "self-elitism evidence", meaning a person cannot be forced to testify against themselves. Thus, Article 20(3) directly covers the prohibition of self-incrimination.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 20(1) → Protection against ex-post-facto laws
☛ Article 20(2) → Protection against double jeopardy
☛ Article 20(3) → Protection against self-incrimination
☛ Article 22 → Protection against arrest and detention
☛ Article 17 → Abolition of untouchability

q: Under which article can the High Courts in India issue a writ (order)?
qs.e: Article 226 of the Indian Constitution empowers the High Courts to issue writs for the enforcement of fundamental rights and for any other purpose within their territorial jurisdiction. Writs include habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari, and quo warranto. In contrast, Article 32 gives writ jurisdiction only to the Supreme Court. Article 131 deals with the original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court, and Article 143 provides for consultation with the Supreme Court. Therefore, the correct provision for High Courts is Article 226. This article makes High Courts powerful guardians of fundamental rights and ensures judicial review of administrative actions.
qs.kf:
☛ Article granting writ power to High Courts → Article 226
☛ Article granting writ power to Supreme Court → Article 32
☛ Types of writs under Article 226 → 5 types
☛ Territorial scope of writ jurisdiction → State territory
☛ Nature of writ jurisdiction under Article 226 → Discretionary power

q: What kind of democracy is the primary purpose of fundamental rights?
qs.e: The primary purpose of Fundamental Rights is to establish Political Democracy. These rights ensure individual liberty, equality, and justice, which are the foundation of democratic governance. In the Indian Constitution, Fundamental Rights are enshrined in Part III, protecting individuals from arbitrary state action. Political democracy allows citizens to participate in elections, enjoy freedom of speech, and form associations. Fundamental Rights are justiciable, meaning they can be enforced by courts, thus strengthening democracy. They ensure that the government remains accountable to the people and that individual rights are safeguarded against majority tyranny.
qs.kf:
☛ Which part of the Indian Constitution contains Fundamental Rights? → Part III
☛ What type of democracy do Fundamental Rights promote? → Political Democracy
☛ Which articles relate to the Right to Equality? → Articles 14-18
☛ Which country's constitution inspired Fundamental Rights? → USA
☛ Are Fundamental Rights absolute? → No, subject to reasonable restrictions

q: The Supreme Court of India can issue order in respect to which of the following?
qs.e: Under Article 32 of the Indian Constitution, the Supreme Court has the power to issue writs for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights. This provision empowers citizens to directly approach the Supreme Court for the protection of their fundamental rights. Article 226 empowers High Courts to issue writs for both fundamental and legal rights, but the Supreme Court's jurisdiction is limited to fundamental rights. Article 32 is often referred to as the 'soul of the Constitution' and is a crucial tool for judicial review. The Supreme Court can issue five types of writs: Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, and Quo Warranto. The President of India cannot apply for a writ under Article 32 as it is a fundamental right only for citizens.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 32 → Right to move Supreme Court for enforcement of fundamental rights
☛ Article 226 → High Court can issue writs for both fundamental and legal rights
☛ Dr. Ambedkar called Article 32 the heart and soul of the Constitution
☛ Five writs of Supreme Court → Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, Quo Warranto
☛ President cannot apply for writ under Article 32

q: Article 24 of the Indian Constitution prohibits the employment of children below the age of _____ years in any factory, mine or other hazardous activities.
qs.e: Article 24 of the Indian Constitution prohibits the employment of children below the age of 14 years in factories, mines, or other hazardous activities. This provision is part of the Fundamental Rights and aims to protect children from exploitation and dangerous working conditions. Article 24 directs the state to make laws against child labor. The Factories Act, 1948 and the Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986 are key legislations in this regard. This prohibition is a crucial step towards eliminating child labor and ensuring the physical and mental development of children.
qs.kf:
☛ What is the age limit prescribed in Article 24? → 14 years
☛ Under which part does Article 24 fall? → Part III (Fundamental Rights)
☛ Which constitutional provision prohibits child labor? → Article 24
☛ What activities are prohibited under Article 24? → Factory, mine, and hazardous activities
☛ Which is the main law regulating child labor in India? → Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (05/06/2025) Shift 3
q: Which Article of the Indian Constitution explicitly declares laws violating Fundamental Rights as void?
qs.e: Article 13 of the Indian Constitution explicitly declares laws that are inconsistent with or violate Fundamental Rights as void. This provision is part of Part III of the Constitution and ensures that any law made by the State does not infringe upon fundamental rights. Article 13 also states that pre-constitutional laws, if contrary to fundamental rights, shall be void to the extent of such inconsistency. This article grants the power of judicial review, enabling the judiciary to examine the constitutional validity of laws.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 13 → Declares laws violating Fundamental Rights as void
☛ Article 143 → Advisory jurisdiction of Supreme Court on President's reference
☛ Article 226 → Power of High Courts to issue writs
☛ Article 32 → Right to move Supreme Court for enforcement of Fundamental Rights
☛ Judicial Review → Power to examine constitutionality of laws under Article 13

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (06/06/2025) Shift 3
q: The power to issue writs for enforcement of Fundamental Rights is vested in the Supreme Court under which Article of the Indian Constitution?
qs.e: Article 32 of the Indian Constitution empowers the Supreme Court to issue writs for enforcement of Fundamental Rights. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar called it the heart and soul of the Constitution. Under this article, the Supreme Court can issue five types of writs: Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Quo Warranto, and Certiorari. It is itself a fundamental right and cannot be suspended except during a national emergency. High Courts also have similar powers under Article 226, but the Supreme Court's jurisdiction under Article 32 is a guaranteed right.
qs.kf:
☛ Who called Article 32 the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution? → Dr. B.R. Ambedkar
☛ How many writs can be issued for enforcement of Fundamental Rights? → Five
☛ Which articles are not suspended during an emergency? → Articles 20 and 21
☛ Under which Article do High Courts have writ jurisdiction? → Article 226
☛ Under which Article does the Supreme Court have original jurisdiction? → Article 32

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (18/06/2025) Shift 1
q: Which Fundamental Right was subjected to additional restrictions by the First Amendment Act of 1951?
o: Right to Freedom of Speech and Expression
qs.e: The First Amendment Act of 1951 imposed additional restrictions on the Right to Freedom of Speech and Expression under Article 19(1) (a). It amended Article 19(2) to include new grounds for restriction such as public order, sovereignty and integrity of India, and friendly relations with foreign states. The amendment aimed to curb misuse of free speech and protect democracy. It also introduced the Ninth Schedule to shield land reform laws from judicial review.
qs.kf:
☛ Year of First Amendment → 1951
☛ Fundamental Right affected → Freedom of Speech and Expression
☛ Article amended → 19(2)
☛ New grounds for restriction → Public order, sovereignty, friendly relations
☛ Schedule added → Ninth Schedule (for land reforms)

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (21/06/2025) Shift 2
q: Which of the following statements is INCORRECT about the Fundamental Rights of the Indian Constitution?
o: Cultural and educational rights are fundamental rights.
These are subject to reasonable restriction.
These may be enforced by the courts.
qs.e: The Fundamental Rights in the Indian Constitution are not absolute; they are subject to reasonable restrictions. Under Article 13, the state cannot make laws that violate Fundamental Rights, but it can impose reasonable restrictions for reasons such as public order, morality, and health. Cultural and educational rights (Articles 29-30) are indeed part of Fundamental Rights. Fundamental Rights are justiciable, meaning they can be enforced by courts. Any person can file a petition in the High Court or Supreme Court if their Fundamental Rights are violated. Thus, the statement that Fundamental Rights are absolute is incorrect.
qs.kf:
☛ Which part of the Indian Constitution deals with Fundamental Rights? → Part 3
☛ How many categories are Fundamental Rights divided into? → 6 categories
☛ Which articles cover cultural and educational rights? → Articles 29-30
☛ Which article deals with the Right to Equality? → Articles 14-18
☛ Under which article can Fundamental Rights be suspended? → Article 359

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (21/06/2025) Shift 2
q: In which year was the Right to Property removed from the Fundamental Rights of the Constitution of India?
qs.e: The Right to Property was removed from the Fundamental Rights (Articles 19(1)(f) and 31) by the 44th Amendment Act, 1978. This amendment was proposed in 1977 and came into force in 1978. Post this amendment, the Right to Property became a legal right under Article 300A of the Constitution. The change occurred during the tenure of Prime Minister Morarji Desai. The objective was to remove property rights from Fundamental Rights to give the state more flexibility in implementing welfare schemes and land reforms.
qs.kf:
☛ Which amendment removed Right to Property from Fundamental Rights? → 44th Amendment, 1978
☛ Under which article is Right to Property now? → Article 300A
☛ When was the 44th Amendment enacted? → 1978
☛ Who was the Prime Minister during this amendment? → Morarji Desai
☛ What type of right is Right to Property now? → Legal right

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (23/06/2025) Shift 3
q: How many writs mentioned in the Constitution of India enforce Fundamental Rights?
qs.e: Under Article 32 of the Indian Constitution, five writs are mentioned for enforcing Fundamental Rights. These writs are: Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Quo Warranto, and Certiorari. Article 32 is known as the 'Right to Constitutional Remedies' and was described by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar as the 'heart and soul of the Constitution'. While the Supreme Court can issue these writs under Article 32, High Courts have similar powers under Article 226. These writs are essential for protecting citizens' fundamental rights against arbitrary state action.
qs.kf:
☛ Number of writs for enforcing Fundamental Rights → Five
☛ Article 32 is known as? → Right to Constitutional Remedies
☛ Article 226 gives power to? → High Courts to issue writs
☛ Meaning of Habeas Corpus writ → Release from illegal detention
☛ Dr. Ambedkar called Article 32 as? → Heart and soul of the Constitution

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (23/06/2025) Shift 3
q: Which of the following writs protects the right to life and personal liberty mentioned in the Constitution of India?
qs.e: This writ is issued to release a person from illegal detention. Article 21 protects the right to life and personal liberty. Habeas Corpus means 'produce the body'. The court orders the detaining authority to present the detained person before the court and examines the legality of detention. If the detention is found illegal, the court orders immediate release. This writ is enforceable under Article 32 (Supreme Court) and Article 226 (High Courts). Mandamus is issued to perform a public duty, Prohibition to stop a court from exceeding its jurisdiction, and Certiorari to quash the order of a lower court. Habeas Corpus is considered the bulwark of personal liberty in India.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 32 deals with? → Right to Constitutional Remedies
☛ Habeas Corpus cannot be issued against? → Valid detention
☛ Prohibition writ is issued to which court? → Inferior court
☛ Mandamus is directed against? → Public bodies
☛ Certiorari is issued on grounds of? → Lack of jurisdiction or error of law

q: What is the minimum age for employment in factories or mines or other hazardous employment, according to Article 24 of the Indian Constitution?
qs.e: Article 24 prohibits the employment of children in factories, mines, and other hazardous occupations. It sets the minimum age at 14 years. This provision is part of the Fundamental Rights and aims to prevent child exploitation. The Factories Act, 1948 and the Mines Act, 1952 also enforce the same age limit. It ensures that children are not deprived of education and health necessary for their development. The Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986 also specifies the minimum age as 14 years. Note that Articles 23 and 24 deal with human trafficking and child labour.
qs.kf:
☛ Minimum age for hazardous employment under Article 24 → 14 years
☛ Minimum age under Child Labour Prohibition Act → 14 years
☛ Definition of child under Factories Act → below 14 years
☛ Right to Education under Article 21A → 6-14 years
☛ Article dealing with child labour in Constitution → 24

q: Which part of the Constitution of India contains Fundamental Rights of the citizens of India?
qs.e: Part 3 of the Indian Constitution (Articles 12 to 35) contains the Fundamental Rights of citizens. These rights are justiciable, meaning individuals can approach the Supreme Court or High Courts for their enforcement. The Fundamental Rights include Right to Equality (Articles 14-18), Right to Freedom (Articles 19-22), Right against Exploitation (Articles 23-24), Right to Freedom of Religion (Articles 25-28), Cultural and Educational Rights (Articles 29-30), and Right to Constitutional Remedies (Article 32). These rights are inspired by the United States Constitution. Fundamental Rights are not absolute and can be restricted for reasons of national security, public order, etc.
qs.kf:
☛ What is the title of Part 3? → Fundamental Rights
☛ Which country's constitution inspired Fundamental Rights? → USA
☛ Which Article deals with Right to Constitutional Remedies? → Article 32
☛ To whom are Fundamental Rights applicable? → All citizens (some to foreigners too)
☛ Which Article is NOT related to Right to Equality? → Article 19

q: Which of the following is NOT a fundamental right as per the Constitution of India?
o: Equal Justice and Free Legal Aid
qs.e: Under the Constitution of India, Fundamental Rights (Articles 12-35) include Right to Equality (Articles 14-18), Freedom of Speech and Expression (Article 19(1)(a)), and Right to Constitutional Remedies (Article 32). Equal Justice and Free Legal Aid is mentioned under Article 39A, which is a Directive Principle of State Policy (DPSP), not a Fundamental Right. DPSPs are non-justiciable, while Fundamental Rights are justiciable. Thus, Option 1 is not a Fundamental Right.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Article deals with Equal Justice and Free Legal Aid? → Article 39A
☛ Which Articles cover Right to Equality? → Articles 14-18
☛ Which Article covers Right to Constitutional Remedies? → Article 32
☛ Which Part contains Fundamental Rights? → Part III
☛ Which Part contains Directive Principles of State Policy? → Part IV

q: What are the fundamental rights that are inherent to all human beings?
qs.e: Fundamental rights are those rights that every human being is born with. These rights are natural, inalienable, and basic, which no government can take away. These rights protect human dignity and freedom. In the Indian Constitution, fundamental rights are mentioned in Articles 12-35. These rights are justiciable and can be challenged in court. Fundamental rights include the right to equality, freedom, against exploitation, freedom of religion, cultural and educational rights, and constitutional remedies.
qs.kf:
☛ Where are fundamental rights mentioned? → Part 3 of the Constitution
☛ Which articles contain the right to equality? → Articles 14-18
☛ Which articles contain the right to freedom? → Articles 19-22
☛ Which article contains the right to constitutional remedies? → Article 32
☛ Which fundamental right did Dr. Ambedkar call the 'heart and soul of the Constitution'? → Article 32

q: In which of the following cases did the Supreme Court mention that the Fundamental Right to Primary Education is the Right to Life under Article 21 of the Indian Constitution?
o: P Sambamurthy vs Union of India
Navtej Singh Johar vs Union of India
Unni Krishnan vs State of Andhra Pradesh
Shreya Singhal vs Union of India
qs.e: In the 1993 case of Unni Krishnan vs State of Andhra Pradesh, the Supreme Court held that the fundamental right to primary education is part of the Right to Life under Article 21. The Court interpreted Articles 21, 39(e), 45, and 46 together to reach this conclusion. This judgment paved the way for the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002, which made education a fundamental right under Article 21A. The case dealt with admission and fee issues in private educational institutions.
qs.kf:
☛ Case that included primary education under Article 21 Right to Life → Unni Krishnan vs State of Andhra Pradesh (1993)
☛ Amendment making education a fundamental right → 86th Amendment, 2002
☛ Article for Right to Education → Article 21A
☛ Articles read together in Unni Krishnan case → 21, 39(e), 45, 46
☛ RTE Act came into force on → 1 April 2010

q: Which of the following rights is NOT part of the Right to Life under Article 21 of the Indian Constitution?
qs.e: Article 21 of the Indian Constitution protects Right to Life and Personal Liberty. The Supreme Court has given it a wide interpretation, encompassing many rights such as Right to Privacy, Right to Free Legal Aid, Right to Livelihood, Right to a Clean Environment, Right to Live with Dignity, etc. However, the Right to Property was originally a fundamental right under Article 31 but was removed by the 44th Amendment (1978) and is now a legal right under Article 300A. Hence, the Right to Property is not part of the Right to Life under Article 21.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 21 → Protects life and personal liberty
☛ Right to Privacy → Integral part of Article 21 (Puttaswamy case)
☛ Right to Free Legal Aid → Under Article 21 (Khatri vs Bihar)
☛ Right to Property → Now a legal right under Article 300A
☛ Right to Livelihood → Included in Article 21 (Olga Tellis)

q: The Indian Constitution guarantees Fundamental Rights to its citizens under which of the following Articles?
qs.e: Fundamental Rights are enshrined in Part III of the Indian Constitution, which spans from Article 12 to Article 35. Article 12 defines the term 'State', Article 13 deals with the doctrine of judicial review of laws, and Articles 14 to 32 enumerate specific rights such as right to equality, freedom, protection against exploitation, religious freedom, cultural education, and constitutional remedies. Articles 33 to 35 contain special provisions like restrictions on rights for armed forces, martial law, and enforcement of rights. Therefore, the entire spectrum of Fundamental Rights is covered under Articles 12 to 35.
qs.kf:
☛ Starting article of Fundamental Rights? → Article 12
☛ Range of articles for Fundamental Rights? → Articles 12 to 35
☛ Article for constitutional remedies? → Article 32
☛ Article 13 relates to? → Judicial review of laws
☛ Title of Part III? → Fundamental Rights

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (05/06/2025) Shift 1
q: The Supreme Court can issue writs under Article 32 only for which specific purpose?
o: To review decisions of statutory tribunals
To enforce the Directive Principles of State Policy
qs.e: Article 32 of the Indian Constitution guarantees the right to move the Supreme Court directly for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights. It is itself a Fundamental Right. Under this article, the Supreme Court can issue five types of writs: Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, and Quo Warranto. These writs can be issued only for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights, not for other legal or constitutional purposes. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar called Article 32 the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution. This provision ensures that citizens have a constitutional remedy when their Fundamental Rights are violated.
qs.kf:
☛ How many types of writs can be issued under Article 32? → Five: Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, and Quo Warranto
☛ Who called Article 32 the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution? → Dr. B.R. Ambedkar
☛ Under Article 32, which court can be approached? → Supreme Court
☛ What type of right is Article 32? → Fundamental Right
☛ Which article empowers High Courts to issue writs similarly? → Article 226

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (17/06/2025) Shift 1
q: Which Article of the Constitution of India permits minorities based on language to establish educational institutes?
qs.e: Article 30 of the Indian Constitution grants minorities based on language or religion the right to establish and administer educational institutions. It is a fundamental right that protects the educational and cultural interests of minority communities. Article 30(1) states that all minorities shall have the right to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice. Article 30(2) prohibits the state from discriminating against such institutions in granting aid. Article 29 deals with cultural and educational rights, Article 28 with religious instruction, and Article 32 with constitutional remedies. This provision ensures that minorities can preserve their language, culture, and education system.
qs.kf:
☛ Right of minorities to establish educational institutions → Article 30
☛ Article 30 is which type of right → Fundamental Right
☛ Article 30(2) prohibits what → Discrimination by state in granting aid
☛ Cultural and educational rights of minorities → Articles 29 and 30
☛ Article 30 applies to which communities → Linguistic and religious minorities

q: Which of the following Articles of the Constitution of India guarantees the protection of certain rights regarding the freedom of speech?
qs.e: Article 19 of the Indian Constitution guarantees six fundamental rights, including freedom of speech (Article 19(1)(a)). It also allows the state to impose reasonable restrictions on these rights for reasons such as security of the state, foreign relations, public order, decency, or morality. Article 19 specifically protects certain rights regarding freedom of speech, such as expression, peaceful assembly, forming associations, movement, residence, and profession. Article 14 deals with equality, Article 21 with right to life, and Article 22 with protection against arrest.
qs.kf:
☛ Article for freedom of speech → 19(1)(a)
☛ Number of rights under Article 19 → 6
☛ Basis of restrictions under Article 19 → Reasonable restrictions
☛ Article 19 can be suspended → During national emergency (Article 358)
☛ Article 19 relates to → Fundamental rights

q: Which of the following is not the original Fundamental Duty?
o: Development of Scientific Thinking, Humanity and Curiosity
qs.e: The Fundamental Duties are enshrined in Part IV-A, Article 51A of the Indian Constitution. Originally, 10 duties were added by the 42nd Amendment in 1976, including protecting the country's rich heritage, protecting public property, and developing scientific thinking and humanity. The Right to Constitutional Remedies under Article 32 is a Fundamental Right, not a duty. The 11th duty was added by the 86th Amendment in 2002, requiring parents to provide education opportunities to children aged 6-14 years. Thus, the Right to Constitutional Remedies is not an original Fundamental Duty.
qs.kf:
☛ Which amendment added Fundamental Duties? → 42nd Amendment, 1976
☛ How many Fundamental Duties are there currently? → 11
☛ Which article deals with Fundamental Duties? → Article 51A
☛ In which part are Fundamental Duties? → Part IV-A
☛ When was the last duty added? → 2002, by 86th Amendment

q: Where is the provision of fundamental rights in the Indian constitution taken from the Constitution?
qs.e: The provision of Fundamental Rights (Part III, Articles 12-35) in the Indian Constitution is borrowed from the United States Constitution. The concept of civil liberties enshrined in the U.S. Constitution influenced India's fundamental rights. These rights include equality, freedom, protection against exploitation, freedom of religion, cultural and educational rights, and constitutional remedies. This provision was drafted by the Drafting Committee headed by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar. Fundamental rights are justiciable, meaning citizens can approach the Supreme Court for their enforcement. These rights protect individuals from arbitrary government actions.
qs.kf:
☛ Fundamental Rights in India are borrowed from which country? → United States
☛ Which part of Indian Constitution deals with Fundamental Rights? → Part III
☛ Articles covering Fundamental Rights? → Articles 12-35
☛ Which Article provides the Right to Constitutional Remedies? → Article 32
☛ Who enforces Fundamental Rights? → Supreme Court

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (06/06/2025) Shift 3
q: Which Article of the Constitution of India allowed citizens to reside and settle in any part of the territory of India?
qs.e: Article 19(1)(e) of the Indian Constitution grants all citizens the right to reside and settle in any part of the territory of India. It is part of the Right to Freedom under fundamental rights. However, this right is subject to reasonable restrictions imposed in the interest of security of the State, interests of foreign nationals, or protection of Scheduled Tribes. Article 15 deals with prohibition of discrimination on grounds of caste, religion, sex, etc., Article 18 deals with abolition of titles, and Article 22 deals with protection against arrest and detention.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Article gives right to reside and settle? → Article 19(1)(e)
☛ Article 19(1)(e) is available to whom? → Only citizens
☛ How many freedoms are under Article 19? → 6
☛ Grounds for restrictions on Article 19(1)(e)? → Security of State, interests of foreign nationals, protection of Scheduled Tribes
☛ Which Article prohibits discrimination? → Article 15

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (19/06/2025) Shift 2
q: In March 2025, what important decision did the Supreme Court of India make regarding disability rights?
o: It allowed only private companies to hire persons with disabilities.
It said disability rights are a part of fundamental rights.
It removed reservations for persons with disabilities.
It banned all exams for persons with disabilities.
qs.e: In March 2025, the Supreme Court of India delivered a landmark judgment declaring that disability rights are an integral part of fundamental rights under the Constitution. The Court ruled that discrimination against persons with disabilities violates Articles 14, 19, and 21. This decision was based on the interpretation of the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016. The Court emphasized that the state has a duty to ensure equal opportunities for persons with disabilities in both public and private sectors. The judgment strengthened access to education, employment, and public services for disabled individuals. It also affirmed that affirmative action and reservations are essential to fulfill fundamental rights.
qs.kf:
☛ Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 → When was it enacted? → 2016
☛ Article 21 → Which right does it relate to? → Right to life and personal liberty
☛ Reservation for persons with disabilities → What percentage in government jobs? → 4%
☛ Judgment declaring disability rights as fundamental rights → In which year? → 2025
☛ Article 14 of the Constitution → Which principle is it related to? → Right to equality

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (24/06/2025) Shift 2
q: Which of the following Articles of the Indian Constitution states about the appointment of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India?
qs.e: Article 148 of the Indian Constitution deals with the appointment, oath, and conditions of service of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India (CAG). The CAG is appointed by the President and takes an oath before the President before assuming office. This provision falls under Part V of the Constitution. The CAG acts as the guardian of India's public financial system, and his reports are submitted to the President, who then places them before Parliament. Article 149 defines the duties and powers of the CAG, while Article 150 deals with the form of accounts of the Union and States. The term of the CAG is 6 years or until the age of 65, whichever is earlier. The removal procedure is the same as that of a High Court judge.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Article deals with CAG? → Article 148
☛ Who appoints the CAG? → President
☛ What is the term of CAG? → 6 years or 65 years
☛ Removal procedure of CAG is similar to which position? → High Court judge
☛ Which Article defines the duties of CAG? → Article 149

q: Which two articles of the Constitution of India most clearly express the power of judicial review?
qs.e: Judicial review refers to the power of the judiciary to examine the constitutionality of laws or executive orders and declare them void if they violate the Constitution. In the Indian Constitution, Article 32 and Article 226 most clearly embody the power of judicial review. Article 32 empowers the Supreme Court to issue writs for the enforcement of fundamental rights, while Article 226 confers similar power on the High Courts. These articles are part of the 'Right to Constitutional Remedies' and enable the judiciary to review legislative and executive actions. They are considered the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, as they ensure that fundamental rights are not violated.
qs.kf:
☛ Which articles provide the power of judicial review? → Article 32 and Article 226
☛ Article 32 empowers which court? → Supreme Court
☛ Article 226 empowers which court? → High Courts
☛ Which article is called the 'Right to Constitutional Remedies'? → Article 32
☛ What writs can be issued under Articles 32 and 226? → Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, Quo Warranto

q: What does the writ 'Habeas- Corpus' in the Indian Judicial system literally mean?
qs.e: Habeas Corpus is a Latin term which literally means 'You shall have the body'. It is a writ issued to bring a detained person before the court to check the legality of the detention. This writ protects individuals from unlawful detention and is a fundamental right under Article 32 and Article 226 of the Indian Constitution. Any person who is illegally detained can approach the court for release through this writ. It is a powerful tool for enforcing the right to personal liberty.
qs.kf:
☛ Literal meaning of Habeas Corpus → You shall have the body
☛ Under which articles is this writ used? → Article 32 and 226
☛ Main purpose of Habeas Corpus → Protection against illegal detention
☛ Under which law is this writ issued? → Code of Civil Procedure
☛ Which article empowers the Supreme Court to issue this writ? → Article 32

q: Under which article, the minorities have the right to open educational institutions and to handle their administration?
qs.e: Article 30 of the Indian Constitution grants minorities the right to establish and administer educational institutions. This right is given to religious or linguistic minorities to preserve their culture and language. According to Article 30(1), all minorities have the right to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice. Article 30(2) ensures that the state shall not discriminate in granting aid to such institutions. This is a fundamental right that protects the cultural and educational interests of minorities. Article 30 is part of the cultural and educational rights (Articles 29-30). Article 29 deals with protection of interests of minorities, while Article 30 specifically gives the right to establish institutions. Article 26 relates to freedom to manage religious affairs, and Article 25 deals with freedom of conscience and religion. Thus, the correct answer is Article 30.
qs.kf:
☛ Which article gives minorities the right to establish educational institutions? → Article 30
☛ Article 30 is related to which right? → Educational rights of minorities
☛ What does Article 30(2) ensure? → No discrimination by state in granting aid
☛ What does Article 29 provide? → Cultural and educational rights
☛ What is Article 26 about? → Right to manage religious affairs

q: Which of the following Articles of the Indian Constitution states that all minorities, whether based on religion or language, shall have the right to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice?
qs.e: Article 30 of the Indian Constitution grants minorities the right to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice. This right is provided to both religious and linguistic minorities. Under Article 30, minorities have the freedom to set up educational institutions to preserve their language, script, and culture. This article protects the educational rights of minorities and helps them maintain their identity. Article 29 deals with cultural and educational rights but does not specifically grant the right to establish institutions. Article 28 relates to religious instruction, and Article 31 was about the right to property (now repealed). Hence, the correct answer is Article 30.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 30 → Right of minorities to establish educational institutions
☛ Article 29 → Cultural and educational rights of minorities
☛ Article 28 → Freedom from religious instruction in certain institutions
☛ Article 31 → Right to property (repealed)
☛ Minority rights → Part III (Fundamental Rights) of the Constitution

q: Which of the following Acts under the Indian Constitution is described by Article 21A?
qs.e: Article 21A of the Indian Constitution provides the fundamental right to free and compulsory education for children aged 6 to 14 years. It was added by the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act of 2002. For its implementation, the Right to Education Act, 2009 was enacted and came into force on April 1, 2010. This article makes education a fundamental right and directs the state to provide it. The Right to Information falls under Article 19(1)(a), while the Right to Freedom of Religion is covered under Article 25. Representation of the People relates to election processes.
qs.kf:
☛ What does Article 21A relate to? → Right to Education
☛ Which amendment added the Right to Education? → 86th Amendment, 2002
☛ When did the RTE Act come into force? → April 1, 2010
☛ What age group is specified in Article 21A? → 6 to 14 years
☛ Under which Article does Right to Information fall? → Article 19(1) (a)

q: Which of the following articles is concerned with the Comptroller Auditor General of India?
qs.e: Article 148 of the Indian Constitution deals with the Comptroller and Auditor General of India (CAG). This article provides for the appointment, oath, and conditions of service of the CAG. The CAG is appointed by the President and takes an oath before the President before assuming office. The salary and other service conditions of the CAG are similar to those of a Judge of the Supreme Court. The term of office of the CAG is 6 years or until the age of 65, whichever is earlier. Article 149 describes the duties and powers of the CAG. The other options: Article 142 (Supreme Court's power to do complete justice), Article 135 (jurisdiction of Supreme Court), Article 154 (executive power of Governor) are not related to CAG.
qs.kf:
☛ Who appoints the CAG? → President
☛ What is the tenure of CAG? → 6 years or 65 years of age
☛ Whose salary is equal to CAG? → Supreme Court Judge
☛ Which article deals with CAG? → Article 148
☛ Which article describes duties of CAG? → Article 149

q: The concepts no double jeopardy, no self incrimination and no ex post facto are mentioned under _____ of the Indian Constitution.
qs.e: Article 20 of the Indian Constitution provides protection against conviction in certain cases. It includes three key safeguards: no ex post facto law, no double jeopardy, and no self-incrimination. This article protects individuals from being punished for an act that was not an offense at the time it was committed. It ensures that no person is prosecuted and punished for the same offense more than once, and that no person accused of any offense shall be compelled to be a witness against themselves. Article 21 deals with the right to life and personal liberty, Article 19 with freedom of speech, and Article 23 with the prohibition of human trafficking.
qs.kf:
☛ No double jeopardy → Under Article 20(2)
☛ Right against self-incrimination → Enshrined in Article 20(3)
☛ Prohibition of ex post facto law → Article 20(1)
☛ Article 20 is a Fundamental Right → Part of Part III
☛ Article 20 applies only in criminal cases → Not civil cases

q: Right to life is guaranteed under ______ of the Constitution of India.
qs.e: Article 21 of the Indian Constitution guarantees the right to life and personal liberty. It states that "No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law." This is a fundamental right available to both citizens and foreigners. The Supreme Court has given a wide interpretation to this article, including the right to live with dignity, right to a clean environment, right to privacy, and right to a speedy trial. The rights under Article 21 can be suspended only during a national emergency. It is a key provision in Part III of the Constitution.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Article deals with Right to Life and Personal Liberty? → Article 21
☛ Which right is not included under Article 21? → Right to vote
☛ During which emergency is Article 21 suspended? → National emergency
☛ Which case expanded Article 21? → Menaka Gandhi vs Union of India (1978)
☛ What does "procedure established by law" under Article 21 mean? → Fair procedure made by law

q: Consider the following statements.
1. Article 13 provides for judicial review of both pre-constitutional and post-constitutional laws.
2. Article 13 declares that all laws inconsistent with or in derogation of the Fundamental Rights shall be null and void. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
qs.e: Article 13 is a crucial provision in Part III of the Constitution. Statement 1 is correct because Article 13(1) provides for judicial review of pre-constitutional laws, while Article 13(2) provides for judicial review of post-constitutional laws. Statement 2 is also correct because Article 13(2) declares that the State shall not make any law that violates Fundamental Rights, and if such a law is made, it shall be null and void. Thus, both statements are correct.
qs.kf:
☛ What does Article 13(1) relate to? → Judicial review of pre-constitutional laws
☛ What does Article 13(2) relate to? → Judicial review of post-constitutional laws
☛ Under which Article can a law be declared void? → Article 13
☛ What is the status of a law violating Fundamental Rights? → Null and void
☛ Which part of the Constitution deals with Fundamental Rights? → Part III

q: The power of High Courts to issue writs for purposes beyond Fundamental Rights is given under __________.
qs.e: Article 226 of the Indian Constitution empowers the High Courts to issue writs for the enforcement of any legal right, not just fundamental rights. This power is broader than Article 32, which allows the Supreme Court to issue writs only for the enforcement of fundamental rights. The High Courts can issue writs like habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari, and quo warranto. Article 245 deals with the extent of laws made by Parliament and state legislatures, while Article 227 gives High Courts the power of superintendence over subordinate courts.
qs.kf:
☛ Article for writs for fundamental rights → Article 32
☛ Article giving High Courts wider writ power → Article 226
☛ How many types of writs are there → 5 (habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari, quo warranto)
☛ Article 227 deals with → High Court's superintendence over subordinate courts
☛ Article 245 deals with → Extent of laws made by Parliament and state legislatures

q: Which of the following categories of fundamental rights is NOT correctly matched with their respective articles from the Constitution of India?
o: Right to freedom of religion : Articles 25–28
qs.e: The Right to Equality is enshrined in Articles 14 to 18 of the Indian Constitution, not 15–21. Article 14 provides equality before law, Article 15 prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, etc., Article 16 ensures equality of opportunity, Article 17 abolishes untouchability, and Article 18 abolishes titles. Articles 19–22 cover the Right to Freedom, Articles 23–24 cover the Right against Exploitation, and Articles 25–28 cover the Right to Freedom of Religion. Hence, Option 4 is incorrectly matched.
qs.kf:
☛ Right to Equality → Articles 14-18
☛ Right to Freedom → Articles 19-22
☛ Right against Exploitation → Articles 23-24
☛ Right to Freedom of Religion → Articles 25-28
☛ Right to Constitutional Remedies → Article 32

q: Under the Right to Equality, of the Indian Constitution, which type of equality is ensured in public employment?
qs.e: Article 16 of the Indian Constitution ensures equality of opportunity in public employment. It provides that all citizens shall have equal opportunity in matters of employment or appointment to any office under the State. No citizen can be discriminated on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, descent, place of birth, or residence. However, the State can make reservations for backward classes. This right is an extension of the general right to equality under Article 14.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 16 → Equality of opportunity in public employment
☛ Article 15 → Prohibition of discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, etc.
☛ Article 14 → Equality before law
☛ Article 17 → Abolition of untouchability
☛ Article 18 → Abolition of titles

q: Which of the following is a key feature of the Right to Information Act?
o: Only MPs can ask for information
Citizens must get court approval to ask questions
Citizens can access government records and decisions
qs.e: The Right to Information Act (RTI Act) 2005 is a landmark Indian law that empowers citizens to access government records and decisions. It promotes transparency and accountability in public administration. Any citizen can legally request information from public authorities without needing court approval. Officials must provide information within 30 days or face penalties. The Act is not limited to MPs; it applies to all citizens. While most information is accessible, certain exemptions exist, such as those related to national security. The RTI Act ensures that government functioning is open to public scrutiny, thereby strengthening democracy.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the RTI Act enacted? → 2005
☛ What is the time limit to provide information? → 30 days
☛ Which information can be withheld? → Related to national security
☛ What is the purpose of RTI? → Transparency and accountability
☛ Who can seek information? → Any citizen

q: Article 23 of the Indian Constitution prohibits which of the following?
o: Prohibition of traffic in human beings and forced labour
Prohibition of discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth
Prohibition of solemnisation of child marriages
Prohibition of employment of children in factories, etc.
qs.e: Article 23 of the Indian Constitution prohibits traffic in human beings and forced labour. It is a fundamental right that protects citizens from exploitation. Under Article 23, practices like beggary and bonded labour are also prohibited. The article allows the state to make laws to enforce this prohibition. This fundamental right applies to both Indian citizens and foreigners. Article 23 aims to protect vulnerable sections of society and uphold human dignity. Article 24 deals with the prohibition of child employment, while Article 15 prohibits discrimination.
qs.kf:
☛ What does Article 23 prohibit? → Traffic in human beings and forced labour
☛ What practices are included under Article 23? → Beggary and bonded labour
☛ Does Article 23 apply to foreigners? → Yes
☛ What type of right is Article 23? → Fundamental right
☛ Which article deals with child employment prohibition? → Article 24

q: The Right to Property was removed from Part III of the Indian Constitution and added to _____.
qs.e: The Right to Property was originally a Fundamental Right under Article 31 of Part III of the Indian Constitution. However, the 44th Amendment Act, 1978 removed it from Part III and added it as Article 300A under Part XII, making it a constitutional right rather than a fundamental right. This amendment was introduced to facilitate land reforms and equitable distribution of resources. Now, no person can be deprived of their property except by the authority of law. Being a constitutional right, its violation does not allow direct petition to the Supreme Court under Article 32; instead, one must approach the High Court under Article 226. The amendment came into effect on 20 June 1979.
qs.kf:
☛ When was Right to Property removed? → 1978 by 44th Amendment
☛ Under which Article is Right to Property now? → Article 300A
☛ Under which Part is Right to Property now? → Part XII
☛ What type of right is Right to Property now? → Constitutional right
☛ When was 44th Amendment enacted? → 20 June 1979

q: Which among the following commissions in India has submitted a report titled 'Right to Information: Master Key to Good Governance'?
qs.e: The First Administrative Reforms Commission (ARC-1) was established in 1966 under the chairmanship of Morarji Desai. It submitted a report titled 'Right to Information: Master Key to Good Governance', emphasizing the importance of the right to information for good governance. This report focused on transparency and accountability in public administration. ARC-1 submitted a total of 20 reports covering various administrative reforms. It recommended the enactment of a law on the right to information, which eventually led to the Right to Information Act, 2005. ARC-2 was formed in 2005 under Veerappa Moily, but did not submit this specific report. The Sarkaria Commission dealt with center-state relations, and the Punchhi Commission focused on constitutional relations between the center and states.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the chairman of ARC-1? → Morarji Desai
☛ When was ARC-1 established? → 1966
☛ Who chaired ARC-2? → Veerappa Moily
☛ Sarkaria Commission related to? → Center-state relations
☛ When was Punchhi Commission formed? → 2007

q: Right to free and compulsory education for children aged 6–14 years is provided under which Article?
qs.e: Article 21A of the Indian Constitution provides the right to free and compulsory education to all children aged 6 to 14 years. This article was added by the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002. To implement this right, the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 (RTE Act) was enacted. Earlier, Article 45 (now a Directive Principle) provided for education for children up to 14 years, but it was not a fundamental right. With Article 21A, education became a fundamental right, making it enforceable by law. Article 51A(k) mentions the duty of parents to provide education to their children aged 6-14, while Article 19 deals with freedom rights.
qs.kf:
☛ Amendment that made education a fundamental right → 86th Amendment (2002)
☛ When was RTE Act enforced? → 1 April 2010
☛ Article 45 deals with → Education for children below 6 years (Directive Principle)
☛ Age group covered under Article 21A → 6 to 14 years
☛ Article 51A(k) imposes duty on → Parents/guardians to provide education to children aged 6-14

q: Article 23 specifically prohibits which practice?
o: Compulsory service in the armed forces
qs.e: Article 23 of the Indian Constitution prohibits trafficking in human beings and forced labor (begar). It is a fundamental right under Part III and declares that traffic in human beings, begar, and other similar forms of forced labor are unconstitutional. However, the state may impose compulsory service for public purposes, provided no discrimination is made. Article 24 specifically prohibits employment of children in hazardous industries. Compulsory service in the armed forces or conferring of titles are not covered under Article 23. Thus, Article 23 primarily outlaws human trafficking and forced labor.
qs.kf:
☛ What does Article 23 prohibit? → Human trafficking and begar
☛ Which Part of the Constitution contains Article 23? → Part III, Fundamental Rights
☛ Scope of Article 23? → Applies to all citizens and non-citizens
☛ Exceptions under Article 23? → Compulsory service for public purposes by the state (without discrimination)
☛ Which article prohibits child labor in hazardous industries? → Article 24

q: Article 25 of the Indian Constitution primarily guarantees which of the following rights?
qs.e: Article 25 of the Indian Constitution guarantees the right to freedom of religion. It grants every person the right to freely profess, practice, and propagate their religion, subject to public order, morality, health, and other fundamental rights. Articles 25 to 28 deal with the right to freedom of religion. Article 25 restricts state intervention in religious matters and allows all citizens to follow their own faith. This right is essential for maintaining the secular fabric of India. It is a fundamental right available to all persons, not just citizens. The state can regulate secular activities associated with religious practices for social welfare and reform.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 25 deals with which right? → Freedom of religion
☛ What right is granted under Article 25? → Right to freedom of conscience and right to freely profess, practice, and propagate religion
☛ Freedom of religion is covered under which articles? → Articles 25-28
☛ Article 26 is related to? → Freedom to manage religious affairs
☛ Article 27 deals with? → Prohibition of taxation for promotion of any particular religion

q: The 24th Constitutional Amendment gave the Parliament which of the following powers?
qs.e: The 24th Constitutional Amendment (1971) empowered Parliament to amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights. It amended Articles 13 and 368, clarifying that Parliament would follow the procedure under Article 368 for constitutional amendments, not the ordinary legislative process. This amendment was introduced to overturn the Supreme Court's judgment in the Golaknath case (1967), which held that Parliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights. However, in the Kesavananda Bharati case (1973), the Supreme Court propounded the basic structure doctrine, limiting Parliament's amending power and preventing damage to the Constitution's essential features.
qs.kf:
☛ Golaknath case → 1967 Supreme Court ruled Parliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights
☛ Kesavananda Bharati case → 1973 propounded the basic structure doctrine
☛ Year of 24th Amendment → 1971
☛ Which amendment gave power to amend Fundamental Rights → 24th Amendment
☛ Article 368 deals with → Constitutional amendment procedure

q: Which Fundamental Right explicitly prohibits human trafficking, forced labour, and the employment of children in hazardous occupations?
qs.e: The Indian Constitution enshrines Fundamental Rights in Part III. The Right against Exploitation is covered under Articles 23 and 24. Article 23 prohibits human trafficking, forced labour, and similar forms of exploitation. Article 24 prohibits the employment of children below the age of 14 in hazardous occupations. This right protects citizens from economic and physical exploitation. The Right to Freedom (Articles 19-22) relates to speech, movement, etc. The Right to Equality (Articles 14-18) ensures equality before law. The Right to Education (Article 21A) provides free education to children aged 6-14. Thus, the correct option is the Right against Exploitation.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Article prohibits human trafficking? → Article 23
☛ Which Article prohibits child labour in hazardous industries? → Article 24
☛ Which Fundamental Right is covered under Articles 23-24? → Right against Exploitation
☛ Which right prohibits forced labour? → Right against Exploitation
☛ Right against Exploitation is in which Part of the Constitution? → Part III

q: Which Article authorizes the State to make special provisions for the welfare of women and children?
qs.e: Article 15(3) of the Indian Constitution authorizes the State to make special provisions for the welfare of women and children. This article falls under the Right to Equality (Articles 14-18) and permits the State to take affirmative action for women and children. For instance, laws related to maternity benefits, reservation for women, and prohibition of child labor are made under this provision. It is essential for ensuring gender equality and protecting vulnerable sections.
qs.kf:
☛ Which article allows special provisions for women? → Article 15(3)
☛ Which article deals with special provisions for children? → Article 15(3)
☛ In which part is Article 15(3) located? → Part III (Fundamental Rights)
☛ Articles covering Right to Equality? → 14-18
☛ Purpose of Article 15(3)? → Welfare of women and children

q: What type of democracy is the goal of policy director theory?
qs.e: The goal of the Directive Principles of State Policy is to establish Social and Economic Democracy, not just political democracy. These principles guide the state to ensure welfare, equality, and justice for all citizens. Mentioned in Part 4 of the Indian Constitution (Articles 36-51), they focus on socio-economic justice. The aim is to reduce inequalities, guarantee rights like education, health, and employment, and provide equal opportunities for all. This broader form of democracy goes beyond political rights and emphasizes social and economic justice. It includes principles like equal pay, right to work, and protection of weaker sections. Though not legally enforceable, they are fundamental in governance.
qs.kf:
☛ Which country influenced India's Directive Principles? → Ireland
☛ Which part of the Indian Constitution contains Directive Principles? → Part 4 (Articles 36-51)
☛ Are Directive Principles legally binding? → No, they are non-justiciable
☛ What does Social and Economic Democracy imply? → Democracy based on equality, justice, and welfare
☛ Which principles aim at welfare of weaker sections? → Directive Principles

q: Amendment in the Directive Principle of State Policy is done on the basis of _________.
o: Special majority of parliament with consent of states
Special majority of both the houses of Parliament
qs.e: The Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) are enshrined in Part IV of the Indian Constitution. Under Article 368, amendments to DPSP require a special majority of both houses of Parliament, meaning a two-thirds majority of members present and voting. This amendment procedure differs from Fundamental Rights, which may require consent of states. DPSP aim to establish social and economic justice and are non-justiciable, but they play a crucial role in policy-making. The special majority ensures stability in these principles. Unlike some constitutional amendments, no state ratification is needed for DPSP amendments.
qs.kf:
☛ Which majority is required to amend DPSP? → Special majority of both houses of Parliament
☛ Which Article deals with amendment procedure? → Article 368
☛ In which part of Constitution are DPSP found? → Part IV
☛ What is the nature of DPSP? → Non-justiciable
☛ What is required for amending Fundamental Rights? → Consent of states

q: Read the following and answer the question based on it. The Directive Principles and Fundamental Rights of the state are sections of the Constitution of India. Before that, the section sets the basic obligations of the state to its citizens and the duties of citizens towards the state. The latter sections include the fundamental officer who is entitled to an Indian citizen. Which conclusion comes from the given paragraph?
A. Fundamental rights are only right and not applicable.
B. Directive principle is the right of a citizen and is applicable.
C. Directive principle is liability, which is related to the completion of the state.
D. Directive Principles cancel the Fundamental Officer
qs.e: According to the given paragraph, the Directive Principles set the basic obligations of the state towards its citizens. They guide the state in making policies and implementing laws to achieve its goals. Thus, Directive Principles are a liability of the state, related to the completion of the state. Option C states this correctly. Option A is wrong because Fundamental Rights are enforceable. Option B is wrong because Directive Principles are not a right of citizens but a duty of the state. Option D is wrong because Directive Principles do not cancel Fundamental Rights; they are complementary.
qs.kf:
☛ From which country's constitution are Directive Principles taken? → Ireland
☛ From which country's constitution are Fundamental Rights taken? → USA
☛ How many Fundamental Rights are there in the Indian Constitution? → 6 (originally 7, right to property removed)
☛ Are Directive Principles legally enforceable? → No, they are not enforceable in court
☛ Which articles contain Directive Principles? → Articles 36 to 51

q: According to the Constitution of India, the minimum age requirement for being a member of Panchayat is ________.
qs.e: According to Article 243F of the Constitution of India, the minimum age requirement for being a member of a Panchayat is 21 years. This provision was introduced through the 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992, which granted constitutional status to Panchayati Raj institutions. It is noteworthy that for Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies, the minimum age is 25 years, while for Panchayats it is set at 21 years. This lower age is intended to encourage youth participation in grassroots governance, as Panchayats are units of rural local self-government.
qs.kf:
☛ Minimum age for Panchayat membership → 21 years (Article 243F)
☛ 73rd Amendment gave constitutional status to Panchayati Raj → 1992
☛ Minimum age for Lok Sabha/Vidhan Sabha membership → 25 years
☛ Age limit for Panchayat chairperson → No separate provision, same as member: 21 years
☛ Age to contest Panchayat elections → Must have completed 21 years

q: Under the Indian political system, there is reservation for women in the:
qs.e: Under the Indian Constitution, the 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendment Acts of 1992 provide for reservation of one-third (33%) seats for women in Panchayati Raj Institutions and Municipalities. This reservation applies not only to members but also to the positions of chairpersons. In contrast, there is no constitutional reservation for women in Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies, though the Women's Reservation Bill (2023) proposes 33% reservation in Lok Sabha and State Assemblies, but it has not yet been implemented. Similarly, Rajya Sabha has no such reservation. Therefore, currently, only Panchayati Raj Institutions have constitutional reservation for women.
qs.kf:
☛ 73rd Amendment → Provides women reservation in Panchayati Raj Institutions
☛ 74th Amendment → Provides women reservation in Municipalities
☛ Women's Reservation Bill 2023 → Proposes 33% reservation in Lok Sabha and State Assemblies
☛ Reservation percentage in Panchayats → One-third (33%)
☛ Year of women reservation in Panchayati Raj → 1992

q: Which Indian state was the first to establish the institution of Panchayat raj?
qs.e: India's first Panchayati Raj system was established in Rajasthan on 2 October 1959. It was based on the recommendations of the Balwant Rai Mehta Committee. The then Chief Minister of Rajasthan was Mohan Lal Sukhadia. The system was inaugurated in Nagaur district. Later, Andhra Pradesh adopted it on 11 November 1959. The Panchayati Raj system is a three-tier structure: Gram Panchayat, Panchayat Samiti, and Zila Parishad. The 73rd Constitutional Amendment in 1992 gave it constitutional status.
qs.kf:
☛ First Panchayati Raj system → Rajasthan, 2 October 1959
☛ Recommending committee → Balwant Rai Mehta, 1957
☛ Inauguration site → Nagaur, Rajasthan
☛ 73rd Amendment → 1992, constitutional status to Panchayats
☛ Three-tier structure → Village, Intermediate, District levels

q: To uphold and protect the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India is a the:
qs.e: Under Article 51A of Part IVA of the Indian Constitution, fundamental duties list the obligations of citizens. One of these duties is 'to uphold and protect the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India'. This duty was added by the 42nd Amendment in 1976. Fundamental duties are non-justiciable in nature, meaning they cannot be enforced by courts, yet they underline citizens' responsibility towards the nation. Initially there were 10 duties, later the 86th Amendment (2002) added an 11th duty. These duties are inspired by the Constitution of Russia (Soviet Union).
qs.kf:
☛ Which Article contains Fundamental Duties? → Article 51A
☛ Which amendment added Fundamental Duties? → 42nd Amendment, 1976
☛ Fundamental Duties are inspired from which country? → Russia (Soviet Union)
☛ Total number of Fundamental Duties? → 11 (after 86th Amendment)
☛ Are Fundamental Duties enforceable in court? → No, they are non-justiciable

q: According to which article of the Constitution of India, it is the fundamental duty of every citizen to protect the natural environment?
qs.e: The Fundamental Duties of Indian citizens are enshrined in Part IVA of the Constitution, added by the 42nd Amendment (1976). Article 51A (g) specifically states that it is the duty of every citizen to protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers, and wildlife, and to have compassion for all living creatures. This duty complements the Directive Principles and Fundamental Rights to ensure environmental protection. While Article 48A directs the State to protect the environment as a Directive Principle, Article 51A imposes a duty on citizens. Therefore, the correct answer is Article 51A.
qs.kf:
☛ Which amendment added Fundamental Duties? → 42nd Amendment (1976)
☛ In which part of the Constitution are Fundamental Duties listed? → Part IVA
☛ Which Directive Principle deals with environmental protection? → Article 48A
☛ How many Fundamental Duties are there? → 11
☛ Article 51A (g) mentions compassion towards whom? → All living creatures

q: The Directive Principles of State Policy are mentioned in which of the following parts of the constitution of India?
qs.e: The Directive Principles of State Policy are mentioned in Part 4 (Articles 36-51) of the Indian Constitution. These principles are inspired by the Irish Constitution and guide the state in making policies. They are non-justiciable, meaning they cannot be enforced by courts, but are considered fundamental in the governance of the country. Their objective is to establish social and economic justice. Part 4 includes provisions such as formation of village panchayats, equal pay for equal work, right to education, environment protection, etc. These principles serve as policy guidelines for the government.
qs.kf:
☛ Which part contains the Directive Principles of State Policy? → Part 4
☛ In which articles are the Directive Principles found? → Articles 36-51
☛ Which country's constitution inspired the Directive Principles? → Ireland
☛ Are the Directive Principles enforceable by courts? → No, they are non-justiciable
☛ What is the aim of Part 4? → To establish social and economic justice

q: Which article of Indian Constitution says, 'The state shall take steps to separate the judiciary from the executive in the public services of the state'?
qs.e: Article 50 of the Indian Constitution is one of the Directive Principles of State Policy. It states that the State shall take steps to separate the judiciary from the executive in the public services of the State. This principle is meant to ensure judicial independence, which is a fundamental pillar of democracy. Article 50 is part of Part IV of the Constitution (Directive Principles of State Policy). These principles are not enforceable by any court, but they are fundamental in the governance of the country. The separation of the judiciary from the executive ensures impartial justice and prevents misuse of power. Other options are incorrect: Article 25 deals with freedom of religion, Article 35 with rights of Scheduled Castes and Tribes, and Article 55 with election of the President.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 50 → Separation of judiciary from executive
☛ Which Part? → Part IV (Directive Principles)
☛ Enforceable? → No, not enforceable by courts
☛ Purpose → Ensure judicial independence
☛ Related Article → Article 50

q: Part V of the Indian Constitution is related with _____.
qs.e: Part V of the Indian Constitution (Articles 52 to 151) deals with the Union Government. It includes provisions for the President, Vice President, Prime Minister, Council of Ministers, Parliament (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha), and the Supreme Court. This part defines the structure, powers, and functions of the central government. Other options: Election (Part XV), Panchayat (Part IX), Fundamental Duties (Part IV-A) are related to different parts.
qs.kf:
☛ Part V extends → Articles 52-151
☛ Organs of Union Government → President, Vice President, Prime Minister, Council of Ministers, Parliament, Supreme Court
☛ President related Articles → 52-62
☛ Prime Minister related Articles → 74-75
☛ Parliament related Articles → 79-122

q: ______ is related to the separation of the judiciary from the executive.
qs.e: Article 50 of the Indian Constitution is part of the Directive Principles of State Policy. It provides for the separation of the judiciary from the executive to ensure judicial independence and impartiality. Under this article, the State shall take steps to separate the judiciary from the executive in the public services. This provision is crucial for maintaining the independence of the judiciary, which is a cornerstone of democratic governance. Article 50 strengthens the principle of rule of law and judicial review in India.
qs.kf:
☛ Which article deals with the separation of judiciary from executive in India? → Article 50
☛ Article 50 is part of which part of the Constitution? → Part IV (Directive Principles)
☛ Which Directive Principle ensures judicial independence? → Article 50
☛ What is the main purpose of Article 50? → Separation of judiciary from executive
☛ Article 50 comes under which category of principles? → Directive Principles of State Policy

q: Which article is related to uniform civil code for all citizens of the country?
qs.e: Article 44 of the Indian Constitution is part of the Directive Principles of State Policy. It states that the State shall endeavor to secure a Uniform Civil Code for all citizens throughout India. The aim is to eliminate discrimination based on religion, caste, gender, etc., and to apply a common law to all citizens. However, it is non-justiciable, meaning courts cannot enforce its implementation. Article 44 is mentioned in Part IV of the Constitution. This article is based on the principles of equality and justice.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 44 → Relates to Uniform Civil Code
☛ Article 46 → Protection of educational and economic interests of SC/ST
☛ Article 48 → Organization of agriculture and animal husbandry
☛ Article 50 → Separation of judiciary from executive
☛ Uniform Civil Code → Implemented in Goa

q: How many fundamental duties are there in Article 51A of the Indian Constitution?
qs.e: Article 51A of the Indian Constitution lists 11 fundamental duties. These were added by the 42nd Amendment (1976) based on the recommendations of the Swaraj Singh Committee. Originally there were 10 duties, but the 86th Amendment (2002) added one more duty (providing opportunities for education to children aged 6-14). These duties remind citizens of their responsibilities towards the nation, such as abiding by the constitution, respecting national symbols, and protecting the environment. However, these duties are non-justiciable, meaning they cannot be enforced by law, yet they are crucial for civic morality.
qs.kf:
