q: Protection of environment and wildlife is mentioned in which Article of the Indian Constitution?
qs.e: The protection of environment and wildlife is mentioned under Article 48A of the Indian Constitution. This article was added by the 42nd Amendment Act of 1976. It directs the State to protect and improve the environment and safeguard forests and wildlife. Under the same amendment, Article 51A(g) was added as a fundamental duty of citizens to protect the environment. Article 48A is part of the Directive Principles of State Policy, which are non-justiciable but act as guiding principles for governance. The Supreme Court has used Article 48A to interpret environmental laws strictly and expand the scope of the right to life under Article 21.
qs.kf:
☛ Article for environment protection → Article 48A
☛ Year of 42nd Amendment → 1976
☛ Fundamental duty for environment → Article 51A(g)
☛ Nature of Article 48A → Directive Principle of State Policy
☛ Wildlife protection related law → Wildlife Protection Act, 1972

q: Which of the following Directive Principles of State Policy is provided under Article 43A of the Indian Constitution?
o: Participation of workers in industrial management
qs.e: Article 43A of the Indian Constitution directs the State to take steps to secure the participation of workers in the management of industries by suitable legislation or other means. It is one of the Directive Principles of State Policy included in Part IV of the Constitution. This article was added by the 42nd Amendment (1976). Its objective is to promote industrial democracy by involving workers in decision-making processes. Right to education is covered under Article 21A, promotion of international peace under Article 51, and living wage for workers under Article 43.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 43A → Participation of workers in industrial management
☛ Article 43 → Living wage for workers
☛ Article 51 → Promotion of international peace and security
☛ Article 21A → Right to education (6-14 years)
☛ 42nd Amendment (1976) → Added Articles 43A, 39A, 48A

q: Which Article of the Indian Constitution directs the State to promote the welfare of the people?
qs.e: Article 38 of the Indian Constitution directs the State to promote the welfare of the people. It falls under the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP). According to Article 38, the State shall strive to secure a social, economic, and political justice and minimize inequalities in income, resources, and opportunities. This reinforces the concept of a welfare state. Article 43 deals with equal pay for workers, Article 47 with nutrition and health standards, and Article 42 with just and humane working conditions.
qs.kf:
☛ Main objective of DPSP → Establish social and economic democracy
☛ Article 38 is based on → Directive Principles of Irish Constitution
☛ Article related to welfare state → Article 38
☛ Article 38 deals with → Social, economic and political justice
☛ Article 38 is known as → Directive Principle of State Policy

q: Which of the following Directive Principles of State Policy was added by the Fortyfourth Amendment Act, 1978?
o: Protection and improvement of the environment and wildlife
Provision for free legal aid to the poor
Participation of workers in industrial management
Reduction of inequalities in income and status among individuals and groups
qs.e: The Forty-fourth Amendment Act, 1978 added clause (2) to Article 38 of the Directive Principles of State Policy. This principle directs the State to reduce inequalities in income and status among individuals and groups. It was introduced to promote social and economic justice. Among the other options, protection of environment and wildlife (Article 48A) was added by the 42nd Amendment, free legal aid (Article 39A) was also added by the 42nd Amendment, and workers' participation in management (Article 43B) was added by the 42nd Amendment. Therefore, only the reduction of income inequality principle was added by the 44th Amendment.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the 44th Amendment enacted? → 1978
☛ Which amendment added Article 38(2)? → 44th Amendment
☛ Which DPSPs were added by the 42nd Amendment? → Articles 39A, 43A, 48A
☛ Article 39A relates to? → Free legal aid
☛ Article 43B relates to? → Workers' participation

q: The Directive Principles of State Policy aim to establish:
qs.e: The Directive Principles of State Policy, enshrined in Part IV (Articles 36-51) of the Indian Constitution, aim to establish a welfare state. These principles direct the state to promote social and economic justice, improve living standards, ensure basic amenities like education and health, and reduce inequalities in income and wealth. Inspired by the Irish Constitution, these principles are non-justiciable (not enforceable by courts) but serve as guiding lights for the government in policy-making. Their goal is to achieve social democracy, not a capitalist or police state. They emphasize the state's responsibility to secure a just and equitable society for all citizens.
qs.kf:
☛ From which country's constitution were the Directive Principles borrowed? → Ireland
☛ What is the nature of Directive Principles? → Non-justiciable and advisory
☛ Which articles cover Directive Principles? → Articles 36-51
☛ What is the main aim of Directive Principles? → Establishment of a welfare state
☛ Who ensures the implementation of Directive Principles? → Government (Legislature and Executive)

q: Which of the following is the Directive Principle of State Policy mentioned under Article 48A of the Indian Constitution?
o: Protection and improvement of the environment
qs.e: Article 48A of the Indian Constitution is a Directive Principle of State Policy. It directs the State to protect and improve the environment and safeguard forests and wildlife. This provision was added by the 42nd Amendment Act of 1976. Environmental protection includes safeguarding natural resources, air, water, and land. This principle encourages the State to adopt eco-friendly policies. Among the other options, Organization of Gram Panchayats is covered under Article 40, Raising the level of nutrition is under Article 47, and Legal aid for weaker sections is under Article 39A.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 48A is related to? → Protection of environment
☛ Which amendment added Article 48A? → 42nd Amendment
☛ What is the subject of Article 40? → Organization of Gram Panchayats
☛ Article 47 deals with? → Nutrition level and public health
☛ What is the objective of Article 39A? → Equal justice and free legal aid

q: Which of the following Articles was introduced by the 86th Amendment to impose a duty on parents to educate children?
qs.e: The 86th Constitutional Amendment (2002) made the right to education a fundamental right. It introduced Article 21A, providing free and compulsory education for children aged 6-14. Additionally, it added a new fundamental duty under Article 51A(k), which imposes a duty on parents or guardians to provide opportunities for education to their children aged 6-14. Thus, the 86th Amendment not only made education a fundamental right but also made it a duty of parents. Article 45 was modified to focus on early childhood care instead of education. This amendment ensured a dual responsibility: the state's duty to provide education and the parents' duty to ensure their child's attendance.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the 86th Amendment passed? → 2002
☛ Right to Education is under which Article? → Article 21A
☛ Duty of parents is under which Article? → Article 51A(k)
☛ Free education is for which age group? → 6-14 years
☛ Which Article was modified by the 86th Amendment? → Article 45

q: Which of the following is a socio-economic Directive Principle?
qs.e: The Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSPs) in Part IV of the Indian Constitution aim to establish social and economic justice. Article 39(d) specifically provides for equal pay for equal work for both men and women, which is a socio-economic directive principle. It focuses on eliminating gender-based wage discrimination and ensuring economic fairness. Other options: Promotion of international peace (Article 51) is a global principle, while Separation of powers and Independence of the judiciary are political and constitutional principles, not socio-economic in nature.
qs.kf:
☛ Equal pay for equal work → Provided under Article 39(d)
☛ Directive Principles of State Policy → Part IV, Articles 36-51
☛ Promotion of international peace → Article 51
☛ Separation of powers → Inspired by US Constitution, not explicitly in Indian Constitution
☛ Independence of judiciary → Part of constitutional framework, not a DPSP

q: Provision for securing just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief comes under which Article of the Indian Constitution?
qs.e: Article 42 of the Indian Constitution directs the State to make provisions for securing just and humane conditions of work and for maternity relief. It is a part of the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP), which are non-justiciable but fundamental in governance. This article aims to promote workers' welfare and protect women during childbirth. Article 39A deals with equal justice and free legal aid, Article 45 with care and education of children, and Article 47 with nutrition level and public health.
qs.kf:
☛ Provision for just and humane work conditions → Article 42
☛ Provision for maternity relief → Article 42
☛ Equal justice and free legal aid → Article 39A
☛ Child care and education → Article 45
☛ Nutrition and public health → Article 47

q: Which Article of the Indian Constitution states that Directive Principles are not enforceable by any court?
qs.e: In the Part IV of the Indian Constitution, Articles 36 to 51 contain the Directive Principles of State Policy. Article 37 explicitly states that these principles are not enforceable by any court, but they are fundamental in the governance of the country and shall be applied in making laws. This article makes the Directive Principles non-justiciable, meaning no legal action can be taken in court for their violation. They serve as guidelines for the state to establish social and economic justice.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 36 → Defines Directive Principles
☛ Article 37 → Non-justiciable nature of DPSPs
☛ Article 38 → Social order for welfare
☛ Article 39 → Principles of policy
☛ Article 40 → Organisation of village panchayats

q: Which of the following Directive Principles of State Policy is provided under Article 40 of the Indian Constitution?
o: Promotion of cottage industries in rural areas
Provision for a uniform civil code
Organisation of agriculture and animal husbandry
qs.e: Article 40 is enshrined in Part IV (Directive Principles of State Policy) of the Indian Constitution. This Article directs the State to take steps to organise village panchayats and endow them with necessary powers to function as units of self-government. This principle promotes rural self-governance and strengthens local democracy. Among the other options, 'Promotion of cottage industries in rural areas' falls under Article 43, 'Provision for a uniform civil code' under Article 44, and 'Organisation of agriculture and animal husbandry' under Article 48.
qs.kf:
☛ Organisation of village panchayats → Article 40
☛ Promotion of cottage industries → Article 43
☛ Uniform civil code → Article 44
☛ Organisation of agriculture and animal husbandry → Article 48
☛ Directive Principles of State Policy → Part IV (Articles 36-51)

q: Which Article of the Indian Constitution directs the State for promotion of cottage industries in rural areas?
qs.e: Part IV of the Indian Constitution contains the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP). Article 43 directs the State to promote cottage industries in rural areas on an individual or cooperative basis. This article is based on Gandhian principles and focuses on strengthening the rural economy and creating employment. Other options: Article 41 deals with the right to work, education, and public assistance; Article 36 defines the State; Article 55 relates to the election of the President.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 43 → Directs promotion of cottage industries in rural areas.
☛ Article 43A → Ensures workers' participation in management of industries.
☛ Article 43B → Promotes voluntary formation of cooperative societies.
☛ Gandhian principles → Reflected in Articles 40, 43, 46, and 48.
☛ Rural development → Article 43 emphasizes rural development and employment generation.

q: Equal pay for equal work is ensured under which Article?
qs.e: The provision for 'Equal pay for equal work' is enshrined in Article 39(d) of the Indian Constitution. It is a part of the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP), which aim to ensure social and economic justice. Article 39(d) specifically states that the State shall ensure equal pay for equal work for both men and women. This principle is crucial for promoting gender equality and preventing workplace discrimination. Other options include Article 43 (proper working conditions), Article 42 (humane conditions of work), and Article 39(a) (right to livelihood).
qs.kf:
☛ Which article provides equal pay for equal work? → Article 39(d)
☛ Article 39(d) is part of which principle? → Directive Principles of State Policy
☛ What is the main objective of Article 39(d)? → Prevent gender discrimination
☛ Article 43 relates to which aspect? → Proper working conditions and wages
☛ What does Article 42 ensure? → Humane conditions of work and maternity relief

q: A minimum of _____ seats have been ensured for women in Panchayats.
qs.e: Under the 73rd Constitutional Amendment (1992) of India, at least one-third (33%) of the total seats in Panchayati Raj Institutions are reserved for women. This reservation applies to seats filled by direct election, and states have the option to increase it. For example, Bihar and Uttarakhand have 50% reservation for women. The provision is crucial for women empowerment and enhancing women's participation in local governance. Article 243D of the Indian Constitution specifically mentions this reservation at all levels of Panchayats.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the 73rd Amendment enacted? → 1993
☛ Which article provides women reservation in Panchayats? → Article 243D
☛ Which state has 50% women reservation in Panchayats? → Bihar
☛ The 73rd Amendment deals with which institutions? → Panchayati Raj
☛ Main objective of women reservation in Panchayats? → Women empowerment

q: Which of the following is the aim of the Directive Principles of State Policy?
qs.e: The Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) are enshrined in Part IV (Articles 36-51) of the Indian Constitution. These principles guide the state in making laws, but they are not enforceable by any court. The aim of DPSP is to establish social and economic democracy. Article 51 specifically emphasizes promoting international peace and security. The other options, such as Right to Constitutional Remedies (Article 32) and Freedom of speech (Article 19), are Fundamental Rights, while Custody against arrest is also a Fundamental Right (Article 22). Thus, one of the key aims of DPSP is to promote international peace and security.
qs.kf:
☛ In which Part are DPSP found? → Part IV
☛ Which Article deals with international peace? → Article 51
☛ From which country are DPSP borrowed? → Ireland
☛ Are DPSP justiciable? → No, they are non-justiciable
☛ What is the first Article of DPSP? → Article 36

q: Which of the following Directive Principles reflects Gandhian ideology?
o: Separation of judiciary from the executive
qs.e: Article 40 of the Indian Constitution, under Part IV, directs the state to organise village panchayats as units of self-government. This Directive Principle reflects Gandhian ideology as Gandhi advocated for Gram Swaraj (village self-rule). Among the given options, equal pay for equal work is a socialist principle, uniform civil code is liberal, and separation of judiciary is a western democratic concept. Thus, only the organisation of village panchayats is rooted in Gandhian philosophy.
qs.kf:
☛ Gandhian Directive Principles → Articles 40, 43, 46, 47, 48
☛ Article related to village panchayats → Article 40
☛ Article for equal pay → Article 39(d)
☛ Article for uniform civil code → Article 44
☛ Article for separation of judiciary → Article 50

q: When is National Panchayati Raj Day observed in India?
qs.e: National Panchayati Raj Day is observed every year on 24th April. This day commemorates the enactment of the 73rd Constitutional Amendment in 1993, which gave constitutional status to Panchayati Raj Institutions in India. The amendment provides for a three-tier system: Gram Panchayat, Block Panchayat, and District Panchayat, along with the Gram Sabha. The first National Panchayati Raj Day was celebrated in 2010. Panchayati Raj plays a crucial role in strengthening grassroots democracy and decentralizing power to local communities.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the 73rd Constitutional Amendment enacted? → 24th April 1993
☛ How many tiers does the Panchayati Raj system have? → Three (Village, Block, District)
☛ Which articles cover Panchayati Raj? → Articles 243 to 243-O
☛ When was the first Panchayati Raj Day observed? → 24th April 2010
☛ Which committee recommended Panchayati Raj? → Balwant Rai Mehta Committee

q: Maintenance of International Peace and Security is the main purpose of which of the following Units/Organisations?
qs.e: The United Nations Organization (UNO) has the primary purpose of maintaining international peace and security as stated in its Charter. NATO is a military alliance, WHO deals with health, and WTO deals with trade. UNO was established in 1945 after World War II. Its headquarters is in New York. The Security Council passes resolutions to maintain peace. Peacekeeping missions and diplomatic interventions are its main tools. Although NATO and other organizations contribute to peace, UNO's main and global objective is to maintain international peace and security.
qs.kf:
☛ UNO's main purpose → Maintenance of international peace and security
☛ UNO establishment year → 1945
☛ UNO headquarters → New York, USA
☛ UN body responsible for peace → Security Council
☛ UN Charter signed on → 26 June 1945 in San Francisco

q: Which of the following statements related to the Constitution of India is true?
o: Fundamental Rights set social and economic democracy, while Directive Principles establish political democracy.
Fundamental Rights are moral and political sanctions, but Directive Principles are legal sanctions.
Fundamental Rights are justiciable, whereas Directive Principles of State are non-justiciable.
Fundamental Rights promote the welfare of the community, while Directive Principles promote individual welfare.
qs.e: In the Indian Constitution, Fundamental Rights (Articles 12-35) are enforceable by courts, meaning if violated, citizens can approach the High Court or Supreme Court. In contrast, Directive Principles of State Policy (Articles 36-51) are non-justiciable, meaning they cannot be enforced by courts. They serve as guiding principles for the state while making laws. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar called them 'instruments of instructions to the government'. While Fundamental Rights ensure individual freedom and political democracy, Directive Principles aim to establish social and economic democracy. Thus, Fundamental Rights are justiciable, whereas Directive Principles are non-justiciable.
qs.kf:
☛ Under which Article are Fundamental Rights enforceable? → Articles 32 and 226
☛ From which country's constitution are Directive Principles borrowed? → Ireland
☛ Who can suspend Fundamental Rights? → President (during emergency)
☛ What is the purpose of Directive Principles? → Establish socio-economic justice
☛ On what basis are Directive Principles implemented despite being non-justiciable? → Political and moral pressure

q: Which section of the Constitution of India discusses about the responsibility of states towards international peace and security?
qs.e: Part IV (Articles 36-51) of the Indian Constitution contains the Directive Principles of State Policy. Article 51 specifically discusses the responsibility of states towards international peace and security. It directs the state to promote international peace and security, maintain just and honourable relations between nations, and respect international law and treaty obligations. Although these principles are non-justiciable, they are fundamental in the governance of the country. Article 51 reflects the principles of the United Nations Charter and underscores India's commitment to global peace. The Directive Principles aim to establish a welfare state and guide the government in policy-making.
qs.kf:
☛ Article related to international peace → Article 51
☛ Source of Directive Principles → Irish Constitution
☛ Purpose of Article 51 → Promote international peace and security
☛ Total articles in Part IV → Articles 36 to 51
☛ Nature of Directive Principles → Non-justiciable but fundamental

q: Under which of the following Parts of the Indian Constitution were Article 36 to 51 listed?
qs.e: Part IV of the Indian Constitution contains Directive Principles of State Policy from Articles 36 to 51. These principles are inspired by the Irish Constitution and guide the state in policy-making. They are not enforceable by courts but are fundamental in governance. They cover social justice, economic welfare, international peace, and environmental protection. Article 36 provides definitions, while Article 37 states they are not justiciable. Articles 38-51 include policies like equal justice, right to work, education, and environmental protection. These principles aim to establish a welfare state and are crucial for understanding the socio-economic goals of India.
qs.kf:
☛ Part IV of Indian Constitution deals with? → Directive Principles of State Policy
☛ Article 36 deals with? → Definition
☛ Directive Principles are inspired from which country? → Ireland
☛ Are Directive Principles justiciable? → No
☛ Article 37 states? → They are not enforceable by courts

q: The __________________ direct(s) and guide(s) the nation/state for equitable society and provide(s) module to the government in formulating policies and enactment of laws.
qs.e: The Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) enshrined in Part IV (Articles 36-51) of the Indian Constitution guide the government in formulating policies and enacting laws. They aim to establish a just and equitable society. Though non-justiciable (Article 37), they are fundamental in governance. DPSP were inspired by the Irish Constitution and promote the concept of a welfare state. They direct the state to secure social, economic, and political justice.
qs.kf:
☛ Main objective of DPSP → Establish social and economic justice
☛ Inspiration for DPSP → Ireland
☛ Nature of DPSP → Non-justiciable, only guiding principles
☛ Total articles in DPSP → 36 to 51 (16 articles)
☛ Main aim of DPSP → Welfare state and equitable society

q: Which of the following parts of the Indian Constitution deals with the Fundamental Duties?
qs.e: The Fundamental Duties are enshrined in Part IV A of the Indian Constitution, which was added by the 42nd Amendment Act of 1976. Originally there were 10 duties; the 86th Amendment (2002) added one more duty (providing educational opportunities for children aged 6-14), making a total of 11 Fundamental Duties. These duties are covered under Article 51 A. They remind citizens of their responsibilities towards the nation, emphasizing respect for the Constitution, national symbols, and social harmony. This part is distinct from Fundamental Rights (Part III) and Directive Principles (Part IV).
qs.kf:
☛ Article dealing with Fundamental Duties → 51 A
☛ Amendment that added Fundamental Duties → 42nd Amendment (1976)
☛ Total number of Fundamental Duties → 11
☛ 86th Amendment related to → Right to education and one new duty
☛ Fundamental Duties inspired from → Constitution of Russia (USSR)

q: Which of the following Articles of the Indian Constitution states that it is the duty of every citizen of India to safeguard public property and to abjure violence?
qs.e: The Fundamental Duties of Indian citizens are enshrined in Part IVA of the Constitution under Article 51A. These were added by the 42nd Amendment in 1976. Clause (i) of Article 51A states: "It shall be the duty of every citizen of India to safeguard public property and to abjure violence." This duty emphasizes the responsibility of citizens to protect national assets and promote non-violent behavior. Among the options, clause (k) relates to the right to education, clause (i) deals with environmental protection, and clause (d) pertains to defending the nation. Hence, the correct answer is Article 51A (i).
qs.kf:
☛ Which amendment added Fundamental Duties? → 42nd Amendment (1976)
☛ Fundamental Duties are in which Article? → Article 51A
☛ How many Fundamental Duties are there? → 11
☛ Which clause deals with safeguarding public property? → Article 51A (i)
☛ Which clause deals with abjuring violence? → Article 51A (i)

q: Which of the following is NOT provided in Part IV A (Fundamental Duties) of the Indian Constitution?
o: To preserve the rich heritage of our composite culture
To promote spirit of brotherhood amongst all people of India
To respect our parents and teachers
qs.e: Part IV A (Article 51A) of the Indian Constitution lists the Fundamental Duties, which were added by the 42nd Amendment in 1976. Currently, there are 11 Fundamental Duties. These include respecting the National Flag and National Anthem, preserving the rich heritage of India's composite culture, and promoting the spirit of brotherhood among all people of India. However, respecting parents and teachers is not listed as a Fundamental Duty. It is a moral or social duty, not a constitutional one. Fundamental Duties impose obligatory responsibilities on citizens, but they do not include family or academic respect. Therefore, the fourth option is NOT provided in Part IV A.
qs.kf:
☛ Total number of Fundamental Duties → 11
☛ Title of Part IV A → Fundamental Duties
☛ Amendment that added Fundamental Duties → 42nd Amendment (1976)
☛ Country whose constitution inspired Fundamental Duties → Soviet Union (USSR)
☛ Nature of Fundamental Duties → Non-justiciable (not enforceable)

q: Which of the following is NOT included in the Fundamental Duties enshrined in the Indian Constitution?
o: To cherish and follow the noble ideals that inspired the national struggle for freedom
To value and preserve the rich heritage of the country's composite culture
To safeguard public property and to abjure violence
qs.e: The Fundamental Duties are enshrined in Part IV-A of the Indian Constitution under Article 51A. There are 11 Fundamental Duties for citizens. Options 1, 3, and 4 are included in various clauses of Article 51A. Option 1 relates to 'to cherish and follow the noble ideals that inspired the national struggle for freedom' (clause b), Option 3 to 'to value and preserve the rich heritage of the country's composite culture' (clause f), and Option 4 to 'to safeguard public property and to abjure violence' (clause i). However, To pay taxes is not listed among the Fundamental Duties. Tax payment is a legal obligation, but the Constitution does not mention it as a Fundamental Duty.
qs.kf:
☛ How many Fundamental Duties are under Article 51A? → 11
☛ Fundamental Duties are inspired by which country? → Russia (former USSR)
☛ When were Fundamental Duties added to the Constitution? → 1976 by the 42nd Amendment
☛ Which article deals with the duty to protect the environment? → Article 51A(g)
☛ Are Fundamental Duties justiciable? → No, they are non-justiciable

q: Which of the following states in India was the first to implement the Panchayati Raj system?
qs.e: India implemented the Panchayati Raj system first in Rajasthan on 2 October 1959 in Nagaur district. Based on the recommendations of the Balwant Rai Mehta Committee, the system was inaugurated by then Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru. Following Rajasthan, Andhra Pradesh adopted Panchayati Raj later in 1959. Rajasthan adopted a three-tier structure consisting of Gram Panchayat, Panchayat Samiti, and Zila Parishad. This step was taken to promote rural development and local self-governance. The system marked a significant milestone in India's democratic decentralization.
qs.kf:
☛ First state to implement Panchayati Raj → Rajasthan
☛ Prime Minister who inaugurated Panchayati Raj → Jawaharlal Nehru
☛ Committee that recommended Panchayati Raj → Balwant Rai Mehta Committee
☛ Year of implementation → 1959
☛ First Panchayat location in Rajasthan → Nagaur district

q: On which document is the Concept of Directive Principles of State Policy based?
qs.e: The Directive Principles of State Policy, enshrined in Part IV (Articles 36-51) of the Indian Constitution, are inspired by the Constitution of Ireland. The Irish Constitution contained principles of social justice, economic welfare, and international peace, which India adopted as guiding principles for governance. These principles are non-justiciable, meaning they are not enforceable by courts, but they serve as fundamental guidelines for the state in policy-making. The aim is to establish a social and economic democracy.
qs.kf:
☛ Who called Directive Principles the 'conscience of the Constitution'? → Dr. B.R. Ambedkar
☛ Which Article begins the Directive Principles? → Article 36
☛ Which Article provides for equal justice and free legal aid? → Article 39A
☛ What is the nature of Directive Principles? → Non-justiciable
☛ Which amendment gave precedence to Directive Principles over Fundamental Rights? → 42nd Amendment (1976)

q: Which amendment of the Indian Constitution asserted a list of 'Fundamental Duties'?
qs.e: The Fundamental Duties were added to the Indian Constitution by the 42nd Amendment (1976), based on the recommendations of the Swaran Singh Committee. This amendment introduced Part IV-A and Article 51A, initially listing 10 duties. Later, the 86th Amendment (2002) added an 11th duty (providing education opportunities to children aged 6-14). These duties aim to promote patriotism and social harmony among citizens. Fundamental Duties are non-justiciable, meaning they cannot be enforced by courts. The 42nd Amendment is often called the 'Mini-Constitution' due to its wide-ranging changes.
qs.kf:
☛ Which amendment added Fundamental Duties? → 42nd Amendment, 1976
☛ Under which Article are Fundamental Duties? → Article 51A
☛ Total number of Fundamental Duties? → 11 (10 original + 1 by 86th Amendment)
☛ Which committee recommended Fundamental Duties? → Swaran Singh Committee
☛ Which 2002 amendment is related to Fundamental Duties? → 86th Amendment

q: Under which part of the Indian Constitution are the Fundamental Duties placed?
qs.e: The Fundamental Duties are enshrined in Part IVA of the Indian Constitution. This part was added by the 42nd Amendment Act (1976) on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee. Article 51A in this part lists 11 fundamental duties for citizens, such as respecting the national flag and the Constitution, following the ideals of the freedom struggle, and protecting the environment. These duties are moral and legal obligations but are not enforceable by courts. Part III deals with Fundamental Rights, Part I with the Union and its territory, and Part IV with Directive Principles of State Policy.
qs.kf:
☛ Under which part are Fundamental Duties placed? → Part IVA (Article 51A)
☛ Which amendment added them? → 42nd Amendment (1976)
☛ How many Fundamental Duties are there? → 11
☛ Which committee recommended them? → Swaran Singh Committee
☛ Are Fundamental Duties enforceable by courts? → No

q: Dr. BR Ambedkar described which part of the Indian Constitution as its ‘novel features', while Granville Austin referred to it as the ‘Conscience of the Constitution’?
qs.e: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar described the Directive Principles of State Policy (Part IV) as the 'novel features' of the Indian Constitution, as they are not found in any other democratic constitution. These principles direct the state to frame policies and enact laws, but are non-justiciable. On the other hand, renowned constitutional expert Granville Austin called them the 'Conscience of the Constitution', because they reflect the socio-economic objectives of the Constitution. These principles are inspired by the Irish Constitution and aim to establish a welfare state. They act as a guide for the government and are fundamental in the governance of the country.
qs.kf:
☛ Which part of the Indian Constitution contains the Directive Principles? → Part IV (Articles 36-51)
☛ From which constitution are the Directive Principles borrowed? → Irish Constitution
☛ Are the Directive Principles justiciable? → No, they are not enforceable by courts
☛ Who called the Directive Principles the 'Conscience of the Constitution'? → Granville Austin
☛ Which feature did Dr. Ambedkar call 'novel features'? → Directive Principles of State Policy

q: Which Constitutional Article specifically provides for free legal aid to the poor?
qs.e: Article 39A of the Indian Constitution directs the State to ensure equal justice and provide free legal aid to the poor. It is part of the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP). This article aims to ensure that economically weaker sections have access to justice without any hindrance. Article 21 deals with the right to life, Article 32 with the right to constitutional remedies, and Article 44 with the Uniform Civil Code. Therefore, the specific provision for free legal aid is in Article 39A.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 39A → Equal justice and free legal aid
☛ Article 21 → Right to life and personal liberty
☛ Article 32 → Right to constitutional remedies (writs)
☛ Article 44 → Uniform Civil Code
☛ DPSP → Articles 36 to 51, Directive Principles of State Policy

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (09/06/2025) Shift 3
q: Which Article of the Constitution of India deals with the application of the Directive Principles of the State Policy?
qs.e: Article 37 of the Indian Constitution deals with the application of the Directive Principles of State Policy. It states that these principles are not enforceable by any court, but they are fundamental in the governance of the country. The government is obliged to apply these principles while making laws. These principles promote social welfare, economic justice, education, health, employment, and equality. Article 36 defines Directive Principles, Article 38 focuses on promoting social welfare, and Article 39 deals with livelihood, resources, and labor. Thus, Article 37 is the basis for the application of Directive Principles.

☛ What does Article 38 relate to? → Social welfare
☛ What topics does Article 39 focus on? → Livelihood, resources, labor

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (10/06/2025) Shift 2
q: Which Article of the Constitution of India states about the directive for states to make provision for public assistance in cases of unemployment?
qs.e: Article 41 of the Indian Constitution directs the state to make effective provision for public assistance in cases of unemployment, old age, sickness, and disablement. This article is part of the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP), which embody socialist principles. Under Article 41, the state is obligated to secure the right to work, the right to education, and public assistance during unemployment. It aims to protect citizens facing economic distress. Although these directives are non-justiciable, they are fundamental in the governance of the country. In contrast, Article 39 deals with equal justice and prevention of poverty, Article 42 covers just and humane conditions of work, and Article 40 pertains to organisation of village panchayats.

q: Which Directive Principle of State Policy is NOT added by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act of the Constitution of India?
o: Protection of the environment, forests and wildlife
Promotion of democratic control of co-operative societies
Promotion of equal justice and to provide free legal aid to the poor
Secure participation of workers in the management of industries
qs.e: The 42nd Amendment (1976) added four new DPSPs: Article 39A (equal justice and free legal aid), Article 43A (participation of workers in management of industries), Article 48A (protection of environment, forests and wildlife), and Article 43B (promotion of co-operative societies) was added by the 97th Amendment (2011). Hence, 'Promotion of democratic control of co-operative societies' was NOT added by the 42nd Amendment.

q: Which Article of the Constitution of India states about the directive for the state to secure a social order for the promotion of welfare of the people?
qs.e: Article 38 of the Indian Constitution directs the state to secure a social order for the promotion of the welfare of the people. It is a part of the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP), which guide the government in policy-making. Article 38 specifically emphasizes social, economic and political justice. It mandates the state to strive to minimize inequalities in income, status, facilities and opportunities. This article is placed under Part IV of the Constitution and is non-justiciable, meaning it cannot be enforced by courts, but it is fundamental in the governance of the country. The concept of a welfare state is embodied in this directive.

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (19/06/2025) Shift 2
q: Which of the following Directive Principles is mentioned in Article 44 of the Constitution of India?
o: Organisation of agriculture and animal husbandry
Uniform civil code for the citizens
Equal justice and free legal aid
qs.e: Article 44 of the Constitution of India is one of the Directive Principles of State Policy. It directs the State to endeavor to secure a Uniform Civil Code for all citizens throughout the territory of India. This provision aims to replace the personal laws based on religions with a common set of laws governing marriage, divorce, inheritance, and adoption. The Uniform Civil Code promotes national unity and gender equality. However, being a Directive Principle, it is not enforceable by courts. The inclusion of Article 44 reflects the vision of a secular and progressive society. Goa is the only Indian state that has a Uniform Civil Code in practice. This article is part of the socialist and secular principles of the Constitution.
qs.kf:

☛ Which Indian state has a Uniform Civil Code in practice? → Goa

q: Which Article of the Constitution of India mentions the Fundamental Duty of safeguarding public property and abjuring violence?
qs.e: Article 51A of the Indian Constitution deals with Fundamental Duties. It lists 11 duties for citizens. Article 51A (i) states that it is the duty of every citizen to safeguard public property and abjure violence. This duty was added by the 42nd Amendment Act of 1976. Its purpose is to instill patriotism and a sense of commitment towards the nation. q: In which year was the provision for the free legal aid to the poor added to the Directive Principles of the State Policy of the Constitution of India?
qs.e: The provision for free legal aid to the poor was added to the Directive Principles of State Policy through the 42nd Amendment (1976). This amendment introduced Article 39A, which ensures equal justice and free legal aid. It was enacted during the Emergency (1975-77) and brought many significant changes, including adding the words 'socialist', 'secular', and 'integrity' to the Preamble. Under Article 39A, the State shall ensure that no citizen is denied opportunities for justice due to economic or other disabilities. This provision is crucial for promoting social justice and ensuring access to justice for the underprivileged.

q: The concept of ‘directive principles’ in Indian Constitution has been taken from:
qs.e: The concept of Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) in the Indian Constitution is derived from the Constitution of Ireland. These principles are enshrined in Part IV (Articles 36-51) of the Indian Constitution. They are non-justiciable, meaning they cannot be enforced by courts, but they serve as guidelines for the state in policy-making. The DPSPs aim to establish a welfare state by ensuring social, economic, and political justice. They include Gandhian principles like promotion of cottage industries, prohibition of intoxicating drinks, and organization of village panchayats.

q: Which article of the Indian Constitution lays down Directive Principles of State Policy on promotion of International Peace and Security?
qs.e: Article 51 of the Indian Constitution, part of the Directive Principles of State Policy, directs the State to promote international peace and security. It instructs the State to foster respect for international law and treaty obligations, encourage settlement of international disputes by arbitration, and maintain just and honorable relations between nations. This article also emphasizes cooperation with international organizations like the United Nations to promote world peace. Though non-justiciable, Article 51 serves as a guiding principle for India's foreign policy, emphasizing peaceful coexistence and global cooperation. It reflects India's commitment to resolving conflicts through dialogue and upholding international legal frameworks.

q: Which of the following is related to the fundamental duties ?

qs.e: The Fundamental Duties are enshrined in Part IV A of the Indian Constitution under Article 51A. These duties apply only to the citizens of India, not to foreigners or tourists. Originally, 10 duties were added by the 42nd Amendment in 1976, later increased to 11 by the 86th Amendment in 2002. These duties reflect moral and civic responsibilities, such as respecting the Constitution, national flag, national anthem, protecting the environment, etc. Fundamental duties are non-justiciable in nature, but the government can make laws to enforce them.

q: What does the state's policy mean by directive principles?

They are inspired by the Constitution of Ireland and aim to establish socio-economic justice. DPSP are non-justiciable, meaning they cannot be enforced by courts, but they are fundamental in the governance of the country. They differ from Fundamental Rights, which are justiciable. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar described DPSP as the soul of the Indian Constitution.

q: What are the goals of state policy director principles?
qs.e: The Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) are enshrined in Part IV of the Indian Constitution. These principles guide the state in making laws and aim to establish social, political and economic justice. Social goals include education, health and equality; political goals focus on protecting democratic values; and economic goals emphasize equitable distribution of wealth and improving living standards. DPSP are borrowed from the Irish Constitution and are not enforceable by courts, but are fundamental in the governance of the country.

q: Which Article states that the State shall strive to promote the welfare of the people?
qs.e: Article 38 of the Indian Constitution directs the State to promote the welfare of the people. This article also emphasizes minimizing inequalities in income, status, facilities, and opportunities. It is a guiding principle for the government in policy-making, though it is not enforceable by courts. Article 38 reflects the socialist inspiration of the Constitution and is included in Part IV.

q: Which Article of the Indian Constitution provides for the promotion of international peace and security as a directive principle?

This article is non-justiciable, meaning it cannot be enforced by courts, but it serves as a guiding principle for policy-making. It reflects India's commitment to global peace and forms the foundation of its foreign policy. q: Which Article of the Constitution of India mentions the Fundamental Duty of defending the country and rendering national service when called upon to do so?
qs.e: The Fundamental Duties are enshrined in Part IV-A of the Indian Constitution under Article 51A. Clause (d) of Article 51A states that it is the duty of every citizen to defend the country and render national service when called upon to do so. These duties were added by the 42nd Amendment Act of 1976 on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee. Other clauses include (a) respecting the Constitution, (b) cherishing ideals of freedom struggle, (c) upholding sovereignty, (e) promoting harmony, etc. There are currently 11 fundamental duties. Clause (d) specifically emphasizes patriotism and national security.

q: As of December 2020, how many fundamental duties are enumerated in the Constitution of India?
qs.e: Fundamental duties were added to the Indian Constitution by the 42nd Amendment in 1976. Originally, there were 10 duties. As of December 2020, there are 11 fundamental duties, which include respecting the national flag and anthem, protecting the unity and integrity of India, safeguarding public property, and protecting the environment. q: Which of the following articles of the Indian Constitution is directed to establish right to work, to education and to public assistance in certain cases?
qs.e: Article 41 of the Indian Constitution directs the State to establish right to work, education, and public assistance in certain cases. Under Article 41, the State is required to provide public assistance in cases of unemployment, old age, sickness, and disablement. This article is based on socialist principles and aims to secure the socio-economic rights of citizens. Although it is non-justiciable, it holds significant importance for the welfare functions of the State. q: In which of the following elections are one-third of the seats reserved for women?
qs.e: The 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments (1992) mandated reservation of one-third (33%) of seats for women in Panchayati Raj Institutions (Gram Panchayat, Block Panchayat, District Panchayat) and urban local bodies. This reservation applies to directly elected seats. In contrast, Lok Sabha, Legislative Assemblies, and Rajya Sabha currently have no such reservation, although the Nari Shakti Vandan Act (2023) proposes one-third reservation for women in Lok Sabha and state assemblies, but it is not yet implemented. Therefore, as of now, only Panchayati Raj elections have one-third seats reserved for women.

☛ 74th Constitutional Amendment → Women reservation in urban local bodies

q: In which of the following elections are one-third of the seats reserved for women?
qs.e: In India, the 73rd Constitutional Amendment (1992) mandates that one-third (33%) of seats in Panchayati Raj Institutions are reserved for women. This reservation applies to both elected positions and chairperson positions. The aim is to enhance women's political participation at the grassroots level. However, there is no such mandatory reservation for women in Rajya Sabha, Lok Sabha, or Legislative Assemblies. The Women's Reservation Bill for Parliament and state assemblies is still pending. Panchayati Raj reservation has already been implemented and has significantly empowered women in local governance.

q: To prohibit the slaughter of cows is a Directive Principle mentioned in _____ of the Indian Constitution.
qs.e: Part IV of the Indian Constitution contains the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP). Article 48 directs the State to organize agriculture and animal husbandry on modern and scientific lines, and in particular to prohibit the slaughter of cows, calves, and other milch animals. This principle is inspired by the Irish Constitution. Article 48 is based on Gandhian principles emphasizing animal welfare and agrarian reform. q: The Fundamental Duties in the Indian Constitution have a resemblance to which of the following international declarations?
o: International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights
qs.e: The Fundamental Duties were added to the Indian Constitution by the 42nd Amendment in 1976, based on the recommendations of the Swaran Singh Committee. These duties are inspired by the spirit of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR), which also emphasizes citizens' responsibilities alongside rights. Article 29 of the UDHR states that everyone has duties to the community. The Indian Constitution originally listed 10 Fundamental Duties; the 11th was added by the 86th Amendment (2002). It is important to note that these duties are non-justiciable, meaning they are not enforceable by courts. The concept of duties was also influenced by the Constitution of the former Soviet Union.

q: Dr. BR Ambedkar described which part of the Indian Constitution as its ‘novel features', while Granville Austin referred to it as the ‘Conscience of the Constitution’?
qs.e: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar described the Directive Principles of State Policy as the 'novel features' of the Constitution because they are a unique and fundamental characteristic of the Indian Constitution. These principles are enshrined in Part IV (Articles 36-51) of the Constitution. Granville Austin called them the 'Conscience of the Constitution' as they guide the state towards achieving socio-economic justice. These principles are non-justiciable, meaning they cannot be enforced by courts, but they are fundamental in the governance of the country. They are inspired by the Irish Constitution and are based on the concept of a welfare state. They aim to establish social and economic democracy in India.

qs.e: The Indian Constitution incorporates several new features that distinguish it from other constitutions. The Directive Principles of State Policy were borrowed from the Irish Constitution, representing a novel concept. These principles guide the government in policy-making but are not enforceable by courts. Fundamental Rights were taken from the USA, Emergency Provisions from Germany, and Fundamental Duties were added by the 42nd Amendment in 1976. q: Which of the following is NOT found in every Gram Panchayat in India?
qs.e: In India, the structure of Gram Panchayat includes mandatory posts like Sarpanch, Upsarpanch, and Panchayat Secretary, but the post of Treasurer is not compulsory in every state. For instance, states like Tripura, West Bengal, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Gujarat, and Rajasthan do not provide for an elected treasurer. This post is generally found in larger panchayats or states with special provisions. Functions of Gram Panchayat include development planning, tax collection, and public services. According to the 73rd Constitutional Amendment, Sarpanch and Upsarpanch are present in every panchayat, while the Panchayat Secretary is appointed by the state government. q: Free legal aid is part of which part of the Indian Constitution?
qs.e: Part IV of the Indian Constitution contains the Directive Principles of State Policy (Articles 36-51). Article 39A directs the State to provide free legal aid to ensure equal justice and equal opportunity. This principle is not enforceable by courts but is fundamental in the governance of the country. It aims to ensure access to justice for the poor and weaker sections of society. Free legal aid is not a Fundamental Right under the Directive Principles; however, the Supreme Court has later held it to be part of Article 21 (Right to Life) as a Fundamental Right. Thus, free legal aid is primarily enshrined in the Directive Principles of State Policy.

q: Which of the following policy adoptions by the Government of India is NOT guided by the 'Directive Principles of State Policy?

Article 44 calls for a uniform civil code. Article 47 includes prohibition of consumption of alcoholic liquor. Building by-laws, such as construction regulations, are framed by local bodies or municipal planning authorities, and are not part of DPSP. q: Which of the following Articles of the Indian Constitution provides for a Uniform Civil Code (UCC)?
qs.e: Article 44 of the Indian Constitution deals with the Uniform Civil Code (UCC). It is part of the Directive Principles of State Policy, which are contained in Part IV (Articles 36-51). Article 44 states that the State shall endeavor to secure a Uniform Civil Code for all citizens throughout India. This provision is already implemented in Goa, which has a common civil code since the Portuguese era. However, it is not enforceable by any court, but serves as a guiding principle for law-making. The UCC aims to replace personal laws based on different religions with a common set of laws. It is rooted in the principles of equality and secularism.

q: "The State shall endeavour to secure for the citizens a uniform civil code throughout the territory of India" is a provision mentioned in which of the following Parts of the Constitution of India?
qs.e: The provision of Uniform Civil Code is mentioned in Part IV (Directive Principles of State Policy) of the Constitution of India under Article 44. q: The Directive Principles of State Policy in the Indian Constitution ____________.
o: Are not enforceable by any court
qs.e: The Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) enshrined in Part IV (Articles 36-51) of the Indian Constitution are non-justiciable, meaning they cannot be enforced by any court. These principles serve as guidelines for the state in formulating policies and laws, but their violation cannot be challenged in a court of law. Article 37 explicitly states that DPSP are not enforceable by any court. Inspired by the Irish Constitution, they aim to establish a welfare state. q: According to L. M. Singhvi, what are the Directive Principles of State Policy considered as?
qs.e: According to L. M. Singhvi, the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) are considered as the 'life-giving provisions of the Constitution.' These principles are enshrined in Part IV (Articles 36-51) of the Indian Constitution and aim to establish social and economic justice. They are non-justiciable but serve as guiding principles for state policy. Singhvi emphasized that DPSP are the soul of the Constitution and should be implemented in balance with Fundamental Rights. While DPSP are also referred to as 'moral rights,' Singhvi's key contribution is terming them as 'life-giving provisions.' In the Kesavananda Bharati case, the Supreme Court held that DPSP are part of the basic structure of the Constitution.

They serve as guidelines for the legislature and executive in making laws and policies. The statement that they are legally enforceable by courts is incorrect. According to Article 37, the provisions of DPSP are not enforceable by any court. Therefore, option 4 is the incorrect statement. Hence, the correct answer is option 4.

☛ Article 40 → Organisation of village panchayats
☛ Article 39A → Equal justice and free legal aid
☛ Article 43A → Participation of workers in management of industries
☛ Article 42 → Just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief
☛ Article 41 → Right to work, education and public assistance

q: Which of the following provisions in the Indian Constitution deals with the duty of the State to separate the judiciary from the executive?
qs.e: Article 50 of the Indian Constitution is part of the Directive Principles of State Policy. It deals with the separation of the judiciary from the executive in public services. This provision aims to ensure judicial independence by preventing interference from the executive branch. It is a guiding principle for policy-making, though not enforceable by courts. Article 50 is found in Part IV of the Constitution. Other options: Article 44 relates to Uniform Civil Code, Article 48A relates to environment protection, and Article 51 relates to international peace and security.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 50 deals with? → Separation of judiciary from executive
☛ Article 50 is part of which Part? → Part IV (Directive Principles)
☛ Article 44 relates to? → Uniform Civil Code
☛ Article 48A relates to? → Protection of environment
☛ Article 51 relates to? → International peace and security

q: Which of the following objectives is mentioned in Article 39 of the Indian Constitution?
o: To organise agriculture and animal husbandry
To ensure equal justice and provide free legal aid
To promote equal pay for equal work for both men and women
qs.e: Article 39 is part of the Directive Principles of State Policy in the Indian Constitution. It directs the State to ensure equal standard of living and adequate means of livelihood for all citizens. Specifically, it mandates equal pay for equal work for both men and women, promoting gender equality and preventing workplace discrimination. Other options like organising agriculture, free legal aid, and village panchayats are covered in different parts of the Constitution.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Article deals with equal pay for equal work? → Article 39
☛ Which part of the Indian Constitution contains Directive Principles? → Part IV
☛ Article 39 is based on which principle? → Social justice
☛ Equal pay provision applies to which gender? → Both men and women
☛ Directive Principles are borrowed from which country's constitution? → Ireland

q: According to the Gandhian principles incorporated in the Directive Principles of State Policy, the State shall endeavor to promote:
o: Cottage industries on an individual or cooperative basis in rural areas
qs.e: The Directive Principles of State Policy in Part IV of the Indian Constitution include Gandhian principles. Article 43 directs the State to promote cottage industries on an individual or cooperative basis in rural areas. This is based on Mahatma Gandhi's economic philosophy emphasizing decentralization and village self-reliance. Gandhian principles focus on self-sufficient villages, small-scale industries, and local production. Options like large-scale corporate farming or industrialization in urban areas do not align with Gandhian ideals. These principles aim to reduce inequality and promote rural development.
qs.kf:
☛ Which articles contain Gandhian principles? → Articles 40, 43, 46, 47, 48
☛ Which article deals with cottage industries? → Article 43
☛ What is the aim of Gandhian principles? → Rural development and self-reliance
☛ From which constitution are DPSPs borrowed? → Constitution of Ireland
☛ Gandhian principles include → Village panchayats, cottage industries, prohibition

q: Which of the following Articles of the Indian Constitution directs the State to ensure equal pay for equal work for both men and women?
qs.e: Article 39(d) of the Indian Constitution is part of the Directive Principles of State Policy under Part IV. It directs the State to ensure equal pay for equal work for both men and women. This provision aims to promote gender equality and eliminate wage discrimination based on sex. Although Directive Principles are not enforceable by any court, they are fundamental in the governance of the country. Article 39(d) complements the fundamental right to equality (Article 14) but specifically addresses wage parity. It was included to uphold the dignity of labor and ensure fair treatment of women in the workplace.
qs.kf:
☛ Equal pay for equal work → Article 39(d)
☛ Article 39(d) is in which part → Part IV (Directive Principles)
☛ Men and women equal pay → Article 39(d)
☛ Article 42(b) → Just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief
☛ Article 15 → Prohibition of discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, etc.

q: Which among following fundamental duties is INCORRECT related towards the protection and promotion of scientific and cultural values?
o: To safe guard the public property and to abjure violence
To value and preserve the rich heritage of our composite culture.
To develop the scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform.
To strive towards excellence in all spheres of individual and collective activity.
qs.e: Article 51A of the Indian Constitution lists fundamental duties. Duty (i) 'To safeguard public property and to abjure violence' relates to social and national security, not to the protection and promotion of scientific and cultural values. Duties related to scientific and cultural values are duty (j) 'To value and preserve the rich heritage of our composite culture', duty (h) 'To develop the scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform', and duty (k) 'To strive towards excellence in all spheres of individual and collective activity'. Among these, duty (k) is directly linked to scientific and cultural progress by promoting excellence. Hence, duty (i) is incorrectly related.
qs.kf:
☛ Under which article are fundamental duties listed? → Article 51A
☛ Which duty is about developing scientific temper? → Duty (h)
☛ Which duty relates to preserving cultural heritage? → Duty (j)
☛ Which duty is about striving for excellence? → Duty (k)
☛ Total number of fundamental duties? → 11

q: Which among the following changes were made in the Indian Constitution by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act ?
o: Introduction of Fundamental Duties under Article 51A.
Inserted Right to Privacy in the Article 21 of Indian Constitution.
Increased Lok Sabha seats from 525 to 545.
qs.e: The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act was enacted in 1976. It introduced Fundamental Duties in the Indian Constitution under Article 51A, providing a list of 10 duties for citizens, such as to defend the nation and protect public property. This amendment also added the words 'Socialist', 'Secular' and 'Integrity' to the Preamble. It attempted to reduce the power of judicial review, but the Supreme Court later upheld it. Nationalization of land ceiling laws or the Right to Privacy were not part of this amendment. The 42nd Amendment is often called the 'Mini Constitution' due to its extensive changes.
qs.kf:
☛ Which words were added to the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment? → Socialist, Secular, Integrity
☛ Under which Article are Fundamental Duties mentioned? → Article 51A
☛ When was the 42nd Amendment enacted? → 1976
☛ How many Fundamental Duties are there originally? → 11 (one added later)
☛ What is the 42nd Amendment also known as? → Mini Constitution

q: Which Article of the Indian Constitution was given practical effect through the 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992, leading to the establishment of the Panchayati Raj System in India?
qs.e: Article 40 of the Indian Constitution, a Directive Principle of State Policy, directs the state to organize village panchayats. The 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992 gave practical effect to this article by granting constitutional status to Panchayati Raj Institutions across India. This act added Part IX (Articles 243 to 243O) to the Constitution, dealing with panchayats. It came into force on April 24, 1993, celebrated as National Panchayati Raj Day. While Article 40 existed in the original Constitution, the 73rd Amendment strengthened it by providing a uniform structure for local self-government.
qs.kf:
☛ Part added by 73rd Amendment → Part IX (Articles 243-243O)
☛ Basis of Panchayati Raj → Article 40
☛ 73rd Amendment enforced on → 24 April 1993
☛ Three-tier system of Panchayats → Village, Intermediate, District
☛ Subjects in 11th Schedule → 29 functional subjects

q: Which of the following Articles of the Indian Constitution contains the fundamental duties?
qs.e: The fundamental duties were added to the Indian Constitution by the 42nd Amendment in 1976. They are enshrined in Article 51A under Part IVA. There are 11 fundamental duties that guide citizens in their responsibilities towards the nation, such as respecting the national flag and anthem, protecting the sovereignty and integrity of India, safeguarding public property, and preserving the environment. Originally, there were 10 duties; the 86th Amendment (2002) added an 11th duty related to providing educational opportunities for children aged 6-14. These duties are non-justiciable but serve as moral obligations for citizens.
qs.kf:
☛ Which amendment added Fundamental Duties? → 42nd Amendment (1976)
☛ Under which Article are Fundamental Duties mentioned? → Article 51A
☛ Which Part of the Constitution contains Fundamental Duties? → Part IVA
☛ How many Fundamental Duties are there currently? → 11
☛ Which duty was added by the 86th Amendment? → Providing educational opportunities

q: How many Fundamental Duties were originally added to the Indian Constitution in 1976?
qs.e: The Fundamental Duties were added to the Indian Constitution by the 42nd Amendment in 1976, under Part IV-A, Article 51A. Originally, 10 duties were included. Later, in 2002, the 86th Amendment added one more duty, making the total count 11. These duties remind citizens of their responsibilities towards the nation. The concept of Fundamental Duties was inspired by the Constitution of the Soviet Union. They were incorporated on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee. These duties are non-justiciable, meaning they cannot be enforced by courts.
qs.kf:
☛ Which article contains Fundamental Duties? → Article 51A
☛ Which amendment added Fundamental Duties? → 42nd Amendment (1976)
☛ How many Fundamental Duties are there currently? → 11
☛ From which constitution were Fundamental Duties inspired? → Constitution of the Soviet Union
☛ Which committee recommended Fundamental Duties? → Swaran Singh Committee

q: Article 47 deals with which of the following?
o: Raising the level of nutrition and public health
qs.e: Article 47 of the Indian Constitution is part of the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP). This article directs the State to raise the level of nutrition and the standard of public health, and to prohibit the consumption of intoxicating drinks and drugs which are injurious to health. It also directs the State to organize agriculture and animal husbandry on modern and scientific lines. This article focuses on promoting social welfare and improving the living standards of citizens. Protection of the environment is covered under Article 48-A.
qs.kf:
☛ What does Article 47 mainly deal with? → Raising the level of nutrition and public health
☛ What does Article 48 deal with? → Organization of agriculture and animal husbandry
☛ What does Article 48-A deal with? → Protection of environment and wildlife
☛ What does Article 43-A deal with? → Participation of workers in management of industries
☛ Article 47 is under which Part? → Part IV (Directive Principles of State Policy)

q: Which of the following is not contained in Article 51?
o: Just and honourable relations between nations
Promotion of international peace and security
Protection of forests and wildlife of India
Respect for international law and treaty obligations
qs.e: Article 51 is part of the Directive Principles of State Policy in the Indian Constitution. This article promotes international peace and security, maintains just and honourable relations between nations, fosters respect for international law and treaty obligations, and encourages settlement of international disputes by arbitration. It directs the State to endeavour to preserve international peace and security. The protection of forests and wildlife is covered under Article 48A, which deals with environmental protection, not Article 51. Hence, option 3 is not contained in Article 51.
qs.kf:
☛ What does Article 51 relate to? → Promotion of international peace and security
☛ What is included in Article 51? → Just and honourable relations between nations
☛ What does Article 48A relate to? → Protection and improvement of environment
☛ Which part is Article 51 in? → Part IV (Directive Principles of State Policy)
☛ What is NOT in Article 51? → Protection of forests and wildlife

q: The 86th Amendment added a new Fundamental Duty related to which of the following?
qs.e: The 86th Constitutional Amendment (2002) added a new Fundamental Duty under Article 51A, making it the duty of parents or guardians to provide opportunities for education to their children aged 6 to 14 years. This amendment was linked to making education a fundamental right under Article 21A. Originally, the Fundamental Duties were added by the 42nd Amendment in 1976, which introduced 10 duties. Later, the 86th Amendment added an 11th duty related to children's education. This duty emphasizes the importance of education and helps in preventing child labor. It reflects the constitutional commitment to universal elementary education.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the 86th Constitutional Amendment enacted? → 2002
☛ Which Article provides Right to Education as a fundamental right? → Article 21A
☛ Under which Article are Fundamental Duties listed? → Article 51A
☛ How many Fundamental Duties were added by the 42nd Amendment? → 10
☛ How many Fundamental Duties are there in total now? → 11

q: Which Article of the Indian Constitution directs the State to take steps to organize Village Panchayats?
qs.e: Article 40 of the Indian Constitution comes under the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP). This Article directs the State to take steps to organize Village Panchayats as units of self-government. It is included in Part IV of the Constitution, which contains the Directive Principles. Although these are non-justiciable, they are fundamental in the governance of the country. Under Article 40, the State shall endeavor to endow panchayats with necessary powers and authority so that they can function as autonomous bodies. This forms the basis of the Panchayati Raj system, which gained constitutional status through the 73rd Constitutional Amendment in 1992. The amendment added Part IX and the Eleventh Schedule to the Constitution, strengthening local self-governance.
qs.kf:
☛ Article related to Village Panchayats → Article 40
☛ Part containing Article 40 → Part IV (DPSP)
☛ Amendment giving constitutional status to Panchayati Raj → 73rd Amendment 1992
☛ Three-tier system of Panchayati Raj → Gram Panchayat, Block Samiti, Zila Parishad
☛ Nature of Panchayats under Article 40 → Units of self-government

q: Which Article of the Indian Constitution obligates the State to secure equal pay for men and women doing comparable work?
qs.e: Article 39(d) of the Indian Constitution directs the State to ensure equal pay for equal work for both men and women. This Article falls under the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) in Part IV. Though not enforceable by courts, these principles are fundamental in governance. Article 39(d) promotes gender equality and social justice. In contrast, Article 42 deals with just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief, while Article 38(1) focuses on securing a social, economic, and political justice. Article 47(a) does not exist. Thus, the correct Article for equal pay is 39(d), which has been a strong pillar for gender equality since the Constitution's inception.
qs.kf:
☛ Constitutional Article ensuring equal pay for equal work → Article 39(d)
☛ Article 39(d) is part of which Part → Part IV (DPSP)
☛ Article 42 is related to → Just conditions of work and maternity relief
☛ Main objective of Article 38(1) → Secure social, economic and political justice
☛ Nature of DPSP → Not enforceable but fundamental in governance

q: Which Article of the Indian Constitution mandates the provision of humane working conditions and maternity relief?
qs.e: Article 42 of the Indian Constitution directs the State to make provision for securing just and humane conditions of work and for maternity relief. It is part of the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP), which are guidelines for the government in policy-making but are not enforceable by courts. Article 42 aims to promote the welfare of workers and protect the health of women during maternity.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Article deals with humane working conditions and maternity relief? → Article 42
☛ Article 42 falls under which category? → Directive Principles of State Policy
☛ Which Act provides maternity benefits in India? → Maternity Benefit Act, 1961
☛ What does Article 48 relate to? → Organisation of agriculture and animal husbandry
☛ What does Article 41 relate to? → Right to education, employment, and public assistance

q: Which Article of the Directive Principles of State Policy enshrines the principle of equal pay for equal work for both men and women in India?
qs.e: The Directive Principles of State Policy are enshrined in Part IV of the Indian Constitution. Article 39 directs the State to ensure equal pay for equal work for both men and women. This principle promotes social justice and gender equality. Article 44 relates to the Uniform Civil Code, Article 43 deals with living wages and decent working conditions for workers, and Article 41 concerns the right to work, education, and public assistance. Thus, the correct answer is Article 39.
qs.kf:
☛ Which article ensures equal pay for equal work? → Article 39
☛ What does Article 44 deal with? → Uniform Civil Code
☛ What is the subject of Article 43? → Living wages for workers
☛ What does Article 41 provide? → Right to work, education, and public assistance
☛ Where are the Directive Principles located? → Articles 36-51 of Part IV

q: Which of the following Articles of the Indian Constitution are concerned with the protection of environment and wildlife?
qs.e: Article 48A of the Indian Constitution is related to the protection of the environment and wildlife. It is a Directive Principle of State Policy and states that the State shall protect and improve the environment and safeguard the forests and wildlife of the country. This article was added by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976. The same amendment also added Article 51A(g), which makes it a fundamental duty of every citizen to protect the environment. Article 48A directs the State to enact laws for environmental protection. Articles 38A, 41A, and 42A do not exist in the Indian Constitution.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 48A → Concerned with environment and wildlife protection
☛ 42nd Constitutional Amendment, 1976 → Added Article 48A
☛ Article 51A(g) → Fundamental duty of citizens to protect environment
☛ Directive Principles of State Policy → Article 48A belongs to this part
☛ Articles 38A, 41A, 42A → Not present in the Constitution

q: Which of the following reflects the Gandhian ideals incorporated as Directive Principles of State Policy in the Constitution of India?
o: Raising the standard of living and public health
Promoting cottage industries in rural areas
qs.e: The Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) in the Indian Constitution include Gandhian ideals. Article 43 directs the State to promote cottage industries in rural areas, reflecting Mahatma Gandhi's vision of gram swaraj and self-reliance. Other options, such as raising standard of living and public health (Article 47), safeguarding children against exploitation (Article 39), and securing employment (Article 39), are more aligned with socialist or liberal principles. Gandhian principles focus on rural development and decentralization, making promotion of cottage industries a direct reflection of Gandhian thought.
qs.kf:
☛ Article related to Gandhian DPSP → Articles 40, 43, 46, 47, 48
☛ Article promoting cottage industries → Article 43
☛ Main goal of Gandhian principles → Strengthen rural economy
☛ Article 40 deals with → Formation of village panchayats
☛ Article 48 deals with → Prohibition of cow slaughter

q: After a Constitution Amendment Bill relating to the Directive Principles of State Policy is passed by the Parliament, what is the next mandatory constitutional step for it to become a law?
qs.e: According to Article 368 of the Indian Constitution, after a Constitution Amendment Bill is passed by Parliament, the next mandatory step is obtaining the President's Assent. Unlike amendments that affect the federal structure, amendments related to the Directive Principles of State Policy do not require ratification by state legislatures. The President must give assent to the bill, after which it becomes an Act and is then notified in the Gazette. Approval by the Supreme Court is not a routine step; it is only sought in cases involving the basic structure doctrine. Thus, the President's Assent is the crucial next step for the bill to become law.
qs.kf:
☛ Whose assent is required after a Constitution Amendment Bill is passed? → President
☛ Which amendments require ratification by states? → Those affecting federal structure
☛ Which article deals with the amendment process? → Article 368
☛ Where are the Directive Principles located? → Part IV
☛ Can the President withhold assent to a Constitutional Amendment Bill? → No, he must give assent

q: Who is the Chairman of the NITI Aayog?
qs.e: NITI Aayog (National Institution for Transforming India) was established on 1 January 2015, replacing the Planning Commission. Its chairman is the Prime Minister of India. It is a non-constitutional body that promotes cooperative federalism between the Centre and states. It has a Vice Chairman, Chief Executive Officer, and full-time members. Currently, Prime Minister Narendra Modi is the chairman. NITI Aayog's headquarters is in New Delhi.
qs.kf:
☛ First Vice Chairman of NITI Aayog → Arvind Panagariya
☛ Year of establishment of NITI Aayog → 2015
☛ Headquarters of NITI Aayog → New Delhi
☛ Current CEO of NITI Aayog → B.V.R. Subrahmanyam (as of 2025)
☛ Ministry under which NITI Aayog functions → None (independent body)

q: The administrative reforms commission was initially chaired by _______.
qs.e: The Administrative Reforms Commission (ARC) was set up by the Government of India on 5 January 1966 to recommend measures for reforming the administrative system. The first ARC was chaired by Morarji Desai, who was then the Deputy Prime Minister of India. The commission submitted its report in 20 volumes covering recommendations on administrative efficiency, civil services, financial management, and grievance redressal. Later, in 2005, the second ARC was constituted under the chairmanship of Veerappa Moily. The first ARC was a landmark reform initiative that strengthened the foundation of Indian administration.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Administrative Reforms Commission (ARC) established? → 1966
☛ Who chaired the second ARC? → Veerappa Moily
☛ How many volumes did the first ARC submit? → 20
☛ What was the objective of ARC? → Recommend administrative reforms
☛ What position did the first ARC chairman hold? → Deputy Prime Minister

q: Who is the Chairman of the National Development Council?
qs.e: The National Development Council (NDC) is a vital constitutional body in India, established in 1952. Its main purpose is to strengthen the country's development plans and promote center-state cooperation. The Prime Minister serves as the chairman of this council. The NDC includes all state chief ministers, administrators of union territories, and members of the union cabinet. The council works in coordination with the Planning Commission (now NITI Aayog) and provides final approval to the five-year plans. The President is the formal head of the state, but the chairman of the NDC is the Prime Minister. This council coordinates policies for economic and social development.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the National Development Council formed? → 1952
☛ What is the main objective of the NDC? → Coordination of development plans
☛ Who are the members of the NDC? → Chief ministers, union ministers, and administrators
☛ Who gives final approval to five-year plans? → National Development Council
☛ In which year was NITI Aayog formed? → 2015

q: President's Ordinance can be issued __________.
o: As a Parliamentary Act on the provisions with same limits
On the specially mentioned provisions of the President
On any provision of the Constitution
qs.e: The President's Ordinance can only be issued when Parliament is not in session, and it has the same force and effect as a Parliamentary Act.
