However, it is subject to the same limitations as a Parliamentary Act, meaning it can only cover subjects within the legislative competence of Parliament. The ordinance cannot be issued on any provision of the Constitution arbitrarily; it must comply with the constitutional limits on legislative power. The ordinance must be approved by Parliament within six weeks of reassembly, otherwise it ceases to operate. Thus, option 1 is correct as it reflects that the ordinance is equivalent to a Parliamentary Act with the same limits.
qs.kf:
☛ When can President's Ordinance be issued? → When Parliament is not in session
☛ What is the maximum duration of an Ordinance? → 6 weeks after Parliament reassembles
☛ Under which Article is the ordinance-making power? → Article 123
☛ Can an ordinance be revoked by Parliament? → Yes
☛ Is the ordinance subject to judicial review? → Yes

q: Who among the following was elected unopposed as the President of India?
qs.e: Neelam Sanjiva Reddy was the sixth President of India, elected unopposed in 1977. He is the only President of India to have been elected unopposed, as opposition parties did not field any candidate against him. V.V. Giri was elected in 1969 but not unopposed. Giani Zail Singh was elected in 1982, and Dr. S. Radhakrishnan was elected in 1952 and 1957 but faced opposition candidates. Hence, Sanjiva Reddy is the sole President elected unopposed. He served as President from July 25, 1977, to July 25, 1982.
qs.kf:
☛ Only unopposed President → Neelam Sanjiva Reddy (1977)
☛ Sixth President of India → Neelam Sanjiva Reddy
☛ First President → Dr. Rajendra Prasad
☛ Youngest President → Neelam Sanjiva Reddy
☛ Prior to presidency, served as Lok Sabha Speaker → Neelam Sanjiva Reddy

q: Members of the Union Public Service Commission is _______.
o: Are appointed by the Home Ministry
qs.e: Members of the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) are appointed by the President of India. This provision is given in Article 316 of the Indian Constitution. UPSC is a constitutional body that conducts examinations for recruitment to civil services. The chairman and other members are appointed by the President and hold office for a term of 6 years or until the age of 65, whichever is earlier. They work with independence and impartiality. The President also has the power to remove members on grounds of misconduct or incapacity, as per Article 317.
qs.kf:
☛ Who appoints UPSC members? → President
☛ Under which Article is UPSC constituted? → Articles 315 to 323
☛ What is the tenure of UPSC chairman? → 6 years or 65 years
☛ Who can remove UPSC members? → President
☛ What type of body is UPSC? → Constitutional

q: Has the President of India declared a ﬁnancial emergency thus far?
qs.e: The President of India has never declared a Financial Emergency (Article 360) so far. This provision is part of the Indian Constitution but has never been used. Financial Emergency can be proclaimed when the financial stability or credit of the nation is threatened. During such an emergency, the central government can interfere in the financial matters of states. While President's Rule (Article 356) and National Emergency (Article 352) have been invoked several times, the Financial Emergency has never been imposed.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Article deals with Financial Emergency? → Article 360
☛ When is Financial Emergency imposed? → When the financial stability or credit of India is threatened
☛ What happens during Financial Emergency? → Centre controls state finances
☛ How many times has Financial Emergency been imposed so far? → Never
☛ What are the other types of emergencies? → National (Article 352) and President's Rule (Article 356)

q: The term of office of the President in India is?
qs.e: The term of office of the President of India is five years, as mentioned in Article 56 of the Constitution. The President holds office from the date of taking the oath and continues for five years, but can resign earlier by addressing the Vice President. The President can also be removed through impeachment for violation of the Constitution, which requires a special majority in both Houses of Parliament. The President is elected by an Electoral College and is eligible for re-election. There is no limit on the number of terms a President can serve.
qs.kf:
☛ Term of President → 5 years
☛ Minimum age for President → 35 years
☛ Removal process of President → Impeachment
☛ Election method for President → Single Transferable Vote
☛ President as constitutional head → Executive head of the Union

q: Who appoints the Chief Justice of India?
qs.e: According to Article 124 of the Indian Constitution, the President appoints the Chief Justice of India. Before making the appointment, the President may consult with other judges and political leaders, but the final decision lies with the President. This process is designed to ensure the independence of the judiciary. The Chief Justice holds office until the age of 65. The Prime Minister or Home Minister do not directly appoint; they only recommend. A Parliamentary Committee is not involved in the appointment.
qs.kf:
☛ Who appoints the Chief Justice of India? → President
☛ Which Article deals with the composition of the Supreme Court? → Article 124
☛ What is the tenure of the Chief Justice of India? → Until age 65
☛ Whom does the President consult before appointment? → Judges and ministers
☛ What is the role of the Prime Minister in appointing the CJI? → To recommend

q: Who is the caretaker President of India in the absence of the President?
o: The most senior member of the Rajya Sabha
qs.e: According to Article 65 of the Indian Constitution, in the absence, death, or removal of the President, the Vice-President acts as the caretaker President. This provision ensures continuity in the office of the President. The Vice-President remains the acting President until a new President assumes office. This constitutional arrangement is a crucial part of India's democratic framework. It is important to note that the Speaker of Lok Sabha, the most senior member of Rajya Sabha, or the Chief Justice of India are not authorized for this role.
qs.kf:
☛ Article related to acting President → Article 65
☛ Who appoints the acting President → Automatically the Vice-President
☛ How long does the acting President serve during a vacancy → Until the new President assumes office
☛ What oath does the Vice-President take as acting President → Oath of the President's office
☛ Who else can become acting President besides the Vice-President → No one

q: Without sanctioning a bill by the President and not returning it, it is called __________, to be kept pending for an indeﬁnite period of time.
qs.e: When the President neither approves a bill nor returns it, but keeps it pending for an indefinite period, it is called Pocket Veto. This concept is borrowed from the US Constitution. Under Article 111 of the Indian Constitution, the President has three options: give assent, return the bill, or withhold it. In Pocket Veto, the President takes no action, leaving the bill in abeyance. This power is particularly useful when the government is in a minority or the bill is constitutionally questionable. Suspensive Veto involves returning the bill for reconsideration, Absolute Veto means outright rejection, and Qualified Veto is used only in some countries.
qs.kf:
☛ From which country is Pocket Veto borrowed? → USA
☛ Which article of the Indian Constitution deals with the President's veto power? → Article 111
☛ In which veto does the President neither accept nor return the bill? → Pocket Veto
☛ In which veto can Parliament pass the bill again after reconsideration? → Suspensive Veto
☛ How many types of veto does the President of India have? → Three (Pocket, Suspensive, Absolute)

q: If the President returns the bill for reconsideration of the Parliament then it is called _____
qs.e: When the President returns a bill to the Parliament for reconsideration, it is called a Suspension Veto. This is a type of veto power where the President suspends the bill by sending it back with suggestions. If the Parliament passes the bill again, the President is bound to give his assent. The Suspension Veto applies only to ordinary bills, not to money bills. It limits the President's power because once the Parliament re-passes the bill, the President must accept it. This veto is a unique feature of the Indian Constitution, balancing the powers between the executive and the legislature.
qs.kf:
☛ On which bills does Suspension Veto not apply? → Money Bills
☛ What action is required from the President after Parliament re-passes a bill? → Must give assent
☛ How many types of veto does the Indian President have? → Three – Suspension, Pocket, Absolute
☛ What happens in a Pocket Veto? → President takes no action on the bill
☛ When is Absolute Veto used? → When the President rejects the bill entirely

q: Who is the Chairman of the Zonal Council?
qs.e: Zonal Councils in India were established to promote cooperation and coordination among states. They were set up under the States Reorganisation Act, 1956. Currently, there are five Zonal Councils: Northern, Central, Eastern, Western, and Southern. The Chairman of each Zonal Council is the Union Home Minister. The Vice-Chairman is the Chief Minister of the concerned states, who hold office on a rotational basis. Members include Chief Ministers, Deputy Chief Ministers of the states, and representatives of Union Territories. The primary objective of Zonal Councils is to discuss regional development plans and policy issues, and to strengthen Centre-State relations. They serve as a forum for resolving inter-state disputes and fostering mutual understanding.
qs.kf:
☛ Who is the Chairman of the Zonal Council? → Union Home Minister
☛ Under which Act were Zonal Councils established? → States Reorganisation Act, 1956
☛ How many Zonal Councils are there in India? → 5
☛ Who is the Vice-Chairman of a Zonal Council? → Chief Ministers of concerned states (rotational)
☛ What is the main purpose of Zonal Councils? → To promote cooperation and coordination among states

q: Under which article of the Indian Constitution, can the President issue the Ordinance?
qs.e: Article 123 of the Indian Constitution empowers the President to promulgate ordinances when both Houses of Parliament are not in session. This power is exercised when immediate action is necessary. An ordinance has the same force as an Act of Parliament, but it must be approved by Parliament within six weeks of reassembly, or it ceases to operate. This provision allows the executive to address urgent legislative needs without waiting for Parliament to convene.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 72 → Power of President to grant pardons
☛ Article 143 → President can seek Supreme Court's opinion
☛ Article 123 → President can issue ordinances
☛ Article 76 → Attorney General of India
☛ Maximum life of an ordinance → 6 weeks after Parliament reassembles

q: Who acted as the interim Prime Minister of India immediately on the death of Jawaharlal Nehru?
qs.e: Upon the death of Jawaharlal Nehru on 27 May 1964, Gulzarilal Nanda, who was the Deputy Prime Minister, took over as the interim Prime Minister of India. Nanda was a senior politician and the Minister of Labour. He held the position until Lal Bahadur Shastri was elected as the next Prime Minister by the Congress Party. Similarly, after Shastri's death in 1966, Nanda again served as the interim Prime Minister. His role as a caretaker leader was crucial in maintaining stability during transitions. Nanda was a respected figure in Indian politics and a member of the Indian National Congress.
qs.kf:
☛ Who became interim PM after Nehru's death? → Gulzarilal Nanda
☛ Which ministry did Gulzarilal Nanda head? → Ministry of Labour
☛ Who served as interim PM after Shastri's death? → Gulzarilal Nanda
☛ Which party did Gulzarilal Nanda belong to? → Indian National Congress
☛ When was Gulzarilal Nanda born? → 4 July 1898

q: The President of India is elected by ________.
o: The Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha at a joint sitting
qs.e: According to the Indian Constitution, the President is elected indirectly by an Electoral College. This Electoral College consists of the elected members of both Houses of Parliament (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) and the elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of all states. The election is conducted through the system of proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote. The voting takes place by secret ballot. The President is not directly elected by the people but through their representatives. The election process is governed by the Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952. Article 54 of the Constitution deals with the composition of the Electoral College for the election of the President.
qs.kf:
☛ Basis of Presidential election → Indirect election
☛ Composition of Electoral College → Elected members of Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha, and state legislatures
☛ Voting method → Single transferable vote
☛ Constitutional article → Article 54
☛ Term of President → 5 years

q: Who appoints the Chief Justice of India?
qs.e: According to Article 124 of the Indian Constitution, the Chief Justice of India is appointed by the President. Before making the appointment, the President may consult with judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts. This process is designed to ensure the independence of the judiciary. The appointment is based on the principle of seniority, though this is not a constitutional requirement. The President may also seek advice from the Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers before appointing. This appointment plays a crucial role in maintaining the independence of the judiciary and the integrity of the judicial system.
qs.kf:
☛ Who appoints the Chief Justice of India? → President
☛ Whose advice is taken before appointment? → Judges of Supreme Court and High Courts
☛ Under which article is this appointment made? → Article 124
☛ On which principle is the appointment based? → Principle of seniority
☛ Whose consultation is also taken by the President? → Prime Minister and Council of Ministers

q: The President of India has a tenure of
qs.e: The President of India has a tenure of 5 years, as per Article 56 of the Indian Constitution. The President resides in the Rashtrapati Bhavan and serves as the Supreme Commander of the Indian Armed Forces. The President is elected by an Electoral College consisting of elected members of both Houses of Parliament and state legislative assemblies. If the President vacates office prematurely, the Vice-President acts as President. The President can also be removed through impeachment for violation of the Constitution. This tenure and election process ensures stability and democratic representation.
qs.kf:
☛ President's tenure → 5 years
☛ President's Electoral College → Parliament + Assemblies
☛ Removal process of President → Impeachment
☛ President's residence → Rashtrapati Bhavan
☛ Supreme Commander → Armed Forces

q: Who governs the Union Territories in India?
qs.e: According to Article 239 of the Indian Constitution, each Union Territory is administered by the President of India. The President exercises this power through an Administrator or Lieutenant Governor. Union Territories are directly under the control of the central government, unlike states which have Governors. Some Union Territories like Delhi and Puducherry have their own Legislative Assembly and Council of Ministers, but ultimate authority remains with the President. This system ensures direct administrative control of the central government over Union Territories for effective governance.
qs.kf:
☛ Who administers Union Territories in India? → President of India
☛ Which Article deals with administration of Union Territories? → Article 239
☛ Through whom does the President administer Union Territories? → Administrator or Lieutenant Governor
☛ Which Union Territories have a Legislative Assembly? → Delhi and Puducherry
☛ Where does the ultimate authority of Union Territories lie? → President of India

q: Which of the following is NOT a power of the president of India?
o: Appointment of the Chief Minister of States
qs.e: The President of India has the power to declare a national emergency (Article 352), appoint the Chief Justice (Article 124), and appoint Governors (Article 155). However, the President does NOT appoint the Chief Minister of a state. The Governor of the state appoints the Chief Minister, who is the leader of the majority party in the state legislative assembly. The President is the constitutional head of the Union executive and acts on the advice of the Union Council of Ministers. State administration is primarily the domain of the Governor, while the President's powers are focused at the federal level. Therefore, the appointment of Chief Ministers is not a power vested in the President. Thus, the correct answer is the 'Appointment of the Chief Minister of States'.
qs.kf:
☛ Who declares a national emergency? → President
☛ Who appoints the Chief Justice? → President
☛ Who appoints Governors of States? → President
☛ Who appoints the Chief Minister of a state? → Governor
☛ Under which article does the President declare emergency? → Article 352

q: Who is the first woman Chief Minister of India?
qs.e: Sucheta Kriplani was the first woman Chief Minister of India. She served as the Chief Minister of Uttar Pradesh from 1963 to 1967. She was a member of the Indian National Congress and actively participated in India's freedom struggle. Born on 25 June 1908, she also served as a member of the Constituent Assembly and contributed to the drafting of the Indian Constitution. She was a prominent politician and social activist.
qs.kf:
☛ First woman Chief Minister of India → Sucheta Kriplani
☛ State of Sucheta Kriplani → Uttar Pradesh
☛ Tenure of Sucheta Kriplani → 1963-1967
☛ First woman Governor of India → Sarojini Naidu
☛ First woman Prime Minister of India → Indira Gandhi

q: Which Article of Indian Constitution gives the procedure for impeachment of the President?
qs.e: Article 61 of the Indian Constitution deals with the procedure for impeachment of the President. It states that the President can be impeached for violation of the Constitution. The impeachment process can be initiated in either House of Parliament. The charge must be signed by at least one-fourth of the total members of that House, and a 14-day notice must be given. The resolution must be passed by a two-thirds majority of the total membership of that House. Then the other House investigates the charge, and if it also passes the resolution by a two-thirds majority, the President is removed. Article 48 relates to agriculture and animal husbandry, Article 42 to work and maternity leave, and Article 59 to qualifications of the President.
qs.kf:
☛ Presidential impeachment procedure → Article 61
☛ Ground for impeachment of President → Violation of Constitution
☛ Notice period for impeachment motion → 14 days
☛ Majority required to pass impeachment resolution → Two-thirds
☛ Initiation of impeachment → Any House of Parliament

q: Which of the following former Indian Presidents served for the shortest duration?
qs.e: Dr. Zakir Husain was the third President of India and served the shortest tenure (approximately 2 years). He became President on 13 May 1967 and died in office on 3 May 1969. Dr. Rajendra Prasad is the longest-serving President with about 12 years. R. Venkataraman served from 1987 to 1992, and Neelam S. Reddy from 1977 to 1982. Dr. Zakir Husain was also the first Muslim President of India. He was a renowned educationist and politician and served as Vice President of India before becoming President.
qs.kf:
☛ Longest-serving President of India → Dr. Rajendra Prasad (approx. 12 years)
☛ First Muslim President of India → Dr. Zakir Husain
☛ Shortest-serving President of India → Dr. Zakir Husain (approx. 2 years)
☛ Third President of India → Dr. Zakir Husain
☛ Only President to die in office → Dr. Zakir Husain

q: Who has the power to proclaim the state of emergency in India?
qs.e: Under Article 352 of the Indian Constitution, the President has the power to proclaim a state of emergency. A national emergency can be imposed when the security of India is threatened by war, external aggression, or armed rebellion. The President issues such a proclamation based on the recommendation of the Council of Ministers. The proclamation must be approved by both houses of Parliament within two months. So far, three national emergencies have been declared in India: in 1962, 1971, and 1975.
qs.kf:
☛ Under which Article is emergency declared? → Article 352
☛ Effect of national emergency on Fundamental Rights? → They can be suspended under Articles 358 and 359
☛ During emergency, who can make laws on subjects in Union List? → Parliament
☛ Maximum duration of national emergency? → Indefinite, but requires parliamentary approval every 6 months
☛ When was the first national emergency declared in India? → 1962 (India-China war)

q: Which of the following is dealt in Article 78 of the Constitution?
o: President's power to send advisory messages to the Parliament
President's power to get information from the Council of Ministers
Prime Minister's duty regarding keeping the President informed about the government's decisions and policies
qs.e: Article 78 deals with the duties of the Prime Minister. It states that the Prime Minister shall keep the President informed about all decisions of the Council of Ministers relating to the administration of the affairs of the Union and proposals for legislation. This article ensures coordination between the executive and the President under the parliamentary system. It also requires the Prime Minister to furnish such information as the President may call for. Article 78 is not about the President's emergency powers or his power to send messages; it specifically lays down the Prime Minister's duty to communicate. It is part of Part V of the Constitution dealing with the Union Executive.
qs.kf:
☛ What does Article 78 describe? → Prime Minister's duty to inform the President
☛ Article 78 is in which part of the Constitution? → Part V
☛ Which article deals with PM's duty to communicate? → Article 78
☛ What is the constitutional provision for keeping the President informed? → Article 78
☛ Which article links the Council of Ministers and the President? → Article 78

q: Which of these Indian Prime Ministers did NOT face the parliament?
qs.e: Charan Singh was the fifth Prime Minister of India, serving from 28 July 1979 to 14 January 1980. He is the only Indian PM who never faced the parliament because no session of parliament was held during his tenure. His government fell before he could prove his majority in the Lok Sabha. Other options like Morarji Desai, V.P. Singh, and Chandrasekhar all faced parliament and won confidence votes. Charan Singh's tenure was very short and he never got the opportunity to face the parliament.
qs.kf:
☛ Charan Singh's tenure → 28 July 1979 to 14 January 1980
☛ His party → Janata Party (Secular)
☛ Parliament session during his tenure → No session held
☛ Prime Minister before him → Morarji Desai
☛ Prime Minister after him → Indira Gandhi

q: What is the minimum age required to become the Prime Minister of India?
A. 21 Years
B. 25 Years
C. 30 Years
D. 35 Years
qs.e: The minimum age required to become the Prime Minister of India is 25 years. This requirement is specified in Article 75 of the Indian Constitution, which states that the Prime Minister must be a member of the Lok Sabha. The minimum age for Lok Sabha membership is 25 years, as per Article 84. Therefore, the same age limit applies for becoming Prime Minister. Option A (21 years) is for Rajya Sabha membership, while 30 years (C) and 35 years (D) are for other constitutional positions.
qs.kf:
☛ Minimum age for Prime Minister → 25 years
☛ Minimum age for Lok Sabha member → 25 years
☛ Minimum age for Rajya Sabha member → 30 years
☛ Minimum age for President → 35 years
☛ Provision for appointment of PM → Article 75 of Constitution

q: Who is the Railway Minister who presented the 2016 Rail Budget?
A. Suresh Prabhu
B. Arun Jaitley
C. Manoj Sinha
D. Jayant Sinha
qs.e: The 2016 Railway Budget was presented by Suresh Prabhu, who served as the Railway Minister of India. He presented it in Parliament on February 24, 2016. The budget focused on the modernization of railways and safety measures. Key announcements included the redevelopment of over 150 stations, provision of Wi-Fi at railway stations, and installation of CCTV cameras in trains. Notably, there was no increase in passenger fares. Suresh Prabhu held the portfolio of Railway Minister from November 2014 to August 2017.
qs.kf:
☛ Who presented the 2017 Railway Budget? → Suresh Prabhu
☛ When was the merger of Railway Budget with General Budget announced? → 2016
☛ What was the main focus of the 2016 Railway Budget? → Safety and modernization
☛ How many Railway Budgets did Suresh Prabhu present? → Three (2015, 2016, 2017)
☛ Was there any fare hike in the 2016 Railway Budget? → No

q: Which of the following statements is not true?
A. The Constitution says that the Chief Minister shall be appointed by the Chief justice of the High Court.
B. The governor elects only those people as ministers, who have been nominated by the Chief Minister.
C. The Chief Minister is the chairman of a state’s Planning Board
D. The governor of a state cannot dismiss a Chief Minister as long as the CM receives the support of the majority in Vidhan Sabha(state’s Lower House)
qs.e: According to Article 164 of the Indian Constitution, the Governor appoints the Chief Minister, not the Chief Justice of the High Court. The Chief Minister is the leader of the majority party in the state legislative assembly. Statement B is true because the Governor appoints ministers on the advice of the Chief Minister. Statement C is correct as the Chief Minister is the chairman of the State Planning Board. Statement D is true since the Governor cannot dismiss the Chief Minister as long as he enjoys the majority support in the Vidhan Sabha. Hence, only statement A is false.
qs.kf:
☛ Who appoints the Chief Minister? → Governor
☛ Who is the chairman of the State Planning Board? → Chief Minister
☛ On whose advice are ministers appointed? → Chief Minister
☛ When can the Governor dismiss the Chief Minister? → When he loses majority in the assembly
☛ Article 164 deals with? → Appointment of Chief Minister

q: Why is it remarked that the “pocket of the Indian President is bigger than that of the American President” in reference to Pocket Vetro Power of the president?
A. The power of the Indian President not to take any action (either positive or negative) on the bill for an indefinite period.
B. The President of the USA has to return the bill for reconsideration within 10 days, as against 30 days for the Indian President.
C. The President of the USA has to return the bill for reconsideration within 10 days, as against 20 days for the Indian President.
D. The President of the USA can't return the bill for reconsideration if he kept it for more than 10 days, while that is not the case with the Indian President.
qs.e: The remark that the "pocket of the Indian President is bigger than that of the American President" refers to the pocket veto power. In India, under Article 111, the President can withhold assent, return the bill for reconsideration, or take no action, effectively killing the bill indefinitely without any time limit. This is known as a pocket veto. In the USA, the President also has a pocket veto, but it applies only when Congress is adjourned within 10 days of presenting the bill. If Congress is in session, the bill automatically becomes law after 10 days if not signed. Hence, the Indian President's pocket veto is absolute, giving him more power to block legislation, while the American President's power is limited by congressional sessions. Thus, the Indian President's 'pocket' is bigger.
qs.kf:
☛ Type of veto power of Indian President → Suspensive veto
☛ When does US President's pocket veto apply? → When Congress is adjourned
☛ Time limit for Indian President to act on a bill → No limit
☛ Time limit for US President to return a bill → 10 days (if Congress in session)
☛ Time limit for Indian President to return bill for reconsideration → 30 days (except Money bills)

q: The first woman to serve as the President of India was:
qs.e: The first woman to serve as the President of India was Pratibha Patil, who held the office from 25 July 2007 to 25 July 2012. She was a member of the Indian National Congress and had previously served as the Governor of Rajasthan. During her tenure, several important legislations were enacted, including the Women's Reservation Bill and the Right to Education Act. Her presidency was marked by adherence to constitutional norms and dignity.
qs.kf:
☛ First woman President of India → Pratibha Patil
☛ Pratibha Patil's tenure → 2007-2012
☛ Pratibha Patil's previous post → Governor of Rajasthan
☛ Key bill approved by Patil → Women's Reservation Bill
☛ Pratibha Patil's political party → Indian National Congress

q: According to question, who has the ultimate command of the Union Defense Forces?
qs.e: According to Article 53 of the Indian Constitution, the President is the Supreme Commander of the Union Defense Forces. This provision ensures civilian supremacy over the military. The Minister of Defense and the Prime Minister play administrative roles, but the ultimate command lies with the President. The Chief of Army Staff is only the head of the respective force. The President also has the power to declare war and conclude peace, though this power is exercised on the advice of the Council of Ministers.
qs.kf:
☛ Which article of the Indian Constitution makes the President the Supreme Commander of the armed forces? → Article 53
☛ On whose advice does the President exercise military powers? → Council of Ministers
☛ Which forces are included in the Union Defense Forces? → Army, Navy, and Air Force
☛ What is the role of the Defense Minister? → Defense policy and administration
☛ To whom is the Chief of Army Staff responsible? → Defense Minister and Prime Minister

q: In a parliamentary system, the legislative, judicial and emergency powers are in reality used by the President only on the advice of the_______.
qs.e: In the Indian parliamentary system, the President is the constitutional head of the state, but the real executive power lies with the Council of Ministers. The President exercises legislative, judicial, and emergency powers only on the advice of the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister. Article 74 of the Indian Constitution provides that there shall be a Council of Ministers with the Prime Minister at its head to aid and advise the President. The President cannot reject the advice of the Council; he can only send it back for reconsideration. If the Council reiterates its advice, the President is bound to accept it. Thus, all powers—legislative, judicial (e.g., pardoning power), and emergency powers—are effectively exercised by the Council of Ministers.
qs.kf:
☛ Body that advises the President → Council of Ministers
☛ Real executive head in India's parliamentary system → Prime Minister
☛ Article 74 → Council of Ministers to aid and advise the President
☛ Article 75 → Appointment of Prime Minister and formation of Council of Ministers
☛ On whose advice does the President impose emergency → Council of Ministers

q: The deputy prime minister of India (from 1977 to 1979) was:
qs.e: The deputy prime minister of India from 1977 to 1979 was Jagjivan Ram. He served under Prime Minister Morarji Desai in the Janata Party government. Jagjivan Ram, popularly known as 'Babuji', was a prominent dalit leader and a key figure in Indian politics. He participated in the freedom struggle and later left the Congress party after the Emergency to join the Janata Party. As deputy prime minister, he handled important portfolios including defence and agriculture.
qs.kf:
☛ By what name is Jagjivan Ram popularly known? → Babuji
☛ Which party did Jagjivan Ram belong to? → Janata Party
☛ Which portfolios did Jagjivan Ram handle as deputy PM? → Defence and Agriculture
☛ When did Jagjivan Ram leave Congress? → After the Emergency in 1977
☛ Which community did Jagjivan Ram belong to? → Dalit

q: Who was the first and only acting PM of India?
qs.e: Gulzarilal Nanda was the first and only acting Prime Minister of India. He assumed office on 27 May 1964 after the death of Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru and served until 9 June 1964 when Lal Bahadur Shastri became Prime Minister. He again served as acting Prime Minister in 1966 after the death of Lal Bahadur Shastri, making him the only person to hold this position twice. Nanda is credited as the first acting Prime Minister of India and remains the sole individual to have held this temporary role.
qs.kf:
☛ First acting PM → Gulzarilal Nanda
☛ Acting PM after Nehru → Gulzarilal Nanda
☛ Acting PM twice → Gulzarilal Nanda
☛ Acting PM after Shastri → Gulzarilal Nanda
☛ Only acting PM → Gulzarilal Nanda

q: Who is the highest Law Officer of the Government of India?
o: Comptroller and Auditor General of India
qs.e: The highest Law Officer of the Government of India is the Attorney General for India. This position is established under Article 76 of the Constitution and is appointed by the President. The Attorney General advises the Government of India on legal matters and represents the government in the Supreme Court and High Courts. It is a constitutional post and is considered the first Law Officer of India. The Attorney General holds office during the pleasure of the President and can participate in the proceedings of both Houses of Parliament but cannot vote. Other options: Major General of the Gendarmerie is a military rank, Advocate General of the State is the highest law officer at the state level, and Comptroller and Auditor General of India is the head of financial audit.
qs.kf:
☛ Under which Article is the Attorney General for India appointed? → Article 76
☛ Who appoints the Attorney General of India? → The President
☛ What is the tenure of the Attorney General? → During the pleasure of the President
☛ Can the Attorney General vote in Parliament? → No
☛ Who was the first Attorney General of India? → M. C. Setalvad

q: Who among the following has not been India's Finance Minister?
qs.e: India has had several prominent figures as Finance Minister. Yashwant Sinha (1998-2002), Arun Jaitley (2014-2019), and T T Krishnamachari (1956-1958 and 1964-1966) all served as Finance Ministers. V K Krishna Menon served as India's first Defence Minister (1957-1962) but never held the Finance portfolio. He was also India's representative to the United Nations. Hence, option 2 is the correct answer.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the first Finance Minister of India? → R K Shanmukham Chetty
☛ Who served the longest as Finance Minister? → Manmohan Singh (1991-1996)
☛ Who was the first woman to present the Union Budget as Finance Minister? → Indira Gandhi (1970)
☛ Who was the youngest Finance Minister of India? → P Chidambaram
☛ For which ministry is V K Krishna Menon known? → Defence Minister

q: Who among the following is NOT a Cabinet Minister?
o: Minister of State in the Ministry of Defence
qs.e: In India, the Council of Ministers has three levels: Cabinet Minister, Minister of State (Independent Charge), and Minister of State. Cabinet Ministers head important departments and attend Cabinet meetings. Minister of Home Affairs, Minister of External Affairs, Minister of Defence, and Minister of Law and Justice are all Cabinet Ministers. The Minister of State in the Ministry of Defence is not a Cabinet Minister; he works under the Defence Minister. Therefore, the Minister of State in the Ministry of Defence is NOT a Cabinet Minister.
qs.kf:
☛ Requirement to become a Cabinet Minister → Must be a member of Parliament
☛ Minister of State (Independent Charge) is equivalent to → Cabinet Minister
☛ Who appoints Cabinet Ministers → President on the recommendation of Prime Minister
☛ Highest level of Council of Ministers in India → Cabinet Minister
☛ Minister of State is responsible to → Cabinet Minister of the concerned department

q: Who among the following is NOT appointed by the President of India?
qs.e: As per the Constitution of India, the President appoints Judges of High Courts, Governors of States, and the Chief Justice of India. However, the State's Chief Minister is not appointed by the President. The Chief Minister is appointed by the Governor of the state, who is the President's representative. The Governor appoints the leader of the party that commands a majority in the state legislative assembly as the Chief Minister. Therefore, the Chief Minister is appointed by the Governor, not directly by the President.
qs.kf:
☛ Post appointed by the President → Judges of High Courts
☛ Post appointed by the President → Governor of State
☛ Post appointed by the President → Chief Justice of India
☛ Post appointed by the Governor → State's Chief Minister
☛ Post NOT appointed by the President → State's Chief Minister

q: Who was the first Vice-President of India to be elected as President by second preference count of votes in the presidential elections?
qs.e: India's fourth President VV Giri (1969-1974) was the first Vice-President to be elected as President by second preference votes. He won the 1969 election against the official Congress candidate Neelam Sanjiva Reddy. Giri, a socialist leader, was also the first full-time Labour Minister of India. Before becoming President, he served as Vice-President (1967-1969). The 1969 presidential election is historically significant due to the single transferable vote system and the role of second preference counts in his victory. Giri was supported by Prime Minister Indira Gandhi, who advocated for a progressive candidate.
qs.kf:
☛ Who is known as India's first full-time Labour Minister? → VV Giri
☛ Who supported VV Giri in the 1969 presidential election? → Indira Gandhi
☛ In which year did VV Giri become President? → 1969
☛ Which voting system uses second preference votes? → Single Transferable Vote
☛ Who was the President before VV Giri? → Zakir Husain

q: The constitutional head of the Executive of the Union of India is the:
qs.e: According to Article 53 of the Indian Constitution, the executive power of the Union is vested in the President and is exercised by him either directly or through officers subordinate to him. The President is the constitutional head of the Union Executive, while the Prime Minister is the real executive head. The President is elected by an electoral college consisting of elected members of both Houses of Parliament and state legislative assemblies. He is also the Supreme Commander of the Indian Armed Forces, but his powers as executive head are limited by the Constitution and the advice of the Council of Ministers. Thus, the President is the constitutional head of the Union Executive.
qs.kf:
☛ Executive power vested → Article 53
☛ President's election → Single Transferable Vote by Electoral College
☛ Real administrative head → Prime Minister
☛ Supreme Commander → President
☛ Impeachment of President → Parliament under Article 61

q: The procedure for impeachment of the President of India is mentioned in ________ of the Constitution of India.
qs.e: The procedure for impeachment of the President of India is mentioned in Article 61 of the Constitution of India. Impeachment can be initiated only on the ground of violation of the Constitution. The process can be started in either House of Parliament with a resolution signed by one-fourth of its members. The resolution must be passed by a two-thirds majority in both Houses for the President to be removed. A mandatory 14-day notice is required before introducing the impeachment motion. Articles 30, 77, and 66 deal with minority educational institutions, executive business, and Vice-President election respectively.
qs.kf:
☛ Ground for impeachment of President → Violation of Constitution
☛ House to initiate impeachment → Either Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha
☛ Majority required for removal → Two-thirds majority
☛ Notice period for impeachment → 14 days
☛ Article related to President impeachment → Article 61

q: Who was NOT a member of the Cabinet Mission?
qs.e: The Cabinet Mission was a high-level delegation sent to India in 1946 by the British government. It consisted of three members: Lord Pethick-Lawrence (Secretary of State for India), Sir Stafford Cripps (President of the Board of Trade), and AV Alexander (First Lord of the Admiralty). The mission aimed to discuss the transfer of power and constitution-making with Indian leaders. It proposed a federal system with provincial autonomy and a weak centre on 16 May 1946. Sir John Simon was not a member of this mission; he had earlier headed the Simon Commission (1928) that reviewed constitutional reforms in India.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the chairman of the Cabinet Mission? → Lord Pethick-Lawrence
☛ When did the Cabinet Mission come to India? → 1946
☛ When was the Cabinet Mission plan announced? → 16 May 1946
☛ Who was the chairman of the Simon Commission? → Sir John Simon
☛ When did the Simon Commission come to India? → 1928

q: Who among the following was the oldest at the time of taking the oath of Prime minster for the first time?
qs.e: Morarji Desai was the oldest at the time of taking the oath as Prime Minister for the first time. He took the oath on 24 March 1977 at the age of 81. Chaudhary Charan Singh took the oath in 1979 at age 76, VP Singh in 1989 at age 58, and Atal Bihari Vajpayee first took the oath in 1996 at age 71. Morarji Desai was the fifth Prime Minister of India and the first non-Congress Prime Minister. He was born on 29 February 1896 and died on 10 April 1995 at the age of 99.
qs.kf:
☛ Age of Morarji Desai when he first took oath as PM? → 81 years
☛ Year Morarji Desai became Prime Minister? → 1977
☛ Age of Chaudhary Charan Singh when he became PM? → 76 years
☛ Oldest Prime Minister of India? → Morarji Desai
☛ Age of Atal Bihari Vajpayee at his first oath? → 71 years

q: Who is the Chairman of the NITI Ayog?
qs.e: NITI Aayog (National Institution for Transforming India) was established on 1 January 2015, replacing the Planning Commission. Its aim is to foster cooperative federalism in government policies. The Prime Minister serves as the Chairman of NITI Aayog, holding the highest decision-making authority. Additionally, there is a Vice Chairperson (currently Suman Bery), full-time members, and all state Chief Ministers and Lieutenant Governors of Union Territories are ex-officio members. The headquarters of NITI Aayog is located in New Delhi. It plays a crucial role in policy formulation and monitoring development goals.
qs.kf:
☛ Who is the Vice Chairperson of NITI Aayog? → Suman Bery
☛ When was NITI Aayog established? → 1 January 2015
☛ Who was the first Vice Chairperson of NITI Aayog? → Arvind Panagariya
☛ How are state Chief Ministers members of NITI Aayog? → Ex-officio members
☛ Where is the headquarters of NITI Aayog located? → New Delhi

q: As of October 2020, who is the Vice President of India?
qs.e: As of October 2020, the Vice President of India was M Venkaiah Naidu. He assumed office on 11 August 2017. He is the 13th Vice President of India. Before this, he served as the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. His term lasts for five years. He is a senior leader of the Bharatiya Janata Party.
qs.kf:
☛ First Vice President of India → Dr. Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan
☛ Office of Vice President → Constitutional post (Article 63)
☛ Term of Vice President → 5 years
☛ Current Vice President (2024) → Jagdeep Dhankhar
☛ Election of Vice President → By members of both Houses of Parliament through single transferable vote

q: Constituent Assembly drafted the Constitution for Independent India. It was set up under:
o: The Government of India Act of 1919
The Government of India Act of 1909
qs.e: The Constituent Assembly of India was set up under the Cabinet Mission Plan of 1946. The Cabinet Mission was sent by the British government to India and consisted of three members. According to this plan, members of the Constituent Assembly were elected by the provincial assemblies. The Assembly had a total of 389 members, of which 292 were from provinces, 93 from princely states, and 4 from chief commissioner provinces. The first meeting of the Constituent Assembly was held on 9 December 1946. Dr. Rajendra Prasad was elected as its permanent Chairman. The Assembly adopted the Constitution on 26 November 1949 and it came into effect on 26 January 1950.
qs.kf:
☛ Basis for formation of Constituent Assembly → Cabinet Mission Plan 1946
☛ Date of first meeting of Constituent Assembly → 9 December 1946
☛ Permanent Chairman of Constituent Assembly → Dr. Rajendra Prasad
☛ Total members of Constituent Assembly → 389 (later 299)
☛ Date of adoption of Constitution → 26 November 1949

q: Which Cabinet Mission proposed a constituent assembly to frame the Constitution of India?
qs.e: The Cabinet Mission that arrived in India in 1946 proposed the formation of a Constituent Assembly to frame the Constitution. The mission consisted of three British ministers: Lord Pethick-Lawrence, Stafford Cripps, and A.V. Alexander. It presented its plan on May 16, 1946, suggesting a 389-member Constituent Assembly indirectly elected by provincial assemblies. The first meeting of the Constituent Assembly was held on December 9, 1946. The mission also recommended a federal government and provincial autonomy. This was followed by the Indian Independence Act of 1947.
qs.kf:
☛ Members of the Cabinet Mission → Three British ministers: Pethick-Lawrence, Cripps, Alexander
☛ Total members of the Constituent Assembly → 389 (elected by provincial assemblies)
☛ First meeting of the Constituent Assembly → December 9, 1946
☛ Date of Cabinet Mission Plan submission → May 16, 1946
☛ Key suggestions of the Cabinet Mission → Federal government and provincial autonomy

q: The forms of oaths of office for a Minister for the Union in India is contained in the:
qs.e: The Third Schedule of the Indian Constitution contains the forms of oaths or affirmations for Ministers of the Union, Members of Parliament, Judges, etc. This schedule is primarily related to Article 75(4), which requires ministers to take an oath before the President before assuming office. The First Schedule relates to the list of states and union territories, the Second Schedule deals with salaries and allowances, and the Fifth Schedule pertains to scheduled areas. The Third Schedule contains 12 forms, with Form III and Form IV for central and state ministers respectively.
qs.kf:
☛ How many oath forms are in the Third Schedule? → 12
☛ Oath form number for central ministers → Form III
☛ Oath form number for state ministers → Form IV
☛ Which Article is the Third Schedule related to? → Article 75(4)
☛ Which Schedule of the Constitution contains salaries and allowances? → Second Schedule

q: Who administers the oath to the President of India?
qs.e: According to Article 60 of the Indian Constitution, the oath of office to the President is administered by the Chief Justice of India. This oath is taken before the President assumes office. During the oath, the President pledges to uphold the Constitution and serve the nation. In the absence of the Chief Justice, the senior-most judge of the Supreme Court performs this duty. This process reflects the independence of the judiciary in India.
qs.kf:
☛ Constitutional provision for President's oath → Article 60
☛ Election of President → By Electoral College (Article 54)
☛ Procedure for removal of President → Impeachment (Article 61)
☛ Power of President → Pardoning power (Article 72)
☛ Term of President → 5 years (Article 56)

q: In India, impeachment process is NOT applicable to ________ for removal from office.
qs.e: In India, the impeachment process is applicable only to certain constitutional authorities such as the President, Vice President, judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts, Chief Election Commissioner, and other constitutional office holders. The Prime Minister is a member of Parliament and is not removed by impeachment but by a vote of no-confidence in the Lok Sabha. The Prime Minister holds office as long as he enjoys the confidence of the majority in the Lok Sabha. Impeachment involves levying charges of constitutional violation, but this process does not apply to the Prime Minister. Therefore, among the given options, only the Prime Minister is not subject to impeachment for removal from office.
qs.kf:
☛ Who can be impeached in India? → President, Vice President, Judges, Chief Election Commissioner
☛ How can the Prime Minister be removed? → Vote of no-confidence
☛ What is the ground for impeachment? → Violation of the Constitution
☛ Which article deals with impeachment of President? → Article 61
☛ Can the Chief Election Commissioner be impeached? → Yes

q: Who among the following shall communicate to the President all the decisions of the council of ministers under article 78?
qs.e: Article 78 of the Indian Constitution deals with the duties of the Prime Minister. It states that it is the duty of the Prime Minister to communicate to the President all decisions of the Council of Ministers relating to the administration of the affairs of the Union and proposals for legislation. This provision ensures coordination between the executive and the President in the parliamentary system. The Prime Minister is the head of the government and presides over cabinet meetings. Thus, under Article 78, the responsibility of informing the President about cabinet decisions lies with the Prime Minister, not the Foreign Minister, Vice-President, or Home Minister.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 78 → PM's duty to communicate council decisions to President
☛ Article 74 → Council of Ministers with PM as head aids and advises President
☛ Article 75 → PM appointed by President; other ministers on PM's advice
☛ Prime Minister → Head of executive and chairperson of Council of Ministers
☛ President → Constitutional head, but executive powers exercised by PM and Council

q: Under whose administration is the Department of Atomic Energy?
qs.e: The Department of Atomic Energy (DAE) in India functions directly under the administrative control of the Prime Minister's Office. This department is responsible for the research, development, and utilization of atomic energy for peaceful purposes. Established in 1954, DAE formulates policies related to nuclear power and radiation technologies. It works under the guidance of the Atomic Energy Commission, which reports directly to the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister of India serves as the ex-officio Chairman of the Atomic Energy Commission. DAE operates various research centres and nuclear power plants across the country.
qs.kf:
☛ Administrative control of DAE → Prime Minister's Office
☛ Chairman of Atomic Energy Commission → Prime Minister
☛ Establishment year of DAE → 1954
☛ Main objective of DAE → Peaceful use of atomic energy
☛ Atomic Energy Regulatory Board → Works under DAE

q: Which of the following declares the policies of the government on the House of Parliament?
qs.e: The Prime Minister declares the policies of the government in the House of Parliament. The Prime Minister is the head of the government and presents the government's policies and programs in Parliament. This declaration often occurs through the President's Address but the Prime Minister is the one who directly announces the policies. The Chairman (Speaker) conducts the proceedings of the House, the President is a part of Parliament but does not declare policies, and the Vice President is the ex-officio Chairman of Rajya Sabha.
qs.kf:
☛ What is the term of the Prime Minister of India? → 5 years
☛ Who is the main person to declare government policies in Parliament? → Prime Minister
☛ When does the President address the Parliament? → After every general election
☛ Who appoints the Prime Minister? → President
☛ Which House does the Vice President chair? → Rajya Sabha

q: Chief Election Commissioner is appointed-
qs.e: The Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) of India is appointed by the President. This provision is made under Article 324 of the Indian Constitution. The President appoints the CEC and other Election Commissioners. The CEC holds office for a term of 6 years or until the age of 65 years, whichever is earlier. The CEC can only be removed through impeachment. The Election Commission is an independent body that conducts elections in India.
qs.kf:
☛ Who appoints the Chief Election Commissioner? → President
☛ Which Article deals with the Election Commission? → Article 324
☛ What is the term of CEC? → 6 years or up to age 65
☛ How can CEC be removed? → Impeachment
☛ What type of body is the Election Commission? → Independent

q: The President of India has a tenure-
qs.e: The tenure of the President of India is five years, as specified under Article 56 of the Indian Constitution. The President holds office for a term of five years from the date of taking the oath of office. The President can resign before the completion of the term by writing to the Vice President. Additionally, the President may be removed through impeachment for violation of the Constitution. Even after the term ends, the President continues in office until a successor assumes charge. The President is the first citizen of India and the head of the executive branch of the government.
qs.kf:
☛ Tenure of President → Five years
☛ Relevant Article → Article 56
☛ Resignation addressed to → Vice President
☛ Impeachment provision → Yes, in Constitution
☛ President's status → First citizen and executive head

q: Who is the Chairman of National Integration Council in India?
qs.e: The National Integration Council (NIC) is an important body of the Government of India, established in 1961 by then Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru. Its objective is to promote national integration and maintain communal harmony in the country. The Chairman of the Council is the Prime Minister. The NIC includes members such as Union Ministers, Chief Ministers of states, leaders of political parties, and prominent personalities. The Council advises the government on matters related to national unity and guides policy formulation. Neither the President nor the Chief Minister serves as its Chairman.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the National Integration Council established? → 1961
☛ What is the objective of the Council? → To promote national integration and communal harmony
☛ Who are the members of the Council? → Prime Minister, Union Ministers, Chief Ministers, political party leaders
☛ When was its first meeting held? → 1962
☛ What is the nature of the Council? → Advisory body

q: Which of the following is the head of the Indian Republic?
qs.e: The head of the Indian Republic is the President. The Constitution of India declares the President as the first citizen of the country and the supreme commander of the armed forces. The President is elected by an electoral college consisting of elected members of both houses of Parliament and the legislative assemblies of the states. The term of office of the President is five years. While the Vice President is the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, the Prime Minister is the head of government, and the Chief Justice is the head of the judiciary.
qs.kf:
☛ Head of Indian Republic → President
☛ Election of President → By electoral college
☛ Term of President → Five years
☛ Supreme Commander of Armed Forces → President
☛ First President of India → Dr. Rajendra Prasad

q: Who is the Chairman of all the Zonal Councils?
qs.e: India has five Zonal Councils: Northern, Eastern, Western, Southern, and Central. The Union Home Minister is the Chairman of all these Zonal Councils. These councils were established to promote inter-state cooperation and coordination. Besides the Home Minister, each council includes the Chief Ministers and Governors of the concerned states as members. This arrangement helps in resolving disputes between states and implementing development plans smoothly. The concept of Zonal Councils is based on the recommendation of the States Reorganisation Commission.
qs.kf:
☛ Chairman of Zonal Councils → Union Home Minister
☛ Members of Zonal Councils → Chief Ministers and Governors of concerned states
☛ First Zonal Council formed → Northern Zonal Council (1956)
☛ Purpose of Zonal Councils → Inter-state coordination and cooperation
☛ Basis of formation → States Reorganisation Act, 1956

q: An ordinance passed by the President ceases to operate _______ from the reassembly of Parliament.
o: on the expiry of six months
on the expiry of six weeks
qs.e: Under Article 123 of the Indian Constitution, the President has the power to promulgate ordinances when Parliament is not in session. An ordinance ceases to operate at the expiry of six weeks from the reassembly of Parliament, unless it is approved by both Houses. This provision ensures the supremacy of the legislature over the executive. If Parliament approves the ordinance, it becomes an act; otherwise, it lapses automatically. This is a constitutional safeguard to prevent misuse of legislative power by the executive. The ordinance must be laid before both Houses when Parliament reconvenes.
qs.kf:
☛ Article related to ordinance-making power → 123
☛ Duration of ordinance after Parliament reassembles → 6 weeks
☛ Who can promulgate an ordinance → President
☛ Who must approve the ordinance to make it law → Parliament
☛ When can President issue ordinance → When Parliament is not in session

q: According to the plan proposed by the British Council, the Constituent Assembly was formed after the arrival of which mission?
qs.e: The Cabinet Mission, which arrived in India in 1946, proposed the plan for the formation of the Constituent Assembly. The mission consisted of three British cabinet members: Lord Pethick-Lawrence, Sir Stafford Cripps, and A.V. Alexander. According to the mission's proposal, the members of the Constituent Assembly were elected by the provincial legislative assemblies. The Assembly had a total of 389 members, with 292 from provinces, 93 from princely states, and 4 from chief commissioner provinces. This assembly was formed to draft the Constitution of India. The Cabinet Mission aimed to preserve India's unity and facilitate a smooth transfer of power.
qs.kf:
☛ Who headed the Cabinet Mission? → Lord Pethick-Lawrence
☛ When did the Cabinet Mission arrive in India? → 1946
☛ Who were the members of the Cabinet Mission? → Pethick-Lawrence, Cripps, and Alexander
☛ Who was the first president of the Constituent Assembly? → Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha (interim)
☛ Who was the permanent president of the Constituent Assembly? → Dr. Rajendra Prasad

q: Who can remain in the post at the pleasure of the Governor?
qs.e: The provision of holding office during the pleasure of the Governor applies to the Chief Minister and other ministers. According to Article 164 of the Indian Constitution, ministers hold office during the pleasure of the Governor, meaning the Governor can dismiss them at any time. IAS officers, police officers, and High Court judges do not hold office at the Governor's pleasure. IAS officers are under the control of the central government, police officers are under state government, and High Court judges can be removed only through impeachment. This provision ensures accountability of ministers to the Governor.
qs.kf:
☛ Who holds office during the pleasure of Governor → Minister
☛ Who appoints ministers → Governor
☛ Article 164 deals with → Council of Ministers
☛ Process to remove High Court judge → Impeachment
☛ IAS officers are under control of → Central Government

q: Which of the following is the supreme commander of the Indian Defense Forces?
qs.e: According to Article 53 of the Indian Constitution, the President is the supreme commander of the Indian Defense Forces. This provision gives the President command over the Army, Navy, and Air Force. Only with the President's consent can war be declared or peace treaties signed. The Prime Minister and Council of Ministers advise the President, but the ultimate commander is the President. The Chiefs of the three services are heads of their respective forces but function under the President's authority. The Cabinet Secretary is a civil servant and not a commander of the defense forces. Therefore, the correct answer is President.
qs.kf:
☛ Who is the supreme commander of the Indian Defense Forces? → President
☛ Which article deals with the executive power of the Union and command of the President? → Article 53
☛ Under which article are the military powers of the President given? → Article 53
☛ What is the collective body of the three service chiefs called? → Chiefs of Staff Committee
☛ Who declares war in India? → President (on the advice of the Council of Ministers)

q: Who is the head of the Council of Ministers?
qs.e: According to Article 74 of the Indian Constitution, the Prime Minister is the head of the Council of Ministers. The Council of Ministers includes the Prime Minister and other ministers. The Prime Minister is appointed by the President and presides over the meetings of the Council of Ministers. The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha, but the Prime Minister leads it and determines policies. The President is the constitutional head, but the real executive head is the Prime Minister. Thus, the head of the Council of Ministers is the Prime Minister.
qs.kf:
☛ Who is the head of the Council of Ministers? → Prime Minister
☛ Which article of the Indian Constitution deals with the Council of Ministers? → Article 74
☛ Who appoints the Prime Minister? → President
☛ To whom is the Council of Ministers responsible? → Lok Sabha
☛ Who is the constitutional head of India? → President

q: Which of the following is the second highest post in India?
qs.e: According to the Indian Constitution, the President is the highest constitutional post in the country. The Vice President is the second highest post, coming after the President. The Vice President is the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha and performs the duties of the President in their absence. The Prime Minister is the head of the government but ranks below the Vice President in the constitutional order. The Governor is the constitutional head of a state and ranks lower than the Vice President at the national level. Therefore, the second highest post is the Vice President.
qs.kf:
☛ What is the highest post in India? → President
☛ What is the second highest post in India? → Vice President
☛ Which house does the Vice President chair? → Rajya Sabha
☛ Who acts as President in their absence? → Vice President
☛ What is the rank of Prime Minister in constitutional order? → Third

q: Who has the power to declare a national emergency in India?
qs.e: Under Article 352 of the Indian Constitution, the President has the power to declare a national emergency. This emergency can be proclaimed on grounds of war, external aggression, or armed rebellion. The President exercises this power only on the written recommendation of the Union Cabinet, headed by the Prime Minister. The proclamation must be approved by both houses of Parliament within one month. It can remain in force indefinitely, but requires parliamentary approval every six months. During a national emergency, the federal structure becomes unitary, with the central government gaining authority to issue directions to states. Fundamental Rights under Article 19 are automatically suspended, and other rights can be suspended under Article 359. The President's role is crucial as the constitutional head, ensuring the decision is based on cabinet advice.
qs.kf:
☛ Under which article is national emergency declared? → Article 352
☛ What happens to Fundamental Rights during national emergency? → They can be suspended under Article 359
☛ How many times has national emergency been imposed in India? → Three times (1962, 1971, 1975)
☛ What is the effect of national emergency on state governments? → Central government can issue directions to states
☛ Does Parliament review the national emergency? → Yes, every six months

q: Which of the following was the Labor Minister in the first Cabinet of independent India?
qs.e: India's first Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru formed the cabinet on August 15, 1947. Jagjivan Ram was appointed as the Labor Minister. He belonged to the Dalit community and was a leader from Bihar. In this cabinet, Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel was Deputy Prime Minister and Home Minister, Maulana Abul Kalam Azad was Education Minister, and Dr. B.R. Ambedkar was Law Minister. John Mathai was the Railways and Transport Minister, and Asaf Ali was the Railways Minister. Liaquat Ali Khan was the Prime Minister of Pakistan. Jagjivan Ram later served as Defence Minister and Deputy Prime Minister.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the Finance Minister in the first cabinet? → R.K. Shanmukham Chetty
☛ Who was the Defence Minister in the first cabinet? → Baldev Singh
☛ Who was the Education Minister in the first cabinet? → Maulana Abul Kalam Azad
☛ Who was the Law Minister in the first cabinet? → Dr. B.R. Ambedkar
☛ Who was the Home Minister in the first cabinet? → Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel

q: Which of the following proposals can the Council of Ministers resign?
o: Suspension Proposal for Non-Resident Day Passed in Parliament
qs.e: According to Article 75(3) of the Indian Constitution, the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha. If the Lok Sabha passes a no-confidence motion against the Council of Ministers on any policy or action, the Council must resign. A no-confidence motion is a dispute resolution proposal that expresses disagreement with the government's policies. Other options like Attendance Resolution, Slander Resolution, or Suspension Proposal for Non-Resident Day do not compel the Council of Ministers to resign. This provision ensures the accountability of the government in a parliamentary democracy.
qs.kf:
☛ Collective responsibility of Council of Ministers → Enshrined in Article 75(3)
☛ Where can a no-confidence motion be passed → Only in Lok Sabha
☛ Majority required to pass no-confidence motion → Simple majority
☛ Rajya Sabha cannot pass no-confidence motion → Because Council is responsible only to Lok Sabha
☛ Procedure to introduce no-confidence motion → Support of at least 50 members required

q: Which of the following is the article related to the power of issuing the President's Ordinance?
qs.e: Article 123 of the Indian Constitution confers upon the President the power to issue ordinances. This power can be exercised only when both Houses of Parliament are not in session and immediate action is necessary. An ordinance has the same force and effect as a law passed by Parliament, but it must be approved by Parliament within six weeks of reassembly. Article 143 deals with the President's power to consult the Supreme Court, Article 153 deals with the appointment of Governors, and Article 133 deals with appeals to the Supreme Court from High Courts. Hence, only Article 123 is related to the President's ordinance-making power.
qs.kf:
☛ When can the President issue an ordinance? → When Parliament is not in session
☛ What is the maximum duration of an ordinance? → Six weeks after the reassembly of Parliament
☛ Can an ordinance be revoked? → Yes, by Parliament
☛ Under which part of the Constitution is Article 123? → Part V (The Union Executive)
☛ Who has the power to issue ordinances? → The President

q: Who is the real executive secretary of India?
o: Chief Justice of the Supreme Court
qs.e: According to the Indian Constitution, the President is the constitutional head of the state, while the Prime Minister is the real executive head. The Prime Minister leads the Council of Ministers and plays a key role in all policy decisions of the central government. The President acts on the advice of the Prime Minister, giving the Prime Minister actual executive power. The Chief Justice of the Supreme Court is the head of the judiciary, not the executive. The Vice President is the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha and does not hold executive powers. Thus, the Prime Minister is the real executive secretary of India.
qs.kf:
☛ Constitutional head of India → President
☛ Real executive head of India → Prime Minister
☛ Who appoints the Prime Minister → President
☛ Head of the Council of Ministers → Prime Minister
☛ Real center of executive power → Prime Minister

q: Who is the presiding officer of the Rajya Sabha?
qs.e: The presiding officer of the Rajya Sabha is the Vice President of India. According to Article 89 of the Indian Constitution, the Vice President serves as the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. The Vice President conducts the proceedings of the House, gives permission to members to speak, and casts a casting vote in case of a tie. The Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha is elected by its members. Article 91 of the Constitution outlines the functions of the Vice President. The term of the Vice President is 5 years, and he can resign by submitting his resignation to the President. The maximum strength of the Rajya Sabha is 250 members.
qs.kf:
☛ Who is the Chairman of Rajya Sabha? → Vice President
☛ What is the term of Vice President? → 5 years
☛ What is the maximum strength of Rajya Sabha? → 250
☛ Who elects the Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha? → Members
☛ To whom does the Vice President submit resignation? → President

q: The Governor of the State may remain in his position as per the wish of __________.
qs.e: The Governor of a state is appointed by the President of India and holds office during the pleasure of the President. According to Article 155, the Governor is appointed by the President, and under Article 156, he holds office during the President's pleasure. This means the President can remove the Governor at any time without assigning any reason. The normal term of a Governor is 5 years, but he remains in position only as long as the President wishes. This provision is part of the Constitution to strengthen center-state relations. The Governor is a constitutional head of the state and acts on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers, except in certain discretionary matters.
qs.kf:
☛ Who appoints the Governor of a state? → President
☛ During whose pleasure does the Governor hold office? → President
☛ Who has the power to remove the Governor? → President
☛ What is the normal term of the Governor? → 5 years
☛ Which article deals with the appointment of Governor? → Article 155

q: India's Finance Commission is formed-
qs.e: The Finance Commission of India is a constitutional body formed by the President of India. Under Article 280 of the Constitution, the President constitutes the Finance Commission every five years or earlier if necessary. Its main function is to recommend the distribution of tax revenue between the Centre and the States. The Chairman and other members of the Commission are also appointed by the President. The recommendations of the Finance Commission are not binding on the government, but it is customary to follow them. Thus, the Finance Commission is formed by the President, not by the Prime Minister, Finance Minister, or NITI Aayog.
qs.kf:
☛ Who forms the Finance Commission? → President
☛ Which constitutional article relates to the Finance Commission? → Article 280
☛ What is the tenure of the Finance Commission? → 5 years
☛ Nature of Finance Commission recommendations? → Advisory (not binding)
☛ Which is the current (2024) Finance Commission? → 16th Finance Commission

q: The Chairman of 'Central Public Service Commission' can be removed by whom?
qs.e: The Chairman of the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) can only be removed by the President of India. According to Article 317 of the Constitution, the President can remove the Chairman or any other member of UPSC after the Supreme Court, on a reference, has conducted an inquiry and found them guilty of misbehaviour or incapacity. This removal process requires a Supreme Court investigation, and the President acts based on its findings. This ensures the commission's independence and impartiality. The Prime Minister, Speaker of Lok Sabha, or Vice President do not have this authority, as the final power for removal of constitutional office bearers rests with the President.
qs.kf:
☛ Removal authority of UPSC Chairman → President
☛ Procedure for removal of UPSC member → Supreme Court inquiry
☛ Appointment of UPSC Chairman → President
☛ Tenure of UPSC Chairman → 6 years or until age 65
☛ Articles related to UPSC → Articles 315 to 323

q: Which of the following can nominate Anglo-Indian members in the Lok Sabha?
qs.e: According to Article 331 of the Indian Constitution, the President can nominate two members of the Anglo-Indian community to the Lok Sabha if the President feels that the community is not adequately represented. This provision was made to ensure representation for the community. The 104th Constitutional Amendment (2020) abolished the reservation and nomination of Anglo-Indian members in the Lok Sabha and state legislative assemblies. However, the term of existing nominated members in the Lok Sabha was not affected. The President had this power under the Constitution, and no other authority like the Chief Minister, Prime Minister, or Speaker of Lok Sabha has this power. This was a special provision for the Anglo-Indian community, which was the only community in India to have such nominated representation.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 331 → Authorizes the President to nominate Anglo-Indian members in Lok Sabha
☛ 104th Amendment → Abolished the nomination of Anglo-Indian members in Lok Sabha and state assemblies
☛ Nominated members by President → Maximum 2 Anglo-Indian members could be nominated
☛ Anglo-Indian community → Was the only community with special representation in the Constitution
☛ Purpose of nomination → To ensure adequate representation for the community

q: Who is the head of government in the parliamentary system?
qs.e: In a parliamentary system, the head of government is the Prime Minister. This system is based on the Westminster model, where the executive authority is led by the Prime Minister, who is appointed from among the members of the legislature. The Prime Minister heads the cabinet and determines government policies. In contrast, the President is the head of state, performing ceremonial duties. According to Articles 74 and 75 of the Indian Constitution, the Prime Minister is the head of the Council of Ministers. The government in a parliamentary system is accountable to the legislature, and the Prime Minister must maintain the confidence of the majority in parliament.
qs.kf:
☛ Head of government in parliamentary system → Prime Minister
☛ Head of state → President
☛ Head of Council of Ministers → Prime Minister
☛ Appointment of Prime Minister → By President
☛ Tenure of Prime Minister → During pleasure of President

q: The Prime Minister of India can use his powers only in consultation with ______.
qs.e: According to Article 74 of the Indian Constitution, the Prime Minister heads the Council of Ministers, which aids and advises the President. The Prime Minister exercises powers only in consultation with the Council of Ministers because the Indian parliamentary system is based on collective responsibility. Individual ministers like the Home Minister, Cabinet Secretary, or External Affairs Minister cannot provide binding advice alone; the entire council must concur. This ensures that decisions reflect collective wisdom and accountability to the Lok Sabha. The Council of Ministers, led by the Prime Minister, is collectively responsible for governance, and any exercise of power without its consultation would violate constitutional principles.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 74 → Council of Ministers aids Prime Minister
☛ Article 75 → Council is collectively responsible to Lok Sabha
☛ Prime Minister → Head of the Council of Ministers
☛ President → Acts on aid and advice of Council
☛ Collective responsibility → Core of Indian parliamentary system

q: Who was the first Vice-President of independent India-
qs.e: The first Vice-President of independent India was Dr. Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan, who served from 1952 to 1962. He was a renowned philosopher, scholar, and statesman who later became the second President of India. The Vice-President is elected indirectly by members of Parliament and serves as the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. Article 63 of the Indian Constitution provides for the office of Vice-President. Dr. Radhakrishnan was born on September 5, 1888, and his birthday is celebrated as Teacher's Day in India. The Vice-President's term is 5 years, and the impeachment process requires a resolution passed by the Rajya Sabha.
qs.kf:
☛ First Vice-President of India → Dr. Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan
☛ Term of Vice-President → 5 years
☛ Vice-President is ex-officio Chairman of → Rajya Sabha
☛ Vice-President is elected by → Members of Parliament
☛ Resolution to remove Vice-President must be passed by → Rajya Sabha

q: If the parliament does not approve, the maximum period of ordinance is ________.
qs.e: According to Article 123 of the Indian Constitution, the President can promulgate ordinances when Parliament is not in session. The ordinance must be laid before both Houses of Parliament within 6 weeks of reassembly. If Parliament does not approve it, the ordinance ceases to operate at the end of 6 weeks from reassembly, but the maximum period of the ordinance from promulgation to the end of 6 weeks after reassembly is 6 months and 6 weeks. This period includes the time from issuance to the next session plus 6 weeks. If Parliament disapproves, the ordinance lapses and cannot be extended beyond 6 months and 6 weeks.
qs.kf:
☛ Authority to promulgate ordinance → President
☛ Constitutional article for ordinance → Article 123
☛ Time to present ordinance before Parliament → 6 weeks
☛ Maximum period of ordinance without approval → 6 months and 6 weeks
☛ Governor's ordinance power in state → Article 213

q: Who can remove the members of the State Human Rights Commission?
qs.e: The members of the State Human Rights Commission can be removed only by the President. This provision is given under Section 31 of the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993. The removal process requires an inquiry by the High Court. The President can remove members only after proven misconduct or incapacity. The Governor does not have this power.
qs.kf:
☛ Who appoints the chairperson of State Human Rights Commission? → Governor
☛ What is the tenure of State Human Rights Commission members? → 3 years or up to age 70
☛ Who can remove members of National Human Rights Commission? → President (on recommendation of Supreme Court)
☛ When was the Protection of Human Rights Act enacted? → 28 September 1993
☛ Whose report is required to remove a member of State Human Rights Commission? → Chief Justice of High Court

q: Who became president of 'Central Legislative Assembly' in 1925?
qs.e: In 1925, Vithalbhai Patel became the president of the Central Legislative Assembly. He was the first Indian to hold this position. Vithalbhai Patel was the elder brother of Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel and a prominent leader of the Indian National Congress. He was a member of the Swaraj Party and advocated against British rule. He defeated the government nominee in the election. The Central Legislative Assembly was established under the Government of India Act 1919 and served as the lower house of the British Indian legislature.
qs.kf:
