Judicial reviews are conducted by the judiciary, supervision of state legislatures is done by the Governor, and the power to declare war rests with the President. The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha and plays a key role in policy formulation and governance.
qs.kf:
☛ Who holds the real executive power in India? → Union Council of Ministers
☛ Who does the President act on the advice of? → Council of Ministers (Article 74)
☛ To whom is the Union Council of Ministers responsible? → Lok Sabha
☛ Who has the final authority in policy making and administration? → Council of Ministers
☛ Who declares war in India? → President (on the advice of the Council of Ministers)

q: Which Article of the Indian Constitution deals with the impeachment procedure of the President?
qs.e: Article 61 of the Indian Constitution deals with the impeachment of the President. The President can be impeached for violation of the Constitution. The process begins in either House of Parliament with a charge preferred after 14 days' notice. The resolution must be passed by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the total membership of that House. It is then sent to the other House, which investigates the charge. If the other House also passes the resolution by a two-thirds majority, the President is removed from office. Article 52 provides for the office of President, while Article 54 and 66 deal with the election of President and Vice-President respectively.
qs.kf:
☛ Ground for impeachment of President → Violation of Constitution
☛ Majority required for impeachment resolution → Two-thirds of total membership
☛ House initiating impeachment → Any House of Parliament
☛ Article dealing with President's impeachment → Article 61
☛ Article for removal of Vice-President → Article 67

q: In which year was the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) initially constituted under the Chairmanship of the Prime Minister of India by an executive order?
qs.e: The National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) was initially constituted by an executive order of the Government of India on 31 May 2005. It was established to formulate policies, plans, and guidelines for disaster management. The Prime Minister is the ex-officio Chairperson of NDMA. Later, it was given statutory status under the Disaster Management Act, 2005. NDMA coordinates prevention, preparedness, and mitigation efforts for disasters at the national level.
qs.kf:
☛ When was NDMA formed? → 31 May 2005
☛ Who is the Chairperson of NDMA? → Prime Minister
☛ Which Act gave NDMA statutory status? → Disaster Management Act, 2005
☛ Where is the headquarters of NDMA? → New Delhi
☛ What is the state-level disaster management body? → State Disaster Management Authority (SDMA)

q: Which Article of the Indian Constitution provides for the Council of Ministers at the Union level?
qs.e: Article 74 of the Indian Constitution provides for a Council of Ministers at the Union level. It states that there shall be a Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister to aid and advise the President. This article establishes the real executive authority in the Council of Ministers. The Council is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha. The interpretation of Article 74 has limited the President's powers, making him bound by the advice of the Council. It is the cornerstone of the parliamentary system, where the actual executive power lies with the Council of Ministers. The 42nd Amendment clarified that the President must act on the advice of the Council, strengthening the cabinet system.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 75 → Appointment and terms of ministers
☛ Article 74 → Council of Ministers at Union level
☛ Article 85 → Sessions, prorogation and dissolution of Parliament
☛ Article 65 → Vice-President to act as President
☛ Council of Ministers collectively responsible → to Lok Sabha

q: Which Article of the Indian Constitution mentions the Council of Ministers to aid and advise the President?
qs.e: Article 74 of the Indian Constitution provides for a Council of Ministers to aid and advise the President. It states that there shall be a Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister to assist the President in the exercise of his functions. The President is bound to act on the advice of the Council, and this became mandatory after the 42nd Amendment. Article 74 is fundamental to the parliamentary system, where the real executive power lies with the Council of Ministers. Article 75 deals with the appointment and responsibility of ministers. This ensures collective responsibility and democratic governance.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 74 → Council of Ministers to aid and advise the President
☛ Article 75 → Appointment and collective responsibility of Ministers
☛ Article 78 → Prime Minister's duty to inform the President
☛ Article 53 → Executive power of the Union vested in the President
☛ Article 77 → Conduct of business of the Government of India

q: According to the principle of collective responsibility in India’s parliamentary system, a successful no-confidence motion against a single Union Minister requires which action?
o: The Lok Sabha is immediately dissolved.
The entire Council of Ministers must resign.
Only the targeted minister must resign.
The President dismisses only the targeted minister.
qs.e: In India's parliamentary system, the principle of collective responsibility is enshrined in Article 75(3). It means the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha. If a no-confidence motion passes against a single minister, it is considered a vote of no-confidence against the entire government. This is because ministers make decisions collectively and are accountable for each other's actions. Consequently, a successful no-confidence motion against one minister requires the resignation of the entire Council of Ministers. This system ensures executive accountability and maintains government stability. Dissolving the Lok Sabha or dismissing only the targeted minister contradicts this principle.
qs.kf:
☛ Which article deals with collective responsibility? → Article 75(3)
☛ To whom is the Council of Ministers responsible? → Lok Sabha
☛ What happens if a no-confidence motion is passed? → The entire Council of Ministers must resign
☛ From which country did India adopt the parliamentary system? → United Kingdom
☛ Who leads the Council of Ministers? → Prime Minister

q: Who was the first Finance Minister of Independent India?
qs.e: The first Finance Minister of Independent India was R K Shanmugham Chetty, who served from 1947 to 1949. He presented India's first budget for the year 1947-48. He played a key role in the formation of the Reserve Bank of India and contributed to framing India's first Industrial Policy in 1948. As Finance Minister, he focused on economic stability and laid the foundation for India's economic framework.
qs.kf:
☛ First Finance Minister of Independent India → R K Shanmugham Chetty
☛ India's first budget → 1947-48, presented by R K Shanmugham Chetty
☛ India's first Industrial Policy → 1948, under R K Shanmugham Chetty
☛ Role in RBI formation → R K Shanmugham Chetty
☛ Tenure of first Finance Minister → 1947–1949

q: Which authority can dissolve the Council of Ministers at the state level?
qs.e: Under Article 164 of the Indian Constitution, the Governor is the authority who can dissolve the Council of Ministers at the state level. The Governor is the constitutional head of the state and the Council of Ministers aids and advises the Governor in the exercise of his functions. The Chief Minister is appointed by the Governor and the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Governor. If the Council loses majority or if the Governor believes it is not functioning according to the Constitution, he can dissolve it. This power is exercised by the Governor without the advice of the Prime Minister or the President, but it is usually invoked only in a constitutional crisis. Hence, the Governor holds the power to dissolve the state Council of Ministers.
qs.kf:
☛ Who appoints the Governor? → President
☛ Who is the executive head at the state level? → Governor
☛ To whom is the Council of Ministers responsible? → Governor
☛ Article 164 deals with? → State Ministers and Council of Ministers
☛ Who can remove the Governor? → President

q: Which of the following is NOT a role of the President of India?
qs.e: The roles of the President of India include passing bills into laws, appointing the Prime Minister, and summoning and dissolving Parliament. However, conducting elections is not a role of the President; it is the responsibility of the Election Commission of India. The President is the head of state and performs certain executive, legislative, and judicial functions under the Constitution. He summons and dissolves the two houses of Parliament, appoints the Prime Minister after the Lok Sabha elections to form the government, and gives assent to bills passed by Parliament to make them laws. The Election Commission ensures free and fair elections independently.
qs.kf:
☛ Who elects the President of India? → Electoral college (Elected members of Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha, State Assemblies)
☛ How many types of veto powers does the President have? → Three: Absolute, Suspensive, Pocket
☛ Under which Article can the President promulgate ordinances? → Article 123
☛ Under which Article can the President grant pardons? → Article 72
☛ Who was the first President of India? → Dr. Rajendra Prasad

q: Under Article 254(2) of the Indian Constitution, a State law repugnant to a Central law can prevail in the State only if:
o: it is passed by a special majority in the State Legislature
It is published in the State Gazette after legislative approval
it is reserved for the President’s consideration and gets his assent
it is certified by the Governor as necessary for public welfare
qs.e: Under Article 254(2) of the Indian Constitution, if a State Legislature makes a law on a subject in the Concurrent List that is repugnant to a Central law, it can prevail in that State only if it is reserved for the President's consideration and receives the President's assent. This provision allows the State to deviate from the Central law, but the President's assent ensures that national interests are safeguarded. Once the President gives assent, the State law overrides the Central law in that State. However, Parliament can later make a law on the same subject to supersede the State law.
qs.kf:
☛ Purpose of Article 254(2) → Allows State to make law differing from Central law
☛ Effect of President's assent → State law overrides Central law
☛ Under Article 254(1) → Central law prevails in case of repugnancy
☛ Condition for President's assent → State law must be reserved for President's consideration
☛ Parliament's power → Can later make a law to nullify the State law

q: Which Article establishes the office of the President?
qs.e: Article 52 of the Indian Constitution establishes the office of the President. It states that there shall be a President of India. The President is the first citizen and the head of state of the Indian Republic. The President is elected by an Electoral College consisting of elected members of both Houses of Parliament and the Legislative Assemblies of the states. Other important conditions for the President's office are given in Articles 57, 58, and 59. The term of the President is five years. The President can be removed through impeachment under Article 61. The President holds executive, legislative, and judicial powers.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 52 → Establishes the office of President
☛ Article 61 → Impeachment of President
☛ President's term → 5 years
☛ Presidential Electoral College → Parliament + State Assemblies
☛ President's powers → Executive, Legislative, Judicial

q: Which of the following Acts abolished the Dyarchy at the provincial level during the colonial period in India?
qs.e: The system of Dyarchy was introduced at the provincial level by the Government of India Act, 1919 (Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms). Under this system, provincial departments were divided into reserved (controlled by the Governor) and transferred (under ministers responsible to the legislature). This created a dual government in provinces. The Government of India Act, 1935 abolished dyarchy and introduced provincial autonomy. It established responsible government in provinces, where the council of ministers was accountable to the legislature. Thus, the 1935 Act is credited with ending dyarchy at the provincial level.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Act introduced Dyarchy at provinces? → Government of India Act, 1919
☛ Which Act introduced provincial autonomy? → Government of India Act, 1935
☛ Under Dyarchy, 'transferred' subjects were given to whom? → Ministers
☛ Under Dyarchy, who controlled 'reserved' subjects? → Governor
☛ What type of government was established in provinces by the Act of 1935? → Responsible government

q: Which Article gives the President of India the power to grant pardons and reprieves?
qs.e: Article 72 of the Indian Constitution empowers the President to grant pardons, reprieves, respites, or remissions of punishment. This power applies to persons convicted under union laws or sentences by court-martial. For state offenses, the Governor has similar power under Article 161. The President's clemency power is subject to judicial review, as established in the Maru Ram vs. Union of India case. It is an executive power exercised on the advice of the Council of Ministers. The scope includes pardon (complete remission), reprieve (temporary stay), respite (less severe substitute), remission (reduction), and commutation (change to lighter punishment).
qs.kf:
☛ Article for presidential pardon → Article 72
☛ Governor's clemency power → Article 161
☛ Meaning of pardon → Complete remission of sentence
☛ Meaning of reprieve → Temporary stay of execution
☛ Landmark judicial review case → Maru Ram vs. Union of India

q: Which of the following is NOT true regarding the President of India?
o: He is the Supreme Commander of the defence forces.
He appoints the Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers.
The President is the first citizen of the nation.
qs.e: The President of India has the power to proclaim a national emergency under Article 352. The statement that he cannot declare national emergency is false. The President is the Supreme Commander of the defence forces (Article 53), appoints the Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers (Article 75), and is considered the first citizen of the nation. The President is part of Parliament and the head of the executive. The emergency proclamation is made by the President in writing and must be approved by Parliament. This power is a key feature of the Indian Constitution, allowing the central government to assume extraordinary powers during threats to the nation.
qs.kf:
☛ Under which Article is national emergency declared? → Article 352
☛ Which Article makes President Supreme Commander? → Article 53
☛ Who appoints the Prime Minister? → President (Article 75)
☛ Is the President the first citizen? → Yes
☛ Is the President part of Parliament? → Yes (Article 79)

q: Article 76 of the Indian Constitution deals with which of the following?
qs.e: Article 76 of the Indian Constitution deals with the Attorney General of India. This article provides for the appointment of the Attorney General by the President, their qualifications, term of office, and functions. The Attorney General is the highest law officer of India and advises the government on legal matters. Article 76 is part of Part V of the Constitution (Articles 52-78) which deals with the Union Executive. Other options: Appointment of Vice-President is covered under Article 63, President under Article 52, and Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) under Article 148.
qs.kf:
☛ Which article deals with the Attorney General of India? → Article 76
☛ Who appoints the Attorney General of India? → The President
☛ Can the Attorney General participate in Parliament? → Yes, but cannot vote
☛ What is the term of the Attorney General? → Not fixed; holds office during the pleasure of the President
☛ How can the Attorney General be removed? → The President can remove at any time

q: Which of the following acts in India was based on report of a committee headed by the British Prime Minister Lord North?
qs.e: The Regulating Act of 1773 was based on the report of a committee headed by the British Prime Minister Lord North. This Act marked the first direct involvement of the British government in controlling the affairs of the East India Company. It created the position of Governor-General of Bengal, with Warren Hastings becoming the first to hold the office. The Act also established a Supreme Court in Calcutta. Its main objective was to bring transparency and accountability to the Company's administration. This Act was a significant step towards administrative reforms in British India. It aimed to regulate the Company's political and administrative functions, thereby laying the foundation for future governance acts.
qs.kf:
☛ In which year was the Regulating Act passed? → 1773
☛ Who became the first Governor-General under this Act? → Warren Hastings
☛ Which city saw the establishment of a Supreme Court by this Act? → Calcutta
☛ The Act was based on the recommendations of which committee? → Lord North Committee
☛ This Act increased British government control over which entity? → East India Company

q: Who acts as the President of India when both, the President and the Vice-President are unavailable?
qs.e: According to Article 65 of the Indian Constitution, when both the President and Vice-President are unavailable, the Chief Justice of India assumes the office of the President. This provision ensures continuity of governance during emergencies. The Chief Justice performs the duties until a new President or Vice-President is elected. This arrangement maintains constitutional stability. Article 65 states that the Vice-President acts as President in case of vacancy, but when both are unavailable, the Chief Justice steps in. This procedure strengthens India's democratic framework. The Chief Justice's role in such circumstances is crucial for the smooth functioning of the executive branch. This constitutional provision has been used in the past and remains a key part of India's governance structure.
qs.kf:
☛ Who acts as President when both President and Vice-President are unavailable? → Chief Justice of India
☛ Which Article provides for the Chief Justice to act as President? → Article 65
☛ Who was the first Chief Justice of India? → Hiralal J. Kania
☛ Who is the current Chief Justice of India? → Sanjiv Khanna (as of January 2025)
☛ What is the minimum age required to be President of India? → 35 years

q: In the absence of the President of India, who would take charge of the President's office?
o: Ex-officio Chairperson of the Rajya Sabha
Senior most judge of the Supreme Court
qs.e: According to Article 65 of the Indian Constitution, in the absence of the President, the Vice-President discharges the functions of the President. The Vice-President is the ex-officio Chairperson of the Rajya Sabha. If the President's office falls vacant due to death, resignation, or impeachment, the Vice-President can act as President for a maximum of six months, during which a new President is elected. The Chief Justice of India or Prime Minister does not have this power. Only the Vice-President assumes the President's duties in his absence.
qs.kf:
☛ Who takes charge in the absence of the President? → Vice-President
☛ What is the Vice-President's role in Rajya Sabha? → Ex-officio Chairperson
☛ Which Article deals with the President's functions? → Article 65
☛ How long can Vice-President act as President if office vacant? → Maximum 6 months
☛ Who elects the new President? → Electoral College

q: Arrange the names of the following Indian presidents in the descending order of their tenure. A. Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed
B. Neelam Sanjiva Reddy C. Dr. Zakir Hussain D. Giani Zail Singh
qs.e: To arrange the Indian presidents in descending order of their tenure, we need to know the duration of their terms. Giani Zail Singh (D) served from 1982 to 1987, about 5 years. Neelam Sanjiva Reddy (B) served from 1977 to 1982, also about 5 years. Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed (A) served from 1974 to 1977, about 3 years. Dr. Zakir Hussain (C) served from 1967 to 1969, about 2 years. Thus, the descending order is D (Zail Singh), B (Sanjiva Reddy), A (Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed), C (Zakir Hussain).
qs.kf:
☛ Longest-serving President → Dr. Rajendra Prasad (12 years)
☛ Shortest-serving President → Dr. Zakir Hussain (2 years)
☛ Presidents who died in office → Dr. Zakir Hussain and Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed
☛ Only person to serve two terms as President → Dr. Rajendra Prasad
☛ Who administers the oath to the President → Chief Justice

q: Which Article of the Constitution of India provides that there shall be a Council of Ministers with the Prime Minister as its head to aid and advice the president, who shall exercise his/her functions in accordance to the advice?
qs.e: Article 74(1) of the Constitution of India provides that there shall be a Council of Ministers with the Prime Minister as its head to aid and advise the President, who shall exercise his/her functions in accordance with the advice. This Article is the cornerstone of the parliamentary system of government, where the President is the formal head and real power lies with the Council of Ministers. The 42nd Amendment Act (1976) clarified that the President is bound by the advice of the Council of Ministers. Article 74(1) defines the structure and functioning of the Council of Ministers, while Article 75 deals with the appointment and responsibility of the Prime Minister and other ministers.
qs.kf:
☛ Who is the head of the Council of Ministers that aids and advises the President? → Prime Minister
☛ Which constitutional amendment clarified Article 74(1)? → 42nd Amendment
☛ How many times can the President ask for reconsideration of the advice? → Once
☛ Which Article deals with the appointment and collective responsibility of ministers? → Article 75
☛ What system of government does India follow? → Parliamentary system

q: The power of the President to promulgate ordinance during recess of the parliament is given in which article of the Indian Constitution?
qs.e: Article 123 of the Indian Constitution empowers the President to promulgate ordinances when the Parliament is not in session. This power is exercised when immediate action is required. An ordinance has the same legal effect as an Act of Parliament, but it must be laid before both Houses within 6 weeks of reassembly, and ceases to operate if not approved within that period. This power is limited to urgent situations. Article 352 relates to National Emergency, Article 63 to the Vice President, and Article 52 to the President of India.
qs.kf:
☛ Power to promulgate ordinance → Article 123
☛ Maximum life of an ordinance → 6 months (if approved)
☛ Time limit to present ordinance before Parliament → 6 weeks
☛ Article related to National Emergency → 352
☛ Article related to Vice President → 63

q: What is the maximum validity of an ordinance issued by the President of India?
qs.e: Under Article 123 of the Indian Constitution, the President has the power to promulgate ordinances when both Houses of Parliament are not in session and immediate action is necessary. Once issued, an ordinance must be approved by both Houses of Parliament within six weeks of reassembly. If not approved, it ceases to operate at the expiration of six weeks from the date of reassembly. Additionally, the ordinance has a maximum lifespan of six months from the date of its promulgation. Therefore, the maximum validity of an ordinance is six months and six weeks. This ensures that executive legislation remains temporary and subject to parliamentary approval. The ordinance power is a significant constitutional provision.
qs.kf:
☛ Constitutional provision for ordinance → Article 123
☛ Condition for issuing ordinance → Parliament not in session
☛ Maximum lifespan of ordinance → 6 months + 6 weeks
☛ Validity after Parliament reassembles → 6 weeks
☛ Ordinance approval by → Both Houses of Parliament

q: With which of the following does Article 72 of the Constitution of India deal?
o: Composition and jurisdiction of Supreme Court of India
qs.e: Article 72 of the Indian Constitution grants the President the power to grant pardons, reprieves, respites, or remissions of punishment, and to suspend, remit, or commute sentences. This power applies to offenses against Union laws, sentences by court-martial, and death sentences. The President's pardoning power is subject to judicial review, as established in the case of Kehar Singh vs Union of India. It differs from the Governor's pardoning power under Article 161, as the President can pardon death sentences while the Governor cannot. Article 72(1) details this power, which is a key feature of the executive authority of the President.
qs.kf:
☛ Which article deals with the President's pardoning power? → Article 72
☛ Which landmark case is related to the President's pardoning power? → Kehar Singh vs Union of India
☛ Which article deals with the Governor's pardoning power? → Article 161
☛ Is the President's pardoning power subject to judicial review? → Yes
☛ Which sentences can the President pardon? → Union offenses, court-martial, death sentences

q: The President of India is elected by:
qs.e: The President of India is elected by an Electoral College consisting of elected members of both Houses of Parliament (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) and elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of states. The election follows the system of proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote. Voting is conducted by secret ballot. The value of votes of MPs and MLAs is not equal; it is determined based on the population of states. The Supreme Court is the final authority to decide disputes related to the Presidential election. This indirect election method ensures fair representation of both the states and the Union.
qs.kf:
☛ What is the voting system in Presidential election? → Single transferable vote
☛ How many types of voters are in Presidential election? → Two: MPs and MLAs
☛ How is vote value determined in Presidential election? → Based on population
☛ Who is the final authority for Presidential election disputes? → Supreme Court
☛ What type of voting is used in Presidential election? → Secret ballot

q: Who was the fourth President of India?
qs.e: The fourth President of India was Varahagiri Venkata Giri, who served from 24 August 1969 to 24 August 1974. He was also the first acting President of India. His predecessor was Dr Zakir Husain (third President). Venkata Giri was the first President of India elected without a unanimous vote. He contributed significantly to judicial independence and workers' rights.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the first President of India? → Dr Rajendra Prasad
☛ Who was the second President of India? → Dr Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan
☛ Who was the third President of India? → Dr Zakir Husain
☛ Who was the fourth President of India? → Varahagiri Venkata Giri
☛ Who was the fifth President of India? → Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed

q: Who among the following is the chairman of the National Development Council (NDC)?
qs.e: The National Development Council (NDC) was established in 1952. It is an apex policy-making body that provides guidance to the Planning Commission (now NITI Aayog). The Prime Minister of India is the ex-officio chairman of the NDC. Its members include all Chief Ministers of states, administrators of union territories, and members of the central cabinet. The NDC's primary functions are to coordinate and evaluate development programs at the national level. The Finance Minister, President, or Vice President does not chair the NDC.
qs.kf:
☛ Establishment year of NDC → 1952
☛ Permanent members of NDC → All Chief Ministers and central ministers
☛ Main function of NDC → Coordination and evaluation of national development plans
☛ Chairperson of NDC meetings → Prime Minister
☛ NDC is associated with → NITI Aayog (formerly Planning Commission)

q: Who can make the rules related to peace, prosperity and good governance in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands?
qs.e: The Andaman and Nicobar Islands is a Union Territory of India. Under Article 240 of the Indian Constitution, the President has the power to make rules for the peace, prosperity, and good governance of certain Union Territories, including the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. These rules are laid before Parliament and have the force of law. This provision ensures that the administration of these territories remains under central control. The Prime Minister, Vice President, and Chief Justice of India do not have this specific power. The President's authority is crucial for maintaining effective governance in these strategically important islands.
qs.kf:
☛ Who makes rules for Andaman and Nicobar Islands? → President
☛ Which Article deals with rules for Union Territories? → Article 240
☛ Where are the President's rules laid? → Before Parliament
☛ What type of territory is Andaman and Nicobar? → Union Territory
☛ What is the purpose of the President's rule-making power? → Peace, prosperity, and good governance

q: How many members of the Rajya Sabha can be nominated by the President of India?
qs.e: According to Article 80 of the Indian Constitution, the President can nominate 12 members to the Rajya Sabha. These members are people having special knowledge or practical experience in fields like art, literature, science, and social service. The total strength of the Rajya Sabha is 245, of which 233 members represent states and union territories, while 12 are nominated by the President. This provision ensures expertise and diversity in Parliament. Nominated members have the same rights and privileges as elected members, but they can be removed by the President. Their term is also six years, subject to the usual rules of retirement.
qs.kf:
☛ What is the total strength of Rajya Sabha? → 245
☛ What is the term of nominated members? → 6 years
☛ How many members represent states in Rajya Sabha? → 233
☛ From which fields are nominated members chosen? → Art, literature, science, social service
☛ Can nominated members vote in Presidential elections? → Yes

q: Who is the only nominal power in the Government of India?
qs.e: According to the Indian Constitution, the President is the constitutional head of the state, but his powers are nominal. The real executive powers lie with the Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers. The President acts according to the constitution and laws, and is bound to act on the advice of the Council of Ministers. Article 74 states that there shall be a Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister to aid and advise the President. The President has some emergency powers, but under normal circumstances, he is only a symbolic head. Thus, the President is the only nominal power in the Government of India.
qs.kf:
☛ Which article of the Indian Constitution relates to the President's nominal powers? → Article 74
☛ Who advises the President? → Council of Ministers
☛ Who is the real executive head of India? → Prime Minister
☛ What powers does the President lack? → Real executive powers
☛ On whose advice must the President act? → Council of Ministers

q: Who is the supreme law officer of India?
qs.e: The supreme law officer of India is the Attorney General of India. This office is established under Article 76 of the Indian Constitution. The Attorney General is appointed by the President and represents the government in the Supreme Court. To be eligible, a person must be qualified to be appointed as a judge of the Supreme Court. The Attorney General can participate in the proceedings of both Houses of Parliament but cannot vote. They advise the government on legal matters referred by the President. This position is distinct from the Chief Justice of India, who is the head of the judiciary.
qs.kf:
☛ Supreme law officer of India → Attorney General of India
☛ Who appoints the Attorney General → President
☛ Constitutional article for Attorney General → Article 76
☛ Tenure of Attorney General → During pleasure of President
☛ Courts where Attorney General can appear → All Indian courts

q: Who is the first citizen of India from among the following?
qs.e: According to the Constitution of India, the President is considered the first citizen of the country. This is a ceremonial position symbolizing the unity and integrity of the nation. The President is also the Supreme Commander of the Indian Armed Forces. The Prime Minister is the head of government, while the President is the head of state. The Chief Justice is the head of the judiciary, and the Governor is the constitutional head at the state level. Under Article 53 of the Constitution, the executive powers are vested in the President. The President is elected by an Electoral College consisting of members of Parliament and state legislative assemblies.
qs.kf:
☛ Who is the first citizen of India? → President
☛ Who is the Supreme Commander of the Indian Armed Forces? → President
☛ Who elects the President? → Electoral College
☛ Under which article are executive powers vested in the President? → Article 53
☛ Who was the first President of India? → Dr. Rajendra Prasad

q: The real Head of the Government of India is
qs.e: In India's parliamentary system, the President is the constitutional head, while the Prime Minister is the real head of the government. The Prime Minister leads the Council of Ministers and exercises executive powers. According to Articles 74 and 75 of the Indian Constitution, the Prime Minister advises the President, which is binding on him. The Prime Minister is appointed by the President but leads the majority in the Lok Sabha (elected by the people). This system is based on the British model. The Prime Minister is accountable to Parliament and plays a central role in all policy decisions of the government.
qs.kf:
☛ Real head of government in India → Prime Minister
☛ Constitutional head of India → President
☛ Who appoints the Prime Minister → President
☛ Head of the Council of Ministers → Prime Minister
☛ Who actually exercises executive power in India → Prime Minister

q: Which of the following can make laws for peace, progress and good government of Lakshadweep?
qs.e: Lakshadweep is a Union Territory of India. Under Article 240 of the Indian Constitution, the President has the power to make regulations for the peace, progress, and good government of certain Union Territories, including Lakshadweep, Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Dadra and Nagar Haveli, Daman and Diu. These regulations can repeal or amend any law made by Parliament in relation to these territories. The President exercises this power on the advice of the Council of Ministers. Thus, the authority to legislate specifically for Lakshadweep rests with the President, not with the Vice President, Prime Minister, or Chief Justice.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Article empowers the President to make regulations for certain UTs? → Article 240
☛ Is Lakshadweep a state or an UT? → Union Territory
☛ Can Parliament override President's regulations under Article 240? → Yes, by making a law
☛ Name the UTs covered under Article 240? → Andaman, Lakshadweep, Dadra, Daman, Diu (and Puducherry in some cases)
☛ Who heads the administration of Lakshadweep? → An Administrator appointed by the President

q: The five year term of the President is calculated from the
o: First day of the month he assumes charge
First day of the month following the month he assumes charge
qs.e: According to Article 56 of the Indian Constitution, the term of the President is five years, and it is calculated from the date on which he assumes charge of his office. This is explicitly stated to ensure clarity and certainty. The term begins on the day of assuming office, not from the election result or any other date. If the President resigns or is removed before completing five years, the Vice President or the Chief Justice acts as President. This provision maintains continuity and stability in the highest office of the country.
qs.kf:
☛ From which day is the President's term calculated? → The day he assumes charge.
☛ What is the minimum age to be President? → 35 years.
☛ How many years must one be a citizen of India to be President? → By birth or at least 5 years.
☛ Who elects the President? → Electoral College.
☛ Who administers the oath to the President? → Chief Justice of India.

q: After which Prime Minister was a sports award named in India?
qs.e: In India, the Rajiv Gandhi Khel Ratna Award (now renamed as Major Dhyan Chand Khel Ratna Award) was named after former Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi. This award was instituted in 1991-92 to recognize outstanding performance by sportspersons. However, in 2021, it was renamed in honor of hockey legend Major Dhyan Chand. Rajiv Gandhi served as the Prime Minister of India from 1984 to 1989 and was the youngest person to hold the office. The award includes a medal, a certificate, and a cash prize. It is considered one of the highest honors in Indian sports. The award is conferred by the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports.
qs.kf:
☛ What is the current name of the Khel Ratna award? → Major Dhyan Chand Khel Ratna Award
☛ When was the Rajiv Gandhi Khel Ratna Award started? → 1991-92
☛ When was Rajiv Gandhi Prime Minister? → 1984 to 1989
☛ Rajiv Gandhi belonged to which party? → Indian National Congress
☛ Which ministry awards the Khel Ratna? → Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports

q: Which former Indian Prime Minister was Deputy Prime Minister under Morarji Desai?
qs.e: Morarji Desai served as the fourth Prime Minister of India from 1977 to 1979. During his tenure, Charan Singh held the position of Deputy Prime Minister. Charan Singh, a prominent farmer leader, later briefly served as Prime Minister himself in 1979.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was Deputy Prime Minister under Morarji Desai? → Charan Singh
☛ Who was India's first Deputy Prime Minister? → Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel
☛ Which party did Charan Singh belong to? → Janata Party (Secular)
☛ Which party did Morarji Desai belong to? → Janata Party
☛ When was Charan Singh's tenure as PM? → 28 July 1979 to 14 January 1980

q: Which of the following statements is FALSE?
o: According to Article 77, all executive actions of the Government of India shall be exeucted in the name of the President.
According to Article 74, the President will act only on the advice of the Council of Ministers.
All members of the Council of Ministers hold office during the pleasure of the President.
Article 76 provides for a Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister.
qs.e: This statement is false because Article 76 deals with the Attorney General of India, not the Council of Ministers. The Council of Ministers is provided under Article 74 and Article 75. Article 74 states that there shall be a Council of Ministers with the Prime Minister at the head to aid and advise the President. Article 75 deals with the appointment, tenure, and responsibility of ministers. According to Article 77, all executive actions of the Government of India shall be taken in the name of the President. All members of the Council of Ministers hold office during the pleasure of the President.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 74 → Council of Ministers headed by Prime Minister
☛ Article 75 → Appointment and responsibility of ministers
☛ Article 76 → Attorney General of India
☛ Article 77 → Executive actions in President's name
☛ President's pleasure → Tenure of Council of Ministers

q: Who is the head of Union Executive in India?
qs.e: According to Article 53 of the Indian Constitution, the executive power of the Union is vested in the President. The President is the constitutional head of the Union Executive. He is the first citizen and the symbol of the nation. The President is elected by an electoral college consisting of elected members of both Houses of Parliament and the Legislative Assemblies of states. Although the President is the head of the executive, he acts on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers (Article 74). The Prime Minister is the real executive head, while the President is the formal head. The Governor is the head of the state executive, and the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court is the head of the judiciary.
qs.kf:
☛ Constitutional head of Union Executive → President
☛ Real head of Union Executive → Prime Minister
☛ President's election basis → Electoral College (Parliament + Assemblies)
☛ Article 53 → Executive power vested in President
☛ President bound by Cabinet advice → Article 74

q: Who among the following had the shortest tenure as the President of India?
qs.e: As the President of India, Zakir Husain had the shortest tenure. He assumed office on 13 May 1967 and served until his death on 3 May 1969, a period of just under 2 years. Rajendra Prasad served the longest tenure (about 12 years). Jawaharlal Nehru and Lal Bahadur Shastri were Prime Ministers, not Presidents. Zakir Husain was the third President and the first Muslim to hold the office.
qs.kf:
☛ President with shortest tenure → Zakir Husain
☛ Zakir Husain's tenure → 13 May 1967 - 3 May 1969
☛ First Muslim President of India → Zakir Husain
☛ Zakir Husain awarded Padma Vibhushan → in 1954
☛ President with longest tenure → Rajendra Prasad

q: Who among the following holds office during the pleasure of the President?
o: Comptroller and Auditor General of India
Chairman of the Union Public Service Commission
qs.e: According to Article 76 of the Indian Constitution, the Attorney General of India holds office during the pleasure of the President. This means the President can remove him at any time. This provision is different from other constitutional office holders. The Speaker of the Lok Sabha (Article 94) holds office until he becomes a member of the Lok Sabha or resigns. The Comptroller and Auditor General of India (Article 148) can only be removed by the President through the process of impeachment. The Chairman of the Union Public Service Commission (Article 316) can be removed by the President only on grounds of misbehaviour or incapacity, following the same procedure as removal of a High Court judge. Thus, only the Attorney General holds office at the pleasure of the President.
qs.kf:
☛ Holds office during pleasure of President → Attorney General of India
☛ Appointment of Attorney General → By President (Article 76)
☛ Term of Speaker of Lok Sabha → As long as he is a member of Lok Sabha
☛ Removal of CAG → Through impeachment (Article 148)
☛ Removal of UPSC Chairman → On grounds of misbehaviour/incapacity (Article 316)

q: Which of the following is the highest law officer in the Government of India?
qs.e: The Constitution of India under Article 76 designates the Attorney General of India as the highest law officer of the Government of India. Appointed by the President, the Attorney General advises the government on legal matters, represents the government in the Supreme Court, and has the right to speak in both Houses of Parliament without the right to vote. He/she is also eligible to become the Chief Justice of India. In contrast, the Chief Justice of India is the head of the judiciary, not a law officer for the government, and the Judges of the Supreme Court or High Court are judicial officers, not law officers for the executive. Thus, only the Attorney General holds the title of the highest law officer.
qs.kf:
☛ Who is the highest law officer in India? → Attorney General of India
☛ Who appoints the Attorney General of India? → The President
☛ Can the Attorney General speak in Parliament? → Yes, but cannot vote
☛ What is the term of the Attorney General? → At the pleasure of the President (no fixed term)
☛ Who administers the oath to the Attorney General? → The President

q: How many members of Rajya Sabha are nominated by the President of India?
qs.e: According to Article 80 of the Indian Constitution, the Rajya Sabha has a total of 245 members, out of which 233 members are elected from states and union territories, and 12 members are nominated by the President. These nominated members are persons having special knowledge or practical experience in fields such as literature, science, art, and social service. This provision ensures that the Parliament benefits from expertise and diversity. The term of nominated members is 6 years, and they enjoy the same rights and privileges as elected members. The President's power of nomination helps in bringing eminent personalities into the legislative process.
qs.kf:
☛ Total seats in Rajya Sabha? → 245
☛ Number of nominated members in Rajya Sabha? → 12
☛ Which article deals with Rajya Sabha nomination? → Article 80
☛ Term of nominated Rajya Sabha members? → 6 years
☛ Who nominates Rajya Sabha members? → President

q: Who is the Chairperson of NITI Aayog?
qs.e: NITI Aayog (National Institution for Transforming India) was established on 1 January 2015, replacing the Planning Commission. The Chairperson of NITI Aayog is the Prime Minister of India. It also includes a Vice-Chairperson, a Chief Executive Officer (CEO), and other members. The main objective of NITI Aayog is to foster cooperative federalism and coordinate policy-making among states. It plays a crucial role in shaping the national development agenda and providing long-term policy frameworks. The Prime Minister heads the governing council, which includes Chief Ministers of all states and Union Territories.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the first Vice-Chairperson of NITI Aayog? → Arvind Panagariya
☛ Where is the headquarters of NITI Aayog located? → New Delhi
☛ Who was the first CEO of NITI Aayog? → Sindhushree Khullar
☛ When was NITI Aayog established? → 1 January 2015
☛ What is the full form of NITI Aayog? → National Institution for Transforming India

q: Consider the following statements. 1. Elections are held every five years for the Lok Sabha and each Legislative Assembly. 2. The President can dissolve the Lok Sabha even before the completion of 5 years of the government, if the Prime Minister makes such a recommendation to the President.

3. The Council of Ministers automatically gets dissolved due to the death or resignation of the Prime Minister. 4. The Lok Sabha elections are conducted according to the 'first past the post' system. Select the correct statement.
qs.e: All four statements are correct. The first statement is correct as per Articles 83 and 172 of the Constitution, which fix the tenure of Lok Sabha and Legislative Assemblies at five years. The second statement is correct because the President can dissolve the Lok Sabha on the recommendation of the Prime Minister. The third statement is correct; the Council of Ministers automatically dissolves upon the death or resignation of the Prime Minister (though ministers hold office during the pleasure of the President under Article 75(2), the council cannot function without the Prime Minister). The fourth statement is correct as Lok Sabha elections in India are conducted using the first-past-the-post system.
qs.kf:
☛ What is the tenure of Lok Sabha? → Five years
☛ Who has the power to dissolve Lok Sabha? → The President
☛ What happens to the Council of Ministers on the death of the Prime Minister? → It automatically dissolves
☛ Which electoral system is used for Lok Sabha elections in India? → First-past-the-post
☛ What is the tenure of a Legislative Assembly? → Five years

q: Who among the following served as India's first Deputy Prime minister?
qs.e: India's first Deputy Prime Minister was Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel. He served from 1947 to 1950. He was also the first Home Minister and Minister of Information and Broadcasting. Sardar Patel is credited with the integration of over 565 princely states into India. His strong leadership and determination played a crucial role in nation-building. His birth anniversary on October 31 is celebrated as National Unity Day. The post of Deputy Prime Minister is political and not constitutional.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the first Deputy Prime Minister of India? → Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel
☛ For how many years did Sardar Patel serve as Deputy Prime Minister? → 1947-1950
☛ Who is credited with the integration of princely states into India? → Sardar Patel
☛ What is celebrated on Sardar Patel's birth anniversary? → National Unity Day (31 October)
☛ Is the Deputy Prime Minister's post constitutional or political? → Political

q: Which of the following articles of Indian Constitution deals with the executive power of the Union?
qs.e: Article 53 of the Indian Constitution deals with the executive power of the Union. It states that the executive power of the Union shall be vested in the President and shall be exercised by him either directly or through officers subordinate to him in accordance with the Constitution. The President is also the Supreme Commander of the armed forces. This article falls under Part V which focuses on the Union Executive. Article 52 provides for the office of the President, Article 54 deals with the election of the President, and Article 55 covers the procedure for the election. Therefore, the source of executive power is Article 53.
qs.kf:
☛ In which Article is the executive power of the Union vested? → Article 53
☛ Who is the Supreme Commander of the armed forces under Article 53? → President
☛ Which Article provides for the office of the President? → Article 52
☛ Which Article deals with the election of the President? → Article 54
☛ Which Article prescribes the procedure for election of President? → Article 55

q: Which Article of the Indian Constitution is related to the appointment of 'Attorney General of India'?
qs.e: Article 76 of the Indian Constitution deals with the appointment, tenure, and functions of the Attorney General of India, who is the highest legal officer of the Government of India. The Attorney General is appointed by the President and must be a person qualified to be appointed as a Judge of the Supreme Court. The Attorney General holds office during the pleasure of the President and has no fixed tenure. They have the right to participate in the proceedings of both Houses of Parliament but do not have the right to vote. Article 73 deals with the extent of executive power of the Union, Article 74 with the Council of Ministers, and Article 75 with the appointment of the Prime Minister and other ministers.
qs.kf:
☛ Who appoints the Attorney General of India? → President
☛ Which Article is related to the Attorney General of India? → Article 76
☛ In which houses of Parliament can the Attorney General participate? → Both houses
☛ What is the qualification to become Attorney General? → Qualification to be a Supreme Court judge
☛ What is the tenure of the Attorney General? → Not fixed; holds office during the pleasure of the President

q: When was a member of the British Cabinet appointed as a 'Secretary of State for India' and made responsible for all matters related to the governance of India?
qs.e: In 1858, a member of the British Cabinet was appointed as the Secretary of State for India. This was part of the reorganization of British rule in India. The Government of India Act 1858 ended the rule of the East India Company and established direct rule by the British Crown. The Secretary of State was made responsible for all matters related to the governance of India and was accountable to the British Parliament. The Governor-General was given the title of Viceroy. Lord Canning became the first Viceroy of India. This system continued until 1947.
qs.kf:
☛ Government of India Act 1858 → Also called the 'Act for the Good Government of India'.
☛ First Secretary of State for India → Lord Stanley
☛ East India Company rule ended → Transferred to British Crown in 1858
☛ First Viceroy of India → Lord Canning (1858-1862)
☛ Role of Secretary of State → Supervise all matters related to the governance of India

q: The power to issue an ordinance when Parliament is NOT in session is given to the President under which Article?
qs.e: Article 123 of the Indian Constitution empowers the President to promulgate ordinances when Parliament is not in session. This power is similar to Article 213 which allows the Governor to issue ordinances during the recess of the state legislature. An ordinance has the same force and effect as an Act of Parliament. However, it must be approved by Parliament within 6 weeks of reassembly; otherwise, it ceases to operate. It is important to note that an ordinance can only be issued when the President is satisfied that immediate action is necessary. Article 72 deals with the power of pardon, Article 110 defines money bills, and Article 356 relates to President's rule.
qs.kf:
☛ Under which Article can the President issue ordinances? → Article 123
☛ Under which Article can the Governor issue ordinances? → Article 213
☛ Within how many weeks must an ordinance be approved by Parliament? → 6 weeks
☛ What does Article 72 deal with? → Power of pardon
☛ What does Article 356 deal with? → President's rule

q: What is the maximum number of Ministers allowed in the Council of Ministers, including the Prime Minister, as per the 91st Amendment Act?
qs.e: The 91st Amendment Act of 2003 amended Articles 75 and 164 of the Indian Constitution. It limits the total number of ministers, including the Prime Minister, in the Council of Ministers to 15% of the total membership of the Lok Sabha. This provision applies equally to the central government and state governments. The amendment was introduced to restrict the size of the cabinet, improve administrative efficiency, and reduce financial burden caused by an excessive number of ministers. It also aims to ensure political stability and prevent the misuse of power through inflated councils.
qs.kf:
☛ 91st Amendment → Enacted in 2003
☛ Article 75 → Limits size of Union Council of Ministers
☛ Maximum limit → 15% of Lok Sabha strength
☛ Prime Minister → Included in this count
☛ For states → 15% of Legislative Assembly strength

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (09/06/2025) Shift 2
q: In the ministerial hierarchy in India, Ministers of State generally have:
o: . no executive responsibility in any of the portfolios
secondary rank within the portfolios assigned to Cabinet Ministers
equal standing with Cabinet Ministers in their assigned portfolios
qs.e: In India's Council of Ministers, Ministers of State (MoS) work under Cabinet Ministers. They do not hold independent charge but assist in the departments assigned to Cabinet Ministers. Their rank is secondary to Cabinet Ministers, and they are given subordinate responsibilities in departmental work. According to Article 74 of the Indian Constitution, the Council of Ministers is headed by the Prime Minister. Cabinet Ministers play a key role in policy-making, while Ministers of State assist in implementation under their guidance.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Article of the Indian Constitution deals with the Council of Ministers? → Article 74
☛ Who is the most senior member of the Cabinet? → Prime Minister
☛ When is a Minister of State given independent charge? → When they are assigned separate departments
☛ What is the main difference between a Cabinet Minister and a Minister of State? → Cabinet Ministers attend Cabinet meetings, Ministers of State do not
☛ How is the size of the Council of Ministers determined in India? → It depends on the discretion of the Prime Minister

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (10/06/2025) Shift 3
q: Who among the following was the President of the Board of Control at the time of Charter renewal in 1793 in India?
qs.e: At the time of the Charter Act of 1793, the President of the Board of Control was Henry Dundas. The Board of Control was established by the Pitt's India Act of 1784 to oversee the political and administrative affairs of the East India Company. Henry Dundas served as its President from 1793 to 1801 and was often referred to as the 'Manager of India' due to his significant influence. The Charter Act of 1793 renewed the Company's charter for a period of 20 years, with no major changes to the existing system. Dundas played a key role in shaping British policy in India during this period.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Act established the Board of Control? → Pitt's India Act, 1784
☛ Who was the first President of the Board of Control? → Henry Dundas
☛ For how many years was the charter renewed under the Charter Act of 1793? → 20 years
☛ By which title was Henry Dundas known? → Manager of India
☛ How many members were in the Board of Control? → Six members

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (20/06/2025) Shift 2
q: The Union Council of Ministers in India, as the Chief Executive Organ, implicates which of the following?
o: Ministers leave all work operations to be done by civil servants
Centralisation of power in local bodies
Each minister is the political head of his/her ministry
The abolition of the role of the Secretary
qs.e: The Union Council of Ministers in India is the chief executive organ, where each minister acts as the political head of his/her ministry. This system is based on the parliamentary form of government, where ministers are responsible for policy-making and administrative decisions. Ministers are assisted by civil servants, but they do not leave all work to them. Options like centralisation of power in local bodies or abolition of the Secretary's role are not implications of the Council of Ministers. The Council advises the President and is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha. This ensures a close link between the legislature and the executive.
qs.kf:
☛ Who is the head of the Council of Ministers? → Prime Minister
☛ To whom is the Council of Ministers responsible? → Lok Sabha
☛ Who is the formal head of the executive in India? → President
☛ Under which Article is the Council of Ministers formed? → Article 74
☛ Ministers are the ________ of their ministries? → political heads

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (20/06/2025) Shift 3
q: 'Reward for loyalty' as a factor for ministerial selection in India refers to:
o: ensuring each geographic region gets equal representation
verifying the educational background of candidates
qs.e: The 'reward for loyalty' factor in ministerial selection in India refers to the practice of rewarding leaders who have shown long-term loyalty to the party or its leader. This is a common practice in political appointments, where loyalty is given more importance than merit or representation. The purpose is to maintain unity within the party and encourage support. This factor is distinct from monetary rewards, regional balance, or educational background. Recognising longstanding support is a key political strategy in cabinet formation, strengthening power structures. It ensures that loyalists are rewarded, thereby reinforcing the party hierarchy and ensuring continued allegiance.
qs.kf:
☛ 'Reward for loyalty' factor in ministerial selection → Recognising and rewarding longstanding support
☛ Key factors in Indian cabinet formation → Loyalty, caste, regional balance
☛ Term 'reward for loyalty' used for → Prioritising loyalty in political appointments
☛ Purpose of 'reward for loyalty' in ministerial selection → Maintain party discipline and support
☛ Effect of rewarding loyalty → Promotes political loyalty over merit

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (20/06/2025) Shift 3
q: 5 What specific provision concerning the President of India is outlined in Article 59(3) of the Constitution of India?
o: Salary and privileges of the President
qs.e: Article 59(3) of the Indian Constitution deals with the salary and privileges of the President of India. It states that the President receives such emoluments, allowances, and privileges as may be determined by Parliament, and these are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India. Additionally, the salary and allowances of the President cannot be diminished during their term of office. This article also grants certain privileges, such as the right to official residence and travel allowances. This provision ensures the independence and dignity of the President.
qs.kf:
☛ On which fund is the President's salary charged? → Consolidated Fund of India
☛ Can the President's salary be reduced during their term? → No
☛ What does Article 59(3) relate to? → Salary and privileges of the President
☛ Who determines the President's salary? → Parliament
☛ Which article grants the President's right to residence? → Article 59(3)

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (21/06/2025) Shift 1
q: Who is responsible for preparing the inaugural speech of the President of India in Indian Parliament?
qs.e: According to the Indian Constitution, the inaugural speech (address) of the President in Parliament is prepared by the Council of Ministers. This speech outlines the policies and programs of the government. The President delivers the speech, but its content is determined by the Union Cabinet. Article 87(1) of the Constitution mandates that the President addresses both Houses of Parliament at the first session after each general election and at the beginning of the first session each year. The speech reflects the government's agenda and is drafted by the Prime Minister and their team. The President cannot make changes to the speech, as they are the constitutional head and act on the advice of the Council of Ministers.
qs.kf:
☛ Who prepares the President's address to Parliament? → Council of Ministers
☛ Article related to President's address? → Article 87(1)
☛ When does the President address Parliament? → First session after general election and first session of the year
☛ What is included in the President's address? → Government's policies and programs
☛ Which Houses are addressed by the President? → Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha (joint session)

q: Who among the following was the youngest President of India?
qs.e: The youngest President of India was Shri Neelam Sanjiva Reddy. He was born on 19 May 1913 and became President on 25 July 1977 at the age of 64. He was the sixth President of India and the first person to serve as Chief Minister, Lok Sabha Speaker, and President. He hailed from Andhra Pradesh and was a member of the Congress party. Prior to becoming President, he also served as the Speaker of the Lok Sabha. His tenure (1977-1982) included the post-Emergency period. Dr. Rajendra Prasad became President in 1950 at age 65, Dr. S. Radhakrishnan in 1962 at age 74, and Dr. Zakir Hussain in 1967 at age 70. Thus, Neelam Sanjiva Reddy was the youngest.
qs.kf:
☛ Youngest President of India → Neelam Sanjiva Reddy
☛ Tenure of Neelam Sanjiva Reddy → 1977-1982
☛ Birth year of Neelam Sanjiva Reddy → 1913
☛ First person to hold posts of → Chief Minister, Lok Sabha Speaker, and President
☛ Age at becoming President → 64 years

q: Who among the following has been the longest-serving chief minister of an Indian state?
qs.e: Pawan Kumar Chamling was the Chief Minister of Sikkim and holds the record for being the longest-serving chief minister of any Indian state. He served from 1994 to 2019, a continuous tenure of 24 years and 165 days. This is the longest tenure for any chief minister in India. Mulayam Singh Yadav served as Chief Minister of Uttar Pradesh but his term was shorter. Narendra Modi was Chief Minister of Gujarat before becoming Prime Minister. Shivraj Singh Chouhan served as Chief Minister of Madhya Pradesh but his tenure is shorter than Chamling's. Under Chamling's leadership, Sikkim saw significant development and progress.
qs.kf:
☛ Who is the longest-serving Chief Minister of Sikkim? → Pawan Kumar Chamling
☛ How many years did Pawan Kumar Chamling serve as CM? → 24 years
☛ Who holds the record for the longest-serving CM in India? → Pawan Kumar Chamling
☛ Which state did Pawan Kumar Chamling serve as CM? → Sikkim
☛ Which Indian state has the longest-serving CM record? → Sikkim

q: Which of the following statement is correct?
o: The Council of Ministers of a State is collectively responsible to the Legislative Assembly of the State.
The Council of Ministers of a State is collectively responsible to the Vice-President.
The Council of Ministers of a State is collectively responsible to the Legislative Council of the State.
The Council of Ministers of a State is collectively responsible to the Council of States.
qs.e: According to Article 164 of the Indian Constitution, the Council of Ministers in a state is collectively responsible to the Legislative Assembly of the state. This provision is based on the parliamentary system, where the executive is accountable to the legislature. If the council loses the majority in the Assembly, it must resign. The other options are incorrect because the council is not responsible to the Vice-President, the Legislative Council, or the Council of States (Rajya Sabha).
qs.kf:
☛ Collective responsibility of state cabinet → Enshrined in Article 164
☛ State cabinet is responsible to → State Legislative Assembly
☛ In parliamentary system, executive → Accountable to legislature
☛ Tenure of state cabinet → As long as it enjoys confidence of Assembly
☛ Appointment of Chief Minister → By the Governor

q: Which of the following is not true with regard to lokayukta?
o: He/she can investigate into the grievance of citizens due to injustice and hardship caused by maladministration
Lokyukta can't question Prime Minister on the allegation of abuse of power
He/she can supervise the citizen grievance investigation
He/she can ask for an inquiry into the allegation of abuse of power by public servants
qs.e: This statement is false because Lokyukta can question the Prime Minister on allegations of abuse of power, though in some states the Prime Minister may be exempted from the jurisdiction of Lokyukta. Lokyukta is an anti-corruption institution that operates at the state level and can investigate cases of abuse of power by public servants. It can investigate citizen grievances, supervise investigations, and order inquiries into allegations. The first Lokyukta was established in Maharashtra in 1971, and the institution aims to bring transparency in administration. Lokyukta is appointed by the Governor and submits its report to the Governor.
qs.kf:
☛ Which state first established the office of Lokyukta? → Maharashtra (1971)
☛ Who appoints the Lokyukta? → Governor
☛ To whom does Lokyukta submit its report? → Governor
☛ Who investigates corruption cases against the Prime Minister? → Lokpal
☛ What category of office is Lokyukta? → Constitutional office (State level)

q: Who is the first full time female Defence Minister of India?
qs.e: Nirmala Sitharaman is the first full time female Defence Minister of India. She took charge of the Ministry of Defence on 3 September 2017. Earlier, Indira Gandhi had held the defence portfolio as additional charge while serving as Prime Minister, but she was not a full time Defence Minister. Nirmala Sitharaman is a Rajya Sabha member from Rajasthan and a senior leader of the Bharatiya Janata Party. She has also served as the Finance Minister. Her appointment symbolizes women empowerment in Indian politics.
qs.kf:
☛ First full time female Defence Minister → Nirmala Sitharaman
☛ First female Defence Minister (additional charge) → Indira Gandhi
☛ Nirmala Sitharaman's Rajya Sabha constituency → Rajasthan
☛ Birthplace of Nirmala Sitharaman → Madurai, Tamil Nadu
☛ Year of becoming full time Defence Minister → 2017

q: In India, impeachment process is NOT applicable to _____ for removal from office.
qs.e: In India, the impeachment process is applicable only to the President, Vice President, judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts, and the Chief Election Commissioner. The Prime Minister is an elected member of Parliament and can be removed not by impeachment but by a no-confidence motion in the Lok Sabha. Impeachment is a judicial process for removal on grounds of violation of the Constitution. The Prime Minister's tenure depends on the majority support in Lok Sabha. Hence, the impeachment process is not applicable to the Prime Minister.
qs.kf:
☛ Under which Article is the impeachment of the President of India? → Article 61
☛ Who orders the removal of Supreme Court judges? → President
☛ What is required to remove the Prime Minister from office? → Majority in Lok Sabha
☛ Which position is not subject to impeachment? → Prime Minister
☛ Impeachment is an example of which process? → Judicial review

q: Who was the 1st Indian woman to preside over Indian National Congress?
qs.e: Sarojini Naidu was the first Indian woman to preside over the Indian National Congress. She chaired the 1925 session held in Kanpur. She was a renowned poet and freedom fighter, known as the 'Nightingale of India'. Earlier, in 1917, Annie Besant became the Congress president, but she was of Irish origin, not Indian. Vijaya Laxmi Pandit and Rajkumari Amrit Kaur were also prominent women leaders, but they never held the Congress presidency. After India's independence, Sarojini Naidu became the first woman governor of Uttar Pradesh, making history again.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the first woman president of Congress? → Annie Besant (1917)
☛ Who was the first Indian woman president of Congress? → Sarojini Naidu (1925)
☛ What is Sarojini Naidu's nickname? → Nightingale of India
☛ Which state did Sarojini Naidu become the first woman governor of? → Uttar Pradesh
☛ Where was the 1925 Congress session held? → Kanpur

q: Which office of the government of India is the governing department of nuclear energy?
qs.e: In India, the Department of Atomic Energy (DAE) is governed by the Office of the Prime Minister. The department functions directly under the Prime Minister and is responsible for the peaceful use, research, and development of nuclear energy. The DAE was established in 1954 and operates under the policy guidance of the Atomic Energy Commission. Its major institutions include Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC), Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research (IGCAR), and Atomic Minerals Directorate for Exploration and Research (AMD). The Ministry of Power, Office of the Home Minister, and Office of the Defence Minister have no jurisdiction over the DAE.
qs.kf:
☛ Which department governs nuclear energy in India? → Department of Atomic Energy under PMO
☛ Who chairs the Atomic Energy Commission? → Prime Minister
☛ India's first nuclear reactor was? → Apsara (1956)
☛ When was the Department of Atomic Energy established? → 1954
☛ Where is Bhabha Atomic Research Centre located? → Mumbai

q: On whose approval can the Lok Sabha be dissolved by the President?
qs.e: Under Article 85 of the Indian Constitution, the President can dissolve the Lok Sabha on the advice of the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister heads the Council of Ministers, and his advice is binding on the President as per Article 74. The Lok Sabha normally has a term of 5 years, but the President can dissolve it prematurely only on the Prime Minister's recommendation. The Chief Justice of India, Parliament, or Chief Secretary have no authority in this matter. This power ensures that the executive remains accountable to the legislature.
qs.kf:
☛ Who has the power to dissolve Lok Sabha? → President on PM's advice
☛ Article 85 deals with? → Sessions, prorogation, and dissolution of Parliament
☛ Article 74 states? → President is bound by Council of Ministers' advice
☛ Maximum term of Lok Sabha? → 5 years
☛ On whose recommendation does President dissolve Lok Sabha? → Prime Minister

q: How long does the governor's tenure take place?
o: Up to a certain period of five years
At the will of the President
qs.e: According to Article 156 of the Indian Constitution, the governor's tenure is normally 5 years, but it is not a fixed term. The governor holds office at the pleasure of the President, meaning the President can remove the governor at any time. The governor's tenure is indefinite and continues until the President decides otherwise. This provision makes the governor a representative of the central government. The governor submits his resignation to the President. Thus, the governor's tenure depends on the will of the President.
qs.kf:
☛ Who appoints the governor? → President
☛ What is the normal term of the governor? → 5 years
☛ Who can remove the governor from office? → President
☛ To whom does the governor submit his resignation? → President
☛ At whose pleasure does the governor hold office? → President

q: In the Indian Parliament, the Prime Minister is appointed by which house of Parliament?
o: At the discretion of the President
Higher or lower can be done by any House.
qs.e: According to Article 75 of the Indian Constitution, the Prime Minister is appointed by the President. The President appoints the person who, in their opinion, is the leader of the majority in the Lok Sabha. This appointment is not made by either house of Parliament but is based on the President's discretion. However, the Prime Minister must prove majority support in the Lok Sabha. If no party has a clear majority, the President may use their discretion. Thus, the Prime Minister is not directly appointed by any house of Parliament, but by the President.
qs.kf:
☛ Who appoints the Prime Minister? → President
☛ Which article deals with appointment of Prime Minister? → Article 75
☛ In which house must the Prime Minister prove majority? → Lok Sabha
☛ Can a Rajya Sabha member become Prime Minister? → Yes
☛ Which article describes duties of Prime Minister? → Article 78

q: What type of veto (veto) does the President have in relation to any state act which has been stopped by the Governor?
qs.e: The President has three types of veto power over state bills: absolute veto, suspension veto, and pocket veto. When a Governor reserves a state bill for the President's consideration, the President can exercise an absolute veto, meaning he can completely reject the bill, and the state legislature cannot override it. This power comes under Articles 200 and 201 of the Indian Constitution. However, the President may also return the bill for reconsideration or grant assent. An absolute veto is the strongest form where the bill is rejected outright and cannot be passed again by the state legislature.
qs.kf:
☛ President's veto that cannot be overridden by state legislature → Absolute Veto
☛ Article allowing Governor to reserve bill for President → Article 200
☛ President's power to reject a bill outright → Absolute Veto
☛ President's power to withhold decision indefinitely → Pocket Veto
☛ Suspension Veto applies only to → single-chamber states

q: Who is the ex - officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha?
qs.e: As per Article 64 of the Indian Constitution, the Vice President is the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. The Vice President holds a term of 5 years and presides over the proceedings of the Rajya Sabha, casts a casting vote in case of a tie, and maintains discipline in the House. This provision is derived from the British parliamentary system where the Vice President serves as the presiding officer of the upper house. Due to the permanent nature of the Rajya Sabha, which is never dissolved, the Vice President is made its ex-officio Chairman. In contrast, the Speaker of the Lok Sabha is elected by its members. Thus, the correct option is 'Vice President'.
qs.kf:
☛ Who is the ex-officio Chairman of Rajya Sabha? → Vice President
☛ What is the term of the Vice President? → 5 years
☛ Article 64 relates to? → Vice President to be Chairman of Rajya Sabha
☛ Who gives the casting vote in Rajya Sabha? → Vice President
☛ How is the Speaker of Lok Sabha elected? → By members

q: What should be the minimum age for becoming the President of India?
qs.e: According to Article 58 of the Indian Constitution, the minimum age for becoming the President of India is 35 years. This provision ensures that the President possesses sufficient experience and maturity. In comparison, the minimum age for a member of the Rajya Sabha is 30 years and for the Lok Sabha is 25 years. The higher age requirement for the President is because they are the supreme constitutional head of the country. Additionally, the candidate must be a citizen of India and must not hold any office of profit under the Central or State government.
qs.kf:
☛ Minimum age for President of India → 35 years
☛ Constitutional Article → 58
☛ Minimum age for Lok Sabha member → 25 years
☛ Minimum age for Rajya Sabha member → 30 years
☛ Citizenship requirement for President → Indian citizen

q: After the death of which prime minister did Gulzarilal Nanda take over as the acting prime minister for the second time?
qs.e: Gulzarilal Nanda served as acting Prime Minister twice. The first time was after the death of Jawaharlal Nehru (27 May 1964) and the second time after the death of Lal Bahadur Shastri (11 January 1966). On both occasions, he remained acting Prime Minister until the election of a new Prime Minister. After Nehru's death, Shastri became Prime Minister; after Shastri's death, Indira Gandhi assumed the office. Gulzarilal Nanda was a senior leader in Indian politics and held key positions such as Home Minister.
qs.kf:
☛ When did Gulzarilal Nanda first take oath as acting PM? → 27 May 1964
☛ Where did Lal Bahadur Shastri die? → Tashkent, Uzbekistan
☛ Who became PM after Shastri? → Indira Gandhi
☛ Which ministry did Gulzarilal Nanda handle? → Home Ministry
☛ Who was India's first acting Prime Minister? → Gulzarilal Nanda

q: Who chairs the Defence Acquisition Council (DAC)?
qs.e: The Defence Acquisition Council (DAC) is the highest decision-making body under the Ministry of Defence of India, responsible for formulating policies related to defence procurement and acquisitions. It is chaired by the Defence Minister, currently Rajnath Singh. The DAC was constituted in 2001 with the aim of streamlining and bringing transparency to the defence procurement process. Its members include the Defence Secretary, the Chiefs of the three armed forces, the Secretary of Defence Production, and the Finance Secretary (Defence). The DAC plays a crucial role in the modernization of the Indian armed forces and strengthening strategic capabilities.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the DAC formed? → 2001
☛ What is the main function of DAC? → Formulating defence procurement and acquisition policies
☛ Who are members of DAC? → Defence Minister, Defence Secretary, Service Chiefs, etc.
☛ Which ministry does DAC belong to? → Ministry of Defence
☛ Who is the current chairperson of DAC? → Rajnath Singh

q: As per Article 78, it is the duty of the Prime Minister to communicate all decisions of the Council of Ministers to whom?
qs.e: According to Article 78, it is the duty of the Prime Minister to communicate all decisions of the Council of Ministers to the President. This provision is part of Part V of the Indian Constitution. Additionally, the Prime Minister must furnish any information that the President may request and submit any decision taken by a minister to the President if required. This ensures that the President, as the constitutional head, remains informed about the functioning of the executive in the parliamentary system. This provision strengthens transparency in government functioning and the President's oversight role.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 78 deals with? → Duties of Prime Minister
☛ To whom does the PM communicate decisions of Council of Ministers? → President
☛ Article 78 is in which part? → Part V
☛ Which article imposes a duty on PM to furnish information to the President? → Article 78
☛ What is the purpose of providing information to the President under Article 78? → Transparency and awareness

q: Who among the following is NOT appointed by the President of India?
