Rajya Sabha is the upper house of Parliament representing the states. The first Rajya Sabha was formed in 1952 after the first Lok Sabha elections, completing the full formation of the Parliament. Rajya Sabha is a permanent house that is never dissolved, but one-third of its members retire every two years. Members of Rajya Sabha are indirectly elected by the elected members of state legislative assemblies.
qs.kf:
☛ Maximum strength of Rajya Sabha → 250
☛ First Chairman of Rajya Sabha → Dr. Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan
☛ First Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha → S. V. Krishnamurthy Rao
☛ Term of Rajya Sabha members → 6 years
☛ Representation of states in Rajya Sabha → Based on population

q: Which of the following states has the highest number of Lok Sabha seats?
qs.e: The allocation of Lok Sabha seats is based on the population of states. India has a total of 543 Lok Sabha seats, of which the highest number, 80 seats, are allocated to Uttar Pradesh. This state is the most populous in the country, hence it has the maximum representation. It is followed by Maharashtra (48 seats), West Bengal (42 seats), and Tamil Nadu (39 seats). This distribution is periodically revised by the Delimitation Commission. The last delimitation based on population was done in 1976, after which it was frozen until 2002.
qs.kf:
☛ Total Lok Sabha seats → 543
☛ State with highest Lok Sabha seats → Uttar Pradesh (80)
☛ Second highest state → Maharashtra (48)
☛ Third highest state → West Bengal (42)
☛ States/UTs with minimum seats → Lakshadweep, Daman & Diu, Dadra & Nagar Haveli (1 each)

q: How many Anglo-Indian members can be nominated in the Lok Sabha?
qs.e: Under Article 331 of the Indian Constitution, the President can nominate two members of the Anglo-Indian community to the Lok Sabha if he believes the community is not adequately represented. This provision was in effect from 1950 when the Constitution came into force until 2020. The 104th Constitutional Amendment (2020) abolished the nomination of Anglo-Indian members in the Lok Sabha and state legislatures. Therefore, currently, no Anglo-Indian members can be nominated. However, in the context of the question, based on the old provision, the correct answer is 2.
qs.kf:
☛ Which article dealt with Anglo-Indian nomination? → Article 331
☛ Which amendment ended Anglo-Indian nomination? → 104th Amendment
☛ How many seats were reserved for Anglo-Indians in Lok Sabha? → 2 (by nomination)
☛ What is the limit for Anglo-Indian nomination in Rajya Sabha? → 12 members, but not mandatory for Anglo-Indians
☛ When was the 104th Amendment enacted? → 2020

q: If a person is elected to both the Parliament House, then the person should inform about working in the desired hall of the house within ________.
qs.e: If a person is elected to both houses of Parliament (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha), they must inform within 10 days in which house they wish to serve, as per Article 101 of the Constitution. This provision prevents dual membership and ensures a person can only be a member of one house at a time. Failure to notify within the stipulated period results in automatic vacation of both seats. This rule is a key part of parliamentary procedure to maintain clarity and efficiency in legislative functioning.
qs.kf:
☛ Time limit for informing choice of house when elected to both → 10 days
☛ Constitutional article governing dual membership → Article 101
☛ Consequence of not informing within time → Membership automatically vacated
☛ Can a person be a member of both Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha simultaneously → No
☛ To whom the information must be given → Chairman (Rajya Sabha) or Speaker (Lok Sabha)

q: The Council of State is also called _________.
qs.e: Under Article 80 of the Indian Constitution, the Council of State is called the Rajya Sabha. It is the upper house of Parliament, while the Lok Sabha is the lower house. Members of Rajya Sabha are indirectly elected by the elected members of state legislative assemblies, and 12 members are nominated by the President. Rajya Sabha is a permanent house; it cannot be dissolved, and one-third of its members retire every two years. Its maximum membership is 250, currently 245. The Chairman of Rajya Sabha is the Vice President of India.
qs.kf:
☛ What is the maximum membership of Rajya Sabha? → 250
☛ What is the term of a Rajya Sabha member? → 6 years
☛ Who is the Chairman of Rajya Sabha? → Vice President
☛ How many members are nominated by the President in Rajya Sabha? → 12
☛ Which article provides for the formation of Rajya Sabha? → Article 80

q: Who is the convenor of the session while absent as the Speaker to conduct a joint session of the Parliament?
qs.e: The joint session of Parliament is presided over by the Speaker of the Lok Sabha. In the absence of the Speaker, the Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha conducts the joint session. This provision is under Article 108 of the Indian Constitution. A joint session is called when a bill passed by one house is rejected or amended by the other house. In such a case, the President convenes a joint sitting of both houses. Neither the Deputy Speaker nor any other member can preside if the Speaker is absent; the Deputy Speaker acts as the convenor. The joint session has a quorum of one-tenth of the total membership.
qs.kf:
☛ Who presides over a joint session of Parliament? → Lok Sabha Speaker
☛ Who conducts the joint session in absence of the Speaker? → Lok Sabha Deputy Speaker
☛ Under which Article is the joint session mentioned? → Article 108
☛ Who convenes the joint session? → President
☛ Which house has more members in a joint session? → Lok Sabha

q: When did the Indian National Congress's Lucknow session take place in which the Narmada Dal and the Nationalist Party of the Hot Dal (Furious) got organized in the Indian National Congress?
qs.e: The Lucknow session of the Indian National Congress took place in 1916. This session is significant because it marked the reunion of the Moderates (Naram Dal) and the Extremists (Garam Dal), who had split in the 1907 Surat session. The session was presided over by Ambika Charan Mazumdar. During this session, the Lucknow Pact was also signed between the Congress and the Muslim League, promoting Hindu-Muslim unity. This session symbolized the unity of nationalist forces and set the stage for the Home Rule Movement.
qs.kf:
☛ 1907 Surat session → Split of Congress into Moderates and Extremists
☛ 1916 Lucknow session → Reunion of Moderates and Extremists
☛ President of Lucknow session → Ambika Charan Mazumdar
☛ Lucknow Pact → Congress-Muslim League agreement in 1916
☛ 1916 event → Establishment of Home Rule League (Annie Besant and Tilak)

q: How many constituencies are there in India?
qs.e: The lower house of the Indian Parliament, the Lok Sabha, has a total of 543 elected members. These members are chosen from 543 parliamentary constituencies across the country. Each constituency represents a specific geographic area. In addition, the President can nominate 2 members from the Anglo-Indian community, but the number of constituencies remains 543. The number is determined by the Delimitation Commission based on population. For Rajya Sabha, members are elected from different states, but for direct elections to Lok Sabha, there are 543 constituencies.
qs.kf:
☛ How many elected members are in Lok Sabha? → 543
☛ How many members can the President nominate to Lok Sabha? →2
☛ Who delimits constituencies? → Delimitation Commission
☛ Which house has direct elections? → Lok Sabha
☛ What is the total strength of Rajya Sabha? → 245

q: The Chairman and Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha comes under, which schedule of the Indian Constitution?
qs.e: The provisions regarding the Chairman and Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha are covered under the Second Schedule of the Indian Constitution. The Second Schedule specifies the salaries, allowances, and privileges of various constitutional functionaries, including the President, Vice-President, Governors, Speaker, Deputy Speaker of Lok Sabha, Chairman and Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha, and judges of High Courts and Supreme Court. The Chairman of Rajya Sabha is the Vice-President, while the Deputy Chairman is elected by the members. Thus, these positions fall under the Second Schedule, not the Tenth, Third, or First Schedule.
qs.kf:
☛ What does the Second Schedule contain? → Salaries of President, Vice-President, Governors, Speaker, Deputy Speaker, Chairman, Deputy Chairman, Judges
☛ What does the First Schedule contain? → List of states and union territories
☛ What does the Third Schedule contain? → Forms of oath and affirmation
☛ What does the Tenth Schedule relate to? → Anti-defection law
☛ Who is the Chairman of Rajya Sabha? → Vice-President

q: The Parliament of India is involved in ________.
o: Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha and President of India
qs.e: The Indian Parliament consists of three components: Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha, and the President of India. According to Article 79 of the Constitution, the President is an integral part of Parliament. The President summons and prorogues sessions, and can dissolve the Lok Sabha. They also give assent to bills passed by both houses, which is essential for them to become law. Thus, Parliament is not just bicameral but includes the President as well. Option 4 is correct.
qs.kf:
☛ What are the three parts of Indian Parliament? → Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha, and President
☛ Which article defines the composition of Parliament? → Article 79
☛ Why is President part of Parliament? → Because they give assent to bills and summon sessions
☛ What is the term of Lok Sabha? → 5 years
☛ How long is the term of Rajya Sabha members? → 6 years

q: All the representatives have been jointly elected / administered, guided and guided by the Indian Government.
qs.e: The provision described in the question pertains to the functioning of the Indian Parliament. According to the Indian Constitution, the election, administration, direction and guidance of all elected representatives in the Parliament (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) is jointly carried out by the Government of India. This process is managed through the Election Commission and other constitutional bodies. The Parliament is the supreme legislative body of India and consists of the President, Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha. The Judiciary, Chief Minister and Chief Justice of India are not responsible for this task. Hence, the correct answer is Parliament.
qs.kf:
☛ Names of the two houses of Indian Parliament → Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha
☛ What is the maximum strength of Lok Sabha? → 552
☛ What is the term of Rajya Sabha members? → 6 years
☛ Which part of the Indian Constitution mentions Parliament? → Part V
☛ Who summons the Parliament session? → President

q: The first hour of each parliamentary meeting is kept for whom?
qs.e: In parliamentary democracy, the first hour of every sitting is reserved for Question Hour. During this time, members of parliament can ask questions to ministers regarding government policies and actions. The purpose of Question Hour is to hold the government accountable and ensure transparency. After Question Hour comes Zero Hour, where members can raise issues without prior notice. Privilege Hour deals with breaches of privilege of any member. Question Hour is a crucial part of parliamentary proceedings and a means of democratic control.
qs.kf:
☛ What is the duration of Question Hour? → One hour
☛ What types of questions can be asked in Question Hour? → Starred, unstarred, and short notice questions
☛ Which right is related to Question Hour? → Right of MPs to ask questions
☛ Which period comes after Question Hour? → Zero Hour
☛ What is the main purpose of Question Hour? → Ensuring government accountability

q: Member of Parliament, Radheshyam Biswas belongs to which state?
qs.e: Radheshyam Biswas is an Indian politician associated with the state of Assam. He represents the Barpeta parliamentary constituency in the Lok Sabha. He is affiliated with the Assam United Democratic Front (AUDF), a major regional party in Assam. His political career has focused on social and economic development in Assam, with efforts to improve education and infrastructure in his constituency. Barpeta is located on the banks of the Manas River and is known for its cultural and historical significance.
qs.kf:
☛ Which party does Radheshyam Biswas belong to? → Assam United Democratic Front (AUDF)
☛ What is his Lok Sabha constituency? → Barpeta, Assam
☛ What is the main agenda of the AUDF party? → Upliftment of minorities and backward classes
☛ Which river flows through Barpeta? → Manas River
☛ How many Lok Sabha constituencies are there in Assam? → 14

q: On the basis of anti-defection law, who decides disqualification in the case of Rajya Sabha?
qs.e: Under the anti-defection law (10th Schedule), the disqualification of Rajya Sabha members is decided by the Chairman of Rajya Sabha (the Vice-President of India). This law was added by the 52nd Constitutional Amendment (1985). The Chairman's decision in this matter is final and cannot be challenged in court (similar to Article 122). For Lok Sabha, the decision is made by the Speaker.
qs.kf:
☛ Which amendment added the anti-defection law? → 52nd Constitutional Amendment (1985)
☛ Which schedule contains the anti-defection law? → 10th Schedule
☛ Who decides disqualification in Lok Sabha? → Speaker
☛ Who appoints the Chairman of Rajya Sabha? → Vice-President is ex-officio Chairman
☛ How many members are required to avoid defection? → At least 2/3 of the original party

q: The term of the post of member of the Rajya Sabha is ______.
qs.e: The Rajya Sabha is the upper house of the Indian Parliament. The term of a member of the Rajya Sabha is 6 years. Rajya Sabha is a permanent house, meaning it is never dissolved, but one-third of its members retire every two years. This provision is given in Article 83 of the Constitution. Members of Rajya Sabha are indirectly elected. The maximum strength of Rajya Sabha is 250, of which 238 members represent states and union territories, and 12 members are nominated by the President.
qs.kf:
☛ Term of a Rajya Sabha member → 6 years
☛ Nature of Rajya Sabha → Permanent house, never dissolved
☛ Retirement of one-third members → Every 2 years
☛ Maximum strength of Rajya Sabha → 250
☛ Articles related to Rajya Sabha → Article 80 (membership) and Article 83 (term)

q: Which Indian state has the largest number of Lok Sabha seats?
qs.e: Out of the total 543 Lok Sabha seats in India, Uttar Pradesh has the highest number with 80 seats. This is followed by Maharashtra (48), West Bengal (42), Bihar (40), and Tamil Nadu (39). The allocation of Lok Sabha seats is based on population, and Uttar Pradesh is the most populous state in India. Rajasthan has 25 seats, Kerala has 20, and Bihar has 40 seats. This information is crucial for competitive exams. The large number of seats gives Uttar Pradesh significant representation in the Lok Sabha.
qs.kf:
☛ What is the total number of Lok Sabha seats? → 543
☛ How many Lok Sabha seats does Uttar Pradesh have? → 80
☛ How many Lok Sabha seats does Maharashtra have? → 48
☛ How many Lok Sabha seats does Bihar have? → 40
☛ How many Lok Sabha seats does Rajasthan have? → 25

q: Which of the following parliamentary forum was formed first?
o: Parliamentary Forum for Water Conservation and Management
qs.e: The Indian Parliament has established several parliamentary forums to focus on specific issues. The first such forum to be formed was the Parliamentary Forum for Water Conservation and Management, established in the year 2005. Following this, the Parliamentary Forum for Youth was formed in 2006, the Parliamentary Forum for Children in 2007, and the Parliamentary Forum for Disaster Management in 2008. These forums enable MPs to discuss and contribute to policy-making on particular topics. The Water Conservation Forum aims to address issues related to water resource conservation and management.
qs.kf:
☛ First parliamentary forum formed → Water Conservation and Management (2005)
☛ Parliamentary Forum for Youth established in → 2006
☛ Parliamentary Forum for Children established in → 2007
☛ Parliamentary Forum for Disaster Management established in → 2008
☛ Purpose of parliamentary forums → Facilitate discussion and policy-making on specific issues

q: In relation to the Finance Bill, which can be disposed of taxation, a bill can be introduced in which house of Parliament?
qs.e: According to Article 109 of the Indian Constitution, a Finance Bill can only be introduced in the Lok Sabha. It is different from a Money Bill as it may contain provisions related to taxation along with other financial matters. After being passed by the Lok Sabha, the Finance Bill is sent to the Rajya Sabha for consideration, which has 14 days to make recommendations. However, the Rajya Sabha cannot reject the bill; it can only suggest amendments. The Lok Sabha may accept or reject these recommendations. This process ensures that the Lok Sabha, being directly elected by the people, retains ultimate control over taxation matters. The Finance Bill is a key instrument for implementing the government's annual budget proposals.
qs.kf:
☛ Where is the Finance Bill introduced? → Lok Sabha
☛ Within how many days can Rajya Sabha return a Finance Bill? → 14 days
☛ Which Article defines a Money Bill? → Article 110
☛ Which Article deals with the Finance Bill? → Article 109
☛ What can Rajya Sabha do with a Finance Bill? → Send recommendations

q: In the politics, the "Whip" office is mentioned in what?
qs.e: In the Indian parliamentary system, the office of 'Whip' is not mentioned in any written document but is a part of Parliamentary Tradition. The whip is responsible for directing party members to vote according to the party line. This practice is borrowed from the British Parliament and adopted in India as a parliamentary convention. It is not mentioned in the Constitution or the Rules of Procedure of the House. The whip is an informal tool of party discipline that ensures smooth functioning of parliamentary proceedings. Violating a whip can lead to disqualification, but it is not a legal compulsion. Thus, the whip office is entirely based on Parliamentary Tradition.
qs.kf:
☛ Where is the Whip office mentioned? → Parliamentary Tradition
☛ What is the function of Whip? → Maintain party discipline
☛ Main purpose of Whip? → Ensure members vote on party lines
☛ Types of Whip? → Single whip, double whip, triple whip
☛ What happens if a whip is violated? → Disqualification action may be taken

q: When was the Public Accounting Committee formed in India?
qs.e: The Public Accounts Committee was formed in India in the year 1921. It is a standing committee of the Parliament that examines the financial accounts of the government. Its objective is to ensure that public funds are used only for the purposes approved by Parliament. The committee consists only of Lok Sabha members. Its formation was recommended by the Indian Financial Committee in 1921. This committee plays a crucial role in ensuring financial discipline of the government.
qs.kf:
☛ Who is the chairman of the Public Accounts Committee? → Leader of Opposition
☛ How many members are in the Public Accounts Committee? → 22 members
☛ What is the main function of the Public Accounts Committee? → To examine government expenditure
☛ From which house are the members of the Public Accounts Committee? → Only Lok Sabha
☛ When was the first Public Accounts Committee formed? → 1921

q: How many members are there in the Lok Sabha according to the Constitution?
qs.e: According to Article 81 of the Indian Constitution, the maximum strength of the Lok Sabha is fixed at 552. This includes 530 members elected from states, 20 members from Union Territories, and 2 members nominated by the President from the Anglo-Indian community. This provision was part of the Constitution enacted in 1950. However, the 104th Amendment (2020) abolished the nomination of Anglo-Indian members, but the constitutional maximum remains 552. Currently, the Lok Sabha has 543 members (530 states + 13 UTs), but the constitutional upper limit is still 552.
qs.kf:
☛ What does Article 81 determine? → Maximum 552 members in Lok Sabha (530 states + 20 UTs + 2 nominated)
☛ How many members are elected from states to Lok Sabha? → 530
☛ How many seats are allocated to Union Territories in Lok Sabha? → 20
☛ Which Amendment abolished Anglo-Indian nominated members? → 104th Amendment, 2020
☛ What is the current actual strength of Lok Sabha? → 543

q: What is the minimum age limit for becoming Lok Sabha member of Parliament?
qs.e: According to Article 84 of the Indian Constitution, the minimum age to become a member of the Lok Sabha is 25 years. This provision was established by the Constituent Assembly to ensure that MPs have sufficient maturity and experience. In contrast, the minimum age for Rajya Sabha membership is 30 years, which is higher because Rajya Sabha is considered the upper house. To contest Lok Sabha elections, a candidate must also be a citizen of India and fulfill other eligibility criteria. This age limit is also explicitly mentioned in the Representation of the People Act, 1951.
qs.kf:
☛ Minimum age for Lok Sabha membership → 25 years
☛ Minimum age for Rajya Sabha membership → 30 years
☛ Related Article of Indian Constitution → Article 84
☛ Minimum age for State Legislative Assembly membership → 25 years
☛ Minimum age for President of India → 35 years

q: Which committee was entrusted with the responsibility to inspect the estimates included in the budget and suggest public spending on the 'economies'?
qs.e: In India, the responsibility to inspect the estimates included in the budget and suggest public spending on the 'economies' is entrusted to the Estimates Committee. This is a standing committee of the Lok Sabha, consisting of 30 members. Its primary function is to examine the expenditure estimates of various ministries and departments of the government and ensure efficient use of funds. The committee can also suggest savings or reappropriations in expenditure. It plays a crucial role in promoting financial discipline and efficiency in public spending. The committee examines whether the money is being used optimally and can recommend changes in budget allocations.
qs.kf:
☛ How many members are in the Estimates Committee? → 30
☛ From which house are the members of the Estimates Committee drawn? → Only Lok Sabha
☛ Who appoints the Chairman of the Estimates Committee? → Lok Sabha Speaker
☛ How many members are in the Public Accounts Committee? → 22 (15 Lok Sabha + 7 Rajya Sabha)
☛ What is the main function of the Public Accounts Committee? → To examine the reports of the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG)

q: Which of the following is the permanent house of the Indian Parliament?
qs.e: The Indian Parliament consists of two houses - Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha. Lok Sabha (Lower House) is temporary and can be dissolved. However, Rajya Sabha (Upper House) is a permanent house and cannot be dissolved. One-third of its members retire every two years. Members of Rajya Sabha are indirectly elected by the elected members of state legislative assemblies. The maximum strength of Rajya Sabha is 250, out of which 238 are elected and 12 are nominated by the President. The Vice President is the ex-officio Chairman of Rajya Sabha.
qs.kf:
☛ Permanent house of Indian Parliament → Rajya Sabha
☛ How many members are nominated by the President in Rajya Sabha? → 12
☛ Who elects the members of Rajya Sabha? → elected members of state legislative assemblies
☛ Who is the ex-officio Chairman of Rajya Sabha? → Vice President
☛ How many elected members represent states and union territories in Rajya Sabha? → 238

q: Which financial provisions of the savings constitution, like the amount sent to banks and judicial deposits, fall under?
qs.e: India's Public Account falls under Article 266(2) of the Constitution. It includes all moneys received by or on behalf of the Government of India that are not part of the Consolidated Fund. This includes amounts sent to banks, judicial deposits, provident funds, small savings, etc. These funds belong to the depositors and can be used without parliamentary approval. In contrast, the Consolidated Fund (Article 266(1)) includes all revenues and loans received by the government, and its withdrawal requires parliamentary sanction. The Contingency Fund (Article 267) is used for emergency expenditures pending parliamentary approval.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 266(2) → Related to Public Account
☛ Included in Public Account → Judicial deposits, provident funds
☛ Withdrawal from Public Account → No parliamentary approval needed
☛ Consolidated Fund → Under Article 266(1)
☛ Contingency Fund → Under Article 267

q: Voting for Demands for Grants is ________
o: By the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court
qs.e: According to the Constitution of India, voting on Demands for Grants and Money Bills is done only by the Lok Sabha. The Rajya Sabha cannot vote on these; it can only make recommendations. The President's recommendation is required before introducing a Money Bill in the Lok Sabha. Voting on Demands for Grants is a crucial part of the budget process, where the Lok Sabha approves or rejects each ministry's demands. This procedure ensures parliamentary control over finances and accountability to the people.
qs.kf:
☛ In which House is a Money Bill introduced? → Lok Sabha
☛ Who votes on Demands for Grants? → Lok Sabha
☛ What is the Rajya Sabha's power over Money Bills? → Only recommendations
☛ Which stage of budget involves voting on demands? → Voting on Demands for Grants
☛ When does voting on Demands for Grants occur? → Budget session

q: Which is the fund used by the President in unexpected situations?
qs.e: The Contingency Fund of India was established under Article 267 of the Constitution. This fund is used by the President in unexpected or emergency situations when Parliament's approval cannot be obtained immediately. The current corpus of this fund is ₹500 crore. The President can make advances from this fund, which are later recouped to the Consolidated Fund of India after obtaining parliamentary approval. This fund is distinct from the Public Account or Consolidated Fund, as it is specifically meant for unforeseen expenditures.
qs.kf:
☛ Who administers the Contingency Fund of India? → Finance Secretary
☛ Who controls the Contingency Fund? → President
☛ What is the maximum amount of the Contingency Fund? → ₹500 crore
☛ Who can make advances from the Contingency Fund? → President
☛ Under which Article was the Contingency Fund created? → Article 267

q: What year was set up as an autonomous body of the Indian Parliamentary Group?
qs.e: The Indian Parliamentary Group (IPG) was established in 1949 as an autonomous body. Its objective is to promote parliamentary practices and democratic values among members of Parliament. IPG is an informal organization of the Indian Parliament and is affiliated with the Inter-Parliamentary Union (IPU). It provides opportunities for Members of Parliament to interact and share experiences with parliaments of other countries. Since its establishment in 1949, the group has been playing a significant role in strengthening parliamentary democracy.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Indian Parliamentary Group formed? → 1949
☛ Which organization is IPG affiliated with? → Inter-Parliamentary Union (IPU)
☛ What is the main objective of IPG? → To promote parliamentary practices and democracy
☛ Where is the headquarters of IPG? → New Delhi
☛ Who are the members of IPG? → Members of the Indian Parliament

q: The offices of the Speaker and Deputy Speaker were established under which of the following Acts?
qs.e: The Government of India Act 1919, also known as the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms, established a bicameral legislature consisting of the Council of State (upper house) and the Legislative Assembly (lower house). This act for the first time created the offices of Speaker and Deputy Speaker in the Indian legislature. The Speaker presided over the proceedings of the house and maintained discipline. This provision was made to make the legislative process more orderly. The Government of India Act 1909 (Morley-Minto Reforms) increased Indian membership in the councils but did not establish the office of the Speaker.
qs.kf:
☛ Other name of Government of India Act 1919 → Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms
☛ Which house was established by this act → Bicameral legislature: Council of State and Legislative Assembly
☛ When was the office of Speaker first created → By the 1919 Act
☛ Other name of Government of India Act 1909 → Morley-Minto Reforms
☛ Meaning of bicameral system → Legislature with two houses

q: According to the Constitution, how much is the number of members in the Rajya Sabha?
qs.e: According to Article 80 of the Indian Constitution, the maximum strength of the Rajya Sabha is fixed at 250 members. Out of these, 238 members are elected representatives of states and union territories, while 12 members are nominated by the President. These nominated members are individuals having special knowledge or practical experience in fields such as literature, art, science, and social service. Currently, the actual strength of the Rajya Sabha is 245 members, but the constitutional provision allows a maximum of 250. Rajya Sabha is a permanent house and its members have a term of 6 years.
qs.kf:
☛ What is the maximum strength of Rajya Sabha? → 250
☛ How many members are nominated in Rajya Sabha? → 12
☛ What is the term of Rajya Sabha members? → 6 years
☛ By which electoral system are Rajya Sabha members elected? → Single Transferable Vote
☛ Who is the Chairman of Rajya Sabha? → Vice President of India

q: The Lok Sabha is also known as _____.
qs.e: The Lok Sabha is the lower house of the Indian Parliament, known as the House of the People because its members are directly elected by the citizens of India. According to Article 81 of the Constitution, the maximum strength of the Lok Sabha is 552 members, of which 530 represent states, 20 represent union territories, and 2 were earlier nominated by the President from the Anglo-Indian community (this provision has been abolished). The normal term of the Lok Sabha is 5 years, but the President can dissolve it earlier. The presiding officer of the Lok Sabha is called the Speaker.
qs.kf:
☛ Alternative name of Lok Sabha → House of the People
☛ Maximum strength of Lok Sabha → 552
☛ Normal term of Lok Sabha → 5 years
☛ Presiding officer of Lok Sabha → Speaker
☛ Anglo-Indian nomination in Lok Sabha → Abolished (by 104th Amendment, 2020)

q: How is the minimum age for becoming a member of the Rajya Sabha?
qs.e: According to Article 84(b) of the Indian Constitution, the minimum age to become a member of the Rajya Sabha is 30 years. This is higher than the minimum age of 25 years for the Lok Sabha, as the Rajya Sabha is designed to be a house of more experienced and mature members. The Rajya Sabha is a permanent house and its members are elected for a term of 6 years. Members of Rajya Sabha are elected by the elected members of state legislative assemblies. The Vice President of India is the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.
qs.kf:
☛ Minimum age for Lok Sabha membership → 25 years
☛ Minimum age for Rajya Sabha membership → 30 years
☛ Minimum age for President → 35 years
☛ Term of Rajya Sabha member → 6 years
☛ Ex-officio Chairman of Rajya Sabha → Vice President

q: How many sessions are there in a year in Parliament?
qs.e: The Indian Parliament holds three sessions in a year: Budget Session, Monsoon Session, and Winter Session. The Budget Session is from February to May, the Monsoon Session from July to September, and the Winter Session from November to December. The duration of each session is not fixed and is decided by the government. The Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs plans these sessions. The President addresses both houses at the beginning of each session. The Budget Session is the most important session as the Union Budget is presented during it. Each session has multiple sittings, and the government can also call a special session if needed.
qs.kf:
☛ Number of regular sessions in Indian Parliament → 3
☛ Longest session → Budget Session
☛ Shortest session → Winter Session
☛ Who summons the sessions → President
☛ Who presides over the sessions → Speaker (Lok Sabha) or Chairman (Rajya Sabha)

q: Which of the following determines whether a member of the Lok Sabha is disqualified or not?
qs.e: The Speaker of Lok Sabha determines whether a member of the Lok Sabha is disqualified. This is provided in Article 103 of the Indian Constitution, which makes the Speaker or Chairman the final authority in matters related to disqualification of members. Although the President may be consulted, the decision rests with the Speaker. Grounds for disqualification include defection under the Anti-Defection Law (10th Schedule), holding an office of profit, or other legal disqualifications. The Vice President is the Chairman of Rajya Sabha, while the Prime Minister and Chief Minister are executive heads and have no role in this decision.
qs.kf:
☛ Lok Sabha Speaker → Determines member disqualification
☛ Article 103 → Disqualification of members
☛ Anti-Defection Law → 10th Schedule
☛ Rajya Sabha Chairman → Vice President
☛ Final disqualification decision → Speaker/Chairman

q: At present, the maximum strength of Rajya Sabha is-
qs.e: Rajya Sabha is the upper house of the Indian Parliament. According to Article 80 of the Constitution, the maximum strength of Rajya Sabha is fixed at 250. Out of these, 238 members represent the states and union territories, while 12 members are nominated by the President. Currently, the actual strength of Rajya Sabha is 245, but the constitutional maximum limit remains 250. This limit was set during the framing of the Constitution and has not been amended. Rajya Sabha is a permanent house and its members have a tenure of 6 years.
qs.kf:
☛ What is the maximum strength of Rajya Sabha? → 250
☛ How many elected members are there in Rajya Sabha? → 238
☛ How many nominated members are there in Rajya Sabha? → 12
☛ What is the tenure of Rajya Sabha members? → 6 years
☛ Under which Article of the Constitution is Rajya Sabha described? → Article 80

q: The elections for Lok Sabha are held every ______ years.
qs.e: According to Article 83 of the Indian Constitution, the term of the Lok Sabha is five years, unless extended during a national emergency by one year at a time. General elections are held every five years, unless the Lok Sabha is dissolved earlier. The President has the power to dissolve the Lok Sabha, leading to mid-term elections. The first Lok Sabha was constituted in 1952. The maximum strength of the Lok Sabha is 552 members, including 530 from states, 20 from union territories, and 2 nominated from the Anglo-Indian community. The elections are conducted by the Election Commission of India using universal adult suffrage.
qs.kf:
☛ Normal term of Lok Sabha → 5 years
☛ Power to dissolve Lok Sabha → President
☛ First Lok Sabha formed → 1952
☛ Maximum members in Lok Sabha → 552
☛ Election method for Lok Sabha → Direct election

q: One-third of Rajya Sabha members retire after every
qs.e: The term of a Rajya Sabha member is 6 years, but one-third of its members retire every 2 years. This provision is mentioned in Article 83 of the Constitution. Rajya Sabha is a permanent house and cannot be dissolved. Retiring members are replaced by newly elected members, ensuring continuity of the house. Members of Rajya Sabha are elected by the elected members of state legislative assemblies using the single transferable vote system.
qs.kf:
☛ Rajya Sabha term → 6 years
☛ Retirement interval → 2 years
☛ One-third members retire → every 2 years
☛ Rajya Sabha formation → Article 80
☛ Rajya Sabha seats → maximum 250

q: The President of India is elected by
o: Elected members of Parliament, State Assemblies and Union Territories
Elected members of State Assemblies only
qs.e: According to Article 54 of the Indian Constitution, the President is elected by an Electoral College. This Electoral College consists of the elected members of both Houses of Parliament (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha), the elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of all States, and the elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of the Union Territories of Delhi and Puducherry. Nominated members do not participate in this election. The election is conducted using the single transferable vote system with secret ballot. Thus, the President is not directly elected by the people but indirectly through these elected representatives.
qs.kf:
☛ Basis of Presidential election → Article 54
☛ Members of Electoral College → Parliament, State Assemblies and 2 UTs (Delhi, Puducherry)
☛ Voting system → Single transferable vote
☛ Method of election → Secret ballot
☛ Not eligible to vote in Presidential election → Nominated members

q: The Vice-President is the ex-officio chairman of the -
qs.e: According to Article 63 of the Indian Constitution, the Vice-President is the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. He presides over the meetings of Rajya Sabha and conducts its proceedings. As the Chairman of Rajya Sabha, the Vice-President has the right to vote only in case of a tie. The Vice-President's term is 5 years and he holds the second highest office after the President. This provision is a key part of India's bicameral parliamentary system. The Vice-President is not the chairman of Lok Sabha, National Development Council, or Planning Commission.
qs.kf:
☛ Who is the ex-officio chairman of Rajya Sabha? → Vice-President
☛ When can the Vice-President vote in Rajya Sabha? → in case of a tie
☛ What is the term of the Vice-President? → 5 years
☛ What is the minimum age for Vice-President? → 35 years
☛ Who presides over Rajya Sabha in absence of Vice-President? → Deputy Chairman

q: Rajya Sabha consists of ______ members representing states and union territories.
qs.e: Rajya Sabha is the upper house of the Parliament. As per Article 80 of the Constitution, the maximum strength of Rajya Sabha is 250, of which 238 members represent states and union territories and 12 members are nominated by the President. Currently, Rajya Sabha has 245 members, out of which 233 members represent states and union territories and 12 are nominated. Representation of states is based on population, while union territories are represented as determined by Parliament. Members of Rajya Sabha are indirectly elected.
qs.kf:
☛ What is the maximum strength of Rajya Sabha? → 250
☛ How many members are nominated in Rajya Sabha? → 12
☛ What is the term of a Rajya Sabha member? → 6 years
☛ Who is the ex-officio Chairman of Rajya Sabha? → Vice-President
☛ On what basis are states represented in Rajya Sabha? → Proportional to population

q: Who is the present Speaker of Lok Sabha?
qs.e: The present Speaker of Lok Sabha is Sumitra Mahajan, who served from 2014 to 2019. She is a member of the Bharatiya Janata Party from the Indore constituency in Madhya Pradesh. The Speaker's term usually ends with the term of the Lok Sabha. This position is the presiding officer of the lower house of the Indian Parliament, responsible for conducting the business of the house and maintaining discipline among members. Sumitra Mahajan was the 16th Speaker of Lok Sabha and the second woman to hold this office.
qs.kf:
☛ First Speaker of Lok Sabha → Ganesh Vasudev Mavalankar
☛ First woman Speaker of Lok Sabha → Meira Kumar
☛ Longest serving Speaker of Lok Sabha → Balram Jakhar
☛ Who elects the Speaker of Lok Sabha → Members of Lok Sabha
☛ Term of Speaker of Lok Sabha → During the term of Lok Sabha

q: Which of the following is known as the lower house of the Indian Parliament?
qs.e: The lower house of the Indian Parliament is known as the Lok Sabha. It is directly elected by the people of India. The term of the Lok Sabha is 5 years. Its members are called Members of Parliament (MPs). The maximum strength of the Lok Sabha is 552 seats, of which 530 represent states, 20 represent union territories, and 2 are nominated from the Anglo-Indian community. The Lok Sabha has the authority to pass money bills and its presiding officer is the Speaker. The Rajya Sabha is known as the upper house.
qs.kf:
☛ Term of Lok Sabha → 5 years
☛ Maximum seats in Lok Sabha → 552
☛ Minimum age for Lok Sabha membership → 25 years
☛ Presiding officer of Lok Sabha → Speaker
☛ Method of formation of Lok Sabha → Direct election

q: Which of the following states has the largest number of representatives in the Lok Sabha?
qs.e: Among the given states, Uttar Pradesh has the highest number of representatives in the Lok Sabha with 80 seats. It is the most populous state in India, and Lok Sabha seats are allocated based on population. After Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra has 48 seats, Bihar has 40 seats, and Madhya Pradesh has 29 seats. This allocation ensures proportional representation based on population, as per the Constitution. The larger the population of a state, the more representatives it sends to the Lok Sabha. Thus, Uttar Pradesh, being the most populous, has the maximum representation.
qs.kf:
☛ State with maximum Lok Sabha seats → Uttar Pradesh (80)
☛ State with second highest Lok Sabha seats → Maharashtra (48)
☛ State with third highest Lok Sabha seats → Bihar (40)
☛ Basis of Lok Sabha seat allocation → State population
☛ Total seats in Lok Sabha → Maximum 552 (currently 543)

q: Which House of the Indian Parliament is more powerful?
o: Both Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha
qs.e: In the Indian Parliament, the Lok Sabha is more powerful because it is directly elected by the people. The Lok Sabha has exclusive authority over money bills, which the Rajya Sabha can only delay for 14 days. The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible only to the Lok Sabha, and if the Lok Sabha passes a no-confidence motion, the government must resign. The Rajya Sabha is a permanent house but cannot block money bills or remove the government. In constitutional amendments, both houses have equal power, but in ordinary legislation and control over the executive, the Lok Sabha dominates.
qs.kf:
☛ What is the term of Lok Sabha? → 5 years
☛ What is the maximum strength of Lok Sabha? → 552
☛ What is the term of Rajya Sabha members? → 6 years
☛ Which article defines a Money Bill? → Article 110
☛ How many members are required to support a no-confidence motion in Lok Sabha? → 50

q: Can the Rajya Sabha be dissolved?
o: at the discretion of the President
qs.e: The Rajya Sabha is the Upper House of the Parliament of India and is a permanent house. This means that the Rajya Sabha cannot be dissolved. While the Lok Sabha can be dissolved by the President, the Rajya Sabha continues to exist permanently. One-third of its members retire every two years and new members are elected, ensuring its continuity. This feature makes it similar to the US Senate. The main reason for the permanent nature of the Rajya Sabha is that it represents the federal structure and protects the interests of the states.
qs.kf:
☛ Term of a Rajya Sabha member → 6 years
☛ Provision for dissolution of Rajya Sabha → None (permanent house)
☛ Maximum strength of Rajya Sabha → 250
☛ Representation of states in Rajya Sabha → Unequal (based on population)
☛ Chairperson of Rajya Sabha → Vice President of India

q: In which year was the 'No Confidence Motion' introduced for the first time in the Lok Sabha?
qs.e: The first No Confidence Motion in the Lok Sabha was introduced in the year 1963. It was moved against the then Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru but was subsequently rejected. A No Confidence Motion is a crucial tool in parliamentary democracy, allowing the opposition to express lack of confidence in the government. Under Article 75 of the Constitution, the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha. Such a motion can only be introduced in the Lok Sabha, not in the Rajya Sabha. If passed, the government must resign.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the first No Confidence Motion introduced in the Lok Sabha? → 1963
☛ Which Article is related to No Confidence Motion? → Article 75
☛ In which House can a No Confidence Motion be introduced? → Lok Sabha
☛ What majority is required to pass a No Confidence Motion? → Simple majority
☛ Can a No Confidence Motion be introduced in the Rajya Sabha? → No

q: Which type of government system has been adopted in the Indian Constitution?
qs.e: The Indian Constitution has adopted a Parliamentary system of government, which is based on the British model. In this system, the President is the constitutional head, while the Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers are the real executive heads. The executive is accountable to the legislature in the parliamentary system. India has a bicameral legislature consisting of the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha. The Prime Minister is appointed by the President, and the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha. This system ensures government stability and democratic accountability.
qs.kf:
☛ India's system of government is based on → British Parliamentary model
☛ Executive responsibility in parliamentary system → accountable to legislature
☛ Constitutional head of India → President
☛ Real executive head of India → Prime Minister
☛ Term of Lok Sabha → 5 years

q: Who appoints the temporary Speaker of the Lok Sabha?
o: By former Speaker of Lok Sabha
qs.e: According to Article 94(1) of the Indian Constitution, when the office of the Speaker of the Lok Sabha is vacant, the temporary Speaker (Pro tem Speaker) is appointed by the President of India. This procedure is followed during the formation of a new Lok Sabha, until a permanent Speaker is elected. The President usually appoints one of the most senior members of the Lok Sabha as the Pro tem Speaker. The main duties of the Pro tem Speaker include administering oaths to the newly elected members and conducting the election process for the permanent Speaker.
qs.kf:
☛ Who appoints the Pro tem Speaker of Lok Sabha? → President of India
☛ Who is appointed as Pro tem Speaker? → One of the senior most members of Lok Sabha
☛ What is the role of Pro tem Speaker? → Administer oaths to new members and conduct election of permanent Speaker
☛ How is the permanent Speaker of Lok Sabha elected? → By the members of Lok Sabha among themselves
☛ Which Article deals with vacancy in the office of the Speaker? → Article 94(1)

q: What is the maximum strength of the Rajya Sabha as per the Indian Constitution?
qs.e: As per Article 80 of the Indian Constitution, the maximum strength of the Rajya Sabha is 250. Out of these, 12 members are nominated by the President from persons having special knowledge or practical experience in literature, science, art, and social service. The remaining 238 members are indirectly elected by the elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of States and Union Territories. Currently, the Rajya Sabha has 245 members, including 229 representing states, 4 representing Union Territories, and 12 nominated members. This is less than the maximum limit prescribed by the Constitution.
qs.kf:
☛ What is the maximum strength of Rajya Sabha? → 250
☛ How many members are nominated in Rajya Sabha? → 12
☛ How are Rajya Sabha members elected? → Indirectly
☛ What is the term of a Rajya Sabha member? → 6 years
☛ Who is the Chairman of Rajya Sabha? → Vice President

q: According to the Constitution, which body is responsible for creating or abolishing a legislative council in a state?
qs.e: According to Article 169 of the Indian Constitution, the power to create or abolish a Legislative Council in a state lies with the Parliament. The process begins when the state's Legislative Assembly passes a resolution with a special majority (majority of total members and at least two-thirds of members present and voting). Subsequently, the Parliament enacts a law to give effect to the resolution. Neither the President, the Governor, nor the Supreme Court has any direct role in this matter. This provision reflects the federal balance and parliamentary supremacy in the Indian Constitution.
qs.kf:
☛ Which body passes the resolution for creating a Legislative Council? → State Legislative Assembly
☛ Which Article deals with abolition of Legislative Council? → Article 169
☛ What majority is required for resolution in the Legislative Assembly? → Majority of total members and two-thirds of those present and voting
☛ How many states currently have a Legislative Council? → 6 (Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Karnataka, Maharashtra)
☛ Who presides over the Legislative Council? → Chairman (Sabhapati)

q: With regards to the Constitutional Amendment Bill, which of the following is correct?
o: It is mandatory to be passed in both houses of Parliament to become an Act.
It is mandatory to be passed in Lok Sabha only to become an Act.
It is mandatory to be passed in Rajya Sabha only to become an Act.
It is mandatory to be passed in either house of Parliament to become an Act.
qs.e: According to Article 368 of the Indian Constitution, a Constitutional Amendment Bill must be passed by both houses of Parliament (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) with a special majority to become an Act. This procedure ensures that any change to the Constitution is made with broad consensus. After being passed separately by both houses, the bill is sent to the President for assent. For certain amendments, ratification by state legislatures is also required. Thus, passing in only one house is insufficient. The special majority requires more than 50% of the total membership of the house and at least two-thirds of the members present and voting.
qs.kf:
☛ Majority required to pass constitutional amendment bill → Special majority (majority of total members and at least two-thirds of members present and voting)
☛ Role of President → President's assent is mandatory; cannot withhold it
☛ Word used in Article 368 → 'passed by both Houses'
☛ Types of amendments under Article 368 → Simple majority, special majority, and amendments requiring state consent
☛ First Constitutional Amendment → was done in 1951

q: Which of the following committees is responsible for examining the conduct of Members of Parliament?
qs.e: The responsibility of examining the conduct of Members of Parliament lies with the Committee on Privileges. This committee investigates cases of breach of privilege or contempt of the House. In the Indian Parliament, both Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha have their own committees on privileges. It considers complaints related to the conduct of members and recommends appropriate action. Other committees like the Public Accounts Committee examine financial matters, while the Committee on Rules deals with parliamentary procedure rules.
qs.kf:
☛ Main function of Committee on Privileges → Investigating breach of members' privileges
☛ Function of Public Accounts Committee → Audit of government accounts
☛ Function of Committee on Rules → Determining parliamentary rules
☛ Committee on Public Undertakings → Examining public sector enterprises
☛ Membership of Committee on Privileges → 15 in Lok Sabha, 10 in Rajya Sabha

q: Which of the following authorities decides, how far the fundamental rights can apply to the members of the armed forces in India?
qs.e: Article 33 of the Indian Constitution empowers the Parliament to determine the extent to which fundamental rights apply to members of the armed forces, paramilitary forces, intelligence agencies, and police forces. This provision ensures discipline and the proper discharge of duties by restricting certain fundamental rights through legislation. The Parliament can enact laws that abrogate or restrict the fundamental rights of these forces. The President, Supreme Court, or the armed forces themselves do not have this authority. This power is exclusive to Parliament to maintain national security and operational efficiency. The purpose is to balance individual rights with the needs of the armed forces.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 33 → Parliament can restrict fundamental rights for armed forces.
☛ Article 34 → Allows restriction of fundamental rights during martial law.
☛ Article 35 → Parliament has power to make laws implementing fundamental rights.
☛ AFSPA → Enacted by Parliament, gives special powers to armed forces in disturbed areas.
☛ Restriction on fundamental rights → Only Parliament can impose through law, not executive.

q: Which of the following parts of the Indian Constitution outlines the powers and procedures of the Parliament?
qs.e: Part V (Articles 52-151) of the Indian Constitution deals with the Union Executive, Legislature, and Judiciary. It specifically outlines the powers, structure, and procedures of the Parliament, including the formation of Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha, qualifications of members, sessions, legislative process, money bills, joint sittings, and parliamentary committees. This part also covers the President's powers and election, as the President is an integral part of Parliament. Articles 79 to 122 detail parliamentary affairs such as the Speaker and Deputy Speaker, privileges of members, and the procedure for lawmaking. Hence, Part V is the core section defining Parliament's authority and functioning.
qs.kf:
☛ Which part covers Parliament's powers? → Part V
☛ Article 85 provides for? → Sessions of Parliament
☛ Definition of Money Bill is in? → Article 110
☛ Article 93 deals with? → Election of Lok Sabha Speaker
☛ Parliamentary privileges are in? → Article 105

q: Which of the following do NOT participate in the election of the President of India?
o: Elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of Delhi and Puducherry
Elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of states
Nominated members of both Houses of Parliament and Members of Jammu and Kashmir Legislative Assembly
Elected members of both Houses of Parliament
qs.e: In the election of the President of India, only elected members are eligible to vote. Nominated members of both Houses of Parliament (Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha) do not participate because they are not elected by the people. Members of the Jammu and Kashmir Legislative Assembly also do not participate, as Jammu and Kashmir has lost its statehood and is now a Union Territory. In contrast, elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of Delhi and Puducherry do participate, as per Article 54 of the Constitution, which includes elected members of state assemblies and both Houses of Parliament. Nominated members are excluded from the electoral college to maintain the principle of direct election by the people's representatives.
qs.kf:
☛ Who participates in Presidential election? → Elected members of state assemblies and both Houses of Parliament
☛ Who does NOT participate? → Nominated members and Jammu & Kashmir Assembly members
☛ Role of Delhi and Puducherry? → Their elected MLAs vote in the election
☛ Why J&K Assembly members excluded? → Because J&K lost statehood status
☛ What does Article 54 state? → It includes elected members in Presidential election

q: Who among the following appoints the Speaker Pro Tem of the Lok Sabha?
o: The Speaker of the previous Lok Sabha
qs.e: The Speaker Pro Tem of the Lok Sabha is appointed by the President. This appointment typically takes place before the first session of the newly elected Lok Sabha. The primary duty of the Speaker Pro Tem is to administer oaths to the new members and to oversee the election process for the Speaker. Usually, the most senior member of the House is chosen for this role. This process follows the provisions of the Indian Constitution, which grants certain powers to the President regarding the functioning of the Lok Sabha. The Speaker Pro Tem holds office until a regular Speaker is elected.
qs.kf:
☛ Who appoints the Speaker Pro Tem of Lok Sabha? → The President
☛ Main duty of Speaker Pro Tem? → Administer oaths to new members and conduct Speaker election
☛ Who is usually made Speaker Pro Tem? → The most senior member
☛ How long does Speaker Pro Tem serve? → Until a new Speaker is elected
☛ Which article deals with this? → Article 93 and related provisions

q: __________ has the power to amend the Constitution of India.
qs.e: The power to amend the Constitution of India rests with the Parliament. This power is outlined in Article 368 of the Constitution. An amendment bill must be passed by both houses (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) with a special majority. For certain amendments affecting the federal structure, ratification by at least half of the state legislatures is also required. The President gives assent to the amendment bill but does not have the power to propose amendments. Thus, Parliament holds the primary authority in the amendment process.
qs.kf:
☛ Who has the power to amend the Constitution? → The Parliament
☛ Which article deals with the amendment process? → Article 368
☛ What majority is required for an amendment bill? → Special majority
☛ When is state ratification required? → For amendments related to federal structure
☛ What is the President's role? → To give assent to the amendment bill

q: To pass a Constitutional Amendment Bill in the Lok Sabha, which of the following correctly states the minimum support required?
o: Two-thirds majority of the total membership of the House
Simple majority of Lok Sabha members and two-thirds of Rajya Sabha members present and voting
Unanimous vote of all Members of Parliament
Majority of the total membership and two-thirds of members present and voting
qs.e: As per Article 368 of the Indian Constitution, a Constitutional Amendment Bill requires the fulfillment of two conditions for passage in each House of Parliament. First, the bill must be supported by a majority of the total membership of that House. This means that more than half of the total members of the House must vote in favor of the bill. Second, the bill must be supported by a two-thirds majority of the members present and voting. This special majority ensures broad consensus for the amendment. Thus, both conditions must be satisfied simultaneously for the bill to pass. Option 1 only requires a two-thirds majority of total membership, which is incorrect. Option 2 incorrectly combines a simple majority in Lok Sabha with two-thirds in Rajya Sabha. Option 3 demands a unanimous vote, which is not constitutionally required.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Article provides for Constitutional Amendment? → Article 368
☛ What type of majority is required for Constitutional Amendment? → Majority of total membership and two-thirds of members present and voting
☛ What majority is needed to pass a Money Bill? → Simple majority
☛ What is the procedure for Constitutional Amendment in Rajya Sabha? → Same dual condition as Lok Sabha
☛ Is President's prior assent required for a Constitutional Amendment Bill? → No, but President's assent is required after passage

q: Which of the following Acts marked the beginning of British parliamentary control over the East India Company?
qs.e: The Regulating Act of 1773 marks the beginning of British parliamentary control over the East India Company. This Act introduced government oversight into the Company's affairs. It transformed the Governor of Bengal into the Governor-General and appointed Warren Hastings as the first Governor-General. The Act also established a Supreme Court at Calcutta. Prior to this, the Company operated with considerable independence.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Regulating Act passed? → 1773
☛ Who became the first Governor-General? → Warren Hastings
☛ Which court was established by this Act? → Supreme Court (Calcutta)
☛ Whose control did this Act impose on the Company? → British Parliament
☛ Was the Board of Control formed under this Act? → No (it was formed under Pitt's India Act 1784)

q: Which of the following Parliamentary Committees of India is considered a ‘Financial Committee’?
o: Committee on Welfare of SCs and STs
qs.e: The Indian Parliament has three Financial Committees: Estimates Committee, Public Accounts Committee, and Committee on Public Undertakings. The Estimates Committee was established in 1950 and consists of 30 members, all from Lok Sabha. Its main function is to examine government budget estimates and suggest efficiencies. It reviews expenditures of ministries and departments and reports to Parliament. Among the other options, the Committee on Welfare of SCs and STs, Committee on Petitions, and Committee on Privileges are not financial committees.
qs.kf:
☛ Three Financial Committees of India → Estimates Committee, Public Accounts Committee, Committee on Public Undertakings
☛ Members of Estimates Committee → 30 (all from Lok Sabha)
☛ Function of Estimates Committee → Examines budget estimates
☛ Year of establishment of Estimates Committee → 1950
☛ Members of Public Accounts Committee → 22 (15 Lok Sabha + 7 Rajya Sabha)

q: Which of the following Articles of the Indian Constitution defines the money bill?
qs.e: Article 110 of the Indian Constitution defines a money bill. A money bill is a bill that contains provisions such as imposition of taxes, borrowing of money, expenditure from the Consolidated Fund, or expenditure from the Contingency Fund of India. According to this article, a money bill can only be introduced in the Lok Sabha and requires prior recommendation of the President. The Rajya Sabha can only delay the bill for 14 days and cannot amend it. If the Rajya Sabha does not return the bill within 14 days, it is deemed passed. Article 112 deals with the budget, Article 117 deals with special procedures for financial bills, and Article 105 deals with privileges of members of Parliament.
qs.kf:
☛ Article defining money bill → Article 110
☛ House where money bill is introduced → Only Lok Sabha
☛ Time limit for Rajya Sabha on money bill → 14 days
☛ Article related to budget → Article 112
☛ Article related to financial bills procedure → Article 117

q: After its 1971 electoral victory, Indira Gandhi’s government amended the Constitution to remove legal obstacles to abolishing which of the following privileges?
o: Privy purses of former princely rulers
qs.e: After a landslide victory in the 1971 general election, Prime Minister Indira Gandhi's government moved to abolish the privy purses and privileges of former princely rulers. These privileges were enshrined in Articles 291 and 362 of the Indian Constitution. However, the Supreme Court in 1971 ruled that the law abolishing privy purses was unconstitutional. In response, the government passed the 26th Constitutional Amendment (1971), which deleted Articles 291 and 362 and derecognized the princely states. This amendment removed all legal obstacles to ending the privy purses and other privileges.
qs.kf:
☛ 26th Constitutional Amendment → Passed in 1971
☛ Privy purses were related to → Former princely rulers
☛ Which article dealt with privy purses? → Article 291
☛ Prime Minister who abolished privy purses → Indira Gandhi
☛ Articles repealed by 26th Amendment → Articles 291 and 362

q: According to Article 79 of the Indian Constitution, the Parliament of India consists of:
o: only Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha
Prime Minister, Lok Sabha, and Rajya Sabha
President, Lok Sabha, and Rajya Sabha
President, Vice President, and Prime Minister
qs.e: Article 79 of the Indian Constitution states that the Parliament of India consists of three components: the President, Lok Sabha, and Rajya Sabha. The President is an integral part of Parliament, though not a member of either house. He summons, prorogues, and dissolves Parliament. Lok Sabha is the lower house, directly elected by the people, while Rajya Sabha is the upper house, indirectly elected. Thus, option 3 is correct. Other options are incorrect as the Prime Minister or Vice President are not parts of Parliament as per Article 79.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 79 → Parliament consists of President, Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha
☛ Article 74 → Council of Ministers aids the Prime Minister
☛ Tenure of Lok Sabha → 5 years
☛ Maximum strength of Rajya Sabha → 250
☛ President's role in Parliament → Part of Parliament but not a member

q: Which of the following is NOT an instrument of parliamentary control over the executive in India?
o: Question Hour in the Lok Sabha
Approval of government bills (laws) by the Parliament
No-confidence motion against the Council of Ministers
qs.e: In India, instruments of parliamentary control over the executive include Question Hour, approval of government bills, and no-confidence motion. These enable Parliament to oversee the executive. Judicial review is the power of the judiciary to examine the constitutionality of executive actions, which is not a parliamentary instrument. It is a function of the judiciary, not Parliament. Parliamentary control ensures the executive is accountable to Parliament.
qs.kf:
☛ Purpose of Question Hour → To obtain oral answers from ministers
☛ No-confidence motion → Means to remove the executive
☛ Approval of bills → Control over government policies
☛ Judicial review → Examination of laws under Constitution
☛ Parliamentary control → Ensures accountability of executive

q: The All India Services in India are created under which Article of the Constitution?
qs.e: The All India Services in India are created under Article 312 of the Constitution. This article empowers the Parliament to create All India Services for services of national importance. Currently, there are three All India Services: Indian Administrative Service (IAS), Indian Police Service (IPS), and Indian Forest Service (IFoS). Under Article 312, to create a new All India Service, a resolution must be passed by the Rajya Sabha with at least a two-thirds majority of members present and voting. This provision is part of Part XIV (Articles 308 to 323) of the Constitution. Article 320 deals with the Union Public Service Commission, while Article 206 and 107 relate to state finances and bills respectively.
qs.kf:
☛ Constitutional basis of All India Services → Article 312
☛ Number of current All India Services → 3
☛ Majority required in Rajya Sabha for new service → Special majority (2/3)
☛ Not included in All India Services → Indian Revenue Service (IRS)
☛ Article 312 is in which Part → Part XIV

q: Who presides over the sessions of the Vidhan Sabha in a State?
o: The Chief Minister of the State
qs.e: According to Article 178 of the Indian Constitution, the Vidhan Sabha elects a Speaker and a Deputy Speaker from among its members. The Speaker presides over the sessions of the Vidhan Sabha. In their absence, the Deputy Speaker presides. The Governor is not a member of the house; they summon the session and deliver the address. The Chief Minister leads the government but does not preside over the house. The Speaker ensures the orderly conduct of business, maintains discipline, and grants members the opportunity to speak. Thus, the sessions of the Vidhan Sabha are presided over by the Speaker elected by its members.
qs.kf:
☛ Who elects the Vidhan Sabha Speaker? → Members of Vidhan Sabha
☛ Who presides in the absence of Speaker? → Deputy Speaker
☛ When does the Governor address the Vidhan Sabha? → At the start of the session
☛ To whom does the Speaker submit resignation? → Deputy Speaker
☛ Under which Article is the Speaker elected? → Article 178

q: What did the Supreme Court decide in the Kesavananda Bharati case (1973) about the powers of Parliament to amend the Constitution of India?
o: The President of India has the ultimate authority to approve or reject constitutional amendments independently.
The Parliament cannot amend any part of the Constitution under any circumstances.
The Parliament can amend the Constitution, but it cannot change or destroy its basic structure or essential features.
The Parliament has unlimited power to amend any part of the Constitution, including the Fundamental Rights.
qs.e: In the Kesavananda Bharati case (1973), the Supreme Court propounded the Basic Structure Doctrine. The Court held that while Parliament has the power to amend the Constitution, it cannot destroy or alter its basic structure. The basic structure includes supremacy of the Constitution, rule of law, separation of powers, judicial review, secularism, federalism, and fundamental rights. This ruling limited Parliament's amending power and empowered the judiciary to review constitutional amendments. The doctrine safeguards the democratic and essential features of the Indian Constitution.
qs.kf:
☛ Which case established the Basic Structure Doctrine? → Kesavananda Bharati (1973)
☛ How many judges were in the Kesavananda Bharati bench? → 13 judges
☛ What is included in the basic structure? → Supremacy of Constitution, rule of law, separation of powers, judicial review, secularism, federalism
☛ Can Parliament amend Fundamental Rights? → Yes, but cannot violate the basic structure
☛ Which case established judicial review of amendments? → Kesavananda Bharati

q: Which of the following Committees is a Standing Committee of the Parliament?
qs.e: The Public Accounts Committee (PAC) is a Standing Committee of Parliament, established in 1921 under the Government of India Act 1919. It examines the annual audit reports of the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) of India. The PAC consists of 22 members: 15 from Lok Sabha and 7 from Rajya Sabha. The Chairman is appointed by the Speaker of Lok Sabha, and by convention, the Chairman is from the opposition party. Other options like Delimitation Commission are not a permanent body, while Joint Parliamentary Committee on 2G Spectrum and Select Committee on a Bill are ad hoc committees. Standing Committees are permanent and constituted every year or periodically.
qs.kf:
☛ Total members in PAC → 22
☛ Chairman of PAC is appointed by → Speaker of Lok Sabha
☛ Year of establishment of PAC → 1921
☛ Total Standing Committees in Parliament → 24
☛ PAC examines reports of → CAG

q: Under what conditions can the Parliament legislate on matters in the State List according to constitutional provisions?
o: When the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution.
During a national emergency declared under Article 352.
If the President signs a proclamation without Parliament's involvement.
If a Governor requests it due to a financial emergency in the state.
qs.e: Under Article 249 of the Constitution, if the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution by a 2/3 majority of members present and voting that it is necessary in the national interest for Parliament to legislate on a matter in the State List, Parliament can do so. The resolution remains valid for a maximum of one year and can be renewed. During a national emergency under Article 352, Parliament can also legislate on State List subjects, but the question specifically refers to conditions under constitutional provisions, and Article 249 is the primary provision. Other options, like the President's proclamation or a Governor's request, are not constitutional provisions for such legislation. Thus, the correct condition is when the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 249 → Allows Parliament to legislate on State List if Rajya Sabha passes a resolution.
☛ Majority required for Rajya Sabha resolution → 2/3 of members present and voting.
☛ Maximum duration of resolution → One year, extendable.
☛ Article 352 → National emergency empowers Parliament to legislate on State List.
☛ Article 250 → Parliament's power to legislate on State List during emergency.

q: What is the primary function of the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) of the Indian Parliament?
o: To assist in the election of the Speaker
qs.e: The Public Accounts Committee (PAC) is a key standing committee of the Indian Parliament, constituted in 1921. Its primary function is to examine the audit reports of the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG). The committee ensures that public funds are used legally, efficiently, and for the intended purposes. It identifies financial irregularities in ministries and departments and reports its findings to Parliament. The PAC consists of 22 members, with 15 from the Lok Sabha and 7 from the Rajya Sabha. The chairman is appointed by the Speaker of the Lok Sabha. The committee plays a vital role in ensuring financial accountability of the executive.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the PAC constituted? → 1921
☛ How many members are in the PAC? → 22
☛ Who appoints the chairman of PAC? → Speaker of Lok Sabha
☛ Whose reports does the PAC examine? → CAG audit reports
☛ How many Lok Sabha members are in PAC? → 15

q: What was the main objective of the Pitt’s India Act of 1784, passed by the British Parliament?
qs.e: The Pitt's India Act of 1784, passed by the British Parliament, aimed to address the maladministration of the East India Company. Its main objective was to establish a dual system of government in India by creating a Board of Control in Britain to oversee political and military affairs, while the Company's Court of Directors retained commercial functions. This act amended the Regulating Act of 1773 and increased British government control over Indian affairs. By separating commercial and political powers, it sought to curb the company's mismanagement and introduce greater parliamentary supervision. Thus, establishing a dual government was the core purpose of the Pitt's India Act, making 'establish dual government' the correct answer.
qs.kf:
☛ When was Pitt's India Act passed? → 1784
☛ Who headed the Board of Control? → British Chancellor of the Exchequer
☛ What system did Pitt's India Act introduce? → Dual government
☛ Which act did Pitt's India Act amend? → Regulating Act of 1773
☛ Which two bodies comprised the dual government? → Court of Directors and Board of Control

q: In India, how many sessions of Parliament are held in a year?
qs.e: The Indian Parliament holds three sessions in a year: Budget Session, Monsoon Session, and Winter Session. The Budget Session runs from February to May, the Monsoon Session from July to September, and the Winter Session from November to December. These sessions are summoned by the President under Article 85 of the Constitution. Each session includes sittings of both Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha. The Budget Session is the longest session, during which the General Budget and Railway Budget are presented.
qs.kf:
☛ What are the three sessions of Parliament? → Budget, Monsoon, Winter
☛ Which is the longest session? → Budget Session
☛ Who summons the sessions? → President
☛ Under which article are sessions summoned? → Article 85
☛ When does the Monsoon Session take place? → July to September

q: The maximum interval between two sessions of state assembly can be ____.
qs.e: According to Article 174 of the Indian Constitution, the maximum interval between two sessions of a state legislative assembly cannot exceed 6 months. This provision is similar to Article 85 for the Parliament. The Governor summons and prorogues the sessions of the state assembly from time to time. This ensures that the assembly meets at least twice a year, maintaining democratic accountability. If the gap between two sessions exceeds 6 months, it would be considered a constitutional violation. The provision aims to ensure continuous legislative oversight and prevent executive overreach.
qs.kf:
☛ Maximum gap between state assembly sessions → 6 months
☛ Article 174 → related to sessions of state legislature
☛ Similar provision for Parliament → Article 85
☛ Power of Governor → summon and prorogue assembly sessions
☛ Minimum meetings per year → at least two

q: Speaker of Lok Sabha Sumitra Mahajan represents which constituency?
A. Amethi
B. Varanasi
C. Indore
D. Patna
qs.e: Sumitra Mahajan served as the Speaker of the Lok Sabha and represented the Indore constituency in Madhya Pradesh. She was a member of the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and held the position of Speaker from 2014 to 2019. Indore is a major urban parliamentary constituency in Madhya Pradesh. She was affectionately known as 'Mai' and was elected as a Member of Parliament eight times consecutively.
qs.kf:
☛ First Speaker of Lok Sabha → Ganesh Vasudev Mavalankar
☛ First Woman Speaker of Lok Sabha → Meira Kumar
☛ State represented by Sumitra Mahajan → Madhya Pradesh
☛ Political party of Sumitra Mahajan → Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP)
☛ Current Speaker of Lok Sabha → Om Birla

q: How many members are nominated by the President of India in the Lok Sabha from the Anglo-Indian community?
qs.e: According to Article 331 of the Indian Constitution, the President can nominate a maximum of 2 members from the Anglo-Indian community to the Lok Sabha if the community is not adequately represented. This provision existed since the Constitution came into effect in 1950. However, the 104th Constitutional Amendment Act (2020) abolished the nomination and reserved seats for the Anglo-Indian community in the Lok Sabha and state legislative assemblies. Despite this, based on the original provision, the answer remains 2. This nomination was intended to ensure representation for a minority community that otherwise had limited electoral presence.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 331 → Deals with nomination of Anglo-Indian members in Lok Sabha
☛ 104th Amendment (2020) → Ended Anglo-Indian reservation and nomination
☛ Maximum nominated members → 2
☛ This provision → Not applicable to Rajya Sabha
☛ 110th Amendment → Similar provision existed for state assemblies

q: The Right to Free and Compulsory Education Act was passed by Parliament in the year ______
qs.e: The Right to Free and Compulsory Education Act (RTE Act) was passed by the Indian Parliament in 2009. It came into force on 1 April 2010. The act aims to provide free and compulsory education to all children aged 6 to 14 years. It implements the right to education as a fundamental right, which was added by the 86th Constitutional Amendment (2002). Under this law, private schools must reserve 25% of seats for children from economically weaker sections. Monitoring mechanisms at district and state levels ensure compliance.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the RTE Act passed by Parliament? → 2009
☛ When did the RTE Act come into force? → 1 April 2010
☛ Which age group does the RTE Act cover? → 6-14 years
☛ Which constitutional amendment made education a fundamental right? → 86th Amendment, 2002
☛ What percentage of seats are reserved in private schools under RTE? → 25%

q: The upper house of Indian parliament is:
qs.e: The Indian Parliament is bicameral, with the Rajya Sabha as the upper house and Lok Sabha as the lower house. Rajya Sabha is also known as the Council of States. Its members are indirectly elected, and its maximum strength is 250, of which 238 represent states and union territories and 12 are nominated by the President. Rajya Sabha is a permanent house and cannot be dissolved; one-third of its members retire every two years. The Vice President of India is the ex-officio Chairman of Rajya Sabha.
qs.kf:
☛ Who is the Chairman of Rajya Sabha? → Vice President of India
☛ What is the term of a Rajya Sabha member? → 6 years
☛ What is the maximum strength of Rajya Sabha? → 250
☛ How many members of Rajya Sabha are nominated by the President? → 12
☛ Under which Article is Rajya Sabha constituted? → Article 80

q: Who was the first chairman of the Rajya Sabha?
qs.e: Dr. Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan was the first Vice President of India (1952-1962), who serves as the ex-officio Chairman of Rajya Sabha. Hence, he became the first Chairman of Rajya Sabha. He assumed office on 13 May 1952. Dr. Radhakrishnan was a renowned philosopher and educationist, who later served as the second President (1962-1967). His birthday (5 September) is celebrated as Teacher's Day in India.
