Other options: Shri M Hidayatullah was the sixth Vice President, Dr. Zakir Husain was the first Muslim President, and Shri VV Giri was the fourth President.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the first Chairman of Rajya Sabha? → Dr. Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan
☛ Who was the first Vice President of India? → Dr. Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan
☛ Who was the second President of India? → Dr. Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan
☛ When is Teacher's Day celebrated in India? → 5 September
☛ Who holds the office of Chairman of Rajya Sabha? → Vice President of India

q: A parliamentary executive is:
o: where the parliament functions as the executive
an executive where there is a parliament
an executive elected by the parliament
an executive who is dependent on the support of the majority in the parliament
qs.e: A parliamentary executive is a system in which the executive (council of ministers) depends on the support of the majority in the lower house of parliament for its existence and tenure. This system is based on the Westminster model, followed in countries like India, the United Kingdom, Canada, and Australia. In this system, the President or Monarch is the nominal head, while the Prime Minister is the real executive head. The council of ministers is collectively responsible to the parliament. If the government loses a confidence vote, it must resign or call for new elections. This arrangement ensures the stability and accountability of the government.
qs.kf:
☛ Who is the real executive head in a parliamentary system? → Prime Minister
☛ From which country did India adopt the parliamentary system? → United Kingdom
☛ To whom is the council of ministers responsible? → Parliament
☛ What type of head is the President considered? → Nominal head
☛ What happens if the government loses a confidence vote? → Resignation or new elections

q: The Central Government is bound to present the 'Annual Financial Report/Statement' as per ________ of the Constitution of India.
qs.e: Article 112 of the Indian Constitution mandates the Central Government to present an Annual Financial Statement (Budget) before Parliament for each financial year. It is called the Annual Financial Statement or Budget. It contains estimates of income and expenditure. Article 110 deals with Money Bills, Article 111 deals with President's assent to bills, and Article 113 deals with demands for grants. The Annual Financial Statement under Article 112 comprises three parts: Consolidated Fund, Contingency Fund, and Public Account. This statement is discussed and voted upon in Parliament.
qs.kf:
☛ Article for presenting Annual Financial Statement → Article 112
☛ Article related to Money Bill → Article 110
☛ Article related to President's assent to bills → Article 111
☛ Article related to demands for grants → Article 113
☛ Three parts of Budget → Consolidated Fund, Contingency Fund, Public Account

q: A civil servant is NOT allowed to become which of the following?
o: Private Secretary to Minister of the Union
qs.e: In India, civil servants (e.g., IAS, IPS officers) are required to maintain political neutrality under the Constitution and service rules. They cannot participate in active politics, which includes becoming a member of Parliament or state legislature. This restriction applies during their service tenure, while after retirement they can join politics. Positions like Private Secretary to a Union Minister, Cabinet Secretary, or Vice-Chancellor of a university are within the government service framework, so they can hold these. The key principle is that civil servants must stay away from political offices to ensure impartiality and neutrality.
qs.kf:
☛ Civil servants cannot hold political offices → Cannot become MP/MLA during service
☛ Allowable positions for civil servants → Private Secretary to Minister, Cabinet Secretary, Vice-Chancellor
☛ Political neutrality of civil servants in India → Ensured by Article 19 of Constitution and service rules
☛ After retirement, civil servants → Can join politics
☛ To become Member of Parliament, a civil servant must → First resign from service

q: What is the maximum time gap between two successive sessions of the Parliament?
qs.e: The maximum gap between two successive sessions of the Indian Parliament is six months, as per Article 85 of the Constitution. This constitutional requirement ensures that Parliament meets at least twice a year, and the interval between sessions does not exceed six months. This provision maintains continuity and accountability in democratic governance. There are three sessions of Parliament: Budget Session (February-May), Monsoon Session (July-September), and Winter Session (November-December). This rule is derived from the British parliamentary tradition.
qs.kf:
☛ What is the maximum gap between two sessions of Parliament? → 6 months
☛ Which Article of the Indian Constitution deals with this? → Article 85
☛ Which is the longest session of Parliament? → Budget Session
☛ How many sessions are held in a year in the Indian Parliament? → Three sessions
☛ Who addresses the first sitting of each session of Parliament? → The President

q: How many days can the Rajya Sabha delay the finance bill passed by the Lok Sabha?
qs.e: Under Article 110 of the Indian Constitution, a finance bill is defined. It is a special type of money bill related to taxation, government expenditure, and financial matters. According to Article 109, after being passed by the Lok Sabha, the finance bill is sent to the Rajya Sabha. The Rajya Sabha can delay this bill only for 14 days. If the Rajya Sabha does not return the bill or pass it within 14 days, it is deemed to have been passed by both houses. This provision ensures the financial supremacy of the Lok Sabha. Note that this period differs for ordinary bills. The finance bill cannot be amended by the Rajya Sabha; it can only recommend changes.
qs.kf:
☛ Which article defines the Finance Bill? → Article 110
☛ What is the maximum period for which Rajya Sabha can delay a Finance Bill? → 14 days
☛ Which article deals with Money Bills? → Article 109
☛ What is the difference between a Finance Bill and a Money Bill? → Finance Bill deals with financial matters while Money Bill is a specific type.
☛ What happens if Rajya Sabha does not return a Finance Bill within 14 days? → The bill is deemed passed.

q: The quorum required in the Rajya Sabha is:
qs.e: The quorum required for the proceedings of the Rajya Sabha is one-tenth of the total membership of the House. The maximum strength of the Rajya Sabha is 250, out of which 238 members represent states and union territories, and 12 members are nominated by the President. Currently, the total membership of the Rajya Sabha is 245. Thus, one-tenth of 245 is 24.5, which is taken as 25. If there is no quorum, the Chairman may adjourn the House or suspend the proceedings. This provision is given under Article 100 of the Constitution.
qs.kf:
☛ What is the maximum strength of Rajya Sabha? → 250
☛ How many nominated members are there in Rajya Sabha? → 12
☛ What is the quorum required in Lok Sabha? → 55
☛ Under which Article is the quorum provision mentioned? → Article 100
☛ What is the current strength of Rajya Sabha? → 245

q: Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the:
qs.e: According to Article 75(3) of the Indian Constitution, the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha. This is a fundamental principle of the parliamentary system of government, where the executive (Council of Ministers) is accountable to the legislature (Lok Sabha). If the Lok Sabha passes a vote of no-confidence against the Council of Ministers, the entire council must resign. The President is the constitutional head but acts on the advice of the Prime Minister. The Rajya Sabha cannot bring a no-confidence motion. The Prime Minister is the head of the council, but collective responsibility is towards the Lok Sabha.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Article deals with collective responsibility of Council of Ministers? → Article 75(3)
☛ In which house can a no-confidence motion be moved? → Only in Lok Sabha
☛ Which house cannot pass a no-confidence motion against the Council of Ministers? → Rajya Sabha
☛ What type of government system does India follow? → Parliamentary system
☛ After which amendment is the President bound to follow the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers? → 42nd Amendment

q: Who presided over the first session of Indian National Congress?
qs.e: The first session of the Indian National Congress was held on 28 December 1885 at Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College in Bombay (now Mumbai). It was presided over by Womesh Chandra Bannerjee (W.C. Bannerjee), a prominent Indian lawyer and nationalist leader. A total of 72 delegates attended this session. The Congress was founded by A.O. Hume, a retired British civil servant. Dadabhai Naoroji presided over the second session (1886, Calcutta). S.N. Banerjee was one of the co-founders but not the president of the first session.
qs.kf:
☛ When was Congress founded? → 1885
☛ Who was the president of the first session? → W.C. Bannerjee
☛ Venue of the first session? → Bombay (Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College)
☛ Who was the founder of Congress? → A.O. Hume
☛ President of the second session? → Dadabhai Naoroji

q: When was the RTI Act passed by the Indian Parliament and when did it get the Presidential assent?
qs.e: The Indian Parliament passed the RTI Act in May 2005 and it received the President's assent in June 2005. This Act provides the Right to Information, ensuring transparency and accountability in government functioning. It came into full force on 12 October 2005. The RTI Act strengthens freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a) of the Indian Constitution. It covers government institutions and public authorities, enabling citizens to access any government document or information.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the RTI Act passed? → May 2005
☛ When did the RTI Act get Presidential assent? → June 2005
☛ When did the RTI Act come into full force? → 12 October 2005
☛ Which article of the Constitution is related to RTI Act? → Article 19(1)(a)
☛ Full form of RTI? → Right to Information Act

q: Who presides over the first meeting of a newly constituted Lok Sabha?
qs.e: The first meeting of a newly constituted Lok Sabha is presided over by the Protem Speaker. According to Article 94 of the Constitution, when the Lok Sabha is dissolved or newly elected, the President appoints one of the senior-most members as the Protem Speaker. The Protem Speaker administers the oath of office to the newly elected members and conducts the election of the new Speaker. Until the permanent Speaker is elected, the Protem Speaker manages the proceedings of the House. This practice ensures a smooth transition and upholds democratic traditions in the functioning of the lower house of Parliament.
qs.kf:
☛ Who appoints the Protem Speaker? → The President
☛ Which article deals with the Protem Speaker? → Article 94
☛ Who does the Protem Speaker swear in? → Newly elected MPs
☛ How long does the Protem Speaker serve? → Until the Speaker is elected
☛ Who elects the Speaker of Lok Sabha? → Members of Lok Sabha

q: Who among the following publishes the 'Economic Survey' in India?
qs.e: In India, the Economic Survey is published by the Ministry of Finance under the Department of Economic Affairs. It is presented in Parliament before the budget as per Article 112 of the Constitution. The Economic Survey provides an annual review of the country's economy, focusing on growth, inflation, employment, and fiscal policy. The Chief Economic Advisor plays a key role in its preparation. NITI Aayog, the Central Statistical Organisation (now part of Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation), or RBI do not publish the Economic Survey. Hence, the correct option is Ministry of Finance.
qs.kf:
☛ When is the Economic Survey presented? → In Parliament before the Union Budget.
☛ Which article mandates the Economic Survey? → Article 112 of the Constitution.
☛ Who drafts the Economic Survey? → A team led by the Chief Economic Advisor.
☛ What does the Economic Survey cover? → Analysis of various sectors and assessment of government schemes.
☛ What is the main objective of the Economic Survey? → To present an annual record of the nation's economic performance.

q: What is the duration of the term of a Rajya Sabha MP?
qs.e: The Rajya Sabha is the upper house of the Indian Parliament. The term of its members is six years. It is a permanent house and one-third of its members retire every two years. Members of Rajya Sabha are indirectly elected by the elected members of the state legislative assemblies. The President nominates 12 members for their special contributions in fields like art, literature, science, and social service. Rajya Sabha is constituted under Article 80 of the Constitution.
qs.kf:
☛ Term of a Rajya Sabha member → Six years
☛ How many members are in Rajya Sabha? → Maximum 250 (245 currently)
☛ Who elects Rajya Sabha members? → Elected members of state legislative assemblies
☛ Number of nominated members in Rajya Sabha → 12 (by President)
☛ How many members retire every two years in Rajya Sabha? → One-third

q: The Vice-President of India is elected by the:
o: members of both houses of parliament
members of the houses of parliament and state legislative assemblies
qs.e: The Vice-President of India is elected by the members of both houses of Parliament (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha). The election is conducted through proportional representation by means of single transferable vote. The Vice-President serves a term of 5 years and acts as the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. It is important to note that members of state legislative assemblies do not participate in this election; only members of Parliament are eligible to vote. This process is governed by Article 66 of the Indian Constitution.
qs.kf:
☛ Who elects the Vice-President? → Members of both houses of Parliament
☛ What is the election system? → Proportional representation via single transferable vote
☛ What is the term of Vice-President? → 5 years
☛ Which house does the Vice-President chair? → Rajya Sabha
☛ Which article deals with the election process? → Article 66

q: Election of Lok Sabha Speaker happens-
o: By elected members of the Legislative Assembly
qs.e: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha is elected by the members of the Lok Sabha from among themselves. This procedure is laid down under Article 93 of the Indian Constitution. The election is conducted by simple majority, and the Speaker presides over the proceedings of the Lok Sabha. To remove the Speaker, a resolution passed by a majority of all the members of the Lok Sabha is required. The term of the Speaker is usually the same as that of the Lok Sabha, but they may continue in office until a new Speaker is elected. The position of Speaker is crucial in Indian democracy as they ensure the impartial conduct of House proceedings.
qs.kf:
☛ Who elects the Lok Sabha Speaker? → Lok Sabha members
☛ Which Article provides for the election of Lok Sabha Speaker? → Article 93
☛ What majority is required to remove the Lok Sabha Speaker? → Majority of all members
☛ What is the term of the Lok Sabha Speaker? → Usually same as Lok Sabha term
☛ How is the Lok Sabha Speaker appointed? → By election

q: Which of the following provisions of the Indian Constitution can be amended only by the general majority of the two Houses in the Parliament?
o: Election of Parliament and State Legislature
qs.e: Article 368 of the Indian Constitution describes the amendment procedure. Provisions that can be amended by a simple majority of both Houses include the Election of Parliament and State Legislature, covered under Articles 327 and 328. Other options: Directive Principles of State Policy and Fundamental Rights require a special majority, while Representation of States in Parliament also requires ratification by states. A simple majority means the majority of members present and voting. This provision is related to the electoral system, which can be changed through a simpler procedure.
qs.kf:
☛ Which articles can be amended by simple majority of both Houses? → Articles 327 and 328
☛ Which article outlines the amendment procedure? → Article 368
☛ What majority is required to amend Fundamental Rights? → Special majority
☛ What is required to amend Representation of States in Parliament? → Ratification by states
☛ What does simple majority mean? → Majority of members present and voting

q: What is the maximum number of members of the Rajya Sabha?
qs.e: The Rajya Sabha is the upper house of the Indian Parliament. According to Article 80 of the Constitution, the maximum strength of the Rajya Sabha is fixed at 250 members. Out of these, 238 members represent the states and union territories, while 12 members are nominated by the President. These nominated members are persons having special knowledge or practical experience in fields such as art, literature, science, and social service. Currently, the sanctioned strength of the Rajya Sabha is 245, which includes 233 elected members and 12 nominated members. It is a permanent house, and one-third of its members retire every two years.
qs.kf:
☛ What is the maximum strength of the Rajya Sabha? → 250
☛ How many members are nominated in the Rajya Sabha? → 12
☛ What is the tenure of a Rajya Sabha member? → 6 years
☛ How are Rajya Sabha members elected? → Indirect election
☛ Who is the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha? → Vice President

q: Who among the following was elected unopposed as the Deputy Speaker of the 8th Arunachal Pradesh Legislative Assembly?
qs.e: Kardo Nyigyor was elected unopposed as the Deputy Speaker of the 8th Arunachal Pradesh Legislative Assembly. He is a member of the Bharatiya Janata Party and serves in this important role that helps in the smooth functioning of the House. His election was unanimous, reflecting his widespread acceptance and political acumen. The Deputy Speaker plays a crucial role in presiding over the sessions in the absence of the Speaker and maintaining order.
qs.kf:
☛ Deputy Speaker of 8th Arunachal Pradesh Legislative Assembly → Kardo Nyigyor
☛ Political party of Kardo Nyigyor → Bharatiya Janata Party
☛ Total seats in Arunachal Pradesh Legislative Assembly → 60
☛ Chief Minister of Arunachal Pradesh (2024) → Pema Khandu
☛ Governor of Arunachal Pradesh (2024) → Kaiwalya Trivikram Parnaik

q: In which of the following years was the Ethics Committee in the Rajya Sabha constituted?
qs.e: The Ethics Committee of the Rajya Sabha was constituted in 1997. This committee examines the ethical conduct of members and investigates cases of misconduct. It is a parliamentary committee that directs members to follow the code of conduct. Members of this committee are nominated by the Chairman of Rajya Sabha. Based on the recommendations of this committee, action can be taken against members.
qs.kf:
☛ Rajya Sabha Ethics Committee formation year → 1997
☛ Lok Sabha Ethics Committee formation year → 2000
☛ Rajya Sabha Ethics Committee chairman appointment → By Chairman of Rajya Sabha
☛ Ethics Committee member strength → 10 (in Rajya Sabha)
☛ First Ethics Committee chairman → Krishan Kant (Rajya Sabha)

q: Which house of the parliament has the most powers in matters of Money bills?
qs.e: A money bill deals with taxation, government expenditure, loans, etc. According to Articles 109 and 110 of the Indian Constitution, a money bill can only be introduced in the Lok Sabha. The Rajya Sabha can only delay it for 14 days and suggest amendments, but cannot reject it. If the Rajya Sabha fails to act within 14 days or recommends amendments, the Lok Sabha can accept or reject them, and the bill is deemed passed. Thus, the Lok Sabha holds supreme authority over money bills, with the Rajya Sabha having only a suspensive veto. This ensures that the popular house controls financial matters.
qs.kf:
☛ Which article defines a money bill? → Article 110
☛ How many days can Rajya Sabha delay a money bill? → 14 days
☛ Where can a money bill be introduced? → Only in Lok Sabha
☛ Can Rajya Sabha reject a money bill? → No, only suggest amendments
☛ Who has the final say on a money bill? → Lok Sabha

q: Which of the following is NOT a part of the electoral college for the election of the President?
o: Elected members of the Lok Sabha
Nominated members of the Rajya Sabha
Elected members of the State Assembly
Elected members of the Rajya Sabha
qs.e: The electoral college for the election of the President of India consists of elected members of both Houses of Parliament (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) and elected members of State Legislative Assemblies. Nominated members of the Rajya Sabha are NOT part of this electoral college as they are not elected. This provision is under Article 54 of the Constitution. The purpose is to ensure democratic representation in the presidential election. The President is elected through the system of Single Transferable Vote and secret ballot.
qs.kf:
☛ Article related to Presidential election → Article 54
☛ Who is not part of the electoral college → Nominated members of Rajya Sabha
☛ Method of Presidential election → Single Transferable Vote
☛ Type of voting in Presidential election → Secret ballot
☛ Minimum age for President → 35 years

q: In which House of Parliament can a money bill be introduced?
qs.e: According to Article 109(1) of the Indian Constitution, a Money Bill can only be introduced in the Lok Sabha. A Money Bill deals with matters such as the imposition, abolition, alteration, or regulation of taxes; government expenditure; withdrawal or deposit of money from the Consolidated Fund of India; or the custody of the Consolidated Fund. The Rajya Sabha can only recommend amendments to a Money Bill and must return it within 14 days; otherwise, it is deemed to have been passed by both Houses. The Rajya Sabha cannot reject a Money Bill. The Speaker of the Lok Sabha certifies whether a bill is a Money Bill. This provision ensures that the Lok Sabha, being directly elected by the people, has exclusive control over financial matters.
qs.kf:
☛ Where can a Money Bill be introduced? → Lok Sabha
☛ How long can Rajya Sabha delay a Money Bill? → 14 days
☛ Who certifies a Money Bill? → Speaker of Lok Sabha
☛ What matters does a Money Bill deal with? → Taxes, expenditure, Consolidated Fund
☛ Can Rajya Sabha reject a Money Bill? → No

q: Former Lok Sabha MP from Assam Ramen Deka was appointed as Governor of which of the following states of India in July 2024?
qs.e: In July 2024, the Government of India reshuffled governors of several states. Former Lok Sabha MP from Assam Ramen Deka was appointed as the Governor of Chhattisgarh. He is a leader of the Asom Gana Parishad and served as a Lok Sabha MP from 2014 to 2019. This appointment was part of the central government's strategy to include experienced politicians in the gubernatorial role. The previous governor of Chhattisgarh was Anusuiya Uikey, whose term ended before Ramen Deka took charge.
qs.kf:
☛ Which state was Ramen Deka appointed Governor of in July 2024? → Chhattisgarh
☛ Ramen Deka was a former MP from which state? → Assam
☛ Which political party does Ramen Deka belong to? → Asom Gana Parishad
☛ Who was the previous Governor of Chhattisgarh? → Anusuiya Uikey
☛ What was Ramen Deka's Lok Sabha tenure? → 2014-2019

q: Which Article of the Indian Constitution deals with the composition of the Rajya Sabha?
qs.e: Article 80 of the Indian Constitution deals with the composition of the Rajya Sabha. It specifies that the Rajya Sabha shall consist of not more than 250 members, of which 238 are representatives of states and union territories, and 12 are nominated by the President from persons having special knowledge or practical experience in literature, science, art, and social service. The representatives of states are elected by the members of the state legislative assemblies using the single transferable vote system. The Rajya Sabha is a permanent body and is not subject to dissolution.
qs.kf:
☛ Maximum strength of Rajya Sabha → 250
☛ Nominated members by President → 12
☛ Term of Rajya Sabha members → 6 years
☛ Chairperson of Rajya Sabha → Vice President
☛ Jammu & Kashmir special provision → Had 4 seats before Article 370 abrogation

q: Which of the following statements is correct regarding the Money Bill in the Parliament?
o: Money Bill can be introduced in the Lok Sabha only.
Money Bill can be introduced in either of the Houses of the Parliament
Money Bill cannot be introduced in the Lok Sabha.
Money Bill can be introduced in the Rajya Sabha only.
qs.e: As per Article 110 of the Indian Constitution, a Money Bill can only be introduced in the Lok Sabha, not in the Rajya Sabha. The Rajya Sabha cannot amend a Money Bill; it can only make recommendations within 14 days. If it fails to do so, the Bill is considered passed. The Lok Sabha may accept or reject the recommendations. The President must give assent to a Money Bill and cannot return it for reconsideration. This provision ensures the lower house's supremacy in financial matters, as it is directly responsible to the people. The Speaker of the Lok Sabha certifies whether a Bill is a Money Bill, and that decision is final.
qs.kf:
☛ In which House is a Money Bill introduced? → Only Lok Sabha
☛ How many days does Rajya Sabha have to recommend changes to a Money Bill? → 14 days
☛ Which Article deals with Money Bill? → Article 110
☛ Who gives the final approval to a Money Bill? → President
☛ Can Rajya Sabha reject a Money Bill? → No

q: Who among the following are involved in the election of the President of India?
1. Elected members of the Lok Sabha
2. All members of the Rajya Sabha
3. Elected members of the State Assembly
4. Elected members of the State Legislative Council
qs.e: The election of the President of India involves only the elected members of Lok Sabha and elected members of State Legislative Assemblies. All members of Rajya Sabha (including nominated) and members of State Legislative Councils do not participate in this election. The election is conducted through the single transferable vote system based on the principle of proportional representation. Only elected members can vote in the Presidential election; nominated members of Rajya Sabha and members of Legislative Councils are not entitled to vote. This provision is laid down in Article 54 of the Indian Constitution.
qs.kf:
☛ Electors in Presidential election → Elected members of Lok Sabha and State Assemblies
☛ System of Presidential election → Single transferable vote with proportional representation
☛ Constitutional Article → Article 54
☛ Nominated members' right → No vote in Presidential election
☛ State Legislative Council → Not involved in Presidential election

q: The President has the power to dissolve which house of Parliament?
o: Both Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha
qs.e: The President of India has the power to dissolve the Lok Sabha (House of the People). This power is granted under Article 85(2)(b) of the Indian Constitution. The Lok Sabha has a term of 5 years, but the President can dissolve it before the expiry of its term. Rajya Sabha is a permanent house and cannot be dissolved; one-third of its members retire every two years. On dissolution, the President, on the advice of the Prime Minister, orders fresh elections. This power is a key feature of the parliamentary democracy in India.
qs.kf:
☛ Who has the power to dissolve the Lok Sabha? → President
☛ Why cannot Rajya Sabha be dissolved? → It is a permanent house
☛ What is the normal term of Lok Sabha? → 5 years
☛ On whose advice does the President dissolve Lok Sabha? → Prime Minister
☛ Under which article is the dissolution of Lok Sabha provided? → Article 85

q: Which Article provides Ministers the right to participate in parliamentary proceedings but without voting rights?
qs.e: Article 88 of the Indian Constitution provides ministers the right to participate in the proceedings of either House of Parliament, but without the right to vote. This provision applies to ministers who are not members of Parliament. For instance, a person who becomes a minister but fails to become a member of Parliament within six months ceases to be a minister. Under this article, ministers can take part in debates, defend policies, and answer questions, but cannot vote on any matter. This ensures coordination between the executive and legislature in a parliamentary democracy.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 88 → Ministers can participate in parliamentary proceedings without voting rights.
☛ Article 53 → Executive power of the President.
☛ Article 77 → Conduct of business of the Government of India.
☛ Article 78 → Prime Minister's duty to inform the President.
☛ Non-member minister → Must become a member of Parliament within 6 months.

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (10/06/2025) Shift 3
q: What is a major drawback of the parliamentary system in terms of governance stability?
o: Elections are held only once every decade.
The President can dismiss the Prime Minister at any time.
The judiciary frequently overrules executive decisions
Governments may collapse due to no-confidence motions or coalition disputes
qs.e: A major drawback of the parliamentary system is the lack of stability in governance. The system makes the executive accountable to the legislature, allowing a no-confidence motion to bring down the government. Especially in multi-party coalition governments, disagreements and disputes among allied parties lead to instability. This causes frequent changes in government, policy uncertainty, and administrative paralysis. For example, in India during the 1990s, several coalition governments collapsed repeatedly, highlighting this flaw. Thus, instability is the key negative aspect of the parliamentary system.
qs.kf:
☛ What is the main defect of the parliamentary system? → Instability of governance
☛ In which system is a no-confidence motion found? → Parliamentary system
☛ What is the main cause of instability in coalition governments? → Disputes among parties
☛ In a parliamentary system, who is the executive accountable to? → Legislature
☛ In which decade was the fall of coalition governments common in India? → 1990s

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (11/06/2025) Shift 1
q: Why does the parliamentary system prevent executive despotism?
o: Because the Prime Minister has unlimited power
Because the judiciary can override executive decisions without checks
Because executive authority is dispersed among a group of ministers accountable to the Parliament
Because the military can intervene in governance
qs.e: In a parliamentary system, the executive power is vested in the Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers, which is collectively responsible to the Parliament. This distribution of power prevents any single individual from becoming despotic. The principle of collective responsibility ensures that ministers act as a team and are accountable to the legislature. If the government loses the confidence of the Parliament, it can be removed via a vote of no-confidence. Unlike a presidential system, the executive here derives its legitimacy from the legislature and remains under its constant scrutiny. Thus, the parliamentary system acts as a check on executive despotism by ensuring accountability and diffusion of power.
qs.kf:
☛ Who is the executive accountable to in a parliamentary system? → Parliament
☛ What mechanism removes a government in a parliamentary system? → Vote of no-confidence
☛ Under which article of the Indian Constitution is the Council of Ministers mentioned? → Article 74
☛ Key feature of parliamentary system? → Collective responsibility
☛ Which country is the origin of the Westminster system? → United Kingdom

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (20/06/2025) Shift 1
q: In the Indian parliamentary system, who has the authority to dissolve the Lok Sabha before its term expires?
o: The Prime Minister advises the President to dissolve it.
The Council of Ministers passes a resolution.
The Chief Justice of India orders dissolution.
The Speaker of Lok Sabha takes the decision.
qs.e: According to Article 85(2)(b) of the Indian Constitution, the President has the power to dissolve the Lok Sabha. However, this power is exercised on the advice of the Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers. The Prime Minister recommends dissolution, and the President formally accepts it. The President’s role is ceremonial, and he cannot reject the advice. The normal term of Lok Sabha is five years, but it can be dissolved earlier. This can only happen on the Prime Minister’s advice.
qs.kf:
☛ Who has the formal power to dissolve Lok Sabha? → President
☛ Who advises the dissolution of Lok Sabha? → Prime Minister
☛ Under which article can Lok Sabha be dissolved? → Article 85(2)(b)
☛ What is the normal term of Lok Sabha? → 5 years
☛ Can the President reject the Prime Minister's advice on dissolution? → No

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (20/06/2025) Shift 3
q: What is one of the key advantages of the parliamentary system in ensuring smooth governance?
o: The judiciary controls both the legislature and the executive.
The executive has absolute power over the legislature.
The Prime Minister can dissolve the legislature at will.
It ensures harmony and cooperation between the legislature and the executive.
qs.e: In a parliamentary system, the executive (council of ministers) is drawn from the legislature (parliament) and is accountable to it. This creates a close coordination between the two branches, facilitating smooth implementation of policies and laws. The government remains stable because the executive commands a majority in the legislature. At the same time, the legislature exercises control over the executive through mechanisms like the no-confidence motion. This ensures that governance runs smoothly and there is harmony between the two organs. Thus, the key advantage of the parliamentary system is the cooperation between the legislature and the executive, which aids in quick decision-making and effective governance.
qs.kf:
☛ Who is the head of the executive in a parliamentary system? → Prime Minister
☛ Where did the parliamentary system originate? → Britain
☛ In India, the council of ministers is responsible to which house? → Lok Sabha
☛ In a presidential system, the executive and legislature are? → Separate
☛ What is the tool for the legislature to remove the executive in a parliamentary system? → No-confidence motion

q: What is the maximum strength of the members of the Lok Sabha?
qs.e: Under Article 81 of the Indian Constitution, the maximum strength of the Lok Sabha is fixed at 550. This includes 530 members representing the states, 20 members from the Union Territories, and 2 members nominated by the President from the Anglo-Indian community. This is the constitutional upper limit, though the current actual strength of the Lok Sabha is 543. The first Lok Sabha in 1952 had 489 members. Seat allocation is revised periodically through constitutional amendments based on population changes.
qs.kf:
☛ What is the maximum strength of Lok Sabha? → 550
☛ How many members represent states in Lok Sabha? → 530
☛ How many members from Union Territories in Lok Sabha? → 20
☛ How many members are nominated from Anglo-Indian community? → 2
☛ What is the current strength of Lok Sabha? → 543

q: In which year was The Environment (Protection) Act passed by the Parliament of India?
qs.e: The Parliament of India passed the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986. This act was introduced after the Bhopal Gas Tragedy (1984), which highlighted the need for a comprehensive law for environmental protection. The act was enacted to protect and improve the quality of the environment and to control pollution. It empowers the central government to regulate industries and other activities, set environmental standards, and take action against polluters. The act is also known as the Environment Protection Act (EPA).
qs.kf:
☛ Which was India's first environmental law? → Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974
☛ When was the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act passed? → 1981
☛ Which is the main agency for pollution control under the Environment (Protection) Act? → Pollution Control Boards
☛ When was the National Green Tribunal established in India? → 2010
☛ When was the Environment (Protection) Act amended? → 1991

q: Who presides over the joint sitting of the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha?
o: A member nominated by the President of India
The senior most member of the Rajya Sabha
qs.e: Under Article 118(4) of the Constitution, the joint sitting of Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha is presided over by the Speaker of Lok Sabha. This provision helps resolve deadlocks between the two Houses on a bill. The joint sitting is summoned by the President, but it is chaired by the Lok Sabha Speaker. In the Speaker's absence, the Deputy Speaker of Lok Sabha presides. The President is part of Parliament but does not chair joint sittings. This procedure ensures smooth legislative functioning in the Indian parliamentary system.
qs.kf:
☛ Who summons a joint sitting? → President
☛ Who presides over a joint sitting? → Lok Sabha Speaker
☛ Who presides in the Speaker's absence? → Deputy Speaker of Lok Sabha
☛ When is a joint sitting called? → When a bill is deadlocked between the two Houses
☛ What is the quorum for a joint sitting? → 1/10th of total members of both Houses

q: Who was the first Chairman of Rajya Sabha?
qs.e: The Rajya Sabha was constituted on 13 May 1952. Dr. Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan, who was also the first Vice President of India, became the first Chairman of Rajya Sabha. The Vice President is the ex-officio Chairman of Rajya Sabha. He served as Chairman from 13 May 1952 to 12 May 1962. After his tenure, he became the second President of India. Rajya Sabha is the upper house of the Indian Parliament, representing the states. The Chairman presides over the proceedings of Rajya Sabha.
qs.kf:
☛ When was Rajya Sabha constituted? → 13 May 1952
☛ Who was the first Chairman of Rajya Sabha? → Dr. Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan
☛ Who is the ex-officio Chairman of Rajya Sabha? → Vice President
☛ For how many years did Dr. Radhakrishnan serve as Chairman? → 10 years (1952-1962)
☛ What is the tenure of the Chairman of Rajya Sabha? → No fixed limit, traditionally 5 years

q: Which of the following Articles of the Constitution of India provides provisions for a joint sitting of both Houses of Parliament?
qs.e: Article 108 of the Indian Constitution provides for a joint sitting of both Houses of Parliament (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha). It is summoned by the President when a bill passed by one House is pending in the other House for more than six months, is rejected, or both Houses disagree. Decisions are taken by majority of the total membership of both Houses. Only three bills have faced joint sittings so far: Dowry Prohibition Bill (1961), Banking Service Commission Bill (1977), and Prevention of Terrorism Bill (POTA, 2002). Other options: Article 164 deals with appointment of Chief Minister by Governor, Article 118 with rule-making power of Parliament, and Article 129 with Supreme Court being a court of record.
qs.kf:
☛ Who has the power to summon a joint sitting? → President
☛ Which Article defines Money Bill? → Article 110
☛ Who presides over a joint sitting under Article 108? → Speaker of Lok Sabha
☛ How many joint sittings have been held in India so far? → Three
☛ What does Article 118 deal with? → Procedure for rule-making by Parliament

q: Which majority can be amended in parliamentary laws?
o: By the absolute majority in Parliament
By the general majority of parliament
qs.e: Under Articles 107 and 108 of the Indian Constitution, to pass ordinary laws, a simple majority of the members present and voting in each House of Parliament is required. This means that more than half of the members present and participating in the vote must support the bill. It is important to note that an absolute majority refers to more than 50% of the total membership of the House, which is a different process. For amending parliamentary laws, a simple majority is sufficient, unless the Constitution specifically requires another type of majority. Thus, ordinary bills and amendments need a simple majority to be passed.
qs.kf:
☛ Majority required for ordinary laws → Simple majority of members present and voting
☛ Meaning of absolute majority → More than 50% of total membership
☛ Majority for constitutional amendments → Special majority (2/3 members present and voting)
☛ Article 107 → Procedure for passing bills
☛ Article 368 → Procedure for constitutional amendments

q: What is the first hour of the parliamentary meeting in the following?
qs.e: The first hour of a parliamentary meeting is called Question Time, during which members ask questions about government policies and administration. It is a crucial parliamentary procedure that ensures government accountability. Zero Hour follows Question Time, where members raise issues without prior notice. Half-hour Discussion and Short-duration Discussion are other procedures held at different times. In Question Time, members ask starred and unstarred questions, and ministers provide answers. This practice enhances transparency and responsibility in a democracy.
qs.kf:
☛ Time of Question Hour → First hour of the sitting
☛ Zero Hour begins → After Question Hour
☛ Purpose of Question Hour → To question ministers
☛ Types of questions in Question Hour → Starred and Unstarred
☛ Significance of Question Hour → Ensures accountability of government

q: President of India is elected-
o: By the members of Legislative Assembly of Members and States from both Houses of Parliament
qs.e: The President of India is elected indirectly. The electoral college consists of elected members of both Houses of Parliament (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) and elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of states. This system is based on the principle of proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote. The election is conducted by the Election Commission of India and the voting is secret. The value of each vote is determined based on the population of the state, ensuring equal representation. Article 54 of the Constitution provides for the election of the President. Members of Legislative Councils are not part of the electoral college. This system balances the representation of the Centre and the states.
qs.kf:
☛ Who are the electors for President election? → Elected members of both Houses of Parliament and elected members of state Legislative Assemblies
☛ What is the voting system used? → Proportional representation by single transferable vote
☛ Who is excluded from the electoral college? → Members of Legislative Councils
☛ Which Article deals with President election? → Article 54
☛ What determines the value of a vote? → Population of the state

q: Who is the lower house of the Indian Parliament?
qs.e: The Indian Parliament consists of two houses: the upper house (Rajya Sabha) and the lower house (Lok Sabha). Lok Sabha is directly elected by the people and is responsible to the government. The term of Lok Sabha members is 5 years, unless dissolved earlier. Currently, Lok Sabha can have a maximum of 552 members, including 530 from states, 20 from union territories, and 2 nominated by the President. The presiding officer of Lok Sabha is called the Speaker. Lok Sabha has special powers over money bills and only Lok Sabha can introduce a no-confidence motion against the government.
qs.kf:
☛ Term of Lok Sabha Speaker → Usually 5 years or until dissolution
☛ How many members are nominated by the President in Lok Sabha → 2
☛ When was the first Lok Sabha formed → 17 April 1952
☛ Where is a money bill introduced → Only in Lok Sabha
☛ Who is the Leader of Lok Sabha → Prime Minister

q: How many houses are there in the Parliament of India?
qs.e: The Parliament of India is a bicameral legislature consisting of two houses: the Lok Sabha (House of the People) and the Rajya Sabha (Council of States). Lok Sabha members are directly elected by the people, while Rajya Sabha members are indirectly elected by state legislative assemblies. This bicameral system strengthens the federal structure and ensures thorough scrutiny of laws. The President is not a member of Parliament but is an integral part of it. Joint sittings of both houses are rare, occurring only in specific circumstances. The Indian parliamentary system is inspired by the British and US models, providing representation to both the people and the states.
qs.kf:
☛ Houses of Indian Parliament → Two: Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha
☛ Tenure of Lok Sabha members → 5 years
☛ Maximum strength of Rajya Sabha → 250
☛ Tenure of Rajya Sabha members → 6 years
☛ Maximum strength of Lok Sabha → 552

q: In 1950, the first estimate committee was formed on the recommendation of?
qs.e: The first Estimates Committee was formed in 1950 on the recommendation of John Mathai, who was the first Finance Minister of India. He suggested the formation of this committee to strengthen parliamentary oversight over government expenditure. The Estimates Committee examines the budget estimates and suggests ways to improve efficiency and economy in public spending. It is a standing committee of the Lok Sabha, and its members are elected from the Lok Sabha. The first chairman of the Estimates Committee was Shri M.V. Krishnappa. This committee plays a vital role in ensuring financial discipline and accountability in government finances.
qs.kf:
☛ First chairman of Estimates Committee → M.V. Krishnappa
☛ Year of formation of Estimates Committee → 1950
☛ Members of Estimates Committee are elected from → Lok Sabha
☛ Estimates Committee was formed on whose recommendation → John Mathai
☛ Main function of Estimates Committee → Examine government expenditure

q: Parliamentary committees are:
qs.e: Parliamentary committees are of two types: Standing committees (e.g., Finance Committee, Public Accounts Committee) and Ad hoc committees (e.g., Estimates Committee, Proposals Committee). Standing committees function regularly, while ad hoc committees are formed for specific tasks. This classification ensures efficiency and thorough scrutiny in parliamentary proceedings. In the Indian Parliament, these committees play a vital role in reviewing legislative matters and controlling government expenditure.
qs.kf:
☛ Types of parliamentary committees → Two types - Standing and Ad hoc
☛ Example of Standing committee → Public Accounts Committee
☛ Example of Ad hoc committee → Estimates Committee
☛ Chairperson of Public Accounts Committee → Member from opposition
☛ Finance Committee members → 15 from Lok Sabha, 7 from Rajya Sabha

q: Budget of a state under President's rule is presented to -
qs.e: When President's rule is imposed in a state, the budget of that state is presented before the Lok Sabha. This arrangement is governed by Article 266 of the Constitution of India and the rules of financial procedure. During President's rule, the state legislative assembly may be suspended or dissolved, and the legislative powers of the state vest in the Parliament. Consequently, the state budget is presented in the lower house of Parliament, i.e., the Lok Sabha. While the Rajya Sabha can only recommend amendments to finance bills, the Lok Sabha has the final authority to pass them. This process is part of India's financial control and center-state relations.
qs.kf:
☛ During President's rule, the state budget is presented to? → Lok Sabha
☛ When President's rule is imposed, state legislative powers vest in? → Parliament
☛ Which Article of the Constitution deals with the state budget? → Article 266
☛ What is the role of Rajya Sabha in finance bills? → Only to recommend
☛ During President's rule, the state government is controlled by? → Central government

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (12/06/2025) Shift 2
q: What type of majority is required to pass laws under Articles 2 and 3, as per Article 4(2) in Indian parliament?
qs.e: As per Article 4(2) of the Indian Constitution, laws made under Articles 2 and 3 can be passed by a simple majority in Parliament. Article 2 deals with the admission or establishment of new states, while Article 3 deals with the reorganization, boundary alteration, or name change of existing states. These bills are not considered constitutional amendments, so a simple majority is sufficient for their passage. However, for bills under Article 3, the President must refer them to the concerned state legislature for its views, but the state's consent is not binding. This provision provides flexibility to Parliament in reorganizing states.
qs.kf:
☛ Majority required for bills under Articles 2 and 3 → Simple majority
☛ Article 4(2) specifies that laws under Articles 2 and 3 → are not constitutional amendments
☛ Who refers the bill under Article 3 to state legislature → President
☛ What does Article 2 deal with → Admission or establishment of new states
☛ What does Article 3 deal with → Reorganization, boundary change, or name change of states

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (13/06/2025) Shift 2
q: Who has the authority to make laws for multi-state co-operative societies?
qs.e: Multi-state co-operative societies operate across more than one state, hence their regulation and control require a national framework. According to the Indian Constitution, the authority to make laws for multi-state co-operative societies rests with the Parliament. This power derives from Article 246 and the Concurrent List. The primary legislation governing them is the Multi-State Co-operative Societies Act, 2002, enacted by Parliament. State legislatures can only legislate on co-operative societies within their respective states. The District Collector and High Court are not law-making bodies; they have executive and judicial roles respectively. This division ensures uniform legal standards for societies operating across state boundaries.
qs.kf:
☛ Who regulates multi-state co-operative societies? → Central Government and Parliament
☛ When was the Multi-State Co-operative Societies Act passed? → 2002
☛ Who is the registrar for multi-state co-operative societies? → Central Registrar of Co-operative Societies
☛ What is the supreme authority in a multi-state co-operative society? → General Body
☛ Where do appeals lie for multi-state co-operative society matters? → Central Co-operative Tribunal

q: The Jammu and Kashmir Reorganization Bill, 2019 was introduced in Rajya Sabha by the Minister of Home Affairs, Mr. Amit Shah. When did this act of Parliament receive the assent of the President?
qs.e: The Jammu and Kashmir Reorganization Bill, 2019 was introduced in Rajya Sabha on August 5, 2019. It was subsequently passed by Lok Sabha as well. The President gave his assent to this bill on August 9, 2019. Under this act, the state of Jammu and Kashmir was divided into two union territories: Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh. This reorganization came into effect on October 31, 2019. Additionally, the special status granted to Jammu and Kashmir under Article 370 was also revoked.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganization Bill introduced? → August 5, 2019
☛ When did the President give assent? → August 9, 2019
☛ Which union territories were created? → Jammu and Kashmir, Ladakh
☛ When did the reorganization take effect? → October 31, 2019
☛ Under which article was the special status revoked? → Article 370

q: There are different types of Bills introduced in the Lok Sabha. Which of the following is NOT one of them?
qs.e: In the Indian Parliament, three main types of Bills are introduced in the Lok Sabha: Ordinary Bills, Money Bills, and Financial Bills. A Revenue Bill is not a separate category; it is included under Financial Bills. Money Bills (Article 110) deal only with taxation, government expenditure, etc., and can only be introduced in the Lok Sabha. Financial Bills (Article 117) contain financial matters other than those in Money Bills. Ordinary Bills deal with non-financial subjects. Hence, Revenue Bill is not an independent type of Bill in the Parliament.
qs.kf:
☛ Under which Article is Money Bill defined? → Article 110
☛ Which Article relates to Financial Bills? → Article 117
☛ Which Bill can only be introduced in Lok Sabha? → Money Bill
☛ How many days can Rajya Sabha hold a Money Bill? → 14 days
☛ Under which Articles do Ordinary Bills fall? → Articles 107 and 108

q: What is the maximum number of members in the Lok Sabha?
qs.e: According to Article 81 of the Indian Constitution, the maximum strength of the Lok Sabha is fixed at 552 members. This includes 530 members representing the states, 20 members representing the Union Territories, and 2 members nominated by the President from the Anglo-Indian community. However, the 104th Constitutional Amendment (2020) abolished the Anglo-Indian reservation, but the constitutional maximum limit remains 552. Currently, the effective strength is 543 (530+20+0 nominated). This limit ensures parliamentary representation and the democratic framework. The allocation is based on population and territorial representation, as per the Delimitation Commission orders.
qs.kf:
☛ Maximum strength of Lok Sabha → 552
☛ Number of members from states in Lok Sabha → 530
☛ Number of members from Union Territories in Lok Sabha → 20
☛ Amendment that removed Anglo-Indian reservation → 104th Constitutional Amendment (2020)
☛ Article related to Lok Sabha membership → Article 81

q: By which word is the postponement of work done during the proceedings of Parliament?
qs.e: During the proceedings of Parliament, the postponement of work is known as Suspension. It refers to temporarily halting the parliamentary proceedings for a specific period, after which the House resumes its sitting. A motion for suspension can be moved by any member and requires the approval of the House. Suspension is usually done when there is a need for discussion on a serious issue or to ensure smooth functioning of the House. This procedure is an important part of parliamentary proceedings as it allows for democratic debate and deliberation. Suspension differs from adjournment, which marks the end of a sitting. The Speaker or Chairperson plays a key role in managing the suspension process.
qs.kf:
☛ What is suspension in Parliament? → Temporary halt of proceedings
☛ Who can propose a suspension motion? → Any member of the House
☛ When does the House resume after suspension? → At a specified time or as per the Speaker's order
☛ What is the purpose of suspension? → To allow discussion on urgent matters
☛ Difference between suspension and adjournment? → Suspension is temporary; adjournment ends the sitting

q: What is the maximum number of Rajya Sabha members?
qs.e: Rajya Sabha is the upper house of the Indian Parliament. According to Article 80 of the Constitution, the maximum number of members of Rajya Sabha is fixed at 250. Out of these, 238 members represent the states and union territories, while 12 members are nominated by the President. These nominated members are persons having special knowledge or practical experience in fields such as literature, art, science, and social service. Currently, the maximum membership of Rajya Sabha is 250, but the actual number of members may be less. This provision was included in the original Constitution framed by the Constituent Assembly.
qs.kf:
☛ What is the maximum number of Rajya Sabha members? → 250
☛ How many nominated members are there in Rajya Sabha? → 12
☛ Under which Article is Rajya Sabha constituted? → Article 80
☛ What is the term of office of Rajya Sabha members? → 6 years
☛ Who is the Chairman of Rajya Sabha? → Vice President

q: Who among the following can propose a Government Bill?
o: Member of the Treasury Bench in Lok Sabha
A Member of Parliament who is not a Minister
Minister in either House of Parliament
qs.e: A Government Bill is a bill introduced by a Minister. According to the Indian Constitution, any Minister, whether a member of the Lok Sabha or the Rajya Sabha, can propose a Government Bill. It is important to note that only Ministers can introduce such bills, not ordinary Members of Parliament. The option 'Member of the Treasury Bench in Lok Sabha' also refers to Ministers, but it is limited to the Lok Sabha, whereas a Minister in either House can propose a bill. Hence, the correct answer is 'Minister in either House of Parliament'.
qs.kf:
☛ Who can propose a Government Bill? → Any Minister
☛ Who introduces a Private Member's Bill? → Ordinary MP (not a Minister)
☛ Who can propose a Money Bill? → Only a Minister in Lok Sabha
☛ Can a Government Bill be introduced in Rajya Sabha? → Yes, by a Minister
☛ Which Articles deal with bills in the Constitution? → Articles 107-111

q: Which of the following statements is INCORRECT?
o: Amit Shah assumed charge as Union Home Minister and Minister of Cooperation in June 2024.
Om Birla is elected as the Speaker of the 18th Lok Sabha.
Narendra Modi took oath as the Prime Minister of India in June 2024.
Sonia Gandhi became the Leader of Opposition in the 18th Lok Sabha.
qs.e: The Leader of Opposition in the 18th Lok Sabha is Rahul Gandhi, not Sonia Gandhi. Sonia Gandhi is a member of the Rajya Sabha, not the Lok Sabha. To become Leader of Opposition in Lok Sabha, one must be a member of the Lok Sabha. Amit Shah assumed charge as Home Minister and Minister of Cooperation in June 2024, Om Birla was elected Speaker of the 18th Lok Sabha, and Narendra Modi took oath as Prime Minister in June 2024 - all these statements are correct.
qs.kf:
☛ Who became Leader of Opposition in 18th Lok Sabha? → Rahul Gandhi
☛ Who is the Speaker of 18th Lok Sabha? → Om Birla
☛ Who became Union Home Minister in 2024? → Amit Shah
☛ When did Narendra Modi take oath as PM? → June 2024
☛ Which house is Sonia Gandhi a member of? → Rajya Sabha

q: Which of the following is related to Article 84 of the Constitution?
qs.e: Article 84 of the Indian Constitution, under Part V, lays down the qualifications for becoming a member of Parliament. It requires a person to be a citizen of India, must have completed 25 years of age for Lok Sabha and 30 years for Rajya Sabha, and must possess other qualifications as prescribed by Parliament. This article is crucial for understanding the eligibility criteria for MPs. In contrast, Article 102 deals with disqualification of members, Article 112 with the Annual Financial Statement (Budget), and Article 123 with the President's ordinance-making power. Hence, Article 84 is directly related to qualifications for membership of Parliament, making it the correct answer.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 84 → Qualification for Parliament membership
☛ Article 102 → Disqualification for membership
☛ Article 112 → Annual Financial Statement
☛ Article 123 → President's ordinance power
☛ Minimum age for Lok Sabha member → 25 years

q: As per Constitution of India, if for a period of ________ days a member of either House of Parliament is, without permission of the House, absent from all meetings thereof, the House may declare his seat vacant.
qs.e: According to Article 101(4) of the Constitution of India, if a member of either House of Parliament is absent from all meetings for a period of 60 days without the permission of the House, the House may declare his seat vacant. This provision ensures that members attend Parliament regularly and fulfill their duties. However, the House may excuse the absence if it considers the reasons satisfactory. This rule applies to both Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha. The period of 60 days is calculated continuously, and the House has the discretion to condone the absence in genuine cases. This helps maintain discipline among legislators.
qs.kf:
☛ Article providing for vacation of seat due to absence → Article 101(4)
☛ Minimum absence period for declaring seat vacant → 60 days
☛ Can the House condone absence? → Yes, if reasons are satisfactory
☛ Which Houses are covered? → Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha
☛ Does this apply to state legislatures? → Yes, similar provision exists for state assemblies

q: The Parliament does not have the power to legislate on the subject in List 2 of the Seventh Schedule. Which of the following is an EXCEPTION in this general law?
o: If the Prime Minister asks the Parliament to do so
If the Judiciary asks the Parliament to do so
if the Governor of the state certifies the requirement
If the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution to this effect
qs.e: Under Article 249 of the Indian Constitution, if the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution by a two-thirds majority that it is necessary in the national interest for Parliament to legislate on a matter in the State List, then Parliament can do so. This resolution remains valid for a maximum of one year and can be renewed repeatedly. Other options: The Prime Minister's or Judiciary's request does not have constitutional backing. The Governor's certificate is only effective during President's Rule under Article 356. Thus, the Rajya Sabha resolution is the correct exception to the general rule that Parliament cannot legislate on State List subjects.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 249 → Parliament can legislate on State List if Rajya Sabha passes a resolution
☛ Required majority in Rajya Sabha → Two-thirds of members present and voting
☛ Validity of resolution → Maximum one year, can be extended repeatedly
☛ Article 356 → Parliament can legislate on State List during President's Rule
☛ Article 252 → Parliament can legislate on State List if two or more states request

q: Money bill can be introduced _________.
o: by neither Lok Sabha nor Rajya Sabha
qs.e: According to Article 109 of the Indian Constitution, a Money Bill can only be introduced in the Lok Sabha. The Rajya Sabha has no power to reject or amend a Money Bill; it can only make recommendations within 14 days. If the Rajya Sabha fails to act within 14 days, the bill is deemed passed in the form as passed by the Lok Sabha. The definition of a Money Bill is given in Article 110, covering matters such as taxation, government expenditure, borrowing public money, etc. The prior recommendation of the President is required for introducing a Money Bill in the Lok Sabha.
qs.kf:
☛ In which house is a Money Bill introduced? → Only in Lok Sabha
☛ Within how many days must Rajya Sabha act on a Money Bill? → 14 days
☛ Which article defines a Money Bill? → Article 110
☛ Whose recommendation is required to introduce a Money Bill? → President
☛ Which house of Parliament cannot reject a Money Bill? → Rajya Sabha

q: One-third of the members of the Rajya Sabha retires after every _________ year.
qs.e: Rajya Sabha is a permanent house that is never dissolved. One-third of its members retire after every second year. This provision is made under Article 83 of the Constitution. The term of a Rajya Sabha member is 6 years, but to maintain continuity, one-third of the members retire every two years. Thus, every two years, new members are elected or nominated. This process ensures that experienced members are always present in the house.
qs.kf:
☛ Term of Rajya Sabha members → 6 years
☛ Retirement cycle of Rajya Sabha → One-third every 2 years
☛ Maximum strength of Rajya Sabha → 250
☛ Chairman of Rajya Sabha → Vice President of India
☛ Representation of states in Rajya Sabha → In proportion to population

q: What does the word 'sine die' mean in the context of indefinite postponement?
qs.e: 'Sine die' is a Latin term meaning 'without a day fixed'. It is used in parliamentary proceedings to adjourn a meeting or session indefinitely. When a house is adjourned 'sine die', it means the house is postponed without setting a date for the next meeting, effectively suspending it until the next session. This differs from a regular adjournment, where the next meeting date is specified. In the Indian Parliament, adjourning the Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha 'sine die' implies that the house is adjourned until the next session. The term is commonly used in legislative bodies and legal contexts to indicate an indefinite postponement.
qs.kf:
☛ From which language is the term 'sine die' derived? → Latin
☛ What does 'sine die' mean in parliamentary procedure? → Adjournment indefinitely
☛ In Indian Parliament, 'sine die' adjournment lasts until when? → Next session
☛ Is the next meeting date fixed in a 'sine die' adjournment? → No
☛ What is the key difference between regular adjournment and 'sine die'? → Regular adjournment fixes date; 'sine die' does not

q: How many years is the tenure of the members of the Lok Sabha?
qs.e: According to Article 83 of the Indian Constitution, the tenure of the Lok Sabha is five years from the date of its first sitting. The President can dissolve the Lok Sabha before the completion of its term. During a national emergency, the Parliament can extend the term by up to one year at a time, but not beyond six months after the emergency ends. Lok Sabha members are elected through direct elections by the people. This provision ensures democratic representation and accountability.
qs.kf:
☛ Normal tenure of Lok Sabha → Five years
☛ Who can dissolve Lok Sabha → President
☛ Maximum extension of Lok Sabha term during emergency → One year at a time
☛ Mode of election of Lok Sabha members → Direct election
☛ Article related to Lok Sabha tenure → Article 83

q: Which of the following members of the House should not be less than 25 years?
qs.e: According to Article 84 of the Indian Constitution, the minimum age for a member of Lok Sabha is 25 years. For Rajya Sabha, the minimum age is 30 years. Gram Sabha and Perina House have no constitutional relevance. Lok Sabha is the lower house formed by direct elections, with a term of 5 years. This age limit ensures that members have maturity and experience.
qs.kf:
☛ Minimum age for Lok Sabha member → 25 years
☛ Minimum age for Rajya Sabha member → 30 years
☛ Minimum age for President → 35 years
☛ Term of Lok Sabha → 5 years
☛ Term of Rajya Sabha member → 6 years

q: Which of the following authorities constitute the Ethics Committee in the Rajya Sabha?
o: the Speaker of the Lok Sabha
The Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
qs.e: The Ethics Committee in the Rajya Sabha is constituted by the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. This committee examines matters related to the conduct and ethics of members. It was first formed in 1997. The committee consists of 10 members, who are nominated by the Chairman. It plays a crucial role in ensuring transparency and accountability in parliamentary democracy. The tenure of the committee is one year.
qs.kf:
☛ Who constitutes the Ethics Committee in the Lok Sabha? → The Speaker of the Lok Sabha
☛ How many members are in the Rajya Sabha Ethics Committee? → 10
☛ When was the Ethics Committee formed? → 1997
☛ Who is the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha? → The Vice President
☛ What is the tenure of the Ethics Committee? → 1 year

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (16/06/2025) Shift 3
q: How does the parliamentary system ensure a “responsible government”?
o: By allowing the President to dismiss the Prime Minister at any time
By giving the judiciary the power to review executive decisions
By permitting the military to oversee governance
By making the council of ministers collectively accountable to the Parliament
qs.e: In a parliamentary system, the key mechanism ensuring a responsible government is the collective accountability of the council of ministers to the Parliament. This means the executive (council of ministers) is answerable to the legislature (Parliament), and if it loses a vote of confidence, it must resign. Thus, the government is indirectly accountable to the people, as Parliament is elected by them. This prevents arbitrary rule and ensures democratic control. The President's powers are limited, the judiciary is independent, and the military has no role in governance. Collective accountability is a core feature of the Westminster model, making the government responsive to public opinion through its representatives.
qs.kf:
☛ In a parliamentary system, the executive is accountable to which body? → Legislature (Parliament)
☛ What does collective accountability of the council of ministers mean? → Government must retain Parliament's confidence
☛ What principle governs government responsibility in India? → Collective responsibility
☛ Which institution is supreme in a parliamentary system? → Parliament
☛ What does a responsible government imply? → Government is accountable to the people

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (18/06/2025) Shift 3
q: For which of the given bills can the President of India summon a joint sitting of both Houses of Parliament?
1. Ordinary Bill
2. Money Bill
3. Constitutional Amendment Bill
qs.e: According to Article 108 of the Indian Constitution, the President can summon a joint sitting of both Houses of Parliament only for an Ordinary Bill. This happens when one House rejects a bill passed by the other, disagrees on amendments, or does not pass it for more than six months. A joint sitting cannot be called for a Money Bill because the Rajya Sabha can only recommend changes, and the Lok Sabha's decision is final. For a Constitutional Amendment Bill, a joint sitting is also not allowed, as it must be passed separately by each House with a special majority.
qs.kf:
☛ Which article provides for a joint sitting? → Article 108
☛ For which bills is a joint sitting not allowed? → Money Bill and Constitutional Amendment Bill
☛ Who presides over a joint sitting? → Speaker of Lok Sabha
☛ How many joint sittings have been held so far? → Three (1961, 1978, 2002)
☛ What is required for a Constitutional Amendment Bill? → Special majority in each House

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (24/06/2025) Shift 1
q: Which type of legislative bills must be introduced in the Lok Sabha only after obtaining the prior approval of the President of India?
qs.e: According to Article 117 of the Indian Constitution, Money Bills can only be introduced in the Lok Sabha with the prior recommendation of the President of India. A Money Bill deals with matters such as the imposition, abolition, alteration, or regulation of taxes; the borrowing of money; the custody of the Consolidated Fund; or the appropriation of money from the Consolidated Fund. The requirement for presidential approval ensures that the government controls financial legislation. Money Bills are introduced only in the Lok Sabha, and the Rajya Sabha can only make recommendations but cannot reject them. The Rajya Sabha must return a Money Bill within 14 days, and the Lok Sabha may accept or reject its recommendations. The President's assent is final.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 117 → Relates to President's recommendation for Money Bills
☛ Money Bill definition → Given in Article 110 of the Constitution
☛ Who introduces a Money Bill → Only a minister in the Lok Sabha
☛ Rajya Sabha's role → Can recommend changes but cannot reject Money Bill
☛ Finance Bill vs Money Bill → Finance Bill often requires President's recommendation but is not the same

q: How many members are there in Rajya Sabha?
qs.e: The Rajya Sabha is the upper house of the Indian Parliament with a maximum strength of 250 members. Out of these, 238 members represent the states and union territories, while 12 members are nominated by the President for their expertise in fields like art, literature, science, and social service. Rajya Sabha is a permanent house and one-third of its members retire every two years. The maximum membership of Rajya Sabha is fixed at 250 under Article 80 of the Indian Constitution. Currently, the actual strength is 245 members (including 12 nominated).
qs.kf:
☛ What is the maximum strength of Rajya Sabha? → 250
☛ How many elected members are in Rajya Sabha? → 238
☛ How many nominated members are in Rajya Sabha? → 12
☛ What is the term of a Rajya Sabha member? → 6 years
☛ Who is the Chairman of Rajya Sabha? → Vice President

q: Currently, which state has the maximum number of Lok Sabha seats?
qs.e: Distribution of Lok Sabha seats is based on population. Currently, Uttar Pradesh has 80 Lok Sabha seats, the highest in the country. Maharashtra has 48 seats, Gujarat has 26, and Rajasthan has 25. Uttar Pradesh's largest number of seats is due to its huge population, which is the largest in India. The allocation of Lok Sabha seats is adjusted periodically as per the Constitution. The last delimitation was done in 2008.
qs.kf:
☛ State with highest Rajya Sabha seats → Uttar Pradesh (31)
☛ State with lowest Lok Sabha seats → Goa, Sikkim, Manipur (just 1)
☛ Total Lok Sabha seats → 543
☛ Number of Anglo-Indian members in Lok Sabha → 0 (removed from 2020)
☛ Number of Lok Sabha seats in Uttar Pradesh → 80

q: After passing a Money Bill in the Lok Sabha, the Rajya Sabha can return the bill to the Lok Sabha within a maximum of ______ days.
qs.e: According to Article 109 of the Indian Constitution, after a Money Bill is passed in the Lok Sabha, it is sent to the Rajya Sabha. The Rajya Sabha must return the bill to the Lok Sabha within 14 days with its recommendations. If the Rajya Sabha fails to return the bill within 14 days, it is deemed to have been passed in the form originally passed by the Lok Sabha. The Lok Sabha can accept or reject any or all of the recommendations of the Rajya Sabha. A Money Bill can only be introduced in the Lok Sabha and requires the prior approval of the President. The Rajya Sabha cannot amend a Money Bill; it can only make recommendations.
qs.kf:
☛ Maximum time for Rajya Sabha to return a Money Bill → 14 days
☛ Money Bill can be introduced only in which House → Lok Sabha
☛ Definition of Money Bill is under which Article → Article 110
☛ Rajya Sabha can only give ___ on a Money Bill → recommendations
☛ If Rajya Sabha does not return the bill in 14 days, it is → deemed passed

q: The provisions related to the federal structure of the state system given in the Constitution can be modified by whom?
o: Constitutional frame time for voting only for Union Ministers
Special majority in Parliament with the consent of half of the state legislatures by a simple majority
qs.e: The provisions related to the federal structure of the state system in the Indian Constitution, such as changes to state boundaries, names, or territories, can be amended under Article 368 through a special procedure. This requires a special majority in Parliament, meaning a majority of the total membership of each House and at least two-thirds of the members present and voting. Additionally, at least half of the state legislatures must give their consent by passing the bill with a simple majority. This process safeguards the federal structure and ensures states' involvement in major constitutional changes.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Article provides for amendment of federal structure? → Article 368
☛ What majority is required in Parliament for such amendments? → Special majority (two-thirds of members present and voting plus majority of total membership)
☛ How many states must consent? → At least half of the states
☛ What majority is needed in state legislatures for consent? → Simple majority
☛ Is state consent mandatory for federal structure amendments? → Yes

q: Which of the following can make "additional regional law" ?
qs.e: Under Article 355 and the federal structure of the Indian Constitution, the power to make "additional regional law" lies solely with the Parliament. This law can be made for the whole of India or any part thereof, especially for Union Territories or specific regions of states. President, Home Minister, or Prime Minister cannot individually enact such laws. Parliament's legislative power is derived from Articles 245 and 246, which also permit the Centre to legislate on state list subjects if it is in the national interest.
qs.kf:
☛ Who can make additional regional law? → Parliament
☛ Under which articles does Parliament derive legislative power? → Articles 245 and 246
☛ Which part of the Constitution deals with Centre-State relations? → Part XI
☛ For which region can additional regional law be made? → Whole of India or any part
☛ Who can legislate on state list subjects for national interest? → Parliament

q: What is the number of members present in the Rajya Sabha?
qs.e: The Rajya Sabha is the upper house of the Indian Parliament. According to the Constitution, the maximum strength of the Rajya Sabha is 250, out of which 238 members represent the states and union territories, and 12 members are nominated by the President. Currently, the total number of members in the Rajya Sabha is 245 because some seats are vacant or not allocated. This number may change over time due to elections and nominations. The Rajya Sabha is a permanent house and one-third of its members retire every two years. The term of a Rajya Sabha member is 6 years. The Vice President is the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.
qs.kf:
☛ What is the maximum strength of the Rajya Sabha? → 250
☛ How many nominated members are in the Rajya Sabha? → 12
☛ What is the term of a Rajya Sabha member? → 6 years
☛ Who is the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha? → Vice President
☛ How many Rajya Sabha members retire every two years? → One-third

q: Who among the following was the Speaker of the Second Lok Sabha?
qs.e: The Speaker of the Second Lok Sabha (1957-1962) was M. Ananthasayanam Ayyangar. He had also served as the Deputy Speaker of the First Lok Sabha. The Speaker is the presiding officer of the lower house of Parliament. The Second Lok Sabha was formed after the 1957 general elections. Bali Ram Bhagat, K. S. Hegde, and Bal Ram Jakhar were Speakers of later Lok Sabhas.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the Speaker of the First Lok Sabha? → G. V. Mavalankar
☛ Who was the Speaker of the Third Lok Sabha? → Sardar Hukam Singh
☛ What is the term of the Lok Sabha Speaker? → 5 years
☛ Who was the first Deputy Speaker of Lok Sabha? → M. Ananthasayanam Ayyangar
☛ Who elects the Lok Sabha Speaker? → Members of Lok Sabha

q: Who was the first speaker of the Indian Parliament?
qs.e: The first Speaker of the Indian Parliament was Ganesh Vasudev Mavlankar. He was elected as the first Speaker of the Lok Sabha in 1952 and served until 1956. Earlier, he also served as the President of the Constituent Assembly from 1946 to 1947. Mavlankar laid the foundation of parliamentary procedures and is often called the 'Father of the Lok Sabha'. Rajendra Prasad was the first President of India, BR Ambedkar was the chief architect of the Constitution, and KM Munshi was a member of the Constituent Assembly.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the first Speaker of Lok Sabha? → GV Mavlankar
☛ Full name of GV Mavlankar → Ganesh Vasudev Mavlankar
☛ Term of Lok Sabha Speaker → 5 years
☛ Current Lok Sabha Speaker → Om Birla (as of 2024)
☛ When was the first Lok Sabha formed? → 1952

q: The time gap between two sessions of the Parliament should NOT exceed:
qs.e: According to Article 85 of the Indian Constitution, the gap between two sessions of the Parliament should not exceed 6 months. This means that the Parliament must meet at least twice a year, and the maximum interval between two sessions is six months. This provision ensures that the Parliament functions regularly and does not remain adjourned for a long period. It strengthens the democratic process by ensuring continuous legislative oversight.
qs.kf:
☛ What is the maximum gap between two sessions of Parliament? → 6 months
☛ Under which Article is this provision? → Article 85
☛ How many times must Parliament meet in a year? → At least twice
☛ What is the longest possible interval between sessions? → 6 months
☛ What type of governance does this provision ensure? → Democratic

q: As per the Constitution of India. Which of the following is NOT an eligibility criteria for the appointment of a state Governor?
