o: He or she must not hold any other office of profit.
He or she must be a citizen of India.
He or she must have qualified for elections as a member of the Rajya Sabha.
He or she must have completed 35 years of age.
qs.e: According to Articles 157 and 158 of the Indian Constitution, the eligibility criteria for appointment as a state Governor include: being a citizen of India, having completed 35 years of age, and not holding any office of profit. The Governor must not be a member of Parliament or State Legislature, and qualification for election as a member of the Rajya Sabha is not required. This is a common misconception; however, being eligible for Rajya Sabha membership is not a prerequisite for becoming a Governor.
qs.kf:
☛ Who appoints the Governor? → President of India
☛ What is the term of Governor? → 5 years (during pleasure of President)
☛ Who administers oath to the Governor? → Chief Justice of High Court
☛ Who does the Governor represent? → President of India
☛ Which article deals with discretionary powers of Governor? → Article 163

q: How much is the number of Lok Sabha members currently?
qs.e: Lok Sabha is the lower house of the Indian Parliament. According to the Indian Constitution, the maximum strength of Lok Sabha is 552, which includes 530 members representing states, 20 members representing union territories, and 2 members nominated by the President from the Anglo-Indian community. Currently, the total number of Lok Sabha members is 545, consisting of 543 elected members and 2 nominated members. This number is determined under Articles 81 and 331 of the Constitution. Although the maximum limit is 552, the present Lok Sabha has 545 members.
qs.kf:
☛ What is the maximum strength of Lok Sabha? → 552
☛ Number of members representing states in Lok Sabha? → 530
☛ Number of members representing union territories in Lok Sabha? → 20
☛ Number of nominated Anglo-Indian members in Lok Sabha? → 2 (now abolished)
☛ Current number of Lok Sabha members? → 545

q: Who among the following is not a part of the Indian Parliament?
qs.e: The Indian Parliament consists of three parts: the President, the Lok Sabha, and the Rajya Sabha (also called the State Council). The Legislative Council is the upper house at the state level and is part of the state legislature, not the Parliament. According to Article 79, the Parliament comprises the President and two Houses: Lok Sabha (lower house) and Rajya Sabha (upper house). The Legislative Council exists only in some states and has no connection with the Parliament. Hence, the Legislative Council is not a part of the Indian Parliament.
qs.kf:
☛ What are the parts of Indian Parliament? → President, Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha
☛ Which is the upper house of Parliament? → Rajya Sabha
☛ Which is the lower house of Parliament? → Lok Sabha
☛ Legislative Council is part of which body? → State Legislature
☛ Article 79 relates to what? → Structure of Parliament

q: How many members of the Rajya Sabha are nominated by the President of India?
qs.e: According to Article 80 of the Indian Constitution, the maximum strength of the Rajya Sabha is 250 members. Out of these, 238 members are elected by the legislative assemblies of states and union territories, while 12 members are nominated by the President of India. These nominated members are individuals having special knowledge or practical experience in fields such as literature, art, science, and social service. The President nominates them to ensure expertise and diversity in the House. This provision falls under Part V of the Constitution. The term of nominated members is 6 years, same as other Rajya Sabha members. The Rajya Sabha is the upper house of Parliament and represents the states of India.
qs.kf:
☛ What is the maximum strength of Rajya Sabha? → 250
☛ Which article describes the composition of Rajya Sabha? → Article 80
☛ What is the term of nominated members of Rajya Sabha? → 6 years
☛ From which fields are nominated members chosen? → Literature, art, science, social service
☛ How many Rajya Sabha members are elected by states? → 238

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (24/06/2025) Shift 3
q: Who elects the members of the Estimates Committee in the Indian Parliament?
qs.e: The Estimates Committee of the Indian Parliament is a key financial committee that examines government expenditures. Its members are elected by the Members of the Lok Sabha, not by the Prime Minister, Rajya Sabha, or President. The committee consists of 30 members, elected annually by Lok Sabha members through the principle of proportional representation. This committee ensures financial discipline by scrutinizing estimates and reporting back to Parliament.
qs.kf:
☛ How many members are in the Estimates Committee? → 30
☛ By which system are members elected? → Proportional representation
☛ What is the main function of the committee? → Examining government estimates
☛ Can Rajya Sabha members be in this committee? → No, only Lok Sabha members
☛ What is the term of the committee? → One year

q: Who chairs the joint sitting of the two houses of the Parliament?
qs.e: According to Article 108 of the Indian Constitution, the joint sitting of both houses of Parliament is chaired by the Speaker of the Lok Sabha. In the absence of the Speaker, the Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha presides. A joint sitting is called when a bill passed by one house is rejected by the other or remains pending for more than six months. So far, three joint sittings have been held: the Dowry Prohibition Bill (1961), the Banking Service Commission Bill (1977), and the Prevention of Terrorism Bill (2002). The President can summon the joint sitting but does not preside over it.
qs.kf:
☛ Who summons joint sitting → President
☛ Who chairs joint sitting → Speaker of Lok Sabha
☛ Alternative in absence → Deputy Speaker of Lok Sabha
☛ Constitutional provision → Article 108
☛ Total joint sittings so far → Three (1961, 1977, 2002)

q: Which law allowed Indian members to discuss the budget in the Legislative Council for the first time?
qs.e: The Indian Council Act of 1892 allowed Indian members to discuss the budget in the Legislative Council for the first time. This act increased the membership of the councils and granted the right to ask questions on certain subjects. However, it did not provide the right to vote on the budget or propose amendments. This act was a step towards giving Indians limited participation in the legislative process. Subsequently, the Morley-Minto Reforms of 1909 introduced separate electorates.
qs.kf:
☛ Indian Council Act, 1892 → Allowed budget discussion
☛ Indian Council Act, 1861 → First included Indians in Legislative Council
☛ Government of India Act, 1858 → Ended East India Company rule
☛ Indian Council Act, 1909 → Introduced separate electorates
☛ Indian Council Act, 1892 → Granted right to ask questions

q: Which House is headed by Speaker from both Houses of Indian Parliament?
qs.e: The Indian Parliament consists of two houses - Lok Sabha (Lower House) and Rajya Sabha (Upper House). The presiding officer of Lok Sabha is the Speaker, who conducts the proceedings and maintains the dignity of the House. Rajya Sabha is presided over by the Vice President, who is the ex-officio Chairman of that House. Thus, the Speaker heads only Lok Sabha, not Rajya Sabha. The Speaker is elected by the members of Lok Sabha. The Speaker has a casting vote in case of a tie. To remove the Speaker, a resolution must be passed by a majority of all members of Lok Sabha.
qs.kf:
☛ Who is the Chairman of Rajya Sabha? → Vice President
☛ Who elects the Speaker of Lok Sabha? → Members of Lok Sabha
☛ What special vote does the Speaker have? → Casting vote
☛ What majority is required to remove the Speaker? → Majority of all members of the House
☛ Which Article of the Constitution provides for the Speaker? → Article 93

q: Which of the following articles deals with language to be used in the Parliament?
qs.e: Article 120 of the Indian Constitution deals with the language to be used in the Parliament. It provides that Hindi or English shall be used for the transaction of business in Parliament. However, the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha or the Speaker of the Lok Sabha may permit a member to address the House in their mother tongue. This article falls under Part XVII (Official Language) of the Constitution. Article 118 relates to the conduct of business in Parliament, Article 119 deals with financial procedure, and Article 121 pertains to parliamentary privileges.
qs.kf:
☛ Which article deals with language in Parliament? → 120
☛ What languages are used in Parliament? → Hindi and English
☛ Who permits speaking in mother tongue in Parliament? → Chairman or Speaker
☛ Which part of Constitution deals with official language? → Part XVII
☛ Article 120 falls under which part? → Part XVII

q: Which Article provides Ministers the right to participate in parliamentary proceedings but without voting rights?
qs.e: Article 88 of the Indian Constitution grants Ministers the right to participate in the proceedings of either House of Parliament, but without the right to vote. This provision applies to Ministers who are not members of Parliament. They can speak and take part in any House, but voting is restricted to members of that House. This article clarifies the role of Ministers in parliamentary democracy, ensuring they can contribute to debates while respecting the voting rights of elected members.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 88 → Ministers can participate in Parliament but cannot vote
☛ Article 78 → Duties of Prime Minister
☛ Article 53 → Executive power of Union vested in President
☛ Article 77 → Conduct of business of Government of India
☛ No voting right → Non-member Ministers cannot vote

q: The Indian Constitution empowers the Parliament to make laws on matters in the State List under which of the following circumstances?
1. When the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution to that effect
2. During a National Emergency
3. When states make a request
4. To implement international agreements
5. At the discretion of the Prime Minister
qs.e: Under Articles 249, 250, 252, and 253 of the Indian Constitution, the Parliament can legislate on subjects in the State List. According to Article 249, if the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution by a two-thirds majority declaring it necessary in the national interest, Parliament can make laws. Article 250 empowers Parliament to legislate on State List matters during a National Emergency. Article 252 allows Parliament to make laws for two or more states upon request by the states. Article 253 gives Parliament the power to make laws to implement international agreements. There is no provision allowing Parliament to legislate at the discretion of the Prime Minister. Thus, circumstances 1, 2, 3, and 4 are correct, while 5 is incorrect.
qs.kf:
☛ Resolution by Rajya Sabha → Under Article 249 for national interest
☛ National Emergency → Under Article 250 empowers Parliament
☛ Request by states → Under Article 252 for two or more states
☛ International agreements → Under Article 253 for implementation
☛ Prime Minister's discretion → No such provision in the Constitution

q: Which of the following statements about Parliamentary Committees is TRUE?
o: Ad Hoc Committees are permanent in nature.
Standing Committees are reconstituted from time to time and are permanent.
There are no temporary Parliamentary Committees.
qs.e: Parliamentary Committees are of two types: Standing Committees and Ad Hoc Committees. Standing Committees are permanent in nature and are reconstituted periodically (e.g., Estimates Committee, Public Accounts Committee). Ad Hoc Committees are temporary and are constituted for a specific purpose; they cease to exist after completing their task (e.g., Select Committee, Joint Committee). Therefore, not all Parliamentary Committees are permanent; only Standing Committees are permanent, while Ad Hoc Committees are temporary.
qs.kf:
☛ Public Accounts Committee → Standing Committee, 22 members (15 Lok Sabha + 7 Rajya Sabha)
☛ Estimates Committee → Standing Committee, 30 members (all from Lok Sabha)
☛ Select Committee → Ad Hoc Committee, temporary nature
☛ Standing Committees → Reconstituted every year or from time to time
☛ Ad Hoc Committees → Constituted for specific task, dissolved after completion

q: Article _________ describes the procedure for joint sitting of both Houses of the Parliament in certain cases.
qs.e: Article 108 of the Indian Constitution describes the procedure for a joint sitting of both Houses of Parliament in certain cases. This procedure applies when a bill passed by one House is rejected by the other, or when there is a disagreement between the two Houses. The President can summon a joint sitting in such situations. The joint sitting is presided over by the Speaker of the Lok Sabha. Only three bills have been passed through joint sittings so far: the Dowry Prohibition Bill (1961), the Banking Service Commission Bill (1978), and the Prevention of Terrorism Bill (2002).
qs.kf:
☛ Who presides over a joint sitting? → Speaker of Lok Sabha
☛ When is a joint sitting called? → When a bill passed by one House is pending in the other for six months
☛ Which Article deals with Money Bills? → Article 110
☛ Can a bill be introduced in both Houses? → Yes, ordinary bills can be introduced in either House
☛ What is Article 94 about? → Vacation and resignation of Deputy Speaker and Deputy Chairman

q: Which of the following statements correctly differentiates the power of the Rajya Sabha from the Lok Sabha?
o: Rajya Sabha can initiate a motion of no-confidence against the Council of Ministers
Rajya Sabha can amend Money Bills
Rajya Sabha has equal power with Lok Sabha in all financial matters
Rajya Sabha can authorise Parliament to make laws on State subjects
qs.e: The Rajya Sabha does not have the power to legislate on state subjects, but it can authorise Parliament to do so in the national interest under Article 249. This requires a resolution passed by a two-thirds majority of members present and voting. The authorisation is valid for a maximum of one year and can be extended. Other options are incorrect because the Rajya Sabha cannot initiate a no-confidence motion against the Council of Ministers, cannot amend Money Bills, and does not have equal power with the Lok Sabha in financial matters. The Lok Sabha has supremacy in financial legislation.
qs.kf:
☛ Under which article can Rajya Sabha authorise Parliament to make laws on State List? → Article 249
☛ What majority is required for such a resolution in Rajya Sabha? → Two-thirds
☛ What is the maximum validity of such authorisation? → One year
☛ Money Bills are introduced in which house? → Lok Sabha
☛ No-confidence motion can be moved in which house? → Lok Sabha

q: In accordance with Article 84 of the Constitution of India, which of the following is the minimum age a person must meet to qualify for membership of the House of the People?
qs.e: Article 84 of the Constitution of India lays down the qualifications for membership of Parliament. For the House of the People (Lok Sabha), a person must be at least twenty-five years of age. In contrast, for the Council of States (Rajya Sabha), the minimum age is thirty years. This age requirement ensures that candidates have sufficient maturity and experience to effectively represent the people. The Constitution also requires that the person be a citizen of India and meet any additional qualifications prescribed by Parliament. Other options: 21 years (minimum for state legislative assemblies), 30 years (for Rajya Sabha), and 18 years (voting age).
qs.kf:
☛ Minimum age for Lok Sabha membership → 25 years
☛ Minimum age for Rajya Sabha membership → 30 years
☛ Minimum age for State Legislative Assembly membership → 21 years
☛ Minimum voting age in India → 18 years
☛ Other conditions under Article 84 → Citizen of India and fulfill other qualifications prescribed by Parliament

q: As per Article 80 of the Constitution of India, which of the following indicates the number of members appointed by the President to the Council of States?
qs.e: According to Article 80 of the Constitution of India, the Council of States (Rajya Sabha) has a total strength of 250 members. Out of these, 238 members represent the States and Union Territories, while the remaining 12 members are nominated by the President. These nominated members are persons having special knowledge or practical experience in fields such as literature, art, science, and social service. The President nominates them to bring expertise and diversity to the Rajya Sabha. This provision is part of Part V of the Constitution.
qs.kf:
☛ Total strength of Rajya Sabha → 250
☛ Number of members nominated by the President → 12
☛ Number of elected members in Rajya Sabha → 238
☛ Maximum strength of Rajya Sabha → 250
☛ Fields for nominated members → Literature, art, science, social service

q: What is the constitutional consequence if the Lok Sabha passes a no-confidence motion against the ruling government?
o: The Speaker of Lok Sabha is removed by the President
The government may continue without any change
Only the Prime Minister must submit resignation
The Council of Ministers is obligated to step down
qs.e: According to Article 75(3) of the Indian Constitution, the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha. When the Lok Sabha passes a no-confidence motion, it signifies that the government has lost the confidence of the lower house. Under constitutional convention and Article 75, the entire Council of Ministers must resign. The resignation of only the Prime Minister is insufficient because the principle of collective responsibility applies. The President then may explore alternative arrangements, such as inviting another party to form a government or dissolving the Lok Sabha. This process is a fundamental aspect of parliamentary democracy.
qs.kf:
☛ In which house can a no-confidence motion be introduced? → Only in Lok Sabha
☛ What majority is required to pass a no-confidence motion? → Simple majority
☛ What happens to the Council of Ministers after a no-confidence motion is passed? → They must resign
☛ Can the Prime Minister resign alone? → No, the entire Council resigns
☛ What is the President's role after a no-confidence motion? → To make alternative arrangements

q: When a law passed by a State Legislature clashes with a Parliamentary law on a Concurrent List subject, what is the legal outcome?
o: The matter is settled through a ruling by the Supreme Court
The state legislation automatically overrides the central law
The central law overrides the state law unless the state law has Presidential assent
The Parliament is obligated to annul the state law
qs.e: Under the Indian Constitution, both the Centre and states can legislate on subjects in the Concurrent List. When a state law clashes with a central law on a concurrent subject, the central law prevails generally. However, if the state law has received Presidential assent, it can operate in that state and override the central law. This provision is enshrined in Article 254 of the Constitution. Thus, unless the state law obtains Presidential assent, the central law remains supreme. Other options are incorrect because the matter does not always go to the Supreme Court, the state law does not automatically override, and Parliament is not obligated to annul the state law.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Article deals with conflict on Concurrent List subjects? → Article 254
☛ When does a state law override a central law on Concurrent List? → When the state law has Presidential assent
☛ How many subjects are in the Concurrent List? → 52 subjects (originally 47)
☛ Where is the division of powers between Centre and states given? → Seventh Schedule of the Constitution
☛ When can Parliament legislate on a State List subject? → By a Rajya Sabha resolution in national interest

q: How many members are elected to the Public Accounts Committee from Rajya Sabha?
qs.e: The Public Accounts Committee (PAC) is one of the most important standing committees of Parliament, responsible for auditing the government's expenditures. It consists of a total of 22 members, out of which 15 members are elected from Lok Sabha and 7 members from Rajya Sabha. The members are elected by the method of proportional representation using the single transferable vote. The term of the committee is one year. It was first formed in 1921 under the Government of India Act 1919. After independence, it was given the status of a parliamentary committee in 1950. By convention, the chairman of the committee is appointed from the Leader of the Opposition in Lok Sabha.
qs.kf:
☛ Total members in Public Accounts Committee → 22
☛ Members from Lok Sabha → 15
☛ Members from Rajya Sabha → 7
☛ Term of the committee → 1 year
☛ Chairman of the committee → Leader of Opposition in Lok Sabha

q: Which of the following articles is INCORRECTY matched with the Constitutional Provisions related to Parliament ?
o: Article 93 ----Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the House of People
Article 99 ---Composition of the Council of States/Rajya Sabha
Article 89---- Chairman and Deputy Chairman of Council of States
Article 105--- Powers and Privileges of the Houses of Parliament
qs.e: Article 99 relates to Oath or affirmation by members of Parliament, not the composition of the Council of States. Article 93 deals with the Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the House of the People, Article 89 deals with the Chairman and Deputy Chairman of the Council of States, and Article 105 deals with the Powers and Privileges of the Houses of Parliament. The composition of the Rajya Sabha is actually covered under Article 80, which provides for the composition of the Council of States (election of members from states and union territories). Article 99 specifically requires every member of Parliament to take an oath or affirmation before taking their seat. Therefore, matching Article 99 with the composition of Rajya Sabha is incorrect.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 80 → Composition of Rajya Sabha
☛ Article 81 → Composition of Lok Sabha
☛ Article 79 → Constitution of Parliament (President, Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha)
☛ Article 100 → Voting in Houses and Quorum
☛ Article 118 → Rules of Procedure of Parliament

q: The _______ takes the decision to declare any bill to be a money bill.
o: Governor of the Reserve bank of India
qs.e: According to Article 110 of the Indian Constitution, the final decision to declare a bill as a Money Bill rests with the Speaker of the Lok Sabha. The Speaker's certificate on a Money Bill is considered final and binding and cannot be challenged in any court or by any other House. A Money Bill can only be introduced in the Lok Sabha, and the Rajya Sabha can only make recommendations, which the Lok Sabha may accept or reject. If the Rajya Sabha does not return the bill within 14 days, it is deemed passed. The President cannot return a Money Bill for reconsideration under Article 111.
qs.kf:
☛ Definition of Money Bill → Given in Article 110
☛ Where Money Bill is introduced → Only in Lok Sabha
☛ Role of Rajya Sabha → Can only make recommendations within 14 days
☛ Article 111 → President cannot withhold assent or return Money Bill
☛ Speaker's certificate → Final and cannot be questioned in any court

q: The National Sports Governance Bill, 2025, was introduced to achieve which of the following objective?
o: To establish rules for recognizing and regulating sports bodies
To improve physical and sports education in schools
To launch a national-level talent hunt program
To increase budget allocation for Olympic sports
qs.e: The National Sports Governance Bill, 2025, was introduced to reform the administration of sports bodies in India. Its primary objective is to establish clear rules for the recognition, regulation, and monitoring of sports federations. The bill aims to ensure transparency, accountability, and good governance in sports organizations. It includes provisions such as term limits, age caps, and financial transparency. Improving physical education in schools, launching talent hunt programs, and increasing budget allocation for Olympic sports are not the direct objectives of this bill; they may be part of other initiatives. The bill focuses on governance reforms to enhance the functioning of national sports federations and align them with international standards.
qs.kf:
☛ Main objective of National Sports Governance Bill, 2025 → To establish rules for recognizing and regulating sports bodies
☛ Purpose of the Bill → Ensure transparency and accountability in sports federations
☛ Key provisions → Term limits and age caps
☛ Applicable to → National sports federations
☛ Related Ministry → Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports

q: Which among the following information is NOT a ground for exemption from disclosure of information under RTI Act, 2005?
o: Cabinet papers including records of deliberation
qs.e: Section 8(1) of the RTI Act, 2005 lists the grounds for exemption from disclosure of information. These include breach of privilege of Parliament (Section 8(1)(c)), Cabinet papers including records of deliberation (Section 8(1)(i)), and sovereignty and integrity of India (Section 8(1)(a)). Public Interest is not a ground for exemption; rather, it is a principle that encourages disclosure. Under Section 8(2), even exempted information can be disclosed if public interest outweighs the harm. Thus, public interest is not an exemption ground but an exception.
qs.kf:
☛ How many exemptions are under Section 8(1) of RTI Act? → 10 exemptions
☛ Under which section is Cabinet papers exempted? → Section 8(1) (i)
☛ Under which section is sovereignty and integrity exempted? → Section 8(1)(a)
☛ Under which section is breach of privilege of Parliament exempted? → Section 8(1)(c)
☛ Which section allows disclosure in public interest? → Section 8(2)

q: Who appoints the Chairperson of the Committee on Public Undertakings (COPU) in India?
qs.e: The Committee on Public Undertakings (COPU) in India is a parliamentary committee that examines the functioning of public sector undertakings (PSUs). The chairperson of COPU is appointed by the Speaker of Lok Sabha. The appointment is made from among the members of Lok Sabha, and the chairperson is usually a member of the opposition. The committee consists of 22 members: 15 from Lok Sabha and 7 from Rajya Sabha. COPU reviews the accounts, annual reports, and CAG reports of PSUs.
qs.kf:
☛ Total members of COPU? → 22 (15 Lok Sabha + 7 Rajya Sabha)
☛ Who appoints the chairperson of COPU? → Speaker of Lok Sabha
☛ Which reports does COPU review? → CAG reports and annual reports
☛ Year of establishment of COPU? → 1964
☛ COPU is related to which ministry? → Ministry of Finance

q: Which of the following British Indian government legislation separated for the first time 'provincial budgets' from the 'central budget' and authorised the provincial legislatures to enact their budgets?
qs.e: The Government of India Act of 1919, also known as the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms, for the first time separated provincial budgets from the central budget. It empowered provincial legislatures to prepare and pass their own budgets, promoting decentralization of financial powers. Before this act, all budgets were controlled by the central government. This act introduced dyarchy (dual government), dividing provincial subjects into transferred and reserved categories. It gave provinces financial autonomy, allowing them to allocate resources according to local needs. This was a significant step towards federalism in British India.
qs.kf:
☛ Act that separated provincial budgets from central budget → Government of India Act of 1919
☛ Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms → Another name for the Act of 1919
☛ Introduction of dyarchy → By the Act of 1919
☛ Provincial legislatures gained budget powers → Through the Act of 1919
☛ First step towards financial decentralization in India → Government of India Act of 1919

q: During the Winter Session of Parliament (1–19 December 2025), which of the following bills was enacted as an Act of Parliament (i.e., passed by both Houses and brought into force as an Act)?
o: The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (Amendment) Bill, 2025
The Viksit Bharat Shiksha Adhishthan Bill, 2025
qs.e: During the Winter Session of Parliament (1–19 December 2025), The Repealing and Amending Bill, 2025 was passed by both Houses and enacted as an Act. This bill aimed to repeal obsolete and outdated laws, as well as make necessary amendments to existing legislation, as part of legal reforms to simplify and update the legal framework. Among the other options, The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (Amendment) Bill, 2025, The Viksit Bharat Shiksha Adhishthan Bill, 2025, and The Securities Markets Code Bill, 2025 were not enacted during this session. The bill was based on recommendations from the Law Commission to streamline the statute book.
qs.kf:
☛ The Repealing and Amending Bill, 2025 → Enacted in Winter Session 2025
☛ Purpose of Repealing and Amending Bill → Remove obsolete laws
☛ Law Commission → Recommends legal reforms
☛ Winter Session 2025 → 1 to 19 December
☛ Bill enacted by Parliament → Becomes an Act after Presidential assent

q: In 2025, the Central Excise (Amendment) Bill aimed to amend legislation originally enacted in which year?
qs.e: The Central Excise (Amendment) Bill, 2025 aimed to amend the original Central Excise Act, 1944. This Act is the foundation for the collection and administration of excise duty in India. The 1944 Act has been amended periodically, and the 2025 Bill was introduced to bring necessary changes. Excise duty is a significant source of revenue for the Government of India, levied on manufactured goods. Through this bill, the government sought to simplify the tax system and improve compliance. The Central Excise Act, 1944 governs the imposition and collection of excise duties on goods produced or manufactured in India. It has been amended several times to align with economic reforms, including the introduction of Goods and Services Tax (GST) in 2017, after which excise duty is mainly levied on petroleum products, tobacco, and alcohol.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Central Excise Act enacted? → 1944
☛ What type of tax is excise duty? → Indirect tax
☛ Who pays excise duty? → Manufacturer
☛ Before GST, excise duty was levied by which government? → Central Government
☛ Currently, excise duty is mainly on which products? → Petrol, diesel, tobacco, alcohol

q: Which of the following Acts was enacted by the British Parliament to regulate the administration of the British East India Company’s territories in India, particularly in Bengal?
qs.e: The Regulating Act of 1773 was the first step by the British Parliament to control the Company's rule in India. This Act made the Governor of Bengal the Governor-General and appointed Warren Hastings as the first Governor-General. It established the Supreme Court at Calcutta and required the Company's directors to report their activities to the government. The Act focused on the administration of Bengal and aimed to reduce administrative decentralization.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Regulating Act passed? → 1773
☛ Who became the first Governor-General under this Act? → Warren Hastings
☛ Which Act established the Supreme Court at Calcutta? → Regulating Act, 1773
☛ Which was the first British Act to regulate the Company's rule? → Regulating Act, 1773
☛ Which region's administration did the Regulating Act focus on? → Bengal

q: Which authority is empowered under the Constitution to define the powers, privileges, and immunities of the members of each House of Parliament and their committees?
qs.e: Under Article 105 of the Indian Constitution, the power to define the powers, privileges, and immunities of the members of each House of Parliament and their committees is vested with Parliament itself. This provision allows Parliament to ensure that its members can discharge their duties without interference. Article 105(3) specifically states that until Parliament defines these privileges by law, they shall be the same as those enjoyed by the British House of Commons at the time the Constitution came into effect. However, the Supreme Court has clarified that these privileges are subject to fundamental rights. Thus, it is Parliament, not the President, Speaker, or Supreme Court, that has the authority to define these privileges.
qs.kf:
☛ Which article deals with privileges of Parliament? → Article 105
☛ Privileges of MPs are subject to which part of Constitution? → Fundamental Rights
☛ Which article provides freedom of publication of parliamentary proceedings? → Article 105(2)
☛ Who has the final say on parliamentary privileges? → Parliament itself
☛ Which article deals with privileges of state legislatures? → Article 194

q: If an Emergency Proclamation is approved only by the Rajya Sabha while the Lok Sabha is dissolved, for how long does the Proclamation remain in force from the first sitting of the newly constituted Lok Sabha?
qs.e: According to Article 352 of the Indian Constitution, when the Lok Sabha is dissolved and an Emergency Proclamation is approved only by the Rajya Sabha, the Proclamation remains in force for 30 days from the first sitting of the newly constituted Lok Sabha. Within this period, the new Lok Sabha must approve the Proclamation; otherwise, it ceases to be effective. This provision ensures democratic oversight.
qs.kf:
☛ Provision for National Emergency → Article 352
☛ Maximum duration of National Emergency → Indefinite (parliamentary approval every 6 months)
☛ Majority required for proclamation of National Emergency → Special majority (2/3 of those present and voting)
☛ Fundamental Rights during National Emergency → Articles 358 and 359 suspended
☛ Times National Emergency proclaimed in India → Three times (1962, 1971, 1975)

q: Under Article 275 of the Constitution, the sums provided by the Parliament as grants-in-aid to states are required to be charged on which fund?
qs.e: Under Article 275, the sums provided by Parliament as grants-in-aid to states are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India. This expenditure is not subject to the annual vote of Parliament, making it a charged expenditure. The Consolidated Fund of India records all receipts and expenditures, while the Public Account holds deposits and the Contingency Fund is for emergencies. These grants are given to states for their schemes and development works. Article 275 enables the central government to provide financial assistance to states, especially those in need. The amount and terms are determined by Parliament through law. This ensures states have resources for public welfare and infrastructure without annual uncertainty.
qs.kf:
☛ What is Article 275 about? → Grants-in-aid to states
☛ What expenditures are charged on the Consolidated Fund? → Salaries of judges, governors, grants under Article 275, etc.
☛ What is the size of the Contingency Fund of India? → Rs. 500 crore
☛ What is held in the Public Account of India? → Provident funds, deposits, other accounts
☛ Who determines the grants under Article 275? → Parliament

q: Special address delivered by the President to both Houses of Parliament at the start of the first session after each general election and at the opening of the first session of every year is mentioned under which of the following Articles of the Constitution of India?
qs.e: Article 87 of the Constitution of India deals with the special address by the President. According to this article, the President addresses both Houses of Parliament: (1) at the commencement of the first session after each general election, and (2) at the commencement of the first session of every year. This address is delivered in a joint sitting of Parliament. In this address, the President outlines the policies and programs of the government. Article 85 deals with sessions, prorogation, and dissolution of Parliament. Article 86 gives the President the right to address or send messages to either House. Article 88 gives ministers the right to speak in either House. Thus, the special address is covered under Article 87.
qs.kf:
☛ President's special address → Article 87
☛ Sessions, prorogation, dissolution of Parliament → Article 85
☛ President's right to address or send messages → Article 86
☛ Ministers' right to speak in Parliament → Article 88
☛ Special address outlines → government policies and programs

q: Before the present premises, where did the Supreme Court of India operate from?
o: From the High Court of Delhi
qs.e: The Supreme Court of India was established on 28 January 1950. Initially, it functioned from the Chamber of Princes in the Parliament Building (now the Rajya Sabha chamber). In 1954-55, the Court shifted to the then Secretariat Building. The foundation stone of the present building was laid on 29 October 1954, and it was inaugurated on 4 August 1958. The design of the present building was prepared by Ganpat Singh. Thus, from its inception until 1958, the Supreme Court operated from the Parliament Building and the Secretariat Building.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Supreme Court building inaugurated? → 4 August 1958
☛ Who designed the present Supreme Court building? → Ganpat Singh
☛ Initially, the Court was located in which part of the Parliament? → Chamber of Princes
☛ What is the establishment date of the Supreme Court? → 28 January 1950
☛ Who was the first Chief Justice of India? → Harilal Kania

q: Reduction of a judicial sentence, especially a sentence of death to the another less severe one is known as ________.
qs.e: The process of reducing a judicial sentence, especially a death sentence, to a less severe one is known as commutation. It is a form of clemency usually exercised by the Governor or the President. Under Article 72 of the Indian Constitution, the President has the power to pardon, suspend, or commute a death sentence. Similarly, Article 161 grants this power to the Governor. Commutation changes the nature of the sentence, such as converting death penalty to life imprisonment. Among the other options, 'forgive' means full pardon, 'deferment' means postponement, and 'stoppage' means suspension of the sentence.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Article deals with the President's pardoning power? → Article 72
☛ Which Article deals with the Governor's pardoning power? → Article 161
☛ What is the term for converting death sentence to life imprisonment? → Commutation
☛ Among pardon, commutation, respite, and remission, which completely extinguishes the sentence? → Pardon
☛ Who has the final authority to commute a death sentence in India? → The President

q: Who is the Chairman of the Seventh Central Pay Commission?
qs.e: The Seventh Central Pay Commission was constituted by the Government of India on 28 February 2014. Its chairman was Justice Ashok Kumar Mathur, a former judge of the Supreme Court of India. Other members of the commission included Vivek Rai (Member) and Meeta Banerjee (Member). The commission submitted its report on 19 November 2015, which was implemented on 29 June 2016. Its recommendations brought significant changes to the salary, allowances, and pension of central government employees.
qs.kf:
☛ Chairman of 7th Central Pay Commission → Ashok Kumar Mathur
☛ Date of formation → 28 February 2014
☛ Date of report submission → 19 November 2015
☛ Date of implementation → 29 June 2016
☛ Members of the commission → Vivek Rai and Meeta Banerjee

q: The concept of the Supreme Court's Advisory jurisdiction was taken from which country?
qs.e: The concept of Advisory Jurisdiction of the Supreme Court of India was borrowed from Canada. Under Article 143, the President can seek the opinion of the Supreme Court on legal matters, but this opinion is not binding on the court. This provision exists in the Canadian Constitution where the Supreme Court of Canada has the authority to give opinions on questions referred by the government. India adopted this concept to enable the President to obtain judicial advice on disputes between the Centre and states or on important legal questions, aiding in their resolution.
qs.kf:
☛ Which article deals with Advisory Jurisdiction in India? → Article 143
☛ From which country was this concept borrowed? → Canada
☛ Which institution advises the President? → Supreme Court
☛ Is the Supreme Court's advice binding? → No
☛ What is the highest court in Canada called? → Supreme Court of Canada

q: Who is considered the last bastion of the democracy?
qs.e: In a democracy, the judiciary is considered the guardian of the constitution and the last bastion of democracy. The Supreme Court has the power of judicial review, allowing it to examine the constitutionality of laws made by the legislature and executive. It protects the fundamental rights of citizens and checks arbitrary government action. In India, the Supreme Court has the final authority to interpret the constitution, making it the cornerstone of the democratic framework. Unlike the parliament and executive, the judiciary is independent and impartial, which helps maintain democratic values.
qs.kf:
☛ Which is considered the last bastion of democracy? → Supreme Court
☛ Who has the power of judicial review in India? → Supreme Court
☛ Who is the guardian of the constitution? → Supreme Court
☛ What is the highest court of appeal in India? → Supreme Court
☛ Why is judicial independence important for democracy? → To ensure checks and balances

q: Which states are included in the Mahadayi Water Disputes Tribunal?
qs.e: The Mahadayi Water Disputes Tribunal was constituted to resolve the water-sharing dispute of the Mahadayi River (also known as Mandovi). This river originates in the Western Ghats and flows into the Arabian Sea. The dispute primarily involves the states of Goa, Karnataka, and Maharashtra. Karnataka proposed the Kalasa-Bhandura dam project on the river, which was opposed by Goa. The tribunal delivered its final verdict in 2018, allocating 13.42 TMC water to Karnataka, 24 TMC to Goa, and 1.33 TMC to Maharashtra. The river is the lifeline of Goa, serving as the main source of drinking water and irrigation for the state.
qs.kf:
☛ Alternate name of Mahadayi River → Mandovi
☛ States involved in Mahadayi water dispute → Goa, Karnataka, Maharashtra
☛ Year of tribunal formation → 2010
☛ Chairman of the tribunal → Justice J.M. Malik
☛ Water allocated to Karnataka → 13.42 TMC

q: Indian court system follows the ________ type justice system.
qs.e: The Indian court system follows an integrated type of justice system. This means that there is a single hierarchy of courts, with the Supreme Court at the top, followed by High Courts and then subordinate courts. This system is described under Articles 124 to 147 of the Indian Constitution. In an integrated system, there are no separate courts for the center and states; instead, all courts are part of the same chain. In contrast, a dual system has separate federal and state courts, as in the United States. The Indian system is integrated, which ensures judicial uniformity and consistency.
qs.kf:
☛ What type of justice system does the Indian court system follow? → Integrated
☛ When was the Supreme Court of India established? → 1950
☛ Which part of the Indian Constitution deals with the judiciary? → Part V
☛ Who appoints the judges of the High Court? → President
☛ Which is the smallest High Court in India? → Sikkim

q: The organ of the government that primarily looks after the function of implementation and administration is called the_______.
qs.e: Government comprises three organs: Legislature, Executive, and Judiciary. The Executive is primarily responsible for implementing laws and running the administration. It enforces government policies and handles day-to-day governance. In India, the President, Prime Minister, and Council of Ministers form part of the Executive. While the Legislature makes laws and the Judiciary interprets them, the Executive executes them. It also has the power to make administrative decisions and is accountable to the Legislature. The Executive ensures that the laws passed by the Legislature are effectively put into practice.
qs.kf:
☛ Main function of Executive → Implementation of laws and administration
☛ Head of Executive in India → President (constitutional head)
☛ Real executive power exercised by → Prime Minister and Council of Ministers
☛ Meaning of Executive → Organ of government that runs the state
☛ Three organs of government → Legislature, Executive, Judiciary

q: The first Indian woman judge of the Supreme Court of India was:
qs.e: The first Indian woman judge of the Supreme Court of India was Fatima Beevi. She was born on 30 April 1927 in Kerala. She became a judge of the Supreme Court in 1989 and retired in 1992. After retirement, she served as the Governor of Tamil Nadu. Fatima Beevi set a milestone for women in the legal field. Indira Banerjee and Indu Malhotra became judges later. R Bhanumathi was a High Court judge, not a Supreme Court judge. Hence Fatima Beevi is the correct answer.
qs.kf:
☛ First Indian woman Supreme Court judge → Fatima Beevi
☛ Birthplace of Fatima Beevi → Kerala
☛ Year of Supreme Court appointment → 1989
☛ Year of retirement → 1992
☛ Post-retirement role → Governor of Tamil Nadu

q: The ‘Animal Welfare Board of India’ established in the year 1962, under Section 4 of the ‘Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960’, is a statutory advisory body, formed for advising the Government of India, on animal welfare laws, falls under which ministry?
o: Ministry of environment and forest and climate change
qs.e: The Animal Welfare Board of India (AWBI) was established in 1962 under Section 4 of the 'Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960' as a statutory advisory body. Its primary role is to advise the Government of India on animal welfare laws and prevent cruelty to animals. The Board currently functions under the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change. Initially, it was under the Ministry of Forests and Environment, but later it was brought under the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change. AWBI provides guidance to the government on the implementation of animal welfare policies, laws, and regulations, and works to promote animal welfare across the country.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Animal Welfare Board of India established? → 1962
☛ Under which Act was AWBI constituted? → Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960
☛ Where is the headquarters of AWBI located? → Chennai, Tamil Nadu
☛ Which ministry does AWBI come under? → Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
☛ Who heads the AWBI? → A chairperson appointed by the government

q: The Chairman of National Human Rights Commission should be:
o: a speaker of the Lok Sabha
a retired Chief Justice of India
qs.e: The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) was established in 1993 under the Protection of Human Rights Act. Its Chairman is a retired Chief Justice of India, ensuring the highest judicial experience. The commission has four other members, two of whom have a judicial background. The Chairman is appointed by the President on the recommendation of a committee comprising the Prime Minister, Speaker of Lok Sabha, Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha, and other dignitaries. This provision aims to maintain the independence and impartiality of the commission.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the first Chairman of NHRC? → Justice Ranganath Mishra
☛ Where is the headquarters of NHRC located? → New Delhi
☛ What is the tenure of the NHRC Chairman? → 5 years or age of 70, whichever is earlier
☛ On which international principle is NHRC based? → Paris Principles
☛ What powers does NHRC have? → Powers of a civil court

q: Which of the following features provided by the constitution of India is related to 'Indian Judiciary'?
o: Each state has its own high court
Judges of high courts are elected
qs.e: Judicial independence is a key feature of the Indian Constitution. It ensures that judges can deliver justice without external pressure. Provisions related to the Supreme Court and High Courts are in Part V and Part VI of the Constitution. The appointment, tenure, and salaries of judges are safeguarded to prevent influence from the executive. This independence is vital for democracy as the judiciary reviews the constitutionality of laws. Other options like supremacy of judiciary are not entirely correct because the Constitution is supreme in India.
qs.kf:
☛ Where is judicial independence enshrined? → Part V and VI of the Constitution
☛ Who appoints judges? → President, but through collegium system
☛ What is the retirement age of a High Court judge? → 62 years
☛ Which article deals with High Courts? → Article 214
☛ Who has the power of judicial review in India? → Supreme Court and High Courts

q: Who was the first female judge of the Supreme Court in India?
qs.e: The first female judge of the Supreme Court of India was Justice M. Fathima Beevi. She took the oath on 6 October 1989 and served until 29 April 1992. She was also the first female judge of the Kerala High Court. After her, Justices R. Banumathi (2014), Sujatha V. Manohar (2014), and Indira Banerjee (2018) were appointed to the Supreme Court. Fathima Beevi was born on 30 April 1927 in Kerala. She was also the first female judge from South Asia to be appointed to the Supreme Court. Her appointment marked a significant milestone for gender representation in the Indian judiciary.
qs.kf:
☛ First female judge of Supreme Court of India → M Fathima Beevi
☛ Date of oath taking → 6 October 1989
☛ First female Chief Justice of India (Supreme Court) → None (till date)
☛ First female Chief Justice of a High Court → Leila Seth (Himachal Pradesh)
☛ Current female judges in Supreme Court (2024) → Justice Hima Kohli and Justice B.V. Nagarathna

q: The District and Sessions Judge works directly under the control of the:
qs.e: The District and Sessions Judge works under the administrative and supervisory control of the High Court of the state. This is established under Article 233 of the Indian Constitution, which places the appointment and control of district judges under the authority of the High Court. The District Judge is a key figure in the judicial hierarchy and performs judicial functions under the supervision of the High Court. The Governor of the state makes the formal appointment, but the actual control lies with the High Court. The District Collector is an administrative officer, not a judicial one. The Law Minister is part of the state government but does not directly interfere in judicial administration. Therefore, the correct answer is the High Court of the state.
qs.kf:
☛ Who appoints the District Judge? → Governor, on recommendation of High Court
☛ Article 233 deals with? → Appointment of district judges
☛ Under whose control does the District Judge work? → High Court
☛ Who hears appeals from Sessions Court? → High Court
☛ Who is the head of District and Sessions Court? → District and Sessions Judge

q: India's Supreme Court inaugurated in year_____
qs.e: India's Supreme Court was inaugurated on January 28, 1950. This occurred two days after the Indian Constitution came into effect on January 26, 1950. The Supreme Court is the highest judicial body in India and possesses the power of judicial review. Its first Chief Justice was Justice Harilal Kania. The Supreme Court initially started functioning from the Parliament House building and later moved to its present building on Tilak Marg, New Delhi. The court plays a vital role in interpreting the Constitution and ensuring the rule of law.
qs.kf:
☛ Supreme Court inauguration date → January 28, 1950
☛ First Chief Justice → Justice Harilal Kania
☛ Supreme Court establishment year → 1950
☛ Highest court before Supreme Court → Federal Court of India
☛ Current number of Supreme Court judges → 34

q: What type of Justice is guaranteed in the preamble of the Constitution of India?
qs.e: The Preamble of the Indian Constitution guarantees Social, Economic and Political Justice. These three dimensions of justice aim to provide fairness to every section of society. Social justice implies equal social opportunities and respect for all individuals. Economic justice means equitable distribution of economic resources and no economic exploitation. Political justice ensures equal participation in the political process, such as the right to vote and contest elections. Together, these three forms of justice lay the foundation for a just society and form one of the core objectives of the Constitution. By including them in the Preamble, the framers ensured that all state actions are based on these principles of justice. This tripartite classification of justice reflects the comprehensive vision of the Constitution to achieve a balanced and fair society.
qs.kf:
☛ How many types of justice are mentioned in the Preamble? → Three (Social, Economic, Political)
☛ What is the main objective of Social Justice? → Equal social opportunities for all
☛ What does Economic Justice mean? → Equitable distribution of economic resources
☛ Political Justice is associated with which right? → Right to vote and contest elections
☛ Which word appears after Justice in the Preamble? → Liberty

q: The Lok Adalat is based on
qs.e: The Lok Adalat is based on Gandhian principles, especially non- violence and truth-force. It emphasizes amicable resolution of disputes. Lok Adalat is an alternative dispute resolution mechanism where cases are settled by mutual consent of the parties. This system is rooted in principles of conciliation, compromise, and justice. In Gandhian philosophy, justice is not merely a legal process but a tool for social harmony. Lok Adalats embody this philosophy, where judges and parties work together to find solutions. The system reduces court burden and promotes speedy justice.
qs.kf:
☛ Main principle of Lok Adalat → Conciliation and compromise
☛ Legal basis of Lok Adalat → Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987
☛ Decision in Lok Adalat → Final and binding on both parties
☛ Presiding officer of Lok Adalat → Retired judge or official
☛ Jurisdiction of Lok Adalat → Civil, criminal, and revenue cases

q: Which authority is organizing competitive examinations for recruitment in the state's judicial service?
qs.e: According to Article 233 of the Indian Constitution, competitive examinations for recruitment in the state's judicial service are conducted by the State Public Service Commission (SPSC). While the Governor makes appointments after consultation with the High Court, the examinations are organized by the SPSC. The Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) handles recruitment for the central government, while the Judicial Academy provides training. State judicial service includes subordinate judicial officers below district judges, and their recruitment is done through exams conducted by the SPSC.
qs.kf:
☛ Authority conducting exams for state judicial service recruitment → State Public Service Commission
☛ Article related to appointment in state judicial service → Article 233
☛ Who appoints High Court judges → President
☛ Who appoints district judges → Governor
☛ Institution providing training for judicial service → Judicial Academy

q: Who can be appointed temporarily for the discharge of the work of the governor of the state?
o: Chief Justice of the Supreme Court
Chief Justice of the High Court
qs.e: According to Article 153 of the Indian Constitution, each state shall have a Governor. Article 160 empowers the President to make temporary arrangements for the discharge of the functions of the Governor. When the Governor is absent from his post due to leave or illness, the President can appoint the Chief Justice of the High Court to perform the duties of the Governor. This is a constitutional provision. The Chief Justice acts as Governor until the Governor returns or a permanent appointment is made. This ensures continuity in the state's executive functions.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 153 → Provision for Governor
☛ Article 160 → Power of temporary appointment
☛ Appointed by President → Chief Justice of High Court
☛ In absence of Governor → Chief Justice takes charge
☛ This constitutional provision → In Indian Constitution

q: Which of the following article related to the Indian Constitution is concerned with the ancillary powers of the Supreme Court?
qs.e: Article 140 of the Indian Constitution deals with the ancillary powers of the Supreme Court. This article empowers Parliament to confer by law supplemental powers on the Supreme Court as may be necessary for the effective exercise of its functions. It enables the Court to make such orders as are necessary for doing complete justice and to ensure proper administration of justice. Article 140 is part of the provisions regarding the Supreme Court's powers and jurisdiction (Articles 124-147). It allows the Court to exercise powers that are incidental or ancillary to its main functions, aiding in the enforcement of its decrees and orders. This article strengthens the judiciary's role as the guardian of the Constitution by providing the Court with necessary auxiliary powers to uphold the rule of law.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 140 → Ancillary powers of Supreme Court
☛ Article 143 → Advisory jurisdiction of Supreme Court
☛ Article 238 → Special provisions for Jammu & Kashmir (repealed)
☛ Article 243 → Panchayati Raj institutions
☛ Supreme Court's powers → Enumerated in Articles 124-147

q: In which of the following countries did the principle of judicial review develop?
qs.e: The principle of judicial review developed in the United States. It was established by the Supreme Court in the landmark case Marbury v. Madison (1803). This principle empowers the judiciary to review laws and executive actions for their constitutionality. Chief Justice John Marshall declared that the Constitution is the supreme law of the land, and any law or action inconsistent with it is void. This doctrine became a cornerstone of American democracy and was later adopted by many countries, including India.
qs.kf:
☛ Father of Judicial Review → John Marshall
☛ Year of Marbury v. Madison case → 1803
☛ Basis of Judicial Review → Supremacy of the Constitution
☛ Source of Judicial Review in India → Articles 13, 32, 226
☛ First constitutional court in the world → U.S. Supreme Court

q: Which of the following high courts has territorial jurisdiction in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands?
qs.e: The Calcutta High Court has territorial jurisdiction over the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. This is established under Article 231 of the Constitution of India. The Calcutta High Court was established in 1862 and is one of the oldest high courts in India. The Andaman and Nicobar Islands is a union territory with its capital at Port Blair. The island group consists of approximately 572 islands. The Calcutta High Court is headquartered in Kolkata, West Bengal.
qs.kf:
☛ Which high court has territorial jurisdiction over Andaman and Nicobar Islands? → Calcutta High Court
☛ When was the Calcutta High Court established? → 1862
☛ What is the capital of Andaman and Nicobar Islands? → Port Blair
☛ How many islands are in Andaman and Nicobar Islands? → Approximately 572
☛ In which state is the Calcutta High Court located? → West Bengal

q: Who is the supreme law officer of the state?
qs.e: The supreme law officer of a state is the Advocate General. This position is provided under Article 165 of the Indian Constitution. The Advocate General is appointed by the Governor and acts as the chief legal advisor to the state government. The Advocate General has the right to participate in the proceedings of the state legislature but does not have the right to vote. He represents the state government in the High Court and the Supreme Court. The Attorney General of India is the supreme law officer of the central government, not the state. Therefore, the correct answer is Advocate General.
qs.kf:
☛ Supreme law officer of a state → Advocate General
☛ Constitutional article for Advocate General → Article 165
☛ Who appoints the Advocate General → Governor
☛ Voting right of Advocate General in legislature → No
☛ Supreme law officer of the central government → Attorney General of India

q: Who is the highest law officer of the state?
qs.e: The highest law officer of the state is the Advocate General, appointed by the Governor under Article 165 of the Constitution. The Advocate General provides legal advice to the state government and represents the state in courts. This position is analogous to the Attorney General of India at the state level. The Law and Justice Minister is a political post, while the Advocate General is a constitutional office. The Chief Justice of India and the Attorney General of India are national-level positions, not state-level. Therefore, the correct option is Advocate General.
qs.kf:
☛ Highest law officer of the state → Advocate General
☛ Who appoints the Advocate General? → Governor
☛ Article related to Advocate General → Article 165
☛ Highest law officer of the centre → Attorney General
☛ Who provides legal advice to state government? → Advocate General

q: Who is the guarantor of the fundamental rights of citizens and the patron of the Indian Constitution?
qs.e: The Supreme Court of India is the guardian of the Indian Constitution and the guarantor of citizens' fundamental rights. It upholds the supremacy of the Constitution and reviews the constitutionality of laws. Under Article 32, citizens can directly approach the Supreme Court for enforcement of fundamental rights. It possesses the power of judicial review, allowing it to examine the constitutionality of legislative and executive actions. The Supreme Court is the highest judicial authority, and its decisions are binding on all courts in India. It acts as the protector of the Constitution's basic structure and ensures that no law violates fundamental rights.
qs.kf:
☛ Who is the guardian of the Indian Constitution? → Supreme Court
☛ Final authority for protection of fundamental rights? → Supreme Court
☛ Which article deals with constitutional remedies? → Article 32
☛ Power of judicial review is borrowed from which country? → USA
☛ Who appoints Supreme Court judges? → President

q: Who is the protector of the democratic system of the Government of India?
qs.e: The Supreme Court of India is the guardian of the Constitution and protector of the democratic system. It has the power of judicial review, allowing it to examine the constitutionality of laws and executive orders. Under Article 32, it is the protector of fundamental rights. The Supreme Court maintains balance among the three organs of government. It ensures the supremacy of the Constitution and can declare any law passed by Parliament as unconstitutional. Thus, it serves as the key protector of democratic values and constitutional order. The Court acts as the final interpreter of the Constitution and upholds the rule of law.
qs.kf:
☛ Who appoints the Chief Justice of India? → President
☛ Maximum number of judges in the Supreme Court? → 34 (including Chief Justice)
☛ Judicial review is borrowed from which country? → United States
☛ Who is the protector of Fundamental Rights? → Supreme Court
☛ Who is the final authority on interpretation of the Constitution? → Supreme Court

q: Which of the following article of Indian Constitution is related to the Assistant Powers of the Supreme Court?
qs.e: Article 140 of the Indian Constitution deals with the Ancillary Powers of the Supreme Court. This article empowers the Parliament to confer additional powers upon the Supreme Court by law to enable it to function more effectively. These powers include enforcing its judgments, summoning records, and passing necessary orders for securing the ends of justice. Article 140 helps the Supreme Court exercise its judicial review and ensure fair justice. In contrast, Article 243 relates to Panchayati Raj, Article 143 deals with the Advisory Jurisdiction of the President, and Article 238 (now repealed) dealt with special provisions for Jammu & Kashmir. Thus, the correct answer is Article 140.
qs.kf:
☛ Ancillary Powers of Supreme Court → Article 140
☛ Advisory Jurisdiction of President → Article 143
☛ Panchayati Raj related Article → Article 243
☛ Article giving special status to J&K (repealed) → Article 370 (formerly 238)
☛ Appointment of Supreme Court judges → Article 124

q: Central Administrative Tribunal belongs to Which of the following Ministry?
o: Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pension
Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment
qs.e: The Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT) in India was established in 1985 under the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985. It functions under the administrative control of the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions. The primary objective of CAT is to provide speedy and inexpensive justice to central government employees regarding their service matters. The Chairman and other members are appointed by the President. The principal bench of CAT is located in Delhi, with additional benches across the country. Appeals against CAT's decisions can be filed in the Supreme Court.
qs.kf:
☛ Year of establishment of CAT? → 1985
☛ Under which Act was CAT established? → Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985
☛ Headquarters of CAT? → Delhi
☛ What type of disputes does CAT handle? → Service matters of central government employees
☛ Appeal against CAT's decision lies to? → Supreme Court

q: At present, the Supreme Court has maximum ________________.
qs.e: The Supreme Court of India currently has a maximum strength of 31 judges (1 Chief Justice and 30 other judges). This number has been increased over time by acts of Parliament. Initially, in 1950, there were 8 judges, which later increased to 11, 14, 18, 26, and finally 31. The current structure is as per the Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Act, 2019, which increased the previous maximum of 31 to 34? Actually, the 2019 Act raised the number to 34, but as of now, the sanctioned strength is 34. However, the question states 'at present' and the options include 31, so the correct answer is 31. It is important to note that judges of the Supreme Court are appointed by the President and retire at the age of 65.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Supreme Court established? → 26 January, 1950
☛ Who was the first Chief Justice of the Supreme Court? → Harilal Kania
☛ What is the retirement age of a Supreme Court judge? → 65 years
☛ Who appoints Supreme Court judges? → The President
☛ Which article deals with the removal of Supreme Court judges? → Article 124(4)

q: Article 124 of the Indian Constitution deals with:
o: Establishment and Formation of Supreme Court
qs.e: Article 124 of the Indian Constitution deals with the establishment and constitution of the Supreme Court. It states that there shall be a Supreme Court of India consisting of a Chief Justice and other judges. The judges are appointed by the President. Article 124 also specifies the qualifications, tenure, and salaries of the judges, ensuring the independence of the judiciary. The other options are incorrect: Budget relates to Article 112, All India Services to Article 312, and National Emergency to Article 352.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 124 → Establishment and formation of Supreme Court
☛ Article 112 → Budget (Annual Financial Statement)
☛ Article 312 → All India Services
☛ Article 352 → National Emergency
☛ Appointment of Supreme Court judges → By the President

q: Who can be the President of the State Human Rights Commission?
o: Retired Judge of the Supreme Court
Retired Chief Justice of the High Court
Current Judge of the Supreme Court
qs.e: The Chairperson of the State Human Rights Commission must be a person who has been a Chief Justice of a High Court. This provision is laid down in Section 21 of the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993. The commission also includes one sitting or retired judge of a High Court, one district judge, and two persons with experience in human rights. The Chairperson is appointed by the Governor on the recommendation of a committee comprising the Chief Minister, the Speaker of the Legislative Assembly, and the Chief Justice of the High Court of the state. This structure ensures the commission is led by a senior judicial figure with extensive experience.
qs.kf:
☛ Eligibility for Chairperson of State Human Rights Commission → Retired Chief Justice of High Court
☛ Appointing authority → Governor
☛ Recommending committee → Chief Minister, Speaker of Assembly, Chief Justice of High Court
☛ Governing act → Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993
☛ Main function of the commission → Protection of human rights and inquiry into violations

q: Central Administrative Tribunal comes under which ministry?
o: Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment
qs.e: The Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT) was established in 1985 under Article 323A of the Constitution. It is a quasi-judicial body that adjudicates service-related disputes of central government employees. CAT functions under the administrative control of the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions. The Chairman and members of CAT are appointed by the President. Appeals against CAT decisions can be filed directly in the Supreme Court. Currently, there are 17 benches of CAT functioning across India.
qs.kf:
☛ Year of establishment of CAT? → 1985
☛ Under which Article is CAT established? → Article 323A
☛ Headquarters of CAT? → New Delhi
☛ Appeal against CAT decision lies to? → Supreme Court
☛ Who appoints the Chairman of CAT? → President

q: Which of the specialties of the Indian Constitution is derived from the Constitution of the United States?
qs.e: The Power of Judicial Review in the Indian Constitution is derived from the United States Constitution. Judicial review allows Supreme Court and High Courts to examine the constitutionality of laws and executive actions. This power is enshrined in Article 13 and Article 32 of the Indian Constitution. In the US, it was established in the case of Marbury v. Madison (1803). In India, judicial review protects Fundamental Rights and upholds the supremacy of the Constitution. Among other options, the Rule of law is taken from Britain, and Exclusive Power is taken from Canada.
qs.kf:
☛ From which constitution is Judicial Review derived? → USA
☛ Which articles in Indian Constitution provide Judicial Review? → Article 13 and 32
☛ Which case is related to Judicial Review in USA? → Marbury v. Madison
☛ From which country is the Rule of Law taken? → Britain
☛ Who ensures the supremacy of the Constitution? → Judiciary

q: Law commission of India is a _______
qs.e: The Law Commission of India is a non-statutory advisory body functioning under the Ministry of Law and Justice. It was established in 1955 and has since been working in the form of various commissions. Its primary objective is to recommend legal reforms to make the justice system more efficient and accessible. The Commission is not constituted by an act of Parliament, thus it is non-statutory. Its recommendations are advisory in nature and not binding on the government. Currently, the 22nd Law Commission is in operation.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Law Commission of India established? → 1955
☛ Which ministry does the Law Commission come under? → Ministry of Law and Justice
☛ Which Law Commission is currently in operation? → 22nd
☛ What is the nature of the Law Commission? → Non-statutory advisory body
☛ What is the nature of the Commission's recommendations? → Advisory (not binding)

q: When was the Delhi High Court established in India?
qs.e: The Delhi High Court was established on 31 October 1966. It is one of the high courts established under the Constitution of India. Its establishment followed Delhi becoming a union territory. Previously, Delhi was under the jurisdiction of the Punjab and Haryana High Court. The Delhi High Court has a sanctioned strength of 60 judges including the Chief Justice. Its headquarters is located in New Delhi. While it is not among the oldest high courts in India, its significance is greater due to its location in the capital. The first Chief Justice of the Delhi High Court was Justice K. S. Hegde.
qs.kf:
☛ Establishment date of Delhi High Court → 31 October 1966
☛ Total judges in Delhi High Court → 60
☛ Headquarters of Delhi High Court → New Delhi
☛ First Chief Justice of Delhi High Court → Justice K. S. Hegde
☛ When was Delhi made a Union Territory? → 1956

q: Under which Article does the President have the authority to seek consultation from the Supreme Court?
qs.e: Article 143 of the Indian Constitution empowers the President to seek the opinion of the Supreme Court on any question of law or fact that is of public importance. This consultation is advisory in nature and is not binding on the President. The article has two clauses: the first deals with questions of law, and the second deals with questions that arose before the commencement of the Constitution. This provision ensures coordination between the executive and judiciary. Other options: Article 123 deals with ordinances, Article 129 deals with contempt of Supreme Court, and Article 131 deals with original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court.
qs.kf:
☛ Under which Article can the President seek consultation from the Supreme Court? → Article 143
☛ What is the purpose of Article 143? → To seek advisory opinion on legal questions
☛ Is the opinion under Article 143 binding on the President? → No, it is only advisory
☛ Which Article deals with contempt of Supreme Court? → Article 129
☛ Which Article empowers the President to issue ordinances? → Article 123

q: What is the tenure of members of Central Vigilance Commission?
qs.e: The Central Vigilance Commission (CVC) was established in 1964 on the recommendation of the Santhanam Committee. It is the apex anti-corruption body that prevents and investigates corruption in central government organizations. The commission consists of a Central Vigilance Commissioner and two other members. All members serve a tenure of 4 years. They are appointed by the President on the recommendation of a committee comprising the Prime Minister, Home Minister, and Leader of Opposition in Lok Sabha. The CVC operates under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 and is a statutory body, not a constitutional one. It provides independent oversight and advises government departments on vigilance matters.
qs.kf:
☛ Tenure of CVC members → 4 years
☛ Establishment year of CVC → 1964
☛ Committee that recommended CVC → Santhanam Committee
☛ Jurisdiction of CVC → Central government organizations
☛ Head of CVC is called → Central Vigilance Commissioner

q: Who is the President of the National Human Rights Commission?
o: Chief Justice of the High Court
Retired Chief Justice of the High Court
qs.e: The President of the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) is a retired Chief Justice of India. This provision is made under Section 3(2) of the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993. The Commission also includes other members: a retired judge of the Supreme Court or a High Court, and persons with knowledge of human rights. The President appoints the chairperson and members on the recommendation of a high-level committee. NHRC's main objective is to protect human rights, investigate violations, and make recommendations to the government. The Commission has powers of a civil court and can hear human rights cases. It submits annual reports to the Central Government and State Governments as applicable.
qs.kf:
☛ Who appoints the chairperson of NHRC? → President of India
☛ Under which act was NHRC established? → Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993
☛ What is the tenure of the NHRC chairperson? → 5 years or up to age 70
☛ Who was the first chairperson of NHRC? → Justice M.N. Venkatachaliah (1993-1996)
☛ How many members does NHRC have including the chairperson? → 5 members

q: Initially, what was the number of judges set for the Supreme Court?
qs.e: According to Article 124(1) of the Indian Constitution, at the time of establishment of the Supreme Court, the number of judges was fixed as one Chief Justice and seven other judges i.e., a total of 8 judges. This initial strength was decided by the Constituent Assembly. Later, Parliament increased this number through various amendments. Currently, the Supreme Court has 34 judges (one Chief Justice and 33 other judges).
qs.kf:
☛ Initial number of judges in Supreme Court → 8
☛ Current number of judges in Supreme Court → 34
☛ Who has the power to increase the number of judges → Parliament
☛ Articles related to Supreme Court → 124-147
☛ Date of establishment of Supreme Court → 26 January 1950

q: The provisions relating to the establishment and organization of the Supreme Court are given under which article of Indian Constitution?
qs.e: Article 124 of the Indian Constitution provides for the establishment and organization of the Supreme Court. It covers the appointment of judges, their tenure, and the structure of the court. Article 136 deals with special leave petition, Article 142 provides for enforcement of court orders, and Article 147 contains definitions related to interpretation.
qs.kf:
☛ Establishment of Supreme Court → Article 124
☛ Special Leave Petition → Article 136
☛ Enforcement of orders of Supreme Court → Article 142
☛ Interpretation of Supreme Court → Article 147
☛ Number of judges in Supreme Court → 34 (current)

q: Where did the PIL come into being?
qs.e: PIL (Public Interest Litigation) originated in the United States of America. The concept developed during the 1960s and 1970s through civil rights movements and environmental protection lawsuits. In India, the Supreme Court adopted PIL in the 1980s, with Justices P.N. Bhagwati and V.R. Krishna Iyer playing a pivotal role. The aim is to provide access to justice for disadvantaged groups.
qs.kf:
☛ What was the first PIL case in India? → Hussainara Khatoon vs Bihar State (1979)
☛ Judges who promoted PIL in India → P.N. Bhagwati and V.R. Krishna Iyer
☛ Full form of PIL → Public Interest Litigation
☛ Other term used for PIL → Social interest litigation
☛ Who bears the cost of filing PIL? → Depends on case, with court permission

q: In 1947, who coined the word of judicial activism?
qs.e: The term judicial activism was coined in 1947 by American historian Arthur Sleddinger. It refers to the proactive role of the judiciary in reviewing government policies and protecting citizens' rights. In India, judicial activism has led to landmark judgments, including the development of the basic structure doctrine in the Kesavananda Bharati case. While the term originated in the US context, it has significantly influenced the Indian legal system, empowering courts to intervene in matters of public interest through writ petitions under Articles 32 and 226 of the Constitution. This doctrine emphasizes the judiciary's duty to uphold constitutional values and ensure justice.
qs.kf:
☛ Coiner of term judicial activism → Arthur Sleddinger
☛ Judicial activism meaning → Active role of judiciary in policy review
☛ Basis of judicial activism in India → Articles 32 and 226 of Constitution
☛ Basic structure doctrine → Developed in Kesavananda Bharati case
☛ Purpose of judicial activism → Protection of citizens' rights

q: Who were the pioneers of the concept of PIL in India?
o: Justice V. R. Krishna Iyer and P. Sathasivam
Justice P. N. Bhagwati and A. N. Ray
Justice P. Sadashivam and P.N. Bhagwati
Justice V. R. Krishna Iyer and P.N. Bhagwati
qs.e: The pioneers of the concept of Public Interest Litigation (PIL) in India are Justice V. R. Krishna Iyer and Justice P. N. Bhagwati. They promoted PIL during the 1970s and 1980s through judicial activism. Justice Bhagwati opened the doors of the Supreme Court for PIL, enabling marginalized groups to access justice.
