This ensures that death penalty cases undergo additional judicial scrutiny, reducing the possibility of judicial errors and maintaining the highest standards of justice.
qs.kf:
☛ Section for confirmation of death sentence? → Section 366, CrPC
☛ What happens after Session Court awards death penalty? → Mandatory High Court confirmation
☛ Minimum bench size for confirmation? → Bench of two judges
☛ Is High Court confirmation needed for life imprisonment? → No
☛ What is capital punishment also called? → Death sentence

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (13/06/2025) Shift 3
q: When appointing judges to the High Courts, the President of India is required to consult which officials apart from the Chief Justice of India and the Chief Justice of the respective State?
o: The members of the State Legislature
qs.e: According to Article 217 of the Indian Constitution, the President appoints judges to the High Courts. In this process, the President must consult the Chief Justice of India, the Chief Justice of the respective State, and the Governor of the State. This consultation is mandatory, though the President is not bound by it. The Governor, as the constitutional head of the state, provides important input regarding the appointment. Other options, such as local district magistrates, members of the State Legislature, or the Union Cabinet, are not part of this consultation process. The Governor's role ensures that the state's perspective is considered in judicial appointments.
qs.kf:
☛ Under which article are High Court judges appointed? → Article 217
☛ How many authorities are required to be consulted for High Court judge appointments? → Three (Chief Justice of India, Chief Justice of the State, Governor)
☛ Is the President bound by the consultation? → No
☛ Who appoints High Court judges? → The President of India
☛ Who appoints the Governor? → The President of India

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (13/06/2025) Shift 3
q: In India, judicial review is considered as:
o: The power of the judiciary to pronounce upon the constitutionality of laws and executive orders
the power of the judiciary to question the wisdom of the executive orders after they are passed by the Union cabinet
the power of the judiciary to review all the legislative enactments before they are assented to by the President
the power of the judiciary to question the wisdom of the laws enacted by the legislatures
qs.e: In India, judicial review refers to the power of the judiciary to examine the constitutionality of legislative laws and executive orders. This power is vested in the Supreme Court and High Courts to ensure that no law or order violates the Constitution. Judicial review is essential for maintaining the supremacy of the Constitution and protecting fundamental rights. It is derived from Articles 13, 32, and 226 of the Indian Constitution. Through judicial review, courts can declare any law or executive action unconstitutional if it infringes upon constitutional provisions. This power acts as a check on the legislature and executive, preventing arbitrary actions and upholding the rule of law.
qs.kf:
☛ Which article deals with judicial review? → Article 13
☛ Who has the power of judicial review in India? → Supreme Court and High Courts
☛ What is the basis of judicial review? → Supremacy of the Constitution
☛ Which article protects fundamental rights via the Supreme Court? → Article 32
☛ On which principle is judicial review based? → Separation of powers

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (18/06/2025) Shift 1
q: The President's power to seek the Supreme Court's opinion on questions of law comes under ___________.
qs.e: The President's power to seek the Supreme Court's opinion on questions of law comes under Article 143. This is an advisory jurisdiction, where the Court gives its opinion, which is not binding. Article 131 deals with original jurisdiction, Article 136 with special leave to appeal, and Article 226 with the power of High Courts to issue writs. The Government of India Act 1935 gave similar power to the Privy Council. The President can refer any question of law or fact of public importance to the Supreme Court for its opinion.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Article deals with the President's advisory power? → Article 143
☛ Is the Supreme Court's opinion binding on the President? → No, it is not binding
☛ Article 131 is related to which jurisdiction? → Original jurisdiction
☛ Article 136 deals with which power? → Special leave to appeal
☛ Article 226 gives which power to High Courts? → Power to issue writs

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (14/06/2025) Shift 2
q: The Indian High Courts Act was passed in the year ______.
qs.e: The Indian High Courts Act was passed by the British Parliament in 1861. This act established High Courts in Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras, replacing the earlier Supreme Courts and Sadar Diwani/Faujdari courts. It was a significant step towards unifying the judicial system in India. Each High Court was to consist of a Chief Justice and up to 15 other judges. The act was introduced after the Government of India Act 1858, which ended the rule of the East India Company. The High Courts exercised original and appellate jurisdiction over civil and criminal cases within their respective provinces.
qs.kf:
☛ Where was India's first High Court established? → Calcutta
☛ When was the Indian High Courts Act passed? → 1861
☛ How many High Courts were established under this act? → Three
☛ What was the maximum number of judges in a High Court? → 15
☛ After which act was the Indian High Courts Act passed? → Government of India Act 1858

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (16/06/2025) Shift 1
q: The award (decision) made by the Lok Adalats is deemed to be a decree of a civil court and is final and binding on all parties because:
o: An appeal can be filed in the Supreme Court
A review petition can be filed
An appeal can be filed in the High Court
qs.e: Lok Adalat's award is deemed to be a decree of a civil court and is final and binding because no appeal lies against it. Lok Adalat is an alternative dispute resolution mechanism where cases are settled with mutual consent. Under the Legal Services Authorities Act, the award of a Lok Adalat has the force of a decree and is not appealable. Although in exceptional cases, a Special Leave Petition may be filed in the Supreme Court, but as a rule, no appeal is permitted. This ensures speedy and final settlement of disputes, avoiding prolonged litigation. The parties voluntarily submit to the jurisdiction of Lok Adalat, making the binding nature of the award essential.
qs.kf:
☛ Lok Adalat award → final and binding
☛ Against Lok Adalat award → no appeal lies
☛ Lok Adalat award → deemed decree of civil court
☛ Lok Adalat → alternative dispute resolution
☛ Case in Lok Adalat → with mutual consent

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (16/06/2025) Shift 2
q: Which landmark case first established the principle of judicial review in constitutional law?
qs.e: The principle of judicial review in constitutional law was first established in the landmark U.S. Supreme Court case Marbury v. Madison (1803). In this case, Chief Justice John Marshall wrote the opinion, declaring that any law that conflicts with the Constitution is void, and it is the duty of the judiciary to invalidate such laws. William Marbury had petitioned for his judicial commission, but the Court ruled that a part of the Judiciary Act of 1789 was unconstitutional. This case laid the foundation for judicial review, empowering the judiciary to check the constitutionality of actions by the legislative and executive branches. It established the judiciary as a co-equal branch of government and solidified the system of checks and balances.
qs.kf:
☛ Which case established the principle of judicial review? → Marbury v. Madison (1803)
☛ Who delivered the judgment in Marbury v. Madison? → Chief Justice John Marshall
☛ Which Indian case introduced the basic structure doctrine? → Kesavananda Bharati case (1973)
☛ Which Indian case cited Marbury v. Madison? → Kesavananda Bharati case
☛ Which article of Indian Constitution embodies judicial review? → Article 13 and 32

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (18/06/2025) Shift 2
q: The doctrine of judicial review originated in which country?
qs.e: The doctrine of judicial review originated in the United States of America. It was first established by the Supreme Court in the case of Marbury v. Madison (1803), where Chief Justice John Marshall ruled that courts have the power to declare laws unconstitutional. This doctrine ensures the supremacy of the constitution and acts as a check on the legislature and executive. While many countries, including India, adopted judicial review, its roots lie in the U.S. In India, Articles 13, 32, and 226 empower courts to exercise judicial review.
qs.kf:
☛ Who is considered the father of judicial review? → John Marshall
☛ When was the Marbury v. Madison case decided? → 1803
☛ Articles related to judicial review in India → 13, 32, 226, 227
☛ Which country has the widest scope of judicial review? → India
☛ What is the basis of judicial review in the UK? → Parliamentary sovereignty

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (19/06/2025) Shift 2
q: When appointing judges to the Supreme Court, the President must consult which of the following?
qs.e: According to Article 124(2) of the Indian Constitution, the President appoints judges to the Supreme Court. In this process, the President must consult the Chief Justice of India (CJI). This consultation is mandatory to ensure the independence of the judiciary. Although the President may also consult other judges and the Law Minister, the CJI's advice is binding in the appointment process. This provision prevents the executive from making unilateral decisions and upholds judicial independence. The Constitution gives the CJI a crucial role in judicial appointments to maintain a balance of power.
qs.kf:
☛ Under which Article are Supreme Court judges appointed? → Article 124
☛ Whose consultation is mandatory for the President in judicial appointments? → Chief Justice of India
☛ Who determines the number of Supreme Court judges? → Parliament
☛ What is the retirement age of Supreme Court judges? → 65 years
☛ How many senior judges are part of the Collegium system? → 5

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (23/06/2025) Shift 3
q: Under which Act was the National Legal Services Authority (NALSA), which conducts Lok Adalats along with other Legal Services Institutions, constituted?
qs.e: National Legal Services Authority (NALSA) was constituted under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, which came into force on 9 November 1995. NALSA is a statutory body responsible for providing free legal aid to the poor and weaker sections of society. It also organizes Lok Adalats, which are forums for amicable and speedy settlement of disputes. The headquarters of NALSA is in New Delhi. The Chief Justice of India serves as its Patron-in-Chief. This Act provides a framework for legal assistance across the country.
qs.kf:
☛ Under which Act was NALSA constituted? → Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987
☛ Who is the head of NALSA? → Chief Justice of India
☛ Who organizes Lok Adalats? → NALSA and other legal services institutions
☛ When did the Legal Services Authorities Act come into force? → 9 November 1995
☛ Where is the headquarters of NALSA? → New Delhi

q: Which is the oldest High Court in India?
qs.e: The oldest High Court in India is the Calcutta High Court, established in 1862. It was set up under the Indian High Courts Act of 1861 and was originally known as the 'High Court of Judicature at Fort William'. The Bombay High Court and Madras High Court were also established in the same year, but the Calcutta High Court is considered the oldest. The Allahabad High Court was established later in 1866. The Calcutta High Court is located in Kolkata, West Bengal. It has jurisdiction over the state of West Bengal and the Union Territory of Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
qs.kf:
☛ Oldest High Court in India → Calcutta High Court (1862)
☛ Second oldest High Court → Bombay High Court (1862)
☛ Third oldest High Court → Madras High Court (1862)
☛ Establishment year of Allahabad High Court → 1866
☛ Indian High Courts Act passed in → 1861

q: Who has the distinction of serving as the Chief Justice of India, President and the Vice president?
qs.e: Justice Mohammad Hidayatullah is the only person in India to have served as Chief Justice of India, Vice President, and President. He served as the Chief Justice from 1968 to 1970. In 1977, he became the Vice President, and in 1979, he became the acting President of India. This unique distinction remains unmatched in Indian constitutional history. His tenure as acting President was brief, but his contributions to Indian judiciary and governance are significant. This fact is crucial for understanding the highest offices in India.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the first Chief Justice of India? → Harilal J. Kania
☛ Who was the first Vice President of India? → Dr. Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan
☛ Who was the first Chief Justice to become President? → Justice M. Hidayatullah
☛ Which President had the shortest term in India? → Justice M. Hidayatullah (acting)
☛ Who is the only Chief Justice to become Vice President? → Justice M. Hidayatullah

q: The first high court of India was established in _______.
qs.e: The first high court of India was the Calcutta High Court, established on July 1, 1862, under the Indian High Courts Act 1861. It was followed by the Bombay and Madras High Courts later in the same year. The Calcutta High Court was originally located at Fort William and later renamed as the Kolkata High Court. It is one of the oldest high courts in India and its jurisdiction covers West Bengal and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
qs.kf:
☛ Where was the first high court of India established? → Calcutta (Kolkata)
☛ When was the Calcutta High Court established? → July 1, 1862
☛ Under which act were high courts established in India? → Indian High Courts Act 1861
☛ What was the original name of the Calcutta High Court? → Fort William High Court
☛ Which other high courts were established in 1862? → Bombay and Madras High Courts

q: In which of the following cases did the Supreme Court of India enunciate the ‘Doctrine of Basic Structure’?
qs.e: The Supreme Court of India enunciated the Doctrine of Basic Structure in the Keshvanand Bharti case in 1973. According to this doctrine, Parliament can amend the Constitution but cannot destroy or alter its basic structure. This landmark judgment limited Parliament's amending power and strengthened judicial review. The basic structure includes the supremacy of the Constitution, democratic and republican form of government, federal structure, separation of powers, and fundamental rights. In the Golaknath case (1967), the Court had held that Parliament cannot amend fundamental rights, but Keshvanand Bharti went further to establish the basic structure doctrine. This case is a cornerstone of Indian constitutional law.
qs.kf:
☛ Keshvanand Bharti case (1973) → Doctrine of Basic Structure was propounded.
☛ Golaknath case (1967) → Parliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights.
☛ Menka Gandhi case (1978) → Interpretation of procedure under Article 21.
☛ AK Gopalan case (1950) → Narrow interpretation of Article 21.
☛ Basic Structure includes: Supremacy of Constitution, Democracy, Republic, Federalism, Separation of Powers.

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (17/06/2025) Shift 3
q: Which of the following systems was abolished by the Nineteenth Amendment Act, 1966?
qs.e: The Nineteenth Amendment Act, 1966 abolished the system of election tribunals. Earlier, election petitions were heard by election tribunals appointed by state governments. After this amendment, the jurisdiction to hear election petitions was transferred exclusively to the High Courts. This amendment relates to Article 324 of the Constitution and aimed to make the electoral process more judicial and transparent. Previously, decisions of election tribunals could be appealed to the High Court, but now petitions are directly filed in the High Court. This change ensured uniformity and faster resolution of election disputes.
qs.kf:
☛ Which amendment abolished election tribunals? → 19th Amendment, 1966
☛ Where are election petitions filed after the 19th Amendment? → High Courts
☛ Which Article provides for universal adult suffrage in India? → Article 326
☛ Under which Article is the Election Commission established? → Article 324
☛ Which amendment abolished the privy purse system? → 26th Amendment, 1971

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (24/06/2025) Shift 2
q: Which of the following can be settled in a Lok Adalat?
qs.e: Lok Adalat is an alternative dispute resolution mechanism that can settle only compoundable offences and civil cases. Compoundable offences are those where the parties can reach a compromise, such as cheque bounce cases, accident claims, etc. Murder and constitutional matters are non-compoundable; they cannot be brought before a Lok Adalat. Public interest litigation also falls outside its scope. Lok Adalats are established under the Legal Services Authority Act, 1987, and their decisions are final and binding. This system helps reduce the burden on regular courts and provides speedy justice.
qs.kf:
☛ Under which Act is Lok Adalat established? → Legal Services Authority Act, 1987
☛ What is the nature of Lok Adalat's decision? → Final and binding on both parties
☛ Which cases cannot be settled in Lok Adalat? → Non-compoundable offences
☛ What is the main objective of Lok Adalat? → Reduce court burden and promote compromise
☛ Where was the first Lok Adalat held in India? → Gujarat (1982)

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (23/06/2025) Shift 2
q: Under its original jurisdiction, the Supreme Court of India can adjudicate disputes between:
o: The Centre and one or more states
Two private citizens from different states
Two municipal corporations of different states
A state government and a private corporation
qs.e: The original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court of India covers disputes between the Centre and states or between states inter se, as defined under Article 131 of the Constitution. It does not include disputes between two private citizens, municipal corporations, or a state government and a private corporation, as those fall under the jurisdiction of High Courts or other tribunals. The Supreme Court's original jurisdiction is limited to federal disputes involving the Union and states.
qs.kf:
☛ Under which Article does the Supreme Court have original jurisdiction? → Article 131
☛ What types of disputes are covered under original jurisdiction? → Centre-state or inter-state disputes
☛ Can disputes between a state government and a private corporation be filed in the Supreme Court under original jurisdiction? → No
☛ Which parties are excluded from original jurisdiction? → Private individuals and corporations
☛ What is the nature of disputes under Article 131? → Federal in nature

q: The National Green Tribunal is a ________.
A. Fast Track Court
B. Non-Gajeted Organization
C. Central Government Department
D. Private Company
qs.e: The National Green Tribunal (NGT) is a Fast Track Court established for the speedy disposal of environmental cases. It was constituted under the National Green Tribunal Act, 2010. NGT consists of a Chairperson and at least 10 judicial and 10 expert members. It is headquartered in Delhi with regional offices. It is a specialized judicial body, not a government department, non-gazetted organization, or private company.
qs.kf:
☛ When was NGT established? → 2010
☛ Who appoints the Chairperson of NGT? → Central Government
☛ Where is NGT headquartered? → Delhi
☛ How many judicial members are in NGT? → At least 10
☛ Under which Act was NGT constituted? → National Green Tribunal Act, 2010

q: Identify the principal organ of the UN which got suspended in 1994?
qs.e: The Trusteeship Council, one of the six principal organs of the United Nations, was suspended in 1994. It was established to oversee the administration of trust territories and colonies after the World Wars. With the independence of Palau, the last trust territory in 1994, the Council's work was completed. Since then it has been inactive, though not formally dissolved. The other principal organs include the General Assembly, Security Council, International Court of Justice, Secretariat, and Economic and Social Council.
qs.kf:
☛ Which year was the Trusteeship Council suspended? → 1994
☛ How many principal organs does the UN have? → 6
☛ What was the last trust territory under the Trusteeship Council? → Palau
☛ Which UN organ performs judicial functions? → International Court of Justice
☛ How many permanent members are in the Security Council? → 5

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (05/06/2025) Shift 1
q: What is the key difference between the Supreme Court’s original jurisdiction in federal disputes versus its writ jurisdiction?
o: Federal dispute jurisdiction is exclusive to SC, while writ jurisdiction is concurrent with High Courts.
Federal dispute jurisdiction can be exercised suo moto, while writ jurisdiction requires a petition.
Federal dispute jurisdiction applies to civil matters, while writ jurisdiction applies to criminal matters.
Federal dispute jurisdiction is advisory, while writ jurisdiction is binding.
qs.e: Under Article 131 of the Indian Constitution, the Supreme Court has exclusive original jurisdiction over federal disputes between the Centre and States or between States. This means such disputes can only be filed in the Supreme Court, not in any High Court. On the other hand, writ jurisdiction is available both in the Supreme Court (under Article 32) and in High Courts (under Article 226), making it concurrent. Citizens can approach either court for enforcement of fundamental rights through writs. This is the key distinction: federal jurisdiction is exclusive to the Supreme Court, while writ jurisdiction is shared with High Courts.
qs.kf:
☛ Which article deals with Supreme Court's federal dispute jurisdiction? → Article 131
☛ Which article gives writ jurisdiction to the Supreme Court? → Article 32
☛ Which article gives writ jurisdiction to High Courts? → Article 226
☛ Supreme Court's writ jurisdiction is limited to fundamental rights, but High Court's writ jurisdiction is wider. → True
☛ What type of jurisdiction does the Supreme Court have in federal disputes? → Exclusive and original

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (05/06/2025) Shift 1
q: Which type of subordinate court primarily handles disputes related to property ownership and contractual agreements?
qs.e: Civil Courts primarily handle disputes related to property ownership, contractual agreements, debt recovery, land disputes, and other non-criminal matters. These are subordinate courts functioning under the High Court. In the Indian judicial system, civil courts are classified as Civil Judge (Junior Division), Civil Judge (Senior Division), and District Judge. They operate under the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC), 1908. These courts have the jurisdiction to hear and decide suits concerning property and contract matters. The hierarchy ensures that minor cases are handled by lower courts, while major cases go to higher civil courts.
qs.kf:
☛ Under which code do Civil Courts function? → Code of Civil Procedure (CPC), 1908
☛ What is the highest level of subordinate civil courts? → District Judge
☛ Property disputes are filed in which court? → Civil Court
☛ First appeal in civil matters lies to which court? → District Judge's court
☛ Who presides over a Civil Court? → Civil Judge

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (18/06/2025) Shift 3
q: In which landmark case did the Supreme Court of India rule that the Council of Ministers DOES NOT cease to hold office even after the dissolution of the Lok Sabha?
o: Kesavananda Bharati vs. State of Kerala, 1973
SR Bommai vs. Union of India, 1994
qs.e: In this landmark case, the Supreme Court ruled that the Council of Ministers does not cease to hold office even after the dissolution of the Lok Sabha. The decision pertained to the powers of the President under Article 74. The Court held that the Council of Ministers continues in office until a new government is formed. This ruling was essential to avoid a constitutional crisis. It ensured the continuity of government in a parliamentary democracy. This precedent is crucial for maintaining stability in the exercise of executive powers at the centre. The case clarified that the Council of Ministers acts as an advisory body to the President even during the interim period.
qs.kf:
☛ What did the UNR Rao vs. Indira Gandhi, 1971 case decide? → The Council of Ministers continues even after Lok Sabha dissolution
☛ What does Article 74 provide for? → Council of Ministers to aid and advise the President
☛ Which constitutional question was resolved in the UNR Rao case? → Continuity of the executive
☛ What was the Kesavananda Bharati case about? → Basic structure of the Constitution
☛ What did the SR Bommai case address? → President's rule in states

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (19/06/2025) Shift 1
q: Which court in the subordinate judiciary has unlimited pecuniary jurisdiction in civil cases?
qs.e: In the subordinate judiciary, the Judge of District Court has unlimited pecuniary jurisdiction in civil cases. This court is the highest civil court at the district level and can entertain suits of any value. In contrast, the Small Causes Court has limited jurisdiction (usually up to 5,000 rupees). The Court of Munsiff also has limited jurisdiction (up to a few lakh rupees). The Nyaya Panchayat is a village-level court with jurisdiction over small civil and criminal cases. Hence, only the District Judge's court has unlimited pecuniary jurisdiction.
qs.kf:
☛ Pecuniary jurisdiction of District Judge → Unlimited
☛ Maximum pecuniary limit of Small Causes Court → 5,000 rupees
☛ Jurisdiction of Munsiff Court → Limited (up to a few lakhs)
☛ Level of Nyaya Panchayat → Village level
☛ Highest subordinate civil court → District Court

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (19/06/2025) Shift 1
q: The Recorder’s Court was later replaced by the ______.
qs.e: The Recorder's Court was later replaced by the Supreme Court. The Recorder's Court was a judicial system established during the British period in presidency towns like Madras, Bombay, and Calcutta. Its primary function was to hear criminal cases. Later, as part of the reform of the Indian judicial system, it was transformed into the Supreme Court under the Regulating Act of 1773 and the Charter Act of 1793. This change was made to strengthen judicial independence and the rule of law. The Supreme Court was the highest court in each presidency and eventually paved the way for the modern judiciary.
qs.kf:
☛ Where was the Recorder's Court first established? → Madras
☛ What replaced the Recorder's Court? → Supreme Court
☛ What type of cases did the Recorder's Court handle? → Criminal cases
☛ Which act established the Supreme Court? → Regulating Act of 1773
☛ In which cities was the Recorder's Court located? → Madras, Bombay, Calcutta

q: Who was the first Muslim female judge to higher judiciary?
qs.e: Justice M. Fathima Beevi was the first Muslim female judge appointed to the higher judiciary in India. She was sworn in as a judge of the Kerala High Court in 1989 and later elevated to the Supreme Court of India in 1992, becoming the first Muslim woman to hold that position. Her appointment marked a significant milestone in the history of the Indian judiciary, promoting gender and religious diversity. She actively contributed to cases related to women's rights and social justice. Her legacy remains as a trailblazer for women in law.
qs.kf:
☛ First female judge of Supreme Court of India → Justice R. Banerjee (not Fathima Beevi; Banerjee was first woman judge in 1989)
☛ Fathima Beevi was from which state? → Kerala
☛ Which High Court did she start her career in? → Kerala High Court
☛ Year she became Supreme Court judge → 1992
☛ Second Muslim female judge in higher judiciary after Fathima Beevi → None (only one so far)

q: In March 2021, whose name was recommended by Chief Justice of India SA Bobde as his successor?
qs.e: In March 2021, the then Chief Justice of India SA Bobde recommended the name of Justice NV Ramana as his successor. This recommendation was made according to the convention of appointing the most senior judge as the next Chief Justice. Justice Ramana became the 48th Chief Justice of India on 24 April 2021. His tenure lasted until 26 August 2022. At the time of this recommendation, Justice Rohinton Fali Nariman and Justice Uday U Lalit were also senior judges, but Justice Ramana was the most senior in the order of seniority.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the 47th Chief Justice of India? → SA Bobde
☛ Which number Chief Justice was Justice NV Ramana? → 48th
☛ On what principle is the Chief Justice appointed? → Seniority
☛ When did Justice Ramana's tenure end? → 26 August 2022
☛ Who became the 49th Chief Justice of India? → Justice Uday U Lalit

q: Which court in India is responsible for handling civil cases like property disputes, divorce and consumer problems?
qs.e: In India, the Civil Court handles civil cases such as property disputes, divorce, consumer problems, contract disputes, etc. It adjudicates matters involving private rights and obligations. The hierarchy of civil courts ranges from the tehsil level to the Supreme Court. The procedure is governed by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. To file a suit, the plaintiff must prove the violation of their rights. Consumer problems are dealt with by Consumer Forums, which are quasi-judicial bodies, but civil courts also have jurisdiction in certain cases.
qs.kf:
☛ Which court hears civil cases? → Civil Court
☛ Which act governs procedure of civil courts? → Code of Civil Procedure, 1908
☛ Where are divorce cases filed? → Family Court (a type of civil court)
☛ Consumer disputes are resolved by? → Consumer Forums
☛ Highest civil court in India? → Supreme Court

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (24/06/2025) Shift 3
q: How are the proceedings and status of a Lok Adalat treated under Indian law?
o: Proceedings are judicial and Lok Adalat is deemed a civil court under CrPC.
Proceedings are advisory and Lok Adalat is not considered a civil court.
Proceedings are not judicial and have no legal standing in courts.
Proceedings are informal and not recognised under any law.
qs.e: Under Indian law, the proceedings of a Lok Adalat are treated as judicial in nature and it is deemed to be a civil court under the Code of Civil Procedure (CrPC). This provision is derived from the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987. The award passed by a Lok Adalat is final and binding, and no appeal lies against it. It functions similarly to a civil court in terms of enforcing its decisions. The main objective is to promote conciliation and speedy resolution of disputes. The award of a Lok Adalat is considered a decree and can be executed through a regular civil court.
qs.kf:
☛ What is the nature of Lok Adalat proceedings? → Judicial
☛ Under which Act is Lok Adalat recognized? → Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987
☛ Is an appeal against Lok Adalat award possible? → No
☛ The award of Lok Adalat is equivalent to what? → Decree of a civil court
☛ Under which code is Lok Adalat deemed a civil court? → Code of Civil Procedure (CrPC)

q: Which court has the power to issue order for common law rights?
qs.e: The power to issue orders for common law rights lies with the High Court. This authority is granted under Article 226 of the Constitution, which allows High Courts to issue directions, orders, or writs to any person or authority for enforcement of fundamental rights as well as for other purposes. Unlike the Supreme Court, which under Article 32 can issue writs only for fundamental rights, the High Court has wider jurisdiction, including common law rights. Subordinate courts do not possess such writ jurisdiction. Thus, the High Court is the correct answer.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 226 → Empowers High Courts to issue writs
☛ Article 32 → Supreme Court's writ jurisdiction for fundamental rights
☛ Common law rights → High Court can enforce these via orders
☛ Types of writs → Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, Quo Warranto
☛ Subordinate Courts → Cannot issue writs

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (21/06/2025) Shift 3
q: Which of the following disputes is excluded from the original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court?
o: A commercial contract dispute between Gujarat and a private company
A disagreement between Punjab and Haryana over territorial boundaries
A dispute between Maharashtra and the Centre over a constitutional law issue
A dispute between Karnataka and Tamil Nadu over water sharing
qs.e: Under Article 131 of the Indian Constitution, the original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court extends only to disputes between states and the Centre, or between states inter se, involving legal or factual questions. However, inter-state water disputes are governed by the Inter-State Water Disputes Act, 1956, which provides for the constitution of a Water Disputes Tribunal for adjudication, thereby excluding them from the Supreme Court's original jurisdiction. Thus, the Cauvery water dispute between Karnataka and Tamil Nadu is excluded. The other options—constitutional disputes between a state and Centre, boundary disputes between states—fall within original jurisdiction. Disputes with private parties are also excluded, but the correct answer is the water dispute.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 131 → Original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court
☛ Inter-State Water Disputes Act, 1956 → Tribunal for water disputes
☛ Article 262 → Parliament may provide for adjudication of inter-state water disputes
☛ Cauvery water dispute → Between Karnataka and Tamil Nadu
☛ Original jurisdiction covers → Legal disputes between states or state vs Centre

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (19/06/2025) Shift 1
q: Who among the following first coined the term 'judicial activism'?
qs.e: The term 'judicial activism' was first coined by Arthur Schlesinger Jr. in 1947 in an article published in Fortune Magazine. It refers to the propensity of the judiciary to actively interpret the Constitution, particularly when the legislature or executive fails to perform its duties. In India, Justice P.N. Bhagwati and Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer are considered proponents of judicial activism, but they did not coin the term. D.A. Desai was an Indian judge but not directly associated with coining the term. Judicial activism emerged as a key concept in U.S. constitutional law before spreading to other jurisdictions.
qs.kf:
☛ Who coined the term 'judicial activism'? → Arthur Schlesinger Jr.
☛ Where and when was it first used? → Fortune Magazine, 1947
☛ Who are regarded as pioneers of judicial activism in India? → Justice P.N. Bhagwati and Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer
☛ Landmark case associated with judicial activism in India → Kesavananda Bharati case (basic structure doctrine)
☛ What is the opposite of judicial activism? → Judicial restraint

q: Which of the following Acts is related to the establishment of High Courts in India?
qs.e: The Indian High Courts Act, 1861 was passed to establish High Courts in India, replacing the Supreme Courts and Sadar Adalats in the presidency towns. It created three High Courts at Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras. Each High Court consisted of a Chief Justice and up to 15 judges. This act unified the judicial system in British India and was a significant step in administering justice during the colonial period. The High Courts became the highest judicial authorities in their respective regions, with powers to hear appeals and original cases.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Indian High Courts Act passed? → 1861
☛ Which were the first three High Courts? → Calcutta, Bombay, Madras
☛ Which courts were abolished by this act? → Supreme Courts and Sadar Adalats
☛ What was the maximum number of judges in a High Court? → 15
☛ Which High Court was established later in 1866? → Allahabad

q: Which of the following Parts of the Indian constitution deals with District Judiciary of India?
qs.e: Part VI (Articles 152 to 237) of the Indian Constitution deals with the structure and functioning of the states, and Chapter 6 (Articles 233 to 237) specifically addresses the District Judiciary. Article 233 provides for appointment and promotion of district judges, Article 234 regulates recruitment to judicial service, and Article 235 gives control over subordinate courts to the High Court. Parts III (Fundamental Rights), IV (Directive Principles), and V (Union Executive) do not relate to district judiciary.
qs.kf:
☛ Articles related to District Judiciary → 233-237
☛ Appointment and promotion provision → Article 233
☛ Recruitment to judicial service → Article 234
☛ Control by High Court → Article 235
☛ Definition of district judge → Article 236

q: Who among the following is considered as the first Law Officer of Government of India?
o: Senior most Advocate of Supreme Court
qs.e: According to Article 76 of the Indian Constitution, the Attorney-General is the highest law officer of the Government of India. He is appointed by the President and advises the government on legal matters. The Attorney-General has the right to participate in the proceedings of Parliament but cannot vote. He represents the government in the Supreme Court. The Solicitor-General works under the Attorney-General. The senior-most advocate of the Supreme Court is a title, while the Chief Justice of India is the head of the judiciary, not a law officer of the government. Thus, the first Law Officer of the Government of India is the Attorney-General.
qs.kf:
☛ Who appoints the Attorney-General? → President
☛ What is the tenure of Attorney-General? → Not fixed by Constitution; holds office during pleasure of President
☛ Does Attorney-General have voting rights in Parliament? → No
☛ Who does Solicitor-General assist? → Attorney-General
☛ Who was the first Attorney-General of India? → Motilal C. Setalvad

q: Puducherry comes under the jurisdiction of which High Court?
qs.e: Puducherry is a Union Territory located in the southern part of India. Its judicial administration falls under the jurisdiction of the Madras High Court. The Madras High Court is the highest judicial body for the state of Tamil Nadu and the Union Territory of Puducherry. It is based in Chennai and was established in 1862. Although Puducherry is a small territory, its legal matters are handled by the Madras High Court. Other options like Calcutta, Hyderabad, and Guwahati High Courts are geographically distant and have no jurisdiction over this region.
qs.kf:
☛ Which High Court has jurisdiction over Puducherry? → Madras High Court
☛ When was Madras High Court established? → 1862
☛ For which state is Madras High Court primarily? → Tamil Nadu
☛ What is the area of Puducherry? → 492 sq km
☛ What is the state animal of Puducherry? → Squirrel

q: Which Article of the Indian Constitution permits the Supreme Court to review its judgement or order?
qs.e: Article 137 of the Indian Constitution empowers the Supreme Court to review any of its judgments or orders. This is a special power that allows the Court to reconsider a case if it believes that it is necessary in the interest of justice. This provision is a crucial part of judicial review and ensures that the Court can correct any mistakes. Article 137 grants the Supreme Court the authority to review its decisions, but this power is not available to lower courts. Petitions filed under this Article are called 'review petitions'. According to the Supreme Court Rules, a review petition is accepted only in exceptional circumstances, such as when there is an error apparent on the face of the record or a miscarriage of justice. The review power is not an appeal but a reconsideration of the same case.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Article gives review power to the Supreme Court? → Article 137
☛ What is the time limit to file a review petition? → 30 days
☛ Who can review a Supreme Court judgment? → The Supreme Court itself
☛ On what ground is a review petition filed? → Error or miscarriage of justice
☛ Under Article 137, review is accepted only in? → Exceptional circumstances

q: The _______ has the authority to punish for contempt of court in India.
qs.e: Under Articles 129 and 215 of the Indian Constitution, the Supreme Court and High Courts have the authority to punish for contempt of court. Contempt is of two types: civil contempt (willful disobedience of a court order) and criminal contempt (acts that scandalize or lower the authority of the court). This power is essential to maintain the independence and dignity of the judiciary. Though Parliament enacted the Contempt of Courts Act in 1971, the power to punish remains with the courts. The President or Lok Adalat does not possess this power.
qs.kf:
☛ Which articles deal with contempt of court power? → Articles 129 and 215
☛ What is civil contempt? → Willful disobedience of court orders
☛ What is criminal contempt? → Acts harming court's prestige
☛ Can Parliament punish for contempt of court? → No, only courts have this power
☛ When was the Contempt of Courts Act enacted? → 1971

q: Who among the following was the first-ever Supreme Court Justice against whom a motion for removal was initiated?
o: Hon'ble Mr. Justice Jitendra Vir Gupta
qs.e: The first Supreme Court judge against whom a motion for removal was initiated in India was Justice V. Ramaswamy. The impeachment motion was moved in the Indian Parliament in 1991 due to alleged misconduct. However, the motion lapsed after the Lok Sabha was dissolved. This event is significant in Indian judicial history as it highlighted the accountability of the judiciary and the impeachment process. Later, Justice Ramaswamy resigned from his position. The process involved allegations of financial irregularities and misuse of office, making it a landmark case in the Indian judiciary.
qs.kf:
☛ First judge against whom impeachment motion was initiated → Justice V. Ramaswamy
☛ Year of impeachment motion → 1991
☛ Motion lapsed due to → Dissolution of Lok Sabha
☛ Article for removal of judges → Article 124(4)
☛ Impeachment motion starts in → Lok Sabha

q: How do subordinate courts support the overall judicial system in India?
o: By providing accessible, prompt, and localized justice
By centralizing legal power in the higher judiciary
qs.e: Subordinate courts in India, including district courts and magistrates' courts, form the backbone of the judicial system. They provide accessible, prompt, and localized justice at the grassroots level, reducing the burden on higher courts. These courts hear cases in local languages and deliver justice close to the people. They operate under the supervision of the High Courts, and their decisions can be appealed to higher courts. Subordinate courts do not enact new legislation; they enforce existing laws. By ensuring that justice is accessible, speedy, and local, they strengthen the overall judicial system and uphold the rule of law.
qs.kf:
☛ Who supervises subordinate courts? → High Courts
☛ Lowest civil court in India? → Munsif Court
☛ Under which Articles do subordinate courts fall? → Articles 233-237
☛ What cases does the District Court handle? → Civil and Criminal cases
☛ Who appoints judges of subordinate courts? → Governor

q: Consider the following statements regarding the Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT) and select which is/are correct.
1. It exercises original jurisdiction in matters related to recruitment and service conditions of public servants.
2. Members of the defence forces, Supreme Court officers, and Parliamentary staff are also covered.
3. Members of CAT are appointed based on the recommendation of a high-powered committee chaired by the Prime Minister.
qs.e: The Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT) was established in 1985 under the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985. It exercises original jurisdiction in matters related to recruitment and service conditions of public servants, so statement 1 is correct. Statement 2 is incorrect because members of defence forces, Supreme Court officers, and Parliamentary staff are excluded from CAT's jurisdiction. Statement 3 is also incorrect: members of CAT are appointed by the President based on the recommendation of a selection committee comprising the Chief Justice of India, the Speaker of Lok Sabha, and a Union Minister. The Prime Minister is not part of this committee.
qs.kf:
☛ When was CAT established? → 1985
☛ Under which act was CAT established? → Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985
☛ Who is excluded from CAT's jurisdiction? → Defence forces, Supreme Court officers, Parliamentary staff
☛ Who appoints members of CAT? → President
☛ Who are on the selection committee for CAT members? → Chief Justice of India, Speaker of Lok Sabha, Union Minister

q: Which of the following Acts provides statutory status to Lok Adalats in India?
qs.e: Lok Adalats in India were granted statutory status by the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987. This Act was amended on November 9, 1995, giving legal recognition to Lok Adalats. Lok Adalats settle disputes through amicable settlement, and their awards are deemed to be decrees of a civil court, with no appeal allowed. This system provides speedy, inexpensive and justice-oriented resolution of cases. The Act also established the National Legal Services Authority (NALSA) and state-level authorities to implement legal aid programs.
qs.kf:
☛ Act providing statutory status to Lok Adalats? → Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987
☛ Lok Adalat award is equivalent to? → Decree of a civil court
☛ Types of disputes settled in Lok Adalat? → Civil, family, and other compoundable cases
☛ Can Lok Adalat award be appealed? → No, it is final and binding
☛ When was NALSA constituted? → December 5, 1995

q: Which of the following laws stipulated the establishment of Supreme Court in 1774 in Calcutta in India?
qs.e: The Regulating Act of 1773 was the first law passed by the British Parliament to regulate the affairs of the East India Company. Under this Act, a Supreme Court was established in Calcutta (now Kolkata) in 1774. The court consisted of a Chief Justice and three other judges. Its jurisdiction was limited to Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa. The court administered English law and its main objective was to control the malpractices of Company officials. This Act also created the position of Governor-General of Bengal, with Warren Hastings as the first incumbent. The establishment of the Supreme Court marked the beginning of the modern judicial system in India.
qs.kf:
☛ First Supreme Court in India → Established in Calcutta in 1774
☛ Regulating Act 1773 passed by → British Parliament
☛ First Chief Justice of Supreme Court → Sir Elijah Impey
☛ Purpose of Regulating Act → Control Company's administration
☛ First Governor-General under Act of 1773 → Warren Hastings

q: Which Article deals with the original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court?
qs.e: Article 131 deals with the original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court in the Indian Constitution. Original jurisdiction means certain disputes can be directly brought to the Supreme Court without going through lower courts. This article primarily covers disputes between the Centre and states, or between two or more states. Article 32 is for enforcement of fundamental rights. Article 124 establishes the Supreme Court. Article 141 makes the Supreme Court's decisions binding on all courts.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Article deals with original jurisdiction of Supreme Court? → Article 131
☛ Article 32 is related to? → Enforcement of fundamental rights
☛ Article 124 is about? → Establishment of Supreme Court
☛ What does Article 141 provide? → Binding nature of Supreme Court decisions
☛ What type of disputes are covered under original jurisdiction? → Centre-state and inter-state disputes

q: Which court is considered the highest judicial authority in a district?
qs.e: The highest judicial authority in a district is the District Court. It functions under the High Court of the state and handles civil and criminal cases at the district level. The District Judge heads this court. The District Court has civil jurisdiction, while the Sessions Court (part of the District Court) handles criminal cases. The Munsif Court is a lower court, Family Court deals with specific matters, and High Court is the apex state-level court. Hence, the District Court is the top judicial body in a district.
qs.kf:
☛ Who heads the District Court? → District Judge
☛ What types of cases does the District Court hear? → Civil and criminal
☛ Under which court does the District Court function? → High Court
☛ Which court deals with criminal cases at the district level? → Sessions Court
☛ Which court is the highest in a district? → District Court

q: Match the Administrative Terms with Their Descriptions Terms /Rulers Descriptions
A. Circle of Justice 1. Concept explaining the interdependence of rulers, soldiers, and peasants
B. Iqta 2. Land granted to governors for revenue collection and military maintenance
C. Razia Sultan 3. Daughter of Iltutmish; faced opposition due to gender
D. Minhaj-us-Siraj 4. Chronicler critical of female rulers
qs.e: 'Circle of Justice' explains the interdependence of rulers, soldiers, and peasants. 'Iqta' was a land grant system for revenue collection and military maintenance during the Sultanate period. Razia Sultan, daughter of Iltutmish, faced opposition due to her gender. Minhaj-us-Siraj, author of 'Tabaqat-i-Nasiri', was critical of female rulers.
qs.kf:
☛ What does 'Circle of Justice' signify? → Interdependence of rulers, soldiers, and peasants
☛ During which period did the Iqta system develop? → Sultanate period
☛ Whose daughter was Razia Sultan? → Iltutmish
☛ Which famous work did Minhaj-us-Siraj write? → Tabaqat-i-Nasiri
☛ What was the main purpose of the Iqta system? → Revenue collection and military maintenance

q: What kind of justice do the Directive Principles of State Policy of the Indian Constitution mainly aim to achieve?
qs.e: The Directive Principles of State Policy (Part IV, Articles 36-51) of the Indian Constitution primarily aim to achieve economic and social justice. These principles guide the state in formulating policies to establish a welfare state. They include provisions for equal pay, right to education, right to work, and public health. Although not enforceable by courts, they are fundamental in governance. Political justice is mainly ensured through Fundamental Rights, while religious justice is part of the secular fabric. Thus, the Directive Principles specifically focus on socio-economic justice to reduce inequality and promote fairness. They were inspired by the Irish Constitution and aim to create a just society.
qs.kf:
☛ Directive Principles are aimed at establishing → Economic and social justice
☛ Part of Constitution containing DPSP → Part IV
☛ DPSP borrowed from which country → Ireland
☛ Are DPSP enforceable by courts → No, they are non-justiciable
☛ Gandhian principles in DPSP include → Prohibition of cow slaughter, village panchayats

q: Which Article of the Indian Constitution empowers the Supreme Court to review any judgment pronounced or order made by it?
qs.e: Article 137 of the Indian Constitution empowers the Supreme Court to review any judgment or order pronounced by it. This power allows the Court to correct its own errors and ensure justice. A review petition is typically filed when new evidence or a legal error is discovered. Article 136 deals with special leave petitions, Article 141 makes Supreme Court decisions binding, and Article 145 governs the Court's procedure. The review power is a key aspect of judicial review, maintaining the balance of judicial authority.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Article gives the Supreme Court the power of review? → Article 137
☛ Which Article deals with special leave petition? → Article 136
☛ Which Article makes Supreme Court decisions binding? → Article 141
☛ Which Article describes the procedure of the Supreme Court? → Article 145
☛ When is a review petition filed? → Based on new facts or legal errors

q: Which of the following objectives is stated in Article 38 of the Indian Constitution?
o: To establish military rule for national security
To establish a social order based on justice—social, economic, and political
To guarantee employment to all citizens
To provide equal education opportunities for all
qs.e: Article 38 of the Indian Constitution is part of the Directive Principles of State Policy. It directs the State to strive to establish a social order based on social, economic, and political justice. This provision aims to create a just society where all citizens have equal opportunities. It is mentioned in Part IV of the Constitution. Other options like establishing military rule, guaranteeing employment, or providing equal education opportunities are not covered under Article 38 but under other articles. This article is non-justiciable, meaning it cannot be enforced by courts but serves as a guiding principle for governance.
qs.kf:
☛ What does Article 38 deal with? → Social order based on social, economic, and political justice
☛ Which part of the Constitution contains Article 38? → Part IV (Directive Principles of State Policy)
☛ What does 'State' mean in Article 38? → Public authorities including government and Parliament
☛ Which aspects of justice are emphasized in Article 38? → Social, economic, and political justice
☛ What type of right is Article 38? → Non-justiciable (cannot be enforced by courts)

q: Under which Article does the Supreme Court have the power of judicial review?
qs.e: Article 32 of the Indian Constitution grants the Supreme Court the power of judicial review. Under this article, any individual can directly approach the Supreme Court for enforcement of fundamental rights. It is considered the 'soul of the Constitution'. Article 32 empowers the court to issue writs such as habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto, and certiorari. This forms the basis of judicial review, allowing the court to examine the constitutionality of laws. Other options: Article 30 deals with minority educational institutions, Article 72 with the President's pardoning power, and Article 124 with the establishment of the Supreme Court.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 32's primary function → Protection of fundamental rights
☛ Article 32 also called → Right to Constitutional Remedies
☛ Writs under Article 32 → Habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto, certiorari
☛ Article 32 comparable to → Article III of the US Constitution
☛ Who called Article 32 'soul of the Constitution' → Dr. B.R. Ambedkar

q: The power to issue writs for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights is vested in_____.
qs.e: Under Article 32 of the Indian Constitution, the Supreme Court has the power to issue writs for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights. Similarly, Article 226 empowers the High Courts to issue writs for the same purpose. There are five types of writs: Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, and Quo Warranto. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar called Article 32 the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution. Thus, the power to issue writs for enforcing Fundamental Rights is vested only in the Supreme Court and High Courts, not in Lok Adalat, District Courts, or Session Courts.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 32 → Gives writ jurisdiction to Supreme Court.
☛ Article 226 → Gives writ jurisdiction to High Courts.
☛ Number of writ types → Five (Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, Quo Warranto).
☛ Dr. Ambedkar said Article 32 is the heart and soul of the Constitution.
☛ Writ concept → Originated from British law.

q: Which legislation forms the legal basis for the creation and operation of the Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT)?
qs.e: The Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT) was established under the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985. This Act gives effect to the provisions of Article 323A of the Constitution of India, which empowers Parliament to establish tribunals for the adjudication of service disputes of central government employees. CAT aims to provide speedy and specialized justice in service matters, thereby reducing the burden on High Courts. It handles cases related to recruitment, promotion, pay, discipline, and other service conditions. The principal bench of CAT is located in New Delhi, with additional benches in various cities across the country.
qs.kf:
☛ Under which Act was CAT established? → The Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985
☛ Which constitutional article governs CAT? → Article 323A
☛ Where is the headquarters of CAT located? → New Delhi
☛ What types of cases does CAT adjudicate? → Service disputes of central government employees
☛ In which year was the Administrative Tribunals Act enacted? → 1985

q: Which of the following officially determines the constitutional validity of any legislation?
o: The Parliament of India through a special resolution
The Supreme Court of India through judicial review
The President of India through constitutional discretion
The Union Cabinet through executive interpretation
qs.e: In India, the official authority to determine the constitutional validity of any legislation rests with the Supreme Court, exercised through the power of judicial review. Judicial review allows the court to examine whether a law or executive order is consistent with the Constitution. If a law violates constitutional provisions, the Supreme Court can declare it unconstitutional. This power is enshrined in Article 13, 32, and 131-136 of the Constitution. The Supreme Court is also known as the Guardian of the Constitution.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Article grants the power of judicial review? → Article 13
☛ Who is the interpreter of the Constitution in India? → Supreme Court
☛ Which Article provides for enforcement of fundamental rights? → Article 32
☛ Where is the Supreme Court of India located? → New Delhi
☛ From which country is the concept of judicial review borrowed? → USA

q: Which of the following British Indian government legislations provided for the establishment of a Supreme Court at Calcutta, comprising one chief justice and three other judges?
qs.e: The Regulating Act of 1773 was the first legislation passed by the British Parliament to regulate the administration of the East India Company in India. This act provided for the establishment of a Supreme Court at Calcutta, consisting of one chief justice and three other judges. The court had jurisdiction over civil, criminal, and admiralty matters in Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa. Additionally, the act laid down the foundation for the British government's control over the Company's affairs. It also appointed Warren Hastings as the first Governor-General of Bengal.
qs.kf:
☛ First regulatory act → Regulating Act of 1773
☛ Supreme Court established at → Calcutta in 1774
☛ First Chief Justice → Sir Elijah Impey
☛ Purpose of the act → To reform Company's administration
☛ Governor-General of Bengal → Warren Hastings

q: Which of the following 1973 landmark judgments of the Supreme Court of India provided that Parliament cannot amend the ‘basic structure’ of the Constitution through amendments?
qs.e: In the 1973 landmark case of Kesavananda Bharati, the Supreme Court of India ruled that Parliament cannot amend the basic structure of the Constitution. This doctrine limited the amending power of Parliament, protecting core principles like democracy, secularism, judicial review, and federalism. The decision was made by a 13-judge bench with a 7:6 majority. It overruled the Golakhnath Case (1967), which had held that fundamental rights could not be amended. The case was filed by a Kerala monastery, Kesavananda Bharati, and became a cornerstone in safeguarding the Constitution's integrity. The basic structure doctrine has since been reaffirmed in subsequent cases like Minerva Mills (1980) and Waman Rao (1981).
qs.kf:
☛ Which case established the basic structure doctrine? → Kesavananda Bharati (1973)
☛ How many judges were in the Kesavananda Bharati case? → 13
☛ Year of Golakhnath case? → 1967
☛ Which case reaffirmed the basic structure doctrine? → Minerva Mills (1980)
☛ What did the Champakam Dorairanjan case deal with? → Article 15(4) and reservations

q: Which Articles in the Indian Constitution deal with the Supreme Court’s organisation and powers?
qs.e: Articles 124 to 147 in Part V of the Indian Constitution deal with the organisation, independence, jurisdiction, and powers of the Supreme Court. Article 124 establishes the Supreme Court and provides for the appointment of judges. Article 126 deals with the appointment of an acting Chief Justice. Article 131 confers original jurisdiction, Articles 132-136 cover appellate jurisdiction (including special leave petition under Article 136), and Article 143 provides advisory jurisdiction. The number of judges is determined by Parliament; currently, there are 34 judges including the Chief Justice. Articles 146 and 147 deal with the officers, servants, and interpretation of the Court's powers.
qs.kf:
☛ Articles dealing with Supreme Court → Articles 124 to 147
☛ Article on original jurisdiction of Supreme Court → Article 131
☛ Articles on appellate jurisdiction of Supreme Court → Articles 132-136
☛ Article on advisory jurisdiction → Article 143
☛ Article on service conditions of Supreme Court judges → Articles 146-147

q: What action did the Supreme Court take regarding mining near national parks and wildlife sanctuaries on November 13, 2025?
o: Banned mining activities within one km
qs.e: On November 13, 2025, the Supreme Court banned mining activities within one kilometer of the boundaries of national parks and wildlife sanctuaries. This decision was taken to protect wildlife habitats and the ecosystem. The court stated that mining poses a threat to wildlife and negatively impacts biodiversity. The order was issued under the Wildlife Protection Act, 1972. Earlier, the protected zone was 0.5 km, which has now been extended to 1 km. This ruling strengthens environmental conservation and helps preserve natural habitats for wildlife. It ensures a buffer zone to minimize human interference in sensitive ecological areas.
qs.kf:
☛ Distance of mining ban near national parks → 1 km
☛ Act under which the decision was taken → Wildlife Protection Act, 1972
☛ Previous protected distance → 0.5 km
☛ Main objective of the mining ban → Wildlife habitat conservation
☛ Date of the Supreme Court decision → November 13, 2025

name: Set 1 · Q1–42
sub: Polity - State Government, Governor & Union Territories

q: Which Commission examined the Centre and state relationship?
qs.e: The Sarkaria Commission was established in 1983 to examine Centre-State relations in India. It was chaired by Justice R.S. Sarkaria. The commission submitted its report in 1988, making recommendations on the balance of powers between the Centre and states, the role of the Governor, the use of Article 356, and financial relations. Out of the 247 recommendations made by the Sarkaria Commission, most were accepted by the government. Other options: The M.M. Punchhi Commission (2007) also examined Centre-State relations, but it came after the Sarkaria Commission.
qs.kf:
☛ First commission to examine Centre-State relations → Sarkaria Commission (1983)
☛ Chairman of Sarkaria Commission → Justice R.S. Sarkaria
☛ Year Sarkaria Commission submitted its report → 1988
☛ Total recommendations of Sarkaria Commission → 247
☛ Second commission on Centre-State relations → M.M. Punchhi Commission (2007)

q: The Republic of India has _____ states and _____ Union Territories.
qs.e: India currently has 28 states and 8 Union Territories. Under the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019, Jammu and Kashmir was converted from a state to a Union Territory, and Ladakh was made a separate Union Territory. This reduced the number of states from 29 to 28. Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu were merged into a single Union Territory. Thus, the number of Union Territories increased from 7 to 8. This division is governed by Article 1 of the Constitution, which defines the territory of India.
qs.kf:
☛ Number of states in India → 28
☛ Number of Union Territories → 8
☛ Year of Jammu & Kashmir reorganisation → 2019
☛ Largest state by area → Rajasthan
☛ Smallest Union Territory by area → Lakshadweep

q: How many parliamentary constituency seats are there in the Union Territory of Puducherry?
qs.e: Puducherry is a Union Territory with its own unicameral legislature. As per the Indian Constitution, Puducherry is allocated one seat in the Lok Sabha. This seat represents the entire Union Territory. Similar to Puducherry, other small Union Territories like Lakshadweep, Daman and Diu, and Dadra and Nagar Haveli also have only one parliamentary seat each. The single Lok Sabha constituency in Puducherry is called the Puducherry Lok Sabha constituency. It is not reserved for Scheduled Castes but is a general category seat.
qs.kf:
☛ How many Lok Sabha seats does Puducherry have? → 1
☛ What type is the Puducherry Lok Sabha seat? → General category
☛ What type of legislature does Puducherry have? → Unicameral
☛ Which Union Territories have the fewest Lok Sabha seats? → Puducherry, Lakshadweep, Daman and Diu, Dadra and Nagar Haveli (1 each)
☛ How many Union Territories are there in India? → 8

q: Which of the following has the right to make parliamentary law in relation to Scheduled Areas?
qs.e: Under Article 244 of the Indian Constitution, the Governor has the right to make parliamentary laws related to Scheduled Areas. The Governor can issue special regulations for the welfare of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes. Parts IX and IX-A of the Constitution empower the Governor to regulate the functioning of Panchayats and Municipalities in these areas. The Governor can also decide which laws of the state legislature apply to Scheduled Areas, with modifications if needed. This power ensures the protection and development of tribal communities. The Fifth Schedule deals with the administration of Scheduled Areas, while the Sixth Schedule covers tribal areas in northeastern states. The Governor's role is crucial in safeguarding the rights and interests of these vulnerable groups.
qs.kf:
☛ Authority to make laws for Scheduled Areas → Governor
☛ Article 244 deals with → Scheduled and Tribal Areas
☛ Who controls Panchayats in Scheduled Areas → Governor
☛ Fifth Schedule contains → Administration of Scheduled Areas
☛ Sixth Schedule contains → Administration of Tribal Areas

q: Who was the chairperson of the commission which was set up to determine the relationship between the Center and the states?
qs.e: In 2007, the central government set up a commission under the chairmanship of M.M. Punchhi to review the relationship between the Centre and states. The commission was formally called the Commission on Centre-State Relations. It submitted its report in 2010, offering suggestions on the division of powers, the role of the governor, and the use of Article 356. Earlier, the R.S. Sarkaria Commission (1983-88) had also reported on the same subject. The Punchhi Commission recommended clear guidelines for the appointment and tenure of governors, among other things. Its recommendations remain important for understanding federal dynamics in India.
qs.kf:
☛ First commission on centre-state relations → Rajamannar Commission (1969)
☛ Chairperson of Sarkaria Commission → R.S. Sarkaria (1983)
☛ Year of Punchhi Commission formation → 2007
☛ Year of Punchhi Commission report → 2010
☛ Key recommendation on governor appointment → Consult central and state governments

q: Who has the right to provide permanent residency to the local residents of Jammu and Kashmir?
qs.e: The right to provide permanent residency to local residents of Jammu and Kashmir lies with the State Legislature. This power is granted under Section 6 of the Jammu and Kashmir Constitution. The State Legislature can enact laws to define who qualifies as a permanent resident. Although the abrogation of Article 370 changed this provision, originally this authority rested with the legislature, not the Chief Minister, President, or Parliament.
qs.kf:
☛ Who had the power to grant permanent residency in Jammu and Kashmir? → State Legislature
☛ Which section of J&K Constitution deals with permanent residency? → Section 6
☛ Article 370 was related to what? → Special status of Jammu and Kashmir
☛ Who is a permanent resident of Jammu and Kashmir? → A person settled before May 14, 1954
☛ What is the current legal basis for J&K? → Indian Constitution

q: Which State comes under the Article 370 of the Constitution?
qs.e: Article 370 of the Indian Constitution granted special autonomous status to the state of Jammu and Kashmir. It was added to the Constitution on 17 October 1949 and was abrogated on 5 August 2019. Under this article, Jammu and Kashmir had its own constitution, flag, and exemption from many central laws. The central government had jurisdiction only over defense, foreign affairs, and communications. Other states like Haryana, Mizoram, and Arunachal Pradesh were never covered under Article 370.
qs.kf:
☛ Which state was granted special status under Article 370? → Jammu and Kashmir
☛ When was Article 370 abrogated? → 5 August 2019
☛ When was Article 370 added to the Constitution? → 17 October 1949
☛ How was J&K reorganized after the abrogation? → Into two Union Territories: Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh
☛ Which subjects were under central jurisdiction under Article 370? → Defense, foreign affairs, and communications

q: Which of the following states has the highest number of Assembly seats in India?
qs.e: The number of Assembly seats in Indian states is based on population. Uttar Pradesh has the highest number of 403 Assembly seats, making it the largest state in this regard. It is followed by West Bengal (294), Maharashtra (288), and Bihar (243). Madhya Pradesh has 230 seats and Tamil Nadu has 234 seats. This distribution is governed by Article 170 of the Indian Constitution, which provides for the delimitation of Assembly constituencies in states. The Delimitation Commission periodically reallocates seats based on population changes.
qs.kf:
☛ State with highest Assembly seats → Uttar Pradesh (403)
☛ State with second highest Assembly seats → West Bengal (294)
☛ State with lowest Assembly seats → Sikkim (32)
☛ Basis of Assembly seats allocation → Population (Article 170)
☛ Function of Delimitation Commission → Reallocation of seats

q: In which of the Union Territories does the Panchayati Raj system NOT exist?
qs.e: The Panchayati Raj system in India was established by the 73rd Constitutional Amendment, 1992. This amendment provides provisions related to Panchayats under Articles 243 to 243-O. However, this amendment is not applicable to certain areas, including the Union Territories of Delhi, Chandigarh, and Lakshadweep. Delhi does not have a Panchayati Raj system; instead, it has urban local bodies like Municipal Corporations, Municipal Councils, and Nagar Panchayats. The reason is Delhi's urban character. Among the given options, only Delhi does not have Panchayati Raj. Other Union Territories like Daman and Diu, and Dadra and Nagar Haveli have Panchayats.
qs.kf:
☛ Constitutional Amendment for Panchayati Raj → 73rd Amendment, 1992
☛ Articles related to Panchayats → 243 to 243-O
☛ Union Territory without Panchayati Raj → Delhi and Chandigarh
☛ Local government in Delhi → Municipal Corporations and Councils
☛ Union Territories with Panchayats → Daman and Diu, Dadra and Nagar Haveli

q: Which of the following created the office of Governor General of India?
qs.e: The Charter Act of 1833 created the office of the Governor General of India. This act made the Governor General of Bengal the Governor General of India and granted him administrative authority over all British Indian provinces. Prior to this, the Governor General was only the head of the Bengal Presidency. The act also conferred legislative powers on the Governor General, allowing him to make laws. This laid the foundation for centralized administration in India. The Governor General also gained control over financial matters. This act was a significant step towards the unification of British rule in India.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the first Governor General of India? → William Bentinck
☛ Under Charter Act, 1833, what was the source of Indian law? → British law
☛ Which commission was established under Charter Act, 1833? → Indian Law Commission
☛ Who was the Governor General of India at the time of Charter Act, 1833? → Lord William Bentinck
☛ Which act was repealed by Charter Act, 1833? → Government of India Act, 1800

q: Which of the following parts of the Constitution is associated with the Union territories?
qs.e: Part VIII (Articles 239 to 242) of the Indian Constitution deals with Union territories. This part provides for the administration of Union territories by the President through an Administrator, and also allows for the establishment of a legislature and council of ministers for certain Union territories under Article 239A. Part VI deals with States, Part IV with Directive Principles of State Policy, and Part IX with Panchayats. Union territories include Delhi, Puducherry, Chandigarh, etc. Article 239A was inserted by the 14th Amendment to provide legislatures for some Union territories.
qs.kf:
☛ Which articles are in Part VIII? → 239 to 242
☛ Who administers Union territories? → The President
☛ Which article provides for legislature in Union territories? → Article 239A
☛ Delhi is what type of Union territory? → National Capital Territory
☛ Which amendment gave legislature to Puducherry? → 14th Amendment

q: The governor of a state of India is appointed for a term of-
qs.e: According to Article 156 of the Indian Constitution, the Governor of a state is appointed by the President for a term of five years. The term begins from the date the Governor assumes office. However, the President can remove the Governor at any time, and the Governor can also resign. If the Governor's term ends before a successor is appointed, they may continue in office until the successor takes over. The standard term is five years, but it is subject to the pleasure of the President.
qs.kf:
☛ What is the term of office of a Governor? → Five years
☛ Who appoints the Governor? → The President
☛ Who can remove the Governor? → The President
☛ To whom is the Governor accountable? → The President
☛ Which article deals with the Governor's term? → Article 156

q: ______ was the last Governor General of India before the Indian Constitution came into existence.
A. Chakravarti Rajagopalachari
B. The Viscount Mountbatten
C. Dr. Rajendra Prasad
D. The Viscount Wavell
qs.e: Chakravarti Rajagopalachari was the last Governor General of India, serving from 21 June 1948 to 26 January 1950. The Indian Constitution came into effect on 26 January 1950, after which the position of Governor General was abolished and Dr. Rajendra Prasad became the first President of India. Rajagopalachari was a prominent freedom fighter and statesman. He was not only the last Governor General of India but also later served as Chief Minister and Governor.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the last Governor General of India? → Chakravarti Rajagopalachari
☛ Who was the first President of India? → Dr. Rajendra Prasad
☛ When did the Indian Constitution come into effect? → 26 January 1950
☛ Who was the last Viceroy of India? → Lord Mountbatten
☛ Which award was given to Chakravarti Rajagopalachari? → Bharat Ratna

q: Which of the following is not a Union Territory?
A. Puducherry
B. Chandigarh
C. Lakshadweep
D. Sikkim
qs.e: India has 8 Union Territories: Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Chandigarh, Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu, Lakshadweep, Delhi (NCT), Puducherry, Jammu and Kashmir, and Ladakh. Sikkim is a state, which became the 22nd state of India in 1975. Union Territories are directly administered by the Central Government, while states have their own governments. Puducherry, Chandigarh, and Lakshadweep are Union Territories.
qs.kf:
☛ Total Union Territories in India → 8
☛ Year Sikkim became a state → 1975
☛ Head of Union Territory administration → President (through Administrator)
☛ Largest Union Territory (area) → Ladakh
☛ Smallest Union Territory (area) → Lakshadweep

q: The states of Chhattisgarh, Uttarakhand and Jharkhand were created in the year _____.
qs.e: Chhattisgarh, Uttarakhand, and Jharkhand were formed in November 2000. These three states were carved out of Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh, and Bihar respectively. Chhattisgarh was formed on 1 November 2000, Uttarakhand (then Uttaranchal) on 9 November 2000, and Jharkhand on 15 November 2000. Thus, the year 2000 is significant in the reorganization of Indian states, with three new states created simultaneously. Later, Telangana was formed in 2014 and Jammu & Kashmir was reorganized in 2019.
qs.kf:
☛ Date of formation of Chhattisgarh? → 1 November 2000
☛ Date of formation of Uttarakhand? → 9 November 2000
☛ Date of formation of Jharkhand? → 15 November 2000
☛ Which commission was involved in formation of these states? → State Reorganisation Commission
☛ Which new state was formed in 2014? → Telangana

q: Which of the following Articles of the Constitution of India provides provisions for creation of Legislative Councils in States?
qs.e: Article 169 of the Indian Constitution provides for the creation or abolition of Legislative Councils (upper house) in states. It empowers Parliament to create or abolish a Legislative Council in a state based on a resolution passed by the state's Legislative Assembly. The Legislative Council is a permanent house with members partly elected and partly nominated. Currently, only 6 states (Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana) have a Legislative Council. In contrast, Article 216 deals with High Courts, Article 151 with audit reports, and Article 195 with the qualification of Assembly members.
qs.kf:
☛ Provision for Legislative Council → Article 169
☛ Provision for Legislative Assembly → Article 170
☛ Appointment of Governor → Article 155
☛ State Council of Ministers → Article 163
☛ State Legislature structure → Article 168

q: Who threw a bomb in the Central Legislative Assembly on 8 April 1929?
o: Ram Prasad Bismil and Prafull Das
Chandra Shekhar Azad and Raushan Singh
qs.e: On 8 April 1929, Bhagat Singh and Batukeshwar Dutt threw a bomb in the Central Legislative Assembly. The aim was to draw the government's attention and highlight revolutionary activities. After throwing the bomb, they were arrested and tried. The British government sentenced them to life imprisonment. This act added a new chapter to the Indian freedom struggle. Both were active members of the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (HSRA). The incident shook the nation and ignited a wave of revolution among the youth.
qs.kf:
☛ Date of bomb throwing in Central Legislative Assembly → 8 April 1929
☛ Organization of Bhagat Singh and Batukeshwar Dutt → Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (HSRA)
☛ Name of leaflets thrown after the bomb → Inquilab Zindabad
☛ Date of Bhagat Singh's execution → 23 March 1931
☛ Sentence given to Batukeshwar Dutt → Life imprisonment

q: Who headed the Commission appointed in April 2007 to suggest measures for improvement in centre-state relations in India?
qs.e: In April 2007, the Government of India constituted a commission to suggest measures for improvement in centre-state relations, known as the Punchhi Commission. It was headed by Justice M.M.
