qs.e: The Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) of India can be removed from office only through a process similar to that of a Supreme Court judge. According to Article 324 of the Constitution, the CEC can be removed by the President only after an address by both Houses of Parliament with a special majority. This process is known as impeachment. The removal is allowed only on grounds of proven misbehavior or incapacity. This provision ensures the independence and impartiality of the Election Commission. The CEC is not removable by the Union Council of Ministers or by the President alone.
qs.kf:
☛ Who appoints the Chief Election Commissioner? → President
☛ What is the tenure of the Chief Election Commissioner? → 6 years or up to 65 years of age, whichever is earlier
☛ How many members are in the Election Commission? → Chief Election Commissioner and two Election Commissioners
☛ Where is the removal motion for CEC introduced? → In either House of Parliament
☛ What majority is required to remove the CEC? → Special majority (two-thirds of members present and voting)

q: Which is not true for the Government of India Act 1919?
A. The Act had a separate preamble.
B. This Act has made the Central Legislature liable.
C. The Act has provided the Public Service Commission in India.
D. The Act covered 20 years from 1919 to 1939.
qs.e: The Government of India Act 1919, also known as the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms, had a separate preamble stating the British government's aim to establish responsible government in India. This Act did not make the Central Legislature responsible; rather, it introduced dyarchy in provincial governments. It provided for the establishment of a Public Service Commission, which was later set up in 1926. The Act did not cover 20 years from 1919 to 1939; it was replaced by the Government of India Act 1935. Thus, option D is incorrect.
qs.kf:
☛ What is the other name of Government of India Act 1919? → Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms
☛ What system of government did this Act introduce? → Dyarchy
☛ Into how many parts were provincial subjects divided under this Act? → Two (Reserved and Transferred)
☛ Which Commission was provided for under this Act? → Public Service Commission
☛ Which Act was replaced by the Government of India Act 1919? → Government of India Act 1909

q: Which of the following is related to the 61st Amendment of the Constitution of India?
o: Advancement of economically weaker sections of citizens
Extended the period of reservation of seats
Incorporation of Goa, Daman and Diu as a union territory
Lowered the voting age of elections
qs.e: The 61st Amendment (1988) to the Indian Constitution reduced the voting age from 21 to 18 years for elections to the Lok Sabha and state legislative assemblies. It amended Article 326, which defines adult suffrage. This amendment aimed to empower youth and increase political participation. Other options: Advancement of economically weaker sections relates to the 103rd Amendment; extension of reservation period is linked to 23rd, 45th, 62nd, 79th, 95th Amendments; and incorporation of Goa, Daman and Diu as a union territory is associated with the 12th Amendment (1962).
qs.kf:
☛ 61st Amendment (1988) → Reduced voting age from 21 to 18 years
☛ Article 326 → Right to vote in Lok Sabha and Assembly elections
☛ 103rd Amendment (2019) → 10% reservation for economically weaker sections
☛ 23rd Amendment → Extended SC/ST reservation period (1969)
☛ 12th Amendment (1962) → Incorporation of Goa, Daman and Diu into India

q: Match the following political parties with their respective founding years. Political Parties Founding Years A) Indian National Congress
1. 1980 B) Bharatiya Janata Party
2. 1964 C) Bahujan Samaj Party
3. 1885 D) Bhartiya Communist Party
qs.e: The Indian National Congress was founded in 1885 by A.O. Hume. The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) was founded in 1980 by Atal Bihari Vajpayee and L.K. Advani. The Bahujan Samaj Party (BSP) was founded in 1984 by Kanshi Ram. The Communist Party of India was founded in 1964 by E.M.S. Namboodiripad and other leaders. Thus, the correct matching is A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2.
qs.kf:
☛ Indian National Congress founding year → 1885
☛ Bharatiya Janata Party founding year → 1980
☛ Bahujan Samaj Party founding year → 1984
☛ Communist Party of India founding year → 1964
☛ Communist Party of India (Marxist) founding year → 1964

q: Which of the following states did NOT hold assembly elections in March-April 2021?
qs.e: In March-April 2021, assembly elections were held in four states: Kerala, West Bengal, Assam, and Tamil Nadu. Manipur did not hold elections during this period; its previous assembly election was held in 2022. Kerala's election for 140 seats was won by the LDF. West Bengal's 294-seat election was won by the Trinamool Congress. Assam saw a victory for the BJP-led alliance. Tamil Nadu's election was won by the DMK-led alliance. Manipur's 60-member assembly elections were held in 2022, resulting in a BJP majority.
qs.kf:
☛ States holding assembly elections in March-April 2021 → Kerala, West Bengal, Assam, Tamil Nadu
☛ Winner in Kerala assembly election 2021 → LDF (Left Democratic Front)
☛ Winner in West Bengal assembly election 2021 → Trinamool Congress
☛ Winner in Assam assembly election 2021 → BJP-led alliance
☛ Next Manipur assembly election held in → 2022

q: The normal tenure of the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) of India is ______ years.
qs.e: The Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) of India holds office for a term of 6 years as per Article 148 of the Constitution. The CAG is appointed by the President and remains in office for a period of 6 years or until reaching the age of 65 years, whichever is earlier. The CAG heads the Indian Audit and Accounts Service and oversees the financial management of the government, ensuring transparency and accountability in the use of public funds. The removal process of the CAG is similar to that of a judge of the Supreme Court, ensuring independence. Key functions include auditing accounts of the Union and State governments.
qs.kf:
☛ What is the tenure of CAG? → 6 years
☛ Who appoints the CAG? → President of India
☛ Under which Article is CAG mentioned? → Article 148
☛ What is the retirement age of CAG? → 65 years
☛ CAG removal process is similar to that of which position? → Supreme Court Judge

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (23/06/2025) Shift 2
q: What is the term for elected members serving on the board of a co-operative society?
qs.e: The board of a co-operative society plays a vital role in its management. As per the Indian Co-operative Societies Act, the term of elected members on the board is 5 years. This duration ensures stability in the society's administration and allows for regular elections to maintain democratic functioning. After the term ends, fresh elections are conducted to elect new members.
qs.kf:
☛ Term of co-operative society board members → 5 years
☛ Maximum term under Co-operative Societies Act → 5 years
☛ Time for board re-constitution → After 5 years
☛ Election interval in co-operative societies → 5 years
☛ Regular election period for co-operative society → 5 years

q: India had _____ during the period between 2009 and 2014.
A. All party government B. Coalition government C. Single party government D. National party government
qs.e: Between 2009 and 2014, India had a coalition government led by the United Progressive Alliance (UPA). The Prime Minister was Dr. Manmohan Singh. The UPA was formed after the 2009 Lok Sabha elections, where the Indian National Congress emerged as the single largest party but fell short of a majority, so it allied with several regional parties like DMK, NCP, RJD, and others. This arrangement is a classic example of a coalition government, where multiple parties share power. Hence, the correct answer is coalition government.
qs.kf:
☛ Which coalition government was in power in India from 2009 to 2014? → UPA (United Progressive Alliance)
☛ Who was the Prime Minister during this period? → Dr. Manmohan Singh
☛ Which party won the most seats in the 2009 Lok Sabha elections? → Indian National Congress
☛ How many seats did Congress win in 2009? → 206 seats
☛ What was the tenure of the UPA government? → 2004 to 2014

q: Which of the following statements is true with regard to the Election Commission of India?
o: It is Constituted every four years.
It is a Permanent constitutional body.
It is Constituted every six years.
It is Constituted every five years.
qs.e: The Election Commission of India is a permanent constitutional body established under Article 324 of the Indian Constitution. It is not constituted periodically but continues to function indefinitely. The members are appointed by the President and hold office for a fixed term or until the age of 65 years, whichever is earlier. The primary role of the Election Commission is to conduct free and fair elections in the country. The other options are incorrect because the Election Commission is not constituted every four, five, or six years; it is a permanent institution that operates continuously.
qs.kf:
☛ Under which Article is the Election Commission constituted? → Article 324
☛ Who appoints the Chief Election Commissioner of India? → The President
☛ What is the term of office of an Election Commissioner? → 6 years or age of 65, whichever is earlier
☛ What type of body is the Election Commission? → Permanent constitutional body
☛ When was the Election Commission of India established? → 25 January 1950

q: Who is the Vice Chairman of the NITI Ayog (As of 2018)?
qs.e: Dr. Rajiv Kumar was appointed as the Vice Chairman of NITI Aayog in 2017. He is an economist and has served in various capacities in the Government of India. NITI Aayog is a policy think tank of the Government of India, established in 2015 to replace the Planning Commission. Its first Vice Chairman was Dr. Arvind Panagariya, followed by Dr. Rajiv Kumar. Dr. Y.V. Reddy served as RBI Governor, Dr. Vijay Kelkar as Finance Commission Chairman, and Dr. M.K. Jain as RBI Deputy Governor. Hence, the correct answer is Dr. Rajiv Kumar.
qs.kf:
☛ Establishment of NITI Aayog → 1 January 2015
☛ First Vice Chairman of NITI Aayog → Dr. Arvind Panagariya
☛ Vice Chairman of NITI Aayog (as of 2018) → Dr. Rajiv Kumar
☛ Main objective of NITI Aayog → Promote cooperative federalism
☛ Former CEO of NITI Aayog → Amitabh Kant

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (06/06/2025) Shift 3
q: What is the total full-time strength of personnels in the National Human Rights Commission, India?
qs.e: The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) of India was established under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993. Initially, it consisted of a Chairperson and four members, but after an amendment in 2000, the number of members was increased to five, making the total strength Chairperson and five members (total 6). It is mandatory to include a woman member. The Chairperson is typically a former Chief Justice of India. Among the members, two must have experience in human rights. The Commission makes recommendations to the central government and investigates complaints of human rights violations.
qs.kf:
☛ When was NHRC established? → 1993
☛ When was the NHRC Act amended? → 2000
☛ Who is the Chairperson of NHRC? → Former Chief Justice of India
☛ Is a woman member mandatory in NHRC? → Yes
☛ Where is the headquarters of NHRC? → New Delhi

q: The term polyarchy was used by Robert Dahl to describe a form of government in which?
o: It reduces the multitudinous differences of opinion to relatively simple alternatives
It takes individual as the basic unit of democratic model
People can participate through their representations
People act both through the electoral system and the group process
qs.e: Robert Dahl used the term polyarchy to describe a form of government where power is distributed among multiple groups. It is a practical model of representative democracy where citizens participate through both the electoral system (voting for representatives) and group processes (such as interest groups and pressure groups). According to Dahl, polyarchy involves both participation in government decisions and public contestation. Hence, people act both through the electoral system and the group process. Option 1 refers to majority rule, Option 2 takes an individualistic perspective, and Option 3 focuses only on representation, which does not fully capture the concept of polyarchy.
qs.kf:
☛ Who coined the term polyarchy? → Robert Dahl
☛ What is the main feature of polyarchy? → Decentralization of power among multiple groups
☛ How do citizens participate in polyarchy? → Through both electoral system and group process
☛ Polyarchy is a model of which type of democracy? → Representative democracy
☛ What does polyarchy include according to Dahl? → Participation and public contestation

q: Which of the following Articles of the Indian Constitution is related to Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG)?
qs.e: Article 148 of the Indian Constitution deals with the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG). It provides for the appointment, oath, service conditions, and term of office of the CAG. The CAG is appointed by the President and holds office for a term of 6 years or until the age of 65 years, whichever is earlier. The CAG audits all accounts of the Government of India and state governments. It is responsible to the Parliament and state legislatures. The removal procedure of the CAG is similar to that of a judge of the Supreme Court.
qs.kf:
☛ Who appoints the CAG? → President
☛ What is the term of CAG? → 6 years or until age 65
☛ Removal procedure of CAG is similar to whom? → Supreme Court judge
☛ Whose accounts does CAG audit? → Government of India and state governments
☛ Under which part of Constitution is CAG? → Part V (Chapter V)

q: Of the following, CEC means ______.
A. Chief Election Controller
B. Central Election Commission
C. Chief Election Commissioner
D. Common Election Code
qs.e: CEC stands for Chief Election Commissioner. The Chief Election Commissioner is the head of the Election Commission of India, a constitutional body responsible for conducting and overseeing elections in the country. The Chief Election Commissioner is appointed by the President and holds office for a term of 6 years or up to the age of 65, whichever is earlier. They ensure transparency and fairness in the electoral process. Options like Chief Election Controller, Central Election Commission, or Common Election Code are not standard terms in the Indian electoral system.
qs.kf:
☛ First Chief Election Commissioner of India → Sukumar Sen
☛ Establishment of Election Commission → 25 January 1950
☛ Term of Chief Election Commissioner → 6 years or 65 years
☛ Number of members in Election Commission → 3 (1 Chief + 2 Commissioners)
☛ Appointing authority of CEC → President

q: Which of the following statements is/are correct about a non-Constitutional body, Reserve Bank of India (RBI)? (1) RBI performs several crucial functions like regulating and supervising the banking system, managing the currency and credit system and managing foreign exchange reserves. (2) RBI was established on April 1, 1935 in accordance with the provisions of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934. (3) The Central Office of the RBI was initially established in Kolkata but was permanently moved to Mumbai in 1937
qs.e: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) is a non-Constitutional body established on April 1, 1935 under the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934. Its key functions include regulating and supervising the banking system, managing currency and credit, and managing foreign exchange reserves. The Central Office was initially set up in Kolkata but was permanently moved to Mumbai in 1937. Hence, all three statements are correct.
qs.kf:
☛ When was RBI nationalized? → 1949
☛ Who was the first Governor of RBI? → Sir Osborne Smith
☛ Who was the first Indian Governor of RBI? → C.D. Deshmukh
☛ Where is the head office of RBI located? → Mumbai
☛ When did RBI become the central bank? → After nationalization in 1949

q: In 1964, who chaired the Committee on Prevention of Corruption and suggested the Central Vigilance Commission be established?
qs.e: In 1964, the Government of India appointed a committee under the chairmanship of K. Santhanam to study the problem of corruption. This committee is known as the Santhanam Committee. In its report, the committee made several recommendations for the prevention of corruption, one of which was the establishment of the Central Vigilance Commission (CVC). The CVC was subsequently set up in 1964 itself. The Santhanam Committee emphasized administrative and legal reforms to curb corruption. It played a crucial role in laying the foundation for anti-corruption institutions in India.
qs.kf:
☛ Who chaired the Committee on Prevention of Corruption (1964)? → K. Santhanam
☛ When was the Central Vigilance Commission established? → 1964
☛ Who was the first Chief Vigilance Commissioner of India? → N. Srinivasan
☛ Which commission was suggested by the Santhanam Committee? → Central Vigilance Commission
☛ When was the Prevention of Corruption Act enacted? → 1988

q: Which among the following statements is INCORRECT related to the Right to Information Act, 2005?
o: The Central Information Commission is a constitutional body.
It covers all constitutional authorities, including the President and the Supreme Court.
All the non-governmental organizations (NGOs) that are financed by the government come under the purview of RTI Act.
The Act mandates that the information be provided within 30 days of the request in normal cases.
qs.e: Under the Right to Information Act, 2005, the Central Information Commission is a statutory body, not a constitutional one. It is constituted under Section 12 of the Act. Other statements are correct: the Act covers all constitutional authorities, including the President and the Supreme Court. All non-governmental organizations financed by the government come under its purview. In normal cases, information must be provided within 30 days, though for matters concerning life and liberty, the time limit is 48 hours.
qs.kf:
☛ When was RTI Act enacted? → 12 October 2005
☛ Tenure of CIC Chairperson? → 5 years
☛ What does 'public authority' include under RTI? → Parliament, Judiciary, Executive
☛ Which bodies are exempted from RTI? → Intelligence agencies (IB, RAW)
☛ Time limit for first appeal? → 30 days

q: In India, which of the following is NOT considered as a constitutional body?
qs.e: The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) is a statutory body, established in 1993 under the Protection of Human Rights Act. It is not created by the Constitution but by an act of Parliament. In contrast, the Election Commission of India (Article 324), Union Public Service Commission (Articles 315-323), and Finance Commission of India (Article 280) are constitutional bodies because they are directly mentioned in the Constitution, and their powers, composition, and functions are defined by it. NHRC is a statutory body formed by the government to protect human rights but does not have constitutional status.
qs.kf:
☛ What is a constitutional body? → A body created directly by the Constitution
☛ What type of body is NHRC? → Statutory body
☛ Constitutional basis of Election Commission → Article 324
☛ Constitutional basis of UPSC → Articles 315-323
☛ Constitutional provision for Finance Commission → Article 280

q: The provision related to the constitution of the Central Information Commission (CIC) in the RTI Act, 2005 is contained in which of the following sections?
qs.e: Section 12 of the RTI Act, 2005 deals with the constitution of the Central Information Commission (CIC). As per this section, the central government appoints a Chief Information Commissioner and up to ten Information Commissioners. The CIC is headquartered in Delhi and hears complaints against public authorities for failure to provide information. Section 15 pertains to the State Information Commission (SIC), while Sections 4 and 5 relate to disclosure of information and right to information, respectively. The CIC is an independent body established after the act came into force.
qs.kf:
☛ Section for CIC constitution → Section 12
☛ Section for SIC constitution → Section 15
☛ Maximum Information Commissioners in CIC → 10
☛ Total sections in RTI Act → 31
☛ RTI Act came into force → 12 October 2005

q: Which action attracts disqualification of an independent MP under the Anti-Defection Law introduced by the 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1985?
o: Joining any political party after their election
qs.e: The 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1985 added the Tenth Schedule, introducing the Anti-Defection Law. Under this law, an independent MP is disqualified if they join any political party after their election. However, they may support a coalition government without becoming a member. Voting differently from the party whip applies only to party members, not independents. Remaining neutral during debates does not attract disqualification.
qs.kf:
☛ Which amendment introduced the Anti-Defection Law? → 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1985
☛ Which schedule contains the Anti-Defection Law? → Tenth Schedule
☛ When is an independent MP disqualified? → If they join any political party after election
☛ Can an independent MP support a coalition government? → Yes, without joining a party
☛ Who decides on defection matters? → Presiding Officer of the House (Speaker/Chairman)

q: Before each general election to the House of the People or to a State Legislative Assembly, the President may appoint Regional Commissioners after:
o: consultation with the Speaker of the Lok Sabha
consultation with the Chief Justice of India
qs.e: According to Article 324(4) of the Indian Constitution, the President may appoint Regional Commissioners before each general election to the House of the People or a State Legislative Assembly after consultation with the Election Commission. These Regional Commissioners assist the Election Commission in the smooth conduct of elections. The Election Commission is an independent constitutional body responsible for administering election processes at both national and state levels. This provision ensures that the appointment is made based on the advice of the Election Commission, which has the expertise and authority over electoral matters. The consultation does not involve the Speaker of Lok Sabha, Chief Justice of India, or the Prime Minister.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Article deals with the appointment of Regional Commissioners? → Article 324(4)
☛ Who heads the Election Commission of India? → Chief Election Commissioner
☛ Who was the first Chief Election Commissioner of India? → Sukumar Sen
☛ When was the Election Commission of India established? → 25 January 1950
☛ Under which Article does the President appoint Regional Commissioners? → Article 324

q: What is the term of office of the Chief Election Commissioner of India?
o: Six year term or continue till the age of 70, whichever is earlier.
Four year term or continue till the age of 60, whichever is earlier.
Five year term or continue till the age of 65, whichever is earlier.
Six year term or continue till the age of 65, whichever is earlier.
qs.e: The term of office of the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) of India is defined under Article 324 of the Constitution. The CEC is appointed by the President and holds office for a term of 6 years or until the age of 65 years, whichever is earlier. This provision ensures the independence of the Election Commission. The CEC can be removed only through a process similar to that of a Supreme Court judge, requiring an impeachment passed by both Houses of Parliament. This term limit is crucial for maintaining free and fair elections in Indian democracy.
qs.kf:
☛ Term of Chief Election Commissioner → 6 years or till 65 years (whichever earlier)
☛ Who appoints the Election Commissioner? → President
☛ Service conditions of CEC are similar to which judge? → Supreme Court judge
☛ Removal procedure of CEC → Impeachment by both Houses of Parliament
☛ Article for Election Commission formation → Article 324

q: How many languages are there in Indian constitution?
qs.e: The Eighth Schedule of the Indian Constitution currently includes 22 languages. Initially, at the time of adoption in 1950, there were 14 languages. These were gradually increased through amendments. The 21st Amendment (1967) added Sindhi. The 71st Amendment (1992) added Konkani, Manipuri, and Nepali. The 92nd Amendment (2003) added Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, and Santhali. Thus, the total now stands at 22 languages. These languages represent the official or major languages of various states and reflect India's cultural diversity. The list continues to be updated as per linguistic demands.
qs.kf:
☛ Languages in the Eighth Schedule → 22
☛ Latest added languages (2003) → Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, Santhali
☛ Language added in 1967 → Sindhi
☛ Languages added in 1992 → Konkani, Manipuri, Nepali
☛ Original number of languages → 14

q: Which of the following languages has been declared as the oﬃcial language of the Government of India?
qs.e: According to Article 343(1) of the Indian Constitution, Hindi written in Devanagari script is the official language of the Government of India. This provision came into effect on 26 January 1965. Under the Official Language Act, 1963 and its amendments, English is recognized as a co-official language alongside Hindi. Articles 346 and 347 lay down rules for communication between states and the Centre. The Eighth Schedule of the Constitution lists 22 languages, but only Hindi is the official language of the Union. Hence, option 4 is correct.
qs.kf:
☛ Constitutional article for official language Hindi → 343(1)
☛ Script of Hindi → Devanagari
☛ Year Hindi was declared official language → 1965
☛ Co-official language → English
☛ Number of languages in Eighth Schedule → 22

q: Which of the following parts of the Indian Constitution contains the provision of emergency?
qs.e: The Part XVIII (Eighteen) of the Indian Constitution deals with emergency provisions. It describes three types of emergencies: National Emergency (Article 352), State Emergency or President's Rule (Article 356), and Financial Emergency (Article 360). National Emergency can be imposed on grounds of war, external aggression, or armed rebellion. State Emergency is imposed when the state government is unable to function according to the constitutional machinery. Financial Emergency is imposed when the financial stability of India is threatened. These provisions are covered under Articles 352 to 360 in Part XVIII. This part grants extensive powers to the central government during extraordinary circumstances.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Article deals with National Emergency? → Article 352
☛ Which Article deals with President's Rule? → Article 356
☛ Which Article deals with Financial Emergency? → Article 360
☛ Which Part of Constitution contains emergency provisions? → Part XVIII
☛ How many times has National Emergency been imposed? → Three times (1962, 1971, 1975)

q: Which amendment act added the Fundamental duties in the constitution?
qs.e: The Fundamental Duties were added to the Indian Constitution by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act (1976). This amendment was based on the recommendations of the Swaran Singh Committee. The Fundamental Duties are listed in Part IV-A of the Constitution under Article 51A. Initially, there were 10 duties; later, the 86th Amendment (2002) added one more duty (providing opportunities for education to children aged 6-14 years), making a total of 11 Fundamental Duties. These duties remind citizens of their responsibilities towards the nation and create a balance with fundamental rights.
qs.kf:
☛ Amendment that added Fundamental Duties → 42nd Amendment (1976)
☛ Article describing Fundamental Duties → Article 51A
☛ Total number of Fundamental Duties → 11
☛ Duty added by 86th Amendment → Providing education opportunities to children aged 6-14
☛ Committee that recommended Fundamental Duties → Swaran Singh Committee

q: The powers, rights and duties of Panchayats were included in the 11th Schedule of the Constitution by ______.
qs.e: The 73rd Amendment Act of 1992 granted constitutional status to the Panchayati Raj institutions in India. It added Part IX and the 11th Schedule to the Constitution. The 11th Schedule lists 29 subjects related to the powers, rights, and duties of Panchayats. This amendment aimed to strengthen rural local self-government and promote decentralization. The 74th Amendment deals with urban local bodies (municipalities).
qs.kf:
☛ Constitutional status to Panchayati Raj → given by 73rd Amendment
☛ Total subjects in 11th Schedule → 29
☛ 73rd Amendment came into effect → 24 April 1993
☛ Part of Constitution related to Panchayati Raj → Part IX
☛ Amendment dealing with municipalities → 74th Amendment

q: Which Constitutional Amendment Act was given to Sikkim as the full state of the Union of India?
qs.e: The 36th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1975 was enacted to grant Sikkim the status of a full state within the Union of India. Prior to this, the 35th Amendment Act, 1974 had made Sikkim an 'Associate State' of India. On May 16, 1975, Sikkim officially became the 22nd state of India. This amendment modified the First Schedule of the Constitution to include Sikkim as a full state, thereby ensuring its representation in both the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha. The amendment was a significant step in the integration of Sikkim into the Indian Union.
qs.kf:
☛ Amendment that made Sikkim an Associate State → 35th Amendment, 1974
☛ Amendment that made Sikkim a full state → 36th Amendment, 1975
☛ Sikkim became which number state of India → 22nd state
☛ Date when Sikkim became a state → May 16, 1975
☛ Number of Lok Sabha seats for Sikkim → 1 seat

q: Abdul Kalam served as the President of India during-
qs.e: Dr. Abdul Kalam served as the 11th President of India from 25 July 2002 to 25 July 2007. He was a renowned scientist and is known as the 'Missile Man of India'. During his tenure, the country made significant progress in science and technology. After his presidency, he remained active in teaching and writing. He authored several books, including 'Wings of Fire' and 'My Journey'. During his tenure, India achieved several milestones in space and defense sectors. Dr. Kalam passed away on 27 July 2015 while delivering a speech in Shillong.
qs.kf:
☛ Dr. Abdul Kalam is known by which nickname? → Missile Man of India
☛ Where was Dr. Kalam born? → Rameswaram, Tamil Nadu
☛ When did Dr. Kalam's presidential term end? → 25 July 2007
☛ Which award was conferred upon Dr. Kalam? → Bharat Ratna
☛ Where did Dr. Kalam pass away? → Shillong, Meghalaya

q: Under which Article of the Constitution of India can the President take over the administration of a state, in case its constitutional machinery breaks down?
qs.e: Article 356 of the Indian Constitution empowers the President to take over the administration of a state if the constitutional machinery fails. This is known as President's Rule or state emergency. Under this article, the President can dismiss the state government and place the state's functions under the control of Parliament. It is part of Part XVIII of the Constitution, which deals with emergency provisions. Article 343 pertains to the official language, Article 352 to national emergency, and Article 83 to the duration of Parliament sessions.
qs.kf:
☛ Under which article is President's Rule imposed? → Article 356
☛ Which article deals with national emergency? → Article 352
☛ Which article is related to the official language? → Article 343
☛ Article 356 is part of which part of the Constitution? → Part XVIII
☛ What does Article 83 deal with? → Duration of Parliament sessions

q: Which community gets special provision for certain services in Article 336?
qs.e: Article 336 of the Indian Constitution provides special provision for the Anglo-Indian community in certain services, particularly in appointments to departments like railways, postal, and customs. This provision was originally intended for 20 years from the commencement of the Constitution, but was later extended. It was abolished by the 126th Constitutional Amendment Act in 2019. The provision granted reservation to the Anglo-Indian community in government jobs. Its aim was to ensure the socio-economic upliftment of this minority community. Under Article 336, this special provision was exclusively for the Anglo-Indian community and not for any other community.
qs.kf:
☛ What does Article 336 deal with? → Special provision for Anglo-Indian community in certain services
☛ Which Amendment abolished Anglo-Indian reservation? → 126th Constitutional Amendment (2019)
☛ Originally, how many years was this provision for? → 20 years
☛ In which services was this provision applicable? → Railways, postal, customs, and other central services
☛ When did the reservation under Article 336 end? → 2020

q: What does the Ashoka's wheel in the Indian National Flag represent?
o: Wheel of the law of dharma
qs.e: The Ashoka Chakra in the Indian National Flag represents the Wheel of Law (Dharma Chakra). It is derived from the Lion Capital of Ashoka at Sarnath. The chakra has 24 spokes, symbolizing 24 hours and the movement of life. It signifies justice, progress, and truth. The chakra is placed in the center of the white band of the flag in navy blue. The wheel implies dynamism and change, representing the nation's continuous progress. Although associated with Buddhism, in the national flag it stands for secularism and moral values. The chakra was adopted on 22 July 1947 during the Constituent Assembly session.
qs.kf:
☛ How many spokes does the Ashoka Chakra have? → 24 spokes
☛ From which pillar is the Ashoka Chakra taken? → Sarnath pillar
☛ On which band of the Indian flag is the Ashoka Chakra placed? → White band
☛ What is the colour of the Ashoka Chakra? → Navy blue
☛ When was the Ashoka Chakra incorporated into the Indian flag? → 22 July 1947

q: What is the 99th amendment of the constitution about?
A. Starting GST in India.
B. Establishment of National Judicial Appointments Commission.
C. Empowering the Governor of Karnataka to take steps for the development of Hyderabad-Karnataka region.
D. Agreement on the land border between Bangladesh and India.
qs.e: The 99th amendment of the Indian Constitution was passed in 2014. Its main objective was to establish the National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC), a new body for appointing judges to the Supreme Court and High Courts. Previously, appointments were made under the collegium system. NJAC was to comprise the Chief Justice, two senior judges, the Union Law Minister, and two eminent persons. However, in 2015, the Supreme Court declared this amendment unconstitutional, thus restoring the collegium system.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the 99th amendment passed? → 2014
☛ How many members were in NJAC? → 6 members
☛ Who struck down the 99th amendment? → Supreme Court (2015)
☛ What was the earlier system for judge appointments? → Collegium system
☛ Which articles are related to the 99th amendment? → Article 124 and 217

q: Which amendment of the constitution provides 27% reservation for other backward classes as private higher education institutions in government?
A. 91st amendment
B. 92nd Amendment
C. 93rd amendment
D. 94th amendment
qs.e: The 93rd Constitutional Amendment, enacted in 2005, added Article 15(5) to the Constitution. This amendment provides 27% reservation for Other Backward Classes (OBCs) in government-aided private higher education institutions. It was introduced to ensure social justice and equal opportunities for OBCs in education. Prior to this, the Supreme Court in the Indra Sawhney case (1992) had ruled that reservations cannot exceed 50% of total seats. The 93rd amendment was crafted within this limit. It is a landmark amendment that expanded reservation policy to private institutions receiving government aid, thereby strengthening affirmative action for educationally backward classes.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the 93rd Amendment enacted? → 2005
☛ Which article is related to the 93rd Amendment? → Article 15(5)
☛ Which class gets reservation under the 93rd Amendment? → Other Backward Classes (OBC)
☛ Which institutions are covered under the 93rd Amendment? → Government-aided private institutions
☛ Which Supreme Court case is related to the 93rd Amendment? → Indra Sawhney case (1992)

q: Since the commencement of the constitution, which act has provisions relating to citizenship and loss of citizenship?
A. Citizenship Act, 1950
B. Citizenship Act, 1952
C. Citizenship Act, 1955
D. Citizenship Act, 1954
qs.e: After the commencement of the Indian Constitution, the provisions relating to acquisition and loss of citizenship are contained in the Citizenship Act, 1955. This act defines the rules for obtaining, losing, and renouncing citizenship. The Constitution in Part II (Articles 5 to 11) provides initial provisions, but detailed regulations are in this act. The act covers citizenship by birth, descent, registration, and naturalization. It came into force in 1955 and has been amended several times, notably in 1986, 2003, and 2019 with the Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA). The act also specifies grounds for loss of citizenship, including renunciation, termination, and deprivation.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Citizenship Act enacted? → 1955
☛ Which part of the Constitution deals with citizenship? → Part II (Articles 5-11)
☛ Main modes of acquiring citizenship? → Birth, descent, registration, naturalization
☛ Grounds for loss of citizenship? → Renunciation, termination, deprivation
☛ When was CAA (Citizenship Amendment Act) passed? → 2019

q: _______ enacted during an emergency imposed by Mrs. Indira Gandhi, is also known as mini constitution because of important & large number of changes made to it.
A. 42nd Amendment Act
B. 44th Amendment Act
C. 74th Amendment Act
D. 73rd Amendment Act
qs.e: The 42nd Amendment Act was passed in 1976 during the Emergency imposed by Mrs. Indira Gandhi in 1975. It is known as the 'Mini Constitution' because it made sweeping changes to many parts of the Indian Constitution. This amendment added the words 'Socialist', 'Secular', and 'Integrity' to the Preamble. It also introduced Fundamental Duties (Part IVA) and strengthened the powers of the central government. Additionally, it made the President bound by the advice of the Council of Ministers. The 44th Amendment was passed in 1978 to undo the distortions caused during the Emergency. The 73rd and 74th Amendments relate to Panchayati Raj and Municipalities respectively.
qs.kf:
☛ Which words were added to the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment? → Socialist, Secular, Integrity
☛ Which Part was added by the 42nd Amendment? → Part IVA (Fundamental Duties)
☛ What was the main purpose of the 44th Amendment? → To correct the excesses of the Emergency
☛ The 73rd Amendment relates to which institution? → Panchayati Raj
☛ The 74th Amendment relates to which institution? → Municipalities

q: Which of the following languages was not included in the 8th schedule of Indian Constitution through the 92nd amendment act?
A. Maithili
B. Bodo
C. Santhali
D. Kannada
qs.e: The 92nd Amendment Act (2003) added four new languages to the 8th Schedule of the Indian Constitution: Maithili, Bodo, Santhali, and Dogri. Kannada was already included in the 8th Schedule since the original constitution and thus was not added through this amendment. Prior to the 92nd amendment, the 8th Schedule contained 18 languages; after the amendment, it increased to 22 languages. The 8th Schedule currently recognizes 22 official languages. The 92nd amendment was significant in recognizing the linguistic diversity of India, especially languages from the northeastern and eastern regions. Note that the 92nd amendment is sometimes called the 91st amendment in some older documents, but it is officially the 92nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003.
qs.kf:
☛ Languages added by 92nd Amendment → Maithili, Bodo, Santhali, Dogri
☛ Total languages in 8th Schedule currently → 22
☛ Dravidian languages already in 8th Schedule → Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam
☛ Year of 92nd Amendment → 2003
☛ Which language was added by 21st Amendment (1967) → Sindhi

q: Name the committee, appointed to identify the creamy layer among the OBCs, which submitted its report in 1993 and was accepted?
A. Dr. K M Munshi Committee
B. G V Mavalankar Committee.
C. Ram Nandan Committee.
D. Swaran Singh Committee
qs.e: The Ram Nandan Committee was appointed to identify the creamy layer among the OBCs (Other Backward Classes). It submitted its report in 1993, which was accepted by the government. The creamy layer refers to the economically well-off members among OBCs who do not need reservation benefits. Based on this committee's recommendations, the government set an income limit for the creamy layer in OBC reservations. The Ram Nandan Committee is a crucial part of OBC reservation policy, ensuring that benefits reach the truly needy.
qs.kf:
☛ OBC creamy layer identification committee → Ram Nandan Committee
☛ Report submission year → 1993
☛ Creamy layer meaning → Economically well-off OBCs
☛ Income limit for creamy layer → Based on Ram Nandan Committee's recommendation
☛ Committee chairman → Justice Ram Nandan

q: In which year was the 'National Human Rights Commission' established in India?
qs.e: The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) of India was established on 12 October 1993 under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993. It is a statutory body that investigates human rights violations. Its formation aligns with the Paris Principles adopted by the United Nations in 1991. The first chairman of NHRC was Ranganath Mishra, a former Chief Justice of India. The commission consists of a chairman and four members, including two judges. Its headquarters is located in New Delhi. NHRC also makes recommendations to the government for the protection and promotion of human rights.
qs.kf:
☛ NHRC establishment year → 1993
☛ Act that created NHRC → Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993
☛ First chairman of NHRC → Ranganath Mishra
☛ NHRC headquarters → New Delhi
☛ Nature of NHRC → Statutory body

q: Which article of the Constitution of India gives the parliament the power to amend the constitution?
qs.e: Article 368 of the Constitution of India grants the parliament the power to amend the constitution. It is part of Part XX and lays down the procedure for amendments. An amendment bill can be introduced in either house of parliament and must be passed by a special majority in each house. Certain amendments, especially those affecting federal provisions or fundamental rights, require ratification by at least half of the state legislatures. The Kesavananda Bharati case (1973) established the doctrine of basic structure, limiting parliament's power to alter the constitution's fundamental framework. Thus, Article 368 is the cornerstone for constitutional amendments.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 368 → Deals with constitutional amendment procedure
☛ Part XX → Contains Article 368
☛ Special majority → Required to pass amendment bills
☛ Kesavananda Bharati case → Propounded basic structure doctrine
☛ Article 368(2) → Mandates state ratification for certain amendments

q: The President can nominate two members of which community to the Lok Sabha?
qs.e: Under Article 331 of the Indian Constitution, the President can nominate two members of the Anglo-Indian community to the Lok Sabha if he/she feels that the community is not adequately represented. This provision was effective from 1950. However, the 104th Constitutional Amendment (2020) abolished the reservation for Anglo-Indian members in the Lok Sabha and state legislative assemblies, effective from 2020. Prior to this, the provision was in force until 2019. Anglo-Indians are Indian citizens whose father is of European descent and mother is Indian. This community is a minority in India, and the provision was made to protect their interests. The amendment also removed the nomination of Anglo-Indians in states.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 331 → President nominates Anglo-Indians
☛ 104th Amendment 2020 → Ended Anglo-Indian reservation
☛ Anglo-Indian definition → Father European, mother Indian
☛ Maximum nomination number → 2 members in Lok Sabha
☛ State Assembly nomination → Governor under Article 171

q: Which constitutional amendment gave the Directive Principles precedence over Fundamental Rights?
qs.e: The 42nd Constitutional Amendment, enacted in 1976 and often called the 'Mini Constitution', gave precedence to Directive Principles over Fundamental Rights. It shielded laws implementing Directive Principles from judicial review on the ground of violating Fundamental Rights. The amendment added four new Directive Principles: equal justice, healthy development of children, opportunity for work, and workers' participation in industry management. It expanded Article 31C, making laws implementing Directive Principles immune to challenges based on Fundamental Rights. However, in 2007, the Supreme Court clarified that this precedence is subject to the 'basic structure' doctrine, particularly Articles 14, 19, and 21. The amendment also added 'Socialist' and 'Secular' to the Preamble.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the 42nd Amendment enacted? → 1976
☛ Which government passed the 42nd Amendment? → Indira Gandhi government
☛ Which amendment added 'Socialist' and 'Secular' to the Preamble? → 42nd Amendment
☛ Which Article was expanded by the 42nd Amendment? → Article 31C
☛ Which amendment is known as 'Mini Constitution'? → 42nd Amendment

q: How many languages are enlisted in the eighth schedule of the Indian Constitution?
qs.e: The Eighth Schedule of the Indian Constitution originally listed 14 languages, which have been expanded through amendments. Currently, there are 22 languages enlisted. These languages are recognized for official purposes, education, and cultural preservation. The 21st Amendment (1967) added Sindhi; the 71st Amendment (1992) added Konkani, Manipuri, and Nepali; and the 92nd Amendment (2003) added Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, and Santhali. The Eighth Schedule reflects India's linguistic diversity.
qs.kf:
☛ Total languages in Eighth Schedule → 22
☛ Most recently added languages → Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, Santhali (92nd Amendment, 2003)
☛ Sindhi added by which amendment → 21st Amendment, 1967
☛ Konkani, Manipuri, Nepali added by which amendment → 71st Amendment, 1992
☛ Original number of languages in Eighth Schedule → 14

q: Hindi was declared as the official language of Union under Article _______ of Indian Constitution.
qs.e: Article 343 of the Indian Constitution declares Hindi in Devanagari script as the official language of the Union. This provision falls under Part XVII (Official Language). Article 343(1) states that the official language of the Union shall be Hindi in Devanagari script. Article 343(2) provided that for a period of 15 years (until 1965), English would continue to be used for official purposes. Article 343(3) empowers Parliament to continue the use of English beyond that period. Article 345 allows states to adopt their own official language, while Articles 333 and 334 deal with reservations for Anglo-Indians and SC/STs.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Article declares Hindi as the official language of the Union? → 343
☛ What is the script of Hindi as per the Constitution? → Devanagari
☛ Which Part of the Constitution deals with Official Language? → Part XVII
☛ For how many years was English allowed as an additional official language? → 15 years (until 1965)
☛ Which Article allows states to adopt their own official language? → 345

q: Which one among the following languages is one of the six official languages of the United Nations?
qs.e: The six official languages of the United Nations are Arabic, Chinese, English, French, Russian, and Spanish. Chinese (Mandarin) is one of the most widely spoken languages globally and has been an official language of the UN since its founding. It is used in the UN General Assembly, Security Council, and other bodies. Among the options, Urdu, Japanese, and Hindi are not official languages of the UN, though Hindi is recognized as a spoken language at the UN.
qs.kf:
☛ Total official languages of UN → 6
☛ Which are the UN official languages? → Arabic, Chinese, English, French, Russian, Spanish
☛ Main form of Chinese language → Mandarin
☛ Most used language in UN → English
☛ Status of Hindi at UN → Spoken language (not official)

q: Which Constitutional Amendment led to inclusion of Sikkim in the Indian Union?
qs.e: The 36th Constitutional Amendment Act of 1975 led to the inclusion of Sikkim as a full-fledged state of the Indian Union. Prior to this, Sikkim was a protectorate state with special treaty relations with India. This amendment inserted Article 371F into the Constitution, which contains special provisions for Sikkim. The amendment came into effect on 26 April 1975, following a referendum in Sikkim that voted for merger. With this amendment, Sikkim became the 22nd state of India.
qs.kf:
☛ Amendment that included Sikkim in Indian Union? → 36th Amendment
☛ Special provision for Sikkim under which Article? → Article 371F
☛ When did the 36th Amendment come into effect? → 26 April 1975
☛ Sikkim became which state of India? → 22nd state
☛ Status of Sikkim before merger? → Protectorate state

q: Kesavananda Bharti Case in 1973 stemmed the question that the Preamble can _______.
qs.e: The Kesavananda Bharti case (1973) was a landmark judgment in Indian constitutional history. The Supreme Court propounded the 'Basic Structure Doctrine' in this case. According to this doctrine, the Parliament can amend the Constitution but cannot alter its basic structure. The Preamble is considered an integral part of the Constitution. The judgment clarified that the Preamble can be amended, but not completely changed. The 42nd Amendment (1976) added the words 'Socialist, Secular and Integrity' to the Preamble, which was consistent with this doctrine. Thus, the Preamble is amendable, but subject to the basic structure. This case established that the Preamble can be amended but cannot be completely rewritten. The basic structure includes supremacy of the Constitution, democratic governance, federal framework, and judicial review.
qs.kf:
☛ Kesavananda Bharti case (1973) → Basic Structure Doctrine was propounded.
☛ Amendment to Preamble → Done by 42nd Amendment (1976).
☛ Elements of Basic Structure → Supremacy of Constitution, Republican form of Government, Federal character, Judicial review.
☛ Berubari Union case (1960) → Preamble was not considered part of the Constitution.
☛ Minerva Mills case (1980) → Reaffirmed the Basic Structure Doctrine.

q: Which among the following Articles of the Indian Constitution deals with financial emergency?
qs.e: Article 360 of the Indian Constitution deals with financial emergency. The President is empowered to proclaim a financial emergency if he is satisfied that the financial stability or credit of India is threatened. During such an emergency, the Central government can interfere in the financial matters of states, such as reducing salaries and allowances of state employees. The proclamation must be approved by both Houses of Parliament within two months. It is one of the three types of emergency powers, the others being national emergency (Article 352) and President's rule in states (Article 356). So far, financial emergency has never been imposed in India.
qs.kf:
☛ Article related to Financial Emergency → Article 360
☛ Article related to National Emergency → Article 352
☛ Article related to President's Rule in states → Article 356
☛ Time limit for parliamentary approval after financial emergency proclamation → Two months
☛ Has financial emergency ever been imposed in India → Never

q: Article 368 of the Indian constitution is related to:
o: election to the post of president
qs.e: Article 368 of the Indian Constitution deals with the power of Parliament to amend the Constitution and the procedure for doing so. It allows amendments to any part of the Constitution, but certain basic features (like democracy, secularism, federalism) cannot be destroyed, as established by the basic structure doctrine in the Kesavananda Bharati case. An amendment bill must be passed by each house of Parliament with a special majority (2/3 of members present and voting). Some amendments also require ratification by at least half of the state legislatures. As of now, there have been 105 constitutional amendments.
qs.kf:
☛ Which article governs the amendment procedure? → Article 368
☛ What majority is required for a constitutional amendment? → Special majority (2/3)
☛ Which case established the basic structure doctrine? → Kesavananda Bharati case
☛ How many constitutional amendments have been made so far? → 105
☛ Who can introduce a constitutional amendment bill? → Either house of Parliament

q: Who is popular for designing the Indian Flag?
qs.e: The credit for designing the Indian National Flag goes to Pingali Venkayya. He was an Indian freedom fighter and agricultural scientist. In 1921, he presented a flag design to Mahatma Gandhi in Vijayawada. It had three stripes - white, green and red, with a spinning wheel in the center. Later, in 1931, it was modified and saffron was added. On 22 July 1947, the Constituent Assembly adopted it as the national flag. Pingali Venkayya is also known as the 'flag maker'.
qs.kf:
☛ Date of adoption of National Flag → 22 July 1947
☛ Length to width ratio of National Flag → 3:2
☛ Meaning of saffron color in National Flag → courage and sacrifice
☛ Number of spokes in the Ashoka Chakra → 24
☛ Designer of the Indian National Flag → Pingali Venkayya

q: Which of the following languages does NOT enjoy the status of a Scheduled language of India?
qs.e: The Eighth Schedule of the Indian Constitution currently recognizes 22 languages as Scheduled languages. Among the options, Maithili (added in 2003), Dogri (added in 2003), and Nepali (added in 1992) are included. Garhwali has not yet been granted the status of a Scheduled language. Garhwali is a major language of Uttarakhand but lacks constitutional recognition. The 22 Scheduled languages include Assamese, Bengali, Bodo, Dogri, Gujarati, Hindi, Kashmiri, Kannada, Konkani, Maithili, Malayalam, Manipuri, Marathi, Nepali, Odia, Punjabi, Sanskrit, Santali, Sindhi, Tamil, Telugu, and Urdu.
qs.kf:
☛ Which schedule lists the official languages? → Eighth Schedule
☛ Total number of Scheduled languages → 22
☛ When was Maithili added to the Eighth Schedule? → 2003
☛ When was Dogri added to the Eighth Schedule? → 2003
☛ When was Nepali added to the Eighth Schedule? → 1992

q: In which year the Article 35A was added to the Indian Constitution?
qs.e: Article 35A was added to the Indian Constitution in 1954 through a Presidential Order. This article granted special rights to the state of Jammu and Kashmir, including permanent residency, land acquisition, and employment reservations. It was abrogated on 5 August 2019. Article 35A was incorporated under Part XXI of the Constitution. It applied exclusively to Jammu and Kashmir and was added by the President rather than Parliament, which remained a controversial issue. The provision allowed the state legislature to define permanent residents and their special privileges.
qs.kf:
☛ Year of addition of Article 35A? → 1954
☛ Article 35A was added by which Presidential Order? → Presidential Order of 1954
☛ Which state was Article 35A related to? → Jammu and Kashmir
☛ When was Article 35A abrogated? → 5 August 2019
☛ Under which part of Constitution was Article 35A? → Part XXI

q: Which of the following was introduced as the 101st Amendment of the Constitution of India on July 1, 2017?
o: Land boundary agreement between India and Bangladesh
qs.e: The 101st Amendment of the Constitution of India, which came into effect on July 1, 2017, was introduced to implement the Goods and Services Tax (GST). This amendment was a major reform in the indirect tax system of India, consolidating multiple central and state taxes into a single unified tax. The GST was approved by the President on September 8, 2016, and became effective from July 1, 2017. The amendment empowers both Parliament and state legislatures to levy tax on goods and services, with the Centre imposing CGST and states imposing SGST. It created a nationwide tax on the supply of goods and services, fostering economic integration.
qs.kf:
☛ 101st Amendment effective from → July 1, 2017
☛ Central tax under GST → CGST
☛ State tax under GST → SGST
☛ Integrated tax under GST → IGST (inter-state supply)
☛ Chairperson of GST Council → Union Finance Minister

q: Which of the following is related to the Arvind Subramanian Committee?
qs.e: The Arvind Subramanian Committee was formed to recommend the framework for the implementation of Goods and Services Tax (GST) in India. The committee drafted a model law for GST and suggested tax rates, a simplified tax structure, and the compensation mechanism for states. GST is a landmark indirect tax reform that subsumed numerous central and state taxes like VAT, service tax, and excise duty. Arvind Subramanian, then Chief Economic Advisor to the Government of India, chaired the committee that laid the groundwork for the rollout of GST on 1 July 2017. The committee's recommendations were instrumental in shaping the final GST structure.
qs.kf:
☛ Which committee drafted the model GST law? → Arvind Subramanian Committee
☛ When was GST implemented in India? → 1 July 2017
☛ Which country first implemented GST? → France
☛ Who is the chairman of the GST Council? → Union Finance Minister
☛ How many GST tax slabs are there in India? → 5%, 12%, 18%, 28%

q: Select the legislation that does NOT deal with the protection of environment.
qs.e: This Act deals with the management and operation of ports, not environmental protection. The Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 restricts deforestation and ensures forest conservation. The Water (Cess) Act, 1977 imposes a cess on water consumption to control water pollution. The Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991 provides immediate relief to victims of accidents involving hazardous substances and is related to environmental damage.
qs.kf:
☛ Forest (Conservation) Act → Enacted in 1980, regulates diversion of forest land
☛ Water (Cess) Act → Enacted in 1977, imposes cess for water pollution control
☛ Public Liability Insurance Act → Enacted in 1991, relief for victims of hazardous substance accidents
☛ Port Laws Amendment Act → Enacted in 1997, relates to port management
☛ Environment Protection Act → Enacted in 1986, comprehensive law for environmental protection

q: Which of the following Constitution Amendment Act has reduced voter age from 21 years to 18 years?
qs.e: The 61st Constitution Amendment Act, passed in 1988, reduced the voting age from 21 years to 18 years. It amended Article 326 of the Constitution. This amendment was enacted during the tenure of Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi and came into effect on 28 March 1989. The aim was to increase youth participation in the democratic process. Earlier, the 44th Amendment Act (1978) had retained the voting age at 21 years. The 61st Amendment was passed by both Houses of Parliament with a special majority. It significantly expanded the electorate by including younger citizens.
qs.kf:
☛ Amendment reducing voting age to 18 → 61st Constitution Amendment (1988)
☛ Article amended → Article 326
☛ Date of effect → 28 March 1989
☛ Prime Minister at the time → Rajiv Gandhi
☛ Previous voting age → 21 years

q: Which amendment act is called the Mini Constitution of India?
qs.e: The 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 is known as the 'Mini Constitution of India' because it brought extensive changes to the Constitution. Enacted during Indira Gandhi's prime ministership, this amendment added the words 'socialist', 'secular', and 'integrity' to the Preamble. It introduced Fundamental Duties, enhanced the power of the executive over the judiciary, and strengthened the central government. The amendment attempted to limit the power of constitutional amendments under Article 368, which was later challenged by the basic structure doctrine in the Kesavananda Bharati case. This Act is one of the most controversial and significant amendments in Indian constitutional history.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the 42nd Amendment enacted? → 1976
☛ Which amendment added 'socialist' to the Preamble? → 42nd Amendment
☛ Which amendment introduced Fundamental Duties? → 42nd Amendment
☛ Which amendment restricted judicial review? → 42nd Amendment
☛ Under whose prime ministership was the 42nd Amendment passed? → Indira Gandhi

q: The right to form cooperative societies, a fundamental right has been provided in ____.
qs.e: The 97th Amendment (2011) to the Indian Constitution made the right to form cooperative societies a fundamental right. It amended Article 19(1)(c) to include the right to form cooperative societies and added Part IXB (Articles 243ZH to 243ZT), which provides for the functioning, administration, and auditing of cooperative societies. This amendment was aimed at providing constitutional protection to the cooperative sector. Earlier, the right was limited to forming associations or unions. The 97th Amendment was a significant step to strengthen the cooperative movement in India. It came into effect from 15 February 2012.
qs.kf:
☛ Constitutional amendment related to cooperative societies → 97th Amendment (2011)
☛ Fundamental right for cooperative societies under which Article → Article 19(1)(c)
☛ Part added by 97th Amendment → Part IXB
☛ Articles for cooperative societies → 243ZH to 243ZT
☛ 97th Amendment came into effect on → 15 February 2012

q: India's Constituent Assembly adopted the National Flag.
qs.e: India's Constituent Assembly adopted the National Flag on July 22, 1947. The flag was designed by Pingali Venkayya and is called the Tricolor. It has three horizontal stripes: saffron (courage and sacrifice), white (peace and truth), and green (faith and fertility). In the center is the Ashoka Chakra with 24 spokes. The flag was first hoisted on August 15, 1947 at independence. The Constitution was adopted on November 26, 1949, and came into effect on January 26, 1950.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the National Flag adopted? → July 22, 1947
☛ Who designed the National Flag? → Pingali Venkayya
☛ Order of colors in the flag → Saffron, white, green
☛ Number of spokes in Ashoka Chakra → 24
☛ When was the Constitution adopted? → November 26, 1949

q: What is the term for the Emergency declared in a country due to war, external attack, or armed rebellion?
qs.e: In the Indian Constitution, the emergency declared due to war, external aggression, or armed rebellion is called a National Emergency. It is imposed under Article 352. The President can proclaim such an emergency when the security of India or any part thereof is threatened by war, external aggression, or armed rebellion. During a National Emergency, fundamental rights can be suspended, and the central government gains more control over states. India has imposed National Emergency three times: in 1962 (Indo-China war), 1971 (Indo-Pakistan war), and 1975 (due to internal disturbance). It is important to note that 'State Emergency' (President's Rule) and 'Financial Emergency' are different types of emergencies under Articles 356 and 360 respectively.
qs.kf:
☛ Under which article is National Emergency imposed? → Article 352
☛ Which rights are suspended during National Emergency? → Fundamental Rights (Article 19)
☛ How many times has National Emergency been imposed in India? → Three times
☛ Why was the 1975 National Emergency imposed? → Internal disturbance
☛ What is State Emergency commonly known as? → President's Rule (Article 356)

q: The term socialist in the Preamble was added in which amendment of the Indian Constitution?
qs.e: The term 'socialist' was added to the Preamble of the Indian Constitution by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976, also known as the 'Mini Constitution'. This amendment, passed during the Emergency under Indira Gandhi's government, also added the words 'secular' and 'integrity' to the Preamble. It changed the description of India from 'sovereign democratic republic' to 'sovereign socialist secular democratic republic'. The 42nd Amendment brought several other significant changes, including the addition of Fundamental Duties and alterations to the powers of the judiciary. It remains one of the most controversial amendments in Indian constitutional history.
qs.kf:
☛ Which amendment added 'socialist' to the Preamble? → 42nd Amendment (1976)
☛ What is the 42nd Amendment also called? → Mini Constitution
☛ Which amendment added 'secular' to the Preamble? → 42nd Amendment (1976)
☛ Which amendment added 'integrity' to the Preamble? → 42nd Amendment (1976)
☛ Who was the Prime Minister during the 42nd Amendment? → Indira Gandhi

q: A significant step towards providing elementary education to all children in the age group of 6-14 years by 2010 was
qs.e: Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (SSA) is a flagship program of the Government of India, launched in 2001. Its primary objective was to provide elementary education to all children in the 6-14 age group and achieve universal primary education by 2010. This program became a key vehicle for implementing the Right to Education (RTE) Act, 2009. Under SSA, various facilities were provided including school construction, teacher recruitment, free textbooks, and mid-day meals. The mission also contributed to reducing gender and social disparities. Thus, SSA was a historic step towards ensuring elementary education for all children aged 6-14 years.
qs.kf:
☛ When was Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan launched? → 2001
☛ What is the main objective of SSA? → Providing elementary education to 6-14 year old children
☛ When was the Right to Education Act enacted? → 2009
☛ Key facilities under SSA → Free textbooks, mid-day meals
☛ Target year for universal primary education under SSA → 2010

q: When did the 86th Constitution Amendment Act come into force?
qs.e: The 86th Constitution Amendment Act, related to the Right to Education, came into force in the year 2002. This amendment inserted Article 21A in the Constitution, making education a fundamental right for children aged 6 to 14 years. It also modified Article 45 under the Directive Principles of State Policy to emphasize early childhood education. This amendment was a significant step toward ensuring free and compulsory education. Subsequently, the Right to Education Act (RTE) was enacted in 2009 and came into effect on 1 April 2010.
qs.kf:
☛ 86th Amendment is related to? → Right to Education (Article 21A)
☛ Which amendment made education a fundamental right? → 86th Amendment, 2002
☛ When did RTE Act come into force? → 1 April 2010
☛ Which article was added by 86th Amendment? → Article 21A
☛ Age group for fundamental right to education? → 6 to 14 years

q: _____ Is related to article 352 of the Indian Constitution.
qs.e: Article 352 of the Indian Constitution deals with National Emergency. It empowers the President to declare that a grave emergency exists whereby the security of India or any part thereof is threatened by war, external aggression or armed rebellion. Such a proclamation can be made only on the recommendation of the Cabinet and must be approved by Parliament. During a National Emergency, Fundamental Rights (except Articles 20 and 21) can be suspended and the distribution of powers between Centre and States shifts in favour of the Centre. So far, National Emergency has been imposed three times: in 1962 (China war), 1971 (Pakistan war), and 1975-77 (internal disturbance). Emergency under Article 352 is called National Emergency, whereas Articles 356 and 360 deal with State and Financial Emergencies respectively.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 352 → National Emergency
☛ Article 356 → State Emergency (President's Rule)
☛ Article 360 → Financial Emergency
☛ Grounds for National Emergency proclamation → war, external aggression, armed rebellion
☛ Fundamental Rights not suspended during National Emergency → Articles 20 and 21

q: Panchayati raj generally refers to the system of local self-government in India, it started in a ______ by a constitutional amendment
qs.e: The Panchayati Raj system in India was given constitutional status through the 73rd Constitutional Amendment passed in the year 1992. This amendment came into effect on 24 April 1993. It added Part IX and Articles 243 to 243O to the Constitution. The Act made a three-tier structure mandatory: Gram Panchayat, Panchayat Samiti, and Zila Parishad. It also provided reservations for women and Scheduled Castes/Tribes.
qs.kf:
☛ When did the 73rd Amendment come into force? → 24 April 1993
☛ What is the main purpose of Panchayati Raj institutions? → To promote local self-government
☛ Which article deals with Gram Sabha? → Article 243A
☛ What is the tenure of a Panchayat? → 5 years
☛ What is the minimum reservation for women in Panchayats? → 33%

q: How many times has the financial emergency been declared in India?
qs.e: Under Article 360 of the Indian Constitution, the President has the power to declare a financial emergency if the financial stability of the country is threatened. As of 2024, a financial emergency has never been declared in India. Unlike the national emergency (Article 352) and President's rule in states (Article 356), the financial emergency has never been invoked. Under this provision, the central government can interfere in the financial matters of states, impose salary cuts, and suspend financial provisions. The financial emergency remains a dormant provision in the Indian Constitution.
qs.kf:
☛ Article related to financial emergency → Article 360
☛ Number of times financial emergency declared in India → Never
☛ Which Article deals with National Emergency? → Article 352
☛ What orders can be issued during financial emergency? → Salary cuts and suspension of financial provisions
☛ Maximum duration of financial emergency → Indefinite (parliamentary approval needed every year)

q: In the year ____, the word 'integrity' was added in the preamble of the Indian Constitution.
qs.e: The word 'integrity' was added to the Preamble of the Indian Constitution in 1976 by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment. This amendment also added the words 'socialist' and 'secular' to the Preamble. Before this amendment, the Preamble described India as a 'sovereign', 'democratic', 'republic'. The 42nd Amendment is the most comprehensive amendment to the Indian Constitution, often called the 'Mini-Constitution'. It also introduced the Fundamental Duties. The term 'integrity' emphasizes the unity and integrity of the nation.
qs.kf:
☛ When was 'integrity' added to the Preamble? → 1976
☛ In which year was the 42nd Constitutional Amendment? → 1976
☛ Which three words were added to the Preamble in 1976? → Socialist, Secular, Integrity
☛ What is the 42nd Amendment also known as? → Mini-Constitution
☛ Which amendment introduced Fundamental Duties? → 42nd Amendment

q: In which year was the exchange of the regions between India and Bangladesh by their constitutional amendment take place?
qs.e: The exchange of regions between India and Bangladesh through constitutional amendments took place in 2015. It was done under the India-Bangladesh Land Boundary Agreement (LBA). Both countries amended their constitutions to transfer the enclaves. India passed the 100th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2015 to facilitate this. Under this agreement, India transferred 111 enclaves to Bangladesh, and Bangladesh transferred 51 enclaves to India. This resolved the long-standing border dispute and clarified the international boundary. The historic agreement was signed during the tenure of Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
qs.kf:
☛ Year of India-Bangladesh enclave swap → 2015
☛ Indian constitutional amendment → 100th Amendment
☛ Enclaves transferred by India → 111
☛ Enclaves transferred by Bangladesh → 51
☛ Name of the agreement → Land Boundary Agreement (LBA)

q: Konkani, Manipuri, and Nepali languages were included in the eighth schedule of the Indian Constitution in which year?
qs.e: The Eighth Schedule of the Indian Constitution originally listed 14 languages. Sindhi was added in 1967 by the 21st Amendment. Later, in 1992, the 71st Constitutional Amendment Act included Konkani, Manipuri, and Nepali. This increased the number of scheduled languages to 18. Subsequently, the 92nd Amendment in 2003 added Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, and Santhali, bringing the total to 22 languages. The 71st Amendment is significant for strengthening the rights of linguistic minorities under Articles 344 and 351 of the Constitution.
qs.kf:
☛ Number of languages originally in Eighth Schedule → 14
☛ Amendment adding Sindhi → 21st Amendment, 1967
☛ Amendment adding Konkani, Manipuri, Nepali → 71st Amendment, 1992
☛ Amendment adding Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, Santhali → 92nd Amendment, 2003
☛ Total languages in Eighth Schedule currently → 22

q: Which of the following decisions was given to the Sikh and Anglo-Indian people in separate India as a separate constituency?
qs.e: The Communal Award was announced in 1932 by British Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald. It provided for separate electorates for minorities including Sikhs and Anglo-Indians. The award aimed to ensure political representation for minority communities. However, Mahatma Gandhi opposed separate electorates for Dalits, leading to the Poona Pact. This decision was made after the Round Table Conferences. Other options - Regulating Act (1773), Indian Councils Act (1909), and Pitts India Act (1784) - are unrelated to this issue.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Communal Award announced? → 1932
☛ Who announced the Communal Award? → Ramsay MacDonald
☛ Which communities got separate electorates in the Communal Award? → Muslims, Sikhs, Anglo-Indians, Dalits
☛ Which pact opposed the Communal Award for Dalits? → Poona Pact (1932)
☛ Between whom was the Poona Pact signed? → Gandhi and Ambedkar

q: The Indian citizen who is normally living outside India and have an Indian passport,
qs.e: An Indian citizen who lives outside India and holds an Indian passport is called a Non-Resident Indian (NRI). NRI status applies to those who are ordinarily residing abroad for employment, business, or other purposes. Overseas Citizenship of India (OCI) is for foreign nationals of Indian origin, not Indian citizens. 'Multi-Country Citizens' is not an official term. 'Inner Line Permit' is a document required for entry into certain northeastern states. NRIs have voting rights and can invest in India under specific schemes.
qs.kf:
☛ Definition of NRI → Indian citizen living abroad
☛ Full form of OCI → Overseas Citizenship of India
☛ PIO card → Merged with OCI now
☛ Income tax rule for NRI → Stay abroad >182 days qualifies as NRI
☛ Indian passport holder → Only NRI, not OCI

q: Which part of the Indian Constitution is related to special provisions given to the states?
qs.e: Part-21 of the Indian Constitution (Articles 369 to 392) deals with Temporary, Transitional, and Special Provisions. This part provides special status and provisions to certain states such as Jammu and Kashmir, Sikkim, Mizoram, Arunachal Pradesh, and Goa. It includes Article 370 (special status for Jammu and Kashmir, now abrogated) and Articles 371 to 371-J (special provisions for various states). This part is one of the concluding parts of the Constitution and was included to accommodate states with special needs at the time of the Constitution's formation.
qs.kf:
☛ Which part provides special provisions for states? → Part-21
☛ Article 370 was part of which part? → Part-21
☛ How many articles are in Part-21? → Articles 369 to 392 (24 articles)
☛ Which article contains special provisions for Sikkim? → Article 371-F
☛ Which article contains special provisions for Mizoram? → Article 371-G

q: The first 'Backward Classes Commission' was appointed in _____.
qs.e: The first Backward Classes Commission in India was appointed in 1953, known as the Kaka Kalelkar Commission. It was constituted by a Presidential Order with Kaka Kalelkar as its chairman. The commission was tasked with identifying the backward classes in India and recommending measures for their upliftment. The commission submitted its report in 1955, identifying backward classes based on social and economic criteria. Although the government did not fully implement its recommendations, it laid the foundation for backward class policy. Later, in 1979, the second Backward Classes Commission (Mandal Commission) was appointed.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the first Backward Classes Commission appointed? → 1953
☛ Who was the chairman of the first Backward Classes Commission? → Kaka Kalelkar
☛ When did the Kaka Kalelkar Commission submit its report? → 1955
☛ When was the second Backward Classes Commission appointed? → 1979
☛ Who was the chairman of the Mandal Commission? → B.P. Mandal

q: Which of the following constitutional amendment is related to the Goods and service tax (GST)?
qs.e: The 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016 was enacted to introduce the Goods and Services Tax (GST) in India. It added a new Article 246A to the Constitution, granting powers to Parliament and state legislatures to levy taxes on goods and services. This amendment also removed the power of states to levy taxes on certain goods and established the GST Council. It came into effect on 1 July 2017, implementing the concept of One Nation, One Tax and unifying the indirect tax system across the country.
qs.kf:
☛ Which constitutional amendment is related to GST? → 101st Amendment
☛ Under which article was the GST Council formed? → Article 279A
☛ Date of GST implementation in India? → 1 July 2017
☛ Which amendment limited states' taxing powers? → 101st Amendment
☛ Which new article was added by the 101st Amendment? → Article 246A

q: When was the fundamental duties involved in the constitution of India?
qs.e: The Fundamental Duties were added to the Indian Constitution in 1976 through the 42nd Amendment. This amendment inserted Article 51-A under Part IV-A of the Constitution, listing 11 fundamental duties of citizens. These duties were based on the recommendations of the Swaran Singh Committee. The original Constitution did not include fundamental duties; they were added later to instill a sense of responsibility among citizens towards the nation.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Amendment added Fundamental Duties? → 42nd Amendment (1976)
☛ Fundamental Duties are in which Part of the Constitution? → Part IV-A
☛ Which Article deals with Fundamental Duties? → Article 51-A
☛ How many Fundamental Duties are there currently? → 11
☛ Which committee recommended Fundamental Duties? → Swaran Singh Committee

q: Basically, how many seats were reserved for Scheduled Tribes in the Lok Sabha?
qs.e: Originally, 47 seats were reserved for Scheduled Tribes (ST) in the Lok Sabha. This provision was made under Article 330 of the Indian Constitution, which provides for the reservation of seats for STs in the Lok Sabha. The objective is to ensure adequate representation of India's Scheduled Tribes in the lower house of Parliament. The number of reserved seats changes over time based on the population figures determined by the Delimitation Commission. Initially, 47 seats were fixed for STs. This provision also applies to Scheduled Castes (SC), for which separate seats are reserved. The reservation aims to enhance political participation and representation of marginalized communities.
qs.kf:
☛ Constitutional provision for ST reservation in Lok Sabha → Article 330
☛ Original number of seats reserved for SC in Lok Sabha → 79
