☛ Which article was added for women reservation in Lok Sabha? → Article 330A (Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam, 2023)

q: What major change was made by the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002?
o: Declared education as a Fundamental Right
qs.e: The 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002 made education a Fundamental Right. It inserted Article 21A, which provides free and compulsory education for children aged 6 to 14 years. It also modified Article 45 to focus on early childhood care and education, and added Article 51A(k) making it the duty of parents to provide educational opportunities to their children. This amendment was a historic step towards ensuring the right to education as a fundamental right.
qs.kf:
☛ Article added by 86th Amendment → 21A
☛ Age group covered by Right to Education → 6-14 years
☛ Articles affected by this amendment → 21A, 45, 51A
☛ Type of right education became → Fundamental Right
☛ Date Article 21A came into effect → 1 April 2010

q: Which Article of the Constitution provides special provisions for the State of Nagaland?
qs.e: Article 371A of the Indian Constitution provides special provisions for the State of Nagaland. This article grants Nagaland exemption from parliamentary laws on matters related to religious or social practices, Naga customary law and procedure, and ownership and transfer of land and its resources. It was added at the time of Nagaland's formation in 1963 to protect the unique cultural and social traditions of the Naga people. Under Article 371A, any law passed by Parliament concerning Nagaland will apply only if the state's Legislative Assembly passes a resolution to that effect. This gives Nagaland a special status compared to other states.
qs.kf:
☛ Special provision for Nagaland → Article 371A
☛ Capital of Nagaland → Kohima
☛ Governor of Nagaland → La Ganesan (current)
☛ Chief Minister of Nagaland → Neiphiu Rio (current)
☛ Year of formation of Nagaland → 1963

q: Which Article of the Constitution states, 'no person shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law'?
qs.e: Article 300A of the Indian Constitution states that "no person shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law". This article was added by the 44th Amendment Act, 1978. Previously, the right to property was a fundamental right under Article 31, but the 44th Amendment removed it and made it a constitutional/legal right. Under Article 300A, the government can only take away a person's property if it is authorized by law and due process is followed. This article is placed in Part XII (Finance, Property, Contracts and Suits) under Chapter IV. It ensures that property rights are protected from arbitrary executive action.
qs.kf:
☛ Which article originally contained the right to property? → Article 31 (now repealed)
☛ When was the 44th Amendment Act enacted? → 1978 (effective 1979)
☛ Article 300A falls under which Part of the Constitution? → Part XII
☛ What is required to deprive a person of property under Article 300A? → Authority of law
☛ How many fundamental rights are there now in the Constitution? → 6 (Articles 14-30)

q: What does ‘dyarchy’ mean in the context of the 1919 Act?
o: Power to the judiciary and legislature
qs.e: The Government of India Act 1919 (Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms) introduced dyarchy at the provincial level. Under this system, provincial subjects were divided into two categories: reserved subjects (under the control of the Governor and his executive council) and transferred subjects (under the control of responsible ministers). This established a dual control in provinces, where some subjects were administered by the Governor, while others were managed by elected ministers. The system proved unworkable and was abolished by the Government of India Act 1935.
qs.kf:
☛ Main objective of 1919 Act → First step towards self-governance in India
☛ Dyarchy relates to → Reserved and transferred subjects in provinces
☛ Examples of transferred subjects → Education, health, local self-government
☛ Examples of reserved subjects → Police, finance, justice
☛ End of dyarchy → Abolished by Government of India Act 1935

q: The 44th Amendment (1978) removed which of the following from the list of Fundamental Rights, converting it into a mere legal right under Article 300A?
qs.e: The 44th Amendment (1978) removed the Right to Property (Article 31) from the list of Fundamental Rights and made it a legal right under Article 300A. Previously, it was a Fundamental Right enforceable in courts. After this amendment, no person can be deprived of their property except by authority of law. This change was made to facilitate land reforms and other welfare measures by the state. The Right to Property is now a constitutional legal right, not a Fundamental Right. This amendment was a major step in balancing individual property rights with social welfare objectives.
qs.kf:
☛ Which right was removed from Fundamental Rights by the 44th Amendment (1978)? → Right to Property
☛ Under which Article is the Right to Property now a legal right? → Article 300A
☛ When was the Right to Property a Fundamental Right? → Before the 44th Amendment (Article 31)
☛ Which amendment made the Right to Property a legal right? → 44th Amendment, 1978
☛ In which year was the 44th Amendment passed? → 1978

q: Women play a significant role in rural livelihoods and household management. What is the minimum percentage of seats reserved for women in Panchayati Raj Institutions?
qs.e: Under the 73rd Constitutional Amendment (1992), Panchayati Raj Institutions must reserve at least 33% of seats for women. This reservation applies at all three levels (village, intermediate, and district panchayats). The aim is to empower women in local governance and ensure their participation in decision-making. The provision is enshrined in Article 243D. Additionally, sub-reservation applies for women from Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. Several states have increased this reservation to 50%.
qs.kf:
☛ Minimum women reservation in Panchayati Raj → 33%
☛ Three tiers of Panchayati Raj → Village, Intermediate, District
☛ Year of 73rd Amendment → 1992
☛ Constitutional article for women reservation → Article 243D
☛ States with 50% women reservation → Bihar, Uttarakhand

q: Which Constitutional Amendment Act restored the Parliament's power to amend Fundamental Rights?
qs.e: The 24th Amendment Act, 1971 restored Parliament's power to amend Fundamental Rights. Prior to this, in the Golaknath case (1967), the Supreme Court had ruled that Parliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights. The 24th Amendment overturned this decision by amending Articles 13 and 368. It clarified that Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights. It also added a provision that a constitutional amendment is not an ordinary law, thus protecting it from judicial review. This amendment was crucial in reasserting Parliament's sovereignty in constitutional amendments. It paved the way for the 25th Amendment and later led to the basic structure doctrine in the Kesavananda Bharati case (1973).
qs.kf:
☛ Golaknath case → 1967 Supreme Court ruling that Fundamental Rights cannot be amended
☛ 24th Amendment → Passed in 1971, reversed Golaknath decision
☛ Article 13 → Deals with judicial review of laws
☛ Article 368 → Procedure for constitutional amendment
☛ Basic Structure Doctrine → Established in Kesavananda Bharati case (1973)

q: Which of the following laws provides reservation in education and employment to the Economically Weaker Sections (EWS)?
qs.e: The 103rd Constitutional Amendment (2019) provides 10% reservation in education and government jobs for the Economically Weaker Sections (EWS) among the general category. It amends Articles 15 and 16 of the Indian Constitution to enable the state to make special provisions for the economically weaker sections. Before this amendment, reservation was available only for socially and educationally backward classes (SC/ST/OBC). The 103rd Amendment is the first constitutional amendment to provide reservation based solely on economic criteria. It was passed on 12 January 2019 and received presidential assent the same day. The EWS category includes individuals with an annual family income of less than 8 lakh rupees. This amendment does not affect existing reservations for SC/ST/OBC categories.
qs.kf:
☛ Amendment providing EWS reservation → 103rd Constitutional Amendment, 2019
☛ Articles amended by the 103rd Amendment → Articles 15 and 16
☛ Reservation percentage for EWS → 10%
☛ Annual income limit for EWS category → Less than 8 lakh rupees
☛ Date of enactment of 103rd Amendment → 12 January 2019

q: Which constitutional amendment gave constitutional status to the Panchayati Raj system in India?
qs.e: The 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992 granted constitutional status to the Panchayati Raj system in India. This amendment was introduced to strengthen rural local self-government. It added Part IX and Schedule 11 to the Constitution. The Act ensures elections, tenure, powers, and financial resources of panchayats. The 74th Amendment deals with urban local self-government (municipalities). The 73rd Amendment provided a three-tier structure: Gram Panchayat, Kshetra Panchayat, and Zila Panchayat.
qs.kf:
☛ Amendment giving constitutional status to Panchayati Raj → 73rd Constitutional Amendment, 1992
☛ Part added by 73rd Amendment → Part IX
☛ Schedule added by 73rd Amendment → Schedule 11
☛ Minimum age for panchayat membership → 21 years
☛ Tenure of panchayats → 5 years

q: Which of the following Articles deals with the amendment procedure of the Constitution?
qs.e: Article 368 of the Indian Constitution deals with the procedure for amending the Constitution. It grants Parliament the power to add, change, or repeal any part of the Constitution. The amendment process requires the bill to be passed by a special majority in both Houses of Parliament. For certain amendments, ratification by at least half of the state legislatures is also required. Several amendments have been made under Article 368, making it a crucial provision for constitutional evolution.
qs.kf:
☛ Who has the final authority for constitutional amendments? → Parliament
☛ Where can a constitutional amendment bill be introduced? → Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha
☛ What is the special majority requirement? → 2/3 majority of members present and voting plus majority of total membership
☛ Which articles can be amended without following Article 368? → Articles 5, 169, 239AA, 370, etc.
☛ Which is the latest constitutional amendment? → 106th Amendment (2023)

q: Which Constitutional Amendment introduced the Goods and Services Tax (GST) in India?
o: One Hundred and First Amendment Act, 2016
One Hundred and Second Amendment Act, 2018
qs.e: The Goods and Services Tax (GST) was introduced in India through the 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016. This amendment came into effect on 1 July 2017, empowering both the central and state governments to levy taxes concurrently through the GST Council. It added new articles 246A, 269A, and 279A to the Constitution. The Act subsumed multiple indirect taxes like central excise, service tax, VAT, and others into a unified tax system. This reform was a landmark step in implementing the One Nation, One Tax principle, simplifying the tax structure and boosting economic integration across states.
qs.kf:
☛ When was GST implemented in India? → 1 July 2017
☛ Which country first introduced GST? → France
☛ Who chairs the GST Council? → Union Finance Minister
☛ What are the GST tax slabs in India? → 5%, 12%, 18%, and 28%
☛ What does GST stand for? → Goods and Services Tax

q: What was the primary objective of the 88th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003?
qs.e: The 88th Amendment Act, 2003 inserted a new Article 268A in the Constitution, empowering the central government to levy and collect service tax. The proceeds of this tax were distributed between the centre and the states. This amendment was a crucial part of India's indirect tax system, later subsumed under the Goods and Services Tax (GST). Service tax was initially introduced in 1994, but it received constitutional status only in 2003 through this amendment. The primary objective was to provide a constitutional backing to service tax, which had been imposed through finance acts until then.
qs.kf:
☛ Which article was added by the 88th Amendment? → Article 268A
☛ When was service tax first introduced? → 1994
☛ When did service tax get constitutional status? → 2003
☛ Which amendment constitutionalized service tax? → 88th Amendment
☛ In which tax is service tax now subsumed? → GST

q: In which landmark case did the Supreme Court of India impose a three-month deadline for the President to give assent to State Bills reserved under Article 201?
o: Minerva Mills vs. Union of India (1980)
SR Bommai vs. Union of India (1994)
State of Tamil Nadu vs. Governor of Tamil Nadu (2023)
Kesavananda Bharati vs. State of Kerala (1973)
qs.e: In this landmark case, the Supreme Court ruled that the President must give assent to state bills reserved under Article 201 within three months. The Court directed the Governor to decide within three months on a bill passed by the Tamil Nadu Assembly to oust authorities. This judgment strengthens the sovereignty of state governments and prevents arbitrary delays by the Governor. The Court clarified that the Governor acts as an agent of the President and that his powers under the Constitution are not unlimited. It also emphasized the need for judicial review of the Governor's actions to ensure accountability. The case reaffirmed the federal balance and the importance of timely decisions on state legislation.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 201 → President can assent, withhold, or reserve state bills.
☛ Role of Governor → Link between state government and President.
☛ SR Bommai case (1994) → Deals with President's rule.
☛ Minerva Mills (1980) → Related to basic structure of Constitution.
☛ Kesavananda Bharati (1973) → Established the basic structure doctrine.

q: Which Constitutional Amendment introduced a cap on the size of the State Council of Ministers?
qs.e: The 91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003 introduced a cap on the size of the State Council of Ministers. According to this amendment, the total number of ministers, including the Chief Minister, in a state shall not exceed 15% of the total number of members of the Legislative Assembly. Additionally, the minimum number of ministers in a state is fixed at 12. This amendment was made to Article 164 of the Constitution. Its objective was to control the size of the government and enhance administrative efficiency. Before this amendment, there was no constitutional limit on the size of the Council of Ministers. This amendment is significant for promoting political stability and good governance.
qs.kf:
☛ Amendment that capped the size of State Council of Ministers → 91st Amendment, 2003
☛ Maximum number of ministers as per 91st Amendment → 15% of total assembly members
☛ Minimum number of ministers as per 91st Amendment → 12
☛ Article amended by 91st Amendment → Article 164
☛ Purpose of 91st Amendment → To control the size of the government

q: Which Constitutional Amendment reduced the voting age from 21 years to 18 years in India?
qs.e: The 61st Amendment Act, 1988 reduced the voting age from 21 years to 18 years in India. This amendment modified Article 326 of the Constitution, which deals with the eligibility for voting in elections to the Lok Sabha and state legislative assemblies. The primary aim was to give youth a participation in the political process and strengthen democracy. The amendment was passed during the tenure of Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi and came into effect on 28 March 1989. Before this, the voting age was 21 years as originally set in the Constitution. Other options: the 52nd Amendment relates to anti-defection, the 86th Amendment to the right to education, and the 44th Amendment to emergency provisions.
qs.kf:
☛ Which article was amended by the 61st Amendment? → Article 326
☛ When did the voting age reduction come into effect? → 28 March 1989
☛ Under which Prime Minister was this amendment passed? → Rajiv Gandhi
☛ What was the original voting age in the Constitution? → 21 years
☛ In which year was the 61st Amendment passed? → 1988

q: Which of the following Constitutional Amendments introduced the Goods and Services Tax (GST) in India?
qs.e: The Goods and Services Tax (GST) was introduced in India by the 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016, which came into effect on 1 July 2017. GST subsumed multiple indirect taxes like VAT, service tax, excise duty, etc., into a unified tax system. This amendment added a new Article 246A to the Constitution, empowering both the Centre and States to levy GST. It also established the GST Council, a federal body that decides tax rates and policies. The 101st Amendment was a landmark reform in India's indirect tax structure.
qs.kf:
☛ Constitutional Amendment for GST → 101st Amendment (2016)
☛ Date of GST implementation → 1 July 2017
☛ New Article added for GST → 246A
☛ Constitutional body for GST → GST Council
☛ Taxes subsumed under GST → VAT, service tax, excise duty, etc.

q: Which Article allows the President to appoint a Commission to investigate the condition of socially and educationally backward classes?
qs.e: Article 340 allows the President to appoint a Commission to investigate the condition of socially and educationally backward classes. This Commission reports on the condition of backward classes and recommends measures for their welfare. Article 330 and 332 deal with reservation of seats for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies respectively. Article 342 relates to the notification of Scheduled Tribes.
qs.kf:
☛ Commission for backward classes investigation → Article 340
☛ Reservation for SCs in Lok Sabha → Article 330
☛ Reservation for STs in State Assemblies → Article 332
☛ Notification of Scheduled Tribes → Article 342
☛ President appoints commission under → Article 340

q: What is the main feature of the Waqf (Amendment) Act, 2025?
o: Implementation of Uniform Civil Code Guidelines
Inclusion of Muslim women and all sects on boards
Nationalisation of all registered Waqf properties
Abolition of all existing Waqf Boards
qs.e: The main feature of the Waqf (Amendment) Act, 2025 is to bring transparency and inclusivity in Waqf Boards. The amendment mandates the inclusion of Muslim women and non-Muslim members in Waqf Boards. Previously, these boards consisted only of Muslim men, leading to a lack of representation for women and other communities. This amendment promotes gender equality and secularism in the management of Waqf properties. It also includes provisions for ensuring diversity in the composition of the board. This step is crucial for making Waqf institutions more accountable and effective. The act aims to modernize the administration of Waqf properties and ensure broader participation.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Waqf (Amendment) Act, 2025 passed? → In 2025
☛ What is the main objective of the act? → Inclusion of women and non-Muslims in Waqf Boards
☛ Who were previously included in Waqf Boards? → Only Muslim men
☛ What does this amendment promote? → Gender equality and secularism
☛ Whose participation is mandated in the act? → Muslim women and non-Muslims

q: Which amendment abolished the privy purse and privileges of the former rulers of princely states?
qs.e: The Twenty-Sixth Amendment to the Indian Constitution was enacted in 1971. It abolished the privy purse and privileges granted to former rulers of princely states. The amendment removed Articles 291 and 362 from the Constitution. The privy purse was an annual payment made to former rulers as part of the merger agreements. This move was taken under Prime Minister Indira Gandhi's leadership to reinforce the principles of equality and republicanism. After this amendment, former rulers lost all special privileges and became equal to ordinary citizens. The amendment was challenged in the Supreme Court but was upheld.
qs.kf:
☛ Amendment that abolished privy purse → 26th Amendment (1971)
☛ Articles removed by 26th Amendment → 291 and 362
☛ Basis of privy purse → Merger agreements with princely states
☛ Prime Minister during 26th Amendment → Indira Gandhi
☛ Purpose of abolishing privy purse → Promote equality and secularism

q: The provision of early childhood care and education to children below six years of age was introduced by which Constitutional Amendment?
qs.e: The 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002 was enacted to make education a fundamental right in India. It inserted Article 21A, providing free and compulsory education to children aged 6 to 14 years. It also amended Article 45, directing the state to endeavor to provide early childhood care and education for all children until they complete the age of six years. Additionally, a new fundamental duty (Clause K) was added under Article 51A, imposing a duty on parents or guardians to provide opportunities for education to their children aged 6 to 14. This amendment was a landmark step towards ensuring universal access to education and laying the foundation for the Right to Education Act, 2009.
qs.kf:
☛ Which amendment made education a fundamental right? → 86th Amendment, 2002
☛ Article 21A deals with? → Free education for 6-14 years
☛ What does Article 45 provide? → Early childhood care for children below 6 years
☛ Which fundamental duty was added by 86th Amendment? → Article 51A, Clause K
☛ When did the 86th Amendment come into force? → 1 April, 2010

q: Which of the following Amendments made Education a subject in the Concurrent List?
qs.e: The 42nd Constitutional Amendment of 1976 transferred education from the State List to the Concurrent List. This was done to ensure uniformity in education policy across the country. This amendment is often called the 'Mini-Constitution' because it introduced numerous changes to the Constitution. Later, the 86th Amendment (2002) made education a fundamental right (Article 21A), but it was the 42nd Amendment that moved education to the Concurrent List. The 44th Amendment primarily dealt with changes to emergency provisions.
qs.kf:
☛ Amendment that brought education under Concurrent List → 42nd Amendment (1976)
☛ Amendment that made education a fundamental right → 86th Amendment (2002)
☛ List under both Centre and State jurisdiction → Concurrent List
☛ 42nd Amendment is also known as → Mini-Constitution
☛ Total subjects in Concurrent List → 47 (originally 52, now 47)

q: The introduction of English education in India was promoted through which of the following documents?
qs.e: The introduction of English education in India was primarily promoted through Macaulay's Minute of 1835. This document, authored by Lord Macaulay, recommended the allocation of government funds for English-medium education rather than traditional Indian languages. Its objective was to create a class of 'Indians in blood and colour, but English in taste and intellect' who would assist in British administration. This policy reshaped the Indian education system, making English the medium of higher education and government jobs. Macaulay's Minute is considered the foundation of modern English education in India.
qs.kf:
☛ When was Macaulay's Minute presented? → 1835
☛ What was the purpose of Macaulay's Minute? → To promote English education in India
☛ Which language was prioritized under Macaulay's Minute? → English
☛ Who authored Macaulay's Minute? → Lord Macaulay
☛ What educational policy did Macaulay's Minute lay the foundation for? → Western education

q: Which Amendment gave Constitutional recognition to the National Commission for Backward Classes (NCBC)?
qs.e: The 102nd Amendment Act, 2018 granted constitutional status to the National Commission for Backward Classes (NCBC). This amendment added Article 338B to the Constitution, which provides for the constitution, powers, and functions of the NCBC. It also added Article 342A, which empowers the central and state governments to prepare lists of backward classes. The amendment aimed to give the NCBC the same constitutional status as the National Commission for Scheduled Castes and the National Commission for Scheduled Tribes. Previously, the NCBC was a statutory body established in 1993 under the National Commission for Backward Classes Act, 1993.
qs.kf:
☛ Amendment granting constitutional status to NCBC → 102nd Amendment Act, 2018
☛ Article added by 102nd Amendment → Article 338B
☛ Article related to backward classes list → Article 342A
☛ Year of establishment of NCBC (as statutory body) → 1993
☛ Who appoints the Chairperson of NCBC → President

q: Which Constitutional Amendment Act abolished the provision for nominating members from the Anglo-Indian community to the State Legislative Assemblies?
qs.e: The 104th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2019 abolished the provision for nominating Anglo-Indian members to the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies. This amendment was made by amending Article 334, which deals with the duration of reservation. It also extended the reservation of seats for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies until 2030. The Act removed Article 331, which empowered the President to nominate two Anglo-Indian members to the Lok Sabha. Additionally, the power of the Governor to nominate an Anglo-Indian member to the State Legislative Assembly under Article 333 was also terminated. This amendment marked the end of a 70-year-old provision that had been in place since the adoption of the Constitution in 1950.
qs.kf:
☛ Amendment that ended Anglo-Indian nomination → 104th Amendment Act, 2019
☛ Duration of Anglo-Indian reservation → 1950 to 2020 (70 years)
☛ Number of Anglo-Indian members → Maximum 2 in Lok Sabha, 1 in State Assembly
☛ Reservation extended by 104th Amendment → SC/ST seats until 2030
☛ Constitutional definition of Anglo-Indian → Article 366(2)

q: What special provision is granted under Article 371J of the Indian Constitution?
o: Provision for official language use in Goa and Daman and Diu
Special status for the Hyderabad–Karnataka region
Creation of a common High Court for the northeastern states
Special powers to the Governor of Manipur for law and order
qs.e: Article 371J of the Indian Constitution provides special provisions for the Hyderabad-Karnataka region of Karnataka state. This article was added by the 92nd Amendment Act, 2003. It mandates separate budget allocation and reservation for the region's development. A separate development board for the Hyderabad-Karnataka region is constituted to ensure educational and economic progress. This is one of several articles (371, 371A, 371B, 371C, 371D, 371E, 371F, 371G, 371H, 371I, 371J) granting special status to different states. The provision applies specifically to the Hyderabad-Karnataka region, not the entire state of Karnataka.
qs.kf:
☛ Which state is related to Article 371J? → Karnataka
☛ By which amendment was Article 371J added? → 92nd Amendment (2003)
☛ What status does the Hyderabad-Karnataka region have? → Special status
☛ Which board is formed under Article 371J? → Hubli-Dharwad and Gulbarga Development Board
☛ How many articles grant special status? → More than 12

q: The introduction of English education in India was promoted through which of the following documents?
qs.e: The introduction of English education in India was primarily promoted through Macaulay's Minute of 1835. Lord Macaulay, a member of the Executive Council under Governor-General Lord William Bentinck, advocated for the adoption of Western education in the Indian education system. His proposal was accepted, and the government decided to make English the medium of instruction. The objective was to create a class of Indians who would be 'Indian in blood and colour, but English in taste, opinions, morals, and intellect.' While the Charter Act of 1813 allocated funds for education, Macaulay's Minute formally pushed for English education. This decision had a lasting impact on India's educational landscape.
qs.kf:
☛ Year of Macaulay's Minute → 1835
☛ Governor-General at that time → Lord William Bentinck
☛ Name of the policy proposed by Macaulay → English Education Policy
☛ Class Macaulay aimed to create → 'Class of interpreters'
☛ Earlier act that allocated funds for education → Charter Act of 1813

q: Which Amendment of the Citizenship Act introduced the provision that an illegal migrant cannot acquire citizenship by naturalisation or registration?
qs.e: The Citizenship Act of 1955 was amended in 2003, which is one of the most significant amendments. It introduced the definition of 'illegal migrant' for the first time and stipulated that such a person cannot acquire citizenship by naturalisation or registration. According to this amendment, an illegal migrant is a person who enters India without valid documents or stays beyond the permitted period. The 2003 Amendment also introduced the concept of dual citizenship, later replaced by the Overseas Citizenship of India (OCI) scheme. This amendment is distinct from the 1986, 1992, and 2005 amendments because it includes strict provisions against illegal migrants. Thus, the 2003 Amendment prevents illegal migrants from obtaining citizenship.
qs.kf:
☛ Which amendment first introduced the definition of 'illegal migrant' in the Citizenship Act 1955? → 2003 Amendment
☛ What new concept did the Citizenship (Amendment) Act 2003 introduce? → Dual citizenship (later OCI)
☛ Which amendment prohibits illegal migrants from acquiring citizenship? → 2003 Amendment
☛ According to the 2003 Amendment, who is an illegal migrant? → Person entering without valid documents or overstaying
☛ Under the Citizenship Amendment Act 2003, who cannot be granted citizenship by registration? → Illegal migrants

q: Which state has special constitutional provisions to protect its tribal customs and laws under Article 371A?
qs.e: Article 371A provides special constitutional provisions to protect the tribal customs, traditional laws, land ownership, and justice system of Nagaland. Under this article, any law passed by the Parliament applies to Nagaland only if the state's Legislative Assembly passes a resolution to that effect. This provision was introduced as part of the 13th Amendment Act, 1962, following the formation of Nagaland as a state. It ensures the preservation of the cultural identity and autonomy of the Naga people. Other options like Assam, Mizoram, and Tripura have their own special provisions under different articles, but Article 371A is exclusively for Nagaland.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 371A is for which state? → Nagaland
☛ When do Parliament laws apply in Nagaland? → Only if state legislature passes a resolution
☛ What does Article 371A protect? → Tribal customs, traditional laws, land ownership
☛ Which amendment introduced Article 371A? → 13th Amendment Act, 1962
☛ What is the capital of Nagaland? → Kohima

q: Which of the following Constitutional provisions can be amended by an ordinary Act of Parliament (simple majority), rather than through the special procedure under Article 368?
o: Article 2 (Parliament may by law admit new states)
qs.e: Certain provisions of the Indian Constitution can be amended by an ordinary Act of Parliament passed by a simple majority, rather than through the special procedure under Article 368. Article 2 empowers Parliament to admit or establish new states by a simple legislative act. Such provisions include Article 3 (alteration of state boundaries), Article 4 (amendments to the First and Fourth Schedules), Article 169 (abolition or creation of Legislative Councils), and Article 239A (creation of local legislatures for Union Territories). These provisions are not part of the Constitution's basic structure, so they require only a simple majority. In contrast, Article 356 and Article 368 require special majorities, and Article 14 is a fundamental right that can only be amended under Article 368.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 3 → Changes to state boundaries and names by simple majority
☛ Article 169 → Creation or abolition of Legislative Councils by simple majority
☛ Article 239A → Legislature for Union Territories by simple majority
☛ Article 4 → Amendments to First and Fourth Schedules by simple majority
☛ Article 368 → Amendment procedure requires special majority and state consent

q: Article 371A of the Indian Constitution grants special provisions for the state of ____________.
qs.e: Article 371A of the Indian Constitution grants special provisions for the state of Nagaland. This article provides special protection to Nagaland in matters of religious or social practices, Naga customary law and procedure, administration of criminal justice in Nagaland, and ownership and transfer of land and its resources. Additionally, the Parliament cannot make laws on these matters without the consent of the Nagaland Legislative Assembly. This provision was designed to preserve the cultural and social identity of the Naga people. The special status under Article 371A was part of the agreement when Nagaland was formed as a separate state in 1963.
qs.kf:
☛ For which state is Article 371A provided? → Nagaland
☛ Which article deals with Assam’s special provisions? → Article 371B
☛ Article 371C grants special provisions for which state? → Manipur
☛ Article 371D provides special provisions for which state? → Andhra Pradesh
☛ Article 371F is related to which state? → Sikkim

q: Which Article of the Indian Constitution states that a person who had voluntarily acquired the citizenship of a foreign State shall NOT be considered a citizen of India at the commencement of the Constitution under Articles 5, 6, or 8?
qs.e: Article 9 of the Indian Constitution states that if a person has voluntarily acquired the citizenship of a foreign State, they shall not be considered a citizen of India at the commencement of the Constitution (26 January 1950) under Articles 5, 6, or 8. This article reinforces the principle of single citizenship followed in India. Article 5 deals with citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution, Article 6 addresses citizenship of migrants from Pakistan, and Article 8 covers citizenship of persons of Indian origin residing outside India. Article 9 ensures that no person can enjoy dual citizenship. It is a crucial provision in Indian citizenship law.
qs.kf:
☛ What is the main purpose of Article 9? → To terminate Indian citizenship upon acquiring foreign citizenship
☛ What does Article 5 relate to? → Citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution
☛ What does Article 6 relate to? → Citizenship of migrants from Pakistan
☛ What does Article 8 relate to? → Citizenship of Indian origin persons living abroad
☛ What type of citizenship is followed in India? → Single citizenship

q: Which special representation in the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies was discontinued by the 104th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2020?
qs.e: The 104th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2020 discontinued the reservation of seats for the Anglo-Indian community in the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies. This reservation was originally provided under Article 331 for the Lok Sabha, allowing the President to nominate two Anglo-Indian members, and under Article 333 for State Assemblies, allowing the Governor to nominate members. The amendment came into effect on 25 January 2020. While it extended the reservation for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes until 2030, it completely removed the Anglo-Indian reservation, marking the end of a special representation that had been in place since the Constitution's adoption.
qs.kf:
☛ Which community's reservation was abolished by the 104th Amendment? → Anglo-Indian
☛ Under which articles was Anglo-Indian reservation provided? → Articles 331 and 333
☛ How many Anglo-Indians were nominated in Lok Sabha? → 2
☛ When did the 104th Amendment come into force? → 25 January 2020
☛ Which reservation was extended to 2030? → SC and ST reservation

q: Which of the following constitutional mechanisms ensures political representation for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in the Indian Parliament?
qs.e: Article 330 and 332 of the Indian Constitution provide for reservation of seats for Scheduled Castes (SC) and Scheduled Tribes (ST) in the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies respectively. This is the constitutional mechanism ensuring political representation. Articles 15 and 16 deal with social equality and equal opportunity in public employment. Articles 341 and 342 define the lists of SCs and STs. Articles 338 and 339 establish the National Commission for SCs and the National Commission for STs. Thus, for parliamentary representation, Articles 330 and 332 are correct.
qs.kf:
☛ Article providing SC/ST reservation in Lok Sabha → Article 330
☛ Article providing SC/ST reservation in State Assemblies → Article 332
☛ Articles defining SC and ST lists → Articles 341 and 342
☛ Article for National Commission for SCs → Article 338
☛ Article for National Commission for STs → Article 339

q: Which Fundamental Right was removed from the Indian Constitution by the 44th Amendment Act, 1978?
qs.e: The 44th Amendment Act, 1978 removed the Right to Property from the list of Fundamental Rights in the Indian Constitution. It was downgraded to a legal right under Article 300A. This amendment was enacted by the Morarji Desai government to balance individual property rights with the needs of land reforms and social welfare. Now, no person can be deprived of their property except by authority of law. The removal aimed to reduce litigation and support equitable distribution of resources.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Article was removed by the 44th Amendment? → Article 31
☛ Under which Article is the Right to Property now? → Article 300A
☛ When was the 44th Amendment enacted? → 1978
☛ Right to Property is now a ___ right. → Legal right
☛ Who was PM during the 44th Amendment? → Morarji Desai

q: Which part of the Indian Constitution deals with special provisions for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, and other backwards classes?
qs.e: Part XVI of the Indian Constitution, comprising Articles 330 to 342, deals with special provisions for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, and Other Backward Classes. It includes reservation of seats in the Lok Sabha and state legislative assemblies for these groups, special representation for the Anglo-Indian community, and provisions for the President to prepare reports regarding Scheduled Castes and Tribes. This part was enacted to ensure social justice and equality.
qs.kf:
☛ How many articles are in Part XVI? → 13 (Articles 330-342)
☛ Which article provides reservation for Scheduled Castes? → Article 330
☛ Which article deals with Other Backward Classes? → Article 340
☛ Which article provides special representation for Anglo-Indians? → Article 331
☛ Under which article is the President's report on SCs and STs prepared? → Article 338

q: Which of the following subjects is addressed by the Tenth Schedule of the Indian Constitution?
qs.e: The Tenth Schedule of the Indian Constitution deals with anti-defection provisions. It was added by the 52nd Amendment Act of 1985. The main objective is to prevent elected members from switching parties arbitrarily, thereby ensuring political stability. According to the Schedule, a member can be disqualified if they voluntarily give up party membership or vote against party directions. The Presiding Officer of the House (Speaker/Chairman) has the final authority to decide disqualification cases. In the landmark Kihoto Hollohan case (1992), the Supreme Court ruled that the Speaker's decision under the Tenth Schedule is subject to judicial review. The Schedule aims to curb the practice of defection, which was destabilizing governments.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Tenth Schedule added? → 1985 (52nd Amendment)
☛ What is the purpose of anti-defection law? → Maintain political stability
☛ Who decides on defection cases? → Presiding Officer of the House
☛ Which case related to Tenth Schedule? → Kihoto Hollohan case (1992)
☛ What constitutes defection? → Voluntary resignation or voting against party

q: Which of the following States enjoys special provisions under Article 371A due to its unique customary law and land ownership practices?
qs.e: Article 371A provides special provisions to the state of Nagaland. This article was added in 1963 when Nagaland was granted statehood. Its main purpose is to protect the customary law, land ownership, and socio-religious practices of the Naga people. Under this provision, laws passed by Parliament will apply to Nagaland only if the state's legislature adopts them. This ensures the preservation of Nagaland's unique cultural identity and traditional governance system. Similar special provisions exist for other northeastern states like Mizoram (Article 371G) and Assam (Article 371B), but Nagaland enjoys the most autonomy under Article 371A.
qs.kf:
☛ Which state is related to Article 371A? → Nagaland
☛ When was Article 371A added? → 1963 (13th Amendment)
☛ What does Article 371A protect? → Customary law and land ownership
☛ What is the purpose of special provisions for Nagaland? → Preservation of Naga culture and traditions
☛ Which state is related to Article 371G? → Mizoram

q: Article 6 deals with persons who migrated to India from _____.
qs.e: Article 6 of the Indian Constitution deals with persons who migrated to India from Pakistan after the partition. It grants citizenship to those who came from Pakistan before 26 January 1950 and have taken up permanent residence in India. This article was enacted to address the humanitarian crisis caused by the partition and to provide a legal framework for the citizenship of migrants. Article 6 is part of the citizenship provisions under Articles 5 to 11. It is distinct from Article 7, which deals with persons who migrated to Pakistan. The core intent of Article 6 is to ensure that those who migrated from Pakistan due to partition are considered Indian citizens if they fulfilled certain conditions.
qs.kf:
☛ What does Article 6 deal with? → Persons who migrated to India from Pakistan
☛ Which date is important for citizenship under Article 6? → 26 January 1950
☛ What does Article 7 deal with? → Persons who migrated to Pakistan
☛ What does Article 8 deal with? → Persons of Indian origin residing outside India
☛ Which articles of the Indian Constitution contain citizenship provisions? → Articles 5 to 11

q: Which of the following is a mode of losing Indian citizenship?
qs.e: According to the Citizenship Act, 1955, there are three modes of losing Indian citizenship: Renunciation, Termination, and Deprivation. Renunciation means a person voluntarily gives up their Indian citizenship. Birth, Registration, and Naturalization are modes of acquiring citizenship, not losing it. After renunciation, the person ceases to be an Indian citizen and loses certain rights.
qs.kf:
☛ Under which act does renunciation fall? → Indian Citizenship Act, 1955
☛ When does termination occur? → When a person voluntarily acquires citizenship of another country
☛ Who can order deprivation? → Government of India (on grounds of fraud, etc.)
☛ Modes of acquiring citizenship → Birth, Descent, Registration, Naturalization, Territorial Incorporation
☛ Which schedule of the Constitution originally dealt with citizenship? → Second Schedule (Part II now replaced by the Act)

q: Under which Article of the Indian Constitution is citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution defined?
qs.e: Article 5 of the Indian Constitution defines citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution. It grants citizenship to persons born in India, or either of whose parents was born in India, or who have been ordinarily resident in India for at least five years immediately before the commencement of the Constitution. Article 6 deals with citizenship of migrants from Pakistan, Article 10 ensures the continuance of citizenship rights, and Article 11 empowers Parliament to regulate citizenship by law. This article lays the foundation for citizenship provisions and is crucial for understanding the initial citizenship framework of India.
qs.kf:
☛ Article for citizenship at commencement → Article 5
☛ Article for migrants' citizenship → Article 6
☛ Article for continuance of citizenship → Article 10
☛ Article for Parliament's power on citizenship → Article 11
☛ Citizenship Act enacted under → Article 11

q: Which Constitutional Amendment added the words 'Socialist', 'Secular' and 'Integrity' to the Preamble of the Indian Constitution?
qs.e: The words 'Socialist', 'Secular', and 'Integrity' were added to the Preamble of the Indian Constitution by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act (1976). Enacted during the Indira Gandhi government, this amendment is often called the 'Mini Constitution' due to its extensive changes. 'Socialist' and 'Secular' were inserted between 'Sovereign' and 'Democratic Republic', while 'Integrity' was added after 'Unity of the Nation'. Besides the Preamble, the 42nd Amendment also added Fundamental Duties (Part IV-A) and altered the balance of power between the judiciary and the executive. It is one of the most significant amendments in Indian constitutional history, aimed at clarifying the ideological stance and strengthening the central government.
qs.kf:
☛ Words added to Preamble by 42nd Amendment → Socialist, Secular, Integrity
☛ 42nd Amendment is known as → Mini Constitution
☛ Year of 42nd Amendment → 1976
☛ Part added by 42nd Amendment → Part IV-A (Fundamental Duties)
☛ Prime Minister during 42nd Amendment → Indira Gandhi

q: Which Article was inserted into the Constitution by the 103rd Amendment Act to provide for EWS reservation?
qs.e: The 103rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 2019 provided 10% reservation for Economically Weaker Sections (EWS) in educational institutions and government jobs. This amendment inserted Article 15(6) and Article 16(6) into the Constitution. Article 15(6) allows the state to make special provisions for EWS in educational admissions, while Article 16(6) provides for reservation in public employment. This reservation is in addition to existing SC/ST/OBC quotas and was initially valid for 10 years. The amendment marked a shift by basing reservation on economic criteria, unlike previous reservations based on social and educational backwardness. The EWS reservation has been upheld by the Supreme Court (2022) subject to certain conditions.
qs.kf:
☛ EWS reservation percentage → 10%
☛ Duration of EWS reservation → 10 years
☛ Articles inserted by 103rd Amendment → 15(6) and 16(6)
☛ Income limit for EWS (Central govt) → Rs 8 lakh per annum
☛ First state to introduce EWS reservation → Gujarat (2016)

q: If an RTI applicant is aggrieved by the Public Information Officer’s decision (or lack of response), within how many days must the first appeal be filed under Section 19 of the RTI Act?
qs.e: Under Section 19(1) of the RTI Act, 2005, if an applicant is aggrieved by the decision (or lack of response) of the Public Information Officer (PIO), they can file a first appeal. This appeal must be filed within 30 days from the date on which the decision is received or should have been received by the applicant. If the appellant provides a satisfactory reason for the delay, the appellate authority may admit the appeal even after 30 days, but the total period cannot exceed 45 days. The first appeal is made to an appellate authority, who is a senior officer to the PIO. The appeal can be filed in physical or electronic form. This provision ensures that applicants have a timely remedy against unsatisfactory responses from PIOs.
qs.kf:
☛ Under which section of RTI Act is the first appeal provision? → Section 19(1)
☛ What is the normal time limit for filing first appeal? → 30 days
☛ Can first appeal be filed after 30 days? → Yes, with valid reason up to 45 days
☛ Before whom is the first appeal filed? → Appellate authority (senior officer to PIO)
☛ What is the time limit for second appeal under RTI Act? → 90 days from the decision of first appeal

q: Which of the following Articles deals with the rights of citizenship at the commencement of the Indian Constitution?
qs.e: Article 5 of the Indian Constitution defines the rights of citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution (January 26, 1950). It states that every person who has his domicile in India and who was born in India, or either of whose parents was born in India, or who has been ordinarily resident in India for not less than five years immediately before such commencement, is a citizen of India. Article 6 covers citizenship of migrants from Pakistan, Article 7 deals with citizenship of migrants to Pakistan, Article 8 covers persons of Indian origin residing outside India, Article 9 provides that a person who voluntarily acquires citizenship of a foreign state shall cease to be a citizen, Article 10 ensures continuity of citizenship rights, and Article 11 empowers Parliament to make laws regarding citizenship.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 5 → Citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution
☛ Article 6 → Citizenship of migrants from Pakistan
☛ Article 7 → Citizenship of migrants to Pakistan
☛ Article 8 → Citizenship of persons of Indian origin residing outside India
☛ Article 11 → Power of Parliament to make citizenship laws

q: Which of the following Ministries is responsible for granting Indian citizenship by naturalisation?
qs.e: According to the Citizenship Act, 1955, the authority to grant Indian citizenship by naturalisation lies with the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA). This ministry handles all matters related to citizenship including registration, naturalisation, and issuance of citizenship certificates. Although the Ministry of External Affairs deals with Overseas Citizens of India (OCI) and Non-Resident Indians (NRI) matters, the power of naturalisation rests solely with the Ministry of Home Affairs. Additionally, the Citizenship Amendment Act, 2019 was also implemented under MHA. Hence, the responsibility of granting Indian citizenship by naturalisation falls under the Ministry of Home Affairs.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Act governs citizenship in India? → Indian Citizenship Act, 1955
☛ What is the residency requirement for citizenship by naturalisation? → 11 years (5 years for persons of Indian origin)
☛ Which Part of the Indian Constitution deals with citizenship? → Part II (Articles 5-11)
☛ What is the official name of the Home Ministry? → Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA)
☛ Which ministry issues OCI cards? → Ministry of Home Affairs

q: Which of the following statements is correct regarding the Tenth Schedule of the Indian Constitution?
o: It deals with the allocation of seats in the Rajya Sabha.
It defines the distribution of powers between the Union and States.
It contains provisions regarding Official Languages.
It provides for disqualification of members on grounds of defection.
qs.e: The Tenth Schedule of the Indian Constitution is also known as the Anti-Defection Law. It was added in 1985 by the 52nd Constitutional Amendment. Its purpose is to prevent Members of Parliament and Legislative Assemblies from switching political parties, thereby ensuring government stability. The schedule provides for the disqualification of a member if they voluntarily leave their party or vote against party instructions. However, there are exceptions such as party mergers or decisions by the Speaker/Chairperson. The final authority to decide on disqualification lies with the Speaker or Chairperson, and their decision can be challenged in court through judicial review.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Tenth Schedule added? → 1985
☛ Which amendment added the Tenth Schedule? → 52nd Constitutional Amendment
☛ Who decides on disqualification under the Tenth Schedule? → Speaker or Chairperson
☛ What is the main objective of the Tenth Schedule? → To prevent defection and ensure government stability
☛ Can the Speaker's decision be challenged in court? → Yes, judicial review is possible

q: Which of the following is NOT a mode of acquiring Indian citizenship under the Citizenship Act, 1955?
qs.e: The Citizenship Act, 1955 provides five modes of acquiring Indian citizenship: By birth, By descent, By registration, By naturalization, and By incorporation of territory. By adoption is NOT recognized as a mode of acquiring citizenship under this Act. Although adoption can grant certain rights, it does not automatically confer citizenship. For example, a foreign child adopted by Indian citizens must go through registration or naturalization to acquire citizenship. Thus, option 2 is the correct answer.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Citizenship Act, 1955 amended? → 1986, 1992, 2003, 2005, and 2019
☛ What is the condition for citizenship by birth? → Born in India on or after 26 January 1950
☛ Who gets citizenship by descent? → A person born outside India if either parent is an Indian citizen
☛ Who can get citizenship by registration? → Persons of Indian origin residing in India for at least 7 years
☛ Under which Article is the Citizenship Act, 1955 enacted? → Article 11

q: Which Constitutional Amendment Act added the Ninth Schedule to the Constitution of India?
qs.e: The Ninth Schedule to the Indian Constitution was added by the First Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951. This schedule was created to protect land reform and certain other laws from judicial review. Under Article 31B, laws placed in the Ninth Schedule cannot be challenged in court even if they violate fundamental rights. This amendment also added Article 31A, which provides protection to land reform laws. However, in the landmark case of Kesavananda Bharati (1973), the Supreme Court established that laws in the Ninth Schedule can still be subject to judicial review if they violate the basic structure of the Constitution. Later, in the I.R. Coelho case (2007), the court clarified that any law added to the Ninth Schedule after 1973 must not violate fundamental rights.
qs.kf:
☛ Which amendment added the Ninth Schedule? → First Amendment Act, 1951
☛ What is the purpose of the Ninth Schedule? → Protect land reform laws from judicial review
☛ Article 31B relates to? → Validity of laws in the Ninth Schedule
☛ What did Kesavananda Bharati case rule? → Ninth Schedule laws are subject to judicial review
☛ When was the First Amendment enacted? → 1951

q: Which of the following Articles of the Indian Constitution empowers Parliament to make laws relating to the acquisition and termination of the Indian Citizenship?
qs.e: Article 11 of the Indian Constitution empowers Parliament to make laws regarding the acquisition and termination of citizenship. Part II of the Constitution (Articles 5 to 11) deals with citizenship. Articles 5 to 10 determine citizenship at the time of commencement of the Constitution, while Article 11 gives Parliament the power to regulate citizenship by law. Under this power, Parliament enacted the Citizenship Act, 1955, which lays down rules for acquisition (by birth, descent, registration, naturalization, incorporation of territory) and termination (renunciation, termination, deprivation) of citizenship. Article 12 defines the State, and Article 10 relates to the continuance of citizenship under a foreign citizenship ordinance. Hence, the correct answer is Article 11.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Articles deal with Citizenship? → Articles 5 to 11
☛ When was the Citizenship Act enacted? → 1955
☛ What does Article 10 relate to? → Foreign citizenship ordinance
☛ What does Article 12 define? → State
☛ What is the main source of citizenship in India? → Citizenship Act, 1955

q: The 91st Amendment of the Indian Constitution was enacted in which year?
qs.e: The 91st Amendment of the Indian Constitution was enacted in the year 2003. The main objective of this amendment was to limit the size of the Council of Ministers and strengthen provisions against defection. Under this, the total number of ministers in the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies cannot exceed 15% of the total membership of the House. Additionally, if a member of a party defects, they can be disqualified from membership of the House. This amendment was brought to make the Tenth Schedule (Anti-Defection Law) more effective.
qs.kf:
☛ 91st Amendment enacted year → 2003
☛ Maximum size of Council of Ministers → 15% of total membership of the House
☛ Objective of the amendment → Limit size of Council of Ministers and prevent defection
☛ Articles amended by this amendment → Article 75 and 164
☛ Tenth Schedule → Related to Anti-Defection Law

q: The First Backward Classes Commission was appointed in which year?
qs.e: The First Backward Classes Commission was appointed by the Government of India in 1953 under Article 340 of the Constitution. Its purpose was to identify socially and educationally backward classes and recommend measures for their welfare. The commission was chaired by Kaka Kalelkar. It submitted its report in 1955, listing approximately 2,399 castes as backward. However, the government did not accept the report. This commission is considered the foundation of backward class policy in India.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the chairman of the First Backward Classes Commission? → Kaka Kalelkar
☛ Under which Article was the First Backward Classes Commission constituted? → Article 340
☛ When did the First Backward Classes Commission submit its report? → 1955
☛ When was the Second Backward Classes Commission constituted? → 1979
☛ When was the Mandal Commission constituted? → 1979

q: The 105th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2021, is related to which of the following?
o: Creation of a National Judicial Commission
Powers of state governments to identify OBCs
qs.e: The 105th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2021, empowers state governments to identify and list Other Backward Classes (OBCs). This amendment was enacted after a Supreme Court ruling that held that states do not have the power to create OBC lists. The act amended Articles 342A, 366, and 367 of the Constitution. Previously, the list of OBCs was prepared based on the advice of the National Commission for Backward Classes. Now, states can create their own lists. This amendment strengthens federalism by granting states the authority to identify OBCs according to local conditions. It ensures that states have the autonomy to include or exclude communities based on regional social and educational backwardness.
qs.kf:
☛ When did the 105th Constitutional Amendment Act come into effect? → 2021
☛ Which articles were amended by this act? → 342A, 366, and 367
☛ Whose advice was previously taken for OBC identification? → National Commission for Backward Classes (NCBC)
☛ What is the purpose of this amendment? → To give states the power to prepare OBC lists
☛ Which court's decision led to this amendment? → Supreme Court

q: Under Article 5 of the Indian Constitution, which of the following is NOT required for a person to be considered a citizen at the commencement of the Constitution?
o: Having at least one parent born in India
Having domicile in the territory of India
qs.e: Article 5 of the Indian Constitution specifies citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution (January 26, 1950). It requires either birth in India, at least one parent born in India, or ordinary residence in India for at least 5 years immediately before the commencement. Holding an Indian passport is not a requirement under Article 5; passports are issued after citizenship is acquired and do not determine citizenship. Article 5 only covers those who were citizens at the start of the Constitution, not later acquisition or registration. The other three options—birth in India, parentage, or domicile—are directly mentioned in Article 5.
qs.kf:
☛ Articles 5 to 11 → Citizenship provisions at the commencement
☛ Conditions in Article 5 → Three conditions: birth, parentage, or domicile
☛ Article 6 → Citizenship of persons migrating from Pakistan
☛ Article 7 → Citizenship of migrants to Pakistan returning
☛ Article 8 → Citizenship of persons of Indian origin residing outside India

q: Which Constitutional Amendment removed the Right to Property from the list of Fundamental Rights in India?
qs.e: The 44th Amendment Act (1978) removed the Right to Property (Article 31) from the list of Fundamental Rights and made it a legal right under Article 300A. It was passed by the Morarji Desai government. Earlier, the 39th Amendment (1975) and 42nd Amendment (1976) had restricted property rights. The 44th Amendment eliminated it as a fundamental right to allow the state to acquire property by law, provided compensation is paid. This amendment came into effect on June 20, 1979. It also introduced Article 300A to ensure no person shall be deprived of property save by authority of law.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Article was removed from Fundamental Rights? → Article 31
☛ Under which Article is the Right to Property now a legal right? → Article 300A
☛ When did the 44th Amendment come into force? → June 20, 1979
☛ Under which Prime Minister was the 44th Amendment passed? → Morarji Desai
☛ Which Amendment removed property right from the basic structure? → 44th Amendment, 1978

q: Which of the following Articles of the Indian Constitution provides for the power of the President to specify the Scheduled Tribes under the Constitution?
qs.e: Article 342 of the Indian Constitution empowers the President to specify the Scheduled Tribes. Under this article, the President, after consultation with the Governor, may specify tribes or tribal communities as Scheduled Tribes in relation to a state or union territory. Article 341 provides a similar provision for Scheduled Castes. Article 343 deals with the official language, while Article 336 makes special provisions for the Anglo-Indian community, and Article 340 deals with the appointment of a commission to investigate the conditions of backward classes.
qs.kf:
☛ Provision for specifying Scheduled Castes → Article 341
☛ Provision for separate administration of Scheduled Tribes → Article 244
☛ The President can amend the list of Scheduled Tribes → by a law of Parliament
☛ The definition of Scheduled Tribes does not include → tribal communities
☛ The term 'tribe' in Article 342 → is not explicitly defined in the Constitution

q: As of June 2025, how many languages are listed in the Eighth Schedule of the Indian Constitution?
qs.e: The Eighth Schedule of the Indian Constitution currently lists 22 languages. These languages are recognized as official languages and are used for government work, education, and cultural development. Originally, the Constitution included 14 languages, but through amendments, 8 more languages were added later. These languages represent the cultural diversity of different states and regions. Inclusion in the Eighth Schedule grants constitutional recognition and allows the language to be used in government exams and official functions. It is important to note that this number has remained unchanged as of June 2025. The addition of languages was made through the 21st and 71st Constitutional Amendments, among others. Some languages like Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, and Santhali were added in 2003.
qs.kf:
☛ How many languages in the Eighth Schedule? → 22
☛ How many languages originally? → 14
☛ Which was the last language added? → Santhali
☛ Which amendment added languages? → 21st and 71st
☛ Which language is NOT in the Eighth Schedule? → English

q: A person who migrated from Pakistan after 19 July 1948 could become an Indian citizen, only if:
o: he was registered by an officer of the Dominion of India
he was a resident of Pakistan in 1948
he took an oath of allegiance
he was born in India before 1947
qs.e: According to Article 5 of the Indian Constitution, on 26 January 1950, a person was a citizen of India if they were born in India, or either of their parents was born in India, or they had been ordinarily resident in India for 5 years. Article 6 makes special provisions for migrants from Pakistan. Those who migrated before 19 July 1948 automatically became citizens. Those migrating after that date had to register as citizens, provided they were born in India or their parents or grandparents were born in India. Thus, the correct answer is 'he was born in India before 1947'.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 6 → Citizenship for migrants from Pakistan
☛ 19 July 1948 → Key date for migration from Pakistan
☛ Article 5 → Citizenship on 26 January 1950
☛ Registration → Requirement for post-1948 migrants
☛ Birth-based citizenship → Birth in India or parent's birth in India required

q: Which Amendment of the Indian Constitution added Article 39A (free legal aid)?
qs.e: The 42nd Amendment of the Indian Constitution (1976), also known as the 'Mini-Constitution', added Article 39A which directs the State to provide free legal aid to economically weaker citizens. This amendment was included in Part IV (Directive Principles of State Policy) of the Constitution. Additionally, the 42nd Amendment added the words socialist, secular, and integrity to the Preamble, and also introduced the Fundamental Duties (Article 51A). It was enacted during the Emergency period under the prime ministership of Indira Gandhi. This amendment made significant changes to the Constitution, affecting its basic structure.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 39A deals with? → Free legal aid
☛ When was the 42nd Amendment enacted? → 1976
☛ The 42nd Amendment is known as? → Mini-Constitution
☛ Which amendment added 'socialist' to the Preamble? → 42nd Amendment
☛ Fundamental Duties were added by which amendment? → 42nd Amendment

q: Which of the following changes would need the approval of at least half of all State Legislatures?
o: Amending the Emergency provisions in Part XVIII
Changing the Guarantee of Fundamental Rights
Altering the Union List of subjects
qs.e: According to Article 368 of the Indian Constitution, certain amendments require approval by at least half of the state legislatures in addition to a two-thirds majority in Parliament. The Emergency provisions (Part XVIII) are among those parts that need state ratification. Other options like rewriting the Preamble or changing Fundamental Rights require only a special majority in Parliament, as they do not affect the federal structure. Altering the Union List also does not require state consent. This procedure ensures protection of the federal character and involves states in significant constitutional changes.
qs.kf:
☛ Constitutional amendments requiring state ratification → Parts III, V, VI, VIII, XII, XVII, XVIII, XX, XXI (partly)
☛ Majority required for state ratification → Simple majority of at least half of state legislatures
☛ Amendment procedure under Article 368 → Special majority in both Houses and sometimes state ratification
☛ Emergency provisions (Part XVIII) include Articles → 352 to 360
☛ Amendment of Preamble requires → Only special majority in Parliament, no state ratification

q: Which amendment granted constitutional status to Panchayati Raj institutions?
qs.e: The 73rd Amendment Act, 1992 granted constitutional status to Panchayati Raj institutions in India. It added Part IX and Articles 243 to 243-O to the Constitution, relating to Panchayats. The amendment came into force on 24 April 1993. It ensured the formation, functions, powers, and financial authority of Panchayats. The Gram Sabha was given constitutional recognition, and provisions were made for reservation for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, and women. The 74th Amendment deals with urban local bodies, while the 86th Amendment relates to the Right to Education.
qs.kf:
☛ Amendment that gave constitutional status to Panchayati Raj → 73rd Amendment Act, 1992
☛ Part added by the 73rd Amendment → Part IX
☛ Date of enforcement of the 73rd Amendment → 24 April 1993
☛ Amendment that provided for Gram Sabha in Panchayati Raj → 73rd Amendment
☛ Amendment giving constitutional status to urban local bodies → 74th Amendment Act, 1992

q: Which of the following commissions was appointed to look into the question of states based on language?
qs.e: The question of reorganisation of states on linguistic basis was first referred to the Dhar Commission (Linguistic Provinces Commission) in 1948. This commission was appointed by the Government of India under the chairmanship of Justice S. K. Dhar. The commission rejected the idea of language as the sole basis for state reorganisation. Subsequently, the Fazal Ali Commission was formed in 1953, leading to the States Reorganisation Act of 1956. Gadgil Commission is related to river water disputes, Sarkaria Commission to centre-state relations, and Swaran Singh Committee to fundamental duties.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the chairman of Dhar Commission? → Justice S. K. Dhar
☛ When was the States Reorganisation Commission formed? → 1953 (Fazal Ali Commission)
☛ When was the States Reorganisation Act passed? → 1956
☛ Gadgil Commission is related to? → River water disputes
☛ Sarkaria Commission is related to? → Centre-state relations

q: Which Constitutional Amendment granted constitutional status to Co-operative Societies in India?
qs.e: The 97th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2011 granted constitutional status to co-operative societies in India. It added Part IXB (Articles 243ZH to 243ZT) dealing with the formation, functioning, and management of co-operative societies. It also inserted Article 43B in the Directive Principles of State Policy, directing the state to promote voluntary formation, autonomous functioning, and democratic control of co-operative societies. This amendment aimed to strengthen the co-operative sector and promote rural development.
qs.kf:
☛ Amendment granting constitutional status to co-operative societies → 97th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2011
☛ Part added by 97th Amendment → Part IXB (Articles 243ZH-243ZT)
☛ Article added by 97th Amendment → Article 43B (Directive Principles)
☛ 73rd Amendment relates to → Panchayati Raj institutions
☛ 74th Amendment relates to → Urban local bodies

q: Which Amendment is considered a near rewrite of the Constitution and made changes to the Preamble, Schedule VII and 53 Articles?
qs.e: The 42nd Amendment (1976) is the most comprehensive amendment to the Indian Constitution, often called the 'Mini-Constitution'. It added the words 'Socialist', 'Secular', and 'Integrity' to the Preamble. It made changes to Schedule VII (Union, State, and Concurrent Lists). A total of 53 Articles were amended, including the addition of Fundamental Duties (Article 51A), extension of President's rule duration, and curtailment of judicial review. This amendment gave the executive greater control over the judiciary. Later, the 44th Amendment (1978) reversed many of its provisions.
qs.kf:
☛ In which year was the 42nd Amendment passed? → 1976
☛ Which three words were added to the Preamble? → Socialist, Secular, Integrity
☛ Under which Article were Fundamental Duties added? → Article 51A
☛ Under which Prime Minister was the 42nd Amendment passed? → Indira Gandhi
☛ What is the 42nd Amendment also known as? → Mini-Constitution

q: Which of the following duties was added by the Constitution (Eighty-sixth Amendment) Act, 2002?
o: To uphold and protect national unity
To provide education to children aged six to fourteen years
qs.e: The Constitution (Eighty-sixth Amendment) Act, 2002 added a new duty among the Fundamental Duties. Article 51A was amended to insert clause (k), which states that it is the duty of parents or guardians to provide opportunities for education to their children aged 6 to 14 years. This amendment was a step towards making Right to Education a fundamental right, which was later implemented as the Right to Education Act (RTE) in 2009. Other options such as developing a scientific temper (clause h), upholding national unity (clause c), and protecting the environment (clause g) were already existing duties in the Constitution.
qs.kf:
☛ Which fundamental duty was added by the 86th Amendment? → To provide education to children aged 6-14 years (Article 51A(k))
☛ Which article was amended by the 86th Amendment? → Article 51A, adding clause (k)
☛ Right to Education is a fundamental right under which article? → Article 21A
☛ In which year was the 86th Amendment enacted? → 2002
☛ When was the RTE Act implemented? → 2009

q: Which Article of the Indian Constitution describes the provisions related to financial emergency?
A. Article 148
B. Article 143
C. Article 360
D. Article 72
qs.e: Article 360 of the Indian Constitution deals with the provisions related to financial emergency. It empowers the President to proclaim a financial emergency if the financial stability or credit of India or any part thereof is threatened. During such an emergency, the Union government can give directions to states regarding financial matters, including reduction of salaries and allowances of state employees. This provision is part of Part XVIII of the Constitution. Notably, a financial emergency has never been declared in India. Other options: Article 148 (Comptroller and Auditor General), Article 143 (Consultation with Supreme Court), Article 72 (President's pardoning power).
qs.kf:
☛ Article related to financial emergency → Article 360
☛ Article related to national emergency → Article 352
☛ Article related to state emergency (President's rule) → Article 356
☛ Maximum duration of financial emergency → Indefinite, subject to parliamentary approval
☛ Provision for reduction of state salaries during financial emergency → Article 360(4)

q: By which of the following Amendments of the Constitution, Fundamental Duties of the citizens were added to the Constitution of India?
qs.e: The Fundamental Duties of citizens were added to the Indian Constitution by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976. This amendment inserted Article 51-A under Part IV-A of the Constitution, listing 11 fundamental duties. It was based on the recommendations of the Swaram Singh Committee. Fundamental duties serve as a reminder to citizens that they have certain responsibilities towards the nation along with their rights. These duties are non-justiciable, meaning they are not enforceable by courts.
qs.kf:
☛ Which amendment added Fundamental Duties? → 42nd Amendment, 1976
☛ Fundamental Duties are covered under which Article? → Article 51-A
☛ Fundamental Duties are in which Part of the Constitution? → Part IV-A
☛ Which committee recommended Fundamental Duties? → Swaram Singh Committee
☛ How many Fundamental Duties are there? → 11

q: The English Language continued to be used for official purposes of the Union via section 3 of the Official Language Act which came into force in the year :
qs.e: The Official Language Act, 1963 received the President's assent on May 10, 1963, but came into force on January 26, 1965. Section 3 of this Act provided that the English language would continue to be used for official purposes of the Union even after January 26, 1965. This was necessary because Article 343 of the Constitution had originally allowed English to be used for official purposes for 15 years (1950-1965) while Hindi was declared the official language. After 1965, there was strong opposition from non-Hindi speaking states to the complete switchover to Hindi, leading to the continuation of English as a co-official language. The Act aimed to balance linguistic diversity and administrative convenience. Its Section 3 specifically ensured that no language imposition occurred and both Hindi and English would be used for official work until a consensus was reached.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Official Language Act passed? → 1963
☛ When did the Official Language Act come into force? → January 26, 1965
☛ Section 3 deals with? → Continued use of English
☛ Which Article deals with official language? → Article 343
☛ How was English retained after 1965? → As a co-official language

q: Currently, how many languages are listed in the eighth schedule of the Constitution?
qs.e: The Eighth Schedule of the Indian Constitution currently lists 22 languages. These languages are covered under Articles 344(1) and 351 of the Constitution. Initially, only 14 languages were included, which were later increased through amendments. The 21st Amendment in 1967 added Sindhi. The 71st Amendment in 1992 added Konkani, Manipuri, and Nepali. The 92nd Amendment in 2003 added Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, and Santali, bringing the total to 22. These languages represent India's diversity and the government promotes their development.
qs.kf:
☛ Total languages in Eighth Schedule → 22
☛ Most recently added languages → Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, Santali (2003)
☛ First language added after original (1967) → Sindhi
☛ Languages added by 71st Amendment (1992) → Konkani, Manipuri, Nepali
☛ Articles referencing Eighth Schedule → Articles 344 and 351

q: Which of the following is NOT correct with respect to amendments in the Constitution of India ?
o: 72nd amendment - to make provisions for setting up Rent Control Tribunals
101st amendment - to introduce goods and service tax
61st amendment - to reduce the voting age from 21 to 18 years
102nd amendment - to give constitutional status to the National Commission for Backward Classes
qs.e: The 72nd Amendment is incorrect because it was the 75th Amendment (1994) that provided for setting up Rent Control Tribunals. The 101st Amendment (2016) introduced the Goods and Services Tax (GST). The 61st Amendment (1988) reduced the voting age from 21 to 18 years for Lok Sabha and state legislative assemblies. The 102nd Amendment (2018) granted constitutional status to the National Commission for Backward Classes (NCBC). Thus, the 72nd Amendment does not relate to Rent Control Tribunals.
qs.kf:
☛ Which amendment set up Rent Control Tribunals? → 75th Amendment (1994)
☛ Which amendment introduced GST? → 101st Amendment (2016)
☛ Which amendment reduced voting age from 21 to 18? → 61st Amendment (1988)
☛ Which amendment gave constitutional status to NCBC? → 102nd Amendment (2018)
☛ What is the 72nd Amendment related to? → Extension of reservation for SC/ST in legislatures

q: Article 21A was added to the Constitution of India by which constitutional amendment act?
qs.e: Article 21A was added to the Indian Constitution by the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002. This article provides the right to free and compulsory education for all children between the ages of 6 and 14 years. It transformed education from a Directive Principle into a Fundamental Right under Part III of the Constitution. Along with this, Article 45 was amended to reflect the state's responsibility for early childhood care. The 86th Amendment was a landmark step to ensure every child's right to education, later enforced by the RTE Act, 2009. This amendment marked a significant shift in India's educational policy.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Article of the Indian Constitution provides the right to free and compulsory education? → Article 21A
☛ In which year was the 86th Constitutional Amendment passed? → 2002
☛ Which age group does Article 21A cover? → 6-14 years
☛ Which Act enforced the right to education in 2009? → RTE Act, 2009
☛ Who was the Prime Minister of India during the 86th Amendment? → Atal Bihari Vajpayee

q: Who designed the National Flag of India?
qs.e: The National Flag of India, the Tricolour, was designed by Pingali Venkaya in 1916 at Machilipatnam, Andhra Pradesh. It was first presented at the Congress session in Bezwada (now Vijayawada) in 1921. The original flag had saffron, white, and green stripes with a charkha (spinning wheel). The tricolour was officially adopted in the Karachi session of 1931. Subsequently, on 15 August 1947, it was adopted as the national flag upon independence. Pingali Venkaya's design has been a symbol of India's freedom struggle and national pride.
qs.kf:
