☛ Who designed the National Flag of India? → Pingali Venkaya
☛ When and where was the flag first presented? → 1921 in Bezwada
☛ What is the length-to-width ratio of the flag? → 3:2
☛ What does the saffron colour represent? → Courage and sacrifice
☛ When was the flag officially adopted? → 22 July 1947 by the Constituent Assembly

q: Which article of the Indian Constitution declares Hindi as the language of the Union?
qs.e: Article 343 of the Indian Constitution deals with the official language of the Union. Article 343(1) declares that Hindi in Devanagari script shall be the official language of the Union. This article is part of Part 17 (Official Language). Article 343(2) provides for the continued use of English for 15 years, while Article 29 pertains to the linguistic rights of minorities.
qs.kf:
☛ Which part of the Constitution deals with official language? → Part 17
☛ Which article declares Hindi as the official language? → Article 343(1)
☛ What does Article 343(2) provide for? → Temporary use of English
☛ What does Article 29(1) grant? → Protection of language and script for minorities
☛ Which article provides for the formation of Official Language Commission? → Article 344

q: Which article of the Indian Constitution had been impacted by the 44th Amendment (1978)?
qs.e: The 44th Amendment (1978) of the Indian Constitution primarily impacted Article 300A. This amendment removed Article 19(1)(f) (right to property) and transformed the right to property from a fundamental right to a constitutional right. The new Article 300A provides that no person shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law. This amendment was introduced by the Morarji Desai government and was significant in reversing the changes made during the Emergency (1975-77).
qs.kf:
☛ Which article is related to the 44th Amendment? → Article 300A
☛ In which year was the 44th Amendment enacted? → 1978
☛ Which right was transferred to Article 300A? → Right to property
☛ Which government introduced the 44th Amendment? → Morarji Desai government
☛ What type of right is property under Article 300A? → Constitutional right

q: Apart from the 22 scheduled languages in the Constitution of India, which other two languages have been recognised by the Sahitya Academy?
qs.e: The Eighth Schedule of the Indian Constitution includes 22 languages that receive official recognition. In addition to these, the Sahitya Akademi has recognised two more languages: Rajasthani and English. Rajasthani is a major regional language spoken in Rajasthan and surrounding areas, while English is a global language with a significant contribution to Indian literature. The Sahitya Akademi grants awards and recognition to literary works in these languages, promoting linguistic diversity and encouraging writers. This recognition helps preserve and promote the cultural heritage associated with these languages.
qs.kf:
☛ Which schedule of the Constitution lists the scheduled languages? → Eighth Schedule
☛ How many languages are in the Eighth Schedule? → 22
☛ Which two additional languages are recognised by the Sahitya Akademi? → Rajasthani and English
☛ Rajasthani is primarily spoken in which state? → Rajasthan
☛ For which languages does the Sahitya Akademi give awards? → Multiple languages including Rajasthani and English

q: Which of the following amendment granted financial powers to the panchayats and helped to strengthen the local government?
qs.e: The 73rd Constitutional Amendment, 1992 gave constitutional status to the Panchayati Raj institutions in India. It granted financial powers to panchayats, such as the authority to collect taxes, fees, and other revenues. The amendment directed state governments to constitute a State Finance Commission to transfer funds to panchayats. This strengthened local government and promoted rural development. The 73rd Amendment added provisions under Articles 243 to 243O and recognizes the Gram Sabha as the foundation of the panchayat system.
qs.kf:
☛ When did the 73rd Amendment come into force? → 24 April 1993
☛ Which articles are related to the 73rd Amendment? → Articles 243 to 243O
☛ What is the basic unit of Panchayati Raj? → Gram Sabha
☛ Which amendment established the State Finance Commission? → 73rd Amendment
☛ Who supervises panchayat elections under the 73rd Amendment? → State Election Commission

q: Article 51A containing Fundamental Duties was inserted by which constitutional amendment?
qs.e: Fundamental Duties were added to the Indian Constitution by the 42nd Amendment (1976). This amendment was introduced by the Indira Gandhi government during the Emergency (1975-77). It inserted Article 51A, listing 10 fundamental duties for citizens, including respecting the Constitution, national flag and anthem, defending the country, promoting communal harmony, and protecting public property. Later, the 86th Amendment (2002) added an 11th duty to provide educational opportunities for children aged 6-14. The 42nd Amendment is considered the most comprehensive amendment, also adding the words 'Socialist', 'Secular' and 'Integrity' to the Preamble.
qs.kf:
☛ Amendment adding Fundamental Duties → 42nd Amendment (1976)
☛ Total number of Fundamental Duties → Originally 10, now 11
☛ Amendment adding 11th duty → 86th Amendment (2002)
☛ Amendment adding 'Socialist, Secular' to Preamble → 42nd Amendment
☛ Prime Minister during 42nd Amendment → Indira Gandhi

q: In which of the following years did the Constitution of India, through the 86th amendment, introduce Article 21-A to provide free and compulsory education to all children in the age group of 6 to 14 years as a Fundamental Right?
qs.e: The 86th Amendment to the Constitution of India was enacted in the year 2002. It introduced Article 21-A, making free and compulsory education a Fundamental Right for all children in the 6 to 14 years age group. The amendment also modified Article 45 under the Directive Principles of State Policy and added Article 51A(k), which imposes a duty on parents or guardians to provide opportunities for education to their children. This amendment laid the constitutional foundation for the Right to Education Act (RTE), 2009, which came into effect on 1 April 2010.
qs.kf:
☛ 86th Amendment passed in which year? → 2002
☛ Article 21-A → Free and compulsory education for children aged 6-14
☛ RTE Act enforced on? → 1 April 2010
☛ Which article was modified by 86th Amendment? → Article 45
☛ Education as a Fundamental Right linked to which amendment? → 86th Amendment

q: Which ministry does the care of India's National Archives?
qs.e: The National Archives of India is under the care of the Ministry of Culture. It is the premier archival institution of the Government of India, responsible for preserving and managing public records. Established in 1891 as the Imperial Record Department in Kolkata, it was moved to New Delhi after the capital shift in 1911. It operates under the Public Records Act, 1993. Being under the Ministry of Culture, it formulates policies for the preservation of historical documents and government archives. The National Archives houses a vast collection of documents from the Mughal period to modern times, serving as a vital resource for researchers and historians.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the National Archives established? → 1891
☛ Where is the headquarters of the National Archives? → New Delhi
☛ Which act governs the National Archives? → Public Records Act, 1993
☛ What is the main function of the National Archives? → Preservation and management of public records
☛ Who is the head of the National Archives? → Director General

q: How many times has 'Financial Emergency' been declared in India so far?
qs.e: Article 360 of the Indian Constitution empowers the President to proclaim a Financial Emergency if the financial stability or credit of India is threatened. To date, India has never declared a Financial Emergency. In contrast, a National Emergency (Article 352) has been imposed three times: in 1962, 1971, and 1975. A State Emergency (President's Rule) under Article 356 has been invoked many times. The provisions of a Financial Emergency include central control over financial matters of states. This fact is important for competitive exams as it highlights a unique aspect of Indian federalism where the provision exists but has never been used.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Article deals with Financial Emergency? → Article 360
☛ How many times has Financial Emergency been declared in India? → Never
☛ Which Article deals with National Emergency? → Article 352
☛ How many times has National Emergency been declared? → Three times
☛ Which Article deals with State Emergency? → Article 356

q: When was the internal emergency declared in India during the period of Indira Gandhi as Prime Minister?
qs.e: The internal emergency was declared in India on June 25, 1975 during the tenure of Prime Minister Indira Gandhi. It was imposed under Article 352 of the Constitution on grounds of internal disturbance. The emergency lasted for 21 months, ending on March 21, 1977. During this period, civil liberties were suspended, press censorship was imposed, and opposition leaders were arrested. This emergency is considered a controversial chapter in Indian political history.
qs.kf:
☛ Which article of the Constitution deals with emergency? → Article 352
☛ When was the first emergency declared in India? → 1962 (China war)
☛ How long did the internal emergency last? → 21 months
☛ Which judge opposed the emergency? → Justice H. R. Khanna
☛ Which government came to power after the emergency? → Janata Party

q: Banwarilal Purohit is the present Governor of-
qs.e: Banwarilal Purohit is an Indian politician who currently serves as the Governor of Tamil Nadu. He assumed office on 18 September 2021. Prior to this, he was the Governor of Assam. Born in Madhya Pradesh, he has been associated with the Bharatiya Janata Party. As Governor of Tamil Nadu, he fulfills constitutional duties.
qs.kf:
☛ Banwarilal Purohit is the Governor of which state? → Tamil Nadu
☛ When did Banwarilal Purohit assume office? → 18 September 2021
☛ Which state was Banwarilal Purohit Governor of previously? → Assam
☛ Who is the current Governor of Tamil Nadu? → Banwarilal Purohit
☛ Which political party is Banwarilal Purohit associated with? → Bharatiya Janata Party

q: In which of the following years was the Overseas Citizenship of India Scheme introduced by amending Citizenship Act 1955?
qs.e: The Overseas Citizenship of India (OCI) Scheme was introduced in the year 2005 by amending the Citizenship Act of 1955. This scheme allows persons of Indian origin living abroad to live and work in India indefinitely, but they do not get voting rights or the right to hold constitutional offices. OCI cardholders are granted multiple-entry visas and certain economic rights. The amendment was aimed at strengthening ties with the Indian diaspora and involving them in the country's development. The OCI scheme was fully implemented in 2006.
qs.kf:
☛ Year of OCI scheme introduction? → 2005
☛ What rights are not granted to OCI cardholders? → Voting and government posts
☛ What type of visa do OCI holders get? → Multiple-entry visa
☛ Which act was amended for OCI? → Citizenship Act 1955
☛ When was OCI fully implemented? → 2006

q: Which Amendment has made the Right to Education a Fundamental Right?
qs.e: The 86th Amendment (2002) to the Indian Constitution made the Right to Education a Fundamental Right. It inserted Article 21A, which guarantees free and compulsory education for children aged 6 to 14 years. The amendment also modified Article 45 to focus on early childhood care and education, and added a new Fundamental Duty under Article 51A(k), making it the duty of parents to provide education to their children. The Right to Education Act, 2009 was enacted to implement this constitutional amendment.
qs.kf:
☛ Amendment that made Right to Education a Fundamental Right → 86th Amendment (2002)
☛ Article 21A → Right to free and compulsory education for children aged 6-14
☛ RTE Act came into force → 1 April 2010
☛ Fundamental Duty added by 86th Amendment → Article 51A(k) (parent's duty to provide education to child)
☛ Policy related to Right to Education → National Education Policy 2020

q: Which of the following authorites in India have the power to terminate the citizenship of an individual under certain circumstances?
qs.e: In India, the power to terminate citizenship rests solely with the Union Government, as per Section 10 of the Citizenship Act, 1955. This power is exercised under specific circumstances such as fraud, false representation, or disloyalty to the country. State Governments, the Supreme Court, or the Delhi Government do not have this authority. Before issuing a termination order, the Union Government must provide the individual an opportunity of a hearing. Other grounds for termination include continuous residence abroad for five years or voluntarily acquiring citizenship of another country. The provision ensures that citizenship is revoked only after due process.
qs.kf:
☛ Which act provides for termination of citizenship? → Citizenship Act, 1955, Section 10
☛ Who has the power to terminate citizenship? → Union Government
☛ What is required before issuing a termination order? → Giving the individual an opportunity of hearing
☛ What happens if a person voluntarily acquires another country's citizenship? → Indian citizenship terminates automatically
☛ Who else can terminate citizenship besides Union Government? → No one

q: In which of the following countries is the policy of dual citizenship accepted?
qs.e: Dual citizenship means a person is a citizen of two countries simultaneously. The US allows dual citizenship, although it does not officially encourage it. The UK also accepts dual citizenship, but it is listed as an option. China and India do not permit dual citizenship. India provides the Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) card, which is not full citizenship. China's law explicitly denies dual citizenship. Thus, among the given options, only the US accepts dual citizenship.
qs.kf:
☛ Country allowing dual citizenship → US, UK, Canada, Australia
☛ Country not allowing dual citizenship → India, China, Japan
☛ India's OCI card → Foreign citizenship, not full citizenship
☛ US citizenship basis → Birthright (jus soli)
☛ Indian Constitution Article 9 → Voluntary acquisition of another country's citizenship terminates Indian citizenship

q: Which of the following Acts regulates the acquisition of Indian Citizenship?
qs.e: The acquisition and determination of Indian citizenship is governed by the Indian Citizenship Act, 1955. This act came into force on 26 January 1950 and prescribes five ways to acquire citizenship: by birth, by descent, by registration, by naturalization, and by incorporation of territory. Part II (Articles 5-11) of the Indian Constitution provides provisions related to citizenship, but the detailed rules are contained in this Act. The acts of 1960, 1948, and 1947 are not related to Indian citizenship.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Indian Citizenship Act enacted? → 1955
☛ How many ways to acquire citizenship? → Five
☛ Which part of the Constitution deals with citizenship? → Part II
☛ Which article covers citizenship by naturalization? → It is covered in Sections 5 and 6 of the Act, not in specific articles.
☛ When were the major amendments to the Citizenship Act? → 1986, 1992, 2003, 2005

q: Which of the following Fundamental Duties was added by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment, 1976?
o: To uphold and protect the harmony and the spirit of common brotherhood amongst all the people of India
Amend the Constitution and its ideals
qs.e: The 42nd Constitutional Amendment, 1976 added the Fundamental Duties (Article 51A) to the Indian Constitution. Originally, there were 10 duties, one of which is 'To uphold and protect the harmony and the spirit of common brotherhood amongst all the people of India'. Other duties include abiding by the Constitution, respecting the national flag and anthem, defending the country, and protecting public property. This duty promotes national unity and integrity. Later, the 86th Amendment (2002) added an 11th duty (opportunity for education). Thus, Fundamental Duties define the responsibilities of citizens towards the nation.
qs.kf:
☛ Under which Article are Fundamental Duties? → Article 51A
☛ Which amendment added Fundamental Duties? → 42nd Amendment, 1976
☛ Which duty includes respecting the national flag? → To abide by the Constitution and national symbols
☛ Which duty was added by the 86th Amendment? → Duty to provide opportunities for education
☛ From which country were Fundamental Duties inspired? → USSR (Soviet Union)

q: In 1978, the _________ Amendment to the Constitution removed the right to the property from the list of the fundamental rights and converted it into a simple legal right under Article 300A.
qs.e: The 44th Amendment to the Constitution, passed in 1978, removed the right to property from the list of fundamental rights (Articles 19(1)(f) and 31) and converted it into a simple legal right under Article 300A. This amendment was introduced by the Morarji Desai government to limit property rights and promote socialist policies. After this, the right to property became only a statutory right, allowing the government to regulate it by law. The 44th Amendment also corrected the misuse of rights during the Emergency.
qs.kf:
☛ Which amendment removed the right to property from fundamental rights? → 44th Amendment (1978)
☛ Article 300A relates to which right? → Legal right to property
☛ Which government introduced the 44th Amendment? → Morarji Desai government
☛ Which amendment had originally included the right to property in fundamental rights? → Original Constitution; later removed by 44th Amendment
☛ The 42nd Amendment is related to what? → Fundamental duties and emergency powers (1976)

q: Which of the following Amendments has added the 11th Fundamental Duty in the Indian Constitution?
qs.e: The 86th Amendment Act, 2002 added the 11th Fundamental Duty in the Indian Constitution. This duty is added under Article 51A which states that "it shall be the duty of every parent or guardian to provide opportunities for education to his child between the age of six and fourteen years". This amendment is also known for making Right to Education a fundamental right by adding Article 21A. It also amended Article 45. The 11th Fundamental Duty imposes responsibility on parents/guardians to provide education to their children.
qs.kf:
☛ 86th Amendment → Added 11th Fundamental Duty
☛ Article 51A → Deals with Fundamental Duties
☛ Article 21A → Right to Education (6-14 years)
☛ Year of 86th Amendment → 2002
☛ 11th Fundamental Duty → Parent/guardian providing education to child

q: How many of the following ways of losing citizenship have been prescribed in the Citizenship Act, 1955?
qs.e: The Citizenship Act, 1955 prescribes three ways of losing citizenship: Renunciation, Termination, and Deprivation. Renunciation refers to voluntarily giving up citizenship. Termination occurs when a person voluntarily acquires the citizenship of another country. Deprivation is imposed by the government due to fraud, false representation, or anti- national activities. These provisions are defined under the Indian Constitution and citizenship law.
qs.kf:
☛ Types of losing citizenship → Renunciation, Termination, Deprivation
☛ What is renunciation? → Voluntarily giving up citizenship
☛ When does termination occur? → Upon acquiring another country's citizenship
☛ Who can deprive citizenship? → Government of India
☛ Year of Citizenship Act → 1955

q: Which part of the Indian Constitution is related to citizenship?
qs.e: Part II (Articles 5 to 11) of the Indian Constitution deals with citizenship. This part covers citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution, citizenship of migrants from Pakistan, citizenship of persons of Indian origin residing abroad, voluntary acquisition of foreign citizenship, and the power of Parliament to regulate citizenship. Article 5 defines citizenship at the commencement, Article 6 covers citizenship of migrants from Pakistan, Article 7 covers citizenship of migrants to Pakistan, Article 8 covers citizenship of persons of Indian origin living abroad, Article 9 deals with voluntary acquisition of foreign citizenship, Article 10 ensures continuance of citizenship rights, and Article 11 empowers Parliament to make laws regarding citizenship. The Citizenship Act, 1955 was enacted by Parliament under Article 11.
qs.kf:
☛ Part of Constitution dealing with citizenship → Part II (Articles 5-11)
☛ Article for citizenship at commencement → Article 5
☛ Article for migrants from Pakistan → Article 6
☛ Power to make citizenship law → Parliament (Article 11)
☛ Citizenship Act year → 1955

q: Which one of following countries is NOT included in the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019?
qs.e: The Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019 (CAA) provides expedited citizenship to religious minorities from Afghanistan, Bangladesh, and Pakistan who faced persecution. The eligible communities include Hindus, Sikhs, Buddhists, Jains, Parsis, and Christians who entered India on or before 31 December 2014. Bhutan is not included in this list. The act aims to protect persecuted minorities, but Bhutan is not considered a country of persecution for these groups under CAA.
qs.kf:

☛ Religions covered under CAA 2019 → Hindu, Sikh, Buddhist, Jain, Parsi, Christian
☛ Cut-off date for CAA 2019 → 31 December 2014
☛ Countries NOT covered under CAA → Bhutan, Myanmar, Sri Lanka
☛ CAA excludes Muslims → because these are Muslim-majority countries

q: Which Article discusses people born in the Indian province, people with either of their parents born in India and people who typically became Indian residents for five or more years instantaneously before the implementation of the Constitution?
qs.e: Article 5 of the Indian Constitution deals with citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution (January 26, 1950). It specifies three categories of persons who are deemed citizens of India: those born in India, those with either parent born in India, and those who have been ordinarily resident in India for at least five years immediately before the commencement of the Constitution. This article defines the initial eligibility for citizenship, while Article 8 covers persons residing outside India, Article 10 ensures the continuance of citizenship rights, and Article 4 deals with the reorganization of states. Hence, the three categories mentioned in the question directly fall under Article 5.
qs.kf:
☛ What does Article 5 relate to? → Citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution
☛ What does Article 6 relate to? → Citizenship of migrants from Pakistan
☛ What does Article 7 relate to? → Citizenship of migrants to Pakistan
☛ What does Article 8 relate to? → Citizenship of persons residing outside India
☛ What does Article 11 relate to? → Power of Parliament to regulate citizenship by law

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (09/06/2025) Shift 1
q: Which Indian Constitutional Amendment Act has NOT amended anything in the Directive Principles of the State Policy?
qs.e: The Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) are enshrined in Part IV of the Indian Constitution. The 42nd Amendment (1976) made several changes to the DPSP, adding Article 39A (equal justice), Article 43A (participation in industry management), and Article 48A (environment protection). The 86th Amendment (2002) added Article 21A (right to education), converting a DPSP into a fundamental right, and amended Article 45. The 97th Amendment (2011) added Article 43B (promotion of cooperative societies). The 48th Amendment Act (1984) primarily amended Article 356 (President's Rule) provisions and did not make any changes to the DPSP articles.
qs.kf:
☛ Articles added to DPSP by 42nd Amendment → 39A, 43A, 48A
☛ DPSP Article linked to 86th Amendment → Article 45 (child education)
☛ Article added by 97th Amendment → Article 43B
☛ Main subject of 48th Amendment → Amendment of Article 356
☛ Amendment making most changes to DPSP → 42nd Amendment

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (09/06/2025) Shift 1
q: Which authority decides citizenship for people in newly added territories?
qs.e: According to the Indian Constitution, the authority to decide citizenship for people in newly added territories rests with the Union Government (Central Government). This power is vested in the Parliament, which acts through the Union Government. Under Article 7 of the Constitution and the Citizenship Act, 1955, the Union Government has the authority to grant or deny citizenship to residents of territories that are annexed or acquired. The Election Commission deals with election conduct, the Supreme Court performs judicial review, and the State Government does not have the power to decide citizenship. Thus, the Union Government is the supreme authority in this matter.
qs.kf:
☛ Who has the authority to decide citizenship? → Union Government
☛ Which is the main act related to Indian citizenship? → Citizenship Act, 1955
☛ Which articles of the Constitution deal with citizenship? → Articles 5-11
☛ Who determines citizenship upon annexation of new territories? → Union Government
☛ Can a State Government grant citizenship? → No

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (09/06/2025) Shift 1
q: Which languages were added to the Eighth Schedule by the 71st Amendment Act, 1992?
qs.e: The Eighth Schedule of the Indian Constitution originally included 14 languages. The 71st Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992 added Konkani, Manipuri and Nepali, increasing the total number of languages to 18. This amendment was made to recognize linguistic diversity. Konkani is spoken in Goa and Karnataka, Manipuri is the main language of Manipur, and Nepali is spoken in Sikkim and West Bengal. Later, the 92nd Amendment (2003) added Bodo, Santhali, Maithili and Dogri.

☛ Languages added by 71st Amendment (1992) → Konkani, Manipuri, Nepali

☛ Last group of languages added to Eighth Schedule → Four languages in 2003

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (09/06/2025) Shift 1
q: What prompted changes in the State Co-operative Societies Acts?
qs.e: The amendments to the State Co-operative Societies Acts were primarily prompted by the poor quality of functioning of cooperative societies. Issues such as lack of transparency, financial irregularities, and inefficient management were prevalent. To address these, the government introduced reforms to strengthen the regulatory framework and improve administrative efficiency. The objective was to enhance the accountability and performance of cooperatives, ensuring better service to members. Other options like limited number of societies, political interests, or rise in taxes were not the main drivers for these changes.

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (09/06/2025) Shift 2
q: Which agreement is linked to the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 1985?
qs.e: The Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 1985 was introduced as a result of the Assam Accord. This accord was signed in 1985 between the Government of India and leaders of the Assam Movement to address the issue of illegal immigrants in Assam. The Act granted citizenship to foreign nationals who entered Assam between 1966 and 1971. It relaxed the eligibility criteria for citizenship specifically for the state of Assam. The Assam Accord aimed to identify and deport illegal immigrants who entered after 1971. Other options are incorrect: Shimla Agreement is between India and Pakistan, Indo-Sri Lanka Pact is related to Tamil issues, and Kashmir Agreement pertains to Jammu and Kashmir. Thus, the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 1985 is directly linked to the Assam Accord.
qs.kf:
☛ Which agreement is linked to the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 1985? → Assam Accord
☛ In which year was the Assam Accord signed? → 1985
☛ Which period of immigrants were granted citizenship under the Assam Accord? → 1966-1971
☛ Between whom was the Assam Accord signed? → Government of India and leaders of Assam Movement
☛ What was the objective of the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 1985? → To identify and deport illegal immigrants in Assam

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (09/06/2025) Shift 3
q: What provision was extended under the 104th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2020?
qs.e: The 104th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2020 extended the reservation of seats for Scheduled Castes (SCs) and Scheduled Tribes (STs) in the Lok Sabha and state legislative assemblies until 2030. Earlier, this reservation was set to expire in 2020. The amendment modified Article 334 of the Constitution. It also abolished the provision for nominated members from the Anglo-Indian community in the Lok Sabha and some state assemblies. This amendment aimed to continue the policy of reservation for these communities.
qs.kf:
☛ Which article was amended by the 104th Amendment? → Article 334
☛ How long was the SC/ST reservation extended? → From 2020 to 2030

☛ In which parliamentary session was it passed? → Budget Session 2020

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (10/06/2025) Shift 1
q: What provision was introduced by the Sixty-fifth Amendment Act of 1990 for the welfare of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes?
qs.e: The Sixty-fifth Constitutional Amendment Act of 1990 amended Article 338 to replace the single Special Officer (Commissioner) for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes with a multi-member National Commission for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. This commission was empowered to investigate matters of discrimination, advise on planning, and submit annual reports to the President. It consisted of a Chairperson, Vice-Chairperson, and five other members. Later, the 89th Amendment Act of 2003 bifurcated it into two separate commissions: one for Scheduled Castes and one for Scheduled Tribes. This change strengthened the institutional mechanism for safeguarding the rights of these communities.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 338 → Provides for National Commission for SCs and STs
☛ 65th Amendment Act, 1990 → Established a multi-member National Commission
☛ 89th Amendment Act, 2003 → Split into two separate commissions: one for SCs and one for STs
☛ Chairperson of National Commission for SCs → Appointed by the President

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (10/06/2025) Shift 2
q: Which principle of citizenship did India start following more strictly after the 2003 Amendment?
qs.e: Before the 2003 Amendment, India followed the principle of Jus soli (citizenship by birth), where anyone born in India could acquire citizenship. After the 2003 Amendment to the Citizenship Act 1955, the principle of Jus sanguinis (citizenship by blood) was implemented more strictly. Under this principle, a child's citizenship is determined by the citizenship of their parents, not by the place of birth. This amendment aimed to curb illegal immigration and prevent misuse of citizenship. Jus sanguinis grants citizenship based on lineage or blood relation, while Jus soli grants it based on birthplace. The change made India's citizenship policy more aligned with the blood-based principle, making it harder for children born in India to parents who are not Indian citizens to automatically get Indian citizenship.
qs.kf:
☛ In which year was the Citizenship Act 1955 amended? → 2003
☛ What does Jus sanguinis mean? → Citizenship by blood
☛ What does Jus soli mean? → Citizenship by birth
☛ Which principle became stricter after the 2003 Amendment in India? → Jus sanguinis
☛ What is the main law governing citizenship in India? → Citizenship Act 1955

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (11/06/2025) Shift 1
q: How can a foreigner who has lived in India for 12 years acquire Indian citizenship?
qs.e: Indian citizenship can be acquired through five modes under the Citizenship Act, 1955: by birth, by descent, by registration, by naturalisation, and by incorporation of territory. A foreign national who has lived in India for 12 years can acquire citizenship through naturalisation. The applicant must fulfill conditions such as residence, good character, and language proficiency. For naturalisation, the person must have resided in India for at least 9 years out of the 12 years immediately preceding the application. This process is governed by the Third Schedule of the Citizenship Act.
qs.kf:
☛ How many modes of acquiring citizenship are there under the Citizenship Act, 1955? → Five
☛ What is the minimum residence period for citizenship by naturalisation? → 12 years (with 9 years immediately preceding)
☛ Is Indian father required for citizenship by birth? → Yes (for births before 1987)
☛ Who can get citizenship by registration? → Persons of Indian origin or married women
☛ Is Indian father sufficient for citizenship by descent? → Yes (for births before 1992)

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (16/06/2025) Shift 3
q: Which of the following communities was NOT included for fast-track citizenship under Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA) of 2019?
qs.e: The Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA) of 2019 was enacted to grant citizenship to illegal immigrants from Pakistan, Afghanistan and Bangladesh belonging to six religious minority communities: Hindus, Sikhs, Buddhists, Jains, Parsis and Christians. These communities are considered persecuted in their home countries due to religious reasons. However, Muslims are specifically excluded from this Act, as the government argues that these are Muslim-majority nations and thus Muslims do not face religious persecution there. The CAA expedites the citizenship process for eligible migrants, reducing the residency requirement from 11 years to just 5 years. This Act has been a subject of widespread debate and legal challenges regarding its constitutional validity and secular principles.
qs.kf:
☛ Which countries are covered under CAA 2019? → Pakistan, Afghanistan and Bangladesh
☛ How many religious communities are included in CAA 2019? → 6 (Hindus, Sikhs, Buddhists, Jains, Parsis and Christians)

☛ What is the full name of CAA? → Citizenship Amendment Act, 2019
☛ Which community is excluded from CAA 2019? → Muslims

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (19/06/2025) Shift 3
q: What powers and responsibilities were granted to Panchayati Raj Institutions through the 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act of 1992?.
o: Direct control over the armed forces in rural areas
Power to override state legislations in matters of local importance
qs.e: The 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act of 1992 granted constitutional status to Panchayati Raj Institutions. Before this, panchayats were dependent on state governments, but now they were included in the 11th Schedule of the Constitution. This act made panchayats units of local self-government and empowered them to prepare plans for economic development and social justice. It recognized the Gram Sabha as the foundational body. It mandated regular elections and provided reservation for women, Scheduled Castes, and Scheduled Tribes. The act gave panchayats constitutional protection, making them stronger and more independent.
qs.kf:

☛ Which Article provides reservation for panchayats? → Article 243D
☛ Which Article mentions Gram Sabha? → Article 243A
☛ What is the tenure of a panchayat? → 5 years
☛ How many subjects are in the 11th Schedule? → 29 subjects

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (19/06/2025) Shift 3
q: What was the cutoff date for migrants to be eligible under the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019 (CAA)?
qs.e: Under the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019 (CAA), migrants belonging to Hindu, Sikh, Buddhist, Jain, Parsi, and Christian communities from Pakistan, Afghanistan, and Bangladesh who entered India on or before December 31, 2014 are eligible for Indian citizenship. This cutoff date is specified in Section 2 of the CAA. The Act was enacted to provide citizenship to persecuted religious minorities from these three neighboring countries. It does not apply to Muslims, as they are considered the majority community in those nations. The CAA reduces the residency requirement for naturalization from 11 years to 5 years for these eligible migrants.

☛ Which countries are covered under CAA? → Pakistan, Afghanistan, Bangladesh
☛ Which religions are covered under CAA? → Hindu, Sikh, Buddhist, Jain, Parsi, Christian

q: The 9th Amendment Act, 1960, was enacted to give effect to which of the following agreements?
qs.e: The 9th Amendment Act, 1960, was enacted to give effect to the Indo-Pak Agreement of 1958. This agreement was signed between India and Pakistan to resolve certain border disputes, particularly concerning the Berubari region and other areas. The amendment made necessary changes in the Constitution to transfer the rights of certain territories to Pakistan as per the agreement. It was the 9th Amendment to the Constitution, passed in 1960.

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (23/06/2025) Shift 1
q: Which Article of the Indian Constitution empowers Parliament to regulate the right of citizenship by law?
qs.e: Article 11 of the Indian Constitution empowers Parliament to regulate the right of citizenship by law. While Articles 5 to 10 deal with citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution, Article 11 gives Parliament the power to make any provision regarding citizenship. Under this article, the Citizenship Act, 1955 was enacted, which provides for acquisition and termination of citizenship. Thus, Article 11 grants legislative power to Parliament on citizenship matters.

☛ Citizenship Act, 1955 → Enacted under Article 11

q: According to the Indian constitution, how many languages have been given the status of official language? A. 15
qs.e: The Eighth Schedule of the Indian Constitution currently recognizes 22 languages. Originally, there were 14 languages, which were increased through amendments. 21st Amendment (1967) added Sindhi; 71st Amendment (1992) added Konkani, Manipuri, and Nepali; and 92nd Amendment (2003) added Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, and Santhali. These languages are not official languages but scheduled languages. Hindi (in Devanagari script) is the official language of the Union, and English is the co-official language. It is important to note that these 22 languages are given the status of scheduled languages, not official languages.
qs.kf:

☛ Which amendment added Sindhi? → 21st Amendment, 1967
☛ Which amendment added Konkani, Manipuri, and Nepali? → 71st Amendment, 1992
☛ Which amendment added Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, and Santhali? → 92nd Amendment, 2003
☛ What is the official language of the Union? → Hindi (Devanagari script)

q: According to Article 348(1) of the Constitution, which of the following languages are used for proceedings in the High Courts of India?
o: Official language of the state (area) in the jurisdiction of the High Count.
qs.e: Article 348(1) of the Indian Constitution prescribes that all proceedings in the High Courts, including judicial judgments, orders, and decrees, shall be in the English language. This provision has been in effect since the commencement of the Constitution. However, under Article 348(2), the Governor of a state, with the prior consent of the President, may authorize the use of Hindi or the official language of the state in the High Court proceedings. Nevertheless, the primary provision mandates English as the language of the High Courts. Hence, the correct answer is English.

☛ Article 348(1) applies to which courts? → High Courts
☛ What alternative language may be used in High Courts? → Official language of the state or Hindi (Article 348(2))

q: Under which Amendment, Article 75 of the Constitution of India inserted the total number of Ministers, including the Prime Minister, in the Council of Ministers shall NOT exceed fifteen percent of the total number of members of the House of the People?
qs.e: The 91st Amendment to the Indian Constitution inserted the provision in Article 75 that the total number of Ministers, including the Prime Minister, shall not exceed 15% of the total number of members of the Lok Sabha. This amendment was enacted in 2003 to control the size of the Council of Ministers and ensure efficiency. It also applied similar limits to state governments, restricting the number of ministers to 15% of the legislative assembly membership. The amendment aimed to prevent excessively large cabinets and promote good governance.

☛ Article 75 → Deals with appointment and number of Ministers
☛ Year of 91st Amendment → 2003
☛ Maximum Lok Sabha strength → 552
☛ Purpose of 91st Amendment → To avoid oversized cabinets

q: Article 368 is related to the amendment of the Constitution, it is covered under which part of the constitution?
qs.e: Article 368 of the Indian Constitution deals with the procedure for amending the Constitution and falls under Part XX (20th Part). This article empowers the Parliament to amend the Constitution through a process that may require a simple majority, special majority, or ratification by states. Part XX contains only one article, Article 368, which outlines the amendment process while preserving the basic structure of the Constitution. The Supreme Court, in the Kesavananda Bharati case, established that the Parliament cannot alter the basic structure. Thus, Article 368 serves as the guide for constitutional amendments, ensuring flexibility while protecting core principles.

☛ Which case propounded the basic structure doctrine? → Kesavananda Bharati

☛ How many parts are there in the Indian Constitution? → 22 parts

q: The maximum number of members of the Council of Ministers was determined by the Constitution Amendment Act?
qs.e: The 91st Constitutional Amendment Act (2003) determined the maximum number of members of the Council of Ministers. According to Article 164(1A), the total number of ministers, including the Chief Minister, in a state shall not exceed 15% of the total number of members of the Legislative Assembly of that state. For the Union, Article 75(1A) states that the total number of ministers, including the Prime Minister, shall not exceed 15% of the total number of members of the Lok Sabha. This amendment was enacted to control the size of the cabinet and ensure political stability. It came into effect on January 1, 2004.

☛ What is the maximum limit for State Council of Ministers? → 15% of Legislative Assembly strength
☛ What is the maximum limit for Union Council of Ministers? → 15% of Lok Sabha strength

q: Which languages are mentioned in the Constitution for the editing of Parliament?
qs.e: Under Article 120 of the Indian Constitution, the business in Parliament can be conducted in Hindi and English. Similarly, Article 210 provides for state legislatures. For the editing and publishing of parliamentary documents and proceedings, these two languages are primarily used. It is important to note that this is separate from the Eighth Schedule languages. The Constituent Assembly designated Hindi as the official language while retaining English as an associate language for a transitional period. Editing here refers to the language used in preparation and publication of parliamentary records. Historically, both Hindi and English have been the primary languages for legislative functioning. This provision ensures accessibility and continuity in parliamentary work across the country.
qs.kf:

☛ What was the Constituent Assembly's approach to language? → Hindi as official language, English as associate language

q: Respect for national flag and national anthem
qs.e: Respecting the National Flag and National Anthem is one of the Fundamental Duties of Indian citizens, as enshrined in Part IV-A of the Indian Constitution. These duties were added by the 42nd Amendment (1976) based on the recommendations of the Swaran Singh Committee. There are currently 11 Fundamental Duties under Article 51A. The other options like Basic Manual and Directive Principles are in Part IV, while Fundamental Rights are in Part III. It is the duty of every citizen to uphold the dignity of national symbols.

☛ Under which Article are Fundamental Duties listed? → Article 51A
☛ Which committee recommended Fundamental Duties? → Swaran Singh Committee
☛ Respect for National Flag comes under which duty? → Article 51A(a)

q: According to clause (2) of Article 239A, any law created by the Parliament for Puducherry shall NOT be considered an amendment to the Constitution for the purposes of which Article?
qs.e: Article 239A of the Indian Constitution provides special provisions for Puducherry (a Union Territory). According to clause (2) of this article, any law enacted by Parliament for the governance or administration of Puducherry, even if it modifies any provision of the Constitution, shall NOT be considered an amendment to the Constitution for the purposes of Article 368. This means such a law does not require the special amendment procedure (like two-thirds majority) prescribed under Article 368. This provision grants a special status to Puducherry, allowing flexibility in its administration. Other options include Article 371 (special provisions for certain states), Article 356 (President's rule), and Article 370 (special status of Jammu and Kashmir), which are not relevant in this context.

☛ Clause (2) of Article 239A is an exception to which Article? → Article 368
☛ Article 368 deals with what? → Constitutional amendment procedure

☛ Article 370 was related to which state? → Jammu and Kashmir

q: Which of the following Constitutional amendments inserts the Special officer for linguistic minorities, who is known as the Commissioner for Linguistic Minorities in India (CLM), to investigate all the matters relating to the safeguards provided for the linguistic minorities in India under the Constitution and report to the President?
qs.e: The 7th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1956 introduced the post of Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities (CLM) in the Indian Constitution. This officer investigates matters related to the safeguards provided for linguistic minorities and reports to the President. The amendment was enacted under Article 350B of the Constitution. Before this, there was no specific mechanism to protect the rights of linguistic minorities. This amendment was a crucial step in preserving linguistic diversity and empowering minority communities. The office of CLM functions under the Department of Official Language and ensures that linguistic minorities receive fair representation in education and administration.

q: Which Constitutional Amendment conferred the constitutional status upon the National Commission for Scheduled Tribes (NCST)?
qs.e: The 89th Constitutional Amendment Act (2003) conferred constitutional status upon the National Commission for Scheduled Tribes (NCST). It established NCST under Article 338A. Earlier, a single commission existed for both Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. The 89th Amendment amended Article 338 and inserted Article 338A to create a separate commission for Scheduled Tribes. NCST is responsible for monitoring constitutional safeguards for STs and making recommendations for their welfare. The commission submits its report to the President. The amendment was a significant step to address the specific issues of tribal communities.

q: Which Article of the Indian Constitution allows the State to make special provisions for the advancement of any socially and educationally backward class?
qs.e: Article 15 of the Indian Constitution prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth. However, its clause (4) allows the State to make special provisions for the advancement of any socially and educationally backward classes, as well as for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. This provision was added by the First Constitutional Amendment Act of 1951 to give constitutional validity to policies like reservation for backward classes. Additionally, clause (5) of this article provides for reservation in private educational institutions. Article 16 deals with equality of opportunity in public employment, Article 17 abolishes untouchability, and Article 18 deals with the abolition of titles.

q: What powers were reinstated to the States by the 105th Constitutional Amendment Act?
o: Power to identify Socially and Educationally Backward Classes (SEBCs), including Other Backward Classes (OBCs)
qs.e: The 105th Constitutional Amendment Act was passed in 2021. Earlier, the 102nd Amendment had transferred the power to identify SEBCs (including OBCs) from states to the National Commission for Backward Classes (NCBC). The 105th Amendment reversed this, restoring the power to states. Now, states can maintain their own lists separate from the central list. The amendment modified Articles 338B and 342A of the Constitution. This gave state governments autonomy in identifying OBC/SEBC groups. The amendment was crucial to uphold federal principles and state rights.
