q: What happens when an Indian citizen renounces their citizenship?
qs.e: Under Article 9 of the Indian Constitution, any person who voluntarily acquires citizenship of another country automatically loses Indian citizenship. The process of renunciation is governed by Section 8 of the Citizenship Act, 1955. When an Indian citizen renounces their citizenship, their minor children also lose Indian citizenship, although they may resume it upon reaching adulthood. After renunciation, the person becomes a foreign citizen and needs a visa or OCI card to stay in India. They lose all rights associated with Indian citizenship, such as voting, holding government jobs, or occupying constitutional positions. Renunciation is a voluntary act and does not involve any penalty; it simply terminates the citizenship status.
qs.kf:
☛ Which article deals with loss of Indian citizenship by acquiring foreign citizenship? → Article 9
☛ Which section of the Citizenship Act governs renunciation? → Section 8 of the Citizenship Act, 1955
☛ What happens to minor children when a parent renounces citizenship? → They also lose citizenship but can resume it as adults
☛ Can renounced citizenship be reacquired? → Yes, under certain conditions
☛ What document is issued after renunciation? → Certificate of Renunciation

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (06/06/2025) Shift 1
q: When was the protection and improvement of environment and safeguarding of forests and wildlife as a directive added in the Constitution of India?
qs.e: The provisions related to environmental protection in the Indian Constitution were added through the 42nd Amendment (1976). This amendment introduced Article 48A (Directive Principle) and Article 51A(g) (Fundamental Duty). Article 48A directs the state to protect and improve the environment and safeguard forests and wildlife. Article 51A(g) makes it a duty of every citizen to protect the natural environment. This amendment was passed during the tenure of Indira Gandhi's government and also added words like socialist, secular, and integrity to the Constitution. Before 1976, there was no explicit constitutional provision for environmental protection.
qs.kf:
☛ Articles for environmental protection → 48A and 51A(g)
☛ When was the 42nd Amendment enacted → 1976
☛ 42nd Amendment is also known as → Mini Constitution
☛ Article 48A was borrowed from which constitution → Russian Constitution
☛ Fundamental Duties were inspired by which country → Russia (Soviet Union)

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (06/06/2025) Shift 1
q: Article 31B was introduced to protect which type of laws from court challenges?
qs.e: Article 31B was added to the Indian Constitution by the First Amendment in 1951. Its purpose was to protect land reform laws from judicial review. Laws placed in the Ninth Schedule under Article 31B cannot be challenged on the grounds of violation of fundamental rights. Initially, 13 laws were added to the Ninth Schedule in 1951. Over time, many more laws were included through various amendments. However, in 2007, the Supreme Court ruled that laws violating the basic structure of the Constitution are not immune to judicial review even if placed in the Ninth Schedule. This landmark judgment was given in the I.R. Coelho case.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 31B → Protects land reform laws from court challenges
☛ Ninth Schedule → List of laws protected under Article 31B
☛ First Amendment → Introduced Article 31B in 1951
☛ Basic Structure Doctrine → Established in Kesavananda Bharati case (1973)
☛ I.R. Coelho v. Tamil Nadu → 2007 verdict: Ninth Schedule protection not absolute if basic structure violated

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (06/06/2025) Shift 2
q: What does OCI stand for in the context of Indian citizenship?
qs.e: OCI stands for Overseas Citizen of India. It is a special status given to foreign citizens of Indian origin, granting them certain rights in India, such as the ability to travel and engage in economic activities. However, OCI holders do not have political rights like voting or contesting elections. This status is not full citizenship under the Indian Constitution but provides permanent residency and privileges. OCI cardholders can work, study, and buy property in India, except agricultural land.
qs.kf:
☛ Full form of OCI → Overseas Citizen of India
☛ Which right is not available to OCI holders → Right to vote
☛ OCI card is for whom → Foreign citizens of Indian origin
☛ What can OCI holders not purchase → Agricultural land
☛ What type of status is OCI → Permanent residency and privileges

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (13/06/2025) Shift 1
q: With reference to the 40th Amendment Act, 1976, which category of maritime zones came under the legislative jurisdiction of the Parliament?
qs.e: The 40th Amendment Act of 1976 added an entry related to maritime zones in the Union List of the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution. This amendment brought territorial waters, continental shelf, Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ), and maritime boundary areas under the legislative jurisdiction of the Parliament. The aim was to bring marine resources and jurisdiction under central control. Inland rivers and lakes fall under the State List, while inter-state river waters and groundwater reserves remain under state jurisdiction. Hence, only territorial waters and EEZ came under Parliament's legislative jurisdiction.
qs.kf:
☛ Which list got maritime zones via 40th Amendment? → Union List
☛ Width of territorial waters? → 12 nautical miles
☛ Width of EEZ? → 200 nautical miles
☛ Continental shelf is under whose jurisdiction? → Parliament
☛ Inland waters are in which list? → State List

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (13/06/2025) Shift 2
q: Which of the following is NOT mentioned in Part IV of the Indian Constitution?
o: Promotion of international peace and security
Promotion of Hindi language as a medium of expression
Provision for free and compulsory education for children
Organisation of agricultural and animal husbandry
qs.e: Part IV of the Indian Constitution (Articles 36-51) contains the Directive Principles of State Policy. It includes promotion of international peace and security (Article 51), provision for free and compulsory education for children (Article 45), and organisation of agriculture and animal husbandry (Article 48). Promotion of Hindi language as a medium of expression is NOT mentioned in Part IV; it is part of the Fundamental Duties (Part IV-A, Article 51A). Hence, option 2 is the correct answer.
qs.kf:
☛ How many articles are in Part IV of the Indian Constitution? → Articles 36 to 51
☛ Which article deals with promotion of international peace and security? → Article 51
☛ Which article deals with free and compulsory education for children? → Article 45
☛ Which article deals with organisation of agriculture and animal husbandry? → Article 48
☛ In which part is the promotion of Hindi language included? → Part IV-A (Fundamental Duties)

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (13/06/2025) Shift 3
q: Which of the following is NOT allowed under the Citizenship Act, 1955?
qs.e: The Citizenship Act, 1955 provides four ways to acquire citizenship: by birth, descent, registration, and naturalisation. However, dual citizenship is not allowed under this Act. The Indian Constitution provides for single citizenship. Although the government introduced the Overseas Citizenship of India (OCI) scheme in 2005, it does not grant full citizenship rights. OCI holders cannot vote, hold government jobs, or run for political office. Thus, dual citizenship is not legally recognized in India.
qs.kf:
☛ Ways to acquire citizenship under Citizenship Act, 1955 → Birth, descent, registration, naturalisation
☛ Type of citizenship in India → Single citizenship
☛ Full form of OCI → Overseas Citizenship of India
☛ When was OCI introduced → 2005
☛ Right not available to OCI holder → Right to vote

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (14/06/2025) Shift 1
q: Which Article of the Indian Constitution promotes the spread and development of Hindi?
qs.e: Article 351 of the Indian Constitution promotes the spread and development of the Hindi language. It imposes a duty on the Union to promote the spread of Hindi and develop it so that it may serve as a medium of expression for all the composite culture of India. It also emphasizes that while developing Hindi vocabulary, words from other Indian languages should be incorporated. This article is part of Part 17 (Official Language). Other options: Article 350 (language for redress of grievances), Article 348 (language in High Courts), and Article 349 (special procedure for language bills).
qs.kf:
☛ Article promoting Hindi spread → Article 351
☛ Article 351 is in which Part → Part 17 (Official Language)
☛ Article 350 deals with → Language for redress of grievances
☛ Article 348 deals with → Language in High Courts
☛ Article 349 deals with → Special procedure for language bills

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (14/06/2025) Shift 1
q: Which Constitutional Amendment recognised the right to form cooperative societies as a part of Fundamental Rights?
qs.e: The 97th Constitutional Amendment (2011) granted constitutional status to cooperative societies and made the right to form them a part of Fundamental Rights. It clarified the right to form cooperative societies under Article 19(1)(c). Additionally, it added Part IX-B (Articles 243-ZH to 243-ZT), providing provisions for the formation, operation, and management of cooperative societies. This amendment emphasized making cooperative societies democratic, transparent, and accountable. It was a significant step towards strengthening the cooperative movement in India.
qs.kf:
☛ Amendment that gave constitutional recognition to cooperative societies → 97th Amendment (2011)
☛ Part added by 97th Amendment → Part IX-B (Articles 243-ZH to 243-ZT)
☛ Entry added in Concurrent List → Entry 32 (Cooperative Societies)
☛ Articles amended by 97th Amendment → Article 19(1)(c) and added Article 43-B
☛ Directive Principle for cooperative societies → Article 43-B (State shall promote voluntary formation of cooperative societies)

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (16/06/2025) Shift 1
q: Where can people of Indian origin living abroad apply for Indian citizenship under Article 8?
o: Indian Embassy at their country of living
qs.e: Under Article 8 of the Indian Constitution, people of Indian origin living abroad who wish to obtain Indian citizenship can apply at the Indian Embassy or Consulate in the country where they reside. This provision is part of Part II of the Constitution, which deals with Citizenship. Article 8 specifically applies to persons of Indian origin who migrated from India before January 26, 1950. Therefore, they do not need to travel to Delhi or any other specific location; they can submit their application at the Indian diplomatic mission in their country of residence. This ensures ease of access for such individuals.
qs.kf:
☛ What does Article 8 relate to? → Citizenship of persons of Indian origin residing abroad
☛ Where to apply under Article 8? → Indian Embassy or Consulate in the country of residence
☛ Which part of the Indian Constitution deals with citizenship? → Part II
☛ Before which date does Article 8 apply to migrants? → January 26, 1950
☛ Who is eligible for citizenship under Article 8? → Persons of Indian origin living abroad

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (16/06/2025) Shift 1
q: What major tax reform was introduced by the 101st Amendment Act, 2016?
qs.e: The 101st Amendment Act, 2016 paved the way for the introduction of Goods and Services Tax (GST) in India. This was a comprehensive indirect tax reform that subsumed multiple taxes like excise duty, service tax, VAT, entry tax, luxury tax, etc. GST aimed to implement the 'One Nation, One Tax' concept. This amendment gave concurrent powers to the Parliament and state legislatures to make laws on GST. GST was implemented nationwide on 1 July 2017. It is considered the biggest indirect tax reform in India's fiscal history.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Amendment Act introduced GST? → 101st Constitution Amendment Act, 2016
☛ When was GST implemented in India? → 1 July 2017
☛ What is the full form of GST? → Goods and Services Tax
☛ Who is the Chairman of the GST Council? → Union Finance Minister
☛ How many main tax components are there in GST? → Three (CGST, SGST, IGST)

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (16/06/2025) Shift 1
q: Which Fundamental Right was introduced by the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act of 2002 specifically for children?
o: Right of children to free and compulsory education
qs.e: The 86th Constitutional Amendment Act of 2002 was enacted to introduce the fundamental right to education for children in India. It added Article 21A, which guarantees free and compulsory education to all children aged 6 to 14 years. Additionally, it amended Article 45 and inserted Article 51A(k), making it a fundamental duty of parents to provide opportunities for education to their children. This right is part of Part III of the Constitution under Fundamental Rights. Subsequently, the Right to Education Act (RTE Act) was passed in 2009 to enforce this right. This amendment made education a fundamental right, ensuring that every child has access to schooling without any cost.
qs.kf:
☛ Article for free and compulsory education → Article 21A
☛ Fundamental duty added by 86th Amendment → Article 51A(k)
☛ RTE Act came into effect on → 1 April 2010
☛ Age group covered under Right to Education → 6-14 years
☛ Year of 86th Amendment → 2002

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (16/06/2025) Shift 2
q: What is the Forty-Second Amendment of the Indian Constitution commonly known as?
qs.e: The Forty-Second Amendment (1976) to the Indian Constitution is commonly known as the Mini-Constitution. Brought by the Indira Gandhi government, it was the most comprehensive amendment, introducing widespread changes. It added the words Socialist, Secular, and Integrity to the Preamble. It introduced Fundamental Duties (Part IVA) and curtailed judicial review, enhancing Parliament's supremacy. The amendment was passed during the Emergency (1975-77). Many of its provisions were later repealed by the 44th Amendment in 1978. The amendment also increased the power of the central government and made directive principles overriding fundamental rights in some cases.
qs.kf:
☛ Which three words were added to the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment? → Socialist, Secular, Integrity
☛ When was the 42nd Amendment enacted? → 1976
☛ Which part was added by the 42nd Amendment? → Part IVA (Fundamental Duties)
☛ Which amendment largely nullified the 42nd Amendment? → 44th Amendment
☛ Who was the Prime Minister during the 42nd Amendment? → Indira Gandhi

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (16/06/2025) Shift 2
q: Which of the following documents are NOT required under CAA 2019 to apply for Indian citizenship?
qs.e: Under CAA 2019, the required documents for applying for Indian citizenship include Passport and Visa, Aadhaar Card, and Voter ID Card. These documents verify the applicant's identity and their entry into India. Birth Certificate is NOT required because CAA applies to migrants who came from Pakistan, Afghanistan, and Bangladesh due to religious persecution and may not have birth certificates. This act provides citizenship to those who arrived before 31 December 2014.
qs.kf:
☛ Which religions are covered under CAA 2019? → Hindu, Sikh, Buddhist, Jain, Parsi, and Christian
☛ What is the minimum residency period for citizenship under CAA 2019? → 5 years (previously 11 years)
☛ Which countries are covered under CAA 2019? → Pakistan, Afghanistan, and Bangladesh
☛ Which act was amended by CAA 2019? → Citizenship Act, 1955
☛ When was CAA 2019 passed? → 11 December 2019

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (18/06/2025) Shift 2
q: What is Lord Thomas Babington Macaulay best known for in the context of British India?
o: Drafting the Indian Penal Code and promoting English education
Framing the Government of India Act, 1858
qs.e: Lord Macaulay is best known for his education policy (1835) and drafting the Indian Penal Code (IPC). He advocated for English as the medium of instruction in India, aiming to create 'a class of persons Indian in blood and colour, but English in taste, opinions, morals and intellect.' His Minute on Education (1835) laid the foundation for Western education in India. Additionally, he is credited with drafting the Indian Penal Code, which came into effect in 1860 and remains the basis of criminal justice in India.
qs.kf:
☛ Macaulay's Minute → Passed in 1835
☛ Indian Penal Code → Enacted in 1860
☛ Macaulay's aim → Creation of 'a class of interpreters'
☛ Governor-General → Lord William Bentinck (implemented education policy)
☛ IPC drafter → Lord Macaulay Committee

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (21/06/2025) Shift 2
q: Prior to 1992, what was the status of Local Governments in India?
o: Directly controlled by the Central Government
qs.e: Before the 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments of 1992, local governments (panchayats and municipalities) in India did not have constitutional status. They functioned under laws enacted by state governments, which meant their powers and existence were entirely dependent on state legislatures. This position is referred to as statutory status under State Law. The 1992 amendments granted constitutional status to local governments, making them constitutional institutions of self-governance. Prior to this, state governments had full authority to dissolve local bodies or interfere in their functioning. The amendments introduced Part IX (Panchayats) and Part IX-A (Municipalities) in the Constitution, ensuring regular elections, devolution of powers, and financial autonomy for local bodies.
qs.kf:
☛ 1992 Constitutional Amendment → 73rd (Panchayats) and 74th (Municipalities)
☛ When did local governments get constitutional status? → 1992
☛ Previously, local governments were under → State Government
☛ Objective of 73rd Amendment → Constitutional recognition of Panchayati Raj
☛ Objective of 74th Amendment → Constitutional status for Municipalities

q: According to the Constitution, the ratio between the length and breadth of the national tricolor should be
qs.e: According to the Indian Constitution, the ratio of length to breadth of the national flag (Tiranga) is 3:2. This ratio is mandated by the Flag Code of India, which came into effect on 26 January 2002. The flag consists of three horizontal stripes: saffron (courage), white (peace), and green (prosperity), with a navy blue Ashoka Chakra in the center having 24 spokes. The 3:2 ratio ensures a consistent and dignified appearance for the flag in all official and public uses. Any deviation from this ratio, such as 3:1 or 2:1, is considered unconstitutional. The design and specifications are strictly adhered to in government institutions and national events.
qs.kf:
☛ Ratio of national flag → 3:2
☛ Order of stripes in Tiranga → Saffron, White, Green
☛ Spokes in Ashoka Chakra → 24
☛ Color of Ashoka Chakra → Navy Blue
☛ Flag Code effective from → 26 January 2002

q: The national song of India was composed by-
qs.e: The national song of India is 'Vande Mataram', which was composed by Bankim Chandra Chatterjee. It was part of the novel 'Anandamath' published in 1882. Rabindranath Tagore composed the national anthem 'Jana Gana Mana', while Pingali Venkayya designed the national flag. Pydirnarri Venkata Subba Rao is not associated with the national song. 'Vande Mataram' was first sung at the 1896 Congress session. The national song was granted equal status with the national anthem by the Constitution of India in 1950.
qs.kf:
☛ The national song 'Vande Mataram' is from which novel? → Anandamath
☛ Who composed the national song? → Bankim Chandra Chatterjee
☛ When was the national song given official status? → 1950
☛ Who composed the national anthem 'Jana Gana Mana'? → Rabindranath Tagore
☛ Who designed the Indian national flag? → Pingali Venkayya

q: 'Right to Property' was removed from the list of Fundamental Rights by which amendment to the Constitution of India?
qs.e: The 44th Amendment to the Constitution of India, passed in 1978, removed the right to property from the list of Fundamental Rights (Article 19(1)(f) and 31) and made it a legal right under Article 300A. This amendment was enacted by the Morarji Desai government and came into effect on 20 June 1979. It stated that no person shall be deprived of his property except by authority of law. This change reduced the scope of judicial review in property matters and transformed the right from a fundamental right to a constitutional right, thereby allowing the government to acquire property for public purposes more easily.
qs.kf:
☛ Amendment that removed right to property from Fundamental Rights → 44th Amendment (1978)
☛ Article under which right to property is now protected → Article 300A
☛ Prime Minister during 44th Amendment → Morarji Desai
☛ Date of enforcement of 44th Amendment → 20 June 1979
☛ Amendment that added Fundamental Duties → 42nd Amendment (1976)

q: A revised version of the 'India-Bangladesh Land Boundary Agreement' was adopted by the two countries under which amendment to the Construction of India?
qs.e: The revised version of the India-Bangladesh Land Boundary Agreement (LBA) was adopted under the 100th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2015. This amendment modified the First Schedule of the Indian Constitution, enabling adjustment of borders in northeastern states like Assam, West Bengal, Meghalaya, and Tripura. It facilitated the exchange of enclaves (adversely possessed territories) and resolved long-standing border disputes. Approximately 162 enclaves were exchanged, granting citizenship to displaced residents. The amendment was passed during the tenure of Prime Minister Narendra Modi and marked a historic milestone in India-Bangladesh relations.
qs.kf:
☛ Which constitutional amendment adopted the India-Bangladesh Land Boundary Agreement? → 100th Amendment, 2015
☛ Which schedule was amended by the 100th Amendment? → First Schedule
☛ What was the objective of LBA? → Exchange of enclaves and border demarcation
☛ How many enclaves were exchanged between the two countries? → About 162
☛ In which year did the LBA come into effect? → 2015

q: Which of the following options is related to the 124th Constitutional Amendment Bill?
o: Right to free and compulsory education up to the age of fourteen years
10% reservation for economically weaker sections of general category
qs.e: The 124th Constitutional Amendment Bill, passed in 2019 and enacted as the 103rd Constitutional Amendment, introduced Articles 15(6) and 16(6) in the Constitution. It provides 10% reservation in educational institutions and government jobs for economically weaker sections (EWS) of the general category. This reservation is over and above the existing SC/ST/OBC quotas, with an annual income cap of 8 lakh rupees. The amendment aims to ensure social justice for poor general category citizens who were not covered by earlier reservation policies.
qs.kf:
☛ What is the 103rd Constitutional Amendment about? → 10% reservation for EWS of general category
☛ What is the income limit for EWS reservation? → 8 lakh rupees per annum
☛ Under which articles was EWS reservation introduced? → Articles 15(6) and 16(6)
☛ In which year was the 124th Amendment Bill passed by Parliament? → 2019
☛ For which category is EWS reservation meant? → Economically weaker sections of the general category

q: For how many years, from the commencement of the Indian Constitution, was English accepted as an associate language of the Union?
qs.e: When the Indian Constitution came into effect on 26 January 1950, Hindi was declared the official language of the Union. However, to accommodate non-Hindi speaking states, Article 343(2) and 343(3) allowed English to be used as an associate language for a period of 15 years. This period was to end in 1965. Due to strong anti-Hindi agitations, especially in Tamil Nadu, the Official Languages Act of 1963 provided for the continued use of English indefinitely. Today, English remains an associate official language of the Union.
qs.kf:
☛ Official language of Union → Hindi (Article 343)
☛ Initial period for English → 15 years (1950-1965)
☛ Official Languages Act → 1963, continued use of English
☛ Associate language of Union → English (Article 343(2))
☛ Anti-Hindi agitation → 1965 in Tamil Nadu

q: State emergency can be imposed in a state if it fails to run constitutionally. Who can declare state emergency?
o: The Chief Justice of the High Court
qs.e: Under Article 356 of the Indian Constitution, if a state fails to run according to constitutional machinery, the President of India can impose a state emergency (also known as President's Rule). The declaration is made by the President, not by the Governor or any other authority. The Governor can only submit a report to the President recommending such a step. Once the emergency is imposed, the executive and legislative powers of the state are transferred to the central government. This provision is part of Part XVIII of the Constitution. The proclamation must be approved by both Houses of Parliament within two months. State emergency can last for a maximum of three years, with periodic parliamentary approval every six months.
qs.kf:
☛ Under which article is state emergency defined? → Article 356
☛ Who can revoke President's Rule? → President
☛ Maximum duration of state emergency? → 3 years (with approval every 6 months)
☛ First state where President's Rule was imposed? → Punjab (1951)
☛ Which amendment changed Article 356? → 44th Amendment

q: Since the 42nd Constitution Amendment Act came into force?
qs.e: The 42nd Constitution Amendment Act, also known as the 'Mini Constitution', was passed in 1976. It is the most comprehensive amendment to the Indian Constitution, adding the words Socialist, Secular, and Integrity to the Preamble. It came into force on January 3, 1977. This amendment introduced Fundamental Duties, limited judicial review, and increased the powers of the central government. Its provisions significantly impacted the basic structure of the Constitution.
qs.kf:
☛ Which three words were added to the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment? → Socialist, Secular, Integrity
☛ Which Part was added for Fundamental Duties by the 42nd Amendment? → Part IV-A
☛ What is the 42nd Amendment commonly known as? → Mini Constitution
☛ Which Article was used to limit judicial review under the 42nd Amendment? → Article 368
☛ When was the 42nd Amendment passed? → 1976

q: In the Indian constitution, which original duties were added by the Act?
qs.e: The Fundamental Duties were added to the Indian Constitution by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976. This amendment was based on the recommendations of the Swaran Singh Committee. It inserted Article 51A under Part IV-A of the Constitution, which lists 11 fundamental duties for citizens. These duties reflect moral and legal obligations. The 42nd Amendment was the most comprehensive amendment to the Indian Constitution and is often called the 'Mini-Constitution'. The other options: 44th Amendment (changed emergency provisions), 41st Amendment (governor's tenure), and 52nd Amendment (anti-defection law) are unrelated to Fundamental Duties.
qs.kf:
☛ Which amendment added Fundamental Duties? → 42nd Amendment (1976)
☛ Which article contains Fundamental Duties? → Article 51A
☛ Which part contains Fundamental Duties? → Part IV-A
☛ Which committee recommended Fundamental Duties? → Swaran Singh Committee
☛ What is the 42nd Amendment also known as? → Mini-Constitution

q: In which Constitutional Amendment Act were the seats of Lok Sabha increased from 525 to 545?
qs.e: The 31st Constitutional Amendment Act, 1973 increased the number of Lok Sabha seats from 525 to 545. This amendment raised the representation of states from 525 to 543, and allowed the President to nominate 2 members from the Anglo-Indian community. Prior to this, the Lok Sabha had 499 seats in 1952, which later increased to 525. The 31st Amendment redistributed seats among states based on the 1971 Census, resulting in additional seats for some states. Currently, the maximum strength of Lok Sabha is 550 (543 elected + 2 nominated), which has been frozen until 2026 by the 84th Amendment. This amendment was significant in adjusting representation according to population growth.
qs.kf:
☛ Which amendment increased Lok Sabha seats from 525 to 545? → 31st Constitutional Amendment, 1973
☛ Which amendment introduced nominated Anglo-Indian members in Lok Sabha? → 31st Constitutional Amendment, 1973
☛ How many elected seats were in Lok Sabha after the 31st Amendment? → 543
☛ Which amendments fixed the maximum Lok Sabha strength at 543+2? → 31st Amendment (1973) and 84th Amendment (2001)
☛ On which census is the current distribution of Lok Sabha seats based? → 1971 Census

q: Which of the following Constitution Amendments empowers Parliament to establish common High court for two or more than two States?
qs.e: The 7th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1956 was enacted after the reorganisation of states. This amendment empowered Parliament to establish a common High Court for two or more states. Prior to this, each state had its own separate High Court. It inserted Article 231 into the Constitution, which allows the creation of a common High Court. For instance, the Punjab and Haryana High Court serves as a common High Court for both states. The 7th Amendment aligned with the States Reorganisation Act, 1956 and simplified judicial administration. It also amended the First and Fourth Schedules to accommodate the new state boundaries.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the 7th Constitutional Amendment enacted? → 1956
☛ Which Article provides for a common High Court? → Article 231
☛ How many schedules were amended by the 7th Amendment? → First and Fourth Schedules
☛ When was the States Reorganisation Act passed? → 1956
☛ Example of a common High Court? → Punjab and Haryana High Court

q: Which Constitutional Amendment Act is known as the 'Right to Education' Amendment?
qs.e: The 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002 is known as the 'Right to Education' Amendment. It inserted Article 21A, making free and compulsory education a fundamental right for children aged 6 to 14 years. It also modified Article 45 to focus on early childhood care and education, and added Article 51A(k), making it a fundamental duty of parents to provide education opportunities to their children aged 6 to 14. This amendment marked a historic step towards universal education in India by elevating education to a fundamental right.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Right to Education Act implemented? → 2010
☛ Which article embodies the RTE Act? → Article 21A
☛ Which fundamental duty was added by the 86th Amendment? → Article 51A(k)
☛ Which article provides free education under RTE? → Article 21A
☛ How was Article 45 changed by the 86th Amendment? → Focused on early childhood care and development

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (17/06/2025) Shift 3
q: Which Indian Constitutional Amendment Act have decreased the Fundamental Rights from seven to six?
qs.e: The 44th Amendment Act (1978) of the Indian Constitution brought a significant change to Fundamental Rights. Originally, the Constitution listed seven Fundamental Rights, which included the Right to Property (Article 31). The 44th Amendment removed the Right to Property from the list of Fundamental Rights and made it a legal right under Article 300A. This reduced the number of Fundamental Rights from seven to six. The amendment was passed by the Janata Party government and came into effect on 20 June 1979. This was a major constitutional change aimed at ensuring equitable distribution of property.
qs.kf:

☛ Article for Right to Property now → Article 300A (legal right)
☛ 44th Amendment effective from → 20 June 1979
☛ 44th Amendment passed by which government → Janata Party government
☛ Original number of Fundamental Rights → Seven

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (17/06/2025) Shift 3
q: Which of the following Articles of the Indian Constitution states about the Official Language Commission in India?
qs.e: Article 344 of the Indian Constitution provides for the establishment of the Official Language Commission. This commission is appointed by the President and is tasked with making recommendations on the use, extension, and development of the official language. Article 343 declares Hindi as the official language. Articles 341 and 342 deal with Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes respectively. The Official Language Commission was constituted in 1955, and its recommendations led to the Official Languages Act of 1963.
qs.kf:
☛ Article related to Official Language Commission → 344
☛ Article declaring Hindi as official language → 343
☛ Who appoints the Official Language Commission → President
☛ Year of establishment of Official Language Commission → 1955

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (24/06/2025) Shift 1
q: When did the citizenship provisions in the Constitution come into effect?
qs.e: The citizenship provisions in the Indian Constitution came into effect on November 26, 1949. This is the date when the Constituent Assembly adopted the Constitution. While the major part of the Constitution came into force on January 26, 1950, the articles related to citizenship (Articles 5 to 11) were made immediately effective. This was done to address the citizenship issues of people displaced during the partition. Article 5 confers citizenship based on birth or descent. Articles 6 and 7 provide for citizenship to those who migrated from Pakistan. This early enforcement was part of the Constitution's temporary and transitional provisions.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Constitution adopted? → November 26, 1949
☛ Which articles deal with citizenship? → Articles 5 to 11
☛ What does Article 5 deal with? → Citizenship by birth or descent
☛ When did the Constitution fully come into effect? → January 26, 1950
☛ When was the Citizenship Act enacted? → 1955

q: How many times has the National Emergency been implemented in India?
qs.e: Under Article 352 of the Indian Constitution, a National Emergency can be proclaimed. India has imposed a National Emergency three times so far. The first was on 26 October 1962 during the India-China war, the second on 3 December 1971 during the India-Pakistan war, and the third on 25 June 1975 on grounds of internal disturbance. The 1975 Emergency, imposed by Prime Minister Indira Gandhi, was the most controversial and lasted until 1977. No National Emergency has been imposed in India since the third one.
qs.kf:
☛ National Emergency provision → Article 352
☛ Reason for 1962 Emergency → India-China war
☛ Reason for 1971 Emergency → India-Pakistan war
☛ Prime Minister during 1975 Emergency → Indira Gandhi
☛ Longest Emergency → 1975 to 1977

q: In 2002, by which constitution amendment education was included in the original rights?
qs.e: In 2002, the 86th Constitution Amendment Act made education a fundamental right. This amendment inserted Article 21A, which provides free and compulsory education for children aged 6-14 years. It was passed in 2002 and came into effect on April 1, 2010. The amendment also modified Article 45 under the Directive Principles of State Policy and added Article 51A(k), which imposes a duty on parents to provide education to their children. This is a landmark amendment that expanded the scope of fundamental rights in the Indian Constitution.

☛ Inserted Article → 21A
☛ Date of effect → April 1, 2010
☛ Duty of parents added → Article 51A(k)
☛ Age group covered → 6 to 14 years

q: Which amendment converted the right to property from a fundamental right to a simple legal right under article 300A?
qs.e: The 44th Amendment (1978) of the Indian Constitution removed the right to property from being a fundamental right under Article 31 and made it a simple legal right under Article 300A. This amendment was passed by the Morarji Desai government. Article 31 was repealed, and the right to property is now regulated only by law. The change aimed to facilitate land reforms and socialist policies. According to Article 300A, no person shall be deprived of his property except by authority of law. Although it is no longer justiciable as a fundamental right, constitutional remedies are still available. The 44th Amendment also introduced other changes, such as abridging the power to declare a national emergency.
qs.kf:

☛ Article 300A → deals with right to property
☛ Original Article 31 → contained right to property as fundamental right
☛ 44th Amendment passed in → 1978
☛ Prime Minister during 44th Amendment → Morarji Desai

q: When was clause (K) of Article 51(A) inserted in the Indian Constitution?
qs.e: Article 51(A) of the Indian Constitution deals with Fundamental Duties. Originally, there were 10 Fundamental Duties added by the 42nd Amendment in 1976. Later, the 86th Amendment (2002) inserted clause (k), which makes it a duty of parents/guardians to provide educational opportunities to their children aged 6-14 years. This amendment was related to the Right to Education and was enacted in 2002. Thus, Article 51A now contains a total of 11 Fundamental Duties.
qs.kf:

☛ What is the total number of Fundamental Duties now? → 11

q: What happens if an Indian citizen voluntarily becomes a citizen of another country?
qs.e: As per the Indian Constitution and the Citizenship Act, 1955, India does not allow dual citizenship. If an Indian citizen voluntarily acquires citizenship of another country, their Indian citizenship automatically terminates. This provision is covered under Section 9 of the Citizenship Act. It means the person loses the Indian passport and other citizenship rights. No government approval or formality is required; the process is automatic. The Indian Constitution provides for single citizenship, which strengthens national unity. This rule applies regardless of the country whose citizenship is acquired. The person cannot retain Indian citizenship while holding another country's citizenship.
qs.kf:

☛ Type of citizenship in India → Single citizenship (no dual citizenship).
☛ Part 2 of Indian Constitution → Provisions related to citizenship (Articles 5-11).
☛ On acquiring foreign citizenship → Indian passport becomes invalid automatically.
☛ OCI card in India → For former Indian citizens, but it is not dual citizenship.

q: Which Constitutional Amendment explicitly inserted the term 'Cabinet' into the Indian Constitution in the context of Article 352?
qs.e: The term 'Cabinet' was explicitly inserted into Article 352 of the Indian Constitution by the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978. This amendment brought significant changes to the emergency provisions. Prior to this, Article 352 only referred to the 'President' and 'Council of Ministers'. The 44th amendment ensured that a proclamation of emergency could only be issued if the Cabinet (Prime Minister and Cabinet Ministers) gives a written recommendation to the President. This made the procedure for imposing an emergency more stringent. The amendment was introduced to prevent the misuse of emergency powers, ensuring that it could only be declared on the advice of the government. It also replaced the term 'internal disturbance' with 'armed rebellion' as a ground for emergency.
qs.kf:
☛ Which amendment inserted 'Cabinet' in Article 352? → 44th Amendment
☛ What was the purpose of the 44th Amendment regarding emergencies? → To prevent misuse of emergency powers
☛ Which amendment replaced 'internal disturbance' with 'armed rebellion' in Article 352? → 44th Amendment
☛ When was the 44th Amendment enacted? → 1978
☛ Who constitutes the Cabinet? → Prime Minister and Cabinet Ministers

q: Which constitutional amendment, known as 'mini constitution', gave effect to the recommendations of Swaran Singh Committee?
qs.e: The 42nd Constitutional Amendment (1976) is known as the 'mini constitution'. It gave effect to the recommendations of the Swaran Singh Committee. It introduced the words Socialist, Secular and Integrity in the Preamble. It added Fundamental Duties (Part IV-A) and curtailed judicial review. It made the President bound by the advice of the Council of Ministers, expanded the amending power under Article 368, and gave precedence to Directive Principles (Part IV) over Fundamental Rights (Part III). This amendment was controversial, and many of its provisions were later repealed by the 43rd and 44th amendments.
qs.kf:
☛ Known as mini constitution → 42nd Amendment
☛ Based on Swaran Singh Committee recommendations → 42nd Amendment
☛ Words added to Preamble → Socialist, Secular, Integrity
☛ Which amendment added Fundamental Duties → 42nd Amendment
☛ Gave precedence to DPSP over Fundamental Rights → 42nd Amendment

q: What historical decision was made based on the basic structure theory?
qs.e: The basic structure theory is a cornerstone of the Indian Constitution, propounded by the Supreme Court in the 1973 case of Kesavananda Bharati vs. State of Kerala. In this historic decision, the court ruled that while Parliament can amend the Constitution, it cannot destroy or alter its basic structure. This principle reinforced the supremacy of the Constitution and the power of judicial review. Before this, the Golaknath case had held that Parliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights, but Kesavananda Bharati overruled that view. Under this doctrine, any constitutional amendment can be struck down by the court if it violates the basic structure, which includes features like secularism, federalism, and judicial independence.
qs.kf:
☛ Which case propounded the basic structure doctrine? → Kesavananda Bharati case
☛ In which year was the Kesavananda Bharati case decided? → 1973
☛ What was the ruling in the Golaknath case? → Parliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights
☛ What is included in the basic structure? → Supremacy of Constitution, judicial review, separation of powers, secularism
☛ Which case was struck down using the basic structure doctrine? → Minerva Mills case (1980)

q: The maximum limit of the Council of Ministers was fixed under which Constitutional Amendment Act?
qs.e: The 91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003 fixed the maximum size of the Council of Ministers. It added Articles 75(1A) and 164(1A) to the Constitution, stipulating that the total number of ministers including the Prime Minister shall not exceed 15% of the total strength of the Lok Sabha. Similarly, in states, the number of ministers including the Chief Minister cannot exceed 15% of the total members of the Legislative Assembly. This amendment aimed to control the growing number of ministers and reduce government expenditure. It came into effect in 2004.
qs.kf:

☛ What is the maximum number of ministers including Prime Minister? → 15% of Lok Sabha members
☛ Which article limits the Council of Ministers in states? → Article 164(1A)

q: Which Indian state has the largest number of seats reserved for the Scheduled Tribes in the Lok Sabha?
qs.e: Under Article 330 of the Indian Constitution, seats are reserved in the Lok Sabha for Scheduled Tribes (ST). Madhya Pradesh has the highest number of ST reserved seats, with 6 seats. This reflects the high proportion of ST population in the state, approximately 21%. In comparison, Rajasthan has 3, Gujarat has 2, and Andhra Pradesh has 2 ST reserved seats. The reason for Madhya Pradesh having the most ST seats is its large tribal population, including prominent tribes such as Bhil, Gond, and Baiga. This reservation policy is a key aspect of ensuring political representation for Scheduled Tribes in India.

q: After the 97th Constitutional Amendment, for how long can a state co-operative law that is inconsistent with the amendment remain in force?
qs.e: The 97th Constitutional Amendment (2011) gave constitutional status to cooperative societies and added Part IXB to the Indian Constitution. After this amendment, any state cooperative law that is inconsistent with the provisions of the amendment can remain in force for a maximum period of 1 year. This provision is contained in Article 243XH, which allows state governments one year to amend their laws to comply with the amendment. Therefore, any inconsistent state law can remain effective for only one year from the date of the amendment's commencement.

q: Who has been appointed as the Governor of the state of Telangana in Sept, 2019?
qs.e: In September 2019, Tamilisai Soundararajan was appointed as the Governor of Telangana. She is the first woman Governor of Telangana. Previously, she was a leader of the Bharatiya Janata Party and a Rajya Sabha member from Tamil Nadu. Her appointment came after the resignation of the then Governor E.S.L. Narasimhan. q: In which of the following years did the new Indian Flag Code become effective?
qs.e: The Flag Code of India, 2002 came into effect on January 26, 2002. It consolidated, amended, and updated the original flag code that had existed since 1950. The new code clarified rules regarding the display, hoisting, and use of the national flag. Under this code, citizens were allowed to fly the flag at any time in public places. It is divided into three parts. The main objective is to maintain the dignity and honor of the national flag.

q: When was the national anthem of India adopted?
qs.e: The national anthem of India, 'Jana Gana Mana', was officially adopted by the Constituent Assembly on January 24, 1950. It was originally written in Bengali by Rabindranath Tagore and first sung on December 27, 1911. The complete version takes about 52 seconds to sing, while the shortened version takes about 20 seconds. The anthem reflects the unity and diversity of India. It was adopted in its Hindi translation on this date.

q: What amendment act was made by decreasing the age of franchise from 21 years to 18 years?
qs.e: The 61st Constitutional Amendment Act, passed in 1988, reduced the voting age from 21 years to 18 years. It aimed to give youth an opportunity to participate in the political process. The amendment modified Article 326 of the Constitution, which deals with eligibility for voting in Lok Sabha and Legislative Assembly elections. This step significantly increased the number of voters in India. The amendment was passed during the tenure of Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi.

q: Under the Citizenship Act, 1955, for how many years does a person of Indian origin need to reside in India to become an Indian Citizen?
qs.e: Under Section 5 of the Citizenship Act, 1955, a person of Indian origin can acquire citizenship by registration if they have resided in India for 7 years immediately before applying. This provision applies to persons who are of Indian origin but residing abroad. Section 5(1)(a) specifies that such persons must have been resident in India for at least 7 years before the application. In contrast, a foreign national applying for citizenship by naturalization under Section 6 must have resided in India for 11 years. The reduced period of 7 years for persons of Indian origin is intended to facilitate their acquisition of Indian citizenship, recognizing their ancestral connection to India.

q: Which Indian Constitution Act provides for the minimization of inequalities in income, property, facilities and opportunities in the Directive Principles of State Policy?
qs.e: The 44th Constitutional Amendment (1978) added Article 38(2) to the Directive Principles of State Policy, which directs the State to minimize inequalities in income, property, facilities and opportunities. This amendment was brought by the Morarji Desai government to restore democratic values after the Emergency. It specifically mandates that the State shall strive to reduce inequalities in status, facilities and opportunities, not only among individuals but also among groups residing in different areas or engaged in different vocations. Thus, the 44th Amendment is the correct answer as it directly inserts the provision regarding minimization of inequalities in the Directive Principles.

q: The Constituent Assembly adopted Indian national flag on
qs.e: The Constituent Assembly of India adopted the tricolour as the national flag on 22nd July 1947, just days before India's independence. The flag consists of horizontal stripes of saffron, white, and green, with a navy blue Ashoka Chakra in the center of the white stripe. The Ashoka Chakra has 24 spokes. The design was created by Pingali Venkayya. The flag has a ratio of 2:3. The first hoisting of the independent India's flag took place on 15th August 1947.

q: The 100th Amendment (2015) to the constitution of India is related to:
o: a maximum of 10% reservation for the economically weaker sections
establishment of the National Judicial Appointment Commission
ratification of the land boundary agreement between India and Bangladesh
introduction of the Goods and Services Tax
qs.e: The 100th Amendment Act of 2015 to the Indian Constitution is related to the ratification of the Land Boundary Agreement (LBA) between India and Bangladesh. This amendment modified the First Schedule of the Constitution to enable the exchange of enclaves along the India-Bangladesh border. Under this agreement, India transferred approximately 111 enclaves to Bangladesh, while Bangladesh transferred 51 enclaves to India. The LBA resolved long-standing border disputes and provided rights to residents of these enclaves. The amendment was passed under Article 2 and Article 3 of the Constitution, which allow for the admission or establishment of new states and alteration of boundaries. The 100th Amendment is historic as it finalized the land boundary between the two nations.

q: What percentage of seats are reserved for women under the 106th Amendment Act?
qs.e: The 106th Constitution Amendment Act, 2023 reserves 33% of seats in the Lok Sabha and state legislative assemblies for women. Also known as the Women's Reservation Bill, it provides one-third reservation for women within the seats reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. This reservation will be effective for a period of 15 years. The Act stipulates that it will come into force after the delimitation exercise based on the next census. The amendment aims to enhance women's political participation and strengthen gender equality in India's legislative bodies. It marks a significant step towards empowering women in the political sphere.

q: Which part of the Constitution of India has been influenced by the German Constitution?
o: Suspension of fundamental rights during Emergency
qs.e: The emergency provisions of the Indian Constitution are influenced by the German Constitution (Weimar Constitution). The German Constitution had provisions for suspending fundamental rights during an emergency, which was adopted in the Indian Constitution under Article 359. In India, the President can suspend fundamental rights during an emergency, except for Articles 20 and 21. Other options: Single citizenship is influenced by Britain, federal system by Canada, and amendment procedure by South Africa.

q: If the period of Lok Sabha is extended due to the National Emergency and when the Emergency is over, how long will the extended period be?
qs.e: Under Article 83(2) of the Indian Constitution, the normal term of the Lok Sabha is 5 years. However, during a National Emergency, Parliament may extend the term by law for up to 1 year at a time. The extended term can continue only for up to 6 months after the Emergency ceases to operate. This provision ensures that elections are held promptly after the Emergency ends. Thus, the correct answer is 6 months.

q: Which Article, added by the 97th Amendment Act, 2011, promotes the professional management of co-operative societies?
qs.e: The 97th Amendment Act, 2011 added Part IXB to the Constitution to give constitutional status to co-operative societies. Through this amendment, Article 43B was inserted, which directs the state to promote voluntary formation, autonomous functioning, and democratic control of co-operative societies. This article encourages professional management so that co-operative societies can work efficiently. Additionally, provisions like Article 243ZL and 243ZM were added, dealing with elections, audits, and financial discipline of co-operative societies. Article 43B is part of the Directive Principles of State Policy, focusing on strengthening the co-operative movement.

q: Which of the following is the correct method to change any provision of the Constitution of India?
qs.e: The only correct method to change any provision of the Constitution of India is through a Constitutional Amendment. Article 368 of the Constitution lays down the procedure for amendment. A bill must be passed by both Houses of Parliament with a special majority (at least two-thirds of members present and voting). For certain amendments affecting the federal structure, ratification by at least half of the state legislatures is also required. Presidential Ordinance and Executive Order are executive powers that cannot permanently alter constitutional provisions. The Supreme Court can review amendments but cannot initiate them. Thus, only a constitutional amendment is the valid method to change the Constitution.
qs.kf:

☛ Where does an amendment bill originate? → In either House of Parliament
☛ What majority is required for a constitutional amendment? → Special majority (2/3 members present and voting)

☛ How many amendments have been made to the Indian Constitution so far? → 106 (as of 2024)

q: 27% reservation for OBCs in educational institutions was provided through which Constitutional Amendment of the Indian Constitution?
qs.e: The 93rd Amendment to the Indian Constitution was enacted in 2005. It added clause (5) to Article 15, enabling the state to provide 27% reservation for socially and educationally backward classes (OBCs) in educational institutions. This reservation was in addition to the existing reservations for Scheduled Castes (SC) and Scheduled Tribes (ST). The amendment brought private educational institutions under the ambit of reservation, except for minority educational institutions. This was a significant step to promote social justice and equal opportunity in education.

☛ Which groups are covered under this amendment? → Socially and educationally backward classes (OBCs)

qs.e: The Land Boundary Agreement (LBA) between India and Bangladesh was constitutionalized through the 100th Constitutional Amendment in 2015. This amendment modified the First Schedule of the Indian Constitution to enable the exchange of border enclaves. The agreement resolved long-standing border disputes by facilitating the exchange of 162 enclaves between the two countries. The 100th Amendment is notable for being specifically focused on territorial adjustment and is a key example of cooperative boundary resolution. It was passed by both houses of Parliament and ratified by the required number of states.

q: 'Oriya’ was replaced with ‘Odia’ in the Eighth Schedule by which Constitutional Amendment?
qs.e: The Eighth Schedule of the Indian Constitution lists the official languages. In 2011, the 96th Constitutional Amendment replaced 'Oriya' with 'Odia'. This amendment reflected the change in the name of the principal language of Odisha. Previously, the term 'Oriya' was used, but it was replaced with 'Odia' to accurately represent the linguistic identity. The amendment is related to Article 344(1) and 351 of the Constitution. The Eighth Schedule currently includes 22 languages. This change was made to ensure correct representation of the language's name.

q: Which of the following Articles was inserted into the Directive Principles of State Policy of the Indian Constitution by the Constitution (Ninety-seventh Amendment) Act of 2011?
o: Article 48A - Protection and improvement of environment and safeguarding of forests and wild life

qs.e: The Constitution (97th Amendment) Act, 2011 inserted Article 43B into the Directive Principles of State Policy of the Indian Constitution, which promotes voluntary formation, autonomous functioning, democratic control and professional management of co-operative societies. q: The 101st Constitutional Amendment Act of 2016 was related to which of the following?

Exchanging enclaves and making other territorial adjustments between India and Bangladesh
Appointing a Minister in charge of tribal welfare in the states of Chhattisgarh and Jharkhand

qs.e: The 101st Constitutional Amendment Act of 2016 was passed to introduce the Goods and Services Tax (GST) in India. This amendment added new Articles 246A, 269A, and 279A to the Constitution and amended the Union List and State List. GST is an indirect tax aimed at creating a uniform tax system across the country. The Act came into effect on July 1, 2017. It also established the GST Council, comprising the Finance Ministers of the Centre and states, to decide on tax rates and policies. This amendment was a significant change in the federal structure of the Indian Constitution.

q: The Constitution (Ninety‑Fifth Amendment) Act of 2009 extended the reservation of seats in the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, and Anglo‑Indians for how many years?
qs.e: The Constitution (Ninety-Fifth Amendment) Act, 2009 extended the reservation of seats in the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, and Anglo-Indians for a period of ten years (from 2010 to 2020). This amendment modified Article 334, which originally provided for reservation for 10 years from 1950. The 95th Amendment came into effect on 25 January 2010. q: In which year was the 52nd Amendment Act of the Indian Constitution, which introduced the Anti‑Defection Law to prevent elected representatives from switching political parties, passed?
qs.e: The 52nd Amendment Act of the Indian Constitution was passed in the year 1985. This act introduced the Anti-Defection Law, which was added as the Tenth Schedule to the Constitution. Its purpose was to prevent elected representatives from switching political parties, thereby ensuring the stability of governments. The law applies when a member of Parliament or a state legislature voluntarily gives up membership of their party or votes against party directions. Exceptions include party mergers and decisions by the Speaker or Chairman. This amendment is considered crucial for maintaining discipline within political parties and curbing the culture of defection, which had often led to political instability.

To promote harmony among all people of India
To uphold and protect the sovereignty of India
qs.e: The 86th Constitutional Amendment of 2002 made Right to Education a fundamental right under Article 21A and added a new fundamental duty under Article 51A(k). This duty requires parents or guardians to provide opportunities for education to their children aged 6 to 14 years. The amendment was a significant step towards making education compulsory. Earlier, there were 10 fundamental duties added by the 42nd Amendment in 1976. The 86th Amendment increased this number to 11. It emphasized the importance of education as both a right and a duty.

q: Which Constitutional Amendment Act added Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, and Santhali to the Eighth Schedule of the Indian Constitution?
qs.e: The Eighth Schedule of the Indian Constitution originally included 14 languages. Over time, various amendments added more languages. The 92nd Amendment Act, 2003 added Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, and Santhali to the Eighth Schedule, increasing the total number of languages to 22. This amendment came into force on January 7, 2004. Earlier, the 71st Amendment (1992) had added Konkani, Manipuri, and Nepali, and the 21st Amendment (1967) had added Sindhi.
qs.kf:
☛ How many languages are currently in the Eighth Schedule? → 22
☛ Which amendment added Sindhi language? → 21st Amendment Act, 1967
☛ Which amendment added Konkani, Manipuri, and Nepali? → 71st Amendment Act, 1992
☛ Which amendment added Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, and Santhali? → 92nd Amendment Act, 2003
☛ What are the last four languages added to the Eighth Schedule? → Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, Santhali

q: The 44th Amendment Act of 1978 restored the standard term of the Lok Sabha and State Legislature to how many years?
qs.e: The 44th Amendment Act of 1978 was a crucial amendment to the Indian Constitution that reversed changes made during the Emergency. It restored the standard term of the Lok Sabha and State Legislatures to five years. Additionally, it strengthened fundamental rights and judicial review. This amendment was passed by the Morarji Desai government.
qs.kf:
☛ Which articles were amended by the 44th Amendment? → Articles 83 and 172
☛ How long was the Lok Sabha term extended during the Emergency? → One year
☛ Which right was removed by the 44th Amendment? → Right to Property (Article 300A)
☛ When did the 44th Amendment come into force? → 20 June 1979
☛ Which article was re-framed by the 44th Amendment? → Article 359

q: Which of the following parts of the Indian Constitution deals with the Official Languages of the Indian Union?
qs.e: Part XVII of the Indian Constitution (Articles 343 to 351) deals with the official languages of the Union. Article 343 declares Hindi as the official language, while Article 345 allows states to adopt their own official languages. Articles 346 and 347 govern the language of communication between the Union and states. Article 348 specifies the language to be used in the Supreme Court and High Courts. Article 351 directs the promotion of Hindi. Part XV deals with elections, Part XVI with special provisions for certain classes, and Part XX with amendments. Thus, Part XVII is correct.
qs.kf:
☛ Which part of the Constitution deals with official languages? → Part XVII
☛ Which articles relate to official language? → 343-351
☛ Which article declares Hindi as official language? → Article 343
☛ Which article deals with language of High Courts? → Article 348
☛ Which article directs development of Hindi? → Article 351

q: Which of the following Articles of the Constitution of India authorises Parliament to alter the applicability of Fundamental Rights with respect to members of the Armed Forces and the forces entrusted with the maintenance of public order?
qs.e: Article 33 of the Indian Constitution empowers Parliament to restrict or abrogate the application of Fundamental Rights to members of the armed forces, paramilitary forces, police, and forces responsible for maintaining public order. This provision ensures discipline and proper discharge of duties without hindrance. Under Article 33, Parliament can make laws specifying which fundamental rights apply to such forces and to what extent. This is aimed at prioritizing national security and public order. Article 35 deals with enforcement of fundamental rights, while Articles 42 and 45 relate to just conditions of work and child care, respectively. Hence, the correct answer is Article 33.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 33 → Authorises Parliament to restrict Fundamental Rights for armed forces.
☛ Article 34 → Restricts Fundamental Rights during martial law.
☛ Article 35 → Power to make laws for enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
☛ Article 32 → Right to move Supreme Court for enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
☛ Law under Article 33 → Army Act, 1950.

q: In which year was Tamil given the status of classical language by the Constitution of India?
qs.e: The Government of India granted Classical Language status to Tamil in October 2004. This decision recognized Tamil's antiquity and rich literary tradition. Tamil is one of the world's oldest living languages, with a history spanning over 2000 years. The criteria for classical language status include high antiquity, independent literary tradition, and originality. Following Tamil, Sanskrit (2005), Kannada, Telugu, Malayalam, Odia, etc., were also granted this status. The classical status helps in promoting research and preservation of the language.
qs.kf:
☛ Which was the first language declared Classical? → Tamil (2004)
☛ When was Sanskrit given Classical Language status? → 2005
☛ Which is the sixth Classical Language of India? → Odia (2014)
☛ Which ministry grants Classical Language status? → Ministry of Culture, Government of India
☛ What is the oldest Tamil literature called? → Sangam literature

q: What condition must be fulfilled by a person born outside India after December 3, 2004, to be considered an Indian citizen by descent?
o: Both parents must be Indian citizens.
They must reside in India for at least 5 years.
They must renounce any other nationality.
They must reside in India for 10 years.
qs.e: According to Article 8 of the Indian Constitution and the Citizenship Act, 1955, for a person born outside India after December 3, 2004, to be considered an Indian citizen by descent, it is necessary that both parents are Indian citizens. This provision was introduced by the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2003. Previously, if either parent was an Indian citizen, the child could claim citizenship by descent, but after 2004, the condition was tightened. There is no requirement of residency in India or renunciation of any other nationality for this category.
qs.kf:
☛ Condition for citizenship by descent for a person born outside India after Dec 3, 2004 → Both parents must be Indian citizens
☛ When did Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2003 come into force? → December 3, 2004
☛ Year of Indian Citizenship Act → 1955
☛ Articles related to citizenship in Constitution → Articles 5-11
☛ Main ways to acquire Indian citizenship → Birth, descent, registration, naturalization, territorial inclusion

q: A person born in India between 26 January 1950 and 1 July 1987 is automatically considered a citizen of India by:
qs.e: Under the Indian Constitution, any person born in India between 26 January 1950 and 1 July 1987 was automatically considered a citizen of India by birth. This provision is outlined in Section 3 of the Citizenship Act, 1955. During this period, individuals born in India did not require any additional process to acquire citizenship. After 1 July 1987, it became mandatory that at least one parent must be an Indian citizen for a person born in India to be a citizen by birth. Other modes of acquiring citizenship include descent (for those born outside India to Indian parents), naturalisation (for foreigners), and registration (for persons of Indian origin abroad). However, for the specific period mentioned, 'birth' is the correct basis.
qs.kf:
☛ Section 3 of Citizenship Act, 1955 → Citizenship by birth
☛ Born after 1 July 1987 → At least one parent must be an Indian citizen
☛ Citizenship by descent → For persons born outside India
☛ Citizenship by naturalisation → For foreigners through naturalisation process
☛ Citizenship by registration → For persons of Indian origin living abroad

q: The Citizenship Amendment Act, 2019, provides citizenship to individuals belonging to which communities if they entered India before 31st December 2014 from Pakistan or Afghanistan or Bangladesh?
o: Hindu, Sikh, Buddhist, Jain, Parsi, Christian
qs.e: The Citizenship Amendment Act, 2019 (CAA) grants Indian citizenship to immigrants who entered India from Pakistan, Afghanistan, or Bangladesh before 31st December 2014 and belong to the Hindu, Sikh, Buddhist, Jain, Parsi, or Christian communities. This Act amends the Citizenship Act, 1955 and reduces the residency requirement for naturalization from 11 years to 5 years for these communities. The Muslim community is excluded from the Act on the grounds that these countries are Muslim-majority and hence Muslims there do not face religious persecution. The Act has been a subject of debate regarding its conformity with the Assam Accord and the right to equality under Article 14.
qs.kf:
☛ Religions covered under CAA 2019 → Hindu, Sikh, Buddhist, Jain, Parsi, Christian
☛ Cut-off date for entry into India → 31 December 2014
☛ Countries covered under CAA → Pakistan, Afghanistan, Bangladesh
☛ Original Act amended by CAA → Citizenship Act, 1955
☛ Reduction in residency requirement under CAA → 11 years to 5 years

q: Which of the following is a Tibeto-Burman language included in the Eighth Schedule of the Indian Constitution?
qs.e: Bodo language belongs to the Tibeto-Burman language family and is included in the Eighth Schedule of the Indian Constitution. It is primarily spoken in Assam and West Bengal. Santhali is from the Munda family, Maithili is Indo-Aryan, and Konkani is also Indo-Aryan. The Eighth Schedule currently has 22 languages. Bodo was added through the 92nd Amendment in 2003. It is one of the official languages of Assam.
qs.kf:
☛ Languages in Eighth Schedule → 22
☛ Language family of Bodo → Tibeto-Burman
☛ Amendment that added Bodo → 92nd Amendment, 2003
☛ State where Bodo is mainly spoken → Assam
☛ Other Tibeto-Burman language in Eighth Schedule → Manipuri

q: Who among the following composed the National Song of India?
qs.e: The National Song of India is 'Vande Mataram', composed by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay. It was included in his novel 'Anandamath' (1882). It was adopted as the National Song on 24 January 1950 by the Indian Constitution. The song praises the motherland and served as an inspiration during the Indian independence movement. Rabindranath Tagore composed the National Anthem 'Jana Gana Mana', while Sarojini Naidu is known as the 'Nightingale of India'. Sri Aurobindo was a philosopher and yogi. The music for 'Vande Mataram' was set by Rabindranath Tagore. This song is a symbol of Indian culture and nationalism.
qs.kf:
☛ Who composed the National Song 'Vande Mataram'? → Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay
☛ 'Vande Mataram' is part of which novel? → Anandamath
☛ When was the National Song officially adopted? → 24 January 1950
☛ Who composed the National Anthem 'Jana Gana Mana'? → Rabindranath Tagore
☛ Who set the music for 'Vande Mataram'? → Rabindranath Tagore

q: According to the Citizenship Amendment Act of 2019, individuals who entered India on or before _______ and belong to the Hindu, Sikh, Buddhist, Jain, Parsi or Christian community from Pakistan, Afghanistan or Bangladesh are eligible for citizenship.
qs.e: According to the Citizenship Amendment Act, 2019, individuals who entered India on or before 31 December 2014 and belong to the Hindu, Sikh, Buddhist, Jain, Parsi or Christian community from Pakistan, Afghanistan or Bangladesh are eligible for citizenship. This Act was passed on 12 December 2019 and aims to grant Indian citizenship to persecuted religious minorities from three neighbouring countries (Pakistan, Afghanistan, Bangladesh). Under this Act, the cut-off date for migration is set as 31 December 2014. This date is crucial because individuals arriving after this date are not eligible for citizenship under this Act.
qs.kf:
☛ Number of religions covered under CAA 2019 → 6 (Hindu, Sikh, Buddhist, Jain, Parsi, Christian)
☛ Countries included in CAA 2019 → Pakistan, Afghanistan, Bangladesh
☛ Cut-off date for entry under CAA 2019 → 31 December 2014
☛ Which Act is amended by CAA 2019 → Citizenship Act, 1955
☛ When did CAA 2019 come into effect → 10 January 2020

q: The 74th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992, entrusted the Municipalities with ______ functional domains under the Twelfth Schedule of the Constitution.
qs.e: The 74th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992, entrusted Municipalities with 18 functional domains under the Twelfth Schedule of the Constitution. This amendment was enacted to give constitutional status to urban local bodies. The Twelfth Schedule lists 18 subjects including urban planning, land use, water supply, public health, roads, and other essential services. The Act aimed to empower municipalities and provide them with greater autonomy in managing urban affairs. It came into force on June 1, 1993, and added Part IX-A to the Constitution.
qs.kf:
☛ Schedule added by 74th Amendment → Twelfth Schedule
☛ Number of functional domains for Municipalities → 18
☛ Domains for Panchayats under 73rd Amendment → 29 (Eleventh Schedule)
☛ Year 74th Amendment came into effect → 1993
☛ Part of Constitution containing Municipalities → Part IX-A

q: Which among the following is NOT a document related to Good Governance?
qs.e: Key documents related to Good Governance include Citizen Charter, Second Administrative Reforms Commission, and Sevottam Model. The Citizen Charter aims to bring transparency and accountability in government services. The Second Administrative Reforms Commission (2005-2009) submitted reports on administrative reforms. The Sevottam Model was developed for excellence in service delivery. The National Forest Policy, 1988 deals with forest conservation and management, not governance.
qs.kf:
☛ What is Citizen Charter related to? → Transparency and accountability in government services
☛ When was the Second Administrative Reforms Commission formed? → 2005
☛ What is the objective of Sevottam Model? → Excellence in service delivery
☛ What is the main focus of National Forest Policy, 1988? → Forest conservation and management
☛ What are three main principles of Good Governance? → Transparency, Accountability, Participation

q: Which of the following Directive Principles was NOT added to the Indian Constitution as part of the 42nd Amendment Act of 1976?
o: Article 48A: To protect and improve the environment and safeguard forests and wildlife
Article 39A: To promote equal justice and to provide free legal aid to the poor
Article 38: State to minimise inequalities in income, status, facilities and opportunities
Article 39: To secure opportunities for healthy development of children
qs.e: The 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 added four new Directive Principles to the Constitution: Article 39A (equal justice and free legal aid), Article 43A (participation of workers in management of industries), Article 48A (protection of environment and wildlife), and Article 43 (development of libraries). It also added clause (f) to Article 39 to secure opportunities for healthy development of children. Article 38 was originally part of the Constitution; the 42nd Amendment only added a directive to minimise inequalities in income, status, facilities and opportunities alongside social, economic and political justice. Thus, Article 38 was not a new addition but an amendment.
qs.kf:
☛ Directive Principles added by 42nd Amendment → Article 39A, 43A, 48A, 43 (libraries)
☛ Clause added to Article 39 → Article 39(f)
☛ Original form of Article 38 → State to secure a social, economic and political justice
☛ Directive added to Article 38 by 42nd Amendment → Minimise inequalities in income, status, facilities and opportunities
☛ Year of 42nd Amendment → 1976

q: "To provide opportunities for education to his child or ward between the ages of six and fourteen years" was added to the Indian Constitution as the 11th Fundamental Duty through which of the following amendments?
qs.e: The Indian Constitution originally had 10 Fundamental Duties, added by the 42nd Amendment (1976). Later, the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act (2002) added 'to provide opportunities for education to his child or ward between the ages of six and fourteen years' as the 11th Fundamental Duty. This amendment also inserted Article 21-A, making education a fundamental right, and added the new duty under Article 51-A. The amendment was crucial for enforcing the Right to Education.
qs.kf:
☛ Number of Fundamental Duties → Originally 10, now 11
☛ When were Fundamental Duties first added → 42nd Amendment, 1976
☛ Which amendment added the 11th Fundamental Duty → 86th Amendment, 2002
☛ Right to Education is under which Article → Article 21-A
☛ 86th Amendment relates to → Right to Education and Fundamental Duty

q: Which of the following amendments to the Indian Constitution is regarded as a major milestone in the country’s taxation system for introducing the Goods and Services Tax (GST)?
qs.e: The 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016 is considered a major milestone in India's taxation system as it introduced the Goods and Services Tax (GST). This amendment enabled both the Centre and States to levy tax simultaneously, creating a unified tax structure across the country. It provided for the formation of the GST Council, comprising the Union Finance Minister and State Finance Ministers, to recommend rates and rules. The amendment replaced multiple indirect taxes like service tax, VAT, excise duty, etc. with a single GST. The reform came into effect on July 1, 2017, and is famously known as 'One Nation, One Tax'.
qs.kf:
☛ Amendment for GST → 101st Amendment (2016)
☛ Implementation date of GST → July 1, 2017
☛ Chairperson of GST Council → Union Finance Minister
☛ Old taxes subsumed under GST → Service tax, VAT, excise duty, etc.
☛ Slogan of GST → 'One Nation, One Tax'

q: Which of the following is NOT one of the valid ways to acquire Indian citizenship under the Citizenship Act, 1955?
qs.e: Under the Citizenship Act, 1955, there are five ways to acquire Indian citizenship: by birth, by descent, by registration, by naturalization, and by incorporation of territory. Marriage is not a direct mode of acquiring citizenship. A foreign woman marrying an Indian citizen may apply for citizenship through registration or naturalization, but marriage alone does not confer citizenship. Citizenship by birth is granted to persons born in India on or after January 26, 1950 (with some exceptions). Citizenship by descent is for children born outside India to Indian parents. Registration is available for certain categories like persons of Indian origin. Naturalization involves a formal process for foreigners. Incorporation of territory occurs when new land becomes part of India.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Citizenship Act enacted? → 1955
☛ How many modes of acquiring citizenship? → 5
☛ Does marriage automatically grant citizenship? → No
☛ Most common mode of citizenship? → By birth
☛ Constitutional provisions on citizenship? → Part II (Articles 5-11)

q: The term 'Armed Rebellion' was introduced under Article 352 of the Indian Constitution for the proclamation of a National Emergency by which Constitutional Amendment?
qs.e: Originally, Article 352 used the term 'internal disturbance' for proclamation of National Emergency. The 44th Amendment (1978) replaced it with 'armed rebellion' to prevent misuse. This amendment made it harder to impose emergency and added provisions for judicial review. Now, emergency can be declared only on grounds of war, external aggression, or armed rebellion, not internal disturbance. The change was recommended by the Swaran Singh Committee and enacted by the Morarji Desai government.
qs.kf:
☛ Which amendment replaced 'internal disturbance' with 'armed rebellion'? → 44th Amendment, 1978
☛ Under which Article is National Emergency proclaimed? → Article 352
☛ What was the original term in Article 352? → Internal disturbance
☛ Which government passed the 44th Amendment? → Morarji Desai government
☛ Which committee recommended the 44th Amendment changes? → Swaran Singh Committee

q: Words 'Integrity', 'Socialist' and 'Secular' were added to the Preamble of the Constitution of India by which of the following amendments?
qs.e: The words 'Socialist', 'Secular' and 'Integrity' were added to the Preamble of the Indian Constitution by the 42nd Amendment (1976). This amendment was enacted during the Prime Ministership of Indira Gandhi and is often called the 'Mini-Constitution'. It also added Fundamental Duties (Part IV-A).
