In the Preamble, 'Socialist' implies equality and social justice; 'Secular' means religious neutrality; and 'Integrity' signifies national unity. These words reflect the core philosophy of India. The amendment also modified Article 368, which deals with the amendment process. It was a comprehensive amendment that changed many provisions of the Constitution.
qs.kf:
☛ What is the 42nd Amendment known as? → Mini-Constitution
☛ How many times has the Preamble been amended? → Only once (by the 42nd Amendment)
☛ Which amendment added Fundamental Duties? → 42nd Amendment, 1976
☛ What does 'Socialist' mean in the Preamble? → Equality and social justice
☛ Which article was amended by the 42nd Amendment? → Article 368

q: Which of the following articles of the Constitution of India provides for the mechanism and power of Parliament to amend the Constitution?
qs.e: Article 368 of the Indian Constitution grants Parliament the power to amend the Constitution. This article details the amendment procedure, which involves introducing a bill in either House of Parliament and passing it with a special majority. Some amendments also require ratification by at least half of the state legislatures. It protects the basic structure of the Constitution, as established by the Supreme Court in the Kesavananda Bharati case. Other options: Article 372 deals with continuation of pre-existing laws, Article 362 deals with privileges of princely rulers, and Article 356 deals with President's rule.
qs.kf:
☛ Article related to constitutional amendment procedure → Article 368
☛ Majority required to pass an amendment bill → Two-thirds of members present and voting
☛ Amendments requiring state ratification → Those affecting federal structure, election of Governor, etc.
☛ Basic structure doctrine → Propounded in Kesavananda Bharati case (1973)
☛ Article 372 provision → Continuance of pre-existing laws

q: The amendment to the Karnataka Land Reforms Act, 1961, and the Karnataka Land Revenue Act, 1964, is known as:
o: Karnataka Land Reforms and Revenue Law (Amendment) Act, 2025
Karnataka Land Reforms and Certain Other Law (Amendment) Act, 2025
qs.e: The Karnataka government has amended the Karnataka Land Reforms Act, 1961 and the Karnataka Land Revenue Act, 1964 to simplify land reforms. This amendment is named the Karnataka Land Reforms and Certain Other Law (Amendment) Act, 2025. Its objective is to facilitate the use of agricultural land, land transactions, and revenue procedures. The act includes provisions to give farmers more flexibility in land transfers and to promote digitalization. This amendment is a significant step towards making the state's land administration more efficient and transparent.
qs.kf:
☛ Which acts are amended by the Karnataka Land Reforms and Certain Other Law (Amendment) Act, 2025? → Karnataka Land Reforms Act, 1961 and Karnataka Land Revenue Act, 1964
☛ What is the main objective of this amendment? → Simplify and make land administration transparent
☛ What benefit will farmers get under this amendment? → More flexibility in land transfers
☛ What provision is made to promote digitalization? → Digitalization of land records
☛ In which year was this amendment passed? → 2025

q: Which Amendment Act made elementary education a fundamental right under Article 21A, mandating free and compulsory education for all children aged 6 to 14 years?
qs.e: The 86th Amendment Act, 2002 of the Indian Constitution is known for making education a fundamental right. It inserted Article 21A, which provides free and compulsory education to all children aged 6 to 14 years. Along with this, Article 45 was modified to focus on early childhood care and education as a Directive Principle of State Policy. Additionally, a new fundamental duty under Article 51A(k) was added, making it the duty of parents to provide education opportunities to their children. This amendment was a historic step in bringing the right to education into the list of fundamental rights. The enabling legislation, the Right to Education (RTE) Act, was enacted in 2009 and came into effect on 1 April 2010.
qs.kf:
☛ Amendment that made education a fundamental right → 86th Amendment (2002)
☛ Age group for Article 21A → 6 to 14 years
☛ Law related to Right to Education → RTE Act, 2009
☛ Articles amended by 86th Amendment → 21A, 45, 51A
☛ RTE Act implementation date → 1 April 2010

q: Through which Constitutional Amendment were the Fundamental Duties incorporated into the Constitution?
qs.e: The Fundamental Duties were incorporated into the Indian Constitution through the 42nd Amendment (1976). This amendment was enacted during the Emergency period under the government of Indira Gandhi. Based on the recommendations of the Swaraj Singh Committee, 11 Fundamental Duties were defined for citizens. These duties are enshrined in Part IV-A of the Constitution under Article 51A. Originally, there were ten duties, but the 86th Amendment (2002) added a new duty related to providing opportunities for education to children between 6-14 years, raising the count to 11. Fundamental Duties serve as a reminder to citizens of their responsibilities towards the nation.
qs.kf:
☛ Which amendment added Fundamental Duties? → 42nd Amendment, 1976
☛ Which part of Constitution contains Fundamental Duties? → Part IV-A
☛ Which Article mentions Fundamental Duties? → Article 51A
☛ Total number of Fundamental Duties? → 11
☛ Which duty was added by 86th Amendment? → Duty to provide opportunities for education to children aged 6-14 years

q: The 97th Constitutional Amendment provided constitutional status to which of the following?
qs.e: The 97th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2011 granted constitutional status to cooperative societies in India. It added Part IX-B (Articles 243-ZH to 243-ZT) to the Constitution, which governs the formation, functioning, and management of cooperative societies. The amendment also modified Article 19(1)(c) to include the right to form cooperative societies as a fundamental right. Additionally, it inserted Article 43-B under the Directive Principles of State Policy, directing the state to promote voluntary formation of cooperative societies. This amendment aimed to strengthen the cooperative sector and ensure democratic and transparent functioning of cooperatives across the country.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the 97th Constitutional Amendment enacted? → 2011
☛ Which part of the Constitution deals with cooperative societies? → Part IX-B
☛ Which article was amended to include right to form cooperatives? → Article 19(1)(c)
☛ Which Directive Principle article was added for cooperatives? → Article 43-B
☛ What did the 97th Amendment grant constitutional status to? → Cooperative Societies

q: Under the Citizenship Act, 1955, which section governs the grant of citizenship when a new territory becomes part of India?
qs.e: Section 7 of the Citizenship Act, 1955 governs the grant of citizenship to persons who are residents of a new territory when that territory becomes part of India. This section is specifically designed for situations where a new territory (e.g., Goa, Puducherry) is incorporated into India. Upon such incorporation, the central government issues a notification specifying which persons from that territory shall be deemed citizens of India. This section differs from others like Section 5 (citizenship by registration) and Section 6 (citizenship by naturalization) as it is exclusively for territorial acquisitions.
qs.kf:
☛ Section for citizenship on new territory → Section 7
☛ Section for citizenship by registration → Section 5
☛ Section for citizenship by naturalization → Section 6
☛ Section for termination of citizenship → Section 9
☛ Total sections in Citizenship Act, 1955 → 18 sections

q: According to the Citizenship Act, 1955, a person born outside India on or after December 10, 1992, shall be a citizen of India by descent if:
o: Only the father is an Indian citizen
Only the mother is an Indian citizen
Both parents are ordinarily resident in India at the time of birth
Either parent is a citizen of India at the time of birth
qs.e: According to Section 4 of the Citizenship Act, 1955, a person born outside India on or after December 10, 1992, shall be a citizen of India by descent only if at the time of birth, either parent is a citizen of India. Prior to the 1992 amendment, only the father satisfied this condition, but the law was changed to ensure gender equality. This provision applies to individuals born abroad to at least one Indian parent. However, such birth must be registered with the Government of India. If both parents are Indian citizens, the condition still holds. This forms the basis of citizenship by descent under the Act.
qs.kf:
☛ Section 4 of Citizenship Act, 1955 → Deals with citizenship by descent
☛ Born after Dec 10, 1992 → Either parent must be an Indian citizen
☛ 1992 amendment → Changed from only father to either parent
☛ Citizenship by descent → Requires registration of birth
☛ Born outside India → This provision applies under the Act

q: The National Commission for Scheduled Tribes (NCST) was created by which Constitutional Amendment?
qs.e: The National Commission for Scheduled Tribes (NCST) was established by the 89th Constitutional Amendment in 2003. This amendment modified Article 338 to create a separate commission for Scheduled Tribes. Previously, there was a combined commission for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. The 89th Amendment split it into two distinct bodies: the National Commission for Scheduled Castes (Article 338) and the National Commission for Scheduled Tribes (Article 338A). The NCST is responsible for protecting the rights of Scheduled Tribes and advising the government on their welfare.
qs.kf:
☛ Year of NCST formation? → 2003
☛ Which constitutional article deals with NCST? → Article 338A
☛ Which commission existed for both SCs and STs before the 89th Amendment? → Combined National Commission for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes
☛ Which article governs the National Commission for Scheduled Castes? → Article 338
☛ Which new article was inserted by the 89th Amendment? → Article 338A

q: Which amendment made it constitutionally mandatory for municipalities to prepare “District Planning Committees” and “Metropolitan Planning Committees”?
qs.e: The 74th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992 deals with municipalities in India. It gave constitutional status to urban local bodies. This amendment mandated the formation of District Planning Committees (DPCs) and Metropolitan Planning Committees (MPCs) for municipalities. DPCs coordinate planning at the district level, while MPCs plan for metropolitan areas. These committees ensure coordination between rural and urban areas. The 74th Amendment added Part IX-A to the Constitution and includes the Twelfth Schedule, which lists 18 functions of municipalities. Other options: 73rd Amendment relates to Panchayati Raj; 97th Amendment to cooperative societies; 102nd Amendment to the National Commission for Backward Classes.
qs.kf:
☛ Which amendment deals with municipalities? → 74th Amendment
☛ How many functions are listed in the Twelfth Schedule? → 18 functions
☛ District Planning Committee operates at which level? → District level
☛ Metropolitan Planning Committee plans for which area? → Metropolitan area
☛ 73rd Amendment relates to which subject? → Panchayati Raj

q: Which constitutional amendment established an urban local government system in India in 1992?
qs.e: The 74th Constitutional Amendment Act of 1992 established the urban local government system in India. It added Part IX-A and the Twelfth Schedule to the Constitution. This act gave constitutional status to municipalities and defined their composition, powers, and functions. It created three types of municipalities: Municipal Corporations for large urban areas, Municipal Councils for smaller towns, and Nagar Panchayats for transitional areas from rural to urban. The act also mandated reservation of seats for women and Scheduled Castes/Scheduled Tribes in urban local bodies. This amendment was a major step towards strengthening urban local self-government in India.
qs.kf:
☛ 74th Amendment relates to? → Urban local self-government
☛ Part added by 74th Amendment? → Part IX-A
☛ Schedule added by 74th Amendment? → Twelfth Schedule
☛ 73rd Amendment relates to? → Panchayati Raj (Rural)
☛ Types of municipalities under 74th Amendment? → Three types

q: Which constitutional amendment reduced the Parliament’s approval period for National Emergency from two months to one month?
qs.e: The 44th Amendment Act of the Indian Constitution was enacted in 1978 by the Janata Party government. It brought significant changes to the emergency provisions. Previously, the proclamation of National Emergency required parliamentary approval within two months, which was reduced to one month. Additionally, it amended Article 359 to prevent the suspension of fundamental rights during emergency. This amendment aimed to prevent the misuse of emergency powers, as witnessed during the 1975-77 Emergency. It strengthened citizens' rights and limited the executive's authority. The 44th Amendment is considered a major reform to restore democratic safeguards and ensure checks and balances.
qs.kf:
☛ Which amendment reduced emergency approval period? → 44th Amendment, 1978
☛ What is the current approval period for National Emergency? → 30 days (1 month)
☛ Which articles were amended by the 44th Amendment? → Article 352 and 359
☛ Which government enacted the 44th Amendment? → Janata Party government
☛ Main objective of 44th Amendment? → To control emergency powers

q: Which provision addresses citizenship for persons who migrated from Pakistan before India's Constitution commencement?
qs.e: Article 6 of the Indian Constitution deals with citizenship for persons who migrated from Pakistan to India before the commencement of the Constitution. It was specifically designed for those displaced during the partition. Article 5 covers citizenship by birth or residence in India, Article 8 covers persons of Indian origin residing outside India, and Article 10 ensures continuation of rights of citizenship. Hence, the correct provision is Article 6.
qs.kf:
☛ Citizenship for migrants from Pakistan before Constitution → Article 6
☛ Citizenship for persons born in India → Article 5
☛ Citizenship for persons of Indian origin abroad → Article 8
☛ Continuation of rights of citizenship → Article 10
☛ Date of Constitution commencement → 26 January 1950

q: If the Government of India revokes the citizenship of an individual for acting against the interests of the country, which constitutional or statutory provision empowers it to do so?
qs.e: Section 10 of the Citizenship Act, 1955 empowers the government to revoke the citizenship of an individual if it was obtained by fraud, misrepresentation, or if the person has acted against the interests of the country. This provision specifically deals with revocation of citizenship. While Article 11 empowers Parliament to regulate citizenship through law, the specific mechanism for revocation is outlined in Section 10. Section 6A relates to the Assam Accord, and Article 5 defines citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution. Thus, the correct answer is Section 10.
qs.kf:
☛ Which section deals with revocation of citizenship? → Section 10 of the Citizenship Act, 1955
☛ What are grounds for revocation? → Fraud, misrepresentation, or acting against national interests
☛ What does Article 11 empower? → Parliament to make laws on citizenship
☛ What is Section 6A about? → Assam Accord
☛ What does Article 5 define? → Citizenship at commencement of Constitution

q: The Eighth Schedule of the Indian Constitution deals with which of the following subjects?
o: Allocation of seats in the Rajya Sabha
Distribution of powers between the Union and the States
qs.e: The Eighth Schedule of the Indian Constitution contains the list of languages recognized by the Constitution. Initially, there were 14 languages, but through amendments, the number has been increased to 22. These languages include Hindi, English, Urdu, Bengali, Tamil, Telugu, Marathi, Gujarati, Punjabi, Sanskrit, Malayalam, Odia, Kannada, Assamese, Kashmiri, Sindhi, Nepali, Maithili, Dogri, Konkani, Manipuri, and Santali. The purpose of the Eighth Schedule is to grant official recognition to these languages and promote their development. It is associated with Article 344(1) and Article 351 of the Constitution.
qs.kf:
☛ How many languages are in the Eighth Schedule? → 22
☛ Which languages were added most recently? → Santali, Dogri, Maithili, Bodo (by 92nd Amendment in 2004)
☛ Which article mentions the Eighth Schedule? → Article 344(1)
☛ Which language in the Eighth Schedule is not an official language? → English (it is an associate official language)
☛ Which is the official language? → Hindi

q: Which of the following introduced dyarchy by dividing subjects into Reserved and Transferred lists?
qs.e: The Government of India Act, 1919 (Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms) introduced dyarchy in the provinces. Under this system, subjects were divided into Reserved List (under the Governor) and Transferred List (under ministers). Reserved subjects included police, jails, land revenue, and justice, while transferred subjects included education, health, local self-government, and agriculture. This marked a significant step in administrative reforms, though it faced criticism for limited self-governance.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Act introduced dyarchy? → Government of India Act, 1919
☛ Which subject was in Reserved List under dyarchy? → Police
☛ Which subject was in Transferred List under dyarchy? → Education
☛ Where was dyarchy implemented? → In provinces
☛ What is another name for dyarchy reforms? → Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms

q: Which constitutional amendment to the Indian Constitution added the term 'Socialist' to the Preamble?
qs.e: The most comprehensive amendment to the Indian Constitution, the 42nd Amendment (1976), is also known as the 'Mini-Constitution'. It added the terms 'Socialist' and 'Secular' to the Preamble. Additionally, 'Unity of the Nation' was changed to 'Unity and Integrity of the Nation'. This amendment was passed by the Indira Gandhi government during the Emergency. It also made changes to Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles, such as adding Fundamental Duties (Part IV-A). Thus, the inclusion of 'Socialist' in the Preamble is a key feature of the 42nd Amendment.
qs.kf:
☛ Which amendment added 'Socialist' to the Preamble? → 42nd Amendment, 1976
☛ When was the 42nd Amendment enacted? → 1976
☛ What is the 42nd Amendment commonly called? → Mini-Constitution
☛ Which two words were added to the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment? → Socialist and Secular
☛ Who was the Prime Minister during the 42nd Amendment? → Indira Gandhi

q: Which of the following languages is NOT included in the Eighth Schedule of the Indian Constitution?
qs.e: The Eighth Schedule of the Indian Constitution includes 22 languages that are recognized for official purposes. These languages represent the linguistic diversity of India. Among the given options, Sanskrit, Urdu, and Nepali are listed in the Eighth Schedule. However, English is NOT included in the Eighth Schedule, even though it is used as an official language for many government and legal purposes. English was adopted as an associate official language for a transitional period but was never added to the Eighth Schedule. Therefore, English is the correct answer.
qs.kf:
☛ How many languages are in the Eighth Schedule? → 22
☛ Which is the oldest language in the Eighth Schedule? → Sanskrit
☛ Which amendments added new languages to the Eighth Schedule? → 71st and 92nd Amendments
☛ What do the Eighth Schedule languages represent? → India's linguistic diversity
☛ Why is English not in the Eighth Schedule? → It is a foreign language

q: What is the legal consequence if an Indian citizen voluntarily acquires the citizenship of a foreign country after the commencement of the Constitution?
o: He/She ceases to be an Indian citizen
Indian citizenship is suspended for three years
Citizenship is retained subject to conditions
qs.e: According to Article 9 of the Indian Constitution, if any person voluntarily acquires the citizenship of a foreign state after the commencement of the Constitution, they cease to be an Indian citizen. India follows the principle of single citizenship, not dual citizenship. This means an Indian citizen cannot hold citizenship of another country simultaneously. The Citizenship Act, 1955 also provides rules for termination of citizenship. The only exception is the Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) card, which is not full citizenship but a long-term visa.
qs.kf:
☛ Article 9 → Voluntary acquisition of foreign citizenship terminates Indian citizenship.
☛ Type of citizenship in India → Single Citizenship.
☛ OCI (Overseas Citizen of India) → Not full citizenship, only permanent residency.
☛ Citizenship Act, 1955 → Governs acquisition and termination of citizenship.
☛ Dual citizenship → Not permitted in India.

q: Which provision in Part II of the Constitution defines one basis for citizenship at the commencement, specifically that the person’s either parent was born in India?
qs.e: Part II of the Indian Constitution contains Articles 5 to 11, which deal with citizenship. Article 5 defines citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution (January 26, 1950). It states that a person born in India, whose either parent was born in India, or who has been ordinarily resident in India for at least five years immediately before the commencement, is a citizen. This provision establishes the basis for citizenship when the Constitution came into effect. Article 6 provides citizenship to migrants from Pakistan, Article 8 covers persons of Indian origin residing outside India, and Article 9 deals with loss of citizenship upon voluntarily acquiring foreign citizenship.
qs.kf:
☛ Which article defines citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution? → Article 5
☛ Under Article 5, what is the minimum period of residence required for citizenship? → 5 years
☛ How many articles are there in Part II of the Constitution? → Articles 5 to 11 (7 articles)
☛ Which article grants citizenship to migrants from Pakistan? → Article 6
☛ Which article deals with citizenship of persons of Indian origin residing abroad? → Article 8

q: Which constitutional article empowers the Indian Parliament to make laws regarding the acquisition and termination of Indian citizenship after the commencement of the Constitution of India?
qs.e: Article 11 of the Indian Constitution empowers the Parliament to make laws regarding the acquisition and termination of citizenship. While Articles 5 to 10 define citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution on 26 January 1950, Article 11 gives Parliament the authority to modify these provisions and enact new laws. Under this article, the Citizenship Act, 1955 was passed, which details the modes of acquiring citizenship by birth, descent, registration, naturalization, and territorial annexation, as well as termination of citizenship. This article ensures that the Parliament has comprehensive power to regulate citizenship matters as needed.
qs.kf:
☛ Under which article was the Citizenship Act, 1955 enacted? → Article 11
☛ Which articles deal with citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution? → Articles 5 to 10
☛ Which act governs citizenship by birth in India? → Citizenship Act, 1955
☛ Where is the provision for termination of Indian citizenship? → Citizenship Act, 1955
☛ Which part of the Constitution covers citizenship? → Part II (Articles 5-11)

q: According to the Constitution (One Hundred and Sixth Amendment) Act, 2023, what proportion of seats to be filled by direct election in the House of the People (Lok Sabha) is to be reserved for women?
qs.e: The Constitution (106th Amendment) Act, 2023, also known as the Nari Shakti Vandan Act, reserves one-third of the seats in the Lok Sabha and state legislative assemblies for women. This reservation applies to seats filled by direct election. Under this act, one-third of the seats reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes will also be reserved for women. The provision will come into effect after delimitation of constituencies. This amendment is a significant step towards women's political empowerment.
qs.kf:
☛ Which constitutional amendment is related to the Nari Shakti Vandan Act? → 106th Amendment
☛ What proportion of Lok Sabha seats are reserved for women under this act? → One-third
☛ Does this reservation also apply to state legislative assemblies? → Yes
☛ When will this reservation come into effect? → After delimitation
☛ Will there be women's reservation in SC/ST seats? → Yes, one-third

q: Which provisions were inserted into the Constitution by the 103rd Amendment Act, 2019, to enable reservation for Economically Weaker Sections (EWS)?
qs.e: The 103rd Amendment Act, 2019 introduced 10% reservation for the Economically Weaker Sections (EWS) of the general category in educational institutions and public employment. To enable this, Article 15(6) and Article 16(6) were inserted. Article 15(6) allows reservation in educational institutions, while Article 16(6) provides for reservation in public services. This reservation is over and above the existing reservation for SCs, STs, and OBCs. The benefit is available to persons with annual family income less than Rs. 8 lakh and certain asset limits.
qs.kf:
☛ When did the 103rd Amendment come into effect? → January 14, 2019
☛ What is the percentage of EWS reservation? → 10%
☛ EWS reservation is not applicable to which categories? → Already reserved categories (SC/ST/OBC)
☛ What is the maximum annual family income for EWS? → Rs. 8 lakh
☛ EWS reservation is included in which part of the Constitution? → Part III (Fundamental Rights)

q: Under the Constitution (101st Amendment) Act, 2016, who has the exclusive power to make laws on GST, where the supply of goods or services takes place in the course of interstate trade or commerce?
qs.e: The Constitution (101st Amendment) Act, 2016 introduced GST. Under this, the exclusive power to make laws on GST for interstate supply of goods or services lies with Parliament. Article 246A empowers both Parliament and State Legislatures to make laws on GST, but for interstate transactions, only Parliament can legislate. This comes under IGST (Integrated Goods and Services Tax), which is levied and collected by the Centre. States can only impose SGST on intrastate supplies. NITI Aayog or the President of India have no legislative power in this regard; the President only gives assent to bills. Parliament ensures a uniform tax structure across states for interstate trade.
qs.kf:
☛ Who imposes GST on interstate supply? → IGST (Central Government)
☛ Article for GST law-making power → 246A
☛ Full form of IGST → Integrated Goods and Services Tax
☛ Who imposes GST on intrastate supply? → State Government (SGST)
☛ Under which article is GST Council formed? → 279A

q: Which of the following Articles of the Constitution of India has Part XX that deals with the powers of the Parliament to amend the Constitution and its procedures?
qs.e: Part XX of the Indian Constitution consists of a single article, Article 368, which deals with the power of Parliament to amend the Constitution. It lays down the procedure for constitutional amendments, including the requirement that an amendment bill must be passed by each House of Parliament with a majority of total membership and a two-thirds majority of members present and voting. For certain amendments, ratification by at least half of the state legislatures is also required. Article 393 and 395 belong to the concluding parts of the Constitution, while Article 367 deals with interpretation.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Part of the Constitution deals with amendment? → Part XX
☛ What is the majority required for a constitutional amendment in Parliament? → Two-thirds of members present and voting
☛ Which Article provides the procedure for amendment? → Article 368
☛ Where is an amendment bill introduced? → In either House of Parliament
☛ When is state legislature ratification required? → When the amendment affects federal structure

q: What is the minimum length of residency required by the Indian Constitution for an individual of Indian descent to be eligible for registration as an Indian citizen?
qs.e: The Indian Constitution under Articles 5 to 11 provides for citizenship. Under the Citizenship Act, 1955, Section 5(1)(e), individuals of Indian descent residing abroad can acquire citizenship by registration. For this, they must have resided in India for a minimum of 7 years immediately before applying. This residency requirement is explicitly mentioned in the Act. Additionally, the person must not be in the service of the Indian government and must meet other eligibility criteria. This provision allows people of Indian origin to maintain a connection with India and regain citizenship if they wish. The 7-year period is a key eligibility condition for registration as a citizen.
qs.kf:
☛ Which section of Citizenship Act, 1955 applies to persons of Indian origin? → Section 5(1)(e)
☛ What is the minimum residency required for registration as citizen? → 7 years
☛ In which year was the Citizenship Act enacted? → 1955
☛ Which articles of the Constitution deal with citizenship? → Articles 5-11
☛ What are the three main ways to acquire Indian citizenship? → Birth, descent, and registration

q: Which of the following is India's 29th state?
qs.e: Telangana is India's 29th state, formed on 2 June 2014 after the bifurcation of Andhra Pradesh. It is the first state in India created not on linguistic basis but on regional and economic factors. The capital of Telangana is Hyderabad, which also serves as the capital of Andhra Pradesh. Before Telangana's formation, Andhra Pradesh itself was formed in 1956 on linguistic lines. The state came into existence due to the Telangana movement. Currently, India has 28 states and 8 union territories. The formation of Telangana added a new chapter to India's political map. This state is located in southern India and is known for its historical and cultural heritage.
qs.kf:
☛ India's 29th state → Telangana
☛ Formation day of Telangana → 2 June 2014
☛ Capital of Telangana → Hyderabad
☛ Telangana was separated from → Andhra Pradesh
☛ Total states in India → 28

q: Minimum support price is applied on the recommendation of _____.
qs.e: The Minimum Support Price (MSP) is announced by the government to ensure farmers get a minimum price for their produce. It is recommended by the Agricultural Costs and Prices Commission (CACP), a statutory body. CACP makes recommendations based on the cost of production and market prices. The main objective of MSP is to protect farmers from price fluctuations and ensure food security. Currently, MSP is applied to about 23 crops.
qs.kf:
☛ When was CACP established? → 1965
☛ Where is the headquarters of CACP? → New Delhi
☛ Who announces the MSP? → Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs
☛ How many crops are covered under MSP? → 23
☛ Who recommends MSP for Kharif crops? → CACP

q: The credit of proposing the first blueprint of Indian Planning is given to
qs.e: The credit of proposing the first blueprint of Indian Planning goes to M. Visvesvaraya. He published the book 'Planned Economy for India' in 1934, which is considered the first systematic proposal for economic planning in India. Visvesvaraya was a renowned engineer and statesman. He suggested a ten-year plan for the economic development of India. Before him, no other person had presented such a comprehensive economic framework. He is thus regarded as the father of Indian planning.
qs.kf:
☛ Who made the first blueprint of Indian planning? → M. Visvesvaraya
☛ Name of Visvesvaraya's book? → Planned Economy for India
☛ What duration plan did Visvesvaraya suggest? → Ten-year plan
☛ When was the Planning Commission established in India? → 1950
☛ When did the First Five-Year Plan start? → 1951

q: What is the principle to be followed in a cooperative society?
A. Multiple votes
B. One man one vote
C. No vote
D. One share one vote
qs.e: The core principle of a cooperative society is one member one vote. This ensures democratic control, where each member has equal voting rights regardless of the amount of capital or number of shares they hold. This distinguishes cooperatives from other business organizations like companies, where voting is based on shareholding. Multiple votes and one share one vote are against the cooperative principle. No vote is also incorrect because members must participate in decision-making. This principle is one of the cooperative principles recognized by the International Cooperative Alliance (ICA).
qs.kf:
☛ Basic principle of cooperative society → One member one vote
☛ Voting in cooperative society is based on → Membership, not shares
☛ Control of cooperative societies → Democratic
☛ Cooperative principles are formulated by → International Cooperative Alliance (ICA)
☛ One member one vote is applicable in → Cooperative society

q: Provincial Autonomy was provided by _______
A. The Government of India Act 1935
B. The Montague-Chelmsford Report
C. The Government of India Act 1919
D. The Indian Independence Act 1947
qs.e: The Government of India Act 1935 introduced provincial autonomy by abolishing dyarchy in the provinces. Under this Act, provincial governments gained full control over their subjects, and the Governor's powers were limited. It came into effect in 1937, and elections were held in the provinces. The Indian National Congress formed governments in most provinces. The Montagu-Chelmsford Report (1918) and the Government of India Act 1919 had introduced dyarchy, while the Indian Independence Act 1947 granted partition and independence.
qs.kf:
☛ Act that provided provincial autonomy → Government of India Act 1935
☛ Act that abolished dyarchy in provinces → Government of India Act 1935
☛ Year provincial autonomy was implemented → 1937
☛ System introduced by Government of India Act 1935 → Provincial autonomy
☛ System introduced by Government of India Act 1919 → Dyarchy

q: Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan is a Government of India flagship programme, making free and compulsory education to children in the age group of _______.
qs.e: Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (SSA) is a flagship programme of the Government of India that provides free and compulsory education to children in the age group of 6 to 14 years. Launched in 2001, its goal is the universalization of elementary education. The Right to Education (RTE) Act, 2009 gave legal backing to this initiative, making education a fundamental right for children aged 6-14. SSA focuses on improving the quality of education, with special emphasis on girls, Scheduled Castes and Tribes, and disadvantaged groups. The programme has significantly contributed to school infrastructure, teacher training, and curriculum development, aiming to bridge social and gender gaps in education.
qs.kf:
☛ When was Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan launched? → 2001
☛ In which year was the RTE Act enacted? → 2009
☛ What is the age group covered by RTE Act? → 6-14 years
☛ What is the main objective of SSA? → Universalization of elementary education
☛ Which groups are given special emphasis under SSA? → Girls, SC/ST, disadvantaged groups

q: Which one of the following provisions was a part of the Indian Independence Act of 1947?
o: India will be divided into two parts
India will become a part of Britain
All princely states will remain dependent on British
qs.e: The Indian Independence Act of 1947 provided for the partition of India into two independent dominions: India and Pakistan. This Act was passed by the British Parliament on 18 July 1947 and came into effect on 15 August 1947. It ended British rule in India and granted sovereignty to both dominions. The Act also allowed princely states to choose whether to join India or Pakistan. Additionally, it established the position of Governor-General for each dominion and empowered the respective Constituent Assemblies to frame their constitutions. The Act was a key step in the process of decolonization and laid the foundation for independent India and Pakistan.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Indian Independence Act passed? → 18 July 1947
☛ When did the Indian Independence Act come into effect? → 15 August 1947
☛ How many dominions were created under the Indian Independence Act? → India and Pakistan
☛ What option was given to princely states? → Join India or Pakistan
☛ Which position was provided for in the Indian Independence Act? → Governor-General

q: NCSM is an autonomous organization under Ministry of culture. What is the full form of NCSM?
qs.e: The full form of NCSM is National Council of Science Museums. It is an autonomous organization under the Ministry of Culture, responsible for managing science museums and science centers across India. NCSM was established in 1978 with its headquarters in Kolkata. It operates more than 25 science museums and centers nationwide, including the National Science Centre, Delhi and the Birla Industrial and Technological Museum, Kolkata. The organization promotes science communication and popularization among the public.
qs.kf:
☛ Headquarters of NCSM → Kolkata
☛ Establishment year of NCSM → 1978
☛ Total science centers under NCSM → More than 25
☛ NCSM comes under which ministry → Ministry of Culture
☛ Famous science museum in Delhi → National Science Centre

q: Which one of the following Committees in India is related to Tax reforms?
qs.e: The Raja Chelliah Committee was constituted in 1991 by the Government of India to recommend tax reforms. Chaired by Dr. Raja J. Chelliah, the committee focused on simplification of direct and indirect taxes, reduction in tax rates, and widening of the tax base. Its recommendations led to comprehensive tax reforms in the 1990s, including reduction in customs and excise duties. While the Meera Seth Committee deals with child labour, the Ghosh Committee deals with banking reforms, and the Anand Sinha Committee is related to the banking sector. The Raja Chelliah Committee remains a landmark in India's tax reform history.
qs.kf:
☛ Committee for Direct Tax Reforms → Raja Chelliah Committee
☛ Committee for Indirect Tax Reforms → Raja Chelliah Committee
☛ Year of formation of Raja Chelliah Committee → 1991
☛ Chairperson of Raja Chelliah Committee → Dr. Raja J. Chelliah
☛ Committee related to Child Labour → Meera Seth Committee

q: The Muslim League was founded in ________.
qs.e: The All-India Muslim League was founded on December 30, 1906 in Dhaka (now Bangladesh). Its objective was to safeguard the interests of Indian Muslims. Key founders included Nawab Salimullah Khan, Aga Khan, and Mohsin-ul-Mulk. It became a major political party in British India, later demanding the creation of Pakistan.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Muslim League founded? → 1906
☛ Who was the first president? → Sir Adamjee K. Mehta (temporary), later Aga Khan
☛ Who chaired the inaugural session in Dhaka? → Nawab Viqar-ul-Mulk
☛ What was the main aim of the Muslim League? → Protection of Muslim political and social interests
☛ Which movement did the Muslim League oppose? → Swadeshi Movement

q: In India, which of the following organisations is NOT exempted from RTI Act?
qs.e: Under Section 24 of the Right to Information (RTI) Act, 2005, certain intelligence and security agencies are exempted from the Act as listed in Schedule II. These include the Aviation Research Centre, Research and Analysis Wing (RAW), and Intelligence Bureau (IB). These organizations are not required to disclose information that could compromise national security, though they must still provide information related to corruption and human rights violations. On the other hand, the Competition Commission of India (CCI) is a statutory body established under the Competition Act, 2002. CCI is covered under the RTI Act and is not exempted. Hence, among the given options, CCI is the only organization that is NOT exempted from the RTI Act.
qs.kf:
☛ Section 24 of RTI Act → Provides exemption to certain intelligence agencies.
☛ Schedule II agencies → Include IB, RAW, ARC, etc.
☛ Competition Commission of India (CCI) → Comes under RTI, not exempted.
☛ CCI established under → Competition Act, 2002.
☛ RTI Act effective from → 12 October 2005.

q: Which of the following Acts ended the trade monopoly of the Company in India and opened it to all British subjects except tea?
qs.e: The Charter Act of 1813 ended the East India Company's trade monopoly in India, opening the country to all British subjects for trade, except for the monopoly on tea and trade with China. This act marked a significant shift in the Company's rule, allowing British merchants to access Indian markets. Additionally, it provided for educational and religious reforms in India. The act also asserted the sovereignty of the British Crown over Indian territories and allocated funds for the promotion of literature and science.
qs.kf:
☛ Which act ended the Company's monopoly over China trade? → Charter Act of 1833
☛ Which act abolished the Company's tea monopoly in India? → Charter Act of 1833
☛ Who was allowed to trade in India under the Charter Act of 1813? → All British subjects
☛ What monopoly did the Charter Act of 1813 retain? → Tea and China trade
☛ What dividend limit did the Charter Act of 1813 impose on the Company? → 10%

q: Which of the following state has announced to enact legislation for the 'right to water' to ensure availability of minimum 55 litres water in a day per person?
qs.e: The Madhya Pradesh government has announced the enactment of a law on 'right to water' to ensure the availability of a minimum of 55 litres of water per person per day. This move aims to promote water conservation and equitable distribution in the state. The bill intends to provide clean and adequate water to every citizen, benefiting regions facing water scarcity. The state government has also implemented several schemes under the Jal Jeevan Mission, focusing on household tap connections and rejuvenation of water sources. This initiative places Madhya Pradesh among the leading states in water security.
qs.kf:
☛ Minimum water per person per day → 55 litres
☛ State enacting right to water law → Madhya Pradesh
☛ Central mission for water conservation → Jal Jeevan Mission
☛ Objective of Jal Jeevan Mission → Tap connection to every household by 2024
☛ Chief Minister of Madhya Pradesh (2024) → Mohan Yadav

q: The financial powers of the chiefs of which Indian defence segments have been extended by the Home Ministry?
qs.e: The Home Ministry has enhanced the financial powers of the chiefs of Central Armed Police Forces (CAPF). This move aims to provide greater financial autonomy to the heads of forces like Border Security Force (BSF), Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF), Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP), Sashastra Seema Bal (SSB), and Central Industrial Security Force (CISF). This will increase administrative efficiency and help in quick decision-making during emergencies. This decision is a significant step towards strengthening national security.
qs.kf:
☛ Which forces' chiefs got enhanced financial powers by the Home Ministry? → Central Armed Police Forces (CAPF)
☛ Which forces are included in CAPF? → BSF, CRPF, ITBP, SSB, CISF
☛ Under which ministry does CAPF come? → Home Ministry
☛ Which is the largest Central Armed Police Force? → CRPF
☛ What is the main function of BSF? → To protect India's borders

q: During whose tenure was the Factory Act 1881 passed?
qs.e: The Factory Act of 1881 was passed during the tenure of Lord Ripon as Viceroy of India. This act was the first legislation in India aimed at improving labor conditions, particularly for child laborers. It restricted the working hours for children aged 7 to 12 years and mandated better working conditions in factories. The act was a significant step towards labor welfare and set a precedent for future labor laws in India.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the first Factory Act in India passed? → 1881
☛ Under which Viceroy was the Factory Act 1881 enacted? → Lord Ripon
☛ What was the main aim of the Factory Act 1881? → To regulate child labor
☛ Which age group of children was affected by the Factory Act 1881? → 7 to 12 years
☛ Which act is considered the beginning of labor legislation in India? → Factory Act 1881

q: The traditional glove puppet show Pavakoothu belongs to _______
qs.e: Pavakoothu is a traditional glove puppet show from Kerala, India. It is mainly practiced in the Palakkad district of Kerala. The puppets are made of wood and cloth and are worn on the hand like gloves. Performances depict mythological stories, especially from the Ramayana and Mahabharata. This art form is an important part of Kerala's rich folk tradition.
qs.kf:
☛ Pavakoothu is a glove puppet show from which state? → Kerala
☛ What type of puppets are used in Pavakoothu? → Glove puppets
☛ Which district is the main center of Pavakoothu? → Palakkad
☛ Which stories are performed in Pavakoothu? → Mythological, especially Ramayana and Mahabharata
☛ Pavakoothu is part of the folk tradition of which state? → Kerala

q: The separate country of India and Pakistan was formed under _______
qs.e: The formation of India and Pakistan as separate countries was carried out under the Indian Independence Act, 1947. This Act was passed by the Parliament of the United Kingdom and received royal assent on 18 July 1947. It granted independence to India on 15 August 1947 and provided for the partition of the two dominions. The Act repealed the previous Government of India Acts, including the Government of India Act, 1935, and served as an interim constitution. Under this Act, both India and Pakistan were granted the status of Dominions, with the British monarch as the head of state represented by Governor-Generals.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Indian Independence Act passed? → 1947
☛ Which Act did it replace? → Government of India Act, 1935
☛ When did India gain independence? → 15 August 1947
☛ When did Pakistan gain independence? → 14 August 1947
☛ What status was given to India under the Act? → Dominion

q: During the British rule, under which act was the establishment of a Dyarchy system in the Indian provinces?
qs.e: The Government of India Act 1919, also known as the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms, introduced the Dyarchy system in the provinces. Under this system, provincial subjects were divided into Reserved and Transferred categories. Reserved subjects like police, justice, and finance were controlled by the Governor, while transferred subjects like education, health, and local self-government were given to ministers responsible to the provincial legislature. This system aimed at gradual constitutional progress but was largely unsuccessful. The act also established a bicameral legislature at the centre and extended communal representation.
qs.kf:
☛ Which act introduced the Dyarchy system? → Government of India Act 1919
☛ What is the other name of Government of India Act 1919? → Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms
☛ How many subjects were transferred under Dyarchy? → 6 (Agriculture, Education, Health, Public Works, Local Self-Government, Industries)
☛ Who introduced the Dyarchy system? → Lord Chelmsford and Edwin Montagu
☛ When was the Dyarchy system abolished? → By the Government of India Act 1935

q: Which of the following act clarified the difference between the commercial and political functions of East India Company for the first time?
qs.e: The Pitts India Act of 1784 first clearly differentiated between the commercial and political functions of the East India Company. Under this act, the Board of Control was created to handle political matters, representing the British government, while the Court of Directors remained in charge of commercial affairs. This act established greater control of the British government over the company's administration and laid the foundation for dual governance. It was passed during the administration of Lord North and was the first law to formally separate the company's functions into two distinct domains.
qs.kf:
☛ Which act created the Board of Control? → Pitts India Act 1784
☛ Which act first separated the commercial and political functions of the East India Company? → Pitts India Act 1784
☛ Which act introduced dual governance in India? → Pitts India Act 1784
☛ When was the Pitts India Act passed? → 1784
☛ Who was the head of the Board of Control? → The British Finance Minister

q: Which of the following departments does not come under the Ministry of Finance?
o: Department of Industrial Policy and Promotion
qs.e: Under the Ministry of Finance, Government of India, there are five departments - Department of Economic Affairs, Department of Expenditure, Department of Revenue, Department of Financial Services, and Department of Investment and Public Asset Management (DIPAM). The Department of Industrial Policy and Promotion (DIPP) does not fall under the Ministry of Finance; it comes under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry. DIPP deals with industrial policy, foreign direct investment (FDI), and technology transfer. The other departments under the Ministry of Finance handle economic policy, government expenditure, tax collection, and disinvestment of public sector undertakings respectively.
qs.kf:
☛ How many departments are under the Ministry of Finance? → 5
☛ What is the full form of DIPP? → Department of Industrial Policy and Promotion
☛ Under which ministry does DIPP come? → Ministry of Commerce and Industry
☛ Which is the oldest department under the Ministry of Finance? → Department of Revenue
☛ Which department is not under the Ministry of Finance? → Department of Industrial Policy and Promotion

q: Government of India Act 1919 was implemented due to which constitutional reform?
qs.e: The Government of India Act 1919 was implemented as a result of the Montague-Chelmsford Reforms. These reforms were based on the report of the then Secretary of State for India, Edwin Montague, and the Viceroy, Lord Chelmsford. The Act introduced dyarchy (dual government) in the provinces, dividing subjects into reserved and transferred categories. At the centre, a bicameral legislature was established, consisting of the Council of State and the Legislative Assembly. For the first time, the Act recognized communal electorates, which fostered communalism. The Act came into effect in 1921 and remained in force until the 1935 Act.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Act introduced Dyarchy? → Government of India Act 1919
☛ When was the Montague-Chelmsford Report published? → 1918
☛ What type of legislature was established at the centre by the Act of 1919? → Bicameral
☛ Dyarchy is associated with which level of government? → Provincial government
☛ When did the Government of India Act 1919 come into force? → 1921

q: Which charter law eliminated the East India Company's monopoly business in India?
qs.e: The Charter Act of 1813 ended the East India Company's monopoly over trade in India, except for tea and trade with China. The act renewed the Company's charter for 20 years but opened Indian trade to other British merchants. While the Company retained its political and administrative powers, the act marked a significant shift towards free trade. It also permitted Christian missionaries to operate in India and allocated funds for educational purposes. This act was passed by the British Parliament and reflected the growing influence of industrialists who opposed the Company's monopoly.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Charter Act ended the East India Company's trade monopoly? → Charter Act 1813 (except tea and China trade)
☛ For how many years was the Company's charter renewed by the Charter Act 1813? → 20 years
☛ Which act allowed Christian missionaries to enter India? → Charter Act 1813
☛ What sum was allocated for education by the Charter Act 1813? → 1 lakh rupees
☛ Under whose Prime Ministership was the Charter Act 1813 passed? → Lord Liverpool

q: Which Act abolished the double government in India?
qs.e: The Government of India Act 1858 abolished the double government in India. This act ended the Company rule and transferred the governance of India directly to the British Crown. It changed the title of Governor General to Viceroy and created the new position of Secretary of State for India. This act was enacted after the Revolt of 1857 and gave the Secretary of State authority over Indian affairs.
qs.kf:
☛ Act passed after the Revolt of 1857 → Government of India Act 1858
☛ Act that ended Company rule → Government of India Act 1858
☛ Act that changed Governor General to Viceroy → Government of India Act 1858
☛ Act that created Secretary of State for India → Government of India Act 1858
☛ Act that abolished double government → Government of India Act 1858

q: In which year was the Pitt's India Act passed?
qs.e: The Pitt's India Act was passed by the British Parliament in 1784. It is also known as the India Act 1784. The act aimed to reform the administration of the East India Company. It sought to separate the company's political and commercial functions. Under this act, the Board of Control was established to supervise the company's affairs. This act was introduced to address the shortcomings of the Regulating Act of 1773.
qs.kf:
☛ In which year was the Pitt's India Act passed? → 1784
☛ Which body was established under the Pitt's India Act? → Board of Control
☛ What was the objective of the Pitt's India Act? → Reform company administration and separate political-commercial functions
☛ Which act's shortcomings did the Pitt's India Act address? → Regulating Act of 1773
☛ What is the alternative name for the Pitt's India Act? → India Act 1784

q: Reducing penalties without changing the nature of penalties is known as ___________.
qs.e: Penalties Forgive refers to reducing penalties without changing their nature. In legal and administrative contexts, this means the offender receives a lighter punishment of the same type, such as reducing a 10- year sentence to 5 years. It differs from departure (complete forgiveness), reduction (lowering fines), and punishment (generic term). The concept is often applied by executive authorities to show leniency while maintaining the original penalty category. An example is remission of prison time. Understanding these distinctions is important for competitive exams.
qs.kf:
☛ Penalties Forgive → Reducing penalties without changing their nature
☛ Departure → Complete forgiveness of penalty
☛ Reduction → Lowering the amount of fine
☛ Punishment → General term for penalty
☛ Executive authorities grant clemency → Penalties Forgive often involves government officials

q: In which act is the system of open competition selected for the selection of government employees introduced?
qs.e: The Charter Act of 1853 introduced the system of open competition for the selection of civil servants in India for the first time. Earlier, appointments were made through influence or patronage. This act also added two legal members to the Governor-General's Council and extended the charter of the East India Company indefinitely (though it was soon revoked). The actual competitive exams were implemented later in 1854 based on the recommendations of the Macaulay Committee.
qs.kf:
☛ Which act introduced open competition for civil services? → Charter Act 1853
☛ Who recommended competitive exams for Indian civil services? → Macaulay Committee (1854)
☛ In which year was the Macaulay Report submitted? → 1854
☛ Which act extended the East India Company's charter indefinitely? → Charter Act 1853
☛ How many legal members were added to Governor-General's Council in 1853? → 2

q: Who was given full authority over the Indian administration after the Act of 1858 for the Better Government of India?
qs.e: The Act of 1858 for the Better Government of India ended the rule of the East India Company and transferred the administration of India directly to the British Crown. Under this act, the governance of India was now carried out in the name of the British monarch. The Secretary of State for India was designated to control Indian administration on behalf of the Crown, but the supreme authority remained with the Crown itself. The Governor General was given the title of Viceroy, acting as the Crown's representative, not an independent ruler. Thus, after the Act of 1858, full authority over Indian administration was vested in the British Crown.
qs.kf:
☛ What was the main effect of the 1858 Act? → End of East India Company rule and direct rule by the British Crown
☛ Who became the first Viceroy of India? → Lord Canning
☛ Which act created the Secretary of State for India? → The Act of 1858 for the Better Government of India
☛ Who was the representative of the British Crown in India? → Viceroy
☛ What is the 1858 Act also known as? → Government of India Act 1858

q: Who wrote "Our Sonar Bangla"?
qs.e: "Amar Sonar Bangla" ("Our Golden Bengal") was written by Rabindranath Tagore in 1905, which later became the national anthem of Bangladesh. This song was composed in protest of the Partition of Bengal. Tagore also composed its tune himself. The song is in Bengali and was first sung at a public gathering in Calcutta. After Bangladesh's independence in 1971, the song was adopted as the national anthem. Tagore is Asia's first Nobel laureate.
qs.kf:
☛ Who composed "Jana Gana Mana"? → Rabindranath Tagore
☛ For which work did Tagore win the Nobel Prize? → Gitanjali
☛ Where was Tagore born? → Kolkata
☛ What is Tagore's title? → Gurudev
☛ In which year did the Partition of Bengal occur? → 1905

q: The demand for a constitutional meeting is accepted in the form of a theory, it is called ______.
qs.e: The August Offer of 1940 was a proposal by the British government to the Indian National Congress during World War II. For the first time, it theoretically accepted the demand for a constituent assembly. However, it included conditions such as framing the constitution only after the war and requiring the consent of minorities, which the Congress rejected. The offer was presented by Viceroy Lord Linlithgow and is known as the 'August Offer'. It laid the foundation for the process of constitution-making in India.
qs.kf:
☛ Who presented the August Offer? → Lord Linlithgow
☛ What year was the August Offer made? → 1940
☛ What demand was theoretically accepted in the August Offer? → Formation of a constituent assembly
☛ Which proposal is called the 'August Offer'? → The proposal of 1940
☛ Who rejected the August Offer? → Indian National Congress

q: In which field do the government own the highest assets and provide all the services?
qs.e: In the public sector, the government owns the highest assets and provides all services. It includes government-owned enterprises, infrastructure like railways, postal service, defense, education, and healthcare. The government controls and invests in these areas to ensure public welfare. In foreign direct investment, private sector, and public-private partnerships, government ownership is limited. In India, the public sector also extends to industries like coal, oil, banking, and insurance.
qs.kf:
☛ Public sector ownership → Government holds maximum assets and services
☛ Private sector → Owned by individuals or companies
☛ Foreign Direct Investment → Investment by foreign companies
☛ Public-Private Partnership → Collaboration between government and private sector
☛ Examples of public sector in India → Railways, Post, Defense, Education

q: Which of the following was adopted in the emblem of Government of India from the Maurya dynasty?
qs.e: The emblem of Government of India features four lions adopted from the Maurya dynasty. This emblem is derived from the Lion Capital of Ashoka at Sarnath, built by Emperor Ashoka. The four lions stand back to back on a circular abacus, symbolizing power, courage, confidence and pride. The base contains an Ashoka Chakra and other animals. It was officially adopted on 24 January 1950. Other options include chariot wheel, horse, and the words 'Satyameva Jayate', but the central motif is the four lions.
qs.kf:
☛ From where is India's national emblem taken? → Lion Capital of Ashoka at Sarnath
☛ How many lions are there in the emblem? → Four
☛ When was the emblem adopted? → 24 January 1950
☛ What is the motto written below the emblem? → Satyameva Jayate
☛ Where is the Ashoka Pillar located? → Sarnath, Uttar Pradesh

q: Which of the following Acts transferred the power from the British East India Company to the British Crown in India?
qs.e: The Government of India Act, 1858 transferred power from the East India Company to the British Crown, establishing direct British rule in India. Under this Act, the Governor-General of India was given the title of 'Viceroy'. Lord Canning became the first Viceroy. This Act was passed after the Revolt of 1857 and brought Indian princely states under the sovereignty of the British Crown. It also abolished the Board of Control and the Court of Directors.
qs.kf:
☛ Which Act established direct British rule in India? → Government of India Act, 1858
☛ Under which Act did the Governor-General become Viceroy? → Government of India Act, 1858
☛ Who was the first Viceroy of India? → Lord Canning
☛ After which event was the Government of India Act, 1858 passed? → Revolt of 1857
☛ Which Act ended the rule of the East India Company? → Government of India Act, 1858

q: Social or Collective Ownership, Central Planning Authority and Social Welfare are the features of which type of economy?
qs.e: A socialist economy is characterized by social or collective ownership of the means of production. Resource allocation is done by a central planning authority, usually under government control. The primary objective is social welfare rather than profit maximization. Socialism ensures equitable distribution of income and the government runs welfare schemes like health and education. Unlike capitalism, which prioritizes individual profit, socialism focuses on collective well-being. Communism also involves collective ownership but aims for a classless society and the eventual withering away of the state, whereas socialism retains the state as a key player in planning and welfare.
qs.kf:
☛ Who owns resources in a socialist economy? → Social or collective ownership
☛ Who allocates resources in socialism? → Central planning authority
☛ What is the main goal of socialism? → Social welfare
☛ Key difference between capitalism and socialism? → Capitalism: individual profit; Socialism: collective good
☛ Which schemes are common in socialism? → Health, education, and welfare schemes

q: Which state was carved out of Assam as an autonomous state in 1970?
qs.e: Meghalaya was carved out of Assam as an autonomous state on 2 April 1970. Later, on 21 January 1972, it was granted full statehood, becoming the 21st state of India. The creation of Meghalaya aimed to provide a distinct identity to the Khasi, Jaintia, and Garo tribes. Its area is about 22,429 sq km and the capital is Shillong. Among the options, Manipur, Tripura, and Nagaland were also formed at different times, but Meghalaya was the one carved out in 1970.
qs.kf:
☛ When was Meghalaya made an autonomous state? → 2 April 1970
☛ When did Meghalaya get full statehood? → 21 January 1972
☛ What is the capital of Meghalaya? → Shillong
☛ Which are the major tribes of Meghalaya? → Khasi, Jaintia, Garo
☛ Which number state is Meghalaya? → 21st state

q: The Indian Councils Act of 1909 is also known as ________.
qs.e: The Indian Councils Act of 1909 is also known as the Morley-Minto Reforms. This act was enacted during British rule in India, expanding the legislative councils. It introduced communal representation by creating separate electorates for Muslims. The act was named after the then Secretary of State for India Lord Morley and Viceroy Lord Minto. It increased the number of Indian members in legislative councils, but was limited as most members were still appointed by the government. This reform was an attempt to grant partial political rights to Indians. The act also allowed members to ask supplementary questions and move resolutions, but control remained with the British. It was a significant step in the constitutional development of India.
qs.kf:
☛ What is the 1909 Act known as? → Morley-Minto Reforms
☛ What policy was introduced? → Communal representation
☛ Who was the Viceroy? → Lord Minto
☛ Who was the Secretary of State? → Lord Morley
☛ What was the main objective? → Grant political rights to Indians

q: Which of the following is a characteristic of rural settlements in India?
o: Economic activities are mainly based on tertiary sector
qs.e: Rural settlements in India are characterized by limited access to infrastructure such as roads, electricity, education, and healthcare facilities. Economic activities are predominantly based on the primary sector (agriculture, livestock). Population density is low, and high-rise buildings are absent. About 65% of India's population resides in rural areas. Rural settlements often feature kutcha houses and a traditional lifestyle. The tertiary sector is not dominant, unlike urban areas.
qs.kf:
☛ Main economic activity in rural settlements → Primary sector (agriculture)
☛ Population density in rural settlements → Low
☛ Infrastructure status in rural areas → Limited
☛ Percentage of rural population in India → About 65%
☛ Type of housing in rural settlements → Mostly kutcha houses

q: In 1919, when the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms were introduced in India, Lord Chelmsford was the:
qs.e: When the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms (officially the Government of India Act 1919) were introduced in India in 1919, Lord Chelmsford was the Viceroy of India. He served in this position from 1916 to 1921. These reforms are known for introducing the dyarchy system in provinces, dividing subjects into reserved and transferred categories. The Secretary of State for India at that time was Edwin Montagu, who collaborated with Lord Chelmsford to prepare the reform report, known as the Montagu-Chelmsford Report, in 1918.
qs.kf:
☛ Government of India Act 1919 → Based on Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms
☛ Dyarchy → Division of executive departments in provinces
☛ Edwin Montagu → Secretary of State for India (1917-1922)
☛ Lord Chelmsford → Viceroy of India (1916-1921)
☛ Montagu-Chelmsford Report → Published in 1918

q: Which commission was appointed to study the reforms of the Government of India Act, 1919, and suggest further measures for constitutional reforms?
qs.e: The British government appointed the Simon Commission in 1928 to study the implementation of the Government of India Act, 1919 (Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms) and suggest further constitutional reforms. The commission was headed by Sir John Simon and consisted of seven British members. Due to the absence of any Indian member, it was boycotted by the Indian National Congress and the Muslim League. The commission submitted its report in 1930, recommending the abolition of diarchy and the introduction of provincial autonomy. This report formed the basis of the Government of India Act, 1935. Other options: Chatfield Commission was related to defense reforms, Hunter Commission to education reforms, and Floud Commission to naval reforms.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the chairman of the Simon Commission? → Sir John Simon
☛ When did the Simon Commission arrive in India? → 1928
☛ When was the Simon Commission report submitted? → 1930
☛ Which major parties boycotted the Simon Commission? → Indian National Congress and Muslim League
☛ Which act was based on the Simon Commission recommendations? → Government of India Act, 1935

q: An area with a population of over 1 million is classified as a _______.
qs.e: According to the Census of India 2011, an urban area with a population of more than 1 million (10 lakh) is classified as a metropolitan city. These are large urban agglomerations that may include one or more districts. Currently, India has 53 metropolitan cities. The term 'mega city' is used for cities with a population over 10 million (1 crore). A 'district town' is the administrative headquarters of a district, while a 'suburban area' refers to the outer part of a city.
qs.kf:
☛ Most populous metropolitan city in India → Mumbai
☛ Number of metropolitan cities as per Census 2011 → 53
☛ Population threshold for a mega city → over 10 million (1 crore)
☛ Delhi is classified as which type → metropolitan city
☛ Who determines metropolitan cities in India → Census of India

q: Who made the first official demand for the partition of Bengal?
qs.e: The partition of Bengal was carried out in 1905 by Lord Curzon, who was the then Viceroy of India. He proposed the partition on administrative grounds, but the real motive was to weaken the rising nationalist movement in Bengal and divide the Hindus and Muslims. The partition came into effect on 16 October 1905, dividing Bengal into Eastern and Western parts. This sparked widespread protests, leading to the Swadeshi and Boycott movements. The partition was finally annulled in 1911 during the viceroyalty of Lord Hardinge.
qs.kf:
☛ Date of Partition of Bengal → 16 October 1905
☛ Viceroy who annulled Partition → Lord Hardinge
☛ Viceroy at the time of Partition → Lord Curzon
☛ Leaders of Swadeshi movement → Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Lala Lajpat Rai, Bipin Chandra Pal
☛ Partition of Bengal annulled → 12 December 1911

q: Which of the following Acts ended the company rule in India?
qs.e: The Government of India Act, 1858 ended the rule of the British East India Company and transferred the governance of India directly to the British Crown. This act is also known as the 'Act for the Better Government of India'. It replaced the position of Governor-General with that of Viceroy, and Lord Canning became the first Viceroy. The act abolished the Board of Control and the Court of Directors, and established the Council of India headed by the Secretary of State. This act was passed after the Revolt of 1857, with the aim of establishing direct control of the British government over India.
qs.kf:
☛ Which act was passed after the Revolt of 1857? → Government of India Act, 1858
☛ What was the new title of the Governor-General under the Government of India Act, 1858? → Viceroy
☛ Which bodies were abolished by the Government of India Act, 1858? → Board of Control and Court of Directors
☛ Which council was established by the Government of India Act, 1858? → Council of India
☛ What is the Government of India Act, 1858 also known as? → Act for the Better Government of India

q: How many small states of present-day Odisha were integrated into the Indian Union at the time of Partition?
qs.e: At the time of India's Partition, 26 small princely states in the present-day Odisha region were integrated into the Indian Union. These states were not under direct British rule but were governed by local rulers. After independence in 1947, under the leadership of Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, these states merged with India. The state of Odisha was originally formed on 1 April 1936, but its current shape emerged after the merger of these 26 princely states following Partition. This integration was a crucial part of India's unification process.
qs.kf:
☛ When was Odisha state formed? → 1 April 1936
☛ What was the first capital of Odisha? → Cuttack
☛ How many princely states were integrated into Odisha? → 26
☛ Who played a key role in the integration of princely states? → Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel
☛ In which year did present-day Odisha come into existence? → 1949

q: What legal document allowed Princely States to join either India or Pakistan after independence?
qs.e: Under the Indian Independence Act 1947, princely states were given the choice to join either India or Pakistan by signing the Instrument of Accession. This legal document allowed a state to accede to the dominion, surrendering control over only three subjects: defence, foreign affairs, and communications. The Instrument of Accession was the basis for the political integration of India, led by Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel. Most states signed it voluntarily, though some like Junagadh and Hyderabad had to be merged later. The process ensured India's territorial integrity.
qs.kf:
☛ Which act provided for the Instrument of Accession? → Indian Independence Act 1947
☛ Who played the key role in integrating princely states? → Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel
☛ Which three subjects were covered in the Instrument of Accession? → Defence, Foreign Affairs, Communications
☛ Which princely state signed the first Instrument of Accession? → Bilaspur (October 1947)
☛ Which state acceded later due to special circumstances? → Jammu and Kashmir (26 October 1947)

q: Which of the following was the first state to be formed on linguistic basis after severe agitation and the death of a protester?
qs.e: Andhra Pradesh was the first state to be formed on a linguistic basis. The creation of Andhra State in 1953, carved out of the Madras State, followed the death of Potti Sriramulu on 15 December 1952 after a 58-day hunger strike demanding a separate state for Telugu-speaking people. His death sparked widespread protests, forcing the Indian government to announce the formation of a linguistic state. This event set a precedent for the reorganization of states along linguistic lines, culminating in the States Reorganisation Act of 1956, which redefined state boundaries. Andhra Pradesh thus became the first state created primarily due to linguistic agitation.
qs.kf:
☛ First state formed on linguistic basis in India? → Andhra Pradesh
☛ Who died during the agitation for Andhra state? → Potti Sriramulu
☛ When did Potti Sriramulu die? → 15 December 1952
☛ When was Andhra State formed? → 1 October 1953
☛ Which commission recommended linguistic reorganization of states? → States Reorganisation Commission (1956)

q: The Right to Public Services legislation was first introduced by which Indian state?
qs.e: The Right to Public Services legislation ensures timely delivery of government services to citizens. It was first introduced by the Indian state of Madhya Pradesh in 2010, followed by several other states. The law aims to enhance transparency and accountability in public administration. Madhya Pradesh's act, known as the Madhya Pradesh Lok Sewaon Ke Pradan Ki Guarantee Adhiniyam, set a precedent for other states like Karnataka and Maharashtra to enact similar laws. Bihar also implemented it in 2011, making it the second state to do so. This legislation is considered a landmark in governance reforms in India.
qs.kf:
☛ First state to enact Right to Public Services Act → Madhya Pradesh (2010)
☛ Second state to enact Right to Public Services Act → Bihar (2011)
☛ Main objective of Right to Public Services Act → Timely delivery of services and accountability
☛ First country to enact Right to Public Services Act → India
☛ Year of Madhya Pradesh Right to Public Services Act → 2010

q: Which military operation was launched to integrate Hyderabad into India in 1948?
qs.e: In 1948, the Government of India launched Operation Polo to integrate the princely state of Hyderabad into India. The operation lasted from 13 to 17 September 1948. The Nizam of Hyderabad had refused to accede to India and wanted to remain independent. The Indian government decided on a military action. The operation was led by Major General J.N. Chaudhuri. The Indian Army swiftly captured Hyderabad and forced the Nizam to surrender. Subsequently, Hyderabad became an integral part of India.
qs.kf:
☛ When was Operation Polo conducted? → 13-17 September 1948
☛ Who led Operation Polo? → Major General J.N. Chaudhuri
☛ What was the name of the Nizam of Hyderabad? → Osman Ali Khan
☛ In which year was Hyderabad integrated into India? → 1948
☛ Who was the Home Minister of India at the time of Hyderabad's integration? → Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel

q: Which leader played the most crucial role in integrating princely states into India postindependence?
qs.e: After independence, India had over 562 princely states that needed to be integrated into the Indian Union. This crucial task was assigned to the then Home Minister, Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel. He used a combination of diplomacy, pressure, and agreements to ensure the merger of almost all princely states. For his role, he is called the Iron Man of India and the Architect of India's Unity. Sardar Patel, along with V.P. Menon, drafted the instruments of accession and convinced the rulers to join India. In cases like Hyderabad and Junagadh, military action had to be taken. His efforts ensured a unified nation.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the Home Minister during the integration of princely states? → Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel
☛ What title is Sardar Patel known by? → Iron Man of India
☛ Who assisted Sardar Patel in the integration of states? → V.P. Menon
☛ Which princely state was integrated through military action? → Hyderabad
☛ Which princely state was the first to accede to India? → Travancore

q: Which of the following is an example of social legislation introduced by the British during the colonial period in India?
qs.e: During the British colonial period, several social reform laws were introduced, one of which was the Widow Remarriage Act, 1856. This act was passed during the tenure of Lord Dalhousie and legally permitted Hindu widows to remarry. The reform was driven by social reformers like Raja Ram Mohan Roy and Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar. The Rowlatt Act and Vernacular Press Act were repressive laws, while the Indian Councils Act dealt with constitutional reforms. Only the Widow Remarriage Act was a social legislation aimed at improving women's rights.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Widow Remarriage Act passed? → 1856
☛ Which social reformer played a key role in enacting this act? → Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar
☛ Which community's widows were given the right to remarry under this act? → Hindu
☛ Which act promoted women's education during British rule? → Establishment of Bethune School (1849)
☛ Under which act was the practice of Sati banned? → Bengal Sati Regulation, 1829

q: Which Ministry is primarily responsible for implementing most rural development schemes in India?
o: Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment
Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare
qs.e: The primary responsibility for implementing most rural development schemes in India lies with the Ministry of Rural Development. This ministry designs and executes programs aimed at poverty alleviation, livelihood enhancement, infrastructure development, and social security in rural areas. Key schemes include Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA), Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana-Gramin (PMAY-G), Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (PMGSY), Deendayal Antyodaya Yojana-National Rural Livelihoods Mission (DAY-NRLM), and Deen Dayal Upadhyaya Grameen Kaushalya Yojana (DDU-GKY). The ministry coordinates with state governments and Panchayati Raj institutions to ensure effective implementation of these programs.
qs.kf:
☛ Primary objective of Ministry of Rural Development → Rural poverty alleviation and sustainable livelihood
☛ Guaranteed employment days under MGNREGA → 100 days per year
☛ Financial assistance under PMAY-G → ₹1.20 lakh in plain areas and ₹1.30 lakh in hilly areas
☛ Full form of DAY-NRLM → Deendayal Antyodaya Yojana - National Rural Livelihoods Mission
☛ Social security scheme under Ministry of Rural Development → Indira Gandhi National Old Age Pension Scheme (IGNOAPS)

q: Which of the following was one of the last princely states to join the Indian Union?
qs.e: Hyderabad was one of the last princely states to join the Indian Union. Its merger took place on 17 September 1948 through Operation Polo.
