Modern manufacturing was limited to a few sectors, and widespread industrialization did not occur in rural India. Thus, the decline of traditional industries was a deliberate strategy of British rule.
qs.kf:
☛ Impact of British policy on Indian handicraft industry → Systematic decline
☛ Traditional textile export centers in British India → Surat, Murshidabad, Dhaka
☛ Main objective of British colonial policy in India → Make India a source of raw materials and market for finished goods
☛ Consequence of decline of traditional Indian industries → Increased unemployment and poverty
☛ Which industry survived under British rule → Some agro-based industries

q: Privatisation under the 1991 reforms primarily involved:
o: selling government shares in public sector enterprises
qs.e: Privatisation under the 1991 economic reforms primarily involved the sale of government stakes in public sector undertakings (PSUs) to the private sector. This reduced government ownership and control, aiming to improve efficiency, foster competition, and reduce fiscal deficits. It was a key pillar of the New Economic Policy (NEP) 1991, along with liberalisation and globalisation. Increasing agricultural subsidies or reducing bank interest rates are separate policy measures, not part of privatisation. Nationalisation (bringing private companies under government control) is the opposite of privatisation. The disinvestment process began gradually, with the government selling minority stakes in many PSUs to raise revenue and enhance performance.
qs.kf:
☛ What are the three pillars of 1991 NEP? → Liberalisation, Privatisation, Globalisation
☛ What was the main objective of privatisation in India? → Improve efficiency of public sector
☛ In which year did economic reforms start in India? → 1991
☛ What is sold in PSUs under privatisation? → Government shares
☛ What is the antonym of privatisation? → Nationalisation

q: Which institution played a key role in influencing the structural reforms of the industrial sector in India post 1991?
qs.e: In 1991, India faced a severe balance of payments crisis. To address this, the Indian government sought loans from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank. As a condition for these loans, India was required to implement structural reforms. These reforms included dismantling the license raj, encouraging foreign investment, reducing the role of the public sector, and simplifying regulations. Thus, the IMF and World Bank played a decisive role in influencing the structural reforms of the industrial sector in post-1991 India. NABARD is related to agriculture, WTO to international trade, and RBI to monetary policy.
qs.kf:
☛ Chief architect of 1991 economic reforms → Manmohan Singh
☛ When was New Industrial Policy (NIP) announced → 24 July 1991
☛ Full form of FDI → Foreign Direct Investment
☛ Sector most affected by liberalization → Industrial sector
☛ Headquarters of World Bank → Washington D.C.

q: Which of the following is considered a major social development outcome of India’s economic reforms since 1991?
qs.e: The economic reforms of 1991 accelerated India's economic growth, leading to expanded access to healthcare services and a significant improvement in life expectancy. Post-reforms, both public and private healthcare infrastructure expanded. This resulted in reduced infant mortality and improved nutrition, raising the average life expectancy from about 58 years in 1990 to approximately 70 years by 2020. This is considered a major social development outcome. Other options—increase in poverty rate, widening of fiscal deficit, and decrease in literacy rate—are not outcomes of the reforms; in fact, poverty declined, the fiscal deficit was controlled, and literacy increased.
qs.kf:
☛ Life expectancy in India post-1991 reforms → increased from 58 years (1990) to about 70 years (2020)
☛ Literacy rate change → increased from 52% (1991) to 74% (2011)
☛ Poverty rate change → declined from 45% (1993-94) to 22% (2011-12)
☛ Healthcare expansion → increased private sector participation
☛ Infant mortality rate → declined from 88 per 1000 (1990) to 28 per 1000 (2020)

q: What is a key indicator of economic growth that has shown sustained improvement in India since 1991?
qs.e: After the 1991 economic reforms, India's foreign exchange reserves have shown sustained improvement. These reserves indicate a country's ability to finance imports, repay external debt, and maintain economic stability. In January 2024, India's reserves reached $618 billion. Fiscal deficit is a measure of government financial health, not economic growth. Black money is illegal and not a growth indicator. Infant mortality rate is a social development indicator. Thus, the key indicator of sustained economic improvement is foreign exchange reserves.
qs.kf:
☛ What are foreign exchange reserves? → Assets held by a central bank and monetary authority in foreign currencies.
☛ India's highest foreign exchange reserves recorded when? → September 2021 at about $642 billion.
☛ Main components of foreign exchange reserves? → Foreign currency assets, gold reserves, SDRs, and reserve position in IMF.
☛ Foreign exchange reserves are used for? → Exchange rate stability, import payments, and external debt repayment.
☛ India's rank in foreign exchange reserves globally? → Fourth largest after China, Japan, and Switzerland.

q: Which institution played a major role in supporting India’s liberalisation policy during the 1991 crisis?
qs.e: In 1991, India faced a severe balance of payments crisis, with foreign exchange reserves sufficient for only two weeks of imports. To overcome this situation, the Indian government sought a loan from the International Monetary Fund (IMF). The IMF imposed conditions that required India to undertake comprehensive economic reforms, including liberalisation, privatisation, and globalisation (LPG). The IMF's guidance and financial support pushed India towards economic reforms, opening its economy to global markets. Thus, during the 1991 crisis, the IMF played a major role in supporting India's liberalisation policy.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the Finance Minister of India during the 1991 balance of payments crisis? → Manmohan Singh
☛ What is the full form of LPG policy? → Liberalisation, Privatisation, Globalisation
☛ Where is the IMF headquarters located? → Washington D.C., United States
☛ Which currency did India devalue after taking the IMF loan in 1991? → Rupee
☛ In which year did India start economic reforms? → 1991

q: What has been the trend in India’s per capita income since the 1991 reforms?
qs.e: Since the 1991 economic reforms, India's per capita income has shown a gradual increase. The reforms adopted liberalization, privatization, and globalization policies, which accelerated economic growth. In 1990-91, per capita income was around $1,200, which rose to about $2,500 by 2023-24. Although the growth has been slow, it has been positive and steady. India maintained relatively good growth even during global recessions. The increase in per capita income is mainly due to the expansion of the services sector, foreign investment, and technological advancement.
qs.kf:
☛ What were the key components of the 1991 reforms? → Liberalization, Privatization, and Globalization
☛ How is per capita income calculated in India? → By dividing national income by total population
☛ What is India's per capita income (2023) according to the World Bank? → Approximately $2,500
☛ Which sector grew the fastest after the 1991 reforms? → Services sector
☛ What is the impact of rising per capita income on standard of living? → It improves the standard of living

q: Liberalisation reduced government control over economic activities. What did liberalisation in 1991 primarily aim to eliminate?
qs.e: The primary aim of liberalisation in 1991 was to eliminate the industrial licensing and quota system, commonly known as the 'License Raj'. Under this system, private companies required government permission for production, expansion, and investment, which hindered business growth and slowed economic development. As part of liberalisation, most industries were exempted from licensing requirements, except for a few related to environment and security. This move reduced government control over economic activities, promoted private sector participation, and integrated India into the global economy. The reforms marked a shift from a protectionist economy to a market-oriented one, boosting industrial growth and efficiency.
qs.kf:
☛ Who was the Prime Minister of India during the 1991 liberalisation? → P. V. Narasimha Rao
☛ What is 'License Raj' also known as? → Industrial licensing and quota system
☛ Who was the Finance Minister who implemented the 1991 economic reforms? → Manmohan Singh
☛ What was the main objective of liberalisation? → To reduce economic controls and promote the private sector
☛ Which sector benefited the most after the removal of License Raj? → Private sector and industrial development

q: Which of the following best defines globalisation in the context of economic reforms in India, post 1991?
o: Integration of the Indian economy with the global economy
qs.e: Globalisation in the context of post-1991 economic reforms in India refers to the integration of the Indian economy with the global economy. The New Economic Policy (1991) emphasised liberalisation, privatisation, and globalisation. Barriers to trade, investment, and technology were reduced. Foreign investment was encouraged, and import-export policies were liberalised. The goal was to connect India to global supply chains and accelerate economic growth. Multinational companies were allowed to enter Indian markets, increasing competition and efficiency. As a result, India's foreign exchange reserves grew, and the economy became more open and globally integrated.
qs.kf:
☛ What are the three pillars of 1991 economic reforms? → Liberalisation, Privatisation, Globalisation
☛ Which policy promoted globalisation in India? → New Economic Policy, 1991
☛ What was a major objective of globalisation? → Integration of Indian economy with global economy
☛ Which international organisation gained prominence post-1991? → World Trade Organization (WTO)
☛ Which sector grew significantly due to globalisation? → Foreign investment and services sector

q: Which organisation’s support was crucial in India’s globalisation process post 1991 economic crisis?
qs.e: In 1991, India faced a severe economic crisis with foreign exchange reserves depleting to only two weeks of imports. The support of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) was crucial in overcoming this crisis and initiating the globalisation process. India borrowed $2.2 billion from the IMF, which imposed conditions of structural reforms and liberalisation. Consequently, under the leadership of then Finance Minister Dr. Manmohan Singh, India introduced the New Economic Policy of 1991, encompassing privatisation, liberalisation, and globalisation. The IMF's assistance helped India integrate into the international financial markets and attract foreign direct investment, marking a significant shift towards a market-oriented economy.
qs.kf:
☛ How much loan did India take from IMF in 1991? → $2.2 billion
☛ What are the three pillars of India's 1991 economic policy? → Privatisation, Liberalisation, Globalisation
☛ Who was India's Finance Minister in 1991? → Dr. Manmohan Singh
☛ Where is the IMF headquarters located? → Washington D.C., USA
☛ When did globalisation begin in India? → 1991

q: How did the Industrial Revolution alter the British economic interests in India?
o: From trade to industry and raw material use
qs.e: The Industrial Revolution transformed Britain into a factory-based economy, requiring vast quantities of raw materials. India became a source of raw cotton, indigo, jute, and tea for British industries, while British manufactured goods flooded Indian markets. This destroyed India's traditional handicraft industries and restructured the Indian economy as a supplier of raw materials and a consumer of British goods. British policies deliberately de-industrialized India, shifting economic interests from merely trading Indian goods to controlling raw material extraction and industrial markets. Thus, British interests shifted from trade to industry and raw material use.
qs.kf:
☛ Impact of Industrial Revolution on India → India became raw material source and market for British goods
☛ Major raw materials exported from India → Cotton, indigo, jute, tea
☛ Reason for decline of Indian handicrafts → Flood of British manufactured goods
☛ Objective of British policy → De-industrialization of India
☛ Outcome → Indian economy aligned with British interests

q: In which year was the Industrial Policy Resolution that gave importance to the public sector adopted?
qs.e: The Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956 was adopted by the Government of India, giving public sector a dominant role in the economy and laying the foundation of a mixed economy. It classified industries into three categories: Schedule A (exclusive government), Schedule B (both government and private), and Schedule C (exclusive private). This policy aligned with the Second Five-Year Plan and promoted a socialist framework. It strengthened government control over heavy industries, infrastructure, and strategic sectors, aiming for self-reliance and rapid industrialization.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the first Industrial Policy Resolution adopted? → 1948
☛ What were the main reforms of the 1991 Industrial Policy? → Liberalization, Privatization, Globalization
☛ How many categories of industries were in the 1956 resolution? → Three
☛ Which Five-Year Plan was associated with the 1956 policy? → Second Five-Year Plan
☛ Which policy prioritized the public sector? → Industrial Policy Resolution 1956

q: What happened to employment opportunities after the 1991 reforms?
o: Increased, especially in private and service sectors
qs.e: The 1991 economic reforms introduced liberalization, privatization, and globalization in India. The abolition of the license raj and attraction of foreign investment led to expansion of the private sector. The service sector (IT, banking, telecom) saw rapid growth, creating new employment opportunities. While public sector jobs were limited, overall employment increased. Agriculture's share of employment declined.
qs.kf:
☛ Main objective of 1991 economic reforms → Liberalize the economy and boost growth rate
☛ Service sector's contribution to India's GDP → About 60%
☛ Full form of LPG policy → Liberalization, Privatization, Globalization
☛ Prime Minister who implemented 1991 reforms → P. V. Narasimha Rao
☛ Fastest growing sector after 1991 reforms → Service sector

q: A primary goal of LPG reforms was macroeconomic stabilisation. Which indicator improved significantly post-1991 reforms?
qs.e: A primary goal of the 1991 LPG reforms (Liberalization, Privatization, Globalization) was to achieve macroeconomic stabilization. Following these reforms, foreign exchange reserves improved significantly. In 1991, India's foreign exchange reserves were only about 5.8 billion dollars, which increased to over 38 billion dollars by 2000. This growth was driven by export promotion, increased foreign direct investment, and a competitive exchange rate. Revenue deficit and fiscal deficit did not improve; in fact, they worsened. Rural unemployment also did not see any significant improvement. Thus, foreign exchange reserves are the indicator that was most positively impacted by the reforms.
qs.kf:
☛ What was India's foreign exchange reserve in 1991? → About 5.8 billion dollars
☛ When were LPG reforms implemented? → In 1991
☛ Main reason for increase in foreign exchange reserves? → Export growth and FDI
☛ Which reforms opened India's economy? → 1991 economic reforms
☛ Indicator of macroeconomic stability? → Foreign exchange reserves

q: What was a major challenge faced by the Indian manufacturing sector after liberalisation?
qs.e: After the 1991 liberalisation, the Indian manufacturing sector faced a major challenge of increased competition from cheaper imports. The reduction in import tariffs and the abolition of the industrial licensing system allowed foreign companies to easily enter the Indian market. Domestic industries had to compete with affordable and quality products from abroad. Sectors like electronics, textiles, and consumer goods were particularly affected. However, in the long run, this forced Indian industries to become competitive and improve efficiency. Liberalisation eliminated industrial licensing, so high licensing fees were not a challenge. Shortage of raw materials and decline in capital inflow were also not the main issues as foreign investment increased.
qs.kf:
☛ What was the main challenge for manufacturing after liberalisation? → Competition from cheaper imports
☛ How did import tariffs change after 1991 reforms? → Reduced
☛ When was the licensing system abolished? → 1991
☛ Which sectors were most affected by cheaper imports? → Electronics and textiles
☛ What was the long-term impact of liberalisation on manufacturing? → Increased competition and efficiency

q: During the colonial period, the manufacturing sector accounted for only ______.
qs.e: During the colonial period, the Indian economy was predominantly agrarian, with 70-75% of the population dependent on agriculture. The contribution of the manufacturing sector was only 10%, indicating a very low level of industrialization. This sector was mainly confined to cottage industries and small-scale production. British policies led to the decline of Indian handicrafts and textile industries, while modern industrial development remained very slow. The main reason was that the British wanted to make India a source of raw materials and a market for finished goods.
qs.kf:
☛ Contribution of agriculture sector during colonial period → 50-55%
☛ Contribution of service sector during colonial period → 30-35%
☛ Contribution of manufacturing sector → 10%
☛ British policy aimed to make India → Source of raw materials and market for finished goods
☛ Who estimated national income during colonial period → Dadabhai Naoroji

q: What does globalisation mainly mean in economic terms?
qs.e: Economic globalisation refers to the integration of national economies through the free flow of goods, services, capital, technology, and labour across borders. It reduces trade barriers and encourages foreign investment, leading to increased interdependence among countries. This process fosters global supply chains, boosts foreign direct investment (FDI), and expands the role of multinational corporations (MNCs). Developing nations gain access to advanced technology and larger markets, while developed countries benefit from cheaper resources and labour. Globalisation also promotes competition, innovation, and economic growth. Thus, it is the opposite of closing borders or limiting trade; instead, it emphasises connecting to the world economy through international economic cooperation.
qs.kf:
☛ Main economic meaning of globalisation → Connecting to the world economy
☛ Key elements of globalisation → Free movement of trade, investment, technology, and labour
☛ Institution promoting globalisation → WTO (World Trade Organization)
☛ One benefit of globalisation → Technology transfer and economic development
☛ Major driver of globalisation → Multinational corporations (MNCs)

q: Which of the following was NOT a component of globalisation in India's economic reforms?
qs.e: In the 1991 economic reforms, globalisation meant integrating the Indian economy with the global market. Its components included allowing foreign technology, encouraging foreign direct investment (FDI), and liberalising imports, which increased international trade and investment. 'Promoting local-only trade' is opposite to globalisation, as it is a policy of closing the economy and prioritising domestic production, falling under protectionism. The aim of globalisation was to remove barriers, not restrict local trade.
qs.kf:
☛ Key element of globalisation → Economic integration
☛ FDI under 1991 reforms → Encouraged
☛ Meaning of import liberalisation → Reduction in import duties
☛ Protectionism policy → Promoting local-only trade
☛ Opposite of globalisation → Local-only trade

q: What was one of the key effects of globalisation on the Indian economy after 1991?
o: Entry of foreign companies and capital
qs.e: After the 1991 economic reforms, India embraced globalisation, leading to a significant increase in the entry of foreign companies and capital. This was facilitated by liberalisation of foreign direct investment (FDI) and foreign portfolio investment (FPI) policies. As a result, the Indian economy gained access to advanced technology, managerial expertise, and new employment opportunities. Globalisation integrated Indian markets into the global supply chain, boosting both exports and imports. Consequently, foreign exchange reserves increased, rather than decreased, and Indian banks did not close. Thus, the most prominent effect was the influx of foreign companies and capital, which transformed India's economic landscape.
qs.kf:
☛ Who were the architects of India's 1991 economic reforms? → Manmohan Singh and P.V. Narasimha Rao
☛ Full form of FDI? → Foreign Direct Investment
☛ Which sector attracts highest FDI in India? → Services sector
☛ Headquarters of WTO? → Geneva, Switzerland
☛ Which countries are part of NAFTA? → USA, Canada, Mexico

q: Which of the following is an example of globalisation in India post-1991?
o: Entry of multinational companies like Amazon and Apple
qs.e: After the economic reforms of 1991, India embraced globalization by opening its economy to foreign investment and allowing multinational companies (MNCs) to enter. The entry of companies like Amazon and Apple is a clear example of globalization. Nationalisation of banks occurred in 1969 and 1980, unrelated to globalization. Licensing requirements were part of the pre-1991 industrial policy, abolished after reforms. Closure of ports contradicts globalization. Hence, the entry of MNCs is the correct example.
qs.kf:
☛ What are the 1991 economic reforms called? → LPG reforms (Liberalization, Privatization, Globalization)
☛ What is the main objective of globalization? → Integration with the world economy
☛ When was the Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) policy introduced in India? → 1991
☛ Which sector expanded in India due to globalization? → Service sector, especially IT and telecom
☛ Which organization is related to globalization? → WTO (World Trade Organization)

q: In which year did India officially start economic liberalisation?
qs.e: India officially started economic liberalisation in 1991. At that time, the country was facing a severe balance of payments crisis, and foreign exchange reserves had become negligible. Under the leadership of Prime Minister P.V. Narasimha Rao and Finance Minister Dr. Manmohan Singh, the New Economic Policy (NEP) was implemented. It included Liberalization, Privatization, and Globalization (LPG). Reforms were made in industrial policy, trade liberalization, tax reforms, and financial sector reforms. This policy transformed the Indian economy from a closed economy to an open market economy.
qs.kf:
☛ Who is known as the father of economic reforms in India? → Dr. Manmohan Singh
☛ What does 'G' stand for in LPG policy? → Globalization
☛ Who was the Prime Minister during the 1991 crisis? → P.V. Narasimha Rao
☛ In which year did economic reforms start in India? → 1991
☛ When was the New Economic Policy (NEP) implemented? → 1991

q: What is the main aim of globalisation?
o: Integrate the Indian economy with the world
qs.e: The main aim of globalisation is to integrate different national economies into a single global market by reducing barriers to trade, investment, technology, and information flow. For India, globalisation focuses on integrating the Indian economy with the world economy, thereby promoting international trade and investment. This accelerates economic growth and facilitates the exchange of technology and knowledge. Limiting foreign trade or reducing employment contradicts the essence of globalisation. While increasing local production may be a positive outcome, it is not the primary objective of globalisation. The process aims at creating a more interconnected and interdependent global economy, benefiting participating countries through enhanced efficiency and access to global markets.
qs.kf:
☛ Main aim of globalisation → Economic integration globally
☛ Barriers reduced under globalisation → Trade and investment barriers
☛ Start of globalisation in India → Economic reforms of 1991
☛ Organisation related to globalisation → WTO (World Trade Organisation)
☛ Benefit of globalisation → Flow of technology and capital

q: Which of the following was NOT a part of the New Economic Policy reforms introduced in 1991?
qs.e: The New Economic Policy (NEP) of 1991 introduced three main reforms: Liberalisation, Privatisation, and Globalisation (LPG policy). These reforms aimed to make the economy market-oriented, reduce government control, and attract foreign investment. Nationalisation of banks was implemented in 1969 and 1980 to strengthen the public sector, whereas the NEP promoted private sector participation. Hence, nationalisation of banks was not part of the 1991 NEP reforms.
qs.kf:
☛ Under which Prime Minister was the NEP introduced in 1991? → P.V. Narasimha Rao
☛ Which reform under NEP abolished the License Raj? → Liberalisation
☛ What was the main objective of Globalisation? → Promote foreign investment and trade
☛ Under Privatisation, how much stake was sold in government companies? → 49% or more
☛ When was the first nationalisation of banks in India? → 1969

q: How did globalisation impact Indian industries?
o: Gave more competition and modern technology
qs.e: Globalisation positively impacted Indian industries by introducing more competition and access to modern technology. After the economic reforms of 1991, India opened its economy, leading to increased foreign investment and technology transfer. This forced Indian companies to improve efficiency and innovate to compete globally. Consumers benefited from better quality and variety of goods and services. While some sectors faced challenges, overall, globalisation made Indian industries more competitive and technologically advanced.
qs.kf:
☛ When did India begin economic reforms? → 1991
☛ What is the main objective of globalisation? → Integration into the world economy
☛ What was a major result of liberalisation in India? → Increase in foreign direct investment
☛ How did globalisation benefit Indian consumers? → Enhanced quality and choice
☛ Which sector is key to India's globalisation policy? → Services and information technology

q: Which sector was most affected by liberalisation in India?
qs.e: In 1991, India adopted liberalisation policies, which eased import-export, foreign investment, and industrial licensing. This most significantly benefited the industry and services sector as privatisation, foreign competition, and technological advancements boosted growth. The IT sector emerged later but was not the most affected; the broader industrial and services sectors saw the greatest impact. Agriculture remained relatively less affected due to continued government controls. Liberalisation led to increased efficiency, foreign direct investment, and global integration for industries and services, making them the primary beneficiaries.
qs.kf:
☛ Start of liberalisation → 1991, Finance Minister Manmohan Singh
☛ Main objective → Economic reforms, privatisation, globalisation
☛ Most affected sector → Industry and Services
☛ IT sector growth → Post-liberalisation boom
☛ Agriculture impact → Limited, due to Green Revolution and controls

q: Globalization has increased cross-border flows of technology. What policy under globalization encourages technology transfer?
qs.e: Under globalization, the automatic route for FDI is a policy that allows foreign investment without prior government approval, thereby encouraging technology transfer. It is part of liberalization and helps developing countries access advanced technology. In contrast, nationalisation (government control of industries), import substitution policy (focus on reducing imports), and licensing raj (extensive regulation) restrict technology flows. The automatic route permits foreign companies to invest without delays, bringing new technology and knowledge. This is a key aspect of globalization, promoting cross-border flows of technology and capital.
qs.kf:
☛ What is the benefit of automatic route for FDI? → Increased technology transfer and capital inflow
☛ What is the main objective of import substitution policy? → Protect domestic industries
☛ What does nationalisation mean? → Government takeover of industries
☛ What is meant by licensing raj? → Mandatory licenses for trade and investment
☛ Which policy is most important in globalization? → Liberalization and automatic FDI route

q: Which of the following was a major fiscal reform introduced in India as part of the 1991 economic reforms?
o: Introduction of the Modified Value Added Tax
qs.e: As part of the 1991 economic reforms, India implemented several fiscal measures to control the fiscal deficit and boost revenue. One key reform was the introduction and expansion of the Modified Value Added Tax (MODVAT), which was initially introduced in 1986 but significantly strengthened during the 1991 reforms. MODVAT allowed credit for excise duties, making the tax system more efficient. The GST was implemented later in 2017. The FRBM Act was passed in 2003. The abolition of wealth tax occurred in 2015. Thus, MODVAT is closely associated with the 1991 reforms.
qs.kf:
☛ Full form of MODVAT → Modified Value Added Tax
☛ When was MODVAT introduced? → 1986
☛ Main objectives of 1991 reforms → Reduce fiscal deficit and liberalize the economy
☛ When was GST implemented? → 1 July 2017
☛ Purpose of FRBM Act → Ensure fiscal discipline

q: What three-part economic strategy defined India’s policy changes in the 1990s?
qs.e: After the 1991 economic crisis, the Indian government adopted a new economic policy known as the LPG model. It consisted of three pillars: Liberalisation (removing license raj and controls), Privatisation (reducing the role of the public sector and promoting private enterprise), and Globalisation (opening the economy to international trade and investment). This policy transformed India from a closed economy to a market-oriented one. The reforms were implemented by Finance Minister Dr. Manmohan Singh under Prime Minister P.V. Narasimha Rao. The strategy aimed to accelerate economic growth, attract foreign investment, and increase competitiveness.
qs.kf:
☛ Full form of LPG model → Liberalisation, Privatisation and Globalisation
☛ Architect of 1991 economic reforms → Dr. Manmohan Singh
☛ Prime Minister during reforms → P.V. Narasimha Rao
☛ Main objective of Liberalisation → Abolish license raj
☛ Effect of Globalisation → Increase in foreign investment and trade

q: What was the major aim of India’s 1991 economic reforms?
o: To reduce taxes on luxury goods
qs.e: The major aim of India's 1991 economic reforms was to stabilise the economy, which faced a severe balance of payments crisis with foreign reserves dropping to only two weeks of imports. The reforms introduced liberalisation, privatisation, and globalisation (LPG), ending the licence raj, promoting foreign investment, and reducing import tariffs. These market-oriented policies stabilized the economy, led to higher growth rates, and laid the foundation for long-term development. The crisis prompted the government to adopt structural adjustments and fiscal discipline, ultimately transforming India into one of the fastest-growing economies in the world.
qs.kf:
☛ What are the 1991 economic reforms known as? → LPG reforms (Liberalisation, Privatisation, Globalisation)
☛ Who was the Prime Minister of India during the 1991 crisis? → P.V. Narasimha Rao
☛ Who was the Finance Minister responsible for the reforms? → Manmohan Singh
☛ To which institution did India pledge gold during the balance of payments crisis? → Bank of England and Swiss Bank
☛ What was India's growth rate after the 1991 reforms? → Around 6-7% per annum

q: As of October 2020 which of the following enterprises is NOT classified as a Maharatna company?
qs.e: As of October 2020, the Government of India had granted Maharatna status to certain Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs), providing them with greater financial and administrative autonomy. The Maharatna companies included ONGC, IOCL, NTPC, SAIL, GAIL, Coal India, and BHEL. NHPC (National Hydroelectric Power Corporation) was not classified as a Maharatna company until October 2020; it was later granted Maharatna status in 2023. Therefore, among the given options, NHPC was not a Maharatna company.
qs.kf:
☛ First PSU to get Maharatna status → BHEL
☛ Maximum number of Maharatna companies → 12 (as of 2024)
☛ Condition for Navratna status → Net profit of ₹1000 crore for three consecutive years
☛ Minimum global presence for Maharatna → Operations in 4 or more countries
☛ Most recent PSU to become Maharatna → NHPC (2023)

q: Which of the following is NOT a function of Bureau of Indian Standards?
o: Formulating the controlling procedures to ensure safety in the food industry
Formulation, recognition and promotion of Indian standards
Product certification for Indian and foreign manufacturers
qs.e: The Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) is the national standards body of India, responsible for the formulation, recognition and promotion of Indian standards. It provides management system certification and product certification for both Indian and foreign manufacturers. However, formulating controlling procedures to ensure safety in the food industry is the function of FSSAI (Food Safety and Standards Authority of India), not BIS. BIS focuses on standardization, certification, and conformity assessment activities.
qs.kf:
☛ BIS headquarters → New Delhi
☛ BIS Act → 1986
☛ BIS certification mark → ISI mark
☛ Food safety regulator → FSSAI
☛ BIS membership → Founding member of ISO

q: Which of the following is a 'Maharatna' company?
qs.e: The Government of India categorizes Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) into Maharatna, Navratna, and Miniratna based on their performance and global presence. Maharatna status is granted to select PSUs that are global giants and enjoy enhanced financial and administrative autonomy. Bharat Petroleum Corporation Limited (BPCL) is a Maharatna company. Currently, there are 13 Maharatna companies in India, including IOC, ONGC, NTPC, SAIL, Coal India, and BPCL. In contrast, Hindustan Aeronautics Limited, Oil India Limited, and Bharat Electronics Limited are classified as Navratna companies. The Maharatna criteria include an average annual turnover of over ₹25,000 crore and net profit of over ₹5,000 crore in the last three years.
qs.kf:
☛ Total number of Maharatna companies → 13
☛ Maharatna companies include → IOC, ONGC, NTPC, SAIL, Coal India, BPCL, etc.
☛ Navratna company → Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL), BEL
☛ Miniratna company → Oil India Limited (OIL)
☛ Maharatna criteria → Average annual turnover > ₹25,000 crore, net profit > ₹5,000 crore for last 3 years

q: Which Navratna company is fondly called 'Vizag steel'?
qs.e: Rashtriya Ispat Nigam Limited (RINL) is a Navratna public sector enterprise headquartered in Visakhapatnam, Andhra Pradesh. Its Visakhapatnam Steel Plant is India's first coastal integrated steel plant. It is fondly called Vizag Steel. RINL is the second-largest steel producer in India. It was established in 1982.
qs.kf:
☛ Headquarters of RINL → Visakhapatnam
☛ Vizag Steel Plant is located in which state → Andhra Pradesh
☛ Category of RINL → Navratna
☛ India's first coastal steel plant → Visakhapatnam Steel Plant
☛ Establishment year of RINL → 1982

q: Which among the following is NOT a Navratna company?
qs.e: ONGC is a Maharatna company, not a Navratna. The Government of India classifies Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) into Maharatna, Navratna, and Miniratna based on performance and autonomy. ONGC was granted Maharatna status in 2010, which is the highest category. Navratna companies include Oil India Limited, Rural Electrification Corporation (REC), and Hindustan Petroleum Corporation (HPCL). Navratna status is given to profitable PSUs with significant investment capacity. ONGC's Maharatna status grants it greater financial autonomy and investment powers. The classification helps in delegating powers to the boards of these companies for faster decision-making.
qs.kf:
☛ Total Maharatna companies → 12 (as of 2025)
☛ Number of Navratna companies → 16
☛ First Maharatna company → Bharat Heavy Electricals Limited (BHEL)
☛ Committee granting Navratna status → Committee of Principal Secretaries/Secretaries
☛ Miniratna Category I and II → Category I includes profitable, Category II includes loss-making but potentially viable companies

q: Which of the following Central Public Sector Enterprises does NOT have the 'Maharatna' status (as on January 2021)?
qs.e: As of January 2021, the Government of India had granted 'Maharatna' status to only 11 PSUs. These include Bharat Heavy Electricals Limited, Bharat Petroleum Corporation Limited, Coal India Limited, GAIL (India) Limited, Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited, Indian Oil Corporation Limited, NTPC Limited, Oil and Natural Gas Corporation Limited, Power Grid Corporation of India Limited, Steel Authority of India Limited, and Bharat Sanchar Nigam Limited. Oil India Limited had not yet been granted Maharatna status; it only holds the 'Navratna' status. Maharatna status is awarded to PSUs that have a significant global presence and meet certain financial criteria.
qs.kf:
☛ Number of Maharatna PSUs → 11 (as of January 2021)
☛ Example of a Navratna PSU → Oil India Limited
☛ First PSU to get Maharatna status → Bharat Heavy Electricals Limited
☛ Classification of Coal India Limited → Maharatna
☛ Ministry that grants Maharatna status → Ministry of Finance

q: In 1991, in order to make international adjustment the rupee was:
qs.e: In 1991, India faced a severe balance of payments crisis, with foreign exchange reserves nearly exhausted. To tackle this, the government initiated economic reforms, and a key step was the devaluation of the rupee. Devaluation made exports cheaper and imports more expensive, helping to reduce the trade deficit and stabilize foreign reserves. This was done under the conditions set by the International Monetary Fund (IMF). The devaluation reduced the rupee's purchasing power in global markets but was crucial for restoring confidence in the Indian economy. It marked the beginning of India's economic liberalization. The rupee was devalued in two phases, totaling about 18-19% against the US dollar.
qs.kf:
☛ What caused the 1991 economic crisis in India? → Severe balance of payments problem and low foreign exchange reserves
☛ By what percentage was the rupee devalued in 1991? → About 18-19% (in two steps)
☛ Who was the Finance Minister of India at that time? → Dr. Manmohan Singh
☛ What was the effect of devaluation on exports? → Exports became more competitive, leading to an increase
☛ Against which currency did the rupee depreciate after devaluation? → US Dollar

q: Which of the following is against globalisation?
o: Globalisation increases access to global markets.
Globalisation increases the diversification of products.
Globalisation increases the use of advanced technology.
qs.e: Among the arguments against globalisation, the increase in economic disparities is a key concern. Globalisation often benefits wealthy countries and multinational corporations more, leading to greater inequality in developing nations. It promotes unequal distribution of capital and resources. On the other hand, globalisation increases market access, product diversification, and technology use, which are arguments in its favor. Therefore, increasing economic disparities is a primary argument against globalisation.
qs.kf:
☛ Argument against globalisation → Increases economic inequality
☛ Arguments for globalisation → Market access, diversification, technology
☛ Impact of globalisation → Widens gap between rich and poor
☛ Beneficiaries of globalisation → Wealthy nations and MNCs
☛ Cause of inequality → Unequal distribution of resources

q: What significant change was implemented in India's New Economic Policy of 1991 to expand privatisation?
o: Centralising government control over key industries
Increasing the number of industries reserved for public sector control
Establishing more Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) across various sectors
Reducing the list of industries reserved for public sector control
qs.e: Under India's New Economic Policy of 1991, the most significant change to expand privatisation was reducing the number of industries reserved exclusively for the public sector. Previously, 17 industries were reserved for the public sector; this was reduced to 8 and later further decreased. This policy allowed private sector participation in industries that were previously under government monopoly. It increased competition, improved efficiency, and attracted private investment. This was a key component of the economic reforms aimed at liberalising the economy and promoting market-driven growth. The reduction in reserved industries enabled the private sector to enter core areas like telecommunications, power, and mining, which were earlier dominated by public sector undertakings. This shift was crucial in transforming India from a state-controlled to a market-oriented economy.
qs.kf:
☛ How many industries were reserved for the public sector before 1991? → 17
☛ How many industries remained reserved after the 1991 policy? → 8
☛ What was the main objective of privatisation in 1991? → To increase private participation and encourage competition
☛ What are the three pillars of the 1991 economic policy? → Liberalisation, Privatisation, Globalisation
☛ How did the government reduce its stake in PSUs under privatisation? → Through disinvestment

q: Which of the following statements is NOT correct about ‘Globalisation’?
o: It helps to create borderless world
It helps in alleviating problems and increased sustainable development benefits
It is the process of interaction and integration among people
It encourages flows of investment, people and information
qs.e: Globalisation is primarily the process of economic, social, and cultural integration, increasing the flow of goods, services, capital, and information between countries. It helps create a borderless world and enhances interaction among people. However, globalisation itself does not directly promise to alleviate problems or increase sustainable development benefits. In fact, globalisation can lead to increased inequalities and environmental issues. Therefore, this statement is incorrect. The other three statements correctly describe characteristics of globalisation.
qs.kf:
☛ Key elements of globalisation → Flow of goods, services, capital, and information
☛ Effect of globalisation → Economic integration and cultural exchange
☛ Negative aspects of globalisation → Inequality and environmental damage
☛ Globalisation relates to → International trade and investment
☛ Outcome of globalisation → Moves towards a borderless world

q: Which of the following is the definition of Globalisation?
o: Globalisation is an outcome of industrial policies that aim to transform the world towards greater interdependence and integration.
Globalisation is an outcome of a set of various policies aimed at transforming the world towards greater interdependence and integration
Globalisation is an outcome of trading policies that aim to transform the world towards greater interdependence and integration.
Globalisation is an outcome of agricultural policies that aim to transform the world towards greater interdependence and integration.
qs.e: Globalisation is a multidimensional process that increases interdependence and integration among countries. It is not the result of a single policy like industrial, trade, or agricultural policy, but rather an outcome of a set of various policies. These include economic, social, cultural, and political policies. Globalisation involves the free flow of goods, services, capital, and technology across national borders. It facilitates international trade, investment, and exchange of information. Therefore, the correct definition is the one stating that globalisation is the outcome of a set of various policies aimed at transforming the world towards greater interdependence and integration.
qs.kf:
☛ Main objective of globalisation → To increase interdependence and integration among countries
☛ Policies involved in globalisation → Economic, social, cultural, and political
☛ Key elements of globalisation → Free flow of goods, services, capital, and technology
☛ Impact of globalisation → Rise in international trade and investment
☛ Globalisation accelerated in → Late 20th century

q: What is the primary function of development banks in the context of India's industrial growth?
o: Their sole function is to manage the country's foreign exchange reserves.
They are involved only in short-term consumer lending.
They serve as regulatory bodies to enforce industrial standards.
Development banks provide long-term financing and support for industrial projects and infrastructure development.
qs.e: The primary function of development banks is to provide long-term financing, which is essential for industrial and infrastructure projects. These banks play a crucial role in India's industrial growth by offering loans and equity support for capital-intensive projects. Major development banks in India include the Industrial Development Bank of India (IDBI), Industrial Finance Corporation of India (IFCI), and National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD). They differ from commercial banks as they do not provide short-term loans but focus on long-term projects. Development banks are not involved in foreign exchange management, consumer lending, or acting as regulatory bodies. Their primary goal is to provide financial assistance for industrial and infrastructure development, which drives economic growth.
qs.kf:
☛ Which was the first development bank in India? → IFCI (Industrial Finance Corporation of India) established in 1948.
☛ What is the full form of IDBI? → Industrial Development Bank of India.
☛ NABARD works for the development of which sector? → Agriculture and rural development.
☛ What is the main objective of SIDBI? → To provide financing to small-scale industries.
☛ What type of loans do development banks provide? → Long-term loans.

q: Which of the following is Disinvestment?
o: Globalisation of the public sector undertakings by selling off the part of the equity of PSUs to the public is known as disinvestment.
Privatisation of the public sector undertakings by selling off the part of the equity of PSUs to the public is known as disinvestment.
Liberalisation of the public sector undertakings by selling off the part of the equity of PSUs to the public is known as disinvestment.
Liberalisation of the private sector undertakings by selling off the part of the equity of PSUs to the public is known as disinvestment.
qs.e: Disinvestment is a process where the government sells a portion or whole of its stake in public sector undertakings (PSUs) to the private sector or the public. Its main objectives are to raise government revenue and improve efficiency. Disinvestment is considered a form of privatisation as it reduces government control. In India, the Disinvestment Commission and NITI Aayog oversee this process. Unlike globalisation or liberalisation, disinvestment focuses solely on the transfer of ownership.
qs.kf:
☛ What is the main objective of disinvestment? → To raise government revenue and improve efficiency
☛ Who oversees the disinvestment process in India? → NITI Aayog and the Disinvestment Commission
☛ What is the relationship between disinvestment and privatisation? → Disinvestment is a form of privatisation
☛ In which Five Year Plan was disinvestment emphasized? → Eighth Five Year Plan
☛ Which policy was formulated for disinvestment? → National Disinvestment Policy 1999

q: Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) has been upgraded to which status by the Ministry of Finance in 2024?
qs.e: Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) has been upgraded to Maharatna CPSE status by the Ministry of Finance in 2024. Maharatna status is awarded to Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs) that are globally competitive and have excellent financial performance. HAL is India's premier aerospace and defence company, manufacturing fighter jets, helicopters, and aero engines. With Maharatna status, HAL gains greater autonomy in investment decisions and can make large investments without government approval. This move is part of the government's policy to empower CPSEs and enhance their operational efficiency. HAL is now the 12th Maharatna CPSE in India.
qs.kf:
☛ Which CPSE got Maharatna status in 2024? → HAL
☛ Which ministry grants Maharatna CPSE status? → Ministry of Finance
☛ Where is the headquarters of HAL located? → Bangalore
☛ What is the minimum annual net profit required for Maharatna status? → ₹5,000 crore
☛ What is the maximum investment limit for a Maharatna CPSE without government approval? → ₹15,000 crore

q: The Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956 categorised industries into how many groups?
qs.e: The Industrial Policy Resolution (IPR) of 1956 classified industries into three groups based on the role of the state and private sector. Schedule A included industries exclusively under state control, such as defense, atomic energy, coal, and railways. Schedule B consisted of industries where both public and private sectors could operate, but the state would take the lead in setting up new units, including aluminum, fertilizers, and chemicals. Schedule C covered all remaining industries, which were primarily open to the private sector, though subject to licensing and regulation. This classification aimed to establish a socialist pattern of society, with the state controlling the commanding heights of the economy. IPR 1956 remained the foundation of India's industrial policy until the liberalization reforms of 1991.
qs.kf:
☛ How many industry groups did IPR 1956 create? → Three
☛ Which group had exclusive state control? → Schedule A
☛ Which group allowed public-private participation? → Schedule B
☛ Which group was primarily for private sector? → Schedule C
☛ What economic philosophy did IPR 1956 reflect? → Socialist pattern

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (11/06/2025) Shift 3
q: What was the average annual growth rate of industries comprising mining, manufacturing and electricity during the post-reform period between 1991-92 and 2011- 12?
qs.e: During the post-reform period from 1991-92 to 2011-12, the average annual growth rate of industries including mining, manufacturing and electricity was 6.7%. This figure reflects industrial development in the Indian economy. Economic reforms led to a boost in industrial production. The manufacturing sector performed particularly well, while mining and electricity sectors also recorded steady growth. This rate is calculated based on Gross Value Added (GVA). Overall, this growth rate signifies India's industrialization and economic progress.
qs.kf:
☛ When did economic reforms begin in India? → 1991
☛ Key indicator for measuring manufacturing growth? → GVA
☛ Growth rate of mining sector during 1991-2011? → Around 5%
☛ Main reason for highest growth in electricity sector? → Reforms and private investment
☛ Highest contributing sector in industrial growth? → Manufacturing

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (12/06/2025) Shift 1
q: Per capita income is an indicator of economic development. What happened to India’s per capita income post 1991 economic reforms?
qs.e: India initiated economic reforms in 1991, including liberalization, privatization, and globalization. These reforms opened up the economy, attracted foreign investment, and boosted industrial production and the service sector. Consequently, the Gross Domestic Product (GDP) grew rapidly, leading to a significant rise in per capita income. Before 1991, per capita income was around $300, which increased to over $2,500 by 2023. This growth clearly indicates economic development.
qs.kf:
☛ What was the main objective of the 1991 economic reforms? → To resolve the balance of payments crisis and accelerate economic growth
☛ Who was the Finance Minister of India in 1991? → Manmohan Singh
☛ How is per capita income measured? → By dividing total national income by total population
☛ What has been India's average GDP growth rate post-1991? → Around 6-7% per annum
☛ Which Indian state has the highest per capita income? → Goa

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (19/06/2025) Shift 2
q: Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) is a key aspect of globalisation. What is a major benefit of FDI for developing countries like India?
qs.e: Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) brings capital, technology, and managerial expertise to developing countries like India. This fosters innovation in local industries and creates employment opportunities. Increased productivity from FDI boosts economic growth. Options like increase in taxation, trade deficits, and currency depreciation are not direct benefits; instead, FDI helps reduce deficits by improving capital inflows. Therefore, the major benefit of FDI is technology transfer and job creation, which drive sustainable development.
qs.kf:
☛ What is the full form of FDI? → Foreign Direct Investment
☛ What is a major benefit of FDI? → Inflow of capital and technology
☛ Which sector attracts the most FDI in India? → Services sector
☛ How does FDI benefit local firms? → Improves competition and skills
☛ What is a negative impact of FDI? → Pressure on local industries

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (19/06/2025) Shift 3
q: Privatisation can be partial, involving minority shareholding by the private sector. What is the government's shareholding threshold in a PSU for it to be considered privatised?
qs.e: In the process of privatisation, the government reduces its shareholding in a Public Sector Undertaking (PSU) to less than 51%, thereby transferring control to the private sector. In India, if the government holds 51% or more shares, the PSU remains in the public sector. Once the government's shareholding falls below 51%, the entity is considered privatised, even if the private sector holds a minority stake. This constitutes a form of partial privatisation.
qs.kf:
☛ Meaning of privatisation → Transfer of government ownership to private sector
☛ Threshold for PSU privatisation → Government shareholding below 51%
☛ Partial privatisation → Involves minority private sector participation
☛ Disinvestment policy → Reducing government shareholding
☛ Example → Privatisation of Maruti Suzuki

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (20/06/2025) Shift 3
q: Privatisation involves transferring the ownership of enterprises from the public to the private sector. What is the primary goal of privatisation?
o: Improve efficiency and reduce government burden
qs.e: The primary goal of privatisation is to improve the efficiency of public sector enterprises and reduce the financial burden on the government. Government-owned enterprises often suffer from inefficiency due to bureaucracy, political interference, and lack of competition. The private sector, driven by profit motive, ensures better resource allocation, innovation, and cost-effectiveness. Moreover, privatisation relieves the government from subsidising loss-making units, thereby reducing the fiscal deficit. It does not aim to increase monopoly power or enhance public employment; in fact, it fosters competition and leads to competitive pricing. In India, privatisation became a key policy after the 1991 economic reforms, aiming to make the economy more market-oriented and globally competitive.
qs.kf:
☛ Primary objective of privatisation → Improve efficiency and reduce government financial burden
☛ Year privatisation started in India → 1991
☛ Type of competition increased by privatisation → Market competition
☛ Effect of privatisation on fiscal deficit → Decreases
☛ Key sector involved in privatisation → Private sector

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (23/06/2025) Shift 1
q: Which of the following is/are correct with respect to the outcomes of globalisation in the Indian economy?
1. The opening of the economy has led to a rapid decrease in foreign direct investment and foreign exchange reserves.
2. The post-1991 India witnessed a steep decline in its GDP on a continual basis for two decades.
3. The growth of GDP increased from 5.6% during 1980-91 to 8.2% during 2007-12.
qs.e: As a result of globalisation, the Indian economy witnessed an increase in Foreign Direct Investment and foreign exchange reserves, not a decrease, so statement 1 is incorrect. Post-1991, India experienced growth in GDP due to economic reforms, not a decline, so statement 2 is incorrect. Due to globalisation and economic reforms, India's GDP growth rate increased from 5.6% during 1980-91 to 8.2% during 2007-12, making statement 3 correct.
qs.kf:
☛ Impact of globalisation on India → Increase in GDP growth
☛ Result of 1991 economic reforms → Increase in FDI and forex reserves
☛ India's GDP growth rate 1980-91 → 5.6%
☛ India's GDP growth rate 2007-12 → 8.2%
☛ Main benefit of globalisation → Faster economic growth

q: Which of the following is a Maharatna PSU?
qs.e: BHEL (Bharat Heavy Electricals Limited) is a Maharatna category Public Sector Undertaking (PSU). The Maharatna status is granted to PSUs with high financial autonomy and global presence. BHEL is one of India's largest engineering and manufacturing companies, producing power generation equipment. Among the options, BCCL (Bharat Coking Coal Limited) is a Schedule 'A' PSU, CSL (Cochin Shipyard Limited) is a Miniratna PSU, and BSNL (Bharat Sanchar Nigam Limited) is a Schedule 'B' PSU. Hence, only BHEL falls under the Maharatna category.
qs.kf:
☛ Number of branches for Maharatna PSU? → Minimum net profit of Rs 5000 crore over 3 years
☛ Required net profit for Maharatna status → More than Rs 2500 crore for 3 consecutive years
☛ Headquarters of BHEL → New Delhi
☛ Total number of Maharatna PSUs (2023) → 13
☛ Awarding authority for Maharatna status → Ministry of Finance, Government of India

q: What are the criteria to be considered to get Maharatna status?
o: Having positive net profit to net worth ratio
qs.e: Maharatna status is the highest category awarded by the Government of India to Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs). One of the key criteria is that the company must have a significant global presence and international operations, which distinguishes it from lower categories. Additionally, the company must already hold Miniratna Category-I status. Other financial criteria include average annual turnover of over ₹25,000 crore, average annual net profit of over ₹5,000 crore, and average annual net worth of over ₹15,000 crore in the last three years. These criteria ensure that only top-performing CPSEs with global reach are granted this status.
qs.kf:
☛ Minimum annual turnover for Maharatna → ₹25,000 crore
☛ Minimum annual net profit for Maharatna → ₹5,000 crore
☛ Minimum annual net worth for Maharatna → ₹15,000 crore
☛ Number of Maharatna CPSEs currently → 12
☛ Highest CPSE category → Maharatna

q: Privatisation of the public sector undertakings by selling off part of the equity of PSUs to the public is known as:
qs.e: Disinvestment refers to the sale of a portion of the government's equity in public sector undertakings (PSUs) to the public or other investors. It is a form of privatization where the government may retain majority control (over 50% stake) or relinquish complete control. The aim of disinvestment is to raise government revenue, improve efficiency of PSUs through private sector participation, and promote competition. In India, disinvestment is overseen by the NITI Aayog and the Department of Investment and Public Asset Management (DIPAM). It has been a key policy since the 1991 economic reforms under the LPG (Liberalisation, Privatisation, Globalisation) framework. Disinvestment differs from liberalization (deregulation) and globalization (international integration). It is a strategic tool to reduce fiscal burden and enhance productivity of state-owned enterprises.
qs.kf:
☛ What is the main objective of disinvestment? → To raise government revenue and improve PSU efficiency
☛ When did disinvestment policy start in India? → 1991 under economic reforms
☛ Where is disinvestment proceeds used? → National Infrastructure Pipeline (NIP) and social welfare schemes
☛ Which body oversees disinvestment process? → NITI Aayog and DIPAM under Ministry of Finance
☛ Difference between disinvestment and privatization? → Privatization involves complete transfer of control, while disinvestment may involve partial stake sale

q: Which of the following is NOT a PSU?
qs.e: In India, a Public Sector Undertaking (PSU) is a company where the government holds 51% or more equity. SAIL (Steel Authority of India Limited), ONGC (Oil and Natural Gas Corporation), and GAIL (Gas Authority of India Limited) are all central government-owned PSUs. BSNL (Bharat Sanchar Nigam Limited) is a government-owned telecommunications company, but technically it is not considered a PSU, as it has been reclassified as a departmental undertaking or has been removed from the PSU list. In fact, BSNL is a departmental undertaking under the Department of Telecommunications, not a PSU. Therefore, BSNL is NOT a PSU among the given options.
qs.kf:
☛ Example of a Maharatna PSU → ONGC
☛ Name of a Navratna PSU → SAIL
☛ Sector in which GAIL operates → Natural gas
☛ Full form of BSNL → Bharat Sanchar Nigam Limited
☛ Ministry controlling PSUs → Respective ministries

q: Which of the following is NOT a Navratna company?
qs.e: Navratna companies are a category of Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) in India that enjoy greater administrative and financial autonomy. Engineers India Limited, Bharat Electronics Limited, and Oil India Limited are all Navratna companies. The Airports Authority of India (AAI) is a public sector enterprise, but it does not hold Navratna status; it is merely a Central Public Sector Enterprise (CPSE). Navratna status is granted to profitable PSUs that are internationally competitive. Currently, there are 16 Navratna companies, including Bharat Electronics, Engineers India, and Oil India. AAI is not among them, making it the correct answer as the one that is NOT a Navratna company.
qs.kf:
☛ Engineers India Limited Navratna status → Yes
☛ Bharat Electronics Limited Navratna status → Yes
☛ Oil India Limited Navratna status → Yes
☛ Airports Authority of India Navratna status → No
☛ Airports Authority of India category → Central Public Sector Enterprise (CPSE)

q: What is the minimum percentage of shares left for strategic disinvestment?
qs.e: In strategic disinvestment, the government transfers its majority stake in a Public Sector Undertaking (PSU) to a strategic buyer, thereby relinquishing management control. According to current policy, the minimum percentage of shares that must remain with the government after disinvestment is 51 percent, ensuring that the government retains majority ownership. However, in some cases, this threshold can be as low as 26 percent, but the standard requirement is 51 percent. This rule ensures that the government maintains a controlling interest in the enterprise. The objective of strategic disinvestment is to bring in private sector efficiency, reduce the government's financial burden, and improve operational performance.
qs.kf:
☛ Minimum government stake after strategic disinvestment → 51 percent
☛ Purpose of strategic disinvestment → To bring in strategic buyer for management control
☛ Who gains management control → The strategic buyer
☛ Standard threshold for government holding → 51 percent
☛ Expected benefit of strategic disinvestment → Improved efficiency and reduced fiscal burden

q: The Government of India initiated and announced the policy of Special Economic Zones to attract foreign investments in business. This was announced in the year ________.
qs.e: The Government of India announced the policy of Special Economic Zones (SEZs) in the year 2005. The SEZ Act was passed by the Parliament in 2005 and came into effect on February 10, 2006. Although the SEZ policy was initially introduced in 2000, the formal announcement and legal framework were established in 2005. The main objectives of SEZs are to attract foreign investment, promote exports, and generate employment. SEZs are geographically defined areas where economic activities are encouraged through tax and regulatory incentives. Currently, India has 7 central government-operated SEZs and many state-level SEZs.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the SEZ Act passed? → 2005
☛ What is the purpose of SEZ policy? → Attract foreign investment and boost exports
☛ What does SEZ stand for? → Special Economic Zone
☛ When did the SEZ Act come into effect? → February 10, 2006
☛ How many central SEZs are there in India? → 7

q: What was a key feature of the economic reforms in India after 1991?
qs.e: The economic reforms in India after 1991 were initiated to address a severe balance of payments crisis. A key feature of these reforms was the liberalisation of trade policies, which included reduction of import tariffs, promotion of exports, and removal of restrictions on foreign trade. The reforms also dismantled the license raj, increased private sector participation, encouraged foreign investment, and deregulated many industries. This liberalisation integrated the Indian economy with the global economy and led to higher growth rates. The New Industrial Policy of 1991 abolished industrial licensing for most sectors, and foreign investment norms were eased to attract capital and technology.
qs.kf:
☛ Main objective of 1991 economic reforms → Overcoming balance of payments crisis and boosting growth
☛ Key feature of New Industrial Policy 1991 → End of license raj and deregulation of industries
☛ Major steps under trade liberalisation → Reduction of import tariffs and export promotion
☛ Change in foreign investment policy → Automatic route for FDI and FII
☛ Impact of 1991 reforms → Higher economic growth rate and increased globalisation

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (17/06/2025) Shift 2
q: Which of the following are the key factors that are favourable for India for making it a key destination for foreign investments? 1. India’s robust economic fundamentals
2. Ongoing structural reforms
3. Decreasing consumer market position
qs.e: India's robust economic fundamentals, such as stable growth rate, high foreign exchange reserves, and controlled inflation, attract foreign investors. Ongoing structural reforms like GST, Insolvency Code, and liberalization create a favorable investment climate. However, decreasing consumer market position is negative as it indicates falling demand, discouraging investment. Therefore, only factors 1 and 2 are favorable.
qs.kf:
☛ India's rank in FDI inflows (2023) → Among top 5 recipients
☛ Reform boosting FDI in India → Improvement in 'Ease of Doing Business' ranking
☛ Sector receiving highest FDI → Services sector
☛ Top source country for FDI in India → Singapore
☛ Key feature of India's FDI policy → 100% FDI allowed under automatic route in most sectors

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (13/06/2025) Shift 2
q: Which of the following statements regarding the Industrial Sector in India is/are correct?
1. According to National Manufacturing Policy 2011, every job created in the manufacturing sector creates two-three additional jobs in related activities.
2. Industries add value to the existing goods and also to the skill of labour employed in it; therefore, this sector is also considered a transformational sector.
3. As industries employ a large part of the population, industrial development is one of the preconditions for the eradication of unemployment and poverty from our country.
qs.e: All three statements are correct. According to the National Manufacturing Policy 2011, every job in manufacturing creates 2-3 additional jobs in related activities, demonstrating a multiplier effect. Industries add value to raw materials and enhance labour skills, hence they are called the transformational sector. Industrial development generates large-scale employment, which is a precondition for eradicating unemployment and poverty. Thus, the industrial sector is the engine of economic growth.
qs.kf:
☛ National Manufacturing Policy → Launched in 2011, every manufacturing job creates 2-3 additional jobs.
☛ Transformational sector → Industries add value to goods and skills.
☛ Goal of industrial development → Eradication of unemployment and poverty.
☛ Employment multiplier effect → Manufacturing jobs lead to jobs in services.
☛ Industrial policy in India → Liberalization since 1991 economic reforms.

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (13/06/2025) Shift 3
q: Which of the following statements regarding the Industrial Sector in India post the launch of the New Economic Policy in 1991 is/are NOT correct?
1. Compulsory licensing on several industries was abolished.
2. Many industries that were only reserved for the government were dereserved.
3. There was quota and price control for all the goods produced in the industrial sector.
qs.e: The New Economic Policy of 1991 (LPG) focused on liberalization, privatization, and globalization. Statement 1 is correct: compulsory licensing for most industries was abolished, retaining it only for 3 strategic sectors. Statement 2 is correct: industries reserved exclusively for the government were reduced from 17 to 3 (defense, atomic energy, railways). Statement 3 is incorrect: quota and price control were removed for most goods; only a few sensitive items remained under control.
qs.kf:
☛ Which industries retained compulsory licensing after 1991? → 3 industries: defense, atomic energy, railways
☛ How many industries were initially reserved for the public sector? → 17, later reduced to 3
☛ What does MRTP Act deal with? → Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices
☛ Which act replaced FERA? → FEMA in 1999
☛ What was the main objective of New Economic Policy? → To make the Indian economy globally competitive

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (14/06/2025) Shift 2
q: Globalisation refers to the integration of economies worldwide. Which of the following was a major globalisation strategy adopted by the Indian government in 1991?
o: Reducing trade barriers and encouraging foreign investment
qs.e: In 1991, India adopted the Liberalization, Privatization, and Globalization (LPG) policies after a severe economic crisis. The globalization strategy mainly involved reducing trade barriers and encouraging foreign investment, integrating the Indian economy with the global economy. Imposing high export or import tariffs and promoting import substitution industrialization are protectionist policies that were followed before 1991.
qs.kf:
☛ When were the LPG policies implemented in India? → 1991
☛ Main objective of globalization? → Integration with the world economy
☛ Reducing trade barriers is part of which policy? → Globalization
☛ Who was the chief architect of the 1991 economic reforms? → Dr. Manmohan Singh
☛ Encouraging foreign investment is part of which policies? → Liberalization and Globalization

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (16/06/2025) Shift 2
q: Banking reforms were part of the 1991 economic reforms. Which of the following committees recommended banking sector liberalisation in 1991?
qs.e: In 1991, India initiated economic reforms, and the Narasimham Committee (1991) recommended banking sector liberalisation. Its suggestions included deregulation of interest rates, entry of private banks, and stricter capital adequacy norms. The committee played a pivotal role in transforming India's banking sector. The Narasimham Committee-II (1998) further recommended banking reforms. Other committees: Suresh Tendulkar Committee (poverty line), Rangarajan Committee (inflation targeting), Kelkar Committee (tax reforms).
qs.kf:
☛ Committee recommending banking sector liberalisation in 1991 → Narasimham Committee-I
☛ Chairman of Narasimham Committee → M. Narasimham
☛ Year of Narasimham Committee-II → 1998
☛ Committee related to poverty line → Suresh Tendulkar Committee
☛ Committee related to inflation targeting → Rangarajan Committee

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (21/06/2025) Shift 2
q: Labour reforms have remained a key agenda in the post-1991 economic policy landscape. How many labour codes were consolidated by the Indian government under the labour reforms enacted in 2019-2020?
qs.e: The Indian government consolidated 29 central labour laws into four labour codes under the labour reforms enacted in 2019-2020. These four codes are: Code on Wages, 2019; Industrial Relations Code, 2020; Social Security Code, 2020; and Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020. The objective of these codes is to simplify labour laws, reduce compliance costs, and promote employment generation. Consolidation into four codes was aimed at bringing flexibility to the labour market, benefiting both employers and workers. This reform is a significant step under the post-1991 economic policy landscape.
qs.kf:
☛ When was the Code on Wages enacted? → 2019
☛ How many central labour laws were consolidated? → 29
☛ Which year was the Industrial Relations Code passed? → 2020
☛ What does the Social Security Code relate to? → Social security provisions for workers
☛ What is the name of the fourth code? → Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (21/06/2025) Shift 2
q: Disinvestment was adopted as a tool for privatisation in India. Which of the following options best defines disinvestment?
o: Selling government stakes in public sector enterprises
Purchase of private companies by the government
Sale of public assets to foreign governments
qs.e: Disinvestment refers to the process where the government sells its stake (partial or full) in public sector undertakings (PSUs). It is a key tool for privatization, aimed at reducing government ownership and increasing private participation. Disinvestment generates revenue for the government, which can be used to reduce fiscal deficit or fund development projects. In India, disinvestment began after the economic reforms of 1991. It helps improve efficiency and competitiveness of PSUs. Disinvestment does not mean increasing public borrowing, buying private companies, or selling assets to foreign governments.
qs.kf:
☛ What is the main objective of disinvestment? → Reduce government stake and raise revenue
☛ When did disinvestment policy start in India? → After economic reforms of 1991
☛ What benefit does the government get from disinvestment? → Fiscal deficit reduction
☛ Disinvestment is a part of which process? → Privatization
☛ What is the impact of disinvestment on PSUs? → Increased efficiency and competitiveness

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (21/06/2025) Shift 3
q: Which of the following is/are correct regarding the agricultural sector post the reform period of 1991?
1. Quantitative restrictions on imports of agricultural products to India were fully removed from April 2001.
2. There was a huge increase in the import duties on agricultural products to India after 1991.
3. Due to the export-oriented policy after 1991, there was a shift from production for the domestic market towards production for the export market, with more focus on cash crops than food grains.
qs.e: After the 1991 economic reforms, the agricultural sector underwent significant changes. From April 2001, India completely removed quantitative restrictions on imports of agricultural products, aligning with WTO requirements. The export-oriented policy led to a shift towards cash crops (e.g., cotton, sugarcane) as they were more profitable for export, while production of food grains relatively declined. Statement 2 is incorrect because after 1991, import duties on agricultural products were reduced, not increased, to promote trade liberalization. Hence, only statements 1 and 3 are correct.
qs.kf:
☛ When were quantitative restrictions on agricultural imports removed in India? → April 2001
☛ Which type of crops got more focus after 1991 reforms in agriculture? → Cash crops
☛ Under which organization's pressure did India remove agricultural import restrictions? → WTO
☛ What happened to import duties on agricultural products after 1991? → They were reduced
☛ What was the impact of export-oriented policy on agriculture? → Increased production of cash crops

q: In which year did the disinvestment process in Public Sector Enterprises in India start?
qs.e: The disinvestment process in Public Sector Enterprises (PSUs) in India started in the year 1991. This decision was taken under the economic reform policy implemented by the then Finance Minister Dr. Manmohan Singh. The year 1991 marks a significant turning point in India's economic history when the government adopted the Liberalization, Privatization, and Globalization (LPG) policy. The objective of disinvestment was to reduce government ownership, raise capital, and improve the efficiency of public enterprises. In this process, the government sold its stake in PSUs. Initially, disinvestment was carried out on a small scale, and later its scope expanded.
qs.kf:
☛ Year of start of disinvestment policy in India → 1991
☛ When was LPG policy implemented → 1991
☛ Who was the Finance Minister in 1991 → Dr. Manmohan Singh
☛ Main objective of disinvestment → Reduce government ownership and improve efficiency
☛ Name of the first disinvestment policy → Privatization policy

q: Which of the following is NOT correct in the context of PSUs and their year of establishment?
o: Oil and Natural Gas Corporation in 1956
qs.e: The Damodar Valley Corporation (DVC) was established in the year 1948, not 1958. It is India's first multipurpose river valley project. The other options are correct: Oil and Natural Gas Corporation (ONGC) was established in 1956, Airports Authority of India (AAI) in 1995, and Balmer Lawrie & Co. Ltd. in 1867. DVC is a public sector undertaking that works for power generation and flood control.
qs.kf:
☛ ONGC establishment year → 1956
☛ AAI establishment year → 1995
☛ Balmer Lawrie establishment year → 1867
☛ DVC establishment year → 1948
☛ India's first multipurpose river valley project → Damodar Valley Corporation

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I (17/06/2025) Shift 3
q: Which of the following categories of MSMEs constitutes the major share of MSME registration on the Udyam Registration Portal?
qs.e: The Micro category constitutes the largest share of MSME registrations on the Udyam Registration Portal. Under MSME classification, enterprises are categorized as micro, small, and medium. Micro enterprises are those with investment less than ₹1 crore and turnover less than ₹5 crore. Due to government policies and incentives, the majority of MSMEs in India fall under the micro category. They play a vital role in employment generation and production.
qs.kf:
☛ What is the maximum investment limit for Micro MSME? → ₹1 crore
☛ What is the maximum turnover limit for Micro MSME? → ₹5 crore
