Winter rainfall is caused by westerly winds, while subtropical high pressure brings dry summers. It is classified as Cs type in the Köppen classification. Other options: Equatorial climate receives rainfall all year round; Sudan climate has summer rainfall; and Laurentian climate has precipitation throughout the year.
qs.kf:
☛ Main cause of rainfall in Mediterranean climate? → Westerlies in winter
☛ Köppen code for Mediterranean climate? → Cs
☛ Summer condition in Mediterranean climate? → Dry and hot
☛ Vegetation type in Mediterranean climate? → Sclerophyllous
☛ Fruit cultivation in Mediterranean climate? → Citrus fruits

q: Willie-Willie is the local name for the tropical cyclones in which country?
qs.e: Willie-Willie (or Willy-Willy) is the local name for tropical cyclones in Australia, particularly affecting the northern and western coasts. These cyclones originate in the Southern Hemisphere and are known by different names in various regions: hurricanes in the Atlantic, typhoons in the Pacific, and cyclones in the Indian Ocean. In Australia, they are called Willy-Willies, a term derived from Aboriginal languages. These storms are highly destructive, causing strong winds, heavy rainfall, and flooding. They typically occur between November and April during the Australian cyclone season. Understanding local names is important for disaster management and geographical studies.
qs.kf:
☛ Where do hurricanes occur? → Atlantic Ocean and eastern Pacific Ocean
☛ Where do typhoons occur? → Northwestern Pacific Ocean
☛ Where do cyclones occur? → Indian Ocean and South Pacific Ocean
☛ What is the local name for tropical cyclones in the Philippines? → Bagyo
☛ What is the local name for tropical cyclones in Japan? → Taifu

q: Tropical cyclone intensity is high in India during months.
qs.e: Tropical cyclone intensity is high in India during October and November. This period coincides with the retreat of the southwest monsoon, when sea surface temperatures remain above 26-27°C and vertical wind shear is low, creating favorable conditions for cyclone formation. The Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea experience more powerful cyclones during these months. In contrast, during the monsoon season from June to September, high wind shear weakens cyclonic activity. The atmospheric pressure changes and increased moisture content in October-November further enhance cyclone intensity. These months are critical for cyclone preparedness in coastal regions of India.
qs.kf:
☛ Peak cyclone intensity months in India → October and November
☛ Required sea temperature for cyclone formation → 26-27°C
☛ Cyclone-prone period in Bay of Bengal → October-November and May-June
☛ Energy source for tropical cyclones → Latent heat from water vapor
☛ Reason for weak cyclones during monsoon → High vertical wind shear

q: Which of the following places in India receives highest rainfall as of now?
qs.e: Mawsynram, located in Meghalaya, is currently the place that receives the highest rainfall in India, with an average annual rainfall of about 11,872 mm. Although Cherrapunji was traditionally considered the wettest place, Mawsynram has now surpassed it. Both Mawsynram and Cherrapunji are in Meghalaya and receive heavy rainfall due to the monsoon winds and their geographical location. Agumbe in Karnataka is known as the 'Cherrapunji of South India' but has lower rainfall compared to Mawsynram. Thus, Mawsynram is the current record holder for highest rainfall in India.
qs.kf:
☛ Highest rainfall place in India → Mawsynram (Meghalaya)
☛ Average annual rainfall of Mawsynram → About 11,872 mm
☛ Cherrapunji of South India → Agumbe (Karnataka)
☛ Average annual rainfall of Cherrapunji → About 11,430 mm
☛ Mawsynram is in which state → Meghalaya

q: The southern branch of which of the following jet streams (high winds) plays an important role in the winter season in north and northwestern India?
qs.e: The southern branch of the Subtropical Westerly Jet Stream plays a crucial role in the winter season over north and northwestern India. This jet stream flows at about 12-14 km altitude near 30°N latitude and brings western disturbances, which cause winter rainfall and snowfall. The Polar-Night Jet Stream is found over polar regions in winter. The Tropical Easterly Jet Stream is active over India during summer and influences the southwest monsoon. The African Easterly Jet is located over Africa.
qs.kf:
☛ Where is the southern branch of the Subtropical Westerly Jet Stream active? → Over north and northwestern India
☛ Western disturbances are associated with which jet stream? → Subtropical Westerly Jet Stream
☛ In which season is the Tropical Easterly Jet active? → Summer (monsoon)
☛ Where is the Polar-Night Jet Stream found? → Over polar regions in winter
☛ Over which continent is the African Easterly Jet found? → Africa

q: As per Advancing Monsoon in India, which of the following cities receives rainfall the earliest?
qs.e: The monsoon in India arrives from the southwest, first reaching the Kerala coast. It then advances towards the northeast and north. Bengaluru is located in southern India, which causes it to be affected earlier by the monsoon compared to other options. Lucknow, Nagpur, and Chandigarh are in northern and central India, where the monsoon arrives later. Bengaluru receives rainfall from early June, while other cities receive it from late June or July. This is why Bengaluru receives the earliest rainfall among the given cities.
qs.kf:
☛ Earliest monsoon arrival point in India → Kerala coast
☛ Bay of Bengal branch → brings rainfall to Northeast India
☛ Arabian Sea branch → brings rainfall to Western Ghats and North India
☛ Monsoon break → dry period over central India
☛ Retreating monsoon → rainfall in southern India during October-November

q: What is the main feature of the Bhangar region in the Northern Plains?
qs.e: Bhangar is the old alluvial region of the Northern Plains, formed by ancient deposits of rivers. It lies above the flood level and is not affected by floods. The soil of Bhangar contains gravel and calcareous particles, making it less fertile compared to Khadar (new alluvium). This soil is suitable for crops like wheat, gram, and barley. Irrigation in Bhangar is done through wells and canals. The Bhangar region extends across Punjab, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, and Bihar. It is characterized by undulating topography and contains older alluvium with kankar nodules.
qs.kf:
☛ Nature of Bhangar soil → Old alluvial, less fertile
☛ Feature of Khadar → New alluvial, highly fertile
☛ Irrigation source in Bhangar → Wells and canals
☛ Extension of Bhangar → Higher part of Northern Plains
☛ Crop grown in Bhangar → Wheat, gram

q: What is the primary characteristic of the Thar Desert's soil?
qs.e: The Thar Desert, also known as the Great Indian Desert, is characterized by sandy and dry soil. Due to extremely low rainfall, the soil lacks moisture and has poor water retention capacity. The high proportion of sand particles makes the soil easily eroded by wind. Organic matter content is very low, rendering it infertile for agriculture. The soil is predominantly sandy in texture and alkaline in nature. It is also saline in many areas, further limiting plant growth. The soil is prone to wind erosion, leading to shifting sand dunes.
qs.kf:
☛ Soil type of Thar Desert → Sandy soil
☛ Average rainfall in Thar Desert → Less than 250 mm
☛ Nature of soil → Alkaline and saline
☛ Organic matter in soil → Very low
☛ Extent of Thar Desert → Rajasthan, Gujarat, Punjab, and Haryana

q: The Season of Retreating Monsoon occurs during which of the following months in India?
qs.e: The retreating monsoon in India occurs during October-November. It begins after the southwest monsoon withdraws. During this period, monsoon winds weaken and reverse direction, activating northeast monsoon winds. This season brings rainfall mainly to the Peninsular India, especially the coastal regions of Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh. By October-November, most parts of India experience clear skies and reduced cloud cover. This season is also known as the post-monsoon season or retreating monsoon.
qs.kf:
☛ When does the retreating monsoon occur in India? → October-November
☛ Which state receives maximum rainfall from northeast monsoon? → Tamil Nadu
☛ In which season does the retreating monsoon occur? → Autumn
☛ Which winds become active during monsoon retreat? → Northeast trade winds
☛ When does the southwest monsoon end in India? → End of September

q: In which of the following months does an easterly jet stream flow over the southern part of the Peninsula, reaching a maximum speed of approximately 90 km per hour?
qs.e: The easterly jet stream, also known as the Tropical Easterly Jet or Southwest Monsoon Jet, flows over the southern part of the Indian Peninsula with a maximum speed of approximately 90 km/h. This jet stream is active during the summer season, particularly in June, when the southwest monsoon is active across India. This strong wind current carries moisture from the Indian Ocean towards the Indian subcontinent and plays a crucial role in monsoon rainfall. The presence of this jet stream is recorded by the India Meteorological Department. In other months like February (winter), April (onset of summer), or December (winter), this easterly jet stream is either weak or alters its course.
qs.kf:
☛ Maximum speed of easterly jet stream → Approximately 90 km/h
☛ Month when easterly jet stream is active → June
☛ Other names of easterly jet stream → Tropical Easterly Jet or Southwest Monsoon Jet
☛ Where does this jet stream flow? → Over southern part of Indian Peninsula
☛ Relation of this jet stream with monsoon → It influences the southwest monsoon

q: In the summer season (around mid-July), the surface low-pressure belt, known as the Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ), shifts northward to lie roughly parallel to the Himalayas between __________.
qs.e: During the summer season, as the sun's rays shift northward, the ITCZ moves northwards. By mid-July, it lies roughly parallel to the Himalayas between 20° N and 25° N. This shift is the primary cause of the onset of the South-West Monsoon in the Indian subcontinent. The ITCZ is a low-pressure belt where trade winds converge. In summer, it moves north of the equator and brings rainfall to India. During this period, low-pressure centers form over Rajasthan and Punjab, attracting monsoon winds.
qs.kf:
☛ What does ITCZ stand for? → Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone
☛ Where is ITCZ located in July? → Between 20° N and 25° N
☛ Which wind is caused by ITCZ shift? → South-West Monsoon
☛ ITCZ is associated with which pressure? → Low pressure
☛ Which winds converge in ITCZ? → Trade winds

q: Which of the following jet streams brings the western cyclonic disturbances in the northern part of India during the winter months?
qs.e: During the winter months, the western cyclonic disturbances in the northern part of India are brought by the Westerly Jet Stream. This jet stream originates from the Mediterranean Sea and Central Asia, carrying moisture that causes rainfall and snowfall in northwestern India. The Westerly Jet Stream flows south of the Himalayas in winter, while in summer it shifts northward. These disturbances bring precipitation to regions like Punjab, Haryana, and western Uttar Pradesh, benefiting Rabi crops. The Westerly Jet Stream is a feature of temperate latitudes and has an average speed of 160-320 km/h. It is also known as the Subtropical Westerly Jet Stream.
qs.kf:
☛ Source of winter western disturbances in India → Mediterranean Sea and Central Asia
☛ When is the Westerly Jet Stream active over India → Winter (October to March)
☛ Alternative name for Westerly Jet Stream → Subtropical Westerly Jet
☛ Jet stream affecting India in summer → Easterly Jet Stream
☛ Altitude of the Westerly Jet Stream → 12-14 km

q: What type of rainfall occurs along the Western Ghats due to moist air being obstructed and forced to rise along the Ghats?
qs.e: When moist air is obstructed by the Western Ghats and forced to rise, it leads to orographic rainfall. This type of rainfall occurs when moist winds encounter a mountain barrier, causing the air to ascend, cool, and condense, resulting in precipitation on the windward side. The Western Ghats experience heavy rainfall during the monsoon due to this mechanism, while the leeward side remains dry due to the rain shadow effect. Orographic rainfall is common in coastal regions of India, the Himalayas, and the northeastern states.
qs.kf:
☛ Cause of orographic rainfall → Moist air forced to rise over mountains
☛ Rain shadow area is formed → On the leeward side of the mountain
☛ Wettest place in India → Mawsynram (Meghalaya)
☛ Why eastern slope of Western Ghats gets less rain → Due to rain shadow effect
☛ Heavy rainfall in Mumbai is due to → Orographic effect of Western Ghats

q: What was the major reason for the poor performance of the agriculture sector during the 1960s?
qs.e: The poor performance of the agriculture sector in India during the 1960s was primarily due to frequent droughts and famines. The decade witnessed severe droughts in 1965-66 and 1966-67, causing a sharp decline in food grain production and forcing heavy dependence on food imports. At that time, irrigation facilities were limited and farmers relied on traditional methods. This crisis pushed the government to adopt the Green Revolution, focusing on high-yielding seeds, fertilizers, and modern techniques. Although low investment in technology, overdependence on imports, and lack of skilled labor were present, natural calamities were the main cause.
qs.kf:
☛ Main cause of agricultural crisis in 1960s? → Frequent droughts and famines
☛ When did the Green Revolution start? → Late 1960s
☛ Father of Green Revolution in India? → M.S. Swaminathan
☛ Food grain production drop in 1965-66? → About 20%
☛ Main crop in Green Revolution? → Wheat

q: In the Indian tradition, which of the following is NOT one of the six two-monthly seasons?
qs.e: In Indian tradition, there are six seasons: Vasanta (Spring), Grishma (Summer), Varsha (Monsoon), Sharada (Autumn), Hemanta (Pre-winter), and Shishira (Winter). These seasons last two months each and divide the year according to the Hindu calendar. Pravara is not one of the six recognized seasons. Vasanta occurs in March-April, Grishma in May-June, Varsha in July-August, Sharada in September-October, Hemanta in November-December, and Shishira in January-February. This classification is mentioned in ancient Indian texts like the Vedas and Puranas.
qs.kf:
☛ Names of six Indian seasons → Vasanta, Grishma, Varsha, Sharada, Hemanta, Shishira
☛ Vasanta season months → Chaitra and Vaishakha (Mar-Apr)
☛ Sharada season months → Ashvina and Kartika (Sep-Oct)
☛ Hemanta season months → Margashirsha and Pausha (Nov-Dec)
☛ Seasons mentioned in → Rigveda and other ancient texts

q: Which of the following steers the tropical depressions into India especially during the summer season?
qs.e: The Easterly Jet Stream steers the tropical depressions into India during the summer season. This jet stream is active over the Indian Peninsula in summer and is associated with the monsoon trough. The easterly jet stream is a high-altitude wind flow that guides tropical depressions towards India, influencing monsoon rainfall. In contrast, the westerly jet stream is active in winter and causes western disturbances. Thus, it is the easterly jet stream that steers tropical depressions into India during summer.
qs.kf:
☛ Which jet stream steers tropical depressions into India in summer? → Easterly Jet Stream
☛ Where is the easterly jet stream active? → Over Indian Peninsula in summer
☛ When is the westerly jet stream active? → In winter
☛ Western disturbances are associated with? → Westerly Jet Stream
☛ Monsoon trough is linked to which jet stream? → Easterly Jet Stream

q: During the winter season, surface winds blow from the high-pressure centre over ______________, reaching India as a dry continental air mass.
qs.e: During winter, a high-pressure centre develops over central Asia. Surface winds from this high-pressure area blow into India, bringing dry and cold continental air mass. This air mass causes cold waves and fog in northwestern India. The high-pressure centre over central Asia is an extension of the Siberian high, which intensifies during winter. Western disturbances, influenced by this air mass, bring rainfall to India. Thus, the dry winds from central Asia significantly affect India's winter climate. Central Asia's high-pressure system is crucial for understanding India's winter weather patterns, as it directs the flow of dry air into the subcontinent, leading to clear skies and low temperatures in northern India.
qs.kf:
☛ From where does the dry continental air mass come to India in winter? → Central Asia
☛ What type of pressure centre exists over central Asia in winter? → High pressure
☛ The high pressure over central Asia is an extension of which pressure system? → Siberian high
☛ What causes winter rainfall in India? → Western disturbances
☛ Characteristics of continental air mass? → Dry and cold

q: What traditional water harvesting system is used in the semi-arid and arid regions of Rajasthan?
qs.e: In the semi-arid and arid regions of Rajasthan, Tankas is a traditional water harvesting system. These are circular or rectangular pits built near houses or fields to collect rainwater. Tankas are constructed using local materials like stone, lime, and sand, with depths ranging from 3 to 10 meters. They are used for drinking and irrigation purposes. This system is effective for water conservation in low rainfall areas. Other options like Guls (Himalayan region), Bamboo pipes (Northeast India), and Rooftop harvesting (various regions) are not specific to Rajasthan.
qs.kf:
☛ Traditional water harvesting system of Rajasthan → Tankas
☛ Use of Tankas → Drinking and irrigation
☛ Construction material of Tankas → Stone, lime, sand
☛ Guls are prevalent in → Himalayan region
☛ Bamboo pipes are used in → Northeast India

q: The Great Indian Plains are primarily known for:
o: alluvial soils and high agricultural productivity
alluvial soils and low agricultural productivity
qs.e: The Great Indian Plains are primarily known for their alluvial soils brought by the Himalayan rivers. These soils are highly fertile and rich in nutrients, leading to high agricultural productivity. This region is the main food basket of India, yielding large quantities of wheat, rice, sugarcane, and pulses. Mineral resources and sand dunes are characteristic of desert areas, while desert vegetation is found in arid regions. Thus, the identity of the Great Plains is defined by their fertile alluvial soil and high agricultural output.
qs.kf:
☛ Which soil type is the Great Indian Plain known for? → Alluvial soil
☛ Which rivers deposit alluvial soil in the plains? → Himalayan rivers (Indus, Ganga, Brahmaputra)
☛ What is the agricultural productivity of the Great Plains? → High
☛ Which region is the main food basket of India? → The Great Indian Plains
☛ Which states are covered by the Great Plains? → Punjab, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, West Bengal, Assam

q: Which of the following statements is/are correct?
Statement 1: The Peninsular India has a well-defined cold weather season. Statement 2: There is hardly any seasonal change in the distribution pattern of the temperature in coastal areas of India.
o: Both statement 1 and statement 2 are correct.
Statement 1 is correct, while statement 2 is incorrect.
Neither statement 1 nor statement 2 is correct.
Statement 2 is correct, while statement 1 is incorrect.
qs.e: Peninsular India does not have a well-defined cold weather season because it lies in the tropical zone and is influenced by the sea, resulting in moderate temperatures throughout the year. In contrast, coastal areas experience maritime influence, which leads to very little seasonal variation in temperature distribution. Therefore, Statement 1 is incorrect, while Statement 2 is correct.
qs.kf:
☛ Characteristic of cold weather in Peninsular India → Moderate, not well-defined.
☛ Annual temperature range in coastal areas → Less than 5°C.
☛ Where well-defined cold season occurs in India → Northern India (near Himalayas).
☛ Reason for stable temperatures due to maritime effect → High specific heat of water.
☛ Why Statement 1 is incorrect → Peninsular India lacks well-defined cold season.

q: The south-west monsoon is regarded as the continuation of which of the following winds, deflected towards the Indian subcontinent after crossing the Equator?
qs.e: The south-west monsoon is essentially the continuation of the southeast trade winds. These winds blow from the southeast direction in the southern hemisphere and, after crossing the Equator, are deflected to the right due to the Coriolis effect, turning into south-westerly winds that move towards the Indian subcontinent. This seasonal reversal of winds is responsible for the majority of rainfall in India. The southeast trades originate from the subtropical high-pressure belt in the southern Indian Ocean and are drawn towards the low-pressure area over the Indian subcontinent during summer.
qs.kf:
☛ Where does the southwest monsoon originate? → Southern Indian Ocean
☛ What deflects the southeast trade winds after crossing the Equator? → Coriolis effect
☛ When does the monsoon normally arrive in India? → Around June 1
☛ Name the two branches of the southwest monsoon. → Arabian Sea branch and Bay of Bengal branch
☛ Which Indian state receives the first monsoon showers? → Kerala

q: The shift in the position of the Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) in the summer season in India is related to which of the following phenomena?
o: Formation of the westerly jet stream in the north Indian plain
Formation of the easterly jet stream along 25°N latitude
Withdrawal of the westerly jet stream from the north Indian plain
Withdrawal of the easterly jet stream along 15°N latitude
qs.e: The shift in the position of the ITCZ during summer in India is related to the withdrawal of the westerly jet stream from the north Indian plain. In winter, the westerly jet stream flows south of the Himalayas, keeping the ITCZ in a southerly position. As the sun moves northward in summer, the westerly jet stream weakens and retreats northwards, allowing the ITCZ to shift northward, leading to the onset of the monsoon over India. Thus, the withdrawal of the westerly jet stream is the primary cause of the northward movement of the ITCZ. The formation of the easterly jet stream occurs during the monsoon period but is not responsible for the shift of the ITCZ.
qs.kf:
☛ Northward shift of ITCZ in summer → Linked to withdrawal of westerly jet stream
☛ Westerly jet stream in winter → Flows south of the Himalayas
☛ Westerly jet stream in summer → Weakens and retreats northward
☛ Formation of easterly jet stream → Occurs during monsoon season
☛ Shift of ITCZ → Causes Indian monsoon

q: The Terai region is best known for:
o: rich forest cover and marshy land
qs.e: The Terai region is a narrow belt at the foot of the Himalayas, extending across northern India and Nepal. It is best known for its rich forest cover and marshy land, due to the rivers flowing from the Himalayas and their alluvial deposits, which create fertile soil. The dense forests include trees like sal and teak. This area is also famous for wildlife such as tigers, elephants, and rhinoceroses. High rainfall and moisture lead to the development of marshy lands, which are crucial for biodiversity. Other options like salt pans or rocky terrain do not characterize the Terai region.
qs.kf:
☛ Main characteristic of Terai region → Rich forest cover and marshy land
☛ Where is Terai located? → At the foothills of the Himalayas
☛ Major trees found in Terai → Sal and teak
☛ Reason for high rainfall in Terai → Moist winds from the Himalayas
☛ Ecological significance of Terai → Center of biodiversity

q: Which of the following are the main reasons for the excessive cold in north India during the winter season? (1) Presence of moderating influence of sea (2) Snowfall in the Himalayan ranges (3) Coming of cold winds from the Caspian Sea and Turkmenistan
qs.e: The main reasons for excessive cold in north India during winter are snowfall in the Himalayan ranges, which drives cold winds southward, and the inflow of cold winds from the Caspian Sea and Turkmenistan. The moderating influence of the sea (maritime effect) is absent in north India due to its inland location, so option 1 is incorrect. Therefore, reasons 2 and 3 are correct.
qs.kf:
☛ Main source of winter cold waves in north India → Western disturbances and cold winds from Central Asia
☛ Himalayan effect on winter monsoon → Blocking cold winds and causing precipitation
☛ Geographical location of Caspian Sea → Between Europe and Asia in Central Asia
☛ Climate of Turkmenistan → Arid continental, extreme temperatures
☛ Absence of maritime influence → Causes extreme temperature variations in north India

q: The southwest monsoon is believed to engulf the entire subcontinent by mid ________.
qs.e: The southwest monsoon arrives on the Kerala coast in early June and advances northwards gradually. It engulfs the entire Indian subcontinent by mid-July. Factors influencing the monsoon's progress include the position of the Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ), high-pressure winds, and the Himalayan barrier. The full coverage of the monsoon marks the onset of rainfall in different parts of the country. Delays or early arrival affect agriculture and water resources. The monsoon typically withdraws by September or October.
qs.kf:
☛ When does the southwest monsoon arrive in India? → Early June on Kerala coast
☛ By when does the monsoon cover the entire subcontinent? → Mid-July
☛ Which mountain range acts as a barrier for the monsoon? → Himalayas
☛ Which zone influences monsoon progression? → Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ)
☛ What is the primary impact of delayed monsoon? → Affects agriculture and water resources

q: What defines the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) during the monsoon season in India?
o: A cold front over the Himalayas
A high-pressure zone at the Equator
A high-pressure zone over the Indian Ocean
A low-pressure zone over the Gangetic plains
qs.e: During the monsoon season, the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) over India is defined as a low-pressure zone over the Gangetic plains. Due to the northward movement of the sun in summer, the ITCZ shifts northward from the Equator. Intense heating over northern India creates a low-pressure area, which attracts southwest monsoon winds. This low-pressure zone is the primary driver of the Indian monsoon and causes heavy rainfall.
qs.kf:
☛ What is the position of ITCZ during monsoon in India? → Low-pressure zone over Gangetic plains
☛ Why does ITCZ shift northwards? → Due to northward movement of the sun
☛ Main cause of southwest monsoon? → Low pressure over Gangetic plains
☛ Which region receives rainfall from ITCZ? → Indian subcontinent
☛ Role of ITCZ in monsoon? → Attracts monsoon winds

q: During winter months, dry continental winds from Central Asia primarily come in contact with trade winds over which of the following regions of India?
qs.e: During winter months, dry continental winds from Central Asia come in contact with trade winds over northwestern India. These winds originate from land areas and are extremely dry. The trade winds blow from the northeast and bring moisture from the Bay of Bengal. When these two wind systems meet over northwestern India, they sometimes create cyclonic circulation, leading to weak precipitation. This region experiences a drop in temperature and formation of fog. The contact mainly occurs over Punjab, Haryana, Delhi, and surrounding areas. This phenomenon is important for understanding India's winter climate and its regional variations.
qs.kf:
☛ Which winds meet over northwestern India in winter? → Dry continental winds from Central Asia and trade winds
☛ From which direction do these winds blow? → Northeast to southwest
☛ What is winter rainfall in northwestern India called? → Mavath rainfall
☛ What effect does this contact have on temperature? → Temperature drops
☛ What type of rainfall occurs due to this contact? → Weak cyclonic rainfall

q: In India, dryland farming is primarily practiced in regions with which of the following annual rainfall levels?
qs.e: Dryland farming is practiced in regions where the annual rainfall is less than 75 cm. These areas experience moisture deficit and crops primarily depend on rainfall. This type of farming is prevalent in arid and semi-arid climatic regions of India, such as parts of Rajasthan, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, and Madhya Pradesh. Due to low rainfall, irrigation facilities are limited, so farmers cultivate drought-tolerant crops like pearl millet, sorghum, maize, pulses, oilseeds, and cotton. Techniques such as soil conservation, water harvesting, and crop rotation are commonly employed in dryland farming. It is crucial for the livelihood of millions of farmers in rain-dependent regions.
qs.kf:
☛ Rainfall range for dryland farming → Less than 75 cm
☛ Major crop in dryland farming → Pearl millet and sorghum
☛ Largest area under dryland farming → Rajasthan
☛ Water conservation technique used → Mulching and drip irrigation
☛ Soil conservation method for dryland → Contour plowing

q: Which of the following was a significant problem faced by the agricultural sector in India around 1947?
qs.e: At the time of independence in 1947, Indian agriculture was primarily rain-fed and heavily dependent on monsoons. There was a lack of irrigation facilities, leading to erratic crop production. Natural calamities like droughts and floods severely affected farming. High productivity, modern techniques, and surplus production were not possible because agricultural practices were traditional and underdeveloped. Before the Green Revolution, India was not self-sufficient in food grains.
qs.kf:
☛ Major problem of Indian agriculture at independence → Dependence on monsoons and lack of irrigation
☛ When did Green Revolution start → 1960s
☛ Focus of India's First Five-Year Plan → Agriculture and irrigation
☛ Largest contributors to food grain production in India → Uttar Pradesh, Punjab, Haryana
☛ Percentage of rain-fed agriculture in India → about 55-60%

q: What can happen if rocks are not weathered in the context of the movement of Earth's materials?
o: Mass movement would be more frequent
qs.e: Weathering breaks down rocks into smaller particles, providing the material necessary for erosion. If weathering does not occur, rocks remain solid and intact, making their transport by wind, water, or ice nearly impossible. Thus, the process of erosion would stop or become insignificant. Mass movements (such as landslides) also depend on weathering; without it, they would decrease, not increase. Soil fertility also requires weathering, as it releases minerals. Hence, in the absence of weathering, erosion would be insignificant.
qs.kf:
☛ Which process becomes insignificant in the absence of weathering? → Erosion
☛ Weathering provides material for which process? → Erosion
☛ Without weathering, mass movement would be? → Less frequent
☛ Which process is essential for soil fertility? → Weathering
☛ What is the relationship between erosion and weathering? → Weathering supplies material for erosion

q: Which term refers to the pre-monsoon showers that occur with a sudden rise in temperature, especially in southern India?
qs.e: Mango showers, also known as pre-monsoon showers, occur in southern India during the summer season (April-May) after a sudden rise in temperature. These rains are crucial for the ripening of mangoes, hence the name. They are common in states like Kerala, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, and Andhra Pradesh. In contrast, nor'westers affect north-west India, break in monsoon refers to a pause in rainfall, and loo is a hot, dry wind.
qs.kf:
☛ Pre-monsoon showers with sudden temperature rise → Mango showers
☛ Main region of mango showers → Southern India
☛ Season of mango showers → Summer (April-May)
☛ Why named mango showers → Beneficial for mango crop
☛ Similar phenomenon in north-west India → Nor'wester (Kalbaisakhi)

q: Which of the following zones receives vertical rays of the Sun throughout the year?
qs.e: Due to the 23.5° tilt of the Earth's axis, the Sun's rays fall vertically throughout the year only in the region between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn. This region is known as the Tropical Zone. It extends from the equator to 23.5° latitude on both sides. Here, the duration of day and night is nearly equal, and temperatures remain high throughout the year. In the Frigid, Temperate, and Polar zones, the Sun's rays strike obliquely, resulting in lower temperatures and seasonal variations.
qs.kf:
☛ Between which latitudes is the Tropical Zone located? → Tropic of Cancer (23.5° N) to Tropic of Capricorn (23.5° S).
☛ What is the axial tilt of the Earth? → 23.5°.
☛ In which zone do vertical sun rays fall? → Tropical Zone.
☛ How many times does the Sun shine directly overhead at the equator in a year? → Twice (March 21 and September 23).
☛ What is another name for the Tropical Zone? → Torrid Zone.

q: Which of the following is a shallow desert depression formed by wind erosion?
qs.e: A deflation hollow is a shallow desert depression formed by wind erosion (deflation). It occurs when wind removes loose particles from the desert surface, creating a concave-shaped basin. These hollows are typically wide and shallow, and sometimes they reach the water table, leading to the formation of playa lakes. Pediment is a gently sloping rock surface at the base of a hill, playa is a temporary lake, and inselberg is an isolated hill or mountain.
qs.kf:
☛ What is a shallow depression formed by wind erosion called? → Deflation hollow
☛ What is formed when a deflation hollow fills with water? → Playa lake
☛ Pediment is formed by which processes? → Wind and water erosion
☛ What is an inselberg? → An isolated residual hill
☛ Which is the most dominant erosion process in deserts? → Deflation (Wind erosion)

q: What type of rainfall occurs when air is forced to rise over a mountain barrier?
qs.e: When moist air is forced to rise over a geographical barrier like a mountain, it cools, condenses, and causes precipitation. This type of rainfall is called orographic rainfall. It predominantly occurs on the windward slope of mountains. Cyclonic rainfall is associated with low-pressure systems, convectional rainfall results from intense heating, and frontal rainfall occurs when warm and cold air masses meet. Thus, the rainfall caused by a mountain barrier is orographic rainfall.
qs.kf:
☛ On which side does orographic rainfall occur? → Windward slope
☛ Example of orographic rainfall in India → Western side of Western Ghats
☛ Another name for orographic rainfall → Relief rainfall
☛ What causes orographic rainfall? → Topography
☛ What is the rain shadow region? → Dry area on the leeward side of mountain

q: What is the area around the equator called where the trade winds from both hemispheres converge?
qs.e: The area around the equator where the trade winds from the Northern and Southern Hemispheres converge is called the Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ). It is a low-pressure belt encircling the Earth near the equator. This zone is characterized by convective rainfall and thunderstorms due to rising warm air. The position of the ITCZ shifts seasonally following the Sun's north-south movement. It plays a crucial role in the global atmospheric circulation system, influencing rainfall patterns in tropical regions. The ITCZ is also known as the Doldrums due to its calm winds.
qs.kf:
☛ What is the full form of ITCZ? → Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone
☛ What is the pressure zone of ITCZ? → Low pressure
☛ Which winds converge in ITCZ? → Trade winds
☛ How does ITCZ shift seasonally? → Follows the Sun's north-south movement
☛ What is another name for ITCZ? → Doldrums

q: The western cyclonic disturbances that enter the Indian subcontinent from the west and the northwest during the winter months originate from which of the following regions?
qs.e: Western Cyclonic Disturbances are a type of cyclone that brings rainfall to the Indian subcontinent during the winter months. These disturbances originate from the Mediterranean Sea region and are brought towards India by western winds. They primarily cause rain and snowfall in northern India, which is beneficial for Rabi crops, especially wheat. These systems are more active during winter and are known as western disturbances. They play a crucial role in the winter weather patterns of the Indian subcontinent.
qs.kf:
☛ From where do Western Cyclonic Disturbances originate? → Mediterranean Sea
☛ What is the main cause of winter rainfall in India? → Western disturbances
☛ In which season are western disturbances active? → Winter
☛ Which Indian states are most affected by western disturbances? → Northern states (Jammu & Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh, Punjab, Haryana, Uttarakhand, Uttar Pradesh)
☛ Which crops benefit from western disturbances? → Rabi crops (wheat, mustard)

q: Which of the following is not a factor that affects ocean currents?
qs.e: Ocean currents are continuous, directed movements of seawater. They are mainly influenced by wind, temperature differences, salinity differences, and Earth's rotation (Coriolis effect). Wind drives surface currents, temperature differences cause density variations, and Earth's rotation deflects currents. Soil type is unrelated to ocean currents because soil is part of terrestrial ecosystems and has no effect on seawater movement.
qs.kf:
☛ Primary cause of ocean currents → Wind and density differences
☛ Coriolis effect is caused by → Earth's rotation
☛ Gulf Stream is what type of current → Warm water current
☛ Labrador Current is in which ocean → Atlantic Ocean
☛ El Nino is associated with → Pacific Ocean currents

q: Which weathering process involves the peeling of rock layers due to temperature variations?
qs.e: Exfoliation is a type of physical weathering process in which the outer layers of rock peel off due to temperature variations. This process mainly occurs in dry and semi-arid regions or desert areas where there is a large difference between day and night temperatures. During the day, high temperatures cause the rock to expand, and at night, cooling causes it to contract, creating repeated pressure. This pressure weakens the outermost layers of the rock, which eventually peel off like crusts or scales. This process is more commonly observed in rocks like granite and sandstone. Frost action is related to freezing of water, solution to chemical dissolution, and oxidation to chemical reactions.
qs.kf:
☛ Which climate is most suitable for exfoliation? → Dry and semi-arid climate
☛ Which layer of rock peels off in exfoliation? → Outer layer
☛ What type of weathering is exfoliation? → Physical (mechanical) weathering
☛ Which rock is most sensitive to exfoliation? → Granite
☛ What is the main cause of exfoliation? → Temperature variation

q: In the Great Indian Plains of India, which kind of soil is found on a large scale?
qs.e: Alluvial soil is found on a large scale in the Great Indian Plains. This soil is formed by the deposition of sediments brought by rivers and is widely spread across the northern plains. Alluvial soil is classified into Bangar (old alluvium) and Khadar (new alluvium). It is very fertile and is suitable for crops like wheat, rice, sugarcane, and pulses. It is found in states like Uttar Pradesh, Punjab, Haryana, Bihar, and West Bengal.
qs.kf:
☛ Classification of alluvial soil → Bangar (old) and Khadar (new)
☛ Elements found in alluvial soil → Potash, lime, phosphorus
☛ Color of alluvial soil → Light brown to dark brown
☛ Extension of alluvial soil → Northern plains and river valleys
☛ Crops grown in alluvial soil → Wheat, rice, sugarcane, pulses

q: What is the most common cause of a tsunami?
qs.e: The most common cause of a tsunami is a subsea earthquake. When tectonic plates shift beneath the ocean floor, they displace a large volume of water, generating massive waves. These waves travel at high speeds across the open ocean and can cause devastating destruction when they reach the coast. While volcanic eruptions, landslides, and meteor impacts can also trigger tsunamis, they are much rarer. The Pacific Ocean's Ring of Fire experiences the highest frequency of tsunamis. The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, caused by a massive undersea earthquake, was the deadliest in history, killing over 230,000 people. Early warning systems and coastal preparedness are essential for mitigating tsunami risks.
qs.kf:
☛ Most common cause of tsunami? → Subsea earthquake
☛ Speed of tsunami waves in open ocean? → Up to 800 km/h
☛ Major region responsible for tsunamis? → Pacific Ring of Fire
☛ Which ocean had the 2004 tsunami? → Indian Ocean
☛ Origin of the word 'tsunami'? → Japanese

q: The Paris Agreement is a significant agreement aimed at keeping global warming well below Celsius.
qs.e: The Paris Agreement is a global treaty adopted in 2015 at the United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP21). Its primary goal is to limit global warming to well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels, and to pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5°C. The agreement emphasizes that all countries submit nationally determined contributions (NDCs) to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Developed countries are to provide financial and technological support to developing nations. The Paris Agreement is a successor to the Kyoto Protocol and includes 196 parties. It aims to mitigate the impacts of climate change by limiting temperature rise and enhancing adaptive capacity. The agreement is legally binding on reporting and monitoring, and it represents a global consensus on combating climate change.
qs.kf:
☛ What is the main temperature goal of the Paris Agreement? → Below 2°C
☛ In which year was the Paris Agreement adopted? → 2015
☛ Under which UN conference was the Paris Agreement adopted? → COP21
☛ What do countries submit under the Paris Agreement? → Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs)
☛ Which protocol did the Paris Agreement replace? → Kyoto Protocol

q: A flat or gently sloping surface left behind after river erosion, often with some resistant remnants, is known as:
qs.e: Peneplain is a landform formed after prolonged river erosion. It is a nearly flat or gently sloping surface, often with resistant rock remnants called monadnocks. This concept was given by geologist William Morris Davis. Peneplain represents the final stage of the fluvial erosion cycle. A plateau is an elevated flat land, a floodplain forms along river banks, and a monadnock is a resistant remnant on a peneplain. Peneplains are characterized by low relief and are often dissected by later erosion.
qs.kf:
☛ Coined the term peneplain → William Morris Davis
☛ Resistant remnant on a peneplain → Monadnock
☛ Final stage of fluvial erosion cycle → Peneplain
☛ Surface of a peneplain → Nearly flat or gently sloping
☛ Formation of peneplain → Prolonged river erosion

q: Which season in India is characterised by high temperature and low humidity?
qs.e: In India, the hot weather season (March to June) is characterized by high temperature and low humidity. During this period, the sun's rays fall directly, raising temperatures, while the atmosphere remains dry with low moisture content. This pre-monsoon season features hot winds like 'Loo' in northern India. The retreating monsoon (October-November) is humid, the cold weather season (December-February) has low temperatures, and the southwest monsoon (June-September) brings high humidity and rainfall. Thus, the hot weather season uniquely combines high temperatures with low humidity.
qs.kf:
☛ Hot Weather Season duration → March to June
☛ Southwest Monsoon feature → high humidity and rainfall
☛ Cold Weather Season feature → low temperature and dry air
☛ Retreating Monsoon feature → humid and cloudy
☛ Hot Weather Season temperature → can reach up to 45°C in northern India

q: What is the low pressure belt near the equator commonly called?
qs.e: Near the equator, due to direct sunlight, intense heating causes the air to warm and rise, creating a low-pressure zone. This region is known as the Doldrums or the Equatorial Low-Pressure Belt. The winds here are very light and erratic, often resulting in calm conditions, which is why sailors historically avoided it. The Doldrums lie approximately between 5°N and 5°S latitude. This belt is also characterized by convectional rainfall due to rising moist air. It is distinct from other pressure belts like the Horse Latitudes, which are subtropical high-pressure zones. The term "Doldrums" literally means a state of inactivity or stagnation, reflecting the windless conditions.
qs.kf:
☛ The equatorial low-pressure belt is also called? → Doldrums
☛ Between which latitudes do the Doldrums lie? → 5°N to 5°S
☛ What type of rainfall occurs in the Doldrums? → Convectional rainfall
☛ Horse Latitudes are associated with which pressure belt? → Subtropical high-pressure belt
☛ What is the characteristic of winds in the Doldrums? → Light and erratic

q: Which physical feature acts as a barrier to the southwest monsoon winds, causing heavy rainfall on one side and dry conditions on the other?
qs.e: The Western Ghats act as a major orographic barrier for the southwest monsoon winds coming from the Arabian Sea. As the moisture-laden winds hit the Western Ghats, they are forced to rise. This upward movement causes cooling and condensation, resulting in heavy rainfall on the windward (western) side. In contrast, the leeward (eastern) side falls in the rain shadow zone, receiving significantly less rainfall, leading to dry conditions in the Deccan Plateau. The Western Ghats run parallel to the western coast of India and are a continuous mountain range. Other options like Aravalli, Vindhya, and Satpura ranges do not significantly obstruct the monsoon winds as they are either lower in altitude or aligned differently. The phenomenon is known as orographic precipitation.
qs.kf:
☛ Highest peak of Western Ghats → Anamudi
☛ Other name of Western Ghats → Sahyadri
☛ Rain shadow region in Western Ghats → Eastern side (Deccan)
☛ Reason for heavy rainfall in Mumbai → Western Ghats
☛ States covered by Western Ghats → Gujarat to Tamil Nadu

q: In dry areas, water from underground comes up through the soil by capillary action and dries quickly, leaving salts behind. These salts form a hard layer called:
qs.e: In dry regions, groundwater rises to the surface through capillary action and evaporates, leaving behind dissolved salts. Over time, these salts accumulate and form a hard, impermeable layer in the soil, known as hardpans. This layer restricts water drainage and root growth, making the soil less fertile. Hardpans are primarily composed of calcium carbonate, silica, or gypsum. They are a common feature in arid and semi-arid regions. In contrast, pedalfer refers to iron- and aluminum-rich soils found in humid regions, laterite is a tropical soil rich in iron and aluminum, and granite is an igneous rock. Understanding hardpans is important for soil management in dry areas.
qs.kf:
☛ What process forms hardpans? → Capillary action and salt deposition
☛ Main components of hardpans? → Calcium carbonate, silica, gypsum
☛ What is pedalfer? → Acidic soil of humid regions
☛ Where is laterite soil found? → Tropical regions
☛ What type of rock is granite? → Igneous rock

q: Why is wheat grown in the north-western plains of India?
o: Because it lies close to the coastal water bodies
Because it receives heavy rainfall during the monsoon
Because the region has fertile alluvial soil and cool winters
Because the region has red soil with limited annual rainfall
qs.e: The north-western plains of India, particularly Punjab, Haryana, and western Uttar Pradesh, are ideal for wheat cultivation. The alluvial soil here, deposited by rivers, is highly fertile. Wheat is a rabi crop that requires cool temperatures; the region experiences cool winters, which are favorable for its growth. The area depends on irrigation as monsoon rainfall is limited, but canals and tube wells provide adequate water. Wheat needs cool weather for germination and warm weather for ripening, which the climate here offers. Thus, the combination of fertile alluvial soil and cool winters makes this region highly suitable for wheat farming, contributing to India's major wheat production.
qs.kf:
☛ What type of crop is wheat? → Rabi crop
☛ Which soil is best for wheat cultivation? → Fertile alluvial soil
☛ What temperature is required for wheat? → Cool for germination, warm for ripening
☛ What is the ideal rainfall for wheat? → Around 50-75 cm
☛ Major source of irrigation in north-western plains? → Canals and tube wells

q: What is the primary cause of southwest monsoon in India?
o: Differential heating of land and sea
qs.e: The primary cause of the southwest monsoon in India is the differential heating of land and sea. During summer, the Indian subcontinent heats up rapidly while the Indian Ocean remains relatively cooler. This temperature difference creates a low-pressure area over land and a high-pressure area over the sea. The pressure gradient forces moisture-laden winds from the sea towards the land. When these winds encounter obstacles like the Western Ghats, they cause orographic rainfall. The monsoon is also influenced by the northward shift of the jet stream and the movement of the ITCZ. The monsoon typically arrives in Kerala by early June and covers the entire country by July.
qs.kf:
☛ Primary cause of SW monsoon → Differential heating of land and sea
☛ First state to receive monsoon → Kerala (first week of June)
☛ Type of rainfall during monsoon → Orographic rainfall
☛ Winds responsible for monsoon → Trade winds (southwest direction)
☛ Monsoon arrival in North India → By July

q: Which of the following is responsible for causing convectional rainfall?
o: Intense surface heating causing air to rise
Cold and warm air masses meeting
qs.e: Convectional rainfall occurs when the sun's rays intensely heat the Earth's surface, causing the air in contact with it to also heat up, become lighter, and rise. This rising air cools at higher altitudes, condenses to form cumulus clouds, and results in heavy rainfall. This type of rainfall is typical in equatorial regions and tropical areas during summer. It is usually heavy, short-lived, and accompanied by thunder and lightning. The intense heating creates strong updrafts, leading to vertical cloud development and precipitation.
qs.kf:
☛ Main cause of convectional rainfall → Intense surface heating causing air to rise
☛ Main cloud type in convectional rainfall → Cumulus clouds
☛ Major region for convectional rainfall → Equatorial regions
☛ Nature of convectional rainfall → Heavy and short duration
☛ Common phenomenon in convectional rainfall → Thunder and lightning

q: Western disturbances mainly affect the weather of which region in India?
qs.e: Western disturbances are low-pressure weather systems originating from the Mediterranean Sea and West Asia, which mainly affect North-West India. They bring winter rainfall to regions like Rajasthan, Punjab, Haryana, Delhi, and Jammu and Kashmir. This rainfall is crucial for Rabi crops such as wheat and mustard. Western disturbances also moderate temperatures in the northern plains. They remain active during the monsoon season and can extend up to eastern India. Their influence decreases with distance from the sea.
qs.kf:
☛ Where do western disturbances originate? → Mediterranean Sea
☛ Which crop season benefits the most? → Rabi
☛ Which states get the maximum benefit? → Punjab and Haryana
☛ What type of weather system are they? → Low-pressure
☛ In which season are they most active? → Winter

q: Which type of weathering is primarily involved in the enrichment of bauxite and other ores?
qs.e: The enrichment of bauxite and other ores primarily involves chemical weathering. In this process, minerals in rocks react with water, oxygen, and carbon dioxide, leading to their decomposition. In tropical regions, high temperature and rainfall accelerate chemical weathering, removing silica and other soluble elements, while concentrating iron and aluminum oxides. This results in the formation of bauxite from aluminum-rich rocks. Chemical weathering is thus crucial for the formation of residual deposits like bauxite and laterite ores.
qs.kf:
☛ Weathering type for bauxite enrichment → Chemical weathering
☛ Main factor for chemical weathering → Water and temperature
☛ Laterite soil formation → Chemical weathering
☛ Main component of bauxite → Aluminum oxide
☛ Result of silica leaching → Ore concentration

q: The hot weather season in India is generally observed from:
qs.e: The hot weather season in India is generally observed from March to May. This season is characterized by a sharp rise in temperature across the country, especially in northwestern India, leading to heatwaves (loo). During this period, before the arrival of the southwest monsoon, the atmosphere remains dry and temperatures can exceed 40°C. Temperatures start increasing in March and peak in May. This season is suitable for cultivation of summer crops like watermelon, muskmelon, and certain vegetables. According to the India Meteorological Department, the hot weather season extends from March to May and ends with the onset of monsoon rains. This period is also marked by thunderstorms and dust storms in some regions.
qs.kf:
☛ Hot weather season in India → March to May
☛ Typical temperature range during hot season → 30°C to 45°C
☛ Winds blowing during hot season → Dry westerlies
☛ Phenomenon associated with hot season → Heatwave (Loo)
☛ End of hot season → Arrival of southwest monsoon

q: Seasonal unemployment is common in rural economies. Which sector in India experiences the most seasonal unemployment?
qs.e: Seasonal unemployment is most prevalent in the Agriculture sector in India. Agriculture heavily depends on monsoon and crop cycles, leading to a lack of work for laborers between sowing and harvesting seasons. During the gap between Rabi and Kharif crops, unemployment rises significantly. Nearly 50% of India's population relies on agriculture, but employment is available only for 4-6 months a year. To address this, the government launched schemes like MGNREGA, which guarantees 100 days of employment in rural areas. Other sectors like transport, information technology, and manufacturing experience lower seasonal unemployment due to more stable demand patterns.
qs.kf:
☛ Which sector is most affected by seasonal unemployment? → Agriculture
☛ What is the full form of MGNREGA? → Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act
☛ How many days of employment are guaranteed under MGNREGA per year? → 100 days
☛ What is the main cause of seasonal unemployment in India? → Seasonal nature of crops
☛ After agriculture, which sector experiences higher seasonal unemployment? → Horticulture and Fisheries

q: What type of pressure develops over the Indian subcontinent during the summer, attracting monsoon winds?
qs.e: During summer, the Indian subcontinent becomes intensely heated, leading to the development of a low pressure area over land. This low pressure zone attracts moisture-laden monsoon winds from the Indian Ocean, which bring rainfall as the southwest monsoon from June to September. Conversely, high pressure prevails over the ocean. The sun's direct rays near the Tropic of Cancer cause high temperatures, forming a thermal low. This process is the primary cause of the Indian monsoon system.
qs.kf:
☛ Type of pressure over India in summer → Low pressure
☛ Factor attracting monsoon winds → Low pressure over land
☛ Cause of summer low pressure over Indian subcontinent → Intense heating
☛ Duration of southwest monsoon → June to September
☛ Location of thermal low formation → Near Tropic of Cancer

q: Climatic maps are primarily based on data related to:
qs.e: Climatic maps represent long-term weather conditions of a region. They are primarily based on data related to temperature and rainfall, as these two factors are the most important in defining a region's climate. Classifications like the Köppen climate classification rely on temperature and precipitation patterns. While factors like population growth, soil moisture, or industrial zones may influence local changes, they are not the primary basis for climatic maps. Temperature and rainfall data are used to depict climate zones globally.
qs.kf:
☛ Primary basis of climatic maps → temperature and rainfall
☛ Key factors in Köppen climate classification → temperature and rainfall
☛ Two main elements defining climate → temperature and rainfall
☛ Determination of world climate zones → based on temperature and rainfall patterns
☛ Not included in climatic maps → population density

q: Which of the following is a reason for the uneven distribution of rainfall in India during the southwest monsoon?
o: Mountain ranges influence wind direction and intensity
The Himalayas stop all monsoon rainfall.
Southern states alone receive all rainfall.
qs.e: The uneven distribution of rainfall during the southwest monsoon in India is primarily due to mountain ranges like the Western Ghats and Himalayas. These ranges obstruct the monsoon winds, forcing them to rise, cool, and condense, causing heavy rainfall on the windward side and creating rain shadow regions on the leeward side. For instance, the western slopes of the Western Ghats receive heavy rainfall, while the eastern slopes remain dry. Similarly, the Himalayas cause intense rainfall in northeastern India but leave the western part, like Rajasthan, dry. Other options are incorrect because monsoon winds do not blow equally everywhere, the Himalayas do not stop all rainfall, and southern states are not the only ones to receive rainfall.
qs.kf:
☛ Wettest place in India → Mawsynram (Meghalaya)
☛ Example of a rain shadow region → Deccan Plateau
☛ Reason for low rainfall on eastern slopes of Western Ghats → Rain shadow effect
☛ First place to receive monsoon in India → Kerala
☛ Main sources of southwest monsoon in India → Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal

q: How does deforestation lead to desertification?
o: It increases humus in the soil.
It removes the top fertile soil layer, exposing hard, rocky layers.
It increases rainfall in dry regions.
qs.e: Deforestation removes trees whose roots hold the soil together, leading to accelerated soil erosion. The top fertile layer (topsoil) is washed or blown away by wind and water, exposing the underlying hard, rocky, or infertile layers. This destroys soil fertility, making it difficult for vegetation to grow. In dry regions, this process causes desertification, where land gradually turns into desert. The loss of trees also reduces humus content and water retention capacity of the soil. Thus, deforestation removes the protective cover of soil and promotes desertification by exposing the soil to erosion agents.
qs.kf:
☛ What is the main cause of desertification? → Deforestation and soil erosion
☛ Effective measure to prevent soil erosion? → Afforestation and forest conservation
☛ Which regions are most affected by desertification? → Arid and semi-arid regions
☛ What is the top layer of soil called? → Topsoil or fertile soil
☛ What decreases in soil due to deforestation? → Humus and moisture

q: What does the term 'halocline' refer to in oceanography?
o: A layer with a rapid change in pressure
A layer with a rapid change in salinity
A zone with the highest oxygen concentration
A layer with a rapid change in temperature
qs.e: In oceanography, a halocline is a layer in the water column where salinity changes rapidly with depth. This vertical gradient is common in oceans, often with lower salinity at the surface and higher salinity at depth. Below the halocline, salinity remains relatively constant. The halocline is closely related to the thermocline (rapid temperature change) and the pycnocline (rapid density change), as salinity affects density. Studying haloclines helps identify water masses and understand oceanic circulation. Haloclines are particularly prominent in areas where freshwater from rivers or ice melt meets salty seawater, such as estuaries and polar regions.
qs.kf:
☛ What changes rapidly in a halocline? → Salinity
☛ What changes rapidly in a thermocline? → Temperature
☛ What changes rapidly in a pycnocline? → Density
☛ Pycnocline is formed by which two clines? → Thermocline and halocline
☛ The term 'halocline' is derived from which language? → Greek

q: Which of the following local winds is known to bring rain to Tamil Nadu during winter?
qs.e: The local wind that brings rain to Tamil Nadu during winter is the Northeast monsoon. This monsoon is active from October to December and causes rainfall along the eastern coast of southern India, especially in Tamil Nadu and Puducherry. In contrast, the Southwest monsoon brings rain to most parts of India from June to September, but Tamil Nadu receives less rainfall from it. The Jet stream is a fast-moving air current in the upper atmosphere that influences weather systems but does not directly cause local rainfall. Nor'wester are thunderstorms that occur in West Bengal and Bangladesh during summer. Thus, Tamil Nadu's winter rainfall is due to the Northeast monsoon.
qs.kf:
☛ Cause of winter rainfall in Tamil Nadu → Northeast monsoon
☛ Active period of Northeast monsoon → October to December
☛ State receiving highest rainfall from Southwest monsoon → Kerala
☛ Region where Nor'westers occur → West Bengal and Bangladesh
☛ Layer where Jet stream is found → Troposphere

q: Which type of land is most suitable for agriculture in India?
qs.e: Level alluvial land is considered most suitable for agriculture in India. This land is formed by sediments deposited by rivers, making it fertile and rich in nutrients. Major agricultural regions like the Ganga-Yamuna plains, Punjab, and Haryana have this type of land. Crops such as wheat, rice, sugarcane, and others are extensively grown here. The flat terrain facilitates irrigation and mechanization, leading to higher productivity. Other options like mountainous, rocky, and forest land are unsuitable due to poor soil, slopes, or forest cover, which make farming difficult.
qs.kf:
☛ Most fertile soil in India → Alluvial soil
☛ Alluvial soil is formed by? → River deposits
☛ Which soil covers the Gangetic plains? → Alluvial soil
☛ What type of land is Punjab's agriculture based on? → Level alluvial
☛ Best soil for rice cultivation? → Alluvial soil

q: The increase in Earth's average temperature due to trapped gases is called:
qs.e: The greenhouse effect is the process by which certain gases in Earth's atmosphere (such as carbon dioxide, methane, and water vapor) trap heat from the sun, causing the planet's average temperature to rise. These gases are called greenhouse gases. Human activities like burning fossil fuels have increased the concentration of these gases, leading to global warming. While the greenhouse effect is natural, excessive accumulation causes harmful climate changes. It is the primary reason for global temperature rise.
qs.kf:
☛ Major greenhouse gas → Carbon dioxide
☛ Gas with highest greenhouse effect → Water vapor
☛ Main source of greenhouse gases → Burning fossil fuels
☛ International treaty related to greenhouse effect → Kyoto Protocol
☛ Long-term effect of greenhouse effect → Global warming

q: What is the disintegration of rocks into smaller fragments without any change in their chemical composition called?
qs.e: Mechanical weathering, also known as physical weathering, is the process of breaking rocks into smaller fragments without any change in their chemical composition. It occurs due to physical forces such as temperature changes, freeze-thaw cycles, and pressure release. Among the given options, exfoliation (sheet jointing) and block disintegration are specific types of mechanical weathering. Frost action, where water freezes in cracks and expands, is also a mechanical weathering process. The question broadly asks for the general process, which is mechanical weathering. Unlike chemical weathering, mechanical weathering does not alter the mineral composition of rocks.
qs.kf:
☛ Alternate name for mechanical weathering → Physical weathering
☛ Exfoliation is a type of which weathering → Mechanical weathering
☛ Frost action belongs to which weathering → Mechanical weathering
☛ Chemical change in rocks is called → Chemical weathering
☛ Block disintegration is a type of which weathering → Mechanical weathering

q: Slump is a type of:
qs.e: Slump is a type of landslide where a mass of soil or rock rotates along a concave surface and moves downward. It differs from erosion and weathering as it involves quick displacement of material. Landslides occur primarily due to gravity on slopes. In slump, the back surface of the sliding material is concave, forming a scarp. It is a common form of landslide, often observed in saturated soils. Slumps are characterized by rotational movement and are distinct from rock falls, where material free-falls. Understanding slump helps in identifying slope failures and preventive measures.
qs.kf:
☛ What is the main cause of slump? → Gravity and saturation
☛ What type of movement occurs in slump? → Rotational movement
☛ What structure is formed in a slump? → Concave scarp
☛ Slump is a subtype of which phenomenon? → Landslide
☛ Difference between slump and rock fall? → Slump has rotational movement, rock fall has free fall

q: Which of the following places is most likely to experience an equable climate with minimal seasonal variation due to its proximity to the sea?
qs.e: Due to its proximity to the sea, Mumbai experiences an equable climate with minimal seasonal variation in temperature. The maritime influence prevents extreme heat in summer and extreme cold in winter. In contrast, Amritsar, Bhopal, and Delhi are inland locations with a continental climate, characterized by very hot summers and very cold winters. The coastal climate is also known as maritime climate, while the inland climate is called continental climate. Therefore, Mumbai is most likely to have an equable climate with minimal seasonal variation due to its proximity to the sea.
qs.kf:
☛ Main cause of maritime climate → Proximity to sea
☛ City with continental climate → Delhi, Amritsar, Bhopal
☛ Indian city with equable climate → Mumbai, Chennai, Kolkata
☛ Climate type of Mumbai → Tropical humid climate
☛ Maximum seasonal variation where → Inland locations

q: The retreating monsoon causes rainfall mainly in _____.
qs.e: The retreating monsoon moves from north India towards the south during October-November. It causes rainfall mainly in the coastal areas of Tamil Nadu due to the northeast trade winds picking up moisture from the Bay of Bengal. In contrast, Assam, Maharashtra, and Punjab receive rainfall primarily from the southwest monsoon. The retreating monsoon is crucial for Tamil Nadu as it provides the state's main post-monsoon rainfall, which is vital for agriculture and water resources.
qs.kf:
☛ State receiving maximum rainfall from retreating monsoon → Tamil Nadu
☛ Direction of retreating monsoon → From north to south India
☛ Period of retreating monsoon → October to December
☛ Main cause of rainfall in Tamil Nadu → Retreating monsoon
☛ State receiving highest rainfall from southwest monsoon → Kerala

q: Clear skies, rising temperatures, and moist land — conditions commonly referred to as ‘October heat’ — are associated with which of the following in the Indian context?
o: Monsoon Wind striking the Western Coast
Cyclonic Depressions of Bay of Bengal
qs.e: October heat occurs during the retreating monsoon when the south-west monsoon weakens and transitions to north-easterly winds. The skies become clear, temperatures rise, and the land remains moist, resulting in high humidity. This phenomenon is observed in northern India during October and is commonly referred to as 'October heat'. It is associated with the retreating monsoon, which brings an end to the rainy season and leads to a hot, humid spell before winter.
qs.kf:
☛ What is 'October heat' associated with? → Retreating monsoon
☛ What is the sky condition during October heat? → Clear
☛ In which month does October heat occur? → October
☛ From which direction do winds blow during retreating monsoon? → North-east
☛ Where is October heat mainly experienced? → Northern India

q: Where do tropical cyclones occur?
qs.e: Temperate cyclones occur in mid-latitude regions (30° to 60° latitude). They are also called extratropical cyclones or wave cyclones. They form at the boundary between polar air and tropical air. Their extent is 1000-2000 km. They move towards the northeast. Western disturbances are an example of temperate cyclones.
qs.kf:
☛ Where do temperate cyclones originate? → Mid-latitude regions
☛ What are temperate cyclones also called? → Extratropical cyclones
☛ In which direction do temperate cyclones move? → Northeast
☛ Which weather system is an example of a temperate cyclone? → Western disturbance
☛ What is the extent of a temperate cyclone? → 1000-2000 km

q: Which of the following options explains the variation in temperature between coastal and interior parts of India?
qs.e: The variation in temperature between coastal and interior parts of India is primarily explained by continentality. Continentality refers to the difference in heating and cooling rates between land and water. Coastal regions, being near the sea, experience a maritime climate with less temperature fluctuation. In contrast, interior regions have a continental climate, characterized by very hot summers and very cold winters. While altitude, pressure belts, and latitude also affect temperature, the main factor for coastal-interior temperature difference is continentality.
qs.kf:
☛ What is continentality? → The difference in heating and cooling of land and water.
☛ Which Indian city has a continental climate? → Delhi has a continental climate.
☛ What type of climate do coastal areas have? → Maritime climate with moderate temperatures.
☛ Why is Mumbai warmer than Delhi in winter? → Due to maritime influence in Mumbai and continentality in Delhi.
☛ Where is the effect of continentality most pronounced? → In interior parts of continents, e.g., Central Asia.

q: Which of the following mass movements occurs when saturated soil and debris flow down a slope during heavy rainfall?
qs.e: When saturated soil and debris flow rapidly down a slope during heavy rainfall, this mass movement is called mudflow. It is a type of mass wasting where water-saturated soil, rock fragments, and debris combine into a fluid, muddy flow. Mudflows are common in hilly and mountainous regions after heavy rains or rapid snowmelt. Avalanches involve snow and ice; soil creep is an extremely slow, gradual movement; and rockfall is the rapid falling of rocks. Mudflow moves at a fast pace and can carry large amounts of material, making it a destructive geological process.
qs.kf:
☛ What causes a mudflow? → Heavy rainfall leading to water-saturated soil
☛ What is soil creep? → Very slow, imperceptible downslope movement of soil
☛ What does an avalanche involve? → Snow and iceWhat is rockfall? → Rapid falling of rocks from a cliff
☛ What is mass wasting? → Downslope movement of rock, soil, or debris under gravity

q: Most of the _______ are formed by sand and silt deposited by rivers and sea waves.
qs.e: Alluvial soils are formed by sand and silt deposited by rivers and sea waves. They are the most fertile soils in India and are found in the northern plains, river valleys, and coastal areas. These soils are rich in potash and lime but deficient in nitrogen and phosphorus. They are formed by the deposition of sediments brought by rivers, known as alluvium. Alluvial soils are classified into two types: Khadar (new alluvium) and Bhangar (old alluvium). Major crops grown include wheat, rice, sugarcane, and pulses.
qs.kf:
☛ How are alluvial soils formed? → By deposition of sand and silt by rivers and sea waves
☛ Which nutrients are deficient in alluvial soils? → Nitrogen and phosphorus
☛ What are the two main types of alluvial soils? → Khadar (new) and Bhangar (old)
☛ Where are alluvial soils most commonly found? → In the northern plains and river valleys of India
☛ Which major crops are grown in alluvial soils? → Wheat, rice, sugarcane, pulses

q: What is the fragrance of soil generated immediately after the rains?
A. Petrichor
B. Tempus vemum
C. Vrochi
D. Irida
qs.e: The earthy scent produced when rain falls on dry soil is called Petrichor. The term is derived from Greek words 'petra' (stone) and 'ichor' (the fluid that flows in the veins of gods). This smell is primarily caused by a compound called geosmin, which is produced by soil-dwelling bacteria of the genus Streptomyces. When raindrops hit dry soil, they trap tiny air bubbles that carry geosmin upward, releasing the scent into the air. Humans are highly sensitive to this smell. The concept was first described by Australian scientists Isabel Joy Bear and Roderick Thomas in 1964.
qs.kf:
☛ What is the origin of the word Petrichor? → Greek
☛ Which compound is responsible for the smell of Petrichor? → Geosmin
☛ Which bacteria produces geosmin? → Streptomyces
☛ In which year was the term Petrichor coined? → 1964
☛ Who coined the term Petrichor? → Isabel Joy Bear and Roderick Thomas

q: Which of the following is/are contaminated by the wastes produced from factories?
qs.e: Wastes produced from factories include solid, liquid, and gaseous substances that contaminate soil, air, and water. Solid waste like chemical residues mixes with soil, making it infertile. Liquid waste such as industrial chemicals is discharged into water bodies, causing water pollution. Gaseous emissions like carbon dioxide and sulfur dioxide pollute the air and lead to acid rain. Thus, factory waste contaminates all three environmental media.
qs.kf:
☛ Environmental impact of industrial solid waste → Soil pollution
☛ Main consequence of industrial liquid waste → Water pollution
☛ Problem associated with industrial gaseous emissions → Acid rain
☛ Cause of biomagnification → Water-soluble industrial chemicals
☛ Major source of soil pollution → Disposal of industrial waste

q: Select the pair that is matched correctly (the institute to the city it is based in).
o: Central Arid Zone Research Institute - Jodhapur
qs.e: The Central Arid Zone Research Institute (CAZRI) is located in Jodhpur, Rajasthan, and is the premier institute for research on agriculture and ecology in India's arid regions. The other options are incorrect: The Central Leather Research Institute is in Chennai, not Salem; the Central Potato Research Institute is in Shimla, not Dehradun; and the Central Drug Research Institute is in Lucknow, not Kanpur. CAZRI was established in 1959 and operates under the Department of Science and Technology, Government of India.
qs.kf:
☛ Where is Central Arid Zone Research Institute located? → Jodhpur
☛ Where is Central Leather Research Institute located? → Chennai
☛ Where is Central Potato Research Institute located? → Shimla
☛ Where is Central Drug Research Institute located? → Lucknow
☛ When was Central Arid Zone Research Institute established? → 1959

q: Which of the following soil types is rich in soil nutrients such as calcium carbonate, magnesium, potash and lime?
qs.e: Black soil, also known as regur soil, is rich in nutrients like calcium carbonate, magnesium, potash and lime. It is predominantly found in the Deccan Plateau region and is ideal for cotton cultivation. This soil has high water retention capacity and is self-ploughing. Black soil also contains iron, aluminium and lime. In comparison, laterite, yellow and red soils have relatively lower amounts of these nutrients.
qs.kf:
☛ Another name for black soil → Regur soil
☛ Where is black soil mainly found → Deccan Plateau
☛ Which crop is suitable for black soil → Cotton
☛ What is high in black soil → Water retention capacity
☛ What does black soil contain → Calcium carbonate, magnesium, potash, lime

q: Which term is used for the tropical cyclone that originates in the north eastern Pacific and north Atlantic?
qs.e: The term Hurricane is used for tropical cyclones that originate in the north eastern Pacific and north Atlantic Ocean. This term is commonly used in the Caribbean and along the coasts of America. In contrast, Typhoon is used in the northwestern Pacific, and Cyclone in the Indian Ocean and South Pacific. Hurricanes have maximum wind speeds exceeding 74 miles per hour (119 km/h). They form over warm ocean waters (above 26.5°C) and bring devastating winds and heavy rainfall. Hurricanes are classified as a category of tropical cyclones in meteorology. The word Hurricane comes from the Mayan and Carib languages.
qs.kf:
☛ What is the maximum wind speed of a hurricane? → 74 mph (119 km/h)
☛ In which region do typhoons originate? → North western Pacific Ocean
☛ What is the term for tropical cyclones in the Indian Ocean? → Cyclone
☛ What is the minimum sea surface temperature required for hurricane formation? → 26.5°C
☛ From which languages is the word Hurricane derived? → Mayan and Carib languages

q: Laterite soil develops in the area with:
qs.e: Laterite soil develops in regions with high temperature and heavy rainfall. It is found in tropical and subtropical areas. Heavy rainfall causes leaching of lime and silica, leaving behind iron and alumina oxides, which give the soil a red or yellow color. This soil is prone to erosion and has low organic matter. It is mainly found in Kerala, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Madhya Pradesh, and Odisha. It does not form in low temperature or low rainfall areas.
qs.kf:
☛ Color of laterite soil → Red or yellow
☛ Which nutrients are deficient in laterite soil? → Organic matter and nitrogen
☛ Which crops are suitable for laterite soil? → Cashew, tea, coffee
☛ Process of laterite soil formation? → Lateritization
☛ Largest area of laterite soil in India? → Western Ghats

q: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of the Drought Prone Areas programme (DPAP)?
o: It emphasized on land development programmes and afforestation.
It was initiated during the Fifth Five-Year Plan.
It provided employment to the people in drought-prone areas.
qs.e: The Drought Prone Areas Programme (DPAP) was launched in 1973-74 during the Fifth Five-Year Plan. Its primary objective was to focus on land development, afforestation, and employment generation in drought-affected areas. This program did not emphasize irrigation projects; instead, it prioritized activities like water conservation, pasture development, and soil conservation. The program was later revised in 1994-95 based on the recommendations of the National Agriculture Commission. DPAP aimed to mitigate the impact of droughts and ensure sustainable use of natural resources.
qs.kf:
☛ When was DPAP launched? → 1973-74
☛ Under which Five-Year Plan was DPAP initiated? → Fifth Five-Year Plan
☛ What is the main focus of DPAP? → Land development, afforestation, and employment
☛ Which areas does DPAP cover? → Drought-prone areas
☛ What is the objective of DPAP? → To mitigate the impact of drought

q: Old alluvial soil is known as:
qs.e: Old alluvial soil is known as Bangar. This soil is formed from ancient alluvium deposited by rivers and is found on higher floodplains.
